Authors bring forward diverse causes for this name: Adrichomius and Burchard certainly observe that this pool was called 'probatica' from the sheep gate, near which it was: but Jerome and Bede derive that name from the fact that the cattle destined for slaughter were washed there. Others say it was so called because it was situated near the 'probatikon' (sheep) market, where they were sold, or near the house where the sheep were kept. However, the former reason for the name seems preferable: which name Eusebius of Emesa applies to baptism from Cant. 4, 2.

pool) A bathing place. It is called a 'piscina' (fishpond) catachrestically: Frontinus interprets it as a reservoir. It seems that in this and certain other neighboring stagnant waters, the cattle were accustomed to be washed before they were led to the temple, as has been noted by many.

Some gather from Aristeas that a huge quantity of water, flowing down from the brazen sea and basins and countless ablutions through pipes and hidden aqueducts and subterranean passages, constituted that lake or pool.

in Hebrew Bethesda) There is no doubt that the Syrian expressed the true name בית חסדא. Abrabanel renders the same name but with an expressed sense as 'house of mercy'. The Hebrews are accustomed to call every place 'Beth', that is, a house: and it was called 'charitos' (of grace) because the sick were healed there by divine benefit. Gutturals are accustomed to be omitted by the Greeks; and thus 'Bethesda', this is, 'Beth-chesda', just as 'Ben-chesed' in 1 Kings 4, 10, in the Greek is 'Benesed'.

Jerome on Hosea renders it 'house of hunting' by writing with a Zade, others 'house of effusion' by writing with a Sin. But the Syrian interpretation is better. The Latin codices wrongly read 'Bethsaida', as does Tertullian in 'De Baptismo', c. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἐπὶ τῇ προβατικῇ) ἐπὶ ut על Hebræum pro apud. ἐπὶ πριάμοιο θύρῃσι apud Homerum: ad fores Priami. ἐπὶ ποταμῷ Thucidides dixit pro παρὰ ποταμῷ. Subaudiendum autem hic πύλῃ quod expressum legitur Nehem. 2, 1. c. 12, 38. Hac victimæ in urbem ducebantur.

Diversas causas afferunt hujus nominis Autores: προβατικὴν dictam hanc piscinam, à porta gregis, juxta quam illa erat, Adrichomius & Burchardus utique observant: at Hieronymus & Beda nomen istud inde deducunt, quod pecudes mactationi destinatæ istic ablutæ sint. Alii ex eo ita vocatam ajunt, quod juxta forum προβατικὸν sita esset, ubi vendebantur, vel juxta domum eam, ubi servabantur oves. Præferenda tamen videtur prior nominis ratio: Quod nomen Eusebius E- miss. baptismo applicat è Cant. 4, 2.

κολυμβήθρα) Lavacrum. Piscina dicitur καταχρηστικῶς: conceptelam interpretatur Frontinus. Videntur in hoc & aliis quibusdam vicinis stagnis ablui solitæ pecudes antequam ad templum ducerentur, ut à compluribus notatum est.

Nonnulli ex Aristea colligunt, quod ingens aquarum copia ex mari æneo & conchis & innumeris ablutionibus defluens per fistulas & aquæductus occultos, & meatus subterraneos lacum sive piscinam illam constituerit.

ἑβραϊστὶ βηθεσδὰ) Non est dubium quin verum nomen Syrus expresserit בית חסדא. Idem nomen sed sensu expresso reddit Abrabs الرحمة بيت domus gratiæ. Omnem locum בית id est domum vocare Hebræi solent: χάριτος autem ideo vocabatur quod ægroti hic sanarentur divino beneficio. Gutturales à Græcis omitti solent; atque ita βηθεσδὰ, hic est, בית־חסדת quomodo בך־חסר I. Reg. 4, 10. in Græco Βενεσὲδ.

Hieronymus in Hoseam reddit domum venationis per Zade, alii domum effusionis per Sin scribentes. Sed præstat Syri interpretatio. Latini Codd. perperam Bethsaida legunt, ut & Tertullianus de Bapt. c. 5.

## 5:3
Vers. 3. having five porches; in these lay a great multitude of the sick.) As was accustomed to happen in the buildings of the middle; in the old Latin tragedy: The wounded of the children of Aesculapius fill the porches. But ἀσθένεια and ἀσθενεῖν are said of any disease in these books, as Matt. 8, 17. Luke 11, 12. Matt. 10, 8. Mark 6, 56.

Ξηρῶν) That is called ξηρὸν which is destitute of vital influx, like a branch that has withered, Matt. XII, 10. Luke VI, 6. See also I Kings 13, 4. Here, therefore, ξηροὶ are those who have some part defective in motion.

Latin:

Vers. 3. πέντε στοὰς ἔχουσα· ἐν ταύταις κατέκειτο πλῆθος πολὺ τῶν ἀσθενούντων.) Ut solebat fieri in mediorum ædibus; in veteri tragœdia Latina: Æsculapi liberorum saucii opplent porticus. Ἀσθένεια autem & ἀσθενεῖν de quovis morbo in his libris dicitur, ut Matth. 8, 17. Luc. 11, 12. Matth. 10, 8. Marc. 6, 56.

Ξηρῶν) ξηρὸν dicitur quod ab influxu vitali est destitutum, ut ramus qui exaruit, Matth. XII, 10. Luc. VI, 6. Vide & I.Reg. 13, 4. hic ergo ξηροὶ quibus pars aliqua motu defecta.

## 5:4
Vers. 4. for an angel) Not that he was seen, but because it was believed by the Jews that such things are not done by God except through angels, and the presence of an angel was understood from the movement of the water, as from an earthquake Matt. 28, 2.

Nor is that without merit: For that ταραχὴ did not happen by chance, or fortuitously, nor from some hidden or natural property, but was clearly done from the outside, and through it the power of healing, which nevertheless was from God, with the angel acting only ministerially and stirring up the ταραχὴν, so that it might be clear to the sick when they must ascend to the waters. This is not the persuasion of the Jews here, but the assertion of the Evangelist.

Κατὰ καιρὸν) At a certain time around Passover as the ancients believed. However, it seems that the water was accustomed to be moved not only once but more often around that time.

Cyril refers it to the feast of Pentecost, others to the three solemn feasts of the Jews. But the phrase κατὰ καιρὸν, and the fact that only one sick person recovered health, seem to imply that it happened only once a year: which it is likely happened at the feast of Passover, both because it was once ennobled by many prodigies in Egypt, and because at that time Christ, about to be killed by a bloody death, was preparing a pool from his own blood for the healing of all the diseases of souls.

Κατέβαινεν ἐν τῇ κολυμβήθρᾳ) That is, into the pool. Moreover, that καταβαίνειν is accustomed to be said of angels, as Matt. 28, 2. Rev. 10, 1. But that old manuscript has ἐλούετο instead of κατέβαινεν, which I do not disapprove: for those things which are of men are accustomed to be applied to angels.

What is this rashness of abandoning the received reading, and for the sake of a single codex inventing those things which are utterly abhorrent to the text and the custom of Scripture?

ἐτάρασσε τὸ ὕδωρ) Many things concurred, nor could it be believed to be natural medication through water? First, it happened at a stated time. Then, all kinds of diseases were healed; finally, the water was moved beforehand, whereas otherwise that which is calm is sought for remedies. ἐτάρασσε is רָפַשׂ Ezech. 32. v. 2.

We add what Walaeus noted from Gomarus: Tertullian in the book on the soul, chapter 1, when he says: there was also a medicinal lake in Judea before Christ. But he does not indicate when it first began, but he handed down in the book against the Jews, chapter 3, that it ceased shortly after Christ because of the stubbornness of the Jews' unbelief, which was punished by God. The pool, he says, of Bethsaida (for so it is read by the error of the scribes, both here and elsewhere) until the coming of Christ, was healing the infirmities of Israel, it ceased from its benefits, then from the perseverance of their fury, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed by them. But at what time of the year, and how often this miracle happened, is uncertain: because no profane history mentions this miracle (perhaps, as is conjectured by some, because it did not last long: and therefore it was unknown to foreigners) but the Evangelist John alone records it; who also indicates only this, that it happened after the water had been troubled by an angel, κατὰ καιρὸν, which the Vulgate version translated too generally, according to the time, as is also read in Ambrose: but it would be more apt, opportunely or at an opportune and stated time, and therefore Lord Beza translates it at a certain moment. But whether it happened more often; or whether it happened only once every year,

And whether on a feast day, or otherwise, there is nothing certain. However, the opinion of Tertullian in his book On Baptism, ch. V, is probable, when he says one was freed once a year: and of Ambrose in his book On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries, ch. IV, where he speaks of this pool, in which one was healed annually. Heinsius noted from Cyril that this was done at the feast of Pentecost: He seems to have expressed that κατὰ καιρὸν למועד. So that it may be posited that κατὰ καιρὸν τοῦτον is accustomed to be said by the Hellenists, and it may be understood that these waters were moved and sanctified annually at the very feast of Pentecost: Which Cyril confirmed by his own opinion and judgment. Who observes: On the day of Pentecost, Angels descending from heaven moved the water of this pool, the sound of which motion signified that they were present to sanctify the water.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἄγγελος γὰρ) Non quod videretur, sed quod persuasum esset Judæis talia à Deo non nisi per Angelos agi, iraque ex motu aquæ præsentia Angeli intelligebatur, ut ex terræ motu Matth. 28, 2.

Nec id immerito: Nam ταραχὴ illa non casu, aut fortuito, nec ex occulta quadam, aut naturali proprietate, sed extrinsecus plane fiebat, & per illam virtus sanandi, quæ tamen à Deo erat, Angelo tantum ministerialiter agente & ταραχὴν exciante, ut constet ægris, quando ad aquas ascendendum. Non Judæorum hic persuasio, sed Evangelistæ assertio hic habetur.

Κατὰ καιρὸν) Certo tempore circa Pascha ut Veteres crediderunt. Videtur autem circa id tempus non semel tantum sed sæpius aqua moveri solita.

Cyrillus ad festum Pentecostes, alii ad tria solemnia Judæorum festa referunt. Sed vox κατὰ καιρὸν, & quod unus tantum ægrotus sanitatem recuperavit, semel in anno tantum id contigisse, innuere videntur: quod festo Paschatos factum verisimile est, tum quod id olim multis prodigiis in Ægypto nobilitatum, tum quod in illo Christus morte cruenta necandus piscinam ex suo sanguine curandis omnibus animarum morbis paraturus erat.

Κατέβαινεν ἐν τῇ κολυμβήθρᾳ) Id est εἰς τὴν κολυμβήθραν, Solet autem illud καταβαίνειν de Angelis dici ut Matth. 28, 2. Apoc. 10, 1. At manuscriptus vetus ille pro κατέβαινεν habet ἐλούετο, quod non improbo: Solent enim Angelis aptari ea, quæ hominum sunt.

Quæ hæc temeritas deserendi receptam lectionem, & in unius Codicis gratiam ea fingendi, quæ prorsus à textu & consuetudine Scripturæ abhorrent?

ἐτάρασσε τὸ ὕδωρ) Multa concurrebant, nec naturalis per aquam medicatio crederetur? Primum stato tempore fiebat. Deinde sanabantur omnia morborum genera; postremo commota prius aqua, cum alioqui ad remedia quæratur ea quæ tranquilla est. ἐτάρασσε est רָפַשׂ Ezech. 32. v. 2.

Addimus, quæ è Gomaro notavit Walæus: Tertullianus libr. de anima cap. 1. cum ait: fuit etiam Judæa lacus medicus ante Christum. Sed quando primum cœperit, non indicat, desiisse autem brevi post Christum ob incredulitatis Judæorum pertinaciam à Deo vindicatam, tradidit libro adversus Judæos cap. 3. Piscina, inquit, Bethsaida (sic enim vitio descriptorum, & hic & alibi legitur) usque ad adventum Christi, curando invaletudinis ab Israel, desiit à beneficiis, deinde ex perseverantia furoris sui, ne nomen Domini per ipsos blasphemaretur. Quo autem anni tempore, ac quoties hoc miraculum acciderit, incertum est: quia nulla profana historia hujus miraculi meminit (forte, ut a nonnullis conjicitur, quod non diu duravit: ideoque ignotum fuerit exteris) sed solus Evangelista Johannes recenset; Qui etiam hoc tantum indicat, illud factum esse, postquam ab Angelo turbata esset aqua, κατὰ καιρὸν, quod vulgata versio nimis generatim transstulit, secundum tempus, ut etiam apud Ambrosium legitur: sed aptius esset, opportune vel opportuno ac stato tempore, ideoque Dominus Beza vertit certo momento. Verum an illud sæpius; an vero semel tantum quotannis contigerit,

& an in festo, aut alias, nihil est certi. Probabilis autem est sententia Tertulliani libr. de bapt. c. V. cum ait unum semel anno liberatum: & Ambro- sii lib. de his qui initiantur mysteriis cap. IV, ubi de hac piscina ait, in qua unus annuus sanabatur. Id, festo Pentecostes factum è Cyrillo notavit Heinsius: Videtur illo κατὰ καιρὸν למועד ex- pressisse. Ut ponatur κατὰ καιρὸν τῦτον ab Helleni- stis dici solet, & intelligatur, aquas has quotan- nis ipso Pentecostes festo, aut alio motas ac sancti- ficatas fuisse: Quod opinione sua ac sententia Cy- rillus confirmavit. Qui observat: Die Penteco- stes, Angelos de cælo descendentes, piscinæ hujus commovisse aquam, cujus motionis sonum, adesse ipsos ad sanctificandum aquam, significasse.

## 5:5
Verse 5. τριάκοντα ἔτη ἔχων] The admiration is increased by the persistence of the disease, Luke VIII. 43.

ἔχων ἐν τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ] κακῶς ἔχων as it is commonly said and in Matthew XIV. 35.

Latin:

Vers. 5. τριάκοντα ἔτη ἔχων] Augetur admiratio ex per- tinacia morbi, Luc. VIII. 43.

ἔχων ἐν τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ] κακῶς ἔχων ut vulgo dicitur & Matth. XIV. 35.

## 5:6
Verse 6. κατακείμενον] Lying down, because he was unable to move himself.

πολὺν ἤδη χρόνον ἔχει] Supply τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ.

Latin:

Vers. 6. κατακείμενον] Jacentem, quod se movere nequi- ret.

πολὺν ἤδη χρόνον ἔχει] Supple τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ.

## 5:7
Verse 7. κύριε ἄνθρωπον οὐκ ἔχω] He answers tacitly more than if he had answered expressly, as if he were saying, indeed this is the only thing I am striving for, that I might be healed, but I find no one who might have pity on me. He modestly implores the help of Jesus, ἄνθρωπον οὐκ ἔχω. It is a Hebraism for I have no one. To the disease was added poverty, so that he could not even procure a companion for himself. The priests and Pharisees were not touched by his misery.

ἐν ὧ δὲ] As soon as. The word time is understood.

Latin:

Vers. 7. κύριε ἄνθρωπον οὐκ ἔχω] Tacite plus respondet, quam si expresse respondisset, quasi dicat, imo hoc uni- cum ago ut saner, sed neminem invenio, qui mei mise- reatur. Verecunde Jesu opem implorat, ἄνθρωπον οὐκ ἔχω. Hebraïsmus est pro neminem habeo. Ad mor- bum accedebat inopia, ut nec comitem comparare sibi posset. Sacerdotes & Pharisæi non tangebantur ejus mi- seria.

ἐν ὧ δὲ] Simul ac. Subauditur χρόνῳ.

## 5:8
Verse 8. ἔγειραι] Here Jesus shows that whatever is expected from an Angel can be performed by Himself: Christ does not demand faith here as He does elsewhere, because here He had seen nothing of his works, had heard nothing. He does not wish to reap where He has not sown. See below v. 12.

The word itself, which is an imperative, requires faith, which Jesus, the knower of hearts, saw that he (the sick man) had, and the sick man testified by his most prompt obedience. For he would not have attempted to rise, unless he had believed that he could rise at this word.

ἆρον τὸν κράββατόν σε] Thus Matthew 9. 6. It was the custom of Christ that, once a miracle was performed, He would command something for the sake of testimony. He did the same here. But by this testimony of divine power, the Sabbath was sanctified, not profaned. For how much more illustrious is this than to circumcise a boy, or to slaughter victims, which was permitted on the Sabbath. Otherwise, to carry a burden is among the things prohibited on the Sabbath, as Philo notes concerning the Colonies. See also Jeremiah 17. 21. and Origen, On First Principles, book IV, ch. 8, where he recounts the strange quibbles of the Jews over this matter.

Latin:

Vers. 8. ἔγειραι] Ostendit hic Jesus quicquid ab Ange- lo expectatur à se præstari posse: non exigit hic ut alias fi- dem Christus, quia hic nihil operum ipsius viderat, nihil au- diverat. Non vult metere ubi non sævit. Vide infra v. 12.

Verbum ipsum, quod imperativus est, fidem requirit, quam & habere ipsum (ægrotum) Jesus καρδιογνώσης videbat, & ægrotus paritione sua promptissima testabatur. Non enim tentasset surgere, nisi se ad hoc verbum surgere posse credi- disset.

ἆρον τὸν κράββατόν σε] Sic Matth. 9. 6. Mos erat Christi ut peracto miraculo aliquid testimonii causa imperaret. Idem hic fecit. Hoc autem testimonio divinæ potentiæ sabbatum sanctificabatur, non profanabatur. Quanto enim hoc illustrius quam puerum circumcidere, aut vi- ctimas jugulare, quod Sabbato licebat. Alioqui ἀχθο- φορεῖν est inter prohibita Sabbato, ut Philo notat de Colo- niis. Vide & Jerem. 17. 21. & Origenem περὶ ἀρχῶν libr. IV. c. 8. ubi miros recitat Judæorum διεξολισμοὺς super hoc negotio.

## 5:10
Verse 10. Ἰουδαῖοι] From the leaders, as also below v. 15.

οὐκ ἔξεστί σοι ἆραι τὸν κράββατον] Caviling after their custom concerning rites.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἰουδαῖοι] Ex primoribus, ut & infra v. 15.

οὐκ ἔξεστί σοι ἆραι τὸν κράββατον] More suo cavillantes cir- ca ritus.

## 5:11
Verse 12.

He who made me whole, he said to me] He shows that he is neither ignorant of the law of the Sabbath, nor of the opinion accepted among his detractors themselves: that the Sabbath can be violated at the command of a prophet, by the example of those who, at the command of Joshua, attacked Jericho on the Sabbath. He tacitly shows, however, that he considers Jesus a prophet, since he had restored health to him by divine power.

Latin:

Vers. II.

ὁ ποιήσας με ὑγιῆ, ἐκεῖνός μοι εἶπεν] Ostendit se nec Sab- bati legem ignorare, nec receptam apud ipsos obtrectato- res sententiam: ad imperium prophetæ posse violari Sab- batum exemplo eorum, qui ad Josuæ imperium Sabbato Hierichuntem oppugnaverunt. Tacite autem ostendit se Jesum pro Propheta habere, cum is vi divina sanitatem ipsi reddidisset.

## 5:12
Verse 12. Who is the man who said to you, take up your bed] Behold the nature of malice. They do not say who is he who healed you, but who ordered you to take up your bed. They ask, not because they are amazed, but so that they may slander.

Latin:

Vers. 12. τίς ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ εἰπών σοι ἆρον τὸν κράββατον] En malitiæ ingenium. Non dicunt quis est ille qui te sana- vit, sed quis jussit grabbatum tollere. Quærunt, non quod mirentur, sed quod calumnientur.

## 5:13
Verse 13. He withdrew] He slipped away, as this word is used in the Greek version, Judges 18:26, 2 Samuel 2:24, chapter 23:16. And not much differently in Judges 4:18. But also for Euripides, to withdraw is to extricate oneself from evil, likewise to depart from an opinion.

there being a crowd in the place] The reason is given why he went away, because there was a great gathering of people there, whose applause Jesus showed he was not seeking.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἐξένευσεν] Subduxit se, uti vox hæc usur- patur in Græca versione, Jud. XIIX. 26. 2. Sam. II. 24. c. XXIII. 16. Nec multo aliter Jud. IV. 18. Sed & Euripi- di ἐκνεύειν est è malo se explicare, item de sententia a- bire.

ὄχλου ὄντος ἐν τῷ τόπῳ] Ratio redditur cur abiret, quia magnus ibi erat hominum conventus, quorum plausum se non captari Jesus ostendebat.

## 5:14
Verse 14. In the temple] Giving thanks to God in a sacred place, as was the custom, Luke 18:10, Acts 3:1.

Sin no more] Beware of committing such a thing as happened before these 38 years; God shows his divinity, when he saw those things which had happened secretly before his own age. The law, among other things, also threatened diseases to transgressors.

Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 15. Christ saying, Behold you have been made whole, now sin no more, manifests that because of the sin of disobedience, infirmities followed for men. Chrysostom, homily 37. And we are warned that diseases are generated from sins. And in the sermon on the first fall of man. Do not sin after pardon, do not be wounded after a cure, do not be defiled after grace. Consider, he says, O man, that the guilt is heavier after pardon, that a renewed wound hurts worse after a cure, that it is more troublesome for a man to be defiled after grace. Wherefore he is ungrateful for indulgence who sins after pardon. Unworthy of health is he who wounds himself after he has been cured, nor does he deserve to be cleansed who defiles himself after grace.

lest something worse happen to you) Those who have obtained pardon, like this man, are not only not safe against new falls, but can also fall back into a worse state, and are punished more severely on account of the benefit received and despised, Matthew 12:45, 2 Peter 2:20.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ] Gratias Deo reddentem in loco sacro, ut mos erat, Luc. XVIII. 10. Actor. III. 1.

μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε] Cave tale aliquid committas quale ante hos XXXVIII. annos; divinitatem suam Deus osten- dit, cum ea videret quæ ante ætatem suam clam acci- derant. Lex autem inter cætera etiam morbos minabatur transgressoribus.

Irenæus lib. V. cap. 15. Dicens Christus, Ecce sa- nus factus es, jam noli peccare amplius, manifestat, quoniam propter inobedientiæ peccatum subsequti sunt languores hominibus. Chrysost. hom. XXXVII. Et nos monemur, quod ex peccatis morbi generan- tur. Et serm. de laps. prim. hom. Noli peccare post veniam, noli vulnerari post curam, noli sordi- dari post gratiam. Cogita, inquit, ó homo, gravio- rem esse culpam post veniam, renovatum vulnus pe- jus dolere post curam, molestius hominem sordidari post gratiam. Quare indulgentiæ ingratus est, qui post veniam peccat. Sanitate indignus, qui semet- ipsum, postquam curatus est, vulnerat, nec munda- ri meretur, qui semetipsum post gratiam sordi- dat.

ἵνα μὴ χεῖρόν τι σοὶ γένηται) Veniam consecuti, qualis hic, non modo tuti non sunt adversus novos lapsus, sed & in statum pejorem recidere possunt, & ob acceptum con- temtumque beneficium gravius puniuntur, Matth. 12, 45. 2. Petr. 2, 20.

## 5:15
Verse 15. That it is Jesus who made him whole) Celebrating with a grateful heart the author of the benefit, whose name he had learned from those standing by in the temple.

PART II. The apology of Jesus against the Jews persecuting him.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὸν ὑγιῆ) Grato ani- mo celebrans beneficii auctorem, cujus nomen ex adstan- tibus in templo didicerat.

PARS II. Iesu contra Iudæos ipsum persequentes Apo- logia.

## 5:16
Verse 16. They persecuted) See Matthew 5:10.

οἱ Ἰυδαῖοι) The leaders.

ἐζήτουν αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι) They were constructing a capital charge against him, to such an extent was their hatred gradually inflamed. This is therefore omitted here in certain books, because it was believed to be repeated from what follows. But the Syriac and Arabic have it.

ὅτι ταῦτα ἐποίει ἐν Σαββάτῳ) See Matt. 12. 24. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἐδίωκον) Vide Matth. V. 10.

οἱ Ἰυδαῖοι) Primores.

ἐζήτουν αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι) Calumniam capitalem ei strue- bant, in tantum paulatim accenso odio. Hoc ideo hic in quibusdam libris omissum, quia repetitum ex sequentibus credebatur. Sed habent Syrus & Arabs.

ὅτι ταῦτα ἐποίει ἐν Σαββάτῳ) Vide Matth. XII. 24. & alibi.

## 5:17
ἀπεκρίνατο] To the words of those accusing his deed, which are passed over in silence, but can easily be understood.

Vers. 17. ὁ πατήρ μυ ἕως ἄρτι ἐργάζεται] He does not cease by his power to bring men and other living creatures into life even on the Sabbaths. For on the Sabbath he once rested from the creation of the universe and of the kinds. Sophocles in Oedipus at Colonus: τελεῖν τελεῖ ζεῦς τι κατ' ἦμαρ. Philo in the Allegories: παύεται ἐδέποτε ποιῶν ὧν ὁ θεός: ἀλλ' ὥσπερ ἴδιον τὸ καίειν πυρὸς, καὶ χιόνος ψύχειν, ὕτω καὶ θεῦ τὸ ποιεῖν, καὶ πολύ γε μᾶλλον, ὅσῳ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἁπάσιν ἀρχὴ τῦ δρᾷν ἐστίν. And concerning Cain: ἀνάπαυλαι δὲ, ὐ τὴν ἀ πραξίαν καλῶ ἐπειδὴ φύσει δραστήριον τὸ τῶν ὅλων αἴτιον ὐδέ- ποτε ἴσχον τῦ ποιεῖν τὰ κάλλιστα. Maximus Tyrius in the dissertation that the active life is to be preferred to the contemplative: ὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ Ζεὺς σχολὴν ἄγει, ἧ γὰρ ἂν ἐπαύσατο καὶ ὐρανὸς περιφερόμενος, καὶ γῆ τρέφουσα, καὶ ποταμοὶ ῥέοντες, καὶ δεχομένη θάλαττα, καὶ ὧραι διαλαγχάνουσαι, καὶ μῦσαι ἄδυσαι ἐπαύσαντο διὰ τὴν τῶν ἀν- θρώπων ἀρεταί, κὶ ζώων σωτηρίαν, κὶ καρπῶν γένεσις· καὶ τὸ πᾶν τῦτο αὖθις αὖ περὶ αὑτῷ σφαλλόμενον συνεχύθη κὶ συνεπλαράχθη· ἀλλ' ἡ Διὸς πραγματεία ἀτρεπτῶ ὖσα κὶ διηνεκῶς κὶ ἀκοίμητος κὶ μηδέποτε ἀπαγορέυσα μηδὲ ἐπαναχωρῦσα τῦ ἑαυτῆς ἔργυ, αἴτια χορηγεῖ τὴν σωτηρίαν τοῖς ἐσι. That ἕως ἄρτι, Matt. 14, 12. and 1 John 2. 9. signifies until this day.

κἀγὼ ἐργάζομαι] Thus I, by his example, perform the works of divine power on the Sabbath, for the Hebrew ו is accustomed to be placed comparatively: See below v. 21.

Since that former statement about the Father is explained as always working from the creation until this day, by preserving created things, this latter statement about the Son must also be understood in the same way, as one of whom the same thing is asserted for the same reason, and not restricted only to miracles performed on the Sabbath: nor is it to be explained as an imitation of the Father's example, but as an identity of operation: because the power of working is one, the operation of the Father and the Son is one, which the Ancients proved from this passage against the Arians, nor did the Jews themselves understand Christ otherwise, accusing him for this reason of blasphemy: whose sense and understanding Christ does not rebuke, but confirms, and teaches that he is altogether ἴσον esse τῷ Θεῷ. Which Grotius explains too jejunely as ἴσον ἑαυτὸν τῷ Θεῷ, that is, proclaiming that it is permitted to him whatever is permitted to God, and that he is not more bound to the Sabbath. For the Jews did not conclude that, but because he said that he worked just as the Father did, they concluded that he was making himself equal to the Father: which his words also implied entirely: whence that futile gloss of Grotius on verse 19 and δύναται. This is most alien to him: that will never come into his mind. For who does not understand what ἀδύνατον is? Christ is teaching that it is impossible, of course, for the Son to do anything that he has not seen the Father doing, on account of the ὁμοουσία of the Son with the Father, and the origin of the Son from the Father, just as the ancients against the Arians, and we ourselves especially against the Socinians in our Anti-Crellius p. 1050 seqq. vindicate the meaning. Therefore he adds ταῦτα ὁ υἱὸς ὁμοίως ποιεῖ: which imply identity, not imitation and parity of the mode of acting, as Grotius perverts it, and thus also import the same power of acting, and the same essence, because in God power and essence are the same. Therefore the comparison which Grotius introduces here is alien, taken from a disciple imitating his Master, and a Master opening the secrets of his art to a disciple whom he holds dearer than the rest. Which comparison Grotius has from the Socinians, and especially from Joh. Crellius, in whom we refuted it l. c. page 1061, or rather from the Arians, in whom St. Cyril has already refuted it l. 11 in Joh. c. 137. The Father shows the Son what he himself does, not as if depicted on tablets, nor as if helping one who is ignorant with teaching. For the Son as God knows all things: But by painting himself entirely in the nature of the Son, so that whatever he has in himself, he shows in the Son, so that from those things, what the nature of the Father is, is known, from those things also the nature of the Son is demonstrated. This is Cyril. That vision and exhibition must be understood in a manner worthy of God, just as the Holy Spirit is said to hear and receive from the Son, Joh. 16, as the mystery of the most Holy Trinity bears: so that, namely, only the origin is indicated, by which the Son of God has all things from the Father: Just as the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son: which the following verses confirm. For Christ also teaches v. 21 that the life-giving power belongs to the Son by his own authority, just as it does to the Father, as well as the sovereign and universal judgment, so that the Father judges no one ALONE or without the Son, and indeed has even handed over the judicial power to the Son according to his human nature, Acts 17, 3; 1 Pet. 4, 5; and therefore he wants the Son to be honored, even as a man, who has this divine power, with the same honor and worship with which the Father himself is to be honored, verse 23, which are clearer than the sun, and are brought forward elsewhere against heretics, when the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father is asserted. But that explanation, that in verse 22 those are perhaps to be understood by 'no one' to whom the Gospel has been preached, is a mere depravation. For the Father is said to judge NO ONE simply, namely, as I have said, without the Son. For he did not take the judgment away from himself when he granted it to Christ according to the flesh. Nor is this to be taken only concerning the judgment of condemnation with Grotius, nor indeed is it to be explained in general concerning that judgment by which those to be judged are either absolved or condemned, but it is to be understood concerning the universal government, which by the received custom of the Hebrews is designated by the word judgment: that all things which pertain to the rule and government of the universe, the Father does not execute alone without the Son, but as he had said before, the Son works and is occupied in the same things just as the Father, and the Father has also handed over to the Son according to the flesh that power of governing and ruling all things, so that the Son may be honored even as he is a man, just as the Father is honored. Which we showed more fully against the Calvinists in our Examination of the Doctrine concerning the Person of Christ from this passage, page 141 seqq.

Nor could Grotius deny this, who on v. 23 has it thus: ἵνα πάντες τιμῶσι τὸν υἱὸν: So that, namely, men, having known this power of the Son, may worship and revere him, Ps. 2:11-12; Phil. 2:10. The use of the Sabbath is to honor God. Thus also the use of the Sabbath is to honor the Son. τὸν πέμψαντα αὐτὸν: he who treats with injury an ambassador, especially when sent with the fullest power, is considered to treat with injury him whose person the ambassador sustains. See above c. 4:34, below v. 30, 37, 38, c. 7:16, and passim in this book. Christ silently shows how intimate he is to the Father. For God does not grant his honor to a stranger. For also Ps. 2:11-12 concerns the Messiah being worshipped as he is God and man, appointed King on Mount Zion, to whom God gave the nations and all the ends of the earth as an inheritance: and Phil. 2:10, the exaltation and the donation of the name above every name, done out of grace, pertains to Christ according to the flesh, or who according to his human nature, according to which he himself sustains the person of the Father, was an ambassador: which name above every name and glory could not have been granted to him at all, if he were a stranger to the flesh, and not assumed into the very hypostasis of the Son of God, so that he is one subsisting thing with the same, Isa. 42:8. Add what Grotius has on v. 27.

Latin:

ἀπεκρίνατο] Ad verba factum suum accusantium, quæ subtice..tur, sed intelligi facile possunt.

Vers. 17. ὁ πατήρ μυ ἕως ἄρτι ἐργάζεται] Non cessat vi sua homines aliaque animantia ipsis etiam Sabbatis in vitam educere. Nam Sabbato olim quievit à creatione univer- sitatis & generum. Sophocles Oedipode Coloneo: τελεῖν τελεῖ ζεῦς τι κατ' ἦμαρ. Philo Allegoriis : παύεται ἐδέποτε ποιῶν ὧν ὁ θεός: ἀλλ' ὥσπερ ἴδιον τὸ καίειν πυρὸς, καὶ χιόνος ψύχειν, ὕτω καὶ θεῦ τὸ ποιεῖν, καὶ πολύ γε μᾶλλον, ὅσῳ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἁπάσιν ἀρχὴ τῦ δρᾷν ἐστίν. Et de Caino: ἀνάπαυλαι δὲ, ὐ τὴν ἀ πραξίαν καλῶ ἐπειδὴ φύσει δραστήριον τὸ τῶν ὅλων αἴτιον ὐδέ- ποτε ἴσχον τῦ ποιεῖν τὰ κάλλιστα. Maximus Tyrius Dissert tione vitam activam contemplativæ præferendam: ὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ Ζεὺς σχολὴν ἄγει, ἧ γὰρ ἂν ἐπαύσατο καὶ ὐρανὸς περιφερόμενος, καὶ γῆ τρέφουσα, καὶ ποταμοὶ ῥέοντες, καὶ δεχομένη θάλαττα, καὶ ὧραι διαλαγχάνουσαι, καὶ μῦσαι ἄδυσαι ἐπαύσαντο διὰ τὴν τῶν ἀν- θρώπων ἀρεταί, κὶ ζώων σωτηρίαν, κὶ καρπῶν γένεσις· καὶ τὸ πᾶν τῦτο αὖθις αὖ περὶ αὑτῷ σφαλλόμενον συνεχύθη κὶ συνεπλαράχθη· ἀλλ' ἡ Διὸς πραγματεία ἀτρεπτῶ ὖσα κὶ διηνεκῶς κὶ ἀκοίμητος κὶ μηδέποτε ἀπαγορέυσα μηδὲ ἐπαναχωρῦσα τῦ ἑαυτῆς ἔργυ, αἴτια χορηγεῖ τὴν σωτηρίαν τοῖς ἐσι. Illud ἕως ἄρτι, Matth. 14, 12. & 1. Joh. 2. 9. significat usque in hunc diem.

κἀγὼ ἐργάζομαι] Sic ego ipsius exemplo sabbato edo divinæ potentiæ opera, nam Hebræum ו solet comparative poni: Vide infra v. 21.

Quum prius illud de Patre explicetur semper operante inde à creatione usque in hunc diem, conservando res conditas, omnino etiam hoc posterius de Filio, utpote de quo idem eadem ratione effertur, similiter intelligendum erit, ne- que tantum ad miracula restringendum, Sabbato edita: aut de imitatione exempli Patris explican- dum, sed de identitate operationis: quia una est operandi potentia, una operatio Patris & Filii, quod ex hoc loco Veteres contra Arianos evice- runt, nec aliter intellexerunt Judæi ipsi Chri- stum ideo blasphemiæ arguentes: quorum sen- sum & intelligentiam non reprehendit, sed con- firmat Christus, seque omnino ἴσον esse τῷ Θεῷ docet. Quod nimis jejune Grotius ita exponit ἴσον ἑαυτὸν τῷ Θεῷ, id est, sibi licere prædicans quicquid Deo licet, neque magis sabbato se ad- stringi. Nam id non colligebant Judæi, sed quia se æque ut Pater operari semper ajebat, concludebant, quod se Patri æquaret: quod o- mnino etiam verba ejus inferebant: unde glos- sa illa futilis Grotii ad vers. 19. & δύναται. A- lienissimum hoc est ab illo: nunquam id ipsi in mentem veniet. Ecquis enim non intelligit, quid sit ἀδύνατον? Nimirum impossibile esse do- cet Christus, ut quicquam faciat Filius, quod non viderit facientem Patrem, ob ὁμοουσίαν Fi- lii cum Patre, & originem Filii à Patre, uti veteres contra Arianos, nosque adversus Soci- nianos imprimis in Anti-Crellio nostro p. 1050. seqq. sensum vindicamus. Ideo addit ταῦτα δ ὁύος ὁμοίως ποιεῖ: quæ identitatem, non ut per- vertit Grotius, imitationem & modi agendi pa- ritatem inferunt, adeoque etiam eandem agen- di virtutem, eandemque essentiam, quia in Deo potentia, & essentia idem sunt, important. Alie- na ergo est comparatio, quam ingerit hic Gro- tius, sumta à discipulo suum Magistrum imitan- te, & Magistro discipulo, quem præ cæteris inti- mum habeat, arcana suæ artis aperiente. Quam comparationem à Socinianis, & imprimis Joh. Crellio habet Grotius, in quo eam profligavi- mus l. c. pag. 1061. imo ab Arianis, in quibus eam jam confutavit S. Cyrillus l. 11. in Joh. c. 137. Pater Filio demonstrat, quæ ipse facit, non quasi depicta in tabulis nec quasi ignorantem, doctrina juvans. Omnia enim Filius ut Deus novit: Sed totum seipsum in natura Filii sic pingens, ut qua- cunque in se habeat, in Filio demonstret, ita ut ex quibus, quænam sit natura Patris, cognosci- tur, ex illis etiam natura Filii demonstretur. Hæc Cyrillus. Visio illa, & exhibitio θεωπρεπῶς intelligenda est, uti Spiritus S. dicitur audire, & accipere à Filio, Joh. 16. quemadmodum fert mysterium SS. Trinitatis: ut nempe origo solum indicetur, qua Filius Dei omnia habet à Patre: Sicuti S. S. à Patre & à Filio: quod sequentia confirmant. Nam & ζωοποίησιν Filius sibi αὐτε- ξυσίως competere, æque ut Patri, docet v. 21. ac judicium αὐτοκρατορικὸν & universale, adeo ut Pater neminem SOLUS vel sine Filio judicet, imo etiam Filio secundum humanam naturam po- testatem δικαστικὴν tradiderit, Actor. 17, 3. 1. Petr. 4, 5. & Filium honorari ideo vult, etiam qua hominem, qui hanc potestatem divinam habet, eodem honoris cultu, quo Pater ipse honoran- dus, vers. 23. quæ Sole clariora sunt, & alias adferuntur adversus hæreticos, cum ὁμουσία Fi- lii cum Patre adseritur. Illa vero explicatio, quod vers. 22. per ὐδένα forte intelligendi illi sint, quibus Evangelium prædicatum est, mera depra- vatio est. Simpliciter enim NEMINEM ju- dicare dicitur Pater, nempe, ut dixi, sine Filio. Non enim sibi ademit judicium cum Christo se- cundum carnem id concessit. Nec id tandum de judicio condemnationis cum Grotio accipiendum, imo nec in genere de judicio illo, quo vel ab- solvuntur, vel condemnantur judicandi expli- candum, sed de universa gubernatione, quæ recepta Ebræis consuetudine per judicium desi- gnatur, intelligendum: quod omnia quæ ad regimen & gubernationem universi pertinent, non Pater solus sine Filio exequatur, sed ut antea dixerat, Filius operetur, & occupetur in iisdem uti Pater, tradideritque etiam Pater Fi- lio secundum carnem illam potestatem gubernan- di, & regendi omnia, ut Filius honoretur etiam qua homo est, sicut honoratur Pater. Quod con- tra Calvinianos in Exam. Doctrinæ de Pers. Chri- sti ex hoc loco uberius ostendimus pag. 141 seqq.

Neque id negare potuit Grotius, qui ad v. 23. ita habet: ἵνα πάντες τιμῶσι τὸν υἱὸν : Ut scili- cet homines cognita hac Filii potestate eum colant ac revereantur, Psal. II. 11. 12. Phil. II. 10. Usus Sabbati est Deum honorare. Sic & usus Sabbati est honorare Filium. τὸν πέμψαντα αὐτὸν : qui le- gatum, præsertim cum plenissima potestate missum, injuria afficit, is injuria afficere eum censetur cu- jus personam legatus sustinet. Vide supra c. IV. 34. infra v. 30. 37. 38. cap. 7, 16. & passim in hoc libro. Tacite ostendit Christus quam intimus sit Patri. Nam Deus honorem suum extraneo non concedit. Nam & Psal. II. 11. 12. de Messia colendo uti Deus & homo est Rex institutus in monte Zion, cui Deus gentes, omnesque fines terræ in hæreditatem de- dit, agitur: & Phil. II. 10. exaltatio & nominis su- pra omne nomen donatio, ex gratia facta pertinet ad Christum secundum carnem, vel qui secundum humanam naturam, juxta quam ipse Patris per- sonam sustinet, legatus esset: quod nomen supra omne nomen & gloria ei concedi minime potuis- set, si extraneo caro esset, nec assumta in ipsam Filii Dei hypostasin, ita ut unum cum eodem sit ὑφισάμενον, Esa. 42, 8. Adde quæ ad v. 27. Gro- tius habet.

## 5:18
Verse 18. ἔλυε τὸ σάββατον) By their own admission. Concerning the expression see Matt. 5:19.

πατέρα ἴδιον ἔλεγε τὸν Θεὸν] Not commonly with the Jews, who used to say of God, 'our father,' but above the rest, for there is an emphasis in that ἴδιον, as in Rom. 8:32. This is just as if they were accusing him because he called himself Christ, whose surname was held to be the Son of God. We noted this at Matthew 26:63. Add what is below c. 19:17.

It is one thing to be the Son of God, which is a name of person, another to be Christ, which is of office.

ἴσον ἑαυτὸν τῷ Θεῷ) Proclaiming that it was permitted to him whatever is permitted to God, and that he was not bound by the Sabbath. A gross calumny, for the works of divine power were undoubtedly exempted from the Sabbath.

Pelagius has rightly executed these and the following things in this passage. The accusation was twofold: the former concerning the violation of the Sabbath: the latter concerning the consubstantiality or equality with God. Both are diluted in such a way that CHRIST teaches that his person is not subject to the laws of the Sabbath, and at the same time confirms that the Son of God is co-eternal with the Father, working up to this time, that is, always.

He recounts the arguments for his divinity in order, nine in number: First, from the equality of his works, for he does the same things that the Father does, v. 19. Second, from the affection of the Father toward him, who from eternity has shown him all things, by communicating his essence and wisdom through eternal generation, v. 20. Third, from the power of giving life, v. 21. Fourth, from the power of judging, which he has obtained entirely from God, v. 22, 23. Fifth, from the bestowing of eternal rewards, v. 24, 25. Sixth, from the power of raising the dead and distributing to each his reward, from v. 26 up to 29. Seventh, from the testimony of the eternal Father, which is greater than any human testimony, from v. 30 up to 32. Eighth, from the testimony of John, v. 33. Ninth, from the works themselves which strike the eyes and senses of all, v. 36, 37. Therefore, Christ did not say it was a calumny when they asserted that Jesus was making himself equal to God, but by this apology he taught that he is ἰσόθεον (equal to God).

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἔλυε τὸ σάββατον) Ipsorum indicio. De locutio- ne vide Matth. 5, 19.

πατέρα ἴδιον ἔλεγε τὸν Θεὸν] Non communiter cum Ju- dæis, qui de Deo dicebant, pater noster, sed supra cæteros, est enim ἔμφασις in illo ἴδιον, ut Rom. 8, 32. Perinde hoc est, quasi eum accusarent quod Christum se diceret, cujus cognomen habebatur Filius Dei. Notavimus ad Matthæi 26, 63. Adde quod infra c. 19, 17.

Aliud est Filium Dei esse, quod nomen personæ, aliud Christum, quod officii.

ἴσον ἑαυτὸν τῷ Θεῷ) Sibi licere prædicans quicquid Deo licet, neq; magis Sabbato se adstringi. Crassa calumnia, nam divinæ potentiæ opera haud dubie Sabbato eximebantur.

Recte hæc & sequentia exequutus est Pelagius in h. l. Duplex erat accusatio: Prior de Sabbato vio- latio: posterior περὶ τῆ ὁμοουσίᾳ sive ἰσοθέᾳ. Utraque sic diluitur, ut CHRISTUS personam suam legibus Sabbati non esse subjectam doceat, & simul confirmet συναΐδιον esse Dei Filium, cum Patre, usque modo, hoc est, semper operantem.

Argumenta divinitatis ordine recenset novem: Primum ab æqualitate operum, eadem enim se face- re, quæ faciat Pater, v. 19. Secundum ab affectu Pa- tris erga se, qui ab æterno sibi demonstravit omnia, essentiam, sapientiam que per æternam generationem communicando v. 20. Tertium à virtute vivifican- di, v. 21. Quartum à potestate judicandi, quam omnem à Deo consecutus sit, v. 22. 23. Quintum à donatione præmiorum æternorum, v. 24. 25. Sextum à potestate resuscitandi mortuos, & distribuendi cui- que mercedem suam, à v. 26. usque ad 29. Septimum à testimonio Patris æterni, quod major sit omni hu- mano à v. 30. usque ad 32. Octavum à testimonio Jo- hannis, v. 33. Nonum ab ipsis operibus in oculos & sensus omnium incurrentibus v. 36. 37. Non ergo calumniam esse dixit, cum assererent Jesum se pa- rem Deo facere, sed ἰσόθεον se esse docuit, Chri- stus hac apologia.

## 5:19
Vers. 19. ἀπεκρίνατο) Take it as above, v. 17.

ὐ δύναται) This is most foreign to that: it will never come into his mind.

ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ ὐδὲν) מן צבנות נפשה The Syriac: that is, by his own will, without command; thus it is taken below in chap. 7, 17 and chap. 12, 47. But I think ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ is properly opposed here to that which we have learned from another, below c. 18, 34, ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ τοῦτο λέγεις, ἢ ἄλλοι σοι εἶπον περὶ ἐμοῦ; where the Syriac has מן נפשך from your own mind. Compare Matt. 16, 17.

ἐὰν μή τι) ἐὰν μὴ here stands for ἀλλὰ as in Matt. 12, 4; Gal. 2, 16; below c. 15, 4. And τι is redundant after μὴ, as in 2 Cor. 1, 17 and c. 13, 5. And interrogatively in Matt. 7, 16; c. 12, 23; c. 26, 22, 25; Mark 4, 21; c. 14, 19; Luke 6, 39.

Βλέπη τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα) The comparison is taken from a disciple who diligently watches his Master going before him, so that he may be able to imitate him. Thus βλέπειν is used, Heb. II. 9.

ταῦτα καὶ ὁ ὑιὸς ὁμοίως ποιεῖ) He imitates these things. Thus Luke VI. 31, ch. X, 37.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἀπεκρίνατο) Accipe ut supra v. 17.

ὐ δύναται) Alienissimum hoc est ab illo: nunquam id psi in mentem veniet.

ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ ὐδὲν) מן צבנות נפשה Syrus: id est suopte arbitratu, injussu, sic infra sumitur cap. 7, 17. & cap. 12. 47. sed proprie puto ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ hic opponi ei quod ab alio didi- cimus, infra c. 18, 34. ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ τοῦτο λέγεις, ἢ ἄλλοι σοι εἶ- πον περὶ ἐμᾶ. ubi Syrus מן נפשך ex animo tuo. Compa- ra Matth. 16, 17.

ἐὰν μή τι) ἐὰν μὴ hic est pro ἀλλὰ ut Matt. 12, 4. Gal. 2, 16. infra c. 15. 4. Et abundat τι post μὴ, ut 2. Cor 1, 17. & c. 13, 5. Et interrogative Matth. 7, 16. cap, 12, 23. c. 26, 22. 25. Marc. 4, 21. c. 14, 19. Luc. 6, 39.

Βλέπη τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα) Comparatio est sumta à disci- pulo qui Magistrum sibi præeuntem diligenter intuetur, ut imitari possit. Sic βλέπειν sumitur, Hebr. II. 9.

ταῦτα καὶ ὁ ὑιὸς ὁμοίως ποιεῖ) Hæc imitatur. Sic Luc. VI. 31. c. X, 37.

## 5:20
V. 20. φιλεῖ τ' ὑὸν κὶ πάντα δείκνυσιν ἀυτῷ ἃ ἀυτὸς ποιεῖ) A comparison from a Master who holds one disciple dearer than the rest, to whom he opens all the secrets of his art. Thus the Greeks translate the Hebrew ירה sometimes by διδάσκειν, sometimes by δεικνύειν. And what is δεικνύειν here is called διδάσκειν below in ch. 8, 28.

Μείζονα τύτων δείξει ἀυτῷ ἔργα) The Father healed those bitten by the serpent: He healed Hezekiah and others: and thus he showed the Son what he himself ought to do according to the Father's example. It remains that the Son should also imitate greater things, and thus teach by the very deed what has been shown to him. Therefore δείξει here is to be referred to τὴν φάσιν. Such is that NOVI, Gen. XII. 12.

This Arian gloss was refuted long ago by the pious ancients: Cyrill. b. II. on John ch. 135. Those who say that the Father acts first, and then the Son imitates his work, labor under great ignorance: for how will the Father ever work separately and alone without the Son? But the Fathers explain the words of Christ truly with Hilary b. VII. de Trinit. Does the demonstration of works here suggest anything to us other than the faith of his birth, so that we may believe the Son subsisting from the subsisting God the Father, unless perhaps by ignorance the Only-begotten God is to be believed to have needed the demonstration of doctrine? But the rashness of this impious opinion is not admitted. For he who knows whatever he is to be taught does not need to be taught. To demonstrate does not always signify to show in sacred writings; but it is often the same as to exhibit and to give, as Ps. 4, 7. Ps. 85, 8. 2 Tim. 4, 14. likewise 1 Sam. 14, 12. Ps. 71, 20. John 10, 32. ch. 14, 9. Acts 9, 16.

ἵνα ὑμεῖς θαυμάζητε) ἐκβατικὸν, that is, in such a way that it cannot be but that you are astonished.

Latin:

V. 20. φιλεῖ τ' ὑὸν κὶ πάντα δείκνυσιν ἀυτῷ ἃ ἀυτὸς ποιεῖ) Com- paratio à Magistro, qui discipulum unum præ cæteris inti- mũ habeat. Cui omnia artis suæ arcana aperiat. Sic ירה He- bræum interdum per διδάσκειν, interdum per δεικνύειν ver- tunt Græci. Et quod hic est δεικνύειν idem dicitur διδάσκειν infra c. 8, 28.

Μείζονα τύτων δείξει ἀυτῷ ἔργα) Pater sanavit à serpente morsos : Sanavit Ezechiam & alios: atque ita filio monstra- vit, quid & ipsi ad Patris exemplum faciendum esset. Re- stat ut filius etiam majora imitetur, ac sic sibi monstrata re- ipsa doceat. Itaque δείξει hic ad τὴν φάσιν referendum est. Tale est illud NOVI, Gen. XII. 12.

Glossam hanc Arianam jam pridem refutarunt pii veteres : Cyrill. l. II. in Joh. c. 135. Qui dicunt Pa- trem primo facere, deinde operæ ejus imitari Filium, magna imperitia laborant : quomodo enim seorsim ac solus absq́; Filio Pater unquam operabitur? Sic vero explicant Patres verba Christi cum Hilario l. VII. de Trinit. Anne demonstratio operum aliud hic no- bis præterquam nativitatis fidem ingerit, ut subsi- stentem Filium, ex subsistente Deo Patre credamus, nisi forte per ignorationem credendus est Unigenitus Deus doctrinæ demonstrationis eguisse. Sed temeri- tas impiæ hujus existimationis non admittitur. Non enim doceri eget, qui quicquid docendus sit, sciat. Demonstrare non semper in sacris signifi- cat ostendere; Sed sæpe idem est, quod exhibere & dare, ut Psal. 4, 7. Psal. 85, 8. 2. Tim. 4, 14. item 1. Sam. 14, 12. Psal. 71, 20. Job. 10, 32. C. 14, 9. Act. 9, 16.

ἵνα ὑμεῖς θαυμάζητε) ἐκβατικὸν, id est ita ut fieri non pos- sit quin obstupeatis.

## 5:21
Vers. 21. ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ἐγείρει τὲς νεκρὸς) ἐγείρει is to be taken without a definition of time, that is, when he wills, as formerly at the prayers of Elisha. Among the excellent things that are said about God, this is one: to restore life, Deut. 32, 39. 1 Sam. 2, 6. Tob. 13, 2. Wisd. 16, 13.

κὶ ζωοποιεῖ) ההיה is an explanation of what he said ἐγείρει. ὥτω κὶ ὁ ὑὸς ὓς θέλεῖ ζωοποιεῖ) That is, ζωοποιήσει, as the following things declare. The sense is: You will see Lazarus and certain others raised up as a sign of the general resurrection. John is always intent on teaching the excellence of Christ, so that his Father is none other than the Creator of the world, against the errors of his time.

But here he is intent on teaching the ὁμουσίαν of the Son with the Father, and therefore the present verb is not to be taken for the future, but perpetually, for the Son always vivifies when and whom he wills, and he implies not so much the act as the power of vivifying. Therefore Pelargius explained these things more correctly: that phrase WHOM HE WILLS implies three things: 1. Universal power; that he can raise all. For no one can be said to raise the dead whom he wills, unless he has the power of raising all. 2. A certain restriction, with respect to the act of vivifying: For he who is said to vivify whom he wills, although he has the power of raising all, is signified not to exercise it on all, but at least on some whom he chose by his own will to be vivified. 3. The good pleasure of raising some in this age, for the demonstration of his divinity and power. Furthermore, the divinity of the Son is confirmed more illustriously here: For it is proper to God to do all things which he wills, Ps. 115, 3. And the Apostle says of the Holy Spirit that the same Spirit works all things, dividing to each one as he wills: Therefore the Son is also of a most free and omnipotent will: and for that reason of the same essence. He speaks here properly of spiritual vivification: for he will treat of the bodily, both universal and particular, later, as P. Tarnov. rightly observed in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ἐγείρει τὲς νεκρὸς) ἐγείρει sumen- dum est sine temporis definitione, id est cum vult, ut olim ad preces Elisæi. Inter eximia quæ de Deo dicuntnr hoc est vitam reddere, Deut. 32, 39. 1. Sam. 2, 6. Tob. 13, 2. Sap: 16, 13.

κὶ ζωοποιεῖ) ההיה est ἐπεξήγησις ejus quod dixit ἐγείρει. ὥτω κὶ ὁ ὑὸς ὓς θέλεῖ ζωοποιεῖ) Id est ζωοποιήσει, ut sequen- tia declarant. Sensus est : Videbitis suscitari Lazarum & alios quosdam in signum resuscitationis generalis. Johan- nes semper in eo est ut & Christi excellentiam doceat, ut Pa- trem ejus non alium esse quam mundi Conditorem, contra errores sui temporis.

Hic vero in eo est, ut Filii cum Patre ὁμουσίαν doceat, ideoque verbum præsens non pro futuro, sed perpetuo accipiendum, semper enim quando, & quos vult, vivificat Filius, nec tam actum quam potentiam vivificandi innuit. Rectius ergo hæc exposuit Pelargius: πρόθεσις illa verba QUOS VULT, tria innuit 1. Potestatem universalem; quod possit suscitare omnes. Nemo enim dici potest suscitare mortuos, quos vult, nisi qui potestatem ha- bet suscitandi omnes. 2. Restrictionem quandam, respectu actus vivificandi : Qui enim dicitur vivi- ficare quos vult, quamvis potestatem habeat omnes suscitandi, eam non in omnes exercere significatur, sed in aliquos saltem, quos suo arbitrio elegit vivifi- candos. 3. Ἐυδοκίαν excitandi in hoc seculo quos- dam, πρὸς ἐπίδειξιν divinitatis, & potentiæ suæ. Præterea divinitas Filii illustrius hic confirmatur: Proprium namque Dei, quæ velit, facere omnia, Psal. 115, 3. Et de Spiritu S. Apostolus operari omnia dicit eundem Spiritum, dividentem singulis prout vult : Voluntatis ergo liberrimæ & omnipotentis etiam est Filius: & idcirco ejusdem essentiæ. Lo- quitur autem hic proprie de vivificatione spiritu- ali : nam de corporali cum universali, tum parti- culari postea aget, ut probe observavit P. Tarnov. in h. l.

## 5:22
Vers. 22. ὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ κρίνει ὐδένα) To judge the world is God's, Gen. 18, 25. Ps. 82, 1. Formerly he judged the world in the times of Noah, he judged Sodom, he judged his people often: but now he will give judicial power to the Son, Acts 17, v. 31. 1 Pet. 4, 5. namely when he will constitute him king, Rev. 1, 5. for it is for Kings to judge, Ps. 72, 1. and elsewhere passim. But the future is expressed in the present tense for the sake of certainty and proximity. And you might perhaps rightly take that ὐδένα of those to whom the Gospel has been preached. See what is at Matt. 25. But γάρ is well placed; because it is of the same power to absolve and to condemn, and this was rightly added, so that those whom hope does not move may be restrained by evils.

Δέδωκε τῷ υἱῷ) He has decreed to give, the sense is, you will see the judgment of the Son upon this city, which will be a sign of the universal judgment.

To judge in the Hebrew phrase here denotes the supreme power of administering, and supreme authority, or the administration of the kingdom of the Messiah in the Church Ps. 72, 1. Jerem. 23, 5. Dan. 7, 14. Matth. 11, 27. Joh. 17, 2. 1. Cor. 15, 24. Thus, however, Christ concludes: The Father has given all judgment to the Son. Therefore, he does not judge anyone alone and separately, but through the Son, and with him.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ κρίνει ὐδένα) Judicare mundum Dei est Gen. 18, 25. Ps. 82, 1. Olim judicavit mundum tem- porib9 Noæ, judicavit Sodoma, judicavit sæpe & populum fuum: sed nunc judiciariam potestatem Filio dabit, Act. 17. v. 31. 1. Petr. 4, 5. nempe ubi ipsum regem constituet Apoc. 1, 5. nam Regum est judicare, Ps. 72, 1. & alibi passim. Fu- turum autem præsenti tempore effertur ob certitudinem & proximitatem. Et illud ᾠδῖνα recte forte accipias de his qui- bus Evangelium prædicatum est. Vide quæ ad Matth. 25, Bene autem ponitur γάρ; quia ejusdem est potestatis absol- vere & damnare, & recte hoc additum, ut quos spes non movet, malis coërceantur.

Δέδωκε τῷ υἱῷ) Decrevit dare, sensus est, videbitis judi- cium filii in hanc urbem quod signum erit judicii universa- lis.

Judicare Phrasi Ebræa hic denotat summam administrandi potestatem, & summum imperium, sive administrationem regni Messiæ in Ecclesia Ps. 72, 1. Jerem. 23, 5. Dan. 7, 14. Matth. 11, 27. Joh. 17, 2. 1. Cor. 15, 24. Ita autem concludit Christus : Pater omne judicium dedit Filio. E. non judicat quenquam solus & separatim, sed per Filium, & cum eo.

## 5:23
Vers. 23. that all may honor the Son) That is to say, so that men, having known this power of the Son, may worship and revere him, Ps. 2. 11. 12. Phil. 2, 10. The use of the Sabbath is to honor God, thus also the use of the Sabbath is to honor the Son.

The duty of the subjects of the kingdom of Christ and of the converted is expressed here, which is to honor and worship their judge or King, the Son of God no less than the Father, so that in this way ἰσοθεότης or rather ὁμοουσία may be expressed again. For he could not be worshipped with the same honor as the Father, unless he were of the same essence as the Father.

him who sent him) He who does an injury to an ambassador, especially when sent with the fullest power, is considered to do an injury to him whose person the ambassador sustains. See above c. 4, 34. below v. 30. 37. 38. c. 6, 38. c. 7, 16. and passim in this book. Christ tacitly shows how intimate he is with the Father. For God does not grant his honor to a stranger.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἵνα πάντες τιμῶσι τὸν υἱὸν) Ut scilicet homines cognita hac Filii potestate eum colant ac revereantur, Ps. 2. 11. 12. Phil. 2, 10. Usus Sabbati est Deum honorare, Sic & usus Sabbati est honorare Filium.

Officium hic subditorum regni Christi & converso- rum exprimitur, quod est honorare ac colere suum judicem sive Regem, Filium Dei non minus ac Patrem, ut ita denuo exprimatur ἰσοθεότης vel potius ὁμοουσία. Non enim eodem cum Patre ho- nore coli posset, nisi ejusdem cum Patre foret es- sentiæ.

τὸν πέμψαντα αὐτὸν) Qui legatum, præsertim cum ple- nissima potestate missum, injuria afficit, is injuria afficere eum censetur cujus personam legatus sustinet. Vide supra c. 4, 34. infra v. 30. 37. 38. c. 6, 38. c. 7, 16. & passim in hoc libro. Tacite ostendit Christus quam intimus sit Patri. Nam Deus honorem suum extraneo non concedit.

## 5:24
Vers. 24. that he who hears my word and believes him who sent me) He who hears my teaching in such a way that he believes, (for the copula has this force) could have added to me, but for the sake of removing envy he names the Father, whose ambassador he was; but it comes to the same thing whichever you say, below c. 12, 44. But just as elsewhere to trust, so here to believe or to give faith to one speaking, is to be understood with the purpose of obeying, as is clear below v. 29.

has eternal life) See above c. III. 36.

does not come into judgment) He is not subject to condemnation: just as to lead into temptation is to cause one to succumb to temptation.

has passed from death into life) So also in 1. Epist. c. III. 14. where it is attributed to love which here is attributed to faith, but indeed faith effective through love. Before he was a slave of death: now by faith he becomes an heir of life and is as it were transferred into another city. See Eph. 2, 5. Moreover, in the word has passed there is an allusion to the type of this thing, that is, the Passover, as also below c. 12, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ὅτι ὁ λόγον με ἀκούων καὶ πιστεύων τῷ πέμψαντί με) Qui meum dogma sic audit ut credat, (nam copula hanc vim habet) potuerat adjicere mihi sed invidiæ amoliendæ causa patrem nominat, cujus erat legatus; Eodem autem recidit utrum dicas, infra c. 12, 44. Sicut autem alibi confi- dere, ita hic credere sive fidem dicenti adhibere, intelligen- dum est cum obediendi proposito, ut patet infra v. 29.

ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον) Vide supra c. III. 36.

εἰς κρίσιν οὐκ ἔρχεται) Non subjacet damnatione: sicut εἰσενέγκειν εἰς πειρασμὸν est efficere ut tentationi succumba- tur.

μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωὴν) Sic & in 1. Epist. c. III. 14. ubi dilectioni tribuitur quod hic fidei, sed nempe efficaci per dilectionem. Ante erat servus mortis: nunc fide fit hæres vitæ & quasi in aliam civitatem transcribitur. Vide Eph. 2, 5. Est autem in voce μεταβέβηκεν allusio ad ty- pum hujus rei id est Pascha, ut & infra c. 12, 1.

## 5:25
Vers. 25. the hour is coming and now is) A future immediately impending is signified, as above c. 4, 25.

The dead hearing the voice of the Son of God) I think it is said more explicitly here what was signified obscurely above in comm. 21. and all the more so because the things that follow, when compared with similar passages, lead to that. And Christ was accustomed to use his voice in raising, Mark 5. v. 41. Luke 7, 14. John 11, 43.

And those who hear shall live) And they as soon as they have heard shall live, lest anyone think that those who hear are distinguished from those who do not hear. In the same way you may read those who hear Matth. 11. 9. Mark XIV. 1. Acts XXI. 22.

These things do not treat of the particular resuscitation of certain ones to this life, but of the gracious excitation or conversion of all those who hear and embrace his Evangelical voice to spiritual life: That that time of grace is now at hand, 2. Corinth. 6, 2. by which the vivification of those dead in transgressions is perfected through the Son, Ephes. 2, 5. Coloss. 2, 13. The cause of this divine power is rendered in verse 26. according to Tarnovius in this place, exerting itself, namely, in the vivification of the dead, or the conversion of infidels through the Son, and it is according to the divine nature the eternal generation, through which the Father gave to the Son essence and life, which he himself as he has in himself, and by essence or nature, so he gave also to the Son, that in himself, and by essence, or nature he has it, not by grace and by participation as creatures do: According to his human nature is his union with the divine nature, through which to the same, and as the Son of man, was given ἐξουσία, or the power of executing judgment, or of administering the kingdom, Matt. 11:27, ch. 28:18, Heb. 2:18. Not yet, says August. in his book on the City of God, does he speak of the second resurrection, that is, of bodies, which is to be in the end, but of the first. For this, in order to distinguish it, he says: The hour comes, and now is. Bede agrees with Augustine, as does Rupert; and Pelargus approves of that sense as the simpler one, p. 64. Cyril, book 2, ch. 143, refers the former hearing to the last day, the latter, and those who shall hear, will live at that time of Christ, so that he teaches that the time of believing is already present, and Christ promises that the eternal reward of this obedience will be theirs. Thus he grants that faithful hearing is signified (which is of the living, not of those dead corporally) regarding the latter member. But the reason does not appear why a different sense should be established in the former words, and those dead hearing the voice of the Son of God be understood as corporally dead, not spiritually. Most all acknowledge that the resurrection of the dead on the last day is finally dealt with in v. 28, even those who with Theophylact (which was also done by the blessed Chemnitz) refer these to the corporal resuscitation of Lazarus and others. The blessed Ægydius Hunnius urges also those words of promise, κ̓ οἱ ἀκύσαντες ζήσονται: It must be known that these words do not deal with the resuscitation of the dead on the last day. For it is said here that those who have heard the voice of the Son of man will live. But it is certain that the impious on the last day are to be resuscitated not to the resurrection of life, but to the punishment of eternal death. Therefore, Christ prophesies concerning that resuscitation of the dead which is to be through the voice and trumpet of the Gospel: promising and confirming with an oath that all who have obeyed that voice will live again from spiritual death.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἔρχεται ὥρα καὶ νῦν ἐστι) Futurum proxime immi- nens significatur, ut supra c. 4, 25.

Οἱ νεκροὶ ἀκούσαντες τῆς φωνῆς τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Puto hic expli- catius dici quod supra involute significabatur comm. 21. eoq; magis quia quæ sequuntur cum similibus locis collata eo ducunt. Et solebat Christus voce uti in excitando, Marc. 5. v. 41. Luc. 7, 14. Joh. 11, 43.

Καὶ οἱ ἀκούσαντες ζήσονται) Et illi simul atq; audierint vi- vent, ne quis audientes à non audientibus putet distingui. Eodem modo οἱ διακούσαντες legas Matth. 11. 9. Marc. XIV. 1. Act. XXI. 22.

Agunt hæc non de particulari quorundam ad hanc vitam resuscitatione, sed de gratiosa eo- rum omnium, qui vocem ejus Evangelicam audiunt & amplectuntur, ad vitam spiritua- lem excitatione vel conversione: Tempus illud gratiæ jam præsto esse, 2. Corinth. 6, 2. quo vivi- ficatio mortuorum in delictis per Filium perfi- citur, Ephes. 2, 5. Coloss. 2, 13. Causa hujus divinæ potentiæ redditur vers. 26. secundum Tarnovium in b. l. exerenti scil. sese in vivificatione mortuo- rum, sive conversione infidelium per Filium, est- que secundum divinam naturam æterna genera- tio, per quam Pater dedit Filio essentiam & vi- tam, quam ipse ut in seipso, & per essentiam sive naturam habet, ita dedit etiam Filio, ut in seipso, & per essentiam, sive naturam habeat eam, non per gratiam & per participationem ut creaturæ: Secundum humanam naturam est unio ejus cum divina natura, per quam eidem, quatenq; Filio hominis, data est ἐξουσία, sive potestas faciendi judicii, sive administrandi regni, Matth. XI. 27. c. 28. v. 18. Ebr. II. 18. Nondum, inquit August. l. de Civ. Dei, de secunda resurrectione, id est, corporum loquitur, quæ in fine futura est, sed de prima. Hanc quippe, ut distingueret, ait: Venit hora, & nunc est. Augustino annuit Beda, ut & Rupertus; eumque sensum probat Pelargus ceu simpliciorem p. 64. Cyrillus l. II. c. 143. prius audire ad extremum diem refert, posterius, & qui audierint, vivent ad tempus illud Christi, ut jam adesse tempus credendi doceat, & hujus obedientiæ mercedem æternam fore his promittat Christus. Sic largitur auditum fidelem significari (qui viventium est, non mortuorum corporaliter) quod ad membrum posterius. At non apparet ratio, cur diversus sensus statuatur in verbis prioribus, ac mortui vocem Filii Dei audientes intelligantur corporaliter mortui, non spiritualiter. De mortuorum resuscitatione in die novissima, v. 28. demum agi agnoscunt plerique omnes, etiam qui cum Theophylacto (quod à B. Chemnitio quoque factum) hæc ad Lazari & aliorum corporalem resuscitationem referunt. Urget B. Ægydius Hunnius & verba illa promissionis, κ̓ οἱ ἀκύσαντες ζήσονται: Sciendum hisce verbis non agi de resuscitatione mortuorum in novissima die. Dicitur enim hic, eos, qui audierint vocem filii hominis, victuros. Impios autem in novissima die non ad vitæ resurrectionem, sed ad æternæ mortis supplicium resuscitandos constat. De ea igitur mortuorum resuscitatione, quæ per vocem ac tubam Evangelii futura sit, vaticinatur Christus: promittens & juramento confirmans, omnes, qui voci illi obediverint, ex spirituali morte revicturos.

## 5:26
Verse 26. Ἔχει ζωὴν ἐν ἑαυτῷ) He has the right of giving life within himself, for he himself is also the one who breathed life into man. See above ch. 1:4.

Ἔδωκε κὶ τῷ ὑῗ ζωὴν ἔχειν ἐν ἑαυτῷ) To have it in his power in such a way that he can give it to whom he wishes.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ἔχει ζωὴν ἐν ἑαυτῷ) Jus dandæ vitæ penes se habet, nam & ipse est qui vitam homini inspiravit. Vide supra c. I. 4.

Ἔδωκε κὶ τῷ ὑῗ ζωὴν ἔχειν ἐν ἑαυτῷ) Ita habere in sua potestate ut cui velit eam dare possit.

## 5:27
Verse 27. ἐξουσίαν ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ κὶ κρίσιν ποιεῖν) κρίσιν ποιεῖν here is to condemn to death. See above 22. He also said ποιῆσαι κρίσιν, Jud. 15.

Ὅτι ὑὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐσί) Because this is that Son of man, of whom Daniel foretold that it would come to pass that dominion and a kingdom would be given to him over all nations without end, Dan. 7:13, 14. For what is read there, like the Son of man, is clearly the same expression as that at Phil. 2:7, ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος. In the Greek of Daniel it is χήματι ἐυρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος. These signify that he himself in external appearance bore nothing greater than a man, and indeed a common one. See what was said at Matt. 8:20, and add what follows in the cited place to the Philippians, that because he conducted himself so humbly, therefore he was exalted on high, and a name was given to him above every name, so that every knee should bow to him.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἐξουσίαν ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ κὶ κρίσιν ποιεῖν) κρίσιν ποιεῖν est hic condemnare ad mortem. Vide supra 22. ποιῆσαι κρίσιν dixit & Jud. 15.

Ὅτι ὑὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐσί) Quia hic ille est filius hominis, de quo Daniel prædixit, fore ut ei detur dominatus & regnum in omnes gentes fine fine Dan. VII. 13. 14. Nam quod ibi legitur similis filio hominis plane eadem locutio est quæ ad Phil. II. 7. ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος. In Græco Danielis est χήματι ἐυρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος. Significant hæc ipsum specie externa nihil majus homine & quide plebejo præ se tulisse. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. VIII 20. & adde quod dicto loco ad Philippenses sequitur, quia se tam humilem gessit, ideo eum in sublime evectum, datumque ei nomen super omne nomen, ut omne genu ei curvetur.

## 5:28
V. 28 Μὴ θαυμάζετε τῦτο) Above 3:7, 1 Ep. 3:13. The sense is this: do not marvel at this which I have said, I will tell you more wonderful things.

Ἔρχεται ὥρα) It is not added κ̓ νῦν ἐσιν because this time is further off. Ἔρχεται therefore is, he will come at some time. See 2 Pet. ch. 3:8.

ἐν ᾗ πάντες) Not one and another, but absolutely all.

οἱ ἐν τοῖς μνημείοις) Not only those who are on a little bed, like the young girl, or on a bier, like the widow's son, but those who are in the tombs, i.e., not for a short time like Lazarus, but who have been there for a very long time.

Others more correctly with Augustine, Bede, and Rupert explain these things thus: Do not marvel at this, which I have said concerning spiritual vivification, I will explain to you something much more worthy of admiration, which will be done by me: which will be the resuscitation of all the dead. Thus Pelargus, Tarnovius, as also the blessed Ægyd. Hunnius, as if to say: It is indeed a wonderful work that I can vivify those who are spiritually dead in sins: but that is not less noble in your own judgment, that I will one day bring forth from the lowest depths of the earth those who are not only dead, but have been reduced to dust.

They shall hear his voice) Just as the voice of the Son is the voice of the Father, so the voice of the Archangel is the voice of Christ, who will send him. See I Thess. IV. 16. Add I Cor. XV. 52. & Matth. XXIV. 51. where see what is noted.

Latin:

V. 28 Μὴ θαυμάζετε τῦτο) Supra III. 7. I. ep. III. 13. Sensus hic est: nolite hoc mirari quod dixi, dicam admirabiliora.

Ἔρχεται ὥρα) Non additum est κ̓ νῦν ἐσιν quia hoc tempus abest longius. Ἔρχεται ergo est, veniet aliquando. Vid. 2. Pet. c. III. 8.

ἐν ᾗ πάντες) Non unus & alter, sed omnes plane.

οἱ ἐν τοῖς μνημείοις) Non tantum qui in lectulo sunt, ut adolescentula, aut in feretro, ut viduæ filius, sed qui in sepulchris, scil. non exiguo tempore ut Lazarus sed diutissime fuerunt.

Rectius alii cum August. Beda, Ruperto hæc ita exponunt: Ne miremini hoc, quod dixi de spirituali vivificatione, multo magis admiratione dignum vobis exponam, quod à me fiet: quod erit mortuorum omnium resuscitatio. Sic Pelargus, Tarnovius, ut & B. Ægyd. Hunnius, q. d. Mirandum quidem opus est, quod spiritualiter in peccatis mortuos vivificare possum: sed illud vestro etiam judicio non est ignobilius, quod eos qui non tantum mortui, sed in pulverem redacti sunt, ex imis aliquando terræ visceribus producam.

Ἀκούσονται τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ) Sicut vox Filii est vox Patris sic vox Archangeli est vox Christi, qui eum mittet. Vid. I. Thess. IV. 16. Adde I. Cor. XV. 52. & Matth. XXIV. 51. ubi quæ notata vide.

## 5:29
Vers. 29. And shall come forth) That is, having heard the voice, they shall go. Unto the resurrection of life) Which is תְחִיַּת הַחַיִּים to the Hebrews & by way of excellence often resurrection. Sometimes also the resurrection of the just, XIV. 14. unto the resurrection of judgment) That is, unto punishment, Matth. XXV. 46. Thus the day of judgment 2 Pet. II. 10. is explained by those being punished.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Καὶ ἐκπορεύσονται) Id est audita voce ibunt. Εἰς ἀνάστασιν ζωῆς) Quæ תְחִיַּת הַחַיִּים Hebræis & κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν sæpe ἀνάστασις. Interdum & ἀνάστασις τῶν δικαίων, XIV. 14. εἰς ἀνάστασιν κρίσεως) Id est εἰς κόλασιν, Matth. XXV. 46. Sic ἡμέρα κρίσεως 2. Petr. II. 10. exponitur per κολαζομένους.

## 5:30
Vers. 30. I can of mine own self do nothing) Christ always so tempers those things which he is compelled to declare about himself that he refers all honor to the Father, and removes that charge as if he were making a man equal to the Father. I can of myself here is to be taken as above 19, except that there he speaks of any action whatsoever, here of a judicial one.

as I hear) From the law which the Father has prescribed concerning saving those who believe in me, and condemning those who reject me, I learn by example and voice, and therefore here I hear is the same as above what the Father teaches, and below VIII. 28. as the Father has taught me.

I judge) Present for future, for the preceding things seem to demand that, as above 21, he quickeneth.

and my judgment is just) Conjunction for a rational: my judgment is therefore equitable because I do not depart from the Father's rule. See the prophecy of Is. XI. 4.

Because I seek not mine own will) An epexegesis of the aforementioned: Judges who are devoted to their own affections, advantages, glory, or revenge are often led astray from what is equitable. I am nothing of the sort; I am not led by my own affections, but I care for that which I know to be thanks to the Father. For to seek is to care for, to hold as paramount, below VII. 18. VIII. v. 50.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Οὐ δύναμαι ἐγὼ ποιεῖν ἀπ᾽ ἐμαυτοῦ οὐδὲν) Semper ea quæ de se prædicare cogitur Christus ita temperat ut o- mnem honorem referat ad Patrem, & removeat illud crimen quasi hominem Patri æqualem faciat. δύναμαι δὲ ἀφ᾽ ἑαυ- τοῦ hic sumenda ut supra 19. nisi quod ibi de quavis actione loquitur, hic de judiciali.

καθὼς ἀκούω) Ex lege quam Pater præscripsit de servandis qui in me credunt, damnandis, qui me rejiciunt, discimo ex- emplo & voce, itaque hic ἀκούω idem est, quod supra ἁ ὁ πα- τὴρ διδάσκει, & infra VIII. 28. καθὼς ἐδίδαξέ με ὁ πατήρ.

Κρίνω) Præsens pro futuro, id enim præcedentia videntur exigere, ut supra 21. ζωοποιεῖ.

καὶ ἡ κρίσις ἐμὴ δικαία ἐστὶ) Copula pro rationali : ideo æ- quum est judicium meum quia à Patris regula non discedo. Vide vaticinium Es. XI. 4.

Ὅτι οὐ ζητῶ τὸ θέλημα τὸ ἐμὸν) Epexegesis ante dicti : Judi- ces qui suis affectibus student, commodis, gloriæ, ultioni, sæpe ab æquo transversi aguntur. Nihil tale ego, non ducor meis affectibus, sed id curo, quod Patri gratiam esse scio. Ζητεῖν enim est curare, præcipuum habere, infra VII. 18. VIII. v. 50.

## 5:31
Vers. 31. is not true) It is a proverbial saying among the Hebrews as appears in VIII. 13. נֶאֱמָן which the Greeks often translate as faithful, not rarely they also translate it as true or truthful, it signifies worthy of belief, in Syriac שְׁרִירָא. In this sense he is called a true witness in the Rhetorics to Alexander c. XVI. Thus the Greeks translate that in Deut. XIX. 15. every word shall stand as every word shall be true. This is what the Romans say, that no one is a suitable witness in his own case. It is a Greek adage, a witness from home. Something can be true which is not such by itself alone as to obtain belief. One can say true things about oneself, as Christ says in VIII. v. 14, but unless other things are added, he does not persuade.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ἐκ ἐστιν ἀληθής) Dictum est proverbiale apud Hebræos ut apparet VIII. 13. נֶאֱמָן quod Græci sæpe vertunt πιστὸς, non raro etiam vertunt ἀληθὴς aut ἀληθινὸς, fide di- gnum significat, Syro שְׁרִירָא Hoc sensu μάρτυς ἀληθινὸς, dicitur in Rhetoricis ad Alexandrum c. XVI. Sic Græci il- lud Deut. XIX. 15. stabit omne verbum vertunt ἀληθὲς ἐσται πᾶν ῥῆμα. Hoc est quod Romani dicunt, neminem idoneum esse testem in re sua. Græcum est adagium οἴκοθεν μάρτυς. Potest aliquid esse verum, quod solum per se tale non est ut fidem impetret. Potest quis de se vera dicere, ut ait Christus VIII. v. 14. sed nisi alia accedant non persuadet.

## 5:32
V. 32. There is another) It is very easy for us to take this as referring to John, because the things which follow immediately are about him.

I know that his witness is true.) It is sufficiently certain to me that he is such a witness, because he could not be rejected by us by any right. True here again means worthy of belief.

Chrysostom indeed understands the Baptist by another, but it is more convenient with Cyril to understand the Father, of whom he speaks similarly in John VIII. 18. See B. Chemnit. Harm. c. XLVI.

Latin:

V. 32. Ἄλλος ἐστι) Facillimum est ut de Johanne suma- mus, quia de eo sunt quæ proxime sequuntur.

Οἶδα ὅτι ἀληθής ἐστιν ἡ μαρτυρία.) Satis mihi constat talem esse testem, quia nobis nullo jure possit rejici. Ἀληθὴς hic iterum fide dignus.

Intelligit sane Chrysostomus Baptistam per * ἄλ- λον, sed convenientius est cum Cyrillo intelligere Patrem de quo similiter loquitur Joh. VIII. 18. Vid. B. Chemnit. Harm. c. XLVI.

## 5:33
Vers. 33. ye have sent unto John) You sent to him by public authority, as to a man of venerable holiness, and whom you yourselves esteemed very highly.

Μεμαρτύρηκε τῇ ἀληθείᾳ) Modestly said: he did not say, he bore witness to me, but to the truth, being lawfully called upon. A similar construction is in Luke IX. 22, above III. 26, 28, and Job XXIX. 11. One bears witness concerning someone, who says good or evil about him: to someone, who says good which may profit him.

Latin:

Vers. 33. ὑμεῖς ἀπεστάλκατε πρὸς ἰωάννην) Publica autori- tate ad eum misistis, tanquam ad hominem venerandæ san- ctitatis, & quem ipsi faceretis plurimi.

Μεμαρτύρηκε τῇ ἀληθείᾳ) Modeste dictum: non dixit, mihi perhibuit testimonium, sed veritati, legitime compel- latus. Similis constructio Luc. IX. 22. supra III. 26. 28. & Job. XXIX. 11. de aliquo testimonium perhibet, qui de eo bo- num vel malum dicit: alicui, qui bonum quod ei prosit.

## 5:34
Vers. 34. ἐγὼ παρὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὴν μαρτυρίαν λαμβάνω) λαμβάνειν τὴν μαρτυρίαν has a different sense here than above III. v. 11, 32, 33, and John V. 9. Here λαμβάνω is I require, as below 41, 44, where in the opposite member ζητεῖν is placed as having the same value. Thus in Latin we are said to accept that which we eagerly desire.

Ταῦτα λέγω) I say these things κατὰ συνκατάβασιν, accommodating myself to you.

Ἵνα ὑμεῖς σωθῆτε) He removes from himself the desire for glory; I claim nothing for myself except for your sake, I did not even say who I was, until after John had indicated me. Christ desires, and indeed seriously, the salvation even of those who are not saved: he suffers nothing to be lacking on his part.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ἐγὼ παρὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὴν μαρτυρίαν λαμβάνω) Ali- um hic sensum habet λαμβάνειν τὴν μαρτυρίαν quam supra III. v. 11. 32. 33. & Joh. V. 9. Hic λαμβάνω est requiro ut infra 41. 44. ubi in opposito membro ponitur ζητεῖν ut idem valens, Sic latine accipere dicimur, quod avide appetimus.

Ταῦτα λέγω) Dico hæc κατὰ συνκατάβασιν me vobis attem- perans.

Ἵνα ὑμεῖς σωθῆτε) Amolitur à se gloriæ cupiditatem, nihil mihi vindico nisi vestri causa, ne dixi quidem quis essem, ni- si postquam me Johannes indicaverat. Vult Christus & qui- dem serio salutem etiam eorum qui non servantur: nihil patitur ex sua parte desiderari.

## 5:35
Vers. 35. ἦν) These things seem to have been said after John was captured.

Ὁ λύχνος ὁ καιόμενος καὶ φαίνων) See how he has adapted to John what used to be said of Elijah, sent in the spirit of Elijah, it is said of Elijah. λόγος αὐτοῦ ὡς λαμπὰς ἐκαίετο in Ecclesiasticus XLVIII. 1. Moreover, καίεσθαι here is nothing other than to be kindled, the beginning of τοῦ φαίνειν. Matthew V. 12, Luke XII. 35, Revelation IV. 5, VIII. 10. It is the Hebrew דָּלַק which the Syrian uses. In the temple נֵרוֹת הַמַּעֲרָכָה are for the Greeks λύχνοι τῶν κδυσεων, Ex. XXXIX. 37. To Peter the word of the Prophets is called a λύχνος φαίνων II. I. 19.

Ἀγαλλιαθῆναι πρὸς ὥραν ἐν τῷ φωτὶ αὐτοῦ) Like children who are delighted by the sight of light, but do not have the use of it. Πρὸς ὥραν as in Philem. 15 is not for a long time, and thus you rightly understand that בשמעה which is in Daniel IV. Jesus shows the inconstancy of the Jews who began to despise John after he bore witness concerning Jesus himself.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ἦν) Videntur hæc dicta capto Johanne.

Ὁ λύχνος ὁ καιόμενος καὶ φαίνων) Vide ut, quod de Elia dici solebat, Johanni aptaverit, misso in spiritu Eliæ, de Elia dicitur. λόγος αὐτοῦ ὡς λαμπὰς ἐκαίετο Ecclesiastici XLVIII. 1. Est autem hic καίεσθαι nihil aliud quam accep- di, principium τοῦ φαίνειν. Matth. V. 12. Luc. XII. 35. Apoc. IV. 5. VIII. 10. Hebræum est דָּלַק quo utitur Syrus. In templo נֵרוֹת הַמַּעֲרָכָה Græcis sunt λύχνοι τῶν κδυ- σεων, Ex. XXXIX. 37. Petro sermo Prophetarum dicitur λύχνος φαίνων II. I. 19.

Ἀγαλλιαθῆναι πρὸς ὥραν ἐν τῷ φωτὶ αὐτοῦ) Ut pueri qui de- lectantur visu lucis, sed usum ejus non habent. Πρὸς ὥραν ut Philem. 15. est non multo tempore, & sic recte fumas illud בשמעה quod est apud Danielem IV. Ostendit Jesus Ju- dæorum inconstantiam qui Johannem aspernari cœperunt postquam de ipso Jesu testimonium perhibuit.

## 5:36
Vers. 36. Μαρτυρίαν μείζων τῆς Ἰωάννη) A similar comparison in 1 Ep. V. 9. From which it appears that what was previously noted is true, that there is here an ellipsis of the article, as often elsewhere.
