Τὰ γὰρ ἔργα) He often invokes the testimony of works that are merely divine, against which there was no quibbling. See above c. III. 12. below IX. 32, 33. c. X. 25, 37, 38. c. XIV. 10, 11, c. XV. 24.

Αὐτὰ τὰ ἔργα) An elegant anaphora, such as that: Pallas te hoc vulnere, Pallas Immolat. For this manner of speaking has emphasis.

Ὅτι ὁ Πατὴρ με ἀπέσταλκε) That I come by the command of God.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Μαρτυρίαν μείζων τῆς Ἰωάννη) Similis collatio I. ep. V. 9. Ex quo apparet veram esse quod pridem monitum est, esse hic ἔλλειψιν articuli, ut sæpe alibi.

Τὰ γὰρ ἔργα) Sæpe advocat operum mere divinorum te- stimonium adversus quæ nulla erat cavillatio. Vide supra c. III. 12. infra IX. 32. 33. c. X. 25, 37. 38. c. XIV. 10, 11, c. XV. 24.

Αὐτὰ τὰ ἔργα) Elegans anaphora, qualis illa: Pallas te hoc vulnere, Pallas Immolat. Habet enim emphasin istud loquendi genus.

Ὅτι ὁ Πατὴρ με ἀπέσταλκε) Me venire Dei mandato.

## 5:37
V. 37. Καὶ ὁ πέμψας με πατὴρ μεμαρτύρηκε περὶ ἐμοῦ) I will gladly connect this with the preceding, so that the sense may be that by his works he showed himself to be sent by God and that he does not lack God's testimony. For there preceded: 'But I do not receive testimony from men.' The works are the testimony. The Father is the witness.

Οὔτε φωνὴν αὐτῦ ἀκηκόατε πώποτε, ὔτε εἶδος αὐτῦ ἑωράκατε) The sense is: You have not known him familiarly, as I have known him, and thus you have no need of my indication. See above I. 8. & III. 32. & what is adduced there. It is to be noted that the people themselves once demanded that God should not reveal himself by voice or by form, but through the Prophets, Deut. XVIII, 15. Exod. c. XX. 19.

Latin:

V. 37. Καὶ ὁ πέμψας με πατὴρ μεμαρτύρηκε περὶ ἐμοῦ) Con- nectam libens cum præcedentibus, ut sensus sit operibus ostendi se missum à Deo & se Dei testimonio non carere. Nam præcessit ἐγὼ δὲ οὐ παρὰ ἀνθρώπων τὴν μαρτυρίαν λαμ- βάνω. Opera sunt testimonium. Pater testis.

Οὔτε φωνὴν αὐτῦ ἀκηκόατε πώποτε, ὔτε εἶδος αὐτῦ ἑωρά- κατε) Sensus est: Vos eum non novistis familiariter, ut ego novi, atque ita ut meo indicio opus non habeatis. Vide su- pra I. 8. & III. 32. & quæ ibi adducta. Notandum est ipsum populum id olim postulasse, ut Deus se nec voce nec specie patefaceret, sed per Prophetas, Deut. XVIII, 15. Exod. c. XX. 19.

## 5:38
Vers. 38. Καὶ τὸν λόγον αὐτῦ ἐκ ἔχετε μένοντα ἐν ὑμῖν) And here, as often elsewhere, is 'and yet.' By yourselves you do not know what the nature and will of God is, and yet the commands which he himself sends to you through me, you do not admit within your mind. Μένειν for John is to be in, to be fixed. The same is μένειν here as χωρεῖν below VIII. 37. 'my word does not have a place in you,' it is not admitted. See what was noted above concerning the word μένειν in III. 36.

Ὅτι) This is demonstrative. It appears that what I say is true. Do you stubbornly refuse to have faith in him who has been sent by God? How will he learn the commands of the King, who excludes the ambassador?

Latin:

Vers. 38. Καὶ τὸν λόγον αὐτῦ ἐκ ἔχετε μένοντα ἐν ὑμῖν) καὶ hic ut alibi sæpe, est & tamen. Per vos ipsos non novistis quæ Dei natura ac voluntas sit, & tamen quæ ad vos ipse mandata per me mittit ea intra animum non admittitis. Μένειν Johanni est inesse, infigi. Idem hic est μένειν quod χω- ρεῖν infra VIII. 37. ὁ λόγος ὁ ἐμὸς οὐ χωρεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν locum non ha- bet, non admittitur. Vide quæ de voce μένειν annotata su- pra III. 36.

Ὅτι) Est hic ἀποδεικτικὸν. Apparet verum esse quod di- co. Num ei qui à Deo missus est fidem habere pertina- citer recusatis. Quomodo mandata Regis discet, qui lega- tum excludit?

## 5:39
Vers. 39. Ἐρευνᾶτε) Do not just read, but weigh with an attentive mind. Thus ἐρευνᾷν is taken below VII. 52. 1 Pet. I. 11. It is the same as ἀνακρίνειν τὰς γραφὰς in Acts XVII. 11.

Τὰς γραφὰς) All the writings which you receive as divine.

Ὅτι ὑμεῖς δοκεῖτε ἐν αὐταῖς ζωὴν αἰώνιον ἔχειν) You attribute even more than is right to them. For you think that eternal life is promised to those who observe the precepts of the law, and thus that that life is contained directly in those books. See on Matt. V. 17. XIX. 7. where likewise ζωὴ is simply ζωὴ αἰώνιος. And note that the matter here is not with the Sadducees but with the Pharisees, who called the law the fountain of life, and interpreted the passage of Deuteronomy XXXII. 47 concerning eternal life.

This is false, that they attributed more than is right to the Scripture of the O.T. when the Jews think that they have eternal life in it. Christ does not reject this, but approves it. Nor here only, but also Luke X. 28. nor does the Apostle otherwise Gal. III. 12. who confirms this also 2. Tim. III. 15. Just as we have already noted this Pelagian-Socinian error of Grotius several times.

Grotius, however, rightly takes the word ἐρευνᾶτε in the imperative rather than the indicative, and explains it by ἀνακρίνειν: although the emphasis of the word derived from a scrutiny in metallic veins, as Chrysostom warned, or from the tracking of wild beasts, is not to be neglected, such an investigation as is required first, or at least ought to be joined with ἀνακρίσει: The Syrian, Chrysostom, Augustine, Theophylact, and Maldonatus also explain it in the imperative, saying: If you listen, all serious authors except Cyril. Thus also Dietenberger and Emser, among the Papists, rendered it; the Tigurines and Belgians, among the Reformed: B. Luther and most of our own take it in the same way. Piscator, however, Beza, Polanus, Tossanus, and Camero explain it in the indicative mood: To whom our Erasmus Schmid also joined himself, whom Dn. D. Sebastian Schmid refutes in Coll. Bibl. post. p. 2. urging for the imperative both that there is greater emphasis in the imperative, and that it is not credible that the common people of the Jews, with whom Christ is dealing here, applied such diligence in reading Scripture that they earned this eulogy concerning the searched Scriptures, which does not even suit the Pharisees and Scribes: who are also rebuked here for negligence, as Chrysostom and Euthymius note, i.e., Search the scriptures, which hitherto you have not done as you ought. He adds, however, the cause of the exhortation, because you yourselves think that you have eternal life in them, which opinion of theirs must indeed be true, because he urges them from that to read scripture. Subjoining further: And they are those which testify of me, i.e., that through me and faith in me you may have eternal life: and you are not willing to come to me, so that, i.e., you may have life, whence the use of the Scripture of the O.T. and its perspicuity and perfection is confirmed.

And they are those which testify concerning me) and here is 'but': and understand μαρτυρῦσαι from the following clause that I am he who gives life. Those Scriptures indicate the giver of that life: they reject you to me: when they prophesy concerning the new covenant, when they prophesy concerning the everlasting kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 39. Ἐρευνᾶτε) Non legit tantum, sed attento animo expendite. Sic ἐρευνᾷν sumitur infra VII. 52. 1. Petr. I. 11. idem est ἀνακρίνειν τὰς γραφὰς Act. XVII. 11.

Τὰς γραφάς) Omnia scripta quæ ut divina recipitis.

Ὅτι ὑμεῖς δοκεῖτε ἐν αὐταῖς ζωὴν αἰώνιον ἔχειν) Etiam plus æquo illis tributis. Existimatis enim legis præcepta obser- vantibus promitti vitam æternam, atque ita directe eam vi- tam illis libris contineri. Vide ad Matth. V. 17. XIX. 7. ubi itidem ζωὴ simpliciter est ζωὴ αἰώνιος. Et nota non cum Sadducæis sed cum Pharisæis hic rem esse qui legem voca- bant fontem vitæ, & de vita æterna accipiebant locum Deu- teronomii XXXII. 47.

Falsum hoc, quod plus æquo tribuerint Scripturæ V. T. cum in illa se vitam æternam habere putant Ju- dæi. Non reprobat hoc Christus, sed approbat. Neque hic solum, sed etiam Luc. X. 28. nec aliter Apostolus Gal. III. 12. qui id confirmat quoque 2. Tim. III. 15. Sicut hunc Pelagiano-Socinianum errorem Grotii jam aliquoties notavimus.

Recte autem Grotius in Imperativo potius acci- pit vocem ἐρευνᾶτε, quã Indicativo, & per ἀνακρί- νειν explicat: quamvis non negligenda vocis em- phasis à scrutinio in venis metallicis, ut Chrysostomus monuit, vel investigatione ferarum deducta, qualis indagatio prius requiritur, vel certe conjuncta esse debet cum ἀνακρίσει: In Imperativo etiam expo- nunt Syrus, Chrysost. Augustinus, Theophyl. & Mal- donato dicente: Si audias, omnes graves autores præter Cyrillum. Sic etiam reddidere Dietenberger 9, & Emserus, è Papistis; Tigurini & Belge, è Refor- matis: B. Lutherus & pleriq; nostrates, eodem modo accipiunt. Piscator tamen, Beza, Polanus, Tossanus & Camero indicativo modo exponunt: Quibus se junxit etiam Erasmus Schmidius noster, quem refellit Dn. D. Sebastian. Schmidius Coll. Bibl. post. p. 2. pro Imperativo urgens tum quod major emphasis sit in imperativo, tum quod credibile non sit, quod vulgus Judæorum, cum quo Christus hic agit, tantam in legenda Scriptura diligentiam adhibuerit, ut hoc elogium reportarit, de pervesti- gatis Scripturis, quod ne Pharisaeis & Scribis qui- dem convenit: quietiam hic reprehenduntur ob negligentiam, notante Chrysost. & Euthymio, q. d. Scrutamini scripturas, quod hactenus non fecistis ut debuistis. Addit autem causam adhortationis, quia vos ipsimet putatis, vos habere vitam æternam in ipsts, quam sententiam eorum utique veram esse oportet, quia inde ad scripturam legendam horta- tur. Subjungens porro: Et illae sunt quæ testantur de me, scil. quod per me & fidem in me & vitam æ- ternam habeatis: & non vultis venire ad me, ut scil. vitam habeatis, unde usus Scripturæ V. T. ejus- demque perspicuitas, & perfectio confirmatur.

Καὶ ἐκεῖναί εἰσιν αἱ μαρτυρῦσαι περὶ ἐμῦ) κὰι hic est Atqui: & μαρτυρῦσαι ex commate sequenti intellige ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ δι- δὺς τὴν ζωήν. Scripturæ illæ indicant vitæ istius datorem: ad me vos rejiciunt: cum de novo fœdere, cum de regno sempiterno vaticinantur.

## 5:40
Vers. 40. And you are not willing to come to me that you may have life) and again for 'yet'. And yet, he says, you are not willing to come to me, that you may receive eternal life. For to come is to be taught, below VI. v. 44. 45. when he says, you are not willing, he shows that it stands with them that they do not arrive at life.

Latin:

Vers. 40. Καὶ ἐ θέλετε ἐλθεῖν πρός μείνα ζωὴν ἔχητε) καὶ rursų pro tamen. Et tamen, inquit, non vultis à me dicere, ut accipiatis vitam æternam. Nam ἔρχεσθαι est doceri, infra VI. v. 44. 45. cum dicit, non vultis, ostendit penes ipsos stare quo minus ad vitam perveniant.

## 5:41
Vers. 41. I do not receive glory from men) I do not say what I say about my authority from a desire of obtaining honor from you. See above 34. In that most ancient manuscript, from man, that is, from any man, whoever he may be.

Latin:

Vers. 41. Δόξαν παρὰ ἀνθρώπων ἐ λαμβάνω) Ego quæ dico de mea auctoritate non dico appetitu honoris à vobis adipi- scendi. Vide supra 34. In Manuscripto illo antiquissimo πα- ρὰ ἀνθρώπω, id est ab aliquo hominum, quisquis ille sit.

## 5:42
Vers. 42. But I have known you) But I say this for this reason, because your vice with which you labor and which hinders you from the journey to eternal life is known to me. The emphasis is on that 'you'. Such as you think me to be, such you are.

that you do not have the love of God in yourselves) You have piety and zeal for divine glory in your mouth, not in your mind, below 44. Thus you may read the love of God Luke XI. 42. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 42. Ἀλλὰ ἔγνωκα ὑμᾶς) Sed ideo hoc dico, quod co- gnitum mihi sit vitium vestrum quo laboratis & quod vos ab itinere ad vitam æternam impedit. Emphasis est in illo ὑμᾶς. Qualem me putatis, vos tales estis.

ὅτι τὴν ἀγάπην τῦ Θεῦ ἐκ ἔχετε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς) Habetis in ore non in animo pietatem & studium gloriæ divinæ, infra 44. Sic ἀγάπην Θεῦ legas Luc. XI. 42. & alibi.

## 5:43
Vers. 43. I have come in the name of my Father) With truly divine power.

And you do not receive me) Only because the purity of my doctrine opposes your evil morals and your ambition: of the leaders indeed, because they alone wish to be considered holy among the people, but of the common people, because they fear being betrayed by the leaders. To receive here is the same as above I. 11. 12.

If another comes in his own name) Certainly bringing no signs of such power, by his own authority. For that is what 'name' signifies here, as Acts IV. 7. and often elsewhere. Such was Bar-Cochebas. See at Matth. XXII, 26. Add 2. Thess. II. 10. And 'if' here is 'when': as XII. 32. and elsewhere.

you will receive him) Because he will not uncover your vices: he will flatter you.

Irenaeus in book V, chapter 25, Jerome to Algasia, question XI, Ambrose in book I on the Holy Spirit, chapter 14, Hilary in book IX on the Trinity, Augustine, epistle LXXX, Cyril, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Bede understand this of the Anti-Christ: But because Christ speaks indefinitely, it ought to be taken simply, that place would be given among the Jews rather to impostors and false Christs than to the true Messiah. See Eusebius, book IV, chapter 6, Josephus, book II on the Jewish War, chapter 12, and book XII on the Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 6.

Latin:

Vers. 43. Ἐγὼ ἐλήλυθα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τῦ πατρός μυ) Cum vere divina potestate.

Καὶ ἐ λαμβάνετέ με) Tantum quia dogmatis mei puritas vestris malis moribus, vestræque ambitioni adversatur: Primorum quidem, quia soli apud populum sancti haberi volunt, plebis vero, quia metuit à primoribus traduci. Λαμ- βάνειν hic idem est quo supra I. 11. 12.

Ἐὰν ἄλλος ἔλθῃ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τῷ ἰδίω) Nulla certe talis potestatis signa adferens, propria auctoritate. Id enim va- let hic ὄνομα, ut Act. IV. 7. & alibi sæpe. Talis fuit Barcho- chebas. Vide ad Matth. XXII, 26. Adde 2. Thess. II. 10. Et ἐὰν hic est quando : ut XII. 32. & alibi.

ἐκεῖνον λήψεσθε) Quia vitia vestra non deteget: vobis blandietur.

De Anti-Christo id Iren. l. V. c. 25. Hieronym. ad Algas. q. XI. Ambros. l. I. de S.S. c. 14. Hilar. l. IX. de Trin. August. ep. XXC. Cyrill. Chrysost. Theophyl. & Beda intelligunt: Sed quia indefinite loquitur Christus, simpliciter accipi debet, impostoribus potius, & Pseudo-Christus datum iri locum apud Judæos, quam vero Messiæ. Vid. Euseb. l. IV. c. 6. Josephus l. II. de bell. Jud. c. 12. & l. XII. de antiquit. Jud. c. 6.

## 5:44
Verse 44. How can you believe) He shows not what is simply impossible, but what is not to be expected from them as long as they are of such a mind: and understand, of such a dogma by which your sores are touched. Add what is below XII. 39. and 42. and James IV. 4.

Receiving glory from one another) Seeking, as has just been explained. You hunt for honor, the common people from the leaders, the leaders from the common people.

The glory from God alone not seeking) The glory which can proceed from God alone is that which is rendered to a sincere heart, of which no one is a witness outside of God. Exterior deeds can be many and common to both good and bad men, especially ritual ones which are easily fulfilled, Romans II, near the end: he is a Jew in secret, and circumcision is of the heart in the spirit, not in the letter, whose praise is not from men but from God. Not far from this departs that saying of Ibycus:

Δίδυκα μήτι παρὰ θεοῖς ἀμπλακὼν Τιμὰν πρὸς ἀνθρώπων ἀμείψω.

Latin:

Vers. 44. Πῶς δύνασθε ὑμεῖς πισεῦσαι) Ostendit non quid simpliciter sit ἀδύνατον; sed quid ab illis expectandum non sit quam diu tali sunt animo: & subintellige, tali do- gmati quo vestra ulcera tangantur. Adde quod infra XII. 39. & 42. & Jac. IV. 4.

Δόξαν παρ᾽ ἀλλήλων λαμβάνοντες) Captantes, ut modo expositum est. Plebs à primoribus, primores à plebe hono- rem venamini.

Τὴν δόξαν παρὰ μόνυ Θεῦ ἐ ζητῦντες) Gloria quæ à solo Deo proficisci potest est quæ cordi sincero redditur, cujus testis nemo est extra Deum. Facta exteriora multa bonis malisque esse possunt communia, maxime ritualia quæ facile implentur Rom. II. circa finem: ὁ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ Ἰυ- δαῖος, κὰι περιτομὴ καρδίας ἐν πνεύματι, Ἐ γράμματι, ἷ ὁ ἔπαι- νος ἐκ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ τῦ Θεῦ. Non longe abit hinc Ibyci illud:

Δίδυκα μήτι παρὰ θεοῖς ἀμπλακὼν Τιμὰν πρὸς ἀνθρώπων ἀμείψω.

## 5:45
Verf. 45. Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father) There will be no need for an accuser for me, whom you think is your enemy.

There is one who accuses you, Moses) See also what is in Matt. XII. v. 41.

in whom you have hoped) The Hebrews say that Samuel, when he was called up after death and believed he was being summoned to judgment, drew Moses to him so that he might act as his advocate. And thus they themselves hope that they will have God propitious to them by the grace and recommendation of Moses. But Ἐλπίζειν here is to trust, as in Matt. XII. 12. Judith c. IX. 5 they hoped in the shield of power. Incidentally, it is shown that many defer to Moses: just as we have just had concerning the scriptures.

There is no need for that fable: from where will it be taught that it had already prevailed at the time when Christ had refuted the Jews? But the Jews were sinning in this, that they had hoped in the law of Moses, and believed that by its observance they could attain eternal life. Rom. IX. 31. 32. Therefore Christ teaches that Moses himself rejected them, concerning salvation not to be attained except through Christ.

Latin:

Verf. 45. Μὴ δοκεῖτε ὄτι ἐγὼ κατηγορήσω ὑμῶν πρὸς τὸν πα- τέρα) Nihil me opus erit accufatore, quem vobis inimicum putatis.

Ἔστιν ὁ κατηγορῶν ὑμῶν Μωσῆς) Vide & quæ Matth. XII. v. 41.

εἰς ὃν ὑμεῖς ἠλπίκατε) Ajunt Hebræi Samuelem cum post mortem evocaretur, & crederet se ad judicium vocari, attra- xisse Mofem, ut sibi patrocinaretur. Et sic ipfi sperant seMo- sis gratia ac commendatione Deum habituros propitium. Ἐλπίζειν autem hîc est confidere, ut Matth. XII. 12. Judith. c. IX. 5 ἤλπισαν ἐν ἀσπίδι ἠξουσίᾳ. Obiter oftenduntur plæ- quoMofi deferre: ficut modo de scripturis habuimus.

Non opus est illa fabula: quam tum obtinuisse jam, cum redarguerat Christus Judæos, unde do- cebitur? in eo autem peccabant Judæi, quod in le- gem Mofis sperarint, & per ejus observationem crediderint se posse vitam æternam consequi. Rom. IX. 31. 32. Ideo Christus docet, quod Moses ipse eosdem ad se rejecerit de salute non nisi per Christum consequenda.

## 5:46
Vers. 46. For if you believed Moses) In his writings, as in Luke XVI. v. 31.

for he wrote about me) He gave you signs by which you might distinguish true prophets from false ones, Deut. XVIII. 15. and following. But the signs of a true Prophet correspond remarkably in me. See Acts III, 22. VII. 37. so that I am denoted there as if specifically.

Moses not only handed down signs, from which Christ could be recognized as the true Prophet, but he wrote about Christ, as Christ himself testifies here, 'for he wrote about me,' which cannot be taken otherwise than that Moses bore true witness about Christ, to whom the Jews ought to have given credence. Which is also evident from Deut. XVIII. 18. as interpreted by Peter in Acts II. 22. and Stephen the Protomartyr, Acts VII. 32. Compare what is at Deut. XVIII. 18. Add that many other things are held in Moses concerning Christ, Gen. III. 15. XII. 3. and similar places, from which Christ demonstrated his passion, death, and resurrection from Moses just as from the Prophets, Luke XXIV. And to this end are those things which are added here, or from the very Grotian interpretation, which we append, though first observing the note of Augustine, from book XVI against Faustus the Manichaean, c. 22. Christ does not say, 'Moses also wrote about me,' so that it might be believed that he also wrote other things which do not pertain to Christ, but he says, 'he wrote about me,' so that we might consult the whole intention of that scripture only for the sake of understanding the grace of Christ by searching.

Latin:

Vers. 46. εἰ γὰρ ἐπιστεύετε Μωσῇ) Scriptis ejus, ut Luc. XVI. v. 31.

περὶ γὰρ ἐμῦ ἐκεῖνος ἔγραψεν) Signa vobis dedit quibę ve- ros prophetas à falsis dignosceretis, Deut. XVIII. 15. & feqq. Signa autem veri Prophetæ in me eximie congruunt. Vide Act. III, 22. VII. 37. ita ut ego ibi velut specialiter denoter.

Moses non solum signa tradidit, ex quibus Chri- stus ceu verus Propheta dignosci potuerit, sed de Christo scripsit, utChristus ipse hîc testatur, περὶ γὰρ ἐμοῦ ἐκείνος ἔγραψεν, quod non potest aliter acci- pi, quam quod verum de Christo testimonium perhibuerit Moses, cui fidem habere debuerint Ju- dæi. Quod etiam ex Deut. XVIII. 18. interprete Pe- tro Act. II. 22. & Stephano Protomartyre, Act. VII. 32. constat. Conf. quæ ad Deut. XVIII. 18. Adde quod multa alia in Mose de Christo Gen. III. 15. XII. 3. & locis similibus habeantur, unde Christus ex Mo- se pariter, ut è Prophetis Luc. XXIV. passionem, mortem & resurrectionem fuam demonstravit. At- que huc faciunt quæ addita hîc sunt, vel ex ipsa in- terpretatione Grotiana, quam subjicimus, observa- ta tamen prius Augustini nota, è l. XVI. contr. Faust. Manich. c. 22. Non ait Christus, Moses & de me scri- psit, ut & alia, quæ ad Christum non pertinent,scri- psisse crederetur, sed ait, de me ille scripsit, ut omnem scripturæ illius intentionem non nisi ad intelligendam Christi gratiam per scrutando confuleremus.

## 5:47
V. 47. But if you do not believe his writings) If you do not believe books of such anciently received authority. But to believe here and often elsewhere is not just to believe generally, but specifically by adapting the law to the fact.

how will you believe my words) Not that the authority of Christ is not greater, but that it is less known. In a similar way Peter addresses the Jews, 2 Pet. I, 19. Christ remarkably strips the Jews of two pretexts which they used for rejecting him: the love of God and reverence for Moses.

SECTION III. Concerning the acts pertaining to the third Passover.

Latin:

V. 47. εἰ δὲ τοῖς ἐκείνα γράμμασιν ὐ πισεύετε) Si libris tam antiquitus receptæ auctoritatis non creditis. Credere au- tem hic & alibi sæpe, est credere non generatim modo sed singulatim aptando jus ad factum.

πῶς τοῖς ἐμοῖς ῥήμασι πιστεύσετε) Non quod non major sit Christi auctoritas, sed quod minus cognita. Simili modo Ju- dæos Petrus compellat, 2. Petr. I, 19. Egregie Christus eripit Judæis duos prætextus, quibę ad rejiciendum se utebantur, dilectionem Dei & reverentiam Mosis.

SECTIO III. Acta ad Pascha tertium perti- nentia concernens.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus, crossing the Sea of Galilee as the Passover approached, in the desert, having first instituted a conversation with Philip and Andrew concerning the lack of food, feeds five thousand men with five loaves and two small fish. With 12 baskets of leftovers remaining, he is recognized as the Prophet who is to come into the world: He ascends a mountain in the evening; walking on the sea, he comes to the disciples' boat, and as the people wonder that they find him across the sea, he preaches about the food that does not perish, about faith, the work of God, and about himself as the true heavenly bread, who gives life to the world, having been sent to do the will of the Father, and to grant eternal life to those who believe in him. But to the Jews who hold him in contempt because of his lowly lineage, he testifies again that those drawn to him and coming to the instruction of the Father have eternal life, that he is the bread of life, which whoever eats will live forever: And he warns again and again that his flesh, which he is about to give for the life of the world, is that living bread, and that the Jews who contend among themselves about him, as to how he can offer his flesh to be eaten, cannot have life unless they have eaten the flesh of the Son of God and drunk his blood, and that whoever receives this true food and true drink remains in him and lives because of him. When some called this discourse, which was held in the Capernaum synagogue, hard, he testifies concerning the ascent of the Son of God to where he had been, and concerning the life-giving spirit and the life-giving power of his word: and the disciples, with Peter as their interpreter, profess that he has the words of life, and that they recognize him to be the Christ, the Son of the living God. But Christ singles out one of them, who is a devil, namely Judas Iscariot the traitor.

There are three parts. I. The miraculous feeding of the five thousand, to v. 15. II. Jesus' walking on the sea, to v. 25. III. The Capernaum discourse concerning the food that does not perish, and the heavenly manna, and its consequences, to v. 71.

PART I. The miraculous feeding of the five thousand.

Vers. 1. Μετὰ ταῦτα) Some time later. Our author here passed over many things recorded by the others: nor would he have related this history of the multiplied loaves, which was treated by others, if the excellent discourse of Christ held on this occasion, which it was in the interest of the Church to preserve, had not required it.

Rupert refers these events to the last year of Christ's preaching: but the chronology does not fit.

Πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης τῆς Γαλιλαίας) I think the proper meaning of the word πέραν, which the Syriac expressed as לעברן, can be retained here. For those things which are narrated by others either here or later do not stand in the way. The lake, which was called the Sea of Galilee by Pliny and others, and by the Hebrews at that time, as in Matt. ch. IV. v. 18 and elsewhere.

Τῆς Τιβεριάδος) It denotes more closely the part of the lake which, as is usual, had a proper name from the nearby town. See below 23. Now this part of the lake was almost the lowest, so that the crowd could follow Christ on foot by crossing the Jordan river without a long detour.

Latin:

CAPUT VI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Iesus per mare Galilæum trajiciens, appropin- quante Paschate, in deserto, colloquio prius cum Philippo & Andrea de defectu cibi in- stituto, cibat quinque panibus & duobus pisculis quinq́; millia virorum 12. Cophinis reliquiarum remanentibus, agnoscitur Propheta in mundum venturus: Ascendit in montem vesperi; ad navigium discipulo- rum ambulans in mari venit, & mirante populo, quod eum trans mare inveniat, de cibo non perituro concionatur, de fide, opere Dei, & de se vero pane cælesti, qui dat mundo vitam, misso, ut voluntatem Patris faciat, & credentibus in se vitam æternam donet. Iudæis autem despicatui ipsum, ob vilem prosapiam, habentibus iterum testatur, ad sese pertractum, & in- formationem Patris venientes vitam æter- nam habere, se esse panem vitæ, quem qui edit, æternum vivet: Carnemque suam, quam pro mundi vita daturus est, esse Pa- nem illum vivum, & contendentes de eo inter se Iudæos, quomodo ipse carnem suam manducandam præbere possit, iterum iterumque monet, non posse ipsos habere vi- tam, nisi manducarint carnem filii Dei, bi- berintque sanguinem ejus, qui vero hunc cibum verum, verumque potum percipit, eum in se manere, & propter se vivere. Quem sermonem in Schola Capernaitica habitum, quum nonnulli durum dicerent, de ascensu Filii Dei eo, ubi fuerat, deq; spi- ritu vivificante ac vi vivifica verbi sui te- statur: ac profitentur, interprete Petro, discipuli, quod ipse habeat verba vitæ, quodque agnoscant ipsum esse Christum Filium Dei viventis. Sed Christus ex- cipit unum ex ipsis, qui diabolus sit, Iu- dam sc. Ischariotam proditorem.

Partes sunt tres. I. Miraculosa quinque millium cibatio, ad v. 15. II. Jesu in mari ambulatio, ad v. 25. III. Capernaitica Concio de cibo non perituro, & manna cælesti, ejusque consequentia, ad v. 71.

PARS I. Miraculosa quinque millium cibatio.

Vers. 1. Μετὰ ταῦτα) Aliquanto post tempore. Transiit hic noster multà à cæteris memorata: neq; hanc de auctis panibus historiam ab aliis tractatam referret, nisi id desi- e- raret sermo eximius Christi hac occasione habitus, quem servari Ecclesiæ intererat.

Rupertus ad ultimum hæc refert prædicationis Christi annum: sed non congruit Chronologia.

Πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης τῆς Γαλιλαίας) Puto significationem propriam vocis πέραν, quam expressit Syrus לעברן hic posse retineri. Neque enim obstant quæ ab aliis aut hic post narrantur. Lacus, qui Plinio & aliis Genesara, Hebræis eo tempore dicebatur mare Galilæum, ut Matth. c. IV. v. 18. & alibi.

Τῆς Τιβεριάδος) Propius denotat lacus partem, quæ ab adsito oppido, ut fieri solet, nomen habebat proprium. Vide infra 23. Erat autem hæc pars lacus ferme infima, ita ut non multo ambitu transito amne Jordane plebs Chri- stum pedestri itinere consequi posset.

## 6:2
Vers. 2. Ὅτι ἑώρων ἀυτῶ τὰ σημεῖα) Partly to benefit from the miracle, partly to enjoy the spectacle.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ὅτι ἑώρων ἀυτῶ τὰ σημεῖα) Partim ut beneficio uterentur, partim ut fruerentur spectaculo.

## 6:3
Vers. 3. Ἐις τὸ ὄρος) In the desert of Bethsaida, as it is called. See Luke IX. 10.

Ἐκεῖ ἐκάθητο) For the sake of imparting instruction.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ἐις τὸ ὄρος) In deserto Bethsaidæ quod dicitur. Vide Lucam IX. 10.

Ἐκεῖ ἐκάθητο) Disciplinæ tradendæ causa.

## 6:4
Vers. 4. ἦν δὲ ἐγγὺς τὸ πάσχα.) He interjects this so that it may be understood that the time was opportune for drawing out a multitude: and so that what follows concerning the grass may cohere better.

Latin:

Vers. 4. ἦν δὲ ἐγγὺς τὸ πάσχα.) Hæc ideo interjicit, ut in- telligatur tempus fuisse opportunum ad eliciendam multi- tudinem: & quo melius cohæreat quod de herba sequitur.

## 6:5
Vers. 5. Ἐπάρας ὄν) That ὄν does not always connect continuous things, but also those separated by some interval of time. For these things were done later, after Jesus had descended from the mountain.

Λέγει πρὸς τ Φίλιππον) Since conversation had already been introduced by the Apostles concerning this matter. And he addresses Philip rather than the others as one who was most in need of instruction, still inexperienced and sufficiently confident, as can be seen below XIV. 8. 9.

This reason is rendered by Theophylact: but by Cyril, because Philip was μάλα ζητητικός: by others, because his homeland was Bethsaida, and he had the places more explored than the others.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ἐπάρας ὄν) ὄν illud non semper continua nectit, sed & aliquo intervallo temporis disjuncta. Nam ser us hæc gesta, postquam Jesus à monte descenderat.

Λέγει πρὸς τ Φίλιππον) Cum jam hac de re ab Apostolis sermo injectus esset. Et Philippum magis quam cæteros compellat ut qui institutionis maxime egeret, rudis adhuc & satis confidens, ut videre est infra XIV. 8. 9.

Hæc causa redditur à Theophylacto: A Cyrillo ve- ro, quod Philippus fuerit μάλα ζητητικός: Ab a- liis, quod patria esset Bethsaida, & loca haberet ma- gis explorata, quam alii.

## 6:6
Vers. 6. Πειράζων ἀυτὸν) So that he might make manifest how far he had progressed. To test has this sense when it is said of God in Gen. XXII. 1. and elsewhere. The same is true of it concerning Christ.

ἤδει γι ἔμελλε ποιεῖν) So definitely that it could be hindered by no action of any man whatsoever. Decrees so firm and immutable are fitting to God alone, Acts XV. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Πειράζων ἀυτὸν) Ut apertum faceret quousque profecisset. Hunc sensum habet πειράζειν, um de Deo dici- tur Gen. XXII. 1. & alibi. Eundem eum de Christo.

ἤδει γι ἔμελλε ποιεῖν) Ita definite ut à nulla hominis cujus- quam qualicunq; actione impediri possit. Decreta tam fir- ma & immutabilia Deo soli conveniunt, Act. XV. 18.

## 6:7
Διακοσίων δηναρίων ἄρτοι οὐκ ἀρκέσωσιν αὐτοῖς) For with these, no more than two thousand could be fed. But there were many more.

Βραχύ τι λάβῃ) They would not suffice even for a taste,

Latin:

Διακοσίων δηναρίων ἄρτοι οὐκ ἀρκέσωσιν αὐτοῖς) Nam his non amplius bis mille pasci poterant. Multo autem plures erant.

Βραχύ τι λάβῃ) Ne ad gustandum quidem tam multus sufficerent,

## 6:8
Vers. 8. Ἀνδρέας) More forward in faith than Philip: therefore Philip uses his help in appealing to the Lord, below XII. 22. But it seems Andrew said this after having first taken counsel with the other Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἀνδρέας) Fide profectior Philippo: ideo ejus auxilio utitur Philippus in Domino compellando, infra XII. 22. Videtur autem Andreas dixisse hoc, consilio prius cum aliis Apostolis habito.

## 6:9
Vers. 9. Ἔστι παιδάριον ἓν ὧδε) In the other Evangelists they are said to have what was at hand so that it could be bought. But παιδάριον is very often used by the Greek interpreters for the Hebrew נַעַר.

Πέντε ἄρτους κριθίνους) This signifies the frugality of Christ and the Apostles, who ate nothing but coarse bread.

Καὶ δύο ὀψάρια) The Greek grammarians note that ὄψον is used by way of excellence for fish: whence ὀψοφάγοι. And the Greek interpreters of the sacred books translated דָג, which they translate as ἰχθῦν elsewhere, as ὄψον in one place. Num. XI. 22. Nonnus here said ἰχθύας ὀπταλέους, in which sense the word ὀψάριον appears again below XXI. 9. 10. 13.

Τί ἐστιν εἰς τοσούτους) The loaves were small, so that it was not without a miracle that Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves, 2 Kings IV. 42. 43. 44. By which example Andrew perhaps hoped it might be possible that twenty-five or more men could be satisfied by those loaves through the benefit of Christ. He did not yet dare to conceive anything greater in his mind.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ἔστι παιδάριον ἓν ὧδε) Apud alios Evangelistas dicuntur habere id quod in promtu erat ut emi posset. Παιδάριον autem sæpissime est apud Græcos interpretes pro Hebræo נַעַר.

Πέντε ἄρτους κριθίνους) Significatur frugalitas Christi & Apostolorum qui pane non nisi vili vescebantur.

Καὶ δύο ὀψάρια) Notant Græcorum grammatici ὄψον per excellentiam dici pisces: unde ὀψοφάγοι. Et Græci sacrorum librorum interpretes דָג quod alibi ἰχθῦν vertunt, uno in loco ὄψον verterunt. Num. XI. 22. Nonnus hic ἰχθύας ὀπταλέους dixit, quo sensu vox ὀψάριον interum comparet infra XXI. 9. 10. 13.

Τί ἐστιν εἰς τοσούτους) Exigui erant panes, ita ut non sine miraculo viginti panibus centum homines cibaverit Elisæus 2. Reg. IV. 42. 43. 44. Quo exemplo sperabat forte Andreas fieri posse ut viginti quinque aut plures homines istis panibus Christi beneficio satiarentur. Majus quicquam nondum audebat animo concipere.

## 6:10
Vers. 10. Χόρτος πολὺς) See Mark VI. 40.

Ἀνέπεσον) With the Apostles attending, who, being between hope and diffidence, had nevertheless learned to obey.

Ἄνδρες ὡσεὶ) He counts only the men, as is customary to be done in a census conducted according to the law; but concerning ὡσεὶ see above IV. 6. Other writers also use the same word in this history.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Χόρτος πολὺς) Vide Marc. VI. 40.

Ἀνέπεσον) Curantibus Apostolis, qui, medii inter spem & diffidentiam, parere tamen dedicerant.

Ἄνδρες ὡσεὶ) Viros tantum numerat, ut in censu qui ex lege agebatur fieri solet; at; de ὡσεὶ vide supra IV. 6. eandem vocem in hac historia & alii scriptores usurpant.

## 6:11
Vers. 11. Εὐχαριστήσας) It is the same as εὐλογήσας. See what is said at Matt. XXVI. 28.

Δίδωκε τοῖς ἀνακειμένοις) Since both certain Greek copies have it thus, and the Syriac and the Latin, it is more credible that those words τοῖς μαθηταῖς, οἱ δὲ μαθηταὶ, were added by those who wished to provide a remedy for the contradiction they imagined between this and other writers: which, however, with the reading we have mentioned retained, is none: because he who gives through another also gives: he who does through another does, as above IV. 1.

Without cause, Grotius departs from the received Codices, which are approved by the consensus of most learned men, in favor of the Syriac and Latin, and indulges his own suspicion as is his custom, but a vain and empty one.

Ὅσον ἤθελον) To the point of satiety: as what follows shows.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Εὐχαριστήσας) Idem est quod εὐλογήσας. Vide quæ ad Matth. XXVI. 28.

Δίδωκε τοῖς ἀνακειμένοις) Cum & Græca quædam Exemplaria sic habeant & Syrus & Latinus, credibilius est illas voces τοῖς μαθηταῖς, οἱ δὲ μαθηταὶ, adjectas ab iis qui medicinam adferre voluerunt ei quam sibi fingebant repugnantiæ inter hunc & alios scriptores: quæ tamen, retenta quam diximus lectione, nulla est: quia dat etiam qui per alium dat: facit qui per alium facit, ut supra IV. 1.

Citra causam a receptis & consensu plerorumq; MM. SS. approbatis Codicibus in gratiam Syri & Latini recedit Grotius, suæque pro more indulget suspicioni, at vanæ & inani.

Ὅσον ἤθελον) Ad satietatem usque: ut ostendit quod sequitur.

## 6:12
Vers. 12. Συνάγάγετε τὰ περισσεύσαντα) Everything was so directed by Christ that it was certain regarding the necessity, the truth, and the magnitude of the miracle. Moreover, the loaves seem to have grown between the hands of the disciples, by the wondrous power of Christ, when he caused as much to remain over as would fill a number of baskets equal to the number of the Apostles.

Hilarius, lib. III. de Trin., disputes whether the multiplication took place in the hands of Christ breaking them, or of the disciples distributing them, or of the crowd receiving them; but Christ, by breaking them, multiplied the fragments in such a way that both the Apostles and the crowd saw the power of God in his hands, and afterwards felt it with their own hands. Therefore Christ says, Mark VIII. 19, Do you not remember when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand? And Mark seems to show the manner when he says he divided the two fishes among all, as if to say that from two fishes so many pieces were made that they sufficed for all. As the Lord breaks, a seed-plot of food is made, says Jerome. In which sense Chrysostom, Hom. 50 in Matth., is to be understood: Those five loaves were multiplied in the hands of the disciples and gushed forth like a fountain, so that it not only sufficed, but even superabounded. You would have seen, says St. Ambrose, by a certain incomprehensible irrigation, the pieces which they had not broken fructifying between the hands of those distributing, and fragments creeping forth of their own accord under the fingers of those breaking them, untouched. Just as we see continuous flows issuing from liquid fountains, and whatever you take from them is replaced by a certain usurious flow. Conf. B. Lyserus in Harmon. cap. 77. But the Papists are rash, scrupulously defining the manner; Abulensis quæst. CIII.

The loaves, he says, were multiplied either by creation from nothing, or by the conversion of air or earth into loaves and fishes. Cornelius à Lapide on Matth. XIV. cap. Christ, he says, by this blessing imparts to the loaves a power not physical but moral, namely, his own deputation and ordination for a miraculous multiplication, through which he applied his hand, that is, his divine power, as it were, to the loaves, so that they might immediately multiply in reality, namely, by converting the neighboring air or other matter, to be distributed gradually, but insensibly and continuously, into loaves. For God creates nothing anew from nothing, but produces and transforms all things from matter created at the beginning of the world.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Συνάγάγετε τὰ περισσεύσαντα) Omnia à Christo ita directa, ut & de necessitate & de veritate & de magnitudine miraculi certo constaret. Videntur autem inter discipulorum manus crevisse panes, mira Christi potestate, cum effecit ut tantum superesset, quantum cophinorum numerum Apostolorum numero parem impleret.

Hilarius, lib. III. de Trin. disputat, an multiplicatio facta sit in manibus Christi frangentis, vel discipulorum distribuentium, vel turbæ sumentis, sed Christus frangendo ita multiplicavit fragmenta, ut tam Apostoli quam turbæ in ipsius manibus viderint, & postea suis manibus palparint dei virtutem. Ideo Christus Marc. IIX. 19. Non recordamini, inquit, quando quinque fregi panes in quinque millia? & modum Marcus ostendere videtur, cum inquit, duos pisces divisit omnibus, quasi dicat, ex duobus piscibus tot factas esse particulas, ut sufficerent omnibus. Frangente Domino seminarium fit ciborum, ait Hieronymus. Quo sensu intelligendus Chrysost. Hom. 50. in Matth. Quinque illi panes in discipulorum manibus multiplicabantur ac fontis in morem scaturiebant, adeo ut non sufficerit solum, verum etiam superabundaverit. Vidisses, ait S. Ambrosius, incomprehensibili quodam rigatu, inter dividentium manus, quas non fregerant fructificare particulas, & intacta frangentium digitis sponte sua fragmenta subrepere. Quemadmodum videmus, liquidis fontibus continuos fluere successus, & quicquid de illis auferas, usurario quodam reparari meatu. Conf. B. Lyserus in Harmon. cap. 77. Temerarii vero sunt Pontificii, modum scrupulose definientes; Abulensis quæst. CIII.

Panes, inquit, multiplicati vel per creationem ex nihilo, vel per conversionem aëris, vel terrae, in panes & pisces. Cornelius à Lapide ad Matth. XIV. cap. Christus, inquit, hac benedictione vir- tutem aliquam non Physicam sed Moralem pani- bus indit, sc. deputationem suam & ordinatio- nem ad miraculosam multiplicationem, per quam manum, id est, virtutem suam divinam quasi pa- nibus apposuit, ut illico, reipsa multiplicares, nimi- rum aërum vicinum, vel aliam materiam, sensim nimirum distribuendam, sed insensibiliter, & con- tinue in panes convertendo. Deus enim nihil de novo creat ex nihilo, sed ex materia initio mundi creata, omnia producit, & transformat.

## 6:14
Vers. 14. ὁ ἐποίησε σημεῖον) Greater than what Moses had done, not giving bread but obtaining it from heaven, and indeed mere bread without side-dishes, and of which no remains were left over. The miracles performed before this had profited few; this one profited the multitude of that class of men who provide their sustenance for themselves with difficulty.

Ὅτι ἗τῶ) Ὅτι here, as elsewhere, is redundant. The speech begins as indirect, it is completed as direct.

ὁ προφήτης ὁ ἐρχόμενος) ὁ ἐρχόμενος, that is, he who was to come, as in Matth. XVII, 11. But properly ὁ ἐρχόμενος was understood as the Messiah, Luke VII. 19, whom they had persuaded themselves at that time would be the same and the greatest Prophet. See above c. IV. 25. From him alone were expected greater things than Moses had performed.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ὁ ἐποίησε σημεῖον) Majus quam quod Moses fecerat, panem non dans sed impetrans de coelo, & qui- dem panem merum sine obsonio & cujus nullae superes- sent reliquiae. Miracula antehac edita paucis profuerant; hoc maxime multitudini ejus generis hominum quod vi- ctum sibi difficulter parit.

Ὅτι ἗τῶ) Ὅτι hic ut alibi πλεονάζει. Oratio incipit ut indirecta, impletur ut directa.

ὁ προφήτης ὁ ἐρχόμενος) ὁ ἐρχόμενος, id est qui venire de- bebat, ut Matth. XVII, 11. Proprie autem ὁ ἐρχόμενος intel- ligebatur Messias Luc. VII. 19. quem eundem & maximum Prophetam fore eo tempore sibi persuaserant. Vide supra c. IV. 25. Ab hoc solo expectabantur majora quam Moses praestiteras.

## 6:15
Vers. 15. Γνὺς) Having perceived their plans by divine power.

Ἁρπάζειν αὐτὸν) Even to seize him against his will and lead him away to where he might be inaugurated.

Ἱνα ποιήσωσιν αὐτὸν βασιλέα) By the hope of easy sustenance.

Ἀνεχώρησε πάλιν εἰς τὸ ὄρος) That is, he returned to the mountain from whence he had come, giving an example to the Pastors of the Church of fleeing earthly powers; a similar expression is above at IV. 3.

Let the Roman Bishops, whose advocate Grotius subsequently acted, think that this is said to them. Tertullian, de Idol. c. VIII, says: Christ judged the glory of the world to be alien both to himself and to his own. The seventh of the Apostolic Canons is as follows: Let a Bishop or Presbyter or Deacon by no means assume secular cares; if otherwise, let him be deposed. In the Canon Law, dist. LXXXVIII, it is held: Let Bishops and Ecclesiastics not care for secular things. He fled as an example, says Gregory the Great, part I, cur. pastor. c. 3. Other reasons for the flight are also given. Augustine, tr. XXV in John, says: He fled, lest he should give an opportunity for rebellion and sedition against the Romans. Cyril, l. III, c. 20: He fled, because he was not such a King as would be made by men, but such a King as would give a kingdom to men.

Αὐτὸς μόνος) And indeed, as it seems, he wished to be inconspicuous without any companion, so that he might be further removed from the appearance of a desired kingdom. Here John connects those things which pertain to Jesus, then pursues those which pertain to the disciples. For if we attend to the order of time, the Apostles enter the ship before Jesus arrived at the mountain. But in such matters it is the custom of historians to use their own liberty.

PART II. Jesus' walking on the sea.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Γνὺς) Divina vi introspectis eorum consi- liis.

Ἁρπάζειν αὐτὸν) Etiam invitum rapere & aliquo perdu- cere ubi inauguraretur.

Ἱνα ποιήσωσιν αὐτὸν βασιλέα) Spe facilis alimoniae.

Ἀνεχώρησε πάλιν εἰς τὸ ὄρος) Id est rediit in montem unde venerat, exemplum dans Ecclesiae Pastoribus fugi- endi potestates terrenas similis locutio supra IV. 3.

Id dictum sibi putent Romani Episcopi, quo- rum advocatum deinceps egit Grotius. Tertull. de Idol. c. VIII. Christus, inquit, gloriam seculi & sibi & suis alienam esse judicavit. Inter Apostolicos Canones septimus ita se habet: Episcopus aut Pres- byter aut Diaconus nequaquam seculares curas affu- mat; sin aliter, dejiciatur. In Jure Canonico dist. XXCVIII. habetur: Episcopi & Ecclesiastici secu- laria non curent. Fugit in exemplum, ait Gregorius M. part. I. cur. pastor. c. 3. Redduntur & aliae fugae causae. Augustinus tr. XXV. in Johann. Fugit, in- quit, ne rebellioni & seditioni adversus Romanos an- sam daret. Cyrillus l. III. c. 20. Fugit, quia non erat talis Rex, qui ab hominibus fieret, sed talis Rex, qui regnum hominibus daret.

Αὐτὸς μόνος) Et quidem, ut videtur, inconspicuus sine ullo comite esse voluit, quo longius abesset à cupiti regni specie. Connectit hic Johannes ea, quae ad Jesum perti- nent, deinde persequitur ea, quae ad discipulos. Nam si tem- poris ordinem attendimus, prius navigium intrant Apostoli quam Jesus in montem perveniret. Sed in ejusmodi rebus mos est historicorum libertate sua uti.

PARS II. Jesu in mari ambulatio.

## 6:17
Vers. 17. ἤρχοντο πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης) I shall translate: they were crossing the sea: for it has been noted elsewhere also that ἔρχεσθαι is used for to go. The Syrian: They were going in the crossing: Nonnus: they were traveling to the land on the other side.

Εἰς Καπερναὺμ] For that was the end proposed for the voyage. Otherwise they seem to have landed at Bethsaida.

Σκοτία ἤδη ἐγεγόνει) A time in itself terrible for those sailing.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ἤρχοντο πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης) Vertam: transibant mare: nam ἔρχεσθαι pro ire poni alibi quoque notatum. Sy- rus: Ibant in transitu: Nonnus γαίην ἰς ἀντιπέραιαν ἐπορεύ- μέοντο.

Εἰς Καπερναὺμ] Is enim finis erat propositus navigationi. Alioqui Bethsaidam videntur appulisse.

Σκοτία ἤδη ἐγεγόνει) Tempus per se terribile naviganti- bus.

## 6:18
Vers. 18. Διηγείρετο) It swelled up. Thus ἐξεγείρετο and the Hebrew in Jonah I. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Διηγείρετο) Intumuit. Sic ἐξεγείρετο ויטל Jo- nae I. 13.

## 6:19
Vers. 19. Ἐληλακότες οὖν) See at Mark VI. 48.

Ὡς σταδίους εἰκοσιπέντε ἡ τριάκοντα) A meager progress from evening to the fourth watch of the night, which time other writers note. For a day's journey is estimated at a thousand stadia: and consequently five hundred for the whole day or night.

περιπατοῦντα ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης) Not with the sea dried up, but on the sea itself: so that here too he might surpass Moses.

This emphasis of the words has been rightly observed. One must not say with Damascene, l. III, de O.F. c. 15: Through divine power the water was so arranged that it would not at all dis-

might flow apart, and yield to the gravity of the bodily feet. What the Scholastics seize upon, or what others among them invent, that Christ's body was carried upon the waters, or that Christ for a time bestowed upon his body a certain power similar to that which the bodies of the glorified will have after the resurrection on account of the gift of agility; much less what others philosophize ineptly, that the body of Christ was tempered to an equality of weight, and for this reason was not heavier than the waters, and was able both to float and walk upon them: least of all, finally, is it to be dreamed with the Manichaeans or Valentinians that the body of Christ was a phantasm or formed from celestial matter, and could be carried most easily upon the waters. But that opinion of certain Scholastics does not seem unlike the truth, that Christ suspended the act of gravity in his own and Peter's body, so that the body would not by its gravity press and weigh down the waters. To which the Ancients also incline: See. Justin. q. CXVII. August. Serm. CXXXIX. de tempore. l. III. de miracul. script. c. 8. Serm. XIII. & XIV. de Verb. Dom. Ambros. l. I. de Interpellat. Job. c. 5. And in the fragment de fid. resurr. Also Jerome in chapter XIV of Matthew. And the body, which is heavy by itself, shall become light. Pelargus notes more miracles here: 1. namely, that Christ, as Matthew ch. X relates, remaining on the shore, saw his disciples more than three miles away through the thickest darkness, in great and dangerous peril. 2. That he walked with his feet upon the waters of the sea for more than three miles. 3. That he granted to Peter a similar power against every law of nature, and immediately lifted him up as he was sinking to some extent. 4. That he compressed and calmed all the force of the winds and the turbulent agitation of the sea by his command alone. 5. That having entered the ship, he brought it immediately to the shore without oars and without sails. See Theophylact, and Victor of Antioch on the 6th chapter of Mark. Cyril, book II, Dialogue on the Trinity.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ἐληλακότες οὖν) Vide ad Marc. VI. 48.

Ὡς σταδίους εἰκοσιπέντε ἡ τριάκοντα) Exiguus profectus à vespere ad quartam noctis vigiliam, quod tempus notant alii Scriptores. Nam νυχθημέρυ curfus mille stadiis aestima- tur: ac proinde diei aut noctis totius quingentis.

περιπατοῦντα ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης) Non siccato mari, sed in ipso mari: ut hic quoque Mosen superaret.

Recte haec verborum emphasis observata. Non cum Damasc. l. III. de O.F. c. 15. dicendum: Per di- vinam potentiam ita comparatam aquam, ut minime disslu-

difflueret, pedumque corporeorum gravitati cederet. quod Scholastici arripiunt, vel quod alii ex ipsis fin- gunt, Christi corpus portatum fuisse super aquas, vel quod Christus ad tempus vim quandam suo corpori tribuerit similem ei, quam habitura post resurrectionem glorificatorum corpora propter dotem agilitatis; nedum ut alii inepte philoso- phantur, corpus Christi temporatum fuisse ad æ- qualitatem ponderis, ob hanc causam aquis non fuisse gravius, super illas & nare & ambulare potu- iffe : minime omnium deniq; cum Manichæis aut Valentinianis somniandum, corpus Christi Φάσμα vel e cœlesti materia formatum, facillime super a- quas ferri potuisse. Vero autem non absimilis vi- detur illa quorundam Scholasticorum sententia, quod Christus suspenderit actum gravitatis in suo & Petri corpore, ne corpus sua gravitate urgeret & premeret aquas deorsum. Quo etiam abeunt Veteres : Vid. Justin. q. CXVII. August. Serm. CXXXIX. de tempore. l. III. de miracul. script. c. 8. Serm. XIII. & XIV. de Verb. Dom. Ambros. l. I. de Interpellat. Job. c. 5. Et in fragment. de fid. resurr. Etiam Hieronymus in cap. XIV. Matth. Et leve fiet corpus, quod per se grave est. Plura hic miracula notat Pelargus : 1. videlicet, quod Christus Matthæi c. X. referente in littore manens discipulos suos plus tribus milliaribus inde distantes per densissimas vidit tenebras, vehementer periculoseque periclitantes. 2. Quod pedibus suis super aquas maris amplius tria milliaria ambulavit. 3. Quod Petro similem conces- sit potestatem contra omnem naturæ legem, & aliqua- tenus mergentem confestim eum sublevavit. 4. Quod omnem ventorum vim, turbulentamq; maris agita- tionem solo jussu compressit atque sedavit. 5. Quod navem ingressus sine remigiis sine velificatione ad li- tus illico perduxit. Vide Theophylactus, & Victorem Antiochen. in 6. cap. Marc. Cyrillum l. II. Dial. de Trin.

## 6:21
Verse 21. ἤθελον ἷν λαβεῖν αὐτὸν) Not that they did not receive him, but that they wished to do so very eagerly, as the Syriac indicates.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἤθελον ἷν λαβεῖν αὐτὸν) Non quod non recepe- rint, sed quod cupide admodum, ut Syrus indicat.

## 6:22
V. 22. Ὁ ἑστηκὼς) Who had stood in the place where the miracle was done. Πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης) On this side of that bay. Ὄτι πλοιάριον ἄλλο ὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖ) That there was no other boat: for ἦν stands in place of any past tense. Οἱ μαθηταὶ Ἰησοῦ) Whom they had seen carried away without Jesus. Μόνοι) Alone, that is, without their Master.

Latin:

V. 22. Ὁ ἑστηκὼς) Qui substiterat in loco facti miraculi. Πέραν τῆς θαλάσσης) Citra sinum illum. Ὄτι πλοιάριον ἄλλο ὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖ) Non aliud fuisse navigium: nam ἦν vice est cujusvis præteriti. Οἱ μαθηταὶ Ἰησοῦ) Quos sine Jesu avectos viderant. Μόνοι) Soli, id est sine Magistro.

## 6:23
Verse 23. Ἄλλα δὲ ἦλθε πλοιάρια) This is so that it may be understood how they themselves crossed. Therefore, after a while, other boats arrived from Tiberias.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Ἄλλα δὲ ἦλθε πλοιάρια) Hoc ideo, ut intelli- gatur quomodo ipsi transierint. Ergo post aliquanto alia navigia à Tiberiade advenerunt.

## 6:24
Verse 24. Ὄτε ὖν εἶδεν) A repetition of that which had preceded, ἰδὼν, because of the words inserted and drawn out for a long time, which also occurs in other histories.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Ὄτε ὖν εἶδεν) Repetitio ejus quo præcesserat ἰδὼν, ob interjecta diuque tracta verba, quod & in aliis hi- storiis occurrit.

## 6:25
Verse 25. Πότε ὧδε γέγονας) As if it were understood that he had been there for a long time, they would not doubt the miracle: since it was certain that he had not come by ship: and the journey on foot was very long. But Christ, dissembling this and looking into their hearts, which were more affected by perishable food than by the food of celestial life, does not answer what is asked, but teaches those things about which he was not asked.

PART III. The Capernaitic Sermon concerning the food that does not perish and the celestial manna and its consequences.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Πότε ὧδε γέγονας) Ut si jamdudum ibi fuisse in- telligeretur, non dubitarent de miraculo: quando navi eum non venisse constabat: pedestre autem iter erat longis- simum. At Christus id dissimulans, & corda eorum intro- spiciens quæ caduco quam cœlestis vitæ pabulo magis affi- ciebantur, ad id quod interrogatur non respondet, ea vero docet, de quibus non interrogabatur.

PARS III. Capernaitica Concio de cibo non perituro & manna cœlesti ejusque consequentia.

## 6:26
Verse 26. Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν) I do not speak from conjectures, but from certain knowledge.

Οὐχ ὅτι εἴδετε σημεῖα) Namely, as they are signs, that is, insofar as they pertain to producing faith and lifting minds to celestial things: for in the miracle itself they looked only at the utility of this life.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν) Non ex conjecturis loquor, sed ex certa scientia.

Οὐχ ὅτι εἴδετε σημεῖα) Nempe qua signa sunt, id est, qua- tenus pertinent ad efficiendam fidem & elevandos animos ad cœlestia: nam in ipso miraculo utilitatem tantum hujus vitæ spectabant.

## 6:27
Verse 27. Ἐργάζεσθε μὴ τὴν βρῶσιν) ἐργάζεσθαι βρῶσιν is to take pains to obtain food: as κατεργάζεσθαι σωτηρίαν Phil. II, 12. so in Ecclesiasticus ἐργάζεσθαι ἀλήθειαν. He wishes, therefore, that this is not what should be done primarily.

Τὴν ἀπολλυμένην) Whose utility is temporary. See 1 Cor. VI, 13, where food is said to be destined for destruction, and Gal. VI, 18, where he who sows to the flesh is said to reap φθορὰν (corruption), for all the duties of this life tend toward death.

Τὴν μένουσαν εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον) That is, whose fruit pertains to eternity, as he had said above concerning the water in IV. 14, in his custom of lifting the mind to spiritual things on the occasion of those things which he saw or heard. Nor was this allegory new among the Jews. Philo Alleg. Τὸ γὰρ φαγεῖν σύμβολόν ἐστι τροφῆς ψυ- χικῆς τρέφεται δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ ἀναλήψει τῶν καλῶν καὶ πράξει τῶν καθορ- θωμάτων. More on Matt. XXVI. 26.

Ἣν ὁ υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ὑμῖν δώσει) As much as is on his part. For words are often taken in this way, as above I. v. 9; thus δώσει is used in Acts V. 31; understand this food as the Evangelical dogma.

Ἐσφράγισεν) He acted here with a miraculous and incomparable power, so as to convince them of faith in him, just as Kings are accustomed to do with a seal impressed upon letters. A similar use of the word is above III. 33.

He confirmed, as if by an impressed seal, the King and Prophet, whom he who receives, seals the truth of God, John III. 33; he who despises it, violates the seal of God himself: to Cyril, ἐσφράγισεν is 'anointed' (l. III. c. 23). Chrysostom: He showed and revealed it by his own testimony. Basil understands it of the divine nature of Christ (l. I. against Eunom.), who is the image of God, Heb. I. 3. Bede takes it of Christ separated from sinners as to his human nature: because we are accustomed to seal with a seal those things which we wish to set apart. Tarnovius reports other opinions, understanding the seal as a sign by which our provider may be distinguished from others, with which the Father sealed him, which to him is the ability to perform miracles, to which, however, the testimonies of the Father can be added, as Theophylact and others with Chrysostom refer these to the administration of the office with divine power in doctrine and miracles.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Ἐργάζεσθε μὴ τὴν βρῶσιν) ἐργάζεσθαι βρῶσιν est operam dare ut victum adipiscamur: ut κατεργάζεσθαι σωτηρίαν Phil. II, 12. sic in Ecclesiastico ἐργάζεσθαι ἀλήθειαν. Vult ergo non hoc præcipue agendum.

Τὴν ἀπολλυμένην) Cujus utilitas temporaria est. Vide 1. Cor. VI, 13. ut cibus dicitur destruendus, & Gal. VI, 18. is qui carni studet dicitur reportare φθορὰν, ad mortem enim tendunt omnia hujus vitæ officia.

Τὴν μένουσαν εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον) Id est, cujus fructus ad æternitatem pertinet, ut supra de aqua dixerat IV. 14. more suo ex occasione eorum quæ videbat aut audiebat ad spiri- tualia animum attollens. Nec nova erat apud Judæos hæc allegoria. Philo Alleg. Τὸ γὰρ φαγεῖν σύμβολόν ἐστι τροφῆς ψυ- χικῆς τρέφεται δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ ἀναλήψει τῶν καλῶν καὶ πράξει τῶν καθορ- θωμάτων. Plura ad Matth. XXVI. 26.

Ἣν ὁ υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ὑμῖν δώσει) Quantum ex sua parte est. Nam sic verba sæpe sumuntur ut supra I. v. 9. sic δώσει ponitur Actor. V. 31, cibum hunc intellige dogma Evan- gelicum.

Ἐσφράγισεν) Potestate mirifica, eaque incomparabili hic egit, ut fidem ei conciliaret, quomodo Reges Sigillo literis impresso solent. Similis usus vocis supra III. 33.

Impresso quasi sigillo confirmavit, Regem & Pro- phetam, quem qui recipit, obsignat Dei veritatem, Joh. III. 33. qui contemnit, Dei ipsius sigillum vio- lat: Cyrillo ἐσφράγισεν est unxit l. III. c. 23. Chry- sost. Ostendit suoq; revelavit testimonio. Basilius de divina natura Christi intelligit l. I. contra Eunom. qui imago Dei est Ebr. I. 3. De Christo segregato à peccatoribus quoad humanam naturam Beda acci- pit: quia quæ segregare volumus, sigillo obsigna- re solemus. Alias sententias refert Tarnovius si- gnum, quo noster promus ab aliis dignoscatur, sigillum intelligens, quo eum Pater obsignavit, quod ipsi est facultas miracula faciendi, cui ta- men testimonia Patris addi possunt, uti Theophyla- ctus & alii cum Chrysostomo hæc referunt ad ad- ministrationem officii cum divina potentia in do- ctrina & miraculis.

## 6:28
Vers. 28. Τί ποιῶμεν ἵνα ἐργαζώμεθα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Θεοῦ) They remember that a nourishing power is attributed to the law of Moses, as Deut. XVIII. v. 1, 2, 3. Whence also Eccles. II. 21, πληθύνουσι τῷ νόμῳ. They ask, therefore, whether there is anything else to be prescribed than what the law prescribes. Compare what is in Matt. c. XIX. v. 16, and following. Ποιῶμεν for ποιήσομεν, which is a frequent enallage, especially in questions. Ἔργα Θεοῦ are works especially pleasing to God. Thus, sacrifices of God, Ps. LI. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Τί ποιῶμεν ἵνα ἐργαζώμεθα τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Θεοῦ) Me- minerunt legi Mosis tribui vim alentein, ut Deut. XVIII. v. 1. 2. 3. Unde & Eccles. II. 21. πληθύνουσι τῷ νόμῳ. Quæ- runt ergo, an quid aliud præscribendum habeat, quam quod lex præscribit. Confer quod est Matth. c. XIX. v. 16. & seqq. Ποιῶμεν pro ποιήσομεν, quæ enallage frequens maxime in in- terrogationibus. Ἔργα Θεοῦ sunt opera apprime Deo grata, Sic sacrificia Dei Ps. LI. 19.

## 6:29
Vers. 29. Τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἵνα πιστεύσητε) This trust is also a work, but an internal one; nor is it opposed to any works whatsoever, but to external ones, and indeed to those which can exist without that trust, as those without which that trust can exist: such as especially ritualistic ones, and others common to both the truly good and those who simulate being good. But he demands one thing here, because if this is sincere and solid, it draws with it all other things pleasing to God. For Christ considers those to trust in him who, by the hope of his promises, enter the way shown by him. Thus Rom. III. 27.

Fiducia is a work, or rather not our work but Θεοῦ, of God, who works it in us. But because trust is nothing other than a fiducial apprehension of the grace of God, or the merit of Christ, it is distinguished from works both internal and external: because works have the law as their rule; but trust looks to the Gospel and apprehends the grace offered in the Gospel. Therefore, works are entirely excluded from justification, which is attributed to faith alone: because it is obtained from grace apprehended by faith without any of our works. That definition of trust, however, that it is to enter the way shown by him by the hope of Christ's promises, smacks of the Socinian-Arminian lamp, and has been defeated in our Socinianism and Arminianism. See also what is said about these in the Epistle to the Romans.

Εἰς ὃν ἀπέστειλεν ἐκεῖνος) Modestly. He did not say 'in me': everywhere referring the honor of his office to the Father. But he sent him, understand, with such great and such miraculous power.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἵνα πιστεύσητε) Opus est etiam hæc fiducia, sed internum; neque opponitur operibus quibusvis, sed externis, & quidem iis quæ sine ea fiducia es- se possunt, ut sine quibus ea fiducia esse potest: qualia præ- sertim sunt ritualia, & alia quædam vere bonis, & bonos si- mulantibus communia. Unum autem hic exigit, quia si hoc sincerum solidumque sit, omnia alia Deo placentia secum trahit. Nam Christus eos demum censet sibi confi- dere, qui spe promissorum suorum viam ab ipso monstra- tam ingrediuntur. Sic Rom. III. 27.

Fiducia ἔργον est, vel opus non nostrum sed Θεοῦ, Dei, qui operatur id in nobis. Quia vero fiducia nihil est aliud, quam fiducialis apprehensio gratiæ Dei, vel meriti Christi, distinguitur ab operibus cum internis, tum externis: quia opera pro regula habent legem: fiducia vero respicit Evangelium & apprehendit gratiam in Evangelio oblatam. Ideo excluduntur prorsus opera à justificatione, quæ soli fidei tribuitur: quia ex gratia obtingit fide apprehensa sine ullis operibus nostris. Illa vero fiduciæ definitio, quod sit spe promissorum Christi viam ab ipso monstratum ingredi, Sociniano-Armi- nianam lucernam redolet, & in Socinianismo & Ar- minianismo nostro profligata est. Vid. etiam quæ de his in Epist. ad Roman.

Εἰς ὃν ἀπέστειλεν ἐκεῖνος) Modeste. Non dixit in me: ubique honorem muneris sui ad Patrem referens. Misit autem, intellige cum tanta ac tam mirifica potestate.

## 6:30
Vers. 30. Ἵνα ἴδωμεν καὶ πιστεύσωμέν σοι) That is, that having seen it, we may apply faith to you, and consequently also trust in you. These seem to have been different people than those who had just called him the Messiah, unless it happened to some what is commonly said: Μετὰ τὴν δόσιν τάχιστα γηράσκει χάρις (After the gift, grace ages most quickly). We have said that it is characteristic of the Jews to demand signs, and indeed shamelessly, such as they themselves might desire.

Τί ἐργάζῃ) ποιεῖν seems to be taken for that which has a permanent effect, ἐργάζεσθαι for that which is transient.

Latin:

Vers. 30. Ἵνα ἴδωμεν καὶ πιστεύσωμέν σοι) Id est, ut eo con- specto tibi fidem adhibeamus, ac proinde etiam confida- mus tibi. Alii videntur hi fuisse quam qui modo eum Messiam vocaverant, nisi quibusdam accidit quod vulgo dicitur: Μετὰ τὴν δόσιν τάχιστα γηράσκει χάρις. Diximus Judæorum esse, signa postulare & quidem inve- recunde qualia ipsi cuperent.

Τί ἐργάζῃ) ποιεῖν videtur sumi pro eo, quod habeat effectum permanentem, ἐργάζεσθαι quod transeun- tem.

## 6:31
Vers. 31. Our fathers) They extol Moses. Those fathers of ours who were six hundred thousand and more. Tὸ μάννα ἔφαγον) With Moses procuring it. And when they say Manna, they understand food, to which the name is given from the very wonder of it, as Josephus, the Chaldean, and the Greek interpreters with the Latin take it. Grammarians wrongly seek another origin. There is indeed מָן for 'what' in Chaldean: but the Egyptians also spoke thus, as Hascuni notes, whose idiom still adhered to the Hebrews at that time. Ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) That is, through the whole forty years. Christ had fed them only once. Therefore they soon say: πάντοτε δὸς ἡμῖν τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον, namely, such as you gave once. Ἄρτον ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) That is, from the first heaven, which is commonly the air, often heaven also to the Latins. They recite the Psalm to which they had become accustomed by singing. Concerning Manna, let the special treatise of B. Luther be seen.

Latin:

Vers. 31. Οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν) Extollunt Mosem. Patres illi nostri qui sexcenties mille erant & amplius. Tὸ μάννα ἔφαγον) Procurante Mose. Et cum dicunt Manna, cibum intelligunt, cui ex ipsa admiratione nomen, ut Josephus, Chaldæus & Græci interpretes cum Latino su- munt. Male aliam originem quærunt Grammatici. Est quidem מָן pro quid Chaldaicum: sed & Ægyptii sic loque- bantur, ut notat Hascuni, quorum idioma adhuc eo tem- pore adhærebat Hebræis. Ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) Id est, per totos annos quadraginta. Chri- stus eos semel tantum paverat. Ideo mox ajunt: πάντοτε δὸς ἡμῖν τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον, nempe qualem semel dedisti. Ἄρτον ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) Id est, ex cœlo primo, qui vulgo aër, cœlum sæpe etiam Latinis. Recitant Psalmum cui canendo assueverant. De Manna videatur peculiaris tractat. B. Lu- theri.

## 6:32
Vers. 32. Moses did not give you the bread from heaven) That is, in the highest heaven, which is the third heaven to the Hebrews: From the throne of immortality מכסאי הכבוד. Tὸν ἀληθινὸν) He who deserves to be called the heavenly bread in an excellent way. We said above in chapter I, v. 9, that the word ἀληθινὸς is taken in this way.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Οὐ Μωσῆς δέδωκεν ὑμῖν τὸν ἄρτον ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) Id est in cœlo supremo, quod tertium cœlum Hebræis: Ex so- lio immortalitatis מכסאי הכבוד. Tὸν ἀληθινὸν) Qui excellenter panis cœlestis dici me- retur. Sic vocem ἀληθινὸς sumi diximus supra cap. I. v. 9.

## 6:33
Vers. 33. For the bread of God) That bread which is given by God in an eminent way. Ἔστιν ὁ καταβαίνων ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) He had just called his word bread: now he calls himself bread. For things that befit the Gospel are wont to be attributed to Christ, its promulgator and sanctifier. Concerning the word καταβαίνειν, see above III. 13. Philo in the Allegories: Moses said to them, This is the bread which the Lord has given us to eat; this is the word which the Lord has commanded. You see what the food of the soul is, the continuous word of God, like dew having encompassed everything in a circle, and leaving no part without a share in it. And soon: the soul is fed by the more perfect, by the whole word. In the book he says the worse lies in wait for the better: he calls Manna the most ancient of beings, the divine word. See what is at Matt. XXVI v. 6. Ζωὴν) Namely eternal, as above I. 4. Διδοὺς) As much as is on his part, as we just said. Τῷ κόσμῳ) And not to six hundred thousand only, but to an infinite number: to all if they would, above I. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 33. Ὁ γὰρ ἄρτος τοῦ Θεοῦ) Panis ille qui à Deo da- tur eximie. Ἔστιν ὁ καταβαίνων ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) Modo verbum suum panem vocaverat: nunc se panem vocat. Solent enim quæ Evangelio conveniunt Christo tribui ejus promulgatori & sanctori. De voce καταβαίνειν vide supra III. 13. Philo Allegoriis: εἶπε δὲ αὐτοῖς Μωσῆς. ὗτός ὁ ἄρτος ὃν δέδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ κύριος τοῦ φαγεῖν· Τοῦτο τὸ ῥῆμα ὃ συνέταξε ὁ κύριος. ὁρᾷς τῆς ψυχῆς τροφὴν οἵα ἐςι, λόγος Θεοῦ συνεχὴς, ἐοικὼς δρόσῳ κύκλῳ πᾶ- σαν περιειληφὼς, καὶ μηδὲν μέρος ἀμέτοχον αὐτῷ ἐῶν. Et mox τρέφεται δὲ ἡ μὲν τελειοτέραν ἡ ψυχὴ ὅλῳ τῷ λόγῳ. In li- bro pejorem insidiari meliori ait: καλεῖ μάννα τὸν πρεσβύ- τατον τῶν ὄντων λόγον θεῖον. Vide quæ ad Matth. XXVI v. 6. Ζωὴν) Nempe æternam, ut supra I. 4. Διδοὺς) Quantum ex sua parte, ut modo diximus. Τῷ κόσμῳ) Nec sexcentis tantum millibus, sed infinito numero: omnibus si vellent supra I. 10.

## 6:34
Vers. 34. Lord, always give us this bread) We had the like above IV. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Κύριε πάντοτε δὸς ἡμῖν τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον) Simile habuimus supra IV. 5.

## 6:35
Vers. 35. Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς) The life-giving bread; we have stated in the preceding verse how this is to be understood. Great is the patience of Christ, who does not reproach the fault, but sets out to heal it. Ὁ ἐρχόμενος πρός με) We have spoken of this at Matt. XXIII. 25. Often, by a certain brevity of speech, the terms of a comparison and that which is indicated by the comparison are intermingled. Thus, here the simple statement would have been: He who eats me shall never hunger; and he who drinks me shall never thirst. But because to eat and to drink signifies to believe, therefore the one is explained by coming, the other by believing. For it is the same thing to come to Christ, that is, to devote oneself to him and to believe, as appears below in verse 44. All these things refer to the passage in Isaiah LV. 1, 2. Οὐ μὴ πεινάσῃ) Namely, πώποτε, which is to be repeated from the following clause by way of distinction. To hunger and to thirst are the same thing here. He silently shows how much more excellent his gift is than Manna, which they valued so highly: and he answers the petition, give us always. Καὶ ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ οὐ μὴ διψήσῃ πώποτε) He will have no need to learn anything else by which he may arrive at eternal life, as was said above III. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 35. Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς) Panis vivificus, quomodo hoc sumendum sit diximus commate antece- dente. Magna Christi patientia, qui vitium non exprobrat, sed sanare aggreditur. Ὁ ἐρχόμενος πρός με) Diximus ad Matth. XXIII. 25. Sæ- pe compendio quodã orationis misceri inter se voces com- parationis, & ejus quod comparatione indicatur. Ita hic simplex oratio fuerat. Qui ederit me, nunquam esuriet; & qui biberit me, non sitiet unquam. Sed quia edere & bi- bere significat credere, ideo alternum exponitur pervenire, alterum per credere. Idem enim est venire ad Christum, hoc est, ei se devovere & credere, ut apparet infra commate 44. Respiciunt hæc omnia locum Esaiæ LV. 1. 2. Οὐ μὴ πεινάσῃ) Nempe πώποτε, quod ex sequenti mem- bro repetendum est καθ' ὑποδιαστολὴν. Esurire & sitire idem hic est. Tacite ostendit quanto suum munus Manna sit præstantius, quod tanti faciebant: & respondet ad petitio- nem, da nobis semper. Καὶ ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ οὐ μὴ διψήσῃ πώποτε) Non opus ha- bebit aliud quicquam addiscere, quo ad vitam æternam perveniat, ut dictum supra III. 14.

## 6:36
Vers. 36. I said to you) He had said it not in the same words but in substance, when he said that they themselves were followers of him for the sake of food, not because of miracles, that is, not so that they might trust in him led by miracles. Above 26, it is put in this sense to say, and below XI. 40. Ὅτι ἑωράκατέ με) That is, you have been spectators of the power given to me. Thus also below XIV. 9. Καὶ οὐ πιστεύετε) Kai is 'And yet'. In that old manuscript it is read πιστεύετέ μοι.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Εἶπον ὑμῖν) Dixerat non verbis iisdem sed re, cum dixit sectatores ipsos sui esse victus causa, non ob mira- cula, id est, non ut miraculis adducti ipsi confiderent. Supra 26. hoc sensu dicere ponitur & infra XL 40. Ὅτι ἑωράκατέ με) Id est spectatores fuistis potestatis mihi datæ. Sic & infra XIV. 9. Καὶ οὐ πιστεύετε) Kai est Et tamen. In Manuscripto illo vetere legitur πιστεύετέ μοι.

## 6:37
Vers. 37. Πᾶν) Neuter for masculine or common. Thus τὰ μῶρα 1 Cor. I. 27, πᾶν κοινὸν Apoc. XXI. 27. Christ shows of what great virtue that believing is, which was neglected by them. Ὃ δίδωσί μοι ὁ πατὴρ) Those whom he hands over to me as if into my hand: for διδόναι here is understood with some effect: as the name κλητοὶ 1 Cor. I. 24, and often elsewhere. Thus to open the heart Acts XVI. 14, to fill the heart Acts V. 3, and this very word of giving Acts XI. 18, 1 Tim. II. 25. Nor does Maimonides explain that Deut. XXIX. 4 otherwise. The Father, however, hands over to Christ with effect those who strive for piety, at least after the word has been heard. Preparations for faith are wont to be attributed to the Father as in Matt. ch. XXVI, as the operation of faith to the Son, the sealing to the Spirit.

Grotius understands the handing over with effect, namely of those who strive for piety: at least after the word has been heard: attributing to the Father the preparation for faith, to the Son the operation of faith, to the Holy Spirit the sealing: but to place the striving for piety before faith is to make the effect prior to its cause, the fruit prior to the tree. For the striving for piety is the effect and fruit of faith. Nor does that distribution concerning the Fatherly preparation for faith, the operation of faith proceeding from the Son, and the sealing of the Holy Spirit have a foundation: Because the works of the Trinity ad extra are undivided, nor does the Father and the Holy Spirit work faith any less than the Son: or the Holy Spirit prepares for faith any less than the Father: although those dispositions and preparations for faith smack of Papism and Socinianism. Rather, the grace and mercy of God the Father is noted, from which we are given to the Son, so that indeed through faith we may enjoy his merits, and come to him: because this is not of our virtue and power: But as faith is ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ, so also that we may come to the Son, which Grotius explains by faith, 'they will come to me', that is, 'they will believe in me', God works and effects, from whom both the willing and the performing is ours. Phil. II. 13. Conf. Phil. I. 29.

πρὸς ἐμὲ ἥξῃ) If they believe in me, for the word of coming signifies that. A likeness taken from disciples whom the Father hands over to a teacher, and who willingly frequent him.

Καὶ τὸν ἐρχόμενον πρός με) He who in this way has applied faith to me.

Οὐ μὴ ἐκβάλω ἔξω) ἐκβάλειν ἔξω means to cast out from some place, as in Acts 7:58. Thus it is said of the Synagogue in 9:34, 35. Here it is as if of the School. For that translation has been begun. I will not act like morose Masters, I will not expel him, that is, if he should wish to be mine perpetually, it will not stand by me that he is not.

Latin:

Vers. 37. Πᾶν) Neutrum pro masculino aut communi. Sic τὰ μῶρα 1. Cor. I. 27. πᾶν κοινὸν Apoc. XXI. 27. Ostendit Christus quantæ sit virtutis illud credere, quod ab ipsis ne- gligebatur. Ὃ δίδωσί μοι ὁ πατὴρ) Quos mihi velut in manum tradit: nam διδόναι hic cum effectu aliquo intelligitur: ut nomen κλητοὶ I. Cor. I. 24. & alibi sæpe. Sic aperire cor Actor. XXVI. 14. implere cor Actor. V. 3. & hoc ipsum dandi ver- bum Act. XI. 18. 1. Tim. II. 25. Nec aliter exponit Maimo- nides illud Deut. XXIX. 4. Tradit autem Pater cum effectu Christo eos qui pietati student, saltem post verbum audi- tum. Solent præparationes ad fidem Patri tribui ut Matth. cap. XXVI. ut fidei operatio filio, obsignatio spiri- tui,

Grotius intelligit traditionem cum effectu, eo- rum scilicet, qui pietati student : saltem post verbum auditum : Patri præparationem ad fidem, Filio fidei operationem, Spiritui S. obsignationem tribuens : sed pietatis studium ante fidem ponere, est effe- ctum priorem causa sua, fructum priorem arbore constituere. Nam pietatis studium effectus est & fructus fidei. Neque illa distributio de præpa- ratione ad fidem Paterna, operatione fidei à Filio profecta, obsignatione Spiritus Sancti fundamen- tum habet: Quia indivisa sunt opera Trinitatis ad extra, nec minus fidem operatur Pater & Spiritus Sanctus quam Filius: aut Spiritus Sanctus ad fi- dem præparat, quam Pater: quanquam illæ dispo- sitiones & præparationes ad fidem Papismum & Socinismum oleant. Notatur potius gratia & misericordia Dei Patris, ex qua donamur Filio, ut nempe per fidem ejus meritis fruamur, & ad ipsum veniamus: quia hoc non nostræ est virtu- tis & potestatis: Sed uti fides est ἔργον τꭣ̃ Θεꭣ̃, ita etiam ut ad Filium veniamus, quod Grotius per fidem explicat, ad me venient, id est, mihi cre- dent, operatur & efficit Deus, à quo & velle & perficere nostrum est. Phil. II. 13. Conf. Phil. I. 29.

πρὸς ἐμὲ ἥξῃ) Si mihi credunt, nam id significat veni- endi vox. Similitudo sumta à discipulis quos Pater magi- stro tradit, quique volentes eum frequentant.

Καὶ `τ ἐρχόμενον πρός με) Qui hoc modo fidem mihi ad- hibuerit.

Οὐ μὴ ἐκβάλω ἔξω) ἐκβάλειν ἔξω è loco aliquo ejicere ut Act. VII. 58. Sic de Synagoga dicitur IX. 34. 35. Hic qua- si de Schola. Ea enim cœpta est translatio. Non faciam ut morosi Magistri, non expellam eum, nempe si perpetuo voluerit meus esse, per me non stabit quo minus sit.

## 6:38
Vers. 38. Ὅτι καταβέβηκα ἐκ τꭣ̃ ὀρανꭣ̃) From the end proposed to himself he makes credible what he had said. How should I cast out from my School those for whom I have been appointed to give eternal life: than which no greater benefit can be devised. I descended from heaven, that is, I was sent singularly by the Father, as above in 3:13.

Οὐχ ἵνα ποιῶ τὸ θέλημα τὸ ἐμὸν) That I may act according to pleasure, by private choice, as above in 5:30.

Ἀλλὰ τὸ θέλημα τꭣ̃ πέμψαντός με) There is an ellipsis of the words ἵνα ποιῶ to be repeated from the previous member, because what preceded is affirmative, this is negative: I am sent that I may do all things congruently with the Father's will.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Ὅτι καταβέβηκα ἐκ τꭣ̃ ὀρανꭣ̃) Ex proposito sibi fine facit credibile quod dixerat. Quomodo è Schola mea ejicerem eos quibꝫ ut idem vitam æternam sum constitutus : Quo nullum majus beneficium excogitari potest. Descendi à cœlo, id est à Patre singulariter missus sum, ut supra III. v. 13.

Οὐχ ἵνα ποιῶ τὸ θέλημα τὸ ἐμὸν) Ut agam pro lubitu, pri- vato arbitrio, ut supra V. 30.

Ἀλλὰ τὸ θέλημα τꭣ̃ πέμψαντός με) Est ἔλλειψις vocum ἵνα ποιῶ ex superiore membro repetendarum, quia quod præcessit affirmativum est, hoc negativum: missus sum ut omnia agam congruenter paternæ voluntati.

## 6:39
Vers. 39. Τꭣ̃το δὲ ἐστι `τὸ θέλημα τꭣ̃ πέμψαντός με πατρὸς) This is his general decree which I execute.

Ἵνα πᾶν ὃ δέδωκέ μοι μὴ ἀπολέσω ἐξ αὐτꭣ̃) It is a Hebraism: for πᾶν does not cohere with any verb. In Latin you would say: that of all that which he has given me, I should lose nothing. The neuter again in place of the common, as in 1 Cor. 1:27, 28. To lose here is the opposite of what he said above in verse 33, to give life: not so much in the sense of acting as of allowing, that is, I will not suffer to perish. For among the Hebrews, active verbs often have the signification of allowing.
