Ἀλλὰ ἀναστήσω αὐτὸ) Ἀνάστασις is usually said specially of that which is for eternal happiness, as we have warned above. An elevation into a much more sublime lot. Thus ἀνιστάναι εἰς τὴν ἀρχὴν is said in Greek of one who has been raised to command. Thus the Hebrews use הקים in Ezekiel 26:8.

Ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ) Thus below several times. Συντέλεια τꭣ̃ αἰῶνꝫ is said in Matthew 13:39.

Latin:

Vers. 39. Τꭣ̃το δὲ ἐστι `τὸ θέλημα τꭣ̃ πέμψαντός με πατρὸς) Hoc est decretum ejus generale quod ego exsequor.

Ἵνα πᾶν ὃ δέδωκέ μοι μὴ ἀπολέσω ἐξ αὐτꭣ̃) Est Hebraismus : nam πᾶν cum nullo verbo cohæret. Latine dicas : ut ex omni eo quod mihi dedit, nihil perdam. Neutrum rursus vi- ce communis, ut I. Cor. I. 27. 28. perdere hic est opposi- tum ei quod supra commate 33. dixit vitam dare: non tam agendi quam sinendi sensu, id est non patiar interire. Nam apud Hebræos agentia sæpe sinendi habent significationem.

Ἀλλὰ ἀναστήσω αὐτὸ) Ἀνάστασις specialiter dici solet ea quæ est ad æternam felicitatem ut supra monuimus. Ele- vatio in sortem multo sublimiorem. Sic ἀνιστάναι εἰς τὴν ἀρχὴν qui ad imperium evectus est Græce dicitur. Sic הקים Hebræis Ezech. XXVI. 8.

Ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ) Sic infra aliquoties. Συντέλεια τꭣ̃ αἰῶνꝫ dicitur Matth. XIII. 39.

## 6:40
Vers. 40. Τꭣ̃το δὲ ἐστι) δὲ here is explanatory: namely, that is to say.

Ὁ θεωρῶν `τ ὑὸν κ` πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν) He had just said ἑωράκατε κ` ὐ πιστεύετε. Therefore seeing precedes believing itself, nor will anyone be condemned as an unbeliever unless he has seen, that is, to whom the reasons for believing have been supplied. Yet it is not for nothing that he said θεωρῶν here rather than ὁρῶν. For θεωρεῖν is not to see in any way whatever, but with attention. Thus in the beginning of the first epistle, after ἑωράκαμεν follows ὃ ἐθεασάμεθα. That θεωρεῖν is taken thus, we see both elsewhere and in Luke 23:6, and above 2:23, below 7:3, 20:6. Cicero in Tusculan Disputations V translates θεωρεῖν as to look into studiously. The Hebrew חזה, which the Syrian also placed here, the Greek interpreters very often translate as θεωρεῖν. θεωρεῖν here is nothing other than to be given by the Father: just as believing is nothing other than coming. Believers are the המשכילים in Daniel 12:3.

Videre præcedere fidem, falsum. Beati qui credunt & non vident John 20:29. Faith is `τ & βλεπομένων Hebrews chapter 11, verse 1. Nor does mental vision or the knowledge of faith precede, but it pertains to the constitution of faith. But in order for someone to be an unbeliever, or for an unbeliever to be condemned, there is no need for reasons for believing to have been supplied to him, for which there is not even a need for faith: since faith relies solely on the revelation of God made through the word, nor does it desire reasons for believing: just as in the Socinian school nothing is believed, unless it is demonstrated by reasons that it must be believed. Those are called infidels who are destitute of faith: whether the word of God has been proposed to them in their own person or not. And are not infants condemned on account of ἀπιστίαν, which is the formal cause of condemnation, even if the word of God has not been proposed to them, much less reasons for believing supplied? For the distribution of men into believers and unbelievers is adequate. Those, therefore, of the infants who are not endowed with faith, or are not believers, are reckoned among the unbelievers. There is also only a twofold state after this life; namely, eternal blessedness and eternal condemnation: heaven and hell. A third state is not given. And therefore some are to be saved, others to be condemned, nor can a third class of men be assigned. Namely, only believers are to be saved: but infidels are to be condemned. And therefore those who are not in the number of the saved are certainly to be condemned. But those to whom reasons for believing have not been supplied, they, according to Grotius, do not believe, and therefore are not in the number of the saved. Because to believe, according to Grotius, or to acknowledge the reasons for believing, precedes believing itself.

Ἀναστήσω) It coheres with ἵνα which preceded. It is therefore of the subjunctive mood.

Latin:

Vers. 40. Τꭣ̃το δὲ ἐστι) δὲ hic est explicativum : nimirum, videlicet.

Ὁ θεωρῶν `τ ὑὸν κ` πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν) Modo dixerat ἑωράκατε κ` ὐ πιστεύετε. Ergo videre præcedit ipsum credere, nec ut in- credulus damnabitur nisi qui viderit, id est cui rationes cre- dendi subministratæ sunt. Non tamen de nihilo est quod θεωρῶν hic potius dixit quam ὁρῶν. Est enim θεωρεῖν non quo- vis modo sed cum attentione videre. Sic in epistolæ primæ initio post ἑωράκαμεν sequitur ὃ ἐθεασάμεθα. Sic θεωρεῖν sumi, videmus tum alibi, tum Lucæ 23, 6. & supra II. 23. infr. VII. 3. XX. 6. θεωρεῖν Cicero Tusculanarum V. vertit studiose per- spicere. Hebræum חזה quod & hic posuit Syrus, Græci in- terpretes sæpissime vertunt θεωρεῖν. Non aliud hic est θεωρεῖν quam dari à Patre : sicut credere non est aliud, quam venire. Credentes sunt המשכילים Dan. XII. 3.

Videre præcedere fidem, falsum. Beati qui cre- dunt & non vident Ioh. XX. 29. Fides est `τ & βλεπομέ- νων Ebr. cap. XI. v. 1. Neque visio mentalis seu co- gnitio fidei antecedit, sed ad fidei constitutionem pertinet. Ut autem quis incredulus sit, vel ut in- credulus condemnetur opus non est, ut rationes credendi subministrata illi sint, quibus ne quidem ad fidem opus est: quum sola Dei revelatione per verbum facta nitatur fides, nec credendi rationes desideret: quemadmodum in schola Sociniana nihil creditur, nisi quod per rationes credendum de- monstratur. Infideles dicuntur, qui fide destituun- tur: seu propositum ipsis in persona propria Dei verbum sit, sive non. Et annon infantes damnan- tur ob ἀπιστίαν, quæ formalis damnationis causa est, etsi illis verbum Dei non propositum, nedum rationes credendi subministratæ sint? Ade- quata enim est distributio hominum in fideles & incredulos. Qui ergo ex infantibus fide præditi, aut fideles non sunt, incredulis accensentur. Ge- minus etiam tantum status post hanc vitam est; beatitudo nempe æterna, & æterna condemnatio: cælum & infernus. Tertius status non datur. Id- eoque alii sunt salvandi, alii damnandi, nec ter- tium genus hominum assignari potest. Soli nem- pe fideles salvandi sunt: damnandi vero sunt infi- deles. Ideoque qui non in salvandorum numero sunt, certo sunt damnandi. Quibus vero rationes credendi subministratæ non sunt, illi juxta Gro- tium non credunt, proinde nec in salvandorum numero sunt. Quia credere secundum Grotium seu rationes credendi agnoscere, præcedit ipsum credere.

Ἀναστήσω) Cohæret cum ἵνα quod præcessit. Est ergo modi subjunctivi.

## 6:41
V. 41. ἐγόγγυζον) See Matt. XX. 11.

οἱ Ἰυδαῖοι) This name at that time contained all the descendants of Israel living in the promised land, even the Galileans.

περὶ αὐτῶ) For that reason. Nonnus takes it as masculine.

ὁ ἄρτο­ ὁ καταβὰς ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ) That must be pronounced with an accent, ὁ καταβὰς ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ. For that was properly what they could not digest: not that he had called himself bread, but that he had said he had come from heaven, which they took not concerning power or περὶ τῦ λόγυ, but concerning the whole man.

Latin:

V. 41. ἐγόγγυζον) Vide Matth. XX. 11.

οἱ Ἰυδαῖοι) Nomen hoc eo tempore omnes Israelis po- steros in terra promissa habitantes continebat, etiam Ga- lilæos.

περὶ αὐτῶ) Ob eam rem. Nonnus masculine accipit.

ὁ ἄρτο­ ὁ καταβὰς ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ) Cum accentu pronuncian- dum illud, ὁ καταβὰς ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ. nam id proprie erat, quod concoquere non poterant: non quod panem se di- xiffet, sed quod se dixisset de cœlo venisse, quod illi non de potestate aut περὶ τῦ λόγυ, sed de toto homine accipiebant.

## 6:42
V. 42. ὁ ὑὸς Ἰωσήφ) Luke III. 23. & IV. 23.

ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν) They lived in the vicinity of Nazareth. They sometimes frequented Capharnaum. Above c. II. 12.

πῶς ὖν λέγει ὗτο­ ὅτι ἐξ ὐρανῦ καταβέβηκα) How can that be true, if he was born in the human manner?

Latin:

V. 42. ὁ ὑὸς Ἰωσήφ) Luc. III. 23. & IV. 23.

ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν) Habitabant in proximo Nazarethæ. Ven- titabant interdum Capharnaumum. Supra c. II. 12.

πῶς ὖν λέγει ὗτο­ ὅτι ἐξ ὐρανῦ καταβέβηκα) Quomodo verum id esse potest, si natus est humano more?

## 6:43
V. 43. Μὴ γογγύζετε μετ' ἀλλήλων) For they had begun to be discordant, with some thinking more kindly, others worse, of Christ. See below 52. He shows his omniscience.

Latin:

V. 43. Μὴ γογγύζετε μετ' ἀλλήλων) Discordes enim esse cœperant, aliis benignius, aliis pejus de Christo sentienti- bus. Vide infra 52. omniscientiam se ostendit.

## 6:44
V. 44. Οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐλθεῖν πρός με) To believe in me, and therefore to acknowledge in me that heavenly excellence which I had indicated when I said that I had descended from heaven. See above 35. He shows the hardness of their heart.

He calls the merely active traction ἔλλαμψιν (illumination), the accepted one he calls δεξιν (reception). The words are: 'For thus the illumination from God occurs when our own vision concurs with it; and the works of prayer are the soul's rest and salvation from those things that come from here, and the appropriation of divine goods and communion with the paternal polity.'

To be drawn, for Grotius, is to be endowed with a certain pious affection. This he requires for someone to come to Christ and believe in Him. But the probity of the mind contributes nothing to faith. The Socinians and Arminians require it. Which we have refuted elsewhere. Scripture does not require it; indeed, it makes probity of mind subsequent to faith, and an effect and fruit of faith. God draws, however, not by a violent and irresistible method, as the Calvinists wish, but by a gracious invitation and the granting of the powers of willing and following, which He works not immediately, but through the Word and sacraments, by making those who are unwilling willing, and those who are unable able. Nor does He draw only by a pathetic proposition of things to be believed and done, by preaching, by exciting with consolations, by deterring with threats, etc. as the Pelagians, Arminians, and Socinians wish; since Christ presupposes all these things, and yet still requires the drawing of the Father: and those things are terminated in the teacher, even if the disciple does not obey, but drawing is an action which is not terminated in the one drawing, but in the one drawn: and the drawing is not an act elicited from him who is drawn, such as applause at a speech of Demosthenes' eloquence, but an act commanded on the part of the one drawing, and a passion inflicted on the part of the one drawn, yet ratified by the subsequent consent of him who is drawn, though resistible. And therefore the Savior requires, besides the doctrine sounding outwardly, the impression of that which sounds outwardly into the heart; as the blessed Hülsemann explains in 'De auxil. grat.' p. 254. Concerning which see Augustine, 'De grat. Christ.' book 1, ch. 10, epistles 107 and 143, and 'Contra duas epist. Pelag.' book 1, ch. 19. Christ does not say: unless the Father shall have led him, so that we might understand in some way that the will precedes. Who is drawn, if he was already willing? And yet no one comes, unless he wills. He is drawn, therefore, in wondrous ways so that he may will, by Him who knows how to work within the innermost hearts of men, not so that men (which is impossible) believe while unwilling, but so that they become willing from being unwilling. These are the words of Augustine. That he did not make that drawing and grace of conversion irresistible, which the Calvinists and Calixtines attribute to him, we have shown in a special dissertation on the opinion of Augustine in the Calixtine Syncretism. For he inculcates this a thousand times: that our willing is from the gift of God: but once this gift is posited and received, it is still possible to be unwilling: as the blessed Hülsemann has it, l. c. page 325. By this word 'drawing' is noted both our natural impotence to come to God, and our original repugnance when we are called, so that by this traction that natural repugnance is restrained by the preventing grace of God, and we, who are repugnant by nature, are made not repugnant, with the grace of God working that in us, so that that innate proneness to resist does not burst forth into act through actual and malicious resistance, to which we are inclined by nature, Rom. 8:6; and also the efficacy of grace and the word of grace, through which God works, first that we do not resist, then that we are rendered willing from being unwilling; not only by moral persuasion, but also by physical action, the giving of a new heart, regeneration, and an effective change of our will, yet not by necessity and irresistibly. But that that divine power, which is called drawing, and is as it were the highest degree of converting grace, is not seen in all hearers as to its effect, it does not follow from that that it is not inherent in the nature of every word. For a greater abundance of grace is not conferred upon him who rejected a lesser, which he was able, with the same grace assisting, not to have rejected. And for that reason he is not drawn, who has stubbornly rejected the first habit of preventing divine grace. Then, he who is drawn on the part of God, if he resists, is also dismissed, nor is the drawing continued. Thus Agrippas was being drawn, Acts XXVI. 28, but kicking against the goad he was dismissed. But concerning these things elsewhere in the cited places and in the Polemics.

Ἀναστήσω αὐτὸν) Him who shall have come to me in such a way that he also remains in me.

Latin:

V. 44. Οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐλθεῖν πρός με) Mihi credere, ac proinde agnoscere in me cœlestem illam excellentiam, quam indicaveram cum dicerem ex cœlo me descendisse. Vid. sup. 35. ostendit duritiam cordis eorum.

tractionem mere activam vocat ἔλλαμψιν, acceptatam vocat δεξιν. Verba sunt: ὅτω γὰρ ἡ παρὰ τῶ Θεῦ ἔλλαμψις τῆς παρὰ ἡμῶν ὁράσεως ἀυτῆ συντρεχούσης γίνεται· ἔργα δὲ τῆς δεήσεως ψυχῆς ἄνεσις καὶ σωτηρία ἀπὸ τῶν τῇδε ἰόντων, καὶ συνοικείωσις τῶν θείων ἀγαθῶν καὶ κοινωνία τῆς πατρικῆς πολιτείας.

Trahi Grotio est pio quodam affectu præditum esse. Quod requirit ad id, ut veniat quis ad Christum, eiq; credat. Sed ad fidem nihil facit animi probitas. Requirunt eam Sociniani & Arminiani. Quod alias profligavimus. Scriptura non requirit; imo probitatem animi fide posteriorem facit, & effectum ac fructum fidei. Trahit autem Deus non violenta & irresistibili ratione, ut Calviniam volunt, sed gratiosa invitatione, viriumque volendi & sequendi concessione, quas non immediate, sed per verbum & sacramenta operatur, ex nolentibus volentes, ex non valentibus valentes efficiendo. Neque trahit tantum pathetica rerum credendarum & agendarum propositione, prædicando, consolationibus excitando, comminationibus deterrendo &c. ut Pelagiani, Arminiani, & Sociniani volunt; siquidem hæc omnia Christus præsupponat, & nihilominus tractum Patris adhuc requirat: & terminentur illa in docente, etsi discipulus non pareat, trahere autem actio sit, quæ non terminatur in trahente, sed intraheto: & tractus non sit actus elicitus ex eo, qui trahitur, qualis est applausus ad orationem eloquentiæ Demosthenis, sed actus imperatus ex parte trahentis, & passio illata ex parte tracti, ratihabita autem per subsequentem consensum ejus, qui trahitur, resistibilis tamen. Ideoque requirit Salvator præter doctrinam forinsecus sonantem, ejus, quod foris sonat, impressionem in cor; ut explicat B. Hülsemannus de auxil. grat. p. 254. Quo de Augustin. l. I. de grat. Christ. cap. 10. epist. CVII. & CXLIII. & l. I. contr. duas epist. Pelag. c. 19. Non ait Christus: nisi Pater duxerit illum, ut illis aliquo modo intelligamus præcedere voluntatem. Quis trahitur, si jam volebat? Et tamen nemo venit, nisi velit. Trahitur ergo miris modis ut velit, ab illo, qui novit intus in intimis hominum cordibus operari, non ut homines (quod fieri non potest) nolentes credant, sed ut volentes ex nolentibus fiant. Hæc Augustinus. Quem vero non irresistibilem illum tractum & gratiam conversionis, quod ei Calviniani & Calixtini tribuunt, fecisse, peculiari disputatione de sententia Augustini in Syncretismo Calixtino ostendimus. Nam vel millies hoc inculcat: ut velimus esse ex dono Dei: posito autem & accepto hoc dono, posse tamen Nolle: ut habet B. Hülsemannus l. c. pag. 325. Notatur autem hac tractus voce tum impotentia nostra naturalis, veniendi ad Deum, tum repugnantia originalis, cum vocamur, ut tractione hac repugnantia illa naturalis per gratiam Dei prævenientem cohibeatur, nosque ex natura repugnantibus non repugnantes efficiamur, id in nobis operante gratia Dei, ut ne in actum prorumpat congenita illa repugnandi pronitas per actualem & malitiosam resistentiam, ad quam τῇ φύσει proclives sumus, Rom. VIII. 6. tum efficacia gratiæ & verbi gratiæ, per quod operatur Deus, primum ut non resistamus, tum ut è nolentibus volentes reddamur; non tantum morali suasione, sed etiam physica actione, cordis novi datione, regeneratione, & efficaci voluntatis nostræ mutatione, non tamen necessitate ac irresistibili. Quod autem divina illa vis, quæ tractus dicitur, & est supremus quasi gradus gratiæ convertentis, quoad effectum non spectatur in omnibus auditoribus, inde non sequitur, non inesse naturæ omnis verbi. Nam major copia gratiæ non confertur ei, qui minorem repudiavit, quam poterat, assistente eadem gratia, non repu- diasse. Eaque propter non trahitur, qui primum habitum prævenientis gratiæ divinæ pervicaciter elisit. Deinde qui trahitur ex parte Dei, si refra- getur, etiam dimittitur, nec continuatur tractio. Ita trahebatur Agrippas, Actor. XXVI. 28. sed recal- citrans dimittebatur. Sed de his alias in LL. CC. & Polemicis.

Ἀναστήσω αὐτὸν) Eum qui ad me venerit ita, ut & in me manserit.

## 6:45
Vers. 45. Ἐν τοῖς προφήταις) Isa. LIV. 13. Jer. XXXI. 4. in that place the words exist: in this one, likewise in Ezekiel several times and Micah IV. 2. the sense is the same.

Ἔσονται πάντες διδακτοὶ τῦ Θεῦ) The Hebrew למודי is not a participle, but an adjective, signifying learned, wise. It is joined with the genitive, as in Isa. VIII. 16. בלמדי, that is, among my learned ones: and in that place which is referred to here. But since the genitive can have many meanings, the most congruent to this place of Isaiah is that those are understood who are learned by divine instruction: just as, מכה אלהים Isa. LIII. 4. Smitten of God, that is, smitten by God: ἐνλογημένοι τῦ πατρός, Matt. XXV. 34. that is, blessed by the Father: Therefore δι- δακτοὶ Θεῦ in two words, or διδακτοὶ πνεύματος ἁγίε, as in I. Cor. II. 15, are those who in one word are θεοδίδακτοι: to Paul 1. Thess. IV. v. 9. Homer expresses the same with the word ἀυτοδίδακτος: For that former part of the word excludes only a human teacher; he himself explains, 'I am self-taught, but God has bestowed song upon me.' See Maximus of Tyre in the dissertation 'If anyone might become good by divine lot,' where he weighs that passage of Homer. But understand 'all' in the Prophet as all those to whom the word of the Gospel is announced: all these will turn out to be taught by God, namely if they are willing, if they are eager, if they do not reject the benefit offered and brought forward of its own accord: they will not have need to approach learned men, so that they may draw from them the mysteries of the Old Testament. Thus also in 1. Epist. II. 27. Add 1. Thess. IV. 9. and Jer. XXXI. 34.

ὁ ἀκύων παρὰ τῦ πατρὸς κὰι μαθὼν) He who hears in such a way that he shows himself teachable, that he prepares himself to learn: that he admits the breath of God into his soul. An old manuscript adds 'truth' after μαθὼν.

ἔρχεται πρός με) If he has given to me: which is to believe.

Latin:

Vers. 45. Ἐν τοῖς προφήταις) Esa. LIV. 13. Jer. XXXI. 4. in illo loco verba extant: in hoc, item apud Ezechielem aliquoties & Michæam IV. 2. sensus idem.

Ἔσονται πάντες διδακτοὶ τῦ Θεῦ) למודי Hebræum non par- ticipium est, sed adjectivum, significans peritum, sapien- tem. Conjungitur cum genitivo, ut Esa. VIII. 16. בלמדי, id est inter peritos meos: & eo loco qui hic respicitur. At cum Genitivus plures habere possit significationes, con- gruentissima huic Esaiæ loco est illa ut intelligantur hi, qui periti sunt divina institutione: sicut, מכה אלהים Es. LIII. 4. Percussus Dei, id est, percussus à Deo: ἐνλογημένοι τῦ πατρός, Matth. XXV. 34. id est, benedicti à Patre: Ergo δι- δακτοὶ Θεῦ duabus vocibus, aut διδακτοὶ πνεύματος ἁγίε, ut I. Cor. II. 15, sunt qui una voce θεοδίδακτοι: Paulo 1. Thess. IV. v. 9. Homerus idem exprimit voce ἀυτοδίδακτος: Nam vocis pars illa prior hominem tantum Magistrum excludit; ipse explicat αὐτοδίδακτος δ̓ εἰμὶ, Θεὸς δέ μοι ὥπασεν ἀυδὴν. Vide Maximum Tyrium dissertatione εἰ τις γένοιτο θείᾳ μοίρᾳ ἀγαθὸς, ubi illum Homeri locum expendit. Omnes autem intellige apud Prophetam, omnes eos quibus sermo Evangelii annunciatur: Hi omnes à Deo docti evadent, nempe si velint, si avidi sint, si non respuant oblatum & in gestum ultro beneficium: non opus habebunt adire viros literatos, ut ex illis hauriant mysteria veteris Testamenti. Sic & in 1. Epist. II. 27. Adde 1. Thess. IV. 9. & Jer. XXXI. 34.

ὁ ἀκύων παρὰ τῦ πατρὸς κὰι μαθὼν) Qui ita audit, ut do- cilem se præbeat, ut ad discendum se compatet: ut afflatus Dei admittat in animum. Vetus manuscriptus post μαθὼν adjicit ἀλήθειαν.

ἔρχεται πρός με) Si mihi dedit: quod est credere.

## 6:46
Vers. 46. Οὐκ ὅτι τὸν πατέρα τις ἑώρακε) An interpretation of the things said before, not that anyone is so familiarly conversant with the Father that he understands from him himself what must be done. See above I. 18. V. 37.

εἰ μὴ) Rightly the old 'but,' as here the Syrian אלא: so that the sense may be: No one of you indeed has seen the Father: but the Son has seen him. For thus what follows, 'He' etc., will cohere more correctly.

ὁ ὢν παρὰ τοῦ Θεῦ) ὁ μονογενὴς above 1. 18. who has been granted to us divinely.

Οὗτος ἑώρακε τὸν πατέρα) He as an intimate has known the Father's will thoroughly. Wherefore when he reveals it, then the Father draws, and he who suffers himself to be drawn is brought, so that he may believe, so that he may obey.

Latin:

Vers. 46. Οὐκ ὅτι τὸν πατέρα τις ἑώρακε) Interpretatio ante dictorum, non quod cum Patre quisquam ita versetur familiariter, ut ab eo ipso intelligat, quid faciendum sit. Vi- de supra I. 18. V. 37.

εἰ μὴ) Recte veteris sed, ut hic Syrus אלא: ut sensus: sit: Vestrum quidem nemo Patrem vidit: at vidit eum Fi- lius. Ita enim rectius cohærebit quod sequitur ἗τος &c.

ὁ ὢν παρὰ τοῦ Θεῦ) ὁ μονογενὴς supra 1. 18. qui divini- tus nobis concessus est.

Οὗτος ἑώρακε τὸν πατέρα) Is ut intimus pernovit Patris voluntatem. Quare cum is eam revelat, tunc Pater trahit, & qui patitur se trahi, adducitur, ut credat, ut obediat.

## 6:47
Vers. 47. ὁ πισεύων εἰς ἐμὲ) Elsewhere we have said that to believe Jesus is to have faith in his words, to believe in him is to trust in him: which the Hebrews express by אמן with ב added, as in Isa. XXVIII. 16. But where he who is speaking is dealing with a matter which he himself is about to perform for us, then these two locutions almost amount to the same thing. But understand 'to believe' and 'to trust' in such a way as is fitting, with the intention of fulfilling the proposed conditions.

ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον) He has a right to eternal life, as above c. III. 16. V. 24. He who has a right to a thing, seems to have the thing, say the Jurisconsults.

Latin:

Vers. 47. ὁ πισεύων εἰς ἐμὲ) Alibi diximus credere Jesu, esse verbis ejus fidem habere, credere in eum esse ei confi- dere: quod Hebr. efferunt per אמן addito ב, ut Es. XXVIII. 16. Ubi autem is qui loquitur, agit de re, quam ipse no- bis præstiturus est, tum hæ duæ locutiones ferme in idem recidunt. Credere autem & confidere intellige, ita ut opor- tet, cum animo implendi conditiones propositas.

ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον) Jus habet ad vitam æternam, ut supra c. III. 16. V. 24. Qui jus ad rem habet, rem habere videtur, ajunt Jurisconsulti.

## 6:48
Vers. 48. Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς) Above in verse 35. He repeats the same sense often, both so that it may be fixed in the mind, and so that an opportunity may be given to those wishing to be taught to ask questions.

Latin:

Vers. 48. Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς) Supra commate 35. Sensum eundem sæpe repetit, tum ut infigatur animo, tum ut occasio detur doceri volentibus, interrogandi.

## 6:49
τὸ μάννα ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) He repeats their own words above 49.

καὶ ἀπέθανον) That is, the manna could not provide life for them, except for a short time.

Latin:

τὸ μάννα ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) Repetit ipsorum verba supra 49.

καὶ ἀπέθανον) Id est, non potuit illis manna præstare vi- tam, nisi ad breve tempus.

## 6:50
V. 50. ὁ ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ καταβαίνων) Above 33. He uses a verb of the present tense, because his power flows perpetually from the Father.

ἵνα τὶς ἐξ αὐτῦ φάγῃ κὰι μὴ ἀποθάνῃ) A Hebraism for: That if anyone eats of it, he may not die. Understand this after he has once obtained life itself [not just the right to life]: for the life proceeding from this bread is eternal, as is explained shortly in verses 51 and 54.

ὁ ζῶν) The Hebrews often use Qal for Hiphil: thus חיה for them is both to live and to make alive: by which example the Hellenists often say ζῶν for ζωοποιῦν, thus Acts VII. 38, Heb. IV. 12, 1 Pet. I. 3.

Latin:

V. 50. ὁ ἐκ τῦ ὐρανῦ καταβαίνων) Sup. 33. Verbum præsentis temporis usurpat, quia perpetuo potestas ipsius fluit à Patre.

ἵνα τὶς ἐξ αὐτῦ φάγῃ κὰι μὴ ἀποθάνῃ)Hebraïsmus pro: Ut si quis ex eo ederit, non moriatur. Intellige postquam se- mel vitam ipsam [non jus tantum vitæ] adeptus fuerit: nam vita ex hoc pane procedens æterna est, ita explicatur mox commate, 51. & 54.

ὁ ζῶν) Hebræi sæpe Cal pro Hiphil: itaque חיה ipsis est & ζῆν & ζωοποιεῖν: quo exemplo ζῶν sæpe dicunt Hellenistæ pro ζωοποιῦν, sic Act. VII. 38. Hebr. IV. 12. 1. Petr. I. 3.

## 6:51
V. 51. κὰι ὁ ἄρτος δὲ ὃν ἐγὼ δώσω, ἡ σάρξ με ἐσίν) Not only is my word food for eternal life [which was treated above] but this will also be my death. For the same thing that the word teaches, death also teaches, both by offering testimony to the truth of the word, and by providing an example of those things which the word commands: obedience, patience, humility, and love.

for the life of the world, he says it is bread or food, not death simply, but the merit of his death, which is proposed to us in the word of the Gospel, as food of life, when we enjoy it with true faith, he teaches us to believe. Therefore, to eat is explained as to believe. Compare 47 and 51, concerning which Augustine, tract. XXVI on John: To believe in him, this is to eat the living bread; he who believes in him eats, he is invisibly nourished, because he is invisibly reborn. He certainly does not propose death as martyrdom, by which he offers testimony to the truth, or call it the bread of life for that reason, for thus every death of the martyrs would be the bread of life; nor as an example of obedience, patience, humility, love, or other virtues that suffices for us; for we do not obtain eternal life through such virtues, but solely through the merit of the death of Christ apprehended by faith. Grotius explains the following words themselves ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ζωῆς concerning the merit and acquisition of life: that I may obtain eternal life for the human race: for he died for all, Heb. II. 9. Therefore, those things which Grotius says later in v. 53 are foreign: that the death of Christ is as it were a visible word: and further: Seneca says wisdom is taught in two ways, by precepts and by examples: in the death of Christ there is the most perfect example both of other virtues, and especially of love: which to imitate is a summary of the precepts. See below XIII. 34, XV. 12, 13, Ep. I. II. 6, 9, 10, 11, 1 Cor. XI. 1. See also Col. I. 24. This therefore is to eat and drink, to use the example: how Basil interprets this passage in his apology to the Caesareans. This very thing Augustine calls communicating in the passion of the Lord: for just as food and drink admitted into the body nourish a man, so good examples admitted into the mind confirm it wonderfully. Moreover, Augustine. lib. III. de doctr. Christ. cap. XVI. does not speak of the communication of the passion through the imitation of Christ's example, but through the fiducial application of Christ's merit: It is a figure, he says, commanding that one should communicate in the passion of the Lord and sweetly and usefully store in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us. Who does not see that these things pertain to faith? Basil the Great, Apol. ad Caesar., which is Epist. CXLI. We eat, he says, his flesh, and drink his blood, having been made partakers of him through the incarnation and the sensible life of the Word and Wisdom. For he called his whole mystical conversation in the flesh flesh and blood, and manifested that doctrine which consists of the practical, the natural, and the theological, through which the soul is nourished, and is meanwhile prepared for the contemplation of those things which are. παρασκευάζεται. That conversation embraces primarily the merit of his obedience and passion, which is the principal object of his theological doctrine. By faith in this, the soul is nourished through the remaining chapters of his doctrine, and is prepared and exercised for the contemplation of those things which truly are. Grotius adds: The Syriac has body for flesh, which word is also read in the institution of the Eucharist, to which there is a certain tacit allusion here, as we said above on the third chapter; there food and drink are called body and blood: here body and blood are called food and drink. Indeed, as is the case among ancient writers, the signs and the things signified are reckoned by the same words. And it was the custom for the Prophets to take visible signs from comparisons or common metaphors by which they might more effectively fix a matter in the minds of men. But sacramental and spiritual perception are so confounded: in the Sacrament, the food and drink are not called body and blood, but concerning that which Christ provides when He offers the bread, Christ testifies, "This is my body": concerning that which He provides when He offers the wine, He testifies: "This is my blood": therefore not there is only a sign of the body and blood of Christ there, but the very body and blood of the Lord is truly present, truly offered, but in another manner (namely, the body to be eaten with and under the bread; the blood to be drunk with and under the wine) than here, where we enjoy the body and blood of Christ spiritually through faith. Calvin himself acknowledged this: saying, here, the discourse is not about the supper, but about the perpetual communion which we have outside the use of the supper: and it is clear from v. 54 that this whole passage is wrongly explained as being about the supper. For it would have been inept and untimely to discourse then about the supper, which he had not yet instituted: therefore it is certain that he is treating of the perpetual eating of faith. Pelargus in his Commentary on this passage brings forward eight differences by which this eating is distinguished from the sacramental one. We have dealt with this against the Calixtines in the Calixtine-Heretical Harmony expressly, which should be compared here.

which I will give) And the Father gives and the Son gives: the Father by decree, the Son by voluntary obedience. Thus also παραδιδόναι is sometimes said of the Father, Matt. XVII. 22. and elsewhere: sometimes of Christ, Gal. II. 20. Eph. V. 2. 25. See below chapter X. 17. 18. He is said to give his body who offers it to be vexed, who offers it to be killed, 1 Cor. XIII. v. 3. for σὰρξ and σῶμα are used indiscriminately by interpreters for the Hebrew בשר.

For the life of the world) That I may obtain eternal life for the human race: for he died for all, Heb. II. 9. See above c. I. 29. c. III. 6.

Latin:

V. 51. κὰι ὁ ἄρτος δὲ ὃν ἐγὼ δώσω, ἡ σάρξ με ἐσίν) Non tantum sermo meus est pabulum ad vitam æternam [quod supra tractatum] sed hoc erit & mors mea. Nam idem quod ser- mo docet, docet & mors, tum sermonis veritati testimo- nium præbens, tum exemplum eorum, quæ sermo præci- pit, obedientiæ, patientiæ, humilitatis, dilectionis.

pro mundi vita, panem vel pabulum esse dicit, non mortem simpliciter, sed mortis suæ meritum, quod in verbo Evangelii nobis proponitur, in cibum vitæ, cum vera fide illo fruimur, credere docet. Ideo manducare exponitur per credere. Conf. 47. & 51. de quo Augustin. tract. XXVI. in Joh. Cre- dere in eum, hoc est, manducare panem vivum, qui credit in eum, manducat, invisibiliter agitatur, quia invisibiliter renascitur. Non sane mortem uti martyrium proponit, qua veritati præbet testimo- nium, aut vitæ panem ideo dicit Christus, ita enim omnis martyrum mors panis vitæ esset; nec qua ex- emplum nobis sufficit obedientiæ, patientiæ, humi- litatis, dilectionis aliarumve virtutum; non enim per ejusmodi virtutes vitam consequimur æter- nam, sed unice per meritum mortis Christi fide ap- prehensum. Explicat Grotius ipsa verba sequen- tia ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ζωῆς de merito & acquisitione vitæ: ut vitam æternam impetrem humano generi: pro omnibus enim mortuus est, Ebr. II. 9. Aliena er- go sunt, quæ postea v. 53. Grotius: mortem Chri- sti esse quasi verbum visibile: & porro: Duobus mo- dis sapientiam ait doceri Seneca, præceptis & exem- plis: in Christi morte perfectissimum est exemplum tum virtutum aliarum, tum præcipue dilectionis: quam imitari compendium est præceptorum. Vide inf. XIII. 34. XV. 12. 13. Ep. I. II. 6. 9. 10. 11. 1. Cor. XI. 1. Vide & Col. I. 24. Hoc ergo est edere & bibere, uti ex- emplo: quomodo hunc locum interpretatur Basilius apologia ad Cæsarianos. Hoc ipsum Augustinus vo- cat communicare passioni Domini: nam sicut cibus ac potus in corpus admissi hominem nutriunt, ita bo- na exempla in animum admissa eum mirabiliter confirmant. Cæterum Augustin. lib. III. de doctr. Christ. cap. XVI. non de communicatione passionis per exempli Christi imitationem, sed per meriti Christi fiducialem applicationem loquitur: Figura est, inquit, præcipiens passioni Domini esse commu- nicandum & suaviter atq; utiliter recondendum in memoria, quod pro nobis caro ejus crucifixa & vul- nerata est. Hæc ad fidem pertinere quis non vi- det? Basilius M. Apol. ad Cæsar. quæ est Epist. CXLI. Carnem, inquit, ipsius edimus, ac sangui- nem bibimus consortes ipsius effecti per incarnatio- nem & sensibilem verbi ac sapientiæ vitam. Car- nem enim ac sanguinem totam suam mysticam in carne conversationem vocavit, doctrinamq; illam, quæ ex practica & naturali, & Theologica constat, manifestavit, per quam nutritur anima, & ad eo- rum quæ sunt contemplationem interea præparatur. παρασκευάζεται. Conversatio illa complectitur imprimis meritum obedientiæ & passionis ejus, quod doctrinæ ejus Theologicæ præcipuum objectum est. Eo fide apprehensio nutritur anima per reli- qua doctrinæ ejus capita, ad contemplationem eorum quæ vere sunt, præparatur, & exercetur. Addit Grotius: Pro carne corpus habet Syrus, quæ vox & in Eucharistiæ institutione legitur, ad quam hic ut diximus supra ad caput tertium, tacita qua- dam allusio est, ibi cibus & potus vocantur corpus & sanguis: hic corpus & sanguis appellantur cibus & potus. Nimirum, ut apud veterum est scriptorem, si- gnificantia & significata iisdem vocabulis censentur. Et mos erat Prophetis ex comparationibus, aut translationibus usitatis signa visibilia sumere quibus efficacius rem animis hominum infigerent. Sed ita confunduntur sacramentalis & spiritualis perce- ptio: in Sacramento non vocatur cibus & potus corpus & sanguis, sed de eo quod præbet Chri- stus, cum panem exhibet, testatur Christus, hoc est corpus meum: de eo quod præbet cum vinum exhibet, testatur: Hoc est sanguis meus: non ergo signum tantum illic est corporis & sanguinis Chri- sti, sed vere adest ipsum corpus & sanguis Domini, vere præbetur, sed alia ratione (manducandum nempe corpus, cum & sub pane; bibendus vero sanguis cum & sub vino) quam hic, ubi sspirituali- ter fruimur corpore & sanguine Christi per fidem. Quod agnovit Calvinus ipse: Hic, inquiens, non de cæna habetur oratio, sed de perpetua communica- tione, quæ extra cænæ usum nobis constat: & patet ex v. 54. perperam de cæna exponi totum hunc locum. Nam ineptum fuisset, ac intempestivum de cæna tunc disserere, quam nondum instituerat: ideo de per- petua fidei manducatione eum tractare, certum est. Pelargus in Comment. ad h. l. octo affert differeu- tias, quibus hæc manducatio à sacramentali distin- guatur. Egimus de eo adversus Calixtinos in Har- monia Calixtino-Hæretica ex professo, quæ hic conferatur.

ὃν ἐγὼ δώσω) Et Pater dat & dat Filius: Pater decreto, Filius voluntario obsequio. Sic & παραδιδόναι modo de Pa- tre dicitur Matth. XVII. 22. & alibi: modo de Christo, Gal. II. 20. Eph. V. 2. 25. Vide infra cap. X. 17. 18. Dare corpus dicitur qui vexandum, qui occidendū præbet, 1. Cor. XIII. v. 3. nam σὰρξ & σῶμα promiscue sumuntur apud interpre- tes pro Hebræo בשר.

Ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ζωῆς) Ut vitam æternam impetrem hu- mano generi: pro omnibus enim mortuus est, Hebr. II. 9. Vide supra c. I. 29. c. III. 6.

## 6:52
V. 52. they strove) The Hebrew רוב which the Greeks mostly translate as μάχεσθαι in Gen. XXXI. 36. Neh. XIII. 11. is often to litigate, as the Latin interpreter translates it here. ἀντιλέγειν is translated in Hos. IV. 4. Others thought there was something secret underlying it: the greater part rejected what Christ had said as clearly absurd, See above 41. 43.

saying) A part of them.

how can this man give us his flesh to eat) Take that δύναται not physically but morally. Thus jurists call impossible conditions those which are repugnant to honesty. Thus we have διώκεσθαι in Matt. IX. 15. in this class of impossibles is feeding on human flesh. 'A god is free from disease' to Moschion: an impious feast, said an old tragic poet among the Latins.

Latin:

V. 52. ἐμάχοντο ἦν) רוב Hebræum quod μάχεσθ plenun- que vertunt Græci in Gen. XXXI. 36. Neh. XIII. 11. sæpe est litigare, quomodo hic vertit interpres Latinus. ἀντιλέ- γειν vertitur Os. IV. 4. Alii putarunt subesse aliquid arcani: pars major quod Christus dixerat ut plane absonum rejece- runt, Vide supra 41. 43.

λέγοντες) Pars eorum.

πῶς δύναται ὗτος ἡμῖν δῦναι τὴν σάρκα φαγεῖν) Illud δύναται sume non φυσικῶς sed ἠθικῶς. Sic Jurisconsulti im- possibiles conditiones vocant quæ honestati repugnant. Sic διώκεσθ habemus Matth. IX. 15. in hoc impossibilium genere est vesci humanis carnibus. θεῶν ἄνοσος ἧς Moschioni: im- piam dapem dixit vetus apud Latinos Tragicus.

## 6:53
V. 53. unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood) In order to excite attention and a desire for learning, he seriously affirms that which elsewhere they thought absurd is not only honest, but also necessary to be done, namely by those who would be called through the Gospel. In what sense he called his flesh food we have already said. Here he distinguishes flesh and blood, to signify not just any death, but a violent and bloody one. Clement of Alexandria in the first book of the Pedagogue says the Word himself is called flesh and blood: nor does Tertullian say otherwise in his book on the resurrection of the flesh: but it is true what we have already said, that the death of Christ is as it were a visible word. Seneca says wisdom is taught in two ways: by precepts and by examples: In the death of Christ there is the most perfect example both of other virtues, and especially of love: to imitate which is a compendium of the commandments. See below XIII. 34. XV. 12. 13. 1 Epist. II. 6. 9. 10. 11. 1 Cor. XI. v. 1. See also Coloss. I. 24. This therefore is to eat and drink, to use the example: How Basil interprets this passage in his apology to the Caesareans. This very thing Augustine calls communicating in the passion of the Lord: for just as food and drink admitted into the body nourish a man, so good examples admitted into the soul wonderfully confirm it. The Syrian has body for flesh, which word is also read in the institution of the Eucharist, to which there is a certain tacit allusion here, as we said above at the third chapter: there food and drink are called body and blood: here body and blood are called food and drink. Indeed, as it is in an ancient writer, the things signifying and the things signified are reckoned by the same words. And it was the custom for the prophets to take visible signs from common comparisons or metaphors by which they might more effectively impress a matter upon the minds of men.

you have no life in yourselves) What it is to have life, namely eternal, has been said several times: but that ἐν ἑαυτοῖς after ἔχειν is a Hebraic pleonasm, as Matt. XIII. v. 21. Mark IX. 50. above c. V. 26. 42. 1 Epist. III. 15. the sense is, you have no right to eternal life.

Latin:

V. 53. ἐὰν μὴ φάγητε τὴν σάρκα τοῦ ὑἱοῦ τῶ ἀνθρώπε καὶ πίητε ἀυτᾶ τὸ αἷμα) Ut attentionem & discendi cupiditatem ex- citet, serio affirmat id quod alibi absurdum putabant non tantum honestum esse, sed & factu necessarium, iis scilicet qui per Evangelium vocarentur. Quo sensu carnem suam cibum appellaverit jam diximus. Hic discernit carnem & sanguinem, ut significet mortem non quamvis, sed vio- lentam & cruentam. Clemens Alexandrinus Pædagogo primo ipsum verbum ait vocari carnem & sanguinem: nec aliter Tertullianus libro de resurrectione carnis: sed ve- rum est quod jam diximus mortem Christi esse quasi ver- bum visibile. Duobus modis sapientiam ait doceri Seneca præceptis & exemplis: In Christi morte perfectissimum est exemplum tum virtutum aliarum, tum præcipue dilectio- nis: quam imitari compendium est præceptorum. Vide in- fra XIII. 34. XV. 12. 13. 1. Epist. II. 6. 9. 10. 11. 1. Cor. XI. v. 1. Vide & Coloss. I. 24. Hoc ergo est edere & bibere, utı exemplo: Quomodo hunc locum interpretatur Basilius apologia ad Cæsarianos. Hoc ipsum Augustinus vocat communicare passioni Domini: nam sicut cibus ac potus in corpus admissi hominem nutriunt, ita bona exempla in animum admissa eum mirabiliter confirmant. Pro carne corpus habet Syrus, quæ vox & in Eucharistiæ institutione legitur, ad quam hic ut diximus supra ad caput tertium, ta- cita quædam allusio est: ibi cibus & potus vocantur corpus & sanguis: hic corpus & sanguis appellantur cibus & po- tus. Nimirum, ut apud veterem est scriptorem, significan- tia & significata iisdem vocabulis censentur. Et mos erat prophetis ex comparationibus aut translationibus usitatis signa visibilia sumere quibus efficacius rem animis homi- num insigerent.

ὀυκ ἔχετε ζωὴν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς) Quid sit habere vitam, æter- nam scilicet, dictum est aliquoties: illud autem ἐν ἑαυτοῖς post ἔχειν est πλεονασμὸς Hebraicus, ut Matth. XIII. v. 21. Marc. IX. 50. supra c. V. 26. 42. 1. Epist. III. 15. sensus est, non est vobis jus ad vitam æternam.

## 6:54
Vers. 54.

and I will raise him up) It is an epexegesis of what preceded. He has a right to eternal life, because I will raise him from death, namely to life and glory.

Latin:

Vers. 54.

καὶ ἐγὼ ἀναστήσω ἀυτὸν) Est epexegesis ejus quod præces- sit. Habet jus ad vitam æternam, quia ego eum excitabo ex morte, ad vitam scilicet & gloriam.

## 6:55
Vers. 55.

Ἀληθῶς ἐστι βρῶσις) Most eminent: concerning the force of this word we have already spoken above several times. Such is that, which is the most beautiful pasture of souls.

Latin:

Vers. 55.

Ἀληθῶς ἐστι βρῶσις) Eminentissime: de qua vi hujus vo- cis diximus jam supra aliquoties Tale illud, qui pastus pulo cherrimus est animorum.

## 6:56
Vers. 56. ἐν ἐμοὶ μένει κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ) He is united to me, and I to him, by mutual love: for μένειν, as we have already noted before, is for John to be, to dwell in someone, which is a figure sufficiently common transferred to the mind. The lover is where he loves. But what is here attributed to the eating of the flesh and blood, that is elsewhere attributed to brotherly love, 1 Epist. III. 23, 24, IV. 16, so that it may appear that these amount to the same thing.

It is not only, nor chiefly, a matter of the union of mutual love, but primarily of that mystical union by which he dwells in us through faith, Ephes. III. v. 15, by which we apprehend Christ and his merit, and apply them to ourselves, so that we may enjoy that life-giving flesh, given for the life of the world, and be quickened, nourished, and fed by its efficacy unto eternal life. As we are in Christ through faith, when we are mystically joined and united to him; so Christ is likewise said to be in us, and to dwell through faith. Nor is this ever attributed to brotherly love; even if he who loves his brother is said to remain in God, for he is not in God, or remains, through love, which is too lacking, imperfect, weak, and unclean for us to be or remain in God by its power; but through faith: which indeed is not without love, Gal. V. 6. Therefore, the subject is designated in 1 John IV. 16, but not the cause or medium of remaining in God. That those who love God remain in God is undoubted: but that they remain in God by that by which they love God, and through love, is nowhere taught: Nor is the same thing attributed to love as to the eating of flesh and blood, or to faith.

Moreover, that this discourse of Christ, and especially v. 53, 54, 55, and 56, treats of the Holy Eucharist, the Papists, Calvinists, and the innovators Calixtus and Dreier laboriously contend. But that this does not treat of the substance of the Holy Supper or sacramental perception, but of the spiritual fruition of the body and blood of Christ, which pertains to the end and efficacy of the Holy Supper, and occurs even outside the Supper, and is to be believed as necessary for all who are to be saved in the Old and New Testament, by the force of Christ's assertion in v. 35, is clear both from the whole discourse and as we have proved against Calixtus and Dreier, having discussed the testimonies of the ancients brought to the contrary in the Harmon. Calixtino-Hæretica p. 762. seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 56. ἐν ἐμοὶ μένει κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ) Unitus est mihi, & ego illi, amore mutuo: nam μένειν, ut jam ante notavimus, Johanni est esse, habitare in aliquo, quod figura satis usi- tata ad animum transfertur. Amans est ubi amat. Quod antem hic tribuitur manducationi carnis & sanguinis, id a- libi tribuitur dilectioni fraternæ, 1. Epist. III. 23. 24. IV. 16. ut appareat hæc eodem recidere.

Non tantum, nec præcipue de unione mutui amoris agitur, sed imprimis de unione illa mystica, qua per fidem habitat in nobis, Ephes. III. v. 15. qua Christum ejusque meritum apprehendimus, no- bisque applicamus, ut carne illa vivifica, pro mun- di vita data, fruamur, ejusdemque efficacia vivifi- cemur, vegetemur, & nutriamur ad æternam vi- tam. Ut nos in Christo sumus per fidem, cum ei- dem mystice copulamur & unimur; ita Christus itidem dicitur in nobis esse, & habitare per fidem. Nec id uspiam dilectioni fraternæ tribuitur; etsi ille qui fratrem diligit, manere dicatur in Deo, non enim per dilectionem in Deo est, aut manet, quæ nimis manca, imperfecta, infirma & immunda est, quam ut ejusdem vi in Deo simus, aut maneamus; sed per fidem: quæ vero non est sine dilectione Gal. V. 6. Subjectum ergo 1. Johann. IV. 16. designatur, non vero causa vel medium mansionis in Deo. Quod qui diligunt Deum, in Deo maneant, in- dubium est: sed quod illi, qua diligunt Deum, & per dilectionem in Deo maneant, nuspiam doce- tur: Nec dilectioni idem tribuitur, quod mandu- cationi carnis & sanguinis, vel fidei.

Cæterum hanc Christi concionem & cumpri- mis v. 53. 54. 55. & 56. de S. Eucharistia agere, Pon- tificii, Calviniani & Novatores Calixtus & Dreie- rus operose contendunt. Quod vero hic non de substantia S. cænæ vel perceptione sacramentali, sed de spirituali corporis & sanguinis Christi fruitione, quæ ad finem & efficaciam S. cænæ pertinet, & extra cænam etiam fit, omnibusque salvandis in Veteri & Novo Testamento necessaria credenda est, vi alleve- rationis Christi v. 35. tum ex concione tota liquet, tum adversus Calixtum & Dreierum probavimus, discussis in contrarium adductis veterum testimo- niis in Harmon. Calixtino-Hæretica p. 762. seqq.

## 6:57
Vers. 57. καθὼς ἀπέστειλέ με ὁ ζῶν πατὴρ κἀγὼ ζῶ διὰ τὸν πατέρα) I think this is the first member of the comparison, not the comparison itself. It is, however, an Enallage: the living Father sent me, that is, the Father who sent me lives. God is called living throughout the sacred scriptures, as in Deuter. IV. 33 and elsewhere, because he has the fountain of all life in himself: whence he is called the Father of spirits, Hebr. XII. v. 9. διὰ here and in the following clause, although with the accusative case, denotes the efficient cause, as διὰ τοὺς θεοὺς among Demosthenes, that is, by the benefit of the gods; Hesiod on Jove: Ὅντε διὰ βροτοὶ ἄνδρες ὁμῶς ἄφατοίτε φατοίτε. Thus almost above IV. 41, 42, and Marc. II. 4.

κἀγὼ τρώγων) Here κἀ is thus, as below X. 15, XV. 9, 1 Epist. II. v. 18.

δι' ἐμέ) With me myself giving life, just as the Father gave me life, and the right of quickening.

Latin:

Vers. 57. καθὼς ἀπέστειλέ με ὁ ζῶν πατὴρ κἀγὼ ζῶ διὰ τὸν πατέρα) Puto hoc esse prius membrum comparationis, non comparationem per se. Est autem Enallage: misit me vivens Pater, id est, vivit Pater qui me misit. Passim in sa- cris literis dicitur Deus vivens, ut Deuter. IV. 33. & alibi, quia fontem omnis vitæ in se habet: unde Pater spirituum appellatur, Hebr. XII. v. 9. διὰ hic & sequenti commate quanquam cum casu quarto, causam efficientem denotet, διὰ τοὺς θεοὺς apud Demosthenem, id est, Deorum beneficio, Hesiodus de Jove: Ὅντε διὰ βροτοὶ ἄνδρες ὁμῶς ἄφατοίτε φατοίτε Sic ferme supra IV. 41. 42. & Marc. II. 4

κἀγὼ τρώγων) Hic κἀ est sic, ut infra X. 15. XV. 9. 1. Epist. II. v. 18.

δι' ἐμέ) Me ipsi vitam dante, sicut Pater mihi dedit vi- tam, & jus vivificandi.

## 6:58
Vers. 58. ἐκ τοῦ ὀυρανοῦ καταβὰς) See above c. III. 13.

ὁ καθὼς) A Hebraism: for, not similar to that bread: Thus ὥστε Rom. IV. 18, above c. III. 8, and elsewhere.

κἀ ἀπέθανον) Again a Hebraism placing a conjunction for a relative. Not such bread as that by the eating of which your fathers died.

Latin:

Vers. 58. ἐκ τοῦ ὀυρανοῦ καταβὰς) Vide supra c. III. 13.

ὁ καθὼς) Hebraismus: pro, non similis ei pani: Sic ὥστε Rom. IV. 18, supra c. III. 8. & alibi.

κἀ ἀπέθανον) Iterum Hebraismus copulam ponens pro relativo. Non talis panis qualis ille quo manducato patres ve- stri mortui sunt.

## 6:59
Vers. 59.

ἐν συναγωγῇ διδάσκων) Openly, in a public place, where there were many witnesses to the discourse: this contributes to the credibility of the narrative, as in Acts 26:26.

Latin:

Vers. 59.

ἐν συναγωγῇ διδάσκων) Palam, loco publico, ubi pluri- mi erant testes sermonis: facit hoc ad fidem narrationis ut Act. XXVI. 26.

## 6:60
Vers. 60.

ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν ἀυτοῦ Not from the twelve, but from others who were more frequent followers of Jesus.

σκληρὸς) The Syriac word here: which term is translated everywhere by σκληρὸν by the Greeks, as in Deuteronomy 1:17; it signifies, however, something perplexing or inexplicable.

τίς δύναται ἀυτοῦ ἀκούειν) Who can listen to him patiently? Here, indeed, they accuse themselves, who do not ask the Master about doubtful matters.

Latin:

Vers. 60.

ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν ἀυτοῦ Non ex duodecim, sed ex aliis qui frequentiores erant Jesu sectatores.

σκληρὸς) NWP Syrus hic: quæ vox passim per σκληρὸν vertitur a Græcis, ut Deuter. I. 17. significat autem perple- xum inexplicabile.

τίς δύναται ἀυτοῦ ἀκούειν) Quis patienter audiat? Hic vero semet accusant, qui de dubiis Magistrum non inter- rogent.

## 6:61
Vers. 61. Σκανδαλίζει] It offends you as incredible, as above 52.

Latin:

Vers. 61. Σκανδαλίζει] Offendit vos tanquam incredibi- le, ut supra 52.

## 6:62
Vers. 62. ἐὰν οὖν θεωρῆτε] If you yourselves see it or learn of it by the certain testimony of others. For it also has the meaning of to know, as above c. IV. 19. below c. XII. 19. 45. XIV. 17. Acts XXI. 20. Heb. VII. 4.

ἀναβαίνοντα ὅπου ἦν τὸ πρότερον] Into heaven where he was before. ὁ λόγος when he was πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, above c. I. 1. for the region of God is heaven. Christ attributes to himself what is fitting for the Word: Why not? since we are accustomed to call the soul and the body separately by the name of man. Homer also gives the proper names of men to the souls of the dead. And just now Christ, when he had named his flesh and blood, added me. See below c. XX. 2. 13. There is, however, an Aposiopesis here, as often in any authors, after, What then: Interpreters supply various things. I would supply it thus: Will you not then at least perceive what you do not perceive now, that my words cannot be understood according to popular usage? for with my body removed far away into heaven, there will be no hope of eating it κατὰ κυριολεξίαν (literally).

There is no reason why we should seize upon this connection of the text: but Cyril rendered it more correctly in lib. IV. in John cap. 22. If you think that my flesh cannot bring you (eternal) life, how does it ascend into heaven like a bird: for this is likewise impossible for the human race, but if my flesh shall ascend into heaven contrary to nature, what prevents it from likewise vivifying contrary to nature? for he who made this earthly body heavenly, he also rendered it vivifying, since by its own nature it was corruptible. Chrysostom explains it thus, that they ought not to be offended by these things, but believe what he says: because other things concerning his flesh are also to be believed by them: namely that it is about to ascend into heaven. He is not, therefore, acting to teach that because he will ascend into heaven, it cannot be eaten properly. For the Article concerning the ascension into heaven is not to be opposed to the eating of the body of Christ, accepted κτ' κυριολεξίαν (literally): because in the holy supper he offers us his body to be eaten, and that properly, for there is no reason why we should invent figures here, without prejudice to the truth of his ascension into heaven, as we teach otherwise against the Calvinists. We only repeat here the explanation of the blessed Lyser in Harm. Evang. c. LXXVII. Does this offend you? that I said that I have come down from heaven, and that my flesh must be eaten, so that one may live forever. If therefore you see the Son of man ascending to where he was before, what will you say then? Will I then also seem to have arrogated to myself more than is right? Will you not then, even against your will, acknowledge that I have descended from heaven? Christ therefore, saying these things, did not wish to deny the eating of his flesh in the Sacrament, and to teach that all things were at least to be spiritual and mystical after the ascension into the heavens, (as the Sacramentarians interpret this passage) but he wishes to assert the truth of his sayings in this way, just as he was also accustomed to refer his enemies, who were withdrawing faith from his words, to his resurrection, ascension, and glorification, by which he was about to prove the truth of his sayings, John II. v. 19. Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. John III. v. 13. No one has ascended into heaven, but he who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven. John VIII. 28. When you have lifted up the Son of man, then you will know that I am he, and I do nothing from myself, but as the Father taught me, these things I speak. Matt. XXVI. 64. I say to you, from now on you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of the power of God, and coming in the clouds of heaven. In this way God is accustomed to prove the truth of the preceding things by the event of the subsequent ones. For example: Exod. III. v. 12. when he was sending Moses into Egypt, to lead the Israelites out of the house of bondage, and he himself was hesitating to undertake this work, he gave him this sign by which he confirmed his faith: When you have led my people out of Egypt, you shall sacrifice to God upon this mountain. If in this place Christ wishes to say that he wishes to demonstrate by his return into heaven, both that he is the true God from heaven; and that what he said concerning the efficacy of his flesh is true! For he who can make his flesh, contrary to the nature of flesh, heavenly: the same can also make it the vivifying food of men. This is the blessed Lyser. Nor is the explanation of Flacius inconsistent: The Jews were offended especially by the fact that Christ affirmed that he had come from heaven, that God was his Father, that he was the savior of the world, and that he preferred himself and his own flesh far above that heavenly manna to Moses and the Fathers. Christ proves by his future ascension and glorification that he is both from heaven and the savior. Thus below c. VIII. 28. and elsewhere he refers them to his resurrection and glorification, promising them the sign of Jonah and that they would see themselves at the right hand of power; and above chapter II. he predicted to them the destruction and restoration of the temple of his body. The sense here is as if he were saying: This seems incredible to you now, that I have come from heaven: but when you see me return there again, from there to reign, or coming from there to judge: You will be compelled to assent that I am from there, just as in c. III. v. 13. he had said: No one has ascended into heaven, but the Son of man, who descended from heaven. By his return there, therefore, he proves that that is as it were his fatherland, and that he is the true God.

Latin:

Vers. 62. ἐὰν οὖν θεωρῆτε] Si aut ipsi videritis aut aliorum certo testimonio cognoveritis. Nam & cognoscendi signi- ficatum habet, ut supra c. IV. 19. infra c. XII. 19. 45. XIV. 17. Actor. XXI. 20. Hebr. VII. 4.

ἀναβαίνοντα ὅπου ἦν τὸ πρότερον] In cœlum ubi ante fuit. ὁ λόγος cum esset πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, sup. c. I. 1. nam Dei regio cœlum. Tribuit Christus sibi quod τῷ λόγῳ convenit: Quid ni? cum & animam & corpus seorsim soleamus appellare hominis vocabulo. Etiam animis mortuorum Homerus dat propria hominum nomina. Et modo Christus cum car- nem & sanguinem suum nominasset, subjunxit me. Vide infra c. XX. 2. 13. Est autem hic Aposiopesis, ut sæpe apud quoslibet auctores, post, Quid fit: Varia supplent interpre- tes. Ego sic suppleam: An tunc saltem non percipietis quod nunc non percipitis, verba mea non posse ex usu populari intelligi? nam corpore meo procul in cœlum amoto, nul- la spes erit ejus manducandi κατὰ κυριολεξίαν.

Non est quod hanc συνέχειαν textus arripiamus: rectius autem Cyrillus eam reddidit lib. IV. in Joh. cap. 22. Si putatis carnem meam vobis vitam (æter- nam) afferre non posse, quomodo (ipsa) tanquam vo- lucris in cœlum ascendit: hoc enim similiter generi humano impossibile est, quod si præter naturam caro mea in cœlum conscendet, quid prohibet, ne similiter præter naturam vivificet? nam qui terrestre hoc corpus cœleste confecit, is etiam vivificum reddidit, cum natura sua corruptibile fuerit. Chrysostomus ita explicat, non debere eos hisce offendi, sed illa quæ dicit credere: quia & alia de carne sua ipsis creden- da: utpote quod in cœlum ea conscensura sit. Non itaque id agit ut doceat, quia in cœlum conscen- det, proprie manducari non posse. Non enim op- ponendus est Articulus de ascensione in cœlum manducationi corporis Christi, κτ' κυριολεξίαν acce- ptæ: quia in sacra cœna nobis præbet corpus suum manducandum, idque proprie, nulla enim causa est, cur figuras hic comminiscamur, salva veritate ascensus sui in cœlum, ut alias contra Calvinianos docemus. Repetimus solum hic B. Lyseri expli- cationem Harm. Evang. c. LXXVII. Hoc vos of- fendit? quod dixi, me è cœlo devenisse, & carnem meam manducandam esse, ut quis vivat in æternum. Si ergo videritis Filium hominis ascendentem eo, ubi erat prius, quid tum dicetis? An tum etiam vi- debor mihi plus quam par est arrogasse? Annon tunc reipsa vel inviti agnoscetis me de cœlo descen- disse? Non ergo Christus hæc dicens carnis suæ esum in Sacramento negare, & omnia saltem spiritualia atque mystica post ascensionem in cœlos futura docere voluit, (sicut Sacramentarii hunc locum interpre- tantur) sed veritatem suorum dictorum hoc modo vult asserere, sicut etiam alias solitus est suos hostes, dictis suis fidem subtrahentes, ad resurrectionem, ascensionem, & glorificationem remittere, quibus veritatem dictorum sit comprobaturus, Joh. II. v. 19. Solvite templum hoc, & in tribus diebus excitabo illud. Joh. III. v. 13. Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit de cœlo, Filius hominis, qui est in cœlo. Joh. VIII. 28. Cum exaltaveritis filium ho- minis, tunc cognoscetis, quia ego sum, & à me- ipso facio nihil, sed sicut docuit me Pater, hæc lo- quor. Matth. XXVI. 64. Dico vobis, à modo vi- debitis Filium hominis sedentem à dextris virtu- tis Dei, & venientem in nubibus cœli. Hoc modo solet Deus per eventum subsequentium comprobare veritatem præmissorum. Verbi gratia: Exod. III. v. 12. cum Moysen in Ægyptum mitteret, ad educen- dos Israelitas ex domo servitutis, ipse vero desperfi- ciendo hoc opere hesitaret, ipsi hoc signum quo fidem ejus confirmavit, dedit: Cum eduxeris populum meum de Ægypto, immolabis Deo super montem istum. Si hoc loco vult Christus dicere, se reditu in cœlum velle demonstrare, & se verum esse Deu ex coelo; & quæ de efficacia carnis suæ dixerit, verà esse! Qui enim potest suam carnem, contra carnis naturam, cælestem facere: idem etiam eam cibum hominum vivificum efficere potest. Hæc B. Lyse rus. Nec inconcinna est Flacii explicatio: Offendebantur Judæi potissimùm eo, quod Christus affirmabat se cælitus venisse, Deum esse suum Patrem, se esse servatorem mundi, seg; Moysi & Patribus, suamq; carnem cælesti illi manna longissime præferebat. Christus probat suo futuro ascensu ac glorificatione, se esse tum de cælo, tum servatorem. Sic infrà c. VIII. 28. & alibi eos remittit ad suam resurrectionem, & glorificationem, promittens eis signum Jonæ & quod sint se visuri ad dextram virtutis; & suprà cap. II. eis prædixit solutionem & instaurationem templi corporis sui. Sensus autem hic est, quasi dicat: Hoc vobis nunc incredibile videtur, quod ego de cælo venerim: at ubi videritis me denuo eo redire, inde regnare, aut illinc venientem judicare: Coge mini assentiri me esse inde, sicut c. III. v. 13. dixerat: Nemo ascendit in cóelum, nisi Filius hominis, qui descendit de cælo. Reditu ergo suo illuc probat, illam esse quasi suam patriam, seg; verum Deum esse.

## 6:63
Vers. 63. τό πνεῦμά ἐστι τό ζωοποιῦν) They are things of the spirit, by which eternal life is obtained. We said at Matt. XXVI. 41. that by the word רוח sometimes the ruling faculty is signified, sometimes the whole soul; as below c. XI. 33. XIII. 21. Acts XIX. 21. And it is simpler to take it in this latter sense here.

By πνεῦμα neither the soul itself, nor things of the soul are understood in this place: nor is Christ in the position of teaching that eternal life is obtained by things of the soul (such as perhaps for Grotius are internal virtues, love, obedience, and the like): for what would this have done for the question raised by the Capernaites: But there are two opinions of this among the ancient interpretations. Some, by τό πνεῦμα, which is opposed to flesh here, understand the spiritual divine nature, to which the power of vivifying is proper: namely that flesh indeed left to itself profits nothing, because that vivifying power ζωοποιητικὴ is proper to the spirit, to the divine spiritual nature; yet that his flesh is truly vivifying, and the food of life, provided that it has the same from the Spirit and the divine nature, through and because of the personal union. Others explain it concerning the spiritual sense, and oppose it to the carnal understanding of the Capernaites: that that carnal understanding profits nothing, but the spiritual sense brings life. Grotius accepts it in the former sense: namely, that Christ is giving the reason why his flesh has the power of vivifying: to wit, that it is the Spirit alone that can provide eternal life, but that the flesh alone, and considered by itself, profits nothing at all toward eternal life. Chrysostom and Theophylact interpreted it in the latter sense: which B. Lyserus in his Harmonia and Bernardus in his Locis Communibus on the Supper approve, who in the latter §. 109 has it thus: There exist two interpretations of the ancients on this passage. For some understand it concerning the flesh of Christ, not that it does not profit of itself and by itself, but that it does not profit accidentally, namely, either alone without divinity, or eaten Capernaitically and carnally, or received sacramentally without faith. But others accept the words of Christ concerning the carnal understanding of the hearers. It is afterward: Although indeed neither of these interpretations is opposed to our opinion, (for we concede that the flesh of Christ does not profit if, by hypothesis, it were the flesh of a mere man, or if it were eaten Capernaitically and carnally; indeed, we even concede that the sacramental eating of the body of Christ profits nothing without the spiritual:) Meanwhile, the latter interpretation is to be preferred to the former, since it agrees more with the text. Which latter sense Flacius in his Gloss presents thus at v. 63. He rebukes them for their unbelief, showing its cause, namely that they do not assent to his spiritual doctrine because they are carnal, whereas for it, the spiritual man and the Holy Spirit himself moving the heart of man are required. Just as Chrysostom also understood this passage. Paul does the same and in almost the same words in Rom. VIII: The mind of the flesh is death, the mind of the spirit is life. He also adds the reason why the flesh of man is of no value for understanding and believing the doctrine of Christ, because it is spiritual, and therefore requires a spiritual hearer. Paul has the same reason and almost the same conflict in Rom. VII. 14: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal. And at v. 64, he opposes their unbelieving carnality to his spiritual doctrine, so that it may be manifest that he is not treating the antithesis of spiritual and carnal eating: (as some contend) but the conflict of his spiritual doctrine requiring a spiritual body, and of their carnal unbelief. For that opinion of some of these is clearly impious, who contend that the flesh of Christ itself is said to be useless, which nevertheless he commended expressly throughout this whole chapter, as also at v. 65. From this application of v. 44 to these statements, it appears that Christ in the immediately preceding verses had rebuked their carnal heart as the source of all unbelief, and had required a spiritually and divinely illuminated one to believe his spiritual doctrine: which explanation does not seem to be disapproved. I would, however, prefer to favor the interpretation of Cyril, lib. IV in John, cap. XXIII: The flesh of other men (i.e., of mere men) indeed does not profit anything; but the flesh of Christ, because the only-begotten Son of God dwells in it, alone can give life. To which St. Augustine also tends, tract. XXVII. in John: The flesh does not profit anything; but how did they understand it? They understood the flesh indeed as it is torn apart in a corpse (like common flesh, which is eaten), or sold in a butcher shop, not how it is enlivened by the Spirit. And Paschasius, lib. de corpore & sanguine Christi in Bibl. Patr. Tom. VI. p. 347: Without the Holy Spirit, just as the flesh of Christ does not profit anything, so neither can this sacrament of the flesh profit. Thus, therefore, the Spirit or the spiritual and divine nature is established as the source and origin of vivification. And this proposition can be rendered, like that in John I. v. 1, "God was the Word," where "Word" is the subject, and "God" the predicate: "The Spirit is that which vivifies," that is, that which vivifies, or the principle, cause, source, and origin of vivification and of our life is the Spirit, or that spiritual nature in Christ. This sense is confirmed by (1) the opposition of flesh and Spirit, which does not sound of a mode of understanding, but of a thing and a carnal nature opposed to a spiritual nature; (2) the underlying subject matter: because it is a matter of the power of Christ's vivification, it must therefore be shown whence the flesh has it, namely not from itself and through itself, but from the Spirit, and because of the hypostatic union with the divine nature; (3) the condition of the attribute; because vivification is the property of the Spirit, but not the spiritual sense of any given statement; (4) the comparison of the other sentence, because even if the animal and carnal man and corrupted reason are opposed to the Spirit, yet an explanation or carnal sense is not opposed to it: nor is flesh anywhere a carnal sense, or Spirit a spiritual sense. Rom. VIII. 8, τὸ φρόνημα σαρκὸς is called carnal prudence, or whatever the flesh thinks without the spirit, and from itself, or by its own ingenuity, but the flesh itself is not taken for a carnal sense. If Spirit is a spiritual sense, must it also be taken that way in the following words? The words that I speak are Spirit, that is, they are a spiritual sense. These are the causes that move us to judge that the former sense is to be preferred here entirely.

ἡ σὰρξ ὐκ ὠφελεῖ ὐδὲν) The flesh, not even mine, can give eternal life. For it is temporary food.

This is an impious interpretation, long ago condemned in Zwingli, concerning the flesh of Christ understood: he who eats it has eternal life. Christ expressly called it life-giving; do they not therefore openly contradict Christ, who say that it profits nothing, or make it only temporary food, which does not profit for eternal life? Although therefore the flesh of a mere man (and, if Christ had been such, his flesh also) profits nothing, yet because the flesh of Christ subsists in the hypostasis of the Word, and is a participant of life from the Word, when it was given for the life of the world, it also actually vivifies those who enjoy it through faith, and thus it profits for salvation both by merits and efficacy; those who say that the flesh of Christ profits nothing are not far from blasphemy. That is therefore asserted only κατ’ ἄνϑρωπον: The flesh of a mere man, and destitute of the Spirit, profits nothing: whence the Capernaites ought to have recognized that the flesh of Christ is not ψιλῶ ἀνθρώπε, nor destitute of the vivifying Spirit, which, given for the life of the world, truly gives life, as the bread of life. Thus Cyril explains that the flesh without the spirit, separated from the divinity, does not profit anything for bestowing eternal life.

Τὰ ῥήματα, ἃ ἐγὼ λαλῶ ὑμῖν, πνῦμά ἐσι) My precepts, which will be sanctioned by my death, which I signified by the name of flesh and blood, pertain to the actions of the soul. Therefore πνεῦμα here signifies πνευματικά, just as πνεῦμα is also generally taken in 2 Cor. III. v. 7, signifying Christ's precepts inscribed on the heart, that is, a heart conformed to Christ's precepts.

Tà ῥήματα are not the precepts of Christ: but the word of the Gospel, which he himself preached: nor is his death signified by the name of flesh and blood, because he was made a partaker of flesh and blood, that he might undergo death, and give his flesh for the life of the world, and shed his blood for us. Furthermore, we do not deny that the words of Christ are πνεῦμα in this sense, that they are πνευματικά; it is more emphatic, however, that it is called πνεῦμα, not πνευματικά, because they are animated by the spirit: nor is the bare sound of words, or even the sense, as in any human word, to be regarded here in the words of Christ, but that power of vivifying, regenerating, converting, saving, which it has from the spirit. For the Most Holy Trinity is united with the word, which comes to us through the word, and makes its abode with us, John 14:23, and this is peculiarly attributed to the Holy Spirit, to whom the work of sanctification pertains. This, therefore, is what Christ wishes to teach: it is of one Spirit, or of the divine nature to vivify, without which the flesh would profit nothing: by the power of which my flesh also is vivifying, through and because of the hypostatic union. Thus the words themselves also, which I speak, are not empty, or like the other words of a mere man, but are animated by the divine spirit and heavenly virtue through a mystical union: because not the bare sound and sense, or the material and formal alone, ought to be regarded in them, since they are endowed with divine efficacy, inasmuch as they are πνεῦμα, or united to the divine Spirit, from whom they obtain the divine power of vivifying. Very crude and cold is the gloss of Grotius, 'My words are spirit, that is, my precepts pertain to the actions of the soul.' Concerning which no question was raised here in the Capernaitic school. Nor in 2 Cor. 3:7 are spiritual actions understood by spirit: for how would those vivify? just as neither are carnal actions understood by flesh: but flesh designates the letter of the law, Spirit designates the Gospel and the words of the Spirit: because the law kills, but the Gospel is the word of life.

καὶ ζωή ἐσιν) καὶ for 'therefore'. Because they pertain to the actions of the soul, therefore they can profit toward eternal life, which is procurable by no other thing; but that is called life by which eternal life is procured, as below 12:50, 17:3. Hence they are soon called ῥήματα ζωῆς αἰωνίε, where the genitive, as often, contains the signification of the effect.

That eternal life is obtainable by the actions of our soul is a gross error, already refuted among the Socinians and Papists: in which Grotius errs all the more gravely, because he adds that eternal life is obtainable by no other thing. For thus the merit of Christ is excluded, which alone, apprehended by faith, procures eternal salvation for us; nor is it excluded by the Papists. Moreover, the words of Christ are called spirit and life by hendiadys, because they are a life-giving Spirit, since they are animated by the life-giving Spirit, who, united with the word, bestows upon it a δύναμιν ζωοποιητικὴν [life-giving power], and causes it to be the word of life, Acts 5:20, Phil. 2:16, of eternal life, John 6:68, living and efficacious, Heb. 4:12, the power of God unto salvation, Rom. 1:16, and able to save our souls, James 1:21. Or if it pleases that καὶ [and] is put for ideo [therefore]; therefore because they are Spirit, they are life-giving, because τὸ πνεῦμα ἐςι τὸ ζωοποιοῦν [the spirit is that which gives life], that which gives us life is Spirit, the principle of all life, in whom is that life which is the light of men, John 1:4, from whom also the flesh of Christ has that it is life-giving, and the bread of life, feeding us unto eternal life, and the word of Christ, that it is life.

Latin:

Vers. 63. τό πνεῦμά ἐστι τό ζωοποιῦν) Res sunt animi, quibus vita æterna comparatur. Diximus ad Matth. XXVI. 41. voce רוח modo τό ἡγεμονικόν significari, modo animum totum; ut infrà c. XI. 33. XIII. 21. Act. XIX, 21. Atq; hoc posteriore sensu hîcc sumere simplicius est.

Per πνεῦμα non vel animus ipse, vel res animi intelliguntur hoc loco: neque in eo est Christus, ut doceat, per res animi (quales forte Grotio sunt virtutes internæ, dilectio, obedientia & similia) comparari vitam æternam: quod enim hoc ad quæstionem à Capernaitis motam fecisset: Duæ autem sunt sententiæ hujus apud veteres interpretationes. Aliqui per τό πνεῦμα, qua carni hic opponitur, intelligunt spiritualem divinam naturam, cui propria est vis vivificandi: quod nempe caro quidem sibi relicta nihil profit, quia vis illa vivificandi ζωοποιητικὴ propria est τῷ πνεύματι, naturæ divinæ spiritualis; carnem tamen suam vere vivificam, & cibum vitæ esse, siquidem eadem à Spiritu & divina natura illam habeat, per & propter unionem personalem. Alii de sensu spirituali explicant, eumque carnali intellectui Capernaitarum opponunt: quod carnalis ille intellectus nihil prosit, sensus autem spiritualis vitam adferat. Priori sensu Grotius accipit: quod nempe Christus rationem reddat, unde caro sua vim habeat vivificandi: videlicet Spiritum solum esse, qui vitam æternam præstare possit, carnem autem solam, & per sese consideratam nihil quicquam ad æternam vitam prodesse. Posteriori sensu Chrysost. & Theophylact. interpretati sunt: quem B. Lyserus in Harmon. & Bernardus in LL. CC. de Cœna probant, qui posterior §. 109. ita habet: Duæ extant veterum interpretationes in hunc locum. Quidam enim de carne Christi intelligunt, non quod ex se & per se non profit, sed quod ex accidenti non profit, videlicet vel sola sine divinitate, vel Capernaitice & carnaliter manducata, vel sacramentaliter sine fide accepta. Quidam vero de carnali auditorum intellectu verba Christi accipiunt. Est postea: Quamvis vero neutra harum interpretationum nostræ sententiæ adversetur, (concedimus enim carnem Christi non prodesse, si ex hypothesi esset nudi hominis caro, vel si Capernaitice & carnaliter manducaretur, quin & sacramentalem corporis Christi manducationem absq; spirituali nihil prodesse concedimus:) Interim posterior interpretatio præferenda est priori, cum textui magis congruit. Quem posteriorem sensum Flacius in Glossa ita exhibet ad v. 63. Objurgat eos de incredulitate, monstrans ejus causam, eos nempe ideo non assentiri suae spirituali doctrinae, quia sunt carnales, cum ad eam spiritualis homo & ipse Spiritus S. movens cor hominis, requiratur. Sicut & Chrysostomus hunc locum intellexit. Idem ac eisdem pene verbis Paulus Rom. VIII. Sensus car- nis mors est, sensus spiritus vita. Addit etiam ra- tionem, cur caro hominis nihil valeat ad intelligen- dum credendamq; doctrinam Christi, quia ea sit spi- ritualis, eoque spiritualem auditorem requirat. Eandem rationem & quasi pugnam etiam Paulus habet Rom. VII. 14. Scimus enim legem esse spiri- tualem, at ego sum carnalis. Et ad v. 64. Opponit suae spirituali doctrinae eorum incredulam carnalita- tem, ut manifestum sit eum tractare non antithesin spiritualis & carnalis manducationis: (ut quidam contendunt) sed pugnam sua spiritualis doctrinae re- quirentis spirituale corpus, & eorum carnalis incre- dulitatis. Nam illa quorundam istorum plane im- pia sententia est, qui contendunt, ipsam Christi car- nem inutilem dici, quam tamen ex professo toto hoc capite commendavit, ut & ad v. 65. Ex hac appli- catione v. 44. ad hasce sententias apparet, Christum in proxime praecedentibus eorum carnale cor arguis- se, tanquam fontem omnis incredulitatis, & requi- sivisse spirituale divinitusq; illuminatum, ad cre- dendam suam spiritualem doctrinam: quae explica- tio non videtur improbanda. Malim tamen prae- ferre Cyrilli interpretationem lib. IV. in Job. cap. XXIII. Caro quidem caeterorum hominum (ψιλῶν scil. ἀνθρώπων) quicquam vere non prodest: caro autem Christi, quia in ipsa unigenitus Dei Filius ha- bitat, sola vivificare potest. Quo etiam abit S. Au- gustinus tract. XXVII. in Joh. Caro non prodest quic- quam, sed quomodo illi intellexerunt? Carnem quip- pe sic intellexerunt, quomodo in cadavere dilania- tur, (ut communem carnem, quae manducatur,) aut in macello venditur, non quomodo spiritu vege- tatur. Et Paschasius lib. de corpore & sanguine Christi in Bibl. Patr. Tom. VI. p. 347. Sine Spiritu S. sicut nec caro Christi prodest quicquam, ita nec hoc carnis sacramentum prodesse potest. Ita ergo Spiritus vel natura spiritualis & divina constitui- tur fons & origo vivificationis. Et reddi potest haec propositio, uti illa Joh. I. v. 1.
