V. 36. and to teach the Greeks) That he may spread his dogma not only among the Israelites, but also among the Greeks, that is, those who, although they are not Israelites, dwell in those places, not acknowledging the one God. The Syrian here has לחנפא for the impious. This is what they mean: perhaps he hopes his dogma, which does not attribute much to the rites of the law, will be well-received among foreigners, so that by their help he may easily hope to be safe against the attempts of our countrymen.

what is this saying which he said) For if he means this, what sense does his speech have? For where on earth in Palestine does he hope for protection for himself, when the Romans themselves in these places defer most to the authority of the Sanhedrin, whose judgment is opposed to him? Thus we also see that the Apostles were nowhere less safe than in Judea. But where they thought Jesus was going to go, so that he might avoid their plots, there Jesus now obtaining a safe and glorious place, they themselves were forced to take flight.

Such things are not approved by Salmasius, nor does he want these to be understood of exiles, openly refuting Grotius, even though his name is passed over in silence. Just as, he says, the dispersion of Pontus & Galatia, in Peter, is the region of Pontus & Galatia, which the dispersed Jews inhabited, so in John the dispersion of the Greeks is the region of the Greeks, or even of the Gentiles, which the Jews inhabited, who were dispersed everywhere in the world: To go into the dispersion of the Greeks is nothing else than to go to the Gentiles, and to set out into the region of the Gentiles, which the dispersed Jews inhabit, and there to teach the Gentiles themselves, not the Jews who live dispersed among them, because those people did not want to admit the word of God. Therefore, they were sending Christ away to the Greeks and Gentiles by their conjecture, where he saw that he could accomplish nothing among the Jews. But because Christ was a Jew, who could not go to the Gentiles without it being known to the Jewish brothers residing there in the Diaspora, when he taught the Greeks, John therefore said the dispersion of the Greeks instead of the region of the Greeks. That these things are most true, is evident. Nor does Cyril interpret it otherwise, who explains the region of the Greeks, which is in the Evangelist as the dispersion of the Greeks. For they do not say that he is about to ascend to heaven, but they imagine the region of the Greeks. Add that the Jews wanted to seize an opportunity from there to accuse Christ, because he seemed to want to interpret the law to foreigners, as they conjectured. For to interpret the law to foreigners, says the same Cyril, is not blameless among them. For it was not free from blame among the Jews to expound the law to foreigners. And God rebukes not lightly through the Prophet those who did this, and they read the law to those outside. And this was the cause of the hatred of the Hebrews or true Jews against the Hellenists, i.e., proselytes of Greek origin, because they used the Bible translated into Greek, and thus read the law and interpreted it to those outside, to foreigners and strangers. But that Diaspora of the Jews, lest anyone err, was not of Exiles, but of Colonists, nor forced, but voluntary. Thus the Romans, who occupied various parts of the world subdued by them and specifically parts with colonies, can indeed be seen to have scattered their citizens through the world, not to have punished them with exile. That dispersion which is made through Colonies is understood especially in the nation of the Greeks or Greeks, who, having originated from Thessalonica and Macedonia, filled all of Greece with their colonies, and did not only scatter colonies through Greece as called by them, but also through the rest of Europe and Asia. Therefore the Apostles, lest anyone should understand that dispersion of the Jews as a dissipation and scattering of the nation, brought about through flight and exiles, did not name it the dispersion of the Jews, but of the Greeks, and of other regions, in which the Jews lived so dispersed that they were not considered exiles or banished in them, but colonists and citizens, and enjoying the same right as the original citizens of those places. It is established that they almost always had this in all the cities they chose to inhabit around those times. Indeed, since that nation has always been of incredible fertility for producing offspring, after the return from the Babylonian captivity, it sent out swarms of people in various times to different tracts of the world, which Judea could not support. This is the only reason for their dispersion, as Philo and Josephus report, who name them their colonies, not exiles, nor banishments or relegations. Therefore, as far as I judge, they interpret the dispersion in that place of John wrongly as those regions in which the descendants of Israel were living in exile, whom they even more perversely maintain were all called Exiles by the name of Hellenists. But neither is their sense of John's words, will he go into the dispersion of the Greeks, which they attach, will he go to Antioch or Alexandria where many of the Israelites migrated under the successors of Alexander? Or will they say that by the name of Greeks one must properly understand in John the Antiochians and Alexandrians? Or must those Greeks to whom they conjectured by guessing that Christ wanted to set out to teach be explained only of the Greeks of Alexandria and Antioch? Nor does the reason which that very great man brings forward to construct this interpretation have any weight at all; But this, he says, they ask rather than about the regions under the Parthian, because Syria and Egypt were less far from Judea; and very many from there came to Jerusalem on feast days, not so from the parts of Media. Or because Media and Parthia were situated further from Jerusalem, did those Jews think only of Antioch and Alexandria, as if Christ had it in mind to proceed to those parts that place to be understood by us properly as citizens and inhabitants of Alexandria and Antioch? We have taught that ἕλληνας there ought to be taken not as men of Greek race and language but as all Gentiles or ἐθνικοὺς. Besides Alexandria and Antioch, other regions near to Jerusalem were also at hand, to which Christ could migrate to teach the ἕλληνας, that is, the Gentiles, such as Mesopotamia and Arabia. The island of Cyprus also, not far off, which had inhabitants who were truly called ἕλληνας, that is, ἑλληνίζοντας. But the nearness and distance of regions has no effect here. These are the words of Salmasius, and from him, Walaeus.

PART III. The solemn promise of the Holy Spirit to those who have believed in Him, and the account of the diverse judgments concerning Him.

Latin:

V. 36. κὶ διδάσκειν τὺς ἕλληνας) Ut dogma suum spargat non tantum inter Israëlitas, sed etiam inter Græcos, id est eos, qui cum Israëlitæ non sint, in iis locis habitant, Deum unum non agnoscentes. לחנפא impios habet hic Syrus. Hoc volunt: forte sperat suum dogma, quod ritibus legis non multum tribuit, gratiosum fore apud alienigenas, ita ut eorum ope facile speret tutum se fore adversus conatus no- stratium.

τίς ἐστιν οὗτος ὁ λόγος ὃν εἶπε) Nam si hoc vult quem sen- sum habet sermo ipsius? Ubi enim in terra Palæstinæ præsi- dium sibi sperat, cum Romani ipsi in his locis plurimum de- ferant auctoritati Synedrii, cujus judicium ipsi adversatur? Sic & Apostolos videmus nusquam minus tutos fuisse, quam in Judæa. Sed quo ipsi Jesum iturum putabant, ut ipsorum insidias vitaret, eo Jesu jam locum tutum ac glorio- sum obtinente, ipsi coacti sunt fugam capere.

Non probantur talia Salmasio, nec de exulibus hæc accipi vult, aperte refellens Grotium, etsi no- mine ejus tacito. Quemadmodum, inquit, διασπορὰ Πόντυ & Γαλατίας, apud Petrum regio est Ponti & Galatiæ, quam dispersi incolebant Judæi, ita apud Jo- hannem διασπορὰ τῶν ἑλλήνων, est regio Graecorũ, vel etiam Gentium, quam inhabitabant Judaei, qui ubi- que terrarum erant dispersi: Πορεύεσθαι εἰς τὴν Διασπορὰν τῶν ἑλλήνων, nihil aliud est, quã ad gen- tes ire, & in regionem gentium, quam διασπορευ̃τες Ἰουδαῖοι inhabitant, proficisci, ibique gentes ipsas doce- re, non Judaeos qui inter ipsas dispersi degunt, quia ver- bum Dei admittere isti nolebant. Ad Graecos igitur ac Gentiles Christum sua conjectura amandabant, ubi se apud Judaeos nihil proficere posse ille videret. Quod autem Christus Judaeus esset, qui ad gentiles ire non pos- set, quin ibi consistentibus in Diaspora Judaeis fratribus id notum foret, cum Graecos doceret, ideo διασπορὰν τ̃ ἑλλήνων Iohannes dixit ἀντὶ τ̃ χώρας τῶν ἑλλήνων. Haec esse verissima, praesto. Nec aliter Cyrillus interpre- tatur, qui χώραν τῶν ἑλλήνων exponit quod est apud Evangelistam Διασπορὰ τῶν ἑλλήνων. Οὐ γάρ ὅτι πρὸς ὀυρανὸν ἀναβήσεσθαι φάσιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἑλλή- νων φαντάζονται χώραν. Adde quod Iudaei inde ac- cusandi Christi ansam arripere volebant, quod alieni- genis legem videretur velle, ut conjectabant, interpreta- ri. Τὸ γὰρ ἐξηγεῖσθαι, inquit idem Cyrillus, ἀλλοχρώ- σι τὸ νόμον, ὀυκ ἀνέγκλητον παρ᾽ ἀυτοῖς. Non enim culpa vacabat apud Iudaeos, legem enarrare alienige- nis. Et qui hoc facerent, non leviter increpat Deus per Prophetam, ϰ ἀνέγνωσαν τοῖς ἔξω νόμον, & praelege- runt extraneis legem. Et hec causa odii Hebraeor. sive Iudaeorũ verorum adversus Hellenistas, h. e. Graecige- neris proselytos, quod Bibliis Graece versis uterentur, & sic praelegerent legẽ, & interpretarentur τοῖς ἔξω, alie- nigenis & extraneis. Diaspora autem illa Iudaeorum, ne quis erret, non Exulum fuit, sed Colonorum, nec coa- cta, sed voluntaria. Ita Romani qui varias orbis a se domiti & nominatim partes coloniis occupaverunt, spar- sisse quidẽ per orbem cives suos videri possunt, non exi- lio multasse. Διασπορὰ illa quae per Colonias fit, ma- xime in Graecorum sive ἑλλήνων natione intelligitur, qui a Thessalonia, ac Macedonia orti, totam Graeciam suis coloniis repleverunt, nec per Graeciam tantum a se dictam colonias sparserunt, sed etiam per reliquam Eu- ropam & Asiam. Ideo Apostoli, ne quis διασπορὰν il- lam Iudaeorum de dissipatione ac disjectione gentis ac- ciperet, per fugã & exilia procurata, non Ἰουδαίων δια- σπορὰν eam nominarunt, sed ἑλλήνων, & aliarum regionum, in quibus ita sparsi degebant Iudaei, ut non exules aut relegati in iis censerentur, sed coloni & ci- ves, & eodem jure cum originalibus eorum locorum ci- vibus fruentes. Quod fere semper in omnibus quas cir- ca ea tempora habitandas elegerunt, civitatibus eos habuisse constat. Profecto cum semper illa gens incre- dibilis ad prolem sufficiendam foecunditatis fuerit, post reditum e Babylonica captivitate, exuberantia popu- lorum examina qua Judaea non posset alere, variis tem- poribus in diversos orbis tractus emisit. Hac unica ratio eorum διασπορᾶς, ut Philo & Josephus refe- runt, qui ἀποικίας eorum nominant, non ἐξορίσεις, nec exulationes vel relegationes. Perperam igitur quantum judico, διασπορὰν interpretantur, eo lo- co Iohannis eas regiones, in quibus Israelis posteri exulabant, quos omnes Exules Hellenistarum no- mine appellatos statuunt etiam perversius. Sed nec sensus est eorum Iohannis verborum, μὴ εἰς τὴν διασπορὰν τῶν ἑλλήνων μέλλει πορεύεσθαι, quem adfingunt, ibitne Antiochiam aut Alexan- driam quo multi Israelitarum migrarunt sub suc- cessoribus Alexandri? An dicent nomine ἑλλήνων proprie intelligendos apud Iohannem esse, Antioche- nos & Alexandrinos? An ἕλληνες illi ad quos docen- dos proficisci velle Christum conjectando hariolaban- tur, de solis Alexandria & Antiochia Graecis exponi debent? Nec ratio quam vir ille maximus adfert, ad hanc struendam interpretationem hilum valet; Hoc autem, inquit, potius quaerunt, quam de regionibus sub Partho, quia Syria & Ægyptus minus longe abe- rant à Judæa; & plurimi inde Hierosolyma festis die- bus veniebant, non item ex Mediæ partibus. An quia Media & Parthia longius Hierosolymis dissitæ, ideo de Antiochia tantum, & Alexandria cogitarunt illi Judæi, quasi ad eas partes pergere in animo haberet Christus, ut doceret ἕλληνας ibi consistentes? An ideo ἕλληνες proprie eo loco intelligendi nobis sunt Alexan- driæ & Antiochix cives & incolæ? Ἐλληνας docuimus ibi sumi oportere non Græci generis & sermonis homi- nes sed omnes gentiles sive ἐθνικοὺς. Præter Alexan- driam & Antiochiam aliæ etiam præsto fuere vicinæ Hierosolymis regiones, ad quas migrare potuit Christus doctrina sua ἕλληνας, id est gentes imbuturus, ut Me- sopotamia & Arabia. Cypros insula etiam non longe quæ & vere dictos ἕλληνας, id est ἑλληνίζοντας ha- buit incolas. Sed propinquitas & longinquitas tractu- um nihil hic facit. Hæc Salmasius, & ex eo Walæus.

PARS III. Spiritus Sancti illis, qui in se crediderint, so- lennis promissio & diversorum judi- ciorum de ipso relatio.

## 7:37
V. 37. On the last, the great day of the feast) The first day and the last of the feast were holidays, but the last, on which the ἄφεσις was given to the people, was more celebrated and with a solemn manifestation of joy. For they also, carrying palms and branches then, cried out Hosanna. That day is called מקרא קדש, a holy convocation, Lev. 23:36, likewise עצרת, an ἐξόδιον to the Greeks; there is much about this manifestation of joy in the Talmud, in the tractate Succah.

Jesus stood) He did not deliver this discourse while walking about as at other times, but standing and with an intent voice, so that He might the more excite attention.

If any man thirst, let him come unto me and drink) Christ was accustomed to take the occasion for His discourse from things close at hand; now on that day the people were drawing water from the fountain of Siloam with great pomp, using that song from Isaiah: Ye shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of salvation; having observed this, Christ teaches them who is the truly saving fountain indicated by Zechariah 13:1. He takes these words of His, however, from Isaiah 55:1. The sense is: Whoever is consumed by a desire for happiness (for the Hebrews, like other nations, call that thirsting) let him come to me, and I will quench his thirst.

Add here what Lud. de Dieu and Walaeus bring forward concerning the eighth day of the feast of tabernacles, especially that three הפטרות or Prophetic readings were accustomed to be read on it. The first, 1 Kings 8, how Solomon addressed the people with a loud voice: which was also done here by the true Solomon, Christ. The second from the beginning of Joshua, who is considered the first of the Prophets after the law. The third, the last section of Malachi. Therefore, he says, the Savior rises opportunely at this time, the true Solomon, the true Joshua, the end of the law, the end of the Prophets. And since they were accustomed to delight themselves on this very day with the most cheerful banquets and drinking parties, He conveniently calls the thirsty to Himself and promises them living waters. These things from Buxtorf are also not to be neglected: It was the custom among the Jews at the feast of tabernacles to draw water from the fountain of Shiloah and to pour it out on each day of the feast, which, after they had done, they were exhilarated and leaped for joy. The Savior seems to look back to this custom, as if He were saying: I see you drawing water from the fountain of Shiloah, and with it being brought in through the water gate, rejoicing greatly, and likewise after it has been poured out. But the water, which joy follows, is finally this, which they do not go to seek at the fountain of Shiloah, but at me: and which is drawn so copiously by the bucket of faith that it becomes a fountain of rivers in the faithful. v. 38. Because the Spirit is living water, bringing forth vital joy. Whence this joy is called the joy of the Spirit, and because it is received by faith, it is called the joy of faith, 1 Thess. 1:6, Phil. 1:25.

Latin:

V. 37. ἐν δὲ τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ μεγάλῃ τῆς ἑορτῆς) Primus dies & ultimus τῆς ἑορτῆς erant festi, sed ultimus, quo daba- tur ἄφεσις λαοῖς, celebrior & cum solenni lætitiæ significa- tione. Nam & palmas ramosque tum gestantes panebant Hosanna. Vocatur is dies מקרא קדש κλητὴ ἁγία Lev. XXIII. 36. item עצרת ἐξόδιον Græcis; multa de hac lætitiæ significatione in Thalmode titulo Succah.

εἱστήκει ὁ Ἰησοῦς) Non inter deambulandum ut alias, ser- monem hunc habuit, sed stans & intenta voce, quo magis attentionem excitaret.

ἐάν τις διψᾷ, ἐρχέσθω πρός με καὶ πινέτω) Ex rebus obviis sermonis occasionem capere Christus solebat, eo autem die populus magna pompa ex fonte Siloæ aquam hauriebat, canticum illud ex Esaia usurpans: Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus salutis, hoc conspecto docet eos Christus quis sit fons vere salutaris indicatus à Zacharia XIII. 1. verba autem hæc sua sumit ex Esaia LV. 1. Sensus est; Qui desiderio feli- citatis uritur (nam id sitire vocant Hebræi ut & aliæ gentes) ad me veniat, ego sitim ejus restinguam.

Addenda hic quæ de octavo die festi tabernaculo- rum adfertè Lud. de Dieu Walæus, imprimis quod eodem tres הפטרות sive lectiones Propheticæ legi consueverint. Prima 1. Reg. VIII. quomodo alta voce Salomon populum compellarit: quod hic à vero Salo- mone Christo etiam factum: Secunda ex initio Josuæ, qui primus Prophetarum post legem habetur: Tertia ultima Malachiæ sectio. Opportune itaq;, inquit, hoc tempore exsurgit Servator, verus Salomo, verus Jo- sua, finis legis, finis Prophetarum. Et quum se hoc ipso die hilarissimis conviviis & compotationibus oble- ctare solerent, commode sitientes ad se vocat, vivasq; ipsis aquas pollicetur. Buxtorfiana etiam hæc non negligenda: Moris erat apud Judæos in festo taber- naculorum, aquam ex fonte Schiloah haurire, & li- bare singulis diebus festi, quod postquam fecissent, ex- hilarabantur, & subsultabant. Ad morem hunc re- spicere Salvator videtur, ac si diceret: Video vos a- quam haurire è fonte Schiloah, & cum ea infertur per aquarum portam, summe lætari, similiter quo- que postquam eadem libata est. Verum aqua, quã gaudium subsequitur, hæc demum est, quam non quæsitum eunt ad fontem Schiloah, sed ad me: quæq; situla fidei adeo copiose hauritur, ut in fidelibus fluviorum fons fiat. v. 38. Quia Spiritus est aqua vi- va, vitale gaudium proferens. Unde hoc gaudium χαρὰ πνεύματος, & quia fide accipitur, χαρὰ πί- στεως vocatur, 1. Thess. c. I. 6. Philipp. I. 25.

## 7:38
v. 38. He that believeth in me) He who applies faith to me in such a way that he obeys me and orders his life as I teach, and as Isaiah 58:7 and following describes to some extent.

As the Scripture hath said) Thus John often does when he indicates not one specific passage but the consensus of many, which is why the Syriac here put Scriptures in the plural, just as we have above in v. 39. All the passages that deal with the pouring out of the Spirit pertain to this; for the pouring out has a silent comparison to waters. But I think the place in Isaiah, in the said chapter 58:12, is especially intended: He shall be like a spring of waters whose waters shall not fail; for he seems to be paraphrasing this passage. Rivers shall flow from his belly of living water) At the outlets or springs of waters, stone receptacles were accustomed to be made: they are called ἀγγεῖα by the Greeks, Prov. 5:15; by the Hebrews sometimes בּוֹר and sometimes בְּאֵר: for the Talmudists say these are distinguished in private places, but in public places the terms are mixed. In the middle of these were pipes through which the water leaped out into the public. In the said passage of Proverbs: Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad and streams from the middle of the receptacle. But every middle or innermost part is called בֶּטֶן by the Hebrews and κοιλία by the Greeks, as 1 Kings 7:20; Matt. 12:40. It is therefore said that it will come to pass that those who believe in Him will be so filled with water that it cannot be contained within them, but will leap out on all sides in great streams. By water here He understands the Holy Spirit, as John immediately explains; living water is water flowing continuously, as Servius explains in the Codex Fuldensis, adding that it is an augural word: and the Holy Spirit is deservedly so called, because He is the earnest of eternal life. Rivers are called not only streams but also any abundance of waters, Matt. 7:25, 27. It is, however, a Hebraism: he that believeth and then his, for which the Greeks would say in one word to him that believeth.

Indeed, some of the ancients also refer these things, which are said about the Scripture, to the prophecies concerning the pouring out of the Holy Spirit. So also B. Walther on Isa. 44:4, ch. 58:15. But Franc. Junius, book 1, Parall. 71, to the passage of Isa. 55. D. Georg. König in Vindiciae Locorum 84, to Ps. 147:18. But just as these two latter opinions are rightly rejected by B. Walther, so these things are best of all referred to faith placed in Christ, according to the Scripture: as the Syriac joined it here, without any distinction, whoever believes in me as the Scriptures have said. For the words that follow are the words of Christ, not of any Prophet. Which the Evangelist indicates, saying: But this he said concerning the Spirit: He said this not the Scripture, but Christ. Nor is it beside the point to note in the words καθὼς εἶπεν ἡ γρα- φὴ that the word εἶπεν means 'commanded', because in Deut. XVIII. 18 this is commanded, just as אָמַר among the Hebrews often, and among the Arabs always, denotes 'to command', as Lud. de Dieu observes; who also warns that not only the Syrian, but also the Arab has 'they said of the Scripture'; because they thought that Scripture indefinitely, not this or that passage of Scripture, was indicated, because the scope and command of the whole of Scripture everywhere is that we should believe in Christ. Cf. B. Lyserus & Dan. Heinsius on this passage. This is the interpretation of Chrysostom, Euthymius, Theophylact & Leontius. See also Toletus, Maldonatus & B. Tarnov. on this passage. Nor are we moved by that argument, that in the O.T. the faithful also believed in Christ, and yet rivers of living water did not flow from their bellies: because Christ is not speaking of those who believed in the Messiah in former times, but of those who believe, to wit, that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah: and he specifically promises some good thing, proper to the N.T. under a certain condition, which the faithful are to receive in their own time, namely after his ascension or glorification.

Latin:

v. 38. ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ) Qui mihi fidem ita adhibet ut mihi pareat atque vitam instituat, quemadmodum ego doceo & qualem describit aliquatenus Esaias LVIII. 7. & sequentib.

καθὼς εἶπεν ἡ γραφὴ) Ita sæpe Johannes ubi non unum ali- quem locum sed multorum consensum indicat, quare & Sy- rus pluraliter hic Scripturas posuit, quomodo & supra habe- mus v. 39. Pertinent huc omnes loci qui de effundendo spi- ritu agunt; nam effusio tacitam habet aquarum compara- tionem. Sed præcipue respici puto locum Esaiæ dicto capite LVIII. 12. Erit sicut exitus aquarum cujus aquæ non defi- cient, hunc enim locum videtur παραφράζειν. ποταμοὶ ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας αὐτῦ ῥέσεσιν ὕδατος ζῶντος) Apud exitus sive scaturigines aquarum solebant conceptacula la- pidea fieri: ἀγγεῖα vocantur Græcis Prov. V. 15. Hebræis modo בּוֹר modo בְּאֵר : nam hæc in privatis locis distingui ajunt Thalmudistæ, in publicis vocabula misceri. In horum medio erant tubi per quos aqua in publicum exsiliebat. Di- cto loco Prov. Dispergantur fontes tui foras & fluenta de medio conceptaculo. Omne autem medium aut intimum Hebræis בֶּטֶן Græcis κοιλία dicitur, ut 1. Reg. VII. 20; Matth. XII, 40, dicitur igitur futurum ut sibi credentes ita repleantur aqua ut contineri intra ipsos nequeat, sed undique magnis fluen- tis exsiliat. Aquam autem hic intelligit Spiritum Sanctum, ut statim Johannes explicat, aqua viva est aqua jugiter fluens, ut explicat Servius in Codice Fuldenfi, addens augu- rale esse verbum: merito autem sic vocatur Spiritus San- ctus, quia arrhabo est vitæ æternæ. Ποταμοὶ vocantur non tantum amnes sed & quævis copia aquarum Matth. VII, 25. 27. est autem Hebraismus : ὁ πιστεύων & deinde αὐτῦ, pro quo Græci una voce dicerent τῷ πιστεύοντι.

Referunt quidem etiam veterum nonnulli hæc, quæ de Scriptura dicuntur, ad vaticinia de effusione SS. Sic etiam B. Waltherus ad Ef. XLIV. 4. c. LVIII. 15. Ast Franc. Junius l. 1. Parall. LXXI. ad locum Ef. LV. D. Georg. König ad vindic. Loc. LXXXIV. ad Pf. CXLVII. 18. Sed uti hæ duæ posteriores senten- tiæ recte rejiciuntur à B. Walthero, ita omnium o- ptimè hæc referuntur ad fidem in Christum, juxta Scripturam, collocatam : uti hic conjunxit Syrus, ci- tra ullam distinctionem, quicunque credit in me sic- ut dixerunt Scripturæ. Nam quæ deinde sequun- tur, verba Christi sunt, non Prophetæ alicujus. Quod indicat Evangelista, inquiens : τῦτο δὲ εἶπε περὶ πνεύματος : Hoc dixit non ἡ γραφὴ sed Christus. Nec præter rem notatur in verbis καθὼς εἶπεν ἡ γρα- φὴ vocem εἶπεν esse jussit, quia Deut. XVIII. 18. hoc mandatum est, quemadmodum אָמַר apud Ebræos sæ- pe, apud Arabes semper jubere denotat, observante Lud. de Dieu; qui monet quoque, non Syrum tan- tum, sed etiam Arabem habere dixerunt Scripturæ; quod indefinite Scripturam, non hunc aut illum Scripturæ locum indicari existimarint, quia totius passim Scripturæ scopus est, & mandatum, ut in Chri- stum credamus. Conf. B. Lyserus & Dan. Heinsius in h. l. Est hæc interpretatio Chrysostomi, Euthymii, Theophylacti & Leontii. Vid. etiam Toletus, Maldo- natus & B. Tarnov. in h. l. Neque vero argumento illo movemur, quod in V. T. fideles etiam in Christum crediderint, neq; tamen de ventre ipsorum flumina aquæ vivæ fluxerint : quia non loquitur Christus de illis qui olim in messiam crediderunt, sed de his qui credunt, sc, Jesum Nazarenum, esse Messiam: & speciatim bonum aliquod promittit, N. T. sub cer- ta ratione proprium, quod accepturi sint suo tempo- re fideles, nempe post ascensionem suam, vel glori- ficationem.

## 7:39
V. 39. concerning the Spirit which those who believe were about to receive) Not only the Apostles; but a huge multitude of believers, the beginning of which thing was made in the 120 people at Pentecost. See what [is said] on Mark XVI, 17. and following.

For the Spirit was not yet) I think it was written thus, for ἅγιον, which Greek codices—and not all of them—have, and which the Arab, Syrian, and Latin [versions] and ancient writers do not acknowledge, follows. Therefore it was added for the sake of explanation: just as in some Greek [texts] ἐπ' αὐτοῖς, and in some 'given' to avoid the calumny of the Macedonians, for which, however, there is no need at all. For it must be understood from the preceding [words], 'of those believing in Christ'. This Spirit of those believing in Christ was still to be expected. Others [ask] how the Holy Spirit is also said of the Prophets 2 Pet. I. 21. and of Elizabeth Luke I. 41. and of Zechariah in the same place 67.

because Jesus was glorified) He had not yet ascended into heaven, as is explained in Acts II. 33 [sic] & Eph. IV. 8. For it is the duty of a king who is already reigning to give royal gifts. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho: 'Again, as it was prophesied that gifts would be made, which he gives from the grace of the power of that Spirit to those who believe in him, so let each one understand that it was prophesied that this was about to happen by him after his ascension into the heights'.

We see no sufficiently solid reason for abandoning the received reading of the Greek Codices. That distinction of spirit, however—namely, that the Holy Spirit is not understood here, who was also attributed to the Prophets, but the spirit of those believing in Christ—is worthless: for in the Old Testament, not only the Spirit of prophecy, but also the Spirit of faith and the earnest of eternal life was given: by which, if they were destitute, how could the Patriarchs, Job, David, Joshua, the Prophets, and other faithful of the Old Testament be asserted to have been, with any appearance of truth? But what is said here, that the Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified, must be understood in a certain respect: namely, regarding those singular gifts, by reason of which He was to be poured out upon believers after His ascension into heaven, which was extraordinary and of a certain time. But that the Holy Spirit is the earnest of salvation pertains to believers commonly and of all times.

T. non tantum Spiritus Prophetiæ, sed etiam Spiritus fi- dei, & arrhabo vitæ æternæ datus est: quo destitutos fuiss̄e Patriarchas, Jobum, Davidem, Josuam, Pro- phetas, aliosq; fideles V.T. qua veri specie assereretur? Quod autem hîc dicitur Spiritum S. nondum fuisse, quia Jesus nondum glorificatus erat, κατὰ τι acci- piendum: nempe quoad dona illa singularia, quo- rum ratione effundendus erat super credentes post ascensionem in cœlum, quæ extraordinaria & certi temporis erat. ## 7:49
V. 49. But this crowd? The people of the land, as they used to say, the dregs of the people.

who does not know the law? Who does not devote effort to learn the law exactly according to the interpretations and traditions of the Schools.

they are accursed? עמ הארץ which the Rabbis say very often about the people of the land. This is taken from Deut. xxvii. 26, where those who were unwilling to live according to the law are pronounced accursed or execrable. As if indeed this pertained to those subtleties which could not be learned except in the Schools: and therefore some simple fisherman or craftsman, devoting effort to keeping God's commandments according to common understanding, could not please God.

Not those who were unwilling to live according to the law, but those who have not fulfilled all things which are written in the law completely, are subjected to the curse by the law, Deut. XXVII. 25. Nor are interpretations and traditions regarded here: but the law itself: they despise all others, to be sure, out of incredible arrogance and the persuasion that they alone have the key of interpretation, the Pharisees and the experts in the law, when yet they themselves were blinder than a mole in Scripture. The people were therefore accursed by their judgment, because they were ignorant of the law. Compare Drusius in Waleus at this place.

Quasi vero hoc ad illos apices pertineret qui nisi in Scholis disci non poterant: ideoque simplex aliquis pisca- tor aut opifex secundum communem intellectum dans o- peram servandis Dei præceptis Deo placere non posset.

Non qui noluerint ex lege vivere, sed qui omnia quæ in lege scripta sunt, haud impleverint ex asse, per legem maledictioni subjiciuntur Deut. XXVII. 25. Neque hic interpretationes & traditiones respi- ciuntur: sed lex ipsa: contemnunt nempe alios o- mnes ex incredibili typho & persuasione, quod so- li habeant clavem significationis, Pharisæi & legis- periti, quum tamen ipsi talpa cæciores fuerint in Scriptura. Maledictus ergo erat populus ipsorum judicio, quia ignarus legis. Conf. Drusius apud Waleum ad h. l.

## 7:50
V. 50. He who came by night to him? This is added so that it may be understood that he was both a supporter of Christ and rather timid. Therefore he does not openly champion him.

Being one of them? One from the senate, as appears above III. 1. V. 51. Does our law judge the man? judge, that is, allow to be judged. Does our law, which everywhere commends equity to judges, allow this, that someone should be struck down by prejudice (such as this was concerning arresting Jesus) with the methods of investigating the truth neglected, such as is primarily this, that he himself should be questioned and heard in person? See the Precepts commanding CVI. the man, some man, as above II. 25. unless it hears from him first? Since he is openly present in the same city, and is not suspected of flight. unless here must be translated as if not. and knows what he does? how for as: so that, namely, in that way it may be known what life he lives: who he says he is, by what arguments. V. 52. Are you also from Galilee? Not that they believed this, but that they wished to signify. That Jesus had no other supporters than commoners occupied by faction. See Mark XIV. 70. Luke XXII. 59. search? Revolve the history of all times: they speak as to a learned man. and see? As if they were saying, it is certain: it is established. that a prophet has not been raised from Galilee? Do not take this concerning one, but concerning any Prophet. No Galilean, they say, has ever been gifted by God with a prophetic spirit: it is a nation despised by God. See above I. 46. A mind blinded by hatred answers nothing to that brought forward by Nicodemus concerning equity, but seizes an argument than which none is more fragile, from history negatively, as if no distinguished person could be born from where no other such person was born before. But properly it is said of a Prophet he has been raised, that is, he is excited by God and as it were placed on high. We have noted this at Matt. XI. 10. V. 53. and each went to his own house? A departure was made with the matter unfinished, which it is credible happened because the Sadducees, a part of the senate, approved Nicodemus's opinion. For they were, as Josephus notes, sufficiently exact observers of the law in administering justice: and they willingly contradicted the Pharisees. But they seem to have yielded afterwards when the accusation of Majesty was understood: for they were worshippers of Roman power.

Nostrane lex quæ æquitatem ubique Judicibus commendat hoc patitur, ut præjudicio confodiatur aliquis (quale hoc erat de Jesu prehendendo) neglectis veri indagandi rationibus commodis, qualis est imprimis, ut ipse coram interrogetur & audiatur? Vide Præceptorum jubentum CVI. τὸν ἄνθρωπον, hominē aliquem, ut supra II. 25. ἐὰν μὴ ἀκούσῃ παρ᾽ αὐτῦ πρότερον) Cum in eadem urbe palam versetur, neque de fuga suspectus sit. ἐὰν μὴ hic si non vertendum. καὶ γνῷ τί ποιεῖ) πῇ pro ut: ut scilicet eo modo cognoscatur quam vitam viva : quem se dicat, quibus argumentis. V. 52. Μὴ καὶ σὺ ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας εἶ) Non quod hoc crederent, sed quod significare vellent. Non alios Jesum fautores habere quam populares factione occulpatos. Vide Marc. XIV. 70. Lucæ XXII. 59. ἐρεύνησον) Revolve tectum omnium temporum historiam: loquuntur ut erudito. καὶ ἴδε) Quasi dicant, certum est: constat. ὅτι προφήτης ἐκ Γαλιλαίας ὐκ ἐγήγερται) Non de uno sed de quovis Propheta accipe. Nullus ajunt Galilæus unquam à Deo donatus est spiritu prophetico: gens est Deo despecta. Vide supra I. 46. Occæcatus odio animus nihil ad illud de æquitate à Nicodemo allatum respondet, sed argumentum arripit quo nullum fragilius, ab historia negative, quasi nemo eximius nasci posset, unde non alius talis prior natus sit. Proprie autem de Propheta dicitur ἐγήγερται, id est à Deo excitatur & quasi in sublimi collocatus est. Notavimus ad Matth. XI. 10. V. 53. καὶ ἐπορεύθη ἕκαστος εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ) Discessio facta est re infecta, quod credibile est evenisse quia Sadducæi, pars senatus, Nicodemi sententiam probarunt. Videntur autem postea hi cessisse intellecta Majestatis accusatione: erant enim cultores Romanæ potentiæ.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

An adulteress is presented to Jesus teaching again in the temple, but when he first ordered whoever was without sin to cast a stone at her, and they all hurried away from there, she is absolved by Jesus, though warned not to sin anymore. Jesus testifies that he is the light of the world, and asserts that testimony against the Pharisees, that it is not his alone, but the Father's, whom they do not know, denies that they can come to where he is going, and that they will die in their sins if they do not believe in him, then indeed they will finally know that he is who he is, when the son of man will be exalted. But those who will have remained in his word will be true disciples, and the truth will make them free: Furthermore, to some answering that they are Abraham's seed, and have never been slaves, he professes that they will then finally be truly free, when the Son will have made them free: If they were Abraham's children, they would do the works of Abraham, but they do not do them, while they seek to kill him. Nor are they children of God, because they do not love Him who was sent by the Father, nor do they hear His word; and so they are of the Devil, a murderer and the father of lies. To the Jews blaspheming that He is a Samaritan and has a devil, He replies that He honors His Father and does not seek His own honor. Those who keep His word shall not see death: to them replying that Abraham and the prophets are dead, He Himself appeals to His Father, who honors Him, and to Abraham, who rejoiced to see His day: and finally that He existed before Abraham was; and when for this reason they wished to stone Him, He passed through the midst of them.

There are four parts: I. The absolution of the adulteress, to v. 11. II. The testimony of Jesus concerning himself as the light of the world, and the assertion of the necessity of believing in him under the danger of death, to v. 29. III. Information concerning true liberty, and the true and false seed of Abraham, to v. 42. IV. Confirmation concerning the life-giving truth of the Word of Christ: for whose day Abraham even rejoiced, and that he himself existed before Abraham, to v. 59.

PART I. The Absolution of the Adulteress.

Vers. 1. But Jesus went) There has long been a question concerning the history of the adulteress, and there is now. I clearly think it was written neither by Matthew in the Hebrew Gospel, nor by John in the Greek, at the beginning: but because both these and other Apostles had often narrated this history by word of mouth, it was attached by the Nazarenes of Palestine to the Hebrew Gospel, and by Papias and other disciples of John to the Greek Gospel of John, and approved by the Church, for the reason that it was established by sufficiently certain testimony that it was handed down by the Apostles; therefore the older Greek copies and the Syriac do not have it: but certain Latin ones, later Greek ones, and the Arabic do have it. For it is sufficiently evident from Jerome that it was in the Hebrew of the Nazarenes. I think, however, that it was omitted from being written by the Apostles themselves, because a calumny could easily be seized from it to traduce Christians before magistrates as if they were overturning public judgments, upon which the safety of the Republic seems to stand. For that which some think, that it was erased by the Novatians, is not credible, since it sufficiently appears from Eusebius and Jerome that it was missing before those times.

Grotius thinks that the history of the adulteress was not written by Matthew, nor by John, but was attached by the Nazarenes of Palestine to the Hebrew Gospel, and by Papias and other disciples of John to the Greek Gospel of John. But although we willingly grant that it was not recorded by Matthew—for the Hebrew Gospel of the Nazarenes is not of canonical authority—it must not, however, be conceded that this history was not described by John. For although it is omitted in the Syriac text, it nevertheless occurs in certain Greek and Latin codices, and in the Arabic text: nor is that conjecture of any moment, that it was omitted from being written by the Apostles themselves because a calumny could easily be seized from it to traduce Christians before magistrates, as if they were overturning public judgments: and although perhaps in Jerome's time it was missing in certain codices, Grotius himself acknowledges that it existed in others, referring it to Papias and other disciples of John: but from whom it actually proceeded, it is not likely. For how would they have dared to add anything to the sacred codex which the Apostles did not want added? Its authority was too great for the disciples of the Apostles to presume to add anything to it, or even to change a word in it: concerning which St. John had also taken care, with the most severe threat added in Rev. 22:18. Regarding what they bring forward from Eusebius, book III, last chapter of the Ecclesiastical History, that this history was written by Papias, it is read otherwise in the Greek text of Eusebius: 'He also set forth another history concerning a woman accused of many sins before the Lord, which the Gospel according to the Hebrews contains': where Papias is said not to have written, but to have set forth a history concerning a woman accused; nor is there a word about an adulteress, but about a woman accused of many sins, whence that Grotius-like suspicion concerning Papias being the author of this history rests on no foundation. Nor because it was passed over by Chrysostom and Origen in their explanation does it follow that it was not read in the codices themselves, since many other things undoubtedly read were passed over in their explanation. Add that Chrysostom, homily 60 on John, makes mention of it: and that Jerome observes that it existed in many codices, Tom. II, Dial. 2 against the Pelagians: in the Gospel according to John it is found in many both Greek and Latin codices concerning the history of the adulteress, who was accused before the Lord: which Tatian also read and

Ammonius, by the testimony of the harmony of both, (and from them the Oriental Church, by the testimony of Eusebius), as also Victor of Capua in his Harmony, and also St. Athanasius by the testimony of the Synopsis of Scripture, and Cyril of Alexandria, as also Ambrose, Tom. III, Epist. book VII, Ep. 58 and book IX, Ep. 26, and Augustine in this place, with Prosper, book on the promises, ch. XXII, Gregory the Great, book I, Morals, ch. 6, and book XIV, ch. 15, Idacius, book to Var., Sedulius, and others. The Greek Gospels with the canons of Eusebius, which conduce to discerning the genuine reading of the Evangelists, are received primarily in the Church, in which the same is not neglected. See Selden apud Bald. Walaeum in this place. Who will believe that the Apostles themselves wanted to pass over this history for the sake of avoiding calumny? For what things cannot be seized upon as an argument for calumny? But this had no place here: for what could be brought forward concerning the law of Moses, which decrees capital punishment for an adulteress, as if Christ had acted against it when he did not want to condemn the adulteress, is easily dissolved: because he did not condemn her as if he were contrary to Moses, but because it was not his office to judge such things and to pass sentence upon them. He does not answer, says Grotius, to that which he had said concerning the law, because it was sufficiently established that it did not oblige them to exact penalties, unless where the people were of their own right, or where the rulers gave them the power of that matter. But they themselves, beyond what was granted to them under the Roman Empire, usurped it of their own accord as if out of love for justice: which pretext he takes away from them, by ordering them to descend into themselves, where they would find enough crimes which they could punish. And at v. 10, 'Has no one condemned you?', as if he were to say, if a sentence has been passed upon you, I do not contradict it. It is not unjust to judge the adulteress to death. v. 11, 'Neither do I condemn you,' I do not lend my authority to this, to incite the people, who can abstain from the exaction of such a punishment with a safe conscience, to do so.

To the Mount of Olives) To the village of Gethsemane, where he was accustomed to pray and spend the night, Luke 21:37, Matt. 26:36; but he often dined nearby in Bethany at the house of Lazarus and his sisters.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Jesu iterum in templo docenti sistitur adultera, sed quum primū in eam lapidem projicere juberet, qui absǫ peccato esset, omnesǫ se inde proriporent, absolvitur illa à Jesu, monita tamen ne peccaret amplius. Jesus testatur, se esse lucem mundi, idq́ testimonium contra Pharisæos asserit, non esse suum solum, sed Patris, quem ipsi non norint, negat ipsos eo venire posse, quo abeat, ac morituros in peccatis suis, si in ipsum non crediderint, tum vero demum cognituros, quod ipse sit, cum exaltabitur filiǫ hominis. Qui autē manserint in sermone suo, veros discipulos fore, ac veritatem ipsos liberos reddituram: Cæterum respondentibǫ nonnullis, se Abrahami semen esse, nec unquam servos fuisse, profitetur, tum demum vere liberos fore, cū liberos ipsos fecerit Filius: Si Abrahæ filii essent, Abrahæ opera facturos esse, ea autem non facere, dum se interficere quærunt. Neque Dei esse filios, quia non diligunt eum, qui à Patre missus est, nec verbum ejus audiunt; adeóǫ à Diabolo esse, homicida, & patre mendacii. Blasphemantibus Judæis quod Samarites sit, & Diabolum habeat, reponit, se Patrem suum honorare, non proprium honorem quærere. Verbuḿq́ suum servantos mortem non visuros: Replicantibǫ illis Abrahamum & Prophetas mortuos esse, provocat ipse ad Patrem suum, se honorantem, & Abrahamum ob diem suum gavisum: Ac deniq́ se fuisse antequam Abrahamus esset: & quum ideo ipsum lapidare vellent, per medium ipsorum transit.

Partes sunt quatuor: I. Adultera absolutio, ad v. 11. II. Testificatio Jesu de se mundi luce, ejusque sub mortis discrimine credendi necessitate adser- tio, ad v. 29. III. De vera libertate, veroq; & falso Abrahæ semine informatio, ad v. 42. IV. De Verbi Christi veritate vivifica confirmatio: ob cujus di- em Abraham etiam gavisus, & quod ante Abraha- mum ipse extiterit, ad v. 59.

PARS I. Adulteræ Absolutio.

Vers. 1. Ἰησοῦς δὲ ἐπορεύθη) De historia adulteræ jam olim fuit quæstio & nunc est. Ego plane arbitror initio nec à Mat- thæo scriptam in Hebræo Evangelio, nec à Johanne in Græ- co: sed quia & hi & alii Apostoli viva voce hanc historiam sæpe narraverant, attextam à Nazarenis quidem Palæstinæ Hebræo Evangelio, à Papia autem aliisq; Johannis discipu- lis Græco Johannis, & ab Ecclesia probatam, ideo quod sa- tis certo testimonio constaret ab Apostolis traditam, ideo vetustiora Græca exemplaria & Syriacum non habent: at habent Latina quædam, seriora Græca & Arabicum. Nam in Nazaræorum Hebræo fuisse satis ex Hieronymo constat. Puto autem omissam scribi ab ipsis Apostolis, quod facile inde calumnia arripi posset traducendi Christianos apud Magistratus quasi evertentes publica judicia quibq stare vi- detur Reip. salus. Nam quod quidam putant à Novatianis erasam credibile non est, cum ex Eusebio & Hieronymo sa- tis appareat ante ea tempora desideratam.

Historiam adulteræ nec à Matthæo, nec à Johanne scriptam, à Nazarenis autem Palæstinæ Ebræo Evan- gelio, à Papia autem aliisq, Johannis discipulis Græco Johannis attextam esse, arbitratur Grotius. Sed quamvis libenter largiamur, eam à Matthæo con- signatam non esse: Ebræum enim Nazarenorum Evangelium non est autoritatis Canonicæ: non ta- men concedendum, quod à Johanne ea Historia descripta non sit. Etsi enim in Syro textu omissa sit, occurrit tamen in Græcis & Latinis quibusdam Co- dicibus, & Arabico textu: neque ullius momenti est conjectura illa, omissam esse scribi ab ipsis Apostolis, quod facile inde calumnia arripi posset traducendi Christianos apud Magistratus, quasi evertentes pu- blica judicia: & quamvis forte Hieronymi tem- pore in quibusdam Codicibus desiderata illa fuerit, in aliis tamen eam extitisse agnoscit ipse Grotius, ad Papiam aliosque Johannis discipulos eam refe- rens: à quibus vero illam profectam esse, non sit verisimile. Quomodo enim illi ausi fuissent aliquid Codici sacro adjicere, quod adjectum noluere Apostoli? Major fuit ejus autoritas quam ut quic- quam addere eidem præsumerent Apostolorum discipuli, aut vel verbum in eodem immutare: de quo etiam caverat S. Johannes, addita comminatio- ne severissima Apoc. XXII. 18. De Eusebio quod ad- ferunt è l. III. c. ult. H. E. scriptam hanc Historiam à Papia fuisse, aliter in textu Græco Eusebii legitur: ἐκτέθειται δὲ κὶ ἄλλην ἱστορίαν περὶ γυναικὸς ἐπὶ πολλαῖς ἁμαρτίαις διαβληθείσης, ἣν τὸ κυριακὸν τὸ καθ᾽ ἑβραίους ἐυαγγέλιον περιέχει: exposuit autem & aliam historiam de muliere accusata de multis peccatis apud Dominum, quam Evangelium secundum Hebræos continet: ubi non scripsisse sed exposuisse de muliere accusata historiam dicitur Papias: nec de adulteræ verbum habetur, sed de muliere de multis peccatis accusata, unde nullo fundamenta nititur illa Gro- tiana de Papia autore hujus historiæ suspicio. Nec quia à Chrysostomo, & Origene eadem præterita est in explicatione, sequitur eandem non lectam fuisse in ipsis Codicibus, quum multa alia indubitato le- cta in explicatione præterierint. Adde quod Chry- sost. hom. LX. in Job. mentionem ejus faciat: quodq; Hieronymus observet eam in multis Codicibus exti- tisse, Tom. II. Dial. 2. contr. Pelag. in Evangelio se- cundum Johannem in multis & Græcis, & Latinis Codicibus invenitur de adulteræ historia, quæ accu- sata apud Dominum: quam etiam legit Tatianus &

Ammonius teste utriusque Harmonia, (& ex illis Orientalis Ecclesia, teste Eusebio) ut & Victor Ca- puanus in Harmonia, nec non S. Athanasius teste Synopsi Scripturae, & Cyrillus Alex. ut & Ambros. Tom. III. Epist. l. VII. Ep. 58. & l. IX. Ep. 26. & Au- gust. in h. l. cum Prospero l. de promiss. c. XXII. Gre- gorio M. l. I. Mor. c. 6. & l. XIV. c. 15. Idacio l. ad Var. Sedulio, & aliis. Recepta imprimis in Ecclesia sunt Evangelia Graeca cum Canonibus Eusebii ad dignoscendam Evangelicorum genuinam lectio- nem conducentia, in quibus eadem non negligi- tur. Vid. Seldenus apud Bald. Walaeum in h. l. Calu- mniae vitandae causa Apostolos ipsos praeterire vo- luisse hanc historiam ecquis credet? Quae enim non rapi possunt in calumniae argumentum? Quae vero hic locum minime habebat: quod enim de Mose legis, poenam capitalem sancienti adulterae, adferri posset, quasi Christus ei contravenexit, cum condemnare adulteram noluit, εὐδιάλυτον est: quia non condemnavit quasi Mosi contrarius esset, sed quia sui id non erat officii, talia judicare, & de iis sen- tentiam ferre. Non respondet, inquit Grotius, ad il- lud, quod dixerat de lege, quia satis constabat, non ob- ligare eam ad poenas exigendas, nisi ubi populus sui juris esset, aut ubi imperantes ejus rei potestatem ipsis facerent. Sed ipsi ultra quam sub Romano imperio concessum ipsis erat, ultro usurpabant quasi amore ju- stitiae: quem praetextum illis eripit, jussis in semet de- scendere, ubi satis criminum inventuri essent, quod vindicare possent. Et ad v. 10. ὀδείς σε κατέκρινεν, quasi dicat, si lata est in te sententia, ego ei non contradico. Non est iniquum in adulteram mortis judicium. v. 11. ὀδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω, Ego auctori- tatem meam in hoc non commodo, ut populum, qui salva conscientia talis supplicii exactione abstinere potest, ad id excitem.

Εἰς τὸ ὄρ@ τῶν ἐλαιῶν) In villam Gethsemane, ubi orare & pernoctare solebat, Luc. XXI. 37. Matth. XXVI. 36. coena- bat autem saepe in proximo in Bethania apud Lazarum & ejus sorores.

## 8:3
Vers. 3. οἱ γραμματεῖς, κὴ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι) They who were considered the most learned and most religious of the Jews propose to him a captious question, such as that one was about paying tribute to Caesar, Matt. 22:17.

ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ κατειλημμένη) By two witnesses, as the law requires. Some understand μοιχείαν here as incest, because they deny that adultery was punished by stoning among the Jews, of which we shall speak presently. I clearly think the propriety of the word should be retained.

ἐν μέσῳ) In a conspicuous place. Thus Matt. 14:6, Mark 3:3.

Latin:

Vers. 3. οἱ γραμματεῖς, κὴ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι) Qui doctissimi & religiosissimi Judaeorum audiebant, quaestionem ei propo- nunt captatoriam, qualis illa erat de tributo Caesari solven- do, Matth. XXII. 17.

ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ κατειλημμένη) A duobus testib9 ut lex deside- rat. Quidam μοιχείαν hic incestum intelligunt, ideo quod negent adulterium apud Judaeos lapidatione punitum, de quo mox dicemus. Ego plane arbitror retinendam vocis proprietatem.

ἐν μέσῳ) Loco conspicuo. Sic Matth. XIV. 6. Marc. III. 3.

## 8:4
Vers. 4. Ἐπαυτοφώρῳ) So manifestly that it cannot be denied. It is a forensic Greek word. They indicate that this is not a matter of the suspicion into which the potion of the water of jealousy was established.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἐπαυτοφώρῳ) Tam manifeste ut negari non pos- sit. Vox est Graecatorensis. Indicant non agi hic de suspi- cione in quam constituta erat potio aquae Zelotypae.

## 8:5
V. 5. Μωσῆς ἐνετείλατο ταῖς τοιαύταις λιθοβολείσθαι) Lev. 20:10, Deut. 22:22, the penalty of death is prescribed for the adulterer and the adulteress. But where the law specified nothing, the mildest penalty of death was accepted, that is, strangulation, which the teachers of the Hebrews also acknowledge specifically in the punishment of an adulteress. The penalty of stoning is among the more severe. The man or woman was placed naked in some part and with hands bound on a scaffold as high as twice the stature of a medium man: from there they were thrown down by the witnesses into a lower place: and if they were killed by that fall, that punishment sufficed: if not, a huge stone was thrown onto the back of the one lying there by the witnesses themselves, and if there was need, others by the rest of the bystanders. By what right, therefore, were adulteresses subjected to this more severe punishment? Some say that since in Leviticus 20, at the beginning and end of the chapter, mention is made of stoning, those placed in the middle should also be drawn to the same. But in that same chapter some things are punished by fire, some by cutting off כרת, that is, by a penalty to be inflicted by God if the matter remains hidden: but if the matter is manifest and a warning has preceded, by scourging. Others say that since in Deuteronomy the penalty of stoning is imposed on a corrupted betrothed woman in the following words, by equal or greater reason it ought to be applied to an adulteress as well. But it can be objected that a more severe punishment is directed against a betrothed woman, because she was not in the custody of a husband, just as theft from a pasture is punished more severely than from a sheepfold. I agree with the Hebrews who teach that where the penalty of death is expressed by law, not likewise the kind of death, there the types of punishments were defined by the Sanhedrin according to the circumstances of the times, so that more severe ones might be exacted where it was necessary to meet a spreading example. Wherefore, since adulteries had been frequent before the Babylonian exile, when in exile it was granted to the Jews to have the right of punishing their own people even with death, adulteresses were stoned: which we are taught in Ez. XVI. 40, compared with verse 38. To which passages it is also noted by Kimchi that at some times adulteresses were stoned, and it happened because of this that he who wrote about the history of Susanna falsely said that those who simulated adultery were stoned by the law of retaliation. Similarly, I think that in the times of Hyrcanus and those following, adulteresses were stoned in Judea because of the frequency of the crime. See Rom. II. 22. These words must therefore be taken as if it had been said, Moses commanded such to be punished with death, which death later usage made stoning.

Selden prefers to call this adulteress betrothed. For here there is an express appeal to the law of Moses: who, however, designated the punishment of stoning only for a betrothed virgin, not yet married. They do not look to later usage, but to the express command of Moses: in the law Moses commanded us that SUCH should be stoned. You, therefore, what do you say?

· σὺ ὖν τί λέγεις) The Romans had not so long ago taken away all capital punishments from the Jews, as has been noted elsewhere. In stoning, the people, with the witnesses leading, carried out the judgment, and indeed in these times often without a sentence, as was done to Stephen and to James the kinsman of Jesus, whose history is with Josephus. The people therefore sometimes usurped this right, although the Romans were unwilling, as if it had been granted by God. It is asked of Jesus what he thinks.

Latin:

V. 5. Μωσῆς ἐνετείλατο ταῖς τοιαύταις λιθοβολείσθαι) Lev. XX. 10. Deut. XXII. 22 mortis poena indicitur adultero, & ad- ulterae. At mortis poena, ubi lex nihil exprimebat, accipie- batur mitissima, id est, strangulatio, quam & specialiter in adulterae supplicio agnoscunt Hebraeorum magistri. Lapi- dationis poena est inter atrocrores. Statuebatur vir aut mu- lier nudi parte aliqua & manib9 vincti in catastalta quan- tum bis sex mediocris hominis statura: inde in locum infe- riorem a testibus praecipitabantur: & si eo casu interime- rentur sufficiebat id supplicium: sin minus, superjicieba- tur tergo jacentis saxum ingens ab ipsis testibus, & si opus esser, alia a reliquis adstantib9. Quo igitur jure hoc gravio- re supplicio affectae adulterae? Ajunt quidam cum Levit. xx. initio & fine capitis mentio fiat lapidationis, etiam in med o posita eodem trahenda. Sed eodem in capite quaeda incen- dio puniuntur, quaeda per succifionem כרת id est per poe- nam divinitus infligendam si res lateat: sin manifesta sit res & monitio praecesserit, per verbera Alii dicunt cum in Deu- teronomio sequent bus verbis sponsae corruptae imponatur poena lapidationis, ex pari aut majori ratione debere eam & adulterae aptari. Sed objici potest in sponsam gravius anim- adversum, quia in custodia mariti non erat, sicut & gravius punitur furtum de pascuo quam de ovili. Accedo Hebraeis tradentibus ubi mortis poena lege exprimitur, non item mortis genus, ibi a Synedrio pro ratione temporum genera poenarum definita, ut graviores exigerentur ubi occurren- dum erat gliscenti exemplo. Quare cum crebra fuissent adulteria ante exsilium Babylonicum, ubi in exsilio Judæis concessum fuit in suos jus puniendi etiam morte, lapidatæ sunt adulteræ: quod docemur Ez. XVI. 40. collato com- mate 38. ad quæ loca etiam a Kimchi notatum, nonnullis temporibus lapidatas adulteras, & eo factum ut qui de Su- sannæ historiam scripsit, falso adulterii in simulatores lege talionis lapidatos dixerit. Similiter & Hyrcani sequentibus- que temporibus in Judæa putem lapidatas adulteras ob criminis frequentiam. Vide Rom. II. 22. Sumenda ergo hæc verba, quasi dictum esset, Moses tales præcepit mor- te puniri, quam mortem postremus usus fecit lapidatio- nem.

Adulteram hanc desponsatam mavult dicere Sel- denus. Nam expresse hic ad legem Mosis provoca- tur: qui vero solum in virginem desponsatam, nec- dum nuptam, lapidationis pœnam designavit. Non usus postremum illi respiciunt, sed Mosis disertum præceptum: in lege Moses præcepit nobis, ut TALES lapidentur. Tu ergo quid dicis?

· σὺ ὖν τί λέγεις) Romani non ita dudum omnia capitalia supplicia eripuerant judæis ut alibi notatum est. In lapida- tione populus testibꝫ præeuntibus judicium exsequebatur, & quidem his temporibus sæpe citra sententiam, ut Stepha- no factum & Jacobo Jesu cognato, cujus historia apud Jo- sephum. Usurpabat ergo interdum populus hoc jus quam- vis Romanis nolentibus ut a Deo concessum. Quæritur ex Jesu quid sentiat.

## 8:6
Vers. 6. ἵνα ἔχωσι κατηγορεῖν κατ' ἀυτᾶ) That they might accuse him either before the Romans of diminished majesty, or before the people of diminished liberty,

Ἔγραψεν εἰς τὴν γῆν) Some sentence worthy of being committed to memory. It seems that this was the custom.

Μὴ προσποιέμεν@·) Dissimulating. Thus Thucydides uses μὴ προσποιεῖσθαι, Polybius προσποιεῖσθαι. Understand: that he understood the conversation of the Pharisees and the experts in the Law.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἵνα ἔχωσι κατηγορεῖν κατ' ἀυτᾶ) Ut eum accusa- rent aut apud Romanos imminutæ Majestatis, aut apud po- pulum imminutæ libertatis,

Ἔγραψεν εἰς τὴν γῆν) Sententiam aliquam dignam quæ memoriæ mandaretur. Videtur id moris fuisse.

Μὴ προσποιέμεν@·) Dissimulans. Sic μὴ προσποιεῖσθ ufur- pat Thucydides, προσποιεῖσθ Polybius. Subintellige, intelli- gere se sermonem Pharisæorum & Legisperitorum.

## 8:7
Vers. 7. Ὁ ἀναμάρτητ@· ὑμῶν) Verbal nouns of this kind do not always signify power, as Jerome seems to have thought, but for the most part an act: as ἄπρακτ@·. But ἀναμάρτητ@· is to be understood here as one who is not guilty of adultery or of an equal or greater crime.

Πρῶτος ἳ λίθον ἐπ' ἀυτῆσ βαλέτω) Because stoning was as it were the judgment of the people, he therefore adapted to the people what is usually said about judges. For it is in reality that same saying which is in Paul, Rom. II. 1: You are inexcusable, you who judge: for when you judge another, you condemn yourself, since you, the judge, do the same things. This comes from natural equity. Cicero, Verrina V: Not only the accuser, but not even the reprover is to be endured, who is reproved for the very vice he criticizes in another. Xenophon: Τὶ πϱοσήκει ἀυτῷ ὄντα πονηϱὸν πονηρίας ἕνεκα ἢ βλακείας ἄλλες κολάζειν. Seneca: A sentence cannot have authority where he who is to be condemned condemns. The same, elsewhere: A just judge does not pass one sentence for his own case and another for another's. Pliny: Thus they are angry at the vices of others as if they envied them, and they punish most severely those whom they most imitate. Salvianus de Gub. divina l. II. By this, while they think they are condemning others, they condemn themselves all the more by their own judgment. He names the first stone, because it is the largest and for the most part lethal. Now, Christ’s purpose was to show that there was no reason for the judges or the people to grieve much that the power of punishing had been taken from them, since that matter is very dangerous for those conscious of any guilt, so that it is much better to be relieved of it. He does not respond to that which they had said about the law, because it was sufficiently agreed that it did not oblige them to exact penalties, unless where the people were of their own right, or where the rulers granted them the power for that matter. But they, beyond what was conceded to them under the Roman Empire, were voluntarily usurping it as if out of a love of justice: which pretext he snatches from them, having ordered them to descend into themselves, where they would find enough crimes which they could punish.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ὁ ἀναμάρτητ@· ὑμῶν) Verbalia hujus generis non semper potentiam significant, ut videtur sensisse Hie- ronymus, sed plerumq; actum: ut ἄπρακτ@·. Intelligendꝫ autem hic ἀναμάρτητ@·, qui nec adulterii nec paris aut ma- joris criminis reus est.

Πρῶτος ἳ λίθον ἐπ' ἀυτῆσ βαλέτω) Quia lapidatio erat quasi judicium populi, ideo quod de judicibus dici solet po- pulo aptavit. Est enim reipsa id, dictum, quod apud Paulum Rom. II. 1. Inexcusabilis es tu qui judicas: quia cum alterum ju- dicas temetipsum condemnas, cum tu judex eadem facias. Venit hoc ex naturali æquitate. Cicero Verrina V: Non modo accu- sator sed ne objurgator quidem ferendus est is, qui quod in alio vitium reprehendit, in eo ipso reprehenditur. Xenophon: Τὶ πϱο- σήκει ἀυτῷ ὄντα πονηϱὸν πονηρίας ἕνεκα ἢ βλακείας ἄλλες κολάζειν. Seneca: Non potest auctoritatem habere sententia, ubi qui da- mnandus est damnat. Id. alibi: Neg æquus judex aliam de sua, aliam de aliena causa sententiam fert. Plinius: Sic aliorum vitiis irascuntur, quasi invideant, & gravissime puniunt quos maxime imitantur. Salvianus de Gub. divina l. II. Per hoc dum da- mnare se cæteros putant, ipsos se magis propria animadversione condemnant. Primum autem lapidem nominat, quia is ma- ximus & plerumq; letalis. Propositum autem erat Christo ostendere, non esse quod judices aut populus multum do- lerent ereptam sibi puniendi potestatem, cum ea res valde sit periculosa alicujus culpæ sibi consciis, ita ut exonerari multo sit satius. Non respondet ad illud quod dixerant de lege, quia satis constabat non obligare eam ad pœnas exi- gendas, nisi ubi populus sui juris esset, aut ubi imperantes ejus rei potestatem ipsis facerent. Sed ipsi ultra quam sub Romano Imperio concessum ipsis erat, ultro usurpabant quasi amore justitiæ: quem prætextum illis eripit, jussis in semet descendere, ubi satis criminum inventuri essent, quod vindicare possent.

Vers. 8. Πάλιν κάτω κύψας ἔγραφεν εἰς γῆν) Showing that he had nothing to add, and that it was no concern of his what they did.

Vers. 8. Πάλιν κάτω κύψας ἔγραφεν εἰς γῆν) Ostendens nihil habere se quod adjiceret, neque sua interesse quid a- gerent.

## 8:9
Vers. 9. ὑπὸ τῆς συνειδήσεως ἐλεγχόμενοι) For at that time the morals even of the learned were most corrupt: so that adulteries were also frequent. See the second chapter to the Romans, and Josephus regarding these times.

εἷς καθ' εἷς) We have spoken to Mark XIV. 19.

to the lawyers. For the Apostles were present, and perhaps a crowd as well. Thus we had μόνον above at VI. 22. Ἐν μέσῳ ἑσῶ) Conspicuous to the Apostles, and perhaps to the crowd. Vers. 10. Μηδένα θεασάμενος) Of those who had brought the woman. Οἱ κατήγοροί σε) That is, those who seemed to want to use my authority to punish you. Οὐδείς σε κατέκρινεν) As if he were saying, if a sentence has been passed upon you, I do not contradict it. It is not unjust to judge an adulteress to death. Vers. 11. Οὐδὲ ἐγώ (σε κατακρίνω) I do not lend my authority to this, so as to incite the people, who can with a clear conscience abstain from the execution of such a punishment, to do so. Πορεύε) Go, attend to your own affairs: you have escaped the danger. Καὶ ἀπὸ τᾶ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε) Otherwise you are to be condemned much more severely by GOD. He adds this so that it might not seem to give license to sin. Augustine: For if he were a supporter of sinners, he would say: Neither will I condemn you, go and live as you wish. Be secure regarding my liberation: however much you have sinned, I will free you from every punishment, even from Gehenna and the terrors of hell. He did not say this, but go and sin no more. The ancients rightly noted that in this woman there is a type of the Church to be gathered from idolatrous nations, whose God-given mercy the Jews could not accuse if they themselves examined their own ways.

PART II. The testimony of JESUS concerning himself as the light of the world and the assertion of the necessity of believing in him under the threat of death.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ὑπὸ τῆς συνειδήσεως ἐλεγχόμενοι) Erant enim eo tempore corruptissimi mores etiam eruditorum: ita ut & adulteria essent frequentia. Vide caput secundum ad Romanos, & Josephum circa hæc tempora.

εἷς καθ' εἷς) Diximus ad Marc. XIV. 19.

legisperitis. Nam Apostoli aderant, forte & turba ali- qua. Sic μόνον habuimus supra VI. 22. Ἐν μέσῳ ἑσῶ) Conspicua Apostolis, forte & turbæ. Vers. 10. Μηδένα θεασάμενος) Eorum qui mulierem adduxerant. Οἱ κατήγοροί σε) Id est qui mea auctoritate videbantur velle uti ad te puniendam. Οὐδείς σε κατέκρινεν) Quasi dicat, si lata est in te sen- tentia, ego ei non contradico. Non est iniquum in ad- ulteram mortis judicium. Vers. 11. Οὐδὲ ἐγώ (σε κατακρίνω) Ego auctoritatem meam in hoc non commodo, ut populum, qui salva conscientia à talis supplicii exactione abstinere potest, ad id excitem. Πορεύε) Abi, cura res tuas: evasisti periculum. Καὶ ἀπὸ τᾶ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε) Alioqui multo gra- vius à DEO damnanda. Hoc ideo adjicit ne commea- tum videretur dare peccandi. Augustinus: Nam si pec- catorum fautor esset, diceret: Nec ego te condemnabo, va- de & vive ut vis. De mea liberatione esto secura: ego quantumcunque peccaveris te ab omni pœna, etiam Geben- na, & inferni terroribus liberabo. Non hoc dixit, sed vade & noli amplius peccare. Recte autem notarunt veteres in hac fœmina typum esse Ecclesiæ ex gentibus idolola- tris colligendæ, cui impertitam DEI misericordiam ac- cusare Judæi non possent, si ipsi suos mores inspice- rent.

PARS II. Testificatio IESV de se mundi luce ejusque sub mortis discrimine credendi necessitate adfertio.

## 8:12
Vers. 12. Πάλιν ὖν) At another time, thus above at l. 33. IX. 15. and elsewhere. Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τῶ κόσμε) When various people felt various things about themselves, JESUS modestly professes what ought to be felt about him. It had been said of the Messiah that he would be the light of the nations, Is. XLIX. v. 6. he adapts this to himself. See what is above at l. 5. and following, and Luke II. 32. Ὁ ἀκολυθῶν ἐμοί) He who follows my guidance: for a light is accustomed to be carried before. Οὐ μὴ περιπατήσει ἐν τῇ [σκυτίᾳ] He sees where and in what he must walk, we said above at c. I. v. 4. and Luke cap. II. v. 32. Ἀλλ' ἕξει τὸ φῶς τῆς ζωῆς) He will have that light which goes before him, which leads to eternal life. See above at the stated place c. I. Vers. 13. εἶπον ὖν ἀυτῷ οἱ φαρισαῖοι) Proud and envious men. Σὺ περὶ σεαυτῶ μαρτυρεῖς) You proclaim such magnificent things about yourself, and you want to be believed when you speak. Ἡ μαρτυρία σε ἐκ ἔσιν ἀληθής) It is not worthy to be received. See above V. 31. Vers. 14. Κ' ἄν ἐγὼ μαρτυρῶ περὶ ἐμαυτῶ) Even if there were no preceding testimonies of the Prophets about me, no testimonies of John the Baptist, even if I were the first and only one to proclaim these things about myself. Ἀληθής ἐσιν ἡ μαρτυρία με) Nevertheless my words would have to be received. Ὅτι οἶδα πόθεν κὶ πᾶ ὑπάγω. ὑμεῖς ἐκ οἴδατε πόθεν ἔρχομαι κὼ πᾶ ὑπάγω) It is accepted among all nations that testimonies are admitted according to the quality of the subject matter. And so in those things which are accustomed to be done in secret, those are heard who would not otherwise be heard. He to whom an embassy is entrusted is conscious of it, the rest must learn this from him himself. But if that ambassador seeks no personal advantage in the matter, if he himself endures many evils because of the embassy, but claims no honor for himself, but rather for the one who sent him, and says nothing that is not worthy of the sender, then there is no reason why he should not be believed. That πόθεν ἔρχομαι κὶ πᾶ ὑπάγω is a circumlocution for the embassy, which is accustomed to be received first, and then reported. I know from whom and what commands have been given to me. You cannot know that except through me. Vers. 15. Ὑμεῖς κατὰ τὴν σάρκα κρίνετε) You do not judge the matter by true reason, but from affections, which he called judging according to appearance above at VII. 14. Thus to walk according to the flesh, to follow affections while reason is despised. Κρίνειν here is to profess what you feel about someone: just as these men were professing that they held Jesus to be unworthy of being believed. Ἐγὼ ἐ κρίνω ἐδένα) I say nothing that could be harmful to anyone, in which kind of speech greater proofs are deservedly expected. Κρίνειν here is to say that from which condemnation could follow. Thus both accusers and witnesses are said in Latin to condemn.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Πάλιν ὖν) Alio tempore, sic supra l. 33. IX. 15. & alibi. Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τῶ κόσμε) Cum varii varia de se senti- rent, JESUS de se quid sentiendum sit, sed modeste profi- tetur. De Messia dictum erat futurum eum lucem gen- tium, Es. XLIX. v. 6. hoc sibi aptat. Vide quæ supra l. 5. & deinceps, & Luc. II. 32. Ὁ ἀκολυθῶν ἐμοί) Qui ductum meum sequitur: lux enim præferri solet. Οὐ μὴ περιπατήσει ἐν τῇ [σκυτίᾳ] Videt qua & quo ambulandum sit, diximus supra c. I. v. 4. & Luc. cap. II. v. 32. Ἀλλ' ἕξει τὸ φῶς τῆς ζωῆς) Habebit sibi præviam illam lu- cem, quæ ducit ad vitam æternam. Vide supra dicto loco c. I. Vers. 13. εἶπον ὖν ἀυτῷ οἱ φαρισαῖοι) Superbi & invidi ho- mines. Σὺ περὶ σεαυτῶ μαρτυρεῖς) Tam magnifica de te prædi- cas, & dicenti tibi credi vis. Ἡ μαρτυρία σε ἐκ ἔσιν ἀληθής) Non digna est quæ recipia- tur. Vide supra V. 31. Vers. 14. Κ' ἄν ἐγὼ μαρτυρῶ περὶ ἐμαυτῶ) Etiamsi nulla essent de me prægressa Prophetarum, nulla Johannis Ba- ptistæ testimonia, etiamsi ego primus ac solus hæc de me prædicarem. Ἀληθής ἐσιν ἡ μαρτυρία με) Tamen recipienda essent mea dicta. Ὅτι οἶδα πόθεν κὶ πᾶ ὑπάγω. ὑμεῖς ἐκ οἴδατε πόθεν ἔρχομαι κὼ πᾶ ὑπάγω) Receptum est apud omnes gentes ut testi- monia admittantur pro subjectæ rei qualitate. Itaque in his, quæ solent clam fieri audiuntur, qui alias non audiren- tur. Legationis injunctæ conscius est is cui injuncta est, re- liqui ab ipso hoc debent discere. Quod si is legatus nulla in re sua commoda captet, ipse ob legationem multa mala per- ferat, honorem vero nullum sibi vindicet, sed leganti, nec quicquam dicat quod non legante dignum sit, tunc nulla est ratio cur non ei credatur. Illud πόθεν ἔρχομαι κὶ πᾶ ὑπάγω est circumlocutio legationis, quæ accipi primo, deinde re- nuntiari solet. Ego scio à quo & quæ mihi data sint man- data. Vos id nisi per me id scire non potestis. Vers. 15. Ὑμεῖς κατὰ τὴν σάρκα κρίνετε) Non vera ratione rem dijudicatis, sed ex affectibus quod supra VII. 14. dixit κατ' ὄψιν κρίνειν. Sic κατὰ σάρκα περιπατεῖν, sequi affectus contemta ratione. Κρίνειν hic est profiteri quid de aliquo sentias: sicut isti profitebantur se Jesum habere pro indi- gno cui fides habeatur. Ἐγὼ ἐ κρίνω ἐδένα) Nihil dico quod alicui noxium esse possit, in quo dictorum genere merito majora expectan- tur documenta. Κρίνειν hic est id dicere unde condemnatio sequi possit. Sic & accusatores & testes condemnare Lati- ne dicuntur.

## 8:16
Vers. 16. Kai ἐὰν κρίνω δὲ ἐγὼ) But if I even do that.

Ἡ κρίσις ἡ ἐμὴ ἀληθής ἐστι) The indicative for the subjunctive, in the Hebrew manner. Such a profession of mine would not be to be despised.

Ὄτι μόνος ὀκ εἰμί) What I might say should not be held as the statement of me alone. I am not alone, in such a profession, that is to say.

Ἀλλ' ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πέμψας με πατήρ) What I might say should be considered to be said by the Father, by whom I say I was sent, and who shows me to have been sent by him, both by voice and by so many and such great miracles. However, the embassy having been proven, whatever the ambassador affirms, he who sent him is to be considered to affirm.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Kai ἐὰν κρίνω δὲ ἐγὼ) Quod si etiam id fa- ciam.

Ἡ κρίσις ἡ ἐμὴ ἀληθής ἐστι) Indicativus pro subjunctivo, more Hebræo. Mea talis professio non esset spernenda.

Ὄτι μόνος ὀκ εἰμί) Quod dicerem non habendum es- set pro meo unius dicto. Non solus sum, in tali professione scilicet.

Ἀλλ' ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πέμψας με πατήρ) Quod ego dicerem Pa- ter dicere censendus esset, à quo missum me dico, & qui me à se missum ostendit, & voce & tot tantisque miraculis. Legatione autem probata, quicquid legatus affirmat id censendus est qui legavit affirmare.

## 8:17
Vers. 17. Καὶ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ δὲ τῷ ὑμετέρῳ γέγραπται) What I now say not only accords with natural equity, but it is also written in the law, your law, I say, in which you boast. It is written, however, not in the same words, but to the same effect, Deut. XVII. 6. the very words of which passage are cited in Matt. XVIII. v. 16.

Ὄτι δύο ἀνθρώπων μαρτυρία ἀληθής ἐστι) It is accepted as true, it finds credence, even for the condemnation of some man, for this is what 'the word shall stand' means. But if the consensus of two men is of such value, how much value should be held for the consensus of God and of him who was sent by God?

Latin:

Vers. 17. Καὶ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ δὲ τῷ ὑμετέρῳ γέγραπται) Quod jam dico non naturali æquitati modo congruit, sed scriptum quoque est in lege, vestra inquam lege in qua gloriamini. Scriptum autem est non totidem verbis, sed eadem senten- tia, Deut. XVII. 6. cujus loci ipsa verba citantur Matth. XIIX. v. 16.

Ὄτι δύο ἀνθρώπων μαρτυρία ἀληθής ἐστι) Pro vero recipi- tur, fidem invenit, etiam ad hominis alicujus condemnatio- nem, hoc enim est stabit verbum. Quod si duorum homi- num consensus tanti est, quanti haberi debet consensus Dei & à Deo missi?

## 8:18
Vers. 18. Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ μαρτυρῶν περὶ ἐμαυτῦ) He returns to that from which he had digressed: from the profession concerning his own quality, which could be believed without any harm to anyone. When, however, he says 'I', understand: in whose life there is nothing to be blamed, whose dogmas all pertain to the promotion of God's honor, piety, and holiness.

Καὶ μαρτυρεῖ περὶ ἐμῦ ὁ πέμψας με πατήρ) He establishes credibility for me, he shows himself to have been sent in the way we have said. See above III. 2. V. 32. 36.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ μαρτυρῶν περὶ ἐμαυτῦ) Redit ad il- lud unde digressus erat: à professione de sua qualitate, quæ credi poterat sine ullo damno cujusquam. Cum autem di- cit ego, subintellige. in cujus vita nihil est culpandum, cujus dogmata omnia ad Dei honorem, pietatem & sanctitatem promovendam pertinent.

Καὶ μαρτυρεῖ περὶ ἐμῦ ὁ πέμψας με πατήρ) Is mihi fidem adstruit, ostendit se missum eo quo diximus modo. Vide supra III. 2. V. 32. 36.

## 8:19
Vers. 19. Πῦ ἐστιν ὁ πατήρ συ) Blinded by hatred, they did not understand whom he called his Father, as is explained below v. 27. Where is he? Show him to us, so that we may see what kind of authority he has, what he says.

Οὔτε ἐμὲ οἴδατε, ἔτε τὸν πατέρα με) You are so hindered by your passions that you neither understand my quality, nor whom I say is my Father, although I have explained both quite clearly to you.

εἰ ἐμὲ ᾔδειτε κὲ τὸ πατέρα μυ ᾔδειτε ἂν) If you were to consider that I am a teacher of the most holy dogma, you would easily conceive in your mind that no one other than God is called Father by me. Thus above IV. 10. εἰ ᾔδεις τὴν δωρεὰν τῦ Θεῦ if you understood. And below XIII. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Πῦ ἐστιν ὁ πατήρ συ) Odio excæcati non intel- ligebant, quem Patrem suum diceret, ut explicatur infra v. 27. Ubi est? demonstra eum nobis, ut videamus qualis sit auctoritatis, quid dicat.

Οὔτε ἐμὲ οἴδατε, ἔτε τὸν πατέρα με) Ita affectibus im- pedimini, ut nec meam qualitatem intelligatis, nec quem dicam esse Patrem meum, cum tamen utrumque satis clare vobis exposuerim.

εἰ ἐμὲ ᾔδειτε κὲ τὸ πατέρα μυ ᾔδειτε ἂν) Si consideraretis me doctorem esse sanctissimi dogmatis, facile & hoc con- ciperetis animo non alium à me Patrem appellari quam Deum. Sic supra IV. 10. εἰ ᾔδεις τὴν δωρεὰν τῦ Θεῦ si intel- ligeres. Et infra XIII. 17.

## 8:20
Vers. 20. ἐν τῷ γαζοφυλακίῳ) In a very famous place, and in which even some of the chief priests were accustomed to be; see what is said on Mark XII. 41.

Διδάσκων ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ) That is, since he was teaching now in this, now in that place of the temple.

Καὶ ὐδεὶς ἐπίασεν ἀυτὸν) κὲ for And yet. Concerning the sense, see above VII. 31.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἐν τῷ γαζοφυλακίῳ) Loco valde celebri, & in quo etiam sacerdotum è primoribus quidam versari erant soliti, vide quæ ad Marcum XII. 41.

Διδάσκων ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ) Id est, cum nunc hoc, nunc illo templi loco doceret.

Καὶ ὐδεὶς ἐπίασεν ἀυτὸν) κὲ pro Et tamen. De sensu vide supra VII. 31.

## 8:21
Vers. 21. ἐγὼ ὑπάγω) Since he knew that many of those standing by persisted in the plan of seizing him and procuring his death, he shows the vanity of that plan, as above VII. 33.

Καὶ ζητήσετέ με) That is, although you may wish to harm me greatly, you will not be able to.

Καὶ ἐν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ὑμῶν ἀποθανεῖσθε) It is taken from Ezekiel III. 19, where in the Greek it is ἐν τῇ ἀδικίᾳ αὑτῦ ἀποθανεῖται, from which passage the interpretation of this one must be taken. It will deservedly come to pass that I am placed beyond danger, and you perish most miserably on account of your own faults: because I have indeed performed the office of a monitor properly, but you were unwilling to listen to the one warning you. Moreover, the destruction of the city and the people is indicated: which was a presage of the universal judgment.

Ὄπυ ἐγὼ ὑπάγω ὑμεῖς ὐ δύνασθε ἐλθεῖν) You cannot reach that place, as above V. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐγὼ ὑπάγω) Cum sciret multos adstantium perstare in consilio se capiendi & mortem ipsi procurandi, ostendit ejus consilii vanitatem, ut supra VII. 33.
