Καὶ ζητήσετέ με) Id est, ut maxime velitis nocere mihi non poteritis.

Καὶ ἐν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ὑμῶν ἀποθανεῖσθε) Desumtum est ex Ezech III. 19. ubi in Græco ἐν τῇ ἀδικίᾳ αὑτῦ ἀποθανεῖται, ex quo loco sumenda est hujus interpretatio. Merito eveniet ut & ego extra periculum ponar, & vos ob culpas vestras pessime pereatis: quia ego quidem monitoris officio probe functus sum, vos autem monenti auscultare noluistis. In- dicatur autem urbis & populi excidium: quod universalis judicii præsagium fuit.

Ὄπυ ἐγὼ ὑπάγω ὑμεῖς ὐ δύνασθε ἐλθεῖν) Eo non potestis pertingere, ut supra V. 14.

## 8:22
Vers. 22. Μήτι ἀποκτενεῖ ἑαυτόν) Will he lay hands on himself after the example of Samson, lest we be able to mock him or inflict death upon him? For certain Hebrews thought that was lawful, as also appears from Josephus.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Μήτι ἀποκτενεῖ ἑαυτόν) Num sibi manus inferet Samsonis exemplo, ne nos ei illudere aut mortem inferre possimus? Nam id Hebræi quidam licitum putabant, ut ex Josepho quoque apparet.

## 8:23
Vers. 23. Ὑμεῖς ἐκ τῶ κάτω ἐσὶ) This ἐκ τῶ κάτω he immediately explains as ἐκ τῦ κόσμυ. Which does not signify origin, but affection, as is clear below XV. 19, where the Apostles are denied to be ἐκ τῦ κόσμε, to be occupied with the pursuits of the world.

Ἐγὼ ἐκ τῶ ἄνω εἰμί) Τὰ ἄνω) That is, I set my mind on things above, not on things on the earth, as Paul speaks in Colossians III. 2. And therefore it is no wonder if I am taken up to heavenly things.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Ὑμεῖς ἐκ τῶ κάτω ἐσὶ) Hoc ἐκ τῶ κάτω statim explicat ἐκ τῦ κόσμυ. Quod non originem significat, sed affectum, ut patet infra XV. 19. ubi Apostoli negantur esse ἐκ τῦ κόσμε, mundi studiis operari.

Ἐγὼ ἐκ τῶ ἄνω εἰμί) Τὰ ἄνω) Id est τὰ ἄνω φρονῶ, μὴ τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς γῆς ut loquitur Paulus Colossens. III. 2. Ac proinde non mirum est si ad superna assumar.

## 8:24
Vers. 24. Εἶπον ἖ν ὑμῖν ὅτι ἀποθανεῖσθε ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν) Here he interprets what he had said concerning their punishments to be understood of those who were addicted to their vices, and remained such.

Ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ πιστεύσητε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι) Where ἐγώ εἰμι is placed simply, it is to be understood of that which was being treated before. Thus Luke XXIV. 39, below XIIX. 5, is understood, JESUS. Here, however, the light of the world from verse 12, above chapter IV. v. 26, the Messiah.

Ἀποθανεῖσθε ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν) No better physician for your diseases will arrive. If you do not wish to be healed by me, you are incurable. See below XVI. 8, Hebrews X. 26.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Εἶπον ἖ν ὑμῖν ὅτι ἀποθανεῖσθε ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν) Hic interpretatur quod de pœnis eorum dixerat in- telligendum de iis qui vitiis suis addicti erant, ac tales ma- nebant.

Ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ πιστεύσητε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι) Ubi ἐγώ εἰμι sim- pliciter ponitur, intelligendum id de quo ante agebatur. Sic Luc. XXIV. 39. infra XIIX. 5. subauditur, J E S U S. Hic vero, lux mundi ex commate 12. supra c. IV. v. 26. Messias.

Ἀποθανεῖσθε ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν) Nullus melior morborum vestrorum medicus adveniet. Si à me sanari non vultis, insanabiles estis. Vide infra XVI.8. Hebr. X.26.

## 8:25
Vers. 25. Who are you? That is, what kind of person are you? Therefore Jesus answers with no noun.

Τὴν ἀρχὴν) First: כתחלה which the Greeks translate as τὴν ἀρχὴν: Christ says this, however, because he could have preached many other things about himself besides what he had said, but he is content with this for now.

Scaliger explains these words thus: τὴν ἀρχὴν, that is, first, in the beginning, primarily, ὅτι, but not ὅ τι, in the beginning I have many things to say, many things to preface concerning your stubbornness and unbelief, before I answer you as to who I am. But these things neither agree with the words nor are they relevant: a tautology would thus be committed. Because it is added, I have many things to say and to judge concerning you. Beza's explanation, that which I say to you from the beginning, has pleased many. We acknowledge with Lud. de Dieu that this has a convenient sense. Yet he finds some things lacking in it: First, that τὴν ἀρχὴν occupies the beginning of the sentence rather harshly, and by hyperbaton is construed with λαλῶ. Next, that ὅ, τι, which is a pronoun, is read with a comma; whereas, as Erasmus admits, the Greek codices consistently have ὅτι. Third, that the particle καὶ is useless, which is why Beza did not express it. Finally, that λαλῶ, I speak, is taken for λέγω, I say. Dievius says these things: He also adduces the Syriac interpretation, even if it were, that I had begun to speak with you: and the Arabic, even if I had already begun to speak with you. But he thinks that those do not agree with the Greek text: Beza, however, interprets the Syriac version differently, so as to render a sense consistent with his own exposition: and Paul Tarnovius explains the Arabic thus according to the Erpenian Codex: What I am, I have already begun to say, in conversing with you. Dievius discovered another and new interpretation of the Greek text, namely that ὅτι serves for an interrogation by virtue of the Hebrew כי, in this way: Do I even speak to you at all? or that it signifies ὄντως, really, truly, in the manner of the Hellenists, as in 1 John 3:20, in this sense: Am I even speaking to you at all in the first place? or with the emphasis of the article τὴν; in this fashion: is this the beginning of my even speaking to you? That is, is it now for the first time? Nothing here, in his judgment, is forced, neither the phrase nor the words, provided a mark of interrogation is added, and the sense is considered most convenient. But to us these things seem distorted. Whoever wishes may read many other expositions in Beza and Flacius, who repeated them from there in his Clavis Scripturae under the word 'Beginning'. We believe that this much-vexed answer of Christ can be explained quite conveniently if τὴν ἀρχὴν is an adverbial accusative, and signifies παντελῶς or ὅλως, altogether, plainly, just as Chrysostom in Homily LII, Euthymius, and Theophylact express it by ὅλως: and the most learned Camerarius showed this meaning from Plato, Demosthenes, Theognis, Herodotus, Xenophon, and Suidas, and warned in this place that it occurs so frequently in the writings of the Greeks that it is by no means doubtful or obscure. Moreover, the particle ὅτι can be taken like the Hebrew כי for the pronoun אשר, which (I am) altogether, which I also speak to you: see Glassius's Philologia Sacra, Book III, Tract 11, Canon XV. Thus there will be no need to divide the word and read ὅ, τι instead of ὅτι; and if the particle καὶ is expletive and redundant, the sense will be, I am altogether that which I speak, or say, to you. He had, however, said that he was the light of the world, and therefore the Messiah, according to the prophecy of Isaiah 49:6. Most all interpreters acknowledge that this sense underlies these words, even if they arrive at the same by one reason or another may they root out. Grotius seems to have understood the rest in the same way, he explained only the first word as 'first', whence that sense which he rendered arose: 'I am this first, which I also say to you': which explanation is more convenient than the interpretations of others: but since the adverbial sense of that accusative is more accepted by the Greeks, in the way we have stated, we prefer to understand the words of Christ.

Ὅτι κὴ λαλῶ ὑμῖν) I am this first, which I also say to you, this very thing which I said I am at this very time, that is, the light of the world. The Hebrew word מילה which the Syrian also placed here is accustomed to be translated by λαλεῖν: but the Hebrews explain that as saying something concisely, ἀποφθεγματικῶς, Matt. IX. 18, XIII. 3, 34, Mark II. 2, Luke XXIV. 24, John III. 34, and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Σὺ τίς εἶ;) Quis es, id est qualis es? ideo neutro nomine respondet Jesus.

Τὴν ἀρχὴν) Primum: כתחלה quod τὴν ἀρχὴν ver- tunt Græci: Hoc autem ideo dicit Christus quia multa alia de se prædicare poterat præter id quod dixerat, Sed eo nunc contentus est.

Scaliger hæc verba ita exponit: τὴν ἀρχὴν, id est, primum, principio, imprimis, ὅτι, non vero ὅ τι, principio multa mihi dicenda sunt, multa præfanda de vestra contumacia, & incredulitate, priusquam nobis respondeam quis ego sim. Sed hæc nec verbis congruunt, nec ad rem faciunt: ταυτολογία sic committeretur. Quia additur, multa habeo de vobis loqui, & judicare. Multis placuit Bezæ ex- plicatio id quod à principio dico vobis. Quam com- modum habere sensum cum Lud. de Dieu agnosci- mus. Nonnulla tamen ille in eadem desiderat: Primo quod τὴν ἀρχὴν dure satis initium sententiæ occupat, & per trajectiionem construitur cum λαλῶ. Deinde quod per ὑποδιασολὴν legatur ὅ, τι, quod, pronomen; quum, fatente Erasmo, Græci codices con- stanter habeant ὅτι. Tertio quod particula καὶ inuti- lis sit, quare & Beza eam non expressit. Denique quod λαλῶ loquor, accipiatur pro λέγω, dico. Hæc Dievius: Qui adducit etiam Syriacam interpreta- tionem, etiamsi esset, quod incepissem loqui vobis- cum: & Arabicam, etiamsi ego incepissem jam lo- qui vobiscum. Sed illa textui Græco non conve- nire putat: Aliter tamen interpretatur Syriacam versionem Beza, ut suæ expositioni congruum reddat sensum: & Arabicam ita exponit Paul. Tar- novius juxta Codicem Erpenian: Ego quid sum jam cœpi dicere, in colloquendo vobiscum. Dievius aliam eamque novam interpretationem textus Græci adinvenit, nimirum ὅτι ut Ebræorum כי in- terrogationi inservire virtute, hoc modo: Primumnē etiam loquor vobis? vel more Hellenistarum signi- ficari ὄντως, revera, utique ut 1. Joh. III.20. hoc sensu: Primumne utique etiam vos alloquor? aut cum ἔμ- φάσει articuli τὴν; hoc pacto: hocne principio utique etiam loquor vobis? Id est, an jam primum? Nihil hic, judicio ejus, coactum est, nec phrasis, nec verba, modo signum addatur interrogationis & sensus conve- nientissimus censetur. Sed nobis videntur hæc dis- torta. Plures alias ἐκθέσεις legere apud Bezam, & Flacium, qui inde illas repetiit in Clavi Scripturæ voce Principium, poterit, qui volet. Nos ita expli- cari per commode responsum illud Christi maxi- mopere vexatum posse censemus, ut τὴν ἀρχὴν accusativus sit adverbiascens, ac significet παντελῶς vel ὅλως omnino, plane, quemadmodum Chrysosto- mus Hom. LII. Euthymius & Theophylactus per ὅλως exprimunt:& eruditissimus Camerarius è Pla- tone, Demosthene, Theognide, Herodoto, Xenophonte, Suida significationem istam ostendit, eamque ita frequenter in Græcorum scriptis occurrere, ut nequa- quam dubia aut obscura sit, monuit in h. l. Particula autem ὅτι accipi potest, ut Ebræum כי pro prono- mine אשר, quod omnino (sum) quod & loquor vo- bis: vid. Gramm. Glassii sacra, l. III. tr. 11. Can. XV. Sic non opus erit dividere vocem & loco ὅτι lege- re ὅ, τι; ac si particula κὶ expletiva sit & redundet, sensus erit, omnino id (sum) quod loquor, vel dico vo- bis. Dixerat autem se lucem mundi esse, adeoq; Mes- siam, secundum vaticinium Es. XLIX. 6. Quem sen- sum plerique omnes Interpretes his verbis subesse agnoscunt, etsi alia atque alia ratione eundem eruant. Videtur eodem modo cætera accepisse Grotius, solum primam vocem exposuit primum, unde ille, quem reddidit, sensus ortus: Primum hoc sum, quod & dico vobis: quæ explicatio alio- rum interpretationibus commodior est: sed quum receptior Græcis sit adverbiascens accusativi istius sensus, eo quo diximus modo, verba Christi acci- pere malumus.

Ὅτι κὴ λαλῶ ὑμῖν) Primum hoc sum, quod & dico vobis, hoc ipsum quod me hoc ipso tempore esse dixi, id est lux mundi. Solet מילה Hebræum quod & hic posuit Syrus per λαλεῖν verti: id autem Hebræi explicant, dicere aliquid concise, ἀποφθεγματικῶς Matth. IX. 18. XIII. 3. 34. Marc. II. 2. Luc. XXIV. 24. Ioh. III. 34. & alibi.

## 8:26
Vers. 26.

Πολλὰ ἔχω περὶ ὑμῶν λαλεῖν κὴ κρίνειν) Concerning myself I say only this which I have said: but concerning you I could say many things to mark you out: for that is what it is to judge here, as we said above in chapter 15. As if he were to say: I could say that you are seducers and the causes of darkness.

Ἀλλ’ ὁ πέμψας με ἀληθής ἐστι) Let this suffice against you for this time, that he who sent me is most worthy of faith in all things.

Κ’ἀγὼ ἃ ἤκουσα παῤ αὐτῦ ταῦτα λέγω εἰς τὸν κόσμον) See above III. 32. The sense: He who sent me is worthy of faith, and I say nothing else than what I received from him to be said. Wherefore you ought deservedly to believe me, because since you do not do so, you are inexcusable. He does not, however, say simply 'I say to you', but εἰς τὸν κόσμον, so that he may more confirm what he had said, that he was the light of the world. For even the things he was saying to them, he was saying for this purpose, that they might be scattered more widely, and the place of the treasury itself was in the middle between the open court in which the Jews were, and the open court in which the foreigners were.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

Πολλὰ ἔχω περὶ ὑμῶν λαλεῖν κὴ κρίνειν) De me hoc tantum dico quod dixi: de vobis autem multa possem dicere ad vos notandos: id enim est hic judicare, ut su- pra 15. diximus. Quasi dicat: Possem dicere vos esse se- ductores & causas tenebrarum.

Ἀλλ’ ὁ πέμψας με ἀληθής ἐστι) Hoc adversum vos pro hoc tempore sufficiat, quod ille qui me misit in omnibus rebus fide est dignissimus.

Κ’ἀγὼ ἃ ἤκουσα παῤ αὐτῦ ταῦτα λέγω εἰς τὸν κόσμον) Vi- de supra III. 32. sensus. Qui me misit fide dignus est, & ego nihil dico aliud quam quod ab ipso dicendum accepi. Quare merito mihi credere deberetis, quod cum non facia- tis, estis inexcusabiles. Non dicit autem simpliciter vo- bis dico, sed εἰς τὸν κόσμον ut magis confirmet quod dixerat se esse lucem mundi. Nam & quæ ipsis dicebat, in hoc dice- bat, ut latius spargerentur, & locus ipse gazophylacii erat medius inter subdiale in quo erant Iudæi, & subdiale in quo erant alienigenæ.

## 8:27
Vers. 27.

Οὐκ ἔγνωσαν ὅτι τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῖς ἔλεγε) Understand τὸν πατέρα as God, whom the Hebrews called Father κατ’ ἐξοχὴν; which the Latin rightly expressed by interpreting it here. Most of the hearers did not understand him to be saying these things about God the Father: that God the Father was signified by the voice of him who sent him. For λέγω here is 'I signify', as it is often for the Latins.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

Οὐκ ἔγνωσαν ὅτι τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῖς ἔλεγε) Intellige τὸν πατέρα τὸν Θεὸν, quem Patrem κατ’ ἐξοχὴν Hebræi voca- bant; id quod recte hic interpretando expressit Latinus. Plerique de auditoribus non intelligebant eum hæc de Deo Patre dicere: Deum Patrem ab ipso mittentis voce signifi- cari. Nam λέγω hic est significo ut Latinis sæpe.

## 8:28
Vers. 28. Ὅταν) that is, after that, as Matt. IX. 15, Luke XIV. v. 8.

Ὑψώσητε) By your instigation you will have driven him onto the cross. See above c. III. 14, below XII. 32.

Τὸν ὑὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου) Thus above III. 13, 14.

Τότε γνώσεσθε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι) He had said first that he was the light of the world: what I am besides, he says, you will know after my passion, taking ὅ, τι here for τί. Then you will know that I am the victor over death, from the resurrection, the Lord of heaven and of the Angels from the ascension, the sender of the Holy Spirit himself, and finally the avenger of the rebellious. But you will know it, some by repenting, others so convinced that you will be able to deny it by no pretext.

In the Greek it is ὅτι, not ὅ, τι. Therefore the Vulgate: Because I am. Beza, that I am he, or that I am that one, or who, what I am. Moreover, because he had tacitly professed himself to be the Messiah, when he called himself the light of the world from Isaiah, by that profession he embraced all those things: because the Messiah is the victor over death, the Lord of heaven, the sender of the Spirit, and the avenger of the rebellious. With the prophets as witnesses.

Καὶ ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ ποιῶ ὐδὲν) κὴ for certainly, for indeed; what I said before, that I do nothing without the Father's command, that will then appear.

Ἀλλὰ καθὼς ἐδίδαξέ με ὁ πατὴρ [ταῦτα λαλῶ) See above V. v. 19. I recite the things dictated by the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Ὅταν) id est postquam ut Matth. IX. 15. Luc. XIV. v. 8.

Ὑψώσητε) Vestro incitatu in crucem egeritis. Vide supra c. III. 14. infra XII. 32.

Τὸν ὑὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου) Sic supra III. 13. 14.

Τότε γνώσεσθε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι) Dixerat primum lucem se esse mundi: quid præterea sim, inquit, cognoscetis post meam passionem, ὅ, τι hic sumo pro τί. Tunc cognoscetis me esse victorem mortis, ex resurrectione, Dominum cæli & An- gelorum ex ascensione, ipsius Spiritus Sancti missorem ac postremo vindicem rebellium. Cognoscetis autem alii re- sipiscendo, alii ita convicti ut nulla specie negare possitis.

In Græco est ὅτι, non ὅ, τι. Ideo Vulgata: Quia ego sum. Beza, me eum esse, vel quod ego ille sim, aut quis, quid ego sim. Cæterum quia Mes- siam tacite se professus erat, cum lucem mundi ex Esaia se vocavit, ea professione omnia illa comple- xus est: quia Messias victor mortis, Dominus cæli, missor Spiritus est, & vindex rebellium. Prophetis testibus.

Καὶ ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ ποιῶ ὐδὲν) κὴ pro certe, etenim; quod dixi antehac me nihil injussu Patris facere id tunc appare- bit.

Ἀλλὰ καθὼς ἐδίδαξέ με ὁ πατὴρ [ταῦτα λαλῶ) Vide supra V. v. 19. dictata Patris recito.

## 8:29
Vers. 29.

Καὶ ὁ πέμψας με, μετ’ ἐμᾶ ἐστι) Present for future as soon 31. & κὴ for therefore. Therefore, he says, he who sent me will clearly promote my affairs. For this is what the Hebraism signifies, to be with someone. See Matth. I. 22. & c. XXVIII. v. 19.

Οὐκ ἀφῆκέ με μόνον ὁ πατὴρ) He explains that which he had already said. Thus also below he opposes being alone and the Father being with him c. XVI. v. 32. Similarly that below XIV. 18. οὐκ ἀφήσω ὑμᾶς ὀρφανούς· ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς.

Ὅτι ἐγὼ τὰ ἀρεστὰ αὐτῷ ποιῶ πάντοτε) ποιῶ that is ἐποίησα. Christ's most perfect obedience is placed not only in this place but also elsewhere as the cause of the glory conferred upon him. See Philipp. cap. II. v. 8. And Es. LIII. 10. 11. 12.

The obedience of Christ is proposed not as the cause, but as the antecedent of the glory conferred. For He possessed that glory by reason of κτίσεως before He put on the form of a servant, having been made obedient to the Father, that is to say, as far as the order of nature is concerned: because He freely emptied Himself of the use of the same, as the Apostle testifies, (for the sake of our salvation) and afterwards, having endured the passion, He was exalted to the plenary use of the majesty communicated to Him.

PART III. Information concerning true liberty, and the true and false seed of Abraham.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

Καὶ ὁ πέμψας με, μετ’ ἐμᾶ ἐστι) Præsens pro futuro ut mox 31. & κὴ pro ideo. Ideo, inquit, qui me mi- sit plane res meas promovebit. Hoc enim significat He- braismus, cum aliquo esse. Vide Matth. I. 22. & c. XXVIII. v. 19.

Οὐκ ἀφῆκέ με μόνον ὁ πατὴρ) Explicat id quod jam dixerat. Sic & infra opponit solum esse & Patrem esse cum ipso c. XVI. v. 32. Similiter illud infra XIV. 18. ἐκ ἀφήσω ὑμᾶς ὀρφανός ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς.

Ὅτι ἐγὼ τὰ ἀρεστὰ αὐτῷ ποιῶ πάντοτε) ποιῶ id est ἐποίησα Christi perfectissima obedientia non hoc tantum in loco sed & alibi ponitur ut causa gloriæ ipsi collatæ. Vide Philipp. cap. II. v. 8. Et Es. LIII. 10. 11. 12.

Non ut causa, sed ut antecedens gloriæ col- latæ obedientia Christi proponitur. Gloriam in enim illam habuit ratione κτίσεως antequam ser- vi formam indueret, obediens Patri factus, quan- tum scil. ad naturæ ordinem: quia libere se usu ejusdem evacuavit, teste Apostolo, (nostræ salutis gratia) ac postmodum exantlata passione, ad plenarium usum majestatis communicatæ exaltatus est.

PARS III. De vera libertate, veroque & falso Abrahæ semine Informatio.

## 8:30
Vers. 30.

Πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς ἀυτὸν) That is, they believed he was sent by God, but with a weak faith.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

Πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς ἀυτὸν) Id est crediderunt à Deo missum, sed fide infirma.

## 8:31
Vers. 31.

Πρὸς τὲς πεπιστευκότας ἀυτῷ) Especially for their sake, although he is addressing his speech generally to the crowd.

Ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ) To remain in the word or in the teaching of Christ, as it is said in 2 John 9, is to observe the commandments, to which 'to transgress' is opposed.

The doctrine of Christ does not only embrace the commandments of morals or of a life to be passed piously, but primarily sets forth the Evangelical promises. In respect of which they remain in the doctrine or word of Christ who believe in Christ and persevere in faith.

Ἀληθῶς μαθηταί με ἐστὲ) Those are called disciples who come to hear: but the name of disciples truly belongs to those who propose to themselves what is taught as a norm. Quintilian on precocious talent: 'There is no true strength underneath, nor does it rest on deeply implanted roots.' See what we said above about the word μένειν at III. 36.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

Πρὸς τὲς πεπιστευκότας ἀυτῷ) Eorum præcipue causa, quanquam communiter ad turbam sermonem di- rigens.

Ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ) Μένειν ἐν τῷ λό- γῳ aut ἐν τῇ διδαχῇ Christi ut dicitur epistola II. 9. est ob- servare præcepta, cui opponitur παραβαίνειν.

Doctrina Christi non tantum præcepta com- plectitur morum seu vitæ pie transigendæ, sed imprimis Evangelicas promissiones exhibet. Qua- rum respectu manent in doctrina vel verbo Christi, qui credunt in Christum & in fide perse- verant.

Ἀληθῶς μαθηταί με ἐστὲ) Discipuli dicuntur qui auditum veniunt: vere autem illis discipulorum nomen competit, qui quod docetur sibi tanquam normam proponunt. Quin- tilianus de præcoci ingenio: Non subest vera vis nec penitus immissis radicibus innititur. Vide quæ de voce μένειν di- ximus supra III. 36.

## 8:32
Vers. 32. Καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν) By experiencing it you shall learn what truth is like. See what we said above about the word γινώσκειν at VI. 69. The Platonists establish one kind of knowledge as the mother of love, another as its daughter.

Καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς) That progress in the knowledge of true doctrine will render you free from the dominion of vices, and that both by the purity of the commandments and the excellence of the promises. Hierocles: 'For in ignorance of the better things, it is necessary to be a slave to the worse, from which it is not possible to be freed otherwise than by the turning of the soul to God through recollection.' Marinus on Proclus: 'For truth leads all good things for the gods, and all things for men.'

Of that liberty which we have through Christ, the Gentiles know nothing. And it renders us free not only from the dominion of vices, but primarily from the punishment of sins: both by the merit of his passion and by the efficacy of his word: rendering us free from the guilt of sin in justification, and from its dominion in sanctification: nor do the commandments contribute to our liberty; because from the law comes only the knowledge of sin, Rom. III. 21, and the law begets only εἰς τὴν δουλείαν, Gal. IV. 24.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν) Experiendo discetis, qualis sit veritas. Vide quæ de voce γινώσκειν diximus supra VI. 69. Platonici cognitionem quandam statuunt matrem amoris, alteram filiam.

Καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς) Profectus ille in co- gnitione veri dogmatis, vos liberos reddet à dominio vitio- rum, idque tum præceptorum puritate, tum promissorum præstantia. Hierocles: ἐν γὰρ τῇ ἀγνοίᾳ ̄τ κρειττόνων ἀνάγ- κη δουλεύειν τοῖς χείροσιν, ἂν ἐλευθερῶσαι ἄλλως ̓πχ οἷον τε ̄τῆ τῇ δι, ἀναμνήσεως ἐκ τῶν π̄ζ έ Θεὸν ἐπιστροφῇ. Marinus Proclo: ἀλήθεια γὰρ πάντων μὲν ἀγαθῶν θεοῖς ἡγεῖται, πάντων δὲ ἀνθρώποις.

De illa libertate, quam per Christum habemus nihil norunt gentiles. Nec à dominio vitiorum tantum, sed imprimis à peccatorum supplicio nos li- beros reddit: cum merito passionis suæ, tum efficacia verbi sui: à peccati reatu nos liberos reddens in ju- stificatione, à dominio in sanctificatione: neque ad libertatem nostram faciunt præcepta; quia ex lege tantum agnitio peccati Rom. III. 21. gignitque lex tantum εἰς τὴν δουλείαν Gal. IV. 24.

## 8:33
Vers. 33. σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ ἐσμὲν καὶ ὀυδενὶ δεδουλεύκαμεν πώποτε) As with water and bread, so also with servitude, the words are taken here κατ̓ ἀλληγορίαν, too much κατὰ πόδας. Men became slaves in two main ways: by being born of slaves, or by falling into captivity through the chance of war: they remove both from themselves. We are not born of Canaanites or other servile peoples. But we descend from Abraham through a legitimate path and free-born heads, and indeed no one has reduced us to servitude by war. This is not a matter of the liberty of public status, but of private.

Seldenus distinguishes between mere personal servitude, or a state inherent and intrinsic to the person, and extrinsic servitude, or that which is not entirely opposed to the dignity of liberty (with which, meanwhile, civil obedience, and the rights of blood and of lordship, and of marriage, and other things which belong to men who are free in every way, remain) when joined with it. But indeed, he says, since it is manifest that the negation of servitude in that saying of the Jews pertains as much to the whole nation itself or the seed of Abraham (by which name they wish, according to ancient tradition, only the Israelites to be contained, not the Ishmaelites or Edomites, however much both these and those are in truth from the descendants of Abraham) as to those themselves who were using it, and not to any part of their nation, that intrinsic servitude or that which changes the personal state of a man nor that there were any slaves at all to the Gentiles, whether Egyptians, Babylonians, or Romans, let alone themselves, who served such servitude (as has been said), nor finally did they ever judge that they served any other servitude than that which is not usually opposed to intrinsic is inherent to the person, but consists only in the performance of works and duties and in civil obedience; do they not deny here that they ever served that intrinsic servitude alone, taught by their ancestral discipline, and not that other or extrinsic one, which they acknowledged everywhere in a people either conquered or received into surrender?

How do you say, that you will be made free] The ὅτι is redundant, as it is often elsewhere. Both laws and reason teach that a free man cannot be manumitted.

Latin:

Vers. 33. σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ ἐσμὲν καὶ ὀυδενὶ δεδουλεύκαμεν πώποτε) Ut de aqua & pane, ita & de servitute dicta, κατ̓ ἀλ- ληγορίαν verba sumuntur hic nimium κατὰ πόδας. Duobus maxime modis homines servi fiebant, nascendo ex servis, aut bellico casu incidendo in captivitatem: Utrumque à se removent. Non sumus nati ex Cananæis aliisve ser- vilibus populis. Sed per legitimum tramitem & ingenua ca- pita ab Abrahamo usque descendimus, tum vero nemo nos in servitutem bello redegit. Non agitur hic de libertate status publici sed privati.

Seldenus distinguit inter servitutem mere perso- nalem, seu statum personæ inhærentem & intrinse- cam, & servitutem extrinsecam, seu eam, quæ liber- tatis cum civili interim obedientia conjuncta digni- tati (qua cum & jura sanguinis & Dominii, & nu- ptiarum alia, quæ hominum sunt undiquaque libero- rum, manent) non omnino opponitur. Sed vero, in- quit, cum manifestum sit, servitutis negationem in Judæorum illo dicto, tam ad gentem ipsam attinere to- tam seu Abrahæ semen (quo nomine solos Israëlitas, non Ismaëlitas aut Edomitas contineri ex veteri tra- ditione volunt, utcunque tam hi quam illi revera ex A- brahæ posteris) quam ad ipsos qui illo uterentur, nec eos gentis suæ partem aliquam, servitutem illam intrinsecam seu quæ statum hominis personalem mu- tat, unquam servisse ex disciplina sua admitterent, nec Gentilibus sive Aegyptiis, sive Babylonis, sive Romanis servos omnino aliquos, nedum seipsos, fuisse qui hujusmodi servitutem servirent, (ut dictum est) nec aliam demum servitutem servisse se unquam decernerent, præter illam quæ libertati intrinsecæ seu personæ inhærenti non opponi solet, sed in operis & munerum præstationibus ac obedientia civili tantum consistit; nonne illam solum servitutem intrinsecam serviisse se unquam heic negant, ex disciplina avita edocti, non alteram illam seu extrinsecam, quæ in populo sive devicto sive in deditionem recepto nullibi non agnovere?

Πῶς σὺ λέγεις, ὅτι ἐλεύθεροι γενήσεσθε] Abundat ὅτι ut alibi sæpe. Liberum hominem non posse manumitti & leges & ratio docent.

## 8:34
Ver. 34. Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin] See Matt. VII. 23 for what it means to commit sin. He is a slave of sin because he is carried and driven by that vice to which he is devoted as if he were a captive, אסיר Isaiah XLII. 7. Horace on love: 'For a master not gentle presses the mind and applies sharp goads to the weary.' Cicero in the Paradoxes: 'If slavery is the obedience of a broken and abject mind that lacks its own judgment, who would deny that all the fickle, all the covetous, in short, all the wicked are slaves? Or is he free to me, whom a woman commands,' and what follows there. Philo excellently develops this statement: 'that every good man is free.' Add Rom. ch. VI. 16, 2 Pet. II. 19, and Prov. V. 22. Moreover, Christ's gentleness shines forth in the fact that He pronounces these things without yet naming the persons to whom He was speaking, in case they might be corrected by that means.

Latin:

Vers. 34. Πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν δοῦλός ἐστι τῆς ἁμαρτίας] ποιεῖν ἁμαρτίαν quid sit vide Matth. VII. 23. δοῦλος ἐστι τῆς ἁμαρτίας quia ab illo vitio cui studet tanquam captivus fertur atque agitur, אסיר Esaia XLII. 7. Horatius de amore: Vrget enim mentem dominus non lenis & acres Subjectat lasso stimulos. Cicero Paradoxis: Si servitus sit obedientia fracti animi atque abjecti & arbitrio carentis suo, quis neget omnes leves, omnes cupidos, omnes denique improbos esse servos? An ille mihi liber, cui mulier imperat & quæ ibi sequuntur. Egregie hoc dictum exsequitur Philo: ὅτι πᾶς ὁ σπουδαῖος ἐλεύθερος. Adde Rom. c. VI. 16. 2. Pet. II. 19. & Prov. V. 22. Elucet autem Christi lenitas in eo quod hæc pronuntiat nondum nominatis personis in quas diceret. Si forte ea ratione emendarentur.

## 8:35
Ver. 35. But the slave does not remain in the house forever] לעולם, that is, for the whole time of his life: as in Horace: 'He will be a slave forever who does not know how to use a little.' He does not dwell, that is, he has the right of dwelling in the house: just as we have warned several times above that ἔχειν is taken. Note, however, that the comparison is tacitly changed. For it passes from a slave of the passions to a slave with respect to the house. Thus in Rom. VII, it passes from the death of a husband to the death of him who is as if bound to the law. And many similar things occur in this kind of discourse.

The son remains forever] He has the right of dwelling in the house: for, as the jurists speak, he is as it were the master of his father's property, the young master in the comedies. Cf. Gen. XXI. 28, Gal. IV. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 35. Ὁ δὲ δοῦλος οὐ μένει ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα] לעולם id est toto vitæ suæ tempore: ut apud Horatium: Serviet æternum qui parvo nescies uti. Non habitat id est jus habet habitandi in domo: sicut ἔχειν sumi supra monuimus aliquoties. Nota autem tacite mutari talationem. Nam à servo affectuum transitur ad servum respectu domus. Sic Rom. VII. à morte mariti transitur ad mortem ejus qui legi quasi devinctus est. Et similia multa in hoc genere sermonum occurrunt.

Ὁ υἱὸς μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα] Jus habet in domo habitandi: nam, ut Jurisconsulti loquuntur, est quasi dominus rerum paternarum, herus minor in Comœdiis. Conf. Genes. XXI. 28. Gal. IV. 30.

## 8:36
Ver. 36. If therefore the Son shall make you free] There was in certain cities of Greece, and perhaps used elsewhere, ἀδελφοθεσία, an adoption into brotherhood, which seems to be alluded to here. If the Son makes you free from being slaves, and at the same time co-heirs with Himself. This is attributed here to the Son, which was just now attributed to the truth, because the Son brings it forth.

You shall be free indeed] Not by a false persuasion, but in reality, Luke XXIV. 34, 2 Pet. II. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Ἐὰν οὖν ὁ υἱὸς ὑμᾶς ἐλευθερώσῃ] Erat in Græciæ quibusdam civitatibus, forte & alibi usitata ἀδελφοθεσία adoptio in fratres, quo hic videtur alludi. Si filius vos ex servis faciat liberos, simulque sibi cohæredes. Tribuitur hic Filio, quod modo veritati, quia eam profert Filius.

Ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι ἔσεσθε] Non falsa persuasione, sed reipsa, Luc. XXIV. 34. 2. Petr. II. 18.

## 8:37
Ver. 37. I know that you are Abraham's seed] In that common sense, not in that κατ' ὑπόνοιαν by which those are said to be born of someone who form their mind by his example or precepts. See what is above in chapter III. Σπέρμα, וזרע, is a Hebraism for offspring, Gen. IV. 25, and elsewhere passim.

But you seek to kill me] The emphasis is on με: me, who am innocent, and known to them as nothing but good.

Because my word does not find a place in you] χωρεῖν among the Hellenists is to go, to pass, Wisd. X. 23, 24, and ἐν ὑμῖν for εἰς ὑμᾶς as often in these books, Matt. XVI. 28, Heb. IV. 11. Closest to this locution is that in 1 Thess. I. 8, 'in every place your faith toward God has gone forth.' The sense is: You intend death for me for this reason, because my precepts are too holy to penetrate into your minds, which are overgrown with vices. Christ says this indeed to the whole crowd, but marking those whom He knew wished Him ill, and thus we are accustomed to attribute to the people what applies to some of the people.

Latin:

Vers. 37. Οἶδα ὅτι σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ ἐστε] Sensu illo vulgari, non illo κατ' ὑπόνοιαν quo nati ex aliquo dicuntur qui ejus exemplo aut præceptis animum informant. Vide quæ supra cap. III. Σπέρμα וזרע pro sobole Hebraismus est Gen. IV. 25. & alibi passim.

Ἀλλὰ ζητεῖτέ με ἀποκτεῖναι] Emphasis est in με: me innocentem, nec nisi beneh iis cognitum.

Ὅτι ὁ λόγος ὁ ἐμὸς οὐ χωρεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν] χωρεῖν apud Hellenistas est vadere, transire Sap. X. 23. 24. & ἐν ὑμῖν pro εἰς ὑμᾶς ut sæpe in his libris, Matth. XVI. 28. Hebr. IV. 11. Proximum huic locutioni est illud 1. Thess. I. 8 ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν ἡ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν ἐξελήλυθεν. Sensus est: Ideo mihi mortem intentatis, quia præcepta mea sanctiora sunt, quam ut in animos vestrum vitiis obsitum penetrent. Dicit autem Christus hoc toti quidem turbæ, sed eos notans quos sibi sciebat male velle, & sic solemus quod aliquibus de populo competit, tribuere populo.

## 8:38
Ver. 38. I speak what I have seen with my Father] I say those things which I have learned from the Father. For as ὁρᾷν, so ἀκούειν means to learn.

And you do what you have seen with your father] Some books have ὃ ἑωράκατε and here ἠκούσατε, but as an interpretation, I think. I do not think a certain father is designated here: but this is said: do what you have learned so that it may appear who your Father or Teacher is: whether Abraham, that is, or the wicked spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ἐγὼ ὃ ἑώρακα παρὰ τῷ πατρί μου λαλῶ] Ea dico quæ à Patre didici. Nam ut ὁρᾷν ita ἀκούειν est discere.

Καὶ ὑμεῖς ὃν ὃ ἑωράκατε παρὰ τῷ πατρὶ ὑμῶν ποιεῖτε] Quidam libri ὃ ἑωράκατε habent & hic ἠκούσατε, sed ex interpretamento ut arbitror. Non puto hic certum patrem designari: sed hoc dici: facite quæ didicistis ut appareat quis sit Pater sive Doctor vester: Abrahamne scilicet an spiritus nequam.

## 8:39
Vers. 39. Our father is Abraham] Because Christ had spoken ambiguously about their father, they repeat what they had said, but more effectively, as if to say that they refuse to acknowledge any other father than Abraham, and that they glory in him as their parent. See Matt. III. 9. Therefore Christ now replies more pressingly to this concession.

If you were Abraham's children, you would do the works of Abraham] If you acknowledged him as father and leader, you would do works similar to his works. Among the Hebrews, one is called a father even if one is not born of him, if he conducts himself as if he held him for a father: such as that one: Nor is a goddess your parent, nor is Dardanus the author of your race. See Ezek. XVI. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 39. Ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν Ἀβραάμ ἐστι] Quia ambigue Christus locutus erat de patre ipsorum, repetunt quod dixerant, sed efficacius, quasi dicant, nolle se alium patrem agnoscere quam Abrahamum, eo se parente gloriari. Vide Matth. III. 9. Ideo Christus jam ex hoc concesso pressius respondet.

Εἰ τέκνα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἦτε, τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἐποιεῖτε] Si eum pro patre ac duce agnosceretis opera faceretis ipsius operibus similia. Hebræis pater vocatur etiam ex quo quis natus non est, si hic ita se gerat quasi eum pro patre habeat: qualis & illa: Nec tibi diva parens, generis nec Dardanus auctor Vid. Ezech. XVI. 3.

## 8:40
Vers. 40. But now you seek to kill me] This 'but now' is oppositional; it notes in them two works very contrary to the works of Abraham: hatred of one's neighbor even to the shedding of blood, and contempt for the truth, and indeed divine truth. We said above that these things are said generally, because either in that crowd, or certainly among the people, many were such.

A man] Which itself was enough to commend me to you. For there is among men a certain kinship instituted by GOD, for which reason He willed that all should arise from one. See Acts XVII. v. 26.

Who have spoken the truth to you] The discourse ascends. Not just any man, but one who teaches you the most true things and therefore deserves faith and thanks.

Which I heard from God] It ascends further. Not just any truth, but that which I learned from God. For this is what 'I heard' means, as it has several times above. If every truth is worthy of being loved for its own sake, how much more that which has God as its author?

Abraham did not do this] 'This', that is, such a thing. Abraham was a lover of men: he freed captives: he received strangers with hospitality: he admitted into his mind the truth revealed to him in the name of God, although it seemed less credible. These are the works of Abraham, by which his true posterity is known. Rom. IV. IX. 8. Gal. III. 6. Justin in his dialogue with Trypho: 'But if you, remaining heirs, do not wish to agree with the truth because of the death appointed for the Christians, you will appear to be the cause of it to yourselves and you deceive yourselves, supposing that because you are the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, you will by all means inherit the good things announced to be given by Christ; for no one, not even those, has anything to receive except those who have been made like in mind to the faith of Abraham.'

Latin:

Vers. 40. Νῦν δὲ ζητεῖτέ με ἀποκτεῖναι] Hoc νῦν δὲ est op- positivum; duo in illis notat opera Abrahami operibus val- de adversa, odium proximi ad suffusionem usque sanguinis, & contemptum veritatis & quidem divinæ. Diximus su- pra communiter hæc dici, quia aut in turba ista, aut certe in populo multi tales erant.

Ἄνθρωπον] Quod ipsum satis erat ut me vobis commen- daret. Est enim inter homines cognatio quædam à DEO instituta, ideo omnes ab uno oriri voluit. Vid. Actor. XVII. v. 26.

Ὃς τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὑμῖν λελάληκα] Ascendit oratio. Non quemvis hominem, sed qui verissima vos doceo ac proinde fidem & gratiam mereor.

Ἣν ἤκουσα παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ] Ascendit amplius. Nec quam- vis veritatem, sed eam quam à Deo didici. Hoc enim est ἤκουσα ut supra aliquoties. Si omnis veritas per se amari di- gna est, quanto magis illa quæ Deum habet auctorem?

Τοῦτο Ἀβραὰμ οὐκ ἐποίησεν] τοῦτο id est tale quid. Abra- hamus hominum amans fuit: captivos liberavit: peregri- nos hospitio excepit: veritatem divino nomine sibi revela- tam, quanquam in speciem minus credibilem, admisit in animum. Hæc sunt Abrahami opera, quibus ejus vera po- steritas cognoscitur Rom IV. IX. 8. Gal. III. 6. Iustinus col- loquio cum Tryphone : ἐὰν δὲ ὑμεῖς (κληρονόμοι μένοντες ὦ ἀπὸ σπᾶς τὴν γνώμην διὰ τὸν ἀφορισμένον ταῖς Χριστιανοῖς θάνατον τῇ ἀληθεῖ συντίθεσθαι μὴ βούλησθε, - ἑαυτοῖς αἴτιοι φανήσεσθε καὶ ἐξαπατᾶτε ἑαυτούς, ὑπονοοῦντες διὰ τὸ εἶναι τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ και τὰ σάρκα σπέρμα, πάντως κληρονομήσειν τὰ κατηγγελμένα παρὰ τοῦ Χριστᾶ δοθήσεσθαι ἀγαθά· οὐδεὶς γὰρ οὐδὲ ἐκείνων οὐδε- μόθεν λαβεῖν ἔχει πλὴν οἱ τῇ γνώμῃ᾽ ἐξομοιωθέντες τῇ πίστει τοῦ Ἀβραάμ.

## 8:41
Vers. 41. You do the works of your father] The rebuke proceeds little by little. He sufficiently shows that Abraham is not morally their father. Now he indicates that their father is someone far different, whom, however, he does not yet name, awaiting voluntary repentance.

We were not born of fornication] 'Of fornication' is said here as 'of circumcision' in Acts X. 45, XI. 2, that is, 'of the circumcised' in Gal. II. 7, 8, 9, Ephes. II. 11. The sense is: we were not born of fornicators, that is, idolaters, whom Moses and the Prophets call fornicators in a metaphorical sense. As if to say: if you are dealing not with the birth of the body but of the mind, even so there is nothing you can object against us. We are not children of whoredom, as Hosea speaks in II. 4.

We have one father, God] We do not have many whom we worship: we worship one God: whom we also call by this name of father, Jerem. III. 4. Even idolaters called their gods fathers, whence Jupiter, Marspiter, and the like.

Latin:

Vers. 41. Ὑμεῖς ποιεῖτε τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν] Paulatim procedit castigatio. Satis ostendit Abrahamum moraliter patrem eorum non esse. Jam indicat alium longe diver- sum esse eorum patrem, quem tamen nondum nominat, expectans voluntariam resipiscentiam.

Ἡμεῖς ἐκ πορνείας ὐ γεγεννήμεθα] ἐκ πορνείας hic dictum est ut ἐκ περιτομῆς Act. X. 45. XI. 2. id est ἐκ ἳ περιτετμημένων Gal. II. 7. 8. 9. Ephes. II. 11. Sensus est non nati sumus ex scortatoribus id est idololatris, quos scortatores sensu trala- titio vocant Moses & Prophetæ. Quasi dicant: si non de nativitate corporis sed animi agis, etiam sic nihil est quod nobis objicias. Non sumus בְּנֵי זְנוּנִים τέκνα πορνείας ut loquitur Oseas II. 4.

Ἕνα πατέρα ἔχομεν τὸν Θεὸν] Non plures habemus quos colamus: unum Deum colimus: quem etiam hoc nomine patris appellamus, Jerem. III. 4. Etiam idololatræ Deos suos patres vocabant, unde Jupiter, Marspiter & similia.

## 8:42
Vers. 42. If God were your father] If, as you profess, you sincerely worshipped God as Father.

you would love me] It is fair that he who loves someone should also love those whose works he himself uses, especially for excellent things.

Ἐγὼ γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ Θεᾶ ἐξῆλθον κὴ ἥκω] That is, having come forth, I am here. I am present, sent from God. The word ἐξέρχεσθαι is often used by John in this sense, XVI. 27, 28, 30, XVII. 8. See what was said above at I. 8 concerning the word ἐξέρχεσθαι. The interpretation follows: οὐκ᾿ ἀπ᾿ ἐμαυτοῦ μὲ ἀ- πέστειλε.

Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀπ᾿ ἐμαυτοῦ ἐλήλυθα] As those who falsely arrogate to themselves the office of prophet, Jer. XXIII. 21. Concerning the expression ἀπ᾿ ἐμαυτοῦ, we spoke above at V. 30.

PARS IV. Confirmation of the life-giving truth of the Word of Christ: on account of whose day Abraham also rejoiced, and that He Himself existed before Abraham.

Latin:

Vers. 42. Εἰ ὁ Θεὸς πατὴρ ὑμῶν ἦν] Si, ut profitemini Deum tanquam Patrem sincere coleretis.

ἠγαπᾶτε ἂν ἐμέ] Æquum est, ut qui aliquem amat, amet & eos quorum opera ipse, maxime ad res eximias, utitur.

Ἐγὼ γὰρ ἐκ τοῦ Θεᾶ ἐξῆλθον κὴ ἥκω] Id est ἐξελθὼν ἥκω. Α Deo missus adsum. Vox ἐξέρχεσθαι sæpe apud Johannem est hoc sensu XVI. 27. 28. 30. XVII. 8. Vide quæ supra I. 8. de voce ἐξέρχεσθαι. Interpretatio sequitur οὐκ᾿ ἀπ᾿ ἐμαυτοῦ μὲ ἀ- πέστειλε.

Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀπ᾿ ἐμαυτοῦ ἐλήλυθα] Ut qui falso sibi prophetæ munus arrogant, Jer. XXUI. 21. de locutione ἀπ᾿ ἐμαυτοῦ supra diximus V. 30.

PARS IV. De Verbi Christi veritate vivifica confirma- tio: ob cujus diem Abraham etiam gavisus, & quod ante Abrahamum ipse extiterit.

## 8:43
Vers. 43. Διὰ τί τὴν λαλιὰν ἐμὴν ὐ γινώσκετε] If God is your Father, why do you not recognize in me His ἰδίωμα, His character of speaking? Sons are accustomed to recognize their father's tongue. Thus He calls His own manner of teaching plainly divine.

Ὅτι ὐ δύνασθε ἀκούειν τὸν λόγον ἐμόν] In order for someone's dialect to be recognized, some attention is needed, for instance whether שָׁכַלְתְּ is said or שָׂכַלְתְּ, Jud. XII. 6. You cannot hear, that is, you cannot patiently bear me speaking. Thus they are said to be unable to whom a vehement passion is an obstacle. We spoke at Mark ch. VI. v. 5 regarding ἀκούειν as to hear attentively, Matt. ch. XI. v. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 43. Διὰ τί τὴν λαλιὰν ἐμὴν ὐ γινώσκετε] Si Deus Pa- ter est vester, cur in me non agnoscitis ipsius ἰδίωμα; lo- quendi characterem ? solent filii agnoscere linguam pater- nam. Sic vocat suam docendi rationem plane divinam.

Ὅτι ὐ δύνασθε ἀκούειν τὸν λόγον ἐμόν] Ut agnoscatur dia- lectus alicujus, artentione aliqua opus est, puta שָׁכַלְתְּ dicatur an שָׂכַלְתְּ Jud. XII. 6. Vos non potestis audire id est patienter ferre me loquentem. Sic non posse dicun- tur quibus affectus vehemens obstat. Diximus ad Marc. cap. VI. vers. 5. ἀκούειν attente audire Matth. cap. XI. v. 15.

## 8:44
Vers. 44. You are of your father the devil. By 'devil' on account of those things which will shortly follow, I here understand the genus of devils, just as also 'the Satan' in Matt. XII. 26. Thus 'man' is often the human race, IV. 4, for which 'the son of man' is said in Matt. XII. 8. Thus Acts XIII. 10, 'son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness'; our 1 Epist. III. 8, 'he who does sin is of the devil'.

And you wish to do the desires of your father. 'Desires', that is, what is pleasing to him. Thus 2 Tim. IV. 3, 1 Pet. c. IV. 2, 'to do a desire' as 'to fulfill a desire', Gal. V. 16.

He was a murderer from the beginning. We said above that two things are especially noted by Christ in the Jews: a purpose of slaughter, and a contempt for truth. From these two he proves that they reflect the nature of the devil. The Hellenists place 'from the beginning' where in the Hebrew is מעולם, as Jos. XXIV. 2, Eccl. XIII. 16, 19. Thus Acts XXVI. 4, and 1 Epist. III. 8, 'the devil sins from the beginning'. Moreover, he was a murderer by the same act by which he was a liar, when he enticed the first humans into sin by evil guile, from which death was to follow. 'By the envy of the devil death entered into the world', Wisd. II. 24. But Paul, looking to the same, says: 'through one man sin entered into the world and through sin death', Rom. V. 12. The Rabbis, and Maimonides himself, feel that Adam fell into crime on the very day he was created.

And he has not stood in the truth. Affirmation through the negation of the contrary; the sense is: he has turned away from the truth. Thus Ps. I. v. 1.

Because there is no truth in him. That is, because there is no zeal for truth in him. Thus 1 Ep. II. 21, 'every lie is not of the truth', that is, is not from a zeal for truth; 1 Macc. VII. 18, closer to our phrase: 'there is no truth and judgment in them. For they transgressed the covenant and the oath which they swore'.

When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own. He speaks according to his own nature.

Because he is a liar. It is his custom to deceive: he loves this, therefore he is called רוח שקר, a lying spirit. 1 Kings XXII. 22, 2 Chron. c. XVIII. 21. Porphyry concerning spirits of this kind: 'for a lie is natural to them'.

And his father. The father of the genus of devils is 'the ruler of the demons'; concerning whom we spoke at Matt. IX. 34, 'the ruler of the authority of the air' Eph. II. 2, 'the ruler of this world' below XII. 31, XIV. v. 36, XVI. 11. Here he is called the father of the others because he gave the beginning of falling away, just as the word 'father' is used both elsewhere and in Gen. IV. 20, 21. He who had deceived Adam was not the 'ruler' himself, but someone sent by him: an Angel of Satan as in 2 Cor. XII. 7.

It is not the Father of the Devil that is indicated here, or of the genus of Devils: but 'the devil' is called the Father of the lie, which name is contained in the word 'liar', according to most, which Casaubon illustrates from Num. XXIII. v. 24, 'and I have blessed, and I will not revoke it', i.e., the blessing, which example, however, B. Glassius observed does not fit, in Gramm. S. p. 178. According to Heinsius and Glassius (to whom we add our vote), 'when he speaks a lie' precedes explicitly because he speaks a lie, and his (the lie's) father is [the devil], since it is not new that what is later in order is referred not to that which is nearest, but to that which precedes. Heinsius also brings another explanation: from a book inscribed 'Chronology of the Saints': When he speaks a lie, here it must be understood, 'each one of you speaks from his own': because he is a liar and his father, i.e., the Devil. All of which hold much more correctly than that commentary about the Father of the genus of devils: For as I said, the Devil himself is called the Father here: but by 'devil' Grotius v. 44 understands the genus of Devils: whence this sense will emerge: The Devil, that is, the genus of devils, is a liar, and the Father of the genus of devils. But what is this, the genus of Devils is the Father of the genus of Devils? How many sick dreams have been born from the fact that they gave a father to the Devil from this passage? Epiphanius thinks the Devil is Judas, his father Cain. Others wanted the father of the Devil to be Leviathan, as Jerome notes in Isaiah XXIV: To Grotius, the father of the genus of Devils is 'the ruler of the demons', whom he nevertheless does not want to have deceived Adam. But here the discourse is entirely about the author of the seduction, even by

Grotius's own admission: For thus to v. 44, 'he was a murderer', he was a murderer by the same act by which he was a liar, when he enticed the first humans into sin by evil guile, from which death was to follow. 'By the envy of the devil death entered into the world', Wisd. II. v. 24. But Paul, looking to the same, 'through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death', Rom. V. v. 12. And that the serpent who seduced Eve was the father of the other Demons is sufficiently indicated in Gen. III. 15, when the others are called his seed. See our Commentary on Genesis at that place.

Latin:

Vers. 44. Ὑμεῖς ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς τοῦ διαβόλου ἐστὲ) Διάβολον ob ea quæ mox sequentur hic intelligo genus diabolorum, quomodo & ὁ Σατανᾶς, Matth. XII. 26. Sic ἄνθρωπος sæpe est genus humanum IV. 4. pro quo ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου dicitur Matth. XII. 8. Sic Act. XIII. 10. υἱὲ διαβόλου, ἐχθρὲ πάσης δι- καιοσύνης noster 1. epist. III. 8. ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐκ τοῦ διαβόλου ἐστίν.

Καὶ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν θέλετε ποιεῖν) ἐπιθυ- μίας id est quod ei collibitum est. Sic 2. Tim. IV. 3. 1. Petr. c. IV. 2. ποιεῖν ἐπιθυμίαν ut τελεῖν ἐπιθυμίαν, Gal. V. 16.

Ἐκεῖνος ἀνθρωποκτόνος ἦν ἀπ' ἀρχῆς) Diximus supra duo à Christo in Judæis maxime notari, cædis proposi- tum, & veritatis contemtum. Ex his duobus probat eos referre ingenium diaboli. ἀπ' ἀρχῆς Hellenistæ ponunt ubi in Hebræo est מעולם ut Jos. XXIV. 2. Eccl. XIII. 16. 19. Sic Act. XXVI. 4. & 1. Epist. III. 8. ἀπ' ἐνὶ ἀρχῆς ὁ διάβολος ἁμαρτάνει. Homicida autem fuit eodem actu quo mendax, tum primos homines dolo malo in peccatum illexit, unde mors erat secutura. Invidia diaboli mors intravit in mun- dum, Sap. II. 24. At Paulus eodem respiciens di ind. δι᾽ ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε κὴ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θάνατος, Rom. V. 12. Adamum quo die erat conditus lapsum in cri- men sentiunt Rabbini, & ipse Maimonides.

Καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ οὐκ ἕστηκεν) Affirmatio per negatio- nem contrarii, sensus est: deflexit à veritate. Sic Ps. I. v. 1.

Ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἀλήθεια ἐν αὐτῷ) Id est quia non est in ipso studium veritatis. Sic 1. Ep II. 21. πᾶν ψεῦδος ἐκ τῆς ἀληθείας οὐκ ἔστι, non est ex studio veritatis, 1. Macc. VII. 18. propius ad nostram phrasin : οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀλήθεια καὶ κρίσις. Παρέ- βησαν γὰρ τὴν στάσιν καὶ τὸν ὅρκον ὃν ὤμοσαν.

Ὅταν λαλῇ τὸ ψεῦδος ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων λαλεῖ) Loquitur pro ingenio suo.

Ὅτι ψεύστης ἐστὶ) In more habet fallere: hoc amat, ideo vocatur רוח שקר πνεῦμα ψευδές. I. Reg. XXII. 22. 2. Paral. c. XVIII. 21. Porphyrius de hujus generis spiritibus, τὸ γὰρ ψεῦδος αὐτοῖς οἰκεῖον.

κὴ ὁ πατὴρ αὐτῦ) Pater generis diabolorum est ὁ ἄρχων τῶν δαιμονίων; de quo diximus ad Matt. IX. 34. ὁ ἄρχων τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος Eph. II. 2. ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμου τούτου infra XII. 31. XIV. v. 36. XVI. 11. Hic pater cæterorum dicitur quia deficiendi initium dedit, quomodo vox patris usurpatur tum alibi, tum Gen. IV. 20. 21. Qui Adamum deceperat non fuit ipse ὁ ἄρ- χων, sed aliquis ab eo submissus: Angelus Satanæ ut 2. Cor. XII. 7.

Non hic Pater Diaboli indigitatur, seu generis Diabolorum: sed ὁ διάβολος dicitur Pater mendacii, quod nomen in voce ψεύστης continetur, juxta ple- rosque, quod Casaubonus illustrat ex Num. XXIII. v. 24. & benedixi, nec revocabo illam sc. benedictio- nem, quod vero exemplum non quadrare observa- vit B. Glassius in Gramm. S. p. 178. juxta Heinsium vero & Glassium (quibus calculum adjicimus) διαῤῥήδην antecedit ὅταν λαλῇ τὸ ψεῦδος quia lo- quitur mendacium, & Pater ejus (mendacii) est, si- quidem novum non sit, quod ordine est posterius non ad id, quod proxime, sed tamen quod præces- sit, referri. Adfert & aliam explicationem Hein- sius: ex libro cui inscriptio Chronologia Sanctorum: Cum loquitur mendacium, hic subaudiendum est, unusquisque vestrum, ex propriis loquitur: quia mendax est & Pater ejus, sc. Diabolus. Quæ omnia longe rectius se habent quam commentarius ille de Patre generis diabolorum: Nam ut dixi, ipse Dia- bolus hic Pater dicitur: per διάβολον autem Gro- tius v. 44. intelligit genus Diabolorum: unde hic emerget sensus: Diabolus, id est, genus diabolo- rum mendax est, & Pater generis diabolorum. Quid vero hoc est, genus Diabolorum Pater est generis Diabolorum? Quot etiam ægrorum so- mnia inde nata, quod ex hoc loco patrem de- derint Diabolo? Epiphanius Diabolum Judam esse putat, patrem ejus Cainum. Alii Patrem Diaboli Leviathan esse voluerunt, notante Hie- ronymo in XXIV. Esaiæ: Grotio Pater generis Diabolorum est ὁ ἄρχων τῶν δαιμονίων, quem tamen non vult decepisse Adamum. At hic de autore seductionis omnino sermo est, ipso etiam

Grotio autore: Sic enim ad v. 44. ἐκεῖνος ἀν- θρωποκτόνος ἦν, homicida fuit eodem actu, quo mendax, cum primos homines dolo malo in pec- catum illexit, unde mors erat secutura. Invidia diaboli mors intravit in mundum, Sap. II. v. 24. At Paulus eodem respiciens δι᾽ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρ- τία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε, καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θά- νατος, Rom. V. v. 12. Et serpentem qui seduxit Evam, Patrem aliorum Dæmonum fuisse satis in- dicatur Gen. III. 15. cum cæteri semen ejus di- cuntur. Vid. Commentar. noster in Genesin ad istum locum.

## 8:45
Vers. 45. But because I speak the truth, you do not believe me. It is a Hebraism such as Ps. LXXIII. 28, and elsewhere, for: but you do not believe me, because I speak the truth to you. So alien and averse in spirit are you from the truth: of which vice I have already indicated whose father you have.

Ludov. de Dieu explains the Hebraism. He says that most learned men wish there to be a trajection here, by which ὅτι δὲ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐγὼ λέγω. The Syriac and the Vulgate judged otherwise, as they changed nothing in the order of the words. I approve. For it is a pure Hebraism and Syriasm, where at the beginning of a sentence a nominative is placed absolutely, which then, with other words intervening, is changed by a suffix into an oblique case. That is an elegance in those languages. In Hebrew you would say, ואנכי האמרת אמרתי אינכם מאמינים לי which signifies nothing else than, but to me, because I speak the truth, you do not believe. You would say that less elegantly. You have a similar [construction] in Ps. LXXIII. 28. ואני קרבת אלהים לי טוב that is, word for word ἐγὼ δὲ τὸ προσκολλᾶσθαι τῷ Θεῷ ἀγαθόν μοι, which the LXX, expressing a Grecism, not a Hebraism, translate: ἐμοὶ δὲ τὸ προσκολλᾶσθαι τῷ Θεῷ ἀγαθόν: These are the words of Dievius, which I have chosen to repeat here on account of those who hate Hebraisms.

Latin:

Vers. 45. ἐγὼ δὲ ὅτι τὴν ἀλήθειαν λέγω οὐ πιστεύετέ μοι) Est Hebraismus qualis Ps. LXXIII. 28. & alibi, pro; mihi vero non creditis, quia verum vobis eloquor. Adeo alieno & averso animo a veritate estis: cujus vitii quem patrem habeatis jam indicavi.

Ebraismum explicat Ludov. de Dieu. Traje- ctionem, inquit, hic esse volunt viri doctissimi, quo ὅτι δὲ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐγὼ λέγω. Secus judicarunt Sy- rus & Vulgatus, qui in ordine verborum nihil mu- tarunt. Laudo. Est enim purus Hebraismus & Syriamus, ubi in initio sententiæ nominativus ponitur absolute, qui deinde aliis dictionibus in- tervenientibus, mutatur per affixum in obliquum. Elegantia id est in istis linguis. Hebraice dicas, ואנכי האמרת אמרתי אינכם מאמינים לי quod aliud nihil significat quam, mihi autem, quia ve- ritatem dico, non creditis. Id minus eleganter diceres Simile ולי כי האמרת אמרתי אינכם מאמינים habes Ps. LXXIII. 28. ואני קרבת אלהים לי טוב id est, ad verbum ἐγὼ δὲ τὸ προσκολλᾶσθαί τῷ Θεῷ ἀγαθόν μοι, quod LXX. Græcismum, non He- braismum exprimentes, vertunt, ἐμοὶ δὲ τὸ προσ- κολλᾶσθαι τῷ Θεῷ ἀγαθόν: Hæc Dievius, quæ ob osores Ebraismorum inde repetere placuit.

## 8:46
Vers. 46. Τίς ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐλέγχει με περὶ ἁμαρτίας) If faith is denied to anyone, it must be denied either because the speaker is unworthy of having faith placed in him, or because the thing itself is incredible. He removes the former part here: you cannot convict me of any fault. For this is what ἐλέγχειν means. Thus below XVI. 8. Tit. c. I. v. 9. 13.

Εἰ δὲ ἀλήθειαν λέγω διὰ τί ὑμεῖς ὐ πιστεύετέ μοι) If I say those things which are most worthy of faith: just as we have said that the word ἀληθῆς is taken several times.

Latin:

Vers. 46. Τίς ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐλέγχει με περὶ ἁμαρτίας) Si cui fi- des negetur, oportet eam negari, aut quia loquens indignus est cui habeatur fides, aut quia res per se est incredibilis. Prio- rem partem hic removet: nullius culpæ me convincere po- testis. Hoc enim est ἐλέγχειν. Sic infra XVI. 8. Tit. c. I. v. 9. 13.

Εἰ δὲ ἀλήθειαν λέγω διὰ τί ὑμεῖς ὐ πιστεύετέ μοι) Si ea dico quæ fide perdigna sunt: sicut vocem ἀληθῆς sumi diximus aliquoties.

## 8:47
Vers. 47. Ὁ ὢν ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ) He who loves honest things, and therefore by his nature reflects God, for this is opposed to that, being from the Devil, wherefore it must be interpreted in the same way, Nonnus not badly, εἰς Θεὸν ἀρχιγένεθλον ἔχων νόον.

To be from God is to be born from God. They were boasting that God was their Father, v. 42. Christ refutes that even now, teaching that the boast is vain, because if they were from God, they would hear the word of God.

Τὰ ῥήματα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀκούει) He hears willingly, he hears attentively the discourses pertaining to the honor of God, worthy of God. Above III. 34.

Τὰ ῥήματα τοῦ Θεοῦ) They are not discourses pertaining to the honor of God, but what the words themselves bring, the word of God. For Christ preached nothing other than the word of God.

Διὰ τοῦτο ὑμεῖς οὐκ ἀκούετε, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐκ ἐστὶ) [Something] is understood. But truly. For there is an opposition, But you for this reason are burdened to hear what I say, because you are by nature averse to things that are truly divine.

Latin:

Vers. 47. Ὁ ὢν ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Qui honesta amat, ac proinde ingenio Deum refert, opponiturenim hoc isti, esse ex Dia- bolo, quare parimodo interpretandum, Nonnus non male, εἰς Θεὸν ἀρχιγένεθλον ἔχων νόον.

Ex Deo esse est genitum esse ex Deo. Jactabant Deum Patrem suum esse, v. 42. Id etiamnum refel- lit Christus, vanam esse jactantiam docens, quia si ex Deo essent, verbum Dei audirent.

Τὰ ῥήματα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀκούει) Libenter audit, attente audit sermones ad Dei honorem pertinentes, Deo dignos. Supra III. 34.

Τὰ ῥήματα τοῦ Θεοῦ) Sunt non sermones ad Dei honorem pertinentes, sed quod verba ipsa inferunt verbum Dei. Nihil enim aliud quam verbum Dei prædicabat Christus.

Διὰ τοῦτο ὑμεῖς οὐκ ἀκούετε, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐκ ἐστὶ) Subaudi- tur. At vero. Est enim oppositio, At vos ideo gravamini quæ dico audire, quia ingenio stis averso a rebus vere divinis.

## 8:48
Vers. 48. Οὐ καλῶς λέγομεν ἡμεῖς, ὅτι Σαμαρείτης εἶ (ύ) Do we not deservedly use to say among ourselves? For it is nowhere narrated that this was said openly, that you are a Samaritan; understand not by race but by sense, because you deny that the truth of religion resides with the Jews. See above IV. 20. and following.

Καὶ δαιμόνιον ἔχεις) δαιμονᾷς, See above VIII. 20. below 52. X. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 48. Οὐ καλῶς λέγομεν ἡμεῖς, ὅτι Σαμαρείτης εἶ (ύ) Nonne merito dicere inter nos solemus? Nusquam enim hoc palam dictum narratur, Samaritam te esse; intellige non gente sed sensu, quia negas veritatem religionis esse penes Judæos. Vide supra IV. 20. & sequentibus.

Καὶ δαιμόνιον ἔχεις) δαιμονᾷς, Vid. supra VIII. 20. infra 52. X. 20.

## 8:49
Vers. 49. Ἐγὼ δαιμόνιον οὐκ ἔχω, ἀλλὰ τιμῶ τὸν πατέρα μυ) What I have said, I have not said out of insanity, but by a divine spirit for the honor of God. Regarding what they had said about a Samaritan, as if it were a mere reproach, he passes over it, as if someone now were to call someone a heretic.

Καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀτιμάζετέ με) And yet you attack me with reproaches.

Latin:

Vers. 49. Ἐγὼ δαιμόνιον οὐκ ἔχω, ἀλλὰ τιμῶ τὸν πατέρα μυ) Quæ dixi non præ insania dixi, sed divino spiritu ad Dei ho- norem. De Samaritæ quod dixerant, quasi merum convi- tium præterit, ut si quis nunc aliquem hæreticum vocet.

Καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀτιμάζετέ με) Ettamen vos me convitiis petitis.

## 8:50
Ver. 50. Ἐγω δὲ οὐ ζητῶ τὴν δόξαν μου) That which I so often say and repeat, that the things I teach are true and have proceeded from God, I do not do this out of a desire for human glory, which is easily gathered both from my words and from my deeds.

ἔστιν ὁ ζητῶν καὶ κρίνων) There is a God who wishes to honor me, and who is going to avenge these insults with which you afflict me. See 1 Pet. 2:23. But the passage in Deuteronomy 18:19 is also being looked at, where God promises that He will be the avenger of a despised prophet. Compare 2 Chron. 24:22.

Latin:

Vers. 50. Ἐγω δὲ οὐ ζητῶ τὴν δόξαν μου) Quod toties dico & repeto, quæ doceo vera esse, & a Deo profecta, non id facio cupiditate humanæ gloriæ, quod & ex verbis & ex factis meis facile collectu est.

ἔστιν ὁ ζητῶν καὶ κρίνων) Est qui me honore afficere velit Deus, & qui vindicaturus est has contumelias quibus me afficitis. Vide 1. Petr. II. 23. Sed & Deuteronomii locus respi- citur c. XIIX. 19. Ubi Deus promittit se vindicem futurum contemti prophetæ. Cons. 2. Paral. XXIV. 22.

## 8:51
Verse 51.

ἐάν τις τὸν λόγον ἐμὸν τηρήσῃ) A locution which [is found in] Matt. 19:17, 28:20, Mark 7:9, below ch. 9:16, ch. 14:15, and elsewhere. θάνατον ὐ μὴ θεωρήσῃ εἰς αἰῶνα) Thus ἰδεῖν θάνατον in Luke 2:26, the same immediately as γεύσασθαι θανάτου, as also in Matt. 16:28, ch. 9:1. The sense is, he will obtain that life which is free from death. Thus we explained above, ch. 6:49.

Latin:

Vers. 51.

ἐάν τις τὸν λόγον ἐμὸν τηρήσῃ) Locutio quæ Matth. XIX. 17. c. XXIIX. 20. Marc. VII. 9. infra c. IX. 16. c. XIV. 15. & alibi. θάνατον ὐ μὴ θεωρήσῃ εἰς αἰῶνα) Sic ἰδεῖν θάνατον Luc. II. 26. idem statim γεύσασθαι θανάτου, ut & Matth. XVI. 28. c. IX. 1. Sensus est, eam vitam consequetur quæ morte careat. Sic supra exposuimus. c. VI. 49.

## 8:52
Verse 52.

νῦν ἐγνώκαμεν ὅτι δαιμόνιον ἔχεις) You are clearly insane when you promise such things. A similar locution [is found in] Gen. 22:12, below ch. 16:30. ᾿Αβραὰμ ἀπέθανε καὶ οἱ προφῆται) From Zech. 1:15. Those who observed the word not of man but of God, yet they died. For they understand everything crudely and literally, fascinated by hatred. σὺ σὺ λέγεις) You, who are in no way to be compared to them, dare to say these things. ἐάν τις τὸν λόγον μου τηρήσῃ) The emphasis is on the word μου, for as we have said, it presupposes that the commandments of God were religiously kept by Moses and the Prophets.

Latin:

Vers. 52.

νῦν ἐγνώκαμεν ὅτι δαιμόνιον ἔχεις) Plane insanis cum ta- lia polliceris. Locutio similis Gen. XXII. 12. infra c. XVI. v. 30. ᾿Αβραὰμ ἀπέθανε καὶ οἱ προφῆται) Ex Zach. I. 15. Qui sermonem non hominis sed Dei observarunt, mortui ta- men sunt. Omnia enim intelligunt crasse & κατὰ πόδας, odio fascinati. σὺ σὺ λέγεις) Tu neutiquam illis comparandus hæc audes dicere. ἐάν τις τὸν λόγον μου τηρήσῃ) Emphasis est in voce μου, nam ut diximus supponit, à Mose & Prophetis religiose servata Dei mandata.

## 8:53
Verse 53.

μὴ σὺ μείζων εἶ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν ᾿Αβραὰμ, ὅς τις ἀπέθανε) He who is about to give life to others [is] much more [able to give it] to himself. You profess that you will give life to others: therefore you proclaim much more that you will live forever, which did not happen to Abraham. κὰι οἱ προφῆται ἀπέθανον) Just as the Prophets also died, for the conjunction is accustomed to be taken in that manner. τίνα σεαυτὸν σὺ ποιεῖς) Whom do you claim to be? Thus below ch. 10:33.

Latin:

Vers. 53.

μὴ σὺ μείζων εἶ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν ᾿Αβραὰμ, ὅς τις ἀπέθανε) Qui vitam aliis daturus est multo magis sibi. Tu te vitam aliis daturum profiteris: ergo multo magis te perpetuo victurum pronuntias, quod Abrahamo non conti- git. κὰι οἱ προφῆται ἀπέθανον) Sicut & Prophetæ mortui sunt, nam ad eum modum copula sumi solet. τίνα σεαυτὸν σὺ ποιεῖς) Quem te venditas? Sic infra c. X. v. 33.

## 8:54
Verse 54.

ἐὰν ἐγὼ δοξάζω ἐμαυτὸν) If I arrogate to myself what is not mine. See above, ch. 3:27, ch. 5:41. ἡ δόξα μου οὐδέν ἐστι) That claim is of no value, it will betray itself. Thus 2 Cor. 13:2. ἔστιν ὁ πατήρ μου ὁ δοξάζων με) By miracles: by the testimony of the Baptist. And more hereafter. ὃν ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι Θεὸς ὑμῶν ἐστι) The God who is the maker of the Universe. The God of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and the Prophets, so that you may not think that a demon is being called Father by me,

Latin:

Vers. 54.

ἐὰν ἐγὼ δοξάζω ἐμαυτὸν) Si quod meum non est mihi ar- rogo. Vide supra. c. III. 27. c. V. 41. ἡ δόξα μου οὐδέν ἐστι) Nullius pretii est ista venditatio, se- met prodet. Sic 2. Cor. XIII. 2. ἔστιν ὁ πατήρ μου ὁ δοξάζων με) Miraculis: Baptistæ testi- monio. Et amplius posthac. ὃν ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι Θεὸς ὑμῶν ἐστι) Deus opifex Universi. Deus Abrahami, Isaaci, Jacobi, Mosis & Prophetarum ne quem sorte dæmonem à me patrem appellari censeatis,

## 8:55
Verse 55.

κὰὶ ὐκ ἐγνώκατε αὐτὸν) You do not understand what kind of worship He especially desires and what rewards He promises. See what [was said] above in ch. 1:18. ἐγὼ δὲ οἶδα αὐτὸν) I have known Him thoroughly. See in the said place. οἶδα αὐτὸν κὶλόγον αὐτῦ τηρῶ) And I know what things please Him, and I religiously observe them, never exceeding the commandments.

Latin:

Vers. 55.

κὰὶ ὐκ ἐγνώκατε αὐτὸν) Non intelligitis qualem cultum præcipue desideret & quæ præmia promittat. Vide quæ su- pra c. I. 18. ἐγὼ δὲ οἶδα αὐτὸν) Penitus pernovi. Vide dicto loco. οἶδα αὐτὸν κὶλόγον αὐτῦ τηρῶ) Et scio quæ ei placeant, & ea religiose observo, nusquam mandata excedens.

## 8:56
Verse 56.

Abraham our father) With which father you boast. Thus above c. VIII. 17. He modestly shows that they ought not to wonder if he himself brings greater things than Abraham. ἠγαλλιάσατο ἵνα ἴδῃ τὴν ἡμέραν τὴν ἐμὴν) ἰδὼν ἀγαλλιέσθω θυμῷ. Nonnus here. The Syrian מסות desired my day, that is, my times. Thus Joel II. 1. Amos V. 18. & elsewhere. Compare 1. Petr. I. 12. The sense is that Abraham, when at the beginning of Gen. XI. 35. he had received the promise from God that it would come to pass that even foreign nations would be blessed through his seed, greatly desired to know more closely what that happiness would be. κὰὶ εἶδε κὰὶ ἐχάρη) And he saw something of it, not without great joy, but from afar, Hebr. XI. 13. Doubtless then most of all when he attributed this reward to his trust in God, that he received Isaac as if from the dead. Hebr. XI. 19. For from this he understood what God especially required & how much He could perform. And from that deed flowed that mystical proverb: In the name of the Lord it shall be provided. Abraham is said not to have desired to know more closely what that happiness is which is obtained through his Seed: but he desired to see the day of Christ itself, as Christ expressly testifies here: & he saw something of it, not without notable joy: not only in the accepted offering of Isaac, but in other further promises, and also in the apparitions of the Son of God made to him, Genes. XV. XVII. XXII. Abraham not only knew the happiness itself, which is obtained through the Messiah, as much as was sufficient, and instilled the same into others as a Teacher and Prophet, but he also experienced it himself singularly, as the Father of believers, because through faith in the Messiah we enjoy it.

Latin:

Vers. 56.

᾿Αβραὰμ ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν) Quo vos patre jactatis. Sic supra c. VIII. 17. Modeste ostendit mirari eos non debere si ipse majora adferat quam Abrahamus. ἠγαλλιάσατο ἵνα ἴδῃ τὴν ἡμέραν τὴν ἐμὴν) ἰδὼν ἀγαλλιέσθω θυμῷ. Nonnus hic. Syrus מסות cupiit diem meum id est tempora mea, Sic Joel II. 1. Amos V. 18. & alibi. Confer 1. Petr. I. 12. Sensus est Abraham cum initio Gen. XI. 35. promissum à Deo accepisset, futurum ut etiam exteræ gen- tes per ipsius semen bearentur, valde expetivit propius ali- quid cognoscere, qualis ea futura esset beatitudo. κὰὶ εἶδε κὰὶ ἐχάρη) Et vidit aliquid ejus non sine magno gaudio sed eminus Ebr. XI. 13. Nimirum tunc maxime cum fiduciæ suæ in Deum hoc præmium retulit quod Isaacum quasi è mortuis recepit. Hebr. XI. 19. Hinc enim intellexit quid præcipue Deus requireret & quantum præstare posset. Atque ex eo facto proverbium illud mysticum manavit : In nomine Domini providebitur. Non expetiisse dicitur Abraham, qualis illa beatitudo sit, propius cognoscere, quæ per Semen ejus obtinetur: sed diem ipsum Christi desidera- vit videre, ut expresse hic testatur Christus : & vi- dit aliquid ejus non sine insigni gaudio: non tan- tum in Isaaci suscepta oblatione, sed in aliis ul- terioribus promissionibus, nec non apparitioni- bus Filii Dei ipsi factis, Genes. XV. XVII. XXII. Beatitudinem ipsam, quæ per Messiam obtinetur, non tantum cognovit Abraham, quantum satis erat, aliisque eandem ceu Doctor, & Propheta instillavit, sed expertus etiam ipse est singulariter, tanquam Pater credentium, quia per fidem in Messiam ea fruimur.

## 8:57
Vers. 57.

πεντήκοντα ἔτη ὔπω ἔχεις) It is the custom of all peoples, where there is no reason for us to act restrictively, to take some number from the more noble ones, such as the fifty-year-old among the Hebrews on account of the Jubilee. As if they were saying: certainly you are not yet half-centenarian. Nor does it matter that Christ was far from that age: for they speak more liberally, because all this has nothing to do with those years which were numbered from the age of Abraham.

κ' Ἀβραὰμ ἑώρακας) It usually happens that he who sees us, we also see him. The sense is: how could it happen that you and Abraham saw each other differently? They take everything, as we have said, in the common sense.

Latin:

Vers. 57.

πεντήκοντα ἔτη ὔπω ἔχεις) Mos est omnium populo- rum ubi non est cur restricte agamus numerum sumere aliquem ex nobilioribus, qualis apud Hebræos quinqua- genarius ob Jubilæum. Quasi dicerent: certe nondum se- misæcularis es. Nec refert quod Christus multis inde ab- erat: agunt enim liberalius, quia hoc omne nihil ad eos an- nos qui ab Abrahami ævo numerabantur.

κ' Ἀβραὰμ ἑώρακας) Solet fieri ut qui nos videt eum & nos videamus. Sensus est: quomodo fieri potuit, ut tu & Abraham aliter alterum conspiceretis? Sumunt omnia ut diximus in sensu vulgari.

## 8:58
Vers. 58.

πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι) Before he was. For thus this word is very often taken above chapter I. 6. 30. & this chapter v. 33. c. XX. 27. Act. VII. 38. c. XIII. 5. & elsewhere.

ἐγώ εἰμι) Present for imperfect. I was. Syrian. ἐγώ πιδος Nonnus. Thus in the Greek Psalm XC. 2. πρὸ τῶ ὄρη γενηθῆ- ναι σὺ εἶ, but Jesus had been before Abraham by divine constitution, below c. XVII. 5. Apoc. XIII. 8. 1. Petr. I. 20. This is certain because it had been said mystically of him and his Church when the human race was recent, that it would come to pass that the seed of the woman would crush the head of the serpent: as is explained Rom. XVI. 20. Whence it is understood at the same time that this man Jesus is greater than Abraham, which he prefers to hint at rather than to proclaim.

Christ's words do not treat of divine constitution, but of the true and real ὑπάρξει and subsistence of Christ before Abraham, which both the literal sense or the letter itself, and the connection and context require: because the Jews were conjecturing that he could not have seen Abraham, since he is not yet 50 years old: Christ therefore testifies that he had already been before Abraham, namely, as far as the divine nature is concerned. Nor is he said in John XVII. 4 to have had glory with the Father only by divine constitution, but truly. See what is expressly written, even against Grotius in select exercises, Exercise I. and in the Disputation concerning the pre-existence before the world. The Proto-Evangelium also, Gen. III. 15, is perverted by Grotius, because it treats of Christ not in a mystical sense, but in a proper and literal one: but in no way of the Church: because it is the work of Christ alone to crush the head of the serpent, even if he himself as the God of peace crushes Satan under our feet, which is said in Rom. XVI.

Latin:

Vers. 58.

πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι) Antequam esset. Sic enim hæc vox sæpissime sumitur supra cap. I. 6. 30. & hoc capite v. 33. c. XX. 27. Act. VII. 38. c. XIII. 5. & alibi

ἐγώ εἰμι) Præsens pro imperfecto. Eram. Syrus. ἐγώ πιδος Nonnus. Sic in Græco Psal. XC. 2. πρὸ τῶ ὄρη γενηθῆ- ναι σὺ εἶ, fuerat autem ante Abrahamum Jesus divina con- stitutione, infra c. XVII. 5. Apoc. XIII. 8. 1. Petr. I. 20. Con- stat hoc quia de ipso ipsiusque Ecclesia mystice dictum erat recente humano genere, futurum ut semen muliebre conte- reret caput serpentis: ut exponitur Rom. XVI. 20. Unde si- mul intelligitur hunc hominem Jesum majorem esse Abra- hamo, quod ipse innuere quam prædicare mavult.

Non de divina constitutione, sed de vera, & reali ὑπάρξει & subsistentia Christi ante Abraha- mum verba Christi agunt, quod tum τὸ ῥητὸν vel litera ipsa, tum συνέχεια, & contextus requirit: quia Judæi conjiciebant, ipsum Abrahamum vi- dere non potuisse, siquidem nondum 50. anno- rum sit: Christus ergo testatur, se jam ante Abra- hamum fuisse, scil. quantum ad divinam naturam. Neque Joh. XVII. 4. gloriam apud Patrem habuisse dicitur tantum divina constitutione, sed ἀληθῶς vere. Vide quæ ex professo, etiam adversus Gro- tium in exercit. select. Exercit. I. & in Disput. de προϋπάρξει antemundana. Prot-Evangelium et- iam, Gen. III. 15. pervertitur a Grotio, quod non sensu mystico, sed proprio & literali de Christo agit: nullatenus autem de Ecclesia: quia solius Christi est conterere caput serpentis, etsi conte- rat ipse ceu Deus pacis Satanam sub pedes nostros, quod Rom. XVI. dicitur.

## 8:59
Vers. 59.

ἦραν ὖν λίθους ἵνα βάλωσιν ἐπ' αὐτὸν) Driven by fury, as below c. X. 31. They took it so badly that something was said which seemed to injure the dignity of Abraham.

They did not take up stones because of injured dignity of Abraham, but because they considered what Christ was saying to be blasphemy, which they thought should be punished by stoning, as was done in Acts VII. 59, when the Jews stoned Stephen as a blasphemer.

ἐκρύβη) By a certain miracle, as in Luke 4:30.

ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ τῶ ἱερῶ) For there were several exits.

Διελθὼν διὰ μέσα αὐτῶν) This seems to have been added from the aforementioned passage of Luke for the sake of interpretation, as is also what follows, καὶ παρῆγεν ὕτως, from the beginning of the following chapter. For the most ancient Greek codices do not have it, and it is missing in the Latin ones. But it is written in the Syriac and Arabic.

Beza testifies that all his codices, with one exception, had these, and Theophylact and Nonnus read it so, along with the Syrian and the Arab: and Beza himself acknowledges that those things cohere not badly, if it is said that Christ both withdrew himself from those who were in the temple, and afterwards passed through the midst of those whom he found outside. Cf. Lud. de Dieu,

Latin:

Vers. 59.

ἦραν ὖν λίθους ἵνα βάλωσιν ἐπ' αὐτὸν) Furore perciti, ut in- fra c. X. 31. Adeo ægre ferebant aliquid dici quod Abraha- mi dignitatem lædere videretur.

Non ob læsam Abrahami dignitatem lapides tollebant, sed quod pro blasphemia haberent, quæ dicebat Christus, quam lapidatione vindi- candam censebant, uti Actorum VII. 59. factum, cum Stephanum ceu blasphemum lapidarunt Ju- dæi.

ἐκρύβη) Miraculo quodam, ut Luc. IV. 30.

ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ τῶ ἱερῶ) Erant enim plures exitus.

Διελθὼν διὰ μέσα αὐτῶν) Videtur hoc additum ex dicto Lucæ loco interpretamenti causa, ut & quod sequitur καὶ παρῆγεν ὕτως ex initio capitis sequentis. Nam & vetustissi- mi Codices Græci non habent, & in Latinis deest. At in Syriaco & Arabico adscriptum est.

Codices suos omnes, unico excepto hæc ha- buisse testatur Beza, legitque ita Theophylactus & Nonnus cum Syro & Arabe: nec male illa co- hærere, agnoscit Beza ipse, si dicatur, & ab iis, qui in templo erant se subduxisse Christum, & dein- ceps per eos medios, quos foris reperit transiisse. Conf. Lud. de Dieu,

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

To the man born blind, with clay, when Jesus had spat upon the ground, prepared, and having washed it in Siloam, sight is given on the Sabbath, which he himself reports to others; the Pharisees deny that Jesus is from God, but the blind man affirms that he was blind from birth, but now made seeing by Jesus, and that this has been unheard of from of old. Whence the Pharisees cast him out for professing that Jesus is from God. When Jesus had found him, and had instructed him concerning faith in the Son of God, he testified that he had come so that those who do not see might see, and those who see might be blind. But to the Pharisees asking whether they also are blind, he replies that because they profess that they see, their sin remains.

There are four parts: I. The healing of the man born blind and the narrative of that event with various judgments concerning it, to v. 17. II. A more accurate investigation of the same matter, to v. 27. III. The confrontation of the Jews with the blind man concerning Jesus, and his ejection, to v. 34. IV. The blind man's profession of faith, with Jesus' testimony concerning the purpose of his coming, and the warning to the Pharisees, to v. 41.

PART I.

The healing of the man born blind, and the narrative of that event with various judgments concerning it.

Ver. 1.

Καὶ παράγων Ἰησοῦς εἶδεν] He passed by. Thus παράγειν is taken in Matt. 20:30, Mark 11:21. For this blind man was sitting by the way as was accustomed to be done, Matt. 20:30.

τυφλὸν ἐκ γενετῆς] This is not added in vain, for it is certain that this infirmity is incurable by human aid.

Latin:

CAPUT IX.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Cæco nato luto, cum in terram exspueret Ie- sus, adornato, eoque in Siloa abluto visus donatur in Sabbato, quod aliis ipse refert, Pharisæi Iesum à Deo esse negant, cæcus au- tem se à nativitate cæcum fuisse, jam vero videntem à Jesu redditum affirmat, idque à seculo inauditum esse. Unde Pharisæi Je- sum à Deo esse profitentem ejiciunt. Quem cum invenisset Jesus, & de fide in Filium Dei instituisset, testatus est, se venisse ut non videntes videant, & videntes cæci sint. Pharisæis vero an & ipsi cæci sint quæren- tibus respondet, ideo quod profiteantur se videntes esse, peccatum ipsorum mane- re.
