Partes sunt quatuor: I. Cæci nati sanatio e- jusque rei narratio cum diversis de eo judiciis, ad v. 17. II. Rei ejusdem accuratior indagatio, ad v. 27. III. Judæorum cum cæco de Jesu collatio, hu- jusque ejectio, ad v. 34. IV. Fidei cæci professio, cum Jesu de fine adventus sui testificatione, & Pha- risæorum commonitione, ad v. 41.

PARS I.

Cæci nati sanatio, ejusque rei narratio cum diversis de eo judiciis.

Vers. 1.

Καὶ παράγων Ἰησοῦς εἶδεν] Vicit in transitu. Sic παράγειν sumitur Matth. XX. 30. Marc. XI. 21. Nam cæcus hic sede- bat juxta viam ut fieri solebat, Matth. XX. 30.

τυφλὸν ἐκ γενετῆς] Non frustra hoc additur, nam id vi- tium constat humana ope esse insanabile.

## 9:2
Ver. 2.

τίς ἥμαρτεν; ὗτος] They hold from tradition that blindness and other such bodily infirmities are punishments for sins: which is sometimes true. See above ch. 5:14. They ask, therefore, whether he himself sinned, because many of the Jews believed in the προϋπαρξιν of souls, and even in גלגול נפשות metempsychosis, as appears from Philo, Josephus, the Talmudists, and some places in these books. They propose this, therefore, as a matter of controversy.

or his parents] Both of the parents. How? By sinning against the law in Leviticus 20:18, which sin Ezekiel 18:6 places among the grave ones. From such intercourse, imperfect births are wont to be born, because the female nature, occupied in the discharge, is hindered from giving the proper form to the conception: as the Hebrews note.

It does not appear that the inquiry is specifically about that sin. Nor is the condition of nature considered here, but the inquiry is about that which is sent as a punishment for sin. The disciples erred, however, in this question, partly in the cause of this blindness, as if it were some peculiar sin; partly in the designation of the sin of this blind man, as if his soul had merited before birth by some crime in a preceding body to be sent into a blind body: for some gather that such a μετεμψύχωσιν from the School of Pythagoras commonly clung to the Hebrews, from Matt. 14:7, ch. 16:4, just as Elias Levita in the book Tisbi under the word גלגול hands down the double revolution believed among the Hebrews; one of the bodies of the dead outside the promised land, through the caverns of the earth, until it has arrived there, necessary so that they may be able to rise again: the other, however, of souls: since the Kabbalists hand down that every single soul revolves itself through three bodies of men, and the place of scripture from which they prove this is Job 33:29. Behold, God works all these things three times, whence (as he says;) they say thus that the soul of the first man rolled itself into the body of King David: and from there it is to return into the body of the Messiah. And that this is signified by the letters which are in the word אדם, each one of which constitutes an entire word, Adam, David, Messiah. Thus also they said that the souls of prevaricating men migrate into the bodies of animals, each one according to its sin: as Gomarus brought these things forward from Elias Levita to Walaeus in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

τίς ἥμαρτεν; ὗτος] Ex traditione habeant cæcitatem & a- lia ejusmodi corporis vitia pœnas esse peccatorum: quod interdum verum est. Vide supra c. 5, 14. Quærunt er- go an ipse peccaverit, quia multi Judæorum credebant προϋπαρξιν animarum, imo & גלגול נפשות metem- psychosin, ut apparet ex Philone, Josepho, Thalmudistis & aliquot horum librorum locis. Proponunt ergo hoc tanquam controversum.

ἢ οἱ γονεῖς ἀυτẽ] Uterque Parentum. Quomodo? delin- quendo contra legem Levit. XX. 18. quod peccatum inter gravia ponit Ezech. XVIII. 6. Ex tali concubitu solent nasci partus imperfecti, quia natura muliebris in egestu oc- cupata impe ditur formam justam dare conceptui: ut no- tant Hebræi.

In specie de illo peccato quæri non apparet. Ne- que natura spectatur hic conditio, sed de eo quæ- ritur, quod in pœnam peccati immittitur. Errarunt autem discipuli in hac quæstione, partim in causa hujus cæcitatis, quasi ea fuerit peculiare quoddam peccatum; partim in designatione peccati hujus cæci, quasi anima ipsius ante nativitatem aliquo scelere in antecedenti corpore promerita fuerit, ut in corpus cæcum immitteretur: talem enim μετεμψύχωσιν è Schola Pythagoræ Ebræis com- muniter hæsisse, colligunt nonnulli è Matth. XIV. 7. cap. XVI. 4. quomodo Elias Levita in libro Tis- bi in voce גלגול revolutionem duplicem apud He- bræos creditam tradit; unam corporum mortuorum extra terram promissam, per cavernas terræ, usque dum eo pervenerit, necessariam ut possint resurgere: alteram vero animarum: cum Cabalistæ tradant, unicamquamque animam se volvere per tria corpora hominum, & locum scripturæ unde id probant es- se Job. XXXIII. v. 29. Ecce ista omnia operatur Deus tribus vicibus, unde (ut ait;) sic dicunt quod anima primi hominis volutaverit se in cor- pus David Regis: & inde reversura sit in corpus Messiæ. Idque significari per literas, qua sunt in voce אדם quarum unaquæque integram dictionem constituit, Adam, David, Messias. Sic quoque dixerunt, quod animæ hominum prævaricatorum migrant in corpora animalium, unaquæque secundum peccatum suum: ut ex Elia Levita hæc adduxit Go- marus ad Walæum in h. l.

## 9:3
οὔτε οὗτος ἥμαρτεν] Before he was born he did not exist, wherefore he did not sin.

οὔτε οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ] Nor is there such a thing regarding his parents as you suspect.

ἀλλ' ἵνα] A little word of this kind is understood; but this happens conveniently, so that it may be manifest how magnificent the works of God are, as we have noted elsewhere that ἵνα is often ἐκβατικὸν (consecutive). Thus Ps. LI. 6. Rom. I. 20. which are noted here by Theophylact. Thus also below v. 39. Moreover, ἵνα is accustomed to have such an attraction, as below c. XIII. 18. c. XIV. 31. c. XV. 25.

φανερωθῇ τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ] So that through him it may be manifest what kind and how great the works of God are. He uses the plural for this reason, because from one example it is gathered how much God can do.

Latin:

οὔτε οὗτος ἥμαρτεν] Antequam nasceretur non exstitit quare nec peccavit.

οὔτε οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ] Nec tale quid de parentibus est quale suspicamini.

ἀλλ' ἵνα] Subauditur vocula hujusmodi; sed commode hoc accidit, ut pateat quam magnifica sint Dei opera, ἵνα sæpe esse ἐκβατικὸν alibi notavimus. Sic Ps. LI. 6. Rom. I. 20. quæ hic notata Theophylacto. Sic & infra v. 39. Solet autem ἵνα ἵνα habere talem ἕλκυσιν ut infra c. XIII. 18. c. XIV. 31. c. XV. 25.

φανερωθῇ τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ] Ut per ipsum pateat qualia & quanta sint Dei opera. Ideo plurali utitur, quia ex uno exemplo colligitur quanta Deus possit.

## 9:4
Vers. 4.

ἐμὲ δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πέμψαντός με] To teach through myself and to do good to many. See above c. V. 19. δεῖ, that is, it is right, it is fitting.

ἕως ἡμέρα ἐστὶ] He alludes to the present matter: for to the blind there is perpetual night. He calls his conspicuous presence, beneficial to many, the day. Thus above c. VIII. 56. c. XII. 35.

ἔρχεται νὺξ] The time of bodily absence. Compare Matth. c. IX. 15.

ὅτε οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐργάζεσθαι] When it is not convenient to apply oneself to work. Thus we noted that δύνασθαι is placed in the said passage of Matth. IX. 15. Christ, having been taken away from the sight of men, no longer taught with his voice, nor did he perform miracles by himself.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

ἐμὲ δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι τὰ ἔργα τοῦ πέμψαντός με] Docere per me ipsum ac plurimis benefacere. Vid. supra c. V. 19. δεῖ hoc est, par est, convenit.

ἕως ἡμέρα ἐστὶ] Alludit ad rem præsentem: nam cæcis perpetua nox est. Diem vocat conspicuam suam præsentiam plurimis salutarem. Sic supra c. VIII. 56. c. XII. 35.

ἔρχεται νὺξ] Tempus absentiæ corporalis. Conf. Matth. c. IX. 15.

ὅτε οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐργάζεσθαι] Cum commodum non est operi intendere. Sic δύνασθαι poni notavimus dicto loco Matth. IX. 15. Christus hominum conspectui abreptus non amplius voce sua docuit, neque per se effecit miracula.

## 9:5
Vers. 5.

ὅταν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ὦ, φῶς εἰμι τοῦ κόσμου] He persists in the allusion, and by the deed confirms it to be true what he had said, above chapter VIII. 20. For bodily benefits are an argument for spiritual ones, above chapter 9, 5. Therefore he wished this blind man to bear the image of the world; of which he himself was the light.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ὅταν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ὦ, φῶς εἰμι τοῦ κόσμου] Persistit in allusione, & facto confirmat verum esse quod dixerat, supra cap. VIII. 20. Nam beneficia corporalia spiritualium sunt argumentum supra cap. 9, 5. Ideo hunc cæcum voluit imaginiem gerere mundi; cujus ipse lux erat.

## 9:6
Verse 6.

He spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle] Because water was not at hand, he made mud with saliva.

A truly wonderful cure, says Pelargus; for he composes an eye-salve from spittle and dust of the earth, and with it anoints the eyes of the blind man, and commands him to wash them in the pool or pond of Siloam. If he had wished to blind him, he might perhaps have cast mud into his eyes: but here he uses mud to bring light, because the power of God brings help through contrary remedies. Some, however, maintain that the mud was formed because the blind man appeared to have eyes that were not whole, but broken and crushed, and devoid of humors from birth: therefore, as if from matter, they were newly formed from the earth. Irenaeus, however, in book V, ch. 15, says: from which earth God formed the eyes for the blind man, from this man was fashioned: for it was not logical that the eyes should be fashioned from one source, and the rest of the body from another. Chrysostom contends that the mud had to be washed off so that he might understand that the mud was not necessary for forming the eyes. Augustine believes that the divine word is shadowed forth by the saliva or spittle, because just as saliva originates from the head, so the Word originates from the Father.

And he anointed the clay upon the eyes of the blind man] We have begun to show the reason for this act. Not only is there not in man by his own nature the power to know by himself those things which are divine and spiritual, but also because he is made from clay, he has muddy affections which hinder him, 1 Cor. 2:14.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ἔπτυσε χαμαὶ, καὶ ἐποίησε πηλὸν ἐκ τοῦ πτύσματος] Quia aqua ad manum non erat, lutum saliva fecit.

Cura valde mirabilis, inquit Pelargus; collyrium enim ex sputo terraque pulvere componit, eoque cæci ungit oculos, jubetque eos in piscina vel stagno Siloë, aqua abluere. Excæcare si voluisset, lutum forte oculis immisisset: sed luto hic ad afferendam lucem utitur, quia Dei potentia contrariis remediis opem affert. Lutum autem propterea formatum aliqui volunt, quia cæcus oculos videatur habuisse non integros, sed fractos & comminutos, & humoribus ab ortu vacuos: ex terra igitur veluti materia novos fuisse efformatos. Irenæus autem lib. V. c. 15. ex qua, inquit, terra Deus formavit oculos cæco; ex hac plasmatis est homo: non enim consequens erat, aliunde quidem oculos, aliunde autem reliquum corpus plasmatum esse. Chrysostomus contendit lutum propterea fuisse abluendum, ut intelligat, luto opus non fuisse ad fingendos oculos. Saliva vero, vel sputo, verbum divinum adumbrari credit August. quod quemadmodum saliva à capite, ita verbum ex Patre oriatur.

καὶ ἐπέχρισε τὸν πηλὸν ἐπὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς τοῦ τυφλοῦ] Causam hujus facti ostendere cœpimus. Homini non tantum sua-pte natura non inest vis cognoscendi per se ea quæ divina sunt ac spiritualia, sed & quia ex luto factus est affectus habet luteos, qui ipsum impediunt, 1. Cor. II. 14.

## 9:7
Verse 7.

Wash in the pool of Siloam] eis for en. And Siloam, by the pronunciation of that age, for Siloa. Thus Silo is called Silom, Judges 18:31. From the fountain of Siloah came an aqueduct from which water was collected into this pool; from there, indeed, it was scattered in streams to irrigate the gardens: concerning which matter there is a passage of Timocharis in Eusebius, Praep. 9.

Which is interpreted, Sent] As often as the Evangelists add an interpretation of a word, they show that an allusion is being made to its meaning. The Hebrews maintain that Siloah was so named because water was sent forth from there. But Christ, who everywhere calls himself sent by the Father, above ch. 3, v. 17, 34, ch. 5, 36, 38, and elsewhere throughout, whence he is also called Apostle, Heb. 3:1, by this pool of the Sent One understands his own word, the cleansing word, Eph. 5:26, Acts 15:9. Upon those who despised this, calamities similar to those of which Isaiah had spoken, ch. 8:5, were incumbent; for that prophecy was fulfilled again in the destruction of Jerusalem. Nor is it incredible that John also looked to the famous prophecy of Jacob: where Shiloh, or with the epenthesis Shiloh with an he, not with a cheth, was in ancient codices, as is evidenced by Jerome's version, He who is to be sent.

That it is called the fountain of Siloah, because water was sent forth from there, we readily admit: But how a reference is had through the word Siloah to the Word of God, or at the same time also to Gen. XLIX, 6, does not appear. The ancients more correctly refer it to the water of Baptism, of which also Ephes. V. 26. See Ambros. b. IX. c. LXXVI. b. III. de Sacr. c. II. Tertull. lib. II. de Baptismo, Nyssen. de Baptism. Hieron. in c. VIII. Es. August. tract. XLIV. in Johan. But that the Messiah is called שלח through ח, is plainly to be denied. From the version of Jerome, the fountain of the Hebrew truth is rashly argued to be a corruption. See what we have said on that passage of Genesis.

καὶ ἐνίψατο καὶ ἦλθε βλέπων) Thus first men are cleansed from depraved affections, then they are illuminated, Ephes. I. 18. Hence the name φωτισμῦ for baptism. Here is indicated in passing the obedience of the blind man who refuses nothing, although it seems useless: Naaman is to be preferred in this, who for some time disdained to enter the Jordan. He went away, however, to his parents' house, from where he had not sat far off. See below c. IX. 18.

That we are first cleansed from depraved affections, then illuminated, is this an inverted order? For it is necessary that the illumination of the mind precede, before the purification and sanctification of the heart follows, Acts XXVI. 18. 1 Pet. I. 22. 2 Pet. I. 3. seq.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Νίψαι εἰς τὴν κολυμβήθραν τοῦ Σιλωὰμ] εἰς pro ἐν. Et Σιλωὰμ ejus sæculi pronuntiatione pro Σιλωά. Sic Silo vocatur Σιλὼμ Jud. XVIII. 31. Ex fonte Siloah prodibat aquæductus unde aqua in piscinam hanc colligebatur; inde vero rivis sparsa hortos irrigabat: de qua re locus est Timocharis apud Eusebium, præp. IX.

ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται ἀπεσταλμένος] Quoties vocis interpretationem adjungunt Evangelistæ ostendunt ad ejus significatum alludi. Siloah dictum volunt Hebræi, quod inde aqua emitteretur. At Christus qui ubique se vocat missum à Patre, supra c. 3, v. 17. 34. c. 5, 36 38. & alibi passim, unde & Ἀπόστολος dicitur Hebr. III. 1. per hanc κολυμβήθραν τοῦ ἀπεσταλμένου intelligit verbum suum, verbum emundans, Ephes. V. 26. Act. XV. 9. Quod qui contemnerent, iis incumbebant clades similes iis de quibus locutus erat Esa. VIII. 5. id enim vaticinium iterum completum est in excidio Hierosolymorum. Neque incredibile est respexisse Johannem simul ad celebre Jacobi vaticinium: ubi שִׁילוֹ vel cum epenthesi שִׁילוֹח per ה non per ח in antiquis fuisse codicibus documento est Hieronymi versio, Qui mittendus est.

Fontem Siloah dictum, quod inde aqua emit- teretur, facile admittimus: Sed quomodo per vo- cem Siloah ad Verbum Dei, vel simul etiam ad Gen. XLIX, 6. respectus habeatur, non apparet. Rectius ad aquam Baptismi, de qua etiam Ephes. V. 26. Ve- teres referunt. Vid. Ambros. l. IX. c. LXXVI. l. III. de Sacr. c. II. Tertull. lib. II. de Baptismo, Nyssen. de Baptism. Hieron. in c. VIII. Es. August. tract. XLIV. in Johan. Messiam vero שלח per ח dictum esse, plane negandum est. E versione Hieronymi te- mere arguitur fons Ebrææ veritatis corruptionis. Vid. quæ ad illum Genes. locum diximus.

καὶ ἐνίψατο καὶ ἦλθε βλέπων) Sic primum mundantur ho- mines à pravis affectibus, deinde illuminantur, Ephes. I. 18. Hinc baptismo nomen φωτισμῦ. Indicatur hic obiter obe- dientia cæci qui nihil recusat quanquam in speciem inutile: præferendus in hoc Neemani qui aliquamdiu spernebat in- trare Iordanem. Abiit autem ad domum parentem, unde non longe sederat. Vide infra c. IX. 18.

Mundari nos primum à pravis affectibus, de- inde illuminari, inversus ordo est? Præcedat enim oportet mentis illuminatio, antequam sequatur cordis purificatio, & sanctificatio Actor. XXVI. 18. 1. Petr. I. 22. 2. Petr. I. 3. seq.

## 9:8
Vers. 8.

οἱ ἐν γείτονες) Those who lived in the neighborhood and had seen him daily.

ὅτι προσάιτης ἦν) Since the Latin, Syriac, Arabic, and certain Greek codices agree on this reading, I judge it to be entirely preferred. He had often been seen, because he was imploring the mercy of all in public. See Mark X. 46, Luke XVIII. 35.

Most Greek codices have ὅτι τυφλὸς ἦν, for which there is no reason why it should be changed: the original text is certainly not to be changed from the Latin version, or even the Syriac and Arabic. Nor did Beza change it here, otherwise prone to the corruption of the text. For he did not find that προσαιτης in more than one copy.

ἐκ ὗτός ἐσιν ὁ καθήμενος προσαιτῶν) Is this not that very one? See a similar case in Acts III. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

οἱ ἐν γείτονες) Qui in proximo habitabant atque eum quotidie viderant.

ὅτι προσάιτης ἦν) Cum in hanc lectionem consentiant Latinus, Syrus, Arabs, & quidam Græci codices, omnino præferendam censeo, Sæpe visus erat, quia in publico mi- sericordiam omnium implorabat. Vide Marci X. 46 Luc. XVIII. 35.

Plerique Græci Codices habent ὅτι τυφλὸς ἦν, quod cur mutetur causa nulla est: è Latina certe versione, aut etiam Syriaca & Arabica mutandus textus originalis non est. Nec mutavit hic Beza, pronus alioquin in corruptionem textus. Non enim nisi in uno tantum exemplari illud προ- σαίτης invenit.

ἐκ ὗτός ἐσιν ὁ καθήμενος προσαιτῶν) Nonne hic ille ipse est? Vide simile Act. III. 10.

## 9:9
V. 9. ὅτι ὗτός ἐσιν) Some were plainly affirming it.

ἄλλοι δὲ ὅτι ὅμοιος αὐτῷ ἐσιν) These various opinions pertain to establishing faith in the miracle and showing its magnitude. For those who said he was very similar to him, so as not to believe it was the same person, were restrained by this alone, that they did not think it possible that a blind man could receive sight.

ἐκεῖνος ἔλεγεν, ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι) I am, namely that very one whom you saw blind: how this ἐγώ εἰμι is to be taken we have noted above. By a grateful profession he settles the whole dispute of the others, a most certain witness.

Latin:

V. 9. ὅτι ὗτός ἐσιν) Quidam plane affirmabant.

ἄλλοι δὲ ὅτι ὅμοιος αὐτῷ ἐσιν) Hæ variæ sententiæ perti- nent ad fidem adstruendam miraculo & ostendendam ejus magnitudinem. Nam qui dicebant simillimum ipsi esse, ne eundem crederent, hoc solo abstinebantur quod non co- gitarent fieri posse ut cæcus visum acciperet.

ἐκεῖνος ἔλεγεν, ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι) Ego sum, nempe ille ipse quem cæcum vidistis: quomodo sumi hoc ἐγώ εἰμι supra notavimus. Grata proffessione omne aliorum disputatio- nem dirimit, certissimus testis.

## 9:10
Vers. 10.

πῶς ἀνεῴχθησάν σοι οἱ ὀφθαλμοί) To open the eyes is to cause them to see. See Matt. IX. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

πῶς ἀνεῴχθησάν σοι οἱ ὀφθαλμοί) Aperire oculos est face- re ut videant. Vide Matth. IX. 30.

## 9:11
Vers. 11.

ἄνθρωπος λεγόμενος Ἰησοῦς) A certain man who is called Jesus. We learn from this many circumstances of the event omitted in the previous narrative, such as the blind man being addressed by Jesus: that he learned from him or from those standing by who it was that was addressing him: and what is added immediately after. These things were done on the Sabbath.

Νιψάμενος ἀνέβλεψα) As soon as I washed, I received my sight; this is, however, a catachresis: for ἀναβλέπειν properly belongs to those who at some time had the faculty of seeing; but one is not incorrectly said to receive back what, being commonly attributed to human nature, was absent from himself.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ἄνθρωπος λεγόμενος Ἰησοῦς) Quidam qui appellatur Iesus. Discimus hinc multas facti circumstantias in supe- riori narratione omissas, ut compellatum ab Iesum cæcum: ex ipso aut adstantibus didicisse quis esset qui se compel- laret: & quod mox adjicitur. Sabbato facta hæc.

Νιψάμενος ἀνέβλεψα) Statim ut lavi, accepi visum; est autem catachresis: nam ἀναβλέπειν proprie eorum est qui videndi facultatem aliquando habuerunt; sed nec male recipere quis dicitur quod communiter tributum humanæ naturæ ipsi abfuit.

## 9:12
Vers. 12.

πῦ ἐσιν ἐκεῖνος; λέγει, ἐκ οἶδα) Jesus was accustomed, once a miracle had been performed, to withdraw himself from the place, so that he might not seem to be hunting for glory from the crowd.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

πῦ ἐσιν ἐκεῖνος; λέγει, ἐκ οἶδα) Solebat Iesus miraculo edito se ex loco subducere, ne gloriam ex concursu venari videretur.

## 9:13
Vers. 13.

πρὸς τὲς Φαρισαίυς) By Pharisæos here I understand the Sanhedrin in which there were very many Pharisees. Thus Nonnus said ἀρχιερέας, because they also were in the Sanhedrin. See above c. I. 24. The same are the Jews below v. 18. & 22. that is, the leaders of the Jews, as already several times above.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

πρὸς τὲς Φαρισαίυς) Pharisæos hic intelligo Synedrium in quo plurimi Pharisæi. Sic ἀρχιερέας dixit Nonnus, quia & illi in Synedrio. Vide supra c. I. 24. Iidem infra Iudæi v. 18. & 22. id est primores Iudæorum ut jam supra aliquo- ties.

## 9:16
Vers. 16. Φαρισαίων τινές) The harsher ones.

ἐκ ἔσι παρὰ τῦ Θεῖ, ὅτι τὸ σάββατον ὐ τηρεῖ) He is not sent from God, because it is customary for him to work on the Sabbath. For he had already healed on the Sabbath several times: Pharisaic superstition had numbered the anointing of eyes among works forbidden on the Sabbath: even if this were so, nevertheless, that which pertains to the honor of God is free from the law.

καὶ ἄλλοι ἔλεγον) These were those in whom some goodness remained, who had not yet become callous.

ἄνθρωπος ἁμαρτωλὸς) Understand from the preceding words, one who falsely proclaims himself to be sent by God. For such are excellently called sinners. Thus ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας 2 Thess. II. 3.

τοιαῦτα σημεῖα ποιεῖν) Note τοιαῦτα & σημεῖα: First, things so excellent, divine, and salutary: And indeed as a sign of his mission. God would certainly never permit this, if he were falsely arrogating this to himself. See above c. III. 2.

Σχίσμα) We have spoken above in chapter VII. 43. so also below in chapter X. v. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Φαρισαίων τινές) Duriores.

ἐκ ἔσι παρὰ τῦ Θεῖ, ὅτι τὸ σάββατον ὐ τηρεῖ) Non est à Deo missus, quia solemne illi est operari in Sabbato. Iam enim aliquoties Sabbato sanaverat: Linere oculos Pharisai- ca superstitio operibus Sabbato vetitis annumaverat: quod etsi ita esset, tamen quod ad Dei honorem pertinet, liberum est à lege.

καὶ ἄλλοι ἔλεγον) Hi quibus aliquid bonitatis erat reliquum, qui nondum occalluerant.

ἄνθρωπος ἁμαρτωλὸς) Intellige ex verbis antecedentibus, qui se falso a Deo missum prædicat. Tales enim ex- cellenter peccatores vocantur. Sic ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρ- τίας 2. Thess. II. 3.

τοιαῦτα σημεῖα ποιεῖν) Nota τοιαῦτα & σημεῖα: Primum res tam eximias, divinas salutaresque: Et quidem in signum missionis suæ. Nunquam sane id Deus permitteret, si fal- so hoc sibi arrogaret. Vide supra c. III. 2.

Σχίσμα) Diximus supra cap. VII. 43. sic & infra cap. X. v. 19.

## 9:17
Vers. 17. τῷ τυφλῷ) That is, τῷ πότε τυφλῷ, as John had just spoken; concerning this manner of speaking, see what is at Matthew XXVI. 6.

σὺ τί λέγεις περὶ αὐτοῦ, ὅτι ἤνοιξέ σου τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς) Namely, on the Sabbath. For thus the question is completed.

ὅτι προφήτης ἐσίν) Sent by God. It was accepted among them that the Sabbath could be broken by the command of a prophet.

PART II. A more accurate investigation of the same matter.

Latin:

Vers. 17. τῷ τυφλῷ) Id est τῷ πότε τυφλῷ uti modo lo- cutus erat Johannes, de hoc loquendi genere vide quæ ad Matth. XXVI. 6.

σὺ τί λέγεις περὶ αὐτᾶ, ὅτι ἤνοιξέ σου τες ὀφθαλμὲς) Nem- pe in Sabbato. Ita enim perfecta est quæstio.

ὅτι προφήτης ἐσίν) A Deo missus. Receptum erat inter ipsos mandato prophetæ solvi posse Sabbatum.

PARS II. Rei ejusdem accuratior indagatio.

## 9:18
Vers. 18.

ἕως ὅτε) It does not follow from this that they believed afterwards: but since they did not believe, they wished to inquire into the whole matter from his parents. See what is at Matthew I. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

ἕως ὅτε) Non inde sequitur postea credidisse: sed cum non crederent voluisse eos ex parentibus sciscitari rem omnem. Vide quæ ad Matth. I. 25.

## 9:19
Vers. 19. ὑμεῖς λέγετε) By the very questioning they show what kind of answer they desire, namely, that he had not been truly blind, or at least not born as such, so that the praise of the healing might either be overturned or diminished.

How then does he now see) This alone could not be denied.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ὑμεῖς λέγετε) Ipsa percunctatione ostendunt quale responsum desiderent, nempe non fuisse revera cæ- cum, aut certe non natum talem, ut aut everteretur aut minueretur laus sanationis.

πῶς ὖν ἄρτι βλέπει) Hoc solum negari non pote- rat.

## 9:21
Ver. 21. ἡμεῖς οὐκ οἴδαμεν) We were not present when this was done.

αὐτὸς ἡλικίαν ἔχει) The age which is required by custom for giving testimony: which for the Hebrews is thirteen years.

περὶ ἑαυτῦ) Concerning that which he himself has discovered.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἡμεῖς ἐκ οἴδαμεν) Non adfuimus cum id fie- ret.

αὐτὸς ἡλικίαν ἔχει) Ætatem quæ ex moribus requiritur ad perhibendum testimonium: quæ Hebræis, anni XIII.

περὶ ἑαυτῦ) De eo quod ipsi compertum est.

## 9:22
Vers. 22. ἤδη γὰρ συνετέθεντο) For the greater part had already agreed on this. For previously, because of dissenting opinions, nothing could be decreed, see above c. VII. 53.

ἐάν τις αὐτὸν ὁμολογήσῃ χρίσον) What the healed blind man had said was very close to this. For he had acknowledged him as sent by God. Therefore, nothing else remained but for him to understand from Jesus that Jesus professed himself to be the Messiah. For if he had been sent by God, he ought to be believed in this as well. See below v. 35. 36. 37. 38.

ἀποσυνάγωγος γένηται) He should be excluded from the synagogues and familiar association, namely by נדוי which is properly translated ἀφορισμὸς, Luke VI. 22. For חרם and שמדתא, which is the second degree, began to be decreed against the followers of Jesus only after the resurrection. See what [is written] at Matt. XXIX. 15. & Apoc. XXII. v. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἤδη γὰρ συνετέθεντο) Jam major pars in eo con- venerat. Nam antea ob dissidentes sententias nihil perro- gari potuerat, supra c. VII. 53.

ἐάν τις αὐτὸν ὁμολογήσῃ χρίσον) Quod cæcus sanatus dixerat huic erat proximum. Missum enim a Deo agnove- rat. Quare nihil aliud restabat quam ut ex Jesu intellige- ret, Jesum se profiteri Messiam. Nam si a Deo missus erat, etiam in hoc ei credi debebat. Vide infra v. 35. 36. 37. 38.

ἀποσυνάγωγος γένηται) Excluderetur a Synagogis & fa- miliari convictu, nempe per נדוי quod proprie vertitur ἀφορισμὸς, Luc. VI. 22. nam חרם et שמדתא qui secundus est gradus, in Jesu sectatores decerni demum cœpit post resurrectionem. Vide quæ ad Matth. XXIX. 15. & Apoc. XXII. v. 15.

## 9:23
Vers. 23.

διὰ τῦτο οἱ γονεῖς ἀυτῦ εἶπον) More fearful of men than of God: it is no wonder if such people consult their own interests rather than those of their dearest ones, and thus they push their son into hatred.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

διὰ τῦτο οἱ γονεῖς ἀυτῦ εἶπον) Hominum quam Dei me- tuentiores: quales non mirum est si sibi potius quam caris- simis consulant, itaque filium obtrudunt odio.

## 9:24
Vers. 24.

ἐκ δευτέρω) For they had already heard him before, as has been narrated. But by more pressing interrogation they hoped they might be able to elicit something that would obscure the clarity of the miracle.

δὸς δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ) We explained this formula at Matt. XXVI. 63. Both the Prophets and the Judges of the great Sanhedrin appointed by God use this. In the Talmudic digests under the title concerning the Sanhedrin, Simeon, one of the Senators, addresses King Jannaeus thus: You do not stand before us, but before Him who said, let it be, and the world was made.

ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν ὅτι ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὗτος ἁμαρτωλός ἐσιν) The more they elicit some testimony against Jesus, they say that it is already established to them from elsewhere that he is a false boaster of the prophetic office. See above v. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ἐκ δευτέρω) Jam ante enim eum audiverant, ut narra- tum est. Sed pressiori interrogatione aliquid sperabant se posse elicere quod claritatem miraculi obscuraret.

δὸς δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ) Explicavimus hanc formulam Matth. XXVI. 63. Usurpant hanc & Prophetæ & Judices magni Sy- nedrii a Deo constituti. In Thalmudicis digestis titulo de Synedrio, Simeon Senatorum unus regem Jannæum sic al- loquitur: Non stas coram nobis, sed coram eo qui dixit, fiat & factus est mundus.

ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν ὅτι ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὗτος ἁμαρτωλός ἐσιν) Quo magis eliciant aliquod testimonium in Jesum ajunt sibi jam aliunde constare esse ipsum falsum jactatorem prophetici muneris. Vide supra v. 16.

## 9:25
Vers. 25.

εἰ ἁμαρτωλός ἐστι, ἐκ οἶδα) That which you say is established for you: concerning that, it is not established for me.

ἓν οἶδα) This one thing I know for certain.

τυφλὸς ὢν) ὢν, which I was, as this Syriac has it. A similar manner of speaking. See Eph. II. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

εἰ ἁμαρτωλός ἐστι, ἐκ οἶδα) Quod vos vobis constare dici- tis: de eo mihi non constat.

ἓν οἶδα) Hoc unum certo mihi constat.

τυφλὸς ὢν) ὢν qui eram, ut habet hic Syrus. Simile lo- quendi genus. Vide Eph. II. 5.

## 9:26
Vers. 26.

τί ἐποίησέ σοι; πῶς ἤνοιξέ σε τες ὀφθαλμὲς;) From the very manner of the healing they hoped they would discover something by which it would be established that it had not been true and congenital blindness.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

τί ἐποίησέ σοι; πῶς ἤνοιξέ σε τες ὀφθαλμὲς;) Ex ipso fanationis modo sperabant aliquid deprehensuros se quo constaret non fuisse veram ac nativam cæcita- tem.

## 9:27
Vers. 27.

καὶ ἐκ ἠκέσατε) Thus both the Syriac and the Arab: wherefore I judge this reading to be preferred: but with a mark of interrogation, so that what follows may cohere better: Have you not heard enough?

Grotius rightly prefers this reading, which is also that of the Syriac and the Arabic, even though the Latin Vulgate omits the negative particle, taking this as an interrogative mark so that what follows coheres better: Have you not heard enough? Ludovicus de Dieu explains it thus: They are contradictory, you have heard, and you have not heard. Yet both are true in a different respect. They had heard with the ears of the body, they had not heard with the ears of the mind. For to hear is often to embrace with the mind, as we said above in ch. VIII, v. 43. There is also to listen, to attend, which fits this place well. I have already told you, and you did not attend. τί πάλιν θέλετε ἀκύειν; The Syriac and Arabic did not read πάλιν. Thus the sense would be, when I first told you, you did not attend. From there I gather that you did not wish to hear. Why do you now wish to hear.

μὴ καὶ ὑμεῖς θέλετε αὐτῦ μαθηταὶ γενέσθαι) Could it be that you, who boast that you know everything, would use that man as a teacher?

PART III. The confrontation of the Jews with the blind man, and his expulsion.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

καὶ ἐκ ἠκέσατε) Sic & Syrus & Arabs: quare hanc lectio- nem præferendam censeo: sed cum interrogandi nota, ut melius cohæreat quod sequitur: Annon satis audistis?

Recte hanc lectionem, quæ Syri etiam est, & Arabis, etsi Latina vulgata particulam negantem omittat, præfert Grotius, cum interrogandi nota hæc accipiens, ut melius cohæreat quod sequitur: Annon satis audistis? Ludovicus de Dieu ita ex- plicat: Contradictoria sunt, audistis, & non audi- stis. Utrumque tamen diverso respectu verum. Audiverant auribus corporis, non audiverant au- ribus animi. Audire enim sæpe est animo ample- cti, ut diximus supra c. VIII. v. 43. Est & auscultare, attendere, quod huic loco bene quadrat. Jam dixi vobis, & non attendistis. τί πάλιν θέλετε ἀκύειν; Syrus & Arabs non legerunt πάλιν. Sic sensus esset, quum primum narravi vobis, non attendistis. Inde colligo noluisse vos audire. Cur jam vul- tis audire.

μὴ καὶ ὑμεῖς θέλετε αὐτῦ μαθηταὶ γενέσθαι) Possetne fieri ut vos qui omnia scire vos venditatis, illo magistro uta- mini.

PARS III. Judæorum cum cæco collatio, hujusque ejectio.

## 9:28
Vers. 28. σὺ εἶ μαθητὴς ἐκείνε) You are certainly his supporter, for you speak in his favor.

τῦ Μωσέως ἐσμὲν μαθηταὶ) Content with that teacher, we seek no other.

Latin:

Vers. 28. σὺ εἶ μαθητὴς ἐκείνε) Tu sane ejus fautor es, nam in gratiam ejus loqueris.

τῦ Μωσέως ἐσμὲν μαθηταὶ) Illo magistro contenti alium non quærimus.

## 9:29
Vers. 29. τῦτον δὲ ὐκ οἴδαμεν πόθεν ἐστιν) The opposition of the preceding member shows that πόθεν here signifies mission: we do not know whether he teaches by his own impulse or by the instigation of a demon. See above ch. VII. 29. Therefore it follows immediately εἰ μὴ ἧν παρὰ Θεῦ.

Latin:

Vers. 29. τῦτον δὲ ὐκ οἴδαμεν πόθεν ἐστιν) Oppositio membri præcedentis ostendit πόθεν hic significare missio- nem: nescimus suopte impulsu, an dæmonis instigatu do- ceat. Vide supra cap. VII. 29. ideo mox sequitur εἰ μὴ ἧν παρὰ Θεῦ.

## 9:30
V. 30. ἐν γὰρ ἐν τύτῳ θαυμασόν ἐστιν) That θαυμαστόν is impersonal, as if you were to say: it is a thing for us to marvel at, with ἐν standing for because of. A similar construction is found after θαυμάζειν in Luke I. 21, 2 Thess. I. 10.

ὑμεῖς ὐκ οἴδατε πόθεν ἐστί) You, who have arrogated to yourselves the knowledge of judging between true and false Prophets.

καὶ ἀνέῳξε) καὶ for yet, as above.

Latin:

V. 30. ἐν γὰρ ἐν τύτῳ θαυμασόν ἐστιν) Illud θαυμαστόν im- personale est, quasi dicas: est quod hoc miremur, ἐν pro ob. Similis constructio post θαυμάζειν Luc. I. 21. 2. Thess. I. 10.

ὑμεῖς ὐκ οἴδατε πόθεν ἐστί) Vos qui vobis arrogastis scien- tiam dijudicandi inter Prophetas veros & falsos.

καὶ ἀνέῳξε) καὶ pro tamen, ut supra.

## 9:31
Vers. 31.

ἀμαρτωλῶν ὁ Θεὸς ὐκ ἀκύει) This is indeed quite proverbial, as can be seen in Ps. LXVI. 18, Isaiah I. 15, and elsewhere: but both the preceding and following context require that this be understood of him who falsely asserts that he is sent by God: whom God does not hear, so that he might produce divine signs to give assurance of his mission; indeed, God permits no miracles to be performed by such people, outside of the case of temptation to the worship of false gods, against which the Israelites ought to have been sufficiently fortified. And these very miracles are far removed from what Jesus had done. See what was said at Matt. XXIV. 24.

Augustine does not simply approve of this opinion of the blind man, and says that he was still imperfect and not yet imbued with true faith, and in Book II against the Epistle of Parmenianus, ch. VIII, as also in Book V on Baptism against the Donatists, ch. XXXI, he refutes those who inferred from this that the prayers of those who administer [sacraments] badly lack all efficacy, and he concludes finally: not every sinner is indeed heard, nor is every sinner not heard. However, one must first distinguish between the good things that are sought, which are either bodily or spiritual: it is established that the former are given even to those who do not ask, Matt. V. 41, out of the common goodness of the creator and preserver of all, which nevertheless are sometimes denied even out of his justice, Ps. LXVI. 18, Prov. I. 24, Is. I. 15, Zech. VII. 13. These spiritual things, however, do not befall obstinate sinners, because they arise from the singular grace promised in Christ, and are proper to the penitent or the justified, Job XIV. 14, ch. XV. 7, ch. XVI. 23, 2 Cor. I. 20, Job I. 9. We acknowledge, however, that the saying of the blind man is special, nor do we disagree with the explanation of Grotius, who rightly says of v. 31, ἐάν τις θεοσεβὴς ᾖ καὶ τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ ποιῇ, τούτου ἀκούει: This is also proverbial, as can be seen in Psalm XXXIV. 16 and elsewhere. But this also must be adapted to the present matter: so that it is understood that God willingly grants the power of signs to those who, with a pious mind, carry out the commands of God and have need of signs for this.

ἀκούῃ) This is also proverbial, as can be seen in Ps. XXXIV. 16 and elsewhere, even among the Greeks. εὐχῆς δικαίας οὐκ ἀνήκοος Θεός. Whence that of Ovid in the first book of the Metamorphoses: If, they said, just prayers soften the gods, they relent. But this also must be adapted to the present matter; so that it is understood that God willingly grants the power of signs to those who, with a pious mind, carry out the commands of God and have need of signs for this.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

ἀμαρτωλῶν ὁ Θεὸς ὐκ ἀκύει) Est quidem hoc satis prover- biale, ut videre est Ps. LXVI. 18. Esaæ I. 15. & alibi: sed & præcedentia & sequentia exigunt ut intelligatur hoc de eo qui falso se à Deo missum asseverat: quem Deus non exau- dit, ut divina edat signa ad fidem faciendam suæ missionis, imo nulla miracula fieri Deus talibus permittit, extra cau- sam tentationis ad cultum falsorum Deorum, adversus quem satis muniti esse debebant Israelitæ. Et hæc ipsa mira- cula multum absunt ab eo quod Jesus fecerat. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. XXIV. 24.

Augustinus non simpliciter hanc cæci senten- tiam probat, & adhuc imperfecti nec vera fide im- buti esse, ait, & lib. II. contr. Epist. Parmen. c. VIII. ut & lib. V. de Bapt. contra Donatist. c. XXXI. refel- lit eos, qui inferebant inde, preces administran- tium male carere omni efficacia, & concludit tan- dem: non omnis peccator quidem exauditur, nec omnis peccator non exauditur. Distinguendum au- tem imprimis inter bona quæ petuntur, quæ vel corporalia sunt, vel spiritualia: illa malis etiam non petentibus dari constat Matth. V. 41. ex com- muni creatoris & conservatoris omnium bonita- te, quæ tamen interdum etiam ex ejusdem justitia denegantur Ps. LXVI. 18. Prov. I. 24. Es. I. 15. Zach. VII. 13. Hæc vero spiritualia non obtingunt pecca- toribus pertinacibus, quia ex singulari gratia in Christo promissa oriuntur, & pœnitentium vel justificatorum propria sunt, Job. XIV. 14. c. XV. 7. c. XVI. 23. 2. Cor. I. 20. Job. I. 9. Præsens tamen cæci dictum speciale esse agnoscimus, neque Grotii ex- plicationi abnuimus, qui ad v. 31. ἐάν τις θεοσεβὴς ἦ καὶ τὸ θέλημα αὐτῦ ποιῇ, τύτυ ἀκύει recte: Est & hoc proverbiale, ut videre est Psal. XXXIV. 16. & alibi. Sed & hoc aptandum est ad præsentem mate- riam: ut intelligatur Deus, libenter concedere potesta- tem signorum his qui pio animo Dei mandata exse- quuntur & ad hoc signis opus habent.

ἀκούῃ) Est & hoc proverbiale ut videre est Pf. XXXIV. 16. & alibi etiam apud Græcos. εὐχῆς δικαίας οὐκ ἀνήκοος Θεός. Unde illud Ovidii primo Metamorphoseon: Si precibus, dixerunt, numina justis Victa remollescunt. Sed & hoc aptandum ad præsentem materiam; ut intelliga- tur Deus, libenter concedere potestatem signorum his qui pio animo Dei mandata exsequuntur & ad hoc signis opus habent.

## 9:32
Vers. 32. ἐκ τοῦ αἰῶνος οὐκ ἠκούσθη) As if he were saying: neither did the Prophets do this, nor he himself whom I profess as Master, Moses. And indeed, what reason could the Senators bring forward why they should believe Jesus less than Moses, when they beheld the miracles of the former, and indeed greater ones, while they had only received those of the latter from their fathers? The Midrash on Ps. 146 says that the Messiah will open the eyes of the blind; add Isaiah 42. 7.

τυφλοῦ γεγεννημένου) This is emphatic: for otherwise many lose their sight through disease, who are curable and not completely blind.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ἐκ τοῦ αἰῶνος οὐκ ἠκούσθη) Quasi dicat: neque Prophetæ hoc fecerunt, necipse ille quem Magistrum pro- fitemi i Moses. Et sane quam causam Senatores adferre poterant cur Jesu minus quam Mofi crederent, cum hujus miracula & quidem majora adspicerent, illius vero à patri- bus tantum accepissent? Messiam cæcis aperturum oculos ait Midrasch in Pf. 146. adde Efaiam 42. 7.

τυφλοῦ γεγεννημένου) ἐμφατικῶν hoc est: nam alioqui mor- bo multi visum amittunt, qui sanabiles sunt nec plane cæci.

## 9:33
Vers. 33. παρὰ Θεοῦ) Sent, that is. See above ch. VII 29.

οὐκ ἠδύνατο ποιεῖν οὐδέν) Understand: of those things which he did.

Latin:

Vers. 33. παρὰ Θεοῦ) Missus scilicet. Vide supra cap. VII 29.

οὐκ ἠδύνατο ποιεῖν οὐδέν) Subintellige horum quæ fe- cit.

## 9:34
Vers. 34. ἐν ἁμαρτίαις σὺ ἐγεννήθης ὅλος) It is a hyperbolic expression which signifies that someone has been vicious from his earliest age, Ps. LI. 7, Ps. LVIII. 4, Isaiah 48. 8. And Chrysostom on this passage: ὡσανεὶ ἔλεγον ἐκ πρώτης ἡλικίας ἐν ἁμαρτίαις εἶ. Thus also other things which have been with us from childhood are said to have been with us from the womb, Ps. XXII. 10, Ps. LXXI. 5, 6, Job XXXI. 18. ὅλος, that is, entirely, as much as you are, you are full of sins. A grave insult.

That hyperbole is not necessary if you look at the opinion of the Pharisees and their hypothesis concerning metempsychosis: nor does the same have a place in Ps. LI. 7, Ps. LVIII. 4, Isa. XLVIII. 8, provided that original sin is either described there, or is included at the same time as the cause of depravity. Ps. XXII deals with Christ, who was holy from the womb, or rather from the first moment of conception: See what was said regarding that.

διδάσκεις ἡμᾶς) Us, the teachers and judges of the people and eminent in holiness, whence the Pharisees were so called.

PART IV. The blind man's profession of faith, with Jesus' testimony concerning the end of his coming, and the admonition of the Pharisees.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ἐν ἁμαρτίαις σὺ ἐγεννήθης ὅλος) Locutio est hyperbolica quæ significat aliquem à prima ætate vitiosum fuiffe Pf. LI. 7. Pf. LIIX. 4. Esaiæ 48. 8. Et Chrysostomus ad hunc locum: ὡσανεὶ ἔλεγον ἐκ πρωτῆς ἡλικίας ἐν ἁμαρτίαις ἦσυ. Sic & aliæ res quæ nobis à pueritia adfuerunt dicun- tur ab utero adfuisse Pf. XXII. 10. Pf. LXXI. 5. 6. Job. XXXI. 18. ὅλος id est totus, quantus es scates peccatis. Grave convitium.

Illa hyperbole non opus est, si Pharisæorum re- spicias sententiam & hypothesin de μετεμψυχώ- σει: neque eadem locum habet Pf. LI. 7. Pf. LIIX. 4. Esa. XLIIX. 8. siquidem ibi peccatum originale vel describatur, vel simul ceu causa pravitatis com- prehendatur. Pf. XXII. de Christo agit, qui ab utero, vel potius à primo conceptionis momento sanctus: Vid. quæ ad illum dicta.

διδάσκεις ἡμᾶς) Nos magistros & Judices populi & san- ctitate eximios, unde Pharisæi dicebantur.

PARS IV. Fidei cæci professio, cum Jesu de fine adventus sui testificatione, & Pharisæorum commonitione.

## 9:35
Vers. 35. ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω) They did not dismiss him, but ordered him to be ignominiously cast out of the court of the Sanhedrin by their attendants; thus this word is used in Acts VII. 58, ch. XIII. 50, and elsewhere.

ἤκουσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω) He wished to know this in the human manner, as others were telling it. But Jesus is present for his witnesses who are suffering evils on account of that testimony.

πιστεύεις εἰς τὸν ὑιον τῦ Θεῦ) You place your trust in the Messiah, which all Jews profess to do. Son of God was a common surname for the Messiah, as noted above in ch. I. v. 46. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω) Non dimiserunt, sed per apparito- res è curia Synedrii ignominiofe ejici jusserunt, ita vox hæc usurpatur Act. VII. 58. c XIII. 50. & alibi.

ἤκουσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι ἐξέβαλον αὐτὸν ἔξω) Volebat hoc scire humano more, narrantibus aliis. Præsto autem est Jesus testibus suis ob id testimonium mala ferenti- bus.

πιστεύεις εἰς τὸν ὑιον τῦ Θεῦ) Fiduciam tuam collocas in Messiam, quod omnes Judæi facere se profitentur. Filius Dei cognomen erat usitatum Messiæ, ut notatum supra c. I. v. 46. & alibi.

## 9:36
Vers. 36. ἐκεῖνος) He who had been healed, which the Syriac adds here. καὶ τίς ἐστι κύριε, ἵνα πιστεύσω εἰς αὐτόν) Where is he? has he come already?

Latin:

Vers. 36. ἐκεῖνος) Qui fanatus erat, quod hic addit Syrus. καὶ τίς ἐστι κύριε, ἵνα πιστεύσω εἰς αὐτόν) Ubi est? jamne venit?

## 9:37
Vers. 37. κὰι ἑώρακας αὐτὸν) You have experienced his mighty work: for he is the one through whom you recovered your sight. Thus above ch. VI. 36. below ch. XIV.

καὶ ὁ λαλῶν μετὰ σῦ, ἐκεῑνός ἐστι) He had said that the Messiah was the one who had restored his sight to him; now he adds that he himself is that person.

Latin:

Vers. 37. κὰι ἑώρακας αὐτὸν) Virtutem ejus expertus es: nam is est per quem visum recuperasti. Sic supra cap. VI. 36. infra cap. XIV.

καὶ ὁ λαλῶν μετὰ σῦ, ἐκεῑνός ἐστι) Dixerat Messiam eum fuisse, qui visum ipsi reddidiffet; nunc addit semet eum esse.

## 9:38
Vers. 38. πιστέυω κύριε) I clearly place my hope in him. κὰι προσεκύνησεν αὐτὸν) Not merely as a Prophet, but as the Messiah, to whom the highest honor was owed. Wherefore the Latin and Syriac have expressed here a gesture of extraordinary veneration.

Latin:

Vers. 38. πιστέυω κύριε) Plane in illo spem meam colloco. κὰι προσεκύνησεν αὐτὸν) Non modo ut Prophetam, sed ut Messiam, cui summus honos debebatur. Quare ge- stum eximiæ venerationis hic expresserunt Latinus & Sy- rus.

## 9:39
Vers. 39. εἰς κρίμα ἐγὼ εἰς τὸν κόσμον τῦτον ἦλθον) From the time I came into the world, that is, appeared openly to men (as we explained above ch. I. 9.) the judgments of God shine forth on this occasion: for the εἰς which follows ἵνα, as often elsewhere, are consequential. See what we said at Luke II. 34. κρίμα is taken here, as in Rom. XI. 33.

ἵνα οἱ μὴ βλέποντες) According to his custom he alludes to the event. Those who do not see, understand also those who feel themselves to be such: such as that blind man had been, who arrogated to himself no skill in divine matters. See above v. 25, 30.

βλέπωσι) May they be gifted with knowledge. Compare the passage of Matthew ch. 11, 25, and what is said there.

καὶ οἱ βλέποντες) Those who wish to be considered and called פקחים, seeing ones, which was the name of the wise, such as most of the Pharisees were considered: and such as these very men with whom the matter was wished to be considered, as appears above v. 24, 29, 34.

τυφλοὶ γένωνται) That is, may they appear blind, ignorant of divine matters, as these men, who in every way acted so as not to see what they were seeing, that light had been given to the blind. Thus they were made foolish, Rom. I, 22. According to the custom of the Hebrews who express the declaration of a thing through Hiphil.

Latin:

Vers. 39. εἰς κρίμα ἐγὼ εἰς τὸν κόσμον τῦτον ἦλθον) Ex quo in mundum veni, id est hominibus palam apparui (ut ex- posuimus supra cap. I. 9.) judicia Dei hac occasione elu- cescunt: nam εἰς quod sequitur ἵνα, ut alibi sæpe, sunt ἐκβατικά. Vide quæ diximus Luc. II. 34. κρίμα hic sumi- tur, ut Rom. XI. 33.

ἵνα οἱ μὴ βλέποντες) More suo alludit ad rem gestam. Qui non vident, subintellige & qui tales se esse sentiunt: qualis ille cœcus fuerat, qui nullam sibi rerum divinarum peritiam arrogabat. Vid. supra v. 25. 30.

βλέπωσι) Cognitione donentur. Conf. locum Matthæi c. 11, 25. & quæ ibi dicta.

καὶ οἱ βλέποντες) Qui tales haberi volunt & appellari פקחים videntes, quod erat nomen sapientum, quales ple- rique Pharisæorum habebantur: & quales hi ipsi cum quibus res erat haberi se volebant ut apparet supra v. 24. 29. 34.

τυφλοὶ γένωνται) Id est appareant cœci, ignari rerum di- vinarum, ut hi, qui omni modo hoc agebant, ne viderent quod videbant, cœco lucem datam. Sic ἐμωράνθησαν Rom. I, 22. Ex Hebræorum more qui declarationem rei per Hi- phil enunciant.

## 9:40
Vers. 40.

οἱ ὄντες μετ’ αὐτῶ) Certain of the Pharisees who followed him for this very purpose, that they might catch his words, Luke XV, 2.

μὴ καὶ ἡμεῖς τυφλοί ἐσμεν) They understood well enough that Christ was speaking of blindness of the soul. But they think it unworthy and incredible that they should be placed in that number.

Latin:

Vers. 40.

οἱ ὄντες μετ’ αὐτῶ) Quidam ex Pharisæis qui in hoc ipsum sectabantur ut sermones ejus captarent, Luc. XV. 2.

μὴ καὶ ἡμεῖς τυφλοί ἐσμεν) Satis intelligebant Christum de animi cœcitate loqui. Sed indignum & incredibile putant se in eo numero poni.

## 9:41
Vers. 41.

εἰ τυφλοὶ ἦτε) Just as just now. μὴ βλέποντες were those who acknowledged their own ignorance, so here, if you were blind, is: if you conducted yourselves as such, if you acknowledged the ignorance by which you are held. The opposite member shows this.

οὐκ ἂν εἴχετε ἁμαρτίαν) That is, you would be in some way excusable: for ἁμαρτία is taken here not for any fault, but for a grave and unpardonable crime, as below ch. XV, 22, 24, ch. 16, 8, 9, where likewise to have sin is to be guilty. Here ἁμαρτία, that is רשע, is opposed to ἁγνοία, that is שגגה.

Νῦν δὲ λέγετε ὅτι βλέπομεν) ὅτι is redundant in the Hebrew manner: and λέγειν is to think. But now you think that you are wise: even after your error has been openly shown to you. Add Rom. II, 19.

ἡ οὖν ἁμαρτία ὑμῶν μένει) That is, it does not perish, it is not taken away. Just as μένειν is taken below ch. XV, 11, 1 Corinthians III, v. 14. But I understand to be taken away as to be forgiven because of the member above here opposed. The Syrian has קיים here, which signifies, it is firm, in the sense which we have said.

Latin:

Vers. 41.

εἰ τυφλοὶ ἦτε) Sicut modo. μὴ βλέποντες erant qui ignorantiam suam agnoscebant, ita hic, si cœci essetis, est: si vos pro talibus gereretis, si agnosceretis ignoran- tiam qua tenemini. Ostendit hoc membrum opposi- tum.

οὐκ ἂν εἴχετε ἁμαρτίαν) Id est, essetis aliquo modo ex- cusabiles: nam ἁμαρτία hic sumitur non pro quavis cul- pa, sed pro gravi & incondonabili crimine, ut infra c. XV. 22. 24. cap. 16, 8. 9. ubi itidem habere peccatum est reum esse. Opponitur hic ἁμαρτία id est רשע, ἁγνοία id est שגגה.

Νῦν δὲ λέγετε ὅτι βλέπομεν) ὅτι abundat more Hebræo:& λέγειν id est cogitare. Nunc autem existimatis vos sapere: etiam postquam error vester vobis aperte monstratus est. Adde Rom. II. 19.

ἡ οὖν ἁμαρτία ὑμῶν μένει) Id est non perit, non aufer- tur. Sicut μένειν sumitur infra c. XV. 11. 1. Corinth. III. v. 14. Auferri autem intelligo condonari ob membrum superius hic oppositum. קיים habet hic Syrus, quod significat, firmum est, eo quo diximus sensu.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The parable concerning him who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, who is pronounced a thief and a robber, and the Shepherd, who enters through the door, to whom the doorkeeper opens and the sheep hear his voice, whom he leads out having called them by name, fleeing from a stranger, is explained by Jesus, that he himself is the door, that all who have not entered through him have been thieves and robbers, but that he who enters through him shall be saved and find pastures. Furthermore, Jesus professes that he is that good Shepherd, distinguishing the good shepherd from the hireling, that he knows his own sheep, and lays down his life for them, and that he will bring other sheep to the fold, and that he lays down his life of his own accord, and has power to take up his life again. Whence a dispute concerning him arose among the Jews. At the Feast of Dedication the Jews ask him whether he is the Christ; Jesus affirms it, and appeals to his works, and says that they, because they do not believe, are not his sheep, that he will give eternal life to his sheep, and that they shall not be snatched from his hands, and that he himself is the same with the Father, who is above all: but the Jews wishing to stone him on the pretext of blasphemy, because, being a man, he makes himself God, having been convinced, and warned that they are called gods to whom the word of God came, he testifies that he is the less a blasphemer, inasmuch as he, having been sanctified by GOD the Father and sent into the world, is truly the Son of God, since he does the works of his Father, which testify that the Father is in him and he is in the Father: and when they wished to seize him, he went out of their hands: departing across the Jordan, where many believed in him.

There are four parts: I. The parable of Jesus concerning the door and the sheepfold, to v. 11. II. The discourse concerning his pastoral office, to v. 21. III. The profession, confirmation, and defense that Christ is one with the Father, God and the Son of God sent into the world, to v. 39. IV. The departure into Perea, to v. 42.

PART I. The parable of Jesus concerning the door and the sheepfold.

Ver. 1.

Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν) The occasion for this discourse, as for the previous one, arises from the situation. For because the blind man had been cast out and Christ was regarded as a seducer, he begins from this point to discourse concerning the true shepherd and the door. But just as Christ in the previous discourse, in order to indicate that he was the Messiah, had used a circumlocution and called himself the light of the world, which is an epithet of the Messiah: so now he signifies the same thing by another epithet. For in Ezekiel the Messiah is indicated by the name of one shepherd, ch. 34, 23. Therefore, after this discourse was finished, the Jews ask whether he calls himself the Christ, below v. 24. See 1 Pet. V. 4, where the same passage of Ezekiel is referred to. Also in Xenophon we read, παραπλήσια ἔργα νομέως ἀγαθῦ καὶ βασιλέως ἀγαθῦ.

Grotius acknowledges here that by the one Shepherd in Ezek. 34, 23, Christ is to be understood. But what he acknowledged in his annotations on that passage, he contends there that the discourse is about Zerubbabel. Behold a spirit of giddiness!

Διὰ τῆς θύρας) Through the door of the farmstead where there immediately appeared an open-air space and in it the sheepfold. Eustathius on Odyssey Ξ. πρόδομος ὁ ἔξω μεθ’ ὃν εὐθὺς ἡ αὐλή.

εἰς τὴν αὐλὴν τῶν προβάτων) For there were also other enclosures for goats, of their own.

ἀλλαχόθεν) By breaking through the wall.

κλέπτης ἐστὶ κὰι λῃστής) A thief because he comes to steal what is another's: a robber because he comes to kill. Thus it is explained below v. 10.

Latin:

CAPUT X. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Parœmia de non ingrediente per ostium in ovi- le, qui fur & latro pronunciatur, ac Pa- store, qui per ostium ingreditur, cui ape- rit ostiarius & vocem ejus audiunt oves, quas nominatim vocatas educit, alienum fugientes, explicatur à Jesu, quod ipse sit ostium, omnes, non per ipsum ingressi, fu- res & latrones fuerint, qui vero per i- psum ingreditur, salvetur & pabula inve- niat. Porro profitetur Jesus, se esse bonum illum Pastorem, distinguens pastorem bo- num à mercenario, se novisse oves suas, & vitam pro illis ponere, aliasque oves ad ovi- le adducturum esse, vitam & à semetipso ponere, & potestatem habere vitam resu- mendi. Unde disceptatio de ipso inter Ju- dæos orta. In Encæniis quærunt de ipso Ju- dæi anne Christus sit, Jesus id affirmat, & ad opera sua provocat, eosque, quia non cre- dunt, oves suas non esse, ovibus suis se da- turum vitam æternam, easque non ere- ptum iri è manibus suis ait, quodque ipse cum Patre, qui super omnia est, idem sit: Judæis autem ipsum lapidare volentibus prætextu blasphemiæ, quod cum homo sit, Deum se faciat, convictis, monitisque Deos dici, ad quos sermo Dei factus est, te- statur eo minus blasphemum se esse, utpo- te qui à DEO Patre sanctificatus, & in mundum missus, vere Filius Dei sit, quum opera Patris sui faciat, quæ testentur, quod Pater in se & ipse in Patre sit: & quum apprehendere ipsum vellent, è manibus eo- rum exiit: Trans Iordanem proficiscens, ubi multum in eum credidere.

Partes sunt quatuor: I. Parœmia Jesu de o- stio, & ovili, ad v. 11. II. Concio de Pastorali suo officio, ad v. 21. III. Professio, confirmatio ac de- fensio, quod Christus sit unus cum Patre Deus ac Dei Filius in mundum missus, ad v. 39. IV. Pro- fectio in Pœream, ad v. 42.

PARS I. Parœmia Jesu de ostio & ovili.

Vers. 1.

Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν) Sermoni huic ut & priori occasio ex re nascitur. Quia enim cæcus ejectus erat & Christus pro seductore habitus, hinc de vero pastore & ostio incipit dis- serere. Sicut autem Christus priori sermone, ut Messiam se indicaret, circumlocutione usus se lucem mundi dixe- rat, quod Messiæ est epithetum: Ita nunc alio epitheto idem significat. Nam apud Ezechielem Messias indicatur nomine unius pastoris cap. 34, 23. Ideo post hunc ser- monem absolutum interrogant Judæi, an se Christum di- cat, infra v. 24. Vide 1. Petr. V. 4. ubi idem Ezechie- lis locus respicitur. Etiam apud Xenophontem legi- mus, παραπλήσια ἔργα νομέως ἀγαθῦ καὶ βασιλέως ἀ- γαθῦ.

Agnoscit hic Grotius, quod Ezech. 34, 23. per unum Pastorem Christus intelligendus sit. Quod vero agnovit in annot. ad istum locum conten- dens ibi sermonem esse de Zorobabele. En spi- ritum vertiginis!

Διὰ τῆς θύρας) Per ostium villæ ubi statim apparebat subdiale & in eo caula. Eustathius ad Odysseæ Ξ. πρόδομος ὁ ἔξω μεθ’ ὃν εὐθὺς ἡ αὐλή.

εἰς τὴν αὐλὴν τῶν προβάτων) Nam erant & alia septa hir- corum, suum.

ἀλλαχόθεν) Perrupto pariete.

κλέπτης ἐστὶ κὰι λῃστής) Fur quia venit ut rapiat alienum: latro quia ut occidat. Sic exponitur infra v. 10.

## 10:2
Verse 2.

ὁ δὲ εἰσερχόμενος διὰ τῆς θύρας) He who is chosen for that office.

Grotius thinks that by these words Christ indicated that he was the Messiah. But those words sound rather general, because Christ opposed the description of the true Shepherd to the Pharisees, whom he tacitly implies are thieves and robbers, not true Shepherds. For the Pharisees were not hired by the heavenly Master of the house, nor introduced through the door by the doorkeeper, but had crept into the fold of God of their own accord. The order of the Pharisees was neither instituted by God, nor introduced by the Holy Spirit or the Prophets, but was fabricated by men and erected by their own daring: whence it was easy to conclude that they themselves were not shepherds, but thieves and robbers. Therefore, they also had no care for the sheep; they neither helped them with the sincere doctrine of the divine Word, nor led the way with an honest example of life, but fattened only themselves, allowing the people of God to wander into any errors and any sects whatsoever. B. Lyferus and others observe here five marks of a true Shepherd: 1. A legitimate calling, so that he may enter through the door. 2. The opening by the doorkeeper, who is the Holy Spirit, Acts 13, verse 2, without whose grace no Shepherd can either enter into the fold or feed the sheep. 3. Knowledge and recognition of the sheep: that he may call them by name.

4. The leading out of the sheep; so that he may send them out from the fold to the pastures, and lead them out.

5. The going before of the sheep: since shepherds in the East are accustomed not to follow the flock in our manner, but to go before it, so that the sheep may go before by voice and example, and invite, so that, namely, they may follow to the pastures of the divine word 1 Tim. 4, 12. 16. Tit. 2, 1. et seqq. However, Christ does not yet apply this to himself alone, and in this former address he does not yet indicate or profess himself to be the Messiah.

Compare Prov. 27, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ὁ δὲ εἰσερχόμενος διὰ τῆς θύρας) Qui ad officium illud electus est.

His ergo Christum se Messiam indicasse, cen- set Grotius. Sed illa sonant potius generali- ter, quia Christus Pharisæis, quos fures & la- trones, non veros Pastores esse tacite innuit, opposuit descriptionem veri Pastoris. Pharisæi enim non erant à cœlesti Patrefamilias condu- cti, nec ab ostiario per ostium intromissi, sed suapte sponte in caulam Dei irrepserant. Pha- risæorum ordo, neque à Deo institutus fuit, ne- que à Spiritu sancto vel Prophetis introductus, sed ab hominibus confictus, & proprio ipso- rummet ausu erectus: unde colligere in pro- clivi erat, ipsos non pastores, sed fures ac la- trones esse. Proinde etiam ovium nullam ha- buere curam, eas neque doctrina Verbi divini sincera juverunt, neque honesto vitæ exemplo antecesserunt, sed seipsos solum saginarunt, permittentes populum Dei ad quosvis errores, & quasvis sectas divagari. B. Lyferus aliisque observant hic quinque notas veri Pastoris: 1. Legitimam vocationem, ut per ostium in- tret. 2. Ostiarii apertionem, qui est Spiri- tus sanctus, Actorum XIII. vers. 2. sine cujus gratia nullus Pastor nec in ovile intrare; nec oves pascere potest. 3. Ovium noti- tiam & cognitionem: ut nominatim eas vocet.

4. Ovium eductionem; ut ex ovili easdem ad pabula emittat, & educat.

5. Ovium præitionem: siquidem pastores in O- riente non nostro more sequi consueverint gre- gem, sed antecedere, ut ovis voce & exemplo præeat, & invitet, ut scil. ad pabula verbi divini sequantur 1. Tim. 4, 12. 16. Tit. 2, 1. seqq. Nondum autem hæc ad se solum applicat Christus, in priori hoc alloquio nedum his se Messiam esse indicat aut profitetur.

Conf. Prov. 27, 3.

## 10:3
Verse 3. τούτῳ ὁ θυρωρὸς ἀνοίγει) There is no need in parables to have individual particles to which they correspond. There are many episodic things. Thus, this about the doorkeeper opening is a description of a known man.

καὶ τὰ πρόβατα τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ ἀκούει) Shepherds have certain proper voices, such as the σίτλα in Theocritus, to which the cattle become accustomed. But understand the sheep in the allegory to be those who are of a pious mind and therefore teachable. Below v. 16. These recognize Christ both from the majesty of his words and from the holiness of his teaching.

καὶ τὰ ἴδια πρόβατα καλεῖ κατ᾿ ὄνομα) He in turn knows his own sheep. See Prov. 27, 23. Virgil: 'And twice a day both count the flock.' To call by name is a sign of perfect knowledge, Is. 40, 26. and elsewhere. ἔγνω κύριος τοὺς ὄντας αὐτοῦ, 2 Tim. 2, 19.

ἐξάγει αὐτὰ) He leads them out into the pastures. Not even this requires a special correspondence. For it pertains to the circumlocution of pastoral care.

Latin:

Vers. 3. τούτῳ ὁ θυρωρὸς ἀνοίγει) Nihil opus est in Para- bolis particulas singulas habere, cui respondeant. Multa sunt ἐπεισοδιώδη. Sic hoc de Janitore aperiente, descri- ptio est noti hominis.

καὶ τὰ πρόβατα τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ ἀκούει) Habent pastores voces quasdam proprias ut σίτλα apud Theocritum, quibus assuescunt pecudes. Oves autem in affabulatione intellige eos, qui pio sunt animo ac proinde dociles. Infra v. 16. Hi & ex majestate verborum & ex sanctitate dogmatis Chri- stum agnoscunt.

καὶ τὰ ἴδια πρόβατα καλεῖ κατ᾿ ὄνομα) Ipse vicissim oves suas novit. Vide Prov. 27, 23. Virgilius: Bisq; die numerant ambo pecus. Vocare nomine, signum perfectæ notitiæ, Es. XL. 26. & alibi. ἔγνω κύριος τοὺς ὄντας αὐτοῦ, 2. Tim. 2, 19.

ἐξάγει αὐτὰ) Educit in pascua. Ne hoc quidem requirit specialem ἀνταπόδοσιν. Pertinet enim ad circumlocutionem curæ pastoralis.

## 10:4
V. 4. ἐκβάλῃ) What he had already called ἐξάγειν, he now calls ἐκβάλλειν. Thus פתה is sometimes translated by ἐξάγειν Jerem. 46, 27, sometimes by ἐκβάλλειν, 2 Chron. 13, 9. Jerem. 29, 18.

ἔμπροσθεν αὐτῶν πορεύεται) Shepherds are accustomed not only to follow the flock, but also to go before it. See Psalm 80, 1. and what we said at Matt. 24, 32. Thus Christ went before us by the example of his life, and the true disciples of Christ are types to the flock, 2 Pet. 5, v. 3.

Latin:

V. 4. ἐκβάλῃ) Quod jam dixerat ἐξάγειν, nunc dicit ἐκβάλλ- λειν. Sic פתה modo per ἐξάγειν vertitur Jerem. 46, 27. modo per ἐκβάλλειν, 2. Par. 13, 9. Jerem. 29, 18.

ἔμπροσθεν αὐτῶν πορεύεται) Solent pastores non modo subsequi gregem, sed & præire. Vide. Psal. 80, 1. & quæ diximus Matth. 24, 32. Sic Christus vitæ exemplo nobis præiit, & veri Christi discipuli τύποι sunt τῶ ποιμνίω, 2. Pet. 5. v. 3.

## 10:5
Verse 5. ἐκ οἶδασι τῶν ἀλλοτρίων τὴν φωνὴν) Thus also pious minds recognize the arrogance of false teachers, their pursuit of private gain, and other things alien to piety.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ἐκ οἶδασι τῶν ἀλλοτρίων τὴν φωνὴν) Sic & pii ani- mi agnoscunt falsorum magistrorum arrogantiam, privati commodi studium, & alia a pietate aliena.

## 10:6
Verse 6. τὴν παροιμίαν) The Hebrew משל signifies any figurative speech, Ezek. 20, 9. The Greeks distinguish between παροιμία and παραβολή. But the Hellenists use them for the same thing. Therefore, the book of Solomon, משל, is inscribed with both titles, and just as in Matt. 15, 16, what is properly a παροιμία is called a παραβολή, so here and in ch. 16, 25. 29, it is called a παροιμία, which is properly a παραβολή.

ἐκ ἔγνωσαν τίνα ἦν ἅ ἐλάλει αὐτοῖς) What he meant by this similitude. Thus we had λέγειν above in ch. 2, 21.

Latin:

Vers. 6. τὴν παροιμίαν) משל Hebræum omnem sermonem figuratum significat, Ezech. 20. 9. Distinguunt Græci παροιμίαν & παραβολὴν. Sed Hellenistæ pro eodem usurpant. Itaque liber Salomonis משל utroque titulo in- scribitur & sicut apud Matth. 15, 16. παραβολὴ vocatur quæ proprie est παροιμία ita hic & c. 16, 25. 29. παροιμία appel- latur, quæ proprie est παραβολή.

ἐκ ἔγνωσαν τίνα ἦν ἅ ἐλάλει αὐτοῖς) Quid hac similitudine significaret. Sic λέγειν habuimus supra c. 2, 21.

## 10:7
Verse 7.

I am the door) Having not set forth the previous similitude, he begins another related one, and explains it on the occasion of what he had said about the door. Within the door the sheep are in safety.

In this second discourse, verse 7, Christ compares himself to a door, not using a new similitude or parable, but explaining, for the illustration of the former, what that door is through which it is necessary to enter. For both the sheep enter through Christ as the door, which happens when they are baptized in his name, and are introduced into the Church through Baptism as the first gate of grace, as Augustine calls it: and true pastors [enter] as well: when, namely, they are called in the name of Christ, and are introduced by Christ, who opens himself to them so that they may enter legitimately: and he guards all who have entered, whether they be sheep or pastors, so that they may be safe, just as doors are closed for the sake of security. In order to enter through Christ, besides the calling in the name of Christ and made by his authority, it is necessary that they be endowed with the true knowledge of Christ, and enter to the sheep through Christ as the door, or through the doctrine and proclamation concerning Christ, besides whom the Apostle protested he knew nothing, 1 Corinthians 2:3, in which sense also the blessed Glassius explained this in Exeges. Evangel. text. fer. III. Pentecost. Vol. III, page 551. Furthermore, those are understood to enter through this door who, endowed with the true knowledge of Christ, direct all things to him as the center, the cynosure, and the highest end. But those are said to climb up from elsewhere who neglect this center of salvation, and are entirely lacking in the knowledge of Christ as the sole mediator, or who stubbornly contradict him; and who lead listeners away to foreign means of obtaining eternal life: And thus he reconciles the explanation of Chrysostom, page 561, that Scripture is the door. Rightly, says Chrysostom, does he call the Scriptures the door, since they lead us to GOD, and open to us the knowledge of him; they themselves make the sheep, they themselves guard them, and do not permit wolves to break in. For as a most firm door they ward off heretics, and establish us in safety; nor will they ever allow us to wander, provided we are willing. And unless we break this door, our enemies will never be able to overcome us. Through this door let us, both pastors and all others, enter; for he who does not use the holy Scripture, but climbs up from elsewhere, that is, not by the permitted way, he is a thief. Concerning this interpretation, B. Glassius says: This exposition, he says, seems indeed to be further from the mind of Christ, since he asserts in verses 7 and 9 that he himself, not the Scriptures, is that door. But it can be rightly saved if it is said that these two are not opposites, but amicably subordinated. Christ is the door of the spiritual sheepfold, only insofar as he has revealed himself in the word of Scripture. And conversely, Holy Scripture is the door, insofar as it proposes Christ as the life, the truth, and the way, John 14:6, and thus as the unique gate and cause of salvation, and refers men to him. B. Glassius there also adduces an excellent comparison of the gate and the doorkeeper, instituted by the blessed Wilhelm Lyser: in which, among other things, it is taught how the doorkeeper, the Holy Spirit, opens the door to a good pastor, a minister of the Church: To him, he says on page 568, the Holy Spirit opens the door (1.) IN HIS OWN INTELLECT, so that through devout prayers and a sound understanding of the divine word, he himself may first be able to enter the sanctuary of GOD, and afterwards go out to the listeners through the solid preaching of the word. For if they themselves do not hold the mysteries of salvation and the true foundations of heavenly doctrine, how will they be able to open them and propose them to others? Then happens that which is in Isaiah 29:11, concerning the sealed book, etc. The Apostles received bread from the hands of Christ, and afterwards distributed it to the people, John 6. John in the Apocalypse saw a door opened in heaven, chapter 4:1, and was afterwards able to explain the various mysteries then revealed to him. Consolation must be received from the word of life first, before it is imparted to others, 2 Corinthians 1:4.

(2.) IN THE ECCLESIASTICAL ASSEMBLY, namely through a legitimate calling, lest that saying of Jeremiah 23:21 become true: They ran, and I did not send them. And therefore the voice of the Holy Spirit, through those to whom the right and office of calling belongs, must be humbly awaited before anyone teaches ordinarily in the Church. Compare Acts 13:2, 3, 4; chapter 20:28. He introduces them, however, only through the true door, which is Christ, as it stands in the Gospel, verse 2. (3.) IN THE AFFECTION OF THE LISTENERS. Thus the Holy Spirit opens the heart of Lydia, to hear the word with fruit, Acts 16:14. Compare Acts 14:27, 1 Corinthians 16:9, Colossians 4:3, etc. This is B. Wilhelm Lyser.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Εγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα) Superiori similitudine non ex- posita aliam affinem orditur, atque explicat occasione ejus quod de ostio dixerat. Intra ostium in tuto sunt oves.

In hoc altero alloquio vers. 7. ostio se compa- rat Christus, non nova usus similitudine, vel parabola, sed ad prioris illustrationem, quod- nam ostium illud sit, per quod intrare opor- teat, explicans. Per Christum enim & oves ingrediuntur tanquam ostium, quod fit, cum in nomine ejus baptizantur, & per Baptismum ceu primam gratiæ portam, ut vocat Augusti- nus, in Ecclesiam intromittuntur: & pastores ve- re: cum nempe in nomine Christi vocantur, & à Christo intromittuntur, qui sese ipsis aperit ut ingredi possint legitime: omnesque qui in- gressi sunt, seu oves sint, seu pastores, custo- dit, ut tuti sint, quemadmodum ostia claudun- tur securitatis gratia. Per Christum ut ingre- diantur præter vocationem in nomine Christi, e- jusque autoritate factam, opus est ut vera Chri- sti cognitione præditi sint, & per Christum ad oves ingrediantur, tanquam januam seu per do- ctrinam & præconium de Christo, præter quem nihil se scire protestatus est Apostolus 1. Corinth. 2, 3. quo etiam sensu exposuit hoc B. Glassius in Exeges. Evangel. text. fer. III. Pentecost. T. III. pag. 551. Cæterum per ostium hoc ingredi intelli- guntur, qui Christi vera cognitione præditi, ad ipsum velut æntrum, cynosuram, summumque finem & meam omnia sunt dirigunt. Aliunde autem afcendere dicuntur, qui hoc salutis cen- trum negligunt, & Christi, ut solius mediatoris, cognitione in solidum carent, eive contradicunt præ- fracte; atque ad peregrina obtinenda vitæ æternæ media, auditores abducunt: Atque ita conciliat Chrysostomi explicationem pag. 561. quod Scri- ptura ostium sit. Merito, inquit Chrysostomus, ostium Scripturas appellat, quoniam nos ad DEUM ducunt, & ejus nobis cognitionem aperiunt; ipsæ oves faciunt, ipsæ custodiunt, neque lupos irrumpe- re permittunt. Tanquam enim ostium firmissimum hæreticos arcent, & in tuto nos constituunt; ne- que, modo velimus, aberrare unquam, sinent. Et nisi hoc ostium infringamus, nunquam nos ini- mici nostri poterunt expugnare. Per hoc ostium & pastores, & alii omnes ingrediamur; qui enim sa- crâ non utitur Scripturâ, sed ascendit aliunde, id est, non concessâ via, is fur est. De quâ ἐκδοχῇ B. Glassius: Hæc, ait, expositio videtur quidem à mente Christi longius abesse, cum non Scripturas, sed seipsum ostium illud esse, vers. 7. 9. asserat. Ve- rum salvari rite potest, si dicatur, opposita hæc duo non esse, sed amicabiliter subordinata. Christus o- stium est ovilis spiritualis, non nisi quatenus in ver- bo Scripturæ se patefecit. Et vicissim ostium est Scriptura Sacra, quatenus Christum at vitam, ve- ritatem, & viam Johan. XV. v. 1. 6. adeoque uni- cam salutis januam & causam proponit, & ad ipsum homines remittit. Adducit illic B. Glas- sius & egregiam januæ & ostiarii comparatio- nem, à B. Wilhelmo Lysero institutam: in qua inter alia docetur quomodo ostiarius Spiri- tus sanctus bono Pastori Ecclesiæ ministro ostium aperiat: Huic, inquit pag. 568. aperit Spiritus sanctus ostium (1.) IN PROPRIO INTEL- LECTU, ut precibus devotis, & verbi divi- ni intelligentia sana, ipse prius ingredi sanctua- rium DEI possit, posteaque per verbi prædi- cationem solidam ad auditores exire. Si enim ipsi mysteria salutis, & doctrinæ cælestis fun- damenta vera non teneant, quomodo aliis a- perire ea & proponere poterunt? Contingit tum illud Esa 29, 11. de libro obsignato &c. Aposto- li ex manibus Christi panem accipiebant, post- modumque populo distribuebant, Joh. 6. Jo- hannes in Apocalypsi januam in cælis apertam videbat, cap. 4, 1. variaque mysteria sibi tum re- velata exponere postea potuit. Consolatio ex verbo vitæ prius accipienda, antequam aliis im- pertiatur, 2. Corinth. I. 4.

(2.) IN ECCLE- SIASTICO COETU, per vocationem ni- mirum legitimam, ne verum fiat illud Jerem. 23, 21. Currebant, & non mittebam eos. Ideo- que Spiritus sancti vox, per eos, quibus vo- candi jus & munus competit, expectanda hu- militer, antequam in Ecclesia quis ordinarie doceat. Confer Actor. XIII. 2. 3. 4. cap. XX. 28. Intromittit autem eos non nisi per ostium ve- rum, quod Christus est, ut in Evangelio ex- tat, vers. 2. (3.) IN AUDITORUM AF- FECTU. Sic aperit Spiritus sanctus cor Lydiæ, ad audiendum cum fructu verbum, Actor. 16, 14. Conf. Act. 14, 27. 1. Cor. 16, 9. Col. 4, 3. &c. Hæc B. Wilhelm. Lyserus.

## 10:8
Verse 8.

all who came) before me, which Nonnus and the Arab read, I think is more correctly omitted; since besides the Latin and the Syrian, many Greek copies agree. And it is more credible that this interpretation was added than that it was erased without cause. All who came, understand as those arrogating to themselves that name of the great shepherd, that is, the Messiah.

κλέπται εἰσὶ καὶ λῃσταὶ] That is, they were Theudas, Judas the Galilean, and any impostors like them, who both deceived themselves and exposed the wretched people, whom they had fascinated, to slaughter. There is an allusion to the passage in Jer. XXIII. 1. & Ezech. XXXIV. 2. 3.

As far as the reading is concerned, that which is found in the received codices is to be preferred, retaining the words πρὸ ἐμοῦ, which it is not likely were added as an interpretation, since they seem to create difficulty rather than illustrate the text, nor do many Greek copies omit them, but only a few in respect to those that retain them: which Augustine also retained in book VI against Faustus, chapter 16.

But as far as the meaning is concerned, these things must be understood determinately and according to the subject matter: all who came before me, who, that is, claimed for themselves the name of the door; or before me, that is, before they are introduced by me, who am the door: The phrase, says Tarnovius on page 774, which Christ uses concerning the entry of thieves and robbers, whom he says come before him, who is the door, or the one sending and introducing all true shepherds into the sheepfold, is to be understood from the opposite of mission; those who have a mission enter only when they are sent or introduced by him who is like a door: those who do not have it run before they are sent, Jer. XXIII. 21. compare the same prophet's chapter XIV. 14. Rom. X. 15. Heb. VI. 4. likewise Augustine, book 2 against the adversary of the law, chapter IV. To which contributes that of Nazianzen, when he says of Christ in Oration XXXVI. ὁδός ἐστιν ὡς δι' ἑαυτὸν φέρων ὑμᾶς θύρα δὲ ὡς εἰσαγωγεύς: He is the way, as leading us through himself: the door, as the introducer. Augustine, book XVI against Faustus, c. 12, says that 'to have come before him' is to be understood in this way, because they were not sent, just as Moses and the holy prophets did not come before him, but with him, because they did not wish to precede him through pride, but humbly carried him who spoke through them. Thieves, says Jerome in chapter VII of Hosea, and robbers, who came before the Lord, we must take to be not Moses and the prophets, who are always praised by the mouth of the Savior, but the pseudo-prophets, and later the heretics, who were not sent by the Lord, but came by their own will. Maldonatus notes that some have rightly observed that Christ did not say 'all who were before me,' but 'all as many as came before me,' i.e., who came as shepherds before him: but were not sent, as Augustine [notes in] books I and II against the adversaries of the law and the prophets. and Bede followed him in his exposition, as did Jerome in book II against Pelagius. Which interpretation amounts to the same thing. Nor is it different from what the same Jesuit praises as a different one from Augustine, tract 45 on John: 'all as many as came, certainly besides me.' Because the true prophets did not come besides Christ, but with Christ. Which, however, Maldonatus explains thus: that they came in a certain way with Christ, because they came for the purpose of preaching him, but soon he confuses it with another sense, that they did not come under him as leader. It may be said that that 'before' does not regard the order of time, but the order of nature and causality, who did not come with me as the author, but before me, before they were sent by me: because it was the way of hypothetical wisdom to send the prophets, Luke XI. 49. Erasmus Schmiedius notes that πρὸ ἐμοῦ is not taken temporally, but modally, those who do not follow my footsteps, or do not come ὀπίσω με, but πρὸ ἐμοῦ without me: but because Christ had called himself the door, and had taught that true shepherds ought to enter through the door, the opposites here are not 'before me' and 'after me,' but he says those came before him who did not enter through him as the door; as Leontius also notes; who did not wait for this door to be opened to them, or for it to open itself and introduce them, but before they were sent, they ran and rushed into the sheepfold. Thus these things will sound concerning all who are not legitimately sent or sent in by Christ, not only concerning pseudo-Christs.
