If, however, with Cyril, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius, and in the Greek Catena, Theodore of Heraclea, & Mopsuestia, one prefers to understand these things particularly concerning pseudo-Christs (which also pleased Grotius), according to the underlying matter, as we have said, this discourse will have to be explained: I am the door of the sheep: all who came before me, and thus boasted that they were, namely, the door of the sheep, are thieves. Grotius: who arrogated to themselves the name of the great Shepherd, that is, the Messiah. Which meaning, however, they could not have from the preceding: as he indeed thinks: but it could be gathered from those things which he was about to say further. And B. Tarnovius, page 785, also observes not beside the point that it is not a matter of that singular and exceptionally good Shepherd, but of the door of all true and legitimate shepherds, through which they ought to enter to teach in the Church, therefore that explanation seems to depart from the genuine sense. But it was the mere impiety of the Manichaeans, who abused this passage to reject the Old Testament, as Chrysostom and Theophylact warn.

οὐκ ἤκουσαν αὐτῶν τὰ πρόβατα] They had their own followers, the Zealots, pursuing human advantages, but the lovers of piety were strangers to them.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

πάντες ὅσοι ἦλθον) πρὸ ἐμῦ quod Nonnus & Arabs lege- runt puto rectius omitti; cum præter Latinum & Syrum multa Græcorum Exemplaria consentiant. Et credibilius est adjectum hoc interpretamentum quam sine caussa era- sum. Omnes qui venerunt, intellige sibi arrogantes illud nomen magni pastoris, id est Messiæ.

κλέπται εἰσὶ καὶ λῃσταὶ] Id est fuerunt, Theudas, Judas Gaulonites & si qui his similes impostores, qui & se fagina- runt & miserum populum a se fascinatum cædibus objece- runt. Alluditur ad locum Jer. XXIII. 1. & Ezech. XXXIV. 2. 3.

Quod ad lectionem attinet, præferenda illa est, quæ in receptis habetur codicibus, retinens voces πρὸ ἐμοῦ, quas pro interpretamento adjectas esse non est verisimile, quum difficultatem potius pariant, quam textum illustrare videantur, neque multa Græcorum exemplaria easdem omittant, sed pau- ca respectu earum, quæ retinent: quas etiam Augu- stinus l. VI. contr. Faust. cap. 16. retinuit.

Quod vero ad sensum attinet, determinate hæc, & secundum subjectam materiam intelligenda sunt: omnes qui ante me venerunt, qui sc. ostii nomen sibi vendi- carunt; vel ante me, id est, antequam à me, qui o- stium sum, intromittantur: Phrasis autem, inquit Tarnovius p. 774. qua utitur Christus de ingressu fu- rum & latronum, quos dicit venire ante se, qui est ostium, sive mittens & intromittens pastores omnes- veros in ovile, est intelligenda ex contrario missionis, missionem qui habent, ut ingrediuntur tum demum, quando mittuntur sive intromittuntur ab eo, qui est instar ostii: qui eam non habent, currunt, ante- quam mittuntur, Jer. XXIII. 21. confer ejusdem Pro- phetæ cap. XIV. 14. Rom. X. 15. Hebr. VI. 4. item August. l. 2. contra adversarium legis, cap. IV. Quo facit illud Nazianzeni, cum de Christo ait Orat. XXXVI. ὁδός ἐστιν ὡς δι' ἑαυτὸν φέρων ὑμᾶς θύρα δὲ ὡς εἰσαγωγεύς: Via est, ut per se nos ducens: o- stium, ut introductor. August. l. XVI. contr. Faust. c. 12. ante se venisse, ait, ita vult intelligi, quia missi non sunt, sicut Moses & S. Prophetæ non ante ipsum, sed cum ipso venerunt, quia non eum per superbiam præcedere voluerunt, sed eum per ipsos loquentem hu- militer portaverunt. Fures, inquit Hieron. in c. VII. Oseæ, & latrones, qui venerunt ante Dominum, non Mosen, & Prophetas, qui semper Servatoris ore lau- dantur, sed Pseudo-Prophetas debemus accipere, & postea hæreticos, qui non missi sunt à Domino, sed sua voluntate venerunt. Maldonatus notat, recte quosdam observasse, quod non dixerit Christus omnes qui ante me fuerunt, sed omnes quotquot ante me venerunt, h. e. qui tanquam pastores ante se ve- nerunt: sed non missi, ut Augustinus l. I. & II. contra adversarios legis & Prophet. eumque sequutus est Beda exposit. nec non Hieronym. l. II. adv. Pelag. Quæ interpretatio eodem abit. Nec diversa est, quam ceu diversam ex Augustino tr. XLV. in Joh. idem Jesuita laudat, omnes quotquot venerunt utiq; præter me. Quia veri Prophetæ, non præter Christum, sed cum Christo venerunt. Quam tamen ita expli- cat Maldonatus: quod ita quodammodo cum Christo venerint, quia venêre ideo, ut illum præ- dicarent, mox autem cum altero sensu confundit, quod non sub eo duce venerint. Dici poterit, illud ante non ordinem temporis respicere, sed ordinem naturæ & causalitatis, qui non venerunt me auto- re, sed ante me, antequam à me mitterentur: quia sa- pientiæ hypotheticæ fuit mittere Prophetas, Luc. XI. 49. Erasmus Schmiedius notat πρὸ ἐμοῦ non ac- cipi temporaliter, sed modaliter, qui non mea se- quuntur vestigia, vel non veniunt ὀπίσω με, sed πρὸ ἐμοῦ sine me: verum quia Christus ostium se di- xerat, & veros pastores per ostium ingredi debere docuerat, opposita hic non sunt, ante me, & post me, sed ante se venisse dicit eos, qui per se tanquam o- stium non sunt ingressi; ut Leontius etiam notat; qui non expectarunt, ut aperiretur sibi hoc o- stium, vel se aperiret, & intromitteret eos, sed an- tequam mitterentur, cucurrerunt, & irruerunt in ovile. Ita de omnibus non legitime missis aut a Christo immissis, non solum de Pseudo-Christis haec sonabunt. Si tamen cum Cyrillo, Chrys. Theoph. Euthym. & in Catena Graeca Theod. Heracleont. & Mopsvestano, de Pseudo-Christis haec peculiari- ter intelligere quis malit (quod Grotio etiam pla- cuit) secundum substratam, ut diximus, materiam, haec explicanda erit oratio: Ego sum ostium ovium: omnes qui ante me venerunt, & ita sese jactarunt, quod nempe ovium ostium sint, fures sunt. Grotius: qui sibi nomen magni Pastoris, id est Messiae arroga- runt. Quem vero sensum e praecedentibus habere non potuere: ut ille quidem arbitratur: sed ex iis quae porro dicturus erat, colligi poterat. Nec non praeter rem observat B. Tarnovius pag. 785. non agi de singulari & eximie bono illo Pastore, sed de ostio omnium verorum & leonorum Pastorum, per quod ingredi debent ad docendum in Eccle- sia, ideo videtur, eam explicationem a genuino sensu abire. Impietas autem mera fuit Manichaeo- rum, qui hoc loco abusi Vet. Testamentum reje- cerunt, monente Chrysostomo & Theophylacto.

οὐκ ἤκουσαν αὐτῶν τὰ πρόβατα] Habuerunt suos sectatores Zelotas, humana commoda sectantes, sed pietatis amantes alieni ab ipsis fuerunt.

## 10:9
V. 9. Δι᾽ ἐμὲ ἐάν τις εἰσέλθῃ] Through me he will find a faithful reception with God Rom. V. 1. Heb. X, 19.

σωθήσεται] He will be out of danger.

And he shall go in and out and shall find pasture] That is, wherever he may be, he shall not lack fodder. For such is the custom of speaking among the Hebrews, Deut. XXVIII. 6. Psalm. CXXI. 8. 1. Sam. XXIX. 6. 2. Sam. III. 25. 2. Par. I. 10. Moreover, there is an allusion to that which was in the comparison. For sheep go out of the fold and return into it, νομὴν etc.

To be saved is not only to be out of danger, but to attain eternal salvation and happiness: as is evident from v. 11: that they may have life, and not only have it, but have it abundantly, because according to Grotius, Christ will not only give his own eternal life, but also with that life every kind of happiness; according to Diepius, however, no comparison is instituted between life and something else more excellent than it, but abundant life is promised, and περισσὸν is the same as περισσῶς: just as κομψότερον ἔχε in John IV. 52 is used for κομψοτέρως.

Latin:

V. 9. Δι᾽ ἐμὲ ἐάν τις εἰσέλθῃ] Per me inveniet fidum rece- ptum apud Deum Rom. V. 1. Ebr. X, 19.

σωθήσεται] Extra periculum erit.

καὶ εἰσελεύσεται καὶ ἐξελεύσεται καὶ νομὴν εὑρήσει] Id est ubi- cunque fuerit, pabulo non carebit. Sic enim mos est lo- quendi Hebraeis Deut. XXVIII. 6. Psalm. CXXI. 8. 1. Sam. XXIX. 6. 2. Sam. III. 25. 2. Par. I. 10. Est autem allusio ad id quod erat in comparatione. Nam oves caula exeunt & in eam redeunt, νομὴν וגו׳.

Salvari non est tantum extra periculum esse, sed salutem & felicitatem aeternam consequi: ut e v. 11. constat: ut vitam habeant, nec tantum habeant, sed abundanter habeant, quia juxta Grotium Chri- stus suis non tantum vitam dabit aeternam, sed & cum ea vita omne genus felicitatis; juxta Diepium vero nulla comparatio instituitur inter vitam, & aliud quid ea excellentius, sed abundans vita pro- mittitur, & περισσὸν idem est quod περισσῶς: sicut κομψότερον ἔχε Joh. IV. 52. pro κομψοτέρως.

## 10:10
V. 10. The thief] He who is also a robber, which word he added above, expresses the sense in the following.

that they may have life and have it abundantly] That they may have more: The Syrian. Sheep that are well kept not only have what is necessary to sustain life, but also the delights of a variety of grasses. See concerning the delights of goats the anapests of Eupolis which are read in Macrobius, and compare those things which are in Ez. XXXIV. Thus Christ will not only give his own eternal life but also with that life every kind of happiness. Thus we have had περισσότερον in Matth. V. 37. Luc. XII. 4. Hebr. VI. 17.

Latin:

V. 10. ὁ κλέπτης] Qui & λῃστὴς, quam vocem supra addi- dit, sequentibus sensum exprimit.

ἵνα ζωὴν ἔχωσι καὶ περισσὸν ἔχωσι] Amplius habeant: Syrus. Oves quae bene habentur, non tantum habent, quae neces- saria sunt ad vitam sustentandam, sed & delicias herbarum varietate. Vide de caprarum deliciis Eupolidis anapaestos qui apud Macrobium leguntur, & confer ea quae sunt Ez. XXXIV. Sic Christus suis non tantum vitam dabit aeternam sed & cum ea vita omne genus felicitatis. Sic περισσότερον habuimus Matth. V. 37. Luc. XII. 4. Hebr. VI. 17.

## 10:11
V. 11. I am the good shepherd] On the occasion of the aforementioned, he begins a third comparison, now taking the voice of a shepherd not for the Messiah alone, but for anyone teaching the people. Nor does he here oppose the shepherd, as before, to the thief and robber, but the shepherd, who is the same Lord of the sheep, to the hireling, whom Virgil calls a stranger. This stranger milks these sheep for the keeper at the hour; and the juice is withdrawn from the flock and the milk from the lambs. Homer Od. Π. but bad shepherds destroy the sheep. There is the same opposition of shepherd and hireling in Rabbi Abraham. There, therefore, Christ opposes himself to the Pseudo-Christs, here to any wicked teachers whatsoever. There he looked to Theudas and those whom we have mentioned: Here to the lawyers of his own times and the Pharisees.

He had already called the lawyers and Pharisees thieves and robbers: now he inculcates generally the difference of the good shepherd from the hirelings, and calls himself by antonomasia the good shepherd: inasmuch as he even laid down his life for the sheep, and acquired them for himself with his own blood. Although, therefore, certain general marks of a good shepherd are held here, Christ nevertheless applies them to himself in such a way that he teaches that he is not only a good shepherd but that very good shepherd whom the Holy Spirit had designated in Ezech. XXXIV. Psal. XXIII. Zach. XII. 7. c. XIII. 7. and elsewhere in the O. T. Conf. Ebr. XIII. 20. 1. Petr. II. 25. For he is named not only Shepherd, according to Nazianzen, Orat. V., because of the office which he holds, as one who feeds in a grassy place, provides pasture at the water of rest, is a guide on the way from there, fights against beasts, turns back that which wanders, brings back the lost, binds up the broken, strengthens that which is corrupted by languor, guards the strong, and gathers his own to the fold through the sermons of pastoral Scripture: But he is called with the article ὁ ποιμὴν that shepherd ὁ καλὸς that good one: concerning whom Bernh. Serm. XXXI. in Cantic. Truly good, who gives his own flesh for food, his blood for drink, his soul for a price, his Deity as the reward of eternal enjoyment. But also the characteristics of the Messiah are not obscure here, in that he knows his own intimately, just as he is known by the Father, which is a divine knowledge, and because it is joined with the affection of love, it brings about the divine love of the Son of God, in that he lays down his soul entirely, and that αὐτεξυσίως (by his own authority), as he explains afterwards, v. 17, 18, and that he has the power to take his soul or his life back again, and that he has this command from his Father, that he should, namely, undergo death for us; finally, that he has other sheep still, and is about to bring them, and from both Jews and Gentiles is about to form one flock, and to increase it subsequently, gathering little sheep for himself from the human race, until the consummation of the age. Who could doubt that these are the criteria of the Messiah? Grotius himself certainly explains the words at v. 18, Ταυτην τὴν ἐντολὴν ἔλαβον παρὰ τῶ πατρός μυ, thus: The Father has entrusted this business of saving the sheep to me:

with this observation added: ἐντέλλεσθαι is accustomed to be used among the Greeks even where a command properly so-called does not have a place. But to the business of saving the sheep pertains primarily the redemption of the sheep accomplished by his blood. Which are proper to the Messiah, as such.

τὴν ψυχὴν ἁυτῶ τίθησιν) ψυχὴν τιθέναι signifies in this place not to shrink from death, whether death actually follows or not, which the Hebrews more fully call to put one's life in one's hand. Jud. XII. 3. 1 Sam. IX. 4. XXVIII. 2. Thus παραδιδόναι τὰς ψυχὰς ἁυτῶν Acts XV. 26. Thus παραθέμενοι κεφαλὰς in Homer's Odyssey, book two: and ψυχὰς παραθέμενοι in the third book of the Odyssey: where the Scholiast says ἀφειδήσαντες ἑαυτῶν, Plautus said to the captives, to put one's head in danger.

ὑπὲρ τῶ προβάτων) A type of which thing was in David 1 Sam. XVII. 34 and following. Otherwise it is hardly the case that anyone would expose himself to great dangers for a beast.

These things in the περιστάσει (circumstance) concerning pastors, and when the application is made to pastors bearing the care of souls in general, can be admitted: But when Christ afterwards speaks specifically of himself v. 15, κὲ τὴν ψυχήν μυ τίθημι ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων, he does not only say that he exposes his soul to danger, but indicates entirely that he will also actually lay down his life for the sheep; therefore he adds v. 17 that he will take his life again: which looks to his resurrection, and presupposes death, not just the danger of death.

PART II. Sermon on the Pastoral office of Christ.

Latin:

V. 11. ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλὸς] Occasione antedicto- rum tertiam incipit comparationem, pastoris vocem jam sumens non pro solo Messia, sed pro quovis pouplum do- cente. Neque hic pastorem opponit ut ante furi & latroni, sed pastorem, qui idem Dominus sit ovium, mercenario, quem alienum Virgilius vocat. Hic alienus oves custos his mulget in hora; Et succus pecori & lac subducitur agnis. Homerus Od. Π. αὐτὰρ μῆλα κακοὶ φθείρουσι νομῆες. Est eadem oppositio pastoris & mercenarii apud Rabbinum Abrahamum. Ibi ergo Christus se Pseudo-Christis oppo- nit, hic quibusvis pravis doctoribus. Ibi respexit Theu- dam & eos quos diximus: Hic legisperitos suorum tempo- rum & Pharisaeos.

Legisperitos & Pharisaeos jam fures & Latrones dixerat: nunc γενικῶς Differentiam boni pastoris a mercenariis inculcat, seque κατ᾿ αὐτονομασίαν bonum pastorem dicit: utpote qui etiam animam suam pro ovibus posuit, easque sanguine suo sibi acquisivit. Etsi ergo hic quaedam generales notae boni pastoris habeantur, eas tamen ita sibi appli- cat Christus, ut se non pastorem modo bonum sed illum omnino pastorem bonum esse doceat, quem Ezech. XXXIV. Psal. XXIII. Zach. XII. 7. c. XIII. 7. & alibi in V. T. Spiritus S. designarat. Conf. Ebr. XIII. 20. 1. Petr. II. 25. Nominatur enim non tan- tum Pastor juxta Nazianzenum orat. V. propter of- ficium quod gerit, ut qui loco herbido pabulet, ad aquam quietis pastum praebeat, inde via dux sit, adversus beluas propugnet, reflectat id quod errat, amissum reducat, fractum obliget, languore corru- ptum corroboret, validum custodiat, per sermones pastoritia Scriptura ad caulam suos colligat: Sed vocatur cum articulo ὁ ποιμὴν pastor ille ὁ καλὸς bonus ille: de quo Bernh. Serm. XXXI. in Cantic. Vere bonus, qui dat carnem suam in cibum, sangui- nem in potum, animam in pretium, Deitatem in fruitionis aeterna premium. Sed & Characteres Messiae hic non obscuri sunt, quod suos intime co- gnoscat, uti à Patre cognoscitur, quae divina est co- gnitio, & quia cum affectu dilectionis conjuncta est, divinum infert amorem Filii Dei, quod prorsus animam ponat, idque αὐτεξυσίως, uti post- ea explicat, v. 17. 18. quodque potestatem habeat a- nimam vel vitam suam vicissim sumendi, & quod hoc mandatum à Patre suo habeat, ut scil. pro nobis mortem subeat; denique quod oves alias adhuc habeat, easdemque adducturus sit, & è Judaeis & gentibus unum gregem formaturus, eumque sub- inde aucturus, oviculas sibi de genere humano collecturus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Quae κριτήρια Messiae esse, ecquis ambigat? Gro- tius certe ipse verba ad v. 18. Ταυτην τὴν ἐντολὴν ἔ- λαβον παρὰ τῶ πατρός μυ, ita exponit: Pater hoc negotium ovium servandarum mihi commendavit:

addita hac observatione: solet ἐντέλλεσθαι apud Grae- cos dici etiam ubi imperium proprie dictum locum non habet. Ad negotium autem ovium servanda- rum pertinet imprimis redemtio ovium sanguine ejus facta. Quae Messiae propria, qua tali.

τὴν ψυχὴν ἁυτῶ τίθησιν) ψυχὴν τιθέναι significat hoc loco mortem non defugere, sive reipsa mors sequatur, sive non, quod plenius Hebraei dicunt vitam ponere in manu sua. Jud. XII. 3. 1. Sam. IX. 4. XXVIII. 2. Sic παραδιδόναι τὰς ψυχὰς ἁυτῶν Actor. XV. 26. Sic παραθέμενοι κεφαλὰς apud Homerum Odyssea secundo: & ψυχὰς παραθέμενοι Odysseae tertio: ubi Scholiastes ἀφειδήσαντες ἑαυτῶν, Plau- tus captivis dixit, caput periculo ponere.

ὑπὲρ τῶ προβάτων) Cujus rei typus fuit in Davide 1. Sam. XVII. 34. & sequentibus. Alioqui vix est ut quis se pro pecude magnis periculis objiciat.

Haec in περιστάσει de pastoribus, & cum appli- catio fit ad pastores animae curam gerentes in ge- nere admitti possunt: Sed quando Christus post- ea speciatim de se loquitur v. 15. κὲ τὴν ψυχήν μυ τί- θημι ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων, non tantum dicit se pe- riculo exponere animam suam, sed indicat omnino se etiam vitam reapse positurum pro ovibus; ideo addit v. 17. se iterum vitam sumturum: quod ad resurrectionem ejus spectat, & mortem, non pericu- lum tantum mortis supponit.

PARS II. Concio de Pastorali Christi officio.

## 10:12
Vers. 12. Καί ἐκ ὧν ποιμὴν) Who is not a shepherd by affection. See Phil. II. 21.

Οὗ ἐκ εἰσὶ τὰ πρόβατα ἴδια) Because the beasts are neither his own nor his father's as they were to David: nor is he a partner, as they say. And so the Apostles and those like them are not excluded from the name of a true shepherd, because they cared for the flock of Christ as their own. See 1 Cor. XII. 15.

θεωρεῖ τὸ λύκον ἐρχόμενον κὰι ἀφίησι) That is, if he sees the wolf coming, he deserts the flock by flight. By the wolf, understand imminent cruelty, which it is not always forbidden to flee, but only then, when in that way the flock remains deserted. See what is said at Matt. X. 23.

κὰι ὁ λύκος ἁρπάζει ἀὐτὰ κὰι σκορπίζει τὰ πρόβατα) That is, in such a way that the wolf partly snatches the sheep, partly scatters them: thus the word πρόβατα is repeated to signify the division. And κὰι is of consequence. The opposition of the shepherd and the wolf is adapted to men also in Maximus of Tyre, in the dissertation on what knowledge is: Κύρῶ μὲν ἡγεῖτο Πέρσων ὡς ποιμὴν θρεμμάτων, σώζων τὸ αἰπόλιον κὰι τρέφων, κὰι Μήδοις πολεμῶν κὰι Βαβυλωνίες λαμβάνων, καὶ μηδενὶ ἐφῖναι λύκω βαρβάρῳ καὶ ἀγρίῳ ἀναμιχθῆναι τῇ ἀγέλῃ καμβύσης δὲ ἦν καὶ αὖθις ξέρξης ἐκ ποιμένων ἀγαθῶν πονηροὶ λύκοι.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Καί ἐκ ὧν ποιμὴν) Qui affectu pastor non est. Vid. Phil. II. 21.

Οὗ ἐκ εἰσὶ τὰ πρόβατα ἴδια) Quia nec ipsius sunt pecudes nec paternae ut Davidi: neque est partiarius ut loquuntur. Itaque à veri pastoris nomine Apostoli eorumque similes non excluduntur, quia gregem Christi tanquam suum cu- rabant. Vide 1. Cor. XII. 15.

θεωρεῖ τὸ λύκον ἐρχόμενον κὰι ἀφίησι) Id est si videat lupum venientem, deserit gregem fuga. Lupum intellige saevi- tiam imminentem, quam fugere non semper vetitum est, sed tum demum, cum eo modo grex destitutus manet. Vi- de quae ad Matth. X. 23.

κὰι ὁ λύκος ἁρπάζει ἀὐτὰ κὰι σκορπίζει τὰ πρόβατα) Id est ita ut lupus partim rapjat oves, partim disjiciat: ita vox πρό- ζατα repetitur ad significandam partitionem. Et κὰι est con- secutionis. Oppositio pastoris & lupi hominibus aptata est & apud Maximum Tyrium, dissertatione quid sit scientia: Κύρῶ μὲν ἡγεῖτο Πέρσων ὡς ποιμὴν θρεμμάτων, σώζων τὸ αἰ- πόλιον κὰι τρέφων, κὰι Μήδοις πολεμῶν κὰι Βαβυλωνίες λαμβά- των, καὶ μηδενὶ ἐφῖναι λύκω βαρβάρῳ καὶ ἀγρίῳ ἀναμιχθῆναι τῇ ἀγέλῃ καμβύσης δὲ ἦν καὶ αὖθις ξέρξης ἐκ ποιμένων ἀγαθῶν πο- νηροὶ λύκοι.

## 10:13
Vers. 13. Οὐ μέλει αὐτῷ περὶ τῶν προβάτων) The sheep are not at his heart: because his own interest is not at stake, nor does he value them so highly: The same expression is in Mark 12:14, Luke 10:40.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Οὐ μέλει αὐτῷ περὶ τῶν προβάτων) Non sunt oves ei cordi: quia res ipsius non agitur neque tanti putat: Eadem locutio Marci XII. 14. Luc. X. 40.

## 10:14
Vers. 14. καὶ γινώσκω τὰ ἐμά) Understand πρόβατα from the preceding. But understand 'know' here as: I know how much they value me, as above in 10.

καὶ γινώσκομαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν) They know in turn with what love I pursue them.

Latin:

Vers. 14. καὶ γινώσκω τὰ ἐμά) πρόβατα ex superioribus in- tellige. Novi autem hic intellige: scio, quanti me faciant ut supra 10.

καὶ γινώσκομαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν) Sciunt vicissim, quo amore se prosequar.

## 10:15
V. 15. καθὼς γινώσκει με ὁ πατὴρ) Just as the Father also knows how obedient I am to Him, Matt. 11:27.

κἀγὼ γινώσκω τὸν πατέρα) And I know how much I am valued by the Father, and how much He destines for me. Christ often compares the love between Himself and Christians to that love which is between Himself and the Father: above 6:56, 57, below 17:32. See Matthew in the place already mentioned.

Latin:

V. 15. καθὼς γινώσκει με ὁ πατὴρ) Sicut & Pater scit quam i- psi sim obsequens Matth. XI. 27.

κἀγὼ γινώσκω τὸν πατέρα) Et ego scio quanti sim apud Pa- trem, quanta mihi destinet. Sæpius Christus amorem inter se & Christianos comparat ei amori qui est inter se & Pa- trem: supra VI. 56. 57. infra XVII. 32. Vide Matth. dicto jam loco.

## 10:16
Vers. 16. καὶ ἄλλα πρόβατα ἔχω) I will not expose myself to death for these my kinsmen only, but also for strangers; understand by 'sheep' those who were of a mild disposition and such that there was hope they would not be rejecters of the Gospel made manifest to them. Thus also the word 'people' is taken from the hope of the future, Acts 18:10, and 'harvest' in Matt. 9:37.

ἃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς ταύτης) They are not of this nation.

κἀκεῖνα με δεῖ ἀγαγεῖν) Through my ministers.

καὶ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούσουσι) He shows the great abundance of those who would believe in Him from among the Gentiles.

Μία ποίμνη, ἗ις ποιμήν) It was a proverb: One flock, one Shepherd. See a similar passage in Ezek. 37:24, where the type is a description of the Church to be gathered from everywhere under Christ as head. Before, they were under various teachers: the Jews under the Scribes of the Law, the Greeks under the Philosophers.

Ezech. 37:24, it is not a type that is held, but an open prophecy concerning Christ, as we have shown at that passage.

Latin:

Vers. 16. καὶ ἄλλα πρόβατα ἔχω) Non pro his tantum con- sanguineis meis me morti objiciam sed & pro extraneis, o- ves intellige eos qui miti erant animo ac tali ut spes esset eos Evangelium sibi patefactum non repudiatores. Sic & populi vox sumitur ex spe futuri. Act. XVIII. 10. & messis Matth. IX. 37.

ἃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τῆς αὐλῆς ταύτης) Non ex hac gente sunt.

κἀκεῖνα με δεῖ ἀγαγεῖν) Per ministros meos.

καὶ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούσουσι) Ostendit magnam copiam eo- rum qui in se credituri essent ex gentibus.

Μία ποίμνη, ἗ις ποιμήν) Proverbium fuit Grex unus, unus Pastor. Vide locum similem Ezech. XXXVII. 24. ubi ty- pus est ejus rei descriptio Ecclesiæ undique colligendæ sub capite Christo. Antea erant sub variis doctoribus, Judæi sub Legisperitis, Græci sub Philosophis.

Ezech. XXXVII. 24. non typus habetur, sed va- ticinium apertum de Christo, ut ad locum istum ostendimus.

## 10:17
V. 17. Therefore the Father loves me) נפשו כעובד LIII. 11. & ibidem לכן therefore in Greek διὸ Phil. II. 9.

that I might take it again) This ἵνα is not telic but, as often, ecbatic. As if he had found, I will indeed expose myself to death, but in such a way that I am to receive my life back.

Latin:

V. 17. Διὰ τῦτό με πατήρ με ἀγαπᾷ) נפשו כעובד LIII. 11. & ibidem לכן διὰ τῦτο Græce διὸ Phil. II. 9.

ἵνα πάλιν λάβω αὐτήν) Hoc ἵνα non est τελικὸν sed, ut sæ- pe, ἐκβατικόν. Quasi reperiisset, Objiciam quidem me mor- ti, sed ita ut vitam sim recepturus.

## 10:18
Vers. 18. No one takes it from me) Christ shows something exceptional in himself. Others, even if they could not offer themselves to danger, yet they cannot as often as they wish remove themselves from danger, which he himself could. Therefore he says his life is not snatched from him, that is to say, against his will.

From myself) By my own will, as the Syrian rightly [translates] here.

I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again) ἐξουσία in this place, if I am not mistaken, signifies power, as in Acts I. 7, XXVI. 18. It has this sense in משל and is thus translated in Psalm CXXXVI. 8. To take it again, understand [it as] snatching life from danger already present: which he often did when he rendered himself invisible, and when he softened the hearts of the guards, and when he cast down those sent against him.

But it is not only about the danger of death and the snatching of life from danger: but about death itself and the resurrection here; which even the Socinians themselves do not deny. And that authority and power of taking up life again he had already asserted for himself before. John II. 19. Nor did that commandment, to which he here appeals, look only to this, that he should expose himself to the danger of death, but that he should meet death for us, and give his soul as a ransom and a counter-ransom for all. We have dealt with this passage in a special German writing, that Christ rose from the dead by his own power, opposed to the Socinian Schaffer in the name of the Theological Faculty of the Academy of Königsberg.

this commandment I received from my Father) The Father entrusted this business of saving the sheep to me. It is customary for ἐντέλλεσθαι to be used among the Greeks even where a command properly so-called does not have a place.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Οὐδεὶς αἴρει αὐτὴν ἀπ᾽ ἐμῦ) Ostendit Christus ali- quid in se eximium. Alii etsi periculo se non offerre po- terant, non tamen quoties volunt se periculo possunt exi- mere, quod ipse poterat, Ideo ait sibi non eripi vitam, invi- to scilicet.

Ἀπ᾽ ἐμαυτῦ) Mea voluntate, ut hic recte Syrus.

ἐξουσίαν ἔχω θεῖναι αὐτὴν, καὶ ἐξουσίαν ἔχω πάλιν λαβεῖν αὐ- τήν) ἐξουσία hoc loco, ni fallor, potentiam significat, ut Actor. I. 7. XXVI. 18. hunc sensum habet משל & sic ver- titur Psal. CXXXVI. 8. πάλιν λαβεῖν αὐτὴν, intellige vitam periculo jam præsenti eripere: quod sæpe fecit cum se red- didit inconspicuum, & cum corda satellitum emollivit, & cum in se missos præcipites dedit.

At non de periculo solum mortis, & ereptione vitæ e periculo: Sed de morte ipsa & resurrectione hic agitur: quod ipsimet quoque Sociniani non diffitentur. Et potestatem illam & potentiam vi- tam iterum sumendi antea sibi jam asseruerat. Job. II. 19. nec ἐντολὴ illa, ad quam hic provocat, eo tantum spectabat, ut periculo mortis se objiceret, sed ut mortem pro nobis oppeteret, animamque suam λύτρον & ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus daret. E- gimus de hoc loco peculiari scripto Germanico, quod Christus propria virtute à mortuis resurrexit Schaffero Sociniano nomine Theologicæ Facult. Acad. Regiomontanæ opposito.

ταύτην τὴν ἐντολὴν ἔλαβον παρὰ τῦ πατρός μου) Pater hoc ne- gotium ovium servandarum mihi commendavit. Solet ἐντέλλεσθαι apud Græcos dici etiam ubi imperium proprie di- ctum locum non habet.

## 10:19
Vers. 19. Schism) See above IX. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Σχίσμα) Vide supra IX. 16.

## 10:20
Vers. 20. He has a demon and is mad) The one is explained by the other, as if you were to say: he is driven by furies and is insane. See above VII. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Δαιμόνιον ἔχει καὶ μαίνεται) Alterum per alterum exponitur, quasi dicas: furiis agitatus insanit. Vide su- pra VII. 20.

## 10:21
Vers. 21. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind) This work is of the power of the Creator of things, not of a lesser spirit. Life and sense are the gifts of God alone. Chrysostom: For he did not only fashion the eye for the beginning, but also granted the power to see; which is a proof of that [power] which breathes into the soul, for if that does not work, the eye, even if it be perfected, will never see anything.

PART III. Profession, confirmation, and defense, that Christ is both one God with the Father, and the Son of God sent into the world.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Μὴ δαιμόνιον δύναται τυφλῶν ὀφθαλμὸς ἀνοίγειν) Opus hoc est potestatis rerum opificis, non spiritus mi- noris, Vita & sensus solius Dei sunt munera. Chrysosto- mus: ὁ γὰρ ἔπλασε μόνον ὀφθαλμὸς εἰς ἀνάρξιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ὁρᾷν ἐχαρίσατο· ὅπερ τεκμήριόν ἐστι τῆς τῇ ψυχῇ ἐμφυσώσης ἐ- κείνης γὰρ μὴ ἐνεργύσης, ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς κἄν ἀπηρτισμένος ᾖ οὐ κὰν ἴδῃ πότε οὐδέν.

PARS III. Professio, confirmatio, ac defensio, quod Chri- stus sit & unus cum Patre Deus, ac Dei Fi- lius in mundum missus.

## 10:22
Ver. 22.

Ἐγένετο δὲ τὰ ἐγκαίνια) the day of the dedication. I Macc. IV. 59. Josephus, book XII of the Antiquities, chap. XI: 'Judas celebrated with his fellow citizens the recovery of the sacrifice concerning the temple for eight days, omitting nothing of pleasure, but feasting himself with costly and splendid sacrifices, and honoring God with hymns and psalms, and delighting himself. And he used such pleasure concerning the renewal of the customs, having unexpectedly after a long time come into power over the religion, that he established a law for those after him to celebrate the recovery of the things concerning the temple for eight days. And from that time until now we keep the feast called Lights.' It was called Lights because throughout these whole eight days lamps were lit even at night in the houses, as is handed down in the Talmudic title, in which this deed and the feast of the strong are treated. ἐγκαινίζειν, from which the name ἐγκαίνια comes, is for the Hebrews חנך, which is used for any dedication, whether first or restored. It is found in Deut. XX. 5, 1 Kings VIII. 64, 2 Chronicles VII. 5. We learn from this that it is possible for the people of God piously, even without a special divine command, to institute feast days in memory of some benefit.

καὶ χειμὼν ἦν) on the twenty-fifth of the month of Casleu, which falls in December.

Guilhelmus Vorstius indeed wishes, in his Observations on Zemach David, p. 273, that that decree of the Dedication in 1 Macc. IV. 59 pertained only to the times of the Maccabees, and did not bind all the descendants of the Jews. But that is from poorly understood words of the book of Maccabees, ἵνα ἄγωνται αἱ ἡμέραι ἐγκαινισμῦ τῦ θυσιασηρίε ἐν τοῖς καιροῖς αὐτῶν ἐνιαυτὸν, which must be rendered: 'that the days of the dedication of the altar (which is also of the Temple) may be celebrated in their times,' that is, as often as their times recur annually. For that these Dedications were subsequently solemnities for the Jews also, and are celebrated by them even today, the formula of prayer, as well as the Hymn of the second Sabbath of the dedication, accustomed to be sung in the Synagogues, as also the blessings in the Rituals, teach. See Mahzor Jud. Germ. part 1, fol. 100. 1, Sepher Tephilloth Lasucchoth fol. 101 & 102. Nonnus the Paraphrast, and some among Theophylact, certainly explain these Dedications in John as the annual memory of the dedication of the Solomonic temple. Chrysostom understands them as the feast of the dedication of the Zorobabelian temple returning, in Homily LXI on John, which opinion is also that of Euthymius Zigabenus. Theodore of Mopsuestia, however, wishes it to be designated as the feast accustomed to be celebrated for the restoration of the city of Jerusalem. But the Solomonic Dedications fell in the autumn, the seventh month, Tisri, 1 Kings VIII. 2; the Zorobabelian, however, in the month Adar, a little before the vernal equinox, Ezra VI. 16; but these Dedications were celebrated in winter, John being the witness. Which time agrees with the institution of the Dedications designated in the Maccabean books, by which the 25th day of the month Casleu, or the Ninth, was dedicated: not to mention that it could not be taught that an annual festival in memory of the temple, whether the first or the second, had been instituted before those Hasmonean Dedications; even if Petrus Comestor, and Thomas Aquinas, or whoever that author of the Commentary on this passage may be, say that those former Dedications were once celebrated annually, but were abolished because of these new Maccabean ones. Concerning the feast of the restored city, it is indeed read in Nehemiah VIII. 1, but the Dedications were not celebrated then, where on the first day indeed, with the reading and explanation of the Biblical text, hymns were sung, but on the second day the feast of tabernacles was proclaimed; and that Solemnity fell on the seventh month, the first day of the same. But that an annual memory of it was ever instituted or celebrated, it is established by no document. Wherefore there is no doubt that the Maccabean Dedications are noted here, not indeed instituted by Mattathias, as Drusius, perhaps having a lapse of memory, if not seduced by some book of Jewish prayers, asserted in his notes on the book of Hasmoneans ch. IV. 52 and in his Praeterita book IV on John X. 22; but instituted by his son Judas, two years after the death of Mattathias.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Ἐγένετο δὲ τὰ ἐγκαίνια) ἡμέρα ἐγκαινισμῦ. I. Macc. IV. 59. Josephus libr. XII. Ant. cap. XI. ἑόρταζε δὲ Ἰούδας μετὰ τῶν πο- λιτῶν ἀνάκτησιν τῆς περὶ τὸ ναὸν θυσίας ἐφ᾽ ἡμέρας ὀκτὼ, μηδὲν ἀπολιπὼν ἡδονῆς οὐδ᾽ ἓν, ἀλλὰ πολυτελέσι καὶ λαμπραῖς ταῖς θυσίαις κατευωχῶν αὐτὸς, ὕμνοις δὲ καὶ ψαλμοῖς τὸν Θεὸν μετιμῶν, αὐτός δὲ τέρπων. Τοσαύτῃ δὲ ἐχρήσατο τῇ περὶ τὴν ἀνανέωσιν τῶν ἐθῶν ἡδονῇ, μετὰ χρόνον πολὺν ἀπροσδοκήτως ἐν ἐξου- σίᾳ γενόμενοι τῆς θρησκείας, ὡς νόμον θέσθαι τοῖς μετ᾽ αὐτὸς, ἑορτά- ζειν τὴν ἀνάκτησιν τῶν περὶ τὸν ναὸν ἐφ᾽ ἡμέρας ὀκτώ. καὶ ἐξ ἐκείνου μέχρι δεῦρο τὴν ἑορτὴν ἄγομεν καλουμένην Φῶτα. Vocabatur Φῶτα quia per totos hos octo dies lucernæ noctibus etiam in domibus accendebantur, ut in titulo Thalmudico, quo de hoc facto & festo fortium agitur traditum est. ἐγκαινίζειν unde est nomen ἐγκαίνια Hebræis est חנך quod de quavis dedicatione sive prima sive instaurata usurpatur. Invenitur Deut. XX. 5. 1. Reg. VIII. 64. 2. Paralip. VII. 5. Discimus hinc posse pie à populo Dei etiam sine speciali mandato di- vino in beneficii alicujus memoriam dies festos institui.

καὶ χειμὼν ἧν) πέμπτῃ καὶ εἰκάδι τῦ χασλεῦ μηνὸς, quod in Decembrem incidit.

Vult quidem Guilhelmus Vorstius in Observat. ad Zemach David p. 273. decretum illud Encænio- rum 1. Macc. IV. 59. tantum pertinuisse ad Macca- bæorum tempora, non vero omnes Judæorum po- steros obstrinxisse. Sed id è male intellectis verbis libri Maccabæorum est, ἵνα ἄγωνται αἱ ἡμέραι ἐγ- καινισμῦ τῦ θυσιασηρίε ἐν τοῖς καιροῖς αὐτῶν ἐνι- αυτὸν, quæ reddenda, ut celebrentur dies Encæ- niorum altaris (quæ & Templi) in suis temporibus, hoc est, quoties annuatim recurrent eorum tem- pora. Nam deinceps solemnia etiam Judæis fuisse hæc Encænia, & hodieque ab iisdem celebrari, formula precationis, nec non Hymnus Sabbati secun- di dedicationis, in Synagogis cantari solitus, ut & benedictiones in Ritualibus docent. vid. Mah- zor. Jud. Germ. part. 1. fol. 100. 1. Sepher Tephilloth Lasucchoth fol. 101. & 102. Explicant sane hæc in Johanne Encænia Nonnus Paraphrastes, & aliqui apud Theophylactum, de Encæniorum templi Salomonici anniversaria memoria. Chrysostomus intelligit illa de festo dedicationis templi Zorobabeli- ci redeunte homil: LXI. in Joh. quæ sententia et- iam Euthymii Zigabeni est. Theodorus vero Mo- psvestanus festum pro urbis Hierosolymitanæ in- staurations celebrari solitum designari vult. Sed Encænia Salomonico inciderunt in autumnum, Mensem septimum, Tisri 1. Reg. VIII. 2. Zoroba- beliana vero in Mensem Adar paulo ante æquino- ctium vernale Esdr. VI. 16. hæc vero Encænia in hyeme celebrata sunt, Johanne teste. Quod tem- pus convenit instituto Encæniorum in Maccabaicis designato, quibus dicatus fuit XXV. dies Mensis Casleu seu Noni: ut taceam, quod doceri neque- at, ante Hasmonæica ista Encænia institutam fuisse festivitatem anniversariam in memoriam templi, seu primi, seu secundi; utut Petrus Comestor, & Thomas Aquinas vel quisquis ille auctor sit Com- ment. in h. l. dicant, Encænia illa priora annuatim quondam celebrata, sed propter ista nova Maccabai- ca abolita fuisse. De festo urbis instauratæ legi- tur quidem Nehem. VIII. 1. sed neque Encænia tum celebrata, ubi primo quidem die cum lectio- ne atque explicatione textus Biblici, hymni de- cantati, altero vero die indictum est festum taber- naculorum; & incidit ista Solemnitas in Mensem septimum diem primum ejusdem. Anniversariam vero ejus memoriam sive institutam, sive cele- bratam unquam fuisse, nullo documento constat. Quapropter dubium non est, hic notari Encænia Maccabaica, non quidem à Matathia, ut Dru- seus sens ad librum Hasmonæor. c. IV. 52. & Præteritor. l. IV. ad Johan. X. 22. memoria forte lapsus, si non libro precum Judaicarum aliquo seductus, assir- mavit; sed à filio ejus Juda, biennio post obi- tum Matathiæ, instituta.

## 10:23
Ver. 23.

ἐν τῇ στοᾷ Σολομῶντος) It coheres well with what he says, that it was winter. For in summer they walked in the open air itself; in winter, more in the portico, where the crowd was also denser at that time; which occasion the enemies of Jesus seize. It is called Solomon's portico or Royal, because it had been restored in the same place where he had built it, to the South of the Temple: Josephus describes it in Antiquities VII, chap. II, and XX, ch. 8. But learned men think that there ἀνατολικὴ was written erroneously for νότιον.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

ἐν τῇ στοᾷ Σολομῶντος) Bene cohæret cum eo quod dicit hyemen fuisse. Nam æstate in ipso subdiali ambulabant; hyeme magis in porticu, ubi & tum densior erat multitudo; quam occasionem captant Jesu inimici. Dicitur autem So- lomonis porticus aut Regia, quia eodem loco quo ille suastruxerat erat restituta, ad Meridiem Templi: describit Josephus VII. antiq. cap. II. & XX. c. 8. Sed ibi ἀνατολικὴ mendose pro νότιον scriptum putant viri eruditi.

## 10:24
Ver. 24.

Ἐκύκλωσαν ὖν) With a great gathering, so that there might be more witnesses of that which Jesus was about to say.

ἕως πότε τὴν ψυχὴν ἡμῶν αἴρεις) αἴρειν here is the same as μετεωρίζειν in Luke 12:29, to hold in suspense in doubt.

εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς εἰπὲ ἡμῖν παῥῥησίᾳ) They saw Jesus using circumlocutions tending toward that end, when he called himself the light of the world, when he called himself the excellent shepherd, and indeed the Son of God; but they want him to speak openly, for this is what παῥῥησία is, as appears below in 16:29. Doubtless they knew that by the name of Christ a king was understood, and by that profession they wanted to create danger for him before the Romans.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

Ἐκύκλωσαν ὖν) Magno confluxu, quo plures essent testes ejus quod Jesus esset dicturus.

ἕως πότε τὴν ψυχὴν ἡμῶν αἴρεις) αἴρειν hic est quod μετεωρίζειν Lucæ XII. 29. suspensum tenere in dubio.

εἰ σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς εἰπὲ ἡμῖν παῥῥησίᾳ) Videbant Jesum uti circumlocutionibus eo tendentibus, ut cum se lucem mun- di, cum eximium pastorem imo & Dei Filium vocabat; sed volunt eum aperte loqui, hoc enim est παῥῥησία ut ap- paret infra XVI. 29. Nimirum Christi nomine sciebant re- gem intelligi, atque ea professione periculum ei creare vo- lebant apud Romanos.

## 10:25
Vers. 25.

ἔιπον ὑμῖν) In reality, with words signifying the same thing, although less invidious.

τὰ ἔργα ἃ ἐγὼ ποιῶ) I enlighten the blind, both in a mystical sense, and—so that you may be the more stirred—in a popular sense as well: and I do other things which were predicted concerning the Messiah.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

ἔιπον ὑμῖν) Reipsa, verbis idem significantibus, quanquam minus invidiosis.

τὰ ἔργα ἃ ἐγὼ ποιῶ) Cæcos illumino, & sensu mystico, & quo magis excitemini sensu etiam populari: aliaque fa- cio, quæ de Messia sunt prædicta.

## 10:26
V. 26. ἀλλ᾽ ὑμεῖς ἐκ τῶν προβάτων τῶν ἐμῶν) You are not pious and teachable, such as are fit to become my sheep. See what is above at 16.

καθὼς εἶπον ὑμῖν) I said that they are sheep who hear my voice. Compare what is above at 8:47.

Latin:

V. 26. ἀλλ᾽ ὑμεῖς ἐκ τῶν προβάτων τῶν ἐμῶν) Non estis pii ac do- ciles, quales sunt apti ut oves meæ fiant. Vide quæ supra 16.

καθὼς εἶπον ὑμῖν) Dixi oves esse eos qui vocem meam audiunt. Confer quod supra VIII. 47.

## 10:28
Vers. 28.

κἀγὼ ζωὴν αἰώνιον δίδωμι αὐτοῖς) Lest anyone should think that those who were not sheep could in no way become sheep, he still entices them with the excellence of his promises, so that they might wish to become sheep.

καὶ ὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) They shall never perish utterly. For thus this expression is used below in 13:8 and often elsewhere. Understand, however, that Christ is speaking of sheep as they are and remain such, as above in 3:36.

κὰι ὐχ ἁρπάσει τις αὐτὰ ἐκ τῆς χειρός με) No force, not even the Devil himself, who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14). The spirits of the saints are deposited in the hand of Christ (Acts 7:59). He preserves them until the time of the resurrection: which was predicted by Daniel, believed by the Maccabees, and foreshadowed in the liberation of the people from Antiochus. These prophecies and histories were indeed explained to the people at the time of the Feast of Dedication.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

κἀγὼ ζωὴν αἰώνιον δίδωμι αὐτοῖς) Ne quis putaret qui o- ves non essent oves fieri nullo modo posse, adhuc promis- sorum excellentia eos allicit, ut oves fieri velint.

καὶ ὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) Nunquam peribunt peni- tus. Sic enim locutio hæc ponitur infra XIII. 8. & alibi sæpe. Intellige autem loqui Christum de ovibus qua tales sunt & manent, ut supra III. 36.

κὰι ὐχ ἁρπάσει τις αὐτὰ ἐκ τῆς χειρός με) Nulla vis, nec ipse quidem Diabolus, qui ὁ τὸ κράτος ἔχει τῦ θανάτε Hebr. II. 24. Spiritus Sanctorum deponuntur in manu Christi. Act. VII. 59. Is eos servat ad tempus resurrectionis: quæ prædicta à Daniele, credita à Maccabæis, adumbrata in liberatione populi ab Antiocho. Hæ vero Prophetiæ & historiæ tempore ἐγκαινίων populo explicabantur.

## 10:29
Verse 29.

ὁ πατήρ με ὃς δέδωκέ μοι μείζων πάντων ἐστί) Thus not only the Greeks have it, but also the Syrian and the Arab. Wherefore this reading seems altogether more true. The Father gives believers to the Son to be saved and made alive. See above VI. 36. But the Father is stronger than death and the Devils.

This reading is rightly preferred to that which Beza thinks Tertullian and Augustine followed; as if they had read ὁ πατήρ με ὃ δέδωκέ μοι, μεῖζον πάν- των ἐστί, That which my Father gave me is greater than all, who understood this concerning the Church overcoming all the power of adversaries.

κὰ ὐδεὶς δύναται ἁρπάζειν ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς τῶ πατρός με) κὰ for because, since the Father is more powerful than them, therefore they can snatch nothing from the Father's power.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

ὁ πατήρ με ὃς δέδωκέ μοι μείζων πάντων ἐστί) Sic habent non Græci tantum sed & Syrus & Arabs. Quare omnino videtur hæc verior lectio. Pater credentes Filio servandos & vivificandos dat. Vide supra VI. 36. Pater autem for- tior est morte & Diabolis.

Recte præfertur hæc lectio illi, quam Tertul- lianum & Augustinum sequutos esse Beza putat; quasi legerint ὁ πατήρ με ὃ δέδωκέ μοι, μεῖζον πάν- των ἐστί, Quod Pater meus dedit mihi, majus est o- mnibus, qui id de Ecclesia superante omnem ad- versariorum potentiam intellexêre.

κὰ ὐδεὶς δύναται ἁρπάζειν ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς τῶ πατρός με) κὰ pro ideo, quia Pater potentior illis est, ideo illi nihil possunt e- ripere Patris potestati.

## 10:30
Verse 30.

ἐγὼ κὰ ὁ πατὴρ ἔν ἐσμεν) He connects what he had said with the preceding, If they cannot be snatched from the Father's power, neither will they be able to be snatched from mine: for my power emanates from the Father, and indeed in such a way that it is worth just as much to be guarded by me or by the Father. See Gen. XLI. 25. 27.

This corruption serves the Socinians and Arians: Christ does not only indicate that, that it is worth just as much to be guarded by himself or by the Father, and that comparison of the passage Gen. XLI. 25 is foreign: he professes himself to be one with the Father, so that he may testify to his ὁμόοσιαν or that he is of the same essence with the Father, which the ancients gravely and with great consensus assert against the Arians, concerning which see Tom. III. System. Theolog. Power and essence in God are the same. Therefore he teaches that both power and essence are one for him with the Father, Christ: and for that reason the Jews wanted to stone him v. 31. ἐβάςασαν ἐν πάλιν λίθες, naturally because they understood that Jesus was ascribing divine power to himself, as Grotius himself notes here, and that he was making himself God v. 33. just as before c. VIII. 59. when they understood that he was asserting the divine nature for himself, they already wanted to stone him. In the Synod of Sardica, as reported by Theodoret, Hist. Eccles. book II, ch. II, against the Arians, they say: The interpretation of the Arians is depraved and execrable, who contend that the Savior said, I and the Father are one, because there is consensus and concord between them. For we both believe and affirm, and understand, that holy statement of the Savior concerning the unity of essence, which is one and the same in the Father and the Son, to be wise. See also Basil, book I, adv. Eunom.; Athanasius, Orat. contr. Arian.; Hilary, books VII and VIII, de Trin.; Gregory Nazianzen, tr. XLI, de fide; Jerome, in VI. Es. Augustine, book IV, de Trin., ch. 9, and book V, ch. 3, book VI, ch. 2, and elsewhere passim. Victor Uticensis, book II, de persequ. Vandal.; Fulgentius, book III, ad Trasm. Reg., ch. 6, and ch. Calvin had also poured water here for the Arians, arguing that Christ was not speaking of the unity of substance, but of the consensus which he has with the Father: our blessed Aegidius Hunnius and Pelargus, who later himself retreated to the camp of Calvin, confound the Arianizing Calvin, and in his commentary on John he rejects the gloss of Calvin in these very words: We do not accept this δόξαν, otherwise we would seem to open the gates wide to Arianism. Furthermore, Grotius himself acknowledged that the Jews understood that Christ was making himself equal to God, noting these things on v. 33, ποιεῖς Ὥ Θεὸν: That is, you say, as above VIII. 53, you sell yourself as God. This is because he had called his Father God in a singular way, as we said above V. 18. Wherefore, what they had called equal to God there, here they call God, that is, as it were another God: just as sons are said to be the same as the father even in law. However, the Jews did not gather this in this place from the word Son of God, which he did not use in this conflict, but from those words, I and the Father are one. But those words v. 36, 4' ὅς τᾶ Θεᾶ εἰμὶ, are to be taken as Grotius explained above v. 25, τ' εἶπεν ὑμῖν, by the thing itself, with words signifying the same: namely, in that he had called God his Father v. 25, and had professed himself to be one with the Father. Father and son are relative terms: and when the Son professes himself to be one with the Father, what is this other than what was defined in the Nicene Council, that the Son is ὁμούσιος, i.e., of the same essence with the Father?

Latin:

Vers. 30.

ἐγὼ κὰ ὁ πατὴρ ἔν ἐσμεν) Connectit quod dixerat cum su- perioribus, Si Patris potestati eripi non poterunt, nec meæ poterunt: nam mea potestas à Patre emanat, & quidem l- ta ut tantumdem valeat à me aut à Patre custodiri. Vide Gen. XLI. 25. 27.

Corruptela hæc Socinianis & Arianis velificatur: non id tantum indicat Christus, tantundem va- lere à se, aut à Patre custodiri, & aliena est illa loci Gen. XLI. 25. collatio: unum se esse profitetur cum Patre, ut ὁμόοσιαν suam testetur vel quod e- jusdem sit essentiæ cum Patre, quod graviter & magno consensu veteres adversus Arianos asse- runt, de quo Tom. III. System. Theolog. Potentia & essentia in Deo idem sunt. Ideo unam esse sibi cum Patre & potentiam & essentiam docet Chri- stus: atq; ea de causa lapidare ipsum volebant Iu- dæi v. 31. ἐβάςασαν ἐν πάλιν λίθες, nimirum quod intelligerent Jesum sibi adscribere potestatem di- vinam, ut hic Grotius ipse notat, & quod seipsum Deum faceret v. 33. quemadmodum antea c. VIII. 59. cum divinam naturam eum sibi asserere intelli- gerent, lapidare ipsum jam voluerunt. In Synodo Sardicensi referente Theodoreto l. II. Hist. Eccles. c. II. contra Arian. Depravata, inquiunt, & execra- bilis est Arianorum interpretatio, qui contendunt, Servatorem ideo dixisse, Ego & Pater unum su- mus, quod sit inter eos consensus & concordia. Nos enim & credimus & affirmamus, & intelligimus, sa- cram illam Servatoris sententiam de unitate essentiæ, quæ una est, eademque in Patre & Filio, sapien- dam esse. Vid. & Basil. l. I. adv. Eunom. Athan. Orat. contr. Arian. Hilarius l. VII. & VIII. de Trin. Gregor. Naz. tr. XLI. de fide Hieron. in VI. Es. Au- gust. l. IV. de Trin. c. 9. & l. V. c. 3. l. VI. c. 2. & pas- sim alibi. Victor. Uticensis l. II. de persequ. Vandal. Fulgent. l. III. ad Trasm. Reg. c. 6. & c. Affuderat A- rianis & Calvinus hic aquam, Christum non de uni- tate substantiæ, sed de consensu, quem cum Patre ha- bet, disputare: Arianizantem Calvinum confun- dit B. Ægid. Hunnius noster, & Pelargus, qui po- stea ipse se ad castra Calvini recepit, in comment. in Joh. reprobat glossam Calvini his omnino ver- bis: Non recipimus hanc δόξαν, alioquin bipatentes videremur Arianismo aperire portas. Cæterum agnovit Grotius ipse, quod Judæi intellexerint Christum se Patri æqualem facere, hæc annotans ad v. 33. ποιεῖς Ὥ Θεὸν: Id est dicis, ut supra VIII. 53. pro Deo te venditas. Hoc ideo quia Patrem suum singulari modo Deum dixerat ut diximus supra V. 18. Quare quod ibi dixerant æqualem Deo, hic dicunt Deum, id est quasi alterum Deum: sicut filii idem cum patre esse etiam in jure dicuntur. Non autem id hoc quidem loco ex voce Filii Dei collegerunt Iu- dæi, qua usus in hoc conflictu non est, sed ex verbis illis, Ego & Pater unum sumus. Verba au- tem illa v. 36. 4' ὅς τᾶ Θεᾶ εἰμὶ accipienda ut supra v. 25. τ' εἶπεν ὑμῖν exposuit Grotius, re ipsa, verbis idem significantibus: nempè qua DEUM Patrem suum dixerat v. 25. seque cum Patre unum esse pro- fessus erat. Pater & filius relata sunt: & cum unum se cum Patre profitetur Filius, quid hoc aliud est, quam quod in Niceno Concilio definitum, quod sit Filius ὁμούσιος h. e. ejusdem essentiæ cum Patre?

## 10:31
Vers. 31.

ἐβάςασαν ἐν πάλιν λίθως) Naturally because they understood that Jesus was ascribing divine power to himself, thus above V. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

ἐβάςασαν ἐν πάλιν λίθως) Nimirum quod intelligerent Je- sum sibi adscribere divinam potestatem, sic supra V. 18.

## 10:32
Vers. 32.

πολλὰ καλὰ ἔργα) Beautiful, praiseworthy. שפירא excellent, the Syrian. Thus Matt. V. 16, Mark IV. 6, 1 Tim. V. 10. ἔδειξα ὑμῖν) I have done, and indeed openly. The Hebrews say הראה to make to see. Ps. IV. 7, LX. 5, LXXXV. 8, Eccl. II. 24. ἐκ τῶ πατρός με) He adds this for the sake of modesty and to diminish envy. ἐκ for παρὰ as often. διὰ ποῖον αὐτῶν ἔργων λιθάζετέ με) There is a wonderful δεινότης in these words. ποῖ for which Matt. IX. 18, Luke XII. 39, Rev. III. 3, and elsewhere. You stone, that is, you want to stone. For by these words Christ restrained their perverse minds, lest they should carry out the intended work, showing by the thing itself what he had said, that it was in his power to snatch himself from dangers as often as he wished.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

πολλὰ καλὰ ἔργα) Pulchra laudabilia. שפירא eximia Syrus. Sic Matth. V. 16. Marc. IV. 6. 1. Tim. V. 10. ἔδειξα ὑμῖν) Feci & quidem palam. Hebræi dicunt הראה facere videre. Psal. IV. 7. LX. 5. LXXXV. 8. Eccl. ## 10:34
Vers. 34.

Ἀπεκρίθη ἀυτοῖς) Replying: as below XII. 34. ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ὑμῶν) That is, in those sacred writings which prescribe to you what you ought to believe and do, and therefore they are not wrongly called by the name of law: that is, תורה by which is signified whatever directs a man. Thus below XV. 26, 1 Cor. XIV. 21, but also in the law of Moses itself, the same words do not indeed exist, but the meaning is the same when judges are called Gods.

Ἐγὼ εἶπα Θεοί ἐστε) Ps. LXXXII, which was made concerning the judges of the great Sanhedrin to remind them of their duty.

That Psalm LXXXII pertains to the judges of the great Sanhedrin, Grotius asserted rashly, and not consistently enough, here and in the appendix to the passages concerning the Anti-Christ. For in his explanation of the Decalogue, at the preface, he affirmed that the word אלהים in Psalm LXXXII. 2 was attributed to angels; and he observed that it is a matter of doubt among the most learned of the Hebrews whether angels or magistrates are understood in Psalm LXXXII. 2 and CXXXI. 1. But the Psalmist speaks neither of angels nor of the judges of the great Sanhedrin, but of the magistrates to whom Moses had already attributed the name Elohim in Exod. XXI. 6 and ch. XXII. 8, 9, 28, when the Sanhedrin had not yet been instituted. Who are called Elohim for three reasons: 1. because the word of God was made to them, that is, they received a mandate from the Lord to judge, as is said here; 2. because they administered not the judgments of man, but of God, 2 Chron. XIX. 6; 3. because God himself is present in the conducting of the affairs of government and judgment, Psalm LXXXII. 2. Which reasons apply to any magistrates whatsoever, Rom. XIII. 1, et seqq.

Vers. 34.

Ἀπεκρίθη ἀυτοῖς) Replicans: ut infra XII. 34. ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ὑμῶν) Id est in sacris illis literis quæ vobis præ- scribunt quid credere & facere debeatis, & proinde non ma- le legis nomine appellantur: id est תורה quo significatur quicquid hominem dirigit. Sic infra XV. 26. 1. Cor. XIV. 21. sed & in ipsa Mosis lege non quidem eadem extant ver- ba, sed sensus idem cum judices Dii vocantur.

Ἐγὼ εἶπα Θεοί ἐστε) Psal. LXXXII. qui de judicibus Syne- drii magni factus est ad eos sui officii commonefaciendos.

Ad judices Synedrii magni pertinere Psalm. LXXXII. Grotius temere, nec constanter satis, hic, & in appendice ad loca de Anti-Christo asseruit. In explic. enim Decal. ad præfat. vocem אלהים Angelis attributam esse Psal. LXXXII. 2. affirmavit; Dubiumque esse inter Hebræorum doctissimos, Angeli an Magistratus Psal. LXXXII. 2. & CXXXI. 1. in- telligantur observavit. At Hieropsaltes nec de Angelis, nec de judicibus Synedrii magni, sed de ma- gistratibus, quibus nomen Elohim Moses Exod. XXI. 6. c. XXII. 8. 9. 28. jam tribuerat, cum Sy- nedrium nondum esset institutum, loquitur. Qui Elohim ob tres causas dicuntur 1. quia Dei sermo ad eos factus est, id est mandatum judicandi ac- ceperunt à Domino, ut hic dicitur, 2. quia non ho- minis, sed Dei judicia administrarunt 2. Paral. XIX. 6. 3. quia Deus ipse adest in negotiis imperii & judicii gerendis Psal. LXXXII. 2. Quæ causæ quibuslibet magistratibus conveniunt Rom. XIII. 1. seqq.

XXVI. 32, and what we call mandates in Latin, the Hebrews call דברי. ## 10:36
Verse 36. Whom the Father) To be understood here as 'me', as appears from what follows.

He sanctified) That which is הקדש in Jeremiah I. 5 is ἡγίασεν in the Greek, as also in Ecclesiasticus XLIX. 9; that is translated by Paul, alluding to that passage, as ἀφορίζειν in Gal. I. 15. The Hebrews, in the aforementioned passage of Jeremiah, rightly explain it as to prepare, and that is to say, for a divine ministry. Which, in the ineffable conception of Christ, was done in an exceptional and admirable way; the angel says to the mother, 'that which is born of you is holy,' Luke I. 35. But it is more likely that something is understood here about which it could be sufficiently clear to the hearers, namely, the attribution of the power to perform such great miracles.

And sent into the world) He who receives some mandate from God to carry something out is said to be sent by Him, as above I. 6, III. 17, 34, V. 36, 38, VI. 57, VIII. 42. There is, however, a tacit comparison here. The Senators had received mandates pertaining to one people: I, to the whole human race, as above I. 9, III. 17, IV. 42, VIII. 12.

You say that you blaspheme, because I said I am the Son of God?) He refutes the calumny as if he were saying: if I attribute anything divine to myself, I did not do it by opposing myself to God, but by acknowledging Him as the source, which is shown by the very words of Father and Son which I used.

As for the present apology of Christ, the Socinians rashly conclude from it that Christ is called the Son of God on account of a communication, as it were, of divine power, wisdom, and holiness, or a likeness by reason of the same with God. For one must distinguish between the cause of knowing, or the argument of proof, by which it is confirmed that Christ is the Son of God, and the cause of being, which makes it so that he is the Son of God, and thus between the medium a priori, or from the cause of filiation, and a posteriori, or from the consequent, proving that Christ is the Son of God. The sanctification of Christ, and his mission into the world, is not the cause for which he is the Son of God, but that by which it is taught that he is the Son of God: because just as he is the Son of God by reason of his generation from the Father, so his sanctification, or singular and altogether divine anointing, by which he was anointed with immense and infinite gifts (John 3:34), divine wisdom, omniscience, omnipotence, etc. (John 3:35; Matt. 11:27), and his mission into the world, effected through the incarnation of the Son of God (Gal. 4:4; John 1:14), proved that Jesus is this only-begotten Son of God. For as Christ could not have been anointed by the Holy Spirit from the womb, unless he had been that only-begotten Son of God, true God by nature; so his being sent into the world for redemption implies both the eternal pre-existence of the Son with the Father, before he was sent, and his supreme Deity, because redemption is not the work of man but of the most high God (Isa. 43:11, 24). Furthermore, that the Son of God is understood here not by grace, but by nature, not by authority, but by essence, is evident partly from the interchange of the Name of God and the Son of God: because he is the Son of God in the same way that he is God, from a comparison of verses 33 and 35. But he is God not as regards power, but essence, not by grace, but by nature; "true God, God blessed for ever" (1 John 5:20; Rom. 9:5), and partly from the accusation of the Jews, because they charged the same person with blasphemy, because, being a man by nature, he made himself God. Where they understood true God, God by nature; otherwise they would not have charged Christ with blasphemy; but Christ answers not by denial, but by demonstration of the truth, both from the lesser to the greater, and from the induction of divine works.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ὃν ὁ πατὴρ) Subaudiendum hic, mihi, ut ex se- quentibus apparet.

ἡγίασε) Quod Jeremiæ I. 5. est הקדש in Græco ἡγιά- σεν ut & Ecclesiastici XLIX. 9. id Paulus ad eum locum al- ludens vertitur ἀφορίζειν Gal. I. 15. Hebræi dicto loco Jere- miæ recte exponunt præparare, ac divinum scilicet ministe- rium. Quod in Christi conceptione ineffabili, eximio & admirando modo factum est, τὸ γεννώμενον ἐκ σῦ ἅγιον ait an- gelus matri Luc. I. 35. Sed magis est ut hic aliquid intelli- gatur de quo satis auditoribus constare poterat, attributio scilicet potestatis tanta prodigia faciendi.

καὶ ἀπέστειλεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον) Qui mandatum aliquod à Deo accipit ad aliquid perferendum, is mitti ab eo dicitur, ut su- pra I. 6. III. 17. 34. V. 36. 38. VI. 57. VIII. 42. Est autem hic tacita comparatio. Senatores mandata acceperant ad u- num populum pertinentia: ego ad totum genus huma- num, ut supra I. 9. III. 17. IV. 42. VIII. 12.

Ὑμεῖς λέγετε, ὅτι βλασφημεῖς, ὅτι εἶπον υἱὸς τῦ Θεῦ εἰμί;) Re- fellit calumniam quasi diceret: si quid divini mihi tribui, non id feci me opponens Deo, sed eum ut fontem agno- scens, quod ostenditur ipsis vocibus Patris & Filii quas u- surpavi.

Quod ad apologiam præsentem Christi, teme- re Sociniani ex eadem colligunt, Christum ob com- municationem κατ’ ἔξω divinæ potentiæ, sapientiæ, ac sanctitatis, vel similitudinem ratione ejusdem cum Deo Filium Dei dici. Distinguendum enim inter causam cognoscendi, vel argumentum probationis, quo confirmatur Christum esse Dei Filium, & cau- sam essendi, quæ faciat, ut Filius Dei sit, adeoque inter medium à priori, vel à causa filiationis, & à po- steriori, vel à consequenti, Dei Filium esse Christum e vincens. Sanctificatio Christi, & missio in mundum non est causa, ob quam sit Filius Dei, sed per quam doceatur esse Filius Dei: quia uti Filius Dei est ob generationem à Patre, ita Jesum esse hunc unigeni- tum Dei Filium comprobabat ejus tum sanctifica- tio, seu unctio singularis, & prorsus divina, qua un- ctus fuit donis immensis & infinitis Iohan. III. 34. divina sapientia, omniscientia, omnipotentia &c. Ioh. III. 35. Matth. XI. 27. tum missio in mundum, facta per incarnationem Filii Dei Gal. IV. 4. Ioh. I. 14. Nam ut ungi haud potuisset Christus Spiri- tu S. ἐκ ἐκ μήτρας, nisi fuisset unigenitus ille Dei Fi- lius, verus natura Deus; ita mitti in mundum ad re- demptionem, innuit cum æternam præexisten- tiam Filii apud Patrem, antequam mitteretur, tum Deitatem supremam, quia Redemptio non est o- pus hominis sed Dei summi Es. XLIII. 11. 24. Porro Filium Dei hic intelligi non κατὰ χάριν, sed κατὰ φύ- σιν, non κατ’ ἐξουσίαν, sed κατ’ ὀυσίαν, constat partim ex permutatione Nominis Dei, & Filii Dei: quia ita est Filius Dei, quemadmodum est Deus, è collat. v. 33. & 35. Deus autem est non quoad poten- tiam, sed essentiam, non per gratiam, sed per natu- ram; " Deus verus, Deus benedictus in secula, Ioh. V. 10. Rom. IX. 6, partim è Iudæorum accusatione, quod eundem blasphemiæ postulabant, quod cum na- tura esset homo seipsum Deum faceret. Ubi intelli- gebant Deum verum, natura Deum; alioquin bla- sphemiæ non postulassent Christum, respondet au- tem Christus non per inficiationem, sed per verita- tis demonstrationem, cum à minori ad majus, tum ab operum divinorum inductione.

## 10:37
Verse 37. τὰ ἔργα τῦ πατρός μυ (the works of my Father): Worthy of God, while I heal every kind of disease, I look into thoughts, I bend hearts where I please, I give sight to the blind, I command demons with a nod.

-κὶν πιστεύετέ μοι (if you do not believe me): This is a figure which is called a concession. As if he were to say, if I do not do such things, allow yourselves not to believe, so below 11:41.

- εἰ πὶ ἐμοὶ πιστεύετε (if you do not believe me): Even if you do not wish to believe my words, although uttered with divine majesty.

Vers. 37. τὰ ἔργα τῦ πατρός μυ] Deo digna, dum omne genus morborum sano, cogitationes introspicio, corda fle- cto ubi libuit, cæcis visum do, diablolis nutu impero.

-κὶν πιστεύετέ μοι] Est figura quæ concessio dicitur. Quasi dicat, nisi tanta facio permittam vobis ne credatis, sic in- fra XI. 41.

## 10:38
Verse 38. τοῖς ἔργοις πιστεύσατε (believe the works): Have faith in the deeds: which he said elsewhere, "believe me for the works' sake" (John 14:11).

- ὅτι ἐν ἐμοὶ ὁ πατὴρ (that the Father is in me): By the working power. Thus that saying is explained below, "the Father is in me"; namely, "the Father who abides in me, he does the works" (John 14:10).

- κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ (and I in him): By most perfect obedience. Thus below, "that I am in the Father," is explained by "the words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself." Compare 15:4, 5.

- The orthodox Fathers refer these to the essential perichoresis of the Father in the Son and of the Son in the Father, and deservedly so: nowhere is the Son said to be in the Father through obedience. "Thus is the Father in the Son," says Fulgentius in his discourse on the Arian objection, "as the Son is in the Father; for the unity there is natural, thus it demonstrates both to be equal, so that the immense might beget the immense, and the immense, begotten from the immense, might have nothing less of the paternal immensity." One is in the other through the inconfused perichoresis of the persons among themselves, as Chrysostom, Theophylact, and other Greeks explain.

Latin:

Vers. 38. τοῖς ἔργοις πιστεύσατε] Factis habete fidem: quod alibi dixit διὰ τὰ ἔργα πιστεύετέ μοι. XIV. 11.

- ὅτι ἐν ἐμοὶ ὁ πατὴρ] Per vim operantem. Sic infra exponi- tur dictum illud, πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοὶ ἐστι; nempe ὁ πατὴρ ὁ ἐν ἐμοὶ μένων αὐτὸς ποιεῖ τὰ ἔργα. XIV. 10.

- κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ] Per obedientiam perfectissimam. Sic infra ὅτι ἐγὼ εἰμὶ ἐν τῷ πατρὶ, exponitur τὰ ῥήματα ἃ ἐγὼ λαλῶ ὑμῖν ἀπ’ ἐμαυτῦ ὐ λαλῶ. Conf. XV. 4. 5.

- Hæc ad περιχώρησιν essentialem Patris in Filio & Filii in Patre referunt, & merito, Patres orthodoxi: nuspiam Filius in Patre esse dicitur per obedientiam. Sic est Pater in Filio, inquit, Fulgentius in discurs. object. Arian. sicut est Filius in Patre; unitas enim ibi naturalis, sic æqualem demonstrat utrumque ut immensus immensum gigneret, & immensus ex im- menso genitus immensitatis paternæ nihil minus habe- ret. Alter in altero est διὰ τὴν ὑποστάσεων ἀσύγ- χυτον ἐν ἀλλήλοις περιχώρησιν per inconfusam im- meationem personarum inter se invicem, ut Chrysost. Theoph. & alii Græci explicant.

PARS POSTERIOR EVANGELII S. JOHANNIS Historiam quarti & ultimi Paschatis continens.

SECTIO I. De iis, quæ proxime ante passionem gesta sunt.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

While Lazarus is lying ill in Bethany, his sisters report it to Jesus, who says that he is dead for the glory of God; after two days he betakes himself into Judea, with the disciples dissuading him in vain, to resuscitate Lazarus who is sleeping, which he explains as the sleep of death. Arriving there, however, he finds Lazarus already buried for four days: meeting him, Martha hears that her brother will rise again, and she understands this of the last day. Jesus, however, testifies that he is the resurrection and the life, which Martha professes to believe. Maria, having received the message from Martha, also meets Jesus outside the village, with the Jews accompanying her, and Jesus, as they are weeping, asks where Lazarus has been laid, and having learned this, he orders the stone to be removed, and having given thanks to God the Father for the hearing of his prayer, he calls forth Lazarus, and orders him to be loosed from his bandages and lets him go, with many of the Jews believing, but some reporting this to the Pharisees, who for that reason gather a council, in which Caiaphas advises that it is better that one man die for the people than that the whole people perish; he prophesies that Jesus will die for the people, and that the children of God who are scattered might be gathered together. When, however, they were deliberating about killing him because of this, Jesus betook himself to the town of Ephron, with the Jews anxious as to whether he would come to the feast of the Passover, and an edict having been promulgated that whoever knows where he is should indicate it.

There are three parts: I. The resuscitation of Lazarus in Bethany, to v. 45. II. The consultation of the chief priests and Pharisees concerning Christ, with the prophetic counsel of Caiaphas, to v. 53. III. The anxiety of the Jews while Jesus is staying in Ephron, and the promulgation of the edict concerning indicating his whereabouts, to v. 57.

PART I. The resuscitation of Lazarus in Bethany.

Ἦν δέ τις ἀσθενῶν] ἀσθενεῖν is also said of one who is seriously ill, as in Matt. X. 8, Luke IV. 40, and elsewhere. Thus the Hebrew חלא is translated. ἀπὸ Βηθανίας ἐκ τῆς κώμης] Do not think Bethany is one thing and the village another. For the one is an interpretation of the other. Nor should the inserted preposition move us at all; for thus we also had above at I. 44, ἀπὸ Βηθσαϊδὰ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως Ἀνδρέου; concerning the name, see what is at Luke XVI. 21.

of Mary and of Martha her sister) The Syriac has this a little differently here: but the Arab confirms the Greek reading besides the Latin: thus here Bethany is called the village of Mary and Martha, just as in the place already mentioned Bethsaida is the town of Andrew and Peter. He names these sisters, however, because Christ and the Apostles had very often lodged with them. Μάρθα is read as a Syriac name also in Plutarch as Mario: and in Tacitus it is to be placed twice for Martina in the name of a Syrian woman. It is often asked why the earlier writers of the Gospel did not touch upon this so noble history. This occurs to me, that when they were writing, the resurrected Lazarus was still alive, and there was danger for him from the Jews if what had happened to him were publicly divulged. For it is also narrated soon after, that for this very reason snares were laid for him XII. 10. Wherefore it seemed to them that they could be silent about this for the time being, since other examples of resurrected persons were available. But when Lazarus was dead, since no danger could now arise to anyone from the narration of the event, this was added by John in this collection, as it were, of things passed over. Lazarus survived, however, if we believe Epiphanius who reports the tradition, for XXX years, within which time the three other Evangelists wrote.

Latin:

CAPUT XI. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Lazaro decumbente in Bethania sorores ejus id Jesu denunciant, qui mortuum esse ad gloriam Dei ais, post biduum in Judæam se, nequicquam dissuadentibus discipulis, con- ferens ad resuscitandum Lazarum dor- mientem, quod de somno mortis explicat. Adveniens autem eo invenit Lazarum jam per quatriduum humatum: cui occur- rens Martha audit fratrem resurrectu- rum, idque de novissimo die intelligit. Je- sus autem se resurrectionem & vitam esse testatur, quod se credere profitetur Mar- tha. Maria nuncio à Martha accepto Je- su etiam occurrit extra vicum, comitanti- bus eam Judæis, Jesusque plorantibus ipsis quærit, ubi repositus sit Lazarus, eoque cognito, jubet removeri lapidem, ac gra- tiis Deo Patri pro exauditione actis La- zarum evocat, eumque fasciis solvi ju- bet ac dimittit, credentibus multis è Ju- dæis, quibusdam vero id ad Pharisæos de- ferentibus, qui concilium ideo congregant, in quo Caiphas præstare monet, ut unus pro populo moriatur, quam ut totus popu- lus pereat, vaticinatur Jesum pro populo, & ut filii Dei dispersi congregentur, mori- turum. Quum vero ex eo de ipso inter- ficiendo deliberarent, Jesus in oppidum E- phron se contulit, Judæis solicitis, utrum ad festum Paschatos venturus, & edicto promulgato, ut cui constet, ubi ipse sit, id indicet.

Partes sunt tres I. Lazari in Bethania resuscita- tio, ad v. 45. II. Pontificum & Pharisæorum de Christo consultatio, cum Caiphæ consilio vaticina- torio, ad v. 53. III. Judæorum Jesu in Ebron hæ- rente, solicitudo, & edicti de ipso indicando promul- gatio, ad v. 57.

PARS I. Lazari in Bethania resuscitatio.

Ἦν δέ τις ἀσθενῶν] ἀσθενεῖν etiam de graviter ægroto dici- tur, ut Matth. X. 8. Luc. IV. 40. & alibi. Sic vertitur חלא Hebræum. ἀπὸ Βηθανίας ἐκ τῆς κώμης] Noli aliud Bethaniam putare, aliud vicum. Est enim alterum alterius interpretatio. Ne- que movere nos quicquam debet interjecta præpositio; nam sic & supra habuimus l. 4. ἀπὸ Βηθσαϊδὰ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως Ἀνδρέου; D: h:: nomine vide quæ ad Luc. XVI. 21.

Μαρίας καὶ Μάρθας τῆς ἀδελφῆς αὐτῆς) Habet hic paulo ali- ter Syrus: sed Græcam lectionem præter Latinam Arabs confirmat: ita hic Bethania dicitur vicus Mariæ & Marthæ, quomodo jam dicto loco Bethsaida oppidum Andreæ & Petri. Nominat autem sorores has quod sæpissime apud eas divertisssent Christus & Apostoli. Μάρθα Syriacum nomen etiam apud Plutarchum Mario legitur: & apud Tacitum pro Martina bis ponendum Martha in Syræ mulieris nomi- ne. Quæri solet, cur hanc tam nobilem historiam priores Evangelii scriptores non attigerint. Mihi hoc succurrit, cum illi scriberent vixisse resuscitatum Lazarum, & periculum ei fuisse à Judæis si quod ipsi acciderat palam vulgaretur. Nam etiam mox narratur, ob hoc ipsum structas ei insidias XII. 10. Quare visum illis hoc ad tempus subticere posse cum alia exempla resuscitatorum suppeterent. At mortuo Lazaro cum jam nemini periculum ex rei narratione fieri posset, additum hoc à Johanne in hac quasi prætermissorum collectione. Supervixit autem Lazarus, si Epiphanio traditionem referenti credimus, annos XXX. intra quod tempus tres alii Evangelistæ scripserunt.

## 11:2
Ver. 2.

the one who anointed) Not that this was done before the sickness of Lazarus, but that this was done and known to all when these things were being written: clearly just as in Luke VI. 16 it is written of Judas: who also became a traitor, and of Simon, who is called Peter, Matt. IV. 18, X. 2. Thus Theodore of Mopsuestia and Leontius explain it. Concerning the matter itself, see what we said at Matt. XXVI. 6. and wiped his feet with her hair) A hysteron proteron. For she first wiped them, then anointed them with ointment. Luke VII. 38, below XII. 3. It is evident from a comparison with ch. XII. 3 that these things are said proleptically. But we have shown at Matt. XXVI. 6 that this Mary is different from that one in Luke VII.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ἡ ἀλείψασα) Non quod hoc ante Lazari morbum esset gestum, sed quod gestum hoc esset & notum omnibus cum hæc scriberentur: planέ ut Luc. VI. 16. de Juda scriptum est: ὃς καὶ ἐγένετο προδότης, & de Simone, ὁ λεγόμενος Πέτρος Matth. IV. 18. X. 2. Sic exponunt Theodorus Mopsuefte- nus & Leontius. De reipsa vide quæ ad Matth. XXVI. 6. κὴ ἐκμάξασα τὺς πόδας αὐτῦ ταῖς θριξὶν αὑτῆς) ὕστερον πρό- τερον. Nam prius abstersit, deinde unguento perfudit. Luc. VII. 38. infra XII. 3. Προληπτικῶς hæc dici è collatione c. XII. 3. li- quet, At diversam hanc Mariam esse ab illa Luc. VII. ad Matth. XXVI. 6. ostendimus.

## 11:3
Ver. 3.

They sent word) They sent a messenger who would say. Saying) Through a messenger. See Matt. VIII. 5. he whom you love is sick) Doubtless hoping that it would come to pass that Jesus, arriving, would heal him, as appears below 21. Compare above IV. 49. Even those dear to God are not without their miseries.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ἀπέστειλαν ἷν) Nuntium miserunt qui diceret. Λέγυσα) Per nuntium. Vide Matth. VIII. 5. ὃν φιλεῖς ἀσθενεῖ) Nimirum sperantes fore, ut Jesus adve- niens eum sanaret, ut apparet infra 21. Confer supra IV. 49. Etiam Deo cari suis non carent miseriis.

## 11:4
Ver. 4.

is not unto death) By the word death here, understand a remaining in death. See Rom. VI. 23, 1 Cor. XV. 24 and following. The same is called Hades elsewhere. Something similar in Matt. IX. 24. Christ shows that what was being indicated to him as if he were ignorant was known to him. But for the glory of God) And here you may rightly supply, it happens conveniently, so that from it the glory of God may be illustrated. See what we said above IX. 3. that the Son of God may be glorified) Whose every glory returns to the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

ὐκ ἔσι πρὸς θάνατον) Mortis voce hic intellige permansio- nem in morte. Vide Rom. VI. 23. 1. Corinth. XV. 24. & sequentibus. Idem alibi ᾴδης dicitur. Simile quid Matth IX. 24. Ostendit Christus notum sibi quod tanquam nescienti indicabatur. Ἀλλ’ ὑπὲρ τῆς δόξης τῦ Θεῦ) Et hic recte subaudias, commo- de evenit, ut inde illustretur Dei gloria. Vide quæ diximus supra IX. 3. ἱνα δοξασθῇ ὁ ὑὸς τῦ Θεῦ) Cujus omnis gloria ad Patrem redit.

## 11:5
Ver. 5.

Now Jesus loved) He loved those by whom he was accustomed to be received with hospitality: as once Elijah 1 Kings XVII. 9, Elisha 2 Kings IV. 8; thus the kindness which is shown to the Saints does not perish. Matt. X. 41. Nonnus: he loved the hospitable women with Jesus. For the mystical sense, see Prov. VIII. 17.

Vers. 5.

Ἠγάπα δὲ ὁ Ἰησῦς) Amabat eos à quibus hospitio excipi solebat: ut olim Elias 1. Reg. XVII. 9. Elisæus 2. Reg. IV. 8. ita non perit beneficium quod Sanctis præstatur. Matth. X. 41. Nonnus φιλαξείνυς δὲ γυναῖκας σὺν Ιησῦς ἠγάπαζε. Mysti- cum sensum. Vide Prov. VIII. 17.

## 11:6
Ver. 6.

Then indeed he remained in the place where he was for two days) There is a μὲν here without a δὲ as in Acts XIX. 4. He stayed, however, for two days, although loving Lazarus, so that there could be less doubt about his death. Therefore it is noted soon after that he had been four days dead.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Τότε μὲν ἔμεινεν ἐν ὧ ἦν τόπῳ δύο ἡμέρας) Est hic μὲν sine δὲ ut Act. XIX. 4. Substitit autem per duos dies quanquam amans Lazari, ut de morte minus dubitari posset. Ideo mox no- tatur eum fuisse τεταρταῖον.

## 11:7
Verse 7.

into Judea again) Further inward from the Jordan towards the city.
