Vers. 7.

εἰς τὴν Ιυδαίαν πάλιν) Introrsum longius à Jordane ver- sus urbem.

## 11:8
Verse 8.

Now they were seeking) It is not long ago: the Latins now say 'just now'. Thus below XXI. 10. and you are going there again) With ill-advised love they wish to remove him from danger, as Peter did in Matthew XVI. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Νυν ἐζήτυν) Non diu est: jam modo dicunt Latini. Sic infra XXI. 10. καὶ πάλιν ὑπάγεις ἐκεῖ) Inconsulto amore volunt eum a periculo removere, ut Petrus Matth. XVI. 22.

## 11:9
Verse 9.

Are there not twelve hours of the day) That is, the last hour belongs to the day no less than the first. And so a journey is usually made during it as well: just as he had said above concerning work in IX. 4. Compare Luke XIII. 32. Hugo understands it thus, that just as the hours of the day change, so the counsels and wills of mortals can change into hours, and therefore there is nothing to be feared. Lyranus notes that there was a proverb among the Hebrews, such as is now common among many, when they wish to signify that what could not be done in the past or present can be done at another time. This is Theophylact's explanation, that the days of his life are certain and defined, which no one can diminish any more than the twelve hours of the day, which are certain and established. Rupertus says almost the same:

that no one will bring it about that the sun sets before the twelfth hour: that Christ is the sun, but it will not happen that he dies before his hour. To this also returns the opinion of Arias Montanus, that Christ warns by this similitude; that the task of his office and ministry was given to him not by chance but by divine counsel, and that he has his own time divinely prescribed for fulfilling all the parts of his actions; and that, functioning and running in this light, he cannot be hindered and disturbed by certain stumbling blocks offered by adversaries, or demons, or men, since these things, by the benefit and virtue of the light which he used, can be foreseen, avoided, declined, and even removed and overcome. Grotius loves to be singular. he who stumbles) He walks safely. He sees where he is going, below XII. 35. See what is said there. because he sees the light of this world) He is illuminated by the light of the sun, the apodosis is not added but is easy to understand from those words 'the light of this world'. How much more safely, therefore, do I walk who have a supercelestial and divine light shining before me, the knowledge of the Father's purpose? Verse 10. because the light is not in him) In his eyes. For vision occurs by the reception of light and images. The allegorical sense, which is injected incidentally and by occasion, is that those who do not look to the will of God fall into sins. Verse 11. He has fallen asleep) We have spoken about this locution by euphemism at Matthew IX. 24. Among the Syrians it is 'dmk', which is used for dying, not only in Isaiah XIV. 8. as has been noted before, but also 2 Samuel VII. 12. In both places the Greeks render it by 'koimasthai'. that I may awaken him) The modesty of Christ shines forth in this, that when he had said he was sleeping, he added that he would awaken him; soon, when he says he is dead, he adds nothing of the sort. 'ur' is translated 'exupnizein' in Job XIV. 12, although in another sense: but if for the Hebrews 'to sleep' was to die, Christ did not depart from common speech when he said 'exupniso' instead of 'to bring back from death to life', which was just as easy for him as it was for others to wake a sleeper. Verse 12. if he has fallen asleep he will be saved) It appears from the book of the Mishnah that this was in the mouth of the people, that sleep in a sick person is a sign of health: because it is shown by it that the disease has remitted. The disciples try in every way to call the Lord away from that journey. Therefore they use all arguments. If he is sleeping, why is it that he should be awakened? ἵνα πιστεύσητε) This is a παρέλκυσις (pleonasm): for what follows coheres with what went before. That you may believe, that is, that you may believe the more, that you may believe the more firmly that I am the giver of life. Thus to believe is used above in II. 11. and elsewhere. ὅτι οὐκ ἤμην ἐκεῖ) Namely, as Nonnus explains, ὅτε νόσφιν ὁμιλέον γόνον κόσμῳ. He tacitly signifies that, had he been on the spot, he could scarcely have honestly refused his aid, which was available to all, to keep a friend in life or to recall him immediately from death: either of which would have diminished either the deed itself or the credibility of the deed. Now, with him buried for four days, there was no room for evasion. Thus he shows his wisdom now, and is about to demonstrate his power later. Ἄγωμεν πρὸς αὐτόν) In this place he preferred to hint at what he was about to do rather than express it, for the reason we have stated. Vers. 16. Θωμᾶς ὁ λεγόμενος Δίδυμος) That is, he who, living among the Greeks, was called by the word Δίδυμος, which has the same meaning. For some of the Jews among the Greeks took a name of allusive sound, but others of equal meaning. And so the Syrian, who could change nothing, placed the same name here twice. that we may die with him) With Christ or with Lazarus? I prefer the latter, because 'autou' concerning Lazarus had preceded, to which Thomas looks back. John had named Thomas for this reason, because he was about to show below his hesitation in believing, of which he now gave an indication: for it is just as if he says: Let us go indeed, that we may follow Lazarus who is now dead. For what else should we hope? He remembered the danger in which the Lord had recently been in Jerusalem, from where Bethany was a short distance, which for this very reason is expressed soon.

But the former is to be preferred here. Because they preferred to follow Christ in death than Lazarus, and they wanted to die with him, with whom Thomas wanted to set out: therefore the name of Christ, which precedes closer to the 'pros to opisapomenon', is looked back upon.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Οὐχὶ δώδεκα ὧραι εἰσὶ τῆς ἡμέρας) Id est, ultima hora non minus quam prima ad diem pertinet. Itaque ea quoque solet iter fieri: sicut supra de opere dixerat IX. 4. Confer Luc. XIII. 32. Hugo ita intelligit, quod quemadmodum horæ diei mutantur, sic in horas mortalium consilia & vo- luntates mutari posse, ideoque non esse timendum. Lyranus notat apud Ebræos proverbium fuisse, qua- le nunc vulgo apud complures, cum significare volunt, posse alio fieri tempore, quod non potuit præterito aut præsenti. Theophylacti hæc est explicatio, certos definitosque esse vitæ suæ dies, quos non magis mi- nuere quisquam possit, quam horas diei duodecim, quæ certæ sin ac constitutæ. Ita fere etiam Rupertus:

neminem effecturum esse, ut Sol ante horam occum- bat duodecimam: Christum Solem esse, id autem non futurum, ut ante horam suam moriatur. Quo redit quoque Ariae Montani sententia, Christum hac similitudine monere; muneris ac ministerii sui pensum non casu sed consilio divino sibi esse datum, & se suum habere tempus divinitus praescriptum ad sua- rum actionum partes omnes explendas; atque hac luce fungentem & currentem non posse impediri ac perturbari quibusdam offendiculis per adver- sarios, vel daemones, vel homines oblatis, quippe quae lucis, qua uteretur beneficio & virtute praevi- deri, caveri, declinari, atque etiam removeri, su- perarique possint. Grotius singularis esse amat. ὁ προσκόπτω) Tuto ambulat. Videt qua eundem sit, in- fra XII. 35. Vide quae ibi dicta. ὅτι τὸ φῶς τῦ κόσμυ τύτυ βλέπει) Illustratur a Solis lumi- ne, ἀνταπόδοσις non apponitur sed facilis intellectu est ex illis verbis Lucem hujus mundi. Quanto ergo magis tuto ambulo qui praelucentem mihi habeo lucem supracoele- stem ac divinam, cognitionem paterni propositi? Vers. 10. ὅτι τὸ φῶς ὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῷ) In oculis ejus Rece- ptione enim lucis & specierum fit visio. Sensus allegoricus qui obiter & per occasionem injicitur, est, eos qui volunta- tem Dei non respiciunt in peccata labi. Vers. 11. Κεκοίμηται) De hac locutione κατ’ εὐφημισμὸν diximus ad Matth. IX, 24. Apud Syrum est דמך quod pro mori usurpatur, non tantum apud Esaiam XIV, 8. ut anno- tatum est antehac, sed & 2. Sam. VII. 12. Utrobique Graeci reddunt per κοιμᾶσϑαι. ἵνα ἐξυπνίσω αὐτὸν) Modestia Christi in hoc elucet quod cum eum dixisset domire addidit se. eum experrecturum, mox cum mortuum dicit nihil adjicit tale. עור vertitur ἐξυπνίζειν Job. XIV. 12. quanquam alio sensu: sed si Hebraeis ὑπνῶσαι erat mori, nihil a consueto sermone abiit Christus cum dixit ἐξυπνίσω pro a morte ad vitam reducere, quod ipsi aeque erat facile atque alii excitare dormientem. Vers. 12. εἰ πεκοίμηται σωϑήσεται) Ex libro Misnajoth ap- paret fuisse hoc in ore populi, somnum in aegrotante signum esse ad salutem: quia eo ostenditur remississe morbum. Discipuli omni modo quaerunt Dominum ab isto itinere a- vocare. Ideo omnibus utuntur argumentis. Si dormit, quid est quod excitetur? Vers. 13. περὶ τῆς κοιμήσεως τῦ ὕπνε) Stupore quodam & quia potentiam Jesu, utcunque magna ejus effecta viderant, non satis animo comprehendebant. Vers. 14. παῥῥησίᾳ) Id est sermone apertissimo & minime ambigui sensus: ut supra X. 24. infra XVI. 29. Syrus פשיקאית aperte, explicate. Vers. 15. ἵνα πιστεύσητε) Est παρέλκυσις: nam quae se- quuntur cohaerent cum prioribus. Ut credatis, id est quo magis, quo firmius credatis me esse vitae datorem. Sic crede- re usurpatur supra II. 11. & alibi. ὅτι ὐκ ἤμην ἐκεῖ) Nempe ut Nonnus explicat, ὅτε νόσφιν ὁμιλέο γόνον κόσμῳ. Tacite significat se, si in loco fuisset, vix honeste potuisse negare opem suam cunctis obviam, ad amicum aut in vita retinendum, aut statim a morte revo- candum: quorum utrumvis imminuturum fuerat aut rem ipsam aut rei fidem. Nunc in quatuor dies sepulto, nulla e- rat tergiversatio. Ita & nunc sapientiam ostendit suam & post potentiam demonstraturus. Ἄγωμεν πρὸς αὐτόν) Hoc loco quid facturus erat maluit innuere quam exprimere, ob eam quam diximus causam. Vers. 16. Θωμᾶς ὁ λεγόμενος Δίδυμος) Id est qui inter Graecos agens ejusdem significationis vocabulo Δίδυμος vo- cabatur. Nam Judaeorum alii apud Graecos nomen sume- bant alludentis soni, alii vero paris significatus. Itaque Syrus qui nihil mutare potuit bis hic idem posuit nomen. ἵνα ἀποϑάνωμεν μετ’ αὐτῷ) Cum Christo an cum Lazaro? Posterius malo, quia αὐτῷ de Lazaro praecesserat, quo respi- cit Thomas. Thomam ideo nominaverat Johannes, quod infra ostensurus esset ejus in credendo traditatem, cujus jam nunc indicium dedit: perinde enim est quasi dicat: Eamus sane, ut Lazarum jam mortuum sequamur. Quid enim aliud speremus? meminerat periculi in quo nuper fuerat Dominus Hierosolymis, unde Bethania modicum di- stabat, quod hac ipsa de causa mox exprimitur.

At prius hic praeferendum. Quia Christum ma- lebant in morte sequi, quam Lazarum, & cum illo volebant mori, quo cum proficisci volebat Tho- mas: Christi nomen ergo quod πρὸς τὸ ὀπισαπό- μενον propius antecedit, respicitur.

Ver. 19.

ἐκ τῶν Ἰουδαίων] Thus by way of eminence the Jerusalemites are called. to those about Martha and Mary] From a sufficiently well-known Grecism, the Syriac and Latin translators understood it as if it were said to Martha and Mary. It may be doubted, however, whether both they and at the same time their whole family are signified, as in Acts 13:13, those about Paul, Paul and those who were with him. that they might comfort them] Which duty was accustomed to be extended over seven days. Mention of this custom is frequent in sacred history, and in Josephus, and in the Talmudic books.

Vers. 19.

ἐκ τῶν Ἰουδαίων] Sic κατ' ἐξοχὴν vocantur Hierosolymitæ. πρὸς τὰς περὶ τὴν Μάρθαν καὶ Μαρίαν] Ex Græcismo satis noto Syrus & Latinus acceperunt, quasi diceretur ad Mar- tham & Mariam. Dubitari tamen potest, annon & ipsæ & simul tota ipsarum familia significetur, ut Act. XIII. 13. οἱ περὶ τὸν Παῦλον, Paulus & qui ei aderant. ἵνα παραμυθήσωνται αὐτάς] Quod officium per septem dies extendi solebat. Sæpe ejus moris mentio in sacra hi- storia & apud Josephum, & in Thalmudicis libris.

Ver. 20.

ὡς ἤκουσεν ὅτι ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἔρχεται] Caring for the affairs of the family, she was running here and there. And so she received the rumor sooner than Mary, who was receiving visitors in the inner part of the house. See Luke 10:41.

Vers. 20.

Ver. 21.

εἶπε δὲ] Faith indeed, but weak, as one that attributes nothing to Him who is present. Thus above c. 5:49.

Vers. 21.

## 11:22
Ver. 22.

ὅσα ἂν αἰτήσῃ Θεὸν] And here weakness appears. She thinks that He is in favor with God, but not that the fullness of divine power is in Him. He will give you] He will grant to your prayers. She does not dare to say He will raise the dead: because of the magnitude of the request.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

ὅσα ἂν αἰτήσῃ Θεὸν] Et hic infirmitas apparet. Putat il- lum gratiosum esse apud Deum, non autem in illo pleni- tudinem esse divinæ potestatis. Δώσει σοι] Concedet tuis precibus. Non audet dicere mortuum resuscitabit: ob voti magnitudinem.

## 11:23
Verse 23.

Ἀναστήσεται ὁ ἀδελφός σου] Modestly, as is his custom, for he proclaims nothing about himself, unless necessity extorts it.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

Ἀναστήσεται ὁ ἀδελφός σου] Modeste, ut solet, nam de se ni- hil prædicat, nisi necessitate extorquente.

## 11:24
Verse 24.

ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ] The Syrian calls the resurrection a consolation, by a received expression; but concerning this general resurrection, Martha had indeed learned something from the Pharisees, but it was confused, obscure, and not supported by certain testimonies: however, from the discourses of Christ held before this, she had learned something more certain.

The error of Grotius, often noted, recurs, that there was no faith in the resurrection among the Jews before Christ, and that no testimonies existed upon which faith could rely.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ] Syrus ἀνάστασιν vocat παράκλησιν locutione recepta; de hac autem generali resur- rectione Martha aliquid quidem à Pharisæis didicerat, sed confusum, obscurum, neque certis nixum testimoniis: Ex Christi autem habitis antehac sermonibus certius aliquid cogmoverat.

Recurrit error Grotius sæpe notatus, quod fi- des resurrectionis apud Judæos nulla ante Christum fuerit, nulla etiam testimonia de ea extiterint, qui- bus inniti fides potuerit.

## 11:25
Verse 25.

ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις] There is no reason for you to hesitate. I am the author of the resurrection: wherefore I can also represent it. Thus the Hebrews are accustomed to give the name of the effect to the causes, as above in chapter 1, verse 4. In a similar manner Christ is called righteousness, sanctification, redemption, 1 Cor. 1:30. Here that thin opinion of Martha concerning Jesus is refuted.

ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ κἂν ἀποθάνῃ ζήσεται] First he says that those who trust in him will not remain in death: in the following member he adds that they, after they have lived again, will never die. All these things are to be understood concerning the whole person.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις] Non est quod hæsites. Ego auctor sum resurrectionis: quare & repræsentare eam possum. Sic solent Hebræi causis dare nomen effecti, ut supra c. I. v. 4. simili modo Christus dicitur, justitia, sanctificatio, redem- tio, 1. Cor. I. 30. refellitur hic tenuis illa Marthæ de Jesu opinio.

ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ κἂν ἀποθάνῃ ζήσεται] Primum dicit in se confidentes non mansuros in morte: sequente membro adjicit, eos postquam iterum vixerint, nunquam morituros. Hæc omnia de tota persona sunt intelligenda.

## 11:26
Verse 26.

Καὶ πᾶς ὁ ζῶν καὶ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ] A Hebraism signifying this: and whoever living (namely, this life of the world) trusts in me: but it is treated here of a working and constant trust.

ὐ μὴ ἀποθάνῃ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα] Thus above in chapter 6, verse 49 and following.

πιστεύεις τῦτο] Christ for the most part demands faith before a miracle.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

Καὶ πᾶς ὁ ζῶν καὶ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ] Hebraismus hoc signifi- cans: & quisquis vivens (vitam hanc mundi scilicet) mihi confidet: agitur autem hic de fiducia operante & constan- te.

ὐ μὴ ἀποθάνῃ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα] Sic supra cap. VI. v. 49. & sequentibus.

πιστεύεις τῦτο] Christus plerumque ante miraculum fidem exigit.

## 11:27
Ver. 27.

Ναὶ Κύριε] I believe you, now affirming this, that you are the giver of eternal life: for it also affirms the preceding things.

ἐγὼ πεπίστευκα] She gives the reason, for she had also previously believed that you are the Christ. Wherefore it is just that I should believe you saying all things. See above ch. VI. 25.

ὁ εἰς ὴ κόσμον ἐρχόμενος] that is, who was to appear to the world, who was expected, thus above ch. VI. v. 14. See also Matth. XI. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

Ναὶ Κύριε] Credo tibi hoc jam affirmanti te esse datorem vitæ æternæ: nam & præcedentia affirmat.

ἐγὼ πεπίστευκα] Rationem reddit, nam & antehac cre- didit te esse Christum. Quare æquum est, ut omnia di- centi tibi credam. Vide supra c. VI. 25.

ὁ εἰς ὴ κόσμον ἐρχόμενος] id est, qui debebat mundo ap- parere, qui expectabatur, sic supra cap. VI. v. 14. Vide & Matth. XVII. 11.

## 11:28
Ver. 28.

Ἀπῆλθε] Having been ordered by Christ, as the following things show, to call her sister Mary to that place where Christ had stopped, which was nearer to the sepulchre placed outside the village, as was the custom.

ὁ διδάσκαλος] Thus that family called him.

Φωνεῖ σε] He had ordered Mary alone to be called by Christ, lest he should seem to gather a crowd, which, however, he had foreseen would follow of its own accord.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

Ἀπῆλθε] Jussa à Christo, ut sequentia ostendunt, Ma- riam sororem advocare ad eum locum, ubi Christus sub- stiterat, qui propior erat sepulchro extra vicum, ut mos e- rat, posito.

ὁ διδάσκαλος] Sic eum illa familia appellabat.

Φωνεῖ σε] Mariam solam Christum vocari jusserat, ne turbam colligere videretur, quam tamen sponte secuturam præviderat.

## 11:29
Ver. 29.

Ἐγείρεται ταχὺ] With ready obedience.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

Ἐγείρεται ταχὺ] Promto obsequio.

## 11:31
Ver. 31.

Ἰυδαίοι] The inhabitants of Jerusalem.

παραμυθέμενοι] as above 19.

Λέγοντες] thinking, as the Syrian rightly explains here. Hence an interpretation crept into certain Greek contexts. δέξηται. εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον, ἵνα κλαύσῃ ἐκεῖ] For a greater kind of lamentation was accustomed to be stirred up there: as if the grief were renewed.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

Ἰυδαίοι] Hierosolymitæ.

παραμυθέμενοι] ut supra 19.

Λέγοντες] cogitantes ut recte hic exponit Syrus. Hinc in quosdam Graecos contextus irrepfit interpretamentum. δέξηται. εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον, ἵνα κλαύσῃ ἐκεῖ] Solebat enim ibi major quadam planctus excitari: velut renovato dolore.

## 11:32
Verf. 32.

ἔπεσεν εἰς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ] as if venerating a Prophet.

Latin:

Verf. 32.

ἔπεσεν εἰς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ] ut Prophetam venerata.

## 11:33
Verf. 33.

ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι] Tears are accustomed to be stirred up by tears, especially among compassionate souls. Good men are easily moved to tears. It is in Homer: weeping with those who weep. It is Romans XII. 15. Euripides: And they shed tears over the pitiable. Menander: It is indeed a very great thing for those who have fallen to see those who share their pain present nearby. Ἐνεβριμήσατο corresponds to the Hebrew זָעַם: thus it is translated in Lamentations II. 6. רָגַז which also אָנַף signifies any more serious movement of the soul, whether it is from anger, or from fear, or as here, from grief. The Arabic تبهل that is, he groaned: πνεῦμα here is the soul. For often also that part in which the affections are comes under this name, Matthew V. 4. Acts XIX. 21. καὶ ἐτάραξεν ἑαυτόν] This is an exposition of the Hithpael form, which does not always signify an action, but often also a passion within us. The Syrian וְאַרְגִּו that is, he moved himself. The Arabic تحرك which is the same, but so that it may differ from the previous member, I think here is understood a change in the countenance which would indicate an affection of the soul.

Latin:

Verf. 33.

ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι] Solent lachrymae lachrymis excitari praesertim apud animos misericordes. Ἀγαθοὶ δὲ ἀριδάκρυες ἄνδρες. Est apud Homerum: κλαῖον μετὰ κλαιόντων. est Romano- rum XII. 15. Euripides: Ἀμυκτίστοι μαδ' ἐπ' οἰκτροῖσιν δάκρυ Στάζουσι. Menander: Μέγιστόν ἐστιν ἆρα τοῖς πεπτωκόσιν τὸ παρόντας ἐγγὺς τοὺς συναλγοῦντας βλέπειν. Ἐνεβριμήσατο respondet Hebraeo זָעַם: sic vertitur Thren. II. 6. רָגַז quod & אָנַף quemlibet animi motum gra- viorem significat, sive ille ex ira est, sive ex metu, sive ut hic, ex dolore. Arabs. تبهل id est gemuit: πνεῦμα hic est ani- mus. Nam saepe & pars illa, in qua sunt affectus venit hoc nomine, Matth. V. 4. Act XIX. 21. καὶ ἐτάραξεν ἑαυτόν] Expositio est formae Hithphaël, quae non actionem semper significat, sed saepe & passionem in- tra nos. Syrus וְאַרְגִּו id est, commovit se. Arabs تحرك quod idem est, sed ut differat a superiore membro, puto hic intelligi mutationem in vultu quae animi affectum indica- ret.

## 11:34
Verf. 34.

ποῦ τεθείκατε αὐτόν] he wanted to be led by them. Therefore he asks.

Latin:

Verf. 34.

ποῦ τεθείκατε αὐτόν] volebat ab ipsis deduci. Ideo inter- rogat.

## 11:35
Verf. 35.

ἐδάκρυσεν Ἰησοῦς] He did not hold back the rising tears any longer, having seen the heavier weeping of the sisters. Nor is this unworthy of Jesus. See Luke XIX. 41. and XXII. 44. which passages were once poorly tampered with by those who wished to fashion for us a Stoic Christ.

Latin:

Verf. 35.

ἐδάκρυσεν Ἰησοῦς] Lachrymas oborientes non ultra tenuit conspecto sororum fletu graviore. Neque hoc indignum Jesu. Vide Luc. XIX. 41. & XXII. 44. quae loca male olim sollicitata ab iis, qui Christum nobis Stoicum effingere vo- luerunt.

## 11:36
Verf. 36.

Ἴδε πῶς ἐφίλει αὐτόν] In this flows the weeping of Jesus, so that the spectators might perceive him to be very kind, so that he might pity a man not unknown to him, and be touched by other human affections.

Latin:

Verf. 36.

Ἴδε πῶς ἐφίλει αὐτόν] In hoc profluit fletus Jesu ut spe- ctatores benignum valde eo sentirent, ut de homine non nescio misereri, aliisque humanis effectibus tangi.

## 11:36
Vers. 36.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

## 11:37
Verf. 37.

οὐκ ἐδύνατο οὗτος] With a doubtful mind. For they thought well of his own affection toward Lazarus, and the illumination of the blind man was a greater thing than a healing. He notes these things the more diligently, so that it might be established by many testimonies that there was no doubt concerning the death of Lazarus.

Latin:

Verf. 37.

οὐκ ἐδύνατο οὗτος] Animo dubio. Nam & de ipsius ani- mo in Lazarum bene existimabant, & caeci illuminatio ma- jus quiddam erat fanatione. Haec eo diligentius annotat, ut plurimis testimoniis constaret non dubitatum de Laza- ri morte.

## 11:37
Τινες δὲ ἐξ ἀυτῶν] Refer this not to the last words, but to that general term 'Jews'. These must have been impious men; a type of person who is not accustomed to repent even when the resurrection of the dead is witnessed, Luke XVI. 31. For they invent everything, even the most absurd things, rather than lose their own advantages or the favor of men (which it is apparent these men were hunting for).

πρὸς τὺς Φαρισαίυς] The leaders of that sect who were in the Sanhedrin, as the following teaches.

Latin:

Τινες δὲ ἐξ ἀυτῶν] Refer non ad postremas voces, sed ad illud generale Ἰυδαίων. Impios hos fuisse necesse est; quod genus hominum ne conspecta quidem mortuorum refurrectione resipiscere solet, Luc. XVI. 31. Omnia enim, potius etiam absurdissima comminiscuntur, quam sua commoda aut hominum gratiam (quam istos venatos ap- paret) amittant.

πρὸς τὺς Φαρισαίυς] Praecipuos ejus sectae qui in Synedrio erant, ut docent sequentia.

## 11:38
Verf. 38.

πάλιν ἐμβριμώμενος ἐν ἑαυτῷ] With his countenance again testifying to his grief: for what he said more explicitly before, he says more briefly here; grief is accustomed, as we have said, to grow raw again at the sight of the tomb. Σπήλαιον] See what [is said] at Matt. XXVII. 60. Λίθος ἐπέκειτο ἐπ' αὐτῷ] Because the mouth of this cave was higher on one side and lower on the other, in a sloping cavern.

Latin:

Verf. 38.

πάλιν ἐμβριμώμενος ἐν ἑαυτῷ] Vultu iterum dolorem te- stante: nam quod ante explicatius dixit, hic brevius; folet, ut diximus, aspectu sepulchri dolor secrudescere. Σπήλαιον] Vide quae ad Matth. XXVII. 60. Λίθος ἐπέκειτο ἐπ' αὐτῷ] Quia os hujus speluncae parte una sublimius, altera depressius erat, declivi specu.

## 11:39
Verf. 39.

Ἄρατε τὸν λίθον] He was saying this to the servants accompanying Martha and Mary: for it was of some labor, Mark XVI. 3. Κύριε, ἤδη ὄζει] Not holding back hope because of the magnitude of the thing hoped for, as if humanly, she calls the Lord away from the entrance of the cave so that he might not be offended by the unpleasant odor of one already decaying. τεταρταῖος γάρ ἐστι] Thus Aristophanes in the Birds called a boy born five days ago πεμταῖος. But Plutarch, dealing likewise with a dead man, said τριταῖον, in the book on the delay of Divine vengeance: as also Philostratus in the life of Apollonius lib. III, c. XII. Plato likewise concerning a dead man δωδεκαταῖον.

Latin:

Verf. 39.

Ἄρατε τὸν λίθον] Dicebat hoc ministris Martham & Ma- riam comitantibus: erat enim nonnullius laboris, Marc. XVI. 3. Κύριε, ἤδη ὄζει] Spem prae rei speratae magnitudine non te- tinens, quasi humane, avocat Dominum ab introitu spe- luncae ne ingrato jam putrescentis odore offenderetur. τεταρταῖος γάρ ἐστι] Sic Aristophanes Avibus πεμταῖος di- xit puerum natum dies quinque. At Plutarchus de mortuo itidem agens τριταῖον dixit, libro de sera Numinis vindicta: ut & Philostratus vita Apollonii lib. III, c. XII. Plato iti- dem de mortuo δωδεκαταῖον.

## 11:40
Verf. 40.

οὐκ εἶπόν σοι] Not in so many words, but in sense, when he had said that her brother would rise again and that he himself was the Lord of the resurrection to be given, and had asked if she believed this. ἐὰν πιστεύσῃς] Christ required this faith in such benefits: so that we might learn that spiritual benefits are not conferred except upon those trusting in him. τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Θεοῦ] Modestly he did not say his own, but God's, whose majesty is never more seen than in works that are admirable and surpassing nature.

Latin:

Verf. 40.

οὐκ εἶπόν σοι] Non totidem verbis, sed sensu, cum dixe- rat resurrecturum fratrem & se esse resurrectionis dandae Dominum, & rogasset an hoc crederet. ἐὰν πιστεύσῃς] Fidem hanc in talibus beneficiis requirebat Christus: ut disceremus spiritualia beneficia non nisi in i- psum confidentibus conferri. τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Θεοῦ] Modeste non suam dixit, sed Dei, cu- jus majestas nunquam magis, quam in admirandis & supe- rantibus naturam operibus conspicitur.

## 11:41
Verf. 41.

ἦραν οὖν τὸν λίθον] The servants, as we have said. οὗ ἦν ὁ τεθνηκὼς κείμενος] The Latin does not have this, but neither does the Syriac, except that by adding the article it refers itself to that which had been said above. But most Greek copies and the Arabic have it, wherefore I think it should be retained. It departs, therefore, and deservedly so, from the Latin text, (which the Roman Pontiff with the Council of Trent ordered it to be held as authentic) however much the Syriac version may agree with it, or even certain Greek copies. If Grotius had observed this in other places, he would not have relegated the authentic text so rashly nor so frequently. ἦρε τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἄνω) See what we said at Luke XVIII. 13. so also Matthew XIV. 19. Εὐχαριστῶ σοι) For every good thing obtained, תּוֹדָה is owed, that is, thanksgiving, in whatever way it may have come to us, since God is the first author of all things, James I. 17. ὅτι ἤκουσάς μου) God is said to hear someone even when not asked, when He does him a kindness, Ps. IX. 17. Isa. LXV. 24. Christ therefore gives thanks for the power received from God to perform any miracles whatsoever.

Latin:

Verf. 41.

ἦραν οὖν τὸν λίθον] Ministri ut diximus. οὗ ἦν ὁ τεθνηκὼς κείμενος] Latinus hoc non habet, sed nec Syrus, nisi quod arriculo addito refert se ad id quod su- pra dictum erat. At habent pleraque exemplaria Graeca & Arabs, quare retinendum puto. Discedit ergo, idque merito a Latino textu, (quem Pontifex Romanus cum Concil. Trident. pro authentico haberi jussit) utut versio Syriaca ei- dem consonet, imo etiam exemplaria quædam Græca. Id aliis locis si observasset Grotius, non tam temere nec tam frequenter textum authenti- cum posthabuisset. ἦρε τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἄνω) Vide quæ diximus Luc. XVIII *. 13. sic & Matth. XIV. 19. Εὐχαριστῶ σοι) Pro omni bono adepto debetur תּוֹדָה id est, gratiarum actio, quocunque modo id nobis obtige- rit, quando omnium primus auctor est Deus, Jac. I. 17. ὅτι ἤκουσάς μου) Audire aliquem Deus dicitur etiam non rogatus cum ei benefacit, Ps. IX. 17. Esa. LXV. 24. Agit ergo gratias Christus pro accepta divina miraculorum quo- rumvis efficiendorum potestate.

## 11:42
Vers. 42.

ᾔδειν ὅτι πάντοτέ με ἀκούεις] I do not do this because this is a new benefit, as the common people think. Above 22. but because You are always with me. Διὰ τὸν ὄχλον τὸν περιεστῶτα] I do this for this reason, lest they think that I either ascribe the origin of this power to myself, or that I use the Devil as an author, or that I worship and point to anyone other than You, O God. You, I say, whom this people also professes to worship. ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας] So that from this they may gather that I was sent by You, because they see that all things are referred by me to Your praise, that I claim nothing for myself, and that the power of the Devil and of death is destroyed through me.

Latin:

Vers. 42.

ᾔδειν ὅτι πάντοτέ με ἀκούεις] Non hoc ideo facio quod no- vum hoc sit beneficium, ut vulgus putat. Supra 22. sed quia semper mihi ades. Διὰ τὸν ὄχλον τὸν περιεστῶτα] Ideo hoc facio ne putent aut me mihi originem hujus potestatis ascribere, aut Diabo- lo uti autore aliumve quam Te Deum colere ac monstra- re. Te inquam, quem & populus hic colere se profite- tur. ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας] Ut inde me à Te missum colligant, quod videant omnia à me ad tuam laudem referri, nihil me mihi vindicare, Diaboli autem & mortis potestatem per me destrui.

## 11:43
Vers. 43.

Φωνῇ μεγάλῃ ἐκραύγασε] Not with a magical whisper, but openly exerting power; and this is a certain image of the general resurrection, Matthew XXIV. 31. 1 Thess. IV. 16. Λάζαρε δεῦρο ἔξω] He did not say only, arise, as to the girl, Mark V. 41. but what is more, come out of the tomb. Such voices, however, do not act, but signify the acting force, as we said at Mark c. I. 25. Compare Rom. IV. 17.

Why should such voices not act or work, since they are the voices of the almighty Son of God of the same virtue as that which was in the first creation, Let there be light and the like? Whence the Apostle in the cited passage teaches that those things which are not are called by God so that they may be, because by His divine voice He brings it about that they exist.

Latin:

Vers. 43.

Φωνῇ μεγάλῃ ἐκραύγασε] Non magico susurro, sed pa- lam exserens potestatem; & est hic imago quædam gene- ralis resuscitationis Matth. XXIV. 31. 1. Thess. IV. 16. Λάζαρε δεῦρο ἔξω] Non dixit tantum, surge ut ad puel- lam Marc. V. 41. sed quod amplius est, exi e monumento. Tales autem voces non agunt, sed vim agentem significant ut diximus ad Marc. c. I. 25. Confer Rom. IV. 17.

Quidni agerent vel operarentur tales voces, quum voces sint omnipotentis Dei Filii ejusdem virtutis, qualis illa erat, cujus vox in prima crea- tione, Fiat lux & similes? Unde Apostolus loco citato docet à Deo vocari ea quæ non sunt, ut sint, quod voce sua divina id efficiat, ut existant.

## 11:44
Vers. 44.

ἐξῆλθεν] Not only with life, but also with health recovered. Δεδιδεμένος τοὺς πόδας καὶ τὰς χεῖρας κειρίαις] Besides the napkin placed on his head, the rest of the whole body was covered with perpetual wrappings, which both Egyptian icons show and Nonnus in this place: . . . . . καὶ ἐκ ποδῶν ἄχρι καρῆνου Σφιγγόμενοι πλεκτῇσιν ὅλον δέμας εἶχε κειρίαις. Therefore we read below XIX. 4. They took therefore the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths. Wherefore, what is said here about the bound hands and feet, take it in such a way as that of Pliny about infants: They lie bound hand and foot. Augustine: The wrappings with which the whole body of Christ was bound. Nor does Basil seem to have thought otherwise, when he treats this history. Therefore the dead man is said to be συνέσφιξαν, Acts V. v. 6. i.e., to be wrapped, namely in bandages, which Latin word the Syrian uses here to interpret the Greek κειρίαις, just as below the Hebrew word is מרבדים. σουδαρίῳ περιεδέδετο] See also below XX, 7. Nonnus: σουδαρίῳ τόπερ εἶπε Σύρων στόμα. As also below: Σουδάριον τόπερ εἶπε Σύρων ἐπιθήμονα ἄνδη. Rightly. For this word had passed into the Syriac and Jewish idiom, as we noted at Luke XIX, 20. Nor is it a wonder, since the Greeks also had received it from the Latins, as Pollux teaches us. Ruth III. 15. המטפחת a veil, as David Kimchi explains in that place, the Chaldean translates סודרא as in Exod. XXXIV. 33. κάλυμμα which Moses placed on his face, in Hebrew מסוה. Other Rabbis also say that a banner consists of a pole or column and a napkin. In the Talmudic title concerning burial, it is reported that a napkin costing no more than a denarius was added for the wiser men: Maimonides also mentions the napkin with which the head of the dead was wrapped. Servius in the eleventh book on the dead Pallas: He put one of the two garments on the youth, the other covered his head. Add that of Homer concerning Patroclus: They placed him on a bed and covered him with a fine linen cloth from head to foot, and over it a white robe. In the second book of the Odyssey, Penelope is said to have spoken thus: . . . . . . until I finish the shroud (lest my threads perish in vain)

Λαέρτῃ ἥρωϊ ταφήϊον εἶς, ὅτε κέν μιν Μοῖρ’ ὀλοὴ καθέλῃσι τανηλεγέος θανάτοιος Μή τίς μοι κατὰ δῆμον Ἀχαιϊάδων νεμεσήσῃ Αἴκεν ἄτερ σπείρυ κεῖται. To that passage Didymus, σπεῖρον ὕφασμα δυνάμενον σπείρειν καὶ σπαργοῦν τὸ ἀυτῷ περιτιθέμενον.

Λύσατε ἀυτὸν] Untie the bandages with which he had crawled out wrapped.

Ἄφετε ὑπάγειν ] Let him go home. Christ did not wish to go with him, lest he seem to be leading him as if in a triumph.

Latin:

Vers. 44.

ἐξῆλθεν] Non vita tantum, sed & valetudine recuperata. Δεδιδεμένος τοὺς πόδας καὶ τὰς χεῖρας κειρίαις] Præter suda- rium capiti impositum cæterum corpus totum perpetuis involucris tegebatur, quod & icones Ægyptiacæ monstrant & Nonnus hoc loco: . . . . . καὶ ἐκ ποδῶν ἄχρι καρῆνου Σφιγγόμενοι πλεκτῇσιν ὅλον δέμας εἶχε κειρίαις. Ideo infra legimus XIX. 4. Ἔλαβον οὖν τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ ἔδησαν αὐτὸ ἐν ὀθονίοις. Quare quod hic dicitur de vinctis manibus pedibusque ita accipe, ut illud Plinii de infantibus: Iacent pedibus manibusque devinctis. Augustinus: Irsitæ quibus totum corpus Christi alligatum est. Nec aliter sensisse videtur Basilius, ubi hanc historiam tractat. Ideo συνέσφι- ξαν dicitur mortuus, Act. V. v. 6. i. e. involvi, fasciis scili- cet quam vocem Latinam Syrus hic usurpat ut Græcum κει- ρίας interpretetur, ut & infra Hebræa vox est מרבדים. σουδαρίῳ περιεδέδετο] Vide & infra XX, 7. Nonnus: σουδαρίῳ τόπερ εἶπε Σύρων στόμα. Ut & infra: Σουδάριον τόπερ εἶπε Σύρων ἐπιθήμονα ἄνδη. Recte. Nam in Syriacum & Judaicum idioma hæc vox transierat, ut notavimus Luc. XIX, 20. Nec mirum cum & Græci eam à Latinis accepissent, ut docet nos Pollux. Ruth. III. 15. המטפחת flammeum ut David Kimchi eo loco exponit, Chaldæus vertit סודרא ut Exod. XXXIV. 33. κάλυμμα quod vultui suo imposuit Moses מסוה Hebraice. Alii Rabbini etiam vexillum constare dicunt ex pertica si- ve columna & sudario. In Talmudico titulo de sepultura fertur sapientioribus additum sudarium non amplius dena- rio constans: meminit sudarii quo caput mortui obvolve- batur & Maimonides. Servius in XI. de Pallante mortuo: Unam de duabus vestibus induit juveni, altera caput e- jas velavit. Adde illud Homeri de Patroclo: Ἐν λεχέεσσι δὲ θέντες ἑανῷ λιτὶ κάλυψαν Ἐς πόδας ἐκ κεφαλῆς, καθύπερθε δὲ φάρεϊ λευκῷ. In Odysseæ secundo Penelope sic locuta dicitur: . . . . . . εἰσόκε φᾶρος Ἐκτελέσω (μή μοι μεταμώνια νήματ᾽ ὄληται)

Λαέρτῃ ἥρωϊ ταφήϊον εἶς, ὅτε κέν μιν Μοῖρ’ ὀλοὴ καθέλῃσι τανηλεγέος θανάτοιος Μή τίς μοι κατὰ δῆμον Ἀχαιϊάδων νεμεσήσῃ Αἴκεν ἄτερ σπείρυ κεῖται. Ad eum locum Didymus, σπεῖρον ὕφασμα δυνάμενον σπεί- ρειν καὶ σπαργοῦν τὸ ἀυτῷ περιτιθέμενον.

Λύσατε ἀυτὸν] Solvite fascias, quibus involutus prore- pferat.

Ἄφετε ὑπάγειν ] Abeat domum. Noluit Christus cum eo ire ne quasi in triumphum ducere videretur.

## 11:45
Vers. 45.

Ἐπίστευσαν εἰς ἀυτὸν] Drawn both by the magnitude and the certainty of the miracle, they believed not only that he was sent by God, but also that he was the Messiah, as the following will show. See below c. XII. 11. 18.

PART II. The consultation of the chief priests and Pharisees concerning Christ, with the prophetic counsel of Caiaphas.

Latin:

Vers. 45.

Ἐπίστευσαν εἰς ἀυτὸν] Tracti & magnitudine & certitudine miraculi, crediderunt non tantum à Deo missum, sed & Messiam, ut sequentia ostendent. Vide infra c. XII. 11.18,

PARS II. Pontificum & Pharisaeorum de Christo con- sultatio, cum Caiphae consilio vati- cinatorio.

## 11:47
Vers. 47.

οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς] The high priest Caiaphas and his father-in-law Annas, who had previously held the high priesthood, and by whose counsels Caiaphas was almost entirely governed. See Luke III. 2, below XVIII. 13, 24, Acts IV. 6.

καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι] By the impulse of the Pharisees, Annas and Caiaphas had convened the senate by their authority.

τί ποιῦμεν; ] What are we doing? Just as the Latins also speak when they are deliberating.

ὕτω ό ἄνθρωπος] Said contemptuously: as above V. 12.

πολλὰ σημεῖα ποιεῖ] Their minds were so blinded by envy that the very thing which ought to have been an argument for them to believe, served only to incite them to his destruction.

Latin:

Vers. 47.

οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς] Pontifex maximus Caiphas & socer ejus Annas, ante eo functus Pontificatu, & cujus consiliis ser- me regebatur Cajaphas. Vide Luc. III. 2. infra XVIII. 13. 24. Act. IV. 6.

καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι] Pharisaei impulsu, Annas & Cajaphas auctoritate senatum convocarant.

τί ποιῦμεν; ] Quid agimus? quomodo & Latini loquun- tur ubi deliberant.

ὕτω ό ἄνθρωπος] Contemtim dictum: ut supra V. 12.

πολλὰ σημεῖα ποιεῖ] Adeo excaecati erant invidia animi, ut quod argumentum esse debuerat quo ipsi crederent, eo in ipsius perniciem incitarentur.

## 11:48
Vers. 48.

ὁ ἀν ἀφῶμεν ἀυτὸν ὕτω] As if human power could hinder divine.

πάντες πισεύσουσιν εἰς ἀυτὸν] as the Messiah, and consequently as the king of this people.

κὶ ἐλεύσονται οι ῥωμαῖοι κὶ ἄρῦσιν ἡμῶν κὶ τόπον καὶ τὸ ἔθνος] A Hebraism for: the arriving Romans will destroy both the city and the nation. נשא, which is often rendered by αἴρειν, signifies to destroy, Hosea 1:7. Thus αἴρουσι is used in Luke 7, above in chapter 1:29, and elsewhere. τόπος for city, also Acts 6:13, 14; the city destroyed by ruin, the nation by slaughter or dispersion. They say the Romans will be hostile on account of the Messiah: as if Jesus had not openly taught that one must obey rulers of whatever kind, and had not refused the kingdom even when it was offered. But they were expecting a Messiah who was indeed an enemy of the Roman Empire. And in truth, by despising the Messiah, they fell into that which they professed to fear.

Latin:

Vers. 48.

ὁ ἀν ἀφῶμεν ἀυτὸν ὕτω] Quasi humana vis divinam im- pedire possit.

πάντες πισεύσουσιν εἰς ἀυτὸν] ut Messiam ac proinde po- puli hujus regem.

κὶ ἐλεύσονται οι ῥωμαῖοι κὶ ἄρῦσιν ἡμῶν κὶ τόπον καὶ τὸ ἔθνος] Hebraismus pro adventantes Romani delebunt & urbem & gentem. נשא quod saepe per αἴρειν redditur significat delere, Ose. I. 7. Sic αἴρουσι sumitur Luc. VII. supra c. I. 29. &c. alibi.τόπος pro urbe etiam Actor. VI. 13. 14. urbs deletus excidio : Gens internecione aut dispersione. Romanos autem insensos ajunt fore ob Messiam: quasi Jesus non a- perte docuisset obtemperandum qualibuscunque rectori- bus: regnum autem etiam oblatum defugisset. At ipsi Messiam & quidem Romani Imperii hostem expectabant. Et vero Messia comtemto in id inciderunt quod se metuere profitebantur.

## 11:49
Vers. 49.

Ἀρχιερεὺς ὣν τῦ ἐνιαυτῦ ἐκείνε] This is added not because the High Priests were changed annually, but because they were changed frequently: a custom which their own ambition had introduced contrary to the law.

Ὑμεῖς ὐκ οἴδατε ὐδὲν] As if he were saying, you are fools for hesitating in a matter so easy and straightforward.

Latin:

Vers. 49.

Ἀρχιερεὺς ὣν τῦ ἐνιαυτῦ ἐκείνε] Hoc additum non quod in annos, sed quod subinde mutarentur Pontifices: quem morem ipsorum ambitio contra legem invexerat.

Ὑμεῖς ὐκ οἴδατε ὐδὲν] Quasi diceret, stulti estis quod in re tam facili atque expedita haesitatis.

## 11:50
Vers. 50.

ἐδὲ διαλογίζεσθε ὅτι συμφέρει ἡμῖν] A description of the character of that class of men whom they commonly call politicians, who, holding the honest and the just in contempt, look to nothing but utility, and have nothing else on their lips. Utility, I say, which they call public, when in reality it is for the most part merely private.

ἵνα ἗ις ἄνθρωπος ἀποθάνῃ ὑπὲρ τῦ λαῦ] that is, for the salvation of the people. Praxithea in Euripides' Erechtheus: 'For the whole city, one for many, in the laws. How must I destroy this, when it is possible for one to die for all?' Emperor Otho in Xiphilinus: 'For it is much better and more just that one should perish for all, than many for one.' In Virgil: 'One head shall be given for many.' The Muslim teachers dedicated the same sentiment to Selim, as is in Leunclavius's annals. But while this may be praiseworthy in one who voluntarily devotes himself for his country, how can it be excused that an innocent, beneficent man should be oppressed for an imaginary danger, and that by calumny? This is that wisdom of the world. The preposition ὑπὲρ here, as in Gen. IV. 25 & XXX. 2, Exod. VII. 1, Prov. XI. 8, is equivalent to the little word ἀντί, in place of a people otherwise to be destroyed by the Romans, which was Caiaphas's meaning, to which also the particle חֶלֶף in the Syriac version points. In the same sense it must also be understood according to the mind of the Holy Spirit, who prophesied through the mouth of the High Priest, even though Caiaphas did not understand or intend this, which the Holy Spirit did. For Christ died entirely in place of the people, nay, in place of the whole human race, which would otherwise have perished eternally: insofar as He took upon Himself our guilt and punishment, and paid for it; concerning which see in Socinismo profligato, p. 390. Beautifully Ambrose in Ps. CXVIII, serm. 15: 'He spoke indeed with a sinister mind: nevertheless the grace of the Holy Spirit used his mouth to predict the future, even though it did not touch his polluted heart.'

and that the whole nation perish not) καὶ μὴ, that is, lest: as the Hebrews use וְלֹא.

Latin:

Vers. 50.

ἐδὲ διαλογίζεσθε ὅτι συμφέρει ἡμῖν] Descriptio ingenii ejus generis quos vulgo politicos vocant, qui honesto atque justo insuper habito, nihil praeter utilitatem spectant, nec aliud in ore habent. Utilitatem inquam quam publicam vocant, cum reversa plerumque mere privata sit.

ἵνα ἗ις ἄνθρωπος ἀποθάνῃ ὑπὲρ τῦ λαῦ] id est, pro salute populi. Praxitheam Euripidis Erechtheo: Πόλεως δ᾽ ἁπάσης τύτομ’ ἕν’ πολλοῖς δὶ ἔν Νόμοισι. τύτυς πῶς διαφθεῖραι με δεῖ ἐξὸν πρὸ πάντων μίαν ὑπερδῦναι θανεῖν; Otho Imperator apud Xiphilinum πολὺ γάρ πω κὶ κρεῖττον κὶ δικαιότερόν ἐστιν ἵνα ὑπὲρ πάντων, ἢ πολλὺς ὑπὲρ ἑνὸς ἀπολέσθαι, Apud Virgilium: Unum pro cunctis dabitur caput. Eandem sententiam Musulmannici magistri Selimo dicarunt, ut est in Leunclavii annalibus. Sed ut hoc laudabile sit in eo qui sponte se pro patria devovet, illud excusari qui potest ut ob periculum imaginarium homo innocens, beneficus, op- primatur, & quidem per calumniam? Haec est illa mundi sapientia. Præpositio ὑπὲρ hic ut Genes. IV. 25. & XXX. 2. Exod. VII. 1. Prov. XI. 8. æquipollet voculæ ἀντί vi- ce populi alioqui per Romanos destruendi, quæ erat Cajaphæ mens, quo etiam spectat particula חֶלֶף in Syriaca versione. Eodem etiam sensu acci- pienda est ex mente Spiritus S. qui per os Pontificis vaticinatus est, etsi hoc Cajaphas non intelligeret, aut intenderet, quod Spiritus S. Nam Christus omnino mortuus est vice populi, imo vice totius humani generis, alioquin æternum perituri: qua- tenus culpam & pœnam nostram suscepit, & pro ea luit: quo de in Socinismo profligato pag. 390. Pul- chre Ambros. in Ps. CXVIII. serm. 15. Sinistro qui- dem dicebat animo: veruntamen gratia Spiritus S. u- sa est ore illius ad prædicendum futurum, tametsi pol- lutum ejus cor non attigerit.

καὶ μὴ ὅλον τὸ ἔθνος ἀπόληται) καὶ μὴ, id est, ne: ut He- bræis וְלֹא.

## 11:51
Ver. 51. Of himself) Not by chance, not without special divine direction, which appears in the individual words.

Being high priest that year he prophesied) Among Homer, it is said of a certain dream that it was to be despised, unless it had happened to Agamemnon, the leader of leaders. And among the Spartans, only the Ephors were allowed to report dreams. And the Hebrews say that it is a matter of an omen that it should fall from the lips of a prince, even if he is ignorant. Whence the proverb: הוֹיְדָא כְשֶׁנִגְרַת הַיּוֹצֵא מִלִפְנֵי הַשַּׁלִּיט. Reason teaches, of course: if God wished to signify any public business, He would signify it especially to those who preside over the people. Thus, future events were revealed to Pharaoh and to Nebuchadnezzar through a dream. Even to consult Urim & Thummim was the business of the kingdom, or of the highest magistrates among the people of God. But because Caiaphas held the highest dignity among that people, and was as it were the prince of the people, therefore God uses his mouth as an instrument. Our enemies are judges. Deut. XXXII, 31.

that Jesus was about to die for the nation) God was going to permit and ordain His death for the eternal salvation of those among the Jews who had some reverence for God. For through the death of Christ, followed especially by the resurrection, they were made certain of His doctrine, had faith in Him, and converted themselves. See Acts II & following. ἔθνος concerning the Jews, Luke VII. 5, below c. XVIII. 35, Acts X. 22, c. XXIV. 2, 10. Hence Philo calls Abraham τὸν ἐθνοπάτορα. But He is said to have died for the nation because He died for the best part of the nation: for this affection seems to be regarded here, not the occasion alone, as elsewhere.

Latin:

Ver. 51. Ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ) Non casu, non sine speciali directio- ne divina, quæ in singulis vocibus apparet.

Ἀρχιερεὺς ὢν τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ ἐκείνου προεφήτευσεν) Apud Home- rum de somnio quodam dicitur contemnendum fuisse, ni- si evenisset ducum duci Agamemnoni. Et apud Spartanos solis Ephoris licebat somnia referre. Et Hebræi ajunt ominis loco esse quod viro principi etiam ignoranti exciderit. Un- de proverbium הוֹיְדָא כְשֶׁנִגְרַת הַיּוֹצֵא מִלִפְנֵי הַשַּׁלִּיט. Docet scilicet ratio: si quid publici negotii si- gnificari vellet Deus id significaturum maxime iis qui po- pulo præsunt. Sic Pharaoni, sic Nabuchodonosoro ven- tura per somnium patefacta sunt. Etiam Urim & Thumim consulere regnum erat, aut summorum magistratuum in populo Dei. Quia vero Caiphas in eo populo summam ob- tinebat dignitatem, & quasi princeps erat populi, ideo ejus ore tanquam instrumento utitur Deus. Inimici nostri ju- dices. Deut. XXXII, 31.

ὅτι ἔμελλεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀποθνήσκειν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἔθνους) Deus mortem ipsius erat permissurus atque ordinaturus ad salutem æter- nam eorum ex Judæis, quibus aliqua esset Dei reveren- tia. Nam per mortem Christi, secuta maxime resurrectio- ne, certi facti sunt de ejus dogmate, fidem ei habuerunt & se converterunt. Vide Act. II. & seqq. ἔθνος de Judæis Luc. VII. 5. infra c. XVIII. 35. Act. X. 22. c. XXIV. 2. 10. Hinc Abrahamum Philo vocat τὸν ἐθνοπάτορα. Pro gente autem mortuus dicitur, quia pro parte optima gentis est mortuus: nam affectus hic respici videtur, non sola occa- sio, ut alibi.

Ver. 53.

They took counsel) Now clearly and firmly, with every scruple removed, they decided that the matter should not be deferred any longer, but that His death should be hastened by every means. The Evangelist shows that that pretext of public utility seemed so valid to them that it sufficed for decreeing the killing of Christ, for which a color was then sought: thus it appeared to be true what is said: 'It is a grave prejudice which has no judgment.'

PART III.

The solicitation of the Jews, while Jesus was staying in Ephron, and the promulgation of the edict concerning informing on Him.

Verf. 53.

Συνεβουλεύσαντο) Iam plane ac firme, exempto omni scrupulo constituerunt rem non ultra differendam, sed o- mni modo mortem maturandam. Ostendit Evangelista il- lum obtentum publicæ utilitatis tam bellum ipsis visum, ut sufficeret ad decernendam Christi occisionem, cui deinde color quærebatur: ita apparuit verum esse quod dicitur Grave præjudicium est, quod judicium non habet.

Iudæorum, Iesu in Ebron hærente, solicitatio, & edicti de ipso indicando pro- mulgatio.

Ver. 54.

οὐκ ἔτι παῤῥησίᾳ) Openly, plainly, 1 Macc. IV. 18. λάψετε τὰ σκῦλα μετὰ παῤῥησίας.

εἰς τὴν χώραν ἐγγὺς τῆς ἐρήμου) To the eastern part of Judea, not far from Jericho.

εἰς Ἐφραῒμ λεγομένην πόλιν) It is the same as Ε'φραῖμα & Ε'φρὴμ, just as יְרוּשָׁלַם is written ἱεροσόλυμα, and in many other words Patach with Iod is changed into Tzere because of the proximity of pronunciation. This city cannot be Ephron, which is mentioned in the Chronicles and the Maccabean history. For Ephron begins with Ayn: Ephrem in Syriac and Arabic with Aleph: so that this town seems entirely to have been named after the tribe itself: whose remnants, I believe, had betaken themselves there after the slaughter inflicted by Jephthah, Jud. XII. 6.

κἀκεῖ διέτριβε) So that he would not expose himself to hatred before the proper time, and so that his very absence might excite a longing for him among those who were not evil, which the following verses show: and so his subsequent entry into the city was made more majestic by that very expectation.

Latin:

οὐκ ἔτι παῤῥησίᾳ) Aperte, palam, 1. Macc. IV. 18. λάψετε τὰ σκῦλα μετὰ παῤῥησίας.

εἰς τὴν χώραν ἐγγὺς τῆς ἐρήμου) Ad partem Judææ orienta- lem, non procul Hierichunte.

εἰς Ἐφραῒμ λεγομένην πόλιν) Eadem est Ε'φραῖμα & Ε'φρὴμ ut pro יְרוּשָׁלַם scribitur ἱεροσόλυμα & in multis aliis voci- bus Patach cum Iod mutatur in Tzere ob vicinitatem pro- nunciationis. Non potest hæc urbs esse Ephron cujus men- tio in Paralipomenis & Maccabaica historia. Nam Ephron incipit ab Ayn: Ephrem Syro & Arabi per Aleph: ut omni- no videatur hoc oppidum dictum ab ipsa tribu: cujus cre- do reliquiæ illuc se contulerant post cladem ab Jephta illa- tam, Jud. XII. 6.

ἐζήτουν ὖν τὸν Ἰησοῦν) Cupidirate videndi miracula.

οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς κὴ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι) i.e., the Senate, urged on by the Chief Priests and those who were of the Pharisaic faction, with the others adapting themselves to the times.

ἵνα ἐὰν γῷ πῦ ἐςι, μηνύσῃ) Which was accustomed to be done in more atrocious crimes, with curses against those who did not obey. See Sophocles' Oedipus.

Ὅπως πιάσωσιν ἀυτόν) So that they might have him in their power and then decide on the manner of killing him.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

A banquet is celebrated in Bethany, where Jesus is anointed by Mary, and is defended against the murmuring of Judas Iscariot, because she did this for the sake of his burial. But many having gathered there on account of Jesus and also Lazarus, the Pharisees sought to kill the latter. To Jesus, however, as he sets out for Jerusalem, many go to meet him with palms, shouting Hosanna, as he rides upon a donkey according to the prophecy (Zach. IX. v. 9.). Greeks desire to see him, whence Jesus preaches concerning the glorification of the Son of Man, and the fructification of the grain of wheat that has died, and he prays that he might be delivered from that hour and the name of the Father be glorified, having received a response from heaven, concerning which, as different people think different things, he teaches that now the prince of the world will be cast out, and that he, being lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to himself; and the people asking, since Christ remains forever, who that Son of Man is who is to be lifted up from the earth? he commands that they believe in the light, which is still shining for a short time, and he hides himself from them: but they, even though he performed many signs, did not believe in him, so that the prophecy of Isaiah (ch. LIII. & ch. VI. 9.) spoken concerning him might be fulfilled, when Isaiah saw his glory. Some of the leaders, however, even if they believed, did not yet profess him. He testifies that he has come into the world as light, so that he who believes in him might not remain in darkness: but he who does not believe, the word which he has spoken will judge him, because he received from the Father what he does and speaks.

There are five parts: I. The anointing of Jesus at the banquet in Bethany, to v. 11. II. The acclamation made to Jesus, when he was riding an ass and heading to Jerusalem, to v. 19. III. The sermon of Jesus delivered for the sake of the Greeks, to v. 26. IV. The prayer of Jesus, when a voice was heard from heaven, and the information concerning his exaltation and the placing of faith in the true light, while the Jews nevertheless remained in their ἀπιστίᾳ [unbelief], to v. 43. V. The defense of his coming into the world, to v. 50.

PART I. The anointing of Jesus at the banquet in Bethany.

Vers. 1.

Ὁ ὖν Ἰησοῦς [Jesus therefore]) Since others had already gone before and he himself had been expected for some time. It coheres with the previous chapter, 54 and following.

πρὸ ἓξ ἡμερῶν τοῦ πάσχα [six days before the Passover]) This is entirely the same locution that is found in the Greek of Amos 1:1, πρὸ δύο ἐτῶν τοῦ σεισμοῦ [two years before the earthquake], that is, two years before the earthquake, as the Hebrew sense openly holds; thus 2 Cor. 12:2, πρὸ ἐτῶν δεκατεσσάρων [fourteen years ago], that is, fourteen years before this day.

Ludovicus de Dieu notes that the cardinal number is placed for the ordinal, 'before six days of the Passover,' that is, before the sixth day, or before the sixth day from the future Passover had come. Theophylact reports that the Jews on the tenth day of the first month take the sheep to be sacrificed at the Passover, and from that time seek out the things necessary for the feast: and that at the supper six days before, namely on the ninth of the same month, they feasted more broadly and made the beginnings of the festival on that day, and therefore Jesus also dined there in Bethany. Concerning that supper, Arias Montanus says: 'When friends were gathered for the communication of religion and the giving of thanks, of the kind that used to be done according to the ancient custom of the Jews, into which no fewer than three could assemble; and Gentiles or otherwise profane and unclean persons were not admitted into the number of those invited;' and ointments were used by those who had them, and thanks were given to God for the use of all dishes and pleasant or useful things. We read of the entire rite of these suppers in the ancient repetitions in the tractate on blessings, in several chapters.

Ἦλθεν εἰς Βηθανίαν [He came to Bethany]) Before the Sabbath: for he would not have made such a journey on the Sabbath.

ὅπου ἦν Λάζαρος [where Lazarus was]) Where Lazarus lived, and where he had remained, for Jesus had not wished to lead him with himself, to avoid ostentation.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Convivium in Bethania celebratur, ubi à Ma- ria Iesus ungitur, & adversus murmur Iu- dæ Ischariothæ defenditur, quod id fecerit sepulturæ ejus causa. Congregatis autem eo multis ob Iesum atque Lazarum etiam, hunc interficere quærebant Pharisæi. Iesu vero Hierosolymam proficiscenti multi cum palmis obviam euntes Hosianna ac- clamant, equitanti super asina secundum vaticinium (Zach. IX. v. 9.) Græci deside- rant ipsum videre, unde concionatur Ie- sus, de clarificatione Filii hominis, & gra- ni tritici emortui fructificatione, ac preca- tur, ut ex hora illa eripiatur & nomen Pa- tris clarificetur, accepto responso è cælo, de quo diversis diversa censentibus docet, jam principem mundi ejectum iri, seque exalta- tum è terra omnes ad se pertracturum; populoq; quærente, cum Christus æternum maneat, quisnam ille Filius hominis sit è terra exaltandus? jubet, ut in lucem, bre- vi tempore adhuc lucentem, credant, seq́; abscondit ab iis: sed illi, etsi multa ederet signa, non credebant in ipsum, ut imple- retur prophetia Esaiæ (cap. LIII. & c. VI. 9.) de ipso dicta, cum Esaias gloriam ejus videret. Quidam autem primores, etsi crederent, non tamen profitebantur ipsum. Qui se venisse in mundum lucem, testatur, ut qui in se credit, non maneat in tenebris: qui vero non credit, eum verbum, quod locu- tus est judicaturum, quia à Patre accepit, quod agit & loquitur.

Partes sunt quinque: I. Unctio Jesu in convivio Bethaniensi, ad v. 11. II. Acclamatio Jesu facta, cum asinae inequitans Hierosolymam contende- ret, ad v. 19. III. Concio Jesu Graecorum causa ha- bita, ad v. 26. IV. Precatio Jesu, cum voce de coe- lo audita, & informatione, de sui exaltatione, & fide in lucem veram collocanda, manentibus ta- men Judaeis in sua ἀπιστίᾳ, ad v. 43. V. Defens adventus sui in mundum, ad v. 50.

PARS I. Unctio Iesu in convivio Bethaniensi.

Vers. 1.

Ὁ ὖν Ἰησοῦς) Cum alii jam praeiissent & ipse aliquamdiu expectatus esset. Cohaeret cum capite superiori 54. & seqq.

πρὸ ἓξ ἡμερῶν τοῦ πάσχα) omnino eadem est locutio quae reperitur in Graeco Amos I. 1. πρὸ δύο ἐτῶν τοῦ σεισμοῦ, id est, duobus annis ante terraemotum, ut aperte habet sensus Hebraicus, sic 2. Cor. XII. 2. πρὸ ἐτῶν δεκατεσσάρων, id est, annis quatuordecim ante hunc diem.

Ludovicus de Dieu cardinalem notat pro ordina- li positum, ante sex dies Paschatis, id est, ante sextum diem, vel antequam sextus à futuro Pascha- te dies venisset. Theophylactus refert, quod Judaei decimo mensis primi die accipiant ovem immo- landam in Paschate, & ex eo tempore conquirant necessaria ad festum: quodque in coena ante sex dies nona videlicet mensis ejusdem latius fuerint epulati, & initia festivitatis illo die fecerint, ideo & Jesum una coenatum esse in Bethania. De illa coena Arias Montanus. Congregatis, inquit, a- micis ad communicationem religionis, & gratiarum actionem, cujusmodi fieri solebant ex more antiquo Judaeorum, in quam convenire non poterant paucio- res quam tres; & non admittebantur gentiles aut a- lias profani & immundi in numerum invitatorum; & adhibeantur unguenta ab iis qui habebant, ac de omni ferculorum & jucundarum aut utilium rerum usu gratia agebantur Deo. Harum coenarum ritum omnem legimus in repetitionibus antiquis tract. de be- nedictionibus plurib. capp.

Ἦλθεν εἰς Βηθανίαν) Prosabbato: neque enim Sabbato tantum itineris fecisset.

ὅπου ἦν Λάζαρος) Ubi habitabat Lazarus, & ubi manserat, neque enim Iesus eum secum ducere voluerat, vitandae o- stentationis.

## 12:2
Vers. 2.

Ἐποίησαν ὖν αὐτῷ δεῖπνον ἐκεῖ [They made therefore for him a supper there]) Personal for impersonal. A supper was prepared for him, namely at the house of Simon, a kinsman of Lazarus. The Jews were accustomed to entertain themselves and their friends with more solemn suppers before the days of the Passover, especially on the ninth, as Theophylact notes, which then fell on the day of the Sun [Sunday]. ἐκεῖ [there], that is, in Bethany, where the house of Simon was. See what [is written] on Matthew 26:6 and on Luke 7:37, where most of this history is explained.

ἡ Μάρθα διηκόνει [Martha served]) Women were not accustomed to recline at such banquets. Concerning Martha's diligence, see Luke 10:40.

And Lazarus was one of those reclining with him) Proving the truth of the restored life by the very act of eating. See Mark V. 43. below XXI. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἐποίησαν ὖν αὐτῷ δεῖπνον ἐκεῖ) Personale pro impersonali. Parata est ei coena, nempe apud Simonem Lazari consan- guineum. Solebant Iudaei ante Paschatis dies coenis so- lennioribus se & amicos excipere, praesertim nona, ut no- tat Theophylactus, quae tunc incidit in diem Solis. ἐκεῖ id est in Bethania, ubi domus erat Simonis. Vide quae ad Matth. XXVI. 6. & ad Lucam VII. v. 37. ubi pleraque hu- jus historiae explicata.

ἡ Μάρθα διηκόνει) Non solebant in talibus conviviis ac- cumbere foeminae. De Marthae sedulitate vid. Luc. X. 40.

ὁ δὲ Λάζαρος εἷς ἦν τῶν ἀνακειμένων σὺν αὐτῷ) Ipso cibi sumtu vitae redditae veritatem probans. Vide Marc. V. 43. infra XXI. 13.

## 12:3
Vers. 3.

Λίτραν) This word, which the Hebrews also use, is one of those which the Latins received from their Sicilian neighbors, as also λίτρον, ὀγκία, τύγκιον, and many others. For they are mistaken who think these are of primitive Latin origin. The Jews received it from the Macedonians.

Drusius is not pleased that this word was accepted from the Latins. The Hebrews, he says, use this term. For they say ליטרא, which they had received from the Greeks, not from the Latins. Or certainly the Greeks took it from the Phoenicians, whose language was related to the Hebrew. For Galen does not persuade me that λίτρα is a Latin word. I rather agree with those who say it is Greek. Elias Thesbite, in the language of our doctors, זהב ליטרא, a golden pound, and in the plural ליטרין, is a word of the Greek language, which is called libra in Latin, and Pfund in German. καὶ ἐξέμαξε) that is, she had wiped, as we said above XI. 2. ταῖς θριξὶν ἀυτῆς) Which is the highest ornament of beauty, says the Latin poet, and that with which women are most accustomed to boast. See 1 Pet. III. 3. ἐπληρώθη ἐκ τῆς ὀσμῆς) For Nard is very fragrant. Cant. I. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Λίτραν) Haec vox qua & Hebraei utuntur, una est earum, quas à vicinis Siculis Latini acceperunt, ut & λίτρον, ὀγκί- αν, τύγκιον multaque alia. Errant enim qui primitiva ori- gine Latina haec putant. Iudaei eam acceperunt à Mace- donibus.

Non placet Drusio vocem hanc à Latinis acce- ptam esse. Utuntur, inquit, hoc vocabulo Ebraei. Nam dicunt ליטרא quod à Graecis acceperant, non à Latinis. Aut certe Graeci sumserunt à Phoenici- bus, quorum lingua Ebraicae cognata erat. Nam La- tinum vocabulum esse λίτρα mihi non persuadet Ga- lenus. Potius assentior iis qui dicunt Graecum esse. Elias Thesbite, in lingua doctorum nostrum זהב ליטרא libra aurea, & in plurali ליטרין libra vox est linguæ Græcæ, quæ Latinè libra dicitur, & Ger- manicè Pfund. καὶ ἐξέμαξε) id est, absterserat, ut diximus supra XI. 2. ταῖς θριξὶν ἀυτῆς) Quod summum formæ decus est, ait Latinus Poeta, & quo fœminæ maximè se solent jactare. Vide 1. Pet. III. 3. ἐπληρώθη ἐκ τῆς ὀσμῆς) Est enim valdè odorum Nardus. Cant. I. 11.

## 12:4
Vers. 4.

Ἰούδας) He made the beginning of the speech with evil intent: whom others followed more incautiously.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ἰούδας) Is dolo malo sermonis fecit initium: quem alii incautius secuti sunt.

## 12:6
Vers. 6.

Οὐχ' ὅτι περὶ τῶν πτωχῶν ἔμελεν ἀυτῷ) Being treacherous and unmerciful. Judas is an example of many who cloak their private interests with the name of piety. κλέπτης ἦν) Yet permitted by Christ to live among the Apostles: so that we might never hope that the Church would be without evil men. He was embezzling money, either contemplating a departure or foreseeing danger. καὶ τὸ γλωσσόκομον εἶχε) Thus ארון is translated by the Chaldean and Jerusalem Targum, Gen. L. 26, and by the Greeks 2 Chron. XXIV. 8. and following, where others have placed κιβωτὸν. And it is believed to have been properly an oblong and narrow chest which those traveling could carry with them. By this example Christ taught that those things which pertain to the care of this life should not be entrusted to excellent men, Acts VI. 2, 1 Cor. VI. 4. At the same time, it appears from this that a common treasury, from which necessities are purchased, is not an obstacle to a most perfect life. τὰ βαλλόμενα) The monies which were put into that purse: & if anything else was necessary for the journey.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Οὐχ' ὅτι περὶ τῶν πτωχῶν ἔμελεν ἀυτῷ) Quippe perfido & immisericordi. Exemplum est Iudas multorum privatis commodis obtendentium nomen pietatis. κλέπτης ἦν) Permissus tamen à Christo inter Apostolos vivere: ne unquam sine malis speraremus fore Ecclesiam. Subducebat autem pecuniam aut divortium meditans aut periculum prævidens. καὶ τὸ γλωσσόκομον εἶχε) Ita ארון vertitur à Chaldæo & Hierosolymitano, Gen. L. 26. à Græcis 2. Par. XXIV. 8. & seq. ubi κιβωτὸν alii posuerunt. Et creditur propriè fuisse ar- cula oblonga & angusta quam iter facientes ferre secum poterant. Docuit hoc exemplo Christus viris excellen- tibus non esse demandanda ea, quæ ad vitæ hujus curam pertinent, Act. VI. 2. 1. Cor. VI. 4. Simul hinc apparet et- iam perfectissimæ vitæ non obstare commune aliquod æra- riolum, unde necessaria comparentur. τὰ βαλλόμενα) Pecunias quæ isti marsupio indebantur: & si quid aliud ad viam erat necessarium.

## 12:7
Vers. 7.

Ἄφες ἀυτήν) i. e. let her do what she wants. See Matt. XXVII. v. 49. Mark explains it best: why are you troubling her? chap. XIV. 6. ἐις τὴν ἡμέραν τῶ ἐνταφιασμῶ τετήρηκεν ἀυτό) i. e. she has kept this as if for the preparation of the body. Those who did not understand this manner of speaking changed the reading so that it would be, 'Let her keep it for the day of my burial,' which not only Latin codices have, but also some Greek ones; the codex which Nonnus used also had it. But the Syriac is correct: nor is it a new thing for things wrongly understood to be wrongly changed. It is therefore not safe enough to trust the Latin text. Which Grotius ought to have observed elsewhere, as often as he dared to amend Greek codices from the Latin.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Ἄφες ἀυτήν) i. e. agat quod vult. Vide Matth. XXVII. v. 49. Marcus optimè exponit: quid ipsi molesti estis? cap. XIV. 6. ἐις τὴν ἡμέραν τῶ ἐνταφιασμῶ τετήρηκεν ἀυτό) i. e. servavit hoc tanquam ad pollincturam. Qui hoc loquendi genus non intellexerunt, murarunt lectionem ut esset, In diem se- pulturæ meæ servet illud, quod non Latini tantum codices habent, sed & Græci quidam; habuit & codex quo usus est Nonnus. At Syrus rectè: neque novum est perperam in- tellecta perperam mutari. Non ergo satis tutum Latino textui fidere. Quod alibi observasse debebat Grotius, quoties è Latino Græcos codices emendare ausus est.

## 12:8
Vers. 8.

ἔχετε) Present for future, as below XVI. 10. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ἔχετε) Præsens pro futuro, ut infra XVI. 10. & alibi.

## 12:9
Vers. 9.

ἔγνω ὖν) When he had stayed there for a day or two. ἐκ τῶν Ἰυδαίων) From the Jerusalemites, as above several times. Ἀλλ' ἵνα καὶ ὲ Λάζαρον ἴδωσιν) By the same effort. The fame of the arrival of JESUS had revived the fame of Lazarus recalled to life.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

ἔγνω ὖν) Cum hæsisset ibi per diem unum aut alterum. ἐκ τῶν Ἰυδαίων) Ex Hierosolymitis, ut supra aliquo- ties. Ἀλλ' ἵνα καὶ ὲ Λάζαρον ἴδωσιν) Eadem opera. Fama ad- ventus IESU famam Lazari in vitam revocati resuscita- rat.

## 12:10
Vers. 10.

ἐβουλεύσαντο δὲ) βουλέυεσθαι here is not to consult, but to resolve, as in Acts V. 33, XV. 37, 2 Cor. I. 17. οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς) With the other Senators, ἵνα καὶ ὲ Λάζαρον ἀποκτείνωσι) Not Jesus alone. Malice is headlong: and always carries one further. They had already progressed so well in that excellent opinion of Caiaphas, that for the public good anything is permitted, that they did not hesitate to make a man guilty of no fault an addition to their crime to protect their dominion.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ἐβουλεύσαντο δὲ) βουλέυεσθαι non est hic consultare, sed con- stituere, ut Act. V. 33. XV. 37. 2. Cor. I. 17. οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς) Cum Senatoribus cæteris, ἵνα καὶ ὲ Λάζαρον ἀποκτείνωσι) Non Iesum solum. Præ- ceps est malitia: & semper ultra rapit. Tam bene jam profecerant in egregia ista Cajaphæ sententia, pro bono publico quidvis licere, ut non dubitarent hominem nullius culpæ reum adjectamentum facere sui sceleris ad tuen- dam dominationem.

## 12:11
Vers. 11.

Δι ἀυτὸν ὑπῆγον) Having left the city, they were following Jesus. καὶ ἐπίστευον ἐἰς ὲ Ἰησοῦν) Not only as in a Prophet, but also as in the Messiah, as the following history shows.

PART II. The acclamation made to Jesus, when riding upon a donkey he made for Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Δι ἀυτὸν ὑπῆγον) Urbe relicta Iesum sectabantur. καὶ ἐπίστευον ἐἰς ὲ Ἰησοῦν) Non tantum ut in Prophetam, sed & ut in Messiam ut sequens historia ostendit.

PARS II. Acclamatio Jesu facta, cum asina inequitans Hierosolymam contenderet.

## 12:12
V. 12. τῇ ἐπαύριον.

Therefore on the fifth day, as is evident from the collation of v. 1, before the Passover, but on the tenth of the month Nisan, he entered Jerusalem, on which day the Jews were accustomed to separate the lamb and receive it into their house, which they would sacrifice at the Passover, Exod. XII. 6, and on which Joshua, having crossed the Jordan, entered the promised land. ὄχλος πολὺς ὁ ἐλθὼν ἐἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν) For to what pro- The worse the days of the Passover were, the greater the crowd that came into the city.

ὅτι ἔρχεται ὁ Ἰησῦς] From Bethany. History explained at Matt. XXI.

Latin:

V. 12. τῇ ἐπαύριον.

Quinto ergo die, ut è v. 1. collatione patet, an- te Pascha, sed decimæ mensis Nisan ingressus est Jerusalem, qua solebant Judæi agnum separare & in domum suam recipere, quem Paschate macta- rent, Exod. XII. 6. & qua Josua trajecto Jordane terram promissam ingressus fuit. ὄχλος πολὺς ὁ ἐλθὼν ἐἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν) Nam quo pro- piores erant dies Paschatis, eo major turba in urbem venie- bat.

ὅτι ἔρχεται ὁ Ἰησῦς] Ex Bethania. Historia explicata ad Matth. XXI.

## 12:13
Vers. 13. τὰ βαΐα] A sign of joy, see the aforementioned place.

ὁ βασιλεὺς τῦ Ἰσραὴλ] The promised Messiah: thus Christ before his death both gave signs of his kingdom, and showed what kind of kingdom it was, moving souls by divine power to his worship.

Latin:

Vers. 13. τὰ βαΐα] Signum lætitiæ, vide d. l.

ὁ βασιλεὺς τῦ Ἰσραὴλ] Promissus Messias: ita Christus an- te mortem & regni sui indicia dedit, & quale esset regnum ostendit, vi divina in sui cultum animos movens.

## 12:14
V. 14. ἑυρὼν δὲ Ἰησῦς] Having found. For that word is taken in this way, as we said at Luke, loc. 30.

ὀνάριον] A somewhat larger foal of an ass. See the aforementioned place.

ἐκάθισεν] He was sitting: namely, while those things were being done which have already been narrated.

Latin:

V. 14. ἑυρὼν δὲ Ἰησῦς] Nactus. Sic enim vox illa sumi- tur, ut diximus Luc. l. 30.

ὀνάριον] Pullum asinæ majusculum. Vide d. l.

ἐκάθισεν] Insidebat: nempe dum fierent, quæ jam nar- rata sunt.

## 12:15
V. 15. Μὴ φοβῦ θυγάτερ Σιὼν] Be secure, city of Jerusalem. What the Prophet had expressed with a voice of rejoicing, he shows that it ought to be secure, because the King is arriving, good and mild and salutary to them: having nothing arrogant.

Latin:

V. 15. Μὴ φοβῦ θυγάτερ Σιὼν] Secura esto civitas Hiero- solymorum. Quod jubilandi voce Propheta expresserat, Securam autem esse debere ostendit, quia Rex adveniat bo- nus ac mitis & ipsi salutaris: nihil habens fastuosum.

## 12:16
V. 16. ἐχ ἔγνωσαν] They did not understand that that prophecy looked to this matter. Γνώσκειν is often to understand, Matt. XII. 7, ch. XXI. 45, and elsewhere.

τὸ πρῶτον] Recently.

ὅτε ἐδοξάσθη ὁ Ἰησῦς] After he ascended into heaven, as above ch. VII. 39. In the time of the kingdom of heaven. See Matt. XI. 11.

τότε ἐμνήσθησαν] By remembering, they understood the meaning of the Prophet: because, namely, the ascension into heaven and the subsequent mission of the Spirit removed from them the opinion accepted concerning an earthly kingdom: and they taught that this kingdom, humble in the sight of men, is the most sublime of all, and truly a kingdom.

κὴ ταῦτα ἐποίησαν αὐτῷ] That is, they revolved in their minds that these things were done to him: for it is personal for impersonal. He understands the acclamation Hosanna, the spreading of garments, the riding of the donkey, and the entry into the city with such a crowd accompanying.

Latin:

V. 16. ἐχ ἔγνωσαν] Non intellexerunt illud vaticinium ad hanc rem spectare. Γνώσκειν sæpe est intelligere, Matth. XII. 7. c. XXI. 45. & alibi.

τὸ πρῶτον] Recentire.

ὅτε ἐδοξάσθη ὁ Ἰησῦς] Postquam in cœlum ascendit, ut supra c. VII. 39. Tempore regni cœlorum. Vid. Matth. XI. 11.

τότε ἐμνήσθησαν] Reminiscendo rem intellexerunt sen- sum Prophetæ: quia scilicet ascensio in cœlum & secuta missio Spiritus exemerunt illis opinionem de regno terreno acceptam: ac docuerunt regnum hoc in conspectu homi- num humile, esse omnium sublimissimum, & vere regnum.

κὴ ταῦτα ἐποίησαν αὐτῷ] Id est, hæc illi facta esse animo revolverunt: nam personale est pro impersonali. Intel- ligit acclamationem Hosanna, substrationem vestimento- rum, incessionein asini & introitum in urbem tanta turba comitante.

## 12:17
V. 17. ὁ ὢν] Who had been, as we also had above.

ὅτε] Thus the Fabrician Syriac edition: thus the Latin: and the older Greek codices. Those who had been present when Lazarus was raised bore witness among the rest of the crowd that this was he who had done it. μαρτυρεῖν is accustomed to be placed absolutely, where it is understood from what follows to what it should be referred, as above c. I. 32.

Latin:

V. 17. ὁ ὢν] Qui fuerat ut supra quoque habuimus.

ὅτε] Ita Syra editio Fabriciana: ita Latina: & Græci co- dices vetustiores. Qui adfuerant cum Lazarus excitaretur apud cæteram turbam testimonium perhibebant, hunc esse eum qui id fecisset. Solet μαρτυρεῖν absolute poni, ubi ex se- quentibus intelligitur, quo sit referendum, ut supra c. I. 32.

## 12:18
V. 18. διὰ τῦτο κὴ ὑπήντησεν αὐτῷ ὄχλος] It is an explanatory cause, for what he had narrated, that a great crowd had met him, he says happened mostly because of the fame spread about Lazarus.

Latin:

V. 18. διὰ τῦτο κὴ ὑπήντησεν αὐτῷ ὄχλος] Est ἐπαίτιον, nam quod narrarat magnam turbam ei obviam factam, id ait maxime evenisse ob famam sparsam de Lazaro.

## 12:19
V. 19. οἱ ἶν] When they saw his followers growing to such an extent.

ὅτι ἐκ ὠφελεῖτε ἐδέν] Some say to others that nothing is being promoted, nay rather that their affairs are being much corrupted by delaying: so that now greater safeguards must be sought to execute the decree of the Senate. The Syrian reads ὠφελεῖτε, the Latin translates 'we profit,' regarding the sense.

ὁ κόσμος] A huge force of men, just as the Hebrews often use עולם and the Syrian here עלמא:

PART III.

The sermon of Jesus held for the sake of the Greeks.

Latin:

V. 19. οἱ ἶν] Cum sectatores ejus in tantum crescentes viderent.

ὅτι ἐκ ὠφελεῖτε ἐδέν] Alii aliis hoc dicunt nihil promoveri, imo multum corrumpi res suas cunctando: ita ut jam majora præsidia quærenda sint ad exequendum Se- natusconsultum. ὠφελεῖτε legit Syrus, Latinus vertit profici- mus sensum respiciens.

ὁ κόσμος] Vis ingens hominum, quomodo עולם sæpe usurpant Hebræi & hic Syrus עלמא:

PARS III.

Concio Jesu Græcorum causa habita.

## 12:20
V. 20. ἧσαν δέ τινες ἕλληνες] By this name are called all who were neither Israelites nor proselytes, among whom were not a few pious men, worshippers of the one God, σεβόμενοι ἕλληνες Acts XVII. 4. To the Talmudic Hebrews חסידי אומות, the pious from the nations: such as Cornelius the centurion and the eunuch of Candace in the Acts of the Apostles. Such worshipped God in the open court which was called of the Gentiles: from the institution of Solomon 1 Kings VIII. 14. Josephus narrates that among these open courts there was a partition, by which foreigners were forbidden to penetrate further. See Acts XXI. 28. This history pertains to knowing the amplitude of the kingdom of the Messiah. For the most abundant calling of the Gentiles was being preluded. These Gentiles seem to have been Syrophoenicians: for we have noted elsewhere, Mark VII. v. 16, that she is called ἐλληνίδα who to others is a Syrophoenician. And for these, because of proximity, there was easier acquaintance with the Galileans of Bethsaida, because they perhaps ran out from time to time into the parts of Tyre and Sidon.

ἐκ τῶν ἀναβαινόντων] From those for whom it was convenient, because of the proximity of the place, to undertake this journey every year.

ἵνα προσκυνήσωσιν ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ] That they might join their prayers with the people of God.

Cyrillus indeed, Chrysostomus & Theophyl. judge them to have been Gentiles, because they came to Jerusalem to become proselytes. Others, however, wish for Greeks, who were already proselytes, to be designated, because they come to worship. See Croyus in Walæus on this passage. But the opinion of Grotius does not seem to be disapproved, which B. Gerhard also confirms, as do Salmasius and Selden in the same Walæus. And it is evident from Josephus, book VI of the Jewish War, chapter 6, that in the Jerusalem temple there was then also a court of the Gentiles, into which it was lawful for those contaminated by legal uncleanness and for heathens to enter. Compare 2 Macc. III. v. 35. See the Harmony of B. Gerhard, ch. CXLVI.

Latin:

V. 20. ἧσαν δέ τινες ἕλληνες] Hoc nomine vocantur omnes qui nec Israëlitæ erant nec proselyti, inter quos non pauci erant viri pii, unius Dei cultores, σεβόμενοι ἕλληνες Act. XVII. 4. Hebræis Talmudicis חסידי אמור pii ex gentibus: qualis Cornelius centurio & Eunuchus Candaces in Actis Apostolicis. Tales Deum adorabant in subdiali quod voca- batur Gentium: ex instituto Solomonis 1. Reg. VIII. 14. Narrat Josephus inter hæc subdnalia intersepimentum fuis- se, quo alienigenæ interius penetrare vetabantur, Vide Act. XXI. 28. Pertinet autem hæc historia ad cognoscendam amplitudinem regni Messiæ. Nam Gentium uberrimæ vo- cationi præludebatur. Videntur autem hi Gentiles fuisse Syrophœnices: nam & alibi notavimus, Marci VII. v. 16. ἐπνηίδα vocari quæ aliis est Syrophœnissa. Et his ob vicini- tatem facilior notitia cum Galilæis Bethsaïdensibus, quod illæ forte in partes Tyri & Sidonis subinde excurrebant.

ἐκ τῶν ἀναβαινόντων] Ex his quibus commodum erat, ob loci propinquitatem hoc iter quotannis suscipere.

ἵνα προσκυνήσωσιν ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ] Ut preces suas cum populo Dei conjungerent.

Cyrillus sane, Chrysostomus & Theophyl. gentiles fuisse censent, quod Hierosolyma venerint, ut Proselyti fierent. Alii tamen Græcos, qui jam Prose- lyti essent, designari volunt, quia veniunt ut ado- rent. Vid. Croyus apud Walæum in h. l. Non im- probanda autem videtur Grotiana sententia, quam etiam confirmat B. Gerhardus, ut & Salma- sius ac Seldenus apud eundem Walæum. Et patet ex Josepho l. VI. de bello Judaico cap. 6. in templo Hierosolymitano tum etiam fuisse atrium gen- tium, in quod fas fuerit legali immunditie conta- minatis atque Ethnicis introire. Conf. 2. Macc. III. v. 35. Vid. Harmon. B. Gerhardi c. CXLVI.

## 12:21
V. 21. Φιλίππῳ] Perhaps a known person, or because they had happened upon him.

Θέλομεν] We would wish. See what we said on Matt. XXVI. 39, Mark X. 35.

Τὸν ἰησοῦν ἰδεῖν] That is, to meet more closely, to converse with him.

Latin:

V. 21. Φιλίππῳ] Noto forte, aut quod in eum inciderant.

Θέλομεν] Vellemus. Vide quæ diximus Matth. XXVI. 39. Marc. X. 35.

Τὸν ἰησοῦν ἰδεῖν] Id est propius convenire, cum eo collo- qui.

## 12:22
V. 22. Καὶ λέγει τῷ Ἀνδρέᾳ] As one who was prior in order and therefore more familiar.

Ἀνδρέας κὴ Φίλιππος λέγουσι τῷ Ἰησοῦ] Because previously he had forbidden the disciples to go into the borders of the Gentiles in their mission (Matt.
