X. 5), they doubted whether men coming from there, uncircumcised, ought to be admitted to conversation with Christ. And so, as in a doubtful matter, they consult him.

Latin:

V. 22. Καὶ λέγει τῷ Ἀνδρέᾳ] Ut qui ordine prior ac proinde familiarior esset.

Ἀνδρέας κὴ Φίλιππος λέγουσι τῷ Ἰησοῦ] quia antehac in lega- tione discipulos vetuerat ire in fines gentium. Matth. X. 5. dubitabant an homines inde venientes incircumcisi, ad- mitti ad Christi colloquium debeant. Itaque ut in re du- bia, ipsum consulunt.

## 12:23
V. 23. Ἀπεκρίνατο αὐτοῖς] With general words, indeed, but from which it might be sufficiently understood that he had not refused this conversation.

Ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα] It is not far off: it is present: that time is at hand.

ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου] That not only the Jews, but also foreigners may recognize what kind of person he is and how great he is.

Latin:

V. 23. Ἀπεκρίνατο αὐτοῖς] Verbis quidem generalibus, sed unde satis intelligeretur, se hoc colloquii non recusasse.

Ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα] Non longe est: adest: instat tempus il- lud.

ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου] Ut qualis quantusque sit, non Judæi tantum, sed & alienigenæ agnoscant.

## 12:24
V. 24. Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν] Now he shows by what way he and others must go to true glory, namely through ignominy and sufferings, and lest they be offended by the conspiracy of the Pharisees against him, he teaches that worse things still remain.

He does not speak here of others, but of himself: for Christ was, as Augustine says in Tract. LI on John, the grain that was to die in the infidelity of the Jews, to be multiplied in the faith of all peoples. The death of Christ was the death of a most fertile grain, from which a huge harvest of Christians arose for the whole world, which is stored in the heavenly barn. So also Ambros. on Ps. XXXVI, Hieronym. on Hos. XIII, Bernhard. Serm. XV on Cant. Afterwards Christ passes to his own, and wishes his ministers to imitate his example, v. 25. And thus far we approve what Grotius has on v. 26: ἐὰν ἐμοὶ διακονῇ τις: He shows that these general pronouncements pertain not only to himself, but also to his own. Here he tacitly calls himself a King, who has many ministers to promote the affairs of his kingdom. ἐμοὶ ἀκολουθείτω: Let him imitate my example. Thus Mark VIII. 34, Luke IX. 32, Rev. XIV. 4. ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγώ: I am for I shall be. He understands the place of highest happiness τιμήσῃ αὐτὸν ὁ πατὴρ. He adds glory to happiness, so that nothing may be lacking which is accustomed to be desired by men; for temporal loss, eternal reparation is promised, just as Christ himself through death arrived not only at eternal life but also at the perfect possession of the kingdom.

Μόνον μένει] Without fruit. Thus above c. VI. 22. μόνον is said in a certain respect.

Latin:

V. 24. Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν] Iam ostendit qua via sibi a- lîisque ad veram gloriam eundum sit, nempe per igno- miniam & passiones, & ne offendantur Pharisæorum in se conspiratione, docet pejora adhuc restare.

Non de aliis hic loquitur, sed de sese: Erat enim Christus, Augustino dicente tract. LI. in Joh. granum mortificaturum in infidelitate Judæorum, multipli- candum in fide omnium populorum. Mors Christi mors fuit grani fertilissimi, ex qua ingens toti orbi messis Christianorum exorta est, quæ in cæleste re- conditur horreum. Ita & Ambros. in Ps. XXXVI. Hieronym. in Os. XIII. Bernhard. Serm. XV. in Cant. Postea transit Christus ad suos, & vult mini- stros suum imitari exemplum v. 25. & hactenus probamus quæ ad v. 26. habet Grotius: ἐὰν ἐμοὶ δι- ακονῇ τις: Ostendit generalia hæc effata, non ad se tan- tum, sed & ad suos pertinere. Hic tacite Regem se nun- cupat, qui ministros plurimos habeat ad res regni sui promovendas. ἐμοὶ ἀκολουθείτω: Imetetur exemplum meum. Sic Marc. VIII. 34. Luc. IX. 32. Apoc. XIV. 4. ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγώ: Sum pro ero. Intelligit locum sum- mæ felicitatis τιμήσῃ αὐτὸν ὁ πατὴρ. Felicitati ad- dit gloriam, nequid absit quod desiderari ab homini- bus solet, pro temporali jactura æterna promittitur reparatio, sicut ipse Christus per mortem non modo ad vitam æternam sed & ad perfectam regni possessionem pervenit.

Μόνον μένει] Sine fructu. Sic supra c. VI. 22. μόνον dici- tur certo respectu.

## 12:25
V. 25. ὁ φιλῶν τὴν ψυχὴν αὑτοῦ] Namely ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ τούτῳ, as the opposite member shows. ψυχὴν αὑτοῦ, that is, both his own comforts and the honors of this life. He loves, namely, more than divine things. Compare what is in Matt. X. 39. and what was said there.

ἀπολέσει αὐτήν] He will destroy himself.

ὁ μισῶν] Valuing less than those things which pertain to God, as in Luke XIV. 26. and see what was said there.

εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον φυλάξει αὐτήν] He will cause it to arrive at eternal life. φυλάσσειν is opposed to τῷ ἀπολύειν, also below c. XVII. 12.

Latin:

V. 25. ὁ φιλῶν τὴν ψυχὴν αὑτοῦ] Nempe ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ τούτῳ, ut ostendit membrum oppositum. ψυχὴν αὑτοῦ, id est, & sua commoda & honores hujus vitæ. Amat, nempe præ divinis. Confer quæ Matth. X. 39. & ibi dicta.

ἀπολέσει αὐτήν] Semet perdet.

ὁ μισῶν] Minoris faciens quam ea quæ ad Deum perti- nent, ut Luc. XIV. 26. & vide quæ ibi dicta.

εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον φυλάξει αὐτήν] Efficiet ut ad vitam æter- nam perveniat. φυλάσσειν opponitur τῷ ἀπολύειν, etiam infra c. XVII. 12.

## 12:26
V. 26. Ἐὰν ἐμοὶ διακονῇ τις] He shows that these general pronouncements pertain not only to himself, but also to his own. Here he tacitly declares himself King, who has very many ministers to promote the affairs of his kingdom.

Ἐμοὶ ἀκολουθείτω] Let him imitate my example. Thus Mark VIII. 34. Luke IX. 23. Rev. XIV. 4.

ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ] I am, for I shall be. He understands the place of highest happiness. - τιμήσῃ αὐτὸν ὁ πατὴρ] He adds glory to happiness, so that nothing may be lacking which is accustomed to be desired by men; for temporal loss, eternal reparation is promised, just as Christ himself through death arrived not only at eternal life, but at the eternal possession of the kingdom.

PART IV. The prayer of Jesus, with a voice heard from heaven, and information concerning his own exaltation, and faith to be placed in the true light, while the Jews nevertheless remain in their ἀπιστίᾳ.

Latin:

V. 26. Ἐὰν ἐμοὶ διακονῇ τις] Ostendit generalia hæc effata non ad se tantum, sed & ad suos pertinere. Hic tacite Regem se nuncupat, qui ministros plurimos habeat ad res regni sui promovendas.

Ἐμοὶ ἀκολουθείτω] Imitetur exemplum meum. Sic Marc. VIII. 34. Luc. IX. 23. Apoc. XIV. 4.

ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ] Sum, pro ero. Intelligit locum summæ fe- licitatis. - τιμήσῃ αὐτὸν ὁ πατὴρ] Felicitati addit gloriam, ne quid absit, quod desiderari ab hominibus solet, pro temporali jactura æterna promittitur reparatio, sicut ipse Christus per mortem non modo ad vitam æternam, sed ad æternam regni possessionem pervenit.

PARS IV. Precatio Jesu, cum voce de cœlo audita, & in- formatione de sui exaltatione, & fide in lucem veram collocanda, manentibus tamen Iu- dæis in sua ἀπιστίᾳ.

## 12:27
V. 27. νῦν ἡ ψυχή με τετάρακται] Lest those who are invited to imitate him should think that in him there were not natural desires of avoiding pain and disgrace, shows that they were truly in him, the more there was need that he should become our example, Heb. II. 8. c. IV. 15. He uses here the word ταράσσεσθαι, by which also above a vehement affection was indicated chap. XI. 33. In Hebrew נפש תחמי עלי as Ps. XLII. 6. Compare what [is said] at Matth. XXVI. 38. & seqq. & Luke XXII. 44.

These do not indicate natural desires of living, but a horrible perturbation in the mind of Christ, and a sense of divine wrath, than which nothing more terrible can be thought, which Beza acknowledged here. Beautifully Ambrose in c. XXII. Luke. Some wish to seek excuses for this sadness. I nowhere more admire the piety and majesty of Christ; for he would have exalted me less, had he not taken up my affection: He indeed, with the delight of his eternal divinity set aside, is affected by the weariness of my infirmity, and takes up my sadness, that he might bestow his joy upon me. Confidently, therefore, I name this sadness, because I preach his cross. In which way also St. Augustine says, the perturbation of Christ tranquilizes us, and his infirmity strengthens [us].

And what shall I say: Father save me from this hour] I think it is rightly read also by later writers as an interrogation for this clause. For we are accustomed in such discourses to ask first generally. What shall I do? Then to subjoin this or that. He calls this time most dangerous to himself among such powerful and cruel enemies an hour.

But for this cause I came to this hour] He shows that he will not do what he had asked, that he will not pray against death. For ἀλλὰ here signifies 'But yet'. For this, understand, that I might die, which he had indicated in the preceding words, I came here to Jerusalem, I cast myself into the midst of enemies.

Latin:

V. 27. νῦν ἡ ψυχή με τετάρακται] Ne putarent qui ad ipsum imitandom invitantur, in ipso non esse naturalia desideria evitandi dolorem & probra, ostendit eadem in se esse reve- ra, quo magis opus erat ut exemplar nostrum fieret, Hebr. II. 8. c. IV. 15. Utitur hic voce ταράσσεσθαι, qua & supra ve- hemens affectus indicatus est cap. XI. 33. Hebraice נפש תחמי עלי ut Pf. XLII. 6. Confer quæ ad Matth. XXVI. 38. & seqq. & Luc. XXII. 44.

Non hæc naturalia desideria vivendi indicant, sed horrendam conturbationem in Christi mente, iræq; divinæq; sensum, quo nihil terribilius cogitari potest, quod hic agnovit Beza. Pulcre Ambros. in c. XXII. Luc. Nonnulli volunt excusationes quæ- rere hujus tristitiæ. Ego nusquam magis Christi pie- tatem majestatemq; demiror; minus enim extulerat mihi, nisi meum suscepisset affectum: Ille vero seque- strata delectatione divinitatis æternæ, tædio meæ in- firmitatis afficitur, suscipitq; tristitiam meam, ut mihi suam lætitiam largiretur. Confidenter ergo hanc tristitiam nomino, quia crucem ejus prædico. Quo pacto etiam S. Augustinus, Christi, inquit, perturbatio nos tranquillat, & infirmitas firmat.

καὶ τί εἴπω : πάτερ σῶσόν με ἐκ τῆς ὥρας ταύτης] Puto recte etiam postertus hoc membrum per interrogationem legi. Solemus enim in talibus sermonibus primum generaliter interrogare. Quid agam? Deinde subjicere hoc aut illud. ὥραν vocat tempus istud sibi periculosissimum inter tam potentes ac crudeles inimicos.

Ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτο ἦλθον εἰς τὴν ὥραν ταύτην] Ostendit se non facturum quod interrogaverat, non deprecaturum mortem. Nam ἀλλὰ hic valet Atqui. Ob hoc intellige ut moriar, quod superioribus verbis indicaverat, veni huc Hierosoly- ma, in medios inimicos me conjeci.

## 12:28
Vers. 28.

Father glorify thy name] I will suffer anything that may be an honor to thee. They are said to glorify God in an eminent way, who die for the testimony of divine truth, below XXI. 19.

There came therefore a voice from heaven] Which was almost the only kind of oracle that remained in the times of the second temple, they call it בת קול.

What? did not Prophecy have a place from the time of the second temple? And Heinsius observes here, that one is קול and the other is בת קול comparing 1 Sam. XII. 18. which if it were the cause of fear, [was] not thunder, but a voice joined with thunder, a witness equally of the divine presence and majesty.

And I have glorified and will glorify again] I think 'Thee' is to be understood, so that the Father shows that the glory of the Son is dear to him, just as his own glory was to the Son. I have glorified, as by miracles and now specifically by having raised Lazarus. I will glorify by your own resurrection and ascension into heaven.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

πάτερ δόξασόν σου τὸ ὄνομα] Patiar quidvis quod tibi sit ho- norincum. δοξάζειν Θεὸν eximie dicuntur, qui pro divinæ veritatis testimonio moriuntur, infra XXI. 19.

ἦλθεν ὖν φωνὴ ἐκ τοῦ ὀρανῦ] Quod solum ferme oraculi ge- nus temporibus templi secundi restabat, בת קול vocant.

Quid? annon Prophetia à templi secundi tem- pore locum habebat? Et observat Heinsius hic, al- terum esse קול alterum בת קול conferens 1. Sam. XII. 18. quod si causa metus fuerit non tonitru, sed vox cum tonitru conjuncta, divinæ pariter præsentiæ ac majestatis testis.

Καὶ ἐδόξασα κὶ πάλιν δοξάσω] Puto subaudiendum Te, ut Pater ostendat sibi cordi esse Filii gloriam, sicut sua glo- ria erat Filio. ἐδόξασα, ut miraculis & nunc nominatim resuscitato Lazaro. δοξάσω tui ipsius resuscitatione & eve- ctione in cœlum.

## 12:29
Vers. 29.

Said that it had thundered] That part of the crowd which was further away from Christ.

An angel has spoken to him] It was the opinion of many among the Hebrews that God does not speak except by the ministry of angels. Therefore the ten commandments which God is said to have spoken are ascribed to angels Acts VII. 38. Heb. II. 2.

Whatever may be the opinion of the Hebrews, it was sufficiently shown at Exodus XIX that not a created Angel, but the Son of GOD himself (αὐτοπροσώπως) promulgated the Ten Commandments.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

Ἔλεγε βροντὴν γεγονέναι] Pars ista vulgi quæ à Christo lon- gius aberat.

Ἄγγελος αὐτῷ λελάληκεν] Opinio erat multorum apud Hebræos Deum non loqui nisi Angelorum ministerio. Ita- que decem præcepta quæ Deus dicitur elocutus ascribuntur Angelis Act. VII. 38. Hebr. II. 2.

Quicquid de Ebræorum opinione sit, Decem præcepta non Angelum creatum, sed Filium DEI αὐτοπροσώπως promulgasse ad Exod. XIX. satis ostensum fuit.

## 12:30
Verse 30.

Οὐ δι ἐμὲ ἂυτη ἡ φωνὴ γέγονεν] I who am sufficiently certain of the Father's affection toward me.

Δι ὑμᾶς] So that you may see how much the Father values me, even if I am condemned as an impious person and a seducer.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

Οὐ δι ἐμὲ ἂυτη ἡ φωνὴ γέγονεν] Qui satis certus sum de Patris in me affectu.

Δι ὑμᾶς] Ut videatis quanti me Pater faciat, etiamsi pro impio & seductore condemner.

## 12:31
Verse 31.

νῦν κρίσις ἐστὶ τοῦ κόσμε] To judge (κρίνειν) is often among the Hebrews to vindicate into liberty. Those who did this were judges (שופטים). The human race will be vindicated from an unjust possessor, as the following verses explain.

νῦν ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμε ἐκβληθήσεται ἔξω] That is, he will be disturbed from his kingdom. For ἔξω is to be interpreted from the word ἄρχων as 'out of the rule' (ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς). The 'ruler of the world' here and in chapter XIV. 30, chapter XVI. 11, and 'the god of this age' in 2 Cor. IV. 4, is the Devil, who, by introducing idolatry into the greatest part of the world and the flood of vices that accompanies idolatry, reigned as if God were excluded; Paul called them 'world-rulers of this darkness' in Ephesians VI. 12. Therefore, Christ signifies that idolatry and what coheres with it is to be destroyed. Compare the passage above at X. 18, and Colossians II. 15, Acts XXVI. 18.

Augustine (Tractate LI on John) and Gregory the Great (Book XVII of the Morals) also accept these words of Christ regarding the ejection of Satan from the hearts of men through the preaching of the Gospel in this way; but because this concerns the fruit of the death of Christ, and afterwards the drawing of men to Christ through the preaching of the Gospel, these are more correctly explained as the acquisition of victory through the passion, rather than the application through the preaching of the Gospel. See B. Gerhard, Harmony, chapter CXLVII, page 535.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

νῦν κρίσις ἐστὶ τοῦ κόσμε] κρίνειν sæpe apud Hebræos est in libertatem vindicare. Id qui faciebant שופטים. Vin- dicabitur genus humanum ab injusto possessore, ut sequen- tia explanant.

νῦν ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ κόσμε ἐκβληθήσεται ἔξω] Id est, de regno diturbabitur. Nam ἔξω ex voce ἄρχων interpretandum ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς. ἄρχων κόσμυ hic & c. XIV. 30. c. XVI. 11. ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, 2. Cor. IV. 4. Est Diabolus qui inducta in ma- ximam mundi partem idololatria & quæ idololatriam co- mitatur vitiorum colluvie, quasi Deo excluso regnabat, κοσμοκράτορας τοῦ κόσμε τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, dixit Paulus Ephes. VI. 12. Significat ergo Christus destruendam idololatriam & quæ ei cohærent. Confer locum supra X. 18. & Coloss. II. 15. Act. XXVI. 18.

Ita accipiunt etiam Augustin. tr. LI. in Joh. & Gregor. M. lib. XVII. moral. circa hæc Christi ver- ba de ejectione Satanæ ex cordibus hominum per Evangelii prædicationem; sed quia hic de fructu mortis Christi agitur, & postea de tractione homi- num per Evangelii prædicationem ad Christum, re- ctius hæc de acquisitione victoriæ per passionem, quam de applicatione per Evangelii prædicationem exponuntur. Vid. B. Gerhard. Harm. c. CXLVII. pag. 535.

## 12:32
Verse 32.

Ἐὰν ὑψωθῶ] That is, after I have been lifted up on the cross, as above in chapter III. 14; for ἐὰν is 'when,' as the Syriac translates it here. Thus in chapter III. 10. Thus the Hebrew word אם is often taken. πάντας ἑλκύσω πρὸς ἐμαυτὸν] Most Greek codices and the Syriac have πάντας. Understand 'all,' not only Jews, but also foreigners. I will draw to myself, I will draw away from the Devil, I will draw by the power of my resurrection, but understand those who do not resist.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

Ἐὰν ὑψωθῶ] Id est, postquam in crucem evectus fuero, ut supra c. III. 14. nam ἐὰν est quando ut hic vertit Syrus. Sic ep. III. 10. Sic sæpe sumitur Hebræum אם. πάντας ἑλκύσω πρὸς ἐμαυτὸν] πάντας habent plerique Co- dices Græci, & Syrus. Omnes intellige, non Judæos tan- tum, sed & alienigenas. Traham ad me, abstraham a Diabolo, traham vi resurrectionis meæ, sed eos intellige qui non reluctentur.

## 12:33
Verse 33.

Ποίῳ θανάτῳ] Namely, of the cross, which that word ὑψω̂ν implies: see above chapter III. 14 and what was said there.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

Ποίῳ θανάτῳ] Nempe crucis, quod vox illa ὑψω̂ν innuit: vide supra c. III. 14. & quæ ibi dicta.

## 12:34
Verse 34.

We have heard out of the law] From the sacred scriptures, as the word law is taken above in chapter X. 34. We have learned, however, understand it as the teachers of the Law interpreting. I think, however, that Psalm 110 and Daniel 7:14 are especially meant. That the Christ abideth for ever] Because, namely, he is said to be about to reign for ever. The teachers of those times had diligently noted the things which pertain to the exaltation of the Messiah, blind to those things which were said concerning his previous sufferings, both elsewhere and especially in Isaiah chapter 53, the beginning of which is cited presently. See 1 Peter 1:11. Therefore, Grotius must have been blind when he asserted that the illustrious passage of Isaiah 53, according to the letter, treats not of the sufferings of Christ, but of the sufferings of Jeremiah. (See what I have written against that corruption of his in the annotations on the Old Testament on Isaiah 53.) Who properly acknowledged here also that Psalm 110 and Daniel 7:14 treat of Christ: which places he wickedly depraved in the annotations on the Old Testament, as we have said in the animadversions on the same. Add what Grotius has a little later in this place on verse 34 concerning Daniel 7. Who is this Son of man? When we hear the Son of man spoken of, we conceive of him of whom Daniel spoke, and whose eternal kingdom he himself prophesied would be, that is, the Messiah. Do you designate another Son of man? And 53, verse 38. that: that here signifies the event, as often. might be fulfilled: That is, thus it happened what Isaiah had said in that place where he predicts the despised state and evils of Christ. Lord: the Greek interpreters rightly added this for the fullness of the sense, who: how few. hath believed our report: report to the Hellenists is that which is heard, the discourse, as also to Homer report of the Odyssey, etc. Thus Matthew 4:24, chapter 26:6, Galatians 3:2, 1 Thessalonians 2:3. Isaiah adapts this prophecy to the Gospel, and Paul in Romans 10:16. to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed, revealed here is understood with effect, as we noted above concerning the words given and drawn: The sense is, how few have sufficiently rightly noticed those wonderful works of God. For thus the arm is very often taken in the Old Testament, and Acts 13:17, where, however, certain words are cited from the Prophet, the following ones are to be understood, which contain a description of the strong abjection of Christ himself, for instance that he was poor, that he was pre-condemned by the Sanhedrin. Moreover, although the arm of the Lord sometimes denotes the essential power of God, here, however, it is rather to be taken hypostatically concerning the Son of God with Augustine, Bede, and Rupert: as Isaiah 51:5, The isles shall wait for my arm. Chapter 52:10, The Lord hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations. See Blessed Gerhard, Harmony, chapter 147, page 583. and how sayest thou, The Son of man must be lifted up] I entirely agree with those who say that the summary of Christ's words is reported here by John, not the individual words: for these sayings of the people show that Christ, at the same time that he spoke of the exaltation, had named the Son of man, and perhaps had also illustrated the exaltation itself by the likeness of the serpent, as above in chapter 3:14, by which it came about that the people understood death to be indicated by that word.

There is no necessity that we should establish this with Maldonado: because that appellation of the Son of man was known to the common people, which he seems here to cast at him sarcastically: and he had taught not once about his passion and crucifixion or exaltation on the cross, especially in John III. 14. Cf. Tarnov. in h. l. p. 907.

τίς εστιν ὕτος ὁ ὑὸς τῦ ἀνθρώπυ;) When we hear the Son of man mentioned, we conceive of him of whom Daniel spoke, and whose kingdom he himself prophesied would be eternal, that is, the Messiah. Or do you designate another Son of man?

Latin:

Vers. 34.

ἡμεῖς ἠκύσαμεν ἐκ τῶ νόμυ] Ex sacris literis, ut vox νόμυ sumta est supra c. X. 34. didicimus autem, intellige Legis- peritis interpretantibus. Puto autem præcipue intelligi Ps. CX. & Dan. VII. 14. ὅτι ὁ Χρισὸς μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα] Quia scilicet in æternum regnaturus dicitur. Quæ ad evectionem Messiæ pertinent, diligenter annotarant magistri illorum temporum, cæci ad ea quæ de præviis ejus passionibus dicebantur, tum alibi, tum maxime Esa. c. LIII. cujus initium mox citatur. Vid. I. Petr. I. 11. Cæcum ergo & Grotium fuisse oportet, cum locum illustrem Esa. LIII. secundum literam non de Christi, sed de Jeremiæ passionibus agere asse- ruit. (Vid. quæ adversus illam corruptelam ejus in annotatis ad Vetus Testamentum ad Esa. LIII.) Qui probe hic etiam agnovit Ps. CX. & Dan. VII. 14. de Christo agi: quæ loca improbe in annotatis ad Vetus Testamentum depravavit, ut in animadver- sionibus ad eadem diximus. Adde quæ de Dan. VII. paulo post habet h. l. Grotius ad v. 34. Τίς ἐστιν ὅτο̂ ὁ ὑὸς τῶ αἰνθρώπυ; Nos cum filium hominis dici audimus, eum concipimus de quo dixit Daniel, & cujus fore regnum æternum ipse vaticinatus est, id est Messiam. An tu alium filium hominis designas? Et LIII. v. 38. ἵνα: ἵνα hic eventum significat, ut sæpe. πληρωθῆ: Id est sic evenit quod Esaias dixerat eo in loco quo Christi statum despectum & mala prædi- cit. κύριε: hoc recte ad sensus plenitudinem, addi- derunt Græci interpretes, τίς: quotusquisque. ἐπίστευ- σε τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν: ἀκοὴ Hellenistis est id quod au- ditur sermo, ut & Homero ἀκοὴ Odysseæ s. Sic Matt. IV. 24. cap. XXVI. 6. Gal. III. 2. 1. Thess. II. 3. Ev- angelio hoc vaticinium Esaias aptat & Paulus Rom. X. 16. ὁ βραχίων κυρίε τίνι ἀπεκαλύφθη, ἀποκαλύ- πτεαζ hic intelligitur cum effectu, ut de vocibus dari & trahi supra notavimus: Sensus est quotusquisque sa- tis recte advertit admiranda illa Dei opera. Sic enim brachium sæpissime sumitur in veteri fœdere, & A- ctor. XIII. 17. ubi autem verba quædam ex Propheta citantur, subintelligenda sunt & sequentia, quæ con- tinent descriptionem fortis abjecta ipsius Christi, puta quod pauper erat, quod à Synedrio prædamnatus. Cæterum quanquam brachium Domini nonnun- quam essentialem Dei virtutem notet, hic tamen hypostatice potius de Filio Dei accipiendum cum Augustino, Beda & Ruperto: ut Esa. LI. 5. Insulæ brachium meum expectabunt. c. LII. 10. nudavit Dominus brachium sanctum suum oculis omnium gentium. Vid. B. Gerh. Harm. c. CXLVII. p. 583. καὶ πῶς σὺ λέγεις δεῖ ὑψωθῆναι τὸν ὑὸν τῶ ἀνθρώπυ] Omni- no iis accedo, qui à Johanne relatam hic ajunt summam verborum Christi, non verba singula: nam hæc plebis di- cta ostendunt Christum simul cum de evectione diceret no- minasse Filium hominis, forte & ipsam evectionem serpen- tis similitudine illustraverat, ut supra c. III. 14. quo factum ut mortem eo verbo indicari plebs intelligeret.

Nulla est necessitas, ut hoc cum Maldonado sta- tuamus: quia nota in vulgus erat illa Filii homi- nis appellatio, quam videtur hic ei sarcastice obji- cere: & de passione sua & crucifixione vel exal- tatione in cruce non semel docuerat, imprimis Iob. III. 14. Conf. Tarnov. in h. l. p. 907.

τίς εστιν ὕτος ὁ ὑὸς τῦ ἀνθρώπυ;) Nos cum Filium hominis dici audimus, eum concipimus de quo dixit Daniel, & cu- jus fore regnum æternum ipse vaticinatus est, id est Mes- siam. An tu alium Filium hominis designas?

## 12:35
Vers. 35.

ὄτι μικρὸν χρόνον τὸ φῶς μεθ' ὑμῶν ἐςι) When he saw them offended by the mention of his passion, he showed on the contrary that this was all the more reason for them to hasten to enjoy the benefits of his presence.

As the pleasant light of the sun is wont to be, now just about to set.

He calls himself the light as he did several times above. The time of light, his conspicuous presence, which he had also called the day in ch. 9, v. 4.

περιπατῶτε ἕως τὸ φῶς ἔχετε) Make progress in the knowledge of divine things. Light and walking are wont to be joined, as above in ch. 8. 12.

ἵνα μὴ σκοτία ὑμᾶς καταλάβῃ) Lest by chance God should withdraw his word from you, which God could indeed rightly have done immediately after Christ was crucified: but out of his mercy he granted much time still, after which he left the city to its own destruction, having led out the Christians.

κὶ ὁ περιπατῶν ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ ὐκ οἶδε πῦ ὑπάγει) κὶ for 'for'. Therefore use the light: because in darkness it is not known where one must go. And indeed the Jews, abandoned by the Gospel, stumbled most grievously not only against their own law but against civil customs and nature itself, as the history of the siege teaches.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

ὄτι μικρὸν χρόνον τὸ φῶς μεθ' ὑμῶν ἐςι) Cum eos videret of- fendi mentione passionis suæ, contra ostendit hoc magis ipsis festinandum ut sui præsentis beneficiis fruantur.

Ut esse Solis gratum lumen solet Jam jam cadentis.

Se vocat lucem ut supra aliquoties. Tempus lucis, præ- sentiam suam conspicuam, quam & diem dixerat c. 9. v. 4.

περιπατῶτε ἕως τὸ φῶς ἔχετε) Proficite in cognitione re- rum divinarum. Conjungi solent lux & ambulatio ut supra c. 8. 12.

ἵνα μὴ σκοτία ὑμᾶς καταλάβῃ) Ne forte Deus sermonem suum vobis subtrahat, quod jure quidem Deus facere potuit statim post Christum crucifixum: sed pro sua misericordia multum adhuc temporis indulsit, quo elapso urbem reli- quit suæ excitati, eductis Christianis.

κὶ ὁ περιπατῶν ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ ὐκ οἶδε πῦ ὑπάγει) κὶ pro nam. Ideo utimini luce: quia in tenebris nescitur quo eundum sit. Et sane Judæi ab Evangelio derelicti non in suam tantum legem sed in mores civiles & naturam ipsam gravissime impegerunt ut docet obsidionis historia.

## 12:36
Vers. 36.

πιςεύετε) He explains what he had just said figuratively, περιπατῶτε.

ἵνα ὑὶοὶ φωτὸς γίνησθε) Sons of eternal light, that is, participants, as the word 'sons' is wont to be taken among the Hebrews. We said this in Matth. XI. 15. The sense is almost the same as above in chapter 8. 12, where it is promised to those walking in the light that they will have the light of life, that is, eternal life.

ἐκρύβη ἀπ' αὐτῶν) He withdrew to Bethany so that he would not expose himself to dangers before the opportune time. Luke XXI. 37.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

πιςεύετε) Explicat quod modo dixerat figurate περιπατῶτε.

ἵνα ὑὶοὶ φωτὸς γίνησθε) Lucis æternæ filii id est participes ut solet vox filiorum sumi apud Hebræos. Diximus Matth. XI. 15. Sensus ferme idem, qui supra cap. 8. 12. ubi in luce ambulantibus promittitur fore ut habeant lu- cem vitæ, æternæ scilicet.

ἐκρύβη ἀπ' αὐτῶν) Bethaniam secessit ne ante opportu- num tempus se ingereret periculis Luc. XXI. 37.

## 12:37
Vers. 37.

τοσαῦτα δὲ αὐτῦ) This is as it were an epiphonema of the Apostle, supported not by those things which immediately preceded, but by the whole history: τοσαῦτα means 'so many', as above c. 6, 9. Luke XV. 29. The Syriac: 'All these things': he had made wine from water, had enlightened the man born blind, had raised the dead.

ὐκ ἐπίσευσαν εἰς αὐτόν) The greatest part of the Jerusalemites did not acknowledge him as sent by God, for those who had gone out to meet him were few in such a great multitude.

ἔμπροσθεν αὐτῶν) Not secretly, but openly, before the eyes of a great multitude, before the enemies themselves.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

τοσαῦτα δὲ αὐτῦ) Hoc est quasi Epiphonema Apostoli, subnixum non iis quæ proxime præcesserunt sed toti hi- storiæ: τοσαῦτα est tot, ut supra c. 6, 9. Luc. XV. 29. Sy- rus: Hæc omnia: ex aqua vinum fecerat, cæcum natum illuminaverat, mortuum excitaverat.

ὐκ ἐπίσευσαν εἰς αὐτόν) Pars maxima Hierosolymitarum non agnovit eum à Deo missum, nam qui obviam ei pro- cesserant pauci erant in tanta multitudine.

ἔμπροσθεν αὐτῶν) Non clam, sed palam, coram oculis ma- gnæ multitudinis, coram ipsis inimicis.

## 12:38
Vers. 38. ἵνα) ἵνα here signifies the outcome, as it often does.

πληρωθῇ) That is, thus it happened what Isaiah had said in that place where he predicts the despised state and the evils of Christ.

κύριε) The Greek interpreters rightly added this for the fullness of the sense.

τίς) How few.

ἐπίσευσε τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν) ἀκοὴ for the Hellenists is that which is heard, a report, as also in Homer, ἀκοὴ in the fifth book of the Odyssey. Thus Matt. IV. 24, c. XXVI. 6, Gal. III. 2, 5, Thess. II. 13. Isaiah adapts this prophecy to the Gospel, and Paul in Rom. XV. 16.

ὁ βραχίων κυρίε τίνι ἀπεκαλύφθη;) ἀπεκαλύπτεσθαι, here is understood with effect, as we noted above regarding being given and being drawn to you. The sense is: how few sufficiently and rightly notice those admirable works of God. For thus 'arm' is very often taken in the Old Testament, and Acts XIII. 17. Where, however, certain words from the Prophet are cited, the following ones must also be understood, which contain the description of the abject lot of Christ himself, for instance, that he was poor, that he was condemned beforehand by the Sanhedrin.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ἵνα) ἵνα hic eventum significat, ut sæpe.

πληρωθῇ) Id est sic evenit quod Esaias dixerat eo in loco quo Christi statum despectum & mala prædicit.

κύριε) Hoc recte ad sensus plenitudinem addiderunt Græ- ci interpretes.

τίς) Quotusquisque.

ἐπίσευσε τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν) ἀκοὴ Hellenistis est, id quod au- ditur, sermo, ut & Homero ἀκοὴ Odysseæ quinto. Sic Matth. IV. 24. c. XXVI. 6. Gal. III. 2. 5. Thess. II. 13. Evangelio hoc vaticinium Esaias aptat & Paulus Rom. XV. 16.

ὁ βραχίων κυρίε τίνι ἀπεκαλύφθη;) ἀπεκαλύπτεσθαι, hic in- telligitur cum effectu, ut de vobis dari & trahi supra no- tavimus. Sensus est: quotusquisque satis recte advertit admiranda illa Dei opera. Sic enim brachium sæpissime sumitur in veteri fœdere, & Actor. XIII. 17. Ubi autem verba quædam ex Propheta citantur, subintelligenda sunt & sequentia quæ continent descriptionem sortis abjectæ i- psius Christi, puta quod pauper erat, quod à Synedrio prædamnatus.

## 12:39
Vers. 39. διὰ τῦτο ὐκ ἠδύναντο πιςεύειν) Namely, as I said, because of those impediments which Isaiah mentions. 'They could not', that is, it was for them, being endowed with such a character that they admired external things, most difficult to embrace such a Messiah. Thus ἀδύνατον is often taken, Jer. XIII. 23, Mark III. 20, and elsewhere. See also I Cor. XII. 14.

ὅτι πάλιν εἶπεν Ἡσαΐας) That is: for indeed Isaiah had said, for I would prefer to translate this ὅτι as 'for', as also below in verse 49, rather than as 'because'.

Latin:

Vers. 39. διὰ τῦτο ὐκ ἠδύναντο πιςεύειν) Nempe ut dixi ob illa impedimenta quæ memorat Esaias. Non poterant id est erat ipsis tali ingenio præditis, ut externa mirarentur, difficillimum talem Messiam amplecti. Sic ἀδύνατον sæpe sumitur Jer. XIII. 23. Marc. III. 20. & alibi. Vide & I. Cor. XII. 14.

ὅτι πάλιν εἶπεν Ἡσαΐας) Id est: nam vero dixerat Esaias, malim enim hoc ὅτι per nam vertere, ut & infra vers. 49. quam per quia.

## 12:40
Vers. 40. τετύφλωκε) Namely Christ, who is said to have done that to which he gave occasion by his own humility, just as in the Hebrew it is said imperatively to the Prophet himself, acting as an image of Christ: 'Make fat the heart, make heavy the ears, smear the eyes.' Such is that in Ezek. XIV: 'I the Lord have deceived him,' and many similar things. Therefore the Syriac here translates it passively, in the same way as the same passage of the Prophet is read here, Acts XXVIII. 27. See what is in Matth. XIII. v. 15.

καὶ ἐπιστραφῶσι) A passive for a reciprocal active, as above ἐκρύβη. In the Greek of Isaiah it is ἐπιστρέψωσι, just as it is also in Matthew and in the Acts.

καὶ ἰάσομαι αὐτοὺς) So also in the Greek of Isaiah, in the Acts, and in Matthew: namely because in the Prophet GOD is speaking (as Paul notes, Acts XXVIII. 25), the interpreters turned it into the personal: following the sense no more than the words: for in the Hebrew it is 'that he may be healed,' which Mark explains with an excellent paraphrase in chapter IV. 12: καὶ ἀφεθῇ αὐτοῖς τὰ ἁμαρτήματα.

It is not poorly judged that John asserts these things about Christ, τετύφλωκε, because afterwards he speaks from the person of God the Father, or rather introduces the Prophet speaking, καὶ ἰάσομαι αὐτοὺς, with the person changed: he did not, however, blind them only by offering occasion through his own humility, but also by offering his word, which, although it is a means of salvation by the intention of God, nevertheless through the malice of the Jews (by accident) caused their greater hardening, especially in that he reproved them for their blindness and foretold the judgment of God, whence they were blinded more and more; and also by withdrawing grace and handing them over to the power of Satan, which is the punishment for the contempt of grace. Furthermore, the Prophet was not only a type and image of Christ regarding those things which happened in his own time, but a clear prediction exists there, looking toward the times of Christ himself, the fulfillment of which we have here, just as we observed in the Annotations on Isaiah 6.

Latin:

Vers. 40. τετύφλωκε) Nempe Christus, qui fecisse dici- tur id cui sua humilitate occasionem præbuit, sicut in He- bræo imperative dicitur ipsi Prophetæ Christi imaginem agenti: Impingua cor, aggrava aures, obline oculos, Ta- le illud Ezech. XIV. Ego Dominus seduxi eum & similia mul- ta. Ideo Syrus hic vertit passive, quomodo legitur idem hic Prophetæ locus, Actor. XXVIII. 27. Vide quæ Matth. XIII. v. 15.

καὶ ἐπιστραφῶσι) Passivum pro Activo reciprocante ut su- pra ἐκρύβη. In Græco Esaiæ est ἐπιστρέψωσι, quomodo & apud Matthæum & in Actis.

καὶ ἰάσομαι αὐτοὺς) Sic & in Græco Esaiæ, in Actis, & apud Matthæum: nimiram quia apud Prophetam DEUS loquitur (ut notat Paulus Act. XXVIII. 25.) verterunt in- terpretes in personale: non sensum magis secuti quam ver- ba: nam in Hebræo est ut medicetur ipsi, quod Marcus e- gregia paraphrasi explicat cap. IV. 12. καὶ ἀφεθῇ αὐτοῖς τὰ ἁ- μαρτήματα.

Non male hæc Johannes de Christo asserre censetur, τετύφλωκε, quia postea ex Dei Patris persona loquitur, vel loquentem potius intró- ducit Prophetam, καὶ ἰάσομαι αὐτοὺς, mutata persona: non autem tantum humilitate sua occa- sionem præbendo excæcavit, sed etiam verbum su- um offerendo, quod etsi medium sit salutis ex in- tentione Dei, per malitiam tamen Judæorum ad majorem eorum indurationem (ex accidenti) fecit, imprimis qua cæcitatis ipsos arguit, & judicium Dei prædixit, unde magis magisque illi excæcati sunt; nec non gratiam subtrahendo, & in potestatem Satanæ tradendo, quæ pœna est contemtus gratiæ. Cæterum Propheta non tan- tum typus & imago Christi fuit quoad ea, quæ suo tempore contigêre, sed prædictio luculenta ibi ex- stat, respiciens tempora ipsius Christi, cujus complementum hic habemus, quemadmodum in Annot. ad Esa. 6. observavimus.

## 12:41
Vers. 41.

ὅτε εἶδε τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ) The judgment which God, as if sitting on a throne, exercises through the Gospel, with the angels ministering to him in that business, and the remission of sins set forth: for all these things precede in Isaiah, having seen which he was encouraged not to refrain from speaking the commands of God, although he was to be an object of contempt to most. Isaiah is said to have seen the glory of Christ, just as Abraham saw his day, above in ch. 8, v. 56.

Grotius previously wanted Abraham to have seen the day of Christ only from afar; but Isaiah saw the glory of Christ close at hand: for he saw the Lord sitting on a throne, whom the angels served, and whom they celebrated together with the Father and the Holy Spirit with their τρισαγίῳ. Abraham saw the day of Christ in oracles and types, as also in the shadow of the ἐνἀνθρωποποιήσεως, in which he appeared to him in human form: but Isaiah saw the Son of God in the glory of his majesty: whence, against the Socinians and for the προΰπαρξιν of the Son of God before his temporal birth, and for his διόμουσίαν with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and thus for the mystery of the Holy Trinity, we have proven this from this passage, with ancient antiquity leading the way. See Vol. III of the System of Theology and the treatise on the preexistence of the Son of God.

Latin:

Vers. 41.

ὅτε εἶδε τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ) Judicium quod Deus, tanquam Throno insidens, per Evangelium exercet, Angelos ei ne- gotio ministrantes, & expositam peccatorum remissio- nem: nam hæc omnia apud Esaiam præcedunt, quibus conspectis animatus est ne abstineret Dei mandata eloqui, quanquam plerisque contemtui futurus. Dicitur Esaias vi- disse gloriam Christi, sicut Abrahamus diem ejus supra c. 8. v. 56.

Diem Christi Abrahamum eminus tantum vi- disse supra Grotius volebat; ast Esaias vidit glo- riam Christi cominus: nam vidit Dominum in throno sedentem, cui Angeli serviebant, quem- que una cum Patre & Spiritu S. τρισαγίῳ suo celebrabant. Abraham Christi diem vidit in oracu- lis & typis, ut & in umbra ἐνἀνθρωποποιήσεως, quam in humana specie ei apparuit: ast Esaias vidit Fi- lium Dei in gloria majestatis suæ: unde adversus Socinianos & προΰπαρξιν Filii Dei ante nativita- tem temporalem, διόμουσίαν cum Patre & Spiri- tu S. adeoque SS. Trinitatis mysterium ex hoc lo- co, præeunte cana antiquitate, alias probavimus, Vid. Tom. III. Syst. Theol. & tract. de præexistentia Filii Dei.

## 12:42
Vers. 42.

ὅμως μέντοι) Although most people spurned Jesus; some, however, who were less stubborn, had sufficiently understood that he was the Christ.

καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἀρχόντων) He was from those very senators whom we noted are accustomed to be called ἄρχοντας.

ἐπίστευσαν εἰς αὐτὸν) By a contemplative, not an active faith: convinced of the truth, but not so as to also bring their will into his obedience.

διὰ τοὺς Φαρισαίους οὐχ ὡμολόγουν) Because of the Pharisees who were powerful in the Sanhedrin, they did not dare to profess it, lest, at their urging, the decree already made should be exercised against them.

He judges that they were not the princes of the people but senators who are said to have believed in Christ. But that passage which he brings forward for that opinion from Matt. XIX. 15. proves it not at all. See what is said there. The primates are noted here in general, both Ecclesiastical and Political: as in Luke XIX. 18. & ch. XXIII. 25. John VII. 26. &c. The question is more serious, how they are said to have believed in Christ. That distinction between theoretical and practical faith, accepted in the Grotian sense, rests on no foundation. For he seems to understand theoretical as bare assent without trust, but he wishes practical to include not only trust, but also obedience to the precepts of Christ. But in the Scriptures, obedience is distinguished from trust as an effect from a cause, and is established as the fruit of faith: however, such a practical trust, which might include obedience in its formal aspect, is nowhere found in the Holy Scriptures. Nor are those said to believe in Christ who have only knowledge about Christ and offer assent to him: Others, therefore, explain this passage concerning saving faith; inasmuch as the faith of these rulers is opposed to the unbelief of others, v. 37, and this description of believing in Christ belongs only to true and saving faith. These, therefore, say that their faith was indeed true, although weak, such as Illyricus, B. Menzer, Vol. I. Disp. on Ch. 10 of the Epistle to the Romans, th. 47, B. Feuerborn, Assert. Doctr. on sin in the H. S. Disput. 50, thes. 5, B. Affelmann in Hept. illustr. quaestion. Q. V., Bucer, Aretius, Pareus, Maldonatus. But in truth, since true and saving faith always has profession joined with it, Ps. 116:10, Rom. 10:10, 2 Cor. 4:13, and does not intermit it on account of fear of dangers, which was done by these, and indeed for this reason, because they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God, they postponed the glory of God, which is promised to true confessors, Matt. 10:32, and preferred the glory of men, or that which they received from men; of which they could easily be deprived through the confession of Christ, John 9:22. A truer explanation is that of those who maintain that these leaders did indeed acknowledge Christ as the Messiah, but did not embrace Him with true confidence of heart: which is the opinion of the blessed Brentius, the blessed Hunnius, the blessed Chemnitius, Harm. cap. XLV., the blessed Gerhard, Harm. cap. CXLVII., the blessed Paulus Tarnovius, Petrus Martyr, and others. Nor indeed are those phrases in Scripture, to believe someone and to believe in someone, always distinguished in such a way that the former implies mere assent and the latter confidence, as the examples of Exod. XIV. 31, Jac. II. v. 31, Joh. VII. 48, cap. VIII. 30, 31 testify. Augustin. tract. LI. in Johan. says that these princes had the beginning of faith, by which, if they had progressed, they would also have overcome the love of human glory.

ἵνα μὴ ἀποσυνάγωγοι γένωνται] Which was considered very disgraceful.

Latin:

Vers. 42.

ὅμως μέντοι) Quanquam plerique aspernabantur Jesum; quidam tamen minus contumaces satis intellexerant eum esse Christum.

καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἀρχόντων) Erat ex ipsis senatoribus quos ἄρ- χοντας solere dici notavimus.

ἐπίστευσαν εἰς αὐτὸν) Contemplativa non activa fide: con- victi de veritate, sed non ut etiam voluntatem in ejus obse- quium redigerent.

διὰ τοὺς Φαρισαίους οὐχ ὡμολόγουν) Ob Pharisæos potentes in Synedrio non audebant profiteri, ne his urgentibus ex- erceretur adversus ipsos decretum jam factum.

Non principes populi sed senatores fuisse cen- set, qui dicuntur in Christum credidisse. Sed locus ille quem in eam sententiam adducit è Matth. XIX. 15. minime id probat. Vid. quæ illic dicta. Notantur hic primates in genere tum Ecclesiastici, tum Politici: ut Luc. XIX. 18. & c. XXIII. 25. Joh. VII. 26. &c. Gravior est quæstio, Uuu- quomodo credidisse dicantur in Christum. Distinctio illa inter fidem theoreticam & practicam, sensu Grotiano accepta, nullo nititur fundamento. Nam theoreticam de assensu nudo sine fiducia intelligere videtur, practicam vero non fiduciam modo includere vult, sed etiam obedientiam praeceptorum Christi. At in Scripturis obedientia à fiducia tanquam effectus à causa distinguitur, & fructus fidei constituitur: nuspiam autem fiducia ejusmodi practica, quae obedientiam in suo formali includat, in S. literis invenitur. Neque credere in Christum dicuntur, qui notitiam solum de Christo habent, eique assensum praebent: Alii ergo de fide salvifica hunc locum exponunt; Siquidem opponatur fides horum Principum incredulitati aliorum, v. 37. & descriptio haec credere in Christum solius sit verae & salvificae fidei. Hi ergo veram quidem eorum fuisse fidem dicunt, etsi infirmam, utpote Illyricus, B. Menzerus, Tom. I. Disp. de X. cap. ad Rom. th. 47. B. Feuerbornius, affert. Doctr. de pecc. in S. S. Disput. L thes. 5. B. Affelmann. in Hept. illustr. quaestion. Q. V. Bucerus, Aretius, Pareus, Maldonatus. Verum enim vero cum fides vera & salvifica semper conjunctam habeat professionem Psal. CXVI. 10. Rom. X. 10. 2. Cor. IV. 13. neque ob metum periculorum eam intermittat, quod ab his factum, & quidem ideo, quia dilexerunt hominum gloriam magis, quam Dei gloriam, posthabuère gloriam Dei, quae promissa est veris confessoribus Matth. X. 32. & praetulère gloriam hominum, vel quae ipsis ab hominibus contigit; qua privari per confessionem Christi facile poterant, Joh. IX. 22. Verior eorum explicatio est, qui Christum quidem Messiam agnovisse hosce primores statuunt, non autem vera cordis fiducia eundem amplexos esse: Quae B. Brentii, B. Hunnii, B. Chemnitii, Harm. cap. XLV. B. Gerhardi Harm. cap. CXLVII. B. Pauli Tarnovii, Petri Martyr. & aliorum est sententia. Nec vero semper in Scriptura Phrases illae credere alicui & in aliquem ita distinguuntur, ut prior assensum nudum, posterior fiduciam inferat, uti exempla testantur Exod. XIV. 31. Jac. II. v. 31. Joh. VII. 48. cap. VIII. 30. 31. Augustin. tract. LI. in Johan. Principes hos dicit habuisse ingressum fidei, quo si profecissent, amorem quoque humanae gloriae superassent.

ἵνα μὴ ἀποσυνάγωγοι γένωνται] Quod probrosum valde habebatur.

## 12:43
Vers. 43. ἠγάπησαν γὰρ τὴν δόξαν ἀνθρώπων μᾶλλον] δόξα with the genitive in John is that of the one to whom it is shown. And so I understand δόξαν ἀνθρώπων here as their own honor, which they preferred to that honor which is owed to God: which the following words also explain, μᾶλλον ἢ is here one of opposition, not comparison, as also above ch. 3:19.

PART V. Concerning the purpose of his coming into the world.

Latin:

Vers. 43. ἠγάπησαν γὰρ τὴν δόξαν ἀνθρώπων μᾶλλον] δόξα cum genitivo apud Johannem est ejus cui exhibetur. Itaque δόξαν ἀνθρώπων hic intelligo suum honorem, quem ei honori qui Deo debetur praetulerunt: quod & sequentia explanant, μᾶλλον ἢ est hic oppositionis non comparationis, ut & supra c. 3, 19.

PARS V. De fine adventus sui in mundum.

## 12:44
Vers. 44.

Ἰησοῦς δὲ ἔκραξε] When he considered the unbelief of some and the fruitless faith of others, he strives to apply a remedy.

ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ] He trusts not so much in me as in the Father, whose ambassador I am. A similar expression is found in Mark 9:37, 1 Sam. 8:7, 1 Thess. 4:8.

But the following words teach that something more sublime is proposed by these words, namely, that he who believes in Christ believes not in him alone, but in the Father himself, because the majesty and glory of the Son and the Father are one. One worship of faith, which is owed to both the Father and the Son. Whence Fulgentius, lib. 3 ad Trasim. ch. 3, says: for the distinction of the twofold person and the profession of one substance in the Father and the Son, the Son himself said this to be taught: he who believes in me, does not believe in me, but in him who sent me.

Latin:

Vers. 44.

Ἰησοῦς δὲ ἔκραξε] Cum consideraret aliorum incredulitatem, aliorum fidem infructuosam, medicinam studet adhibere.

ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ] Non tam mihi quam Patri confidit, cujus legatus sum. Similis locutio Marc. IX. 37. 1. Sam. VIII. 7. I. Thess. IV. 8.

Atqui sublimius quid proponi hisce verbis sequentia docent, nimirum, quod qui in Christum credit, non in eum solum, sed in ipsum Patrem credat, quia una est Filii & Patris majestas & gloria. Unus cultus fidei, qui & Patri & Filio debetur. Unde Fulgentius lib. III. ad Trasim. cap. 3. ad distinctionem, inquit, geminae personae, & professionem unius substantiae in Patre & Filio, perdo- cendam ipse Filius hoc dixit: qui credit in me, non credit in me, sed in eum, qui misit me.

## 12:45
Vers. 45.

ὁ θεωρῶν ἐμὲ θεωρεῖ τὸν πέμψαντά με] So also below ch. 14:9, as if he were saying, in my works the majesty of the Father shines forth. Heb. 1:3. This was the confession of Lucian the martyr, as we touched upon above. ὁ υἱὸς τῆ Θεῦ ὀυσίας ἧς βυλῆς ἧς δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης ἀπαράλλακτος εἰκών.

If these things are understood κατ' περιχώρησιν, which implies the ὁμουσία of the Son with the Father, as in John XIV. 9, on account of which ὁμουσία he is called ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, the effulgence of the glory of the Father, Heb. I. 3, which the Confession of Lucian the martyr also respects, they are correct. But why is this Paraphrase of Christ's words rendered, 'the majesty of the Father shines in my works'? Christ is not speaking of his works, but of himself: 'he who sees me, sees him who sent me.' Therefore, in Christ himself we have the image of the Father, and the refulgence of his glory, not only in the works of Christ the resplendence of the majesty of God the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 45.

ὁ θεωρῶν ἐμὲ θεωρεῖ τὸν πέμψαντά με] Sic & infra cap. XIV. 9. quasi dicat, in meis operibus resplendet Patris majestas. Hebr. I, 3. Luciani martyris haec erat confessio ut supra attigimus. ὁ υἱὸς τῆ Θεῦ ὀυσίας ἧς βυλῆς ἧς δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης ἀπαράλλακτος εἰκών.

Si haec intelligantur κατ' περιχώρησιν, quam ὁμουσία, Filii cum Patre infert, ut Joh. XIV. 9. ob quam ὁμουσίαν dicitur ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης effulgescentia gloriae Patris Ebr. I. 3. quam respicit etiam Confessio Luciani martyris, recte se habent. Sed cur haec redditur verborum Christi Paraphrasis, in meis operibus resplendet Patris majestas? Non de operibus suis, sed de se loquitur Christus, qui me videt, videt eum qui misit me. In Christo ergo ipso habemus imaginem Patris, & refulgescentiam gloriae ejus, non solum in operibus Christi majestatis Dei Patris resplendentiam.

## 12:46
Verse 46.

ἐγὼ φῶς εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἐλήλυθα] I, the light, have shone upon men: see above c. 1, 9. c. 3, 19. c. 8, 12. Is. XLII. 6.

ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ μὴ μείνῃ] He does not dwell in darkness, in ignorance of good things, and in most grievous errors. We have spoken about the word μένειν in c. 3, 36. c. 8, 31. The opposite is ἐν φωτὶ μένειν, to dwell in the light, 1 Ep. II. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 46.

ἐγὼ φῶς εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἐλήλυθα] Ego lux affulsi hominibus: supra c. 1, 9. c. 3, 19. c. 8, 12. Es. XLII. 6.

ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ μὴ μείνῃ] Non versatur in tenebris, in rerum bonarum ignorantia, gravissimisque erroribus. De voce μένειν diximus c. 3, 36. c. 8, 31. Contrarium est ἐν φωτὶ μένειν versari in luce 1. Ep. II. 10.

## 12:47
Verse 47.

κ' μὴ φυλάξῃ] Some codices have it thus, and that most ancient one in England. The Syriac, the Latin, and Nonnus follow it. Wherefore this reading of the Vulgate, πιστεύσῃ, which the Arabic follows, seems to be preferred, so that this may be said properly of those who were hearing, that is, they believed the sermon of Christ to be true, but did not observe it, that is, they did not profess themselves his disciples. Above v. 42.

The Vulgate reading ἐ μὴ πιστεύσῃ is altogether to be preferred, as it is found in very many and most approved copies, and it also fits best. For just as the only medium through which we are freed from darkness was indicated before, so now the proper and adequate cause of damnation is expressed, which is incredulity; when this is posited, damnation is posited, because through incredulity the satisfaction of Christ is repudiated, by which alone we are freed from damnation, John III. 18, 36, c. XIV. 9, and here below v. 48.

ἐγὼ ὀ κρίνω αὐτὸν] I pronounce nothing harsher against him: as above c. 8, 15.

ὐ γὰρ ἦλθον ἵνα κρίνω τὸν κόσμον] That is not my primary purpose: ὐκ ἐπὶ τῦτο τὸ προηγύμενον, I willingly abstain from such things. Thus above c. 3, 17.

ἀλλ' ἵνα σώσω τὸν κόσμον] This I do uniquely, this I desire, that no one should perish, but that all should come to repentance, so that they may be saved perpetually, 2 Pet. III. 9.

Κρίνειν here does not properly signify to sustain the person of a judge, but to provide the matter for judging and condemning. Indeed, Christ removes judgment and condemnation from himself, and ascribes it to the incredulity of men, because they perish by their own fault; he himself is not the author of their condemnation: he transfers the action of judgment from himself to his sermon, which, if not received by faith, judges, because the neglect or contempt of the word is the cause of condemnation, John XV. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 47.

κ' μὴ φυλάξῃ] Ita habent quidam codices, & ille in Anglia antiquissimus. Sequitur Syrus, Latinus, Nonnus. Quare haec lectio vulgatae πιστεύσῃ quam sequitur Arabs, praeferenda videtur, ut hoc proprie in eos dictum sit qui audiebant, id est, verum credebant Christi sermonem, sed non observabant, id est, se ejus discipulos non profitebantur. Supra v. 42.

Praeferenda omnino vulgata lectio ἐ μὴ πιστεύσῃ, utpote quam habent plurima, & probatissima exemplaria, quae etiam optime congruit. Nam ut antea medium unicum, per quod a tenebris liberamur, indicatum, ita propria jam & adaequata causa damnationis exprimitur, quae est incredulitas; qua posita ponitur damnatio, quia per incredulitatem repudiatur satisfactio Christi, qua sola liberamur a damnatione Joh. III. 18. 36. c. XIV. 9. & hic infra v. 48.

ἐγὼ ὀ κρίνω αὐτὸν] Nihil de illo durius pronuntio: ut supra c. 8, 15.

ὐ γὰρ ἦλθον ἵνα κρίνω τὸν κόσμον] Non id mihi praecipue propositum est: ὐκ ἐπὶ τῦτο τὸ προηγύμενον, libenter talibus abstineo. Sic supra c. 3, 17.

ἀλλ' ἵνα σώσω τὸν κόσμον] Hoc unice ago, hoc desidero, ne quisquam pereat, sed omnes ad resipiscentiam veniant, ut perpetuo serventur, 2. Pet. III. 9.

Κρίνειν hic proprie non significat judicis personam sustinere, sed materiam judicandi & damnandi praebere. Nimirum removet Christus judicium & condemnationem a se, eamque adscribit incredulitati hominum, quod illi propria culpa pereant; ipse vero condemnationis eorum autor non sit: transfert judicii actionem a se ad suum sermonem, qui fide non receptus judicat, quia neglectus vel contemtus verbi causa condemnationis est, Joh. XV. 22.

## 12:48
Verse 48.

ὁ ἀθετῶν ἐμὲ κ' μὴ λαμβάνων τὰ ῥήματά μυ] This is an allusion to the passage in Deut. XVIII. 19. ὃς ἐ' ἂν μὴ ἀκύσῃ ὅσα ἂν λαλήσῃ ὁ προφήτης ἐκεῖνος ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματί μυ, ἐγὼ ἐκδικήσω ἐξ ἀυτῦ, however, λαμβάνειν means to embrace as above in chapter 1, verse 12, and chapter 3, verse 11.

ἔχει τὸν κρίνοντα αὐτὸν] The following words explain what he says; he carries his judge with him, even if I am silent.

ὁ λόγος ὃν ἐλάλησα ἐκεῖνος κρινεῖ αὐτὸν] Just as the Ninevites are said to be future witnesses, Matt. XII. 4, and Moses an accuser, above c. 5, 45, so here the Gospel will condemn the unbelievers, having been spurned, since it contains nothing in itself that is not most worthy of admiration and veneration. See above c. 2, 9, and below c. 15, 22.

Thus some say that the word of Christ will judge by way of a witness and an accuser: that is to say, because they were unwilling to receive through faith the word which they heard from me, therefore that word will stand as a certain witness against them, and will accuse them and cry out, as it were, that they are worthy of condemnation. But he wished rather to express the cause of condemnation, which is unbelief, because they are to be judged on account of the contempt of the word: and also the norm and rule according to which the judgment is to be instituted. But as to the fact that he says his word will condemn them, although it is not the word, but the contempt of the word, that is the cause of condemnation, he wishes to signify by this that the word offered will take away every excuse from the unbelievers. Therefore, also, the judgment will be instituted according to the word or speech of Christ as a certain rule, Rom. II. 16, when the unbelievers are to be judged according to the norm of that word which is held in John III. 36. He who does not believe in the Son will not have life, but the wrath of God will remain upon him, Mark XVI. 15, he who has not believed will be condemned: such things are contained throughout the Apostolic and Prophetic Scriptures, which likewise comprehend the word of Christ, because they have proceeded from the Spirit of Christ. Whence the word of God comprehended in Holy Scripture is deservedly to be acknowledged as the voice of the judge and the norm of judgment, even in controversies of faith. For if the judgment of condemnation on the last day is rightly attributed to the word of Christ proposed in Scripture, then certainly the judgment of discretion to be conducted in the Church in causes of religion will also be deservedly attributed to it. Through which, and in which, Christ speaks with us, and sets forth to us his judgment concerning controversies of faith, that can be called the voice of the judge, and the norm of judgment, and in a sound sense even the judge. That indeed is done through the word, and in the word of Scripture, whence Augustine, lib. de grat. & liber. Arbitr. cap. 18, disputing against the Pelagians, says, Let the Apostle John sit as judge, and II. de nupt. & concupisc. cap. 33. This controversy requires a JUDGE. But who will be the JUDGE? Let Christ judge, let the Apostle judge with him, because Christ himself speaks in the Apostle.

ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῇ ἡμέρᾳ] At which time not only the deeds of all, but also their thoughts will be laid bare, and the vision of Isaiah mentioned above in the former place will be most perfectly fulfilled.

Latin:

Vers. 48.

ὁ ἀθετῶν ἐμὲ κ' μὴ λαμβάνων τὰ ῥήματά μυ] Allusio est ad locum Deut. XVIII. 19. ὃς ἐ' ἂν μὴ ἀκύσῃ ὅσα ἂν λαλήσῃ ὁ προφήτης ἐκεῖνος ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματί μυ, ἐγὼ ἐκδικήσω ἐξ ἀυτῦ, est autem λαμβάνειν amplecti ut supra cap. 1. v. 12. cap. 3. v. 11.

ἔχει τὸν κρίνοντα αὐτὸν] Quid dicat explicant sequentia; secum fert judicem suum vel me tacente.

ὁ λόγος ὃν ἐλάλησα ἐκεῖνος κρινεῖ αὐτὸν] Sicut Ninevitae dicuntur testes futuri, Matth. XII. 4. Moses accusator, supra c. 5, 45. sic hic Evangelium condemnaturum incredulos, spretum scilicet, cum nihil in se habeat quod non admiratione ac veneratione sit dignissimum. Vide supra c. 2, 9. & infra c. 15, 22.

Ita nonnulli sermonem Christi judicaturum ajunt per modum testis, & accusatoris: q.d. quia sermonem, quem a me audierunt, per fidem recipere noluerunt, ideo sermo ille velut testis quidam adversus eos stabit, eosque accusabit ac clamabit quasi, dignos esse condemnatione. Sed causam exprimere potius voluit condemnationis, quae est incredulitas, quod ob comtemtum verbi judicandi sint: nec non normam & regulam, juxta quam judicium instituendum. Quod ve- ro ait sermonem suum condem Naturum ipsos, etsi non sermo, sed comtemtus sermonis causa sit condemnationis, eo significare vult, sermonem oblatum omnem infidelibus excusationem adem- turum. Ideo etiam juxta verbum vel sermonem Christi ceu regulam aliquam instituetur judicium Rom. II. 16. quum increduli juxta normam verbi illius, quod habetur Johan. III. 36. Qui non credit Filio, vitam non habebit, sed ira Dei mane- bit super ipsum, Marc. XVI. 15. qui non crediderit condemnabitur, judicandi sint: qualia passim in Scripturis Apostolicis & Propheticis, quae itidem sermonem Christi comprehendunt, quia a Spi- ritu Christi profecta sunt, continentur. Unde verbum Dei Scriptura sacra comprehensum pro judicis voce & norma judicii, etiam in controver- siis fidei merito agnoscendum. Si enim judicium condemnationis in extremo die sermoni Christi in scriptura proposito recte tribuitur, utique & judicium discretionis in causis religionis in Eccle- sia gerendum ei merito tribuetur. Per quod, & in quo Christus nobiscum loquitur, & suum judi- cium de controversiis fidei nobis exponit, illud vox judicis, & norma judicii, ac sano sensu etiam judex dici potest. Id vero fit per verbum, & in verbo scripturae, unde Augustinus lib. de grat. & liber. Arbitr. cap. 18. contra Pelagianos dispu- tans, Sedeat, inquit, judex Apostolus Johannes, & II. de nupt. & concupisc. cap. 33. Ista contro- versia JUDICEM requirit. At quis JUDEX e- rit? Judicet Christus, judicet cum illo & Aposto- lus, quia in Apostolo ipse loquitur Christus.

ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῇ ἡμέρᾳ] Quo tempore omnium non facta tan- tum, sed & cogitata nudabuntur, & perfectissime adim- plebitur Esaiae visio supra priore loco memorata.

## 12:49
Verse 49.

ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐξ ἐμαυτῦ οὐκ ἐλάλησα] I said it is best translated by 'for', in this sense: For certainly I speak nothing to you as if discovered from myself, but as commanded by the Father: understand, in which matter it was necessary to believe me both because of the works and because of the holiness of the precepts. Take ἀπ' ἐμαυτῦ as above c. 7, 17. and below c. 14, 10.

ὁ πέμψας με πατὴρ αὐτός μοι ἐντολὴν ἔδωκε τί εἴπω καὶ τί λα- λήσω] The Prophets, and among them Isaiah, were moved at certain times by the divine spirit. I, however, always have him in me, so that not only when I teach (for that is what the word אמר signifies to the Hebrews) but when I even speak anything incidentally, I follow the prescription of the Father, ἐντολὴν as above c. X. 18.

These could seem to be distinct, τί εἴπω καὶ λα- λῶ, and by some they are distinguished, but because Christ after the word λαλεῖν comprehends everything, these are more correctly held as synonyms in this place than distinguished: however, ἐντολὴ does not denote the precepts of Christ, in the way that Maldonatus and Salmero attempt to infer from this, that the observance of the commandments of God is the meritorious cause of eternal life, because it is added ἡ ἐντολὴ αὐτοῦ ζωὴ αἰώ- νιός ἐστιν, but by the name of commandment is understood metonymically the doctrine of the Gospel, which he announced to the world from the command of the heavenly Father, as the words themselves sound, he himself gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak; which Grotius also acknowledges, explaining those things in such a way that Christ wishes to say this, that the Gospel is the cause of eternal life. Cf. John VI. 68. c. XVII. 3. Acts V. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 49.

ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐξ ἐμαυτῦ οὐκ ἐλάλησα] Dixi optime verti per nam, hoc sensu: Nam certe nihil vobis tanquam ex me reper- tum, sed tanquam a patre mandatum loquor: subintellige, qua in re credi mihi & ob opera & ob praeceptorum sancti- tatem oportuit. ἀπ' ἐμαυτῦ sume ut supra c. 7, 17. & in- fra c. 14, 10.

ὁ πέμψας με πατὴρ αὐτός μοι ἐντολὴν ἔδωκε τί εἴπω καὶ τί λα- λήσω] Prophetae & inter eos Esaias certis temporibus mo- vebantur divino spiritu. Ego vero eum semper in me ha- beo, ita ut non tantum cum doceo (nam id vox אמר He- braeis significat) sed cum quidvis etiam obiter loquor, se- quar Patris praescriptum, ἐντολὴν ut supra c. X. 18.

Possent haec videri distincta, τί εἴπω καὶ λα- λῶ, & a nonnullis distinguuntur, sed quia Christus post vocem λαλεῖν omnia complectitur, rectius haec pro Synonymis hoc loco habentur, quam distinguuntur: ἐντολὴ autem non notat praecepta Christi, quemadmodum Maldonatus & Salmero hinc inferre conantur, observatio- nem mandatorum Dei esse causam meritoriam vi- tae aeternae, quia additur ἡ ἐντολὴ αὐτοῦ ζωὴ αἰώ- νιός ἐστιν, sed intelligitur mandati nomine meto- nymice doctrina Evangelii, quam ex mandato Pa- tris coelestis mundo annunciavit, ut ipsa verba sonant, ipse mihi mandatum dedit, quid dicam, & quid loquar; quod agnoscit etiam Grotius il- la ita explicans, quod velit Christus hoc dicere, Evangelium esse causam vitæ æternæ. Conf. Joh. VI. 68. c. XVII. 3. Act. V. 20.

## 12:50
Verse 50.

ἡ ἐντολὴ ἀυτῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιός ἐστι] The effect for the cause: for he wishes to say that the Gospel is the cause of eternal life. Thus Christ said he was life, above c. 11, 25. and below c. 14, 6. Thus also the word of God is called life, Deut. XXXIII. 47.

ἃ ὖν λαλῶ ἐγὼ, καθὼς εἴρηκέ μοι ὁ πατὴρ, ὕτω λαλῶ] Understand: and thus they are to be received by you.

Latin:

Vers. 50.

ἡ ἐντολὴ ἀυτῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιός ἐστι] Effectus pro causâ: vult enim dicere Evangelium causam esse vitæ æternæ. Sic Christus se vitam dixit, supra c. 11, 25. & infra c. 14, 6. Sic & verbum Dei vita dicitur Deut. XXXIII. 47.

ἃ ὖν λαλῶ ἐγὼ, καθὼς εἴρηκέ μοι ὁ πατὴρ, ὕτω λαλῶ] Subaudi & sic à vobis accipienda sunt.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

When Jesus knew that the time of his departure to the Father had come, intending to testify his love toward his own, although the Father had delivered all things into his hands, he washed his disciples' feet after supper; which Peter at first refused twice, but being warned that otherwise he would have no communion with the Lord, he sought to have not only his feet, but also his hands and head washed: Jesus, however, testified that they were indeed clean, but not all, because he knew his betrayer: then indeed he exhorted them to the imitation of his example, because a servant is not greater than his master, and again he warned them concerning him who, according to the scripture (Ps. 41:10), was about to trample him with his feet, and concerning receiving him, and being troubled in spirit a third time, he spoke of his betrayer, whereupon he gave the sign of the dipped morsel to the disciple nearest to him, who was asking about it at the prompting of Peter, upon which Satan entered into Judas: but Jesus himself said to his betrayer, what you are going to do, do quickly, but the disciples did not perceive the meaning of what was said. But when Judas went out at night, he preached to his disciples concerning the glorification of the Son of Man and his own imminent departure, and gave them a commandment concerning mutual love, but to Peter, when he protested that he would follow Jesus, he predicted that he would follow him at some time, but now would deny him three times before the cock crowed. There are four parts: I. The washing of the disciples' feet, to v. 17. II. The repeated signification of the betrayal, and the designation of the betrayer, to v. 30. III. A discourse concerning his own glorification and the duty of mutual love, to v. 35. IV. The prediction concerning the triple denial of Peter, to v. 38.

PART I. The washing of the disciples' feet.

Vers. 1.

πρὸ δὲ τῆς ἑορτῆς] It was that evening from which the νυχθήμερον (day and night) of the preparation began.

Understand the preparation not in relation to the Passover of Christ, but of the Jews. For it is evident from Matt. 26:17, Mark 14:12, Luke 22:7 that Christ had already eaten the Passover on the first day of unleavened bread. Casaubon notes here at this place: Those who take the words of John concerning that Passover which Christ himself celebrated do not notice that they are the authors of a most absurd opinion. For if Christ kept the Passover before the feast of the Passover, that is, before its legitimate time had arrived, he therefore did not keep the law, nor was he a fulfiller, but a transgressor of the law, which it is impious even to think, let alone absurd.

Uuu 2

The hour that he should depart] That time suitable to the name of the Passover, which signifies a passing over: a most opportune time for death because of the greatest gathering of the people, by which the matter might be more attested. ἐκ τῦ κόσμυ τύτε πρὸς τὸν πατέρα] By death, of course, which was the first step toward that transition. ἀγαπήσας τὺς ἰδίυς τὺς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ] Those who had received his teaching, especially those twelve. Moreover, it is effectively said, "those in the world," whom he was about to leave in this sea of affairs. Thus below c. 17, 11. εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτὸς] That is, he continued to love them to the end. Thus this expression is used in Psalm 9:19, Psalm 44:34, and elsewhere. The Apostle prefaces this, however, to signify that Christ subjected himself to such a vile ministry for this reason, that he might most evidently show his love. That we have said the ministry is vile appears in 1 Sam. 25:41, which passage Josephus applying says: "Unworthy, he said, even to touch the feet of those of him." In the Oracle given to the Milesians in Herodotus: "And your wives shall wash the feet of the long-haired." Plutarch, to show that Favonius was most obedient to Pompey after the defeat, says thus: "And for the rest, from that time he continued to busy himself and serve him, as much as slaves do masters, even to the washing of feet and the preparation of dinner." The same author on the virtues of women: "They served each other's parents and brothers even to the washing of their feet." Catullus:

Which slave-girl might serve you with pleasant labor, soothing your white feet with liquid waters.

But not to refuse so vile a ministry is of great love, Luke 7:44, 1 Tim. 5:10.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Iesus quum sciret advenisse tempus abitus sui ad Patrem, amorem erga suos testaturus, etsi Pater ipsi omnia tradiderat, discipulis suis post cœnam pedes lavit; quod primum bis renuens Petrus, at monitus, se alias non habiturum communionem cum Domino, non pedes tantum, sed manus etiam & caput ablui expetebat: testatus autem Iesus est, mundos quidem ipsos esse, sed non omnes, quia norat proditorem suum: tum vero eos ad imitationem exempli sui hortatus, quia servus non major est domino, iterumque de eo qui se juxta scripturam (Psal. XLI. 10.) pedibus suis conculcaturus sit, & de se suscipiendo monuit, tertiumque contristatus spiritu, de suo proditore egit, unde discipulo, ei proximo, instinctu Petri de illo quærente, signum intinctus frusti dedit, ad quod in Iudam ingressus est Satanas: Ipse vero proditori suo dixit, quod vis facere fac cito, at dicti mentem haud perceperunt discipuli. Exeunte autem Iuda sub noctem, de glorificatione filii hominis, & de imminente abitu suo discipulis suis prædicavit, eisq; mandatum de dilectione mutua dedit, Petro vero, quum protestaretur se Iesum sequuturum, prædixit, ipsum aliquando sequuturum, jam vero ter se abnegaturum, priusquam Gallus cantarit. Partes sunt quatuor: I. Pedum discipulorum lotio, ad v. 17. II. Iterata proditionis significatio, & proditoris designatio, ad v. 30. III. Concio de sui glorificatione & dilectionis mutuæ debito, ad v. 35. IV. Prædictio de trina abnegatione Petri, ad v. 38.

PARS I. Pedum discipulorum lotio.

Vers. 1.

πρὸ δὲ τῆς ἑορτῆς] Erat vespera illa à qua incipiebat τὸ νυχθήμερον τῆς παρασκευῆς.

Parascceven intellige non ratione Paschatos Christi, sed Judæorum. Nam Christus primo die azymorum jam Pascha manducasse è Matth. XXVI. 17. Marc. XIV. 12. Luc. XXII. 7. constat. Notat hic Casaubonus ad h. l. Qui verba Johannis de eo Paschate accipiunt, quod ipse Christus celebravit autores se esse absurdissimæ sententiæ non animadvertunt. Nam si Pascha egit Christus ante festum Paschatos, hoc est, antequam ejus ritus legitimum tempus advenisset, non igitur servavit legem neque πληρωτὴς, sed παραβάτης τῦ νόμυ, quod etiam cogitare imperium est, nedum absurdum.

Uuu 2

ἡ ὥρα ἵνα μεταβῇ] Tempus illud conveniens nomini Paschatis, quod διάβασιν significat: tempus opportunissi- mum morti ob maximum populi conventum quo res esset testatior. ἐκ τῦ κόσμυ τύτε πρὸς τὸν πατέρα] Per mortem scilicet, qui primus erat ad eum transitum gradus. ἀγαπήσας τὺς ἰδίυς τὺς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ] Eos qui discipli- nam suam receperant, præcipue duodecim illos. Est autem efficaciter dictum τὺς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, quos relicturus erat in hoc rerum salo. Sic infra c. 17, 11. εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτὸς] Id est διατέλη ἀγαπῶν perrexit eos diligere. Sic locutio hæc usurpatur Psal. IX. 19. Psal. XLIV. 34. & alibi. Hoc autem ideo præfatur Apostolus, ut significet ideo tam vili ministerio Christum se subjecisse, ut amorem suum evidentissime ostenderet. Quod diximus vile esse ministerium apparet I. Sam. XXV. 41. quem locum Josephus applicans: ἀναξία μὲν ἔφη κὶ ποδῶν ἅψασθαι τῶν ἐκείνυ. In Oraculo Milesiis dato apud Herodotum: Συὶ δ᾽ ἄλοχοι πολέεσσι πόδας νίψυσι κομήταις. Plutarchus Pompejo Favonium post cladem obsequentissi- mum fuisse ut ostendat sic ait: Καὶ τὸ λοιπὸν ἐκ τύτυ περίσ- πων κὶ θεραπεύων, ὅσα δεσπότας δῦλοι μέχρι τίψεως ποδῶν κὶ δειπνῦ παρασκευῆς διετέλεσεν. Idem de virtutibus mulierum: διηκονῦντο τοῖς ἀλλήλων γονεῦσι κὶ ἀδελφοῖς ἄχρι τῦ κὶ τὺς πό- δας ἀπονίζειν. Catullus:

Quæ tibi jucundo famularet serva labore Candida permulcens liquidis vestigia lymphis.

Tam vile autem ministerium non detrectare magnæ est di- lectionis, Luc. VII. 44. I. Tim. V. 10.

## 13:2
Ver. 2.

And when supper was ended] At that former supper, at which Christ did not indeed eat the slaughtered lamb, but yet as he could, he celebrated the memory of the Passover by the rite of the Babylonian exile: which supper did not have a washing before it: for it was not a proper supper, but an image of a supper. See what [is said] to Matthew.

The former supper seems to Grotius to be the Passover itself, because he says that at that former supper Christ did not indeed eat the slaughtered lamb, but only celebrated the memory of the Passover by the rite of the Babylonian exile: this is, as he explained at Matthew, that he celebrated not a sacrificial Passover but a commemorative one (which invention we have refuted there) in which a Paschal lamb was not accustomed to be eaten, but only something of unleavened bread with bitter herbs. But what the latter supper was, Grotius does not explain, except that he later calls the same a proper supper. I will not say that the Paschal supper is thus confused with the "dismissory" [meal], as they call it, and the second courses, according to the rites which Joseph Scaliger observes from the Rabbis, lib. 6 de emend. tempor. page 372. For he teaches that this supper, which was accustomed to follow the Passover among the Jews, was nothing other than a certain salad of endives and wild lettuces, the juice of which, because it is sad and bitter, they made into a sauce with vinegar and other things, into which the unleavened bread and those bitter herbs were dipped. Although in other solemnities (Pentecost and the Feast of Tabernacles) the Jews would prepare another supper, which they call the dismissory or second courses with sweetmeats, after the feasts of the sacrifice or the slaughtered victim were finished, yet in the Passover the guests were forbidden every kind of sweetmeat, and they were obliged to be content only with that sauce, according to Scaliger: which was followed by the cup of praise or thanksgiving, but after that it was forbidden to take any food or drink. Therefore, that which Grotius wants, that a proper supper was still accustomed to be celebrated after the sacrificial Passover, as also after the commemorative one which he invented, Scaliger teaches that this is contrary to the Paschal Canon of the Jews. But whatever may be the case regarding the rites and canon of the Jews, for we cannot yet agree with Scaliger that the Passover was celebrated by Christ with the same rite as by the Jews, namely that which the Canons in the Talmudic Digests designate, especially since he seems to make the eating of the Paschal lamb the supper, and describes the supper that followed through the dipping of the unleavened bread, according to the Jewish rite; which shadows of the Paschal supper, namely the invention of a Passover by the Jews, and one accustomed to be celebrated without the Paschal lamb (which Grotius calls a commemorative Passover), agree not with the Passover celebrated by Christ: inasmuch as it was performed neither without the Paschal lamb, nor without bitter herbs and unleavened bread, but with the Paschal lamb eaten with bitter herbs and unleavened bread, according to the divine institution. Nor can we add our vote to Scaliger in that which he hands down concerning the repeated washing of feet. For Scaliger has it thus: For no one will deny that this last (Passover) was similar to the remaining preceding ones, and the preceding ones were celebrated by Christ with the same rite as by the Jews. Therefore, both those and this last were celebrated with the rite which we have explained. For the washing was also repeated, as in other Passovers, first indeed from daily custom, so that he might recline and eat the lamb, then when supper was ended, from the rite of the Passover. Peter, therefore, does not marvel that it is necessary to wash again, as one who knew that in the first of the Unleavened Bread this was accustomed to be done, and the washing to be repeated, but that a disciple is served by the Master, a servant by the Lord, a little man by the true God. Again, there is a double supper in succession, since two washings precede each, one ordinary, in which the lamb is also eaten: the other, because of the breaking of the unleavened bread, and the dipping of the unleavened bread in the dish of sauce, John 13:26. Scaliger indeed tries to prove these things, but without success: If, he says, Christ, as certain enemies of good letters maintain, did not bind himself to the rites of the Jews: why therefore are all things done here which exist in the Jewish ritual? Why are all things most similar? But those who are enemies of superstitions and rites introduced by the Jews against the divine law are not going to be enemies of good letters, nor do they believe that Christ, having left the law of God, bound himself to the same. We judge it to be far from the truth that all things which exist in the Jewish ritual were observed by Christ; for as has been said, Christ did not celebrate the Passover without the Paschal lamb, as the Jews celebrate it: nor did he eat the Paschal lamb according to the ritual of the Jews without unleavened bread and bitter herbs: nor is any word found among the Evangelists concerning a double washing of feet, indeed not even concerning a common supper celebrated after the Paschal supper, nor is there a command held in the divine law, nor can anything solid be taught from the Evangelical History: to say nothing of other things, which teach that all things which were observed by Christ are not very similar, but very different. I feel entirely this way, that the sacred text has only been obscured by those who judged that Jewish rites were observed by Christ, and who dug them out from their rituals, whereas with those left aside, it is sufficiently clear and transparent, and thus involved in no difficulties.

τẽ διαβόλε ἤδη βεβληκότ@ [the devil having already put into the heart of Judas] Here also that βεβληκότ@ is to be understood with effect, namely that Judas received this counsel of the Devil. We have already observed a similar manner of speaking several times above. Thus Satan is said to tempt when one succumbs to temptation, I Cor. VII. v. 5.

ἵνα ἀυτὸν παραδῷ [that he might betray him] This also has emphasis. With the plan of betraying already taken, and with the danger so near, he did not omit to testify his care for the disciples, even for that wicked one, if by chance he might still repent.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

κὶ δείπνε γενομένε] Cœna illa priore, qua non agnum quidem mactatum edit Christus, sed tamen ut potuit ritu Babylonici exsilii memoriam Paschatis celebravit: quæ cœ- na non habebat ante se lotionem: nam non erat cœna ju- sta, sed cœnæ imago. Vide quæ ad Matth.

Cœna prior videtur Grotio esse ipsum Pascha, quia cœna illa priore ait non agnum qui- dem mactatum edisse Christum, sed tantum ritu Ba- bylonici exsilii memoriam Paschatis celebrasse: hoc est, ut ad Matthæum exposuit, celebrasse non Pa- scha θύσιμον sed μνημονευτικὸν (quod commen- tum ibi profligavimus) in quo non agnus Pascha- lis comedi consueverit, sed solum aliquid azy- morum herbis amaris. Posterior vero cœna, qualis fuerit, Grotius non explicat, nisi quod eandem cœnam justam postea dicat.
