Then that 'that' is commonly to be referred to 'you ask,' so that it may cohere more correctly with the preceding: whatever you ask, by which the Son and through the Son the Father may be able to be glorified, that I will give effect to for you. 'In my name,' that is, whatever you will pray the Father to do for my sake. The Hebrews, when praying to God, were accustomed to ask that He would benefit the people for the sake of the Fathers, for the sake of Abraham, for the sake of Isaac, for the sake of Jacob, for the sake of David. A new manner of praying is now taught through Christ, Romans 1:8.

There is no reason why that 'that' should not be referred to the immediately preceding 'I will do this,' so that he promises that he will perform or effect all things, so that the Father may be glorified in him: because from this the Father is glorified by the Son, when we acknowledge that we obtain from the Father through the Son the Mediator whatever we ask according to His will. Nor is 'in my name' only 'for my sake,' 'on account of me,' much less to be explained from those prayers when the ancients asked that He would benefit the people for the sake of Abraham, for the sake of Isaac, etc. (in the Grotius sense), because no one merited anything for the people: nor did they ask to be heard for the sake of Abraham, Isaac, etc., in any other sense than that they hoped for a hearing because of the promise made to Abraham and the other Fathers, in which promise the Messiah was entirely included, whence they vowed that their prayers were grateful and ratified for the sake of Christ promised to the Patriarchs: just as Daniel asked to be heard for the sake of the Lord, ch. 9:12. But 'for the sake of Christ' is for the sake of Christ's merit, which is accustomed to be designated by the phrase 'in the name of Christ,' because in the name of Christ the remission of sins and life is communicated and obtained, that is, through the merit of Christ, Luke 24:47, John 20:31, Acts 10:43. Compare John 16:23, Acts 4:12. Therefore, this is not a new manner of praying, except insofar as one must now pray in the name of this Jesus, whereas the ancients, who lived before Jesus was born and did not know him, but longed to see his day, prayed in the name of the promised Messiah: for since Jesus is that promised Messiah, John 20:31, they can be said to have prayed in his name thus far, because they believed, sought, and expected that they would obtain every blessing and every grace not outside the Messiah, but in him: however much they did not know Jesus of Nazareth regarding his human existence, much less believe in him in that way: since he was only to come and manifest himself in the fullness of time.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἀμὴν Ἀμὴν] Pergit consolari.

Τὰ ἔργα ἃ ἐγὼ ποιῶ κ' ἀκεῖνος ποιήσει] Daemonas ejiciet, morbos sanabit, mortuos resuscitabit. Intelligenda au- tem haec promissio secundum ea quae dicta sunt ad Marcum XVI. 17.

Καὶ μείζονα τούτων ποιήσει] Omni genere linguarum lo- quetur ad conversionem omnium gentium. Maximum si- gnum, ut Chrysostomus notat, gloriae Christi quod per ab- sentem fierent quae praesens non effecerat.

Rectius majora intelligit Brentius non ratione formae vel qualitatis, sed ratione efficaciae & fru- ctus praeconii uberioris. Conf. quae ad Act. V. 16. Ita Rupertus de conversione innumerorum per varietatem linguarum, interpretabatur. Origenes Hom. VI. in Es. Opera facietis majora, quia ego feci resurgere ex mortuis corporaliter: Vos resurgere facietis ex mortuis spiritualiter. Ego caecis sensibile hoc lumen infudi: Vos spiritualem lucem non videntibus dabi- tis. Alibi, nimirum Hom. VII. in Num. ita ha- bet Origenes: Vere majus mihi videtur, quod homo in carne positus, fragilis & caducus, fide tamen Christi ac verbo ejus accinctus superet Gigantes & Daemo- niorum legiones; quamvis ipse sit, qui vincit in no- bis, plus tamen est quod per nos, quam quod per se vincit.

Ὅτι ἐγὼ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μυ πορεύομαι; κὴ ὅ, τι ἂν αἰτήση- τε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μυ, τῦτο ποιήσω· ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ] Haec ita uno spiritu legenda sunt & notandi Hebraismi, πορεύομαι κὴ ποιήσω id est profectus efficiam. Similitudo sumta ab eo qui ad regem profectus coram commendat a- micorum desideria. Deinde illud ἵνα communiter referen- dum ad αἰτήσητε ut rectius cum superioribus cohaereat: quic- quid postulaveritis quo Filius & per Filium Pater inclaresce- re possint, id ego pro vobis effectum dabo. ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μυ id est quicquid orabitis Patrem ut mea causa faciat. Solebant Hebraei Deum orantes rogare ut populo benefaceret, ob Patres, ob Abrahamum, ob Isaacum, ob Jacobum, ob Davi- dem. Nova nunc docetur orandi ratio per Christum Rom. 1. 8.

Nulla ratio est, cur non ἵνα illud referendum ad proxime antecedens τοῦτο ποιήσω, ut omnia se praestiturum, vel effecturum promittat, ut glori- ficetur in se Pater: quia hinc a Filio Pater glorifi- catur, cum agnoscimus nos per Filium Mediato- rem a Patre impetrare, quicquid secundum vo- luntatem ejus petimus. Neque ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου est tantum mei causa, ob me, nedum explicandum ex illis precibus, cum rogarunt veteres, ut popu- lo benefaceret ob Abrahamum, ob Isaacum, &c. (sensu Grotiano) quia nemo quicquam populo pro- meruit: nec ob Abrahamum, Isaacum, &c. pe- tebant exaudiri alio sensu, quam quod ob promis- sionem Abrahamo, aliisque Patribus factam spera- rint exauditionem, in qua promissione omnino includebatur Messias, unde ob Christum Patriar- chis promissum gratas, & ratas esse preces suas i- ta vovebant: quemadmodum Daniel petiit exau- diri propter Dominum c. IX. 12. Ob Christum autem est ob Christi meritum, quod phrasi in nomine Christi designari solet, quia in nomine Christi re- missio peccatorum & vita communicatur, & obti- netur, id est, per meritum Christi, Luc. XXIV. 47. Joh. XX. 31. Actor. X. 43. Conf. Joh. XVI. 23. Act. IV. 12. Non ergo nova haec orandi ratio est, nisi quatenus in Jesu hujus nomine orandum nunc est, quum orarint Veteres, qui ante Jesum natum vi- xere, eumque non agnoverunt, sed diem ejus videre exoptarunt, in nomine promissi Messiae: Quum enim Jesus sit promissus ille Messias, Joh. XX. 31. hactenus in ejus nomine orasse dici pos- sunt, quia non extra Messiam, sed in eo omnem benedictionem, omnemque gratiam obtingere crediderunt, expetierunt, & expectarunt: utut Jesum Nazarenum quoad humanam existentiam non noverint, nedum ita in eundem crediderint: quum in temporis plenitudine demum venire, se- que manifestare debuerit.

## 14:14
Verse 14. I will do] He repeats this to confirm their hope more, that he himself, being so well known to them, will have the power to grant all things effected.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ἐγὼ ποιήσω] Repetit hoc ut magis spem eorum confirmet, quod ipse adeo ipsis notus omnia effecta dandi sit habiturus potestatem.

## 14:15
Verse 15. If you love me] Do not show love by mourning, but by obedience.

Keep my commandments] Especially that one concerning mutual love. Thus in Acts 2, before the mission of the Holy Spirit is narrated, it is set before it: 'they were all with one accord in one place.' Therefore, by this way especially they were being prepared to receive that Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με] Ne luctu ostendite amorem, sed obedientia.

Τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσατε] Praesertim illam de mu- tua dilectione. Sic Act. II. antequam narretur missio Spir. S. praeponitur ea, ἦσαν πάντες ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἐπ᾽ τὸ αὐτὸ. Itaque hac praecipue ratione ad accipiendum eum spiritum para- bantur.

## 14:16
Verse 16. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete] And here the latter part is to be repeated in the former. I will pray that he may give you the Spirit, and he will give, namely if you persevere in the obedience of the commandments. 'To ask' for 'to pray' is frequent in these books. Luke 14:18 and elsewhere. But Christ now prays not with suppliant tears in this life, but by that authority which he sought for himself by the obedience of death. 'Paraclete' is a Greek word frequent among the Jews in the Chaldean version and among the Talmudists, not for a comforter, but for one who pleads a cause, and indeed for the defendant. For he who speaks for the accuser is called by another Greek word, κατηγόρος. Therefore, Christ promises another advocate who may plead the cause of his own before the world, just as he himself is about to plead before the Father. For in this sense he himself is a Paraclete, 1 John 2:2, and what he just said, that he would intercede for his own before the Father, is a circumlocution of the office of Paraclete. Moreover, it is the Spirit who is said to speak for the Apostles before kings and nobles; Matt. X. 20. who calls Christ’s words to their memory, below 26. who effectively convinces their adversaries, below XVI. 8. Therefore the ancient Latins called Him Advocate, and it is to be noted that to the Spirit of God who is παράκλητος is opposed the malignant spirit who is κατηγόρος, and is thus called in Apocal. XII. 10.

We admit that the name Paraclete signifies Advocate; which the blessed Gerhard shows at greater length in Harm. chap. CLXXVI. p. 507. et seqq. But because it is the duty of an advocate not only to plead the cause of a client, but also to console and encourage the same, to suggest useful things to the same, and to exhort to the same, and it is peculiarly ascribed to the Holy Spirit

παράκλησις Acts 9:31. The word is also used similarly to παρακλήτωρ for מנחם, comforter, Job 16:2, and λόγοι παρακλητικοί for a gentle and comforting discourse, Zech. 1:13. B. Luther, as well as Erasmus, has not inappropriately interpreted it as comforter from the primary office of an advocate: who, unless he raises up and comforts his clients when they are seen in the most desperate causes, where they might be left to themselves, encourages them when they are diffident of their cause, promotes them when they hesitate, and confirms them when they waver, they will despair utterly, nor will they have any παρρησία, where there is need of it.

Whether, however, the Holy Spirit is an Advocate not only before the world, but also before the Father, not only by comforting, exhorting, exciting, and confirming us, so that we may approach Him with παρρησία and cry out with true faith, Abba Father, Rom. 8:15, but also by interceding for us, just as that is done by the Son, 1 John 2:1, Rom. 8:24, the Doctors differ concerning this. Some think that because Christ promised another paraclete with respect to Himself, who also helped the disciples by His own intercession, He intended to indicate that the same intercession is also to be expected from this other paraclete; especially because ὑπερεντυγχάνειν, which is to meet someone on behalf of another's business, and to intercede for him, is said in Rom. 8:27. Others rightly say that the Holy Spirit is called another paraclete, because He agrees with Christ in other parts of the paraclete's office, and performs the same, even if He does not have this office of interceding before the Father: which they judge to be proper to Christ, and they explain that word ὑπερεντυγχάνειν metalepsis-wise, because He makes us ask, just as groans and sighs are attributed to Him, because He makes us groan and sigh, for whom otherwise there would be unutterable groanings, since we do not know how we ought to pray.

Ambrose seems to favor the former interpretation in this place. 'The Spirit of the Lord does not ask for us in human eloquence, but in the manner of His own nature: for when He speaks of God to God, it is necessary that He speaks in the manner in which He speaks from whom He is. For no one speaks to his fellow citizen in another language. For He pours Himself into our prayers, given to us, so that He may cover our lack of skill and lack of foresight with His own movement, and ask from God for us those things which are profitable to us.' And further: 'He speaks to God, therefore, when He seems to be silent to us; because He both sees when He is not seen, and asks for those things which He knows please God and profit us. Then indeed the same Spirit interposes Himself for us, when He knows that we, through ignorance, not through boasting, are asking for contrary things.' Likewise Gregory the Great, Homily 30 on the Gospel: 'The Holy Spirit is therefore called an advocate, because He intercedes for the error of delinquents before the justice of the Father, while He makes those whom He has filled to be praying.' Although the same Gregory in Book II of the Morals, ch. 40, explains this passage in the latter way. Among the Greeks, Nazianzen seems to attribute intercession properly to the Holy Spirit, Oration 2 on the Son: among the Scholastics, Thomas, Part III, Question 21, Article 4. Among the Jesuits, Cornelius à Lapide especially embraces this opinion in Rom. ch. 8, verse 27: 'The Holy Spirit asks, that is, He explains the desires of His friends, and their unutterable groanings in the consistory of the most holy Trinity as a paraclete, that is, our advocate, with great insistence, great weight, and great authority.' For the Greek ὑπερεντυγχάνῃ signifies all these things, that is, He over-asks; for ὑπέρ denotes the preeminence of the Holy Spirit in asking, as if He Himself were presiding over all who ask, and were as it were the master and prefect of our petitions before God; and the Latin 'to ask' (postulare), says Ulpian in Book I, title 'on asking,' is to exhibit or set forth one's own desire, or that of one's friend, in law before him who presides over jurisdiction. In a similar way, verse 34, the Son is said to intercede for us. To which Tirinus the Jesuit also agrees in this place. Some of our own agree with these, especially B. Gerlach, Vol. I, Disp. 6, p. 604. 'Although,' he says, 'it is true that the Holy Spirit excites the faithful to prayers and groans, and teaches us to pray; yet the Apostle speaks here not of simple prayer, by which the Holy Spirit makes the faithful pray for themselves: but of intercession, by which one intercedes for another, not for himself.' And just as Paul wants intercessions to be made by Christians for others, that is, for all men: so he writes here concerning the Spirit of adoption, that He Himself intercedes for us. And he repeats: 'That He who searches the hearts knows what is the sense of the Spirit: because He intercedes for the saints according to God.' But it is one thing for the Holy Spirit to cause us to pray conveniently to God: and another when it is said that the Holy Spirit intercedes for us. For intercession is made by Him as another, for us: nor is any of the saints said to intercede for himself. But the Holy Spirit does both in us: namely, He makes us groan and cry out. And at the same time He also intercedes for us, in great infirmities. For He is our Paraclete. And indeed, He then most especially helps our infirmity, and sighs for us in our heart, when we, established in the agony of death, fail to pray: or otherwise in great temptations, through the infirmity of the flesh, we almost despair of the grace and help of God: then He Himself, the earnest of our salvation, intercedes for us who are failing. Furthermore, if it is not unworthy for the Holy Spirit to dwell in sinners, to purge the filth of sins, to teach us who are rude, and to comfort the infirm: it will not be alien to Him to intercede and groan for us who are laboring. By which, however, He is not made miserable: but just as sadness is attributed to the Holy Spirit by Paul in a convenient way, when in Eph. 4:30 he says: 'Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God': so also intercession and groaning, without any change of Him, are ascribed to Him. The suffrages of D. Wigand and Hesbusius are added above. Epistle to the Romans 8, p. 258. D. Rungius, Disputation 10 on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 161. D. Wesenbeck on the same chapter, conclusion 9, p. 707. Cyriacus Spangenberg, Sermon 66 on the same chapter, p. 344. B. D. Gerhard in Schola pietatis, p. 592, as also B. Feuerborn, who indeed previously in Fascicle 4, Disputation 6, thesis 31, p. 420, and Disputation 9, thesis 42, p. 561, explained it in the latter sense, yet in the third part of his Syntagma of dissertations, 3, p. 538, contends at length that the Holy Spirit is said to intercede for us properly: urging especially that the Holy Spirit himself is said to ἐντυγχάνειν and ὑπερεντυγχάνειν for us, but it is one thing for the Holy Spirit to cause us to pray appropriately to God, and another when it is said that the Holy Spirit himself intercedes for us, because intercession is made by him as another for us, nor is any of the saints said to intercede for himself.

Sometimes, however, both ancient and more recent Doctors have preferred to explain the ἐντυγχάνειν of the Holy Spirit before God the Father in such a way that he does not himself petition for us, but makes us petition: and to understand these groanings not as divine, but as human, stirred up by the Holy Spirit in the regenerate: which are called ἀλάλητοι because we ourselves cannot ἐκλαλεῖν them, especially when established in the greatest straits and dangers and in the agony of death: since groanings do not befit God, but only one affected by tribulations and miseries: Exodus chapter 2, verse 24; chapter 6, verse 5; Psalm 6, verse 7; as also Romans chapter 8, verse 23. What is it to be always groaning, other than to be always miserable, says Augustine, Volume 6, book 1 against Maximinus, and book 2, chapter 9. Thus among the ancients interpret this: Origen on this place; Augustine, Vol. II, Epistle XXI, ch. 15; Vol. IV, book on the Trinity and the unity of God, ch. 3 & 10; Vol. VI, Sermon against the Arians, ch. 25; Vol. IX, Tractate VI on John. Therefore, the Holy Spirit does not groan in himself, by himself, in that Trinity, in that blessedness, in that eternity of substance, but he groans in us, because he makes us groan. Gregory the Great, book II, Morals, ch. 22, and others: from the more recent ones, Schuvarez, Vol. I, Commentary on the III part of Thomas, q. 21, art. 4, disp. 45, sect. 2, p. 629. William Estius on Romans VIII. Emmanuel Sa, Justinian, Toletus, Adam von Conzen, Menochius, Pererius, who [wrote] Commentary on Romans, disp. XVIII. Even if, he says, our spirit sometimes asks in prayer for things that will harm it, nevertheless the Holy Spirit, breathing into our souls and as it were presiding over our vows and petitions, corrects what was asked for wrongly, as one who is in charge of and presides over all intercessions; he corrects, I say, while he makes us ask for whatever we ask for, only insofar as it conduces to the glory of God and our own utility. Claudius Espencaeus on Christ the Mediator, ch. II, p. 294. Therefore, he says, by his own breathing the Holy Spirit asks, and as if in charge of all the vows of the saints (which excellence the word ὑπὲρ signifies, as Erasmus notes) he moderates them, and breathes into their minds, and stirs up divine motions in us from heaven, and indeed with the greatest zeal: Among our own, after Blessed Luther, Commentary on Genesis, ch. XXX and XXXII and elsewhere passim, Flacius, Blessed Selneccer in Commentary on the Epistle of Paul, p. 176. Christ is the intercessor because he is the mediator and redeemer, appeasing the wrath of the Father: but the Holy Spirit is the intercessor after the wrath has been appeased through the Son, moving us to invocation, compelling our hearts, exciting, and certifying, as an advocate, teaching, instructing, consoling, gladdening, according to that [verse]: I will pour out upon the house of David a spirit of grace and of prayers: And to the following words of Romans VIII. 28. But he who searches the hearts, that is, the Holy Spirit, groans in us or makes us groan, and compels us to invocation according to the will of God ᾗ καρδιογνώση, so that we may ask for those things which make for the glory of God and for our salvation. For although by carnal affection and mouth we often want, desire, and ask for something which, if it were conferred upon us, would not be to our advantage, nevertheless the Sp. Spirit, in the hidden recess of our heart, does not depart from the will of God, but governs, corrects, and directs our prayers, so that they may be acceptable to God and be heard, if not according to our carnal will, yet according to the spiritual will and our salvation. Which explanation is also that of Blessed Brentius in his Commentary on Romans, Luke Osiander, the Weimar Paraphrasts, Blessed Aegidius Hunnius in his Commentary on Romans, p. 278. But when the Holy Spirit is said to intercede for us with inexpressible groanings, this is not to be understood as if the Holy Spirit himself were praying, or were feeling such groanings and affections in himself. But he is said to pray while he makes us pray, while he excites, forms, and directs these very prayers and these groanings in us, inflames our heart to the affection of praying, and provides filial confidence in praying. Just as he explained above: You have received the Spirit of adoption, through whom we cry Abba. Blessed Georg Mylius in his Commentary on Romans, f. 297. But to the Holy Spirit is attributed not a simple intercession, but an ὑπερέντευξις, so that it may be shown that the cause of the intercession is conducted with the greatest zeal and most intense exertion. Which is not to be understood as if the Spirit himself, as regards his essence or person, becomes a suppliant to God by praying: but because he is our guide and author for praying rightly, who suggests both words to the mouth and motions to the heart, and helps and inflames them, so that the prayers may become acceptable to God. In the notation of τῶ πρέπης which is annexed; Augustine says that we labor with a certain learned ignorance. Interpreters say that the groanings are called ineffable because we do not ourselves breathe out what we ask for: But with the Spirit instigating, we conceive those vows in our breast. For it happens not rarely to the pious that they only sigh, and do not discern where they should turn themselves in praying. Meanwhile, while they are thinking nothing of it, indeed while they are ignorant of what is happening, the Holy Spirit moderates those sighs excited by himself within, and brings it about that they come into the sight of God. Our Blessed Weller in his Commentary on Romans, f. 501. These things are said about the Holy Spirit causally and effectively, as the Chorus of the Fathers commonly explained, in this sense: Besides our Helper, who is Christ alone, and who himself intercedes for us, the Holy Spirit makes us cry out, so that God may deliver us. Blessed Glassius, book III, Grammar, tr. III, Can. 22, p. 276. The Holy Spirit is said to pray and groan in the pious (Romans VIII. 26, as also Galatians IV. v. 6) because he excites the δύναμιν of praying and groaning. For he is the Spirit of grace and of prayers, Zechariah XII. 10, in whom we cry Abba Father, Romans VIII. 15. Augustine, Vol. II, on the Trinity of God, ch. 3, it is written that the Holy Spirit groans for us, that is, he makes us groan. Blessed Glassius adds, you will observe the most delightful and most full-of-consolation conjunction of the intercession of the Holy Spirit and the sighs of the pious, and as it were a περιχώρησιν: While contrite souls, addicted to God through Christ, sigh, the Holy Spirit is said to sigh and at the same time to intercede, ὑπερεντυγχάνειν; whatever is lacking in the prayers, the Spirit includes that in the holy groaning in the hearts of the pious. That groaning is not from the powers of nature, but from God, whence it is ἀλάλητα. To which almost all of our own agree, also Blessed Gerhard in his Harmony, ch. CLXXVI, p. 503, where he has this to say about this place in John XIV. A Rule is to be noted in this place, that some things are attributed to the Holy Spirit absolutely in his own person, but some things relatively, not in his own person, but in our person, and that both passively, as in Acts VII. 51, and actively, as in this place. Blessed Danhauer in his Ὁδοσοφίᾳ, p. 940. Otherwise, he says, the Father is said to παρακαλεῖν, otherwise the Son, otherwise the Holy Spirit. The Father, indeed the whole Holy Trinity, asks that we be reconciled to him by a mandatory request, 2 Corinthians V. 20. The Son intercedes by a formal, ἱλασικῇ and mediatorial intercession: The Holy Spirit intercedes by an effective intercession: And afterwards: Therefore that ὑπερέντευξις is effective, transitive, and, if I may say so, Hiphilic. The Spirit groans for us, because he makes us groan, as Augustine roundly explains. In sum, the Sp. He breathes comfort into his client and the defendant who is in despair, encourages those who are diffident about their cause, teaches the one who is ignorant of the manner of praying, adds light to the blind, gives salutary advice to those lacking counsel, defends the accused, rouses the languid to prayer, strengthens the ejaculation of the infirm, purifies the impure, makes the ungrateful grateful, clears the obscured, sharpens the dull, elevates the slothful, and finally leads them to the throne of God: he finally conquers, obtains the cause, attains his vows, fulfills his desire; for that is what ἐντυγχάνειν is, hence τύχη, fortune, as among the Germans Glück from gelingen. This our B. Danhauerus [says] for that common opinion, who nevertheless adds another explanation at the same time, that this ὑπερέντευξις is formal, a divine locution, a celestial language, an intercession worthy of God, proper to the Holy Spirit, who truly prays, but θεοπρεπῶς, which sense he confirms there with the arguments of B. Feurbornius. But how both significations can have a place at the same time does not appear. For if he asks for us, it is that he makes us ask; therefore the same word used once in the same place is not also 'he intercedes' or 'he prays for us' if it is taken effectively, because if it makes us pray, it will certainly not be taken as formal prayer by which he intercedes for us. One or the other interpretation must therefore be embraced, whence our countrymen almost commonly acquiesce in the explanation of St. Augustine.

In this way also, most of the Reformed understand τὸ ὑπερεντυγχάνειν effectively: Peter Martyr, Beza, Pareus, and others, including the annotators of the Belgian Bible version; Joh. Coccejus in his Commentary on Romans ch. 8, p. 448. Just as, he says, the Spirit is said to cry out, Gal. 4:6, so also to groan, namely, because He works both in us, as our own, or as the Paraclete. For that phrase does not simply imply this, that the Spirit works so that we may cry out: but also that the cry and those groans are a sign of τῶ φρονήματος αὐτῶ, or of His own will and zeal. And that this will has the likeness of intercession; because it is the will of the Paraclete, i.e., of Him who has been given to us, and of whom we are the temple. Coccejus does not dare to say that it is intercession, but that it has the likeness of intercession. Grotius, however, observes on Romans 8:26. that ὑπερεντυγχάνειν belongs to advocates who dictate the desires of their clients: And that this is attributed to the Holy Spirit for this reason, because He dictates prayers to God for us.

These things concerning the various explanations of the τῆς ὑπερεντεύξεως of the Spirit by those who understand the same thing concerning the Holy Spirit Himself: but because some think that this does not properly befit the Holy Spirit, nor do they consider the explanation of effective petition to be sufficiently congruent, some interpret it as concerning our own spirit, of which it was treated in verse 16, that it συναντιλαμβάνεται (helps) the infirmity of our flesh, and since our true inner man does not understand what ought to be prayed for, or rather we, because we are still carnal in part, do not know it, that same Spirit intercedes for us; which is not only the exposition of Zwingli and Bucer, but our blessed Brentius also seems to incline toward the same, when he teaches that two sinners concur in us in the petition for bodily things: the affection of the flesh, and the affection of the Spirit; the former seeking external liberation: but the latter interprets the words of prayer before God concerning true and eternal liberation, and that its groaning for the pious who are most grievously afflicted and who invoke God according to the affection of the flesh is ineffable: and thus Estius observes that Chrysostom and his followers—lest, if the Holy Spirit Himself be understood, it should follow that the Holy Spirit, according to the heresy of Macedonius, is a creature and inferior to God, as one praying for us before God—interpret it either as the spirit of man insofar as it has received the grace of prayer from the Holy Spirit, or as the very gift of prayer infused into men by the Holy Spirit: and that Ambrose himself, in Book 3 of De Spiritu Sancto, ch. 12, understands it as spiritual grace. But it seems undoubted to us from the context that the Holy Spirit Himself is understood, and emphatically τὸ αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα. But to whom, because ὑπερέντευξις is attributed, saving His ὁμουσία (consubstantiality) with the Father, we truly judge it to be ἀλάλητον (ineffable) and ἄῥῥητον (unspeakable): nor does it appear, if the Holy Spirit is said to intercede before the Father with a proper and formal prayer, even if θεϊκῶς (divinely), why He should not likewise be said to intercede in such a way before the Son, since He proceeds equally from the Son as from the Father. But since the Son Himself is our intercessor before the Father, and for that end willed to become a partaker of our nature, that He might be our Mediator and intercessor, there seems to be no need for the ἐντεύξει (intercession) of the Holy Spirit before the Son. And since the intercession of the Mediator is a work, will there not thus be two of our Mediators in the divine, the Son and the Holy Spirit, which is repugnant to the Apostle in 1 Timothy 2:2. Finally, since it cannot be explained by any concept what kind of formal ἔντευξις (intercession) and intercession the Holy Spirit might undergo before the Father and the Son simultaneously, lest it obstruct the essential περιχώρησις (indwelling) of the divine persons in the Holy Trinity, and the communion of works and actions in God which do not pertain to the property of the persons, it is better, in our judgment, to acquiesce in the explanation of the blessed Luther and those who have followed him, and to acknowledge the formal ἔντευξιν (intercession) as an act not merely θεϊκὸν (divine), but θεανδρικὸν (theandric), and that it is no other than μεσιτικὸν (mediatorial), and therefore to understand the ἔντευξιν (intercession) of the Holy Spirit which the Apostle points out as effective.

It is helpful to add the reasons which the blessed Feurbornius used in Fasciculus 4, disp. 9, thesis 42, p. 561. Do not, he says, think that the Holy Spirit Himself properly intercedes for us. For (1) He is not only said to intercede for us, but to intercede with ineffable groanings and sighs. But He Himself does not properly groan and utter sighs, because He is an infinite Spirit: but He makes us groan and sigh; as Augustine also explains. (2) He is indeed said to intercede for us, but Holy Scripture does not add that He intercedes πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν (before God), just as Christ is said to be our advocate before God the Father in 1 John 2:1, but κτ᾽ Θεὸν (according to God), Romans ch. 8:27, i.e., He renders us piously praying according to the divine will. (3) Holy Scripture explains this in such a way that it says we cry out through the Holy Spirit, Abba Father, Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6. (4) The Holy Spirit is not our advocate and mediator, but Christ is one and alone, 1 Timothy 2:5 and 1 John 2:1. Therefore, He does not intercede for us in a mediatorial way properly. (5) The Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of grace and of prayers, Zechariah ch. 12:10, for the reason that He both begins and completes the grace of God in our hearts, leading us to Christ, in whom we are κεχαριτωμένοι (graced) Ephesians 1:6, and makes us, from children of wrath, such as we are φύσει (by nature), Ephesians 2:3, children of grace, which He seals and confirms in us, 2 Corinthians 1:22 and Romans 8:16 and 1 John 5:6, and then kindles pious prayers in us, and makes us certain of being heard. For He is a right and firm Spirit, strengthening and consolidating us, Psalm 51:12, 14. Finally (6) because no one can say (piously invoke, and in true justifying faith call upon) the Lord Jesus, except through the Holy Spirit, 1 Corinthians 12:3. Far be it therefore that we should maintain that the Holy Spirit himself properly intercedes for us before God, and thus himself in his own person pours forth prayers for us. For he intercedes for us effectively, that is, he makes us pray piously and rightly. Since we do not know what we are to pray for as we ought (namely, by the powers of nature), but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered, that is, the Holy Spirit makes us pray piously and sigh devoutly to God. This is B. Feuerborn. If ὑπερεντυγχάνειν belongs to advocates, by which they dictate desires to clients, which Grotius wishes, and that is the emphasis of this word, so that it signifies him who is set over the prayers of the saints, which seemed so to Erasmus, and Claud. Espencaeus, as also to B. Dannhauer, there is no reason why we should depart here from the common explanation concerning effective petition. B. Paul. Tarnovius Comment. in Joh. p. 1031. The Holy Spirit, he says, is our paraclete, insofar as he sanctifies us, that is, he leads us to the knowledge of the truth, consoles those who have been led, and teaches our prayers to be carried to the Father through the Son, and therefore it is said in Rom. 8:26 that he intercedes for us, because he excites us to prayers, and as it were dictates the words within. The most learned Camero on the present Johannine passage against Calvin, who contends that the Holy Spirit is our intercessor and advocate before God, both from these words of Christ, because παράκλητον denotes an advocate, and from the Apostolic passage at Rom. 8:26, observes that the word παράκλητον is Attic, by which are signified those whom we summon in danger, that they may assist us with counsel (who for that reason are called Advocates in Latin), even if they do not litigate in court, in our name, and that which happens only by accident, that he should be an Advocate and intercessor, just as Christ is called our παράκλητος: and he explains this word from the Hebrew מליץ, Doctor, or interpreter, and from Job XVI. v. 20. Where in the Targum it is used for comforter, so that the Holy Spirit is called παράκλητος, not on account of prayer or a certain intercession, but because he was to teach the Apostles, and make them fit to answer others and teach them, and that in such a way that he also comforts and brings joy. But in the Apostolic passage Rom. VIII. the Spirit is said to intercede for us, not that the person of the Holy Spirit himself intercedes immediately, but because he excites in us the affection of praying, inasmuch as he intercedes through groanings; but the Spirit does not groan, but we groan: and therefore he intercedes, by causing us to groan, and by exciting in us the affection of praying.

Ἵνα μένῃ μεθ' ὑμῶν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) Not that he may be with you for a few years, as I was, but that he may remain perpetually. For this is to the Hebrews εἰς αἰῶνα. This, however, is to be understood under the condition already stated, of the observation of the commandments.

Latin:

Vers. 16. κ᾿ ἐγὼ ἐρωτήσω ἲ πατέρα κ᾿ ἄλλον παράκλητον δώ- σει ὑμῖν] Et hic posterior pars in priori repetenda. Orabo ut Spiritum vobis det, & dabit, nempe si in obedientia prae- ceptorum perseveraveritis. Ἐρωτᾶν pro peccati frequens in his libris. Luc. XIV. 18. & alibi. Precatur autem jam Christus non cum supplicibus lachrymis in hac vita, sed pro ea auctoritate quam sibi mortis obedientia quaesivit. παράκλητος vox Graeca frequens apud Judaeos in versione Chaldæa & apud Talmudicos, non pro consolatore, sed pro eo qui causam agit, & quidem rei. Nam qui pro ac- cusatore dicit vocatur alia Graeca voce קטגור κατηγόρος. Alium ergo oratorem CHRISTUS pollicetur qui causam suorum agat apud mundum, sicut ipse aucturus est apud Patrem. Nam hoc sensu ipse est παράκλητος I. Joh. II. 2, & quod modo dixit se pro suis interpellaturum Patrem est circumlocutio muneris παρακλήτου. Spiritus autem est, qui pro Apostolis apud reges & proceres loqui dicitur; Matth. X. 20. qui Christi dicta ipsis in memoriam revocat, infra 26. qui adversarios ipsorum efficaciter convincit, in- fra XVI. 8. Ideo veteres Latini Advocatum dixerunt, & notandum Dei Spiritui qui est παράκλητος opponi spiritum malignum qui est κατηγόρος, & sic dicitur Apocal. XII. 10.

Admittimus Paracleti nomen Advocatum signi- ficare; quod prolixius ostendit B. Gerhard. Harm. cap. CLXXVI. pag. 507. seqq. Sed quia advocati est non solum clientis causam agere, sed etiam eundem consolari, & erige- re, eidem suggerere utilia, & ad eadem horta- ri, ac Spiritui Sancto peculiariter adscribitur

παράκλησις Act. IX. 31. vox etiam similis παρα- κλήτωρ pro מנחם consolatore Job. XVI. 2. ac λό- γοι παρακλητικόι pro sermone blando, & consola- torio adhibetur Zach. I. 13. non incommode inter- pretatus est B. Lutherus, ut & Erasmus per consola- torem à præcipuo munere advocati: qui nisi clien- tes suos in causis maxime desperatis visis, ubi sibi relinquantur, erigat, & consoletur, causæ suæ dif- fidentes animet, cunctantes promoveat, nutantes confirmet, desperabunt penitus, nec ullam παῥ- ῥησίαν, ubi ea opus est, habebunt.

Utrum autem Advocatus sit Spiritus S. non tan- tum apud mundum, sed etiam apud Patrem, non tantum nos consolando, hortando, excitando, & con- firmando, ut χ᾿ παῥῥησίας ad eum accedamus, & vera fide clamemus Abba Pater, Rom. IIX. 15. sed etiam pro nobis interpellando, quemadmodum id à Filio fit 1. Job. II. 1. Rom. IIX. 24. de eo variant Do- ctores. Nonnulli quia ἄλλον παράκλητον promi- sit Christus respectu habito ad seipsum, qui inter- cessione etiam sua discipulos juverit, eandem in- terpellationem etiam ab hoc ἄλλῳ παρακλήτῳ expectandam esse indicare voluisse, putant: im- primis quia ὑπερεντυγχάνειν, quod est convenire aliquem super negotio alterius, ac intercedere pro eo, dicitur Rom. IIX. 27. Alii recte alium paracle- tum Sp. S. dici, ajunt, quod in aliis τ̃ παρακλη- τῶν partibus conveniat cum Christo, idemque præstet, etsi hoc intercedendi apud Patrem munus non habeat: quod Christo proprium esse censent, & verbum illud ὑπερεντυγχάνειν explicant metale- ptice, quod postulare nos faciat, quemadmodum gemitus & suspiria ipsi tribuuntur, quod nos geme- re faciat, & suspirare, quibus alias στεναγμοὶ essent ἀλάλητοι, quum nesciamus quomodo orare de- beamus.

Priori interpretationi favere videtur Am- brosius in h. l. Non humanis eloquiis postulare pro nobis dicit Spiritum Domini, sed more naturæ suæ: Cum enim quid de Deo est, Deo loquitur, eo more loquitur necesse est, quo ille loquitur de quo est. Nemo enim cum suo cive alia lingua loquitur. Superfundit enim se precibus no- stris, datus nobis, ut imperitiam, & improvidentiam nostram motu suo operiat, & illa nobis à Deo petat, quæ prosunt nobis. Et porro: Deo ergo loquitur cum nobis tacere videtur; quia & videt cum non videatur, & hæc petit, quæ scit Deo placere, & nobis prodesse. Tunc sane pro nobis interponit se idem Spiritus, cum scit nos per ignorantiam, non per jactantiam contraria postulare. Item Gre- gor. M. homil. XXX. in Evangel. Spiritus S. ideo advocatus dicitur, quia pro errore delinquen- tium apud justitiam Patris intercedit, dum eos, quos repleverit, exorantes facit. Quanquam idem Gregorius l. II. Moral. c. XL. posteriori modo hunc locum explicet. E Græcis Nazianzenus proprie intercessionem Spiritui S. tribuere vide- tur Orat. II. de Filio: è Scholasticis Thomas III. quæst. XXI. artic. IV. E Jesuitis imprimis hanc senten- tiam amplectitur Cornel. à Lap. in Rom. c. VIII. vers. 27. Spiritus Sanctus postulat, id est, desi- deria amicorum suorum, eorumque gemitus inenar- rabiles in consistorio sanctissimæ Trinitatis quasi pa- racletus, id est, advocatus noster exponit magna instantia, magno pondere, & magna auctoritate. Hæc enim omnia significat Græcum ὑπερεντυγχάνῃ, id est, super expostulat; nam ὑπὲρ notat præmi- nentiam Spiritus Sancti in postulando, quasi ipse præsit omnibus postulantibus, sitque quasi magister & præfectus libellorum supplicium nostrorum apud Deum; & Latinum postulare, inquit Ulpianus l. I. tit. de postulando, est desiderium suum, vel amici sui in jure apud eum, qui jurisdictioni præest ex- hibe- ponere. Simili modo v. 34. dicitur Filius interpella- re pro nobis. Cui accedit & Tirinus Jesuita in h. l. His consonant è nostris nonnulli, imprimis B. Gerlachius Tom. I. Disp. VI. p. 604. Etsi, in- quiens, verum sit, quod Spiritus S. ad preces & gemitus fideles excitet, nosque orare doceat; loqui- tur tamen hic Apostolus non de simplici oratione, qua Spiritus S. fideles pro seipsis orare facit: sed de in- tercessione, qua quis pro alio, non pro se intercedit. Et sicut Paulus à Christianis vult fieri intercessiones pro aliis, hoc est, pro omnibus hominibus: ita hic de Spiritu adoptionis scribit, quod ipse intercedat pro nobis. Et repetit: Quod scrutans corda, sciat, quis sit sensus Spiritus: quia secundum Deum intercedat PRO SANCTIS. A- liud verò est, Spiritum Sanctum efficere, ut con- venienter ad Deum oremus: & aliud, cum dicitur, quod Spiritus Sanctus pro nobis intercedat. Nam intercessio ab ipso tanquam alio, pro nobis fit: nec quisquam Sanctorum pro seipso intercedere dicitur. Utrumque autem Spiritus Sanctus in nobis agit: ni- mirum, ingemiscere & clamare nos facit. Et si- mul etiam pro nobis, in magnis infirmitatibus, intercedit. Est enim Paracletus noster. Et qui- dem, tum maxime auxiliatur infirmitati nostræ, & suspirat pro nobis in corde nostro, cum in agone mor- tis constituti ad orandum deficimus: aut alias in ma- gnis tentationibus, per carnis infirmitatem, de gratia & ope Dei quasi desperamus: tum ipse, salutis no- stræ arrha, pro nobis deficientibus interpellat. Ad- hæc, si Spiritui S. indignum non est, in peccatoribus habitare, sordes peccatorum expurgare, nos rudes docere, & infirmos consolari: nec etiam ab ipso a- lienum erit, pro nobis laborantibus intercedere & ingemiscere. Per quod tamen ipse non efficitur miser: sed sicut Spiritui Sancto, modo convenien- te, tristitia à Paulo tribuitur, cum Eph. IV. 30. in- quit; Ne contristetis Spiritum Sanctum Dei: ita quoque intercessio & gemitus, sine omni illius mutatione, ei adscribuntur. Accedunt suffragia D. Wigandi & Hesbusii sup. Epist. ad Rom. IIX. p. 258. D. Rungii Disp. X. in Ep. ad Rom. p. 161. D. Wesenbeck. in idem cap. conc. IX. p. 707. Cyriac. Spangenberg. Conc. LXVI. super idem cap. p. 344. B. D. Gerhardi in Sch. piet. p. m. 592. ut & B. Feuer- bornii, qui antea quidem Fascic. IV. Disp. VI. th. 31. p. 420. & Disp. IX. th. 42. p. 561. posterio- ri sensu exposuit, parte tamen tertia Syntagm. dissert. III. p. 538. prolixe contendit, quod pro- prie Spiritus S. pro nobis interpellare dicatur: id imprimis urgens, quod ipse Spiritus S. dicatur ἐν- τυγχάνειν & ὑπερεντυγχάνειν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, aliud vero sit, Spiritum S. efficere, ut nos convenienter ad Deum oremus, aliud cum dicitur, quod Spiritus S. pse pro nobis intercedat, quia intercessio ab ipso tanquam alio pro nobis fiat, nec quisquam san- ctorum pro seipso intercedere dicatur.

Nonnunquam tamen tum antiqui tum recentio- res Doctores τὸ ἐντυγχάνειν Spiritus Sancti apud Deum Patrem ita maluerunt explicare, quod non ipse postulet pro nobis, sed postulare nos fa- ciat: & gemitus hic intelligere non divinos, sed humanos, à Spiritu Sancto in renatis excitatos: qui ἀλάλητοι dicantur, quod nos ipsi non possimus ἐκλαλεῖν, maxime in summis angustiis, & peri- culis, & in agone mortis constituti: siquidem στεναγμοὶ non DEO competant, sed tantum tribulationibus & miseriis affecto: Exod. cap. II. vers. 24. cap. VI. vers. 5. Ps. VI. v. 7. ut & Rom. c. IIX. v. 23. Quid est aliud semper gemere, quam semper esse miserum, ait Augustinus Tom. VI. l. I. contr. Maximin. & lib. II. cap. 9. Ita inter- pretantur è Veteribus Origenes in h. l. August. T. II. Epist. XXI. c. 15. Tom. IV. lib. de Trin. & unit. Dei, c. 3. & 10. Tom. VI. Serm. contr. Arian. c. 25. Tom. IX. Tract. VI. in Johann. Non ergo Spiritus Sanctus in semetipso apud semetipsum in illa Trinitate, in illa beatitudine, in illa æternitate substantiæ gemit, sed in nobis gemit, quia gemere nos facit. Gregor. M. l. II. Moral. c. 22. & alii: è recentioribus Schuvarez Tom. I. Comment. in III. part. Thom. q. 21. art. 4. disp. 45. sect. 2. p. 629. Guilh. Estius in Rom. IIX. Eman. Saa, Justinian. Toletus, Adamus à Conzen. Menochius, Pererius, qui Comment. in Rom. disp. XVIII. Etiamsi, inquit, Spiritus noster aliquando petit in oratione sibi nocitura, attamen Spiritus Sanctus afflans animas nostras, & quasi præsidens votis & postulatis nostris corrigit quod male petebatur, tanquam præfectus & præsidens cunctis interpellationibus, corrigit, inquam, dum quicquid petimus, eatenus nos petere facit, quatenus ad Dei gloriam, & nostram utilitatem conducit. Claudius Espensæus de Christo Mediat. c. II. p. 294. suo ergo, inquit, afflatu Spiritus Sanctus postulat, ac velut omnibus sanctorum votis præfectus (quam excellentiam tò ὑπὲρ Erasmo annotante significat) & moderatur, eorumque afflat animos, & divinos è cœlis in nobis ciet motus, & quidem summo studio: E nostris post B. Lutherum Comment. in Gen. c. XXX. & XXXII. & alibi passim, Flacius, B. Selneccer. in Comment. in Epist. Pauli p. 176. Christus est interpellator, quia est mediator & redemptor, placans iram Patris: Spiritus S. vero est interpellator post placatam iram per Filium, movens nos ad invocationem, compellens nostra corda, excitans, & certificans, ut advocatus, docens, instituens, consolans, lætificans, secundum illud, effundam super domum David Spiritum gratiæ & precum: Et ad verba sequentia Rom. IIX. 28. Qui vero scrutatur corda, id est, Spiritus S. in nobis gemit seu gemere nos facit, & ad invocationem compellit secundum voluntatem Dei ᾗ καρδιογνώση, ut petamus ea, quæ ad gloriam Dei, & ad salutem nostram faciunt. Etsi enim affectu & ore carnali sæpe aliquid velimus, optemus, & petamus, quod si nobis conferretur, non conduceret nobis, tamen Sp. S. sensus in occulto cordis nostri recessu non discedit a voluntate Dei, sed gubernat, corrigit, & dirigit preces nostras, ut Deo acceptæ sint, & exaudiantur, si non ad voluntatem nostram carnalem, tamen ad voluntatem spiritualem & salutem nostram. Quæ explicatio etiam B. Brentii est in Comment. ad Rom. Luc. Osiandri, Paraphrastarum Vinariensium, B. Ægyd. Hunnii in Comment. ad Rom. p. 278. Quando autem Sp. S. gemitibus inenarrabilibus pro nobis intercedere dicitur, non hoc modo accipiendum est, quasi vel ipse Sp. S. oret, vel tales gemitus & affectus in seipso sentiat. Sed orare dicitur, dum nos orare facit, dum has ipsas preces, hos gemitus in nobis excitat, format, dirigit, cor nostrum ad precandi affectum incendit, & filialem fiduciam in precando subministrat. Sicut supra exposuit: Accepistis Spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus Abba. B. Georg. Mylius in Comment. ad Rom. f. 297. Spiritui autem Sancto non simplex intercessio, sed ὑπερέντευξις tribuitur, ut summo studio atque acerrima contentione causam intercessionis agi ostendatur. Quod non ita accipiendum est, quasi Spiritus ipse, quoad essentiam suam sive personam orando supplex Deo fiat: sed quia ille nobis dux est atque autor ad recte precandum, qui & verba ori, & motus cordi suggerit, eosdemque adjuvat & inflammat, ut preces Deo fiant acceptabiles. In notatione τῶ πρέπης quæ annexa est; Augustinus ait, nos laborare docta quadam ignorantia. Interpretes dicunt, ineffabiles dici gemitus, quia non ipsi efflamur, quod petimus: Sed Spiritu instigan- te vota ista in pectore concipimus. Contingit enim non raro piis, ut tantummodo suspirent, & quo sese precando vertant, non dispiciant. Interim illis mi- nime cogitantibus, imo quid agatur ignorantibus, Spiritus S. suspiria ista a se ipso excitata, intus mode- ratur, atque ut in conspectum Dei veniant, efficit. B. Wellerus noster in Comment. ad Rom. f. 501. Cau- saliter & effective hac de Spiritu S. dicuntur, ut com- muniter Chorus Patrum exposuit, hoc sensu: Præter Opitulatorem nostrum, qui solus Christus est, & pro nobis intercedit ipse, Spiritus S. nos facit cla- mantes, ut Deus nos liberet. B. Glassius l. III. Grammat. tr. III. Can. 22. p. 276. Orare & gemere in piis dicitur Spiritus S. (Rom. IIX. 26. ut & Gal. IV. v. 6.) quia orandi & gemendi δύναμιν excitat. Est enim Spiritus gratiæ & precum Zach. XII. 10. in quo clamamus Abba Pater, Rom. IIX. 15. Augusti- nus Tom. II. de Trin. Dei c. 3. scribitur Sp. S. gemere pro nobis, id est, gementes nos facere. Addit B. Glas- sius, observabic jucundissimam, & consolaminis ple- nissimam intercessionis Spiritus S. & suspiriorum pio- rum conjunctionem, & quasi περιχώρησιν: Dum suspirant contrita, & Deo addictæ per Christum ani- mæ suspirare, & simul intercedere ὑπερεντυγχά- νειν dicitur Sp. S. quicquid precibus deest, id gemitui sancto in piorum cordibus includit Spiritus. Is gemi- tus non est ex naturæ viribus, sed ex Deo, unde ἀλά- λητ␄. Quibus astipulantur è nostris plerique omnes, etiam B. Gerhardus in Harm. c. CLXXVI. p. 503. ubi ita habet de hoc loco Johann. XIV. No- tanda est hoc loco Regula, quod quædam tribuantur Spiritui S. absolute in persona propria, quædam vero relate non in propria, sed in nostra persona, idque tum passive, ut Act. VII. 51. tum active, ut hoc loco B. Danhauerus in Ὁδοσοφίᾳ p. 940. Aliter, inquit, Pater dicitur παρακαλεῖν, aliter Filius, aliter S. S. Pater, imo tota SS. Trinitas rogat, ut sibi reconcilie- mur rogatione mandatoria 2. Cor. V. 20. Filius in- tercedit intercessione formali, ἱλασικῇ & mediatoria: Spiritus S. intercedit intercessione effectiva: Et po- stea: Est igitur illa ὑπερέντευξις effectiva, transiti- va ac, ut sic dicam, Hiphilica. Spiritus gemit pro nobis, quia gementes nos facit, ut rotunde exponit Augustinus. Ad summam Sp. S. clienti suo reoque desperabundo solatia aspirat, causæ suæ diffidentes a- nimat, ignorantem modum precandi docet, cæco lu- men addit, consilii experti suadet salutaria, accusa- tum defendit, languidum ad preces excitat, infir- mæ ejaculationem roborat, impuram defecat, ingra- tam gratam facit, obscuratam serenat, hebetem acuit, ignavam sublimat, ad thronum Dei adducit tan- dam: vincit tandem, obtinet causam, consequitur vota, implet desiderium, id enim est ἐντυγχάνειν, hinc τύχη, fortuna, ut apud Germanos Glück vom ge- lingen. Hæc B. Danhauerus noster pro illa communi sententia, qui tamen alteram explicatio- nem simul addit, quod ὑπερέντευξις hæc formalis sit, locutio divina, lingua cælestis, Deo digna interces- sio, Sp. S. propria, qui vere oret, sed θεοπρεπῶς, quem sensum illic B. Feurbornii rationibus confirmat. Quæ vero utraque significatio quomodo simul lo- cum habere possit, non apparet. Nam si postulat pro nobis, est, postulare nos facit, non ergo idem verbum semel adhibitum in eodem loco etiam est intercedit, vel orat pro nobis, si effective sumitur, quod orare nos faciat, utique non de formali ora- tione, qua pro nobis interpellet, accipietur. Al- terutra ergo interpretatio amplectenda erit, un- de communiter fere nostrates S. Augustini expli- cationi acquiescunt.

Quo pacto etiam è Reformatis plerisque effective τὸ ὑπερεντυγχάνειν intelligunt, Petrus Martyr, Be- za, Pareus, & alii etiam Annotatores ad versionem Bibl. Belgicam: Joh. Coccejus in Comment. ad Ro- man. c. IIX. p. 448. Quemadmodum, inquit, Spiri- tus dicitur clamare, Gal. IV. 6. ita etiam ingemiscere, nempe, quia utrumque operatur in nobis, ut noster, sive ut Paracletus. Neque enim simpliciter hoc innuit ea phrasis, Spiritum operari, ut clamemus: sed et- iam clamorem & eos gemitus esse signum τῶ φρονήμα- τος αὐτῶ sive voluntatis & studii ipsius. Eam vero voluntatem habere instar intercessionis; quia est vo- luntas Paracleti, h. e. ejus qui nobis datus est, & cu- jus nos templum sumus. Non audet Coccejus di- cere, quod sit intercessio, sed quod habeat in- star intercessionis. Grotius vero observat ad Rom. IIX. v. 26. ὑπερεντυγχάνειν esse advocatorum, qui clientum desideria dictant: Idque ideo Spiritui San- cto tribui, quia preces ad Deum nobis dictat.

Hæc de diversis explicationibus τῆς ὑπερεντεύ- ξεως Spiritus eorum, qui de ipfomet Spiritu S. e- andem intelligunt: quam vero quia nec proprie convenire Spiritui S. nonnulli putant, neque sa- tis congruam esse arbitrantur explicationem de ef- fectiva postulatione; de Spiritu nostro, de quo v. 16. actum erat, interpretantur nonnulli, quod carnis nostræ infirmitati συναντιλαμβάνεται & cum verus noster homo non intelligat, quid oran- dum sit, vel potius nos, quia adhuc carnales su- mus ex parte, id nesciamus, idem ille Spiritus pro nobis intercedat, quæ non tantum Zuvinglii & Buzeri est ἔκθεσις, sed videtur etiam inclinare in e- andem B. Brentius noster, cum duos peccatores in petitione corporalium in nobis concurrere docet, affe- ctum carnis, & affectum Spiritus: illum externam li- berationem expetere: hunc autem interpretari verba precationis coram Deo, de vera & æterna liberatione, ejusque gemitum piis gravissime afflictis, & Deum juxta carnis affectum invocantibus, esse inenarrabi- lem: atque ita observat Estius Chrysostomum, ejus- que sequaces, ne si ipse Spiritus Sanctus intellige- tur, consequens sit Spiritum Sanctum secundum hæresin Macedonii creaturam esse, ac Deo mino- rem, utpote orantem pro nobis apud Deum, inter- pretari, vel Spiritum hominis quatenus gratiam o- rationis à Spiritu Sancto accepit, vel ipsum oratio- nis donum hominibus à SpirituSancto infusum: & Ambrosium ipsum l. III. de S. S. c. 12. intelligere gra- tiam spiritualem. Sed indubium nobis è contex- tu videtur, ipsummet Spiritum S. intelligi, & em- phatice τὸ αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα. Cui vero quod ὑπερέν- τευξις, salva ὁμουσίᾳ ejus cum Patre, tribuatur, ve- re ἀλάλητον & ἄῥῥητον censemus: neque apparet, si apud Patrem propria ac formali oratione interce- dere, etsi θεϊκῶς, dicatur Spiritus S. Cur non pari- ter & apud Filium ita intercedere dicendus sit, quum æque à Filio procedat, atque à Patre. Quum autem Filius ipse noster intercessor sit apud Pa- trem, eoque fine naturæ nostræ consors fieri volue- rit, ut Mediator & intercessor noster esset, non opus videtur ἐντεύξει Spiritus S. apud Filium. Et quum in- tercessio Mediatoris sit opus, annon ita duo erunt in divinis Mediatores nostri, Filius & Spiritus S. quod repugnat Apostolo 1. Tim. II. 2. Denique quum nullo conceptu explicari possit, ejusmodi formalis ἔντευξις, & intercessio, quam subeat Spiri- tus S. apud Patrem & Filium simul, ne obstet essen- tiali personarum divinarum περιχωρήσει in S. S. Tri- nitate, & operum atque actionum in Deo, quæ ad proprietatem personarum non pertinent, commu- nioni, præstat, nostro judicio, acquiescere expli- cationi B. Lutheri, & eorum, qui eum sequuti sunt, ac ἔντευξιν formalem agnoscere actum non mere θεϊκὸν, sed θεανδρικὸν, eumque nullum a- lium quam μεσιτικὸν, ac proinde ἔντευξιν Spiritus S. quam indigitat Apostolus effective intellige- re.

Juvat addere rationes, quibus B. Feurbornius Fascisc. IV. usus est; disp. IX. th. XLII. p. 561. No- li, inquit, putare, quod Spiritus S. ipse proprie pro no- bis intercedat. Nam (1) non tantum dicitur pro nobis intercedere, sed intercedere gemitibus & suspiriis indicibilibus. At ille ipse proprie non ge- mit & suspiria promit, quia est Spiritus infinitus: sed nos gementes & suspirantes facit; ut etiam Augustinus explicat. (2) Pro nobis dicitur qui- dem intercedere, at S. Scriptura non addit, quod pro nobis intercedat πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν apud Deum, sicut Christus dicitur noster esse advocatus apud Deum Patrem 1. Joh. II. v. 1. sed κτ᾽ Θεὸν, Rom. c. VIII. v. 27. i. e. juxta divinam voluntatem nos pie precantes reddit. (3.) S. Scriptura hoc explicat ita, ut dicat, nos per Spiritum S. clamare, Abba Pater, Rom. VIII. 15. & Gal. IV. 6. (4) Spiritus Sanctus non est noster advocatus & mediator sed unus & so- lus Christus 1. Tim. II. 5. & 1. Job. II. 1. Ergo neque mediatorie pro nobis proprie intercedit. (5) Spiritus Sanctus dicitur Spiritus gratiæ & precum Zach. c. XII. 10. eo quod tum gratiam Dei in cordibus nostris inchoet & consumet, nos ducendo ad Christum, in quo sumus κεχαριτωμένοι Eph. I. 6. & ex filiis iræ, quales φύσει sumus, Ephes. II. 3. nos faciat filios gratiæ, quam in nobis obsignat & confirmat, 2. Cor. I. 22. & Rom. VIII. 16. & 1. Johan. V. 6. tum preces pias in nobis accendat, & de exauditione nos certos reddat. Est enim Spiritus rectus, & firmus, nos firmans, & consolidans, Ps. LI. 12. 14. Denique (6) quia nemo potest dicere (pie invocare, & in ve- ra justificante fide compellare, Dominum Jesum, nisi per Spiritum Sanctum, 1. Cor. XII. 3. Absit ergo ut statuamus, Spiritum Sanctum ipsum proprie pro nobis interpellare apud Deum, & sic ipsum in sua persona fundere pro nobis preces. Nam pro no- bis intercedit effective, hoc est, nos pie & recte pre- cantes facit. Siquidem hoc ipsum quid oraturi su- mus ut oportet, non novimus (scilicet ex natura vi- ribus) sed ipse Spiritus intercedit pro nobis gemi- tibus inenarrabilibus, h. e. Spiritus Sanctus nos pie precantes & devote ad Deum suspirantes facit. Hæc B. Feuerbornius. Si ὑπερεντυγχάνειν advocato- rum est, qua clientibus desideria dictant, quod Gro- tius vult, & ea vocis hujus emphasis est, ut eum si- gnificet, qui sanctorum votis præfectus est, quod E- rasmo, & Claud. Espensæo, ut & B. Dannhauero vi- sum, nulla causa est, cur ab explicatione communi de effectiva postulatione hic discedamus. B. Paul. Tarnovius Comment. in Joh. p. 1031. Spiritus San- ctus, inquit, est paracletus noster, quatenus nos san- ctificat, hoc est, ad veritatis cognitionem adducit, ad- ductos solatur, & preces nostras ad Patrem per Fi- lium deferendas docet, ideoq́ dicitur Rom. IIX. 26. in- terpellare pro nobis, quia nos ad preces excitat, & velut verba intus dictitat. Doctissim⁹ Camero ad præ- sentem locum Johanneum adversus Calvinum, qui Spiritum Sanctum deprecatorem & advocatum no- strum apud Deum esse contendit, tum ex his Chri- sti verbis, quod παράκλητον advocatum no- tet, tum è loco Apostolico ad Rom. IIX. 26. obser- vat, vocem παράκλητον Atticam esse, qua signi- ficentur illi, quos in periculo accersimus, ut nobis adsint consilio (qui iidem Advocati propterea di- cuntur Latine) etiamsi non litigent in foro, nostro nomine, quodque solum per accidens fiat, ut id Advo- catus & deprecator sit, quomodo Christus πα- ράκλητος noster dicitur: & explicat hanc vocem ex Ebræo מליץ Doctor, vel interpres, & è Job. XVI. v. 20. Ubi in Targum pro consolatore adhibetur, ut ita Spiritus S. dicatur παράκλητος, non ob de- precationem, aut intercessionem quandam, sed edo- cturus esset Apostolos, & redditurus eos idoneos, qui aliis respondeant, & eos edoceant, idque ita, ut soletur etiam, ac gaudium adferat. In loco vero Apostolico Rom. VIII. Spiritum dici interce- dere pro nobis, non quod ipsa Spiritus S. persona immediate intercedat, sed quia excitat in nobis af- fectum precandi, siquidem intercedat per gemitus; non autem gemit Spiritus, sed nos gemimus: adeo- que deprecatur, efficiendo ut gemamus, & exci- tando in nobis precandi affectum.

Ἵνα μένῃ μεθ' ὑμῶν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) Non ut aliquot annis apud vos sit, ut ego fui, sed ut maneat perpetuo. Hoc enim Hebræis est εἰς αἰῶνα. Intelligendum autem hoc sub con- ditione jam dicta, observationis mandatorum.

## 14:17
Vers. 17.

Τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας) i. e. That Spirit the teacher of truth, as is explained below XVI. 13. & 1. Joh. II. v. 27. Opposed to this are πνεύματα πλάνης, 1. Tim. IV. 1.

ὃ ὁ κόσμος οὐ δύναται λαβεῖν) Namely as the world, as it is attached to the things of this age, 1. Cor. II. 14.

ὅτι οὐ θεωρεῖ αὐτὸ) The world cares for nothing except those things which are seen by bodily eyes: such as that Spirit is not.

Οὐδὲ γινώσκει αὐτὸ) And therefore it does not seek him; for there is no desire for the unknown. But it would know him if it showed itself docile and obedient to divine discourses. For that Spirit seeks such hearts. Irenaeus, citing Basil: τοὺς δὲ ἀχαλιναγωγήτως καὶ καταφερομένους εἰς τὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐπιθυμίας, καὶ μηδεμίαν ἔχοντας ἐπιθυμίαν θείου πνεύματος, δικαίως ὁ ἀπόστολος σαρκικοὺς καλεῖ. Conf. ad Coloss. III. 10.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ γινώσκετε αὐτὸ) You know and care for, you seek him. Thus Matth. VII. 23.

ὅτι παρ' ὑμῖν μένει) I think ὅτι is placed here for διὰ τοῦτο or for certainly, as Esa. VII. 9. 1. Joh. III. 20. & elsewhere. For the preceding words seem to indicate that the Spirit, as he is taken here, is first known, then penetrates into man. μένει is inhabits as we said above V. 38. Thus to be in someone 1. Joh. II. 5. is explained by μένειν, ibid. 6. 14. 24.

καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσται) Both inhabits and will inhabit: for ἔσται is the same as μένει: as we have already said.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας) i. e. Spiritus ille doctor verita- tis, ut explicatur infra XVI. 13. & 1. Joh. II. v. 27. Huic op- ponuntur πνεύματα πλάνης, 1. Tim. IV. 1.

ὃ ὁ κόσμος οὐ δύναται λαβεῖν) Nempe qua mundus, qua affixus rebus hujus seculi, 1. Cor. II. 14.

ὅτι οὐ θεωρεῖ αὐτὸ) Mundus non curat nisi ea, quæ ocu- lis corporeis conspiciuntur: quale non est ille Spiritus.

Οὐδὲ γινώσκει αὐτὸ) Ac proinde nec expetit; ignoti enim nulla cupido. Nosset autem si se divinis sermonibus docilem ac morigerum præberet. Nam talia pectora quæ- sit ille Spiritus. Irenæus citante Basilio: τοὺς δὲ ἀχαλιναγω- γήτως καὶ καταφερομένους εἰς τὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐπιθυμίας, καὶ μηδεμίαν ἔχοντας ἐπιθυμίαν θείου πνεύματος, δικαίως ὁ ἀπόστολος σαρ- κικοὺς καλεῖ. Conf. ad Coloss. III. 10.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ γινώσκετε αὐτὸ) Nostis & curatis, expetitis. Sic Matth. VII. 23.

ὅτι παρ' ὑμῖν μένει) Puto ὅτι hic poni pro διὰ τοῦτο aut pro certe, ut Esa. VII. 9. 1. Joh. III. 20. & alibi. Videntur enim præcedentia indicare Spiritum, quomodo hic sumi- tur, prius nosci, deinde in hominem penetrare. μένει est in- habitat ut diximus supra V. 38. Sic esse in aliquo 1. Joh. II. 5. exponitur per μένειν, ibid. 6. 14. 24.

καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσται) Et habitat & habitabit: ἔσται enim idem est, quod μένει: ut jam diximus.

## 14:18
Vers. 18.

Οὐκ ἀφήσω ὑμᾶς ὀρφανοὺς) At the time of my burial you will be as orphans: but you will not remain such: for I, first returning, will be to you as a father, then I will leave you the Spirit, who may be in the place of a father and defender.

ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς) The present tense, as often, for the future. And 'to come' for 'to return'. Thus also below 28 and ἐλθὼν Matthew XII. 44.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Οὐκ ἀφήσω ὑμᾶς ὀρφανοὺς) Tempore sepulturæ meæ eri- tis tanquam pupilli: sed non manebitis tales: nam ego pri- mum rediens vobis ero pro patre, deinde Spiritum vobis, qui vice patris ac defensoris sit, relinquam.

ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Præsens ut sæpe pro futuro. Et veni- re pro redire. Sic & infra 28 & ἐλθὼν Matth. XII. 44.

## 14:19
Verse 19.

ἔτι μικρὸν καὶ ὁ κόσμος με οὐκ ἔτι θεωρεῖ) A Hebraism such as also in Hosea I. 4, Haggai II. 7, for that which we would say: after some time I shall no longer be seen by the world, that is, after death. He understands by 'the world' those alienated from his teaching, which is the greatest part. θεωρεῖ for θεωρήσει, as often in this writer.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ θεωρεῖτέ με) With your own eyes you will see me more than once.

ὅτι ἐγὼ ζῶ) For I shall surely live. The same enallage. You will not see a phantom; you will see me, I say, alive.

καὶ ὑμεῖς ζήσεσθε) They feared that they would be swept away into death with Christ, above ch. IX. 16; now he affirms to them that it will come to pass that, exempted from the most grievous dangers, they shall survive.

By these words, 'because I live, and you shall live,' a reason is rendered for the preceding, namely that the disciples are to see Christ, who promised that he would come to them and would not leave them orphans. As therefore he was about to come to them, not only that he might manifest himself to them on a few occasions and days after his resurrection, but that they might not, I say, be left orphans, and that he might always be with them, even unto the consummation of the age, so that reason, 'because I live, and you shall live,' does not only pertain to his resurrection and the preservation of the disciples in life; but as far as it concerns Christ, it is rightly explained by Cyril, book IX on John, ch. 47: 'I live, since I am life according to nature (or essence), and my temple, filled with life, lives,' whence he teaches not only that he will rise again, but that he will live eternally, and he constitutes his resurrection and life as the cause of our resurrection and life. See Job XIX. verse 25, and therefore those words, 'and you shall live,' are to be understood as meaning that they shall live, both in this life in afflictions and in the future, as Rupert says: 'I live and you shall live: I live and you shall live forever, for this very reason, that I live, having died for you.' Which are also referred by some to spiritual life, or to the sanctification of the Apostles in this life: but B. Paulus Tarnovius rightly judges in his commentary, p. 1034, that they deflect too far from the genuine sense, which the scope indicates.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

ἔτι μικρὸν καὶ ὁ κόσμος με οὐκ ἔτι θεωρεῖ) Hebraismus qualis & Os. I. 4. Agg. II. 7. pro eo quod diceremus post ali- quod tempus mundo non conspiciar amplius, post mortem scilicet. Mundum intelligit, à sua disciplina alienos, quæ pars maxima. θεωρεῖ pro θεωρήσει, ut sæpe in hoc scriptore.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ θεωρεῖτέ με) Vestris oculis vos me non semel videbitis.

ὅτι ἐγὼ ζῶ) Nam sane vivam. Eadem enallage. Non vi- debitis spectrum, me, inquam, vivum videbitis.

καὶ ὑμεῖς ζήσεσθε) Timebant ne cum Christo in mortem raperentur, supra c. IX. 16. nunc illis affirmat futurum ut gravissimis periculis exempti superstites sint.

Verbis hisce, quia vivo ego, & vos vivetis, ra- tio redditur præcedentium, quod nempe visuri sint Christum discipuli, qui ad ipsos venturum se promisit, nec eosdem orphanos relicturum. Ut ergo venturus ad ipsos erat, non tantum ut paucis vicibus & diebus post resurrectionem suam illis se manifestaret, sed ne, inquam, relinquerentur or- phani, & ut semper illis adsit, usque ad consumma- tionem seculi, sic ratio illa, quia vivo ego, & vos vivetis, non tantum pertinet ad resurrectionem ipsius, ac conservationem discipulorum in vita; sed quod ad Christum attinet, recte explicatur à Cy- rillo lib. IX. in Joh. cap. 47. Ego vivo, cum vita sim secundum naturam (vel essentiam) & templum meum vita repletum vivit, unde non modo se re- surrecturum docet, sed æternum victurum, ac re- surrectionem & vitam suam nostræ resurrectio- nis & vitæ causam constituit. Vide Job. XIX. vers. 25. ideoque verba illa, & vos vivetis, intelli- genda, quod victuri sint, cum in hac vita in affli- ctionibus, cum in futura, ut Rupertus; Vivo ego & vos vivetis: vivo & vos in æternum vivetis, pro- pter hoc ipsum, quod vivo mortuus pro vobis. Quæ à nonnullis etiam ad spiritualem vitam referuntur, sive ad sanctificationem Apostolorum in hac vita: sed recte judicat B. Paulus Tarnovius in comment. p. 1034. eos longius à genuino sensu deflectere, quem scopus indicat.

## 14:20
v. 20. ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ) At that time, when I shall now appear to you as the victor over death.

γνώσεσθε ὑμεῖς) Much more perfectly than heretofore: through the open explanation of the ancient prophecies, Luke XXIV. v. 45, and through the experience of the thing itself.

Some refer that day to the day of the resurrection on the last day, with Augustine, Homily 75 on John: 'In that day, when we shall live by that life by which death shall be swallowed up, we shall know that I am in the Father, and you in me, and I in you, because then this very thing will be perfected which is even now begun through him, that he may be in us, and we in him.' Although indeed this is most certain, that in that day this knowledge will be plenary; yet this does not look to the day of the resurrection of Christ's disciples, but to the day of the Lord's resurrection, and consequently to the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and by that argument the disciples are encouraged, namely, that Christ was about to come to them again, as he promised here. Which is rightly observed by Chrysostom, homily LXXIV. To one interpreting thus: when I shall rise again, then you shall know that I am not a stranger to the Father, but of the same power, and that I am always with you, the things themselves crying out my help for you, etc. Cf. Luke XXIV. 45. Which day, however, does not exclude, but includes the time of the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, in which the Apostles knew the divine mysteries more abundantly: whence Theophylact joins these: When he rose again, he delivered a manifest opinion concerning all these things. For the grace of the Spirit after the resurrection taught them all things.

ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐν πατρί μου) That I have remained in all things which the Father had prescribed for me: which the Father showed by the resurrection itself and will show by the ascension into heaven. See below c. XVI. 10.

καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐν ἐμοὶ, κἀγὼ ἐν ὑμῖν) Again, and first for as. You shall know then that I will be most closely joined to you by present help, just as you were most closely joined to me by obedience and faith, Luke XXII. v. 28. Concerning the locution see above VI. 56. Add 1 John IV. 15, 16.

A mystical union of the faithful with Christ is hinted at, which imports much more than Christ's help and the obedience and faith of the faithful: a full description of which the blessed Gerhard has delivered here in Harmon. Evang. around c. CLXXVI, page 551, observing its formal aspect, that on the part of Christ it is more active, on our part more passive. For Christ, he says, is in us in such a way that he may live in us, Gal. II. v. 20, that he may make us partakers of all his goods, of righteousness and eternal life, that he may impart his Holy Spirit to us, that he may rule us by his words and his Spirit, that he may protect and defend us as the apple of his eye. But we are in Christ in such a way that we may receive spiritual life, righteousness, and salvation from him as from the head, that we may be inserted into his mystical body as true and living members, that we may be ruled, sustained, and defended by him. Theophylact on this passage. You are in me, whom I guard; And I in you, that is, I am with you, snatching you from dangers, working miracles through you, and glorifying you through all things. I am in you, as the head in the members, and you in me as members in the head.

Latin:

v. 20. ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ) Illo tempore, quo jam mortis victor vobis apparebo.

γνώσεσθε ὑμεῖς) Multo quam antehac perfectius: per explicationem apertam veterum vaticiniorum Luc. XXIV. v. 45. & per rei ipsius experimentum.

Diem illam referunt nonnulli ad diem resurre- ctionis in novissimo die cum Augustino LXXV. in Joh. in illa die, quando vivemus ea vita, qua mors absorbebitur, cognoscemus, quia IPSE in Patre, & nos in ipso, & ipse in nobis, quia tunc perficietur hoc ipsum, quod & nunc inchoatum est jam per ipsum, ut sit in nobis, & nos in ipso. Quanquam vero hoc certissimum sit, in illa die plenariam fu- turam istam cognitionem; non tamen hic dies re- surrectionis discipulorum Christi, sed dies resur- rectionis Dominicæ, consequenter visibilis effusio- nis Spiritus S. respicitur, ejusque argumento disci- puli eriguntur, quo nempe iterum ad ipsos ventu- rus erat Christus, uti hic promisit. Quod recte observatum Chrysostomo homil. LXXIV. ita in- terpretanti: cum resurgam, tum me non alienum à Patre, sed ejusdem potestatis esse cognoscetis, & me semper vobiscum esse, rebus ipsis meum ergo vos auxilium clamantibus &c. Conf. Luc. XXIV. 45. Quæ tamen dies non excludit, sed includit tem- pus visibilis effusionis Spiritus S. in quo uberius mysteria divina cognoverunt Apostoli: unde hæc conjungit Theophyl. Quando resurrexit, manife- stam de his omnibus sententiam tradidit. Gratia enim Spiritus post resurrectionem omnia docuit illos.

ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐν πατρί μυ) Me mansisse in omnibus quæ Pater mihi præscripserat: quod Pater ipsa resurrectione ostendit & evectione in cœlum ostendet. Vide infra c. XVI. 10.

καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐν ἐμοὶ, κἀγὼ ἐν ὑμῖν) Iterum κὶ primum pro sicut. Cognoscetis tunc me vobis conjunctissimum fore præsente auxilio, sicut vos mihi fuistis conjunctissimi obe- dientia & fide, Luc. XXII. v. 28. De locutione vide su- pra VI. 56. Adde 1. Joh. IV. 15. 16.

Mystica innuitur fidelium cum Christo unio, quæ multo plura importat, quam Christi auxi- lium, & fidelium obedientiam & fidem: cujus ple- nam descriptionem hic tradidit B. Gerhardus in Harmon. Evang. circa formale ejus observans c. CLXXVI. pag. 551. quod ex parte Christi ea magis activa, ex parte nostri magis passiva sit. Christus enim, inquit, ea ratione est in nobis, ut in nobis vi- vat, Gal. II. v. 20. ut omnium suorum bonorum ju- stitiæ & vitæ æternæ nos participes faciat, ut Spiri- tum suum S. nobis impertiatur, ut verba & Spiritu suo nos regat, ut nos tanquam oculi pupillam prote- gat & defendat. Nos vero ea ratione sumus in Chri- sto, ut ab ipso tanquam capite vitam spiritualem, ju- stitiam & salutem percipiamus, ut corpori ipsius my- stico tanquam vera & viva membra inseramur, ut ab ipso regamur, sustentemur, defendamur. Theo- phyl. in h. l. Vos in me estis, quos ego custodio; Et ego in vobis, hoc est, vobiscum sum, vos eripiens ex peri- culis, miracula per vos operans, vosque glorificans per omnia. In vobis sum, ut caput in membris, & vos in me sicut membra in capite.

## 14:21
Vers. 21.

ὁ ἔχων τὰς ἐυτολάς με) Lest anyone should think that He was making promises only to the Apostles, He extends what has been said to all who obey Him. ἔχειν ἐντολὰς, as ἔχειν λόγον, above V. 38, is to receive within, that is, to believe, to have faith.

καὶ τηρῶν ἀυτάς) Otherwise, to believe harms more than it profits.

ὁ δὲ ἀγαπῶν με ἀγαπηθήσεται ὑπὸ τῦ πατρός με) With a subsequent and greater and more fervent love.

καὶ ἐμφανίσω ἀυτῷ ἐμαυτὸν) And after the resurrection I will show myself to others, as to Magdalene, Cleopas, Nathanael, five hundred others, and I will make them partakers of my Spirit. See Ps. XXV. v. 13. Eph. III. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

ὁ ἔχων τὰς ἐυτολάς με) Ne quis putaret solis se Aposto- lis promittere quæ dixerat, extendit jam dicta ad omnes sibi parentes. ἔχειν ἐντολὰς, ut ἔχειν λόγον, supra V. 38. est intus recipere, id est credere, fidem habere.

καὶ τηρῶν ἀυτάς) Alioqui credere nocet magis, quam prodest.

ὁ δὲ ἀγαπῶν με ἀγαπηθήσεται ὑπὸ τῦ πατρός με) Subse- quente eaque majore ac fervidiore dilectione.

καὶ ἐμφανίσω ἀυτῷ ἐμαυτὸν) Et post resurrectionem me aliis ostendam, ut Magdalenæ, Cleophæ, Nathanieli, quin- gentis aliis, & participes faciam Spiritus mei. Vide Ps. XXV. v. 13. Eph. III. 3.

## 14:22
Vers. 22.

Ἰούδας ἐκ ὁ Ἰσκαριώτης) He adds this because He had spoken of him before. Therefore He designates Thaddaeus.

τί γέγονεν) A Hebraism for 'how does it happen'.

ὅτι ἡμῖν μέλλεις ἐμφανίζειν σεαυτὸν καὶ ἐχὶ τῷ κόσμῳ) He wonders at this because, with the others, he was expecting the kingdom of Christ to be conspicuous before the whole world.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Ἰούδας ἐκ ὁ Ἰσκαριώτης) Hoc ideo adjicit quod de eo locutus ante erat. Ergo Thaddæum designat.

τί γέγονεν) Hebraismus pro qui fit.

ὅτι ἡμῖν μέλλεις ἐμφανίζειν σεαυτὸν καὶ ἐχὶ τῷ κόσμῳ) Miratur hoc quia cum cæteris regnum Christi coram toto mundo conspicuum exspectabat.

## 14:23
Vers. 23.

ἐάν τις ἀγαπᾷ με, τὸν λόγον με τηρήσει) These and what follow are again to be read in one breath. Christ says that Judas ought not to wonder if He does not show Himself to all, since it is also the custom of the Father not to reveal Himself except to those who love Him, that is, those who observe His precepts. And that He Himself is an imitator of the Father. See what is at Matt. XI. 25 and above c. VI. 44. He repeats, however, what He had said above at 15, that no love is esteemed by Him and the Father without the observance of the commandments.

καὶ πρὸς ἀυτὸν ἐλευσόμεθα καὶ μονὴν παρ᾿ ἀυτῷ ποιήσομεν) It is a great thing if some king visits a private citizen, more if he wishes to lodge in his house. This honor is held only for those who are well beloved. Thus Christ also shows it to be fair that those signs of closer familiarity are not exhibited by Him and the Father to just anyone, but to those who love Him. See Zech. II. 10 and following.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

ἐάν τις ἀγαπᾷ με, τὸν λόγον με τηρήσει) Hæc & quæ se- quuntur rursum uno legenda sunt spiritu. Ait Christus mi- rari Judam non debere si non omnib. ipse se ostendat, quan- do & Patri is mos sit, se non patefacere nisi sui amantibus, id est præcepta sua observantibus. Se autem Patris esse imitatorem. Vide quæ ad Matth. XI. 25. & supra c. VI. 44. Repetit autem quod supra dixerat 15. dilectionem nullam a se ac Patre æstimari sine præceptorum observantia.

καὶ πρὸς ἀυτὸν ἐλευσόμεθα καὶ μονὴν παρ᾿ ἀυτῷ ποιήσομεν) Multum est, si rex aliquis privatum adeat, plus si in ejus ædibus velit divertere. Hic honos non nisi bene caris ha- betur. Sic æquum etiam ostendit Christus ut illa propioris familiaritatis indicia a se & Patre non exhibeantur qui- busvis, sed sui amantibus. Vide Zach. II. 10. & seqq.

## 14:24
Verse 24.

ὁ μὴ ἀγαπῶν με τὰς λόγες με ἐ τηρεῖ) An inverted statement, for: But those who do not observe my precepts, like worldly men, they do not love me, understand: and therefore they are not worthy of such honor.

κὶ ὁ λόγος ὃν ἀκέετε) Which you have been hearing for these years while you have been visiting me.

ἐκ ἔστιν ἐμὸς ἀλλὰ τῦ πέμψαντός με πατρὸς) It is no wonder, he says, if the Father also does not honor those who despise my precepts, since they did not originally proceed from me, were not discovered by my own ingenuity, but emanate from the Father himself. See above VII. 8. VIII. 28. XII. 49. 50.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ὁ μὴ ἀγαπῶν με τὰς λόγες με ἐ τηρεῖ) Inversa oratio, pro: Qui vero præcepta mea non observant, ut mundani homines, ii me non diligunt, subaudi ac proinde tali ho- nore digni non sunt.

κὶ ὁ λόγος ὃν ἀκέετε) Quem auditis per hos annos dum me festamini.

ἐκ ἔστιν ἐμὸς ἀλλὰ τῦ πέμψαντός με πατρὸς) Non mi- rum est, ait, si & Pater non honoret eos, qui præcepta mea spernunt, cum ea non à me originaliter sint profecta, non meo reperta ingenio, sed ab ipso Patre emanent. Vide su- pra VII. 8. VIII. 28. XII. 49. 50.

## 14:25
Verse 25.

ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν παρ᾿ ὑμῖν μένων) These things I have said to you briefly to console you, as far as the circumstances of time allow: while it is still permitted to be with you and to converse.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν παρ᾿ ὑμῖν μένων) Hæc ad vos con- solandos breviter vobis dixi, quoad fert temporis ratio: dum adhuc vobiscum esse & colloqui licet.

## 14:26
Verse 26.

ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί με) that is, for my sake, as above 13.

ἐκεῖνος ὑμᾶς διδάξει πάντα καὶ ὑπομνήσει ὑμᾶς πάντα ἃ εἶπον ὑμῖν) And these are to be read in one breath, so that the final words may be referred to both clauses. He will teach, that is, he will interpret the obscure, he will recall to memory things given to oblivion; see examples above II. 22. XII. 16.

Which interpretation can be confirmed from a comparison of Matt. XXVIII. v. 20. John XVI. 13. 14., and it clearly cuts the nerve of the argument of the Papists, which they seek from this passage, since the Spirit was not to teach new things, but those which Christ had already delivered.
