Yet Maldonatus does not reject this interpretation: It is doubtful, he says, whether what he says, he will teach all things, should be referred to that word whatsoever I have said to you, as if he were saying that the Holy Spirit would teach nothing else than what he himself had taught before, just as the word he will suggest is certainly referred to that. I will not object if anyone wishes to interpret it in that way; indeed, I will point out those authors by whom they defend their opinion, Augustine, Bede, and Rupert, who seem to have understood it in that way as well. John Ferus also approves of that explanation in this place. Rashly, therefore, do other Papists seek in this passage a defense for traditions, for which Grotius, having become an advocate for the Papists, subsequently also contended.

PART IV. Prediction concerning the threefold denial of Peter.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί με) id est, in meam gratiam, ut supra 13.

ἐκεῖνος ὑμᾶς διδάξει πάντα καὶ ὑπομνήσει ὑμᾶς πάντα ἃ εἶπον ὑμῖν) Et hæc legenda uno spiritu, ut postrema verba ad utrumque membrum referantur. Docebit, id est, inter- pretabitur obscura, in memoriam revocabit oblivioni data; exempla vide supra II. 22. XII. 16.

Quæ interpretatio è collatione Matth. XXVIII. v. 20. Joh. XVI. 13. 14. confirmari potest, & argu- mento Pontificiorum, quod ex hoc loco petunt, nervum plane incidit, siquidem non nova docere debuerit Spiritus, sed ea quæ Christus jam tradi- derat. Nec tamen reprobat hunc interpretatio- nem Maldonatus: Dubium, inquit, an quod dicit, docebit omnia, ad illud verbum quæcunque dixe- ro vobis, referendum sit quasi non aliud docturum Spiritum S. dicat, quam quod ipse ante docuisset, quemadmodum & verbum suggeret eo utique refer- tur. Non repugnabo, si quis ita velit interpretari, quin autores illi, quibus suam sententiam tuentur, Augustinum, Bedam, & Rupertum indicabo, qui ita videntur quoque intellexisse. Approbat eam ex- plicationem quoque Joh. Ferus in h. l. Temere ita- que alii Papistæ patrocinium traditionum, pro qui- bus deinceps etiam dimicavit Papistarum advo- catus factus Grotius, in hoc loco quærunt.

PARS IV. Prædictio de trina negatione Petri.

## 14:27
Verse 27. Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you) About to depart, he bids farewell. For the Hebrews used to say to leave or to give peace, that is, salvation, for that is what שלום signifies. He repeats the same sense twice, just as we are accustomed to say: farewell, farewell.

Not as the world giveth, give I unto you) The world, that is, the greater part of men, imparts salvation to others by the sound of the voice, often thinking nothing of the matter, and if it does think, yet it profits the other nothing. But Christ greets both from the heart and effectively: just as when εὐλογεῖν is attributed to God it signifies to do good; the correlative is missing as above 22. Not Iscariot.

Let not your heart be troubled) Out of pity for me.

Neither let it be afraid) Out of regard for your own danger: these things are to be connected with what follows.

Latin:

Vers. 27. εἰρήνην ἀφίημι ὑμῖν, εἰρήνην τὴν ἐμὴν δίδωμι ὑμῖν) Abiturus valedicit. Nam id Ebræi dicebant relinquere aut dare pacem, id est salutem, Nam id valet שלום, Bis autem eundem sensum repetit, sicut dicere solemus: vale, vale.

ἐ καθὼς ὁ κόσμος δίδωσι, ἐγὼ δίδωμι ὑμῖν) Mundus, id est, major pars hominum, salute alios impertit sono vocis, nihil sæpe de re cogitans, & si cogit &, tameo id alteri ni- hil prodest. At Christus, tum ex animo, tum efficaciter sa- lutat: sicut ἐυλογεῖν cum Deo tribuitur significat benefa- cere; deest ἀνταπόδοτον ut supra 22. ἐκ ὁ Ἰσκαριώτης.

Μὴ ταρασσέσθω ὑμῶν ἡκαρδία) Miseratione mei.

Μηδὲ δειλιάτω) Vestri periculi respectu: connectenda hæc cum sequentibus.

## 14:28
Verse 28.

I go away and come unto you) Above 12 and 19, where I said that ἔρχομαι means I am about to return.

If ye loved me) As much as is fitting, and in the way that is fitting with the judgment of right reason.

Ye would have rejoiced) Just as they did rejoice afterwards, when they beheld the fulfillment of the departure to the Father, Luke 24:52.

For the Father is greater than I) The sender than the sent. This, however, is said so that it may be understood both that he himself would be safe there and that there would be more protection for them in the Father than in his bodily presence.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ὑπάγω καὶ ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς) supra 12. & 19. ubi dixi- mus ἔρχομαι esse rediturus sum.

εἰ ἠγαπᾶτέ με) Quantum oportet, & quomodo oportet cum judicio rectæ rationis.

ἐχάρητε ἂν) Sicut & gavisi sunt postea, cum implemen- tum abitus ad Patrem conspexerunt, Luc. XXIV. 52.

ὅτι ὁ πατήρ με μείζων με ἐστί) Mittens misso. Hoc autem ideo dicitur ut intelligatur & se ibi tutum fore & ipsis in Pa- tre plus futurum præsidii quam in sua corporali præsentia.

## 14:29
Verse 29.

I have told you before it come to pass) I have indicated by these words my ascent into the heavenly region. Thus 13:19, 16:4.

ἵνα ὅταν γένηται πιστεύσητε) so that when it happens you may trust and believe me more and more that what I have foretold will truly come to pass, and the rest, concerning my perpetual help and your being taken up.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

εἴρηκα ὑμῖν πριν γενέσθαι) Indicavi vocis his verbis meum ascensum in regionem cœlestem. Sic XIII. 19. XVI. 4.

ἵνα ὅταν γένηται πιστεύσητε) ut magis magisque mihi con- fidatis & credatis vere futura & cætera quæ prædixi, de au- xilio meo perpetuo & vestri assumtione.

## 14:30
Vers. 30.

ἐκ ἔτι πολλὰ λαλήσω μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν) as if he were saying: the straits of time snatch away words.

ἔρχεται γὰρ ὁ τῷ κόσμε ἄρχων) we spoke above XII. 31. He comes, however, through men full of him, whose power was ἐξουσία τῦ σκότος, Luc. XXII. 53. For that ruler works in the sons of disobedience, Eph. II. 2.

καὶ ἐν ἐμοὶ ἐκ ἔχει ἐδὲν) ἐν ἐμοὶ is the same as πρός με, Acts XXIV. 19 and chapter XXV. 19. Which is more clearly ἔχειν κατηγορῆσαι, Acts XXVIII. 19. It is the devil's work to accuse. In me he has nothing that he can blame. See above VIII. 46. Whence it follows that Jesus is not a debtor to death: for death is the wages of sin, and the devil has the power of death, as noted above v. 4. for but, as Acts X. 28 and elsewhere. Samuel is a figure of Jesus, in his own way ἀνέγκλητος, I Sam. XII. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

ἐκ ἔτι πολλὰ λαλήσω μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν) quasi dicat: temporis angustiæ abripiunt verba.

ἔρχεται γὰρ ὁ τῷ κόσμε ἄρχων) diximus supra XII. 31. ve- nit autem per homines sui plenos, quorum vis erat ἐξουσία τῦ σκότος, Luc. XXII. 53. Nam is ἄρχων ἐνεργεῖ ἐν τοῖς ὑοῖς τῆς ἀπειθείας, Eph. II. 2.

καὶ ἐν ἐμοὶ ἐκ ἔχει ἐδὲν) ἐν ἐμοὶ idem est quod πρός με, Actor. XXIV. 19. & XXV. cap. 19. Quod apertius ἔχειν κατηγορῆσαι, Act. XXVIII. 19. Diaboli opus est accusare. In me nihil habet quod culpare possit. Vide supra VIII. 46. Unde sequitur Jesum non esse mortis debitorem: nam mors stipendium peccati, & Diabolus habet imperium mortis, ut notatum supra v.4. pro sed, ut Act. X. 28. & alibi. Samuel fi- gura Jesu, suo modo ἀνέγκλητος, I. Sam. XII. 5.

## 14:31
Vers. 31.

Ἀλλ᾿ ἵνα γνῷ ὁ κόσμος ὅτι ἀγαπῶ τὸν πατέρα) so that it may be evident to the human race concerning that love with which I love the Father.

κὶ καθὼς ἐνετείλατό μοι ὁ πατὴρ ὕτω ποιῶ) καὶ here is for therefore: as also elsewhere, Therefore, he says, I do all those things which have been entrusted to me by the Father: Therefore I also allow myself to be captured, and led to judgment, and condemned, and ignominiously put to death. Philipp. II. 8. And compare what is above X. 18.

ἐγείρεσθε) Let us rise from the table. For they were accustomed to prolong conversations at the reclining place even after supper. See Mark XVI. 14, Luke XXIV. 33.

Ἄγωμεν ἐντεῦθεν) I do not see what prevents us from believing that the discourses which follow up to chapter XVIII were held by Christ on the very journey, not indeed with all the apostles hearing, but those who, being first in order, were clinging closer to his side, namely Peter, James, and this our John.

This opinion is indeed pleasing to Ammonius and Tatian in their Harmony, to Hilary in book IX of his De Trinitate, as well as to the Venerable Bede, and also to B. Tarnovius and Pelargus. But it neither agrees sufficiently with John XVIII, v. 1, nor does it seem likely that Christ would have delivered so long and arduous a discourse at an unseasonable hour of the night on the road, where He could not be heard by all the disciples. Therefore, Chrysostom thinks that Christ led the disciples away to some other place, where they could hear what still remained to be said without fear; but history contains nothing regarding this. Whence others, including our blessed Gerhard, more correctly judge that after they had risen from the table, Christ still remained for a while in the upper room, as is customary, drawing one discourse from another, and finished the remaining part of this valedictory sermon while standing, and also offered there a προαγωνίσιον prayer to God the Father, and only then undertook his departure out of the city to the garden of Olivet. He commanded them to rise, however, because a change of place and posture is accustomed to stir the minds of the hearers, so that they might thereafter attend more diligently.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

Ἀλλ᾿ ἵνα γνῷ ὁ κόσμος ὅτι ἀγαπῶ τὸν πατέρα) ut generi humano constet de eo amore, quo Patrem amo.

κὶ καθὼς ἐνετείλατό μοι ὁ πατὴρ ὕτω ποιῶ) καὶ hic est pro- pterea: ut & alibi, Propterea, inquit, omnia ea facio, quæ à Patre mihi commendata sunt: Propterea & capi me si- nam, & in judicium adduci, & damnari & ignominose in- terfici. Philipp. II. 8. Et confer, quæ supra X. 18.

ἐγείρεσθε) Surgamus à mensa. Solebant enim sermones in accubitu etiam post cœnam nonnihil produci. Vide Marc. XVI. 14. Luc. XXIV. 33.

Ἄγωμεν ἐντεῦθεν) Non video quid nos impediat credere sermones qui sequuntur ad caput usque XVIII. habitos à Christo in ipso itinere, non quidem Apostolis omnibus ex- audientibus, sed iis qui primi ordine cum essent, ipsius la- teri proprius hærebanr, Petro scilicet, Jacobo & huic nostro Johanni.

Placet quidem ista sententia Ammonio & Ta- tiano in Harm. Hilario l. IX. de Trin. nec non Ve- nerab. Bedæ ut & B. Tarnovio & Pelargo. Sed ne- que satis convenit cum Joh. XVIII. v. 1. neque ve- risimile videtur, Christum tam prolixam atque ar- duam concionem morte intempesta in via habuis- se, ubi ab omnibus discipulis audiri nequivit. Ideo Chrysostomus putat, Christum discipulos in alium quendam locum, in quo sine metu, quæ adhuc dicenda restabant, audire potuerit, abduxisse; sed de eo nihil habet historia. Unde rectius alii censent, etiam B. Gerhardus noster, postquam à mensa surrexissent, aliquantisper adhuc, ut fieri solet, in cœnaculo Christum commoratum es- se, sermonem ex sermone traxisse, ac residuam va- ledictoriæ hujus concionis partem stando absol- visse, orationem etiam προαγωνίσιον ad Deum Pa- trem ibi habuisse, ac tum demum abitionem ex- tra urbem in hortum Oliveti suscepisse. Jussisse autem surgere, quia solet mutatio loci ac situs au- ditorum animos excitare, ut deinceps diligentius attendant.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Jesus teaches concerning the true vine and the branches, and their pruning, that they may bear fruit, for which cause it is necessary to remain in the vine, and that those who do not remain in Christ as the vine will be cast into the fire. To the others, who will both have the word in themselves and obtain the hearing of their prayers, who are to bring forth much fruit, provided they persevere in the love of Jesus, the sign of which is the keeping of the commandment, namely mutual love, from which it may be evident that they are friends of the Lord, who revealed all things to them as his friends, and chose them, and appointed them to this end, that they might bear fruit. He encourages them, moreover, against the hatred of the world by the example of himself, and the cause of the hatred, their election from the world, and also the unbelief of those who hate, for which they even hated him, and that without cause according to Scripture (Psal. XXXV. 13.). Finally, he promises the future testimony concerning himself of the Paraclete, whom he is about to send from the Father, and who proceeds from the Father, with whom they themselves also are to testify.

There are three parts: I. The parabolic discourse concerning the vine and the branches, to v. 8. II. An exhortation to love, to v. 17. III. A forewarning concerning the hatred of the world, and the consolation opposed to it, to v. 23.

PART I. Parabolic discourse concerning the vine and the branches.

Ver. 1.

Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος ἡ ἀληθινή) It is the custom of Christ to take the occasion for his discourse from things close at hand: he had already, after supper, offered his own the last cup, the token of his passion, which history John omitted, having been liberally treated by others: because it was nothing other than a signification through visible things of that which Christ had said in words above in ch. VI. 51. In this offering he had called wine his blood. Hence, sliding into related matters (just as above in ch. X. he called himself first the shepherd, then the door), he calls himself the vine, and indeed with the article, that true vine, just as in ch. X. he had called himself that true shepherd, namely, described in sufficiently well-known places. Therefore, when he calls himself that true vine, he understands that these epithets שורק זרע אמת כל כלה Jer. II. 21, belong to him in an excellent sense at last. ἄμπελον καρποφόρον πᾶσαν ἀληθινήν, as it is in the Greek, where in the Hebrew it is the seed of truth, as here the vine of truth in the Syriac, that is, a genuine, not a wild vine. The vine in the fable of Jud. IX. 12. boasts that God and men are gladdened by its liquor, which is most truly said of the blood of Christ. Wine is the blood of the grape: Gen. XLIX. 11. Deut. XXXII. 14. αἷμα σταφυλῆς, 1. Macc. VI. 34. Clement, Paed. II., concerning Christ: he partook of wine and he himself also blessed the wine, saying, take, drink, this is my blood, the blood of the vine. And a little before: therefore the Scripture called wine a mystical symbol of holy blood.

καὶ ὁ πατήρ μου ὁ γεωργός ἐστι) The genus for the species, γεωργὸς for ἀμπελουργὸς כרם Matth. XXI. 33. God is called οἰκοδεσπότης who planted a vineyard; to Philo also the husbandry of the soul is compared to the working of the earth in his book on that subject. And there are many similitudes taken from agriculture among the Prophets.

Latin:

CAPUT XV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

De vera vite & palmitibus, eorumque purga- tione, ut fructus ferant, cujus causa in vite manere oportet, qui vero in Christo ceu vite non manent, eos in ignem abjectum iri Jesus docet. Ceteris & verbum in se habituris & precum exauditionem consequuturis, qui multos fructus sint prolaturi, modo in cha- ritate Jesu perseverarint, cujus signum est observatio mandati, mutua scilicet dilectio, e qua constet, quod amici sint Domini, qui ipsis ceu amicis suis omnia revelavit, eosque elegit, & ad id posuit, ut fructus ferant. Erigit autem eosdem adversus odium mun- di suiipsius exemplo, & causa odii, electio- ne ipsorum e mundo, nec non incredulitate eorum, qui oderunt, ob quam etiam semet- ipsum, idque gratis secundum Scripturam (Psal. XXXV. 13.) oderint. Denique Para- cleti, quem a Patre missurus est, & qui a Patre procedit, futuram de se testificatio- nem, quo cum & ipsi testificaturi sint, promittit.

Partes sunt tres: I. Parabolica concio de vite, ac palmitibus, ad v. 8. II. Adhortatio ad charita- tem, ad v. 17. III. Præmonitio de mundi odio, & consolatio eidem opposita, ad v. 23.

PARS I. Parabolica de vite ac palmitibus. Concio.

Vers. 1.

Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος ἡ ἀληθινή) Mos est Christi ex re- bus obviis sermonis sui occasionem sumere: propinave- rat jam post cœnam suis ultimum calicem, passionis suæ tesseram, quam historiam ab aliis liberaliter tractatam omisit Johannes: eo quod nihil aliud esset quam significa- tio per res visibiles ejus quod verbis dixerat Christus supra c. VI. 51. In hac propinatione vinum vocarat sanguinem suum. Hinc ad affinia delabens (quomodo supra c. X. se pastorem primum, deinde ostium dixit,) vitem se vocat, & quidem cum articulo, illam veram vitem, sicut cap. X. se dixerat illum verum pastorem, nimirum descriptum locis satis notis. Ergo cum se illam veram vitem vocat, intelli- git sibi demum excellenter competere ista epitheta שורק זרע אמת כל כלה Jer. II. 21. ἄμπελον καρποφόρον πᾶ- σαν ἀληθινήν, ut est in Græco, ubi in Hebræo semen verita- tis, ut hic vitis veritatis in Syriaco, id est, genuina, non fera vitis. Gloriatur vitis in fabula Jud. IX. 12. suo liquore læ- tificari Deum & homines, quod de Christi sanguine ve- rissime dicitur. Vinum sanguis uvæ: Gen. XLIX. 11. Deut. XXXII. 14. αἷμα σταφυλῆς, 1. Macc. VI. 34. Clemens pæd. II. de Christo μετέλαβεν οἴνου καὶ αὐτὸς καὶ εὐλόγησέν γε τὸν οἶνον, εἰπὼν, λάβετε, πίετε, τοῦτο μοῦ ἐστι τὸ αἷμα, αἷμα τῆς ἀμπέλου. Et paulo ante: μυστικὸν ἄρα σύμβολον τῷ γραφῇ αἵματος ἁ- γίου οἶνον ὠνόμασεν.

καὶ ὁ πατήρ μου ὁ γεωργός ἐστι) Genus pro specie γεωργὸς pro ἀμπελουργὸς כרם Matth. XXI. 33. Deus dicitur οἰκο- δεσπότης ὅστις ἐφύτευσεν ἀμπελῶνα, Philoni quoque ψυχῆς γεωργία τῇ γῇς ἐργασίᾳ comparatur libro ejus argumenti. Et multæ sunt apud Prophetas similitudines ab agricultura desumtæ.

## 15:2
v. 2. πᾶν κλῆμα, ἐν ἐμοὶ μὴ φέρον καρπὸν αἴρει αὐτό) ἐν ἐμοὶ, that is, being in me, that is, adhering to me. This cutting off of useless branches the Hebrews call פוס, the Greeks κλάσιν, sometimes κάθαρσιν, the Latins deputationem. See Varro in his book on the Study of Farmers: Theophrastus III. on the Causes of Plants: Cicero on Old Age: The art of farmers, pruning with the knife, restrains the vine creeping with manifold and erratic growth, lest it grow wild with shoots and spread too much in all directions. Thus, those who profess Christianity without pious deeds are taken away, and are held by God as not Christians: however much they may show themselves with green leaves.

καὶ πᾶν τὸ καρπὸν φέρον καθαίρει αὐτό) He purges more and more and renders it more fruitful. This is βλαστολογία to the Greeks, pampinatio to the Latins. But God does this in various ways, especially through afflictions.

ἵνα πλείονα καρπὸν φέρῃ) More and more every day.

Latin:

v. 2. πᾶν κλῆμα, ἐν ἐμοὶ μὴ φέρον καρπὸν αἴρει αὐτό) ἐν ἐμοὶ, id est, ὂν ἐν ἐμοὶ, id est, mihi adhærens. Hanc defractionem inutilium palmitum פוס Hebræi, Græci κλάσιν vocant, in- terdum κάθαρσιν, deputationem Latini. Vide Varronem libro de Studio Agricolarum: Theophrastum III. de Causis Stirpium: Cicero de Senectute: Vitem serpentem multiplici lapsu & erratico ferro, amputans coercet ars agricolarum, ne silvescat sarmentis & in omnes partes nimia fundatur. Sic qui Christianismum profitentur, sine factis piis, tolluntur, ha- bentur a Deo pro non Christianis: utcunque frondibus vi- ridibus se ostentent.

καὶ πᾶν τὸ καρπὸν φέρον καθαίρει αὐτό) Magis magisque purgat & fœcundius reddit. Hæc est βλαστολογία Græcis, Latinis pampinatio. Hoc autem facit Deus variis modis præcipue per afflictiones.

ἵνα πλείονα καρπὸν φέρῃ) Indies magis magisque.

## 15:3
Verse 3.

You are already clean) By the purpose of the mind, as was explained above in chapter XIII, 11. But he says 'already': because the impure Judas had already gone out, never to return to the Apostolic fellowship, a useless branch. But Christ wishes it to be tacitly understood that they are pure, that is, fruit-bearing, in such a way that they must nevertheless be cleansed more and more by the diligent cleansing which he had spoken of above regarding the washing of the feet. For in repeating the words then spoken, he must be considered to have repeated or hinted at those connected to them as well.

Because of the word which I have spoken to you) Understand it as piously admitted and received: which the following words hint at: 'if my words remain in you.' Add what is below in XVII, 17. 19.

That purity which Christ attributes to the disciples 'because of the word,' which they had obtained through His Word, is not to be understood solely as a purpose of the mind, but was situated primarily in true faith: by which our hearts are purified, Acts XV. 9. Which purification is justification itself, consisting in the remission of sins, which is followed by daily renewal, by which, because of the sins to which we are daily liable, we must be cleansed from time to time, and the inner man must be renewed from day to day, 2 Cor. IV. 13. Nor does the particle 'already' look so much to Judas as to the present state of the Apostles, that now some apply faith to His speech, by which their hearts were purified, but there is a need that they persevere in that faith. For Christ foresees that it will shortly come to pass that they will be defiled by the sin of flight and denial. The Apostles are therefore called clean, not because they are entirely free from every sin, for this is repugnant to the Scriptures, Exod. XXXIV. 7. 1 Kings VIII. v. 46. Job IX. 2. Psalm XIX. 13. Prov. XX. 9. Matt. VI. 12. John XIII. 10. James III. 2. 1 John I. 8. but because, having been freed from the error of unbelief through faith, they have obtained the remission of sins, and strive for true purity through the daily mortification and renewal of the old Adam: both of which benefits, of regeneration and justification as well as of renewal, are obtained for us through the word of the Gospel, 1 Pet. I. 23. James I. 18. 21. 'This is the word of faith,' says Augustine, 'which we preach, by which, without doubt, Baptism is consecrated so that it may cleanse.' Compare Eph. V. 26. Tit. III. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ἤδη ὑμεῖς καθαροί ἐστε) Proposito animi, ut explicatum est supra c. XIII, 11. Dicit autem jam: quia impurus Judas jam exierat, nunquam in Apostolicum consortium rediturus, sarmentum inutile. Tacite autem subintelligi vult Christus ita puros esse, id est frugiferos, ut tamen magis magisque purgandi sint solicita purgatione quam pedum lotionem supra dixerat. Nam repetens verba tum dicta, etiam connexa censendus est repetiisse aut innuisse.

διὰ τὸν λόγον ὃν λελάληκα ὑμῖν) Subintellige pie admissum atque receptum: quod innuunt sequentia: ἐὰν τὰ ῥήματά μου ἐν ὑμῖν μείνῃ. Adde quæ infra XVII, 17. 19.

Puritas illa, quam discipulis tribuit Christus διὰ τὸν λόγον, quam per Verbum suum consequuti erant, non est de proposito animi solum intelligenda, sed imprimis in vera fide sita fuit: qua purificantur corda nostra, Actor. XV. 9. quæ purificatio est ipsa justificatio in remissione peccatorum consistens, quam excipit quotidiana renovatio, qua ob peccata, quibus obnoxii quotidie sumus, subinde purgandi sumus, & de die in diem renovandus est homo interior, 2. Cor. IV. 13. Neque particula ἤδη tam Judam respicit, quam statum præsentem Apostolorum, quod nunc quidam adhibeant sermoni suo fidem, qua corda ipsorum purificata erant, opus autem sit, ut in fide illa perseverent. Prævidet enim Christus brevi futurum, ut fuga & abnegationis peccato impureantur. Dicuntur ergo Apostoli mundi, non quod omni prorsus peccato careant, hoc enim Scripturæ repugnat Exod. XXXIV. 7. 1. Reg. VIII. v. 46. Job. IX. 2. Psal. XIX. 13. Prov. XX. 9. Matth. VI. 12. Joh. XIII. 10. Jac. III. 2. 1. Joh. I. 8. sed quod ab errore incredulitatis liberati per fidem consequuti sint remissionem peccatorum, veræque puritati studeant, quotidiana veteris Adami mortificatione & renovatione: quod utrumque beneficium cum regenerationis ac justificationis, tum renovationis obtingit nobis per verbum Evangelii, 1. Petr. I. 23. Jacob. I. 18. 21. Hoc est verbum fidei, inquit Augustinus, quod prædicamus, quo sine dubio ut mundare possit, consecratur & Baptismus. Conf. Eph. V. 26. Tit. III. 5.

## 15:4
Verse 4.

Abide in me) Take care that you are fixed in me: namely, by the purpose of obeying and imitating. 1 Epistle II. 6. See what we said in X. 38. and XIV. 10.

And I in you) Take care that I am fixed in you, through the influx of the Spirit and daily help. See the places already mentioned. But this indicates what will happen if they themselves retain the purpose of obeying and imitating. For these things are connected. A similar manner of speaking is 1 Tim. IV. 12, 'Let no one despise your youth,' that is, take care that you do not give an occasion for yourself to be despised.

In the former part, that which is primary is omitted, namely faith, because through faith we are grafted into Christ as the true vine, and we abide in Christ; which is indeed followed by the purpose of imitating and obedience as the fruit of faith, which fruit-bearing branches grafted into Christ ought to bear, but it is by no means the means of either being grafted into Christ or of remaining in Christ. For by that through which we are grafted into Christ the vine and are implanted, by that same thing we also remain in Christ. But we are grafted in through faith, John I. v. 12. Gal. III. 26. 27. Eph. III. 17. John VI. v. 56. Christ therefore warns of this, that they should not fall away from faith, whether through the cross and sufferings or through mortal sins, and that they should cherish the word, through which faith is ascribed and confirmed, in their heart, and meditate upon it diligently, and strive for true piety, and exercise faith through love, and render it testified to themselves and others that they are and remain in Christ, 2 Pet. I. 10. 1 John III. v. 14. Compare Gal. V. 6. 1. John IV. 15. In the latter member there is rather a promise, as Euthymius observes, than commanded: because Christ does not wish to desert his branches, which remain in him, but to invigorate them and render them fruit-bearing. Whence Maldonatus wrongly concludes from this passage that it is in our power to remain in grace. Conf. 1 Cor. XV. v. 10. 1 Pet. I. 5. c. V. 10. Moreover, Christ remains in us through the communication of spiritual life, the influx and gift of his Spirit, and our confirmation and preservation in grace, as well as protection in adversities and final liberation, Gal. II. 20. 1 John IV. 13. Rom. VIII. 38, 39. 1 Pet. I. 5. 2 Tim. IV. 17, 18. Beautifully Augustine, tr. LXXXI. on John: The branches are in the vine in such a way that they do not confer anything upon the vine, but receive from it that by which they may live: but the vine is in the branches in such a way that it supplies vital nourishment to them, and does not take from them.

which is able to bear fruit of itself) By some power of its own which it might have outside the vine. Thus ἀπ’ ἐμαυτῦ above chapter V. 30. VII. 17. VIII. 28.

unless it remains in the vine) ἐὰν μὴ for but, as above V. 10. that is, only then will the branch bear fruit, if it remains clinging to the vine.

so neither do you, if you do not remain in me) Unless you perpetually retain that purpose in your mind. Otherwise you will slip down to useless rites, or falsely called virtues, and finally to open vices.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

μείνατε ἐν ἐμοὶ) Curate ut mihi infixi sitis: nempe obediendi imitandique proposito. 1. Epistola II. 6. Vide quæ diximus X. 38. & XIV. 10.

κἀγὼ ἐν ὑμῖν) Curate, ut ego nobis insigar, per influxum Spiritus & auxilii quotidiani. Vide dicta jam loca. Hoc autem indicat futurum, si ipsi retinuerit obediendi imitandique propositum. Sunt enim hæc connexa. Simile loquendi genus 1. Tim. IV. 12. μηδείς σου τῆς νεότητος καταφρονείτω, id est, cura, ne tui contemnendi occasionem des.

In priori parte omittitur, quod præcipuum est, fides nempe, quia per fidem Christo ceu veræ viti inserimur, & in Christo manemus; quam sequitur quidem imitandi propositum, & obedientia tanquam fructus fidei, quem palmites frugiferi Christo inserti ferre debent, neutiquam vero est medium vel insitionis in Christum, vel permanentiæ in Christo. Per quod enim Christo viti inserimur, & implantamur, per idem etiam in Christo manemus. At inserimur per fidem Joh. I. v. 12. Gal. III. 26. 27. Eph. III. 17. Joh. VI. v. 56. Id ergo monet Christus, ne fide excidant, seu per crucem & passiones, seu per peccata mortalia, adeoque verbum, per quod fides adscribitur & confirmatur, in corde foveant, & sedulo meditentur, veræque pietati studeant, ac per dilectionem fidem exerceant, ac sibiipsis, aliisque testatum reddant, se in Christo esse & manere, 2. Petr. I. 10. 1. Joh. III. v. 14. Conf. Gal. V. 6. 1. Joh. IV. 15. In posteriori membro promissum potius habetur, ut Euthymius observat, quam mandatum: quia Christus palmites suos, qui in ipso manent, deserere non vult, sed vegeta- re & frugiferos reddere. Unde Maldonatus per- peram concludit ex hoc loco, in nostra esse potesta- te, ut in gratia maneamus. Conf. 1. Cor. XV. v. 10. 1. Petr. I. 5. c. V. 10. Manet autem in nobis Chri- stus per vitæ spiritualis communicationem, Spiritus sui influxum & donationem, nostrique in gratia con- firmationem & conservationem nec non in adver- sis protectionem & finalem liberationem, Gal. II. 20. 1. Joh. IV. 13. Rom. VIII. 38. 39. 1. Petr. I. 5. 2. Tim. IV. 17. 18. Pulchre Augustin. tr. LXXXI. in Joh. Ita in vite palmites sunt, ut viti non conferant, sed inde accipiant, unde vivant: ita vero vitis est in pal- mitibus, ut vitale alimentum subministret eis, non sumat ab eis.

ὃ δύναται καρπὸν φέρειν ἀφ’ ἑαυτῦ) Vi aliqua propria quam habeat extra vitem. Sic ἀπ’ ἐμαυτῦ supra cap. V. 30. VII. 17. VIII. 28.

ἐὰν μὴ μένῃ ἐν τῇ ἀμπέλῳ) ἐὰν μὴ pro sed, ut supra V. 10. id est, ita demum palmes fructum feret, si maneat viti co- hærens.

οὕτως ὐδὲ ὑμεῖς, ἐὰν μὴ ἐν ἐμοὶ μένητε) Nisi perpetuo il- lud propositum in animo retinueritis. Alioqui delabemini ad ritus inutiles, aut falso dictas virtutes, tandem ad aperta vitia.

## 15:5
Verse 5.

I am the vine) He immediately adds a plainer interpretation, as in Matt. XIII. 47.

and I in him, a Hebraism for: and in whom I remain.

this one) This one finally, and no other. Thus James I. 25.

without me you can do nothing) χωρὶς, that is, outside of me, as the preceding words show. Thus Matt. XIV. 21. below XX. 7. Thus without Christ Eph. II. 12. Thus it is translated בלעד Gen XXXI. 1. Numbers XVI. 36. and elsewhere, which in other places is καθ’ ἑαυτὸν, κατὰ μονὰς, καθ’ ἑυτὸ. He who departs from the precepts and example of Christ, from him no good fruit is to be expected. See above VI. 68. Acts IV. 12.

To be outside of Christ is not properly to depart from the precepts and example of Christ, but not to be inserted into Christ, the true vine, through faith, whence we can do nothing without Christ, just as a branch cannot bear fruit without the vine, or one who is not in the vine or inserted into the vine: concerning which Macarius hom. XVII. Just as it is impossible for a fish to lead a life without water, or for anyone to walk without feet, or to behold light without eyes, or to speak without a tongue, or to hear without ears: so also without the Lord Jesus and the efficacy of divine virtue it is not permitted to know the mysteries and wisdom of God, or to be rich, and a Christian. Prosper to Demetr. Is not, he says, the proud branch convinced that it is emptied of all fertility if it is not nourished by the richness of the vine? for who can bear the fruit of justice without the help of grace, or who dares to say that he is not divided from Christ, who denies that Christ works in him? Christ does not say, without me you can do something with difficulty: but χωρὶς ἐμῦ ὐ δύνασθε ἐδὲν, without me you can do nothing. Nor is it so, as if we have the beginning from him alone, or as if, with his grace approaching, we could cooperate through our own powers, but so that we may be taught that all things are to be ascribed to Christ, the beginning, the progress, and the completion; and that we should not attribute the powers by which we cooperate to nature, but to grace, since it is said in this place of the converted themselves, without me you can do nothing. Just as the branch has all its juice, power, and vigor from the vine, and cannot bear any fruit outside of it. Therefore that phrase 'without me' must be understood negatively and exclusively, in that outside of Christ we not only do not have sufficient strength, but we have no strength at all; not as if we indeed have strength through nature with Christ, which however without the grace of Christ would not be sufficient: but that our natural strengths are nothing and we are able to do nothing without Christ. This is to be observed against the Papists, who explain it thus, that without grace assisting us we can do nothing, yet meanwhile, together with grace, or even when assisted by grace, man can do something in spiritual matters from himself and his own natural strengths (See Bellarmine, book V, on free will, chapter XVII). Augustine, book II, against the two letters of the Pelagians, chapter 8: The Lord, he says, in order to answer the future Pelagius, does not say, 'without me you can do something with difficulty,' but, 'without me you can do nothing.' And in order to answer those future ones as well, in that same Evangelical sentence, he does not say, 'without me you can perfect nothing,' but 'do.' For if he had said 'perfect,' they themselves could say that the help of God is not necessary for beginning the good, which is from us, but for perfecting it. When the Lord says, 'without me you can do nothing,' by this one word he comprehends the beginning and the end. And tractate LXXXI on John: Lest anyone should think that the branch could at least bear some small fruit by itself, when he had said, 'this one bears much fruit,' he does not say, 'because without me you can do little,' but 'you can do nothing.' Therefore, whether it be little or much, it cannot be done without him, without whom nothing can be done. Compare the Council of Milevis, Canon 5.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος) Statim subjungit planiorem inter- pretationem, ut Matth. XIII. 47.

κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ, Hebraïsmus pro: & in quo ego maneo.

ὗτος) Hic demum, non alius. Sic Jac. I. 25.

χωρὶς ἐμῦ ὐ δύνασθε ἐδὲν) χωρὶς, id est, extra me, ut osten- dunt præcedentia. Sic Matth. XIV. 21. infra XX. 7. Sic χω- ρὶς Χρισῦ Eph. II. 12. Sic vertitur בלעד Gen XXXI. 1. Nu- mer. XVI. 36. & alibi, quod aliis locis καθ’ ἑαυτὸν κατὰ μονὰς καθ’ ἑυτὸ. Qui à Christi præceptis & exemplo discedit, ab eo nihil bonæ frugis exspectandum est. Vide supra VI. 68. Actor. IV. 12.

Extra Christum esse proprie non est à Christi præceptis & exemplo discedere, sed Christo veræ viti non insertum esse per fidem, unde tam sine Christo nos nihil facere possumus, quam non po- test palmes sine vite, vel qui in vite non est, aut insertus non est viti, fructum ferre: de quo Ma- carius hom. XVII. Quemadmodum piscem absque aqua vitam ducere, aut absque pedibus quemquam progredi, aut absque oculis lumen intueri, aut absque lingua loqui, aut absque auribus audire, impossibile est: sic quoque absque Domino Jesu & virtutis divinæ efficacia non licet cognoscere mysteria & sapientiam Dei, aut esse divitem, & Christianum. Prosper ad Demetr. Nonne, inquit, convincitur palmes ela- tus, quod omni fertilitate vacuetur, si vitis ubertate non alitur? quis enim sine auxilio gratiæ fructum ferre potest justitiæ, aut quis audet dicere, se à Chri- sto non dividi, qui Christum in se diffitetur operari? Non dicit Christus, sine me difficulter quid facere potestis: sed χωρὶς ἐμῦ ὐ δύνασθε ἐδὲν, sine me nihil potestis facere. Nec id ita, quasi ab ipso so- lum initium habeamus, aut quasi accedente ipsius gratia per vires proprias cooperari possimus, sed ut omnia Christo adscribenda esse doceamur, ini- tium, progressum & complementum; nec vires, quibus cooperamur, naturæ, sed gratiæ tribua- mus, quum de ipsis conversis dicatur hoc loco, sine me nihil potestis facere. Quemadmodum pal- mes omnem succum, vim & vigorem habet a vite, nec extra ipsam nullum fructum ferre potest. Ideo illud sine me, negative & exclusive intelligendum, quod extra Christum non modo non sufficientes, sed nullas vires habeamus, non quasi cum Chri- sto quidem gratia habeamus vires per naturam, quæ vero sine gratia Christi non sufficiant: sed quod nullæ nostræ sint vires naturales nihilque valeamus fine Christo. Quod contra Pontificios, ita exponentes, sine gratia adjuvante nos nihil pos- se, interim tamen una cum gratia, vel adjutos à gratia etiam, in spiritualibus ex se, & naturalibus viribus suis hominem aliquid posse (Vide Bellarm. lib. V. de liber. arbitr. cap. XVII.) observandum. Augustin. lib. II. contra duas epist. Pelag. cap. 8. Dominus, inquit, ut responderet futuro Pelagio, non ait, sine me difficile aliquid potestis facere, sed, sine me nihil potestis facere. Et ut responderet futu- ris etiam istis, in eadem etiam ipsa Evangelica sen- tentia, non ait, sine me nihil potestis perficere, sed facere. Nam si perficere dixisset, possent ipsi dicere, non ad incipiendum bonum, quod a nobis est, sed ad perficiendum esse Dei adjutorium necessarium. Do- minus cum ait, sine me nihil porestis facere, hoc uno verbo initium finemque comprehendis. & tract. LXXXI. in Joh. Ne quisquam putaret, saltem par- vum aliquem fructum posse à semetipso palmitem ferre, cum dixisset, hic fert fructum multum, non ait quia sine me parum potestis facere, sed nihil po- testis facere. Sive ergo parum, sive multum sine illo fieri non potest, sine quo nihil fieri potest. Conf. Concilium Milevit. Can. 5.

## 15:6
Verse 6.

Ἐβλήθη ἔξω ὡς τὸ κλῆμα) By these aorists without designation of time it is signified what is accustomed to happen, for which the present is also often used. ἐκβάλλεσθαι ἔξω in the comparison is to be cut off from the vine, in meaning, to be destitute of the grace and favor of Christ. See Matthew XVIII. 12, chapter XXII. 13, XXV. 30.

κὶ ἐξηράνθη) Its uselessness appears: which is excellently described in Ezekiel XV. 2. This will happen on the day of judgment.

κὶ συνάγυσιν αὐτὰ) He changes the number, because the sense is the same. So also Psalm CXI. 10, and it is a Hebraism, 'they gather them' impersonally, that is, 'they shall be gathered.' The Syrian expressed this with another idiom, 'gatherers gather.' 'The tares are gathered,' Matthew XIII. 40.

Καὶ καίεται) It is given to the fire to be consumed. Ezekiel in the cited place concerning the vine-branches, thus concerning the tares in the cited place of Matthew: concerning the useless tree, Matthew III. 10. The explanation is in Matthew in the cited chapter XIII. Moreover, the end of Judas seems to be tacitly indicated so that others may beware for themselves by his example.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ἐβλήθη ἔξω ὡς τὸ κλῆμα) Hi aoristi sine designatione temporis significatur quid fieri soleat, pro quo & præsens sæpe usurpatur. ἐκβάλλεσθαι ἔξω in comparatione est præcidi à vite, in significatione, destitui gratia ac favore Christi. Vide Matth. XVIII. 12. c. XXII, 13. XXV. 30.

κὶ ἐξηράνθη) Apparet ejus inuutilitas: quæ egregie de- scribitur Ezech. XV. 2. Hoc fiet indie judicii.

κὶ συνάγυσιν αὐτὰ) Mutat numerum, quia sensus idem est. Sic & Psal. CXI. 10. & est Hebraismus colligunt ipsa impersonaliter, id est colligentur. Hoc Syrus alio idioti- smo expressit colligunt colligentes. Συνάγεται τὰ ζιζάνια, Matth. XIII. 40.

Καὶ καίεται) Igni datur ad consumendum. Ezechiel dicto loco de sarmentis, Sic de zizaniis dicto Matthæi loco: de arbore inutili, Matth. III. 10. explicatio est apud Mat- thæum dicto capite XIII. Videtur autem tacite Judæ exi- tus indicari ut ejus exemplo cæteri sibi caveant.

## 15:7
Verse 7.

Καὶ τὰ ῥήματά μυ ἐν ὑμῖν μείνῃ) Let them not only stick in the memory, but also in the affection. So above verse 38, 1 Ep. II. 14.

ὃ ἐὰν θέλητε) Namely, pertaining to the honor of God, which restriction was added above in chapter XIV. 13.

Αἰτήσεσθε κὶ γενήσεται ὑμῖν) A Hebraism: for, if you ask, it will happen to you. A similar expression above VII. 39. Thus the Latins: 'A hungry little Greek, if you order him, will go to heaven.'

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Καὶ τὰ ῥήματά μυ ἐν ὑμῖν μείνῃ) Non in memoria tan- tum hæreant, sed & in affectu. Sic supra V. 38. 1. Ep. II. 14.

ὃ ἐὰν θέλητε) Nempe ad honorem Dei pertinens, quæ restrictio addita est supra c. XIV. 13.

Αἰτήσεσθε κὶ γενήσεται ὑμῖν) Hebraismus: pro, si petie- ritis continget vobis. Similis locutio supra VII. 39. Sic Latini: Græculus esuriens in cælum, jusseris, ibit.

## 15:8
Verse 8.

ἐν τύτῳ ἐδοξάσθη ὁ πατήρ μυ) Again the aorist in the sense which we just mentioned; the glory of God becomes manifest from the holy works of His own, Matt. V. v. 16. 1 Cor. VI. 20. ἐν τύτῳ by this.

ἵνα καρπὸν πολὺν φέρητε) ἵνα here is indicative in mood: which in Latin is sometimes expressed by ut, sometimes by si. A similar use of this little word is found above IV. 34. VI. 29. below XVII. v. 3. which meaning the Syrian rightly expressed here.

κὶ γενήσεσθε ἐμοὶ μαθηταί) Thus also the Syrian reads: therefore the sense is: if you bring forth copious fruits, then you will truly be, that is, it will appear that you are my disciples. For it is often said to be that which appears. See above chap. VIII. v. 31. Rom. III. v. 4. Jas. I. 12.

PART II. Exhortation to charity.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

ἐν τύτῳ ἐδοξάσθη ὁ πατήρ μυ) Iterum aoristus sensu, quem modo diximus; ex operibus sanctis suorum inclare- scit Dei gloria, Matth. V. v. 16. 1. Corinth. VI. 20. ἐν τύτῳ per hoc.

ἵνα καρπὸν πολὺν φέρητε) ἵνα hic est modi significativum: quod Latine interdum per ut, interdum per si enunciatur. Similis hujus voculæ usus supra IV. 34. VI. 29. infra XVII. v. 3. quam significationem recte hic expressit Syrus.

κὶ γενήσεσθε ἐμοὶ μαθηταί) Sic etiam Syrus legit: itaque sensus est: si copiosos fructus proferatis, tunc vere eritis, id est apparebitis mei esse discipuli. Sæpe enim dicitur esse id quod apparet. Vide supra cap. VIII. v. 31. Rom. III. v. 4. Jac. I. 12.

PARS II. Adhortatio ad charitatem.

## 15:9
Vers. 9.

Καθὼς ἠγάπησέ με ὁ πατὴρ κἀγὼ ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς μείνατε ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ τῇ ἐμῇ) All these things are to be read in one breath: and ὕτως is understood before μείνατε, as above 3. VI. 57. The sense is: As the Father has loved me and I you, so you in turn love me. What he called here ἀγάπη τῇ ἐμῇ he will immediately call ἀγάπη με. ἀγάπη με is love of me. Thus ἀγάπη Θεῦ, Luke XI. 42. and above c. V. v. 42. and 1 Epist. II. 5. where ἀγάπη Θεῦ explains that which had been said before ἔγνωκα αὐτὸν. and ibid 16. ἡ ἀγάπη τῦ πατρὸς is opposed to that love with which the world is loved. Thus also the same Epist. III. 16. and 17.

Ἐὰν τὰς ἐντολάς μυ τηρήσατει μενεῖτε ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ μυ) that is, thus it will appear that I am loved by you. Thus in the said chap. II. of the epistle, verse 5, and above IV. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Καθὼς ἠγάπησέ με ὁ πατὴρ κἀγὼ ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς μείνατε ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ τῇ ἐμῇ) Omnia hæc ita legenda uno spiritu: & subauditur ante μείνατε, ὕτως, ut supra 3. VI. 57. Sensus est: Sicut Pater me dilexit & ego vos, sic vos me vicissim diligite. Quod hic dixit ἀγάπη τῇ ἐμῇ statim dicet ἀγάπη με. ἀγάπη με est amor mei. Sic ἀγάπη Θεῦ, Luc. XI. 42. & supra c. V. v. 42. & 1. Epist. II. 5. ubi ἀγάπη Θεῦ explicat id quod ante dictum erat ἔγνωκα αὐτὸν. & ibid 16. ἡ ἀγάπη τῦ πατρὸς opponitur ei dilectioni qua mundus diligitur. Sic & eadem Epist. III. 16. & 17.

Ἐὰν τὰς ἐντολάς μυ τηρήσατει μενεῖτε ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ μυ) id est, sic apparebit me à vobis diligi. Sic dicto cap. II. epi- stolæ commate 5. & supra IV. 25.

## 15:10
Ver. 10.

καθὼς ἐγὼ τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ πατρός μου τετήρηκα καὶ μένω αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ) Thus I have shown how greatly I love him. Thus above XIV. 30. That the world may know that the Father is loved by me, as the Father has commanded me, so I do.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

καθὼς ἐγὼ τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ πατρός μου τετήρηκα καὶ μένω αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ) Sic ostendi quantopere ipsum diligam. Sic supra XIV. 30. Vt novit mundus à me diligi Patrem, prout Pater mihi mandavit ita facio.

## 15:11
Ver. 11.

ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν) Therefore I have stirred you up to bring forth much fruit.

ἵνα ἡ χαρὰ ἡ ἐμὴ ἐν ὑμῖν μείνῃ) My joy, the joy because of me, which you have enjoyed while I was present and cherishing you. See below XVII. 13. As if he were to say, these words of mine will supply the place of me being absent in comforting you.

καὶ ἡ χαρὰ ὑμῶν πληρωθῇ) πληροῦσθαι is said of joy, and above c. III, 29. and below in the said passage XVII. 13. 1 Epist. c. I. v. 4. 2 Epist. 12. Phil. II. 2. Not only will my words be a consolation to you here, but that matter will also produce for you most perfect joy in the future life.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν) Ideo vos excitavi ad multum fructum proferendum.

ἵνα ἡ χαρὰ ἡ ἐμὴ ἐν ὑμῖν μείνῃ) χαρὰ ἡ ἐμὴ, gaudium ob me, quo gavisi estis me præsente ac vos fovente. Vide infra XVII. 13. Quasi dicat, hæc mea verba mei absentis vicem supplebent in vobis consolandis.

καὶ ἡ χαρὰ ὑμῶν πληρωθῇ) πληροῦσθαι de gaudio dicitur & supra c. III, 29. & infra dicto loco XVII. 13. I. Epist. c. I. v. 4. 2. Epist. 12. Phil. II. 2. Non hic tantum mea verba vobis so-latio erunt, sed vobis quoque ea res perfectissimum pariet gaudium in vita futura.

## 15:12
Ver. 12.

ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ ἐμὴ) Not of the old law, which neither extends love so widely, nor extends it to that joy. See what is above XIII. 34. He inculcates this very often, as it is most necessary for establishing and maintaining the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ ἐμὴ) Non legis veteris, quæ dilectionem nec tam late porrigit, nec ad eum extendit gaudium. Vide quæ supra XIII. 34. Sæpissime hoc inculcat, ut ad Ecclesiam con-stituendam continendamque maxime necessarium.

## 15:13
Ver. 13.

Μείζονα ταύτης ἀγάπην οὐδεὶς ἔχει) He explains what that is, as I have loved you. No one can show his affection toward friends by a greater deed. Toward friends, I say: for the discourse was to such.

ἵνα) It is an explanation of that ταύτης. See what is above 8.

τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ θῇ ὑπὲρ τῶν φίλων αὐτοῦ) Let him expose himself to the dangers of death. We have spoken of the expression X. 11. and following. Nothing is dearer than life Job II. 4. Euripides: ψυχῆς γὰρ οὐδὲν ἐστι τιμιώτερον. The stories of Pylades and Orestes, of Damon and Pythias are well known, whether fables or histories, beyond which examples of friendship cannot go.

It is not the highest degree of love to expose oneself to death and dangers: for a higher degree is to undergo death in another's place, than to expose oneself to the danger of death merely for another. And Grotius, in his treatise on the satisfaction of Christ, defends with us against Socinus that Christ underwent death in our place. Compare with this passage Rom. V. 8. Gal. II. 20. 1. John III. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Μείζονα ταύτης ἀγάπην οὐδεὶς ἔχει) Explicat quid sit illud, sicut ego vos dilexi. Affectum suum erga amicos nemo ma-jori facto potest ostendere. Erga amicos inquam: nam ad tales sermo erat.

ἵνα) Est expositio illius ταύτης. Vide quæ supra 8.

τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ θῇ ὑπὲρ τῶν φίλων αὐτοῦ) Mortis peri-culis se objiciat. De locutione diximus X. 11. & deinceps. Vita nihil carius Job. II. 4. Euripides: ψυχῆς γὰρ οὐδὲν ἐστι τι-μιώτερον. Notæ sunt de Pylade & Oreste, de Damone & Pythia sive fabulæ sive historiæ, ultra quæ amicitiæ exem-pla progredi non possunt.

Non est is summus gradus amoris, mortis, peri-culis se objicere: superior enim gradus est alterius loco mortem subire, quam pro alio periculo tantum mortis se exponere. Et Christum mortem nostri loco subiisse contra Socinum nobiscum defendit Grotius tr. de satisfact. Christi. Confer cum hoc loco Rom. V. 8. Gal. II. 20. 1. Joh. III. 16.

## 15:14
Verse 14.

You are my friends) Present for future as above VIII. v. 31. thus you will remain my friends: thus it will come to pass that you are always loved by me, and consequently you have nothing not to be expected from so faithful a lover, Rom. V. 8. 9. 10.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ὑμεῖς φίλοι μου ἐστὲ) Præsens pro futuro ut supra VIII. v. 31. ita amici mei manebitis: ita fiet ut semper à me dili-gamini, ac proinde nihil non à tam fideli amante expectan-dum habeatis, Rom. V. 8. 9. 10.

## 15:15
Verse 15.

I no longer call you servants) I say, that is, I hold. I do not now deal with you as with servants, although by my right I could. We have spoken of this in Matt. I. 21.

for a servant does not know what his Lord is doing) Xenophon: for servants ought not to know the nature or the business of masters, to whom nothing more than service belongs. Euripides: You are born a servant, of whom I have a share in the discourse.

is doing) Here it is, what he wishes to do, as above c. X. v. 32. Masters are not accustomed to disclose their plans to servants, but to friends. Seneca: A servant is not the judge of a master's command, but a minister. Not far from this is what is in Plato, that servants are treated by physicians with commands only: but friends, in such a way that the reason for the commands is at the same time rendered to them.

but I have called you friends) And so I call you, and as such I treat you.

because) For as we have also noted elsewhere.

all things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you) The Father's plans which I received from him (thus 'to hear' is taken also above III. 32. & VIII. 26.) I have made open to you, concerning my resurrection, concerning the ascension into heaven, concerning the sending of the Holy Spirit, concerning the calling of the Gentiles, concerning the universal judgment, concerning eternal life. Most of these things God had indeed shadowed forth before, but had not revealed, Eph. III. 5. understand therefore all things which could in any way pertain to your consolation. For thus often universality is restricted by the subject matter of the discourse. A not dissimilar passage, Acts XX. 27. For certain things, such as that his kingdom was merely spiritual, that the law of Moses was ceasing, he taught only afterwards, as he professes he will do below c. XVI. 12.

The whole plan concerning our salvation is without doubt to be understood, to which Christ's passion pertains primarily, nor should other things concerning regeneration, faith, and justification be omitted, without which salvation cannot consist: and those 'all things' extend more widely than the aforementioned plans, nor can those things which Christ heard from the Father be excluded, those things concerning the merely spiritual kingdom of Christ, concerning the abrogation of the ceremonial law, and other things in

the Scriptures handed down. But that Grotius restricts all those things which Christ heard from the Father to those which in any way pertained to the consolation of the disciples of Christ, does not rest on a solid foundation: nay, it is not to be doubted that not only those things which make for consolation, but also those which make for teaching or information, for reproof or refutation, for correction or amendment, and for instruction in righteousness, were handed down by Christ, who did this in his school, so that the Apostles might be complete, equipped for every good work, as the Apostle speaks 2. Tim. III. 16. 17. although they attained a fuller knowledge of them only when they were equipped with power from on high, and the Holy Spirit was poured out upon them: who did not bring a new kind of doctrine, but explained those things which they had heard from Christ, and had not sufficiently understood, impressed their meaning upon their hearts, and confirmed the truth of them within them.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

οὐκέτι ὑμᾶς λέγω δούλους) Dico, id est, habeo. Non ego nunc vobiscum ago tanquam cum servis, quanquam meo jure possem. Diximus Matth. I. 21.

ὅτι δοῦλος οὐκ οἶδε τί ποιεῖ αὐτοῦ ὁ Κύριος) Xenophon: οὐδὲ γὰρ δεσποτῶν φύσιν ἢ πρᾶξιν δούλους δεῖ εἰδέναι, οἷς οὐδὲν πλέον ὑπηρεσίας προσήκει. Euripides: δοῦλος πέφυκας ὧν μετεσ-τί μοι λόγου.

ποιεῖ) Hic est, quid facere velit, ut supra c. X. v. 32. Non solent heri servis sua consilia patefacere, sed amicis. Sene-ca: Servus herilis imperii non censor est, sed minister. Non lon-ge hinc abit, quod apud Platonem est, servos à medicis cu-rari solis præceptis: at amicos, ita ut simul præceptorum ratio ipsis reddatur.

ὑμᾶς δὲ εἴρηκα φίλους) Et sic voco, & ut tales tracto.

ὅτι) Nam ut & alibi monuimus.

πάντα ὅσα ἤκουσα παρὰ τοῦ πατρός μου ἐγνώρισα ὑμῖν) Pa-tris consilia quæ ex ipso accepi (sic audire sumitur & supra III. 32. & VIII. 26.) vobis aperta feci, de mea resurrectio-ne, de ascensione in cœlum, de missione Spiritus S. de vo-catione gentium, de judicio universali, de vita æterna. Horum pleraque Deus antehac adumbraverat quidem, sed non revelaverat, Eph. III. 5. omnia ergo intellige, quæ ul-lo modo ad consolationem vestram pertinere poterant. Sic enim sæpe universalitas ex subjecto sermone restringi-tur. Locus non dissimilis, Actor. XX. 27. Nam quædam, ut regnum suum mere esse spirituale, legem Mosis cessare, postea demum docuit, ut profitetur se facturum infra c. XVI. 12.

Consilium totum de salute nostra sine dubio intelligendum est, ad quod imprimis pertinet Christi passio, nec omittenda alia de regeneratione, fide, justificatione, sine quibus salus constare non potest: & latius patent illa πάντα, quam prædicta consilia, neque eximi possunt illis, quæ a Patre audivit Christus, ista de regno Christi mere spiritua-li, de legis ceremonialis abrogatione, aliaque in

Scripturis tradita. Quod vero omnia illa, quæ au- divit à Patre Christus, restringit Grotius ad ea, quæ ullo modo ad consolationem pertinebant di- scipulorum Christi, solido fundamento haud ni- titur: imo non ea tantum quæ ad consolationem, sed etiam quæ ad διδασκαλίαν vel informationem, ad ἔλεγχον vel confutationem, ad ἐπανόρθωσιν vel correptionem, & ad παιδείαν, τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ vel institutionem in justitia faciunt, à Christo tradita esse, dubitandum non est, qui id egit in Schola sua, ut Apostoli ἄρτιοι essent, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένοι, ut loquitur Apostolus 2. Tim. III. 16. 17. tametsi uberiorem eorum cognitionem assecuti demum sint, cum virtute ex alto instructi sunt, & Spiritus S. in ipsos effusus est: qui non attulit no- vum doctrinæ genus, sed ea, quæ à Christo au- dierant, nec satis intellexerant, declaravit, eorum sensum cordibus ipsorum impressit, & veritatem eorum in ipsis confirmavit.

## 15:16
Verse 16.

οὐχ᾽ ὑμεῖς με ἐξελέξασθε) He commends his love because the beginning of the friendship was made by him, not provoked by any good deeds of theirs toward him. You did not choose me as a friend, but I took you for myself.

Ἀλλ᾽ ἐγὼ ἐξελεξάμην ὑμᾶς) See above VI. 70. XIII. 18.

κὶ ἔθηκα ὑμᾶς) I have also raised you to Apostolic dignity. Thus τιθέναι is also accustomed to be used, Acts XIII. 47. XX. 28. Rom. IV. v. 17. Heb. I. 2. This is elsewhere κατασῆσαι, as Matthew XXV. 23.

ἵνα ὑμεῖς ὑπάγητε κὶ καρπὸν φέρητε) The Syrian [version] as 'that going away you may bring forth.' These particles ὑπάγειν and πορεύεσθαι are often accustomed to be redundant. But here it is more correct that we understand the Apostles to be stirred up by Christ's words, so that they do not wait until men eager for learning come to them, but they themselves of their own accord seek them out.

κὶ ὁ καρπὸς ὑμῶν μένῃ) A Hebraism for, that the fruit may remain, which may be stored in the heavenly barn, not be burned up. See above c. IV. 37. Matthew XIII. 30.

ἵνα ὅ, τι ἂν αἰτήσητε ᾇ πατέρα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί με δῷ ὑμῖν) The Syrian and Latin [versions], and some of the Greeks, read δῷ in the third person. ἵνα here also is used consecutively. It is not the case that God fulfills their prayers as a consequence of diligent fruit-bearing. See Acts IV. 30. See above 7. Matthew XXI. 22.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

οὐχ᾽ ὑμεῖς με ἐξελέξασθε) Commendat amorem suum quod à se amicitiæ factum sit initium, nullis ipsorum in se bene- factis provocato. Non vos me elegistis in amicum, sed ego vos mihi assumpsi.

Ἀλλ᾽ ἐγὼ ἐξελεξάμην ὑμᾶς) Vide supra VI. 70. XIII. 18.

κὶ ἔθηκα ὑμᾶς) Etiam ad Apostolicam dignitatem evexi, Sic & usurpari solet τιθέναι, Act. XIII 47. XX, 28. Rom. IV, v. 17. Heb. I. 2. Hoc alibi est κατασῆσαι, ut Matth. XXV. 23.

ἵνα ὑμεῖς ὑπάγητε κὶ καρπὸν φέρητε) Syrus ut abeuntes afferatis. Solent sæpe hæ particulæ ὑπάγειν & πορεύεσθαι ab- undare. Sed hic rectius est, ut intelligamus Christi verbis excitari Apostolos, ut non expectent dum homines discendi avidi ad se veniant, sed ipsi ultro eos quærant.

κὶ ὁ καρπὸς ὑμῶν μένῃ) Hebraïsmus pro, qui fructus ma- neat, qui in cœleste horreum reponatur, non comburatur, Vide supra c. IV. 37. Matth. XIII. 30.

ἵνα ὅ, τι ἂν αἰτήσητε ᾇ πατέρα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί με δῷ ὑμῖν) δῷ in tertia persona legerunt Syrus & Latinus, & Græcorum nonnulli. ἵνα hic quoque est ἐκβατικῶς. Non hoc consequens est diligenti fructificationi ut preces ipsorum Deus impleat, Vid. Act. IV. 30. Vide supra 7. Matth. XXI. 22,

## 15:17
Verse 17.

ταῦτα ἐντέλλομαι ὑμῖν) I enjoin these things upon you, namely concerning the love with which I anticipated you, which I extended even unto death, and concerning which I hid nothing from you. אמר is also accustomed to be translated by ἐντέλλομαι and דבר which is mostly translated by ἐντέλλομαι through λαλῆν. Thus Ps. XLII. 8. יצוה he will command his mercy, he will indicate, he will signify.

ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλυς) I do not say these things because I am reproaching you with benefits; but so that you, provoked by such a great example, may love one another.

PART III. A forewarning concerning the world's hatred, and a consolation opposed to the same.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ταῦτα ἐντέλλομαι ὑμῖν) Hæc omnia inculco vobis, nem- pe de amore quo vos præveni, quem ad mortem usque ex- tendi, quo nihil vos celavi. Solet & אמר verti per ἐντέλ- λομαι & דבר quod plerumque ἐντέλλομαι per λαλῆν. Sic PS. XLII. 8. יצוה ἐντελεῖται ἔλεος αὑτῦ, indicabit, signi- ficabit.

ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλυς) Non hæc dico quod beneficia ex- probrem; sed ut vos tanto exemplo provocati diligatis alii alios.

PARS III. Præmonitio de mundi odio, & consolatio eidem opposita.

## 15:18
Ver. 18.

εἰ ὁ κόσμος ὑμᾶς μισεῖ) The Apostles already saw that the message of the Gospel could not be taught without incurring the greatest hatreds. For those who professed Jesus to be the Messiah were already forbidden from the assembly; He himself was sought for death. Therefore, against this fear Christ consoles them: moreover, there is an excellent use of the particle, si, where we oppose good to evil.

Γινώσκετε) Recall to mind. Thus γινώσκειν is taken in the same argument, 1 Pet. 5.9.

πρῶτον ὑμῶν) that is πρότερον; before you, as the Syriac explains. See what is above at 1.15. I have paved the way for you; I have received these hatreds first.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

εἰ ὁ κόσμος ὑμᾶς μισεῖ) Videbant jam Apostoli non pos- se sermonem Evangelii doceri ut non maxima odia incurre- rentur. Jam enim conventu prohibiti erant qui Jesum pro- fiterentur Messiam; ipse petebatur ad mortem. Itaque ad versus hunc metum Christus eos solatur: est autem egre- gius usus particulæ, si, ubi malo bonum opponimus.

Γινώσκετε) Animo recolite. Sic γινώσκειν sumitur in eodem argumento, I. Petr. V. 9.

πρῶτον ὑμῶν) id est πρότερον; antequam vos, ut exponit Syrus. Vide quæ supra I. 15. Munivi vobis viam; hæc odia prios excepi.

## 15:19
Ver. 19,

εἰ ἐκ τῦ κόσμυ ἦτε) Endowed with worldly affection, in the same way as being from the Devil and from God is taken, above 8.44, 47.

ὁ κόσμος ἂν τὸν ἴδιον ἐφίλει) That it might love you as its own. For a community of interests is accustomed to avail for friendships: take κόσμον for the totality of those who are devoted to the flesh and the age, who with general hatred persecute only the professors of piety and holiness. See above 7.7 and 1 Ep. 3.14.

ἐξελεξάμην ὑμᾶς ἐκ τῦ κόσμυ) I have separated you from that totality, and set you apart for myself as a peculiar possession: Thus Christians are called ἀποφυγόντες τὰ μιάσματα τῦ κόσμυ, 2 Pet. 2.20. ἐκλέγειν is often used in this sense in the Old Testament, where it treats of the Hebrew people and their fathers, 2 Macc. 1.25, ὁ ποιήσας τὺς πατέρας ἐκλεκτὺς κὶ ἁγιάσας αὐτός.

διὰ τῦτο) As those who reproach their own vices by a contrary way of life.

Latin:

Vers. 19,

εἰ ἐκ τῦ κόσμυ ἦτε) Affectu mundano præditi, quomo- do ex Diabolo esse & ex Deo sumtum, supra VIII. 44.47.

ὁ κόσμος ἂν τὸν ἴδιον ἐφίλει) Vos ut suos diligeret. Solet enim ad amicitias valere studiorum communitas: κόσμον accipe pro universitate eorum, qui carni & seculo student, qui generali odio solos pietatis & sanctitatis professores in- sectantur. Vide supra VII. 7. & I. Ep. III. 14.

ἐξελεξάμην ὑμᾶς ἐκ τῦ κόσμυ) Secrevi ex illa universi- tate, & mihi in peculium seposui: Sic dicuntur Christiani ἀποφυγόντες τὰ μιάσματα τῦ κόσμυ, 2. Pet. II. 20. ἐκλέγειν sæpe hoc sensu in Veteri Testamento usurpatur, ubi agitur de populo Hebræo, eorumque patribus, 2. Maccab. I. 25. ὁ ποιήσας τὺς πατέρας ἐκλεκτὺς κὶ ἁγιάσας αὐτός.

διὰ τῦτο) Tanquam qui sua ipsi vitia contrario vitæ instituto exprobretis.

## 15:20
V. 20. μνημονεύετε) Be mindful. Thus Luke XVII. 32. τῦ λόγε) Of the well-known proverb, ὕ εἶπον ὑμῖν) above XIII, 16, although in a different usage. ὐκ ἔστι δῦλος μείζων) He ought not to take it ill or be surprised if that happens to him which happened to the Lord. In this sense a similar saying is used, Matt. X. 24. εἰ ὲ λόγον με ἐτήρησαν) if they have been listeners to me, expect that they will be to you also. As if he were to say, there is no reason for you to hope for this.

Latin:

V. 20. μνημονεύετε) Memores estote. Sic Luc. XVII. 32. τῦ λόγε) Adagii satis noti, ὕ εἶπον ὑμῖν) supra XIII, 16. quanquam alio usu. ὐκ ἔστι δῦλος μείζων) Non debet ægre ferre aut mirari, si sibi accidat quod Domino. In hunc sensum simile distum usurpatur, Matth. X. 24. εἰ ὲ λόγον με ἐτήρησαν) si mihi audientes fuerint, expe- ctate ut & vobis sint. Quasi dicat, non est quod hoc speretis.

## 15:21
Vers. 21. ταῦτα τάντα ποιήσυσιν ὑμῖν) that they may hate you, vex you, and despise your words. Διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με) This, as elsewhere, is for my sake, so here it is hatred of me, as also Matt. X. 22, which may be explained as ἕνεκεν ἐμῦ, as it is in Matt. V. 11. If you suffer these things for my sake, expect help and reward from me as well. The Apostles felt this consolation afterwards, Acts V. 41. See also 1 Pet. IV. v. 16. ὅτι ὐκ ἴδασι τὸν πέμψαντά με) They do not consider by whom I was sent, blinded by ambition and other worldly affections. See what we said a little earlier regarding the word γινώσκετε, as if he were to say: Why do you wonder if the blind rush upon you.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ταῦτα τάντα ποιήσυσιν ὑμῖν) ut vos odio ha- beant, vexent, dicta contemnant. Διὰ τὸ ὄνομά με) Hoc sicut alibi est in meam gratiam, ita dic est odio mei, ut & Matth. X. 22. quod explicare licet ἕνεκεν ἐμῦ, ut est Matth. V. 11. Si ob me hæc patimini etiam à me auxilium & præmium expectare. Hanc consolatio- nem senserunt postea Apostoli, Act. V. 41. Vide & 1. Petr. IV. v. 16. ὅτι ὐκ ἴδασι τὸν πέμψαντά με) Non considerant à quo missus sim, excæcati ambitione aliisque mundanis affecti- bus. Vide quod paulo ante diximus ad vocem γινώσκετε, quasi dicat: Quid miramini si cæci in vos ruunt.

## 15:22
Vers. 22.

εἰ μὴ ἦλθον) Unless I had shown myself publicly. For that is what ἔρχεσϑαι means, as we have said several times above. καὶ ἐλάλησα αὐτοῖς) And unless I had openly preached to them a doctrine most holy, in which nothing can be reprehended: and had affirmed that this was commanded to me by God, and at the same time confirmed it, not only by the testimonies of the Prophets, but also by a certain extraordinary majesty of speech. Above VII. 46. Ἁμαρτίαν ὐκ εἶχον) They would be without fault, namely in that which they do not know, by whom I was sent. For these things must be connected with the preceding. Νῦν δέ πρόφασιν ὐκ ἔχεσι περὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας) Now they have no pretext to excuse themselves of this fault. In Ps. CXLI. 4. להתעלל עלילות ברשׁע for the making of excuses in sins. Among Juvenal: Dic aliquem, dic Quintiliane colorem. A color is a πρόφασις.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

εἰ μὴ ἦλθον) Nisi publice me ostendissem. Id enim est ἔρχεσϑαι ut supra diximus aliquoties. καὶ ἐλάλησα αὐτοῖς) Et nisi ipsis aperte prædicassem do- gma longe sanctissimum, in quo nihil potest reprehendi: idque affirmassem mihi à Deo mandatum, simul confirmassem, non tantam testimoniis Prophetarum, sed & exi- mia quadam loquendi majestate. Supra VII. 46. Ἁμαρτίαν ὐκ εἶχον) Essent extra culpam, nempe in eo quod ignorant, à quo missus sim. Connectenda enim hæc cum superioribus. Νῦν δέ πρόφασιν ὐκ ἔχεσι περὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας) Nunc nihil habent obtentus ad se purgandum de hac culpa. In Psal. CXLI. 4. להתעלל עלילות ברשׁע τῦ προφασί- ζεσϑαι προφάσεις ἐν ἁμαρτίαις. Apud Juvenalem: Dic aliquem, dic Quintiliane colorem. color est πρόφασις.

## 15:23
Vers. 23.

ὁ ἐμὲ μιζῶν κὰι τὸν πατέρα με μισεῖ) The sense is this: Since they could and ought to have known that I was sent by the Father, whatever they do that is insulting to me, the Father interprets as done to his own insult. It is the custom of Holy Scripture that someone is said to do what he does not properly do, if he does that which is held in the same place by the judgment of God. Thus 1 Sam. X. 19, Matt. XXV. v. 40. Moreover, this aggravation of their fault pertains wonderfully to the comforting of the Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

ὁ ἐμὲ μιζῶν κὰι τὸν πατέρα με μισεῖ) Sensus hic est: Cum scire potuerint ac debuerint me à Patre missum, quicquid in me contumeliosum faciunt, id Pater in suam contume- liam factum interpretatur. Mos est S. Scripturæ ut facere quis dicatur, quod non facit proprie, si id facit quod eodem loco habetur Deo judice. Sic 1. Sam. X. 19. Matth. XXV. v. 40. Hæc autem culpæ illorum aggravatio mirifice perti- net ad consolandos Apostolos.

## 15:24
Vers. 24.

εἰ τὰ ἔργα μὴ ἐποίησα) He brings forward another argument, by which his adversaries are rendered inexcusable: his miracles. But this must be understood in such a way that either one suffices, either the mere proposal of the doctrine, or the works to prove the mission. Therefore this is an ἔκπτωσις: if I had neither spoken to them, nor done such works, they would have been excusable. ἃ ὐδεὶς ἄλλος πεποίηκεν) Especially in that I healed all kinds of diseases, with none excepted, even the natural defect of blindness, by my command alone and by my own authority. Moses did not do this, nor Elias, nor Elisha, whom they believed to have been sent by God. But what they did, I also did and more powerfully, as appears in the resuscitation of the man dead four days, and in the multiplication of the loaves. ἐν αὐτοῖς) Supply ὢν, while I am among them. ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν, as Acts II. 22, in their sight, this Syrian [version]. Ἁμαρτίαν ὐκ εἶχον) Take it as above 22. Νῦν δὲ κὰὶ ἑωράκασι) Those extraordinary works. κὰὶ) and yet. Μεμισήκασι κὰὶ ἐμὲ κὰι τὸν πατέρα με) Me indeed directly, but the Father by interpretation of the Father, because they despise his commands and works, with no probable pretext.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

εἰ τὰ ἔργα μὴ ἐποίησα) Alterum affert argumentum, quo adversarii reddantur inexcusabiles: miracula sua. Hoc autem ita accipiendum est ut utrumvis sufficiat, aut dogma- tis sola propositio, aut opera ad probandam missionem. Itaque hic est ἔκπτωσις: si nec locutus essem ipsis, nec talia opera fecissem erant excusabiles. ἃ ὐδεὶς ἄλλος πεποίηκεν) Præcipue eo quod omnia morborum genera, nullis exceptis, etiam naturale cæcita- tis vitium, solo imperio ac meo jure sanavi. Hoc non fecit Moses, non Elias, non Elisæus quos à Deo missos credide- runt. Quæ autem illi fecerunt, ego quoque feci & poten- tius, ut in resuscitatione mortui quatriduani, in panum multiplicatione apparet. ἐν αὐτοῖς) Supple ὢν, dum inter ipsos ago. ἐν μέσῳ αὐ- τῶν, ut Act. II. 22. in conspectu ipsorum Syrus hic. Ἁμαρτίαν ὐκ εἶχον) Sume ut supra 22. Νῦν δὲ κὰὶ ἑωράκασι) Opera illa eximia. κὰὶ) & tamen. Μεμισήκασι κὰὶ ἐμὲ κὰι τὸν πατέρα με) Me quidem directe, Patrem autem patris interpretatione, quia ipsius mandata atque opera contemnunt, nullo probabili prætextu.

## 15:25
Vers. 25.

Ἀλλ' ἵνα πληρωϑῇ ὁ λόγος) Again an ἔκπτωσις as above, and ἵνα is ἐκβατικὸν: it happens conveniently, that in this way that which David, who bore a type of me, once complained was done to him, might be fulfilled in me. Concerning the word πληρῶσαι we spoke at Matt. I. v. 22. ἐν τῷ νόμῳ αὐτῶν) take νόμον, as X. 34, for it is from Ps. XXXV. 19. Others wish to refer here to Ps. LXIX. 5. Some wish to refer to Ps. CIX. 3. But what prevents us from referring all those passages here? Nor indeed in those is it a question of David according to the letter, which Grotius, with Calvin and Piscator, wishes, but of Christ, which was shown concerning Ps. LXIX. and CIX. in the annotations on the Psalms: nor is it obscure concerning Ps. XXXV. in which not only are the insulting words, with which the Jews mocked Christ hanging on the cross, found, v. 21, but a prophecy is also held, v. 18, concerning the congregation of the Church and the Gentiles. Nor does it fit David, but Christ alone, what is read in v. 27: They shall rejoice and exult in my joy. Compare Isa. XLV. 24. 25.

ὅτι) This ὅτι here means 'namely', and is of the one producing the testimony of the Psalm.

ἐμίσησάν με δωρεὰν) δωρεὰν חנם in Hebrew is 'without just cause'. Therefore elsewhere it is translated ἀδίκως, as Prov. I, 11, 17. See I. Sam. XIX, 5.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

Ἀλλ' ἵνα πληρωϑῇ ὁ λόγος) Iterum ἔκπτωσις quæ supra & ἵνα est ἐκβατικὸν: commode evenit, ut hoc modo in me impleretur, quod olim David, qui typum mei gessit, sibi fieri conquestus est. De voce πληρῶσαι diximus ad Matth. I. v. 22. ἐν τῷ νόμῳ αὐτῶν) νόμον sume, ut X. 34. est enim ex Psal. XXXV. 19. Alii ad Psal. LXIX. 5. Nonnulli ad Psal. CIX. 3. respici hic volunt. Sed quid obstat, quo minus omnia illa loca huc referamus? Nec vero in illis quoad literam de Davide agitur, quod cum Calvi- no & Piscatore Grotius vult, sed de Christo, quod de Psal. LXIX. & CIX. ostensum in annotatis ad Psal- mos: nec obscurum est de Psal. XXXV. in quo tan- tum voces contumeliosæ, quibus Christo in cru- ce pendenti illuserunt Judæi, reperiuntur, v. 21. sed vaticinium etiam habetur, v. 18. de congrega- tione Ecclesiæ & gentibus. Neque Davidi con- venit, sed Christo unice, quod v. 27. legitur: Læ- tabuntur & exultabunt lætitia mea. Confer. Esa. XLV. 24. 25.

ὅτι) Hoc ὅτι hic valet nempe, & est producentis testi- monium Psalmi.

ἐμίσησάν με δωρεὰν) δωρεὰν חנם Hebræis est sine justa causa. Itaque alibi vertitur ἀδίκως, ut Prov. I, 1l 17. Vide I. Sam. XIX, 5.

## 15:26
Vers. 26.

ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ ὁ παράκλητος) He shows that his cause, although subject to such great hatreds, will not lack defenders even in his absence. And first he says the Holy Spirit will come: παράκλητον, that is, an advocate of his cause, as we explained above.

ὃν ἐγὼ πέμψω ὑμῖν) I will cause him to come, just as advocates of causes are accustomed to be sent by him whose cause it is.

παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς) From the house of my Father, from heaven. Thus we say: Let us go to my place.

The place from which he is to be sent is not indicated, nor is the Father confined to a place, or does he have a house or palace in which he dwells, as Grotius seems to imagine, but it is noted that Christ has from the Father that he should send the Holy Spirit, from whom he also has that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, and thus that the Father is that fountain from which that pure and splendid river, the Holy Spirit, flows, Apoc. XXII, 1. Conf. Gen. XIX. 24. Joh. V. 17. Theophyl. in h. l. ὡς ἰσότιμος τῷ πατρὶ πέμψωμεν αὐτὸν Φησὶ, ἀλλὰ παρα τοῦ πατρὸς, τουτέστιν ἐκ ἄντανισάμενος ἐκείνῳ ἀλλ᾽ εὐδοκοῦντος τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ συναποστέλλοντος.

τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας) Since he comes from heaven, he must altogether be held as truthful: to whom nothing can be opposed.

ὃ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐκπορεύεται) If some angel were to offer me testimony, they ought to believe. But now, not some created spirit is about to bear testimony to me and plead my cause; but he who proceeds from the very substance of the Father and emanates from him. ἀπόῤῥοία Θεοῦ, as Athenagoras speaks: ὡς ἀκτὶν ἡλίου ὡς φῶς ἀπὸ πυρός, Justin calls him: ἄνωθεν παρὰ Θεοῦ κατιοῦσαν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἁγίους ἄνδρας δωρεὰν, τὸ πνεῦμα ἅγιον ὀνομάζουσιν οἱ ἱεροὶ προφῆται. In Tertullian against Praxeas he is called: the third divinity of the godhead and the third name of majesty.

ἐκεῖνος μαρτυρήσει περὶ ἐμοῦ) For the gift of tongues (to omit other gifts) served no other end than to plead the cause of Jesus, which, since it could not be except from the Father, the Father most openly approved this cause.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ ὁ παράκλητος) ostendit causam suam, quan- quam tantis odiis obnoxium, non carituram defensoribus etiam se absente. Ac primum dicit Spirit. S. venturum: πα- ράκλητον, id est, actorem causæ suæ, ut supra exposuimus.

ὃν ἐγὼ πέμψω ὑμῖν) Efficiam ut veniat, sicut causarum oratores mitti solent ab eo cujus est causa.

παρὰ τοῦ πατρός) Ex domo Patris mei, ex cœlo. Sic di- cimus: Eamus ad me.

Non locus unde mittendus est, indicatur, neque loco concluditur Pater, aut domum vel regiam ha- bet, in qua habitet, uti fingere videtur Grotius, sed notatur, Christum à Patre habere, ut mittat Spiri- tum S. à quo habet quoque ut procedat ab ipso Spi- ritus S. adeoque Patrem esse fontem illum, à quo purus iste ac splendidus fluvius Spiritus S. profluat, Apoc. XXII, 1. Conf. Gen. XIX. 24. Joh. V. 17. Theo- phyl. in h. l. ὡς ἰσότιμος τῷ πατρὶ πέμψωμεν αὐτὸν Φησὶ, ἀλλὰ παρα τοῦ πατρός, τουτέστιν ἐκ ἄντα- νισάμενος ἐκείνῳ ἀλλ᾽ εὐδοκοῦντος τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ συναποστέλλοντος.

τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας) Qui cum ex cœlo veniat omni- no pro veraci habendus est: cui nihil potest opponi.

ὃ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐκπορεύεται) Si Angelus aliquis mihi te- stimonium præberet, credere deberent. At nunc perhibi- turus est testimonium mihi, causamque meam acturus non creatus aliquis spiritus; sed qui de Patris ipsius substantia procedit & ab ipso emanat. ἀπόῤῥοία Θεοῦ, ut Athenagoras loquitur: ὡς ἀκτὶν ἡλίου ὡς φῶς ἀπὸ πυρός, Justinus vocat: ἄνωθεν παρὰ Θεοῦ κατιοῦσαν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἁγίους ἄνδρας δωρεάν, τὸ πνεῦμα ἅγιον ὀνομάζουσιν οἱ ἱεροὶ προφῆται. Tertulliano ad- versus Praxeam dicitur: tertium numen divinitatis & ter- tium nomen majestatis.

ἐκεῖνος μαρτυρήσει περὶ ἐμοῦ) Donum enim linguarum (ut alia dona omittamus) non alii fini serviebat, quam ad agen- dam Jesu causam, quod cum non posset esse nisi à Patre, apertissime Pater hanc causam probabat.

## 15:27
v. 27. καὶ ὑμεῖς δὲ μαρτυρεῖτε) that is, μαρτυρήσετε, with the received enallage. Just as he was saying a moment ago that even without works his word sufficed to teach his mission, so now he says that even without such gifts the Apostles, men of good life and faith, ought to have been believed. Note that the testimony of the Apostles and of the Spirit himself is joined, as in Acts V. 32.

ὅτι ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ ἐστε) from the beginning, namely from the time I began to perform my office, Acts 1:21. It is customary and right that good men be believed as often as they testify concerning a matter which they profess to have seen with their own eyes, which the Apostles were doing, Acts 2:32, ch. 4:20, ch. 10:41, 2 Pet. 1:16, 1 John 1:1.

Latin:

v. 27. καὶ ὑμεῖς δὲ μαρτυρεῖτε) id est, μαρτυρήσετε recepta enallage. Sicut modo dicebat etiam sine operibus sermo- nem suum sufficere ad docendam suam missionem, ita nunc ait etiam sine talibus donis credi debuisse Apostolis, viris bonæ vitæ ac fidei. Nota conjungi testimonium Aposto- lorum, & ipsius Spiritus, ut Act. V. 32.

ὅτι ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ ἐστε) ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς, nempe ex quo cœ- pi munus meum agere Act. I. 21. Viris bonis credi solet ac debet, quoties testantur de re quam oculis suis conspectam profitentur, quod faciebant Apostoli, Act. II. 32. c. IV. 20. c. X. 41. 2. Petr. I. 16. I. Joh. I. 1.

## 16:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVI. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The Lord further warns of the persecution, excommunication, and killing of the disciples, and of his own departure to the Father, and the fruit of the same, the mission of the Paraclete who is to correct the world, and lead the Apostles into all truth, and announce future things, and that a little time remains in which they will see him, but a little later they will see him again, which he explains to them, and he teaches that their mourning is to be turned into joy by the simile of a woman in labor, he makes them certain that prayers made in his name will be heard, and he confirms their faith concerning his coming forth from the Father and return to the Father, nevertheless predicting their dispersion, but raising them up on account of the overcoming of the world.

There are three parts. I. The prediction of persecution, to v. 4. II. Information concerning the departure to the Father and the consequent mission of the Paraclete, and the joy of the return, to v. 23. III. Consolation concerning the hearing of prayers, peace, and victory over the world, to v. 33.

PART I. The prediction of persecution.

Vers. 1.

Ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν) Concerning the hatred and inconveniences which are imminent for you.

Ἵνα μὴ σκανδαλισθῆτε) Not that I may render you more sorrowful, but that I may fortify you: for foreseen evils strike less, nor ought you to be offended if that happens to you which always happens to the good. Matt. V. 13.

Latin:

CAPUT XVI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Adhuc de persecutione, excommunicatione & interfectione discipulorum, deque abitu suo ad Patrem, ac fructu ejusdem, missione Paracleti mundum correcturi, & Apostolos in omnem veritatem ducturi, ac futura an- nunciaturi, monet Dominus, & pusillum temporis superesse, quo se visuri sint, paulo post autem se iterum visum iri, quod ipsis ex- plicat, ac luctum ipsorum in gaudium con- vertendum esse similitudine puerperæ do- cet, de precibus in nomine suo factis exaudi- endis certos reddit, & fidem eorum de egres- su à Patre, & regressu ad Patrem confirmat, prædicens tamen eorum dispersionem, sed erigens eos ob mundi devictionem.

Partes sunt tres. I. De persecutione prædictio, ad v. 4. II. De abitu ad Patrem & consequente missione Paracleti, reditusque gaudio informatio, ad v. 23. III. De precum exauditione, pace, & mundi victoria consolatio, ad v. 33.

PARS I. De persecutione prædictio.

Vers. 1.

Ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν) De odio & incommodis, quæ vobis imminent.

Ἵνα μὴ σκανδαλισθῆτε) Non ut vos mœstiores reddam, sed ut muniam : prævisa enim mala minus percellunt, nec offendi debetis si vobis accidit quod semper accidit bonis. Matth. V. 13.

## 16:2
v. 2. Ἀποσυναγώγους ποιήσουσιν ὑμᾶς) He begins from a mark that is, as it were, censorial. They will separate you from themselves not only by נדוי but also by חרם. See what we have said above IX. 22. XII. 42.

Ἀλλʼ) This particle here is affirmative, as 'imo' among the Latins. Thus 'ἀλλὰ' is taken in 2 Cor. VII. 11.

ἔρχεται ὥρα) There will be a time, as the Latins say. Thus above V. 25.

ἵνα) This particle here signifies 'when'.

πᾶς ὁ ἀποκτείνας ὑμᾶς) He speaks especially of the Jews, whom the Acts of the Apostles teach to have burned everywhere, even to the point of sedition, for the slaughter of the Apostles.

Δόξη λατρείαν προσφέρειν τῷ Θεῷ) Λατρεία corresponds to the Hebrew עבודה, but as the genus is accustomed to be put for the species, it signifies here קרבן, which the Syriac has, that is, an offering. Thus Exodus XXXII. 29, where Moses says to the Levites who had killed the idolaters: You have consecrated your hands. The Chaldean has 'you have offered a sacrifice.' And Exodus VIII. 16, and 21, X. 7, 24, it appears that λατρεύειν and θύειν are used with the same meaning. See the example of Acts VIII. 3, IX. 1, XXIII. 14.

Latin:

v. 2. Ἀποσυναγώγους ποιήσουσιν ὑμᾶς) Incipit à nota quasi censoria. Separabunt vos à se non tantum per נדוי sed & per חרם. Vide quæ diximus supra IX. 22. XII. 42.

Ἀλλʼ) Hæc particula hic est ajentis, ut imo apud Latinos. Sic ἀλλὰ sumitur 2. Cor. VII. 11.
