ἔρχεται ὥρα) Tempus erit, ut loquuntur Latini. Sic supra V. 25.

ἵνα) Hæc particula hic valet quum.

πᾶς ὁ ἀποκτείνας ὑμᾶς) De Judæis præcipue loquitur, quos ubique ad seditionem usque exarsisse in necem Apostolorum docent Actus Apostoli.

Δόξη λατρείαν προσφέρειν τῷ Θεῷ) Λατρεία respondet Hebræo עבודה sed ut solet genus pro specie poni, valet hic קרבן quod habet Syrus, id est προσφοράν. Sic Exodi XXXII. 29. ubi Moses dicit Levitis qui Idololatras interfecerant : Consecrastis manus vestras. Chaldæus habet sacrificium obtulistis. Et Exodi VIII. 16. & 21. X. 7. 24. apparet eodem significatu poni λατρεύειν & θύειν. Vide exemplum Actuum VIII. 3. IX. 1. XXIII. 14.

## 16:3
v. 3. καὶ) It signifies here 'but': for it is a consolation against the former things, as if Christ were saying: those who will do these things will be more to be pitied, because they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, Rom. X. 3.

ὅτι ὐκ ἔγνωσαν τὸν πατέρα) They do not understand that God is a lover of the human race, nor that He is delighted so much by rituals as by purity of mind.

ὐδὲ ἐμὲ) Nor do they consider those things by which they can be convinced that I was sent by God. Above XV. 22. and following.

Latin:

v. 3. καὶ) Valet hic sed: est enim consolatio adversus priora, quasi dicat Christus: miserandi magis erunt qui ista facient ὅτι ζῆλον Θεῦ ἔχουσιν ἀλλʼ ὐ κατʼ ἐπίγνωσιν, Rom. X. 3.

ὅτι ὐκ ἔγνωσαν τὸν πατέρα) Non intelligunt Deum esse amantem humani generis, nec tam ritibus delectari, quam animi puritate.

ὐδὲ ἐμὲ) Neque considerant ea quibus convinci possunt me à Deo missum. Supra XV. 22. & sequentibus.

## 16:4
v. 4. Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν, ἵνα ὅταν ἔλθῃ ἡ ὥρα μνημονεύητε ἀυτῶν, ὅτι ἐγὼ εἶπον ὑμῖν) That you may learn my faithfulness from such a truthful prediction, and therefore trust in the connected promises. Matt. XXIV. 25. In that most ancient manuscript it is here, ὥρα ἀυτῶν, not badly. See Luke XXII. 53.

ταῦτα δὲ ὑμῖν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὐκ εἶπον) That you would suffer these things from your own kinsmen and under the pretext of piety. For he had predicted many evils more indistinctly. Matt. X. 1. ἐξ ἀρχῆς מן קדים as the Syrian has it, is nothing other than long ago. Ecclesiasticus XXXIX. 28.

ὅτι μεθʼ ὑμῶν ἤμην) And therefore I myself, as the head of this business, was receiving all the hatred upon myself.

Theophylact reconciles by the same reasoning that he had previously predicted the persecution of the Gentiles: but now the persecution of the Jews. But Christ speaks here not only of the persecution of the Jews, but also of the Gentiles: and he had also predicted the persecutions to be brought by the Jews. Matt. V. 12. ch. X. 17. Therefore others explain it more correctly, that he had not predicted such things to them so harshly and bitterly nor so clearly, especially that they were to be killed with the opinion of a singular worship. Chrysostom explains the cause thus: Because you were in safety and it was permitted to ask when you wished, and the whole war was turned against me and it was superfluous to say these things at the beginning.

PARS II. Concerning the departure to the Father and the consequent mission of the Paraclete, and information about the joy of the return.

Latin:

v. 4. Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν, ἵνα ὅταν ἔλθῃ ἡ ὥρα μνημονεύητε ἀυτῶν, ὅτι ἐγὼ εἶπον ὑμῖν) Ut fidelitatem meam discatis ex tam veridica prædictione, eoque & connexis promissionibus confidatis. Matth. XXIV. 25. In Manuscripto illo antiquissimo est hic, ὥρα ἀυτῶν, non male. Vide Lucæ XXII. 53.

ταῦτα δὲ ὑμῖν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὐκ εἶπον) Hæ vos passuros ab ipsis cognatis vestris & sub obtentu pietatis. Nam indistinctius multa mala prædixerat. Matth. X. 1. ἐξ ἀρχῆς מן קדים ut habet Syrus, nihil aliud est quam olim. Ecclesiastici XXXIX. 28.

ὅτι μεθʼ ὑμῶν ἤμην) Ac proinde ipse, ut hujus negotii caput, omnia odia in me excipiebam.

Conciliat eadem ratione Theophyl. quod antehac persecutionem gentium prædixerit : jam vero persecutionem Judæorum. Sed loquitur hic Christus non solum de Judæorum, sed etiam gentium persecutione : & prædixerat etiam persecutiones à Judæis inferendas. Matth. V. 12. c. X. 17. Ideo rectius alii explicant, quod non tam dura & acerba nec tam perspicue eis talia prædixerit, imprimis quod cum opinione cultus singularis interficiendi sint. Cawsam ita exponit Chrysost. Quia in tuto eratis & licitum erat interrogare, cum volebatis, & in me totum bellum vertebatur & superfluum erat hæc principio dicere.

PARS II. De abitu ad Patrem & consequente missione Paracleti, reditusque gaudio informatio.

## 16:5
v. 5. Νῦν δὲ ὑπάγω πρὸς ἳ πέμψαντά με) Now it is necessary for this to be said to you, who will be the leaders of this embassy once I am taken away.

καὶ ὐδεὶς ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐρωτᾷ με, πῦ ὑπάγεις:) You no longer ask, as you ought. For he saw that he was not yet sufficiently understood.

Latin:

v. 5. Νῦν δὲ ὑπάγω πρὸς ἳ πέμψαντά με) Nunc vobis id opus est dici, qui me erepto principes eritis hujus legationis.

καὶ ὐδεὶς ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐρωτᾷ με, πῦ ὑπάγεις:) Non amplius jam interrogatis, ut deberetis. Videbat enim nondum se satis intelligi.

## 16:6
v. 6. Ἀλλὰ ὅτι ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν) My imminent absence and the connected inconveniences.

ἡ λύπη πεπλήρωκεν ὑμῶν τὴν καρδίαν) It has completely occupied your minds. Thus Acts V. 3. it hinders you from asking as before.

Latin:

v. 6. Ἀλλὰ ὅτι ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν) Imminentem absentiam meam & connexa incommoda.

ἡ λύπη πεπλήρωκεν ὑμῶν τὴν καρδίαν) Obsedit plane animos vestros. Sic Act. V. 3. id impedit quo minus ut ante interrogetis.

## 16:7
v. 7. Τὴν ἀλήθειαν λέγω ὑμῖν) He excites attention and faith. Συμφέρει ὑμῖν ἵνα ἐγὼ ἀπέλθω) Namely, that I may receive possession of the heavenly kingdom. ὁ παράκλητος ἐκ ἐλεύσεται πρὸς ὑμᾶς) For this is among those things which are reserved for my heavenly kingdom. See what is above VII. 39. Ἐὰν δὲ πορευθῶ, πέμψω αὐτὸν πρὸς ὑμᾶς) When I have gone, as above XIV. 3. as if I would send him down from the citadel. Acts II. 33.

Latin:

v. 7. Τὴν ἀλήθειαν λέγω ὑμῖν) Attentionem & fidem ex- citat. Συμφέρει ὑμῖν ἵνα ἐγὼ ἀπέλθω) Nempe ut possessionem accipiam regni cælestis. ὁ παράκλητος ἐκ ἐλεύσεται πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Est enim hoc in- ter ea, quæ cælesti meo regno reservantur. Vide quæ su- pra VII. 39. Ἐὰν δὲ πορευθῶ, πέμψω αὐτὸν πρὸς ὑμᾶς) Ubi abiero, ut supra XIV. 3. quasi ex arce demittam. Act. II. 33.

## 16:8
v. 8. And when he is come, he will reprove the world) We have said that παράκλητος is the defender of a cause; his duty is ἐλέγχειν τὲς ἀντιλέγοντας. Tit. I. 9. to convince concerning the righteousness of his cause. It corresponds to the Hebrew יוֹכִיחַ, and just as this is forensic, befitting the person of an advocate of causes, so too are the things that follow. For there are three kinds of causes: public judgments concerning crimes περὶ ἁμαρτίας חַטָאת, private ones from equity and good conscience צְדָקָה δικαιοσύνη, (for to the Hebrews that word signifies equity more than law strictly so called) and private ones having a certain formula from the law מִשְׁפָּט κρίσις.

Latin:

v. 8. κὶ ἐλθὼν ἐκεῖνος, ἐλέγξει τὸν κόσμον) Diximus παράκλη- τον esse defensorem causæ; ejus munus est ἐλέγχειν τὲς ἀντι- λέγοντας. Tit. I. 9. convincere de causæ suæ rectitudine. Re- spondet Hebræo יוֹכִיחַ, sicut autem hoc forense est conve- niens personæ, causarum actori, ita & quæ sequuntur. Tria enim sunt causarum genera, publica judicia de criminibus περὶ ἁμαρτίας חַטָאת privata, privata ex æquo & bono צְדָקָה δικαιοσύνη, (nam Hebræis ea vox æquitatem magis signifi- cat, quam jus stricte dictum) privata certam ex lege for- mulam habentia מִשְׁפָּט κρίσις.

## 16:9
Vers. 9.

περὶ ἁμαρτίας μὲν, ὅτι ἐπιτεύεσιν εἰς ἐμὲ) When all things that I have said about the sending of the Spirit come to pass, it will appear that I am a Prophet, according to the rule of Deut. XVIII. 22. and consequently that those who do not believe in me are to be afflicted with the most severe punishments by the law of public judgment, which exists in the same place, 18. And God will exact these punishments from the Jews before the eyes of the world, by the destruction of the nation.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

περὶ ἁμαρτίας μὲν, ὅτι ἐ πιτεύεσιν εἰς ἐμὲ) Cum evenient omnia, quæ dixi de mittendo Spiritu, apparebit me esse Pro- phetam, secundum regulam Deut. XVIII. 22. ac proinde eos, qui mihi non credunt, gravissimis suppliciis afficien- dos ex lege publici judicii, quæ extat ibidem 18. Et hæc supplicia Deus coram oculis mundi de Judæis exiget, ex- cidio gentis.

## 16:10
Vers. 10.

περὶ δικαιοσύνης δὲ ὅτι πρὸς ἳ πατέρα ὑπάγω κὶ ἐκ ἔτι θεωρεῖτέ με) The nature of equity and good conscience, which is understood by the name of δικαιοσύνης, requires this, that rulers, even if no law has preceded, are accustomed to console good men who have suffered evils with some goods. δίκαιον παρὰ Θεῷ ἀνταποδῦναι τοῖς θλιβομένοις ἄνεσιν 2. Thess. 1. 5. ἐ γὰρ ἄδικος ὁ Θεὸς ἐπιλαθέσθαι τῶ κόπε. Hebr. VI. 10. The Spirit will therefore show that God is a just ruler, in that he has received me beyond all contact of injury (for this is what he says, you will not see me, as above VII. 30.) into the fellowship of his majesty, θεωρεῖτε for θεωρήσετε, an enallage common to others, but especially familiar to this one.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

περὶ δικαιοσύνης δὲ ὅτι πρὸς ἳ πατέρα ὑπάγω κὶ ἐκ ἔτι θεωρεῖτέ με) Natura æqui & boni, quæ δικαιοσύνης nomine intelligitur hoc exigit, ut rectores, etiamsi lex nulla præcesserit, bonos mala passos aliquibus bonis solentur. δί- καιον παρὰ Θεῷ ἀνταποδῦναι τοῖς θλιβομένοις ἄνεσιν 2. Thess. 1. 5. ἐ γὰρ ἄδικος ὁ Θεὸς ἐπιλαθέσθαι τῶ κόπε. Hebr. VI. 10. O- stendet ergo Spiritus Deum æquum esse rectorem, ut qui me extra omnem injuriæ contactum (hoc enim est quod ait non videbitis me, ut supra VII. 30.) in suæ majestatis consortium receperit, θεωρεῖτε pro θεωρήσετε, enallage tum aliis tum huic inprimis familiari.

## 16:11
Vers. 11.

περὶ δὲ κρίσεως ὅτι ὁ ἄρχων τῆ κόσμε τότε κέκριται) Among κρίσεις, that is, judgments which are exercised between parties, is that excellent one concerning retaliation, Levit. XXIV. 20. so that he who has unjustly harmed anyone, may himself bear as much evil. The Devil was the cause of Christ's death: therefore by right, with God condemning him, he has suffered what is for him equivalent to death, being stripped of his kingdom through the destruction of idolatry and other vices, the Holy Spirit performing this. See above XII. 31. In so many ways, therefore, through the Holy Spirit as a most faithful patron, the cause of Christ has been proven, not without the greatest fruit among pious souls.

Grotius's gloss is plainly new and unheard of, and by its own novelty it collapses of its own accord. Those to be convinced of the sin of unbelief were not only the Jews of that time, but all men, ὁ κόσμος, the world at every time, in every age, just as Augustine, Cyril, and Rupert interpret it concerning the whole world: nor was the method of conviction situated in punishments or in the destruction of the nation, but it had to be done by the conviction of the Spirit through the word. St. Augustine, tract. XCV. on John, posits, he says, this sin of infidelity specifically, because while this remains the others remain, and when this departs the others are remitted. And Serm. LX. on the word of the Lord. The medicine of the soul for all wounds and the one propitiation for the offenses of all is to believe in Christ. Therefore, concerning this one sin he wished the world to be reproved by the Holy Spirit, that they do not believe in him, namely, because by believing in him all sins are dissolved, he wished this one to be imputed, by which the others are bound.

But the justice, concerning which the world is likewise to be convinced by the Holy Spirit, is not the equity of GOD the ruler, in that he received Christ beyond all contact of injury into the fellowship of his majesty: For whence will faith be won for that gloss? But it is that justice, which the Holy Spirit preached through the Apostles, and of whose necessity and truth he convinced the world, which is situated in the departure of Christ to the Father, inasmuch as it encompasses his passion, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven Rom. 4:5 wills. Moreover, the Socinian interpretation of Grotius is akin to the gloss in the explanation of the place of Scripture, page 92. Concerning righteousness, because it is or was just that Christ be taken away from the sight of men and never be seen by them, who treated him so unworthily. But everyone sees how inept that is. The interpretation of B. Luther flows from the text itself; the Holy Spirit will convict the world of righteousness, that is, he will convince the world and demonstrate with invincible arguments that by my departure, that is, by my passion, death, resurrection, etc., true righteousness has been restored to the faithful, the confirmation of which see in B. Gerh. Harm. c. CXXXIX. p. 1073.

the whole world, just as it was predicted Ps. 68:19, Joel 2:28.

Furthermore, the Holy Spirit is not called παράκλητος [advocate/comforter] with respect to Christ, because he undertakes the defense of his cause, as Grotius wills, but with respect to us, because he pleads our cause against the world, as Grotius is mistaken above c. XIV. 16.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

περὶ δὲ κρίσεως ὅτι ὁ ἄρχων τῆ κόσμε τότε κέκριται) Inter κρίσεις, id est, judicia quæ inter partes exercentur est exi- mia illa de talione Levit. XXIV. 20. ut qui injuste cuiquam nocuit, ipse tantundem mali ferat. Diabolus causa mor- tis Christi fuit: jure igitur ipse Deo condemnante passus est, quod ipsi est pro morte, exutus regno suo per destru- ctionem idololatriæ aliorumque vitiorum, peragente id Spiritu Sancto. Vid. supra XII. 31. Tot igitur modis per Spiritum Sanctum tanquam fidelissimum patronum pro- bata est Christi causa, non sine maximo fructu apud pios animos.

Glossa Grotii nova plane & inaudita est, & no- vitate sua portentosa ultro concidit. Convincendi de peccato incredulitatis erant non Judæi tantum istius temporis, sed omnes homines, ὁ κόσμος, mundus omni tempore, omni ætate, quemadmo- dum Augustinus, Cyrillus & Rupertus de toto mun- do interpretantur: neque modus elenchi in sup- pliciis situs aut in excidio gentis, sed convictione Spiritus fieri debuit per verbum. S. August. tract. XCV. in Johan. ponit, inquit, hoc peccatum infideli- tatis specialiter, quia hoc manente cætera manent, hoc decedente cætera remittuntur. Et Serm. LX. de verbo Dom. Medicina animæ omnium vulnerum & una propitiatio pro delictis omnium est credere in Christum. Ergo de hoc uno peccato voluit per Spiri- tum S. mundum argui, quod non credant in eum, vi- delicet, quia in eum credendo cuncta peccata solvun- tur, hoc unum imputari voluit, quo cætera colligan- tur.

Justitia vero, de qua convincendus itidem mundus est à Spiritu S. non est æquitas DEI recto- ris, quod Christum extra omnem injuriæ conta- ctum in suæ majestatis consortium receperit: Un- de enim glossæ illi fides conciliabitur? Sed ea justitia, quain Spiritus S. per Apostolos prædi- cavit, & de cujus necessitate ac veritate mun- dum convicit, quæ sita est in abitu Christi ad Pa- trem, utpote, qui complectitur passionem, mor- tem, resurrectionem, ascensionem ejusdem in cœlum Rom. IV. v. vult. Affinis autem est Grotii in- terpretatio Sociniana glossæ in expl. loc. Script. pag. 92. De justitia, quia justum est vel fuit, Christum auferri è conspectu hominum & nunquam ab eis conspici, qui ita indigne eum tractarunt. Quæ vero quam inepta sit, nemo non videt. B. Lutheri interpretatio ex ipso textu fluit; Spiritus Sanct. arguet mundum de justitia, hoc est convin- cet mundum & invictis argumentis demonstrabit per meum abitum, hoc est, per meam passionem, mortem, resurrectionem &c. veram fidelibus restitutam esse justitiam, cujus confirmationem vid. apud B. Gerh. Harm.c. CXXXIX. p. 1073.

totum orbem, quemadmodum prædictum Pfal. LXVIII. 19. Joel. II. 28.

Porro Spiritus S. non dicitur παράκλητος re- spectu Christi, quod causa ejus defensionem susci- piat, uti Grotius vult, sed respectu nostri, quod no- stram causam agat adversus mundum, uti falsus est Grotius supra c. XIV. 16.

## 16:12
v. 12. Ὅτι πολλὰ ἔχω λέγειν ὑμῖν [For I have many things to say to you]) I still have things which I may say to you. Thus the Syriac here very well.

Ἀλλ' οὐ δύνασθε βαστάζειν ἄρτι [But you cannot bear them now]) It is the mark of a good teacher not to heap everything on at once, but to dispense them at their proper times: and to reserve certain things for the greater maturity of the disciples 1 Cor. 3:1, 23, Heb. 5:11.

Latin:

v. 12. Ὅτι πολλὰ ἔχω λέγειν ὑμῖν) Sunt mihi adhuc quæ vobis dicam. Ita hic Syrus optime.

Ἀλλ' 8 δύνασθε βασάζειν ἄρτι) Boni Magistri est non omnia simul ingerere, sed suis dispensare temporibus: & quædam ad majorem discipulorum maturitatem reservare 1. Cor. III. 1.23. Hebr. V. 11.

## 16:13
v. 13. Ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ ἐκεῖνος [But when he comes]) That vicar of mine, the patron of my cause, is a construction κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον [according to the meaning].

Finally, the judgment against the prince of the world, of which the world is to be convicted, is not a judgment of retaliation, such as is held in Lev. 24:20, which certainly cannot be exercised against the Devil, since the Devil cannot sustain those things which he unjustly inflicted upon Christ through his instruments by the law of retaliation, nor can retaliation be had, because he has been stripped of his kingdom through the destruction of idolatry and other vices: which Grotius says is for the death of Satan; but in the law of retaliation, that which is for death is by no means sufficient for death inflicted. And the judgment by which the Holy Spirit teaches and convinces that the prince of the world has been judged is something else, namely that he was judged when, through the death of Christ, he was stripped of the power and ἐξυσίᾳ [authority], or the right of death, which he had over the human race, Heb. 2:14, so that those believing in Christ might seek true righteousness in his departure, which was the apex of Christ's obedience Phil. 1. as also liberation from the power of Satan, exercised in the judgment through the death of Christ against the same. Gen. 3:15, Col. 2:10, whence, having been liberated from the servitude of sin, they ought to serve not Satan, but God: concerning which Eusebius Emissenus: the world, he says, is convicted of judgment, by which the Prince of the world is condemned and the world itself liberated, but ungrateful for such a benefit, it does not yet follow Christ, the author of salvation, but rather the Devil, the deceiver. Theophyl. in h. l. He condemns the idle, slothful world, which does not strive to be conquered by itself from the sin of Satan and the broken, enervated one. If, however, one wishes to allude here to the judgments and kingdoms of the world, the Brentian explanation analogous to ours will fit very well. Christ, he says, uses the verb to convict in that signification in which the Prophet Is. 2:4, he will judge between the nations, he will convict many peoples, c. 11:4, he will judge the poor in righteousness and will convict in uprightness for the meek of the earth; signifying that Christ would receive a kingdom among men, and would administer it in righteousness and judgment, so that the sense is: The Holy Spirit will institute the ministry of the Gospel, through which Christ will reign in the world. There are, however, three parts of the office in a legitimate kingdom. First, to punish crimes, so that an honest life may be preserved. Second, that justice may be done, that is, that the just cause of the good may be approved by public sentences and the good may be defended in their righteousness. Third, that judgment may be done, that is, that the wicked may be restrained, so that they do not harm the good and the injury of enemies may be repelled from the citizens. These three parts are also dealt with in the kingdom of Christ, but in a heavenly manner. In worldly kingdoms, only external crimes are considered as sins: But in the kingdom of Christ, even interior incredulity. In worldly kingdoms, only civil justice is preserved, but in the kingdom of Christ, true righteousness is distributed, which Christ prepared by his departure to the Father. In worldly kingdoms, civil judgments are exercised, but in the kingdom of Christ, true judgment is administered, because Christ conquered Satan, and those who believe in Christ are safe from him. These things Brentius; And although the Holy Spirit did all these things from the beginning of the world, yet poured out visibly upon the Apostles, the teachers of the whole world, he had to do those things in a more illustrious manner through

Nor does the name of vicar of Christ properly befit the Holy Spirit; since Christ, although visibly absent, is truly present with us, nor is the Holy Spirit called so anywhere in the Scriptures, nor is he the Patron of Christ's cause, although he bears witness to the truth about Christ, and testifies concerning him.

ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν) He will guide you into the perfect knowledge of those things which pertain to the establishing of Churches. For the universality must be restricted to that which is being discussed. Tertullian, On the Prescription of Heretics: Adding, 'He himself will lead you into all truth,' he shows that they were ignorant of nothing, whom he had promised would attain all truth through the Spirit of truth: and he certainly fulfilled the promise, as the Acts of the Apostles prove. To this pertains, as we said above, the knowledge of the kingdom of Christ as merely spiritual, and the removal of the ritual law, and looking to this, the Apostles say in the decree, 'It seemed good to us and to the Holy Spirit.' Origen, Against Celsus, book two: I do not think it out of place to set forth a certain saying of Jesus from the Gospel according to John: 'I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now; but when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth; for he shall not speak of himself, but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak.' And we inquire in that place, what were the many things which Jesus had to say to his disciples, which they were not able to bear at that time, and we say, perhaps as Jews and having been brought up with the law of Moses according to the letter, the Apostles were not able to hear what is the true law, and of what things the worship among the Jews was a pattern and shadow, and of what future good things the law concerning foods and drinks and feasts and new moons and sabbaths contained a shadow; and there were many such things which he had to say to them; but seeing that it is altogether difficult to overturn from the soul dogmas that have been almost innate and brought up with one until the age of manhood, and to persuade those who have received them that these things are divine, but that to abandon them is impious; he sought to defer the knowledge of the truth according to the need, until they should prove them to be refuse and loss, as the Apostles have suffered, he deferred it to a more suitable time, or according to his passion, his resurrection.

Where is that restriction in the text? The Holy Spirit had to inform the Apostles not only about those things which pertain to establishing Churches or the polity of the Churches. But to lead them into ALL truth, just as the outcome also proved, because in their sermons and writings, being carried by the Holy Spirit (Φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνέυματος ἁγίς), they proposed not only those things which pertain to the order and decency (τάξιν & εὐσχημοσύνην) of the Church, but primarily those things which pertain to the Christian faith and truth. Cyril, book X, ch. 41: 'This Spirit of truth,' he says, 'will lead you into all truth. For he knows exactly the truth, whose Spirit he is, and he will reveal it not in part, but entirely.' For although we know in part in this life, says Paul, yet not a mangled but an entire truth has shone upon us in this small knowledge. Rightly, however. Ordinary Gloss. He will lead you into all truth necessary for salvation, because other truth is rather vanity, but in Scripture, which is according to godliness, solid and simple truth is found. Tertullian confirms this in the place cited by Grotius, On the Prescription of Heretics: 'Adding, he himself will lead you into all truth, he shows that they were ignorant of nothing, whom he had promised would attain all truth through the Spirit of truth: and he certainly fulfilled the promise, as the Acts of the Apostles prove.' Nor indeed should those preceding words, 'I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them,' be restricted to the constitution of Churches or the knowledge of the kingdom of Christ as merely spiritual, concerning which they had also previously handed down, or to the proposition of the spiritual law, which had already been proposed in the Old Testament with the condition of the kingdom of Christ: or with the Papists to be carried away to traditions, because it will never be proven that anything of the many things which the Apostles could not then bear, and which the Holy Spirit later revealed, is not contained in the Scriptures: But they comprehend generally those things concerning which the disciples were still to be informed, which, although handed down by Christ, they had not yet perceived: which indeed they could by no means grasp then, partly because of their infirmity and rudeness, partly because of preconceived opinion, partly because of the modern sadness and grief of mind, whence Christ promised them the Spirit as Teacher, who was to illustrate all things said by Him, and to inform them more clearly and fully concerning all things. Against the Papists can be opposed the opinion of the Roman Bishop Leo the Great, Sermon II on Pentecost. For that perfection which was to be conferred upon the disciples, a greater grace and more abundant inspiration was reserved; through which they might both receive what they had not yet received and might more excellently possess what they had received, for which reason the Lord was saying, I still have many things to say to you. Therefore, no other truth was to be insinuated, nor other doctrine to be preached, but it was necessary that the capacity of those who were being taught be increased and multiplied by that constant charity which would cast out all fear and would not fear the fury of those persecuting.

'For he shall not speak of himself' Nothing that has not seemed good to God the Father and to me will he invent of himself. He speaks as of an ambassador: Thus above VII. 18. XIV. 10. The Holy Spirit is speaking, to insinuate into minds.

But whatever he shall hear he shall speak) What he shall have received from the Father. Thus above V. 30. VIII. 26.

Concerning this hearing, the Holy Fathers accept it within the most simple complex of the Holy Trinity, or internal, which infers the procession or origin of the Holy Spirit from the Father, not of some external reception: Because the Spirit is not outside of God, but in God; And therefore these things are not only opposed to fabrications, nor are they to be accepted only in such a way as we are accustomed to speak of ambassadors; But they are to be referred to the mystery of the origin of the Holy Spirit from the Father, and indeed also from the Son, because he adds, 'for he shall receive of mine.' Thus Didymus of Alexandria, book II on the Holy Spirit. He does not speak from himself, that is, not without me and without the will of me and the Father, because he is inseparable from my will and the Father's, because he is not from himself, but is from the Father and me; For this very thing, that he subsists and speaks, is to him from the Father and me. Thus Ambrose, book V on the faith, chapter 6. He shall not speak from himself, but he shall speak what he shall hear, so that we might note that whatever the Spirit speaks, the Son also speaks, and whatever the Son speaks, the Father also speaks, because there is one sentiment and operation of the Trinity. Thus St. Prosper in the Sentences, sentence 366, from St. Augustine, book on the Trinity and the unity of GOD, chapter 3. Thus we ought to accept what has been said concerning the Holy Spirit: for he does not speak from himself, but whatever he has heard, he shall speak, so that we may understand that he is not from himself; for the Father alone is not from another. For the Son also is born of the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. But the Father is neither born of another nor proceeds, nor for that reason indeed should any disparity occur to human thought in that supreme Trinity, because both the Son is equal to Him from whom he is born, and the Holy Spirit is equal to Him from whom he proceeds. Bede in the Gospel homily. The Spirit does not speak from himself, that is, without the communion of the Father and the Son: for the Spirit is not diverse and divided from himself; But whatever he shall hear, he shall speak, he shall hear, namely, through the unity of Substance and the property of knowledge: from whom he has essence, from him certainly also knowledge: from him therefore hearing, which is nothing other than knowledge. Alcuin on this passage. The Spirit does not speak from himself, because he is not from himself, but from the Father.

and he will announce to you the things to come) He will foretell what is about to happen either to the world, or to the Jewish people, or to the Church. See examples Acts XI. 28. XIII. 1. ch. XX. 28. ch. XXI. 11. 1 Tim. IV. 1. 2 Tim. III. Eph. IV. 11. 2 Pet. I, 14. and throughout the whole Apocalypse.

Latin:

v. 13. Ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ ἐκεῖνος) Ille vicarius meus, mez cau- sæ patronus, constructio est, κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον.

Denique judicium adversus principem mundi, de quo convincendus est mundus, non est judi- cium talionis, quale Levit. XXIV. 20. habetur, quod in Diabolum utique exerceri nequit, siqui- dem illa, quæ injuste intulit Christo per instru- menta sua, Diabolus ex lege talionis sustinere non possit, nec talio haberi queat, quod regno suo exu- tus per destructionem idololatriæ, aliorumque vitiorum sit: quod pro morte Satanæ esse dicit Grotius; in jure vero talionis, id quod pro morte est, pro morte illata minime sufficit. Et aliud est judicium, quo principem mundi judicatum esse Spi- ritus S. docet, ac convincit, nempe quod judicatus est, cum per Christi morte potestate & ἐξυσίᾳ, vel jure mortis, quod habebat in genus humanum, exutus est Ebr. II. 14. ut in Christum credentes ju- stitiam veram in abitu ejus quærant, qui apex fuit obedientiæ Christi Phil. I. ut & liberationem à potestate Satanæ, in judicio per mortem Christi adversus eundem exercito. Genes. III. 15. Col. II. 10. unde liberati à servitute peccati, non Satanæ, sed Deo servire debent: de quo Eusebius Emissenus: arguitur, inquit, mundus de judicio, quo Princeps mundi est damnatus & mundus ipse liberatus, sed tanti beneficii ingratus, nondum sequitur Christum sive salutis autorem, sed potius Diabolum decepto- rem. Theophyl. in h. l. Condemnat otiosum, desidem mundum, qui Satanæ & fracto enervato non studeat ab se peccato vinci. Si tamen ad judicia & regna mundi, hic alludi quis velit, Brentiana explicatio nostræ analoga optime conveniet. Arguendi, in- quit, verbo Christus utitur in ea significatione, in qua Propheta Es. II. 4. judicabit inter gentes, arguet populos multos, c. XI. 4. judicabit in justitia pau- peres & arguet in rectitudine pro mansuetis terræ; significans Christum accepturum regnum inter ho- mines, illudque in justitia & judicio administratu- rum, ut sit sensus: Spiritus S. instituet ministerium Evangelii, per quod Christus regnabit in orbe terra- rum. Sunt autem tres officii partes in legitimo regno. Primo punire scelera, ut honesta vita conservetur. Secundo ut fiat justitia, hoc est, ut justa bonorum causa publicis sententiis approbetur boni in sua justitia defendantur. Tertio ut fiat judicium, hoc est, ut mali coërceantur, ne bonis noceant & injuria ho- stium à civibus repellatur. De his tribus partibus a- gitur etiam in Christo regno, sed cœlesti ratione. In regnis mundanis externa tantum scelera pro peccatis habentur: Sed in regno Christi etiam interior incre- dulitas. In regnis mundanis civilis cantum justitia conservatur, sed in regno Christi vera justitia distri- buitur, quam Christus suo ad Patrem abitu paravit. In regnis mundanis civilia judicia exercentur, sed in regno Christi verum judicium administratur, quia Christus vicit Satanam, qui in Christum credunt, ab ipso tuti sunt. Hæc Brentius; Etsi autem hæc omnia egerit Spiritus S. inde ab initio mundi, ta- men effusus visibiliter in Apostolos totius mundi doctorcs, illustriori ratione illa agere debuit per

Neque vicarii Christi nomen proprie Spiritui S. convenit; cum Christus, etsi visibiliter absens, nobis vere adsit, neque uspiam inScripturis ita vo- catur Spiritus S. neque causæ Christi Patronus est, etsi veritatem de Christo perhibeat, ac de ipso te- stetur.

ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν) Vos manuducet ad perfectam cognitionem eorum, quæ ad Ecclesias consti- tuendas pertinent. Nam universalitas restringenda ad id, de quo agitur. Tertullianus de præscriptionibus Hæretico- rum: Adjiciens, ipse deducet bos in omnem beritatem, ostendit illos nihil ignorasse, quos omnem beritatem consecuturos per spi- ritum beritatis promiserat: & utique implebis repromissum pro- bantibus Actis Apostolorum. Huc pertinet, ut supra diximus, cognitio regni Christi mere spiritualis, & ablatio legis ri- tualis, & huc respicientes Apostoli indecreto ajunt, Visum est nobis & Spiritui Sancto. Origenes adversus Celsum secun- do: Οὐκ ἄτοπον ἡγῦμαι παραθέαὶ τὸ Ἰησῦ τινα φωνὴν ἀπὸ τὸ κατὰ Ἰωάννην Εὐαγγελία ἔτι πολλὰ ἔχω λέγειν ὑμῖν, ἀλλ' ὦ δύνα- θε βασάζειν ἄρτι· ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ ἐκεῖν, τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀλη- θείας, ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς εἰς ἀλήθειαν πᾶσαν· ὦ γὰρ λαλήσει ἀφ' ἑαυτῶ, ἀλλ' ὅσα ἀκέση λαλήσει. κὶ ζητῆμεν ἐν τῷ τόπῳ, τίνα ἦν τὰ πολλὰ ἃ εἶχε μὲν λέγειν ὁ Ἰησῦς τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἑαυτῦ, ὅκ ἐδύναντο δὲ ἀὐτὰ βασάζειν τότε, καὶ φαμὲν, μὴ ποὺ ὡς Ιὐδαίος κὶ συντραφεῖσι τῷ κατὰ τὸ γράμμα Μωσέως νόμῳτοῖς ἀποσόλοις ὀὐχι μοὶ λέγειν τίς ὁ ἀληθῶς νόμο, καὶ τίνων ἐπεχωσαν ὑποδείγ- ματι κὶ σκιᾷ ἡ παρὰ τοῖς Ἰυδαίοις λατρεία ἐπιτελεῖτη κὶ τί των μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν σκιὰν περιεῖχεν ὁ περὶ βρωμάτων κὶ ποτῶν κὶ ἑορτῶν κὶ νεμηνιῶν κὶ σαββάτων νόμο· κὶ πολλὰ ἦν τοιᾶῦ ἃ εἶ- χεν ἀυτοῖς λέγειν· ὁρῶν δ' ὅτι πᾶντο χαλεπόν ἐσιν ἀπὸ ψυχῆς ἀνα- τρέπειν σχεδὸν συγγενηθέντα, κὶ συντραφέντα δόγμαζα μέχρι τῆς τὲ ἀνδρὸς ἡλικίας κὶ πείσαΐζα τῆς ἀναλαβόντας ἀυτὰ ὅτι ταῦτα μὲν ἔσι θεῖα, τὸ δὲ μέλλασταλῆναι ἀυτὰ ἐσιν ἀσεβές· ἐζήτη ὑπερθέ- χῆ τῆς κατὰ χρείαν τρίτεσι τὴν ἀλήθειαν γνώσεως ἐλέγχην ἀυτὰ σκύβαλα κὶ ζημίαν ὥσε πεπόνθασι τὰς ἀποσόλος, ὑπερετίθετο εἰς ἐπιτηδειότερον, καιρὸν ἢ κατὰ τὸ παθὸν ἡ ἀνάσαση ἀυτῦ.

Ubi illa restrictio in textu? Non tantum de iis, quæ ad constituendas Ecclesias seu politiam Ecclesi- arum faciunt, Apostolos informare debuitSpiritus S. Sed in OMNEM veritatem ducere, quemadmo- dum eventus id etiam comprobavit, quia in con- cionibus & scriptis suis Φερόμενοι ὑπὸ πνέυματος ἁγίς non solum ea, quæ ad τάξιν & εὐσχημοσύνην Ecclesiæ pertinent, proposuere, sed imprimis, quæ faciunt ad fidem & veritatemChristianam. Cyrillus l. X. c. 41. Hic veritatis Spiritus, inquit, ad omnem veritatem vos deducet. Novit enim exacte verita- tem, cujus Spiritus est, & eam non ex parte, sed inte- gre revelabit. Nam etsi ex parte in hac vita agnosci- mus, ait Paulus, non manca tamen sed integra veri- tas in hac parva cognitione nobis refulsit. Recte ta- men. Glossa ordinaria. Deducet vos in omnem veri- tatem saluti necessariam, quia alia veritas potius est vanitas, sed in Scriptura, qua secundum pietatem est, solida & simplex invenitur veritas. Comprobat id Tertullianus loco à Grotio laudato de præscriptio- nibus Hæreticorum: Adjiciens, ipse deducet vos in omnem veritatem, ostendit illos nihil ignorasse, quos omnem veritatem consecuturos per Spiritum veritatis promiserat: & utique implevit repromissum probanti- bus Actis Apostolorum. Nec vero illa præcedentia, habeo adhuc multa vobis dicere, sed non potestis ea por- tare, restringenda ad constitutionem Ecclesiarum aut cognitionem regni Christi meri spiritualis, de quo antea etiam tradiderant, aut propositio- nem legis spiritualis, quæ cum conditione regni Christi jam in Vet. Testamento proposita erat: aut cum Pontificiis ad traditiones abripienda, quia in Scripturis non contineri quicquam τῶν πολλῶν, quæ tum portare nequiverint Aposto- li, quæque revelarit postea Spiritus Sanctus, numquam probabitur: Sed ea generaliter com- prehendunt, de quibus adhuc informandi erant discipuli, quæ, etsi à Christo tradita, ipsi non- dum perceperant: quæ vero tum ob infirmita- tem & ruditatem suam, tum ob præconceptam opinionem, tum ob modernam tristitiam & mœ- rorem animi capere minime poterant, unde promisit Christus ipsis Spiritum Doctorem, qui omnia à se dicta illustraturus, & de omnibus lu- culentius & plenius eos informaturus sit. Pon- tificiis opponi potest Episcopi Romani Leonis M. sententia Sermon. II. Pentecost. Illi perfe- ćtioni, quæ erat discipulis conferenda, major gratia & abundantior inspiratio servabatur; per quam & quæ nondum acceperant sumerent & ex- cellentius possent haberi quæ sumserant, propter quod Dominus dicebat, adhuc multa habeo vo- bis dicere. Non itaque alia insinuanda erat ve- ritas, nec alia prædicanda doctrina, sed oporte- bat capacitatem eorum, qui docebantur augeri & multiplicari constantis illius caritatis, quæ omnem formidinem foras mitteret & furorem persequen- tium non timeret.

'Οὐ γὰρ λαλήσει ἀφ’ ἑαυτῦ) Nihil quod Deo Patri mihi- que visum non fuerit, de se comminiscetur. Loquitur ut de legato: Sic supra VII. 18. XIV. 10. λαλῶν Spiritus S. est, insinuare animis.

Ἀλλ’ ὅσα ἂν ἀκούσῃ λαλήσει) Quæ à Patre acceperit. Sic supra V. 30. VIII. 26.

De ἀκοῇ hæc inter complexum simplicissimum SS. Trinitatis accipiunt Sancti Patres, seu in- terna, quæ processionem vel originem Spiritus Sancti à Patre infert, non de externa quadam ceptione: Quia Spiritus non est extra Deum, sed in Deo; Ideoque non tantum hæc opponun- tur commentis, nec ita solum accipienda, ut de legatis loqui solemus; Sed referenda ad my- sterium originis Spiritus Sancti à Patre, imo & à Filio, quia addit, ὅτι ἐκ τῦ ἐμῦ λήψεται. Ita Didymus Alexandr. l. II. de Spiritu Sancto. Non loquitur à semetipso, hoc est, non sine me & si- ne meo & Patris arbitrio, quia inseparabilis à mea & Patris est voluntate, quia non ex se est, sed ex Patre & me est; Hoc enim ipsum, quod subsistit & loquitur, à Patre & me illi est. Ita Ambrosius l. V. de fide cap. 6. Non loquetur à semetipso, sed quæ audiet loquetur, ut adverte- remus, quod quicquid Spiritus loquitur, loqui- tur & Filius, & quicquid Filius loquitur, loqui- tur & Pater, quia una sententia & operatio Trini- tatis est. Ita S. Prosper in Sententiis sentent. 366. ex S. Augustino l. de Trin. & un. DEI cap. 3. Sic debemus accipere, quod de Spiritu Sancto dictum est: non enim loquitur à semetipso, sed quæ- cunque audivit, loquetur, ut intelligamus non eum esse à semetipso; Pater quippe solus ab alio non est. Nam & Filius de Patre natus est & Spi- ritus Sanctus de Patre procedit. Pater autem nec natus est de alio nec procedit, nec ideo sane aliqua disparitas in summa illa Trinitate cogitationi oc- currat humanæ, quia & Filius ei, de quo natus est, & Spiritus Sanctus, de quo procedit, æqualis est. Beda in homil. Evang. Non loquitur Spiri- tus à semetipso, hoc est sine Patris & Filii com- munione: neque enim diversus ac à se partitus est Spiritus; Sed quæcunque audiet, loquetur, audiet videlicet per unitatem Substantiæ & pro- prietatem scientiæ: à quo illi essentia ab illo utique & scientia: ab illo igitur audientia, quod nihil a- lind est, quam scientia. Alcuinus in h. l. Non loquitur Spiritus à semetipso, quia non est à se- metipso, sed à Patre.

καὶ τὰ ἐρχόμενα ἀναγγελεῖ ὑμῖν) Quæ aut mundo, aut po- pulo Judaico, aut Ecclesiæ eventura sunt, prænunciabit. Exempla vide Act. XI. 28. XIII. 1. c. XX. 28. c. XXI. 11. 1. Tim. IV. 1. 2. Tim. III. Ephes. IV. 11. 2. Petr. I, 14. & per totam Apocalypsin.

## 16:14
Verse 14.

He shall glorify me) By this very thing he will show my glory, that through me the things that are to be are signified beforehand to my own.

because he shall receive of mine) As if from my archives, as ambassadors are accustomed to do.

The holy Fathers teach more correctly concerning this reception of the Holy Spirit from the Son, that it is eternal and signifies the origin of the Holy Spirit from the Son. Augustine, Tractate 99 on John: This reception is eternal, and contains in itself eminently all times and can be accommodated to all. For in that which is everlasting, whatever word of time is placed, whether past, present, or future, it is not taken untruthfully. Athanasius to Serapion: The Spirit receives from the Son according to the voice of the Lord, 'He shall receive of mine and shall announce it to you,' since the Spirit has such an order and nature toward the Son as the Son has toward the Father. The reception is internal and therefore eternal. The Holy Spirit is said to receive from the Son, so that it may be signified that He has His origin from Him. Compare what we have said in System of Theology, Vol. III, concerning this eternal λήψει (reception).

κὰι ἀναγγελεῖ ὑμῖν (and shall announce to you) is an epexegesis of that which had preceded.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ἐκεῖνος ἐμὲ δοξάσει) Hoc ipso meam gloriam ostendet, quod per me meis futura præsignificantur.

ὅτι ἐκ τῦ ἐμῦ λήψεται) Tanquam ex archivis meis, ut legati solent.

Rectius de hac acceptione Spiritus Sancti à Filio S. Patres docent, quod eadem æterna sit & originem Spiritus Sanct. à Filio innuat. August. tr. XCIX. in Johan. Acceptio hæc æterna est, & con- tinet in se eminenter omnia tempora & ad omnia accommodari potest. In eo enim quod sempiter- num est, cujuslibet temporis verbum ponatur si- ve præteriti sive præsentis sive venturi, non men- daciter sumitur. Athanas. ad Serap. Spiritus à Fi- lio accipit juxta Domini vocem, de meo accipiet & annunciabit vobis, siquidem talem ordinem & naturam Spiritus habet ad Filium qualem Filius ad Patrem. Acceptio interna adeoque æterna est. Accipere à Filio dicitur Spiritus Sanctus, ut ab eo originem habere innuatur. Cons. quæ in Syst. Theol. Tom. III. de hac æterna λήψει dixi- mus.

κὰι ἀναγγελεῖ ὑμῖν) est ἐπεξήγησις ejus quod præcesse- rat.

## 16:15
Verse 15.

πάντα ὅσα ἔχει ὁ πατὴρ ἐμά ἐσι (all things that the Father has are mine) Also foreknowledge and decrees concerning future things, insofar as they concern the Church.

Διὰ τῦτο ἔιπον, ὅτι ἐκ τῦ ἐμῦ λαμβάνει (Therefore I said, that he receives of mine) What He receives from the Father, He receives from me. For the Son is another Lord of the Father's things. Luke 15:31. Tertullian: He calls the Holy Spirit the steward (that is, the dispenser) of the Father, the Vicar of Christ. Compare the passage in Acts 2:33. Peleus in Euripides concerning the affairs of his grandson Pyrrhus: 'Those things of his are mine, those things of mine are his.'

If the Son also has all things that the Father has, including foreknowledge and decrees concerning future things whatsoever (does the Father have only those decrees which concern the Church?), it is necessary that He be ὁμούσιος (consubstantial) with the Father; because to all those things which the Father has, the essential divine attributes pertain or belong primarily. If the Holy Spirit therefore received from the Son, just as from the Father, because all things which the Father has are the Son's, it behooves the Holy Spirit to receive also His essence from the Son, through eternal procession, because the Father also has this, that the Holy Spirit should receive essence from Him through eternal procession. Therefore these things do not pertain to that reception of which Acts 2:33 speaks, which was done in time and pertains to that human nature according to which He received from the Father the power of pouring out the gifts of the Holy Spirit, because the reception which is being treated here is eternal, and implies the origin of the Spirit from the Son of God, insofar as He has all things which are the Father's, and is ὁμούσιος (consubstantial) to Him. All of which, however, are to be understood without prejudice to the personal character of the Father and the Son, which is not common to them, but distinguishes the person of the Father and the Son from each other: Concerning which St. Augustine, Sermon 60 on the seasons: While He says 'all things,' He left nothing here which He would have less than the Father: All things, that is, the power, substance, and majesty. Who would not tremble to call him lesser, who equates himself as a truthful witness to the Father generally and in all things. Cf. John 5:17, 19, 26; ch. 10:30; ch. 14:9, 10; ch. 17:5, 10. Therefore, we oppose Grotius with what Augustine has in his treatise C. on John: The Son did not say, 'All things that the Father has are mine,' in the way it was said to that son who is not the only-begotten, but the elder of the two: 'You are with me always, and all that is mine is yours.' And what St. Cyril says in book 11, ch. 1, on John: Since the Son differs from the Father in nothing at all, except that he is not the Father, and since in both the same substance shines forth in the same way, how will they not be common, or rather, the same in both, so that whatever things are in the Father, the same are also in the Son, and whatever things are in the Son, are likewise in the Father also! Therefore, as I think, he used most exquisite language: for he did not say, 'because whatever the Father has, I also have,' lest he seem to be some exterior image formed after a primitive, just as we humans, who were made in the image of God; but he says, 'they are mine,' showing the ultimate identity of substance in the immutable properties in both. Add also Didymus of Alexandria, book 2, On the Holy Spirit (and St. Jerome, who translated his books into the Latin language, is of the same opinion): Although the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father and God gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him, yet because 'all things that the Father has are mine,' the Spirit himself is also mine, and 'he will take from what is mine.' Ambrose, book 2, On the Holy Spirit, ch. 12: He received the Holy Spirit from the Son through the unity of substance, just as the Son received from the Father: 'He,' he says, 'will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine.' What, therefore, is more evident than this unity, that what the Father has, are the Son's, and what the Son has, the Holy Spirit also received. The Grotian gloss is refuted partly by Arians and Photinians, who elide this statement of Christ lest they be forced to admit the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father, and partly by the Greeks, who deny the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. We have dealt sufficiently against both in Vol. 3, Syst. Theol., art. 3, ch. 2, p. 495, and art. 4, ch. 3, p. 813, 830.

We only add here what we said in the demonstration of the Deity of Christ—which, because of various intervening matters, was not brought to an end, let alone made public—for the argument of the infinite Deity of Christ in the present passage being confirmed. Thus, indeed, it is permitted to conclude: He who has all things, whatever the Father has, he possesses the divine essence no less than the Father. But Christ has all things whatever the Father has. Therefore, Christ has the divine essence no less than the Father. The minor proposition is presented in Christ's own words, and therefore needs no proof. The major proposition, however, is clear even from this, that if the Son did not have the divine essence, or what is the same thing, were not by nature true God as the Father is, he could not have professed in any appearance of truth, 'all things whatever the Father has are mine,' because in that way infinite things would remain for the Father as the supreme infinite God, of which Christ would be destitute, as a mere creature, as the adversaries imagine, and by nature only finite, far distant from that supreme God.

Although these things are clear, it is nevertheless helpful for the sake of greater illustration to urge this argument a little further. We wish it to be noted, however: (1) The universal particle 'all' (πάντα), which concludes all things under its scope, excludes nothing. For if anything were excepted, they would not be 'all.' Just as in a similar argument the Holy Spirit himself taught us to urge the force of the universal particle and to insist upon it strictly. The passage is 1 Corinthians 15:27: 'He put all things under his (Christ's) feet: but when he says that all things are put under him, it is manifest that he is excepted who put all things under him.' From Hebrews 2:8: 'For in that he put all things in subjection under him, he left nothing that is not put under him.' In that, therefore, he put all things in subjection to him, he left nothing not subject to him. Similarly we can conclude, and by the leading of the Holy Spirit we ought to, that when Christ said, 'All things, whatever the Father has, are mine,' it is manifest that all things except that which the Father is: And further. In that he testified that he has all those things, he left nothing that is not his from those things which the Father has. (2) The collective particle 'whatever' (ὅσα). For Christ did not only say 'all things that the Father has,' but to express notably all things without any exception, he also adds the collective particle, 'all things WHATEVER the Father has are mine.' Therefore, it is again manifest that 'all things' must be understood in such a way that nothing is left out or excepted. (3) The verb of having: 'Whatever the Father has, are mine,' that is, I have them likewise, just as they are the Father's, because the Father has them. But the Father is said to have not only those things which are comprised under his power, but also those which belong to him by nature. The Father has divine omnipotence, divine omnipresence, divine majesty and glory, divine authority, and to say it in a word, the divine essence, and whatever pertains to the same. Therefore, it is necessary that the Son of God also have all those things by the force of this utterance. Concerning which Athanasius, in the disputation against the Arians at the Council of Nicaea: He did not speak concerning created things when he said, 'all things that the Father has are mine,' but he showed that those things which pertain to the Deity are his own and peculiar to him, namely, immortality, incorruptibility, invincibility, immutability, incomprehensibility, power and the force of foreknowing, and whatever the Father has, those he claimed for himself as his own. (4) The appropriation of all those things which the Father has. For Christ explicitly says of all those things, 'THEY ARE MINE' (ἐμά ἐστι). He does not restrict or limit the reason or manner of having or possessing, but in an equal manner claims and appropriates the same to himself, just as the Father has the same; because he obtains it by the same divine and infinite reason. Cyril of Alexandria on this passage. He used most exquisite language. For he did not say, because whatever the Father has, I also have, lest he should seem to be a certain exterior image formed after the original, just as we men, who were made in the image of GOD; But he says, mine are, showing by identity of substance the ultimate in incommunicable properties in both: which he also says most openly elsewhere regarding the Father. For all mine are thine, he says, and thine are mine. (5) The inference of Christ. Christ proves that the Holy Spirit will receive from his own, which he had said in the preceding verse ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ ἐμοῦ λήψεται, or as some codices read λαμβάνει, because he will receive, or receives, from MINE, and therefore he adds again: All things whatsoever the Father has, are mine, διὰ τοῦτο Wherefore I said, that he will receive from mine. But if the Son had certain things as if he had them, which are the Father's, that inference of his would be faulty, for from a particular there is no inference made: I have certain things, which the Father has: Therefore I also have that ἀξίωμα [axiom/claim], that the Holy Spirit receives from what is mine, just as he receives from the Father. Wherefore it is necessary to understand the particle πάντα [all things] universally, concerning all things in the universe which the Father has. (6) The underlying subject matter. It concerns a matter that is entirely divine, namely the λήψει [reception] of the Holy Spirit, which Christ assumes the Spirit receives from the Father, which he announces. Here, however, he claims for himself the same ἀξίωμα, that the Holy Spirit receives from him, or from his own, for the reason that he himself has all things, whatsoever are the Father's. But he could by no means have professed this, unless he were truly GOD in nature with the Father. For the Holy Spirit receives nothing from any creature: since he himself is one with the Father, 1 John V. 7, and he himself distributes to each one his own, as he wills, 1 Corinthians XII. v. 11; as the spirit of man is in man, says the Apostle 1 Corinthians II. 11, so is the Spirit of God in God. Thus, therefore, Christ has all things, by virtue of this statement, whatsoever the Father has, so that the Holy Spirit receives from him no less than from the Father whatever he receives, even that which he announces to the Apostles: and this within the simplest complex of the divine essence. For this λῆψις [reception] is internal, not external: and because in God there is nothing which is not eternal, therefore this λῆψις in God is not temporary, but eternal. Wherefore it is necessary that the Son of God have the divine essence no less than the Father, otherwise it could not be said that the Holy Spirit receives from him whatever he receives, or even that which he inspires in the Apostles, and that divine wisdom by which he instructed them. For by this very thing is inferred the divine wisdom of knowing divine mysteries, and the omniscience of foreseeing future things: or as the Holy Spirit instructed the Apostles in the knowledge of divine things and in divine wisdom, and inspired in them the knowledge of future things, so that they could predict them. If he received all this from the Son, what is more clear than that the Son of GOD is equally endowed with divine wisdom and omniscience, just as the Father is, since the Spirit himself, the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge, who searches all things, even τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ [the depths of God], 1 Corinthians II. verse 10, receives from him whatever he has of divine wisdom and knowledge, so that he may be able to inspire and communicate it to others. (7) The absurdity of the opposing opinion. Imagine with the adversaries that Christ is a mere creature and a certain finite essence: By what right then will he be able to profess that he himself also has all things which the Father has, when nevertheless they are infinite, infinite in the immense treasury of the Father's infinite power, infinite in the immense treasury of the Father's infinite omniscience, infinite in the immense treasury of the Father's infinite divine majesty, and thus consequently, which are not in the power, knowledge, and majesty of a creature, however finite it may be, and however it may be exalted: since there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite. By what right will the Son be able to claim for himself that ἀξίωμα [axiom/claim], that that Holy Spirit of knowledge and wisdom, who knows all things, and is the author and giver of all wisdom, 1 Cor. chap. XII. verse 11, receives from him and from his own whatever he has, or communicates, of knowledge, if the Son is only a certain creature, and of nothing but a finite essence, and therefore also of only finite wisdom and knowledge. Will the Holy Spirit receive from a creature? By what right, therefore, will he assert for himself in this matter a parity of this dignity with the dignity and eminence of the Father, if his power, dignity, and divinity are in infinite ways inferior to his, as the adversaries contend. (8) The nature of the λήψεως [reception] of the Holy Spirit. For this λῆψις is eternal, just as that ἀκοὴ [hearing], by which he is said to hear from the Father, and from the Son, whatever he inspires in the disciples, is eternal. If, therefore, the Holy Spirit has received and heard from the Son from eternity whatever he has received and heard from the Father, it is necessary that the Son be no less an eternal GOD than the Father. (9) A parallel passage, John chap. XVII. verse 10. All mine are thine, and thine are mine, where Christ used that reciprocity by which he would equate himself to the Father, with no ἐξοχῇ [preeminence] or prerogative left to the Father. For he who can absolutely profess concerning the Father as the supreme and infinite GOD, all thine are mine, and conversely all mine are thine, he must not be in any part inferior, but in all things equal to GOD the Father. But concerning Christ, the former is true, and the latter. Whence Nazianzen, Orat. II. de Theolog.: All things which the Father has are the Son's, just as conversely, what are the Son's, the same are also the Father's. Nothing, therefore, is proper, because all things are common. And Cyril of Alexandria, book XI. on John, chap. 19: All mine are thine, and thine are mine; for where the highest identity of nature shines through, there the glory of perfections is incommunicable, and not divided, but one and the same. For since the Son is substantially the heir of the Father's perfections, he himself possesses all things which are the begetter's: and he shows that the Father in turn has all his own. And book I. on John, chap. 3: The Son, with his speech turned to the Father, says, All mine are thine, and thine are mine. If, therefore, the Son is lesser than the Father, and the Father greater than the Son, as heretics think, since what are the Son's are the Father's, and what are the Father's are the Son's, the lesser itself, which is in the Son, will also be in the Father, and conversely, the greater itself, which is in the Father, will also necessarily be accommodated to the Son. Nothing, therefore, will prevent believing the Father also to be lesser than the Son, and the Father greater than the Son. All of which, since they are most absurd, it is necessary that the Son be altogether equal to the Father, since all things which are the Father's are common to himself with the Son. Epiphanius against Sabellius: But what is that which is the Father's? Unless that the Father is GOD, I am GOD. The Father is life, I am life. All things which are the Father's are mine. Ambrose, book V. de fide, chap. 3: So that you might know the great GOD, and the saving, and omnipotent Son of GOD, he added a sign of his Majesty; by saying, And all mine are thine, and thine are mine. Augustine, tract. IV. on John. It is not right that the saints, of whom he has spoken here, should belong to anyone except Him by whom they were created and sanctified, and by this it is necessary that all things which are theirs should also belong to Him to whom they themselves belong. Therefore, since they belong to both the Father and the Son, he demonstrates that they are equal, to whom they equally belong. Gaudentius de promiss. Paracl. sermon. 14. tract. 14. All your things are mine and my things are yours, through the unity, namely, of the divine substance, which does not know how to have anything of its own that is not of its nature. Compare Basil lib. II. & IV. contr. Eunom. Hilary lib. II. de Trinit. & Athanasius disp. cum Ario coram Probo judice &c. To which finally (10) Regarding this present passage we also add the consensus of the ancient Church. Cyril of Alexandria lib. XI. cap. II. bursts forth in these words. The Son shows himself to be the exact and sincere character of the hypostasis of the Father in these words. For he makes it understood that, since he is the fruit of the substance of the Father, all things which are His, according to nature he draws to himself, so that they both are and are called his own by right. Didymus of Alexandria, Book II, On the Holy Spirit: Beware, he says, when these things are said, lest you fall into a grave error of understanding: and think that it is some thing and a possession which is held by the Father and the Son, but what the Father has according to substance and all eternity, immobility, incorruption, immutable goodness, subsistence from himself and in himself, this same thing the Son also has, and whatever things are the Son's, these same things the Father also has. Athanasius, Oration III against the Arians: The Son is ἐξουσιαστὴς καὶ παντοκράτωρ by the same reason as his Father: For his words are; All things whatsoever my Father has are mine. For it is the property of the Son to possess those things which are the Father's. Hilary, Book IX, On the Trinity: All things which the Father has are mine. And here indeed the present discourse does not signify species of creatures, nor diverse substitutions of the Elements, but unfolding to us the glory of the blessed and absolute divinity, it shows that GOD is to be understood in these things, which are his in virtue, in eternity, in providence, in power, etc. Ambrose, Book II, On the Faith, chapter 3: All things which the Father has are mine. What are all things? He certainly did not speak of created things. For all these things were made through the Son, but those things which the Father has, that is, eternity, majesty, and divinity, he possesses by being born. Augustine, Tractate CVII on John: It sufficiently appears how all things which are the Father's are the Son's. By this certainly, that he himself is also GOD, and was born of the Father to the Father equal. And afterwards: That which he says, when he was speaking of the Holy Spirit; All things which the Father has are mine, I said therefore, because he will receive of mine, etc. he spoke of those things which pertain to the divinity of the Father itself, in which he is equal to him, by having all things which he has. For the Holy Spirit was not about to receive from a creature which is subject to the Father and the Son, that which he says he will receive of mine, but certainly from the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, from whom the Son is also born. Dionysius the Carthusian, in this place: All things which the Father has are mine, not only by fruition, as the heretics said, but by substantial identity and real containment, that is, the Father communicated his whole essence, power, and perfection to the Son, nay, whatever is fitting for the Father, is appropriate for the Son, but with the relation or natural property, in which he is distinguished, excepted. Compare Epiphanius, heresy LXIX, against the Ariomanites. Nazianzen, Oration XLIX. Idacius Clarus, Book III, against Varimundus. Theophylact, in this place, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

πάντα ὅσα ἔχει ὁ πατὴρ ἐμά ἐσι) Etiam præscientiam & decreta de rebus futuris, quatenus Ecclesiam spectant.

Διὰ τῦτο ἔιπον, ὅτι ἐκ τῦ ἐμῦ λαμβάνει) Quod de pa- terno accipit, de me accipit. Filius enim alter Dominus rerum paternarum. Luc. XV. 31. Tertullianus: Spiritum Sanctum vocat villicum (id est, dispensatorem) Patris, Vicarium Christi. Confer locum Actor. II. 33. Peleus apud Euripidem de Pyrrhi nepotis sui rebus : ἐκεῖν’ ἐκείνε τἀμά, τἀκείνε τἐμά.

Si omnia, quæ Pater habet, etiam præscien- tia & decreta de rebus futuris quæcunque (num Pater solum ea habet decreta, quæ Ecclesiam spectant?) habet & Filius, necessum est, ut Pa- tri sit ὁμούσιος; quia ad omnia illa, quæ Pater habet, pertinent vel imprimis attributa divina essentialia. Si ideo à Filio accepit Spiritus Sanct. uti à Patre, quia omnia, quæ Pater habet, Filii sunt, oportet Spiritum Sanctum accipere & es- sentiam à Filio, per æternam processionem, quia & hoc habet Pater, quod ab eo recipiat Spiri- tus Sanctus essentiam per processionem æter- nam. Non ergo spectant hæc ad illam acceptio- nem, de qua Actor. II. 33. quæ in tempore fa- cta & ad humanam illam naturam pertinet, se- cundum quam à Patre potestatem accepit effun- dendi dona Spiritus Sancti, quia acceptio, de qua in præsenti agitur, æterna est, & infert ori- ginem Spiritus à Filio Dei, quatenus is omnia habet, quæ Patris sunt, eique ὁμούσιος est. Quæ tamen omnia intelligenda sunt salvo chara- ctere personali Patris & Filii, qui ipsis com- munis non est, sed personam Patris & Filii distinguit à se invicem: Quo de S. Augusti- nus Serm. LX. de temp. Dum dicit omnia, ni- hil hic reliquit, quod minus haberet à Patre: O- mnia, id est, unius Dei potentiam, substantiam, & majestatem. Quis eum minorem dicere non tre- miscat, qui se Patri generaliter & per omnia ve- ridicus testis exæquat. Conf. Johan. V. 17. 19. 26. cap. X. 30. cap. XIV. 9. 10. c. XVII. 5. 10. Grotio ita- que opponimus, quod tractatu C. in Joh. habet Augustinus: Non sic dixisse Filium, omnia quæ Pa- ter habet mea sunt, quemadmodum dictum est illi filio non unigenito, sed ex duobus majori. Tu me- cum es semper & omnia mea tua sunt. Et quæ S. Cyrillus lib. XI. cap. 1. in Joh. cum nihil à Patre penitus Filius differat, præterquam quod Pater non est, cumque in utraque eadem substantia eodem modo perfulgeat, quomodo non erunt communia imo vero eodem in utrisque, ut quæcunque in Pa- tre sunt, eadem etiam in Filio sint, & quæcunque in Filio, in Patre quoque similiter! Ideo ut ego puto, exquisitissima usus est oratione: non enim dixit, quia quæcunque Pater habet & ego habeo, ne i- mago quædam exterior ad primitivum formata, quemadmodum homines, qui ad imaginem DEI facti sumus, esse videatur, sed mea sunt, ait, iden- titatem substantiæ ultimam in proprietatibus incom- mutabilibus in utrisque ostendens. Adde & Didy- mum Alexandr. l. II. de Spiritu Sancto (& qui li- bros ejus in latinum idioma transtulit ὁμόψηφον S. Hieronymum) Licet à Patre procedat Spiritus ve- ritatis & det DEVS Spiritum Sanctum petentibus se, tamen quia omnia, quæ Pater habet, mea sunt, & ipse Spiritus Patris meus est, & de meo acci- piet. Ambrof. lib. II. de S. S. cap. 12. Accepit Spi- ritum Sanctum de Filio per unitatem substantiæ, sicut accepit à Patre Filius: ille, inquit, me cla- rificabit, quia de meo accipiet. Quid igitur hac unitate evidentius, quæ habet Pater, Filii sunt, quæ habet Filius, accepit & Spiritus Sanctus. Ve- lificatur Grotiana glossa partim Arianis & Photi- nianis hanc Christi sententiam elidentibus, ne ὁμοοσίαν Filii cum Patre admittere cogantur, par- tim Græcis procesfionem Spiritus Sancti à Filio ne- gantibus. Contra utrosque, quantum satis egi- mus. Tom. III. Syst. Theol. art. III. c. II. pag. 495. & art. IV. c. III. p. 813. 830.

Addimus tantum hic, quæ in ἀποδείξει Dei- tatis Christi, utpote propter varia intervenien- tia ad finem haud perducta, nedum publici juris facta, pro argumento infinitæ Deitatis Chri- sti in præsente loco firmando diximus. Ita nem- pe concludere licet: Qui omnia habet, quæ- cunque habet Pater, is non minus essentiam di- vinam obtinet, quam Pater. At Christus omnia habet quæcunque habet Pater. E. Christus non minus essentiam divinam habet quam Pater. Mi- nor propositio διαῤῥήδην afferto Christi exhibe- tur, ideoque probatione non eget. Major autem propositio vel inde liquet, quod si es- sentiam divinam non haberet Filius, vel quod idem esset, non foret natura verus DEUS uti Pater, nulla veri specie profiteri potuit, omnia quæcunque Pater habet mea sunt, quia ita in- finita superessent Patri ceu summo infinito Deo, quibus destitueretur Christus, ceu mera, uti fingunt adversarii creatura, & natura tantum finita longe distans à summo illo DEO.

Hæc quamvis luculenta sunt; Juvat tamen majoris illustrationis causa argumentum hoc paululum adhuc urgere. Notari autem veli- mus. (1) Particulam universalem πάντα O- MNIA, quæ sub ambitu suo cuncta conclu- dit, nihil excludit. Nam si exciperetur quic- quam, non essent omnia. Quemadmodum in simili argumento ipse Spiritus Sanct. nos docuit, vim particulæ universalis urgere, eidemque presse insistere. Locus est 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 27. Omnia ipsi (Christo) subjecit sub pedes ejus: ὅταν δὲ εἴπη ὅτι πάντα ὑποτέτακται, δῆλον ὅτι ἐκτὸς τοῦ ὑποτάξαντος αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα. Quum vero dixerit, quod omnia subjecta sunt ei, MANIFESTUM EST, quod præter eum, qui subjecit ipsi OMNIA. Ex Ebr. II. vers. 8. ἐν γὰρ τῷ ὑποτάξαι αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα, οὐδὲν ἀφῆκεν αὐτῷ ἀνυπότακτον. In eo enim, quod OMNIA ei subjecit, NIHIL dimisit Ei non subjectum. Similiter concludere possumus, & ductu Spiritus Sancti debemus, Quum dixerit Christus, OMNIA, quæcunque habet Pater, mea sunt, MANIFESTUM est, quod omnia præter id quod Pater est: Et porro. In eo quod omnia ea se habere testatus sit οὐδὲν ἀφῆκεν NIHIL DIMISIT, quod SUUM non sit ex his quæ Pater habet. (2) Particulam collectivam ὅσα, quæcunque. Non enim tantum dixit Christus omnia, quæ Pater habet, sed ut notanter exprimeret omnia citra ullam exceptionem, addit etiam collectivam particulam, omnia QUÆCUNQUE habet Pater mea sunt. Iterum ergo manifestum est, ita intelligenda esse omnia, ut nihil dimittatur, aut excipiatur. (3) Verbum habendi: Quæcunque habet Pater, mea sunt, id est ea itidem habeo, quemadmodum ea Patris sunt, quia habet illa Pater. Habere autem Pater dicitur non tantum, quæ sub sua potestate comprehenduntur, sed etiam quæ ipsi per naturam conveniunt. Habet Pater divinam omnipotentiam, divinam omnipræsentiam, divinum majestatem & gloriam, divinam imperium, & ut verbo dicam, divinam essentiam, & quicquid ad eandem spectat. Ea ergo omnia itidem habeat Filius DEI, vi hujus effati, necessum est. Quo de Athanas. disp. contr. Ar. in Concil. Nic. Non propter res creatas loquutus est, cum diceret omnia, quæ Pater habet, mea sunt, sed quæ spectant ad Deitatem, ea sibi propria & peculiaria esse ostendit, nimirum immortalitatem, incorruptibilitatem, invincibilitatem, immutabilitatem, incomprehensibilitatem, potentiam & præcognoscendi vim, & quæcunque Pater habet, ea, ut propria, sibi vendicavit. (4) Appropriationem eorum omnium, quæ Pater habet. Diserte enim Christus de omnibus illis ἐμά ἐστι MEA SUNT. Non restringit, aut limitat rationem, vel modum habendi, aut possidendi, sed pari modo eadem sibi vindicat, & appropriat, prout eadem habet Pater; quia eadem divina & infinita ratione obtinet. Cyrill. Alexandr. in hunc loc. Exquisitissima usus est oratione. Non enim dixit, quia quæcunque Pater habet, & ego habeo, ne imago quædam exterior ad primitium formata, quemadmodum homines, qui ad imaginem DEI facti sumus, esse videant; Sed mea sunt, ait identitate substantiæ ultimam in proprietatibus incommunicabilibus in utriusque ostendens: quod alibi etiam ad Patrem apertissime dicit. Omnia enim mea tua sunt, inquit, & tua mea. (5) Illationem Christi. Probat Christus Spiritum Sanctum de suis accepturum, quod vers. præcedente dixerat ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ ἐμοῦ λήψεται, vel ut nonnulli legunt Codices λαμβάνει, quia de MEO accipiet, aut accipit, ideoque iterum subjungit: Omnia quæcunque Pater habet, mea sunt, διὰ τοῦτο Quapropter dixi, quod de meo accipiet. At si quædam tanquam haberet Filius, quæ Patris sunt, vitiosa esset illa ipsius colle- ctio, à particulari enim nulla fit illatio: Quæ- dam habeo Ego, quæ Pater: Ergo etiam id ἀξίωμα habeo, quod Spiritus Sanct. accipiat de meo, quemadmodum accipit à Patre. Qua- propter oportet universaliter intelligere parti- culam πάντα de omnibus in universum quæ ha- bet Pater. (6) Materia substrata. Agitur de re prorsus divina, nempe de λήψει Spiritus Sancti, quem à Patre accipere quæ annunciat, Christus supponit. Hic vero vindicat sibi idem ἀξίωμα, quod nempe Spiritus S. à se, vel de suo accipiat, ideo quia ipse omnia habeat, quæcunque Patris sunt. At id nequaquam profiteri potuisset, nisi verus esset cum Patre natura DEUS. Nam Spiritus S. à nulla creatura quicquam accipit: quum ipse u- num sit cum Patre 1. Johan. V. 7. & distribuat ipse unicuique suum, prout vult. 1. Corinth. XII. v. 11. ut spiritus hominis in homine est, inquit Apostolus 1. Corinth. II. 11. ita Spiritus Dei in Deo. Sic ergo Christus omnia habet, vi hujus effati, quæcun- que habet Pater, ut ab ipso non minus quam à Pa- tre accipiat Spirit. Sanct. quicquid accipit, etiam id, quod annunciat Apostolis: idque intra simpli- cissimum complexum essentiæ divinæ. Nam λῆψις hæc interna est non externa: & quia in Deo nihil est, quod non æternum sit, ideo λῆψις hæc in Deo non temporaria est, sed æterna. Quapro- pter oportet Filium Dei non minus habere divi- nam essentiam, quam Patrem, alias ab ipso non posset dici accipere Spirit. Sanct. quicquid acci- pit, aut etiam id, quod inspirat Apostolis, & divinam illam sapientiam, qua eosdem instruxit. Hoc ipso enim infertur divina sapientia cogno- scendi mysteria divina, & omniscentia futu- ras res prævidendi: vel uti Spiritus Sanctus A- postolos divinarum rerum cognitione, ac sa- pientia divina instruxit, & futurorum notitiam ipsis inspiravit, ut ea prædicere possent. Si hoc omne à Filio accepit, quid luculentius est, quam Filium DEI divina sapientia & omniscien- tia æque pollere, uti Patrem, quum ab eo- dem Spiritus ipse, Spiritus sapientiæ & scientiæ, qui omnia scrutatur, etiam τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ pro- funditates ipsas DEI 1. Corinth. II. verf. 10. ac- cipiat, quicquid habet sapientiæ & scientiæ di- vinæ, ut aliis inspirare ac communicare pos- sit. (7) Absurditatem sententiæ adversæ. Finge cum adversariis, Christum esse meram tantum creaturam & finitam quandam essentiam: Quo jure tum profiteri poterit, quod omnia, quæ Pater habet, etiam ipse habeat, quum tamen infinita sint, in immenso thesauro potentiæ, Patris infinitæ, infinita in immenso thesauro omniscientiæ Patris infinitæ, infinita in im- menso thesauro majestatis divinæ Patris infini- tæ, atque ita consequenter, quæ in potesta- te, scientia & majestate finita creaturæ, quanta- cunque illa sit, & quomodocunque illa exaltetur, non sunt: quum finiti & infiniti nulla sit propor- tio. Quo jure poterit Filius illud sibi ἀξίωμα vin- dicare, quod nempe S. Spiritus ille scientiæ & sa- pientiæ, qui novit omnia, & omnis sapientiæ au- ctor ac dator est, 1. Cor. cap. XII. verf. 11. abs se & de suo accipiat, quicquid habet, vel commu- nicat, cognitionis, si Filius est tantum crea- tura quædam, nec nisi finitæ essentiæ, adeo- que finitæ etiam tantum sapientiæ & scientiæ. Num Spiritus Sanctus à creatura accipiet? Quo jure ergo paritatem hac in re adseret sibi digni- tatis hujus cum dignitate atque eminentia Pa- tris, si infinitis modis inferior ejus est potestas, dignitas ac divinitas, prout contendunt adver- sarii. (8) λήψεως Spiritus Sanct. indolem. Hac enim λῆψις est sterna, prouti etiam illa ἀκοὴ, qua à Patre audire, & à Filio dicitur, quic- quid inspirat discipulis æterna est. Si ergo ab æterno Spirit. Sanct. à Filio accepit, & audi- vit, quicquid à Patre accepit, & audivit, non minus DEUM æternum oportet esse Filium, quam Patrem. (9) Locum parallelum, Johan. cap. XVII. vers. 10. Omnia mea tua sunt, & tua mea, ubi ea reciprocatione usus est Chri- stus, qua se exæquaret Patri, nulla relicta Patri ἐξοχῇ, vel prærogativa. Qui enim ab- solute profiteri potest de Patre ceu DEO sum- mo & infinito, omnia tua mea sunt, & vicis- sim omnia mea tua sunt, eum oportet non esse ulla parte inferiorem, sed per omnia æqualem DEO Patri. At de Christo verum est prius, & posterius. Unde Nazianzenus Orat. II. de Theolog. Omnia quæ Pater habet Filii sunt, sicut vicissim, quæ Filii sunt, eadem & Patris sunt. Nihil ergo proprium, quia omnia com- munia. Et Cyrill. Alexandr. l. XI. in Johan. cap. 19. Omnia mea tua sunt, & tua mea; ubi e- nim summa identitas naturæ persulget, ibi glo- ria perfectionum incommunicabilis est, nec di- visa, sed una & eadem. Nam cum perfectionum Patris substantialiter Filius hæres sit, omnia i- pse, quæ genitoris sunt, possidet: & Patrem sua rursus habere omnia, ostendit. Et l. I. in Jo- han. cap. 3. Filius ad Patrem versa oratione, Omnia mea, inquit, tua sunt, & tua mea. Si ergo minor Patre Filius est, & Filio Pater major, ut hæretici sentiunt, quoniam quæ Fi- lii sunt, Patris sunt, & quæ Patris Filii, mi- nus ipsum, quod in Filio est, Patri etiam inerit, & è converso, majus ipsum, quod in Patre est, Filio quoque necessario accommodabitur. Nihil ergo prohibebit Patrem quoque minorem Filio cre- dere, & Filio Patre majorem. Quæ omnia cum absurdissima sint, necesse est æqualem omni- no Patri Filium esse, cum omnia quæ Patris sunt, communia sibi cum Filio sint. Epiphan. contra Sabell. Quid vero est ea quæ Patris sunt? Nisi quod DEUS est Pater, DEUS ego sum. Vita est Pater, vita ego sum. Omnia quæ Pa- tris, mea sunt. Ambros. lib. V. de fide cap. 3. Ut scires magnum DEUM, & salutarem, & omnipotentem DEI Filium, indicium suæ Majestatis admiscuit; dicendo, Et mea omnia tua sunt, & tua mea. August. tract. IV. in Johan. Non est fas, ut sancti, de quibus hic lo- cutus est, cujusquam sint, nisi ejus, à quo crea- ti, & sanctificati sunt, ac per hoc & omnia quæ ipsorum sunt, necesse est, ut ejus sint, cujus & ipsi sunt. Ergo cum & Patris & Filii sint, æquales eos esse demonstrat, quorum æqualiter sunt. Gaudentius de promiss. Paracl. sermon. 14. tract. 14. Tua omnia mea sunt & mea tua sunt, per unitatem sc. divina substantiæ, quæ nescit aliquid habere suum, quod naturæ suæ non sit. Confer Basilius lib. II. & IV. contr. Eunom. Hilarius lib. II. de Trinit. & Athanas. disp. cum Ario coram Probo judice &c. Quibus denique (10) Circa hunc præsentem locum etiam addimus antiquæ Ecclesiæ consensum. Cyrill. Allexandr. lib XI. cap. II. in hæc verba prorum- pit. Characterem rursus exactum, atque since- rum hypostaseos Patris his se verbis Filius ostendit. Intelligere namque facit, quia cum sit fructus sub- stantiæ Patris, omnia quæ ejus sunt, secundum naturam attrahit, ita ut propria sua merito & sint & appellentur. Didymus Alexand. l. II. de Spirit. Sanct. Cave, inquit, cum ista dicuntur, ne grave labaris intelligentiae in vitium: & putes, rem ali- quam esse & possessionem, quae habeatur a Patre ac Filio, verum quae habet Pater juxta substantiam & omnem aeternitatem, immobilitatem, incorru- ptionem, immutabilem bonitatem, de se & in se subsistentiam, haec eadem habet & Filius, & quae- cunque sunt Filii, hac eadem habet & Pater. Atha- nas. Orat. III. contra Arian. Filius est ἐξουσιαστὴς καὶ παντοκράτωρ eadem ratione qua Pater ipsius: Ejus enim verba sunt; Omnia quaecunque Pater meus habet mea sunt. Filii enim proprium, ea quae Patris sunt possidere. Hilarius lib. IX. de Tri- nit. Omnia quae Pater habet mea sunt. Et hic quidem non creaturarum species, neque Elemen- torum diversas substitutiones praesens sermo signifi- cat, sed beatae atque absolutae divinitatis nobis gloriam pandens, DEUM in his ostendit intel- ligendum esse, quae sua sunt in virtute, in aeternita- te, in providentia, in potestate, &c. Ambrof. lib. II. de fide cap. 3. Omnia quae Pater habet mea sunt. Quae sunt omnia? Non utique loquutus est de creatis. Haec enim omnia facta sunt per filium, sed ea quae Pater habet, id est, aeternitatem, ma- jestatem, divinitatemque nascendo possidet. Au- gust. tr. CVII. in Johan. Satis apparet, quomodo unigeniti Filii sint omnia, quae sunt Patris. Per hoc utique, quod etiam ipse DEUS est, & de Pa- tre Patri natus est equalis. Et postea. Illud quod ait, cum de Spirit. Sanct. loqueretur; Omnia quae ha- bet Pater mea sunt, Propterea dixi, quia de meo accipiet &c. de his dixit quae ad ipsam Pa- tris pertinent divinitatem, in quibus illi est aequa- lis, omnia quae habet, habendo.
