That καθὼς signifies some, not an all-encompassing congruence, namely in the very dogma which was to be preached, not in authority. Christ proclaims throughout this book that he was sent by the Father, and not rarely in that sense of teaching. See Is. ch. LXI. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Καθὼς ἐμὲ ἀπέστειλας εἰς τὸν κόσμον κἀγὼ ἀπέ- στειλα αὐτοὺς εἰς τὸν κόσμον). Causa redditur cur hi supra alios auxilio divino egeant, quia durum munus susce- pturi sint legationis pro Christo, 2. Cor. V. 20. Eph. VI. v. 20. ἀπέστειλα hic est consuevi mittere, quo sensu & vocem dandi usurpari aliquoties monuimus. Illud καθὼς aliquam, non omnimodam congruentiam signifi- cat, in ipso scilicet dogmate, quod erat prædicandum, non in auctoritate. Christus à Patre se missum passim in hoc libro prædicat, nec raro in illo sensu docendi. Vide Es. c. LXI. 1.

## 17:19
Vers. 19. And for them I sanctify myself) He repeats the word ἁγιάζειν with the sense slightly changed. For קדש ἁγιάζειν among other things also means to offer, and is said both of victims and of other things which are consecrated to GOD, Exod. XIII. 2. Levit. XXII. 2. Ecclesiast. XXXV. v. 8. The same thing therefore is said here, which is said at Hebr. IX. 14. he offered himself. See also X. 10. and 14. ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν here is, that they may be more confirmed in that faith by which they have embraced my word. Thus Eph. III. 13. Col. I. 24.

that they also may be sanctified in truth) Here he explains more that end, which is excellent among others, of the death of Christ, namely that by that example the Apostles may render their life purer day by day, confirmed in the truth.

The particle ὑπὲρ does not here look only to the end, much less to the confirmation of faith, because the death and offering of Christ was not a martyrdom, but a ransom and an expiatory sacrifice, and therefore ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν is in place and instead of us: because he was made a ransom for all, 1 Tim. II. 6. Nor do they speak of the example which the Apostles have in the death of Christ, that they also may be sanctified in truth, but of the consequence and fruit of the satisfaction of Christ: who therefore offered himself for us, that by this one offering he might perfect all who were to be sanctified, Hebr. X. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Καὶ ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἐγὼ ἁγιάζω ἐμαυτὸν) Repe- tit vocem ἁγιάζειν sensu paulum mutato. Nam קדש ἁγιάζειν inter cætera etiam valet προσφέρειν, & dicitur tum de victimis tum de aliis rebus, quæ DEO conse- crantur, Exod. XIII, 2. Levit. XXII. 2. Ecclesiast. XXXV. v. 8. Idem ergo hîc dicitur, quod ad Hebr. IX. 14. ἑαυ- τὸν προσήνεγκε. Vide & X. 10. & 14. ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν hîc est, ut magis confirmentur in ea fide, qua sermonem meum amplexi sunt. Sic Eph. III. 13. Col. I. 24.

ἵνα κὴ αὐτοὶ ὦσιν ἡγιασμένοι ἐν ἀληθείᾳ) Hîc magis ex- plicat finem illum inter cæteros eximium mortis Chri- sti, nimirum ut eo exemplo Apostoli vitam suam red- dant indies puriorem confirmati in veritate.

Particula ὑπὲρ non hîc finem tantum respicit, nedum confirmationem fidei, quia Christi mors & oblatio non martyrium fuit, sed λύτρον & sacrificium expiatorium, ideoque ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν est loco & vice nostri: quia factus est ἀντίλυτρον ὑ- πὲρ πάντων, 1. Tim. II. 6. Neque de exemplo, quod in morte Christi habent Apostoli, lo- quuntur ἵνα κὴ αὐτοὶ ὦσιν, ἡγιασμένοι ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, sed de consequenti & fructu satisfactionis Christi: qui ideo se pro nobis obtulit, ut hac una obla- tione consummaret omnes, qui sanctificarentur, Ebr. X. 14.

## 17:20
Vers. 20. I do not pray for these only) Although he has prayed for certain special things for the Apostles, he shows nevertheless that there are many things which they have in common with other believers, such as confirmation in faith and charity.

Of those who shall believe) Taken for the future.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Οὐ περὶ τούτων δὲ ἐρωτῶ μόνον) Quanquam pro Apostolis specialia quædam precatus est, ostendit ta- men multa esse quæ cum aliis credentibus habeant com- munia, ut confirmationem in fide & caritate.

Τῶν πιστευσόντων) Pro futuro sumtum.

## 17:21
Vers. 21.

that all may be one) That they may be one in faith and charity. He treats, however, of the first Christians, concerning whom see Acts IV. 32. Compare Rom. XII. 5. Eph. IV. 3.

Since this part of the prayer pertains to ALL the faithful who were to believe in Christ through the word of the Apostles, just as the preceding part pertains to the Apostles themselves, it is not to be restricted to the first Christians; because not only they, but all, as many as believe in Christ, believe through the word of the Apostles, until the consummation of the age; and the force of this prayer of agony extends itself to all of them. For it is the same word which we hear and read in the Scriptures, which the first Christians heard and received from the Apostles preaching by living voice. Not through others, says Iren. b. III. ch. I. have we known the disposition of our salvation than through those by whom the Gospel came to us, which indeed they then proclaimed, but afterwards by the will of God handed down to us in the Scriptures to be the foundation and pillar of our faith.

καθὼς σὺ πάτερ ἐν ἐμοὶ κἀγὼ ἐν σοὶ) Just as we promote the Gospel with joined works. See above X. 38. XIV. 10.

κὴ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἡμῖν ἓν ὦσι) ἐν ἡμῖν that is, by obeying us. Thus those who follow his rule are said to be in Christ.

It is not correctly said that the Father and the Son promote the Gospel with joined works: for they are not associate causes: their essence is one, their will is one, their power of working is one, their operation is one. Nor is this phrase intended to designate a conjunction in promoting the Gospel or an operation through the Gospel, but the intimate περιχώρησις of the Son in the Father and of the Father in the Son, as observed before. And the warning of Athanasius in Orat. IV. contr. Arian. is worth noting: It is not said, that they may be one in you, as I am one in you; but that they may be one in us, as I am in you and you in me, so that it might be shown that the Father and the Son are one by nature, but our union is by grace. Conf. Ambros. l. IV. de fid. c. I. August. tract. CX. in Joh. Certainly the spiritual, supreme, and most intimate, holy and sincere unity of the faithful is noted, in the Father and in the Son, and at the same time the mystical union and communion, which with the Father and

They have in the Son, it is designated. Cf. 2 Pet. 1:4, 1 John 1:3, ch. 4:13. We are one with God through faith, one with our neighbor through charity. Ignat. Epist. 7. The whole is faith in one God and love toward one's fellow.

that the world may believe that you sent me) So that others may be enticed by their example to the faith, admiring that supreme constancy in the profession of dogma and mutual love. See what we noted above on 13:35. But it is the same thing to believe that Jesus was sent by God, or to believe the Gospel.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

ἵνα πάντες ἓν ὦσι) Ut sint uni fide & caritate. Agit autem de primis Christianorum, de quibus vide Act. IV. 32. Conf. Rom. XII. 5. Eph. IV. 3.

Quum hæc precationis pars ad OMNES fi- deles, qui credituri erant per verbum Aposto- lorum in Christum, uti præcedens ad Apostolos ipsos, pertineat, restringenda non est ad primos Christianorum; Quia non illi tantum, sed o- mnes, quotquot in Christum credunt, per ver- bum Apostolorum credunt, usque ad consum- mationem seculi; & vis precationis hujus προ- αγωνίας porrigit sese ad illos universos. Idem enim verbum est, quod nos audimus & legimus in Scripturis, quod audiverunt & acceperunt pri- mi Christianorum ab Apostolis viva voce prædi- cantibus. Non per alios, inquit Iren. l. III. c. I. dispositionem salutis nostræ cognovimus quam per eos, per quos Evangelium pervenit ad nos, quod quidem tunc præconiaverunt, postea vero per Dei voluntatem in scripturis nobis tradiderunt funda- mentum & columnam fidei nostræ futurum.

καθὼς σὺ πάτερ ἐν ἐμοὶ κἀγὼ ἐν σοὶ) Sicut nos conjun- ctis operis Evangelium promovemus. Vide supra X. 38. XIV. 10.

κὴ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἡμῖν ἓν ὦσι) ἐν ἡμῖν id est nobis obedsubendo. Sic esse in Christo dicuntur, qui ejus regulam sequun- tur.

Non recte dicitur Pater & Filius conjunctis operis Evangelium promovere: non enim causæ sociæ sunt: una est eorum essentia, una volun- tas, una operandi virtus, una operatio. Nec phrasi hac conjunctio in Evangelio promoven- do aut operatio per Evangelium, sed intima περιχώρησις Filii in Patre & Patris in Filio desi- gnatur, ut antea observatum. Et ἀξιομνημόνευτον est monitum Athanasii Orat. IV. contr. Arian. Non est dictum, ut sint in te unum, sicut ego in te unum sum; sed sint unum in nobis, sicut ego in te & tu in me, ut ostenderetur, quod Pater & Filius sint unum per naturam, nostræ autem unio sit per gratiam. Conf. Ambros. l. IV. de fid. c. I. August. tract. CX. in Joh. Nimirum Vnitas fide- lium notatur spiritualis summa & arctissima, sancta & sincera, in Patre & in Filio, ac simul mystica unio & communio, quam cum Patre &

Filio habent, designatur. Conf. 2. Petr. I. 4. 1. Joh. I. v. 3. cap. IV. 13. Unum cum Deo sumus per fidem, unum cum proximo per charitatem. Ignat. Epist. VII. Tὸ ὅλον ἡ πίςις ἡ εἰς ἳ θεὸν καὶ ἀγάπη πρὸς τὸ ὁμόφυλλον.

ἵνα ὁ κόσμος πιςεύσῃ ὅτι σύ με ἀπέςειλας) Ut cæteri il- lorum exemplo alliciantur ad fidem, admirantes summam illam constantiam in professione dogmatis & mutuam di- lectionem. Vide quæ notavimus supra XIII. 35. Idem au- tem est credere Jesum esse à Deo missum, aut credere Evan- gelio.

## 17:22
Καθὼς ἡμεῖς) Just as I willed the same thing which you had commanded, Father, and you approved my words and held them ratified.

Latin:

Καθὼς ἡμεῖς) Sicut ego idem volui, quod tu præceperas Pater, & tu mea dicta probasti ac rata habuisti.

## 17:22
Ver. 22. And I the glory which you have given me) The power of performing miracles, which is called the glory of Christ above 3:1, and the glory of God, above 11:40. By his own example, who gave this power to them, he commends that which he had asked of the Father for their sanctification. For he is accustomed to distribute tasks, as it were, between himself and the Father in an economical manner.

I have given to them) I have determined to give, as above I sent 18.

that they may be one) So that in that respect also, namely through that influx, they may be connected to me. For I understand here 'in me,' the same as with me.

as we are one) Through that divine power which I have from you. See above 10:38.

Although some explain it concerning the glory of miracles, even the blessed Brentius, yet because that was not given to all ministers of the word, much less to the faithful, it is more correctly explained by the force of the context as the glory of unity, since Grotius acknowledges that the word 'that' (ἵνα) is taken specifically in the former clause and in the latter, 'that the world may know,' it is finally established that it is taken as a purpose; since the faithful cannot aspire to that spiritual unity by their own powers, whence Christ says that he gave to the faithful the glory which the Father gave to his own, which is this, that they may be one in him. That statement, 'the glory which you gave me,' some explain in such a way that that most blessed communion between the Father and the Son, and likewise between the divine and human nature in Christ, is the origin and source of that spiritual unity which Christ here prays for for believers, which is the interpretation of the blessed Gerhard, Harm. Ch. 180, p. 1586. But Christ did not receive that glory of unity, which he merited and gave to believers, from the Father beforehand, but through eternal generation as GOD, or through personal union as man, nor is it one and the same unity which he has through eternal generation and which he has through the hypostatic union; the former is unity with the Father, and essential to him, the latter is the unity of the human nature with the divine nature of the Word, and is personal; therefore that 'which you have given me' refers to a giving done in time, not of the glory of the unity of Christ, but of the faithful among themselves and with God, which the Father had given to Christ, not for possession, so that it might be Christ's own and possessed by him, but for distribution, so that he might grant it to the faithful, just as the Holy Spirit is said to have received the promise for Christ for pouring out, Acts ch. 2, v. 13. St. Cyril, book 11 on John, ch. 12, explains it concerning the unity which the Son of God received in time according to his human nature with God, not concerning the unity which he has from eternity as God with the Father, which is a more suitable exposition, because the same word 'you have given' does not seem to be conveniently taken for a giving done both from eternity and in time simultaneously, nor is that essential unity of the Son with the Father the origin and source of our spiritual unity, but rather that personal union and communion of the human nature with the divine nature of the Word. And to speak more briefly and clearly, he says, he says that it was given to himself, the only-begotten, what was given to his own flesh: but it was given entirely by the Father through him in the Spirit. For the mode of union with God has no other way. For it is understood in Christ, insofar as he appeared as man, by union with the Spirit, by reason of an ineffable conjunction, with his flesh sanctified and thus ascending to union without confusion with God the Word and through him with the Father, by a certain relation, namely, not by nature. This brightness and glory, therefore, he says, Father, which you gave me, which is that I may be one with you, I have given to them that they may be one, just as we are one. If, however, the first 'that' (ἵνα) is also to be taken as a purpose, the glory given to Christ can be understood concerning the goods and gifts which he received for our sake, so that he might give them to us, so that we might receive them from his fullness, to the end that we might be one in Christ among ourselves and with GOD, Ps. 68:19, Eph. 4:8, John 1:16.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Καὶ ἐγὼ τὴν δόξαν ἣν δέδωκάς μοι) Potesta- tem faciendi miracula, quæ gloria Christi dicitur supra III. 1. & gloria Dei, supra XI. 40. Exemplo suo qui hanc illis potestatem dederit, commendat id quod patrem roga- verat pro ipsorum sanctificatione. Solet enim οἰκονομικῶς quasi inter se & Patrem operas partiri.

Δέδωκα ἀυτοῖς) Constitui dare, ut supra ἀπέςειλα 18.

ἵνα ὦσιν ἓν) Ut ea quoque ratione, nimirum per illum influxum, mihi connexi sint. Subaudio enim hic ἐν ἐμοὶ, idem mecum.

καθὼς ἡμεῖς ἓν ἐσμέν) Per divinam illam vim, quam à te habeo. Vid. supra X. 38.

Etsi nonnulli de gloria miraculorum expli- cent, etiam B. Brentius, tamen quia ea non o- mnibus verbi ministris nedum fidelibus data, rectius explicatur vi contextus de gloria unitatis, quum agnoscat Grotius, vocem ἵνα in priori mem- bro εἰδικῶς accipi & in posteriori, ut mundus cognoscat, demum eam τελικῶς accipi constet; Siquidem ad spiritualem illam unitatem suis vi- ribus aspirare nequeant fideles, unde ait Chri- stus, se gloriam, quam dedit suis Pater, dedisse fidelibus, quæ hæc est, ut unum sint in se. Illud ergo, gloriam quam dedisti mihi, nonnulli ita explicant, quod beatissima illa inter Patrem & Filium, itemque inter divinam & humanam na- turam in Christo communio origo & fons sit spi- ritualis illius unitatis, quam Christus h. l. creden- tibus precatur, quæ B. Gerhardi est interpreta- tio Harm. Cap. CLXXX. p. 1586. Sed gloriam illam unitatis, quam credentibus promeruit ac dedit, Christus non accepit prius à Patre, sed per æternam generationem, ut DEUS, seu per unionem personalem ut homo, nec una est ea- demque unitas quam per æternam generationem & quam per hypostaticam unionem habet, illa est unitas cum Patre, eidemque essentialis, hæc est unitas humanæ naturæ cum divina Verbi natu- ra, eademque personalis, ideo illud ἣν δέδωκάς μοι de datione in tempore facta non gloriæ unitatis Christi, sed fidelium inter se & cum Deo, quam dederat Christo Pater, non πρὸς κτῆσιν ad posses- sionem, ut eadem Christi esset propria, & ab ipso possideretur: Sed πρὸς διαίρεσιν ad distributio- nem, ut ea concederet fidelibus, quemadmo- dum Spiritus Sanct. promissum accepisse dicitur Christum πρὸς ἔχυσιν Actor. c. II. v. 13. S. Cyrillus l. XI. in Joh. cap. XII. de unitate, quam in tem- pore accepit Filius Dei secundum humanam na- turam cum Deo explicat, non de unitate, quam ab æterno ut Deus cum Patre habet, quæ ἔκθεσις convenientior, quia de datione cum ab æterno, tum in tempore facta simul verbum idem δέδωκας commode non videtur accipi, ne- que unitas illa essentialis Filii cum Patre est ori- go & fons unitatis nostræ spiritualis, sed potius unio & communio illa personalis humanæ naturæ cum divina τοῦ λόγου. Atque ut brevius dicam & clarius inquit, sibi ipsi datum esse unigenitus ait, quod datum est propriæ carni: Datum autem omnino à Patre per ipsum in spiritu. Modus enim unionis cum Deo aliam viam non habet. Insol- ven- ligitur enim in Christo quatenus apparuit ut homo unione cum spiritu, ratione conjunctionis ineffabili, sanctificata carne atque ita ad unionem fine confusione cum Deo verbo ipsa ascendente & per ipsum cum Patre, habitudine quadam scil. non natura. Hanc igitur, inquit, claritatem & gloriam, Pater, quam dedisti mihi, quæ est, ut tecum unum sim, dedi eis ut sint unum, sicut nos unum sumus. Si tamen prius ἵνα etiam accipiendum τελικῶς sit, gloria Christo data intelligi potest, de bonis & donis, quæ accepit nostri causa, ut nobis daret, ut de plenitudine ejus acciperemus ea. fini, ut nos unum essemus in Christo inter nos, & cum DEO, Ps. LXIIX. v. 19. Eph. IV. v. 8. Joh. I. 16.

## 17:23
Ver. 23. I in them, and you in me) This is an explanation of what preceded, and 'that they may be' is to be repeated, and 'and' stands for 'as,' which is placed below 23.

that they may be perfected into one) That is, 'that they may be perfected in love,' as the same person speaks here in Epistle 1, 4:19, so that they may contribute those common gifts to the common cause. See Heb. ch. 12:23, 11:40.

That ἐγὼ ἐν αὐτοῖς does not only imply an influx of power for miracles: But the mystical union which Christ has with us. For He is in us through communion of nature, because He is ὁμοούσιος to us. Eph. V. 30. through the distribution of His body & blood in the Eucharist, if we spiritually enjoy the same, Joh. VI. 56. through the participation of His spirit, Rom. IIX. 19. which is the spirit of charity & unity, 2. Tim. I. XVII. through gracious indwelling, which happens through faith, Eph. III. 17. and the influence, which as mystical members we have from Christ our head. Concerning which modes St. Cyril discourses elegantly in the loc. cit. The Father, however, is in Christ through essential περιχώρησιν, by which He is considered as God and through the indwelling of the whole fullness of the Godhead in Christ, by which He is man Col. II. 9. We, however, are said to be perfected into one, both by that τελειώσει, which falls into this life, 1. Cor. I. 10. 1. Joh. I. 3. 4. II. 5. not only through mutual love among ourselves, but also through true faith in Christ, by which we are united in Christ to the Father Himself, we are one with God: and also by that which we have through faith, and expect in the other life: as Dionysius explains, that they may be perfected into one, that is, that they may be led to the perfection of mutual union, which is had in the fatherland, where they are connected by inseparable charity, and where God is all in all.

ἵνα ὁ κόσμος πιστεύσῃ ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας) Those signs having been seen, just as above he had attributed the same effect to the concord of the Apostles, 21.

καὶ ἠγάπησας αὐτοὺς) Since by your will that power was granted to them, nor could it have been granted otherwise.

καθὼς ἐμὲ ἠγάπησας) Which among other things you had shown by that divine power of performing miracles given to me. See what is above III. 35. X. 42.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐγὼ ἐν αὐτοῖς, καὶ σὺ ἐν ἐμοί) Explicatio est ejus quod præcessit & repetendum ἵνα ὦ & καὶ pro καθώς, quod positum est infra 23.

ἵνα ὦσι τετελειωμένοι εἰς ἕν) Id est ἵνα ὦσι τετελειωμένοι ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ ut loquitur hic idem Epistola I. IV. 19. ut illa dona communia ad causam communem conferant. Vid. Hebr. c. XII. 23. XI. 40.

Illud ἐγὼ ἐν αὐτοῖς non solum influxum virtutis ad miracula infert: Sed unionem mysticam quam habet Christus nobiscum. Est enim in nobis per naturæ communionem, quia nobis ὁμοούσιος. Eph. V. 30. per corporis & sanguinis sui in Eucharistia distributionem, si iisdem spiritualiter fruamur, Joh. VI. 56. per spiritus sui participationem, Rom. IIX. 19. qui charitatis & unitatis est spiritus, 2. Tim. I. XVII. per gratiosam inhabitationem, quæ fit per fidem, Eph. III. 17. & influentiam, quam ut mystica membra habemus à Christo capite nostro. De quibus modis S. Cyrillus eleganter disserit l. c. Pater autem in Christo est per essentialem περιχώρησιν, qua consideratur ut Deus & per inhabitationem totius plenitudinis Deitatis in Christo, qua homo est Col. II. 9. Nos autem consummati in unum dicimur, tum ea τελειώσει, quæ in hanc vitam cadit, 1. Cor. I. 10. 1. Joh. I. 3. 4. II. 5. non solum per mutuam inter nos invicem dilectionem, sed & per veram in Christum fidem, qua in Christo ipsi Patri unimur, nos unum cum Deo sumus: tum illa quam per fidem habemus, & expectamus in altera vita: quomodo Dionysius explicat, ut sint consummati in unum, id est, ut ad perfectionem mutuæ unionis, quæ habetur in patria, perducantur, ubi inseparabili charitate connexi sunt, & ubi est Deus omnia in omnibus.

ἵνα ὁ κόσμος πιστεύσῃ ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας) Visis signis illis, quemadmodum supra concordiæ Apostolorum eundem tribuerat effectum, 21.

καὶ ἠγάπησας αὐτοὺς) Quandoquidem tua voluntate ipsis ea potestas concessa est, nec aliter concedi potuit.

καθὼς ἐμὲ ἠγάπησας) Quod inter cætera ostenderas data mihi illa divina miraculorum edendorum potestate. Vide quæ supra III. 35. X. 42.

## 17:24
Vers. 24. Πάτερ ὃς δέδωκάς μοι) With effect, so that they have surrendered themselves to me. He prays this not only for the Apostles, but for all believers, as above 20.

This is what he says: where consequently the giving is not to be understood as regards the election and calling of the Apostles, as in v. 16, but a giving through election to eternal life, as in v. 2.

θέλω) I would wish as Marc. cap. VI. v. 25. c. X. v. 35. Matth. c. XII. 38.

ἵνα ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ) That is, where I am to be, in the highest heaven. Above VII. 34 XII. 26. 2. Timoth. cap. II. v. 12.

κἀκεῖνοι ὦσι μετ' ἐμοῦ) After the resurrection, just as I.

ἵνα θεωρῶσι τὴν δόξαν τὴν ἐμὴν) That they may behold in my presence with what honor you have endowed me. For it is a certain part of blessedness to have friends as conscious witnesses of it.

ὧν ἔδωκάς μοι) Which you determined to give me. ὅτι ἠγάπησάς με πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου) See above ch. V. & Matth. XXV. 35.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Πάτερ ὃς δέδωκάς μοι) Cum effectu, ita ut tradiderint se mihi. Hoc non pro Apostolis tantum precatur, sed pro omnibus credentibus, ut supra 20.

Hæc ille: ubi proinde non datio quoad electionem & vocationem Apostolorum intelligenda, ut v. 16. sed datio per electionem ad vitam æternam, ut v. 2.

θέλω) Velim ut Marc. cap. VI. v. 25. c. X. v. 35. Matth. c. XII. 38.

ἵνα ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ) Id est, ubi futurus sum, in cœlo supremo. Supra VII. 34 XII. 26. 2. Timoth. cap. II. v. 12.

κἀκεῖνοι ὦσι μετ' ἐμοῦ) Post resurrectionem, sicut ego.

ἵνα θεωρῶσι τὴν δόξαν τὴν ἐμὴν) Ut coram spectent, quo me honore affeceris. Est enim pars quædam beatitudinis, amicos habere ejus conscios & testes.

ὧν ἔδωκάς μοι) Quam constituisti mihi dare. ὅτι ἠγάπησάς με πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου) Vide supra c. V. & Matth. XXV. 35.

## 17:25
Vers. 25.

πάτερ δίκαιε) He addresses God by this name, because it is consistent with his equity to reward those who, having left the world, have worshipped him.

καὶ ὁ κόσμος σε οὐκ ἔγνω) The thought coheres with the preceding ὅτι ἠγάπησας. Therefore, one should not place a full stop after κόσμος. A great part of mankind does not show by their deeds that you are known to them. For this concerns active knowledge, 1 ep. II. 4. &c. IV. 8.

ἐγὼ δέ σε ἔγνων) I have shown by my teaching.

καὶ οὗτοι ἔγνωσαν ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας) They have shown by their deeds that they believe this.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

πάτερ δίκαιε) Compellat Deum hoc nomine, quia æqui- tati ejus sit conveniens, præmiis afficere eos qui mundo relicto ipsum coluerunt.

καὶ ὁ κόσμος σε οὐκ ἔγνω) Cohæret sententia cum præce- dentibus ὅτι ἠγάπησας. Itaque non est interstinguendum complete post κόσμος. Magna hominum pars non ostendit factis te sibi esse notum. Agitur enim hic de cognitione activa, 1. ep. II. 4. &c. IV. 8.

ἐγὼ δέ σε ἔγνων) Ostendi dogmate meo.

καὶ οὗτοι ἔγνωσαν ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας) Factis ostenderunt se id credere.

## 17:26
Vers. 26.

καὶ ἐγνώρισα αὐτοῖς τὸ ὄνομά σου) Your properties, as above v. 9.

καὶ γνωρίσω) More so in the conversations after the resurrection, Luc. XXIV. 45. Actor. I. 3.

Grotius explains the manifestation as having taken place after the resurrection, Luc. XXIV. 4. Actor. I. 3. But the manifestation made through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit is not to be excluded, nor is this prayer to be restricted to the Apostles: since he prays for all believers, and thus also for those who believe in him through the Apostolic word, v. 20, for whom he has prayed for grace in this life, v. 21, 22, 23, and glory in the next, v. 24, 25, 26. Which Grotius himself acknowledged at v. 24.

ἵνα ἡ ἀγάπη ἣν ἠγάπησάς με ἐν αὐτοῖς ᾖ) That is, that you may love them, being so well instructed about you, just as you love me. Thus 1 epist. IV. 9. ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν is towards us, with which he pursues us.

Christ explains in these words, as interpreted by our blessed Gerhard on page 1622, the end and consequence of that salutary manifestation of which he had spoken: therefore I have made your name known to them and will continue to make it known, [the love] with which you loved me, if [it be] in them; that is, that then the knowledge of your name and also your love may be derived to them through me, your beloved Son, so that through that manifestation of your name, having been led to true faith in me, your beloved Son, they themselves also, as adopted sons, may be loved, so that the more richly and intimately they have known you, the more they may be loved by you as sons, just as you also love me most ardently as your only-begotten Son, so that they may feel in their hearts that incomprehensible charity of yours, with which you love not only me, but also them in me and on account of me.

κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτοῖς) That my dogmas and the example of my life, so well inculcated, may stick more and more in their minds, Gal. IV. 19. and above c. XIV. 33.

Christ does not speak of his own doctrine or life, but of himself: that I, to wit, may be in them, because for this reason he manifests his name to us, that he himself may be and dwell in us, John XIV. 23. namely through the acknowledgment of himself and faith, Ephes. III. 17. in this life and hereafter in the other through a glorious indwelling, by which he will be all in all to us with the Father and the Holy Spirit, 1. Cor. XV. 28. Apoc. XXI. 35. Cf. Cyril on this passage. May this prayer be effective, O Lord Jesus, we pray with Rupert on this passage, in the souls of your people, that they may be one in you and among themselves, that they may see your glory after the miseries of this life, that they may be with you and you in them, and that they may live in your love and that of your Father, to be torn away from it by no heights nor depths, by no ages of ages.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

καὶ ἐγνώρισα αὐτοῖς τὸ ὄνομά σου) Proprietates tuas, ut su- pra v. 9.

καὶ γνωρίσω) Magis in colloquiis post resurrectionem, Luc. XXIV. 45. Actor. I. 3.

De manifestatione explicat Grotius post resur- rectionem facta Luc. XXIV. 4. Actor. I. 3. Sed non excludenda manifestatio facta per effusionem Spi- ritus sancti, nec restringenda hæc oratio ad Apo- stolos: Siquidem orat pro omnibus fidelibus, adeo- que iis etiam, qui per verbum Apostolicum in se credunt vers. 20. quibus gratiam in hac vita v. 21. 22. 23. & gloriam in altera exoravit, v. 24. 25. 26. Quod agnovit ad v. 24. ipse Grotius.

ἵνα ἡ ἀγάπη ἣν ἠγάπησάς με ἐν αὐτοῖς ᾖ) Id est, ut eos tam bene institutos de te ames, sicut me amas. Sic 1. epist. IV. 9. ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν est erga nos, qua nos prosequi- tur.

Exponit Christus his verbis, interprete B. Ger- hardo nostro pag. 1622. finem & consequens saluta- ris illius, de qua egerat, manifestationis, ideo eis no- tum feci ac porro etiam notum faciam nomen tuum, qua me dilexisti, si in eis; id est, ut tum notitia no- minis tui etiam dilectio tua per me dilectum tuum Filium ad ipsos derivetur, ut per manifestationem illam tui nominis ad veram fidem perducti in me dilecto tuo Filio etiam ipsi, ut filii adoptivi, dili- gantur, ut quanto illi te uberius ac intimius cogno- verint, eo magis à te, ut filii diligantur, quemad- modum etiam me, ut Filium tuum unigenitum ar- dentissime diligis, ut cordibus suis sentiant cha- ritatem illam tuam incomprehensibilem, qua non me solum, sed etiam ipsos in me ac propter me diligis.

κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτοῖς) Ut mea dogmata & exemplum vitæ tam bene inculcata magis magisque hæreant eorum mentibus, Gal. IV. 19. & supra c. XIV. 33.

Non de sua doctrina, vel vita loquitur Chri- stus, sed de sese: ut ego scil. sim in ipsis, quia ideo ma- nifestat nobis nomen suum, ut in nobis sit & ha- bitet ipse Joh. XIV. 23. per agnitionem nempe sui & fidem Ephes. III. 17. in hac vita & olim in altera per ἐνοίκησιν gloriosam, qua nobis cumPatre & Spi- ritu sancto erit omnia in omnibus 1. Cor. XV. 28. Apoc. XXI. 35. Conf. Cyrill. in h. l. Efficax sit ô Domine Jesu, precamur cum Ruperto in h. l. in animis tuorum hæc oratio, ut in te & inter se unum sint, ut videant gloriam tuam post vitæ hujus miserias, ut tecum sint & tu in eis, utque in tua dilectione & Patris tui vi- vant, nullis neque sublimitatibus neque profundita- tibus, nullis seculorum seculis ab ea divellendi.

## 18:1 Argument
SECTION II. On the History of the passion of Christ. CHAPTER XVIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

When Jesus had betaken himself through the torrent of Kidron into the garden, which Judas knew, and Judas was seeking him there with a cohort, having met him he prostrated them with a single word, and again making himself known to them, he ordered his own to be dismissed. But he warned Peter, who was striking Malchus, to put back his sword, since indeed it behooved him to drink the cup of the Father. Then, bound, he was led to Annas the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was Pontiff at that time: Peter, having been let into the palace of the Pontiff and asked by a maidservant, denies that he is a disciple of Jesus. Jesus, examined by the Pontiff concerning his disciples and his doctrine, testifies that he has spoken nothing in secret. And therefore that he can be inquired of from his hearers, what he taught; he is struck by an iniquitous servant. There follow those things which were done before Caiaphas the Pontiff, to whom he had been sent back by Annas: where also Peter, asked for the second time by those who were warming themselves by the fire, denied Jesus, as also when he was asked for the third time by a certain friend of Malchus, but Jesus was led to the praetorium. Pilate, inquiring about the cause, orders the Jews to judge him according to their law, but they denying that they can crucify anyone, examines Jesus whether he is the King of the Jews; upon his professing that his kingdom is not of this world, and that he was born for this, that he might testify to the truth, Pilate manifests his innocence to the Jews, and wishes to release him free on account of the feast of the Passover: but they cry out with one voice, that not him, but Barabbas should be released.

There are three parts: I. The Captivity of Jesus in the garden, to v. 12. II. The Examination and Passion of Jesus before the Sanhedrin, with the triple denial of Peter, to verse 27. III. The Accusation and Examination of Jesus in the praetorium, to verse 40.

PART I. The Captivity of Jesus in the garden.

Vers. 1.

Ἐξῆλθε) Outside the city, whose gates were open even at night in great peace, especially on feast days, since there was no room for such a great multitude for rest within the city.

He is said to have gone out, as St. Cyril has it, from that house in which he had instructed his disciples. Therefore the terminus a quo is noted by the word Ἐξῆλθε, but the terminus ad quem is not expressed. For as Augustine and others warn, the whole valedictory discourse and prayer of Christ was made in the upper room, which being finished, he went out into the mount of Olives across the torrent of Kidron.

πέραν τοῦ χειμάῤῥου) To that place which is crossed on foot, as the Syriac here.

τοῦ κέδρων) Thus all the Greek Codices here, and no otherwise in the Greek version, 2 Samuel XV. 13, 1 Kings II. 13. Elsewhere as 2 Kings XXIII. 4, without the article κέδρων, but in such a way that it appears to be an appellative, since otherwise Hebrew names are written with the accent on the last syllable. It is added that Josephus in the sixth book of the Jewish War and elsewhere calls the adjacent valley κεδρῶνα, just as he calls the Mount of Olives ἐλαιῶνα, and just as the Greeks say δαφνῶνα, παλαιῶνα and others of that form, so that there should be no doubt that the banks of this torrent were planted with cedars. Nor should it disturb anyone that some have noted that cedars are called ארזים by the Hebrews, for there are many kinds of cedars so called in a general sense, and among them one from which the Greek name flowed, קדרן, which exists in Genesis 6 in the Chaldean version, which the Rabbis Nathan and Joshua Karchel have expelled קדרונו.

Therefore, to the Hebrews it is called the torrent of Cedron, to the Greeks signified by the same χείμαρ́ρός τω̃ν κέδρων: because in these collective nouns the singular is taken for the plural, as we saw above in ch. XV. 16. Now John is accustomed, where he expresses proper names, to allude to some meaning or history, as here to that by which David, a type of Christ in most things, being attacked in war by his son and migrating from the city, crossed the same torrent, with good men weeping for his calamity, which was so unworthy of him, 2 Sam. XV. 23. Just as the treacherous Achitophel bore the image of Judas, so Absalom, an ungrateful and rebellious son, bore the image of the Jewish people.

Others take it as a proper name, and treat the article τω̃ν as added in imitation of the LXX Interpreters, even though Jerome, in his Hebrew Places, citing these words of the Evangelist, reads τη̃ κέδρων and warns that Cedron was the name of the valley, and of the torrent flowing through the valley. But there appears no reason why we should believe the article and accent were changed by the fault of the scribes, even though Erasmus Schmidius, with Isaac Casaubon in his notes on this passage, may lean toward that, although Casaubon himself is forced to admit that τω̃ν κέδρων has been written here for many centuries. Whence it is surprising that Mr. Dr. Henricus Müllerus, against the consensus of many centuries and all modern codices and the reading of the Greek version of the LXX Interpreters, should here admit a slip of the scribes, which not even Grotius thought should be admitted. I do not see how that squares with his protestation that he reveres the consensus of the codices. For here he could not deny that the codices agree. However, some derive the name קִדְרוֹן rather from obscurity or blackness, because this torrent was obscure, black, and dark, since cedars do not thrive in streams, like willows, planes, or alders, but grow more happily in the mountains, whence Lebanon is ennobled by cedars, 1 Kings IV. 33. We allow everyone here to abound in his own sense regarding the origin of the word. Nevertheless, the opinion of Grotius does not seem improbable.

ὅπυ ἦν κη̃πος) A part of the estate of Gethsemani. See Matt. XXVI. 36.

Latin:

SECTIO II. De Historia passionis Christi. CAPUT XVIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Quum Jesus per torrentem Cidron in hortum, quem Iudas noverat, se contulisset, & Iudas cum cohorte illic eum quaereret, obvius ei factus unica voce illos prostravit, atque iterum se illis notificans suos dimitti jussit. Petrum autem Malchum percutientem monuit, ut recondat gladium, siquidem calicem Patris bibere ipsum oporteat. Dehinc ligatus ad Hannam socerum Caiphe deductus est, qui Pontifex tum erat: Petrus in palatium Pontificis intromissus ab ancilla rogatus, negat se esse Iesu discipulum. Iesus à Pontifice de discipulis, & de doctrina sua examinatus testatur, se nihil in occulto loquutum esse. Ideoque ex auditoribus suis queri posse, quid docuerit; à servo iniquo percutitur. Sequuntur quae coram Caipha Pontifice, ad quem ab Hanna remissus erat, gesta sunt: ubi etiam Petrus secunda vice ab iis, qui juxta ignem se calefaciebant, rogatus Jesum abnegabat, ut & cum tertia vice ab amico quodam Malchi rogaretur, Iesus autem ad praetorium ductus. Pilatus de causa quaerens, Iudaeos eum, juxta legem ipsorum judicare jubet, illis autem negantibus, se quenquam crucifigere posse, examinat Iesum anne Iudaeorum Rex sit; quo regnum suum non esse de hoc mundo, seque ad id natum esse, ut de veritate testetur, profitente, Pilatus Iudaeis innocentiam ejusdem manifestat, eumque ob festum Paschatos liberum dimittere vult: sed illi una voce clamant, non ipsum, sed Barrabam dimittendum esse.

Partes sunt tres: I. Captivatio Jesu in horto, ad v. 12. II. Examen, & Passio Jesu coram Synedrio, cum trina Petri abnegatione, ad vers. 27. III. Accusatio, & Examen Jesu in praetorio, ad vers. 40.

PARS I. Captivatio Jesu in horto.

Vers. 1.

Ἐξῆλθε) Extra urbem, cujus portae etiam noctu patebant alta pace, praesertim festis diebus, cum tantae multitudini locus ad quietem intra urbem non esset.

Egressus dicitur, ut habet S. Cyrillus ex illa domo, in qua suos instituerat discipulos. Notatur ergo terminus a quo voce ἐξῆλθε, non vero exprimitur terminus ad quem. Nam ut Augustinus, & alii monent, tota oratio valedictoria, & precatio Christi in coenaculo facta est, qua expedita egressus est, in montem Oliveti trans torrentem Cedron.

πέραν τοῦ χειμάῤῥου) Ad eum locum qua pedibus transitur, ut hic Syrus.

τοῦ κέδρων) Ita hic Graeci omnes Codices, nec aliter in Graeca versione, 2. Samuel, XV. 13. 1. Reg. II. 13. Alibi ut 2. Reg. XXIII. 4. sine articulo κέδρων, sed ita ut appellativum esse appareat, cum alioqui Hebraea nomina scribantur cum accentu in ultima. Accedit quod Josephus belli Judaici sexto & alibi vallem adstitam κεδρῶνα vocat, quomodo montem Oliveti ἐλαιῶνα, & sicut Graeci dicunt δαφνῶνα, παλαιῶνα & alia ad eam formam, ita ut dubitari non debeat, quin cedris consiti fuerint margines hujus torrentis. Nec movere quenquam debet, quod nonnulli monuerunt, cedros Hebraeis dici ארזים multa enim sunt cedri ita generaliter dictae genera, & inter ea unum unde nomen Graecum fluxit קדרן quod exstat Genes. 6. in Chaldaica versione, quod Rabbini Nathan & Josua Karchel expulerunt קדרונו

Hebraeis ergo dicitur torrens Cedri, Graecis eodem signifi- catus χείμαρ́ρός τω̃ν κέδρων: quia in his collectivis singulare sumitur pro plurali, ut vidimus supra c. XV. 16. Solet autem Johannes ubi nomina propria exprimit ad significationem aliquam aut historiam alludere, ut hic ad eam qua David typus in plerisque Christi, a filio suo bello petitus urbe mi- grans eundem torrentem transiit, bonis tam indignam ejus calamitatem lachrymantibus, 2. Sam. XV. 23. Sicut perfi- dus Achitophel Judae, ita Absolomus ingratus & rebellis filius populi Judaici gessit imaginem.

Alii pro nomine proprio habent, & articulum τω̃ν ex imitatione LXX. Interpp. additum agunt, etfi Hieronymus in locis Hebraic. haec Evangeli- stae verba citans legat τη̃ κέδρων moneatque Ce- dron fuisse nomen vallis, ac torrentis per vallem fluentis. Cur vero articulum & accentum vitio librariorum mutatum credamus, nulla apparet causa, utut Erasmus Schmidius cum Isaaco Ca- saubono in not. ad h. l. eo propendant, cum tamen Casaubonus ipse fateri necessum habeat, τω̃ν κέ- δρων a multis seculis hic scribi. Unde mirari subit quod Dn. D. Henricus Müllerus contra mul- torum seculorum & codicum modernorum o- mnium consensum Graecaeque versionis LXX. In- terpp. lectionem liberariorum lapsum hic admit- tat, quem ne Grotius quidem admittendum cen- suit. Non video quomodo id protestationi ejus, quod consensum codicum veneretur, congruat. Hic enim consentire codices negare haud potuit. Deducunt autem nonnulli nomen קִדְרוֹן potius ab obscuritate, nigredine, quod torrens hic obscu- rus, niger & tenebricosus fuerit, siquidem Cedri non gaudeant rivis, ut salices, platani, alni, sed in montibus felicius nascantur, unde Libanus cedris nobilitatus. 1. Reg. IV. 33. Permittimus hic quem- vis suo abundare sensu, quoad vocis originem. Non improbabilis tamen videtur Grotii senten- tia.

ὅπυ ἦν κη̃πος) Pars villae Gethsemani. Vide Matth. XXVI. 36.

## 18:2
Verse 2.

ὅτι πολλάκις συνήχθη ὁ Ἰησου̃ς ἐκει̃) Jesus was always accustomed to seek solitary places for the sake of prayer. But on these feast days he was accustomed to spend the night there, Luke XXI. 37, ch. XXII. 39. By this act, Christ also shows that he does not flee his enemies, but chooses a place and time that are opportune, according to his Father's counsel and his own. He preferred to be taken in the place of prayer rather than in the place of supper: and at night, so that the fear of his enemies might be shown, who had not dared to attack him by day.

Why he wished to be taken in that place, and why in a garden, St. Cyril explains thus: He arrived at the place in which Christ himself, the Savior of all, and his holy disciples were frequently accustomed to be. He did this again, however, so that he might be found by the traitor without difficulty; the place, moreover, was a garden, bearing the form of the old Paradise. For it was, so to speak, a certain recollection of figures, and a return of all things in one word to their pristine state. For in Paradise was the beginning of all our sadness, but in the garden the passion of Christ also begins, which brings us the amendment of all those ancient things.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ὅτι πολλάκις συνήχθη ὁ Ἰησου̃ς ἐκει̃) Solebat Jesus semper precandi causa loca sola quaerere. His vero festis diebus semper ibi pernoctare solitus erat, Luc. XXI. 37. c. XXII. 39. Ostendit & hoc facto Christus se inimicos non fugere, sed locum & tempus eligere opportuna, Patris suoque consilio. In loco orationis, quam in loco coenae capi maluit: & no- cte, ut ostenderetur hostium formido, qui die illum aggre- di ausi non erant.

Cur eo in loco, & cur in horto voluerit capi, S. Cyrillus ita explicat: Pervenit ad locum, in quo ipse Servator omnium Christus & sancti discipuli frequenter versari solebant. Hoc autem rursus a- gebat, ut a proditore citra negotium inveniretur; Locus autem, hortus erat, veteris Paradisi formam gerens. Erat enim, ut ita dicam, recollectio quae- dam figurarum, & omnium uno verbo in pristinum statum reversio. In Paradiso quippe omnis tristi- tiae nostrae initium fuit, in horto vero Christi quoque passio inchoatur, quae veterum illorum omnium e- mendationem nobis invehit.

## 18:3
Verse 3.

τὴν σπει̃ραν) That which was accustomed to be given by the governor to the Senators during the days of the Passover to preserve the peace of the City and the Temple. See what is said at Matt. XXVI. 45. The commander of this cohort is soon called χιλίαρχος in v. 12. Yet it is not necessary that the whole cohort was present, but a part of it.

καὶ ἐκ τω̃ν ἀρχιερέων καὶ Φαρισαίων ὑπηρέτας) ἐκ that is, given by them themselves. By the name of the Chief Priests and Pharisees he again describes the Senate, because they were most opposed to Jesus on account of private interests. ὑπηρέται are כְּלֵי מִשְׁׁטָר, concerning whom see the cited passage of Matthew. The captain (ὁ στρατηγός) was present with these ministers, as noted in the same place.

That some of the Priests and Elders were also present, Luke clearly testifies in chapter XXII. 52. Therefore, not only Roman soldiers, Gentiles, and ministers of the Priests and Pharisees, but also

the Chief Priests and Elders were present for the sake of authority, and so that the business might be carried out more diligently: and thus Gentiles and Jews, ecclesiastics and politicians, masters and servants, military men and others, conspired against the Lord, together with Christ's own Apostle, Judas.

μετὰ φανῶν κὴ λαμπάδων) The Evangelist shows with what ardor they sought Christ and feared that he might slip away, since, although it was a full moon, they nevertheless brought both torches and lanterns, so that they might creep through every hiding place.

Cyril adds another reason: They were afraid that, as usually happens in the dark, they might strike against stones or fall into pits. For such things usually happen in the dark. But oh, the madness! The wretches do not see, because of their great folly, that they are striking against the stone of which God and the Father says: Behold, I lay in Sion a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal. And those who fear a small pit do not perceive that they are rushing into the fountains of the abyss and the depths of the earth, and those who turn away from the evening darkness do not care about the perpetual and eternal night.

καὶ ὅπλων) This proves the fear which we just noted.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

τὴν σπει̃ραν) Illam quae Paschatis diebus a praeside dari solebat Senatoribus ad servandam Urbis & Templi quie- tem. Vide quaead Matth. XXVI. 45. Hujus cohortis praefe- ctus χιλίαρχος mox vocatur v. 12. Neque tamen necesse est totam cohortem adfuisse, sed ejus partem.

καὶ ἐκ τω̃ν ἀρχιερέων καὶ Φαρισαίων ὑπηρέτας) ἐκ id est ab ipfis datos. Pontificum & Pharisaeorum nomine iterum Senatum describit, quod illi ob privata studia maxime Jesu adversarentur. ὑπηρέται כְּלֵי מִשְׁׁטָר de quibus dicto Matthaei loco. Aderat his ministris ὁ στρατηγός, ut ibidem notatum.

Adfuisse etiam nonnullos e Sacerdotibus & Senioribus, Lucas clare testatur cap. XXII. 52. Non ergo tantum milites Romani, gentiles, & mi- nistri Sacerdotum & Pharisaeorum, sed etiam

Pontifices & Seniores autoritatis causa, & ut diligentius negotium perageretur, adfuerunt: adeoque conspiraverunt adversus Dominum genti- les & Judæi, Ecclesiastici & Politici, heri & ser- vi, militares & alii, cum ipso Christi Apostolo Juda.

μετὰ φανῶν κὴ λαμπάδων) Ostendit Evangelista quanto ardore Christum quæsierint & metuerint ne elaberetur, qui plena luna, tamen & faces & laternas attulerint, ut o- mnes latebras perreptarent.

Addit & aliam causam Cyrillus: Metuebant, ne, ut in tenebris assolet, in lapides impingerent, aut in foveas caderent. Solent enim in tenebris talia fere accidere. Sed o dementiam! Non vi- dent miseri præ multa vecordia se in lapidem of- fendere, de quo Deus ac Pater infit: Ecce pono in Sion lapidem offensionis, & petram scan- dali: Et qui parvam foveam reformidant, in fontes abyssi, in terræ profunda ruere se non sen- tiunt, & qui serotinam obscuritatem aver- santur, perpetuam & æternam noctem non cu- rant.

καὶ ὅπλων) Hoc arguit eam quam modo notavimus for- midinem.

## 18:4
Vers. 4.

εἰδὼς πάντα τὰ ἐρχόμενα ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν) The Evangelist diligently notes both this and the following, to show that Christ came into the hands of his enemies not by powerlessness, but by his own will.

ἐξελθὼν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς, τίνα ζητεῖτε;) He comes forth voluntarily and offers himself. A similar account regarding Elisha is in Josephus, chapter VIII, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

εἰδὼς πάντα τὰ ἐρχόμενα ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν) Et hoc & sequentia diligenter annotat Evangelista, ut ostendat Christum non impotentia sed voluntate suapte in manus venisse inimico- rum.

ἐξελθὼν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς, τίνα ζητεῖτε;) Ultro prodit & se offert. Simile de Elisæo Josephus cap. VIII, 2.

## 18:5
Vers. 5.

ἀπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ· Ἰησοῦν τὸν Ναζωραῖον) They could not recognize him in such great light, being struck with blindness, as the citizens of Sodom once were in Gen. XIX, 11, which was a presage of the city that was to perish in a not dissimilar manner.

Chrysostom notes that the Lord blinded their eyes, because they had lanterns and could have recognized him by his voice, and even if others were ignorant, Judas could not have been ignorant, who had been with him continuously.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ἀπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ· Ἰησοῦν τὸν Ναζωραῖον) Tanta luce agno- scere eum non potuerunt, καταχθέντες ἐν ἀορασίᾳ, ut olim Sodomæ cives Gen. XIX, 11. quo præsagium fuit urbis non dissimilem in modum perituræ.

Chrysostomus excæcasse Dominum ipsorum oculos notat, quia habuere lampades, & è voce eum cognoscere poterant, ac si alii ignorarent, Judas ignorare nequiverit, qui cum ipso continue fuerat.

## 18:6
Vers. 6.

ἐγώ εἰμι) I am he, as we have explained this expression elsewhere.

ἀπῆλθον εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω κὴ ἔπεσον χαμαὶ) There happened to them immediately what David prays for against his enemies from God, Ps. XXXV. 4, let them be turned back, as the Greek version has it there. So also Isaiah XXIX. 15, let them fall backward. Moreover, the power of Jesus seems to be graphically expressed here, as if he had blown away his enemies with his breath alone, which is attributed to God, Job V. 8. See also Dan. X. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ἐγώ εἰμι) Ego is sum, ut alibi hanc locutionem expo- suimus.

ἀπῆλθον εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω κὴ ἔπεσον χαμαὶ) Evenit illis κατὰ πό- δας quod David adversus inimicos suos à Deo precatur, Ps. XXXV. 4. ἀποστραφήτωσαν εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω, ut ibi habet Græ- ca versio. Sic & Esaias XXIX. 15. πέσωσιν ὀπίσω. Videtur autem hic graphice exprimi Jesu potentia, quasi solo ha- litu suos inimicos difflasset, quod Deo tribuitur, Job. V. 8. Vide & Dan. X. 9.

## 18:7
Verse 7.

πάλιν ὖν αὐτὸς ἐπηρώτησε) Since they did not yet repent, though warned by that miracle. A mark of great stubbornness.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

πάλιν ὖν αὐτὸς ἐπηρώτησε) Cum isto miraculo moniti nondum resipiscerent. Magnæ contumaciæ character.

## 18:8
v. 8. εἰ ὖν ἐμὲ ζητεῖτε, ἄφετε τέτες ὑπάγειν) A specimen of a good king, solicitous not for himself but for his own: in which very thing David bore his type, 1 Chron. 21:17, and he shows his power, who commands this as if by his own right.

Latin:

v. 8. εἰ ὖν ἐμὲ ζητεῖτε, ἄφετε τέτες ὑπάγειν) Boni regis spe- cimen, non pro se sed pro suis solliciti: qua & ipsa in re Da- vid ejus typum gessit 1. Paral. XXI. 17. & potentiam suam ostendit qui hoc quasi jure suo imperat.

## 18:9
v. 9. ἵνα πληρωθῇ ὁ λόγος ὃν εἶπεν) Here it is manifest what we have often said, that in such citations of sayings the ἵνα is ecbatic, as also below in ch. 19:24.

ὅτι ὃς δέδωκάς μοι ἐκ ἀπώλεσα ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐδένα) ἀπώλεσα here, like ἀπολέσω above in chapter 6:38, is to cause to perish, in the way that those things which have the Hiphil form among the Hebrews are often to be interpreted, because the Syrian uses this form here. For the words which are repeated here have it thus above, κὴ ἐδεὶς ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀπώλετο, chapter 17:12. Christ wished, as we said there, to ensure with a certain singular care that, apart from one most impure person, no one should be withdrawn from the number of twelve of his witnesses: so that all the others might receive the promised Spirit and begin their office with fruit, and might see the growth of the kingdom of the Messiah.

Latin:

v. 9. ἵνα πληρωθῇ ὁ λόγος ὃν εἶπεν) Hic manifestum est quod sæpe diximus, talibus dictorum citationibus appositum ἵνα ἐκβατικὸν, ut & infra c. XIX. 24.

ὅτι ὃς δέδωκάς μοι ἐκ ἀπώλεσα ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐδένα) ἀπώλεσα hic ut ἀπολέσω supra cap. VI. 38. est fivi perire, quomodo sæ- pe interpretanda sunt ea quæ habent formam Hiphil apud Hebræos, quia forma hic Syrus utitur. Nam verba quæ hic repetuntur, supra fic habent, κὴ ἐδεὶς ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀπώλετο cap. XVII, 12. Voluit Christus ut ibi diximus singulari quadam cura præstare, ne duodenario testium suorum numero præter unum impurissimum quisquam subduceretur: ut cæteri omnes acciperent promissum Spiritum & munus suum cum fructu auspicarentur, viderentque incremen- ta regni Messiæ.

## 18:10
Verse 10.

ἔχων μάχαιραν) According to the custom of travelers in those places. We spoke on Luke 22:38. See the rest at Matthew.

ἦν δὲ ὄνομα τῷ δέλῳ Μάλχος) A frequent name among the Syrians: just as that philosopher was called in his native tongue, who called himself Porphyry in Greek. The Arabs also used it, as appears in Josephus.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ἔχων μάχαιραν) Pro more peregrinantium in iis lo- cis. Diximus ad Luc. XXII. 38. Cætera vide ad Mat- thæum.

ἦν δὲ ὄνομα τῷ δέλῳ Μάλχος) Nomen frequens apud Syrus: quomodo & patrio sermone vocabatur Philosophus is, qui se Græce Porphyrium dixit. Etiam Arabes usurpa- runt, ut apud Josephum apparet.

## 18:11
Verse 11.

Vers. 11. εἰς τὴν θήκην) See the note on Matthew. τὸ ποτήριον ὃ δέδωκέ μοι ὁ πατὴρ) See regarding this expression the note on Matthew XX. 22. ὐ μὴ πίω ἀυτὸ) Do you wish to prevent me from fulfilling what pleases the Father? See a not dissimilar passage, Matt. XVI. v. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Vers. 11. εἰς τὴν θήκην) Vide ad Matthæum. τὸ ποτήριον ὃ δέδωκέ μοι ὁ πατὴρ) Vide de hac locutione ad Matthæum XX. 22. ὐ μὴ πίω ἀυτὸ) Vin'tu prohibere quo minus impleam quod Patri placet. Vide locum non dissimilem, Matth. XVI. v. 23.

## 18:12
Vers. 12.

καὶ ὁ χιλίαρχος) It should have been translated 'prefect of the cohort': for thus the Latins call him whom the Greek writers of Latin history call χιλίαρχος, as Luke also does quite often in the Acts. A tribune, however, is he who is in charge of an entire legion. There were also χιλίαρχοι among the Jews, Num. XXXI. 14. and following, 1 Samuel XVIII. 13, 1 Chronicles XII. 20. But here it concerns him who was leading the Roman cohort. Therefore it follows aptly καὶ οἱ ὑπηρέται τῶν Ἰυδαίων.

καὶ ἔδησαν ἀυτὸν) Warned by Judas to lead him with great circumspection, because he was accustomed at times to slip away from the crowd unnoticed. See Mark XIV. 44.

PART II. The examination and passion of Jesus before the Sanhedrin with the threefold denial of Peter.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

καὶ ὁ χιλίαρχος) Vertendum fuit præfectus cohortis: ita enim Latini vocant quem Græci Latinæ historiæ scriptores χιλίαρχον, ut & Lucas in Actis sæpius. Tribunus vero est qui toti legioni præest. Erant & inter Judæos χιλίαρχοι, Num. XXXI. 14. & seqq. 1. Samuel. XIIX. 13. 1. Paral. XII. 20. Sed hic de eo agitur qui Romanam cohortem ducebat. Ideo apposite sequitur καὶ οἱ ὑπηρέται τῶν Ἰυδαίων.

καὶ ἔδησαν ἀυτὸν) Ab Juda moniti ut cum magna circumspectione eum ducerent, quod solitus esset interdum è turba inconspicuus elabi. Vide Marc. XIV. 44.

PARS II. Examen & passio Jesu coram Synedrio cum trina Petri abnegatione.

## 18:13
Vers. 13.

καὶ ἀπήγαγον ἀυτὸν πρὸς Ἄνναν πρῶτον) Because his house was nearby, and because he was of great authority with his son-in-law Caiaphas, they wanted to learn from him where and how Jesus should be led. See what we shall say below in v. 21.

ἦν γὰρ πενθερὸς τῶ Καιάφα) More advanced in age, joined by affinity, and through whose favor Caiaphas had received the High Priesthood.

Doubtless they wanted to provide some pleasure, ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, to the elder, primary in authority and recently High Priest, by presenting to him that captive who was believed to be a hater and destroyer of the pontifical dignity, so that he too might approve with his own vote the chains cast upon Christ. Chrysostom, hom. XXVIII, notes that they wanted to feed the eyes of the old father-in-law, since they were leading Jesus as if in a triumph, boasting of this matter as if of a trophy set up, as Euthymius has it.

ὃς ἦν ἀρχιερεὺς τῆ ἐνιαυτῶ ἐκείνου) Wherefore as often as ἀρχιερεὺς is said simply below, Caiaphas is to be understood, as also in Matthew and other writers. Why 'of that year' is added, was said above in chapter XI. 49. And when he had just said he was led first to Annas, he indicated tacitly enough that he was led from there to Caiaphas. Because some thought this was missing, they added it to the text, as we learn from Cyril, against all the codices and interpreters that now exist. Add that this is understood well enough from what is said below in v. 15. But then the codex which Cyril also used had other things added as well, as below in chapter XIX. v. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

καὶ ἀπήγαγον ἀυτὸν πρὸς Ἄνναν πρῶτον) Quod ejus domus in proximo esset, & quia is magnæ erat apud generum Cajapham auctoritatis, ex ipso discere voluerunt quonam & quomodo ducendus esset Jesus. Vide quæ infra dicemus v. 21.

ἦν γὰρ πενθερὸς τῶ Καιάφα) Provectior ætate, affinitate junctus, & cujus gratia Cajaphas Pontificatum acceperat.

Nimirum volebant Seni autoritate primario & nuper Pontifici etiam aliquam voluptatem, ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ creare, sistendo ei captivum illum, qui credebatur Pontificiæ dignitatis osor & eversor, ut ipse quoque calculo suo vincula in Christum conjecta comprobaret. Chrysostom. hom. XXVIII. notat, quod voluerint pascere soceri senis oculos, siquidem Jesum velut in triumphum ducebant, hac de re gloriantes, tanquam de trophæo instituto, ut habet Euthymius.

ὃς ἦν ἀρχιερεὺς τῆ ἐνιαυτῶ ἐκείνου) Quare quoties infra ἀρχιερεὺς simpliciter dicitur. Cajaphas est intelligendus, ut & apud Matthæum aliosque scriptores, Cur additum sit, ejus anni, dictum supra cap. XI. 49. Et cum modo dixisset primum ductum ad Annam, tacite satis indicavit, inde ductum ad Cajapham. Quod quum quidam deesse putarent, textui addiderunt, ut ex Cyrillo discimus, contra omnes qui nunc extant codices & interpretes. Adde quod satis hoc dictum intelligitur infra v. 15. Tum vero codex quo usus & Cyrillus alia quoque habebat afficta ut infra cap. XIX. v. 30.

## 18:14
Vers. 14.

ἦν δὲ Καιάφας ὁ συμβουλεύσας) He brings back to memory the saying of this Caiaphas mentioned in chapter 9, so that it may be understood from there how great was the hatred with which he was inflamed against Christ, as one who, with no other cause brought forward, under the pretext of public utility, and an imaginary one at that, dared to say that he should be put to death according to his opinion. Moreover, this pertains to diminishing the authority of the judgment held against Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

ἦν δὲ Καιάφας ὁ συμβουλεύσας) In memoriam reducit dictum hujus Cajaphæ memoratum capite 9. ut inde intelligatur quanto ille odio in Christum incensus fuerit, ut qui nulla alia prolata causa, prætextu utilitatis publicæ, & quidem imaginario, interficiendum eum pro sententia ausus esset dicere. Pertinet autem hoc ad elevandam judicii in Christum habiti auctoritatem.

## 18:15
Vers. 15.

καὶ ὁ ἄλλ@ μαθητής) It is certain that in other books as well as in these the article often abounds, which sense the Syrian also followed here, translating: One of the other disciples, and indeed it is not probable that John himself is understood here (for why, being a Galilean, would he be questioned less by those standing by than Peter?) or any one of the twelve, but some other Jerusalemite, not an equally manifest supporter of Jesus, such as many were in the city, as we learned above in ch. XII. 42. The conjecture of those who think this is the man in whose house Christ had dined, because of what is read in Matt. XXVI. 18, approves itself greatly to me.

ἦν γνωστὸς τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ) Inasmuch as he was a citizen of that city: not a Galilean.

Chrysostomus sane, Cyrillus, Theophylactus, Nicephorus, Lyranus, B. Brentius & others say it was John: But it is not likely that he, after three years of instruction in the School of Christ, would have fostered familiarity with the High Priest, the sworn enemy of Christ. We leave the conjecture of Grotius in its own place: and with August. tr. CXIII. in Joh. we profess that who this disciple is, must not be rashly asserted, because it is passed over in silence.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

καὶ ὁ ἄλλ@ μαθητής) Certum est & in aliis & in his libris sæpe abundare articulum, quem sensum & hic secutus est Syrus, vertens: Vnus ex discipulis aliis, & sane non est probabile aut ipsum Johannem hic intelligi) cur enim Galilæus cum esset minus interrogaretur ab adstantibus quam Petrus?) aut aliquem ex duodecim, sed alium quendam Hierosolymitanum, non æque manifestum fautorem Jesu, quales multi erant in urbe, ut supra didicimus c. XII. 42. Valde mihi se probat conjectura existimantium hunc esse eum, in cujus domo Christus cænaverat, ob id quod legitur Matth. XXVI. 18.

ἦν γνωστὸς τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ) Quippe civis ejus urbis: non Galilæus.

Chrysostomus sane, Cyrillus, Theophylactus, Nicephorus, Lyranus, B. Brentius & alii dicunt Johannem fuisse: Sed eum post triennalem in Schola Christi informationem familiaritatem cum Pontifice jurato Christi hoste aluisse non est verisimile. Conjecturam Grotii suo relinquimus loco: & cum August. tr. CXIII. in Joh. profi- temur, quisnam sit iste discipulus, non temere affir- mandum est, quia tacetur.

## 18:16
Vers. 16.

τῇ θυρωρῷ) It was the custom for the Hebrews to use women as doorkeepers, 2 Sam. IV. 16, in the Greek ἡ θυρωρὸς τὸ οἶκον ἐκάθαιρε πυροῦς.

κὴ εἰσήγαγε τὸν Πέτρον) The doorkeeper herself. For the sense is concise. He said to the doorkeeper that she should allow Peter to enter: which she did.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

τῇ θυρωρῷ) Mos erat Hebræis, etiam feminis uti janitricibus, 2. Sam. IV. 16. in Græco ἡ θυρωρὸς τὸ οἶκον ἐκά- θαιρε πυροῦς.

κὴ εἰσήγαγε τὸν Πέτρον) Ipsa janitrix. Est enim sensus concisus. Dixit ille janitrici, ut intrare pateretur Petrum: quod illa fecit.

## 18:17
Vers. 17.

μὴ κὶ σὺ) Of one affirming among the Hebrews. See what is in Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

μὴ κὶ σὺ) Affirmantis apud Hebræos. Vide quæ apud Matthæum.

## 18:18
Vers. 18.

οἱ δῦλοι) The private servants of the house.

κὴ οἱ ὑπηρέται) Public ministers.

ἀνθρακιὰν πεποιηκότες) A pile of coals for kindling a bright fire. See Mark.

ψύχος ἧν) As on a night in early spring.

ἑστὼς) Sometimes standing, sometimes sitting, uncertain what he should do, what posture he should assume.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

οἱ δῦλοι) Privata domus servitia.

κὴ οἱ ὑπηρέται) Ministri publici.

ἀνθρακιὰν πεποιηκότες) Struem carbonum ad excitan- dum ignem luculentum. Vide Marcum.

ψύχος ἧν) Ut nocte primi veris.

ἑστὼς) Interdum stans, interdum sedens, incertus quid ageret, quem habitum præferret.

## 18:19
Vers. 19.

περὶ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτῦ) Why he gathered disciples and specifically the twelve of the first admission.

κὴ περὶ τῆς διδαχῆς αὐτῦ) What that was, tacitly indicating it to be factious and seditious.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

περὶ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτῦ) Cur discipulos colligeret & nominatim duodecim primæ admissionis.

κὴ περὶ τῆς διδαχῆς αὐτῦ) Quænam ea esset, tacite in- dicans esse factiosam & seditiosam.

## 18:20
Vers. 20.

ἐγὼ παῥῥησίᾳ ἐλάλησα τῷ κόσμῳ) παῥῥησία is openly, as several times above. Openly, he says, before all who wished to hear I taught, which those who stir up seditions do not do.

πάντοτε ἐδίδαξα) As often as any opportunity presented itself.

ὅπε πάντες οἱ Ἰαδαῖοι) Commonly, and here it is πάντοτε, repeated, if I am not mistaken, from the passage above. But the Syrian, Arab, and Latin read πάντες.

κὴ ἐν κρυπτῷ ἐλάλησα ὐδὲν) That is, I took no pains to conceal anything. I taught nothing at home other than what I taught in public, which is a sign of great confidence.

The same words, which were used in Isaiah 45:19, testify that it is the same person who speaks in the Prophet and who speaks here. See the things said at Isaiah in the cited place. Into memory, says Cyril, as it seems, he recalls, even against the will of the leaders of the Jews, that prophecy which the divine Isaiah brought forth as if under the person of Christ: I have not spoken in secret, etc.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ἐγὼ παῥῥησίᾳ ἐλάλησα τῷ κόσμῳ) παῥῥησία est palam, ut supra aliquoties. Palam, inquit, coram omnibus, qui audire vellent docui, quod non faciunt seditionum con- citatores.

πάντοτε ἐδίδαξα) Quoties ulla se dedit occasio.

ὅπε πάντες οἱ Ἰαδαῖοι) Vulgo & hic est πάντοτε, repetitum, ni fallor, ex loco superiore. At πάντες legerunt Syrus, Arabs, Latinus.

κὴ ἐν κρυπτῷ ἐλάλησα ὐδὲν) Id est nihil studui celare. Non aliud domi docui, quam in publico, quod signum est magnæ fiduciæ.

Verba eadem, quæ adhibita Esa. XLV. 19. te- stantur, eandem esse personam, quæ apud Pro- phetam, & quæ hic loquitur. Vide ad Esa. dicta l. c. In memoriam, inquit Cyrillus, ut videtur, vel invitis revocat Judæorum principibus prophetiam illam, quam divinus Esaias tanquam sub per- sona Christi prodidit: Non locutus sum in abscon- dito, &c.

## 18:21
Verse 21.

Why do you ask me? As if he were to say: You have already stirred up the Synagogue against those who believe in me: you have already decreed that I should be captured, and you have not yet inquired into my doctrines; but now at last do you wish to learn them from me? What kind of way of acting is this?

Ask those who have heard. The law commands this, to begin with witnesses: especially where many are available, as here. The Pharisees had heard him so many times.

Behold, these know what I have said. Your own attendants know well what kind of things I have taught: you know what they have reported to you. See chapter 7:46.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

τί με ἐπερωτᾷς) Quasi dicat: Jam Synagoga movistis qui mihi credunt: jam me decrevistis capiendum, & non- dum inquisivistis in mea dogmata; sed nunc demum ex me ea vultis discere? Quis hic mos agendi?

ἐπερώτησον τὺς ἀκηκοότας) Hoc jubet lex, à testibus inci- pi: præsertim ubi multi suppetunt, ut hic. Audierant eum toties Pharisæi.

ἴδε, ὗτοι οἴδασιν ἃ ἔιπον ἐγώ) Ipsi vestri satellites satis no- runt qualia docuerim: scitis quid vobis retulerint. Vide c. VII. 46.

## 18:22
Verse 22.

One of the attendants. Fearing that he himself might be considered a supporter of the accused.

A blow. See what [is said] at Matthew 26:67. This Syrian struck him on the cheek. Those who flatter tyrants are accustomed to do so. See the history in 1 Kings 22:24, where it is similarly in the Hebrew: He struck on the cheek. Josephus says in that place, you will strike.

We add the reasons why the Lord wished to be struck in such a way, from Cyril: That indeed was also predicted by the voice of the Prophet as something that would happen concerning Christ, I gave my back, he says, to the scourges, and my cheeks to the blows: which, having been predicted long ago, is now brought to fulfillment for the condemnation of Jewish pride and the abolition of the ignominy due to us, since we sinned in the first Adam, having trampled upon the divine command. For he sustains the ignominy for us, inasmuch as he himself bears our sins, according to the voice of the Prophet, and suffers for us. For just as by his body being handed over to death he destroyed death, so he wiped away the ignominy [due] to us on account of the transgression and that original sin by the blow inflicted upon Christ through ignominy. For one, as a representative of all, underwent the ignominy for all.

οὕτως ἀπεκρίθη τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ) As he did in Acts XXIII. 4, who said to Paul, 'Do you revile God's high priest?' Reverence is indeed owed to magistrates, but not such as would take away from the accused the freedom to defend themselves.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

἗ις τῶν ὑπηρετῶν) Metuens ne & ipse pro fautore rei ha- beretur.

ῥάπισμα) Vide quæ ad Matth. XXVI. 67. Percussit super maxillam Syrus hic. Sic solent facere, qui Tyrannis adu- lantur. Vide historiam 1. Reg. XXII. 24. ubi est similiter in Hebræo: Percussit super maxillam. ῥαπίσεις ait eo loco Josephus.

Addimus causas, cur percuti ita voluerit Do- minus, è Cyrillo: Istud quidem voce Prophetæ prædictum etiam est tanquam de Christo futurum, dorsum meum dedi, inquit, ad flagella, & genas meas ad alapas: quod olim prædictum, nunc in condemnationem superbiæ Judaicæ, & abolitionem ignominiæ nobis debitæ ad exitum perducitur, quip- pe qui in Adam primo peccavimus, concultato mandato divino. Pro nobis enim sustinet ignomi- niam, quandoquidem ipse peccata nostra portat, juxta Prophetæ vocem, & pro nobis dolet. Quem- admodum enim corpore suo morti tradito mortem destruxit, sic ignominiam nobis propter prævari- cationem & primigenium illud peccatum alapa delevit Christo per ignominiam inflicta. Unus enim instar omnium pro omnibus ignominiam subiit.

οὕτως ἀπεκρίθη τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ) Ut ille Act. XXIII. 4. qui Pau- lo dicebat τὸν ἀρχιερέα τοῦ Θεοῦ λοιδορεῖς. Debetur quidem Magistratibus reverentia, sed non quæ reis se tuendi liber- tatem tollat.

## 18:23
Vers. 23.

εἰ κακῶς ἐλάλησα) If I have spoken anything too contumeliously against the Pontiff. Thus 'you shall not speak evil,' Acts XXIII. 5, as also in the Greek of Exodus XXII. 28.

μαρτύρησον περὶ τοῦ κακοῦ) Show that I have sinned against that law of Exodus. Μαρτυρεῖν means to speak openly, as above in ch. XIII. 21. The Lord could say this confidently, for while He did indeed defend Himself, which was lawful and becoming, yet 'when He was reviled, He did not revile in return; when He suffered, He did not threaten.'

εἰ δὲ καλῶς, τί με δέρεις) Those who are under the power of just judges are also under their protection against all violence outside the court, and they ought to be defended by the ministers of the judges in this matter, not violated. And the things which follow shortly regarding Pilate's examination tacitly show, as the Acts of the Apostles often do, that the Romans were more equitable than the Jews, and consequently that it happened by the just judgment of God that they were subject to the Romans.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

εἰ κακῶς ἐλάλησα) Si quid dixi contumeliosius in Pon- tificem. Sic ἐκ ἐρεῖς κακῶς, Actorum XXIII. 5. ut & in Græco Exod. XXII. 28.

μαρτύρησον περὶ τοῦ κακοῦ) Ostende me in legem illam Exo- di peccasse. Μαρτυρεῖν est palam dicere, ut supra c. XIII. 21. fidenter hoc dicere poterat Dominus qui defendit se qui- dem, quod licebat & decebat: sed λοιδορύμενος οὐκ ἀντελοι- δόρει, πάσχων οὐκ ἠπείλει.

εἰ δὲ καλῶς, τί με δέρεις) Qui in æquorum judicum sunt potestate, iidem & in eorum tutela sunt contra vim omnem extra judicium, & a ministris judicum in hoc defendi, non violari debent. Et quæ mox sequuntur de Pilati cognitio- ne, tacite ostendunt, ut & Acta Apostolorum sæpe, Roma- nos Judæis fuisse æquiores, ac proinde justo Dei judicio ac- cidisse, ut Romanis parerent.

## 18:24
Vers. 24.

ἀπέστειλεν αὐτὸν) The 'oun' is absent from most codices, and more correctly so, I think. But to untie the knot that is usually tied here, translate 'apesteilen' as 'had sent,' just as 'edesen' in Matthew XIV. 3 means 'had bound,' where I have also brought forward other examples. Thus 'ekratese' in Mark VI. 17. Thus also a little below, 'ha apekopse ho Petros to otion,' where the Latin correctly says, 'whose ear Peter had cut off.' But why John should have inserted here what he had omitted earlier in its proper place, we shall understand only if we place the accent of emphasis not on the word 'apesteilen,' but on the word 'dedemenon.' For John, about to narrate Peter's second fall, puts forward the cause: that Peter now saw Jesus remaining bound, which John notes in passing had been done by the order of Annas himself, a grave prejudice against the accused, whereas before that time it could have been ascribed to the imprudence of the guards. This, therefore, took away from Peter all hope of a fair hearing.

We do not disapprove of this explanation of the hysteron proteron. It must certainly not be conceded, as some who cannot find the cause of the recapitulation imagine, that the transposition of this verse was made by the carelessness of a scribe. Blessed Gerhard, however, brings forward another reason in his Harmony on the Passion, ch. VI, p. 62, which can be joined with this one: He had said, he says, in the preceding verses, that a blow had been inflicted upon Christ by the minister of the Pontiff; in order, therefore, to express more fully the atrocity and indignity of this deed, he added, 'Annas had sent him bound [dedemenon], tied and constricted, to Caiaphas,' as if to say, Christ stood before the judgment bound with those chains which Annas had ordered to be placed upon him to his prejudice; most indignantly, therefore, was he treated with that shameful striking of the cheek.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ἀπέστειλεν αὐτὸν) ὖν abest a plerisque codicibus, & rectius ut opinor. Sed ut nodum solvas, qui hic necti solet, ἀπέστειλεν verte miserat, ut ἔδησεν Matth. XIV. 3. vinxerat: ubi & alia attulimus exempla. Sic ἐκράτησε Marc. VI. 17. Sic & paulo infra ἆ ἀπέκοψε ὁ Πέτρος τὸ ὠτίον, ubi Latinus recte, cujus absciderat Petrus auriculam. Cur au- tem hoc, quod ante suo loco omiserat Johannes hic inse- ruerit, ita demum intelligemus, si accentum ἐμφάσεως indi- cem, posuerimus non in voce ἀπέστειλεν, sed in voce δεδεμένον. Narraturus enim Johannes secundum Petri lapsum, causam præmittit, quod Petrus jam Jesum videret manere vin- ctum, quod Johannes notat obiter, factum fuisse ipsius An- næ jussu, gravi in reum præjudicio, cum ante id tempus sa- tellitum imprudentiæ id potuisset adscribi. Hoc igitur Pe- tro omnem spem æquæ cognitionis ademit.

Non improbamus hanc rationem hysterolo- gias. Concedendum utique non est, quod non- nulli causam non invenientes ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως fingunt incuria scribæ transpositionem hujus ver- siculi factam esse. Aliam tamen rationem adfert B. Gerhardus Harmon. in Passion. cap. VI. p. 62. quæ cum ista conjungi potest: Dixerat, inquit, in præcedentibus, alapam a ministro Pontificis esse Christo inflictam; ut igitur facti hujus atrocitatem & indignitatem magis exprimeret, subjunxit, An- nas miserat eum vinctum δεδεμένον ligatum & con- strictum ad Cajapham, quasi dicat, stabat Christus coram judicio constrictus illis vinculis, quæ An- nas in præjudicium ipsi injicere mandaverat in- dignissime igitur cum ipso actum fuit ignominio- sa ista maxillæ percussione.

## 18:25
Vers. 25. ἱστὼς) See what is above in v. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἱστὼς) Vide quæ supra v. 18.

## 18:26
Vers. 26. ἐκ ἐγώ σε εἶδον ἐν κήπῳ) Just as the cause of the second fall was given just now, so now the cause of the third is given: that he felt himself greatly pressured by the mention of the garden, and feared that he might be held guilty of violated authority.

PARS III. The Accusation and Examination of Jesus in the praetorium.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ἐκ ἐγώ σε εἶδον ἐν κήπῳ) Ut modo secundi, ita nunc tertii lapsus causa affertur, quod valde sentiret se pre- mi memoratione horti, & metueret ne violatæ potesta- tis reus ageretur.

PARS III. Accusatio & Examen Jesu in prætorio.

## 18:28
Vers. 28.

Ἄγωσιν) Impersonally, that is, Jesus is led: he is led around through many tribunals, so that his innocence may be the more noted.

ἀπὸ τῦ Καϊάφα) From his house. Thus Mark 5:35, ἀπὸ τῦ ἀρχισυναγώγου. See above ch. 15:26.

into the praetorium) See Matt. XXVII. 27.

ἦν δὲ πρωῒ) Not even this is added in vain. For the extreme haste of the Senators is shown. It was customary to judge after the third hour. They wanted the judgment to be finished before that time, lest, with the Sabbath imminent, something should happen by which the accused might escape.

ἐκ εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον, ἵνα μὴ μιανθῶσιν) Since they could not avoid every conversation with foreigners, they had tempered the matter so that on holy days and days preparatory to holy things, it was not permitted to approach them privately, but they could address them publicly if any business pressed: which was a contrivance of frivolous superstition. Peter also in the Acts of the Apostles first addresses those sent by Cornelius before the doors, and does not bring them into the house until it is known that they are those about whom he had been forewarned by God, Acts 10:21, 22, 23. Others, however, think that the Jews did not enter the praetorium for this reason: lest they should seem to be participants in the condemnation, for it was not permitted to eat holy things immediately after a condemnation, as noted by Maimonides.

Cyril here detests, as is fitting, the hypocrisy of the Jews: They persuade themselves, he says, that stones and the bodies of men of the same kind can defile a man’s soul, yet they think that the foulest of all evils, namely most unjust slaughter, brings no harm upon them at all. And what is more wonderful, or rather more insane than all else, they are not defiled by the slaughter of the lamb, which expresses to us nothing other than a shadow of the mystery of Christ, and while they honor the type of the thing, they undermine the truth itself. For while they pretend to be purified by the lamb, they are defiled by the slaughter of Christ. It does not appear, therefore, why Casaubon should have tortured himself in his notes, as if the sequence of the discourse seemed to demand absolutely that whatever is narrated before verse 24 should be understood as having all taken place at the house of Annas, when verse 15 openly contradicts this, and then verse 18, when compared with 25, clearly argues that the first denial occurred in the same place as the second. Since it is said that he was led first to Annas, the word first indicates that he did not remain there, but was then led elsewhere. To where? That is indicated when it is added that he entered into the hall of the high priest, and since that was not Annas, but Caiaphas, it appears sufficiently that he was led from Annas to Caiaphas. Because that, however, had not been stated openly, but could be gathered from verse 15 and following, it is indicated openly by the particle therefore in verse 24. He had therefore been sent bound from Annas to Caiaphas. That sequence seems to me far more suitable than if, with the renowned Beza following Cyril, the same thing is said to be stated twice. For if in verse 13 it is openly said that Annas sent Christ bound to Caiaphas, what need was there to gather the same thing again through οὖν and state it openly in verse 24? But if we say that it was indicated earlier, and then openly gathered from a more obscure narrative, everything fits correctly, as Lud. de Dieu holds here.

ἀλλ’ ἵνα φάγωσι τὸ πάσχα) Namely, undefiled, without prejudice to their religion; and note τὸ πάσχα regarding those things which we said at Matt. 26:2 and 17.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

Ἄγωσιν) Impersonaliter, id est ducitur Jesus: circumdu- citur per multa tribunalia, quo magis innocentia ejus in- notescat.

ἀπὸ τῦ Καϊάφα) Ab ejus ædibus. Sic Marc. V. 35. ἀπὸ τῦ ἀρχισυναγώγου. Vide supra c. XV. 26.

εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον) Vide Matth. XXVII. 27.

ἦν δὲ πρωῒ) Ne hoc quidem frustra additum. Ostenditur enim summa Senatorum festinatio. Judicari solebat post nonam. Ante id tempus volebant peragi judicium, ne imminente Sabbato aliquid accideret, quo reus elabere- tur.

ἐκ εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον, ἵνα μὴ μιανθῶσιν) Cum non possent omne cum alienigenis colloquium vitare, ita rem temperaverant, ut diebus sacris & præparato- riis ad sacra, eos privatim accedere non liceret, sed publice, si quod urgeret negotium alloqui eos possent: quod com- mentum erat frivolæ superstitionis. Petrus quoque in Actis Apostolicis a Cornelio missos primum pro foribus alloqui- tur, nec in ædes introducit, nisi cognito eos esse, de quibus a Deo erat præmonitus Actorum X. 21. 22. 23. Alii vero existimant, ideo Judæos prætorium non ingressos; ne damnationis participes viderentur, nam statim a da- mnatione sacris vesci non licebat, ut notatum Maimo- nidæ.

Cyrillus detestatur hic, ut par est, hypocrisin Ju- dæorum: Lapides, inquit, & ejusdem generis ho- minum corpora inquinare posse hominis animam sibi persuadent: fœdissimum vero malorum o- mnium, injustissimam nempe cædem nihil pror- sus sibi noxæ putant affingere.
