Et quod mirabi- lius, immo vero cæteris omnibus insanius est, non polluuntur ob agni cædem, qui nihil aliud quam mysterii Christi nobis umbram exprimit, & cum rei typum honorent, ipsam veritatem labe- factant. Nam cum ob agnum lustrari se fingant, Christi cæde inquinantur. Non ergo apparet, cur se torserit Casaubonus in notis, quasi omni- no postulare videatur series orationis, ut quæ- cunque ante versum 24. narrantur, ea intelli- gantur omnia gesta esse apud Annam, quum aperte repugnet vers. 15. deinde v. 18. collatus cum 25. clare arguat, eodem in loco conti- gisse primam negationem, in quo secunda. Quum dicatur reductus primum ad Annam, vox primum indicat ibi non mansisse, sed alio deinde deductum. Quo? indicatur id, quum subjicitur, eum intrasse in aulam summi Sacer- dotis, qui quum non fuerit Annas, sed Caja- phas; satis apparet, eum ab Anna ad Caja- pham deductum. Quia id tamen aperte non fuerat dictum, sed ex vers. 15. & deinceps col- ligi poterat, indicatur aperte per particulam igitur v. 24. Fuerat igitur missus ab Anna ad Cajapham vinctus. Ea sequela mihi longe con- venientior videtur, quam si cum Cl. Beza ex Cyrillo idem bis dicatur. Si enim vers. 13. aper- te dicitur, Annam misisse Christum vinctum ad Cajapham, quid opus erat idem rursus per ἐν col- ligere & aperte dicere vers. 24.? Sed si id prius in- dicatum, deinde ex obscuriori narratione aperte col- lectum dicamus, omnia recte conveniunt, ut hic ha- bet Lud. de Dieu.

ἀλλ’ ἵνα φάγωσι τὸ πάσχα) Scilicet impolluti salva reli- gione; & nota τὸ πάσχα ad ea quæ diximus Matth. XXVI. 2. & 17.

## 18:29
Vers. 29.

ἐξῆλθεν ὖν Πιλάτος πρὸς αὐτὺς) Not as superstitious as they, but more observant of justice, and in this respect better. For all these things have their own importance; he went out, however, into the stadium where he was accustomed to place the tribunal.

τίνα κατηγορίαν) He calls the charge a crime; what crime do you bring that drives you here at an unusual time?

Latin:

Vers. 29.

ἐξῆλθεν ὖν Πιλάτος πρὸς αὐτὺς) Non tam superstitiosus ut illi, sed æqui observantior, & hoc melior. Omnia enim hæc suum habent momentum; exiit autem in stadium ubi tribunal ponere solebat.

τίνα κατηγορίαν) κατηγορίαν vocat crimen; quod crimen adfertis quod vos alieno tempore huc adigit?

## 18:30
Vers. 30.

If this man were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up to you) See the iniquity. What was lacking in proofs they wish to supply by their own authority. At the same time, it is credible that they brought forward some things concerning the Sabbath and the like.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

εἰ μὴ ἦν ὗτος κακοποιὸς, ὐκ ἄν σοι παρεδώκαμεν αὐτόν) Vi- de iniquitatem. Quod probationibus deerat id suppleri volunt sua autoritate. Simul ut credibile est aliqua attu- lerunt de Sabbato & similia.

## 18:31
Vers. 31.

Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law) Instead of kill: for up to this point their power had remained intact after Judea was reduced to a province. See Matt. X, 17. 2 Cor. XI, 24.

It is not lawful for us to put any man to death) They tacitly imply that Jesus is held for such great crimes that they must be atoned for by death entirely. But that was not within their power. For if any were ever killed by the Jews, it was done by a popular uprising, although sometimes a certain prejudice had preceded it, with the Sanhedrin declaring them guilty. See what is at Matt. V, v. 22.

They do not seem here to have generally professed a lack of power and jurisdiction, which they call criminal and absolute authority: But to have excepted the punishment of the cross, to which they wanted Jesus to be subjected as a seditious person, with the cognizance of this case, which concerned the public state, devolved to the Roman governor. For as a blasphemer he could indeed be subjected to capital punishment by the Jews, but that of stoning. Which sense seems to shine forth from the immediately annexed cause:

It is not permitted for us to kill anyone: that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spoke, signifying by what death he was to die, namely, by the solemn punishment of the cross of the Romans or Gentiles, John 18:32. Which the blessed Gerhard teaches in this place, the blessed Hülsemann in the Harmony of Paul and James, chapter 140, and the Bishop of Norwich in Origines Ecclesiasticae, part 1, latter section, 388.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

λάβετε αὐτὸν ὑμεῖς κὲ κατὰ τὸν νόμον ὑμῶν κρίνετε αὐτόν) Lo- co cædite: nam hucusque potestas illis salva permanserat post Judæam in provinciam redactam. Vide Matth. X, 17. 2. Cor. XI. 24.

ἡμῖν ὐκ ἔξεστιν ἀποκτεῖναι ἐδένα) Tacite innuunt Jesum tantorum criminum teneri ut omnino morte luenda sint. Id autem non erat ipsorum potestatis. Nam si qui aliquan- do à Judæis sunt interfecti, id factum est motu populari, quanquam interdum præjudicium quoddam præcesserat Senatus eos reos declarantis. Vide quæ ad Matth. V. v. 22.

Non videntur hic generatim defectum pote- statis & jurisdictionis, quam criminationem, & meri imperii vocant, professi: Sed excepisse de supplicio crucis, cui tanquam seditiosum vole- bant subjici Jesum, cognitione hujus causæ, quæ statum publicum concernebat, ad Romanum præsidem devoluta. Tanquam blasphemus e- nim poterat à Judæis quidem supplicio affici capitali, sed lapidationis. Qui sensus elu- cere videtur ex immediata subnexa causa:

Non licet nobis occidere quenquam: ut sermo Jesu impleretur, quem dixit, significans, qua morte esset moriturus, crucis scil. Romanis seu Gentibus solemni supplicio, Joh. XII. 37. Quod do- cet B. Gerhardus in h. l. B. Hülsemannus Harm. Pauli & Jacobi c. CXL. Et Norvicensis Episcopus Orig. Ecclesiast. 1. part. poster. 388.

## 18:32
Verse 32.

ἵνα) It was done so that what Jesus had said might be fulfilled.

σημαίνων ποίῳ θανάτῳ ἤμελλεν ἀποθνήσκειν) Not by popular sedition, but what was worse, by the sentence of a Gentile man whom they themselves abhorred: but by a sentence extorted by the Jews. See Matthew 20:19 and chapter 26:45. The very kind of punishment by which Christ had indicated he was to be affected. Above chapter 3:14, chapter 12:32. Roman, not Jewish.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

ἵνα) Ita factum est ut impleretur quod Jesus dixe- rat.

σημαίνων ποίῳ θανάτῳ ἤμελλεν ἀποθνήσκειν) Non seditio- ne populari, sed quod pejus erat, sententia hominis genti- lis quem ipsi abominabantur: sed sententia à Judæis, extor- ta. Vide Matth. XX. 19. & c. XXVI. 45. Ipsum supplicii ge- nus quo se afficiendum Christus indicaverat. Supra c. III. 14. c. XII. 32. Romanum non Judaicum.

## 18:33
Verse 33.

εἰσῆλθεν ἓν εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον πάλιν) πάλιν here does not refer to the act of entering (for that was not repeated) but to the place where he had been before he went out. We had a similar way of speaking above in chapter 6:15, chapter 10:17. The Syriac, because this particle was redundant, omitted it. But Pilate entered into the praetorium, that he might interrogate the accused more freely.

σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων) For those delegated by the Sanhedrin had burdened him with this crime in particular: which the other Evangelists narrate. Are you, he says, that king whom the Jews have long promised themselves would come? Or do you proclaim yourself to be him?

Latin:

Vers. 33.

εἰσῆλθεν ἓν εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον πάλιν) πάλιν hic non ad actum intrandi refertur (is enim repetitus non est) sed ad locum ubi fuerat antequam exiret. Simile loquendi genus habuimus supra c. VI. 15. c. X. 17. Syrus quod abundaret hæc particula eam amisit. Intravit autem in prætorium Pilatus, ut reum liberius interrogaret.

σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων) Nam delegati à Synedrio hoc præcipue crimine eum oneraverant: quod alii Evange- listæ narrant. Tune, inquit, es rex ille, quem Judæi jam- pridem venturum sibi pollicentur? aut eum te esse præ- dicas?

## 18:34
Verse 34.

ἀφ' ἑαυτῦ σὺ τῦτο λέγεις ἢ ἄλλοι σοι εἶπον περὶ ἐμῦ) You have acted as governor for so many years now, and you guard the majesty of the Roman Empire not negligently; has anything been discovered by you that would make me suspected of disturbing the empire? But if nothing such has been discovered by you, but others have suggested this, see that you are not deceived by the ambiguity of the word. Thus he prudently wishes to elicit from the governor that which prepares a way for his own further response.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

ἀφ' ἑαυτῦ σὺ τῦτο λέγεις ἢ ἄλλοι σοι εἶπον περὶ ἐμῦ) Tot jam annis præsidem agis, & Imperii Romani majestatem non negligenter tutaris, compertumne est tibi aliquid quod me imperii turbati suspectum faceret? Quod si nihil tibi tale compertum est, sed alii hoc suggesserunt, vide ne vocis am- biguo fallaris. Ita prudenter ex præside id vult elicere, quod ipsi ad ulteriorem responsionem viam paret.

## 18:35
Verse 35.

μήτι ἐγὼ Ἰουδαῖός εἰμι) Can I know what the Jews hope for from their books, or what they promise themselves?

τὸ ἔθνος τὸ σὸν) Your countrymen, as the Syriac here.

καὶ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς παρέδωκάν σε ἐμοί) Exposition of that which preceded: nay, the chief priests themselves, the leaders of the people, understanding these matters, brought you here having already judged you themselves.

τί ἐποίησας) By what deed did you offend them so gravely? This also gives Christ an opportunity to respond.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

μήτι ἐγὼ Ἰουδαῖός εἰμι) Egone scire possum quid Judæi ex suis libris sperent, aut sibi promittant?

τὸ ἔθνος τὸ σὸν) Populares tui, ut hic Syrus.

καὶ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς παρέδωκάν σε ἐμοί) Expositio ejus quod præcesserat: imo ipsi Pontifices proceres populi, istarum rerum intelligentes, te huc adduxerunt à se præjudica- tum.

τί ἐποίησας) Quo facto eos tam graviter offendisti? Hoc quoque Christo occasionem dat respondendi.

## 18:36
Vers. 36.

ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμὴ ὀυκ ἔςιν ἐκ τῶ κόσμου τούτου) The kingdom promised by the Prophets which I claim for myself does not harm the state of the Roman Empire: for it is not of a worldly nature; in which sense that phrase ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου was also used above, ch. VIII. 23, ch. XV. 19. The difference is that there it concerns the vicious morals of the world, here it concerns that power which those who are called kings in the common sense use everywhere. He says the same thing shortly after with ἐντεῦθεν. It is narrated in Eusebius that the relatives of Jesus, when asked by Domitian about his kingdom, replied: that his kingdom is not worldly nor earthly, but happens to be heavenly and angelic.

οἱ ὑπηρέται ἂν οἱ ἐμοὶ ἠγωνίζοντο) If I had aspired to such a kingdom as it concerns you to guard against, I would have gathered for myself armed guards, as is the custom for those who attempt such things. Now I had a few disciples, and most of them unarmed; what are they against such a great force of enemies? And I forbade even these to fight.

ἵνα μὴ παραδοθῶ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις) I would have exhorted my men, as Emperors are wont to do, to fight bravely for me, so that I would not fall into the power of my enemies, in which sense παραδῦναι is used, Matt. IV. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμὴ ὀυκ ἔςιν ἐκ τῶ κόσμου τούτου) Regnum à Prophetis promissum quod mihi vendico, statum Imperii Romani non lædit: non est enim indolis mundanæ; quo serme sensu illa locutio ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου & supra usurpata est c. IIX. 23. c. XV. 19. Hoc interest quod ibi de moribus vitiosis mundi agitur, hic de potestate illa qua ubique utuntur qui reges appellantur sensu vulgari. Idem mox dicit ἐντεῦθεν. Narrantur apud Eusebium Jesu cognati rogati de ipsius re- gno respondisse Domitiano: ὡς ἡ ἀυτῦ βασιλεία ὀυ κοσμικὴ μὲν ὀυδὲ ἐπίγειος, ἐπεράνιος δὲ καὶ ἀγγελικὴ τυγχάνει.

οἱ ὑπηρέται ἂν οἱ ἐμοὶ ἠγωνίζοντο) Si tale regnum affectas- sem, quale cavere ad te pertinet, collegissem mihi stipato- tes armatos ut solent, qui talia conantur. Nunc paucos ha- bui discipulos, & plerosque inermes, quid ad tantam vim inimicorum? & hos ipsos pugnare vetui.

ἵνα μὴ παραδοθῶ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις) Hortatus essem meos ut Imperatores solent, ut pro me fortiter dimicarent, ne in potestatem venirem inimicorum, quo sensu παραδῦναι usurpatur, Matth. IV. 12.

## 18:37
Vers. 37.

ὀυκ ὖν βασιλεὺς εἶ σύ) מרון Syriac, that is, Therefore. Since you distinguish concerning the kingdom, therefore you claim some kingdom for yourself.

σὺ λέγεις) You say it correctly. A Hebraism. I am a king in a certain sense. Pilate's interrogation tacitly posited this. Christ did not wish to simply abdicate the title of king, lest he seem to alienate from himself those famous prophecies about the coming king. This is that καλὴ ὁμολογία, 1 Tim. VI. 13.

ἐγὼ εἰς τῦτο γεγέννημαι) Those who claim a kingdom for themselves are accustomed to say that they were born with that right; Christ also shows himself born for this, that he might reign, Luke I. 32.

καὶ εἰς τῦτο ἐλήλυθα εἰς τὸν κόσμον) For this I showed myself and made myself known to men, above ch. III. 17, 19, ch. IX. 39, ch. XI. 27.

ἵνα μαρτυρήσω τῇ ἀληθείᾳ) Understand: and in this very thing my kingdom is situated; it is not coercive, but persuasive. Concerning the phrase, see v. 33.

The phrases to be born and to come into the world explain each other mutually, namely that Christ was born, so that whereas he was before with the Father Joh. I. 1. in time by being born he came into the world, sent by the Father into the world, Joh. III. 16. See what we have said concerning the προϋπάρξει of the Son of God. Cyril says that he came into the world when he was made man, that he might bear witness to the truth.

πᾶς ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς ἀληθείας) Those who are of a truth-loving disposition. Thus Rom. II. 8. τοῖς ἐξ ἐριθείας, those who are of a contentious disposition. See also above c. IIX. 47.

ἀκούει με τῆς φωνῆς) These obey me as their king of their own accord, compelled by no force. See above chapter X. On the contrary, it is given to be understood that men who are lovers of falsehood (such as the Jews were; above c. IIX. 49) are of a mind alienated from him, nor is it a wonder if he is accused by such, since truth among such people breeds hatred.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

ὀυκ ὖν βασιλεὺς εἶ σύ) מרון Syrus, id est Ergo. Quando- quidem distinguis de regno, aliquod ergo regnum tibi vindicas.

σὺ λέγεις) Recte dicis. Hebraismus. Rex sum certo sensu. Interrogatio Pilati tacite hoc ponebat. Noluit Christus simpliciter à se abdicare regis titulum, ne videretur præclara illa de venturo rege vaticinia à se alienare. Hæc illa καλὴ ὁμολογία, I. Tim. VI. 13.

ἐγὼ εἰς τῦτο γεγέννημαι) Solent, qui regnum sibi vindi- cant, dicere se cum eo jure natos; Christus quoque se osten- dit natum in hoc ut regnaret, Luc. I, 32.

καὶ εἰς τῦτο ἐλήλυθα εἰς τὸν κόσμον) In hoc me ostendi & no- tum feci hominibus, supra c. III. 17. 19. c. IX. 39. c. XI. 27.

ἵνα μαρτυρήσω τῇ ἀληθείᾳ) Subaudi & in hoc ipso situm est regnum meum, non est coactivum, sed persuasivum. De locutione vide v. 33.

Phrases nasci & venire in mundum sese mu- tuo explicant, quod nempe natus Christus sit, ita ut quum antea fuerit apud Patrem Joh. I. 1. in tem- pore nascendo in mundum venerit, a Patre in mundum missus, Joh.an. III. 16. Vide, quæ de προϋ- πάρξει Filii Dei diximus. Cyrillus, Se in mundum venisse, ait, cum factus est homo, ut testimonium perhiberet veritati.

πᾶς ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς ἀληθείας) Qui ingenio sunt veri amante. Sic Rom. II. 8. τοῖς ἐξ ἐριθείας, his qui ingenio sunt conten- tioso. Vide & supra c. IIX. 47.

ἀκούει με τῆς φωνῆς) Hi mihi tanquam regi sua sponte, vi nulla coacti, obediunt. Vide supra cap. X. Ex contrario dat intelligi homines falsi amantes (quales erant Judæi; su- pra c. IIX. 49) alieno a se esse animo, neque mirum, si à talibus accusetur, cum veritas apud tales odium pariat.

## 18:38
Vers. 38. λέγει ἀυτῷ ὁ Πιλάτος, τί ἐστι ἀλήθεια) From Jesus' answer Pilate conceived that the kingdom which Jesus attributed to himself was no more harmful to the Roman empire than that which the Stoics attribute to their wise man. Incidentally, however, he asks of what kind that truth is of which he professes himself to be a Master: but in such a way that he does not insist, as if it were a matter pertaining in no way to the office of a Judge.

πρὸς τοὺς Ἰυδαίυς) To the Chief Priests, with the crowd of the people standing by.

ὀὐδεμίαν αἰτίαν ἐυρίσκω ἐν αὐτῷ) αἰτία here, as often among the Greeks, is a crime. Thus also below chapter XIX. 4. & 6. Thus αἰτία θανάτυ, Acts XIII. 28. a capital crime. The sense is much the same as that which is attributed to Gallio, Acts XVIII. 15. I see indeed that there is some controversy among you, but of such a kind that it is concerned with disputations, which is not for forensic examination: it is not here ἀδίκημα ἢ ῥαδιούργημα.

Latin:

Vers. 38. λέγει ἀυτῷ ὁ Πιλάτος, τί ἐστι ἀλήθεια) Ex Jesu responso Pilatus concepit regnum quod Jesus sibi tribue- ret, non magis imperio Romano obesse quam id quod Stoici sapienti suo tribuunt. Obiter autem quærit, cujus generis sit illa veritas cujus se Magistrum profiteatur: sed ita ut non instet, quasi de re ad Judicis officium nihil per- tinente.

πρὸς τοὺς Ἰυδαίυς) Ad Pontifices, adstante corona po- puli.

ὀὐδεμίαν αἰτίαν ἐυρίσκω ἐν αὐτῷ) αἰτία hic ut sæpe apud Græcos est crimen. Sic & infra cap. XIX. 4. & 6. Sic αἰτία θανάτυ, Actor. XIII. 28. crimen capitale. Sensus est ferme similis ei qui Gallioni tribuitur, Actor. XIIX. 15. Video qui- dem aliquid esse inter vos controversiæ, sed ejus generis, quæ in disputationibus versetur, quæ non sit forensis cogni- tionis: non est hic ἀδίκημα ἡ ῥαδιόργημα.

## 18:39
Vers. 39. ἔστι δὲ συνήθεια ὑμῖν) A custom introduced for your sake. See what [we said] on Matthew.

τὸν βασιλέα τῶν Ἰυδαίων) Contemptuously, as if he were to say, if any of you deem such men worthy of a royal title, we at Rome do not care about that, it pertains nothing to us, we allow you these dreams.

Latin:

Vers. 39. ἔστι δὲ συνήθεια ὑμῖν) Consuetudo in vestri gra- tiam introducta. Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

τὸν βασιλέα τῶν Ἰυδαίων) Contemtim, quasi dicat, si qui vestrum tales homines regio titulo dignantur, nos Ro- mam id non curamus, nihil ad nos id pertinet, permitti- mus vobis hæc somnia.

## 18:40
v. 40. λῃσής) That is, a murderer, as in Acts III. 14. The ringleader of a bloody sedition.

Latin:

v. 40. λῃσής) Id est φονεὺς, ut Actor. III. 14. Caput cru- entæ seditionis.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Jesus is scourged, and a crown of thorns having been placed upon him, clothed in purple he is mocked and struck, yet Pilate testified again concerning his innocence. But the priests crying out, crucify, crucify, and Pilate for the third time bearing witness to his innocence, and they pronouncing that he himself deserved death because he made himself the Son of God, Pilate undertakes a new examination in the praetorium, asking whence he is, and no answer being received, he sets forth to him his own power, both to crucify him and to release him, but being informed that he would have received it not unless from above, and that he is guilty of a greater sin by whom he was delivered, he asks, whom should he release? But the Jews pretending the crime of sedition against Caesar, he ascends the tribunal again, and when the Jews cried out that he must be crucified, [and that] they had no king but Caesar, he condemned him that he should be crucified. He who was led to the place of Golgotha and crucified, in the midst of two thieves, with this inscription placed upon the cross, Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudæorum, in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages, his garments being divided among the soldiers, as also the seamless tunic distributed by lot, according to the Scripture (Psal. XXII. 19.), Jesus commends John to Mary as a son, and Mary to John as a mother, from the cross, concerning his thirst he complains, so that the Scripture (Ps. LXIX. 23.) may be fulfilled, and exclaiming, It is finished, with head bowed he expires. But when the soldiers were breaking the legs of the two thieves, they did not break the legs of Jesus, but one of them pierced his side with a lance, from which blood and water flowed out, so that the Scripture (Exod. XII. 46. Zach. XII. 10.) may be fulfilled. But Joseph of Arimathea obtained the body of Jesus from Pilate, which was buried by him, and Nicodemus bringing spices, after the manner of the Jews, in a new tomb.

There are two parts: I. The continuation of the history of the passion and death of Christ, to which belongs the scourging, the mockery, the accusation concerning blasphemy as well as sedition, and the condemnation to the cross, as also the crucifixion, and what was done concerning it by Pilate and the soldiers, the inscription of the cross, and the division of the garments, then the commendation of John and his mother by Jesus, the complaint about thirst, the exclamation about the completion of all things, and the bowing of the head to expiration, then finally by a certain soldier, who pierced the side of Jesus with a lance, to v. 37. II. The burial of Jesus, to v. 42.

PART II. Continuation of the History of the passion of Christ.

Ver. 1.

Τότε οὖν) Since Pilate profited nothing by that device concerning the feast day. ἐμασίγωσε) As if for the sake of holding an examination, with the intention meanwhile of satisfying the anger of the people, as has been noted at Matthew.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Iesus flagellatur, & corona spineà imposita, purpura indutus illuditur ac percutitur, te- status tamen iterum Pilatus est de innocen- tia ejus. Sacerdotibus autem clamantibus, crucifige, crucifige, tertiumque Pilato in- nocentia ejus testimonium perhibente, illis etiam mortem ipsum meritum esse, quod se Filium Dei fecerit, pronunciantibus, Pila- tus novum examen in prætorio suscipit, quræens undenam sit, nulloque responso ac- cepto, potestatem suam, ipsum & crucifi- gendi & dimittendi ei exponit, sed infor- matus, quod non nisi superne eam accepe- rit, majoris autem culpareus sit is, à quo traditus sit, quærit, quem ipsum dimitte- ret? Iudæis autem seditionis crimen adver- sus Cæsarem prætextentibus, denuo tribu- nal conscendit, & quum clamarent Iudæi ipsum crucifigendum esse, se nullum habe- re regem nisi Cæsarem, condemnavit eum ut crucifigeretur. Qui in locum Golga- tha ductus crucifixus est, in medio duo- rum latronum, inscriptione hac Iesus Na- zarenus Rex Iudæorum cruce imposita lin- gua Ebræa, Græca & Latina, vestibus ejus inter milites divisis, ut & tunica inconsutili per sortem distributa, juxta Scripturam (Psal. XXII. 19.) Iesus Mariæ Iohannem ceu filium, Iohanni Mariam, ceu matrem è cruce commendat, de siti sua queritur, ut Scriptura (Ps. LXIX. 23.) im- pleatur, & exclamans, Consummatum est, capite inclinato expirat. Quum vero mili- tes duobus latronibus crura frangerent, Ie- su tamen non fregerunt crura, sed quidam eorum lancea transfixit latus, unde sanguis & aqua effluxit, ut Scriptura (Exod. XII. 46. Zach. XII. 10.) impleatur. Ioseph vero Arimatheus a Pilato corpus Iesu impetra- vit, quod ab ipso, & Nicodemo adferente aromata, more Iudaeorum, in novo monu- mento conditum.

Partes sunt duæ: I. Continuatio historiæ passionis & mortis Christi, ad quam pertinet flagellatio, illusio, de blasphemia ut & de seditione accusatio, & ad crucem condemnatio, nec non crucifixio, & quæ circa eam gesta sunt à Pilato & militibus, in- scriptio crucis, & vestium divisio, tum à Jesu com- mendatio Johannis & matris, querela de siti, ex- clamatio de omnium consummatione, & inclina- tio capitis ad expirationem, tum denique à milite quodam, qui lancea transfixit latus Jesu, ad v. 37. II. Jesu sepultura, ad v. 42.

PARS II. Continuatio Historiæ passionis Christi.

Vers. 1.

Τότε οὖν) Cum nihil proficeret Pilatus isto commento de die festo. ἐμασίγωσε) Tanquam quæstionis habendæ gratia, con- silio interim satiandi iram populi, ut ad Matthæum est an- notatum.

## 19:2
Ver. 2.

ἱμάτιον πορφυρῦν) Others [call it] a scarlet cloak, the Syrian here ܐܫܒܘܢܐ which corresponds to the Hebrew אַרְגָּמָן which the Greeks were accustomed to translate as πορφύραν. Moreover, the color is either the same as that which is called תולע & שׁני and is translated by the Greeks as κόκκινον, or certainly very close, so that the teachers of the Hebrews interpret both as crimson. And in Isaiah I. 18, where in Greek it is ὡς φοινικοῦν, the Latin version has as scarlet; however, the word ἱμάτιον here has a general meaning, not that special one of a mantle.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ἱμάτιον πορφυρῦν) Chlamydem coccineam alii, Syrus hic ܐܫܒܘܢܐ quod respondet Hebræo אַרְגָּמָן quod πορφύραν vertere solebant Græci. Est autem color aut idem qui תולע & שׁני dicitur & Græcis κόκκινον vertitur, aut sane proximus, ita ut Hebræorum magistri utrumque interpretentur per cramosinum. Et Esaæ I. 18. ubi Græce est ὡς φοινικοῦν, Latina versio habet ut coccinum; ἱμάτιον au- tem vox hic generalem habet notionem, non illam spe- cialem pallii.

## 19:3
Ver. 3. ῥαπίσματα) Blows. See above. Ver. 4. οὐδεμίαν αἰτίαν) That is, not even the slightest thing for which he should have been beaten with scourges. Thus he condemns himself of iniquity, who, complying with the angry people, had granted the punishment of an innocent man.

Latin:

Vers. 3. ῥαπίσματα) Alapas. Vide supra. Vers. 4. οὐδεμίαν αἰτίαν) Id est ne tantillum quidem ob quod flagris cædi debuerit. Ita ipse se iniquitatis damnat, qui populo irato obsequens donaverat pœnam hominis in- nocentis.

## 19:5
Ver. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

## 19:6
ἰδὲ ὁ ἄνθρωπος) See his misery and how ridiculous the charge of affected kingship is in him. See below v. 14.

Ver. 6.

οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ ὑπηρέται) From whom the beginning was made [and] flowed into the people. ἐκραύγασαν) See what [is said] at Matthew. λάβετε αὐτὸν ὑμεῖς καὶ σταυρώσατε) As if he were saying: Do this yourselves if you wish at your own risk, it is not for me to condemn an innocent man. He does not grant the right, but prefers that the crime be another's rather than his own.

Latin:

ἰδὲ ὁ ἄνθρωπος) Videte ejus miseriam & quam ridicu- lum sit in ipso crimen regni affectati. Vide infra v. 14.

Vers. 6.

οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ ὑπηρέται) A quibus initium factum in populum manavit. ἐκραύγασαν) Vide quæ ad Matthæum. λάβετε αὐτὸν ὑμεῖς καὶ σταυρώσατε) Quasi dicat. Vos hoc si libet facite vestro periculo, meum non est damnare in- sontem. Non jus concedit, sed mavult alienum quam suum esse crimen.

## 19:7
Verse 7.

ἡμεῖς νόμον ἔχομεν) Since they could not persuade him of a crime against the Roman empire, they urge their own law, namely that one concerning false prophets, Deut. XIII. 20. ὅτι ἑαυτὸν υἱὸν Θεοῦ ἐποίησας) Son of God, that is, the Messiah, as we noted above c. I. 49, c. X. 36, and at Matth. XXVI. 63. If he who calls himself a prophet when he is not must die, much more must he die who calls himself the Messiah when he is not, since the Messiah must be both a prophet and more than a prophet. See above c. IV. 25. He made himself, that is, he feigned himself to be him. So also above c. V. 18, c. VIII. 53, c. X. 33, and presently 12. Beware of admitting here that Son of God and Messiah are the same. For although the Messiah is none other than the Son of God himself, so that they are materially the same, formally, however, they are not the same, because Son is the name of a person, designating generation from the Father, while Messiah is the name of an office, designating anointing for an office.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

ἡμεῖς νόμον ἔχομεν) Cum non persuaderent crimen ad- versus imperium Romanum, legem suam urgent, nempe illam de Pseudoprophetis Deut. XIII. 20. ὅτι ἑαυτὸν υἱὸν Θεοῦ ἐποίησας) υἱὸν Θεοῦ, id est Messiam ut notavimus supra c. I. 49. c. X. 36. & ad Matth. XXVI. 63. Si mori debet qui prophetam se dicit, cum non sit, mori mul- to magis debet qui Messiam se dicit, cum non sit, cum Mes- sias & Propheta esse debeat, & plusquam Propheta. Vide supra c. IV. 25. Se fecit, id est se eum esse finxit. Sic & supra c. V. 18. c. IIX. 53. c. X. 33. & mox 12. Cave hîc idem esse Filium Dei & Messiam ad- mittas. Nam etsi Messias alius non sit, quam ipse Dei Filius, ut hæc idem omnino sit materialiter, formaliter tamen non idem sunt, quia Filius no- men est personæ, generationem à Patre designans, Messias nomen Officii, unctionem ad officium designans.

## 19:8
Verse 8. μᾶλλον ἐφοβήθη) Fearing, because of the wonderful things heard about him, that perhaps it might be true that he had originated by divine decree, just as

the Romans and Greeks believed concerning their heroes. See what we said at Matth. XXVII. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 8. μᾶλλον ἐφοβήθη) Metuens ob res miras de eo auditas ne forte verum esset ortum eum divino fatu, sicut

Romani & Græci de heroibus suis credebant. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXVII. 14.

## 19:9
Verse 9.

εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον πάλιν) About to institute a new interrogation because of a new accusation.

πόθεν εἶ σύ) That is, from where are you sprung? See what we said above c. VII. 27.

ἀπόκρισιν οὐκ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ) Having followed what he himself had commanded, that pearls should not be cast before swine. See what is at Matthew XXVI. 63. Nothing fair could be expected from him who had ordered him to be scourged for the sake of an angry mob, whom he knew and confessed to be innocent. Nor could Pilate understand what the force of the Hebrew expression, Son of God, was. But indeed, Jesus had already said enough before, when he had professed himself born for this, that he might be king of those who love the truth. Above c. XVIII. 37.

He answered concerning the kingdom, so that he might resolve the suspicion of affected rule, and free Pilate from fear, as Euthymius notes: To this question, however, he answers nothing, both for the stated reasons, and because he had to be silent like a sheep according to the prophetic prophecy, and because he was not there to defend himself, but to be condemned, as Chrysostom has it, homil. XCVII. in Matth.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον πάλιν) Novæ accusationis causa novam instituturus interrogationem.

πόθεν εἶ σύ) Id est, unde ortus? Vide quæ diximus supra c. VII. 27.

ἀπόκρισιν οὐκ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ) Secutus quod ipse præceperat, margaritæ porcis objicerentur. Vide quæ ad Matthæum XXVI. 63. Nihil æqui exspectari poterat ab eo, qui verberari in gratiam plebis iratæ jusserat eum, quem noverat & fatebatur innocentem. Nęc intelligere poterat Pilatus, quæ esset vis Hebraicæ locutionis, filius Dei. Tum vero, quantum satis est, jam ante dixerat Jesus, cum se professus erat in hoc natum, ut rex esse amantium veritatem. Supra c. XIIX. 37.

De regno respondit, ut solveret affectati regiminis suspicionem, metuque Pilatum liberaret, notante Euthymio: Ad hoc quæsitum vero nihil respondet, tum ob dictas causas, tum quia sicut ovis tacere debuit secundum vaticinium Propheticum, tum quia non ibi erat, ut se defenderet, sed ut condemnaretur, ut habet Chrysostom. homil. XCVII. in Matth.

## 19:10
Verse 10.

ὅτι ἐξουσίαν ἔχω σταυρῶσαι) ἐξουσία here is not right properly, but such an efficacy that it easily gives effect to what it wants, whether just or unjust, as above c. X. 18. Thus Eccl. IX. 18, you shall be delivered from a man who has the power to kill. In this sense Cicero used the word to be allowed in his speech for Rabirius, addressing the judges: For if you ask what is allowed, you can remove from the state whom you wish.

ἀπολῦσαί σε) Of dismissing unpunished, as above c. XVIII. 39. Pilate, little mindful of his duty, boasts of what he can do: and condemns himself, who so powerfully and servilely humors the raging mob.

Hear, says Ambrose, sermon XX on Elijah 118, what the Judge of iniquity says: I have power to crucify you, and I have power to absolve you. An evil power to allow what harms, that power is the power of darkness. A good judge does nothing out of whim and the purpose of a private will, but pronounces according to law and rights; he obeys the decrees of the law, he does not indulge his own will.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

ὅτι ἐξουσίαν ἔχω σταυρῶσαι) ἐξουσία hic est non jus proprie, sed efficacia talis, quæ quod vult æquum aut iniquum facile effectum dat, ut supra c. X. 18. Sic Eccl. IX. 18. ἄνσῃς ἀπὸ ἀνθρώπου ὃς ἐξουσίαν ἔχει τοῦ φονεύειν. Hoc sensu vocem licere usurpavit Cicero pro Rabirio. Judices alloquens: Si enim quod liceat quæritis, potestis tollere è civitate quem vultis

ἀπολῦσαί σε) Impunitum dimittendi, ut supra c. XIIX. 39. Pilatus parum memor officii, quid valeat, jactat: & se damnat, qui tam potens plebi furenti serviliter morem gerit.

Audite, inquit Ambros. sermon. XX. in El. CXVIII. quid Judex iniquitatis loquatur: Potestatem habeo crucifigendi te, & potestatem habeo absolvendi te. Mala potestas licere quod noceat, potestas illa potestas tenebrarum est. Bonus Judex nihil ex arbitrio facit, & domesticæ proposito voluntatis, sed juxta legem & jura pronunciat, scitis juris obtemperat, propriæ voluntati non indulget.

## 19:11
Verse 11.

You would have no such power or authority, which you boast of over me; I would easily escape it, as I have previously escaped many traps and seditions.

From there, clearly, whence I have arisen, for he indicates this tacitly: ἄνωθεν is from heaven, מעלה, John 3:4, which is also translated as from on high, Job 31:2; thus above, ch. 3:31, James 1:17, ch. 3:15, 17. But when he says it was given from the places above, he does not signify that common permission which leaves many things to the natural order, but a matter deliberated for most grave reasons in the divine counsel, which had removed all impediments from every side. In this way Pilate has now obtained power over Jesus. Thus he both indicates his own dignity and admonishes Pilate to modesty. See Luke ch. 22, v. 53.

This is a reference to something that is left unsaid, but which can easily be understood from what has been said. Therefore, because I am such a one, for whom God takes such special care, which the Jews can know from the prophecies, you cannot know equally, nor are you equally bound.

Singular for plural, whoever he is, who delivered me to you: those who were the cause why I should be led to you as a criminal: Judas especially, in the second place the Senate, in the third the people.

You are not without guilt, you who not only do not defend an innocent man, but burden him: but you sin less, because it is not as easy for you to know against whom you sin. The quality of the one to whom the injury is inflicted, when known or able to be known, increases the atrocity of the injury. Christ condemns the opinion that holds sins to be equal, as also Luke 12:48, Matthew 10:15.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

οὐκ εἶχες ἐξουσίαν οὐδεμίαν κατ' ἐμοῦ) Non haberes talem potentiam sive facultatem, quam jactas in me; facile eam evaderem, ut antehac insidias & seditiones multas.

εἰ μὴ ἦν σοι δεδομένον ἄνωθεν) Inde scilicet unde ortus sum, tacite enim hoc indicat: ἄνωθεν est ex cælo מעלה Joh. III. 4. quod & ἐξ ὑψίστου vertitur Job. XXXI. 2. sic supra c. III. 31. Jac. I. 17. c III. 15. 17. Cum autem dicit datum è locis superis, non illam communem significat permissio- nem quæ multa relinquit ordini naturali, sed ex gravissimis causis deliberatam rem in consilio divino: quæ omnia impedimenta undique amoverat. Hæc modo nactus est Pilatus potentiam in Jesum. Ita & suam indicat dignitatem & Pilatum modestiæ admonet. Vide Lucam cap. XXII. v. 53.

διὰ τοῦτο) Relatio est ad aliquid quod subticetur, sed quod facile ex dictis intelligi potest. Ideo quia talis sum, cujus curam tam peculiarem gerat Deus, quod scilicet Judæi ex vaticiniis scire possunt, tu non æque potes, nec æque teneris.

ὁ παραδιδούς με σοι) Singulare pro plurali, quisquis is, qui me tibi tradidit: qui causa fuerunt cur ut reus ad te duceret: Judas præcipue, secundo loco Senatus, tertio populus.

μείζονα ἁμαρτίαν ἔχει) Non cares tu culpa qui innocentem non modo non defendis, sed oneras: sed minus delinquis, quia tibi non tam promtum est nosse in quem delinquas. Atrocitatem injuriæ auget cognita aut cognosci quita qualitas ejus cui infertur. Damnat Christus sententiam quæ peccata statuit paria, ut & Luc. XII. 48. Matth. X. 15.

## 19:12
Verse 12.

From which he felt his conscience convicted of sin. For this reason, the Syriac, as also above in chapter 6:66.

Take it in the sense as above in verse 10. He was seeking pretexts by which he might favorably release him.

Οὐκ εἶ φίλος τοῦ Καίσαρος.) You are not a friend of Caesar, that is, you show yourself not to be faithful to Caesar, as εἶναι is often taken for to be shown.

πᾶς ὁ βασιλέα ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν) Whoever in the Roman provinces asserts himself to be king, without the order of the Emperor.

Ἀντιλέγει τῷ Καίσαρι) Ἀντιλέγειν here, as also in Luke 2:34, is to oppose. For to the Hebrews, to say is often to do or to plot. He claims for himself the role of the Roman Emperor, who wishes to reign without his authority.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

ἐκ τούτου) Ex quo conscientiam suam peccati convictam sentiebat. Propter hoc Syrus, ut & supra cap. VI. 66.

ἀπολῦσαι) Sume sensu quo supra commate 10. Quærebat obtentus quibus eum favorabiliter dimitteret.

Οὐκ εἶ φίλος τοῦ Καίσαρος.) Non es amicus Cæsaris, id est ostendis te non esse fidum Cæsari, ut sæpe εἶναι sumitur pro ostendi.

πᾶς ὁ βασιλέα ἑαυτὸν ποιῶν) Quicunque in provinciis Romanis regem se asserit, injussu Imperatoris.

Ἀντιλέγει τῷ Καίσαρι) Ἀντιλέγειν hic ut & Luc. II. 34. est repugnare. Nam Hebræis dicere sæpe est facere aut moliri. Partes Imperatoris Romani sibi vindicat, qui sine ejus auctoritate vult regnare.

## 19:13
Vers. 13.

Ἀκούσας τοῦτον τὸν λόγον) Tiberius was most suspicious, and under him the smallest things came under the charge of high treason, as is most evident from Tacitus and Suetonius. Before such a master, an accusation of any kind brought danger to a provincial: yielding to whose fear, Pilate, just like Caiaphas, prefers to act unjustly rather than to suffer: which is truly the character of those who manage the state.

ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος.) In the Xystus or covered stadium. See what [we said] regarding Matthew.

Λιθόστρωτον) For a similar reason the forum at Constantinople was called πλακωτὸν, because, as Zonaras says to Constantine, it was paved with stone slabs.

Ἑβραϊστὶ δὲ Γαββαθᾶ) By Ἑβραϊστὶ understand the language of that time; it signifies βῆμα, a high place, such as were the tribunals of the Romans. The Syrians often change ת into D. Therefore here גפיפתא. It was the custom of the Roman governors not to pronounce judgment except from the tribunal, which place is also called the law.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Ἀκούσας τοῦτον τὸν λόγον) Suspiciofissimus erat Tyberius, & sub illo minima quæque veniebant in crimen majestatis, ut ex Tacito & Suetonio apertissimum est. Apud talem Dominum qualiscunque provincialem accusatio afferebat periculum: cujus timori succumbens Pilatus, plane ut Cajaphas, injuste agere quam pati mavult: quod vere est ingenium eorum qui rempublicam tractant.

ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος.) In Xysto sive stadio tecto. Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

Λιθόστρωτον) Pari de causa forum Constantinopoli dictum πλακωτὸν, quia nimirum, ut Zonaras Constantino loquitur κατέστρωτο λιθίναις πλαξί.

Ἑβραϊστὶ δὲ Γαββαθᾶ) Ἑβραϊστὶ intellige sermone ejus temporis, significat βῆμα, locum excelsum, qualia erant Romanorum tribunalia. Syri sæpe ת mutant in D. Ideo hic גפיפתא. Mos erat Romanorum præsidum non pronuntiare nisi pro tribunali, qui locus & jus dicitur.

## 19:14
Vers. 14.

ἦν δὲ παρασκευὴ τοῦ πάσχα) And at the same time the day before the Sabbath, Mark 15:40. See what [we said] regarding Matthew. It signifies that the matter was directed in such a way not without the special providence of God, since the death of Christ was truly a preparation for our passage into a better life.

ὥρα δὲ ὡσεὶ ἕκτη) That is, at the time of צהרים when the sun shines most brightly. It is not signified that it was precisely noon, but that part of the day which is between the morning בקר and the evening ערב. See what [we said] regarding Matthew. ὡσεὶ is accustomed, both among others and among our own writers, to have some latitude.

De his etiam vide, quæ in Anti-Grotianis ad Matthæum diximus. Nolumus τὸ πρᾶχθεν πράττειν.

Ἴδε ὁ βασιλεὺς ὑμῶν) He reproaches them because so many among them were so foolish as to have held such a man for a king.

Others more correctly wish to refer to the congratulatory exception made upon his entry into the city in Matthew XXI: as if to say, Do you now dare to demand for crucifixion him whom you accepted as King four days ago?

Latin:

Vers. 14.

ἦν δὲ παρασκευὴ τοῦ πάσχα) Et simul προσάββατον, Marci XV.40. Vide quæ ad Matthæum. Significat non sine speciali Dei providentia rem ita directam, quandoquidem & Christi mors vere erat præparatio ad transitum nostrum in vitam meliorem.

ὥρα δὲ ὡσεὶ ἕκτη) Id est tempore צהרים cum Sol maxime fulget. Non significatur præcise fuisse meridies, sed illa pars diei quæ inter mane בקר & ערב vesperam. Vide quæ ad Matthæum. Solet ὡσεὶ & apud alios & apud nostros scriptores nonnihil habere latitudinis.

De his etiam vide, quæ in Anti-Grotianis ad Matthæum diximus. Nolumus τὸ πρᾶχθεν πράττειν.

Ἴδε ὁ βασιλεὺς ὑμῶν) Exprobrat illis quod tam stulti multi inter ipsos fuerint, qui talem hominem pro rege habuerint.

Rectius alii respici volunt ad exceptionem gratulatoriam sub ingressum in urbem Matth. XXI. factam: q. d. Num eum, quem ut Regem accepistis ante quatriduum, jam ad crucifixionem deposcere audetis?

## 19:15
Vers. 15.

ἆρον, ἆρον,) See what [is said] at Matthew.

οὐκ ἔχομεν βασιλέα, εἰ μὴ Καίσαρα) We have, that is, we acknowledge. It was the custom of the Greeks and Hellenists to call him whom the Romans called Emperor a king: because the power would be similar. With God thus directing matters and words, the Jews both renounce their hope concerning the Messiah and condemn themselves for rebellion on account of the wars stirred up afterwards. Anger has such power that they often say things that harm them the most. They were accustomed to say, we have no King but God: which is in the Talmud.

Rightly therefore Cyril: While other nations scattered throughout the whole world cling tenaciously to their error, and constantly worship those whom they have persuaded themselves are gods, and do not easily fall away from them, nor transfer themselves to other cults: Israel nevertheless recoiled, enslaving itself to the rule of Caesar, and stripped off the kingdom of God. And therefore it was quite justly handed over to the hands of Caesar, and when it had received power at the beginning, it perished badly itself, and with the region overturned, it endured the evils of war and the most grievous calamities.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

ἆρον, ἆρον,) Vide quæ ad Matth.

οὐκ ἔχομεν βασιλέα, εἰ μὴ Καίσαρα) ἔχομεν, id est, agnoscimus. Mos erat Græcorum & Hellenistarum, quem Romani vocabant Imperatorem, appellare βασιλέα: quia potestas erit similis. Deo ita res & verba dirigente Judæi & spem de Messia abdicant, & se ob bella postea excitata rebellionis damnant. Tantum potest ira, ut sæpe dicantur, quæ maxime nocent. Solebant dicere, non habemus Regem nisi Deum: quod est in Thalmude.

Recte ergo Cyrillus: Quum cæteræ gentes per universum terrarum orbem sparsæ errori suo mordicus inhæreant, & constanter colant, quos sibi persuascrint esse Deos, nec ab iis facile deficiant, nec ad alios cultus se transferant: resiliit tamen Israël, Cæsaris imperio seipsum mancipans, & Dei regnum exuit. Ideoque juste admodum Cæsaris traditus est manibus, & cum potestatem initio suscepisset, male ipse periit, & eversa regione belli mala gravissimasque calamitates sustinuit.

## 19:16
Vers. 16.

παρέδωκεν ἀυτὸν ἀυτοῖς) He does not hand him over into their hands: for he was handed over to the soldiers according to Roman custom: but he granted him to their hatred, ἐχαρίσατο Acts XXV. 11. 16.

παρέλαβον δὲ) That is, he was received. For the nominative is understood, those who received, whose duty it was, namely the soldiers.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

παρέδωκεν ἀυτὸν ἀυτοῖς) Non in manus tradit: Nam traditus est militibus ex more Romano: sed largitus est ipsum illorum odio, ἐχαρίσατο Act XXV. 11. 16.

παρέλαβον δὲ) Id est acceptus est. Nam subauditur Nominativus οἱ παραλαβόντες, quorum id erat officium, milites scilicet.

## 19:17
Vers. 17.

ἐξῆλθεν) Outside the city, as in Matthew XXVII. 32. concerning the rest see what [is said] in that place.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ἐξῆλθεν) Extra urbem, ut Matth. XXVII. 32. de cæteris vide quæ eo loco.

## 19:19
Vers. 19.

τίτλον) τίτλος, a small tablet having an inscription, according to Hesychius. Suetonius uses the Latin word in this sense. The Syrian and Arab did not poorly call it a tablet. To the Hebrews it is לוח.

Beautiful are the things which Cyril has here: We were cursed, and condemned by divine judgment, both on account of the transgression in Adam, and the transgression of the law established after him. But this handwriting which was against us, the Savior blotted out, by affixing to his cross the title, by which he clearly signified his death on the cross, which he endured for the life of all the condemned, for he indeed paid the penalties owed for sins for us. For although one was suffering, he was nevertheless above every creature as God, and more valuable than the life of all. Therefore, as the Psalmist says, all iniquity has stopped its mouth, and the tongue of sin is in a way obstructed, no longer able to accuse sinners.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

τίτλον) τίτλος, πτυχίον ἐπίγραμμα ἔχον Hesychio. Latinam vocem hoc sensu usurpat Suetonius. Tabulam non male dixerunt Syrus & Arabs. Hebræis est לוח.

Pulchra sunt, quæ hic habet Cyrillus: Era- mus maledicti, ac divino calculo condemnati, cum propter prævaricationem in Adam, tum prævari- cationem legis post eum constitutæ. Verum hoc, quod adversus nos erat, chirographum Servator de- levit, affixo suæ cruci titulo, quo liquido mortem in cruce suam significabat, quam pro damnatorum universorum vita pertulit, pro nobis quippe exol- vit pœnas peccatis debitas. Etsi enim patiebatur u- nus, erat tamen supra creaturam omnem ut Deus, & universorum vita potior. Idcirco, ut ait Psalmi- sta, omnis iniquitas oppilavit os suum, & lingua pec- cati quodammodo obstructa est, non jam peccatores incusare potis.

## 19:20
Verse 20.

ἐγγὺς ἦν ὁ τόπος τῆς πόλεως) In the suburb, as places of execution were accustomed to be.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

ἐγγὺς ἦν ὁ τόπος τῆς πόλεως) In suburbano, ut solebant esse loca suppliciorum.

## 19:21
Verse 21.

Μὴ γράφε, ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων) For that could be taken in such a way, as if the people of the Jews had held him for their king. Ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐκεῖνος εἶπε) That is, because he had rashly arrogated that title to himself.

Latin:

Vers 21.

Μὴ γράφε, ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων) Id enim ita accipi po- terat, quasi populus Judæorum eum pro rege habuisset. Ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐκεῖνος εἶπε) Id est quod id nominis temere sibi arrogaverit.

## 19:22
Verse 22.

Ὃ γέγραφα, γέγραφα) That is, I have written what I ordered, as above v. ἐμαρτύρησε. The second γέγραφα is for 'I hold as written,' 'I wish what is written to remain.' Similar to the tablet in Matthew V. 37. Agesilaus in Xenophon replied that he would not rewrite what had been written. You see here the inflexibility of Pilate noted by Philo.

More worthy is the observation of Cyril, which I am pleased to add: Pilate did not grant the request of those seeking that the title be changed, not permitting the glory of our Savior to be violated by them in any way, clearly by a divine and ineffable nod. For the kingdom of Christ is stable and free from calumny even against the will of the Jews, who attempt to adulterate the confession of his majesty.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Ὃ γέγραφα, γέγραφα) Id est, scripsi jussi, ut supra v. ἐμαρτύ- ρησε. Secundum γέγραφα est pro scripto habeo, scriptum manere volo. Similis πλακὰ Matth. V. 37. Agesilaus apud Xenophontem ἀπεκρίνατο ὅτι μεταγράψαι μὲν οὐκ ἂν ἀπο- γράψαντο. Vides hic τὸ ἄκαμπτον Pilati Philoni notatum.

Dignior est Cyrilli. observatio, quam adjicere lubet: Pilatus titulum mutari petentibus non an- nuit, non usque quaque Servatoris nostri gloriam ab iis violari permittens, divino videlicet atque ineffabili nutu. Stabile quippe & calumniæ expers vel nolenti- bus Judæis Christi regnum est, qui confessionem ma- jestatis ejus adulterare conantur.

## 19:23
Verse 23.

ἔλαβον τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ) A plural word in a singular sense, as we said at Matthew XXVII. 31 and above XIII. 4; it is the same, however, because the cloak consisted of several pieces.

κὶ ἐποίησαν τέσσαρα μέρη) That could easily be done, because the outer garment of the Jews consisted of four parts, the outermost edges of which are כנפות to the Hebrews, πτερύγια to the Greeks, Deut. XXII. 12. These parts were joined by a clasp.

Ἄῤῥαφος) Without a seam, in a continuous weave, not joined by clasps. Josephus on the tunic of the High Priest: 'This tunic is not made of two pieces so as to be sewn at the shoulders,' etc.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

ἔλαβον τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ) Pluralis vox sensu singulari, ut diximus ad Matth. XXVII. 31. & supra XIII. 4. idem autem ideo quia pallium pluribus patribus constabat.

κὶ ἐποίησαν τέσσαρα μέρη) Facile id fieri potuit, quia Ju- dæorum vestis exterior quatuor partibus constabat, qua- rum extimæ oræ כנפות Hebræis, πτερύγια Græcis Deut. XXII. 12. Hæ partes fibula jungebantur.

Ἄῤῥαφος) Sine commissura, continuo textu, non juncta fibulis. Josephus de Pontificis tunica. ἔστι δὲ ὁ χιτὼν οὗτος οὐκ ἐκ δυοῖν περιτμημάτων ὥστε ῥαπτὸς ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων εἶναι, &c.

## 19:24
Vers. 24.

Μὴ σχίσωμεν αὐτόν) That it would be useless if it were torn.

Ἀλλὰ λάχωμεν περὶ αὐτοῦ) Thus Probus, according to Vopiscus, when a horse had fallen to the common lot in the spoils: he ordered the soldiers to put their names into an urn so that someone, drawn by lot, might receive it. In Virgil and Papinius, a helmet is used instead of an urn.

διεμερίσαντο) David said this of himself proverbially in Psalm 22:19, to indicate that his enemies rejoiced in his spoils. But by the providence of God, it came to pass that these things and others of the same kind were fulfilled in Christ more perfectly, not only according to the proverbial sense, but also literally, so that it might appear that in Him is the fulfillment of all things that had happened to the ancients.

That David prophesied not of himself, but of the Messiah in Psalm 22, and did not utter it proverbially, but understood it as the words sound, I think our defenses of that Psalm have sufficiently taught. For Christ, says Cyril, could not lie, who said through the voice of the Psalmist: 'They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.' All these things, therefore, were usefully foretold, so that by comparing the words with the outcome of events, we might recognize that He is the very one who was foretold, whom we hoped would come for us in our form, and would die for the life of all. I add a mystical meaning from the same Father: Although they divide the Savior's garments into four parts, they nevertheless leave that one indivisible tunic, the ineffable Wisdom of the Only-Begotten so disposing it, that it might be a mystical sign, as it were, of the dispensation by which the four parts of the world were to be brought to salvation. For the four parts of the world have obtained it in a certain way, and they possess the most holy garment of the Word indivisibly, that is, the body of him. For when distributed into minute parts one by one, and the only-begotten, sanctifying the soul of each one with the body through his own flesh, is entirely and indivisibly one in all, existing everywhere. For he is by no means divided, as Paul (1 Cor. 1:13) teaches.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

Μὴ σχίσωμεν αὐτόν) Inutilem futuram si scinderetur.

Ἀλλὰ λάχωμεν περὶ αὐτοῦ) Sic Probus apud Vopiscum cum equus in commune obtigisset in præda: In urnam milites jussit nomen suum mittere ut aliquis eum forte ductus acciperet. Pro urna est galea apud Virgilium & Papinium.

διεμερίσαντο) Dixit hoc David de se proverbialiter Psal. XXII. 19. ut indicaret inimicos lætatos suis spoliis. At Dei providentia factum est, ut hæc & alia ejusmodi in Christo implerentur perfectius, non modo secundum sensum pro- verbialem, sed & κατὰ πόδας, ut appareat, in ipso esse com- plementum omnium, quæ veteribus contigerant.

Davidem non de se, sed Messia Ps. XXII. vatici- natum esse, nec proverbialiter id protulisse, sed ut verba sonant intellexisse, vindicæ nostræ ad illum Psalmum satis opinor docuerunt. Mentiri quippe, inquit Cyrillus, Christus non poterat, qui per Psal- mistæ vocem dixit: Diviserunt sibi vestimenta mea, & super vestem meam miserunt sortem. Hæc igi- tur omnia utiliter prædicta sunt, ut cum rerum e- ventu verba conferentes agnosceremus, eum ipsum esse, qui prædictus est, quem venturum pro nobis in forma nostra, & pro vita omnium moriturum spe- rabamus. Addo mysticam significationem ex eo- dem Patre: In quatuor partes cum Servatoris vesti- menta dividant; tunicam tamen relinquunt unam illam indivisam, ineffabili Sapientia Unigeniti sic disponente, ut id mystica quasi quoddam signum es- set dispensationis, quæ quatuor orbis partes ad salu- tem essent adducendæ. Nam partes orbis quatuor sortitæ sunt quodammodo, & impartibiliter habent Sacrosanctum Verbi indumentum, hoc est, corpus ejus. In minutas enim partes sigillatim distributis, & unius cujusque animam cum corpore sanctificans per suam carnem unigenitus, integre & indivise est in omnibus unus existens ubique. Nequaquam enim divisus est, ut Paulus (1. Cor. I. 13.) docet.

## 19:25
Verse 25.

by the cross) Yet in such a way that, with the crowd of soldiers intervening, they were prevented from approaching closer to the cross, Matt. 27:55.

his mother) Neither deterred by her own danger, nor by the sadness of the spectacle, nor by reproaches, from receiving the final commands of her son, and showing in reality that she was mindful of those things which she had learned from the Angel. A presage of Christian fortitude that would appear even in the weaker sex.

Mary of Clopas) The daughter of Clopas, as the Arabic expressly has it. See what is said at Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

παρὰ τῷ σταυρῷ) Ita tamen ut intercedente militum tur- ba propius ad crucem accedere prohiberentur, Matth. XXVII. 55.

ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ) Neque periculo suo, neque tristitia spe- ctaculi, neque probris absterrita, quo minus filii ultima mandata exciperet, & reipsa ostenderet, memorem se eo- rum quæ ab Angelo didicisset. Præsagium fortitudinis Chri- stianæ etiam in sexu infirmiore apparituræ.

Μαρία ἡ τοῦ Κλωπᾶ) Filia Cleopæ, ut diserte habet Arabs. Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

## 19:26
Verse 26.

the disciple standing by whom he loved) As above 13:23.

Woman) As above 2:4.

behold your son) This one will be in the place of a son to you for me, this one will perform for you the duties of a son, so that thus also in this very thing that which Christ promised to the pious might be fulfilled, Matt. 19:29. Tertullian against the heretics concerning John: whom he entrusted to Mary as a son in his own place.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

Τὸν μαθητὴν παρεστῶτα ὃν ἠγάπα) Ut supra XIII. 23.

Γύναι) Ut supra II. 4.

ἰδοὺ ὁ υἱός σου) Hic tibi pro me filii erit loco, hic tibi filii officia exhibebit, ut sic etiam in ipsa adimpleretur id quod piis Christus promisit Matth. XIX. 29. Turtullianus adver- sus hæreticos de Johanne: quam loco suo filium Mariæ de- mandavit.

## 19:27
Verse 27.

behold your mother) Whom you are to observe as a mother henceforth. Thus in Virgil, Aeneid 9, Ascanius to Euryalus concerning Euryalus's mother: For she shall be a mother to me.

From that hour) The manuscript, which I have already often cited, has from that day.

εἰς τὰ ἴδια) Into his own home. See what is said at Luke II. 49 and above XVI. 32. Thus what is in Hebrew אל ביתו Esther V. 10 and VI. 12 is translated in Greek as εἰς τὰ ἴδια. We have noted elsewhere that Joseph, the husband of Mary, was dead when these things were taking place.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

ἰδοὺ ἡ μήτηρ σου) Quam tu ut matrem posthac observa- turus es. Sic apud Virgilium IX, Æneidos, Ascanius Euryalo de Euryali matre. Namque erit ista mihi geni- trix.

Ἀπ' ἐκείνης τῆς ὥρας) manuscriptus, quem sæpe jam lau- davi, habet τῆς ἐκείνης τῆς ἡμέρας.

εἰς τὰ ἴδια) In domicilium suum. Vide quæ ad Luc. II. 49. supra XVI. 32. Sic quod Hebraice est אל ביתו Esther V. 10. & VI. 12. Græce vertitur εἰς τὰ ἴδια. Notavimus alibi Josephum Mariæ conjugem cum hæc gererentur fuis- se mortuum.

## 19:28
Vers. 28.

ὅτι πάντα ἤδη τετέλεσται) Which pertained to his own humble state, and understand that the past tense is used for the immediate future, as in Matthew XXVI. 28 and what is noted there.

ἵνα) ecbatic, as we have already often noted.

Διψῶ) For he had contracted thirst both from the torture and the flow of blood.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ὅτι πάντα ἤδη τετέλεσται) Quæ ad ipsius statum humilem pertinebant, & intellige præteritum poni pro proxime fu- turo, ut Matth. XXVI. 28. & quæ ibi notata.

ἵνα) ἐκβατικὸν ut jam sæpe notavimus.

Διψῶ) Quippe & cruciatu & sanguinis fluxu sitim con- traxerat.

## 19:29
Vers. 29.

ὄξος) I think it is that artificial wine which used to be provided at the cross. For we noted at Matthew that it is called ὄξος. Moreover, that drink was both bitter in itself and all the more so because it was given during an execution.

Ὑσσώπῳ) With the reed of that tree, as at Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

ὄξος) Puto esse vinum illud factitium quod apponi sole- bat ad crucem. Nam id ὄξος appellari ad Matthæum no- tavimus. Erat autem is potus & per se amarus & eo magis quia in supplicio dabatur.

Ὑσσώπῳ) Calamo ejus arboris, ut ad Matthæum.

## 19:30
Vers. 30.

τετέλεσται) The end of the sufferings is at hand. It is proverbial. Homer says τὰ δὲ νῦν πάντα τελεῖται. Philoxenus, about to die, says in the Comedian: τέλος ἔχει τὰ πάντα μοι.

Κλίνας τὴν κεφαλὴν) As those who are dying are accustomed to do. Ovid: Thus the dying body lies, and the neck, failing in strength, is a burden to itself and reclines upon the shoulder.

παρέδωκε τὸ πνεῦμα) It is a pious expression accepted among those Hebrews who believed in judgment after this life, by which he who is dying is said to deliver up his spirit, namely to God, its author, so that He may determine its fate. See Ecclesiastes XII. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

τετέλεσται) Finis adest passionum. Proverbiale est. Ho- merus τὰ δὲ νῦν πάντα τελεῖται. Piloxenus moriturus apud Comicum: τέλος ἔχει τὰ πάντα μοι.

Κλίνας τὴν κεφαλὴν) Ut solent moribundi. Ovidius, Sic corpus moriens jacet, & defecta vigore Ipsa sibi est oneri cervix, humeroque recumbit.

παρέδωκε τὸ πνεῦμα) Pia est locutio apud Hebræos illos, qui judicium post hanc vitam credebant, recepta, qua qui moritur dicitur spiritum tradere, Deo scilicet ejus autori, ut is de eo statuat. Vide Ecclesiastæ XII. 7.

## 19:31
Ver. 31.

that the bodies might not remain on the cross on the Sabbath) Because by the long remaining of bodies on the gallows the holy land is said to be defiled in the law, Deut. XXI. 23, the experts in the law gathered from the similarity of the reason that even a day, especially one so solemn, would be defiled by such a spectacle. They hasten, however, that they might be taken down, not only before evening, by which the Sabbath begins, but also before the hours immediately following, which were owed to the preparing of souls and bodies for the sacred day. The taking down was indeed to be done not by the Jews, but by the Roman soldiers; but the Jews placed a part of the autonomy granted to them in this, that nothing should be done publicly even by the Romans which was unbecoming to the time. See what [we said] at Matt. XXVI. 5.

since it was the preparation) The very time destined for preparation was now imminent: ערב שבת from which time the whole day by synecdoche had the name. See below 42.

for that day of the Sabbath was great) The most festive day of the Passover fell on the following Sabbath, and so they were hastening not only because of the Sabbath, but also because of the Passover. See Matt. XXVI. 2.

Concerning these things we have spoken at Matthew. Cyril here detests, and not undeservedly, the hypocrisy of the Jews: Behold, Christ having been killed, they make much of the honor of the Sabbath, and with incredible audacity, having violated the author of the Law, they make a show of piety toward the law. They pretend to honor the day of that Sabbath especially great, who killed the Lord of the great day, and they demand a favor worthy only of themselves, namely that their legs be broken, contriving for them a destruction more bitter than death itself with intolerable pain, now that they were nearly dead.

that their legs might be broken) Personal for impersonal, which is expressed in Latin by the passive. That the legs might be broken. Lactantius, whom others follow, says this was done according to Roman custom. Doubtless, for those who were condemned to die on the cross, which is a slow death, it sometimes happened that because of the delay of the punishment, but by way of compensation for no small torture, that is, by leg-breaking, so that there might not be too much of a decrease in the severity of the punishment. Otherwise, leg-breaking was a punishment distinct from the cross.

and might be taken away) So that thus the dead bodies could be taken down from the cross.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

ἵνα μὴ μείνῃ ἐπὶ τοῦ σταυροῦ τὰ σώματα ἐν τῷ σαββάτῳ) Quia longa permansione corporum in patibulo terra sancta con- taminari dicitur in lege, Deut XXI. 23. collegerunt ex si- militudine rationis legisperiti etiam diem præsertim tam solemnem, contaminatum iri tali spectaculo. Festinant autem ut tollantur, non tantum ante vesperam, qua Sab- batum inchoatur, sed etiam ante horas proximas, quæ pa- randis sacro animis ac corporibus debebantur. Erat quidem depositio facienda non per Judæos, sed per milites Ro- manos; verum Judæi partem αὐτονομίας sibi concessæ in eo ponebant, ne quid publice etiam à Romanis fieret, quod tempus dedeceret. Vide quæ ad Matth. XXVI. 5.

ἐπεὶ παρασκευὴ ἦν) Tempus ipsum præparationi desti- natum jam imminebat: ערב שבת ex quo tempore tota dies κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν nomen habebat. Vide infra 42.

ἦν γὰρ ἡ μεγάλη ἡμέρα ἐκείνη τοῦ σαββάτου) In Sabbatum sequens incidebat dies maxime festus Paschatis, itaque fe- stinabant non modo ob Sabbatum, sed & ob Pascha. Vide Matth. XXVI. 2.

De his ad Matthæum diximus. Cyrillus dete- statur hic, nec immerito, hypocrisin Judæorum: Ecce Christo interfecto Sabbati honorem magni fa- ciunt, & incredibili audacia violato Legis autore, pietatem erga legem præ se ferunt. Magnum autem illius præcipue Sabbati diem colere fimulant, qui magna diei Dominum interemerunt, & gratiam se solis dignam flagitant, ut eorum nempe crura frangantur, intolerabili dolore acerbiorem morte ipsa perniciem prope jam mortis molientes.

ἵνα κατεαγῶσιν αὐτῶν τὰ σκέλη) Personale pro imperfo- nali, quod per passivum Latine exprimitur. Vt frangerentur crura. Ait Lactantius, quem sequuntur alii, factum hoc ex more Romano. Nimirum qui damnati erant mori in cruce, quæ lenta mors, iis interdum accidebat ut mora supplicii, sed compensatione non exigui cruciatus, id est crurifragio, ne de pœnæ gravitate nimium decederet. Erat alioqui cru- rifragium pœna distincta à cruce.

καὶ ἀρθῶσιν) Ut ita mortua corpora tolli de cruce pos- sent.

## 19:33
Ver. 33.

When they saw him already dead) They saw from the signs, or also discovered from the report of the standing centurion, who had observed his death. See at Matthew.

Latin:

Verf. 33.

Ὡς εἶδον αὐτὸν ἤδη τεθνηκότα) Viderunt ex indiciis, aut etiam compererunt ex relatu adstantis centurionis, qui e- jus mortem observaverat. Vide ad Matth.

## 19:34
Ver. 34.

He pierced his side with a spear) The Syriac translates 'struck', that is, pierced through, doubtless doubting whether he was truly dead, and wishing to test whether he would move himself by the sensation of the blow. The guards were accustomed to have spears: Suetonius teaches this in Claudius: And the spearmen around Vespasian in Josephus, Jewish War III. c. VIII.

blood and water) The pericardium having been touched, in which there is water and blood around it. The body had not yet grown cold, so that it would easily allow a flow.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

Λόγχῃ αὐτῦ τὴν πλευρὰν ἔνυξε) Percussit vertit Syrus, id est perfodit, nimirum dubitans an vere esset mortuus, & experiri volens an sensu ictus se esset commoturus. Sole- bant autem speculatores habere lanceas : Suetonius Clau- dio id docet: Et λογχοφόροι circa Vespasianum apud Iose- phum belli Iudaici III. c. VIII.

αἷμα κά ὕδωρ) Tacto pericardio, in quo est aqua & san- guis circum. Nondum autem refrixerat corpus, ita ut flu- xum facile ferret.

## 19:35
Verse 35.

κὰ ὁ ἑωρακὼς μεμαρτύρηκε) An inverted expression for what would be: he who testifies has seen, as above VII. 28. and elsewhere. He inculcates this so expressly concerning the certainty of his testimony, so that even if it were not clear from the previous points that Christ had died, it would certainly be clear from this: since that wound, if he had lived, would have been altogether lethal. Quintilian places among the necessary signs of a future event that it is necessary for him to die whose heart is wounded. Galen gives an example of a certain theorem, if anyone is heart-wounded, he will die in vain. It is the custom of John to speak of himself in the third person.

ἵνα ὑμεῖς πιστεύητε) So that you Christians may the more believe that Jesus truly died: and consequently also truly rose from the dead. Thus he has used 'to believe' several times above regarding growth.

Grotius does not acknowledge a miracle, having followed Calvin here. But the pious ancients did acknowledge it. And St. Ambrose observes in chapter XXIII of Luke: In our bodies blood congeals after death, but in this place it is still fluid. Furthermore, since the blood did not drip drop by drop, but flowed forth from the wound immediately like a spring, it cannot be said that heat still remaining, because it happened immediately after death, prevented the coagulation of the blood. That would hold if only a few drops had trickled out: but such a long flow of blood could not have happened without a miracle. Added to this is that the water flowed forth separately, as Gregory Nazianzen says in the tragedy 'Christus patiens': But from the pierced side there flowed immediately an unusual αἷμα τ'ως φορεμένον blood not mixed and wonderful water. St. John distinctly commemorates blood and water, true blood indeed and true water, because the literal sense must be retained entirely in a historical account. Therefore the water was not from the pericardium: since that fluid approaches more to a bilious humor than to natural water. Thomas Bartholinus proves that the serum enclosed in the membrane of the heart is devoid of all resemblance to blood: therefore he contends that the cavity of the chest emitted watery and bloody humors here: which he calls serum, and he thinks it could not have appeared without a mixture of blood or the appearance of a bloody color, especially at this time, when it might imbibe a tincture through the wound and the badly affected parts. But here water and blood are clearly distinguished, and not a mixture of blood, or merely the appearance of a bloody color, is commemorated. Whence Theophylact on John: The Jews also try to treat the dead body with contumely, but the contumely is turned for them into a miracle. And that blood indeed came forth from a dead body is wonderful, yet a sycophant might say that it is likely that a certain vital power was still in the body, but the water removes all controversy by a miracle. Thus Theophylact. And the pious ancients defend this distinct and unconfused flow in such a way that they teach that those two distinct Sacraments of the New Testament also flowed from the side of Christ, because, forsooth, by that flow the same were shadowed forth: among the Greeks Chrysostom, Cyril, Theophylact, and so also Damascene, book IV, on the Orthodox Faith, ch. X; among the Latins Ambrose, book X, on Luke; Augustine, book III, on the Creed, ch. VI; book III, on the City of God, ch. XXVI, etc. To this also some refer the testimony of St. John himself, 1 Epistle V. 6. This is he who came by water and blood; not in water only, but in water and blood. What of the fact that that grave asseveration, which he added here, and indeed immediately to this account, sufficiently indicates that this is something singular and miraculous. For what else would have been the need for such a great asseveration? Which Grotius draws in vain to the certainty of the death of Christ: concerning which it was sufficiently established from the preceding, and could further be established from the following, so that for its sake the same was by no means necessary.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

κὰ ὁ ἑωρακὼς μεμαρτύρηκε) Locutio inversa pro eo quod esset: qui testatur is vidit, ut supra VII. 28. & alibi. Ideo autem hoc de testimonii sui certitudine tam diserte incul- cat, ut etiamsi ex prioribus non constaret, Christum esse mortuum, hinc certe constaret: cum id vulnus, si vixis- set, omnino fuisset lethale. Quintilianus inter signa neces- saria futuri ponit, mori necesse esse eum, cujus cor est vul- neratum. Galenus dat certi theorematis exemplum, εἶ τις έσὶ καρδιότρωτ® εἰκῆ® ἀποθανεῖται. Mos est Iohannis de se in tertia persona loqui.

ἵνα ὑμεῖς πιστεύητε) Quo magis vos Christiani credatis vere mortuum esse Iesum: ac proinde etiam vere à mor- tuis resuscitatum. Sic credere aliquoties supra usurpavit de augmento.

Non agnoscit miraculum Grotius, Calvinum hic sequutus. Sed agnovere pii veteres. Et ob- servat S. Ambrosius in cap. XXIII. Lucæ: In cor- poribus nostris sanguis post mortem congelascit, sed hoc loco adhuc fluidus est. Porro quum non guttatim destillaverit, sed scaturiginis instar con- festim ex vulnere profluxerit sanguis, dici non po- test, calorem adhuc reliquum, quia statim post mortem id accidit, prohibuisse coagulationem sanguinis. Locum id haberet, si guttæ aliquæ solum stillassent: sed tam longus profluxus san- guinis sine miraculo fieri non potuit. Accedit quod aqua seorsim promanavit, ut Gregor. Naz. in Trag. Christus patiens: At latere fixo fluxit il- lico insolens αἷμα τ'ως φορεμένον sanguis non permix- tus & mirabilis aqua. Distincte S. Johannes com- memorat sanguinem, & aquam, verum nempe sanguinem & veram aquam, quia retinendum o- mnino in historica relatione τὸ ῥητὸν. Ideo non de pericardio aqua fuit: siquidem liquor ille magis ad bilosum humorem accedat, quam ad aquam na- turalem. Inclusum membranæ cordis serum omni cruoris destitutum similitudine Thomas Bartholinus probat: ideo contendit thoracis cavum humores aquatos & cruentos hic emisisse: quem serum vo- cat, nec sine sanguinis mixtura vel coloris sanguinei specie apparere potuisse, hoc imprimis tempore, ubi per vulnus maleque affectas partes tincturam imbibat, existimat. Sed hic distinguuntur aperte aqua & sanguis, non vero mixtura sanguinis, vel species tan- tum coloris sanguinei commemoratur. Unde Theo- phyl. in Joh. Judæi etiam mortuum corpus contume- lia afficere conantur, sed contumelia illis in miracu- lum vertitur. Et sanguinem quidem ex mortuo cor- pore prodiisse admirabile est, veruntamen posset quis Sycophantarum dicere, quod verisimile sit, vi- talem quandam virtutem adhuc in corpore fuisse, aqua autem omnem controversiam miraculo tollit. Haec Theophylact. Atque hunc distinctum & in- confusum profluxum ita tuentur pii veteres, ut inde etiam duo illa distincta Sacramenta Novi Test. e latere Christi profluxisse doceant, quia nimirum profluxu illo eadem adumbrata sunt: e Graecis Chrysost. Cyrill. Theophyl. sic & Damasc. lib. IV. de orth. fid. c. X. e Latinis Ambros. l. X. in Luc. Augu- stin. l. III. de Symb. c. VI. l. III. de C.D. c. XXVI. &c. Quo etiam referunt nonnulli ipsius S. Johannis testimonium 1. Epist. V. 6. Hic est, qui venit per aquam & sanguinem; non in aqua solum, sed in aqua & sanguine. Quid quod gravis illa asseveratio, quam hic addidit, & immediate quidem ad hanc relationem, satis indicet, singulare quidpiam, & miraculosum hoc esse. Quid enim alias opus fuisset tanta asseveratione? Quam Grotius nequicquam trahit ad mortis Christi certitudinem: de qua satis constabat ex antecedentibus, & e consequentibus. constare porro poterat, ut ejus gratia eadem mi- nime opus fuerit.

## 19:36
Verse 36.

A bone shall not be broken of him) Most think that the law concerning the Paschal Lamb is being referred to. I would rather believe that the passage of Psalm XXXIV, 21 is being looked to, where the special care of God for a pious man is described.

Grotius is singular after his own custom. But the very words cited from chapter XII of Exodus sufficiently teach that it is being referred to. Special care for every single pious man has nothing to do with the omission of the breaking of the legs: the converted thief also died piously, and yet his legs were broken. And Christ had something singular here, which had been predicted of him, or rather prefigured in the Paschal lamb: therefore one must not depart to sayings concerning the care of pious men in general.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

ὀστοῦν οὐ συντριβήσεται ἀπ' αὐτοῦ) Putant plerique respici le- gem de Agno Paschali. Potius crediderim spectari locum Psalmi XXXIV, 21. ubi specialis Dei cura pro homine pio describitur.

Singularis pro more suo Grotius est. Sed ver- ba ipsa e cap. XII. Exod. allegata satis docent id re- spici. Cura specialis pro unoquoque pio homine nil ad crurifragii intermissionem facit: pie etiam decessit latro conversus, & fracta tamen ei crura sunt. Et singulare quid hic habuit Christus, quod de ipso praedictum erat, vel potius figuratum in a- gno Paschali: Non ergo est abeundum ad dicta cu- ram piorum hominum generatim concernentia.

## 19:37
Verse 37.

They shall look on him whom they pierced) Doubtless some of the Greek versions had it thus; for that reading is also found in many books, from Symmachus, Aquila, or Theodotion. This also, said figuratively by God concerning himself being despised, comes to pass in Jesus literally, as do other prophecies. But they shall see that, taken concerning Jesus, it seems best understood of the day of judgment, because of the passage in Revelation I. 7. See Matthew XXVI, 64, where it is 'you shall see'.

The passage in Zechariah XII does not treat of Christ figuratively, but literally and of Christ, as has been shown in the same place.

PART II. The burial of Jesus.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

ὄψονται εἰς ὃν ἐξεκέντησαν) Sic habuit haud dubie aliqua Graecarum versionum; nam & in multis libris ea lectio re- peritur, a Symmacho, Aquila, aut Theodotione. Hoc quo- que tralatitie dictum a Deo, de se contemto, evenit in Jesu κατα πόδας, ut & alia vaticinia. Videbunt autem illud, de Jesu sumtum, videtur optime intelligi de die judicii, ob locum Apoc. I. 7. Vide Matth. XXVI, 64. ubi est ὄψεσθε.

Locus Zach. XII. non tralatitie de Christo, sed κατα πόδας, & literaliter de Christo agit, ut ibi- dem ostensum.

PARS II. Jesu sepultura.

## 19:38
Verse 38.

Being a disciple) As one who was a disciple, so the Syrian rightly explains.

But hidden because of the fear of the Jews) Such as many of the chief men above in XII. 42. He feared the reproach of excommunication.

ἵνα ἄρῃ) That he might take [it] from the cross: as above 31. See how suddenly the indignity of the punishment has animated the timid; and how, after no interval, the ultimate contempt was followed by some glory: a distinguished man professing the friendship of the dead [man] which he had concealed while he was alive.

καὶ ἐπέτρεψεν Πιλάτος) With the facility common among Roman governors. See what [is said] regarding Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 38.

ὢν μαθητὴς) Ut qui discipulus esset, ita recte Syrus ex- plicat.

Κεκρυμμένος δὲ διὰ τὸν φόβον τῶν ἰουδαίων) Quales mul- ti e primoribus supra XII. 42. metuebat contumeliam ex- communicationis.

ἵνα ἄρῃ) Ut de cruce tollere sibi liceret: ut supra 31. En ut subito supplicii indignitas timidum animaverit; & nullo in- tervallo ultimum contemtum secuta sit aliqua gloria: Viro illustri mortui amicitiam profitente qui vivi dissimulaverat.

καὶ ἐπέτρεψεν Πιλάτος) Facilitate obvia apud Romanos praesides. Vide quae ad Matthaeum.

## 19:39
Vers. 39.

ὁ ἐλθὼν πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν, νυκτὸς τὸ πρῶτον) That is, previously, as the Syriac has it here. πρῶτον for πρότερον as above I. 15.

μίγμα σμύρνης καὶ ἀλόης) Which spices were considered best for this use. In Aëtius there is νεκρῶ σμύρνησις and elsewhere σμυρνισμὸς. μίγμα is in 2 Chron. XVI. 14. The same were used for perfuming the garments of kings, Psalm XLV. 9.

ὡς λίτρας ἑκατόν) A sign both of Nicodemus's opulence and of his not sparing affection. It should be noted, however, that the bodies of the great were accustomed to be laid out in a large heap of spices, as appears in the following verse: and 2 Chron. XVI. 14. Thus also the Hebrews record that the body of the Patriarch Jacob was hardened with spices, so that it was touched by no hand. By comparing these places, it appears that this is a different and more sumptuous embalming than that common one which was done by anointing. Add what [is said] regarding Matt. XXVI, 12.

Besides myrrh and aloes, cedromel, salt, natron, bitumen, and resin were accustomed to be used. But those two species, as being more excellent and precious, are mentioned here. B. Gerhard thinks that Psalm XLV. 9 refers to this: Myrrh, Aloes, and Cinnamon [are] all his garments; and that it is indicated that Christ is to be wrapped and clothed in his burial with Myrrh, Aloes, and other spices, and that in his resurrection he is to come forth glorious from the sepulchre hewn out of the rock, just as any King might come forth from an ivory [palace] conspicuous in beauty. Certainly the whole body of Christ was anointed: since a mass of nearly a hundred pounds was spent by Nicodemus for anointing the body of Christ. Nor indeed does any necessity appear why we should understand by λίτραν in this place, with Erasmus Schmid, not a certain weight, but a kind of coin. For the fact that Nicodemus could not carry so much weight is nothing to the point, since he could have had his own servants: nor is there need that so many pounds were used to anoint the body of the Lord, since it can be said with Salmasius that they were used not so much to anoint the body of the Lord as to embalm it, that is, to wrap it in linen cloths smeared with spices, where, however, it does not seem to be denied that the body itself was also anointed and smeared with them at the same time. But those spices, with which the body of Christ is wrapped, denote the sweet and life-giving odor, overflowing to us from the death and burial of Christ, 2 Cor. II. 15. And because those condiments preserve bodies from putrefaction (although it was impossible that the most holy body of Christ should see corruption), they remind us that we should seek life in Christ even under death, and expect salvation from this dried-up body. Salmasius observes that two very different plants are found under the name of aloes, one aromatic, accustomed to be used for incense: the other an herb from which a very bitter juice is extracted. He determines that most interpreters understand the latter: but that the former is noted here, with Nonnus: both because myrrh and aloes are spices, such as were used alone for embalming, and not that medicinal aloe: and because in sacred writings aromatic aloe is always understood when it is joined with myrrh, in Proverbs, Psalms, and the Canticle: and because the Egyptians used aromatic aloe with myrrh in embalming bodies, as Herodotus testifies.

Latin:

Vers. 39.

ὁ ἐλθὼν πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν, νυκτὸς τὸ πρῶτον) Id est antehac, ut hic habet Syrus. πρῶτον pro πρότερον ut supra I. 15.
