μίγμα σμύρνης καὶ ἀλόης) Quae aromata ad hunc usum optima habebantur. Apud Aëtium est νεκρῶ σμύρνησις & alibi σμυρνισμὸς. μίγμα est 2. Paral. XVI. 14. Eadem ad odo- randas regum vestes adhibita, Psal. XLV. 9.

ὡς λίτρας ἑκατόν) Signum & opulentiae Nicodemi & non parci affectus. Notandum autem in magno aromatum cumulo deponi solita magnatum corpora, ut apparet versu sequente: & 2. Par. XVI. 14. sic & Jacobi Patriarchae corpus Hebraei memorant aromatibus induruisse, ta ut nulla ma- nu tangeretur. Quibus locis collatis apparet aliam hanc esse pollincturam & sumtuosiorem vulgari illa, quae per un- ctionem fiebat. Adde quae ad Matth. XXVI, 12.

Præter myrrham & aloën adhiberi solebant ce- dromel, sal, cicera, bitumen, & resina. Sed illæ duæ species, ceu præstantiores & pretiosiores hîc rese- runtur. B. Gerhardus eo respicere Psal. XLV. 9. censet: Myrrha, Aloë & Cinamomum omnia ve- stimenta ejus; & indicari, quod Christus in se- pultura sua Myrrha, Aloë, atque aliis aromatibus involvendus, ac vestiendus sit, inque resurrectio- ne sua ex sepulchro in petram exciso gloriosus proditurus, quam ex Eburnéa Rex quisquam de- core conspicuus prodeat. Totum certe corpus Christi delibutum fuit: siquidem massa centum fere librarum à Nicodemo corpori Christi un- guendo impensa sit. Neque vero ulla apparet ne- cessitas, cur per λίτραν hoc loco intelligamus cum Erasm. Schmidio non certum ponderis, sed nummi genus. Nam quod Nicodemus non potue- rit tantum ponderis φέρειν, nihil ad rem, quum habere potuerit suos ministros: neque opus, ut corpus Domini unguendum tot libræ adhibitæ sint, quum dici possit cum Salmasio adhibitas non tam ut corpus Domini ungeret, quam ut pol- lingeret, hoc est sapus & sindoni involveret aro- matis delibutis, ubi tamen ipsum etiam corpus iis- dem simul unctum & delibutum fuisse non negan- dum videtur. Aromata autem illa, quibus obvol- vitur corpus Christi, odorem suavem ac vivificum denotant, ex morte & sepultura Christi ad nos re- dundantem 2. Cor. II. 15. Et quia condimenta ista corpora à putrefactione conservant, (quamvis im- possibile fuerit, ut sanctissimum corpus Christi corruptionem videret) commonefaciunt nos, ut vitam in Christo etiam sub morte quæramus, & ex hoc arefacto corpore salutem expectemus. Sal- masius observat duas diversissimas plantas ἀλόης nomine reperiri, alteram aromaticam ad Thymia- mata adhiberi solitam: alteram herbam ex qua suc- cus amarissimus elicitur. Posteriorem Interpp. ple- rosque intelligere: Priorem autem hîc notari cum Nonno statuit: tum quia Myrrha & aloë aromata, qualia sola ad pollincturam adhibita, non vero a- loë illa Medica: tum quia semper in sacris aroma- tica aloë intelligitur, cum Myrrhæ jungitur, in Proverbiis, Psalmis, ac Cantico: tum quod Ægy- ptii ἀλόην adhibuerint cum myrrha in condendis corporibus aromaticam, teste Herodoto.

## 19:40
v. 40. κὰι ἔδησαν αὐτὸν ἐν ὀθονίοις) By ὀθόνια understand those bandages, תכריכין to the Hebrews: with which we said above, XI. 44, that the body was wrapped. Therefore, what is here ἔδησαν, the Syriac translates ܛܪܟܘ that is, they wrapped: using the verb from which that Hebrew name is derived, which I just mentioned. See also what [is said] regarding Matthew.

μετὰ τω̃ν ἀρωμάτων) They did not anoint [him] because of the shortness of time, but they applied the spices, intending to anoint [him] at the first convenient time.

ἐνταφιάζειν) This is to be referred to ὀθόνια: ἐνταφιάζειν is to prepare for burial: whether by wrapping as here, or by anointing, which is properly חנט, as appears from the Syriac and Arabic word ܚܪܘܝܬܐ which signifies a mixture: above XIX. 39.

Piscator also denies that the body of Christ was anointed: both because the shortness of time did not allow for it, and because the Galilean women wished to perform the duty of anointing afterwards; but the words of the Evangelist are clear: κ̓ἔδησαν αὐτό (τὸ σω̃μα ὀθο- νίοις μετὰ τω̃ν ἀρωμάτων καθὼς ἔθος ἐστὶ τοι̃ς ̓Ιε- δαίοις ἐνταφιάζειν. Now the custom of the Jews was not merely to apply spices, but to wrap the body in spices reduced to the form of an ointment, and afterwards to wrap that in a clean linen cloth. John understands this by ὀθόνια, using the plural, because the body of Christ was wrapped not in one, but in several linen cloths, but we have also noted at Matthew that both ὀθόνια and σίνδονα were brought into use. Indeed, ἐνταφιάζειν is even used for the Hebrew חנט among the LXX regarding the anointing with which the dead are seasoned and anointed. bodies, and are prepared for burial. Conf. Matt. XXVI. 12. See also Schindler in Lex. under the word סוך. Grotius himself observes that meaning here from the Syriac and Arabic interpretation, and in his notes on Matt. XXVI. 12. Here τὸ ἐνταφιάσαι is to be interpreted by the ellipsis of the little word ὡσεὶ, he acted as if for my embalming. Which little word the Syriac interpreter prudently added here, as also in this history in Mark. And to John ἡμέρα ἐνταφιασμοῦ is the day as it were of the embalming. The LXX had said ἐνταφιάζειν for to embalm in the last chapter of Genesis, etc. But that the women likewise wished to anoint Christ is to be attributed to the fervor of their charity; or it was done because the anointing of Joseph and Nicodemus was rough and extemporaneous, whence they themselves, because they were sufficiently wealthy, Luke VIII. 3, planned a more accurate and expensive one. Therefore they brought not only myrrh, but also aromatics, because besides liquid ointments they also wished to use precious aromatics. Salmasius observes that it is not said that Nicodemus anointed the body of the Lord with those aromatics, but that he embalmed it, i.e., wrapped it in bandages with aromatics. But the women are said to have bought aromatics and myrrh, in order to anoint. The weight also of the aromatics of Nicodemus is too great to be able to be thought prepared for an anointing. Concerning which, let a judgment be made from those things which we have said.

Latin:

v. 40. κὰι ἔδησαν αὐτὸν ἐν ὀθονίοις) ὀθόνια intell ge illas fa- scias תכריכין Hebræis: quibus corpus involutum fuisse su- pra diximus XI. 44. Itaque quod hîc est ἔδησαν Syrus vertit ܛܪܟܘ id est involverunt: verbo utens unde illud Hebræum nomen est, quod modo dixi. Vide & quæ ad Matthæum.

μετὰ τω̃ν ἀρωμάτων) Non unxerunt ob temporis angustias, sed aromata apposuerunt, uncturi primo commodo tem- pore.

ἐνταφιάζειν) Referendum hoc ad ὀθόνια: ἐνταφιάζειν est præparare ad sepulturam: sive involvendo ut hîc, sive un- gendo, quod proprie חנט, ut apparet ex voce Syriaca & Arabica ܚܪܘܝܬܐ quæ μίγμα significat: supra XIX. 39.

Pollinctum fuisse corpus Christi etiam Piscator negat: tum quod propter temporis brevitatem id non licuerit, tum quia mulieris Galilææ postea ungendi officium exequi voluere; Sed verba Ev- angelistæ clara sunt: κ̓ἔδησαν αὐτό (τὸ σω̃μα ὀθο- νίοις μετὰ τω̃ν ἀρωμάτων καθὼς ἔθος ἐστὶ τοι̃ς ̓Ιε- δαίοις ἐνταφιάζειν. Consuetudo autem Judæorum erat non apponere solum aromata, sed corpus aro- matibus ad formam unguenti redactis obvolvere, idque Sindoni munda postea involvere. Quam per ὀθόνια intelligit Johannes, adhibito plurali, quia non uno, sed pluribus linteis corpus Christi involu- tum fuit, sed & ὀθόνια & σίνδονα in usum vocata ad Matthæum notavimus. Verum etiam ἐνταφιάζειν pro Ebræo חנט apud LXX. adhibetur de unctio- ne, qua condiuntur & pollinguntur defunctorum corpora, ac præparantur ad sepulturam. Conf. Matth. XXVI. 12. Vid. & Schindler. in Lex. in voce סוך. Grotius ipse significationem illam hic obser- vat è Syriaca & Arabica interpretatione, & ad Matt. XXVI. 12. in notat. Hic τὸ ἐνταφιάσαι inter- pretandum est per ἔλλειψιν voculæ ὡσεὶ, fecit quasi ad me pollinciendum. Quam voculam prudenter hic, ut & in hac apud Marcum historia, addidit Sy- rus interpres. Et Johanni ἡμέρα ἐνταφιασμῦ est dies quasi pollincturæ. ἐνταφιάζειν pro pollincire dixerant LXX. capite ultimo Geneseos &c. Quod vero mulieres itidem ungere Christum voluerint fervori caritatis tribuendum; vel factum id, quod unctio Josephi & Nicodemi rudis & extemporanea fuerit, unde ipsæ accuratiorem, & sumtuosiorem, quia satis opulentæ fuere, Luc. VIII. 3. meditatæ sunt. Ideo attulerunt non solum μύῤῥα, sed etiam aromata, quia præter unguenta liquida etiam pre- tiosa aromata adhibere volebant. Salmasius obser- vat, non dici Nicodemum illis aromatis unxisse corpus Domini, sed pollinxisse, h. e. fasciis involvisse cum A- romatis. Mulieres autem dici aromata & myrrham emisse, ut ungerent. Pondus etiam aromatum Nicole- mi nimis magnum esse, quam ut unctioni paratum existimari queat. De quo ex iis, quæ diximus, ju- dicium fiat.

## 19:41
v. 41. ἦν δὲ ἐν τῷ τόπῳ) Τόπος here calls that suburban region. Μνημεῖον καινὸν ἐν ᾧ οὐδέπω ἐτέθη) Lest any other be believed to have risen.

Latin:

v. 41. ἦν δὲ ἐν τῷ τόπῳ) Τόπος hic vocat regionem illam suburbanam. Μνημεῖον καινὸν ἐν ᾧ ἐδέπω ἐτέθη) Ne quis alius surrexisse crederetur.

## 19:42
v. 42. Διὰ τὴν παρασκευὴν τῶν Ἰουδαίων) Refer to ἔθηκαν. They hastened to deposit him there not yet anointed, which they would have done otherwise, had not time pressed. παρασκευὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων is said as above II. 6. 13. & V. 1. Ὅτι ἐγγὺς ἦν τὸ μνημεῖον) It is to be read by way of parenthesis: as if he were to say: do not wonder that he could be deposited there so quickly at the very moment of the feast of the preparation: for the monument was near, at fifty or sixty paces, as they say who have surveyed those places.

SECTION III. The History of the Resurrection of Christ.

Latin:

v. 42. Διὰ τὴν παρασκευὴν τῶν Ἰυδαίων) Refer ad ἔθηκαν. Festinarunt, ibi deponere nondum unctum, quod alioqui facturi, ni tempus urfisset. παρασκευὴ τῶν Ἰυδαίων di- ctum ut supra II. 6. 13. & V. 1. Ὅτι ἐγγὺς ἦν τὸ μνημεῖον) Per παρίνθεσιν legendum: quasi dicat: ne miremini ibi tam cito instante ipso puncto festæ præparationis potuisse deponi: erat enim in proximo mo- numentum, ad quinquaginta aut sexaginta passus, ut ajunt qui ea loca lustrarunt.

SECTIO III. Historia Resurrectionis Christi.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Mary Magdalene, having made a run to the sepulcher and seeing the stone rolled away, complains to Peter and the other disciple that the Lord has been taken away; as they run out to the sepulcher, the other disciple first catches sight of the linen cloths. Peter, however, having entered the sepulcher, also sees the napkin, which the other, having also entered, saw, not yet understanding the Scripture concerning the resurrection of Jesus. But to Mary, weeping before the sepulcher and looking into it, two angels appear; while she complains to them about the Lord being taken away, having caught sight of Jesus, and taking him for the gardener, she asks whither he has carried the Lord, whom she truly recognizes from his address, and is warned not to touch him, but to announce to the disciples the future ascension, which she herself reports to the disciples: but in the evening, the doors being shut, Jesus himself stood in their midst, and having prayed for peace, he shows them his hands and his side: to whom, as they rejoiced, he again gives the gift of peace, sending them, just as he himself was sent by the Father, and with his breath granted the Holy Spirit and the power of loosing and binding sins. Thomas, however, who had been absent, refused to give credence to the report of this apparition, unless he should see the print of the nails in his hands and put his hand into his side, whom, on another Sabbath, the doors being shut, the Lord, having entered to the disciples, ordered to put his finger and hands in, whence Thomas confessed him to be his Lord and his God. Jesus, however, pronounced blessed those who do not see, and believe. The cause is added for the writing of these signs out of many which were performed before the disciples, namely, that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ the Son of God, and through faith may have life in his name.

There are four parts. I. The apparition made to Mary Magdalene, to v. 18. II. The apparition made to the disciples with Thomas absent, to v. 23. III. The apparition made to the disciples for the sake of Thomas, v. 29. IV. The cause of the writing of the signs of the Lord, to v. 31.

PART I. The apparition made to Mary Magdalene.

Ver. 1.

Τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων) Which day, according to the Hebrew custom, had begun from the setting of the sun of the Sabbath.

Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ) He names one principal person for many. Thus Mark 5:2 and 46, if you compare them with Matthew.

The Evangelist speaks here of only one, because his purpose is to describe the first appearance of Christ made to Mary Magdalene; since it was made to her alone, he names her alone; furthermore, he wished to commemorate the running of Peter and the other disciple to the sepulcher, for which Mary provided the occasion.

ἔρχεται πρωὶ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης) She went out at the end of the night; she arrived when it had dawned somewhat. The diligence of the woman is shown, who, with the legitimate impediment of the Sabbath and the natural one of the night removed, allowed no time to call her to duty.

ἠρμένον ἐκ τοῦ μνημείου) Taken away from the mouth of the cave and placed aside. Matt. 28:11. Therefore ἐκ is ἀπὸ, as it is elsewhere.

Latin:

CAPUT XX.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Maria Magdalena excursu facto ad sepul- crum lapidem devolutum videns, Petro & alteri discipulo queritur Dominum ablatum esse, istis ad sepulcrum excurrentibus alter discipulus primum linteamina conspicatur. Petrus autem ingressus sepulcrum etiam sudarium videt, quod alter ingressus quoque vidit, nondum intelligentes Scripturam de resurrectione Jesu. Maria vero coram sepul- cro ploranti, idque introspicienti apparent duo angeli; quibus dum queritur de Domino ablato, Jesum conspicata, & pro hortulano habens, quærit, quorsum Dominum translu- lerit, quem vero ex compellatione agnoscit, moneturque ne ipsum attingat, sed discipu- lis annunciet ascensionem futuram, qua ipsa discipulis refert: at vesperi januis clausis, Jesus ipse stetit in medio eorum, & pacem comprecatus, ostendit ipsis manus & latus suum: quibus gaudentibus iterato pacis do- to mittens eosdem, uti ipse à Patre missus fuit, cum afflatu Spiritum S. & potestatem solvendi & ligandi peccata concessit. Tho- mas vero qui abfuerat, renuit hujus appari- tionis relationi fidem habere, nisi in mani- bus ejus fixuram clavorum viderit, atq; la- teri ejus manum suam immiserit, quem alio sabbato, januis occlusis, ad discipulos ingres- sus Dominus jussit digitum, & manus im- mittere, unde confessus ipsum Thomas est Dominum suum & Deum suum. Jesus verò beatos prædicavit eos, qui non vident, & credunt. Additur causa scriptionis horum signorum è multis, quæ coram discipulis edi- ta fuerint, ut nempe credamus, Jesum esse Christum Filium Dei, & per fidem in nomi- ne ejus vitam habeamus.

Partes sunt quatuor. I. Apparitio Mariæ Mag- dalenæ facta, ad v. 18. II. Apparitio facta discipulis absente Thoma, ad v. 23. III. Apparitio facta discipulis Thomæ gratia, v. 29. IV. Causa scriptionis signorum Domini, ad v. 31.

PARS I. Apparitio Mariæ Magdalenæ facta.

Vers. 1.

Τῇ δὲ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων) Quæ dies more Hebræo cœpe- rat ab occasu Solis sabbati.

Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ) Unam præcipuam nominat pro pluribus. Sic Marc. V. 2. & 46. si cum Matthæo conferas.

De una tantum hic loquitur Evangelista: quia propositum ei est primam apparitionem Christi Mariæ Magdalenæ factam describere: quæ cùm ei soli facta sit, eam solam nominat: adhæc voluit excursum Petri & alterius discipuli ad sepulcrum commemorare: cui occasionem Maria præbuit.

ἔρχεται πρωὶ σκοτίας ἔτι οὔσης) Fine noctis exiit: pervenit ubi non nihil illuxerat. Ostenditur mulieris sedulitas, quæ sublato impedimento legitimo sabbati & naturali noctis, nullum tempus officio vocare permisit.

ἠρμένον ἐκ τοῦ μνημείου) Ablatum ab ore specus & seorsim positum. Matth. XXVIII. 11. Ergo ἐκ est ἀπὸ ut & alibi.

## 20:2
v. 2. τρέχει ἦν) He narrates here briefly only what he will soon execute more fully. For here the occasion is reported which led Peter and John to the sepulcher; soon, how the order of the events was known in detail.

καὶ ἔρχεται πρὸς Σίμωνα Πέτρον, καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἄλλον) To all the disciples indeed, eleven in number, but in such a way that she conferred with these as if they were preeminent.

Mary Magdalene was running from the sepulcher after she had seen the empty sepulcher. For she says, they have taken away my Lord, as is held in this very verse. She did not, however, confer with these in particular; but Peter and John seem to have been excited by this news of the empty sepulcher more than the others, when the rest were little moved by it. Cf. Luke 24:12.

ἦραν τὸν κύριον ἐκ τοῦ μνημείου) A Hebraism, for the Lord has been taken away from the monument. She had indeed seen him, but had believed him to be a phantom, as others also did when she reported it, Luke 24:21, 22, 23, 24, 25.

καὶ οὐκ οἴδαμεν ποῦ ἔθηκαν αὐτόν) Where the body might have been left: on the way, or in another sepulcher.

Mary Magdalene had not yet seen the resurrected Christ when she came to the disciples. For who would have said: they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him, if she had already seen him resurrected? Certainly, when Christ saw her, he immediately manifested himself to her, v. 16, 17. How, therefore, could she doubt that she had seen the Lord himself?

Latin:

v. 2. τρέχει ἦν) Breviter hic tantum narrat quod mox exequetur fusius. Hic enim occasio refertur quæ Petrum & Johannem ad sepulcrum perduxit: mox quomodo rei ge- stæ ordo singulatim cognitus fuerit.

καὶ ἔρχεται πρὸς Σίμωνα Πέτρον, καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἄλλον) Ad omnes quidem discipulos numero undecim, sed ita ut cum his tan- quam eminentibus peculiariter sermonem conferret.

Currebat Maria Magdalena à sepulcro, post- quam sepulcrum vacuum viderat. Dicit enim, tu- lerunt Dominum meum, ut hoc ipso versu habetur. Non autem cum his sermonem peculiariter con- tulit: sed Petrus & Johannes videntur præ aliis hoc nuncio de sepulcro vacuo excitati, quum reliqui parum eo moverentur. Conf. Luc. XXIV. 12.

ἦραν τὸν κύριον ἐκ τοῦ μνημείου) Hebraismus, pro sublatus est Dominus è monumento. Viderat quidem ipsum, sed φάν- τασμα crediderat, ut & ipsa referente alii, Luc. XXIV. 21. 22. 23. 24. 25.

καὶ οὐκ οἴδαμεν ποῦ ἔθηκαν αὐτόν) Ubi relictum sit corpus: in via, an in sepulcro alio.

Nondum viderat Maria Magdalena Christum redivivum, quum ad discipulos veniret. Qui enim dixisset: tulerunt Dominum meum, & nescio, ubi posuerunt eum, si jam vidisset redivivum? Sane quum vidit ipsam Christus, eidem se statim mani- festavit v. 16. 17. Quomodo ergo dubitare poterat ipsum Dominum se vidisse?

## 20:3
v. 3. εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον) Used loosely thus: that is, within the enclosure. See what [is said] regarding Matthew.

Nay, it is necessary that they came to the tomb itself, strictly speaking: since they inspected the monument itself, having thrust their heads into the cave, as Grotius soon admits. For at v. 5 he has: καὶ παρακύψας, having thrust the head into the cave; and at v. 6 he observes that by μνημεῖον, the cave itself is understood, εἰς ἦλθεν εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον) understand μνημεῖον here as the cave itself.

Latin:

v. 3. εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον) Laxius sic dictum: id est intra se- ptum. Vide quæ ad Matthæum.

Imo ad ipsum sepulcrum pressius dictum venis- se oportet: quum monumentum ipsum, capite in specum immisso, ut mox fatetur Grotius, inspexe- rint. Nam ad v. 5. habet: καὶ παρακύψας Capite in specum intromisso; & ad v. 6. observat per μνημεῖον, speluncam ipsam intelligi, εἰς ἦλθεν εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον) μνημεῖον hic intellige ipsam speluncam.

## 20:4
v. 4. προέδραμε τάχιον τοῦ Πέτρου) Swifter in age.

Latin:

v. 4. προέδραμε τάχιον τοῦ Πέτρου) Ætate velocior.

## 20:5
v. 5. καὶ παρακύψας) Having thrust the head into the cave.

τὰ ὀθόνια) Those bandages about which [we spoke] above in the history of Lazarus.

οὐ μέν τοι εἰσῆλθεν) Through a certain youthful lack of attention.

Latin:

v. 5. καὶ παρακύψας) Capite in specum intromisso.

τὰ ὀθόνια) Fascias illas de quibus supra in Lazari historia.

οὐ μέν τοι εἰσῆλθεν) Juvenili quadam ἀπροσεξίᾳ.

## 20:6
v. 6. ἔρχεται ὖν Σίμων Πέτρος) More prudent in age, and therefore exploring everything more diligently,

he entered into the tomb) by tomb here understand the cave itself.

Latin:

v. 6. ἔρχεται ὖν Σίμων Πέτρος) Ætate prudentior, eoque diligentius omnia explorans,

εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸ μνημεῖον) μνημεῖον hic intellige ipsam spe- luncam.

## 20:7
V. 7. the face cloth) See above XI. 44. wrapped up in one place) in one place that is in its own proper and peculiar place. This so accurate arrangement of the linens removed the suspicion of theft. For thieves are in a hurry, and do not do things foreign to their purpose.

Latin:

V. 7. τὸ σουδάριον) Vide supra XI. 44. χωρὶς ἐντετυλιγμένον εἰς ἕνα τόπον) εἰς ἕνα τόπον id est loco proprio & peculiari. Hæc tam accurata collocatio linteo- rum amovebat furti suspicionem. Fures enim festinant, nec agunt aliena à suo instituto.

## 20:8
V. 8. and he saw and he believed) He believed certainly that the body was absent, which he had not believed when Mary Magdalene reported it, and about which he had doubted upon seeing the wrappings.

Latin:

V. 8. κᾀ εἶδε κᾀ ἐπίστευσεν) Credidit certo abesse corpus, quod Mariæ Magdalenæ referenti non crediderat, & de quo conspectis fasciis dubitaverat.

## 20:9
V. 9. for as yet they did not know the scripture) This is an explanatory reason for their running together, as if he were saying: John did not yet believe that that body had been restored to life, for both he and the other disciples had not yet sufficiently grasped that which Scripture had predicted concerning his resurrection. They had indeed often heard the Lord promising this, but the magnitude of the event and the slowness of their understanding stood in the way of their admitting this into their minds. Luke XXIV. 12.

the scripture) That is, the sense of the sacred writers who had indicated this under figures and types, as Ps. II. and XVI. and more openly CX. See Luke XXIV. 27.

Grotius therefore judges here that the sense of Ps. II, XVI, and CX concerns the resurrection of Christ. Which, if he snatches those words from Psalm II, 'I have this day begotten thee,' to the resurrection of Christ with the Socinians, as it appears, is by no means to be conceded: however, the request for the inheritance of the nations granted to him after the resurrection pertains to this, along with all the passages which indicate the inheritance of the nations and the dominion of Christ, and constitute him an eternal king. By which name Ps. CX also pertains to this: in which, however, it is also said that the head of Christ is to be exalted through the resurrection, after he drank from the brook in the way during his passion. But the resurrection of Christ is not wrapped up under figures and types in such prophecies, even if it is elicited by consequence from those things which were predicted there. The same thing is indeed more clearly handed down in Ps. XVI, as also in Hos. VI and XIII, and likewise Is. LIII, as shown in those places in our Anti-Grotian vindications. Concerning that 'he believed,' Theophylact notes that John believed what he had heard from the women, not indeed that Christ had risen, but that he had been taken away from the tomb. So also Augustine.

Latin:

V. 9. οὐδέπω γὰρ ᾔδεισαν τὴν γραφὴν) Est αἰτιολογικὸν τοῦ συν- τρέχειν, quasi dicat: Corpus illud vitæ redditum nondum credebat Johannes, nam & ille & discipuli alii nondum sa- tis perceperant id quod Scriptura prædixerat de ejus resur- rectione. Sæpe quidem audiverant Dominum id pollicen- tem, sed rei magnitudo, & ingenii tarditas obstabant, quo minus hoc in animum admitterent. Luc. XXIV. 12.

τὴν γραφήν) Id est sensum sacrorum scriptorum qui sub figuris & typis hoc indicaverant, ut Ps. II. & XVI. & aper- tius CX. Vide Luc. XXIV. 27.

Censet ergo hic Grotius Ps. II. XVI. & CX. sen- sum subesse de resurrectione Christi. Quod de Psalmo II. si, ut apparet, verba illa, Ego hodie genui te, ad resurrectionem Christi cum Socinianis abri- pit, minime concedendum : postulatio autem hæ- reditatis gentium ipsi post resurrectionem con- cessæ huc facit, cum omnibus locis, quæ gentium hæreditatem, & dominium Christi indicant, eum- que æternum regem constituunt. Quo nomine et- iam huc Ps. CX. facit: in quo tamen etiam exaltan- dum dicitur caput Christi per resurrectionem, post- quam de torrente in via bibit in passione sua. Non autem sub figuris & typis resurrectio Christi invo- luta est in talibus vaticiniis, etsi per consequen- tiam eliciatur ex iis, quæ ibi prædicta sunt. Lucu- lentius vero tradita eadem Ps. XVI. ut & Os. VI. & XIII. nec non Es. LIII. ut istis locis ostensum in vin- diciis nostris Anti-Grotianis. De illo ἐπίστευσεν Theophylactus notat, credidisse Johannem, quod ex fœminis audierat, non quidem Christum resurre- xisse, sed è sepulcro sublatum esse. Ita & Augustinus.

## 20:10
V. 10. The disciples therefore went away again to their own homes) the disciples, that is Peter and John. Take 'again' as above XIX. 4. they returned to the place from whence they had come. 'To their own homes' into that house into which they had turned aside: concerning which manner of speaking see above XVIII. 28.

Latin:

V. 10. Ἀπῆλθον ὖν πάλιν πρὸς ἑαυτὸς οἱ μαθηταὶ) οἱ μα- θηταὶ, id est Petrus & Johannes. πάλιν sume ut supra XIX. 4. redierunt in locum unde venerant. πρὸς ἑαυτὸς in eam domum in quam diverterant: de quo loquendi genere vide supra XVIII. 28.

## 20:11
V. 11. But Mary stood) She had stood. For we judge these things to have been said by way of a return to a previous point. See what is said on Matthew. And in that manner are those things which follow to be interpreted.

ἔξω) Outside the enclosure.

παρέκυψεν) She looked inside the enclosure. Compare Matt.

How remarkably the history is thus distorted by Grotius through an ἐπάνοδον (recapitulation), we have taught at Matthew. There is no reason why εἱστήκει should be rendered in the pluperfect, 'she had stood.' Nor is there any need for any hysteron proteron. It is implied that she was still standing, the two disciples having indeed departed. And thus it is taught that after their departure from the tomb, when Mary Magdalene remained alone at the tomb, and was standing there and weeping, and looking into the monument, she saw two angels; that this ἀγγελοψίαν (angel-vision) is the same as that which the other Evangelists reported, Grotius rashly feigns, perhaps seduced by Maldonatus; how it differs in many ways, we have clearly shown at Matthew. Hence it happened that he had to twist many things in this history, in order to support that fiction about one and the same angelic apparition, just as we warned there.

Latin:

V. 11. Μαρία δὲ εἱστήκει) Steterat. Dicta enim hæc cense- mus per ἐπάνοδον. Vide quæ ad Matthæum. Et ad eum mo- dum interpretanda quæ sequuntur.

ἔξω) Extra septum.

παρέκυψεν) Introspexit intra septum. Confer Matth.

Quam insigniter ita per ἐπάνοδον Grotii perver- tatur historia, ad Matthæum docuimus. Non est, quod reddatur εἱστήκει in plusquamperfecto, ste- terat. Neque ulla ὑστερολογία opus est. Id innuitur, quod adhuc stabat, digressis nempe discipulis duo- bus. Adeoque docetur, post eorum digressionem à sepulcro, cum sola remansit Maria Magdalena ad sepulcrum, ibique staret ac lacrymaret, & in mo- numentum introspiceret, duos angelos ipsam vi- disse, quam ἀγγελοψίαν eandem esse, quam alii Ev- angelistæ retulerunt, temere fingit Grotius, à Mal- donato forte seductus; quam multis modis differre, ad Matthæum luculenter ostendimus. Inde fa- ctum, ut multa in hac historia torquere opus ha- buerit, quo commentum istud de una eademque apparitione angelica sustineret, quemadmodum ibi monuimus.

## 20:12
V. 12. ἐν λευκοῖς) See Matt. XXVIII. 3. Rev. I. 14. περὶ τὴν κεφαλῆ ) At the part where the head had been situated. See at Matt. XXVI. 6.

ὅπου ἔκειτο τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ἰησοῦ) An explanation of what he had said about the head and feet, so that it may be understood that the place of the sitting corresponded to that place from the North to the South, as is believed.

Latin:

V. 12. ἐν λευκοῖς) Vide Matth. XXVIII. 3. Apoc. I. 14. περὶ τὴν κεφαλῆ ) Qua parte caput situm fuerat. Vide ad Matth. XXVI. 6.

ὅπου ἔκειτο τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ἰησοῦ) Explicatio ejus, quod dixerat de capite & pedibus, ut intelligatur locus sessionis ei loco respondisse à Septentrione in Austrum ut creditur.

## 20:13
V. 13. τί κλαίεις;) It is the language of those consoling: as if they were saying: there is no cause for weeping: with the addition of the reason which is read in the other Evangelists.

ἦραν) He has been taken away by thieves, perhaps for the sake of gaining the spices.

In the other Evangelists no mention is made of her weeping, nor is anything held regarding the apparition of angels made to Mary Magdalene: Matthew XXVIII. 5 mentions one angel, who said to the other women: Do not be afraid: for I know that you seek Jesus, who was crucified, he is not here, he has risen. Which are also reported by Mark chap. XVI. 5. ff. But what do these have to do with the present apparition of two angels made to Mary alone? To whom such things were not said.

πῦ ἔθηκαν αὐτὸν) As above. Compare Cant. III. 1.

Latin:

V. 13. τί κλαίεις;) Consolantium est: quasi dicant: nulla causa flendi est: addita ratione quæ apud alios Evangelistas legitur.

ἦραν) Sublatus est à furibus, aromatum forte lucrando- rum causa.

Apud alios Evangelistas nulla ploratus ejus fit mentio, nec de apparitione angelorum Mariæ Magdalenæ facta quicquam habetur: Matthæus XXVIII. 5. unum commemorat angelum, qui aliis mulieribus dixerit: Nolite timere vos: Scio enim quod Jesum, qui crucifixus est, vos quæritis, non est hic, surrexit. Quæ etiam à Marco referuntur cap. XVI. 5. seqq. Quid verò hæc ad præsentem duo- rum angelorum apparitionem soli Mariæ factam? cui talia dicta non sunt.

πῦ ἔθηκαν αὐτὸν) Ut supra. Conf. Cant. III. 1.

## 20:14
V. 14. ἐστράφη εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω) She turned her eyes from the monument to the garden, as those who are anxious are accustomed to do.

κὶ ὐκ ᾔδει ὅτι ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐστι) Full recognition was hindered for a time, as was the perception of his voice, as in Luke XXIV. 16.

Latin:

V. 14. ἐστράφη εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω) Oculos à monumento ad hortum vertit, ut solent anxii.

κὶ ὐκ ᾔδει ὅτι ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐστι) Impediebatur plenus connui- tus ad tempus, ut & vocis perceptio, ut Luc. XXIV. 16.

## 20:15
V. 15. ὁ κηπουρός ἐστι) The cultivator of that garden.

πῦ ἔθηκας αὐτὸν) Him whom you know I am seeking. It seemed very probable that the body was taken away by this person rather than by another, because no one would have freer access.

κὰγὼ αὐτὸν ἀρῦ) If this place is not for him, I will find where he may be honorably buried, lest the body of so great a man be a laughingstock to his enemies.

Latin:

V. 15. ὁ κηπουρός ἐστι) Horti illius colonus.

πῦ ἔθηκας αὐτὸν) Illum quem scis à me quæri. Valde pro- babile videbatur ab hoc potius quam ab alio ablatum cor- pus, quod nemo liberiorem haberet aditum.

κὰγὼ αὐτὸν ἀρῦ) Si hic locus illi non est, inveniam ubi honeste sepeliatur, ne tanti viri corpus inimicis sit ludibrio.

## 20:16
V. 16. Μαρία) She uttered this with a tone that would be easily recognized.

ῥαββυνί) How they were accustomed to call him, Mark 10:50; this was the Hebrew of that time.

Latin:

V. 16. Μαρία) Hoc protulit eo sono, qui facile cognosce- retur.

ῥαββυνί) Quomodo appellare eum solebant Marc. X. 50. erat hoc Hebræum illius temporis.

## 20:17
v. 17. Μὴ μου ἅπτε οὔπω γὰρ ἀναβέβηκα πρὸς τὸν πατέρα με) This passage is similar, if I judge correctly, to that in Matthew 26:29. For just as there the fruit of the vine, or wine, has one meaning in the first clause and another in the second, in which it is considered to be repeated, so here does ἅπτεσθαι. As if Jesus were saying: You wish to touch me, Mary, that is, you wish to enjoy my friendship entirely: that is not permitted now, since I only show myself to be seen economically to strengthen your faith. But when I have ascended to the Father, the time will come when you will be able to enjoy my friendship most perfectly, not by earthly contact, but by such contact as is appropriate to that place, that is, heaven, a spiritual one. Philo: 'of the power established throughout the whole body, which they specifically call touch.' Therefore, enjoyment is best indicated by the word touch. Compare Canticles 3:4.

πρὸς τὺς ἀδελφύς με) With this honorable title he now raises up the mourning disciples. See Matthew 28:10; incidentally, the very words seem to point a finger to the prophecy, Psalm 22:45.

κὰὶ εἰπὲ αὐτοῖς) Report these words of mine to them. For direct speech follows.

πατέρα με κὰι πατέρα ὑμῶν) In whom you can safely place your trust, just as I have placed mine and have been resurrected.

Latin:

v. 17. Μὴ μου ἅπτε οὔπω γὰρ ἀναβέβηκα πρὸς τὸν πατέρα με) Similis est hic locus, si quid recte judico, illi apud Matthæ- um XXVI. 29. Nam ut ibi fructus vitis sive vinum, alium ha- bet significatum in priore membro, alium in secundo in quo repetitum censetur, ita hic ἅπτεσθαι. Quasi dicat Jesus: Vis me tangere, Maria, id est, vis omnino frui amicitia mea: id nunc non licet, cum tantum οἰκονομικῶς ad fidem vestram robo- randam me do conspiciendum. At ubi ad Patrem ascenderò, veniet tempus cum frui mea amicitia perfectissime poteris, non terrestri contactu, sed tali qui loco illi id est cælo con- veniat, spirituali. Philo τῆς ἀνὰ πᾶν τὸ σῶμα συνειδρυμένης δυνά- μεως, ἧς ἰδίως ὀνομάζουσιν ἁφήν. Ideo fruitio voce tactus optime indicatur. Conf. Cant. III. 4.

πρὸς τὺς ἀδελφύς με) Hoc nunc honorifico titulo mœren- tes discipulos erigit. Vide ad Matth. XXVIII. 10. obiter ipsa verba digitum intendere videntur ad vaticinium. Ps. XXII. 45.

κὰὶ εἰπὲ αὐτοῖς) Hæc mea verba ipsis refer. Sequitur enim oratio directa.

πατέρα με κὰι πατέρα ὑμῶν) In quem fiduciam vestram tuto ponere potestis, ut ego posui & resuscitatus sum.

## 20:18
V. 18. ὅτι ἑώρακε ὁ κύριον) That she had seen someone whom she herself had believed to be the Lord. For she was doubting again whether it had been an incorporeal vision.

He undeservedly renders the faith of Mary Magdalene doubtful: as if she herself were still ambiguous and uncertain whether she had seen the Lord himself. For that she believed it was not a specter, but recognized Jesus alive again, and by the naming of Mary, v. 16, it is taught: She, having turned, says to him, Rabboni, which is called Master. And how could she doubt, when Jesus not only told her about his ascension to the Father, but also ordered these things to be reported to his brothers, the Apostles, 'I ascend to my Father,' etc.? Who will allow himself to be persuaded that she doubted whether Jesus had said these things to her, when she hurried to the disciples for this command of his, and professed that she had seen not some specter but the Lord, not whom she had thought to be the Lord, but whom she had truly recognized to be the Lord, and who had said these things himself. She reports, says Cyril, that the Lord had appeared to her, released from the bonds of death, and she heard him speaking, and brought to the disciples the first fruits of true life and the divine Gospels. Furthermore, regarding v. 18, Beza rightly says: Since in Matthew 28:9 the women, to whom Christ likewise appeared as they were hurrying to the city, are said to have grasped his feet—a gesture of worship he by no means rejected—it appears that Christ by no means simply prohibited his contact here, which he even invited his own to later, so that they would no longer doubt his true resurrection, Luke 24:39, but rather wished to gently admonish Mary so that, without delay, she would immediately set out on her way to announce what would refresh the terrified disciples. For she would still have enough space to look at and embrace him, as he would not be departing for the Father so quickly.

PART II. The apparition made to the disciples while Thomas was absent.

Latin:

V. 18. ὅτι ἑώρακε ὁ κύριον) Quod aliquem vidisset quem ipsa Dominum crediderat. Nam dubitabat iterum, annon fuisset visio incorporea.

Immerito fidem Mariæ Magdalenæ dubiam reddit: quasi adhuc ambigua & anceps ipsa fuerit, utrum Dominum ipsummet viderit. Nam quod non spectrum esse crediderit, sed Jesum redivivum agnoverit, & compellatione nominetenus facta Mariæ, v. 16. docetur: Conversa illa dicit ei, Rabbo- ni, quod dicitur Magister. Et quomodo dubitare po- terat, quum Jesus ei de ascensione ad Patrem non tantum dixerit, sed etiam fratribus suis Apostolis hæc referri jusserit, ascendo ad Patrem meum &c. Ecquis persuaderi sibi patietur, eam dubitasse, an Jesus hæc sibi dixerit, quum ad hoc mandatum ejus ad discipulos properarit, & professa ἀνυποδίκτωνῇ sit, quod vidisset non spectrum quoddam sed Do- minum, non quem putarat esse Dominũ, sed quem revera agnoverat Dominum esse, quique hæc ipse dixerit. Renunciat, inquit Cyrillus, Maria sibi visum esse Dominum mortis vinculis exolutum, & quænam eum loquentem audierit, ac discipulis veræ vitæ, divino- rumque Evangeliorum primitias pertulit. Cæterum ad v. 18. recte ita Beza: Cum Matt. XXVIII. 9. dican- tur mulieres, quibus itidem in urbem properantibus Christus occurrit, pedes ejus, hunc cultum minime repudiantis, prehendisse, apparet, Christum minime hic simpliciter prohibuisse sui contactum, quo suos et- iam postea invitavit, ne amplius de ipsius veræ resur- rectione dubitarent, Luc. XXIV. 39. sed Mariam blande commonefacere sic voluisse, ut nihil mora- ta statim sese in viam daret, annunciatura quod di- scipulos perterritos recrearet. Satis enim adhuc il- lam spatii ad illum spectandum & amplectendum habituram, ipso non tam cito ad Patrem abituro.

PARS II. Apparitio facta discipulis absente Thoma.

## 20:19
v. 19. ὔσης ἐν ὀψίας) Already late at night. See what [is said] regarding Mark and Luke.

Τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ μιᾷ τ︮ σαββάτων) On that day which he just named: therefore he repeats the designation.

κᾲ τ︮ θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων, ὅπυ ἦσαν οἱ μαθηταί συνηγμένοι) This is a designation of that which is done in secret, 2 Kings 4:4, Isaiah 26:20, Matthew 6:6, Acts 12:12, 13, 14.

It is not only designated that this apparition was made in secret, but that with the buildings left closed, without the door being opened or unbolted, Jesus suddenly and unexpectedly stood in the midst of the disciples, whence it must be that he entered through the closed doors, which Grotius himself does not deny, annotating thus on the following words.

διὰ τ︮ φόβον τ︮ Ἰυδαίων) This is to be referred to both preceding members. For the reason is given why they held nocturnal meetings, and why with closed doors: namely, lest if they held meetings by day and openly, they might stir up against themselves the hatreds of the Jews and public punishments or sedition. That meetings were often held at night for fear of the Christians is clear from Pliny and Tertullian. It appears also that they were accustomed to assemble with doors closed for a similar reason. Acts 12:13.

ἔση εἰς τὸ μέσον) He stood suddenly among them, so that it did not appear whence he had come. The Solver of Questions to the Orthodox: 'It is necessary for you to understand that things which are equivalent have the same faith when they are permitted, and have the same faith when they are removed; and it is equivalent to walk upon the sea in an immutable body, to entering to the apostles in an immutable body with the doors closed.' Cyril: 'Let no one here ask how the body of the Lord penetrated with the doors closed, when he understands that these things are written not of a naked man, as we are now, but of the omnipotent Son of God.' This was done on the seventh day after the Passover, the kind of day on which the sea had once yielded to the people of Israel, who were a figure of Christ.

See similar things regarding Christ entering through closed doors in Chrysostom, homily on Baptism; Nazianzen, in 'Christ Suffering'; Hilary, book III on the Trinity; Ambrose, sermon X on Psalm 118; Jerome, in the Epistle to Pammachius; Augustine, tractate 121 on John and sermon 121 on the seasons, and also sermon I on the resurrection, Epistles 10 and 23. Pelargus asserted this miracle from antiquity, and in his Commentary on this passage he agreed; but afterwards, having been carried off to the Calvinist camp, he went over to all other opinions.

εἰρήνη ὑμῖν) Greetings. With that voice he confirmed the fearful.

Latin:

v. 19. ὔσης ἐν ὀψίας) Iam multa nocte. Vide quæ ad Marcum & Lucam.

Τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ μιᾷ τ︮ σαββάτων) Ea die quam modo nominavit: ideo nuncupationem repetit.

κᾲ τ︮ θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων, ὅπυ ἦσαν οἱ μαθηταί συνηγμένοι) Designatio est ejus quod clam fit, 2. Reg. IV. 4. Esa. XXVI. 20. Matth. VI. 6. Act. XII. 12. 13. 14.

Non designatur tantum quod clam facta sit hæc apparitio, sed quod clausis relictis ædibus, non aper- to aut referato ostio Jesus subito & ἀπροσδοκήτως steterit in medio discipulorum, unde per clausas fores eum ingressum esse oportet, quod non diffi- tetur Grotius ipse, ad verba sequentia ita annotans.

διὰ τ︮ φόβον τ︮ Ἰυδαίων) Referendum hoc ad utrumque membrum præcedens. Causa enim redditur cur cœtus ha- buerit nocturnos, & cur clausis januis: nimirum ne si cœtus de die & palam haberent, Iudæorum odia & pœnas publi- cas aut seditionem in se commoverent. Noctu habitos sæ- pe præ metu Christianorum cœtus ex Plinio & Tertulliano liquet. Etiam januis clausis convenire solitos ob causam similem apparet. Act. XII. 13.

ἔση εἰς τὸ μέσον) Subito inter ipsos adstitit, ita ut qua venisset non appareret. Solutor quæstionum ad Orthodoxos: χρὴ δὲ ὑμᾶς ἐννοῆσαι ὅτι τὰ ἰσοδύναμα τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχει πίσιν συγχωρομένων αὐτῶν, κᾲ τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχει πίστιν ἀναιρεμένων αὐτῶν ἰσοδυναμεῖ δὲ τὸ περιπατεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν ἐν ἀτρέπτῳ σώματι, τῷ εἰσελθεῖν πρὸς τὼς ἀποσόλως ἐν ἀτρέπτῳ σώματι τῶν θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων. Cyrillus: Hic nullus quærat, quomodo clausis januis corpus Do- mini penetravit, cum intelligat non de homine nudo, ut modo nos sumus, sed de omnipotente Filio Dei hæc scribi. Factum hoc septimo die post Pascha, quali die olim mare cesserat Israe- lis populo, qui figura Christi.

Similia de Christo per fores clausas ingresso vid. apud Chrys. hom. de Baptismo, Nazianz. in Christo patiente, Hilar. l. III. de Trin. Ambros. serm. X. in Pf. CXIIX. Hier. in Ep. ad Pammach. Aug. tr. CXXI. in Joh. & serm. CXXI. de temp. nec non serm. I. de re- surr. Ep. X. & XXIII. Asseruit hoc miraculum ex antiquitate, & cum eodem Pelargus in Comment. ad h. l. Sed postea ad Calviniana castra abreptus in alia omnia ivit.

εἰρήνη ὑμῖν) Salvete Ea voce trepidos confirmavit.

## 20:20
v. 20. ἔδειξεν αὐτοῖς τὰς χεῖρας κᾲ τὴν πλευρὰν αὐτ︮) Also the feet, which Luke added, in which places were the traces of the crucifixion and the piercing.

ἐχάρησαν ὖν οἱ μαθηταὶ) Thus was fulfilled what Christ had predicted [in chapter] 16:22.

ἰδόντες τ︮ κύριον) This has emphasis. Not some image of him: but clearly him himself in the same body.

If the word τ︮ κύριον has emphasis here, why should the same emphasis not obtain in Mary Magdalene's report in v. 18?

Latin:

v. 20. ἔδειξεν αὐτοῖς τὰς χεῖρας κᾲ τὴν πλευρὰν αὐτ︮) Etiam pedes quod addidit Lucas, in quibus locis crucifixionis & transfixionis erant vestigia.

ἐχάρησαν ὖν οἱ μαθηταὶ) Ita impletum est quod Christus prædixerat XVI. 22.

ἰδόντες τ︮ κύριον) Emphasin hoc habet. Non imaginem aliquam ipsius: sed plane ipsum eodem corpore.

Si hic emphasin habet vox τ︮ κύριον, cur non in Mariæ Magdalenæ relatione v. 18. eadem emphasis obtineat?

## 20:21
v. 21. καθὼς ἀπέσταλκέ με ὁ πατὴρ) Namely, for the announcing of the Gospel. Above XVII, 18, he signifies that he has completed his mission.

κᾀγὼ πέμπω ὑμᾶς) I send you. A present tense used for the immediate future.

Latin:

v. 21. καθὼς ἀπέσταλκέ με ὁ πατὴρ) Nempe ad annuntian- dum Evang. Supra XVII, 18. significat se legatione defunctum.

κᾀγὼ πέμπω ὑμᾶς) Mitta brevi præsens pro futuri proximo.

## 20:22
v. 22. κᾲ τῦτο εἰπὼν, ἐνεφύσησε) Just as he prefigured his future passion with suitable signs, so also he prefigured the mission of the Holy Spirit, who is compared to wind in Acts II, 2. By breathing, the spirit of life was given to man. By breathing, the Holy Spirit is promised.

The origin of the Holy Spirit is also adumbrated, namely that he is the breath of the mouth of the Lord, the Son of God: no less the Spirit than the breath, or the Spirit of the mouth of God the Father. Job XXXIII, 4; Ps. XXXIII, 6; Isa. XI, 4; 2 Thess. II, 8. We cannot say, says Augustine, book IV de Trin. c. 29, that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, nor is it in vain that the same Spirit is called the Spirit of both the Father and the Son. Nor do I see what else he could have wished to signify when, breathing into their faces, he says, 'Receive the Holy Spirit'; for that bodily breath, proceeding from the body with the sensation of being touched corporally, was not the substance of the Holy Spirit, but a demonstration through a fitting sign that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father, but also from the Son.

λάβετε πνεῦμα ἅγιον) Be as certain that you will receive the Spirit as you feel this breath, Acts I, 4.

There is no reason why we should depart from the letter, and, since the Holy Spirit is said to be conferred in the present, understand it as referring to his future outpouring. For this breathing was not empty, but joined with effect; and that breath of Christ's mouth was the symbol in which, with which, and through which the Holy Spirit was given, just as the tongues of fire were such a symbol later. The sacred ministry is here committed to the Apostles, therefore the Holy Spirit is breathed into them so that we may know that the ministry is of the Spirit, and that it cannot be given without the grace of the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. XII, 11; 2 Cor. III, 8; 1 John V, 8. Therefore, just as they had already received the Spirit before for the purpose of sanctification, so now they receive him for the purpose of the evangelical ministry, being about to receive the same at the feast of Pentecost for the purpose of miraculous gifts. Cyril on this passage. Wherefore, he says, the saints indeed receive the participation of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as he also breathed on them, saying, 'Receive the Holy Spirit': for Christ cannot lie, nor would he say 'Receive' unless he were bestowing. But in the days of holy Pentecost, when God wished there to be a more express manifestation of grace and a declaration of the Holy Spirit dwelling in them, there appeared as it were fire, tongues, which did not in the least signify the beginning of the gift in them, but rather led to the beginning of speaking. It is written, therefore, that they began to speak in various tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance. Cf. Chrysostom, hom. LXXXVI on John.

Latin:

v. 22. κᾲ τῦτο εἰπὼν, ἐνεφύσησε) Sicut passionem suam futu- ram signis aptis præfiguravit, ita & missionem Spiritus S. qui vento comparatur Act. II, 2. Sufflando datus erat ho- mini spiritus vitæ. Sufflando promittitur Spiritus Sanctus.

Adumbrata etiam origo Sp. S. quod nempe spira- culum sit oris Domini, Filii Dei: non minus Spiritus, quam spiraculum, vel Spiritus oris Dei Patris. Iob. XXXIII. 4. Pf. XXXIII, 6. Ef. XI. 4. 2. Thess. XI. 8. Non possumus dicere, inquit Aug. l. IV. de Trin. c. 29. quod S. S. à Filio non procedat, neque frustra idem Spirit. & Patris & Filii Spiritus dicitur. Nec video quid aliud si- gnificare voluerit, cum sufflans in faciem ait, accipite Spir. S. neque enim flatus ille corporeus, cum sensu cor- poraliter tangendi procedens ex corpore, substantia S. S. fuit, sed demonstratio per congruam significationem, non tantum à Patre, sed & à Filio procedere Spirit. S.

λάβετε πνεῦμα ἅγιον) Tam certi este vos accepturos Spi- ritum, quam sentitis hunc flatum, Act. I. 4.

Nulla est causa cur à litera discedamus, & cum in præsenti conferri dicatur Spir. S. id intelligamus de futura ejusdem effusione. Nam non inanis fuit hæc ἐμφύσησις sed cum effectu conjuncta; & Symbolum in quo, cum quo, & per quod dabatur Sp. S. erat flatus ille oris Christi, sicut deinde Symbolum tale fuere linguæ igneæ. Committitur hic Apostolis sacrum ministerium, ideo inspiratur ipsis Spir. S. ut sciamus Spiritus esse ministerium, nec sine Spir. S. gratia id dari posse, 1. Cor. XII. 11. 2. Cor. III. 8. 1. Ioh. V. 8. uti ergo antea jam acceperant Spiritum ratione san- ctificationis, ita nunc accipiunt ratione ministerii Evangelici, accepturi eundem in festo Pentecostes ratione donorum miraculosorum. Cyrillus in h. l. Quapropter, inquit, Sancti quidem Spiritus partici- pationem accipiunt, quandoquidem & insufflavit eis, dicens, Accipite SpiritumSanctum: nec enim mentiri Christus potest, nec diceret Accipite, nisi traderet. In diebus vero sanctæ Pentecostes, cum expressiorem gra- tiæ manifestationem ac inhabitantis in iis Sancti Spi- ritus declarationem Deus esse vellet, apparuerunt tanquam ignis, linguæ, quæ doni quidem initium in iis minime significabant, sed ad loquendi potius initium deducebant. Scriptum est ergo, cœpisse loqui variis lin- guis, prout Spiritus dabat eloqui illis. Conf. Chrysost. hom. XXCVI. in Joh.

## 20:23
v. 23. ἄν τινων ἀφῆτε τὰς ἁμαρτίας) 'To forgive' is said of the Apostles in one way, and of God in another. For the one is conditional, the other is by promise. The Apostles remitted sins as often as they received those professing faith into the Church through baptism, as in Acts II, 38, 41, or as often as they received the lapsed into their communion after testimony of serious repentance, 2 Cor. II, 10. Cyprian, epistle LXXIII, rightly joined both in his interpretation of this passage.

ἀφίενται αὐτοῖς) Even before God such will be received into favor, provided the judgment has been rightly carried out. And the visible sign of this remission was the healing of diseases which had been inflicted on account of sin, James V, 14.

ἄν τινων κρατῆτε) Either by not imparting baptism, since they are unbelievers, or by excluding them from communion, as the contumacious, 1 Cor. V. Tertullian: 'It is a supreme prejudgment of the future judgment if anyone has so sinned that he is banished from the communication of prayer and assembly and all holy commerce.' See what is said on Luke VI, 22.

κεκράτηνται) God will also hold such people as alienated from his favor; and the signs of that fact will be the blindness sent upon them, Acts XIII, 11; the visible dominion of the devil over them, 1 Cor. V, 5; 1 Tim. I, 20; and other evils.

The Grotian distinction is obscure. God does not merely remit sins by promising remission, but by the very act of pardoning sins. Nor is the remission of God and of the ministers of God to be separated, because it is one action of the Principal and ministerial cause: for in the name of God the ministers of the Word remit sins, and God remits them through them, as through his ambassadors 1 Cor. IV. 1. 2 Cor. V. 20. therefore Christ says, whose sins you remit, they shall be remitted to them, and Matt. XVIII. 18. whatever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven, so that he may testify that that remission and loosing, which is by the ministers of the Word, is ratified before God. Whence Augustine in the book of homilies, last homily, says that these words are more certain than all the edicts and diplomas of Kings. This power of remitting and retaining sins from Matt. XVIII. 18. is called the power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, by which kingdom Pareus and Jansenius understand the kingdom of grace, Brentius, the blessed Ægidius Hunnius, and Mr. Dr. Sebast. Schmiedius in his disputation on the twin Keys understand the kingdom of glory, observing that after the resurrection of Christ, the Church is nowhere read to be denoted by the name of the kingdom of heaven, but only before the same, where the Church was so called on account of the visible presence of its King on earth. But he notes at the same time that it is rightly gathered from this, if those keys have the power to open and shut the kingdom of glory, how much more the kingdom of grace, so that the penitent are received into its communion, and the impenitent are excluded: but by the keys he understands the Word and Sacraments, by the application of which the kingdom of God is opened to us, John III. 5, and when they are taken away it remains shut: so that through the delivery of the keys the ecclesiastical office of teaching the Word of God and administering the Sacraments has been delivered. Conf. Ef. xxii. Regarding the metaphor of binding and loosing, he notes that the similitude is taken from the instruments of prisons, by which men are either bound in chains or loosed from chains, with this paraphrase rendered: And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and also consequently the keys of the eternal prison; and whatever you shall have bound, and shut up in prison, so that the kingdom of heaven is closed to him, that shall be bound in heaven, the kingdom of heaven closed to him: but whatever you shall have loosed from the bonds of the eternal prison, so that you open the kingdom of heaven to him, that shall be loosed in heaven, and the kingdom of heaven opened Schmied also explains how in the common designation of the key that binds and looses, those two tropes concur, a metaphor from keys and from bonds: because, namely, it is not enough for the keys of the Church to open or close heaven, but besides it is required that, because by nature men are bound, so that they cannot enter even into an opened heaven, it should loose those who are bound: and because the sins of men deserve not only the penalty of loss, which the closing of heaven signifies, but also of sense, it should bind those who are loosed. The keys, therefore, are the doctrine of the law and the Gospel, as also the Sacraments, which are the means of leading men out of the misery of sin and the penalty of sin, and introducing them into the kingdom of glory, or on the contrary excluding them from the kingdom and casting them into the prison and bonds of sin and the penalty of sins. The power of the keys, however, is taken either for the virtue which the Keys themselves have (the Word and Sacraments), or as it denotes the power and office, and that an effective (not ineffective) one, of administering the keys of the Church, by opening and closing, binding and loosing. Concerning which, see more fully the cited Disputation.

PART III. The apparition made to the disciples for the sake of Thomas.

Latin:

v. 23. ἄν τινων ἀφῆτε τὰς ἁμαρτίας) Aliter ἀφιέναι dicitur de Apostolis, aliter de Deo. Nam alterum est in conditione, alterum in promissione. Remiserunt Apostoli peccata quo- ties aut profitentes fidem per baptisma receperunt in Ec- clesiam, ut Act. II. 38. 41. aut quoties lapsos post seriæ pœ- nitentiæ testimonium receperunt in suam communionem, 2. Cor. II. 10. Utrumque in interpretatione hujus loci recte conjunxit Cyprianus epist. LXXIII.

ἀφίενται αὐτοῖς) Etiam apud Deum tales recipientur in gratiam, judicio scilicet recte peracto. Et hujus remissionis visibile signum erat sanatio morborum, qui ob peccatum inflicti erant, Iac. V. 4.

ἄν τινων κρατῆτε) Aut baptismum non impertiendo, quip- pe incredulis, aut à communione arcendo, ut contumaces 1. Cor. V. Tertullianus: Summum futuri judicii præjudicium est, si quis ita deliquerit ut à communicatione orationis & con- ventus & omnis sancti commercii relegetur. Vide quæ ad Lu- cam VI, 22.

κεκράτηνται) Etiam Deus tales à suo favore alienos habe- bit; atque ejus rei signum erunt immissa cæcitas Act. XIII. 11. Diaboli in ipsos visibile dominium 1. Cor. V. 5. 1. Tim. I. 20. & mala alia.

Obscura est Grotiana distinctio. Non remittit Deus tantum peccata remissionem promittendo, sed actu ipso peccata condonando. Neque separanda est remissio Dei, & ministrorum Dei, quia una actio est causæ Principalis & ministerialis: nomine enim Dei remittunt Verbi ministri peccata, & Deus re- mittit ea per illos, tanquam per legatos suos 1. Cor. IV. 1. 2. Corinth. V. 20. ideo Christus ait, quorum re- miseritis peccata, remittentur eis, & Matth. XVIII. 18. quicquid in terra solveritis solutum erit in cœlis, ut testetur, remissionem & solutionem illam, quæ sit à ministris Verbi, coram Deo ratam esse. Unde Augustinus l. Lib. homiliarum homil. ult. dicit, ver- ba hæc certiora esse, quam omnia Regum edicta atque diplomata. Hæc potestas remittendi & retinendi peccata è Matth. XVIII. 18. dicitur potestas clavium regni cælorum, per quod regnum gratiæ intelligunt Pareus & Iansenius, gloriæ Brentius, B. Ægid Hun- nius & Dn. D. Sebast. Schmiedius disp. de geminis Clavibus, observans, post resurrectionem Christi, no- mine regni cælorum Ecclesiam notatam esse nuspiam legi, sed solum ante eandem, ubi ita vocata sit Ecclesia ob Regis sui in terris visibilem præsentiam. Sed adver- tit simul, recte hinc colligi, si claves illæ regnum gloriæ aperire & claudere valent, quanto magis regnum gra- tiæ, adeo ut in communionem ejus recipiantur pœ- nitentes, excludantur impœnitentes: per claves vero intelligit Verbum & Sacramenta, quibus adhi- bitis aperitur nobis regnum Dei, Ioh. III. 5. ablatis clausum manet: ut ita per traditionem clavium of- ficium Ecclesiasticum docendi Verbum Dei, & ad- ministrandi Sacramenta traditum sit. Conf. Ef. xxii. De ligationis & solutionis vero metaphora notat, quod similitudo petita sit ab instrumentis carcerum, quibus homines vel in vincula constringuntur, vel è vinculis ligantur, hac reddita paraphrasi: Et dabo tibi claves regni cælorum, nec non consequenter claves æterni carceris; & quicquid tu ligaveris, carcerique incluseris, ita ut regnum cælorum illi claudatur, illud ligatum sit in cælis, regnum cælorum illi clausum: quicquid vero solveris è vinculis æterni carceris, ita ut aperias illi regnum cælorum, illud solutum erit in cæ- lis, regnumque cælorum apertum. Erudite etiam ex- ponit Dn. D. Schmied. quomodo in communi ap- pellatione clavis ligantis & solventis, duo illi tro- pi concurrant, metaphora à clavibus & à vinculis: quia sc. non sufficit claves Ecclesiæ cælum aperire, vel claudere, sed præterea requiritur, ut, quia na- tura homines ligati sunt, ut ne in apertum quidem cælum ingredi possint, ligatos solvat: & quia pecca- ta hominum non tantum damni pœnam, quam occlu- sio cæli significat, sed sensus quoque merentur, solutos li- get. Claves itaque ipsi sunt doctrina legis, & Evange- lii, ut & Sacramenta, quæ sunt media educendi ho- mines è miseria peccati & pœnæ peccati, & intro- ducendi in regnum gloriæ, aut contra excludendi à regno & conjiciendi in carcerem & vincula pec- cati & pœnæ peccatorum. Potestas autem clavium vel pro virtute accipitur, quam ipsæ Claves ha- bent, (Verbum & Sacramenta) vel ut notet potestas clavium potestatem & officium idque efficax (non in- efficax) administrandi claves Ecclesiæ, aperiendo & occludendo, ligando & solvendo. De quibus plenius vid. laudata Disputatio.

PARS III. Apparitio facta discipulis Thomæ gratia.

## 20:24
v. 24. one of the twelve) Thus after the death of Theramenes those who ruled Athens were called the thirty, Xenoph. l. II. was not with them, when Jesus came) Occupied with some business, as is credible. Therefore, when the eleven are named, it is to be understood that this was the name of the college after Judas was removed, as it was before twelve. See Matt. XXVIII. 16.

Latin:

v. 24. εἷς ἐκ τῶν δώδεκα) Sic post mortem Theramentis ii qui Athenas regebant, vocabantur οἱ τριάκοντα Xenoph. l. II. οὐκ ἦν μετ᾿ αὐτῶν, ὅτε ἦλθεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς) Negotio aliquo, ut credibile est, occupatus. Itaque cum undecim nominantur, intelligendum est id post Judam sublatum collegii fuisse nomen ut ante duodecim. Vide Matth. XXVIII. 16.

## 20:25
v. 25. we have seen the Lord) Without doubt they recounted the whole history of the matter in a more ample discourse: But it sufficed for John to hand down the summary.

if I do not see in his hands the print of the nails) The condemned were accustomed to be fixed to the cross with nails. This is called being nailed by the Greeks, to which Paul alluding uses the same word in Col. II. 14. Hence to Apuleius: The fleshy nails of those hanging. And Seneca alluding to this: When they attempt to unfix themselves from their crosses, onto which each one adds his own nails. Lucan said: the steel inserted into the hands: but typos is a Greek word, but one which later Hebrews also use. But this word is used quite properly in this place. Thus Pliny: for whom the impressed clay made a type: there is in Plato, a type is impressed. and I put my finger into the place of the nails) I think this is the true reading, which the Latin followed, and that most ancient manuscript in England shows, and that it is wrongly repeated as typos in others. It seems to be typoi: it is filled by topoi. The Syrian, however, in both places reads place, which likewise I do not approve.

Nor is that to be approved, that he corrects all other codices from one Manuscript. For how much is to be attributed to the Latin, Grotius himself has already declared more than once. Thomas had said before the place of the nails, which he wished both to view with his eyes, and to fill by inserting his finger. Typos is the trace of a wound impressed by nails. By Augustine it is called a scar. Why could a finger not be inserted into such a trace or wound, since the nails were not small?

and I put my hand into his side) For he had learned the whole history of the passion from John and others: and he aptly destines his finger for the smaller wound, his hand for the larger.

that I may not believe) I will not believe that he himself has risen, rather I will think the eyes of all were deceived: that a phantom had appeared. See Luke XXIV. 37.

Latin:

v. 25. ἑωράκαμεν έ Κύριον) Haud dubie ampliori sermone totam rei historiam exsecuti sunt: At Iohanni suffecit sum- mam tradere.

εἰ μὴ ἴδω ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν ἀυτῶ τὸν τύπον τῶν ἥλων) Solebant damnati clavis ad crucem figi. Id προσηλοῦσθαι dicitur Græcis, quo alludens Paulus eadem voce utitur Col. II. 14. Hinc A- pulejo: Carnosi clabi pendentium. Et huc Seneca alludens: Cum refigere se crucibus suis conentur, in quas unusquisque cla- vos suos adjicit. Insertum manibus chalybem, dixit Lucanus: τύπος autem vox Græca est, sed qua & Hebræi posteriores utuntur. Proprie autem admodum hæc vox hoc loco usur- patur. Sic Plinius: quibus impressa argilla typum fecit: ἐνδύε- ται τύπῳ est apud Platonem, imprimitur typus. κὴ βάλω τὸν δάκτυλόν μυ εἰς τὸν τόπον τῶν ἥλων) Puto ve- ram esse hanc lectionem, quam secutus est Latinus, & o- stendit vetustissimus ille in Anglia manuscriptus, & male apud alios repeti τύπον. τύπῳ videtur: τόπῳ impletur. Sy- rus autem utroque loco legit τόπον, quod itidem non probo.

Nec id probandum, quod ex uno Manuscripto omnes alios codices corrigit. Quantum enim La- tino tribuendum sit, jam ipse non semel edixit Grotius. ἗ τόπον τῶν ἥλων antea dixerat Thomas, quem & oculis usurpare volebat, & digito immisso adimplere. τύπος est vestigium vulneris ex clavis impressum. Augustino cicatrix dicitur. Quidni digitus immitti in tale vestigium vel vulnus possit, quum non exigui fuerint clavi?

κὴ βάλω τὴν χεῖρά μυ εἰς τὴν πλευρὰν ἀυτῶ) Omnem enim passionis historiam ex Johanne atque aliis didicerat: & apte minori vulneri digitum, majori manum destinat.

ὁ μὴ πιστεύσω) Non credam, ipsum resurrexisse, potius deceptos putabo omnium oculos: phasma apparuisse. Vide Luc. XXIV. 37.

## 20:26
v. 26. After eight days) The disciples seem to have experienced the presence of the Lord once on the day of the resurrection, and to have dedicated the same day thereafter to solemn assemblies. Acts XX. v. 7. 1 Cor. XVI. 2. Hence it is called the Lord's day, Rev. I. 10.

Jesus comes when the doors were shut) He repeats all things which he had once done, for the sake of Thomas, giving an example of condescension, concerning which see Rom. XV. 1.

Latin:

v. 26. Μεθ᾽ ἡμέρας ὀκτὼ) Videntur discipuli semel resur- rectionis die Domini experti præsentiam, eundem diem in posterum solennibus conventibus dicasse. Actor. XX. v. 7. 1. Cor. XVI. 2. Hinc dicta ἡμέρα κυριακὴ, Apoc. I. 10.

ἔρχεται Ἰησοῦς έ θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων) Omnia quæ semel fecerat, iterat in Thomæ gratiam, exemplum dans συγκα- ταβάσεως, de qua vide Rom. XV. 1.

## 20:27
v. 27. Reach your finger here) He repeats the words of Thomas, so that he may show himself omniscient,

Βάλε εἰς τὴν πλευράν με) I think Thomas did exactly what Christ commanded, and then exclaimed. And here I would refer to that 1 John 1:1, ὃ ἐθεασάμεθα, καὶ αἱ χεῖρες ἡμῶν ἐψηλάφησαν. Tertullian, against Praxeas: He was both heard and seen, and so that he might not be believed to be a phantom, he was even touched.

κὴ μὴ γίνε ἄπιστος) Unbelief has something of the voluntary in it.

πιστός) This word signifies faithful or constant to the Greeks. But to us it also signifies him who believes, and πιστεύοντα. Therefore here we see it opposed to ἀπίστῳ, as also in 2 Cor. 6:5, and it occurs often in this sense: as Acts 10:45, 15:1, 1 Tim. 4:3, 10, 12, 5:16, 6:2.

Latin:

v. 27. Φέρε τὸν δάκτυλόν συ ὧδε) Repetit Thomæ verba, ut se omniscilum ostendat,

Βάλε εἰς τὴν πλευράν με) Omnino quod jubet Christus fecisse Thomam puto, & tum exclamasse. Et huc referam illud 1. Joh. I. 1. ὃ ἐθεασάμεθα, καὶ αἱ χεῖρες ἡμῶν ἐψηλάφησαν. Tertullian. adversus Praxeam: Ipse & auditus & visus, & ne phantasma crederetur etiam contrectatus.

κὴ μὴ γίνε ἄπιστος) Incredulitas aliquid habet de volun- tario.

πιστός) Haec vox Graecis fidelem aut constantem signifi- cat. At nostris etiam eum qui credit, & πιστεύοντα. Itaque hic videmus opponi ἀπίστῳ, ut & 2. Cor. VI. 5. & hoc sensu saepe occurrit: ut Act. X. 45. XV. 1. 1. Tim. IV. 3. 10. 12. V. 16. VI. 2.

## 20:28
v. 28. ὁ Κύριός με) The nominative for the vocative: which is frequent among the Attics, but also among the Hellenists, as appears in this word in Psalm 35:23, Mark 15:34, and in another of the same sense in Psalm 30:1, 35:23. Thus by this word Thomas shows that he wishes to obey him.

Vossius, book III of the Harmony of the Gospels, ch. IV, rightly refuted Theodore of Mopsuestia, who wanted it to be a figurative expression by way of exclamation, i.e., O immortal God! What do I see? What do I touch? Whose opinion, although condemned by the Fifth Council of Constantinople, Act III, ch. II, and in the Edict of the Emperor Justinian on the profession of faith, has nevertheless been resurrected from the dead by the Neo-Photinians, whose mouths we have stopped elsewhere. Vossius notes, however, that it is not so much an Attic usage here of the nominative for the vocative, as it is from emotion, because Thomas used a truncated speech, and it is not clearly said: You are the Lord, You are my God.

κὴ ὁ Θεός με) Here for the first time this word is found in the Gospel narrative attributed to Jesus by the Apostles, after he had clearly proven by his resurrection that he was the one from whom life, and indeed eternal life, ought to be expected. See above 11:25. That custom then remained in the Church, as appears not only in the Apostolic writings, such as Rom. 9:5, and those of the ancient Christians, as can be seen in Justin Martyr against Trypho, but also in Pliny's letter to Trajan, where he says that Christians sang hymns to Christ as to a God.

Satis jejune illa confessio That confession of Thomas, ὁ Κύριός με, is explained quite dryly, as if Thomas had only testified by it that he wished to obey Christ; and the ecclesiastical custom is not spoken of with sufficient piety, because Christ is called God. Here Thomas issued a confession of his faith, after he was no longer an unbeliever, but πιστὸς or πιστεύων, concerning Christ, that he acknowledges him as his Lord and as his God: both of which words, when used by the faithful, denote the one only God: For every believer acknowledges this one as his Lord and as his God, and the name Κύριος corresponds for the interpreters to the word יהוה, but the name Θεὸς to the word אלהים, as we have expressly taught in our treatise on natural and revealed theology. He confesses, therefore, that Christ is truly God by nature. Porro in N. T. Furthermore, in the New Testament the word Κυρίε is accustomed to be used peculiarly of Christ, especially with the pronoun of application, because he is our Lord, not only by right of creation, but also of redemption, who acquired us for himself as a peculiar possession, indeed by reason of government, dominion, and rule, which he himself as God has by his own nature, but as man indeed by another, namely by the grace of the hypostatic union and of his exaltation to the right hand of God, Acts 2:36, Phil. 2:11, whom it behooves us not only to obey with true confidence of heart, but who also rules, protects, cherishes, and guards us by his grace unto eternal glory. Thomas professes all these things about Christ with true faith. But we have dealt with this confession of his against the Socinians more fully elsewhere. Whence these; because hitherto they lie as ἀνέκδοτα in our archives, it will not be irksome to repeat them here for the sake of vindicating an illustrious confession, especially because Neo-Arians are also striving to obscure this confession of Thomas in ways that are altogether unworthy: which was also recently done by Christ. Sandius. Now Thomas calls Christ Κύριον & Θεὸν with the article, which the Socinians allege as a mark, since indeed ὁ Θεὸς occurs, for the signification of the supreme God. See Socin. against Wujeck, page 375. Crellius on the divine attributes, p. 96. Con- he confesses the same as his Lord and his God, which is a word of trust, and teaches him to place all the trust of his heart in Christ, and to trust in the same as God: whence it is added by Christ: Because you have seen me Thomas, YOU HAVE BELIEVED, Blessed are they who do not see and BELIEVE. Thomas knew well τὴν πρώτην πασῶν τῶν ἐντολῶν, which was both repeated and inculcated by Christ, Hear Israel, Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν Κύριος εἷς ἐστι, The Lord our God is one Lord, and you shall love Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου, the Lord your God with all your heart, &c. Deut. VI. v. 4. Mark XII. v. 29. 30. And yet he confesses λευκάδι φωνῇ Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου, that Christ is his Lord and his God. What else was this, than that he acknowledged him to be his ONE LORD? Since our Lord God is ONE LORD? And what is the difference between that Davidic address Ps. XXXIV. 23. attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, and this one of Thomas, my God, and my God. If therefore in that place by the words my God, and my Lord, that one God is denoted, as it is confessed to be denoted, why should not also here by the very same address my Lord, and my God, that one God be denoted.

Regarding this so clear confession of the Deity of Christ, the adversaries have sought various loopholes to escape. I. Enjedinus in explicat. locor. p. 249. denied in these words that Thomas addressed Christ, and called him his Lord and his God, because he saw well that this address befits none but the true God by nature. He feigns therefore that, full of terror and astonishment, and as if rapt out of himself, he exclaims in a manner customary to men, My Lord and my God, and thus at least signifies an unusual thing and his own extreme admiration, just as the Greeks are accustomed to say great Gods, the Latins, great Gods, good Gods, as can be seen in Heliodorus, Catullus, Terence, and the common people when they see something wonderful, exclaim Jesus, Mary, &c.

In this opinion Sandius in Interpret. Paradox. p. 257. also praises Theodore of Mopsuestia, and strives to defend his little exception against Bellarmine. The Nestorians, he says (denying with Paul of Samosata and Photinus that Christ is the true God) said that these words were referred to the Father by an exclamation of Thomas admiring the resurrection of Christ, as is clear from the V. Synod ch. 8. and 12. Theodore of Mopsuestia, and the confession which Thomas made, when he had touched the hands and side of the Lord after the resurrection, saying: My Lord and my God, he says, was not said by Thomas about Christ: for Theodore does not say that Christ is God; but that at the miracle of the resurrection, the astonished Thomas glorified God, who raised up the Lord. To this indeed Bellarmine replies, that in the Greek there is not written ὦ the sign of an exclamation but the article. But the Nestorians could again respond to Bellarmine, Mark XV. 34. that Christ says by exclamation, My God, my God, and Matt. XXVII. 46. Eusebius dem. Evang. X. 8. reads: God my God &c. Thus Ps. XXI. 1. God my God, why have you forsaken me. 2. My God I will cry out by day, XXVII. 1. My God, do not be silent from me. XLV. 8. your throne O God &c. 9. therefore God your God has anointed you. LXXIII. 11. how long shall the enemy reproach O God, and infinite others. These are the words of Sandius. And that this interpretation is true, Enjedinus says it appears even from this, that at that time nothing such was seen by Thomas in Christ, from which he could gather that Christ is God. For the resurrection is accustomed to procure the opinion of divinity not for him who rose, but for the one who raised him: indeed it is certain among all, that God does not die, and therefore has no need of resurrection.

Furthermore II. Franc. David contends that those words can be referred to the Father in this sense: My Lord and my God, how stubborn and incredulous I was, because I did not acquiesce to your word and promise concerning the raising of your Son from the dead, and also to the witnesses, my fellow disciples; because of this my incredulity I would be worthy of punishment; as Socinus reports in Epist. p. 189. III. There were besides, as the same Socinus reports p. 191. who said that there is indeed an ellipsis in the words of Thomas, but that they should be taken in the nominative, not the vocative case, in this or a similar sense, My Lord and my God be praised, who makes me see those things which, although I desired them greatly, I could not bring my mind to believe had happened, and as Socinus confesses ibid. l. c. Nor were there lacking those who indeed confessed that Christ was called God by Thomas, but not rightly. Which opinion, however, Svevius acknowledged to be so foul and impious, that it was held unworthy to be refuted by Erasmus and Gvaltherus.

IV. Enjedinus, however, having granted that these words were directed to Christ, denies that it follows that Christ is the eternal and omnipotent God: since there are many Lords and Gods both in heaven and on earth, 1 Cor. VIII. v. 6. Socinus, however, V. objects in Antivyujek, page 260, that the article in this place does not have the force of signifying the one God because of the pronoun με added to the name ὁ Θεὸς. VI. That the article can be taken in such a way as if it were an adverb of calling, and the name God had been uttered in the vocative case, or as if ὁ Θεὸς had been uttered in the vocative case without any adverb, as in Mark XV. v. 34. VII. That it is hinted by these words that Christ is not only Lord, but a divine Lord, whom he ought to worship and in whom he ought to trust. That Thomas was not only a Jew but also a Christian, and therefore acknowledged not only that one God of Israel, but also Christ the man as his God, that is, as a King given to him by that one God, full of divine power, from whom eternal salvation was to be sought, and whom he ought to treat with divine worship. Johann Crellius repeats most of Socinus's trifles in his book On God and His Divine Attributes, chapter 13, p. 100. That Thomas used the nominative for the vocative, or if his words are even taken in such a way, 'You are my Lord and my God': just as some interpreters have translated, the force of the article is diminished because of the added particle με 'my': but if, finally, it must be granted that it has some force, it is consistent that Thomas, when he saw Christ resurrected by God, wished to say that he is that Lord who had been promised by God to the Israelite people, who is to benefit that nation significantly, and is to liberate it from servitude, and that he could or ought to call him not only his Lord, but also his God: and thus the article would be anaphoric, which refers the mind to a certain, internally known thing. We read similar things in Socinus in his Animadversions on the Posnanian Assertions, p. 56, Defense of the Animadversions, p. 417, Schmaltz's Refutation of the book on the Errors of the Arians, p. 180, Volckel's On True Religion, p. 423, and elsewhere passim.

These cracks, sought in vain, are easily stopped: As to I. the invention of Enjedinus, or rather of Theodore of Mopsuestia, who is its first author, it is worthy of its authors, and reveals the most devilish nature of these men in perverting the most clear sayings of Scripture. For first, no example of such admiration in an unusual matter is held in the sacred writings, especially where not the sign of an exclamation, but the article occurs. For Enjedinus had need to shake out the cabinets of Heliodorus, Catullus, and Terence, finding nothing in the Scriptures. He wished to adjust the holy confession of Thomas to the custom of those authors and of common Christians, so that there might not be lacking that which he might answer. The things which Sandius brings forward from Scripture are ἀλλότρια, Mark XV. v. 34 is not an exclamation of one wondering, but a sigh of one praying, from Psalm XXII. v. 1. it is held. Which must also be said of Psalm XXVII. v. 1, Psalm XLV. v. 8 & LXXXIV. v. 10, likewise there is no exclamation of one wondering, but an address to God in the nominative case, concerning which a little later. Furthermore, not even among gentile writers are examples found, since exclamations of such a kind are not expressed with an article and nominative, but in the vocative, or even with an interjection and vocative, as the examples brought forward by Enjedinus teach, and is known by itself. If the adversaries say: The nominative is here used for the vocative: examples will have to be brought forward by them, where in exclamations made out of wonder this has come into use, and indeed with the article employed, so that it corresponds to the ὦ of the one exclaiming. It is indeed customary in an address for the nominative to be used for the vocative, but in such a way the article takes on the force of one addressing and calling, but not of one exclaiming, which can be seen in Psalm LIX. v. 1, Psalm LX. v. 1, Psalm LXIII. v. 1, Luke XVIII. v. 13. Compare Luke VIII. 54, Eph. VI. v. 1. That this also happens in Matt. XV. v. 34 is manifest, where likewise it has the force of addressing, but not of exclaiming out of wonder. Thirdly, it is too manifest that Thomas is not here exclaiming to God the Father, but addressing Christ, because it is expressly said that he answered Christ, and said these things to him: My Lord and my God, ἡ ἀπεκρίθη ὁ Θωμᾶς, ἡ εἶπεν αὐτῷ. Thomas answered and said: to whom indeed if not to Christ? Enjedinus twists himself here, and invents that this formula of speaking HE SAID TO HIM means the same thing in sacred writings as he said after his words, or having heard his words, Luke XIV. v. 16, John XIV. v. 22, 23. But that he said it after his words, or having heard his words, the Evangelist had already hinted with the word ἀπεκρίθη he answered, now however he indicates to whom he directed the words, he said to him.
