Nor does anything else appear from Luke XIV. 16, John XIV. v. 22, 23 than that by the force of the words he said to him, the words were directed to him who had spoken before, even if others (which is accidental to the sense of these words) were present, and at the same time the words were spoken to them in such a way. Here, however, those words, My Lord and my God, even if spoken in the presence of others, were nevertheless directed to Christ alone, to whom John reports that Thomas said these things. Franc. David objects that some copies do not have and he said to him, but simply, and he said. But Socinus himself answers him in his Epist. page 186. That different reading does not exist, neither in any approved codex, nor in any approved writer: And it is enough that it is said: Thomas answered, because no one answering speaks with another, or directs words to another than to him to whom, or to whose words he answers, especially if he had spoken to him before, and had directed his words to him. Fourthly, Christ had exhorted Thomas: be not faithless, but believing: now indeed Thomas testifies that he believes by this confession of his, he does not exclaim full of terror and stupor, and as if snatched out of himself. What of the fact that Christ himself bears witness to his faith, because you have seen, you have believed. Therefore he accepted his words not as a voice of stupor and terror, but as a confession of faith. Which without doubt moved the adversaries, Socinus, Smalzius, Volckelius, as also Theoph. Nicolaides against Albert. Borckovsky de Eccl. c. 8. and others, to reject the gloss of Enjedinus, and to acknowledge that Christ was addressed by Thomas, and indeed with the interpreter Smalzius against Franz. disp. 12. they held the refuted explanation of Enjedinus to be MOST ABSURD: which Socinus also refutes (although with the name suppressed) in his Epist. p. 191. with these two arguments: First that it would not have been said thus, and Thomas answered. Then that no example of such an exclamation is brought forward from the Holy Scriptures.

The reason which he brings forward for confirming his opinion. Enjedinus is brought forward also by other adversaries, who nevertheless reject the opinion of Enjedinus; and it is more opposed to our interpretation than accommodated to the confirmation of the depravation of Enjedinus. We deny, however, what is assumed, that nothing had been seen by Thomas from which he could gather that Christ was God: since Christ himself brings forward that he believed because he had seen. And Thomas saw entirely and acknowledged, while he saw Christ alive from the dead, that the same is truly the Messiah, that is, truly God, Psalm XLV. 8, Jehovah, Jer. XXIII. v. 6, and by the very work had fulfilled what he had predicted John II. v. 19 and what he had testified John X. 18. But if he who is raised from the dead is gathered to be the true God, could Thomas not conclude from this that Christ is the true God, because he saw that he himself had raised the temple of his body, and had resumed his soul: even if he acknowledged the same to be true man, in which part he was both dead and raised.

II. To the distortion of Franc. David, Socinus himself answers, whom we produce from the loc. cit. p. 189, since the book is held by few. This interpretation of yours, he says, can in no way be sustained, first, because John could not have said simply that Thomas answered, if he had directed his words to another than to Jesus, who had addressed him. Then, because you will find no example of such an ellipsis in the whole Scripture, but perhaps not even in another approved author. Furthermore, since Christ immediately says to the words brought forth by Thomas: Because you have seen, Thomas, you have believed, no one can doubt that it was openly evident from the very words of Thomas that he had already believed. And, if those things are referred to God the Father, that can in no way be evident, since they explain no sentence, and various things can be understood, indeed such things as demonstrate that Thomas neither believed nor wished to believe. For thus someone could supply those words: My Lord and my God, do not permit that I be deceived by these illusions, and that I believe that which is not to be believed. But if it is referred to Christ, all things are plain. These things Socinus.

To III. Response. That ellipsis is entirely arbitrary, supported neither by examples from Scripture nor by any reason. But if an ellipsis of such a kind is to be established or introduced at will, a sense could be affixed to certain words of Scripture. Add that such a fiction is contradicted by the very express words. For it is said that Thomas answered, and said to him, that is to Christ: and not that he celebrated God the Father by a prayer directed to God. Nor did Christ accept the words of Thomas otherwise than as a confession of faith, as is manifest from his response subjoined. Socinus admits from this that it is certain that those words are to be referred to Christ, and that it must be concluded altogether that Christ was called God in those words of Thomas, and indeed with the best right, and not only God, but our God, l. c. p. 192. And he says that the passage at John XIII. 13, ὁ διδάσκαλος ᾄ ὁ Κύριος, is very similar to this place. For just as they acknowledged (these are the words of Socinus concerning the disciples of Christ) and confessed him as Lord, so Thomas, saying to Christ: My Lord and my God, acknowledged and confessed him as his Lord and God. He says, however, that the passage at Tob. VII. 2, εἶπεν αὐτῷ, ὁ τῦ καλῦ ᾄ ἀγαθῦ ἀνθρώπε υἱός, is clearly most similar, and one which could serve for an open explanation of this.

Just as, therefore, Tobias is there manifestly recognized and named by Raguel as the son of an honest and good man, so also here is Christ recognized and named by Thomas as his Lord and his God. Thus far Socinus, whose conclusion is held as valid by all who follow his other tenets.

To (IV.) Response. This confession of Thomas having been obtained and conceded, it is inferred quite invincibly that Christ was recognized as the eternal and omnipotent God, because there is no other God except one, namely that eternal and omnipotent God, as the Apostle testifies in the cited passage, 1 Corinthians 8:4. Although he says there are many gods and many lords, he speaks openly, however, of the so-called lords, who are called such and are gods only in name, and he removes Christ from that same class as that one Lord through whom all things exist, and we through him; and therefore it is only impiously that Christ is referred into the order and census of those many lords and gods.

Regarding (V.) Socinus's exception concerning the article, our demonstration relies not only on the emphasis of the article but also on the evidence of the matter, that there is no God but one, and that neither Thomas nor any other of Christ's disciples recognized, nor ought to have recognized, any other God of his than Jehovah, the one God, whom they were bound by the force of the first commandment to trust with their whole heart, and whom alone they were bound to love with their whole soul. That the pronoun 'my' added does not detract from the emphasis of the article, nor diminish the appellation of God, we have already made plain in Natural and Revealed Theology, chapter 3, page 483 et seqq. Nay, this pronoun confirms for us that the one God is understood. Because nowhere in the Holy Scriptures is the God of any of the faithful called anything except that one God. Whence the invincible inference: the God of the faithful is that one God; but Christ is the God of the faithful, which is established by the example and confession of Thomas, who was already a believer. The major premise, as I have said, is evident from an induction of passages: What is more solemn in the Holy Scriptures than that that one God is described in such a way that He is the God of the faithful? Thus God is called OUR GOD, Luke 1:78, 1 Thessalonians 2:2, chapter 3:9, 2 Thessalonians 1:11-12, Hebrews 12:29, 1 Peter 1:1, Revelation 5:10, chapter 7:3, 10, 12, chapter 12:10, 16, chapter 19:15. YOUR GOD, Mark 12:29, John 8:54, chapter 10:27, Acts 2:39, chapter 3:22, chapter 4:19, chapter 7:37, or their own, 2 Corinthians 6:16, Hebrews 2:16, Revelation 21:3. The pronoun 'your' is also added to the name God when the discourse is about the one God, Matthew 4:7, 10, chapter 22:37, Mark 12:30, Luke 4:8, 12, chapter 10:27, Hebrews 1:9. Likewise this very pronoun 'my', Matthew 27:45, Mark 5:34, John 20:17, Romans 1:8, 1 Corinthians 1:4, chapter 14:18, 2 Corinthians 12:21, Philippians 1:3, chapter 4:19, Philemon 1, Revelation 3:12. And what is more frequent than that that one God is called the God of Israel, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, the God of the Fathers, the God of the people? Likewise the God of the holy Prophets, Revelation 21:6; what doubt can there be that this is the same God of Thomas? Socinus compares in his Epistle, p. 189, with this reasoning of ours in this place, the phrases of Psalm 5:2, 'Attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God,' and Psalm 34:23, 'Arise and attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord,' and (so that there may be a passage exactly corresponding to this one of ours, where indeed the name of Lord is placed before the name of God) Revelation 4:last, 'Worthy art Thou, O Lord, our God, the Holy One, to receive,' etc. Therefore, just as there is no doubt that in those places by the expression 'my God and my Lord,' and likewise 'our Lord and God,' that one true God is understood, so it is also absolutely necessary to understand that one true God here, when Thomas says, 'My Lord and my God,' since the phrases are exactly the same, and the passages correspond to each other exactly; for the judgment is the same for similar things, and one should not rashly depart from the customary and proper meaning of words, which Socinus himself warns here on page 188.

To (VI.) Response. Even if 'the God' is admitted as being said in the sense of calling, the force of the word God is not thereby infringed so as not to designate that one God. For what? Is not the one God indicated when 'the God' or even 'my God' is addressed in the vocative case, Matthew 15:34, Luke 18:11, 13, Revelation 4:last, chapter 11:17, chapter 15:3, chapter 16:7, etc.? Certainly, a mere change of case cannot by itself do anything to diminish the power of the name of God. But nowhere is God addressed in this manner, 'the God,' or even with the added pronoun 'my' or 'our' or a similar addition, without that one true God being always and everywhere understood. Whence it is again invincibly concluded that that one true God is understood, whom Thomas addresses as 'my God.' The antecedent is established from the induction of passages, both of the Old Testament: Numbers 12:13, Judges 16:28, 1 Kings 8:23, 25, 26, 28, 1 Chronicles 17:17, Psalm 3:8, and chapter 5:3, and chapter 7:2, 4, 10, and chapter 10:12, Psalm 34:73, etc., and likewise of the New, Matthew 15:34, Luke 18:11, 13, Revelation 4:last, chapter 11:17, chapter 15:3, chapter 16:7. What if Socinus does not so much refuse to accept the words of Thomas's confession in the nominative case, but at least warns that, even if they are taken in the nominative case as referring to Christ, it is clearly the same confession of the Deity of Christ and the recognition of Him? Nay, what is more straightforward, says Socinus in the cited place, page 192, than to simply understand the substantive verb, as they call it, without any true ellipsis or unusual and uncertain interpretation? In this way, indeed, the sense emerges here: You are my Lord and my God. With this sense standing, it is most evident that the name 'God' is attributed to Christ with the article, and therefore, by the force of the rule of the Socinians themselves, it must be concluded that Christ is that one God.

To (VII.) Response. That explanation is too meager, that Christ is hinted at as a divine Lord. For the Apostle does not confess a divine Lord, but his Lord and his God. Nowhere in the Scriptures is GOD the same as divine. Nowhere does the God of this or that believer, the God of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, or the God of Israel denote a divine man; always and everywhere it denotes that one God, just as the adversaries themselves confess that the God of Israel is that one God. Moreover, the God of Thomas is the same as the God of Abraham, the Father of believers, who is the God of Israel, and not one God and then another, since there is no other God except one even in the New Testament, 1 Cor. 8:4, and that divine axiom is diligently repeated by Christ, Mark 12:29, Hear O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord, and this in such a way that we are commanded to worship that one God religiously. That the Christian religion is different from the Jewish in that, besides that one God of Israel, we ought to worship another who is by nature a mere man, is an impious Socinian fiction, the falsity of which we have demonstrated expressly, as they say, in our assertion of the divine monarchy, Theol. Nat. & Revel. chap. IV.

Nor indeed does this Thomas here profess Christ the King as given by that one God, full of divine power: and he professes him his Lord and his God, and consequently that one true God. Because no one is properly called by the name of God in the Scriptures, unless the one God, nor is God of the faithful, or with the pronoun my, your, our, etc., related to the faithful, indicated anywhere in the whole Scripture, unless Jehovah, the true God by nature, much less is anyone distinguished or addressed by these combined names, my Lord and my God, except the one and only supreme God, as for instance Ps. XXXIV. 23. Apoc. IV. last, etc. Finally, if it be granted that the article is anaphoric in this place, and designates the Lord or that God whose coming was promised to the Israelite people, yet he must be understood not as a mere benefactor and liberator from servitude, but as Jehovah, the true and only God, since the coming of Jehovah himself (which name is accustomed to be expressed by the word Κύριος in the New Testament) and of the God of Israel was promised, as can be read throughout Jer. XXIII. 6. Zach. II. 10. Wherefore there can be no doubt that he was also Thomas's God, and was held by him as his God. And these things for the present concerning the confession of Thomas.

Latin:

v. 28. ὁ Κύριός με) Nominativus pro Vocativo: quod frequens Atticis, sed & Hellenistis, ut in hac voce apparet Psal. XXXV. v. 23. Marci XV. 34. & in alia sensus ejusdem Psal. XXX. 1. XXXV. 23. Sic hac voce ostendit Thomas se ei parere velle.

Vossius l. III. Harm. Evang. c. IV. merito redar- guit Theodor. Mopsvestanum, qui volebat, figura- tum esse sermonem per exclamationem, q. d. o Deum immortalem! quid video? quid tango? Cujus sen- tentia, etsi damnata Synodo Constantinopolitano V. Act. III. c. II. & in Edicto Justiniani Imperatoris de professo fidei; ex inferis tamen resuscitata est a Neo-Photinianis, quibus alibi os obstipavimus. Notat autem Vossius, non tam Atticissmum hic esse posito nominativo pro vocativo, quam ab affectu es- se, quod trunca oratione usus sit Thomas, nec clare dicatur: Tu Dominus, Tu Deus meus.

κὴ ὁ Θεός με) Hic primum ea vox in narratione Evange- lica reperitur ab Apostolis Jesu tributa, postquam scilicet sua resurrectione probaverat se esse, a quo vita & quidem aeterna exspectari deberet. Vide supra XI. 25. mansit de- inde ille mos in Ecclesia, ut apparet non tantum in scriptis Apostolicis, ut Rom. IX. 5. & veterum Christianorum, ut videre est apud Justin. Martyrem contra Tryphonem, sed & in Plinii ad Trajanum Epistola, ubi ait, Christianos Christo, ut Deo, carmina cecinisse.

Satis jejune illa confessio Thomae explicatur ὁ Κύριός με, quasi testatus ea tantum sit Thomas se Christo parere velle; non autem satis pie mos dicitur Ecclesiasticus, quod Christus Deus dici- tur. Edidit hic Thomas fidei suae, postquam non amplius incredulus fuit, sed πιστὸς vel πιστεύων, confessionem de Christo, quod agnoscat eum pro Domino suo, & pro Deo suo: quae utraque vox, cum a fidelibus adhibetur, unicum solum Deum notat: Hunc enim fidelis quisq; pro suo Domino, & pro suo Deo agnoscit, & respondet nomen Κύ- ριος penes Interpretes voci יהוה, nomen vero Θεὸς voci אלהים, ut in tract. de naturali & revela- ta Theologia ex professo docuimus. Confitetur er- go Christum verum natura Deum. Porro in N. T. vox Κυρίε solet peculiariter de Christo adhiberi, cumprimis cum pronomine applicationis, quod Dominus noster is sit, non tantum jure creationis, sed etiam redemtionis, qui nos sibi acquisivit in pe- culium, imo ratione gubernationis, dominii, & re- gaminis, quod ipse ut Deus κατ᾿ αὐτὸ habet, ut ho- mo vero κατ᾿ ἄλλο per unionis nempe hyposta- ticae, & exaltationis ad dextram Dei gratiam, Act. II. 36. Phil. II. 11. cui nos non modo parere oportet cum vera cordis fiducia, sed qui etiam non regit, tuetur, fovet gratia sua, & custodit ad aeternam glo- riam. Haec omnia de Christo vera fide profitetur Thomas. Sed de hac ejus confessione adversus So- cinianos alibi egimus pluribus. Unde ea; quia ha- ctenus in scriniis nostris ἀνέκδοτα jacent, hic vin- dicandae illustris confessionis gratia, repetere non pigebit, imprimis quia indignis prorsum modis hanc confessionem Thomae obfuscare etiam Neo- Ariani satagunt: quod nuper quoque a Christ. San- dio factum. Vocat autem Thomas Christum Κύ- ριον & Θεὸν cum articulo, quod γνώρισμα cum nem- pe ὁ Θεὸς occurrit, Sociniani pro summi Dei signi- ficatione allegant. Vid. Socin. contra Wujeck. pag. 375. Crellius de attribut. divin. p. 96. Con- fitetur eundem Dominum suum & Deum suum, quod verbum fiduciæ est, docetque eum omnem cordis sui fiduciam in Christum collocare, eidemque ceu Deo confidere: unde additur à Christo: Quia vidisti me Thoma, CREDIDISTI, Beati qui non vident & CREDUNT. Noverat probe Thomas τὴν πρώτην πασῶν τῶν ἐντολῶν, à Christo & repetitam & inculcatam, Audi Israel, Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν Κύριος εἷς ἐστι, Dominus Deus tuus Dominus unus est, & diliges Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου, Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, &c. Deut. VI. v. 4. Marc. XII. v. 29. 30. Et profitetur tamen λευκάδι φωνῇ Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου, Dominum Deum suum esse Christum. Quod quid aliud erat, quam quod agnosceret eum UNUM suum DOMINUM esse? Quandoquidem Dominus Deus noster UNUS DOMINUS sit? Et quæ est diversitas inter compellationem illam Davidicam Ps. XXXIV. 23. προσχὲς τῇ κρίσει μου, ὁ Θεός μου καὶ ὁ Κύριός μου, & hanc Thomæam, ὁ Θεός μου, καὶ ὁ Θεός μου. Si ergo illic vocibus ὁ Θεός μου, καὶ Κύριός μου, unus ille Deus denotatur, uti denotari in confesso est, quidni etiam hic eadem prorsus compellatione ὁ Κύριός μου, καὶ ὁ Θεός μου, unus ille Deus denotaretur.

Circa hanc tam luculentam Deitatis Christi confessionem varias quæsivere elabendi rimas adversarii I. Enjedinus in explicat. locor. p. 249. negavit his verbis Thomam Christum compellasse, eumque Dominum suum & Deum suum vocasse, quod probe videret hanc compellationem nonnisi vero natura Deo convenire. Fingit itaque terrore & stupore plenum, & extra se quasi raptum exclamare more hominibus consueto, Dominus meus & Deus meus, adeoque saltem rem inusitatam & admirationem suam summam significare, ut cum Græci dicere solent μεγαλοὶ Θεοὶ, Latini, Dii magni, Dii boni, ut apud Heliodorum, Catullum, Terentium, videre est, & vulgus cum admirabile aliquod videt, exclamat Jesus, Maria, &c.

In hanc sententiam laudat Sandius in Interpret. Paradox. p. 257. etiam Theodorum Mopsvestenum, ejusque exceptiunculam contra Bellarminum tueri satagit. Nestoriani, inquit (cum Paulo Samosateno & Photino negantes Christum esse verum Deum) dicebant verba hæc ad Patrem referri per exclamationem Thomæ Christi resurrectionem admirantis, ut patet ex V. Synodo cap. 8. & 12. Theodorus Mopsvestenus, & confessionem, quam fecit Thomas, cum palpasset manus & latus Domini post resurrectionem, dicens: Dominus meus & Deus meus, inquit, non esse dictum à Thoma de Christo: nec enim dicit Theodorus Deum esse Christum; sed ad miraculum resurrectionis, stupefactum Thomam glorificasse Deum, qui Dominum resuscitavit. Adhæc quidem regerit Bellarminus, quod in Græco non sit scriptum ὦ signum exclamantis sed articulus. Verum Bellarmino Nestoriani rursus respondere possent, Marc. XV. 34. Christum per exclamationem dicere, ὁ Θεός μου, ὁ Θεός μου, & Matth. XXVII. 46. Eusebius dem. Evang. X. 8. legit: ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Θεός μου &c. Sic Ps. XXI. 1. ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Θεός μου, ἵνα τί ἐγκατέλιπές με. 2. ὁ Θεός μου κεκράξομαι ἡμέρας, XXVII. 1. ὁ Θεός μου, μὴ παρασιωπήσῃς ἀπ᾽ ἐμοῦ. XLV. 8. ὁ θρόνος σου ὁ Θεὸς &c. 9. διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέ σε ὁ Θεὸς ὁ Θεός σου. LXXIII. 11. ἕως πότε ὁ Θεὸς ὀνειδιεῖ ὁ ἐχθρὸς, & alia infinita. Hæc Sandius. Atque hanc interpretationem veram esse, vel inde apparere, ait Enjedinus, quod in Christo tunc nihil tale à Thoma visum est, ex quo Christum Deum esse colligere posset. Nam resurrectio non ei, qui resurrexit, sed resuscitatori opinionem divinitatis conciliare solet: imo certum apud omnes, Deum non mori, ac propterea resurrectione non opus habere.

Porro II. Franc. David hoc sensu verba illa ad Pa- trem referri posse contendit: Dominus meus ac Deus meus, quam fui pertinax & incredulus, quod verbo & promissioni tuæ de excitando ex mortuis Fi- lio tuo, & testibus quoque condiscipulis meis non ac- quievi; propter hanc meam incredulitatem dignus essem pœna; ut refert Socinus in Epist. p. 189. III. Fuerunt præterea, qui, referente eodem Socino p. 191. dixerunt, ellipsin quidem esse in verbis Tho- mæ, sed recto tamen, non autem vocandi casu ea ac- cipienda esse, hoc aut simili sensu, Dominus meus & Deus meus laudetur, qui me ea videre facit, quæ licet maxime cuperem, non tamen facta fuisse ani- mum inducere poteram, & profitente ibid. Socin. l. c. Nec defuerunt, qui faterentur quidem Christum à Thoma Deum appellatum fuisse, sed non jure. Quam sententiam tamen adeo fœdam & impiam esse agno- vit Svevius, ut ab Erasmo & Gvalthero confutari indigna habita fuerit.

IV. Enjedinus vero concesso eo, quod verba hæc in Christum directa fuerint, negat consequi, Christum esse æternum & omnipotentem Deum: quandoquidem multi sint Domini & Dii tam in cœlo quàm in terra, 1. Corinth. VIII. v. 6. Socinus autem V. excipit in Antivyujek. pag. 260. Arti- culum non habere hoc loco vim singularis Dei signi- ficandi propter additum nomini ὁ Θεὸς pronomen με. VI. Articulum eum ita accipi posse, ac si esset ad- verbium vocandi, & nomen Deus casu vocativo elatum esset, vel ac si ὁ Θεὸς sine ullo adverbio, vo- candi casu elatum fuisset, ut Marc. XV. v. 34. VII. Innui his verbis, Christum non modo Dominum, sed divinum Dominum esse, quem colere, eique con- fidere deberet. Thomam non modo Judæum sed Christianum quoque fuisse, ac propterea non mo- do unum illum Deum Israëlis, sed etiam Christum hominem suum Deum agnovisse, id est, sibi ab illo uno Deo divinæ potestatis plenum Regem datum, à quo æterna salus expetenda foret, quemque divino cultu afficere deberet. Repetit plerisque Socini φλυαρίας Johan. Crellius lib. de Deo & attrib. di- vin. cap. 13. p. 100. Thomam Nominativo pro Vo- cativo usum esse, vel si ita verba etiam ejus accipi- antur, Tu es Dominus meus & Deus meus: quem- admodum nonnulli verterunt interpretes, articuli vim ob adjectam particulam με meus minui: quod si denique vim aliquam habere concedendum sit, consentaneum esse, Thomam, cum Christũ a Deo resuscitatum videret, dicere voluisse, eum esse illum Dominum, qui à Deo fuerit Israëlitico populo promif- sus, qui ei genti insigniter sit benefacturus, eamque ex servitute liberaturus sit, jure eum non modo Dominum suum, sed & Deum suum appellare pos- sit aut debeat: adeoque articulum fore ἀναφορικὸν, qui mentem ad rem certam, internam notam re- ferat. Similia legimus apud Socin. in animadvers. ad assert. Posnan. p. 56. defens. animadv. pag. 417. Schmaltz. refut. lib. de err. Arian. p. 180. Volckel. de ver. Relig. p. 423. & alias passim.

Facile autem obstruuntur hæ rimæ, frustra quæsitæ: Quod I. ad Enjedini, vel potius Theo- dori Mopsuestani, qui primus ejus autor, com- mentum, dignum id autoribus suis, prodit ho- rum hominum ingenium in pervertendis Scriptu- ræ dictis luculentissimis διαβολικώτατον. Primum enim nullum in sacris literis talis admirationis in re inusitata exemplum habetur, maxime, ubi non ὧ signum exclamantis, sed articulus occurrat. Et- enim scrinia Heliodori, Catulli, Terentii excutere opus habuit Enjedinus, nihil reperiens in Scriptu- ris. Ad illorum & vulgi Christianorum consuetu- dinem sanctam Thomæ confessionem exigere vo- luit, ne deesset, quod regereret. Quæ Sandius adfert è Scriptura, ἀλλότρια sunt, Marc. XV. v. 34. non exclamatio admirantis, sed suspirium invocantis, è Psalm. XXII. v. 1. habetur. Quod etiam de Psal. XXVII. v. 1. dicendum, Psal. XLV. v. 8. & LXXXIV. v. 10. itidem nulla est admirantis exclamatio, sed compellatio Dei in casu nominandi, de quo paulo post. Deinde ne apud gentiles quidem scriptores reperiuntur exempla, quandoquidem exclamationes ejusmodi non cum articulo & nominativo exprimantur, sed in vocativo, vel etiam interjectione & vocativo, ut adducta Enjedini exempla docent, & per se notissimum. Si dicant adversarii: Nominativum hic pro Vocativo usurpari: exempla proferenda ipsis erunt, ubi in exclamationibus præ admiratione factis id usu venerit, & quidem adhibito articulo, ita ut is τῷ ὧ exclaman- tis respondeat. Solet quidem in compellatione nominativus pro vocativo adhiberi, verum ita articulus compellantis & vocantis vim subit, non autem exclamantis, quod Psal. LIX. v. 1. Psal. LX. v. 1. Psal. LXIII. v. 1. Luc. XVIII. v. 13. videre est. Conf. Luc. VIII. 54. Eph. VI. v. 1. Quod etiam Matt. XV. v. 34. fieri, manifestum est, ubi itidem compellandi vim habet, non autem præ admiratione exclamandi. Tertio manifestum nimis est, Thomam hic non exclamare ad Deum Patrem, sed Christum compellare, quia diferte dicitur, Christo respondisse, eique hæc dixisse: Dominus meus & Deus meus, ἡ ἀπεκρίθη ὁ Θωμᾶς, ἡ εἶπεν αὐτῷ. Respondit Thomas & dixit: cuinam vero nisi Christo? Torquet se hic Enjedinus, & comminiscitur, hanc loquendi formulam DIXIT EI idem significare in sacris atque dixit post verba ejus, vel auditis verbis ejus, Luc. XIV. v. 16. Joh. XIV. v. 22. 23. At quod dixerit post verba ejus, vel auditis verbis ejus, jam in- nuerat Evangelista voce ἀπεκρίθη respondit, nunc autem ad quem verba direxerit, in responsione indicat, dixit ei. Nec aliud apparet è Luc. XIV. 16. Joh. XIV. v. 22. 23. quam quod vi verborum dixit ei, ad eum, qui loquutus antea erat, verba directa fuerint, etsi alii (quod ex accidenti est ad horum verborum sensum) adfuerint, simulque ita illis ea dicta fuerint. Hic vero verba illa, Dominus meus & Deus meus, etsi in aliorum præsentia dicta, tamen ad unum tantum Christum, cui dixisse hæc Thomam refert Johannes, directa fuere. Franc. David obvertit, quædam exemplaria non habere & dixit ei, sed simpliciter, & dixit. Respondet autem ei Socinus ipse in Epist. pag. 186. Diversam illam lectionem non extare, neque in ullo probato codice, nec apud ullum probatum scriptorem: Satisque esse quod dicatur: Respondit Thomas, quia nemo respondens cum alio loquatur, sive ad alium verba dirigat quam ad eum, cui, sive ad cujus verba respondet, præsertim, si is antea ipsi loquutus fuerat, ad ipsumque verba sua direxerat. Quarto adhortatus fuerat Christus Thomam: ne incredulus esto, sed credens: jam vero Thomas sese credere hac confessione sua testatur, non terrore & stupore plenus, & extra se quasi raptus exclamat. Quid quod Christus ipse ei testimonium tribuat fidei, quia vidisti, credidisti. Non ergo ut stuporis & terroris vocem, sed ut fidei confessionem verba ejus acceptavit. Quæ sine dubio moverunt adversarios, Socinum, Smalzium, Volckelium, ut & Theoph. Nicolaidem contra Albert. Borckovsky de Eccl. c. 8. aliosq;, ut Enjedini glossam reprobarent, Christumque à Thoma compellatum esse agnoscerent, quin & interprete Smalcio contra Franz. disp. 12. refutati Enjedini explicationem pro INEPTISSIMA haberent: quam refellit etiam (licet supresso nomine) Socin. in Epist. p. 191. his duobus argumentis: Primum quod ita dictum non fuisset, & respondit Thomas. Deinde quod ejusmodi excla- mationis nullum exemplum ex S. literis proferatur.

Ratio quam affert confirmandæ suæ sententiæ. Enjedinus adfertur & ab aliis adversariis, qui ta- men sententiam Enjedini reprobant; magisque ea est opposita nostræ interpretationi, quam ac- commodata confirmationi depravationis Enje- dianæ. Negamus autem, quod assumitur, nihil visum fuisse Thomæ, ex quo colligere poterat Chri- stum Deum esse: quandoquidem ipse Christus ad- ferat, eum credidisse propterea quia viderit. Et vidit omnino Thomas atque agnovit, dum Chri- stum redivivum à mortuis vidit, eundem vere Mes- siam esse, hoc est, vere Deum, Psal. XLV. 8. Jeho- vam, Jer. XXIII. v. 6. ipsoque opere complevisse, quod prædixerat Johan. II. v. 19. quodque testatus erat Joh. X. 18. Quod si is, qui à mortuis resuscitat, verus Deus esse colligitur, annon hinc Christum verum Deum esse concludere poterat Thomas, quod videret, ipsum excitasse templum corporis sui, animamq; suam resumsisse: etsi eundem agno- sceret verum hominem, qua parte & mortuus & resuscitatus fuit.

II. Ad Franc. Davidis detorsionem respondet ipse Socinus, quem producimus è loc. cit. p. 189. quum liber à paucis habeatur. Hæc tua interpre- tatio, inquit, nullo modo sustineri potest, primum, quia non potuisset dicere Johannes simpliciter, Tho- mam respondisse, si ad alium, quam ad Jesum, qui ipsum allocutus fuerat, verba sua direxisset. Dein- de, qui nullum ejusmodi eclipsis exemplum in tota Scriptura, sed neque etiam in alio probato autore for- tassis, invenies. Præterea cum Christus verbis illis à Thoma prolatis statim dicat: Quia vidisti Thoma, credidisti, nemo dubitare potest, quin ex ipsis Tho- mæ verbis aperte constiterit, eum jam credidisse. Atque, si ad Deum Patrem illa referantur, id nullo modo constare potest, cum nullam sententiam expli- cent, & varia possint subaudiri, imo talia, quæ Tho- mam nec credidisse nec credere voluisse demonstrent. Sic enim posset quispiam ea verba supplere: Domi- nus meus & Deus meus, ne permittas, ut his præsti- giis decipiar, & id credam, quod credendum non est. Quod si ad Christum referatur, omnia plana sunt. Hæc Socinus.

Ad III. Resp. Ellipsis illa prorsus arbitraria est, ne Scripturæ exemplis nęc ulla ratione sufful- ta. Quod si autem ellipsis ejusmodi pro arbitrio statuenda, vel introducendæ, quibusdam sensus affingi non poterit verbis Scripturæ. Adde quod refragetur tale commentum ipsis disertis verbis. Dicitur enim respondisse Thomas, & dixisse ei, hoc est Christo: non autem oratione ad Deum di- recta Deum Patrem celebrasse. Nec aliter acce- ptavit Christus Thomæ verba, quam ceu fidei confessionem, ut è responso ejus subjunčto mani- festum est. Fatetur inde Socinus, certum esse ad Christum ea referenda, & omnino concludendum esse, Christum in illis verbis Thomæ, & quidem jure optimo, Deum, nec solum Deum, sed Deum nostrum fuisse appellatum, l. c. p. 192. Et persimilem hoc loco esse locum illum, ait Joh. XIII. 13. ὁ διδάσκα- los ᾄ ὁ Κύριos. Quemadmodum enim Dominum agnoscebant (verba sunt Socini de discipulis Chri- sti) & confitebantur, sic Thomas Christo dicens: Dominus meus & Deus meus, eum Dominum & Deum suum agnovit & confessus est. Locum au- tem plane simillimum dicit, quique pro aperta hujus explicatione esse possit, Tob. VII. 2. εἶ- πεν αὐτῷ, ὁ τῦ καλῦ ᾄ ἀγαθῦ ἀνθρώπε υἱός.

Sicut igitur ibi manifeste Tobias à Raguele ho- nesti & boni viri filius agnoscitur, & nominatur, ita & hic Christus à Thoma Dominus suus & Deus suus agnoscitur & nominatur. Hactenus Socinus, cujus conclusionem ratam habent, quot- quot alia ejus placita sectantur.

Ad (IV.) Resp. Obtenta & concessa hac Thomæ confessione invicte prorfus colligitur, Christum agnitum fuisse æternum & omnipoten- tem Deum, quia non est Deus alius, nisi unus, nimirum æternus illé & omnipotens Deus, ut Apostolus loco citato testatur 1. Corinth. VIII. 4. Quanquam autem multos esse Deos & multos Do- minos dicat, aperte tamen loquitur de Dominis λεγομένοις, qui ita dicuntur, & nuncupative tan- tum dii sunt, eademque classe eximit Christum, ceu unum illum Dominum, per quem omnia sunt, & nos per ipsum, ideoque non nisi impie Christus in ordinem & censum multorum illorum Domino- rum & Deorum refertur.

Quod (V.) ad Socini exceptionem de articulo, non tantum nititur nostra demonstratio emphasi articuli, sed & evidentia rei, quod non sit nisi unus Deus, quod nec Thomas nec quisquam alius di- scipulorum Christi agnoverit, nec agnoscere de- buerit alium Deum suum, quam Jehovam, unum Deum, cui & uni & soli toto corde confidere, quem unum & solum tota anima diligere, vi præ- cepti primi tenebantur. Quod vero pronomen με additum, neque emphasi articuli deroset, ne- que Dei appellationem imminuat, id planum jam fecimus Theolog. nat. & revel. cap. 3. p. 483. seqq. Quin imo pronomen hoc confirmat nos, intel- ligi Deum unum. Quia nuspiam in Sacris Literis ullius fidelium Deus dicitur, præterquam ille unus Deus. Unde invicta illatio: Deus fidelium est unus ille Deus; At Christus est Deus fidelium, quod exemplo & confessione Thomæ jam fide- lis constat. E. Major uti dixi, patet è locorum inductione: Quid solemnius in Sacris Literis, quam unum illum Deum ita describi, quod fide- lium Deus sit. Ita Deus vocatur DEVS ἡμῶν no- ster, Luc. I. v. 78. 1. Thessal. II. v. 2. cap. III. v. 9. 2. Thessal. I. v. 11. 12. Ebr. XII. v. 29. 1. Petr. I. v. 1. Apoc. V. v. 10. c. VII. v. 3. 10. 12. cap. XII. v. 10. 16. cap. XIX. v. 15. DEUS ὑμῶν, DEUS vester, Marc. XII. v. 29. Johan. VIII. v. 54. cap. X. v. 27. Actor. II. v. 39. cap. III. v. 22. cap. IV. v. 19. cap. VII. v. 37. vel αὐτῶν ipsorum, 2. Corinth. VI. vers. 16. Ebr. II. v. 16. Apoc. XXI. v. 3. Additur etiam nomini Θεός pronomen σε tuus, cum sermo est de Deo uno, Matth. IV. v. 7. 10. cap. XXII. v. 37. Marc. XII. vers. 30. Luc. IV. v. 8. 12. cap. X. v. 27. Ebr. I. v. 9. Item hoc ipsum pronomen με meus, Matt. XXVII. v. 45. Marc. V. v. 34. Job. XX. v. 17. Rom. I. v. 8. 1. Corinth. I. v. 4. cap. XIV. v. 18. 2. Corinth. XII. v. 21. Philipp. I. v. 3. cap. IV. v. 19. Philem. v. 1. Apoc. III. vers. 12. Et quid frequentius, quam Deum illum unum dici Deum Israelis, Deum Abrahæ, Deum Isaac, Deum Jacob, Deum Patrum Deum populi. Deum item sanctorum Prophetarum, Apoc. XXI. v. 6. quem eundem esse Deum Thomæ qui dubium esse potest? Confert Socinus in Epist. p. 189. cum hac nostro loco ratione phrases Psal. V. v. 2. Inten- de voci orationis Rex & Deus meus, & Ps. XXXIV. v. 23. Exurgo & intende judicio meo Θεός με ὴ Κύ- ριός με, Deus meus & Dominus meus, & (ut habea- tur locus huic nostro exacte respondens, ubi nimirum nomen Domini Dei nomini præposi- tum sit) Apoc. IV. ult. ἄξιος εἶ ὁ Κύριος, ἢ ὁ Θεὸς ὑμῶν ὁ ἅγιος λαβεῖν &c. Ut ergo nullum dubium, quum illis in locis voce Deus meus & Dominus meus, item Dominus & Deus noster intelligatur unus ille Deus verus, ita necessum quoque omni- no est, eadem voce hic unum illum Deum verum intelligere, cum Thomas ait, ὁ Κύριός με, ὴ ὁ Θεός με, quum phrases prorsus eædem sint, & lo- ca exacte sibi respondeant; de similibus enim idem est judicium, nec temere, quod hic monet Socinus ipse p. 188. à consueta & propria verborum significatione est recedendum.

Ad (VI.) Resp. Etsiamsi ὁ Θεὸς admittatur ceu sensu vocandi dictum, non tamen ideo vis vocis Dei infringitur, ne designet unum illum Deum. Quid enim? Anne Deus unus indigitatur, cum ὁ Θεὸς aut etiam ὁ Θεός με casu vocandi compella- tur, Matth. XV. v. 34. Luc. XVIII. 11. 13. Apocal. IV. v. ult. cap. XI. v. 17. c. XV. v. 3. c. XVI. v. 7. &c. Sola certe casuum enallage non potest per se quicquam facere ad imminutionem potestatis nominis Dei. Sed nec ullibi compellatur Deus hoc pacto, ὁ Θεὸς, vel etiam cum addito prono- mine, με, vel ἡμῶν, aut simili additamento, quin semper & ubiq; intelligatur unus ille verus Deus. Unde iterum invicte concluditur, unum illum verum Deum intelligi, quem ita compellat Tho- mas ὁ Θεός με. Antecedens è locorum inductio- ne constat tum Veteris Testamenti: Num. XII. v. 13. Judic. XVI. v. 28. 1. Reg. VIII. v. 23. 25. 26. 28. 1. Paral. XVII. v. 17. Psal. III. v. 8. & cap. V. v. 3. & cap. VII. 2. 4. 10. & cap. X. v. 12. Psal. XXXIV. v. 73. &c. tum itidem Novi Matth. XV. v. 34. Luc. XVIII. v. 11. 13. Apoc. IV. v. ult. cap. XI. vers. 17. cap. XV. v. 3. cap. XVI. v. 7. Quid quod Socinus non renuat adeo verba confessionis Thomæ casu recto accipere, moneat saltem, etiamsi ad Chri- stum relata recto casu accipiantur, eandem plane esse confessionem Deitatis Christi, & agnitionem ipsius. Imo quid proclivius est, inquit Socinus loco citato pag. 192. quam sine ulla vera ellipsi aut insolente atque incerta interpretatione verbum sub- stantivum, quod vocant, simpliciter subaudire? Ita vero hic sensus prodit: Dominus meus es, & Deus meus. Hoc autem sensu stante, apertissi- mum est, nomen τῶ Θεῷ Christo tribui cum arti- culo, adeoque vi Regulæ ipsorummet Socinia- norum concludendum, Christum esse unum illum Deum.

Ad (VII.) Resp. Nimis jejuna est illa expli- catio, quod Christus divinus Dominus innuatur. Non enim divinum Dominum, sed Dominum suum, & Deum suum confitetur Apostolus. Nus- piam in Scripturis DEUS idem est quod divinus. Nuspiam Deus hujus vel illius fidelis Deus Abra- hæ, Isaaci, Jacobi, aut Deus Israelis hominem di- vinum notat, semper & ubique Deum illum unum, quemadmodum ipsimet adversarii faten- tur Deum Israelis, Deum illum unum esse. Idem autem est Deus Thomæ, qui Deus Abrahæ, Patris credentium, qui Deus Israelis, non autem alius atque alius Deus, quum non sit alius Deus nisi unus etiam in Novo Testamento, 1. Corinth. VIII. v. 4. & repetitur diligenter à Christo illud ἀξίωμα di- vinum, Marc. XII. v. 29. Audi Israel, Dominus Deus noster Dominus unus est, idque ita, ut illum unum religiose colere jubeamur. Christianam ve- ro religionem in eo diversam esse à Judaica, quod præter unum illum Deum Israelis alium natura merum hominem colere debeamus, impium com- mentum est Socinisticum, cujus falsitatem ex pro- fesso, quod dicitur, demonstravimus in μοναρχίας divinæ assertione Theolog. natur. & revel. cap. IV.

Nec vero profitetur hic Thomas Christum Re- gem ab uno illo Deo datum divinæ potestatis ple- num: & profitetur illum Dominum suum & Deum suum, ac proinde unum illum verum Deum. Quia nec Dei nomine proprie quisquam dicitur in Scripturis, nisi unus Deus, nec Deus fidelium, aut pronomine meus, tuus, noster, &c. relato ad fide- les uspiam in tota Scriptura indigitatur, nisi Je- hova verus natura Deus, multo minus conjunctis his nominibus, Dominus meus & Deus meus ullus insignitur aut compellatur, præterquam unus & solus Deus supremus, utpote Ps. XXXIV. 23. Apoc. IV. ult. &c. Denique si concedatur articulum ἀναφορικὸν hoc loco esse, ac Dominum vel Deum illum, cujus adventus populo Israelitico promissus fuit, designare, non tamen nudus tantum benefa- ctor & liberator è servitute, sed Jehova Deus ve- rus & unicus intelligendus erit, quandoquidem promissus sit adventus ipsius Jehovah (quod no- men per verbum Κύριος exprimi consuevit in Novo Testamento) & Dei Israelis, ut passim lege- re est Jer. XXIII. 6. Zach. II. 10. Quare ipsum etiam Thomæ Deum fuisse, & ab eo pro Deo suo habitum, nullum esse potest dubium. Atque hæc in præsenti de confessione Thomæ.

## 20:29
Vers. 29.

ὅτι ἑώρακάς με πεπίστευκας) By the verb of seeing, touch is also included here. Thus also hearing Exod. XX. 18. Jer. II. v. 31. & Mark XV. 4. & in the Greek Ezech. III. 13. Elsewhere smelling Gen. XXVII. 27. πεπίστευκας, that is, you believe. For it is frequent in verbs of emotion that past tenses are put for present ones.

Μακάριοι) that is, they are to be preferred. Thus Luke XI. 27. The positive for the comparative, as 1 Cor. VII. 8.

οἱ μὴ ἰδόντες καὶ πιστεύσαντες) For this is truly of those who rightly think concerning the power and goodness of God, to apply faith to probable testimonies, concerning that matter which pertains to confirming the most holy dogma. Moreover, this aorist is also for the present: but the present for any time. For it is mainly a question of those who will believe by the testimony of the Apostles, and indeed men placed far from Judea. A similar emphasis is in Peter, 1st epistle I. v. 8. ὃν οὐκ εἰδότες ἀγαπᾶτε, and what follows.

PART IV.

The reason for the writing of the signs of the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

ὅτι ἑώρακάς με πεπίστευκας) Verbo videndi hic etiam ta- ctus comprehenditur. Sic & auditus Exod. XX. 18. Jer. II. v. 31. & Marci XV. 4. & in Græco Ezech. III. 13. Alibi odo- ratus Gen. XXVII. 27. πεπίστευκας, id est, credis. Frequens enim est in verbis affectuum, ut præterita pro præsentibus ponantur.

Μακάριοι) id est, præferendi sunt. Sic Luc. XI. 27. Po- sitivus pro comparativo, ut 1. Cor. VII. 8.

οἱ μὴ ἰδόντες καὶ πιστεύσαντες) Nam hoc vere est de Dei potentia ac bonitate recte sentientium, fidem adhibere pro- babilibus testimoniis, de ea re quæ ad sanctissimum dogma confirmandum pertinet. Est autem & hic aoristus pro præ- senti: præsens autem pro quovis tempore. Nam de credi- turis Apostolorum testimonio, & quidem longe positis à Judæa hominibus, præcipue agitur. Similis emphasis apud Petrum I. epist. I. v. 8. ὃν οὐκ εἰδότες ἀγαπᾶτε, & quæ sequuntur.

PARS IV.

Causa scriptionis signorum Domini.

## 20:30
Vers. 30.

πολλὰ μὲν οὖν καὶ ἄλλα σημεῖα) I entirely believe that what follows here is the conclusion of the whole work and that John finished the book he published there. But just as the last chapter of the Pentateuch, and the last chapter of Joshua were added after the death of Moses and Joshua by the Sanhedrin of the Hebrews, so also the chapter which follows was added after the death of John by the Ephesian Church, with this main purpose, that it might be shown that what the Lord had predicted concerning the longevity and non-violent death of John was fulfilled. But the other things which are narrated in that chapter were added to demonstrate the time, place, and occasion of that oracle. It is an argument that at the end of the chapter a clause similar to this is repeated, and indeed in this way: οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀληθής ἐστιν ἡ μαρτυρία αὐτοῦ: by which words the Church shows that it does not doubt in the least concerning the things placed above by John and concerning these things also, which were taken from his private commentaries, whereas otherwise, if John had written this, he would have said as above, κὰκεῖνος οἶδεν ὅτι ἀληθῆ λέγει, c. XIX. 35.

This is a new opinion, resting on no foundation. For although some have held this to be a general clause, which concerns not only the preceding histories, but the whole book of the Johannine Gospel, yet one will hardly find anyone who has asserted that the following chapter proceeded from the Ephesian Church. Nor do they rest on any reason who have said that the last chapter was perhaps added not by John, but by someone else. Which pleased Vossius, Harm. Evang. lib. III. cap. IV. §. 8., otherwise insisting on Grotian footsteps. That (the appearance of the Lord at the sea of Tiberias) was added by John after the first edition: or after his departure by John the presbyter, and the Ephesian Church: which had not only heard it often from the mouth of John the Apostle, but had also found it in his private writings. But that it was added after the death of John the Apostle, I prefer to believe: because of those words in verse 24. We know (οἴδαμεν,) that his testimony is true: For John would rather have said of himself I know (oîda): just as in chapter XIX. 35. he speaks in the singular number about his own testimony. Nor does that matter detract anything from the faith of this last chapter: since in a similar way the final words of the Pentateuch concerning the death of Moses were added after his death. Also in the book of Joshua, which one may read in the Talmud was written by Joshua himself, and from there followed. But there is one reason for the conclusion of the books of Moses and Joshua, which deal with the death of these writers, and thus cannot have been added by those writers themselves, and another for the last chapter of John. But if it was added by the Ephesian Church, drawn from some of John's private commentaries, how can it be considered θεόπνευστος? The argument for this novel and dangerous opinion is extremely weak. For although those things are expressed in the plural (πληθυντικῶς), and as if about a third party: we know (οἴδαμεν) that his testimony is true, it is nevertheless not unusual for St. John to speak of himself as if of some other person: and could these not have been expressed in the plural because he was joining himself with the other Apostles, as in John I. v. 14. 16. 18. 1 John I. v. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. etc.? Can one conclude from the fact that St. John says, and we write these things to you, that John was not the only author of this Epistle? What of the fact that the author of this final chapter speaks not only in the plural, when he embraces the consensus of others at the same time; but also in the singular, when he brings forward something from his own person alone, as when he says in verse 25, I suppose (οἶμαι), I think or I am of the opinion. However, this clause sufficiently teaches that it is not generally a question here of the whole Evangelical book, (even if the end of it is the same) or of any signs whatsoever that Christ performed, but that the preceding histories are primarily regarded, and the signs which Christ performed in the sight not of the whole people, but of his disciples. Whence those seem to be referred to the signs by which Christ manifested himself after the resurrection, which St. Luke reports was done through many proofs (ἐν πολλοῖς τεκμηρίοις) during those forty days, Acts I. v. 3. For thus the word signs (σημεῖα) is accustomed to be used for proof (τεκμηρίῳ). See Matt. XXIV. v. 3. chapter XXVI. v. 48. Luke II. v. 12. The general conclusion of the book is held in c. XXI. v. 25, which regards not only those signs (σημεῖα), but all the miracles of Christ.

in the presence of his disciples (ἐνώπιον τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ) As if he were to say, I have narrated those miracles which were performed while a great crowd was watching. But those which were performed only before his intimates, were few, such as that he entered twice with the doors closed. He submits the reason.

which are not written in this book (ἃ οὐκ ἔστι γεγραμμένα ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τούτῳ) As being by no means necessary.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

πολλὰ μὲν οὖν καὶ ἄλλα σημεῖα) Omnino arbitror quæ hic sequuntur conclusionem esse totius operis & ibi finiisse Jo- hannem librum quem edidit. At sicut caput ultimum Pen- tateuchi, & caput ultimum Josuæ post Mosis & Josuæ mor- tem additum est à Synedrio Hebræorum, ita & caput quod sequitur post mortem Johannis additum ab Ecclesia Ephe- sina, hoc maxime fine, ut ostenderetur impletum, quod de longævitate ac non violenta morte Johannis Dominus prædixerat. Cætera autem, quæ in eo capite narrantur, addita ad demonstrandum tempus, locum & occasionem illius oraculi. Argumento est, quod in fine capitis clausula huic similis repetitur, & quidem hoc modo: οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀληθής ἐστιν ἡ μαρτυρία αὐτοῦ: quibus verbis Ecclesia osten- dit se de supra positis à Johanne & do his etiam, quæ ex pri- vatis ipsius commentariis erant deprompta, minime dubi- tare, cum alioqui si Johannes hoc scripsisset, dicturus fuis- set ut supra, κὰκεῖνος οἶδεν ὅτι ἀληθῆ λέγει, c. XIX. 35.

Nova est hæc sententia, nullo nitens fun- damento. Etsi enim nonnulli hanc pro generali clausula habuerint, quæ non tantum præcedentes historias, sed totum librum Evangelii Johannei concernat, qui tamen sequens caput ab Ecclesia Ephesina profectum esse asseruerit, haud facile in- venietur ullus. Nec ulla ratione nituntur, qui for- te non à Johanne, sed ab alio quopiam caput ul- timum adjectum dixere. Quod placuit Vossio Harm. Evang. lib. III. cap. IV. §. 8. de cætero in- sistenti Grotianis vestigiis. Illa (apparitio Domi- ni ad mare Tiberiadis) addita ab Johanne post edi- tionem primam: vel post ejus excessum ab Johanne presbytero, atque Ecclesia Ephesina: quæ non modo ex ore Johannis Apostoli sæpius audierat, sed cedo etiam in privatis repererat scriptis. A morte vero Johannis Apostoli accessisse, malo credere: propter illa verba vers. 24. Scimus (οἴδαμεν,) quod verum est testimonium ejus: Nam Johannes de se potius scio (oîda) dixisset: quomodo cap. XIX. 35. singulo numero de testimonio suo loquitur. Neque ea res fidei hujus capitis ultimi detrahit quicquam: cum similiter Pentateuchi verba extrema de morte Mosis post mortem ejus addita sint. Josuæ etiam libro, quem ab Josua ipso scriptum fuisse legere est in Talmude, & inde consecutiis. Atqui alia ratio est clausulæ librorum Mosis & Josuæ, quæ de morte Scriptorum horum agunt, adeoque ab ipsis Scriptoribus illis additæ esse non possunt, alia capitis ultimi Johannei. Quod si additum est ab Ecclesia Ephesina, nonnullis ex privatis commentariis Johannis depromptis, quomodo θεόπνευστος haberi poterit? Argumentum hujus novellæ, & periculosæ sententiæ perquam leve est. Etsi enim πληθυντικῶς efferantur illa, & velut de tertio: οἴδαμεν ὅτι ἀληθής ἐστιν ἡ μαρτυρία αὐτοῦ, non insolens tamen est S. Johanni de se tanquam de alio quopiam loqui: & annon in plurali hæc efferri potuere, quod se conjungeret cum aliis Apostolis, uti Johan. I. v. 14. 16. 18. 1. Johan. I. v. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. &c. Num ex eo, quod ait S. Johannes, & hæc scribimus vobis, concludere licet, non solum Johannem fuisse autorem hujus Epistolæ? Quid quod autor hujus postremi capitis non tantum in plurali loquatur, cum aliorum consensum simul complectitur; sed etiam in singulari, cum ex sua solius persona quid profert, ut cum vers. 25. ait, οἶμαι, arbitror vel opinor. Satis autem hæc clausula docet, quod non generaliter hic de toto libro Evangelico agatur, (etsi idem totius ejusdem finis sit) aut de quibusvis, quæ Christus fecit, signis, sed quod respiciantur eadem præcedentes imprimis historiæ, & signa, quæ fecit Christus in conspectu non totius populi, sed discipulorum suorum. Unde illa ad signa ea videtur referenda, quibus post resurrectionem se manifestavit Christus, quod ἐν πολλοῖς τεκμηρίοις per dies illos quadraginta factum esse, S. Lucas perhibet Act. I. v. 3. Nam ita vox σημεῖα usurpari solet pro τεκμηρίῳ. Vid. Matth. XXIV. v. 3. cap. XXVI. v. 48. Luc. II. v. 12. Clausula generalis libri c. XXI. v. 25. habetur, quæ respicit non illa tantum σημεῖα, sed miracula Christi universa.

ἐνώπιον τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ) Quasi dicat, ea miracula narravi, quæ magna turba conspiciente facta sunt. Quæ vero coram familiaribus tantum, pauca, ut quod bis januis clausis intraverit. Rationem subjicit.

ἃ οὐκ ἔστι γεγραμμένα ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τούτῳ) Ut minime necessaria.

## 20:31
but these are written (ταῦτα δὲ γέγραπται) These are not so many, but the principal ones and those regarding some passage of the Old Testament.

that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ the Son of God (ἵνα πιστεύσητε ὅτι ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ) He who was promised to Abraham, Jacob, and David: which he himself openly professed, and added that it might appear both by the miracles performed by him in accordance with the prophecies, and that he would be resurrected.

The opposite of what Grotius says is clearly contained in the words of the Evangelist. For St. John says that the Lord performed many and great signs in the sight of the Disciples. Grotius, on the contrary, says there were only a few signs which he performed before his intimates, such as that he entered twice with the doors closed. For the rest, that these pertain to the signs exhibited after the resurrection, for the faith of the resurrection, has been observed before.

that believing you may have life (ἵνα πιστεύοντες ζωὴν ἔχητε) A right to eternal life, above c. III. 15. 36. c. V. 24. Thus Peter 1. Epistle I. 9. receiving the end of your faith the salvation of souls (κομιζόμενοι τὸ τέλος τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν σωτηρίαν ψυχῶν). Which are to be understood not of faith of any kind, but of active faith: to which the Law and the Prophets lead.

Latin:

ταῦτα δὲ γέγραπται) Hæc non adeo multa, sed præcipua & ad locum aliquem veteris fœderis respicientia.

ἵνα πιστεύσητε ὅτι ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ) Ille Abrahamo, Jacobo, Davidi promissus: quod ipse palam professus est, addiditque ut id appareret & miracula à se factavaticiniis congruentia, & se resuscitatum iri.

Contrarium ejus quod ait Grotius, diserte in verbis Evangelistæ habetur. Multa enim & magna signa fecisse Dominum in conspectu Discipulorum, ait S. Johannes. Grotius ex adverso pauca tantum fuisse signa, quæ coram familiaribus fecerit, ut quod bis clausis januis intraverit. De cætero hæc pertineread signa post resurrectionem exhibita, in fidem resurrectionis antea observatum.

ἵνα πιστεύοντες ζωὴν ἔχητε) Jus ad vitam æternam, supra c. III. 15. 36. c. V. 24. Sic Petri 1. Epist. I. 9. κομιζόμενοι τὸ τέλος τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν σωτηρίαν ψυχῶν. Quæ intelligenda sunt de fide non qualicunque, sed actuosa: ad quam ducunt Lex & Prophetæ.

## 21:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXI. AND THE LAST. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Jesus manifested himself at the Sea of Tiberias to Simon Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two other disciples, after they had fished all night and caught nothing, standing on the shore in the morning, when they had nothing which they could offer him to eat, commanding that they cast the net to the right side of the boat, which being done they enclosed a great number of fish, and the Lord was recognized by John; and the disciples found fish already placed on the coals, and after the net was drawn in, great fish were found to the number of 153. Moreover, while dining, Jesus distributed bread and fish to them. Then indeed, to Simon, having been asked three times whether he loved him, he commits his lambs and sheep to be fed three times; and he predicts the kind of martyrdom, and commands him to follow him: And John also following Jesus, when Peter asked about him, and Jesus answered: If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? and a rumor went out from there that John would not die; it is taught that Jesus did not say he would not die, but if I want him to remain. The Gospel of John is concluded with the confirmation of the testimony of his truth, with an indication of countless other things which Jesus did, omitted here. There are three parts: I. The manifestation of Jesus at the Sea of Tiberias, to v. 14. II. The twofold conversation of Christ with Peter, to v. 23. III. The conclusion of this book, to v. 25.

PART I. The manifestation of Jesus at the Sea of Tiberias.

Vers. 1. Μετὰ ταῦτα) After those things which John had included in his writing. A gloss proceeding from a false hypothesis, which we have already noted: ταῦτα refers to the preceding appearances made to the Apostles, who are called his disciples ἐξοχικῶς (preeminently). Here were present also some from the number of the LXX, less noble, as Grotius notes at v. 2. Or rather μετὰ ταῦτα, when he had shown himself to be seen by all the Apostles, with Thomas absent and then present, now he exhibited himself to some particularly: whence at v. 14 Grotius: τοῦτο ἤδη τρίτον: Refer to the number of days. He appeared first to various ones on the very day of the resurrection: a second time on the eighth day, now a third.

ἐφανέρωσεν ἑαυτὸν) Thus Mark XVI. 14. This is because he was no longer, as before, perpetually with the disciples.

πάλιν) Refer to the place. For the previous showings were made at Jerusalem.

ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης τῆς Τιβεριάδος) In Galilee, where he had said he would come. Matt. XXVIII. 7.

Latin:

CAPUT XXI. ET ULTIMUM. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Iesus ad mare Tiberiadis Simoni Petro, Thomae, Nathanaeli, filiis Zebedaei, aliisque duobus discipulis se manifestavit, postquam illi per totam noctem piscati nihil cepissent, mane ad littus stans, quum nihil haberent, quod manducandum ipsi praeberent, praecipiens, ut rete ejicerent ad dextram navis, quo fa- cto magnum numerum piscium conclusere, Dominusq; a Johanne agnitus fuit; & disci- puli pisces jam impositos prunis invenerunt, post extracto reti inventi sunt magni pisces numero 153. inter prandendum autem panes & pisces distribuit ipsis Iesus. Dehinc vero Simoni, ter rogato ipso, anne se diligeret? tri- bus vicibus agnos, & oves suas pascendas committit; & genus martyrii praedicit, seque sequi jubet: Sequente autem Iesum etiam Io- hanne, cum quaereret de ipso Petrus, & re- sponderet Iesus: Si volo eum manere donec veniam, quid hoc ad te? ac rumor inde exi- ret, Iohannem non moriturum; docetur, Ie- sum non dixisse, non moriturum, sed si volo eum manere. Concluditur Iohannis Evan- gelium veritatis testificationis ejus confir- matione cum indicatione aliorum innume- rorum, quae Iesus egit, hic omissorum. Partes sunt tres: I. Jesu ad mare Tiberiadis ma- nifestatio, ad v. 14. II. Colloquium geminum Chri- sti cum Petro, ad v. 23. III. Libri hujus conclusio, ad v. 25.

PARS I. Iesu ad mare Tiberiadis manifestatio.

Vers. 1. Μετὰ ταῦτα) Post acta ea, quae Johannes scri- pto complexus fuerat. Glossa ex falsa hypothesi, quam jam notavimus, profecta: ταῦτα respiciunt praecedentes appari- tiones Apostolos, qui ἐξοχικῶς discipuli ejus di- cuntur, factas. Hic aderant etiam nonnulli ex LXX. numero minus nobiles, ut ad v. 2. notat Grotius. Aut potius μετὰ ταῦτα, ubi Apostolis, absente ac deinde praesente Thoma, omnibus se visendum praebuit, jam nonnullis particulariter se exhibuit: unde ad v. 14. Grotius: τοῦτο ἤδι τρίτον: Refer ad dierum numerum. Primum apparuit diversis ipso resurrectionis die: iterum die octavo, nunc tertium.

ἐφανέρωσεν ἑαυτὸν) Sic Marc. XVI. 14. Hoc ideo, quia non jam, ut ante, perpetuo cum discipulis erat.

πάλιν) Refer ad locum. Nam priores ostensiones factae Hierosolymis.

ἐπὶ τῆς θαλάσσης τῆς Τιβεριάδος) In Galilaea, quo ven- turum se dixerat. Matth. XXVIII. 7.

## 21:2
v. 2. ἦσαν ὁμοῦ) in one lodging.

καὶ ἄλλοι ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν δύο) From the number of the LXX, less noble, likewise Galileans as it seems.

Latin:

v. 2. ἦσαν ὁμῦ) in uno contubernio.

καὶ ἄλλοι ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν δύο) Ex numero LXX. minus nobiles, itidem Galilaei ut videtur.

## 21:3
v. 3. ὑπάγω ἁλιεύειν) that is, I want to go fishing. While the Spirit was being awaited, there was nothing for the Apostles to do. And among the Jews it was not dishonorable. Sustenance also, as is credible, was not supplied from elsewhere, having hitherto had their nourishment from the company of Christ.

ἐρχόμεθα κὴ ὑμεῖς) We also want to go.

ἐξῆλθον) The letter x is correctly placed before this word, as it is in that old Manuscript. It is wrong for all codices to be placed after a single Manuscript. Nor is that particle necessary. For the sense is sufficiently consistent with itself, even without it being added. Although a copula can also sometimes be understood.

εἰς τὸ πλοῖον) Left behind or borrowed previously.

ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ νυκτὶ) a time opportune for fishing,

ἐπίασαν οὐδὲν) Divine providence, so that it might be established by this that human labor is in vain without divine grace, Psalm CXXVII. The word πιάζειν is also above VII. 30.

Latin:

v. 3. ὑπάγω ἁλιεύειν) id est, volo ire piscatum. Dum ex- pectabatur Spiritus nihil erat quod agerent Apostoli. Et apud Judaeos inhonestum non erat. Victus quoque, ut cre- dibile est, non aliunde suppetebat, hactenus ex comitatu Christi alimoniam habentibus.

ἐρχόμεθα κὴ ὑμεῖς) Volumus & nos ire.

ἐξῆλθον) Huic voci recte praeponitur x, ut est in vetere illo Manuscripto. Male uni Manuscripto postponuntur omnes codices. Neque illa particula opus est. Sensus enim satis sibi constat, ea non addita. Quanquam etiam subaudiri possit nonnunquam copula.

εἰς τὸ πλοῖον) Relictum aut commodatum antehac.

ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ νυκτὶ) tempus piscatui opportunum,

ἐπίασαν οὐδὲν) Providentia divina, ut eo constaret frustra esse humanum laborem sine divina gratia, Psal, CXXVII. Vox πιάζειν est & supra VII. 30.

## 21:4
Vers. 4.

ἔστη ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἰς τὸν αἰγιαλὸν) Signifying that he, through the resurrection, was now on land: they themselves were occupied in the salt sea. οἱ μέντοι ᾔδεισαν οἱ μαθηταὶ ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστι) Hindered from recognizing him, as above XX. 14, 15. they believed him to be a buyer of fish.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

ἔστη ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἰς τὸν αἰγιαλὸν) Significans se per resurre- ctionem jam esse invado: ipsos in salo versari. ὦ μέντοι ᾔδεισαν οἱ μαθηταὶ ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστι) Impediti ne eum agnoscerent, ut supra XX. 14, 15. crediderunt emptorem esse piscium.

## 21:5
Vers. 5.

παιδία) A gentle form of address, 1 Epist. II. 14. 18. προσφάγιον) ὄψον, ὀψάριον, that which is eaten with bread, especially fish,

Latin:

Vers. 5.

παιδία) Blanda compellatio, 1. Epist. II. 14. 18. προσφάγιον) ὄψον, ὀψάριον, id quod eum pane editur, præcipue pisces,

## 21:6
Vers. 6.

Βάλετε εἰς τὰ δεξιὰ μέρη) Closer to the shore as it seems, where there was less hope of catching, as if he were saying, In the very whirlpool where you least think, there will be fish. Thus, among the near-barbarian nations, the catch was more successful than among the Jews.

κὶ εὑρήσετε) As much as is enough. ἀπὸ τῶ πλήθους τῶν ἰχθύων) A presage of the great catch of men to be made by the Apostles. ὁ Κύριός ἐστι) Admonished by the miracle itself. τὸν ἐπενδύτην) Thus the LXX translate in two places מעיל which is a more honorable kind of garment. ἐπένδυμα in Aquila and Symmachus, in Jerome epist. CXXX, an outer tunic. In Theodoret on Exodus, quest. LXVI, χιτὼν ὁ ἔξωθεν. In the martyrology on the 12th of the Kalends of November concerning Hilarion: having a leather ependyten, which is taken from Jerome’s life of the same Hilarion; they translate ἱμάτιον, στολὴν, ποδήρη. Suidas: τὸ ἱμάτιον ἐπάνω. Later Hebrews also use אנפנדא. Peter therefore put this on (for that is tacitly indicated by the word for girding, whence the Syrian; he took the tunic and girded his loins) so that he might appear more respectable before Christ, fearing nothing if he should dampen it somewhat by walking through the waters.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Βάλετε εἰς τὰ δεξιὰ μέρη) Propius littus ut videtur, ubi minor erat spes capiendi, quasi dicat, Quo minime reris gurgite piscis erit. Sic apud gentes prope barbaras felicior quam apud Judæos captura.

κὶ εὑρήσετε Quantum satis. ἀπὸ τῶ πλήθους τῶν ἰχθύων) Præsagium maximæ capturæ hominum per Apostolos faciendæ. ὁ Κύριός ἐστι) Ipso miraculo admonitus. τὸν ἐπενδύτην) Sic vertunt LXX. duobus locis מעיל quod est vestis genus honoratius. ἐπένδυμα Aquilæ & Sym- macho, Hieronymo epist. CXXX. superior tunica. Theodo- reto in Exodum, quæst. LXVI. χιτὼν ὁ ἔξωθεν. In martyro- logio ad XII. Calend. Nov. de Hilarione: pelliceum habens ependyten, quod ex Hieronymo desumtum vita ejusdem Hilarionis; vertunt ἱμάτιον, στολὴν, ποδήρη. Suidas τὸ ἱμάτιον ἐπάνω. Utuntur & Hebræi posteriores אנפנדא. Hanc ergo induit Petrus (id enim succingendi vocabulo tacite in- nuitur, unde Syrus; accepit tunicam & cinxit lumbos suos) quo honestior apud Christum appareret, mhil veritus, si eam per aquas gradiendo nonnihil humectaret.

## 21:7
ἦν γὰρ γυμνὸς) Thus the Hebrews call him who is stripped of his outer garment: who has nothing but τὴν ὑποδύτην, כתונה, as 1 Sam. XIX. 24, 2 Sam. VI. 20, Isa. XX. 7, Acts XIX. 16. Mela says the Germans mostly went naked: Tacitus interprets that as having cast off the outer garment. Thus in Job XXII. 6 and ch. XXIV. 7, a garment is said to be stripped from the naked. Chrysostom to those being baptized: Γυμνός μοι τῶ χιτωνίσκῳ μόνῳ. Thus in Xiphilinus concerning Pseudo-Antony, when γυμνὸς had been used, it follows συνδύα διασείων.

Peter could not reach Christ by walking or wading: since the water was deep, being still about two hundred cubits distant from the shore. A doubt arises here, however, when Peter cast himself into the sea and wished to hasten to the Lord by swimming, why he still girded himself with a tunic, which would have easily caused a hindrance to one swimming? To Blessed Gerhard it is probable that he hastened to Christ by walking miraculously upon the waters. Which is an argument of great faith, strengthened in Peter by the presence of Christ, and also of the divine power of Christ, that He sustained him walking on the sea. But lest that faith be believed to be destitute of a command, it must be said that Peter was stirred by an internal impulse from Christ, just as before this in Matthew 14:29 he was ordered by an express word to enter the sea. Yet there seems no need for us to attribute such a miraculous walking to Peter here. For ἐπενδύτης is not inconveniently understood with Lud. de Dieu, so that it is neither a cloak, as Erasmus, nor a stole, as Fuller in book II, chapter 11 of his Miscellanea wished, or any outer garment whatsoever, which are certainly troublesome and inconvenient to one swimming, nor an undergarment, which the Arab, seeing it, rendered as פיס, whence comes Camisia, in French Chemise (which does not agree with the composition of the word ἐπενδύτης, nor was it suitable for one swimming, both because of its looseness and because it was ankle-length), but a garment intermediate between an undergarment and a stole. For this was the order of garments: first the undergarment, then the shirt with drawers or breeches, third the stole, fourth the cloak. Peter, while he was engaged in fishing in that hot climate, was completely naked (for he was naked), with only his private parts covered, which they are accustomed to do even among the Barbarian Indians, who walk about naked. And when he had heard that it was the Lord who was standing on the shore, neglecting the undergarment, which could have hindered one swimming, he put on the drawers, which could not impede one swimming, and thus he leaped into the sea. ἔβαλεν ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὴν θαλάσσην, which is said not of one walking upon the waters, but of one throwing himself into the sea. Although, however, the undergarment was then an ὑπένδυτον, it nevertheless conveniently retains the name ἐπενδύτης, because it was accustomed to be put on over the shirt: nor is the word διεζώσατο inappropriate. For because the undergarments of Orientals are narrow at the bottom and loose at the top, they are drawn together like a purse, and are again loosened, and are called διαζώννυσθαι when, drawn in at the loins, they gird and constrict them, whence also the undergarments are called διαζώματα. Nor does Dievius think that the Greek-Latin Glossary meant anything else when it renders ἐπενδύτης as instata, superaria, or the Latin-Greek as superaria, ἐπενδύτης. Superaria, which is put on over the shirt, over the first garment. And it was always of light, thin material, mostly cotton and sometimes linen.

Latin:

ἦν γὰρ γυμνὸς) Sic Hebræi vocant eum qui superiore ve- ste exutus est: qui non habet nisi τὴν ὑποδύτην, כתונה, ut 1. Sam. XIX. 24. 2. Sam. VI. 20. Esa. XX. 7. Act. XIX. 16. Germanos Mela plerunque nudos egisse dicit: interpretatur id Tacitus rejecta veste superiore. Sic apud Jobum XXII. 6. & c. XXIV. 7. vestis dicitur nudis detrahi. Chrysostomus ad baptizandos: Γυμνός μοι τῶ χιτωνίσκῳ μόνῳ. Sic apud Xiphilinum Pseudantonio, cum γυμνὸς positum esset sequi- tur συνδύα διασείων.

Non peditando vel vadendo potuit ad Christum pervenire Petrus: siquidem profunda fuerit aqua, à continenti adhuc ducentis quasi cubitis distans. Dubium autem hic incidit, cum Petrus in mare se misit, & natando ad Dominum contendere voluit, cur tunica adhuc se succinxerit, quæ facile remo- ram natanti injecisset? B. Gerhardo verisimile est, quod miraculose super aquas ambulando ad Chri- stump contenderit. Quod argumentum est magnæ fidei, è præsentia Christi roboratæ in Petro, nec non divinæ virtutis Christi, quod eum ambulan- tem in mari sustentarit. Ne autem fides ea desti- tuta credatur mandato, dicendum fuerit, interno impulsu à Christo excitatum fuisse Petrum, uti an- te hac Matth. XIV. 29. expresso verbo jussus est in- trare mare. Non tamen opus videtur, ut Petro talem miraculosam ambulationem hic tribuamus. Nam ἐπενδύτης accipitur non incommode cum Lud. de Dieu, ita ut nec pallium sit, ut Erasmus, nec stola, ut Fullerus lib. II. c. 11 Miscell. voluit, aut quæcunque superior vestis, quæ utique natanti mole- stæ sunt & incommodæ, neque indusium, quod A- rabi visum פיס reddenti, unde Camisia, Gallice Chemise (quæ cum compositione vocis ἐπενδύτης non convenit, neque apta natanti erat, tum ob laxitatem, tum quia talaris fuit) sed vestis media inter indusium & stolam. Hic enim erat vestium ordo: Primum indusium, tum subucula cum sub- ligaculis seu femoralibus, tertio stola, quarto pal- lium. Fuit Petrus, dum piscationi in calido isto climate incumberet, prorsus nudus ἦν γὰρ γυμνὸς) tectis solummodo, quod & inter Barbaros Indos so- lent, qui nudi incedunt, pudendis. Quumque audi- visset Dominum esse, qui in littore staret, neglecto indusio, quod natanti obesse poterat, induit subli- gaculum, quod natantem impedire non poterat, atque ita prosiliit in mare. ἔβαλεν ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὴν θαλάσσην, quod non de ambulante super aquas, sed de projiciente se in mare dicitur. Etsi autem tum subligaculum fuerit ὑπένδυτον, retinet tamen commode nomen ἐπενδύτυ, quia solebat indusio superindui: neque inconveniens est verbum διε- ζώσατο. Nam quia Orientalium subligacula in- terne angusta, superne laxa crumenæ instar con- trahuntur, & rursus laxantur διαζώννυσθαι dicun- tur, quando ad lumbos contracta eos cingunt & constringunt, unde & subligacula διαζώματα. Nec aliud voluisse putat Dievius Glossarium Græ- co-Latinum, cum ἐπενδύτης reddit instata, supera- ria, aut Latino-Græcum superaria, ἐπενδύτης. Su- peraria, quæ supra indusium, supra primam ve- stem induitur. Eratque ex levi semper, tenui- que materia, gossypina plerumque & interdum lin- tea.

## 21:8
Vers. 8. οἱ δὲ ἄλλοι μαθηταὶ, τῷ πλοιαρίῳ ἦλθον) Just as he praises Peter's readiness, so he excuses the others.

ὀ γὰρ ἦσαν μακρὰν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς) They were about to arrive at Christ by a short voyage.

σύροντες τὸ δίκτυον) Dragging with difficulty.

Latin:

Vers. 8. οἱ δὲ ἄλλοι μαθηταὶ, τῷ πλοιαρίῳ ἦλθον) Sicut Petri promptitudinem laudat, ita excusat cæteros.

ὀ γὰρ ἦσαν μακρὰν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς) Brevi navigio erant per- venturi ad Christum.

σύροντες τὸ δίκτυον) Ægre moventes.

## 21:9
Vers. 9. ἀνθρακίαν κειμένην) Christ now shows greater power by creating things out of nothing.

κὶ ὀψάριον) A word comprising a plural meaning with a singular sound. Formerly he had increased a few fish, now he causes them to exist out of nothing.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἀνθρακίαν κειμένην) Majorem jam potestatem Christus ostendit res creans ex nihilo.

κὶ ὀψάριον) Vox singulari sono pluralem significatum comprehendens. Olim pisces paucos auxerat, nunc fa- cit ut ex nihilo existant.

## 21:10
Vers. 10. ἀπὸ τῶν ὀψαρίων ὧν ἐπιάσαντε νῦν) Christ makes a common meal from the fish made by himself and others which the Apostles had caught, so that he might thus show that both those whom he himself had converted and those who were to be converted by the ministry of the Apostles are destined for the same end.

Chrysostom, Leontius, Theophylactus, and Euthymius have noted the same miracle, that Christ produced a fish out of nothing: Cyril wishes it to have been brought out of the sea by a mere command: Theodoret of Heraclea brings forward both opinions as probable. But since he created both fire and bread, it is altogether more likely that the fish was also thus created out of nothing, if indeed they found a roasted fish and bread on the shore, when no food had been there before. Nicephorus, Book I of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 35, says this breakfast was prepared by the hands of Angels. But however it was prepared, whether immediately or by the employment of angelic ministry, Christ demonstrated his divine power in it, since to produce something out of nothing belongs to none but one of infinite power.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ἀπὸ τῶν ὀψαρίων ὧν ἐπιάσαντε νῦν) Christus ex piscibus a se factis, & aliis, quos Apostoli ceperant, com- munes facit epulas, ut sic ostendat, & eos, quos ipse con- verterat & quos Apostolorum ministerio erat conversurus, ad eundem finem destinari.

Notarunt idem miraculum Chrysostom, Leon- tius, Theophylactus, Euthymius, quod Christus piscem ex nihilo produxerit: Quem è mari solo jussu eductum Cyrillus vult: utramque sententiam ceu probabilem adfert Theodoretus Heracleotes. Sed quum & ignem & panem procrearit, verisimi- lius omnino est, & piscem è nihilo ita procrea- tum, siquidem piscem assum & panem invenerint in littore, cum nihil cibi prius illic adfuisset. Ni- cephorus lib. I. Histor. Eccles. cap. 35. Manibus An- gelorum hoc jentaculum præparatum fuisse. Sed quomodocunque præparatum fuerit, an imme- diato, num vero angelico adhibito ministerio, Chri- stus demonstravit eodem divinam potentiam, quum ex nihilo aliquid producere non nisi infini- tæ virtutis sit.

## 21:11
Vers. 11. ἀνέβη) Into the ship. Thus Mark VI. 51, Luke VIII. v. 22.

εἵλκυσε τὸ δίκτυον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) Namely, with the ship now brought to the shore so that the net could now be dragged more easily. Understand, however, that this was done by Peter and his companions: but he himself is named as the leader of the others.

ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα τριῶν) Some note that there are as many kinds of fish, and that it is thereby signified that the catch would be from every kind of man. A figure of the times of David and Solomon, when there were 153,000 proselytes, 2 Chronicles II. v. 17.

τοσύτων) Since there were so many, thus above c. VI. 9.

ἐκ ἐσχίσθη τὸ δίκτυον) A presage of the future unity of those who were to be gathered into the Church through the work of the Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἀνέβη) In navem. Sic Marc. VI. 51. Luc. VIII. v. 22.

εἵλκυσε τὸ δίκτυον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) Quippe nave jam ad littus admota ut facilius jam trahi rete posset. Intellige autem hoc factum à Petro & sociis: sed ipse ut cæterorum dux no- minatur.

ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα τριῶν) Notant quidam tot piscium nu- merari genera, eoque significari, ex omnium hominum genere capturam fore. Figura Davidis & Salomonis tem- poribus, cum CLIII. millia fuere proselytarum, 2. Paral. II. v. 17.

τοσύτων) Cum tot essent, sic supra c. VI. 9.

ἐκ ἐσχίσθη τὸ δίκτυον) Præsagium mitæ unitatis eorum qui per Apostolorum operam in Ecclesiam erant colli- gendi.

## 21:12
Vers. 12. ἀριστήσατε) ἄριστον is the term used for food that is taken even in the morning. Thus, in Homer, it is narrated that an ἄριστον was prepared at the appearance of dawn. It must be understood, however, that Christ took food together with them for the greater assurance of his body, Acts 1:4, ch. 10:41.

ἐδεὶς δὲ ἐτόλμα τῶν μαθητῶν ἐξετάσαι αὐτὸν) Although his appearance was once more majestic.

εἰδότες, ὅτι ὁ κύριός ἐστιν) From his countenance, voice, and deeds.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἀριστήσατε) ἄριστον dicitur cibus etiam qui ma- ne sumitur. Sic apud Homerum narratur paratum ἄριστον ἅμ' ἠοῖ φαινομένῃ. Intelligendum autem est Christum una cum ipsis cibum sumsisse in majorem corporis sui fidem, Act. I. 4. c. X. 41.

ἐδεὶς δὲ ἐτόλμα τῶν μαθητῶν ἐξετάσαι αὐτὸν) Quanquam conspectus erat olim visu augustior.

εἰδότες, ὅτι ὁ κύριός ἐστιν) Ex vultu, voce, factis.

## 21:13
Vers. 13. δίδωσιν ἀυτοῖς) He shows himself to be the head of the household of the Church, whose duty it is to give to each his own portion: which is explained shortly after in the discourse held with Peter and John. Compare what is said in Matthew 25:15.

Latin:

Vers. 13. δίδωσιν ἀυτοῖς) Patremfamilias Ecclesiæ se o- stendit, cujus & suum cuique dimensum dare: quod mox explicatur, sermone habito ad Petrum & Johannem. Con- fer quæ dicta Matth. XXV. 15.

## 21:14
Vers. 14. τοῦτο ἤδη τρίτον) Refer this to the number of days. He appeared first on the very day of his resurrection: again on the eighth day, now the third time.

Others observe that this was the third manifestation which was made to the disciples, and indeed to several of them, as is expressly added τοῖς μαθηταῖς, for he had appeared otherwise also to the women: he had also appeared to Peter, as is held in Luke 24:34. However, the Grotian explanation is found in Augustine: and both can be conveniently joined.

PART II.

A twofold conversation with Peter.

Latin:

Vers. 14. τοῦτο ἤδη τρίτον) Refer ad dierum numerum. Primum apparuit diversis ab ipso resurrectionis die: iterum die octavo, nunc tertium.

Alii observant, quod tertia fuerit hæc manife- statio, quæ facta discipulis, & quidem pluribus, ut expresle additur τοῖς μαθηταῖς, nam alias apparue- rat etiam mulieribus: apparuerat quoque Petro, ut habetur Luc. XXIV. 34. Habetur autem Gro- tiana explicatio apud Augustinum: & conjungi potest commode utraque.

PARS II.

Colloquium geminum cum Petro.

## 21:15
Vers. 15. ὅτε ὖν ἠρίσησαν) Which is the time for conversing. Σίμων Ἰωνᾶ) Concerning this word, see Matthew 16:17. ἀγαπᾷς με πλεῖον τύτων) The wonderful wisdom of Christ, who with so few words brings it about that Peter might satisfy both himself, whom he had denied three times, and his colleagues, whom he had preferred himself over: giving an example of ecclesiastical discipline.

Ναὶ κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε) It sufficed for him, as Augustine says, to bear witness to his own heart; he did not wish to be the judge of another's heart. He did not prefer himself to others as before in Matthew 26:33, and yet he brought forth a testimony of his affection from a sincere heart, such as is required in a pastor of the Church. John used ἀγαπᾷν and φιλεῖν interchangeably here, as he did βόσκειν and ποιμαίνειν shortly after. Nor are subtleties to be sought here. And Peter reverently appeals to Christ's knowledge, to whom he had learned by experience that he was better known than to himself.

Wrongly, says Beza, is this response punctuated thus: Ναὶ, κύριε, as if Peter were assenting to the whole question, affirming that he loved the Lord more than his fellow disciples loved him, which would have been the act of a most impudent man. Therefore, this passage is to be read in one flow, and the particle Ναὶ is that of one affirming what is subjoined concerning Christ's own knowledge, and not of one who was simply assenting to the whole of that about which he was asked: for which reason it is also better to interpret it in this place as 'Certainly' rather than 'Yes'.

βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μυ) Christ teaches in the prince of the Apostles the others, in what best way love for him is demonstrated. Feed, that is, consult for them, not for yourself: persuade, do not compel: sheep not yours, but mine: the force of which words Peter demonstrates that he understood very well in 1 Peter 5:2.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὅτε ὖν ἠρίσησαν) Quod tempus est colloquendi. Σίμων Ἰωνᾶ) De hac voce vide ad Matth. XVI. 17. ἀγαπᾷς με πλεῖον τύτων) Mira Christi sapientia, qui tam paucis vocibus efficit, ut Petrus & sibi satisfaceret quem ter negaverat, & collegis, quibus se prætulerat: exemplum dans disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ.

Ναὶ κύριε, σὺ οἶδας ὅτι φιλῶ σε) Suffecit ei, ut ait Augu- stinus, testimonium perhibere cordi suo, noluit judex esse cordis alieni. Non prætulit se aliis ut ante Matt. XXVI. 33. & ta- men ex corde sincero affectus testimonium protulit, qua- le in Ecclesiæ pastore requiritur. Promiscue hic usurpa- vit Johannes ἀγαπᾷν & φιλεῖν ut mox βόσκειν & ποιμαίνειν. Neque hic quærendæ sunt subtilitates. Et reverenter Pe- trus ad Christi scientiam provocat, cui se notiorem esse quam sibi ipsi, experimento didicerat.

Perperam, inquit Beza, hæc responsio sic inter- pungitur, Ναὶ, κύριε, ac si toti interroganti assentire- tur Petrus, affirmans, se diligere Dominum am- plius quam sui condiscipuli diligerent, quod impu- dentissimi hominis fuisset.
