Vno igitur tenore legen- dus est hic locus, & particula Ναὶ est affirmantis id quod subjicitur de ipsius Christi notitia, non autem ejus, qui simpliciter ei toti, de quo rogatus erat, assen- tiretur: quamobrem etiam præstat hoc loco interpre- tari Certe quam Etiam.

βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μυ) Docet Christus in principe Apostolo- rum cæteros, quo optime modo amor in ipsum demon- stretur. Pasce, id est ipsis, non tibi consule: suade, non co- ge: oves non tuas, sed meas: quam vocum vim optime se intellexisse Petrus demonstrat 1. Petr. V. 2.

## 21:16
Vers. 16. πάλιν δεύτερον) A pleonasm such as in Matthew 26:42. It is shown here that signs of a corrected mind are required in proportion to the magnitude of the fault.

ποίμαινε τὰ πρόβατά μου) What we have said concerning the words βόσκειν and ποιμαίνειν is to be understood likewise of the words προβάτων and ἀρνίων. For these also are used indiscriminately, as appears from a comparison of the passages Matth. X. 16, Luc. X. 3. Compare Zach. XI. 4, and consider the destruction of the Jewish nation, which was properly committed to Peter, Gal. II. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 16. πάλιν δεύτερον) πλεονασμὸς qualis Matth. XXVI. 42. Ostenditur hic emendati animi notas requiri pro culpæ magnitudine.

ποίμαινε τὰ πρόβατά μυ) Quod de voce βόσκειν & ποι- μαίνειν diximus, idem de vocibus προβάτων & ἀρνίων intelli- gendum est. Nam & hæ promiscue usurpantur, ut appa- ret ex collatione locorum Matth. X. 16. Luc. X. 3. Conf. Zach. XI. 4. & cogita exitium Judaicæ gentis, quæ proprie Petro commissa Gal. II. 9.

## 21:17
Vers. 17. ἐλυπήθη ὁ Πέτρο) Because by denying three times he had deserved to be questioned three times.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ἐλυπήθη ὁ Πέτρο) Quod ter negando me- ruisset ter interrogari.

## 21:18
Vers. 18. ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω σοι) He shows that a pastor must consider how difficult a duty he is undertaking, lest he be caught unprepared, Matthew 10:16. It is a matter which consists in the expenditure of liberty and life.

We note these things as being spoken conveniently, and as less suitable to the Oecumenical Episcopate and dominion of the Roman Pontiff, so that it may appear how Grotius has progressed for the worse, when he became a parasite of the Roman curia. From this interpretation, however, it is manifest at the same time how empty and vain is the inference of the Papists from this saying, who seek the chief defense of their very bad cause in this commendation of the sheep made to Peter. Assuredly, this is not peculiar and proper to Peter, but common to all pastors. But for Peter, after his threefold denial and the subsequent threefold profession of love for Christ, there was a proper and peculiar restoration to his sacred office: which, although it was done generally in chapter XX, when it was entrusted to him along with the rest of the Apostles, yet here the Lord repeated or confirmed it to him separately, but with witnesses present, so that every scruple concerning his reception might be removed, and at the same time He taught what is the chief thing προσκείμενον to pastors and ministers of the word, which is their proper duty; the former indeed, to love Christ, but the latter, to feed the lambs, and likewise the sheep; for those subject to Peter are not so committed to him along with the Prelates as if

To the shepherd of shepherds, as the Papists trifle, but all pastors are warned in his person, and that the tender ones or infants are to be nourished with milk as lambs, and the sheep as more perfect ones are to be properly cared for, as Ambrose observes in lib. X. in Luc. Nor indeed did Christ commend ALL SHEEP or ALL LAMBS to Peter: but indefinitely, Feed, he says, my sheep; which is enjoined upon all pastors alike, Acts 20. 28. 1. Pet. 5. 2. But there is no need to pursue these things now. For here Grotius was not yet a pleader or advocate for the Roman Pontiff.

Vers. 18. ὅτε ἧς νεώτερος) ἧς here has an indefinite meaning. For now also he addresses him as a young man with respect to his future age. For all things which Christ says here have an allusion to preceding deeds: The interrogation concerning greater love, to that which Peter had first met Christ through the sea; the excellent command of the Apostolic office, to that which he had drawn the net: so also these words, to that which he had come girded with a linen cloth. And he shows the impending troubles to be the more grievous, because they are to fall upon an age already heavy in itself.

κὶ περιεπάτεις ὅπε ἤθελες) As just now out of the ship and into the ship at your own will.

ὅτ᾽ ἂν δὲ γηράσῃς) When you shall have added nearly forty years to this age.

ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς σε) You will be forced to stretch them out as captives are wont to do.

κὶ ἄλλος σε ζώσει) For also to bind is to gird, as Kimchi notes at Ps. 76. 10, where also Symmachus has περιζωσθὲν. That which will remain of wrath for the Assyrian, that you will bind and restrain so that he may not destroy Jerusalem. Compare with this passage Acts XXI. 11. ἄρας τὴν ζώνην τῦ Παύλε δήσας τε αὑτῶ τὰς χεῖρας. Where you see a belt is taken for a bond.

κὶ οἴσει ὅπε ὐ θέλεις) These words, not those former ones, have the meaning of the punishment of the cross. ὅπε ὐ θέλεις that is, whither you would not be drawn, indicative for subjunctive as above c. XII. 21. Matth. XXVI. 39. It is, however, a witticism, to act concerning that which you would not, that is, to a bad cross. That Peter died by the cross and indeed at Rome, I do not think should be doubted, since we have so many testimonies of the ancients. Tertullian brings it forward as a matter confessed among all, even heretics: Happy is the Church (Roman) to which the Apostles poured out their whole doctrine with their blood, where Peter is made equal to the Lord's passion. Scorpiaco: Then Peter is girded by another when he is bound to the cross. Clem. Strom. VII. ταύτῃ ἄρα τὲς πόνες κὶ τὰς βασάνες κὶ τὰς θλίψεις, ἐχ ὡς παρὰ τοῖς φιλοσόφοις οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι ἐλπίδι δὲ τῶν ἡδέων μεταχῦν, ὑπομένεσ᾽ ἀλλ᾽ ἡ γνῶσις αὐτῷ πεῖσμα βεβαιότα- τον ἐναγώνησε τῆς τῶν μελλόντων ἐλπίδων ἀπολαύσεως. διόπερ ὐ μόνον τῶν ἐνταῦθα κολάσεων, ἀλλὰ κὶ τῶν ἡδέων ἁπάντων κα- ταφρονεῖ· Φασὶν ἦν τὸν μακάριον πέτρον θεασάμενον τὴν ἀυτῶ γυναῖκα ἀγομένην τὴν ἐπὶ θάνατον ἡσθῆναι μὲν τῆς κολάσεως χάριν κὶ τῆς εἰς οἶκον ἀνακομιδῆς· ἐπιφωνῆσαι δὲ ἔυ μάλα προ- τρεπτικῶς τε κὶ παρακλητικῶς ἐξ ὀνόματος προσειπόντα μέμνησο- αὕτη τῷ κυρίε. For so it must be read. To these add Gaius, who lived under Bishop Zephyrinus, and Dionysius, Bishop of Corinth, whose testimonies exist in Eusebius. I omit later authors, who have reported it in great numbers. If, however, anyone wishes to see those who are of exceptional authority, let him read Ambrose on the nativity of the Apostles, Prudentius on the passion of Peter and Paul, Chrysostom in his oration on the same, Theodoret περὶ ἀγάπης.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω σοι) Ostendit pastori consideran- dum quam difficile suscipiat munus, ne imparatus depre- hendatur, Matth. X. 16. Res est, quæ constat libertatis & vitæ dispendio.

Hæc ut commode dicta, & Pontificis Romani Oecumenico Episcopatui, ac dominatui minus con- venientia annotamus, ut quomodo in deterius profecerit Grotius, quando parasitus factus est curiæ Romanæ, appareat. Ex hac autem inter- pretatione patet simul, quam inanis & vana sit Pontificiorum ex hoc dicto illatio, qui præci- puum causæ suæ pessimæ præsidium in hac ovium commendatione Petro facta quærunt. Nimirum non hoc peculiare ac proprium Petro est, sed commune omnibus pastoribus. Petro autem pro- pria & peculiaris erat, post trinam abnegationem, edita trina amoris Christi professione, restitutio in sacrum munus: quæ etsi cap. XX. facta γενικῶς, cum ipsi cum reliquis Apostolis id demandatum, hic tamen seorfim eidem, sed adhibitis testibus, eam denuo, vt omnis de receptione ipsius scrupu- lus eximeretur, repetiit, vel confirmavit Domi- nus, & quod præcipuum sit προσκείμενον Pastorum & ministrorum verbi, quod officium proprium, simul docuit; illud quidem, Christum diligere, hoc vero, agnos pascere, pariter & oves; non enim Petro ita subditi cum Prælatis committuntur ceu

Pastori pastorum, uti nugantur Papistæ, sed mo- nentur in ejus persona pastores omnes, & tenellos sive infantes lacte nutriendos tanquam agnos, & oves tanquam perfectiores probe esse curandas, ut observat Ambrosius lib. X. in Luc. Nec vero u- niversaliter OVES aut AGNOS OMNES, commendavit Petro Christus: sed indefinite Pasce, inquit, oves meas; quod omnibus pastori- bus pariter injungitur Actor. 20. 28. 1. Petr. 5. 2. Sed hæc non opus est jam persequi. Hic enim nondum fuit Grotius Pontificis Romani Causidi- cus, vel Advocatus.

Vers. 18. ὅτε ἧς νεώτερος) ἧς hic habet indefinitam si- gnificationem. Nam nunc quoque eum ut juvenem allo- quitur respectu venturæ ætatis. Omnia enim quæ Christus hic dicit, allusionem habent ad facta præcedentia: Inter- rogatio de majori dilectione, ad id quod Petrus primus per mare Christo occurrerat; mandatum eximium Apo- stolici muneris, ad id quod rete pertraxerat: sic & hæc ver- ba, ad id quod superariam cinctus venerat. Et ærumnas impendentes eo ostendit graviores fore, quod incubitu- ræ sint ætati per se gravi.

κὶ περιεπάτεις ὅπε ἤθελες) Ut modo ex navi & in navem tuopte arbitratu.

ὅτ᾽ ἂν δὲ γηράσῃς) Ubi ad hanc ætatem quadraginta ferme annos adjeceris.

ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς σε) Cogeris extendere ut solent ca- ptivi.

κὶ ἄλλος σε ζώσει) Nam & vincire est cingere ut ad Psal. 76. 10. notat Kimchi, ubi & Symmachus περιζωσθὲν. Quod iræ Assyrio restabit id vincies ac cohibebis ne perdat Hiero- solyma. Confer cum hoc loco Actor. XXI. 11. ἄρας τὴν ζώνην τῦ Παύλε δήσας τε αὑτῶ τὰς χεῖρας. Ubi vides cingulum sumi pro vinculo.

κὶ οἴσει ὅπε ὐ θέλεις) Hæc verba non illa priora, supplicii crucis habent significationem. ὅπε ὐ θέλεις id est quo nolles trahi, indicativus pro subjunctivo ut supra c. XII. 21. Matth. XXVI. 39. Est autem χαριεντισμὸς, agent de quo nolles, id est in malam crucem. Quin cruce Petrus & quidem Romæ obierit, dubitandum non arbitror, cum tot habeamus vete- tum testimonia. Tertullianus tanquam rem apud omnes etiam hæreticos confessam adfert: Statu felix Ecclesia (Ro- mana) cui totam doctrinam Apostoli cum suo sanguine profude- runt, ubi Petrus passioni dominicæ adæquatur. Scorpiaco: Tum Petrus ab altero cingitur cum cruci adstringitur. Cle- men Strom. VII. ταύτῃ ἄρα τὲς πόνες κὶ τὰς βασάνες κὶ τὰς θλίψεις, ἐχ ὡς παρὰ τοῖς φιλοσόφοις οἱ ἀνδρεῖοι ἐλπίδι δὲ τῶν ἡδέων μεταχῦν, ὑπομένεσ᾽ ἀλλ᾽ ἡ γνῶσις αὐτῷ πεῖσμα βεβαιότα- τον ἐναγώνησε τῆς τῶν μελλόντων ἐλπίδων ἀπολαύσεως. διόπερ ὐ μόνον τῶν ἐνταῦθα κολάσεων, ἀλλὰ κὶ τῶν ἡδέων ἁπάντων κα- ταφρονεῖ· Φασὶν ἦν τὸν μακάριον πέτρον θεασάμενον τὴν ἀυτῶ γυναῖκα ἀγομένην τὴν ἐπὶ θάνατον ἡσθῆναι μὲν τῆς κολάσεως χάριν κὶ τῆς εἰς οἶκον ἀνακομιδῆς· ἐπιφωνῆσαι δὲ ἔυ μάλα προ- τρεπτικῶς τε κὶ παρακλητικῶς ἐξ ὀνόματος προσειπόντα μέμνησο- αὕτη τῷ κυρίε. Ita enim legendum. His adde Cajum, qui sub Zephyrino Episcopo vixit & Dionysium Corinthi Epi- scopum, quorum testimonia apud Eusebium exstant. Po- steriores auctores, qui plurimi id tradiderunt, omitto. Si quis tamen eos, qui auctoritatis sunt eximiæ, volet videre, legat Ambrosium in nativitatem Apostolorum, Prudenti- um de passione Petri & Pauli, Chrysostomum oratione de iisdem, Theodoretum περὶ ἀγάπης.

## 21:19
Vers. 19. ποίῳ θανάτῳ δοξάσει τὸν Θεὸν) By a death, namely, violent and excruciating. A magnificent title of Martyrdom, to glorify God. See above c. XIII. 31.

ἀκολύθει μοι) Just as he had just now taken the things done before as signs of things to be said, so now he expresses by a conspicuous sign what he had said. For follow me has both that common meaning, which Peter also obeyed for the present, and another mystical one. He alludes to that which he had said in Matth. X. 38.

Most interpreters agree that Christ prophesied the punishment of the cross to be endured by Peter: although some depart to the contrary opinion, and understand that ποίῳ θανάτῳ only of martyrdom, or violent death. Of those, however, who judge the aforementioned crucifixion to be for Peter, some prefer to seek it in the words ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς σε, others indeed in those ἀκολούθει μοι. Grotius loves to be singular, eliciting it from the words κὶ οἴσει ὅπε ὐ θέλεις. But those are too general, so that the punishment of the cross can hardly be carved out from them. The most learned Casaubon agrees with the former, from the words ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς.

“But another shall gird thee,” gathering: at Rome, he says, the candidates for the cross, to use an Apuleian word, with the fork inserted into their necks, their hands spread out, and tied to the horns of the fork, were carried around through the city, and after that long procession were finally fixed outside the Metian gate to any one of the crosses, which were distributed in that place in great numbers. He notes that this was observed in the same way elsewhere. Rome, however, by no means concedes that Peter suffered there. Since, therefore, he says, the ancients rightly conjectured from that passage in John about the cross of Peter, that they dream he suffered at Rome, I do not know from where they fished it out: for from Christ’s reception into heaven to the fourth year of Nero, it is certain beyond a doubt that Peter did not come to Rome. But because they had read in C. Tacitus and Suetonius that punishment was inflicted upon the Christians under Nero in about the seventh year of his reign, they divined that Peter and Paul, though at different times, were put to death; in which they are certainly mistaken: for Cornelius and Suetonius imply that the Christians were raged against only once, and that they were not punished by the cross, but by the torch, because, being stripped and tied to a stake, with a hook driven into their chin or throat, and with pitch dripping from above, they provided the use of nocturnal lights, a kind of cruelty which Juvenal touches upon. If, therefore, Peter and Paul were condemned at that time, neither did the one perish by the sword, nor the other by the cross; but they shone with the torch in that instance: But neither could it have been at Rome, since he was never at Rome. But it seems he was punished in a provincial magistracy, for instance when he was preaching to the diaspora of Asia, whose metropolis was Babylon, from which he writes his Epistle. It should be known that the Jews had one metropolis of religion or θρησκείας; but there were three metropolises of citizenship, Jerusalem, Babylon, and Alexandria. There were two diasporas, the Asian, to which Peter writes, and the European, which is mentioned in John 7:35. Thus the Jews living among pagans and gentiles were called by one name, which name is found written in the Talmud in this way.... But the Jews, ignorant of Greek and Latin, do not know what that word means. The head of the Asian diaspora was Babylon, and those Jews used, and still use today in their synagogues, the Chaldean paraphrase of Onkelos. Peter writes to them from that very metropolis, Babylon. The metropolis of the European diaspora was Alexandria. Those Jews had a temple almost as great as the Jerusalemites, and they used the Greek paraphrase of the 70 Interpreters. For that reason they were called Hellenists in Acts 6:1 and 11:20, which has been little noticed by all interpreters: for to hellenize is not to live in Greece, as it seemed to the most learned of all, but to use the Greek language. The third kind of citizenship were the Jews assigned to the Jerusalem metropolis, as in the same chapter 6, the Hebrews are distinguished from those who were Hellenists; the former used the Jerusalem paraphrase which exists today. Since, therefore, Peter was sent to the circumcision, it seems he perished in the Asian diaspora, if there is room for conjecture. For as to his arrival in Rome, his 25-year seat, and his supreme capital punishment there, no one who is a little more humane could believe it. Casaubon says these things very learnedly; William, the tutor of Wycliffe, similarly did not hesitate to assert that Peter did not even ever see Rome. See Thomas Waldensis, book 2, on the doctrine of faith, art. 1, and Whitaker on the Roman Pontiff, quest. 3, chap. 3, p. 309. Johannes Aventinus, book 2 of the Annals, p. 21, says that there are not lacking those who entirely deny that Peter was ever alive at Rome, because the province of teaching the worshippers of gods (whose head is Rome) was entrusted to Paul by Christ, and the opportunity of instructing the Hebrews only was given to Peter. Whatever, however, may be the case regarding him, whether Peter was at Rome and even underwent death there, or not: certainly the Papists will never teach that he held the bishopric there. But that has been dealt with in the Papistical Matæologia.

Regarding the testimonies of the Fathers, Casaubon, Witak, Chamier, and others may be consulted.

We must return here to our text: from whose words 'follow me,' Grotius seems to gather the manner of Peter's death among others, while he wishes to allude, as to the mystical sense, to Matt. 10:38, 'He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.' But neither can a double sense have a place in the phrase 'FOLLOW ME,' namely, the common one, concerning the following properly so-called, which happens by walking after another, whom Peter obeyed at the present time, and concerning the following taken metaphorically, which happens by imitating another; nor is the cross to which someone is to be fastened designated precisely or definitely in the words 'take up his cross,' even if it is alluded to, and any cross or calamity of ours has its denomination from the cross of Christ, but rather indefinitely any affliction whatsoever, which GOD imposes upon us for the sake of testing. Gnost. ch. 15, accepted it concerning the punishment of the cross, then Peter is girded by another when he is bound to the cross, he added this critique concerning that explanation: But since hands are extended in other kinds of violent death also than in crucifixion, and since it is added, 'another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish,' it is more simply referred to the constriction by chains, which are accustomed to be imposed on those who are led to punishment. But regarding those words, 'FOLLOW ME,' he has this: Christ had imposed the pastoral office on Peter, and had predicted his martyrdom to him; rising, therefore, he said to Peter, 'follow me,' and thus by that bodily following he signified the same thing which he had previously expressed in words; first he proposes his own example to him in feeding the sheep: then in undergoing death: Comparing John 13:36, 'where I go you cannot follow me now, but you will follow me afterwards,' by which words he certainly indicated that Peter in his own time would receive the same reward from the world that he himself had received, namely, the punishment of the cross. It seems to us that, since the words, 'but he said this, signifying by what death he would glorify God,' were added and subjoined, they refer not to those words 'follow me,' but to the preceding verse 18, 'You will stretch out your hands,' etc. or by the word 'by what death' the species of death, crucifixion, is designated, as in John 12:33, and then it must be gathered from those preceding things, or if that cannot be done from the preceding words, certainly the following words do so much less, since the Evangelist wishes the quality of death to be deduced not from them, but from the things above, and the following of Christ's example in doctrine and martyrdom does not immediately bring about the same kind of martyrdom: Therefore, it is better, with Tertullian, Casaubon, and others, to refer the extension of the hands, the girding, and the violent leading to the custom used in crucifixion, or it must be said that the 'quality' of death denotes not the same species of death, namely crucifixion, but generally a violent death and martyrdom: just as it is still in doubt whether Peter was affected by the punishment of the cross. Blessed Chemnitz in Harmony, ch. 50, p. 518, observes that Origen and Nicephorus note that Peter came to Rome toward the end of his life, in the last years of Nero, and that others add that he was fastened to the cross there with his head downward and his feet inverted. These are the words of Chemnitz. But if it is pleasing to know the opinion of Origen concerning the crucifixion of Peter, and the conjectures which moved the Ancients to it, so that it may be permitted to judge how certain that is, Casaubon must be employed, from whom we shall bring forward some things: The ancient Christians, he says, who grieved that nothing certain existed in Christian history from the end of the Acts of the Apostles to the times of Trajan, in order to fill that gap of time, many things licentiously

and foolishly fabricated about Peter's arrival in Rome and about his first see. But what they left written about Peter's death, and persuaded posterity, that he was affected by the punishment of the cross, although it is true, they did not nevertheless draw it from certain history, but searched for it by conjectures from John 13:36, 'but afterwards you will follow me.' Likewise chapter 21, v. 18. Also the daily usage of those times could teach them that Peter, a man of foreign condition and a despicable person, could not have been affected by the Romans by any other kind of death than the cross, as on the contrary, Paul, a Roman citizen, was punished by the sword. They judged correctly about Peter; about Paul it can be doubted: not even because he was a Roman citizen, he was immediately to be punished by the sword: For even the fratricidal emperor seems to accuse the prefect of ignorance, who did not know whether the seat of Papinian was to be executed by the sword or the axe. Therefore, Paul could also have been struck by the axe. But it was as easy and prone for the ancient Christians to fabricate these things as it was to forge the Epistles of Seneca to Paul, and of the latter to him: and to foist this merchandise upon the good Jerome, who for that reason co-opted Seneca among the Ecclesiastical writers. Some more recent learned and pious men deny that it matters to us by what kind of death Peter finished his life; nor do they think it can be gathered from that passage of John that Peter was put on the cross. Thus far Casaubon, who, however, does not seem to be sufficiently consistent with himself. For if, as he himself says, nothing certain is held in Christian history from the end of the Acts of the Apostles until the times of Trajan, if they searched for what they left written about the death of Peter, and persuaded posterity, only by conjectures from John 13:36 and the present passage, what certainty concerning that punishment of the cross will be obtained from the ancients? Moreover, those words, 'he will lead you where you do not wish,' do not imply that Peter underwent martyrdom entirely unwillingly and compelled, as Grotius wishes, for thus he would not have glorified God by his death, but they indicate only the struggle of flesh and spirit, which remains even in the reborn: because the spirit was willing, even if the flesh was weak to tremble at death, which we naturally abhor. For no one of the saints, as Cyril has it here, suffers willingly, but although bitter death encroaches upon them even against their will, yet, desirous of divine glory, they also renounce this earthly life.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ποίῳ θανάτῳ δοξάσει τὸν Θεὸν) Morte scilicet vi- olenta ac cruciabili. Magnificus Martyrii titulus δοξάζειν τὸν Θεόν. Vide supra c. XIII. 31.

ἀκολύθει μοι) Sicut modo res ante gestas signa dicendo- rum sumsit, ita nunc quod dixerat signo conspicuo expri- mit. Nam sequere me, sensum habet & illud communem, cui etiam Petrus in præsens paruit, & mysticum alterum. Alludit ad id quod dixerat Matth. X. 38.

De crucis supplicio à Petro sustinendo Chri- stum vaticinatum esse, consentiunt plerique in- terpretes: etsi nonnulli in diversum abeant, ac il- lud ποίῳ θανάτῳ tantum de martyrio, vel morte violenta intelligant. Eorum vero, qui crucifixio- nem prædictam Petro censent, alii quidem id in verbis ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς σε, alii vero in illis ἀκο- λύθει μοι, quærere malunt. Grotius singularis esse amat, è verbis κὶ οἴσει ὅπε ὐ θέλεις id eruens. Sed ea nimis sunt generalia, ut crucis supplicium inde exsculpi haud possit. Prioribus accedit eru- ditissimus Casaubonus, è verbis ἐκτενεῖς τὰς χεῖράς

συ ἡ ἄλλο σε ζώσει colligens: Romae, inquit, crucis candidati, ut verbum Apulejanum usurpem, collo furca inserto, manibus dispersis, & ad furcae cornua deligatus, per urbem circumferebantur, & ex diutina traductione illa tandem extra portam Metiam uni ex crucibus cuilibet, quae multae in eo loco distributae erant, affigebantur. Quod etiam alibi sic observatum esse notat. Roma tamen passum esse Petrum minime concedit. Quum igitur, inquit, veteres Christiani de cruce Petri, ex eo loco Johannis recte conjecerint, quod Roma passum somniant, nescio unde expiscati sint: nam à Christi in cœlum receptu ad IV. Annum Neronis certo certius est, Petrum Romam non venisse. Quia vero legerant apud C. Tacitum & Suetonium, supplicium de Christianis sub Nerone sumtum anno VII. circiter imperii ejus, ariolati sunt Petrum & Paulum, diversis tamen temporib. supplicio affectos; in quo sane frustra sunt: nam semel tantum in Christianos sævitum fuisse innuit Cornelius & Suetonius, & non cruce in eos animadversum, sed tæda, quod destituti ad palum, unco in mentum aut guttur impacto, & pice desuper stillante, usum luminum nocturnorum præstiterint, quod genus crudelitatis tangit Juvenalis. Si igitur tunc damnati sunt Petrus & Paulus, neque iste gladio, neque ille cruce perierunt; sed tæda luxerunt in illa: Sed neque Romæ potuit, quum Romæ nunquam fuerit. Sed videtur in provinciali magistratu animadversus, puta quum prædicaret τῇ διασπορᾷ Ἀσίας, cujus metropolis erat Babylon, ex qua scribit Epistolam suam. Sciendum Judæis unam religionis ἢ θρησκείας metropolim fuisse; Tres autem πολιτείας metropoles fuisse, Hierosolyma, Babylonem, Alexandriam. Duæ erant Διασποραὶ, Asiana, ad quam scribit Petrus, Europæa, cujus mentio Johannis VII. 35. Ita uno nomine vocabantur Judæi inquilini inter paganos & gentes, quod nomen invenitur in Talmud ita scriptum.... Sed Judæi, Græce & Latine ignari, quid id verbi sit nesciunt. Asianæ διασπορᾶς caput erat Babylon, iique Judæi utebantur, utunturque adhuc in Synagogis paraphrasi Chaldaici Onkelos. Ad eos scribit Petrus ex ipsa metropoli Babylone. διασπορᾶς Europææ metropolis erat Alexandria. Ii Judæi habebant templum quasi quantum Hierosolymitani, & Græca paraphrasi LXX. Interpretum utebantur. Ob id dicti Ἑλληνισαὶ Actor. VI, 1. & c. XI. 20. quod parum ab omnibus interpretibus animadversum: nam ἑλληνίζειν non est habitare in Græcia, ut doctissimo omnium visum est, sed, Græca lingua uti. Tertium genus πολιτείας, erant Judæi attributi metropoli Hierosolymitana, ut eodem cap. VI. Ἑβραῖοι distinguuntur ab iis, qui ἑλληνισαὶ ii paraphrasi Hierosolymitana quæ hodie exstat, utebantur. Quum igitur Petrus ad περιτομὴν missus est, videtur in διασπορᾷ Asianæ periisse, si conjecturæ locus est. Nam de ejus Romam adventu, sede 25. annorum, & supremo capitis supplicio, ibidem, nemo qui paulo humanior fuerit credere posset. Hæc perquam docte Casaubonus, Guilhelmus Wiclefi præceptor similiter Petrum ne quidem Romam vidisse unquam asserere non dubitavit. Vid. Thom. Waldens. lib. II. doctr. fid. art. 1. & Witackerus de Pontif. Roman. quæst. III. cap. III. p. 309. Johannes Aventinus lib. II. Annal. p. 21. non deesse, ait, qui Petrum Romæ vivum fuisse omnino pernegant, quod Paulo provincia docendi Cultores Deorum (quorum caput Roma) demandata fuerit à Christo, Petro Hebræos duntaxat instituendi copia facta. Quidquid autem de eo sit, seu fuerit Romæ, ibique etiam mortem subierit Petrus, seu non: Certe illic eum Episcopatu functum esse, nunquam docebunt Pontificii. Sed de eo in Matæologia Papistica actum.

De testimoniis Patrum Casaubonus, Witak. Cha- mierus aliique conferri poterunt.

Nobis hic ad textum nostrum redeundum: è cujus verbis sequere me genus mortis Petrinæ in- ter alios videtur colligere Grotius, dum alludi vult, quod ad sensum Mysticum, ad Matth. X. 38. Qui non tollit crucem suam, & me sequitur, non est me dignus. Sed nec geminus sensus in voce SE- QUERE ME locum habere potest, commu- nis nempe, de sequela proprie dicta, quæ ambulan- do post alium fit, cui in præsens paruit Petrus, & de sequela metaphorice accepta, quæ fit imitando alterum, neque in verbis tollat crucem suam desi- gnatur præcise aut definite crux, cui aliquis affi- gendus, etsi ad eum alludatur, & à cruce Christi quælibet nostra crux, vel calamitas denominatio- nem habeat, sed indefinite afflictio quæcunque, quam δοκιμασίας ergo DEUS nobis imponit. B. Gerhardus noster in Harmon. Evang. de Re- surrect. c. VI. adducto Tertulliano, qui verba Chri- sti, extendes manus tuas & c. l. adv. Gnost. c. XV. ac- cepit de crucis supplicio, tunc Petrus ab alio cingi- tur, cum cruci adstringitur, hanc de illa explica- tione adjecit ἐπίκρισιν: Sed cum in aliis etiam vio- lentæ mortis generibus, quam in crucifixione manus extendantur, cumque addatur, alius te cinget & ducet, quo non vis, ideo ad constrictionem per vincula, quæ imponi solent illis, qui ad supplicium ducuntur, simplicius refertur. Ad verba autem illa, SEQUERE ME, hæc habet: Imposuerat Chri- stus Petro pastorale officium, & prædixerat ei mar- tyrium, surgens ergo dixit Petro, sequere me, & sic per illam sequelam corporalem idem significabat, quod verbis prius expresserat; primo exemplum suum in pascendis ovibus ipsi proponit: deinde in obeun- da morte: Conferens Joh. XIII. 36. quo ego vado non potes sequi me modo, sequeris autem postea, quibus verbis certe indicavit, quod Petrus suo tempore idem præmium à mundo relaturus sit, quod ipse retulerit, crucis nempe supplicium. Nobis videtur, quum ver- ba, hoc autem dixit, significans qua morte glorifica- turus esset Deum, addita & subjuncta sint, non ad illa sequere me, sed ad præcedentia v. 18. Extendes manus &c. aut voce ποίῳ θανάτῳ speciem mortis, crucifixionem designatam, uti Joh. XII. 33. atque tum ex illis præcedentibus eam colligendam esse, aut si id fieri non possit è verbis præcedentibus, certe verba sequentia eo multo minus facere, quum Ev- angelista ποιότητα mortis non ex illis, sed è supe- rioribus deduci velit, neque sequela exempli Chri- sti in doctrina, & martyrio statim idem genus mar- tyrii inferat: Quapropter vel præstare, cum Ter- tulliano, Casaubono & aliis, extensionem manuum, cinćturam, & deductionem violentam ad morem usitatum in crucifixione referre, vel dicendum esse, τὶν ποιότητα mortis, non speciem eandem mortis, ni- mirum crucifixionem, sed γενικῶς mortem violen- tam & martyrium notare: quemadmodum etiam adhuc in dubio est, anne Petrus supplicio crucis af- fectus sit? B. Chemnitius in Harmon. c. L. p. 518. observat, Origenem & Nicephorum annotare, Pe- trum circa finem vitæ suæ, ultimis annis Neronis, Romam venisse, reliquos addere, quod ibi demisso ca- pite, & inversis vestigiis cruci affixus sit. Hæc Che- mnitius. Origenem vero sententia de Petri cruci- fixione, & conjecturas, quæ ad eam moverint Vete- res, si cognoscere juvat, ut quam certa illa sit judi- care liceat, adhibendus Casaubonus est, è quo non- nulla adducemus: Veteres Christiani, inquit, quibus à fine Actorum Apostolicorum ad tempora Trajani nihil certi extare in historia Christiana dolebat, ut illum hiatum temporum explerent, multa licenter

& inepte de Petri Romam adventu, deque ejus prima sede fabulati sunt. Quod vero de Petri morte scri- ptum relinquerunt, & posteris persuaserunt, crucis supplicio affectum, quanquam id verum est, non ta- men ex historia certa depromserunt, sed conjecturis ri- mati sunt ex Joh. XIII. 36. ὕστερον δὲ ἀκολουθήσεις μοι. Item cap. XXI. v. 18. Deinde usus quotidianus illorum temporum potuit docere eos, Petrum peregrinæ con- ditionis hominem & despicabilem personam, non alio genere mortis à Romanis, quam crucis affici potuisse, ut contra, Paulum civem Romanum gladio anim- adversum fuisse. De Petro recte judicarunt, de Pau- lo potest dubitari: non etiam quia civis Romanus, statim gladio animadvertendus: Nam & imperator fratricida videtur præfectum ignorantiæ accusare, qui nesciverit utrum sedes Papiniani gladio an secu- ri exsequenda fuerit. Proinde Paulus potuit & se- curi feriri. Sed tam facile & proclive fuit veteri- bus Christianis hæc confingere, quam Epistolas Sene- cæ ad Paulum, & hujus ad eum supponere: & bono Hieronymo hanc mercem obtrudere, qui ob eam rem Senecam scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis cooptavit. Qui- dam recentiores docti & pii negant interesse nostra, quo genere mortis functus sit Petrus; neque putant ex eo loco Johannis colligi posse Petrum in crucem actum esse. Hactenus Casaubonus, qui vero sibi ipsi satis constare haud videtur. Si enim, quod ipse ait, nihil certe à fine Actorum Apostolicorum usque ad tempora Trajani in historia Christiana habetur, si conjecturis tantum id quod de morte Petri scriptum reliquerunt veteres, & posteris persuaserunt, rimati sunt è Joh. XIII. 36. & præsenti loco, quænam de illo crucis supplicio βεβαιότης obtinebitur è veteribus? Cæterum illa, ducet quo non vis, non innuunt, Pe- trum prorsus invitum, & coactum martyrium sub- iisse, uti Grotius vult, ita enim morte sua Deum non glorificasset, sed luctam tantum carnis & spiri- tus, quæ etiam in renatis superest, indicant: quia spiritus promtus fuit, etsi caro infirma ad mortem, quam natura exhorrescimus, trepidaret. Nemo quippe sanctorum, ut hic Cyrillus habet, sponte patitur, sed tametsi mors acerba eis ingruat etiam perinvitis, tamen gloriæ divinæ cupidi vitam quo- que hanc terrenam asuernantur.

## 21:20
Vers. 20. ἀκολουθοῦντα) Because he saw him following Peter. ὃς καὶ ἀνέπεσεν) These things, not usually placed before in the designation of John (for he was designated solely by the note of the disciple whom the Lord loved), are added in this place not without effect. For all those things were coming into Peter's mind, so that he might believe this disciple to be his equal or next in loving Christ. Wherefore, when he himself, after his profession of love, had received the prediction of the death to be borne, after the example of the Lord, by a certain curiosity of human nature he wishes to know what is to become of him.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἀκολουθοῦντα) Quia Petrum subsequi videbat. ὃς καὶ ἀνέπεσεν) Hæc antehac in designatione Johannis poni non solita (sola enim nota dilecti a Domino discipuli designatus est) hoc loco non sine efficacia adduntur. Nam omnia ista Petro in animum veniebant, ut crederet hunc discipulum sibi in diligendo Christo parem esse aut proxi- mum. Quare cum ipse post amoris professionem accepis- set prædictionem ferendæ moris, ad Domini exemplum, curiositate quadam humani ingenii scire vult quid de illo sit futurum.

## 21:21
Vers. 21. ὗτος δὲ τί;) ἔπαθεν. For τί ποιήσεται, what does he suffer? what end will he have?

Latin:

Vers. 21. ὗτος δὲ τί;) ἔπαθεν. Pro τί ποιήσεται, quid patio- tur? quem habebit exitum?

## 21:22
Vers. 22. ἐὰν αὐτὸν θέλω μένειν) In this frail life. Thus Phil. I. 22, 23, 24; 1 Cor. XV. 16. ἕως ἔρχομαι) As if the Emperor were to say: what if I wish him to remain in the garrison until I myself recall him? Thus he obscurely signifies that John, unlike Peter, would not die a violent death, but by such a one as he would be released without the force of men, when Christ had judged the time suitable; which also happened, as most of the ancients agree. Thus Christians often call the time of death a summoning. τί πρός σε) Thus we also say in Latin, what is it to you? As if he were to say: whatever will be of him, that does not pertain to you; take care of what concerns you. This is a part of the washing of Peter's feet, which he himself rightly understanding, later forbade Christians to be ἀλλοτριοεπισκόπους, 1 Pet. IV. 15, just as Paul forbade women to be περιέργους, 1 Tim. V. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἐὰν αὐτὸν θέλω μένειν) In vita hac caduca. Sic Phil. I. 22. 23. 24. 1. Cor. XV. 16. ἕως ἔρχομαι) Quasi Imperator diceret: quid si hunc ve- lim in præsidio manere donec ipse eum revocem? ita ob- scure significat Johannem, non ut Petrum, morte violenta moriturum, sed tali, qua sine hominum vi solveretur, ubi Christus tempus idoneum judicasset; quod & contigit, ut veterum plures consentiunt. Sic tempus mortis accersi- tionem sæpe vocant Christiani. τί πρός σε) Sic & Latine dicimus quid ad te? Quasi dicat: quicquid de illo erit, id ad te non pertinet, cura quod te spe- ctat. Hæc est pars lotionis pedum Petri, quam ipse recte intelligens, postea vetuit Christianos esse ἀλλοτριοεπισκό- πους, 1. Petr. IV. 15. ut & feminas Paulus esse περιέργους, 1. Tim. V. 13.

## 21:23
Vers. 23. ἐξῆλθεν ὖν ὁ λόγος) A Hebraism. See Matt. IX. 26. Add also Luke VI. 22. ὅτι ὁ μαθητὴς ἐκεῖνος ὐκ ἀποθνήσκει) He will not die; the present for the future. They took, namely, the interrogation of Christ for an affirmation, and the coming for the coming to judgment, of which he had often spoken to them before, and indeed with the word ἔρχεσθαι added, as in Matt. XVI. 27 and ch. XXIV. 30. This day they thought was imminent, 1 Thess. 5. And when the day was to be, the day of the resurrection of the dead before, those who were then to live piously they rightly thought would not experience death, 1 Cor. 15:51. And it is credible that Christ in conversations after the resurrection spoke more openly about that day than before, as about the completion of his kingdom, Acts 1:3.

v. 23) And yet, as often elsewhere. οὐκ εἶπεν ἀυτῷ ὁ Ἰησῦς, ὅτι ἐκ ἀποθνήσκει) he had not said that he would never die, as they were interpreting.

ἀλλ' ἐὰν ἀυτὸν θέλω μένειν ἕως ἔρχομαι) This repetition of words up to this point shows that the emphasis is not on that ἐὰν θέλω, but on that ἔρχομαι, by the ambiguity of which the disciples had been deceived, when they ought either to have questioned the Master, or to have left what was said ambiguously as ambiguous, until the outcome declared the meaning. Tertullian, book on the soul: John also died, whose hope that he would remain until the coming of the Lord had been false.

From that repetition of words it cannot be firmly concluded that the emphasis is not on that ἐὰν θέλω, but on that ἔρχομαι. Because Christ wished to repeat his whole words. Those who invent an emphasis on the word ἔρχομαι, some interpret it as the coming of the Lord for a particular judgment against the Jews, but B. Gerhard rightly warned that this is forced, and John lived after the destruction of Jerusalem for about 30 years more: others explain it as the coming of Christ for the summoning of John: with whom Beda agrees, as does Grotius, and also Heinsius. But there would not have been need for a conditional statement in this way, if I will him to remain until I come: and Christ can say categorically about all the pious, even those who undergo martyrdom: I will them to remain until I come: for even they, although they are released by force, are not released, however, except when Christ judges the time suitable, and their death is also a summoning. Wherefore the interpretation of those who seek the emphasis in the added condition ἐὰν θέλω, and explain the coming, in the manner customary in the Scriptures, as the coming to judgment, is more correct, as if Christ were saying, to restrain the περιεργείαν and curiosity of Peter, if I wished this disciple to survive perpetually, until the very day of the final coming, what is that to you? since John himself, by repeating the hypothetical proposition, corrected the opinion that had arisen from Christ's hypothetical speech changed into a categorical one: and through this hypothetical statement thus set forth, Peter's curiosity is more strongly blamed, and the coming of Christ, when placed absolutely in the New Testament, when there is talk about a future coming, is commonly taken as his coming to the final judgment. Cf. B. Gerhard. So St. Cyril in this place. Absurd (outside the bounds of what is fitting) seemed the interrogation of Peter, and of a mind seeking curious rather than useful things, having received knowledge of his own affairs, to scrutinize those of another. For this reason, I think, the Lord did indeed answer something; but not directly to what was asked, but as if turning away the aim of the questioner, he says that John would not be immortal, but if I wish him to live, he says, until I come, what is that to you, I ask? that is, You have heard, O Peter, what pertains to you; why do you inquire into the affairs of others, and untimely scrutinize the knowledge of divine judgments? For even if he does not die at all, he says, will that relieve your concern in any way?

PART III. Conclusion of this book.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐξῆλθεν ὖν ὁ λόγος) Hebraismus. Vide Matth. IX. 26. Adde & Luc. VI. 22. ὅτι ὁ μαθητὴς ἐκεῖνος ὐκ ἀποθνήσκει) Non moriturum præsens pro futuro. Sumserunt scil. interrogationem Christi pro af- firmatione & adventum pro adventu ad judiciu de quo sæ- pe illis antehac locutus erat, & quidem addita voce ἔρχεσθαι, ut Matt. XVI. 27. & c. XXIV. 30. Hunc diem de propinquo imminere existimabant, 1. Thess. V. Et cum dies futurus esset, dies resuscitationis ante mortuorum, qui tum pio- sum victuri essent mortem non sensuros recte existimabant 1. Cor. XV. 51. Et credibile est Christum colloquiis post resurrectionem de illo die apertius quam antea locutum, ut de complemento regni sui, Act. I, 3.

v. 23) Et tamen, ut alibi sæpe. ὐκ εἶπεν ἀυτῷ ὁ Ἰησῦς, ὅτι ἐκ ἀποθνήσκει) non dixerat nun- quam moriturum, ut illi interpretabantur.

ἀλλ' ἐὰν ἀυτὸν θέλω μένειν ἕως ἔρχομαι) Hæc repetitio vo- cum hucusque ostendit emphasin non esse in illo ἐὰν θέλω, sed in illo ἔρχομαι, cujus ambiguitate decepti erant discipu- li, cum debuissent aut Magistrum interrogare, aut quod ambigue dictum erat, pro ambiguo relinquere, donec sen- sum exitus declararet. Tertullianus lib. de animo: Obiit & Iohannes quem in adventum Domini fuisse remansurum fal- sa fuerat spes.

Ex illa vocum repetitione id firmiter colligi non potest, ἔμφασιν esse non in illo ἐὰν θέλω, sed in illo ἔρχομαι. Quia integra sua verba repetere voluit Christus. Qui emphasin in voce ἔρχομαι fingunt, alii de adventu Domini ad judicium par- ticulare contra Judæos interpretantur, sed hoc coactum esse recte monuit B. Gerhardus, & vixit Johannes post excidium Hierosolymitanum ad- huc 30. circiter annis: alii de adventu Christi ad evocationem Johannis explicant: quibus cum Be- da accedit Grotius, ut & Heinsius. Sed ita non fuisset opus conditionata loquutione, si volo eum manere donec veniam: & de omnibus piis, etiam qui martyrium subeunt, categorice dicere po- test Christus: volo eos manere donec veniam: nam & illi, etsi vi solvantur, non solvuntur tamen, nisi cum tempus idoneum judicat Christus, mors- que ipsorum etiam est accersitio. Quapropter rectius se habet illorum interpretatio, qui em- phasin in conditione addita ἐὰν θέλω quærunt, & adventum, usitato in Scripturis modo, de adven- tu ad judicium explicant, quasi dicat Christus, ad coërcendam περιεργείαν & curiositatem Petri, si vellem hunc discipulum superesse perpetuo, usque ad ipsum adventus novissimi diem, quid hoc ad te? siquidem Johannes ipse opinionem ex hypothe- tica Christi oratione in categoricam mutata ena- tam, propositionem hypotheticam repetendo, correxerit: & per hanc hypotheticam ita expo- sitam fortius vitio datur Petri curiositas, ac adven- tus Christi absolute positus in Novo Testamento, cum de futuro adventu sermo est, de adventu ejus ad judicium novissimum communiter acci- piatur. Conf. B. Gerhardus. Ita S. Cyrillus in h. l. Absurda (ἔξω λόγε τῦ πρέποντος) visa est Petri interrogatio, & curiosi potius, quam utilia quærentis animi, accepta suarum rerum notitia a- liena scrutari. Hanc opinor ob causam Dominus respondit quidem aliquid; verum non recta adin- terrogata, sed alio veluti percontantis scopum aver- tens, non immortalem fore Johannem ait, sed si ve- lim eum vivere, inquit, donec veniam, quid hoc ad te, quæso? hoc est, Audisti, o Petre, quæ ad te pertinent; cur aliena sciscitaris, & di- vinorum judiciorum scientiam intempestive scru- taris? Nam etsi non moriatur prorsus, inquit, an tuam curam aliqua in re istud levabit?

PARS III. Libri hujus Conclusio.

## 21:24
Vers. 24. ὁ μαρτυρῶν περὶ τύτων) Peter now being dead, and others who had been present, who could no longer bear witness to these things said.

καὶ γράψας ταῦτα) Who had also left these things, above the others previously published, in private commentaries.

καὶ οἴδαμεν) The Ephesian Church speaks.

ὅτι ἀληθής ἐσιν ἡ μαρτυρία ἀυτῶ) Ἀληθὴς that is, worthy of faith, as above c. 5:31, c. 8:13. We know, they say, that it is worthy of faith, namely from the perpetual purity of his life and the miracles performed by him. We know therefore clearly what kind of death he had, predicted by Jesus,

Grotius imagines that these things and what follows were added by the Ephesian Church after the death of St. John, for he is devoid of any testimony. Nor is there any need for us to admit that John wrote his Gospel after Peter and the other Apostles were already dead, or that these things were recorded in the Ephesian Church: because not even Grotius himself was certain about it. For concerning the place, he says in his preface to John, and the time of writing, authors disagree, some wishing this book to have been written in Patmos, others at Ephesus, and some indeed thirty and odd years, but others sixty or more after Christ's ascension into heaven. Then, if he had written even after the departure of all the Apostles, could there not have been others surviving whose testimony John could have added to his own faith? And indeed the very words of the text openly refute the Grotian hypothesis, as if the Ephesian Church had added this last chapter. For it holds thus: This is that disciple who bears witness of these things, ὁ καὶ γράψας ταῦτα, who also wrote these things. Now these things teach that these were not written by another, but by John, who is introduced by those words, as surviving and living, ὁ μαρτυρῶν, who testifies (in the present) of these things: and he himself bears witness of these things which he wrote by Apostolic authority, as an eyewitness, καὶ ἀξιόπιστος: and thus he secures canonical authority for his Gospel. Which could entirely be done by him, because he was προκεχειροτονημένως ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ μάρτυς, a witness chosen beforehand by God, Acts X. 41. furthermore an eyewitness John XIX. 35. and one who heard for himself 1 John I. 1. and inspired by God John XVI. 13. 2 Pet. I. 21. 2 Tim. III. 16. finally a miracle-working witness, who confirmed the truth of his preaching and writing with miracles. For since very many adulterated writings were being sold at that time as Apostolic, the Gospel according to the Egyptians, the Proto-Evangelium of James, the Gospel of Nicodemus, the Acts of Paul, the History of the Period of Paul and Thecla, the Itinerary of Peter, the Preaching of Peter, the Apocalypse of Peter, the Acts of Andrew, Philip, Thomas, etc. Therefore St. John wished to profess himself openly as the author of this writing, so that he might distinguish it from spurious and adulterated books. For Canonical Scripture is able to secure authority for itself, because it is inspired by God, and divine: just as God himself gives assurance of himself, and needs no other's testimony.

Latin:

Vers. 24. ὁ μαρτυρῶν περὶ τύτων) Petro jam mortuo, & aliis qui adfuerant, qui amplius de his dictis testimonium præbere non poterant.

καὶ γράψας ταῦτα) Qui hæc quoque supra cætera antehac edita in commentariis privatis reliquerat.

καὶ οἴδαμεν) Loquitur Ecclesia Ephesina.

ὅτι ἀληθής ἐσιν ἡ μαρτυρία ἀυτῶ) Ἀληθὴς id est fide di- gna, ut supra c. V. 31. c. VIII. 13. Scimus ajunt fide dignum, ex vitæ scilicet perpetua puritate & miraculis ab ipso edi- tis. Scimus ergo plane qualem habuit mortem prædi- ctam ab Jesu,

Addita hæc & quæ sequuntur ab Ecclesia Ephe- sina, post S. Johannis mortem, fingit Grotius, omni enim testimonio destituitur. Neque vero opus est, ut admittamus, Johannem Petro aliis- que Apostolis jam defunctis, scripsisse Evange- lium suum, aut in Ecclesia Ephesina hæc consi- gnata esse: quia nec ipse Grotius de eo certus fuit. De loco enim, inquit in præloquio in Jo- hannem, & tempore scriptionis dissentiunt autores, aliis in Pathmo scriptum hunc librum volentibus, aliis Ephesi, & aliis quidem triginta & quod excur- rit, aliis vero sexaginta aut amplius post Christi in cœlum evectionem annis. Tum si maxime post excessum Apostolorum omnium scripsisset, an- non alii superstites esse poterant, quorum testi- monium Johannes fidei suæ adjungere potuerit? Et sane verba ipsa textus palam refellunt hypo- thesin Grotianam, quasi Ecclesia Ephesina hoc ca- put ultimum adjecerit. Sic enim habet: Hic est discipulus ille, qui testimonium perhibet de his, ὁ καὶ γράψας ταῦτα, qui & scripsit ista. Hæc autem do- cent, ista non ab alio, sed à Johanne scripta esse, qui verbis illis, ut superstes & vivus, introducitur, ὁ μαρτυρῶν, qui testatur (in præsenti) de his: & testi- monium ipse præbet de his, quæ scripsit Aposto- lica auctoritate, ceu ἀυτόπτης, καὶ ἀξιόπιστος: at- que ita Canonicam autoritatem Evangelio suo conciliat. Quod ab ipso fieri omnino poterat, quia erat προκεχειροτονημένως ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ μάρ- τυς, Actor. X. 41. adhæc ἀυτὲπτης Joh. XIX. 35. καὶ ἀυτήκοος 1. Joh. I. 1. ac θεόπνευστος Joh. XVI. 13. 2. Pet. I. 21. 2. Tim. III. 16. denique θαυματερ- γὸς μάρτυρ, qui miraculis prædicationis & scri- ptionis suæ veritatem comprobavit. Cum enim plurima adulterina scripta tum temporis pro Apo- stolicis venditarentur, Evangelium secundum Ægy- ptios, Prot-Evangelium Jacobi, Evangelium Nico- demi, Acta Pauli, Historia de Periodo Pauli & Te- clæ, Itinerarium Petri, Prædicatio Petri, Apocaly- psis Petri, Actus Andreæ, Philippi, Thomæ, &c. Ideo S. Johannes se autorem hujus Scripti palam pro- fiteri voluit, ut à nothis & adulterinis libris id di- scerneret. Scriptura enim Canonica sibi ipsi au- toritate conciliare valet, ideo quia θεόπνευστος, & divina: quemadmodum Deus ipse fidem sibi facit, nec alterius indiget testimonio.

## 21:25
Vers. 25. κᾲ ἄλλα πολλὰ) Miracles, of which the memory was then still recent, the witnesses having died not so long ago. ἐὰν γράφηται καθ' ἓν) So that nothing of them is omitted. ὀυδὲ ἀυτὸν οἶμαι τὸν κόσμον χωρῆσαι τὰ γραφόμενα βιβλία) Γραφόμενα that is, which ought to be written, and it is a hyperbole not infrequent in the sacred scriptures, as Gen. XI. 4. Num. XXIII. 24. Dan. IV. v. 17. See also above chapter XII. 19. οἶμαι is said here singularly, because the Bishop wrote these things for the Church, just as also in the Apocalypse letters are directed to the Bishop for the Churches. Perhaps that was John the Elder, whose tomb at Ephesus, distinct from that of John the Apostle, Jerome records having seen, and to whom some of the ancients ascribe two epistles.

That conjecture about John the Presbyter, who added this clause, is futile, and rests on no testimony of antiquity. That John the Presbyter, different from John the Apostle, is the author of the two later Epistles, bearing the name of John, although it may have been asserted by some, and Jerome may be alleged for that opinion, he nevertheless does not speak that so much from his own mind as relatively, both concerning the different tomb of John the Apostle and John the Presbyter, and concerning the later Epistles of John, in the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers. The remaining two (Epistles) whose beginning is, The Elder to the elect Lady and her children: and of the following, The Elder to the most beloved Gaius, are asserted to be of John the Presbyter, whose other tomb also today at EPHESUS IS SHOWN (he says it is not that other one, but that it is shown as if it were another, yet at the same time soon subjoining the diverse opinion of others concerning it) & some think there are two memorials of THE SAME John the Evangelist: & under the title PAPIAS from the Catalogue of names recounted by the Pope it is observed, that Papias Astrio of the Lord, and distinguished them from John the Apostle, and he noted that because of the opinion handed down by most, that the two later Epistles of John are not the Apostle's, but the Presbyter's. But as far as Jerome's own opinion is concerned, we have it in Epist. ad Paulin. James, Peter, John, and Jude the Apostles published seven Epistles, as mystical as they are concise and short: and equally long in their sentiments. And in Epist. ad Evagr. which is 85. The trumpet of the son of thunder sounds, whom Jesus loved most, who drank the streams of doctrines from the breast of the Saviour: The Presbyter to the elect Lady, and her children, whom I love in the truth. Annunt. Iren. l. III. c. 13. Didymus, Clemens Alexandr. Athanas. in Syn. Gregor. Nazianz. in carm. de libr. Script. August. l. II. de Doctr. Christ. c. 8. Damasc. l. IV. de Orth. Fid. c. 28. Beda, Oecumenius & other Fathers, and also the Council of Laodicea c. 59. Carthage III. c. 47. Nor does Eusebius disagree. For since it appears from the history which he brought from Clement of Rome l. III. c. 20, that John is called Presbyter absolutely as an Apostle, Eusebius nowhere distinguishes John the Apostle from the Presbyter. And although in c. 21 he asserts that among those things which John wrote after the Gospel, his first Epistle is received without any hesitation both by the more recent and by the ancient, but that the remaining two are contradicted (by some): yet afterwards in l. VII. c. 23 he praises these of Dionysius: But not even in the second, nor the third, which are circulated under John's name, however short the Epistles may be, does John place his name before them, but wrote as the Presbyter without a name.

Regarding the hyperbolic expression, which Cyril, Chrysostom, and Euthymius favor in this clause, B. Gerhard observes that those things were said proverbially: for in proverbs it is customary to add 'as I think': Augustine tract. 124 in John & Isidore of Pelusium l. I. Ep. 269 and others interpret these things in such a way that God did not wish the infirmity of our intellect to be burdened by the mass and abundance of books, but condescending to our infirmity, He selected to be written through the Evangelists only those things from the words and deeds of Christ which would suffice for the salvation of the believer: who therefore take the word 'to contain' (χωρῆσαι) not of the capacity of a place but of the intellect, as Matt. 19:11, John 8:37, 2 Cor. 8:2. If all the words and deeds of Christ had been written, no age of men and no power of genius could suffice to pursue and weigh those books. Nicephorus lib. 1 Hist. Eccl. c. 14 has it thus: The Evangelist superseded pursuing the greatest part of the miracles of Christ, because they would not easily be credible to the common people, and to the world, and those who are held by the studies of this world, and are of a more curious mind than to believe and be persuaded. For I believe that that saying is referred to this, that if all things were written down one by one, not even the world itself would contain the books that would have to be written. Similarly Jerome in chapter 30 of Matthew: The world could not contain them, not that the world could not contain the volumes, which it can contain, however many, in a single small cupboard or one chest: But because it could not bear the MAGNITUDE OF THE MIRACLES in comparison with the miracles and UNBELIEF. Which sense is approved not only by Junius in his animadversions on Bellarmine, book on the Word of God, chapter 10, but also by B. Chemnitz in l. 1 Exam. p. 21 and B. Ægid. Hunnius in this place, as also by B. Tarnovius, but it also seems to be confirmed from the opposition of those things which are written, c. 20:31. But these are written, that you may believe. For not to comprehend or contain, and to believe, are opposites. The world could not have contained them because of the magnitude of the miracles and its own unbelief: and human life would not suffice even for weighing or containing them, because of the variety and multitude of the signs: finally, those things were selected which could suffice for the faith of those who do not exalt themselves against the knowledge of God, but take captive their thoughts (νοήματα) into the obedience of Christ. For those things were chosen to be written which seemed to suffice for the salvation of believers: We conclude with the sentiment and doxology of St. Cyril: For it must be thought that many thousands of miracles were done by the power of our Saviour; nevertheless, only the more illustrious ones were written, as it seems, by the heralds of the Gospels, and through which the hearers could most be strengthened unto an incorrupt faith, and be instructed in the doctrine of both morals and dogmas, so that, conspicuous in right faith, and variously illuminated by works pertaining to piety, and raised to the heavenly city itself, and joined to the firstborn of the Church, they might also penetrate into the kingdom of heaven itself in Christ, through whom, and with whom, to God and the Father be glory, with the Holy Spirit for ever. AMEN.

Latin:

Vers. 25. κᾲ ἄλλα πολλὰ) Miracula, quorum tunc re- cens adhuc erat memoria, non ita dudum mortuis testibus. ἐὰν γράφηται καθ' ἓν) Ita ut nihil eorum omittatur. ὀυδὲ ἀυτὸν οἶμαι τὸν κόσμον χωρῆσαι τὰ γραφόμενα βιβλία) Γραφόμενα id est quæ scribi deberent, & hyperbole est non infrequens sacris literis, ut Gen. XI. 4. Num. XXIII. 24. Dan. IV. v. 17. Vide & supra cap. XII. 19. οἶμαι hic dicitur sin- gulariter, quia pro Ecclesia hæc scripsit Episcopus, Sicut & in Apocalypsi literæ pro Ecclesiis ad Episcopum dirigun- tur. Forte is fuit Johannes ὁ πρεσβύτερος, cujus sepul- chrum se Ephesi distinctum ab illo Johannis Apostoli vi- disse memorat Hieronymus, & cui veterum nonnulli ad- scribunt epistolas duas.

Illa conjectura de Johanne Presbytero, qui hanc clausulam addiderit, futilis est, nulloque nititur antiquitatis testimonio. Johannem Presbyterum, diversum à Johanne Apostolo, auctorem esse dua- rum posteriorum Epistolarum, Johannis nomen præferentium, etsi à quibusdam assertum fuerit, & Hieronymus allegetur in eam sententiam, is ta- men non tam ex mente propria id loquitur, quam relative, tum de sepulcro diverso Johannis Apo- stoli, & Johannis Presbyteri, tum de Epistolis posterioribus Johannis, in Catalogo Scriptor. Ecclesiast. Reliquæ duæ (Epistolæ) quarum prin- cipium est, Senior electæ Dominæ & natis ejus: & sequentis, Senior Cajo charissimo, Johannis Pres- byteri asseruntur, cujus & hodie alterum sepulcrum apud EPHESUM OSTENDITUR (non id alterum esse ait, sed ostendi velut alterum, diver- fam tamen simul aliorum mox subjiciens de eo opinionem) & nonnulli putant duas memorias EJUSDEM Johannis Evangelistæ esse: & sub ti- tulo PAPIAS è Catalogo nominum à Papa re- censitorum observatur, quod Papias Astrionem & Seniorem Johannem discipulos Domini vocarit, & à Johanne Apostolo distinxerit, idque notavit propter opinionem à plerisque traditam, quod duæ posteriores Epistolæ Johannis non Apostoli sint, sed Presbyteri. Quod autem ad propriam Hierony- mi sententiam attinet, eam habemus in Epist. ad Paulin. Jacobus, Petrus, Johannes, & Judas Apostoli septem Epistolas ediderunt, tam mysticas, quam suc- cinclas, & breves: pariter longas in sententiis. Et in Epist. ad Evagr. quæ est XXCV. Clangit tuba filii tonitrui, quem Jesus amavit plurimum, qui de pecto- re Salvatoris doctrinarum fluenta potavit: Presby- ter electæ Dominæ, & filiæ ejus, quos diligo in ve- ritate. Annunt. Iren. l. III. c. 13. Didymus, Clemens Alexandr. Athanas. in Syn. Gregor. Nazianz. in carm. de libr. Script. August. l. II. de Doctr. Christ. c. 8. Damasc. l. IV. de Orth. Fid. c. 28. Beda, Oecu- menius & alii Patres, nec non Concilium Laodice- num c. LIX. Carthaginense III. c. XLVII. Neque discrepat Eusebius. Quum enim Johannem ut A- postolum absolute Presbyterum vocatum, ex hi- storia, quam è Clemente Romano l. III. c. 20. attulit, appareat, nuspiam Johannem Apostolum à Presby- tero distinguit Eusebius. Et quanquam c. 21. inter ea, quæ Johannes scripsit post Evangelium, etiam priorem illius Epistolam cum à recentioribus tum à veteribus, absque ulla hesitatione recipi, reliquis ve- ro duabus contradici (à quibusdam) asserat: postea tamen l. VII. c. 23. Dionysii hæc laudat: Sed ne in altera quidem, nec tertia, quæ sub Johannis nomine circumferuntur, quantumvis brevibus Epistolis no- men suum Johannes præponit, sed sine nomine Pres- byter scripsit.

Quod ad hyperbolicam loquutionem, cui in hac clausula favent Cyrillus, Chrysostom. & Euthymius, B. Gerhard. observat παροιμικῶς illa dicta: in pro- verbiis enim addi solere ὡς οἶμαι: Augustin. tract. cxxiv. in Joh. & Isidorus Pelusiota l. I. Ep. 269. aliiq; ita hæc interpretantur, quod mole & copia librorum infirmitatem nostri intellectus Deus gravari nolue- rit, sed infirmitati nostræ condescendens, ea solum per Evangelistas ex Christi dictis & factis scribenda se- legerit, quæ saluti credentis sufficerent: qui proinde verbum χωρῆσαι de capacitate non loci sed intelle- ctus accipiunt, ut Matth. XIX. 11. Job. VIII. 37. 2. Cor. VIII. 2. Si omnia Christi dicta & facta scripta fuis- sent, ad persequendos & expendendos illos libros, nulla hominum ætas, nullaque ingenii vis sufficerè posset. Nicephorus lib. I. Hist. Eccl. c. 14. ita habet: Evangelista maximam miraculorum Christi par- tem, quod non facile in vulgus probabilia essent, mun- dove, & qui hujus studiis tenentur, curiosiorique men- te sint, quam ut crederent, & persuaderi possent, per- sequi supersederunt. Huc enim referri illud arbi- tror, si omnia sigillatim perscribantur, ne ipsum qui- dem mundum recepturum esse, qui scribendi essent, libros. Similiter Hieronymus in cap. XXX. Matth. Mundus capere non posset, non quod mundus volu- mina capere non potuerit, quæ potest quamvis mul- tiplicia, unicum armariolum, vel unum capere scri- nium: Sed quod MAGNITUDINEM SIGNO- RUM præ miraculis & INCREDULITATE ferre non posset. Qui sensus non tantum Junio animadvers. ad Bellarm. lib. de V. D. cap. X. sed & B. Chemnitio l. 1. Exam. p. 21. & B. Ægid. Hunno in h. l. ut & B. Tarnovio probatur, sed & ex oppositio- ne eorum, quæ scripta sunt, c. XX. 31. confirmari vi- detur. Hæc autem scripta sunt, ut credatis. Nam non comprehendere vel capere, & credere opposita sunt. Mundus capere non potuisset ob miraculorum magnitudinem, & propriam incredulitatem: ac ne quidem illis expendendis, aut capiendis huma- na sufficeret ætas, ob signorum varietatem, & mul- titudinem: denique selecta ea sunt, quæ ad fidem eo- rum, qui non extollunt se adversus cognitionem Dei, sed νοήματα sua captivant sua obedientiam Christi, sufficere possint. Electa enim sunt quæ scriberen- tur, quæ saluti credentium sufficere videbantur: Concludim9 sententia & δοξολογίᾳ S. Cyrilli: Mul- ta quippe miraculorum millia virtute Servatoris no- stri facta esse cogitandum est; veruntamen illustrio- ra tantum ab Evangeliorum preconibus, ut videtur, scripta fuere, & per quæ maxime possent auditores ad incorruptam fidem firmari, & doctrina tam mo- rum quam dogmatum institui, ut recta fide conspi- cui, & operibus ad pietatem spectantibus varie illu- strati, & ad ipsam supernam civitatem evecti, atque primogenitorum Ecclesiæ conjuncti, in ipsum quo- que regnum cælorum penetrarent in Christo, per quem, & cum quo, Deo ac Patri gloria, cum Sancto Spiritu in secula. AMEN.

# Acts

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 1). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
In the Name of Jesus. ANNOTATIONS ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES.

ACTS of the Apostles) The Syrian and Arab retained the Greek word, as they often did with words which they thought would not have the same force if transferred into another language. It is, however, the same thing, whether it is 'Acts' (acta), as the interpreter here, or 'deeds' (actus), as some of the ancients. For 'deeds' (actus) and 'acts' (acta) signify the same thing, as 'effects' (effectus) and 'effects' (effecta), 'events' (eventus) and 'events' (eventa), 'commands' (jussus) and 'commands' (jussa), and many others of that form. It is indeed more accepted that those things which have been recorded in public records are called 'acts' (acta). But Cicero also calls whatever anyone has done, now 'acts' (acta), now 'deeds' (actus). And he says the Sempronian laws are the 'acts' (acta) of the Gracchi. Nor is 'deeds' (actus) in this sense only a word of the poets, for Cicero also said in the first book of Laws, that the likeness of the human race is remarkable not only in right deeds, but also in wrong ones. Of the Apostles, that is, of Peter and Paul. For the others are mentioned only in passing, and after Luke followed Paul, he continues to speak of him alone. Of the acts of the other Apostles, scarcely a faint report has reached us. Whence the name of Luke, who he himself was or what kind of man he was, we have spoken of in his former book, which is commonly called the Gospel.

lest Peter and Paul alone, as it seemed to Grotius, be pointed out. Nor is mention made of the others only in passing, even though the acts of Peter and Paul are especially recounted. Oecumenius says that the Acts of the Holy Spirit are described in this book, namely those things which He did through the Apostles at the beginnings of the Church. For as, he says, the four Evangelists write the Gospel and the acts of Christ, so Luke here describes the Gospel and Acts of the Holy Spirit, which He Himself performed in the Apostles and through the Apostles.

Concerning the author and chronology of the book, Jerome has this in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, under Luke: He also published another excellent volume, which is entitled by the title πράξεις ἀποστόλων, the history of which reaches as far as the two years of Paul staying in Rome, that is, as far as the fourth year of Nero, from which we understand that the book was composed in the same city. Cf. Acts XXVIII, last verse. Thus, therefore, this book embraces the history of the golden age of the primitive Church for about 27 years, as many as from the ascension of Christ into heaven in the year

Latin:

J. N. J. ANNOT. AD ACTA APOSTOLORVM.

ΠΡΑΞΕΙΣ τῶν Ἀποστόλων) Græcam! vocem retinuere Syrus & Arabs, ut sæpe in vocibus quæ transfusæ in sermonem alium vim non eandem habituræ puta- bantur. Perinde autem est, sive Acta veritas, ut hic inter- pres, sive actus, ut veterum nonnulli. Idem enim signi- ficant actus & acta, ut effectus & effecta, eventus & even- ta, jussus & jussa, multaque alia ad eam formam. Est qui- dem receptius ut acta dicantur quæ in publicas tabulas re- lata sunt. Sed etiam Cicero quicquid quisquam egit, id modo acta, modo actus vocat. Et leges Sempronias ait es- se acta Gracchorum. Neque actus hoc sensu Poetarū tan- tum vox est, nam & Cicero primo legum dixit, non solum in rectis, sed etiam in pravis actibus insignem esse humani generis similitudinem. Apostolorum, id est, Petri & Pauli. Nam cæterorum ferme obiter tantum fit mentio, & post- quam Paulum sectatus est Lucas, de eo solo pergit loqui. De cæterorum Apostolorum actibus vix tenuis ad nos fama manavit. Lucæ nomen unde, ipse quis qualisve fuerit, dixi- mus ad librum ejus priorem, qui vulgo Evangelium dicitur.

ne Petrus & Paulus tantum, uti Grotio visum est, indigitantur. Neque obiter tantum cæterorum mentio fit, utut præcipue Petri & Pauli acta refe- rantur. Oecumenius Acta Sp. S. describi hoc li- bro, ait, quæ scilicet per Apostolos sub primordia Ecclesiæ egit. Nam uti, inquit, quatuor Evangelistæ scribunt Evangelium & acta Christi, sic Lucas hic describit Evangelium & Acta Spiritus sancti, quæ ipse in Apostolis & per Apostolos gessit.

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface
PREFACE.

Although the acts of Peter and Paul are primarily described in this book, yet not in the inscription by the name of the Apostles of it [the book] in 34, having occurred, flowed on, up to the fourth year of Nero, which falls in the year of Christ 60. Describing then the foundation of the Church in Judea and Samaria according to the command of Christ c. I. 8. in the first part up to chapter X. mostly accomplished by the works of St. Peter: then the propagation of the Church among the Gentiles through Syria, Lycaonia, Pamphylia, Greece, etc., undertaken primarily by St. Paul, to whom Luke was a companion; after St. Peter had first entered to the Gentiles by divine warning in chapter X. and Paul indeed had been set apart with Barnabas for the propagation of the Gospel. And the Jews at Antioch had rejected Paul and had repelled the word of the Gospel from themselves Acts XIII.

The chronotaxis of the Acts with the order of the chapters described in this book can be exhibited thus. In the year of Christ 34, the ascension of Christ 40 days after the resurrection, and the election of Matthias into the place of Judas occurred Acts I. and the sending of the Holy Spirit at the feast of Pentecost, with three thousand men converted at the first sermon chapter II. Shortly after, the lame man having been healed by a second sermon of Peter, 5000 were converted c. III. and IV. After the imprisonment of Peter and John, and their apology and the prayer of the whole assembly, they were filled with the Spirit and great παῤῥησίᾳ, as is related in the same fourth chapter. Then chapter V. the theft and punishment of Ananias and Sapphira, and after the murmuring of the Greeks against the Hebrews, the creation of the seven Deacons, and the disputation of Stephen against the Jews and his end, the stoning of Stephen the Protomartyr is set forth in chapters VI. and VII. Which is believed to have occurred toward the end of the year.

In the following year 35, the faithful being dispersed on account of persecution through Judea and Samaria, Philip preached in Samaria, and when they accepted the word there, they were confirmed in the faith by Peter and John, and Simon Magus was publicly confounded by Peter: the Eunuch also, a chief man of Ethiopia, was baptized by Philip chapter VIII.

In the year 36, Paul is converted, he preaches at Damascus, (thence he went into Arabia Gal. I. 17. Soon returning again to Damascus, where he stayed for three years: Peter indeed at Lydda heals Aeneas the paralytic, and at Joppa raises Tabitha chapter IX.

In the year 37, warned by a heavenly vision that the conversion of the Gentiles was at hand, St. Peter betakes himself to Cornelius the Centurion at Caesarea, and baptizes him with his family chapter X. and renders an account of that matter Acts XI.

In the year of Christ 39, Paul being sought at Damascus by the Jews, is let down in a basket through the wall, and goes to Jerusalem, that he might see Peter, Gal. I. 18. which history St. Luke inserted in chapter IX.

In the year 42, after Paul had been brought to Antioch by Barnabas and the Church there had received increase through them, both remained there for a year, and preached: Then a famine, predicted by Agabus, arose, and at Antioch they were first named Christians Acts XI.

In the year 44, James was killed by Herod; Peter indeed was imprisoned, but was freed by an Angel Acts XII.

In the year 45, Barnabas and Paul are set apart at Antioch to preach the Gospel among the Gentiles Acts XIII.

In the year 46, when the same had traveled through Seleucia, thence had sailed to Cyprus, had come to Salamis, and had traversed the whole island to Paphos, and having blinded the magician Elymas had converted the Proconsul Sergius, thence they landed in Pamphylia: afterwards they betook themselves to Antioch, and preached there, but being rejected by the Jews they turned themselves to the Gentiles and hastened to Iconium Acts XIII.

In the year 47. In Iconium, many of the Jews and Gentiles were converted through them, and Paul and Barnabas remained there for a long time; but finally in the year 48, because of persecution, they proceeded into Lycaonia, and being taken for gods among the Lystrians, they announced the true God, and a sedition having been stirred up by the Jews, Paul having been stoned, so that he was taken for dead, they came to Derbe, and from there in turn betook themselves to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, and strengthened the disciples, and went through Pisidia and Pamphylia, and preached in Perga, then set out for Attalia: and from there again in the year 49, after a five-year journey, they sailed to Antioch, and remained there for no small time, namely for two years. Acts 14.

In the year of Christ 51, the first Council was held in Jerusalem concerning the controversy stirred up by the Pseudo-Apostles, whether the observance of the law is necessary for salvation? The decision of which Paul, Barnabas, Silas, and Judas carried down to Antioch. Acts 15. But Barnabas, having been separated, contended with John Mark into Cyprus; the Apostle Paul with Silas traveled through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches: Acts 15. And he arrived in Derbe and Lystra, where he circumcised Timothy and joined him to himself as a companion, and passing through Phrygia and Galatia and Mysia, they came to Troas: and there, Paul having been stirred by a vision, they contended for Macedonia. At Philippi, Lydia was converted, and they were imprisoned because of the fortune-telling spirit cast out of a slave girl, and through their miraculous liberation, the keeper of the prison was led to the faith of Christ. Acts 16. From there they traveled through Amphipolis and Apollonia, and came to Thessalonica, and preached there, but being driven from the city by a sedition of the Jews, they set out for Beroea, where many were converted to the faith, but because of the persecution stirred up by the Jews, Paul, having left Silas and Timothy there, contended for Athens, in the year of Christ 52. He announced there the God whom they worshipped as unknown, and converted among others Dionysius with his wife. Acts 17. And from there betaking himself to Corinth, he led many Jews, and among them also Crispus the ruler of the synagogue, and Greeks to the faith, and having been warned by an oracle, he remained there for a year and a half. Acts 18.

In the year of Christ 53, having been dragged by the rioting Jews to the tribunal of Gallio: from there, intending to depart for Syria according to a vow, he shaved his head at Cenchreae, which was the port of Corinth, and arrived at Ephesus.

In the year 54, Paul, having left Aquila with Priscilla at Ephesus, by whom Apollos, having been more fully instructed in the faith, powerfully convinced the Jews, went up to Caesarea, and having greeted the Jerusalem Church, returned to Antioch; having traveled through Galatia and Phrygia, he confirmed the disciples everywhere. Acts 18.

In the year 55, Paul, after he had traveled through the upper regions, came again to Ephesus, and preached there for two years and three months, and performed very many miracles. Acts 19.

In the year 56, at Ephesus, on the occasion of the exorcists of the Jews, many were converted; many also, who had followed magic, brought their books and burned them publicly, and the word of God grew mightily then; Timothy and Erastus were sent away to Macedonia by Paul. Acts 19.

In the year 57, a tumult having been stirred up by Demetrius, who made silver temples of Diana, Paul set out from Ephesus into Macedonia, from there came into Greece, and having stayed there for three months, having set out into Macedonia through lesser Asia, he raised Eutychus from the dead in Troas, finally came to the city of Miletus, and summoning the Ephesian elders there, he delivered a valedictory speech to them. Acts 20.

In the year 58 he came to Caesarea, where Agabus foretold to him the Jerusalem bonds: thence having set out for Jerusalem, when he was purifying himself in the temple, he was seized by the Jews, and rescued by the tribune, Acts 21. He instituted his defense, narrating his conversion, ch. 22, and having been brought to the Sanhedrin, when he testified that he was being accused on account of the resurrection of the dead, a dissension having been made between the Jews themselves, the Pharisees and Sadducees, he escaped judgment, and on account of the snares of the Jews was led away by the tribune to Caesarea, and was accepted by Felix, ch. 23. Who, having heard both sides, Ananias having been sent by the Jews, and Paul, prolonged the cause, heard Paul's address with his wife Drusilla, and left him a captive behind him to his successor Porcius Festus, ch. 24. From whom Paul, when he wished to investigate the cause at Jerusalem for the sake of the Jews, appealed to Caesar, ch. 25, and after he had instituted his defense in the presence of King Agrippa, ch. 26. He is sent into Italy to Caesar, and having suffered shipwreck, but having been saved with all his companions, he arrived at Malta in the year 59, ch. 27. On the island of Malta, having been freed from a viper, and Publius's father and many others having been restored to health, he arrived at Syracuse and Rhegium: and afterwards he stayed for seven days at Puteoli, and thence he headed for Rome: there he explained the reason of his faith to the Jews, and remained for two years under guard in his own rented house, receiving all, and freely preaching Christ, ch. 28, the two years having been completed, he was finally released by Nero in the year of Christ 61.

ITINERARY OF ST. PETER AND ST. PAUL.

It is helpful, however, from there also to exhibit the pilgrimages and journeys of the Apostles, of St. Peter especially, and of St. Paul, with the measurement of the journeys, as the same has been designated by B. Bünting, for the better understanding of this book, and that according to the chronology already proposed.

St. Peter, therefore, with John in the year of Christ 35, betook themselves from Jerusalem into Samaria for eight miles, and there confirmed the newly converted, and disputed with Simon Magus, Acts 8. In the year of Christ 36, Peter at Lydda, which is distant five miles from Jerusalem, healed Aeneas the paralytic, Acts 9, and furthermore, having been summoned to Joppa, distant three-quarters of a German mile from Lydda, he raised Tabitha there, in the same chapter.

From Joppa to Caesarea Stratonis, a distance of nine miles, having been summoned by Cornelius, he came in the year 37, Acts 10.

From Caesarea he returned to Jerusalem, a distance of eight miles, where he excused himself for his entry to the Gentiles, Acts 11.

But after Peter had been freed from the prison into which he had been cast in the days of Unleavened Bread in the year 44, he departed from Jerusalem, but whither, it is not clear, Acts 12, returning there after the death of Herod: if indeed he took part in the Jerusalem council, ch. 15.

These things concerning Peter's journeys designated in the Acts: as regards the journeys of St. Paul described here, from Jerusalem, which is distant 76 miles from his homeland Tarsus in Cilicia, in the year of our Lord 36, he contended for Damascus, 40 miles away, and was converted on the way, Acts 9, soon he betook himself into Arabia, Gal. 1:17, but shortly after he returned again from Arabia to Damascus; until, on account of the persecution of Aretas, he escaped having been let down through a basket, Acts 9:25, 2 Cor. 11, and betook himself to Jerusalem to Peter, Gal. 1:18, Acts 9:26, a journey of forty miles.
