But even there, exposed to the snares of the Jews, having been led by the brothers to Caesarea for eight miles, he came to Tarsus, Acts 9:30, at an interval of sixty-eight miles. Thence he is read to have been found at Antioch in Syria, Acts 11:26, which was distant thirty miles: where he stayed for a year. Afterwards, for 70 miles from Antioch with Barnabas they brought alms to Jerusalem: having completed the ministry of alms, he returned again to Antioch for as many miles. And this was Paul's first pilgrimage for 482 miles.

The second, undertaken with Barnabas when he was sent to the Gentiles, Acts XIII, A.D. 46. From Antioch, the metropolis of Syria, he first came to Seleucia, a journey of six miles, after which they crossed by ship to Salamis in Cyprus, 24 miles, Acts XIII. 4, 5. In the year 46, and proceeding further on that island as far as Paphos for 25 miles: further, they came to Perga, a city of Pamphylia, situated in Asia Minor, at a distance of 37 miles: from there they set out to Antioch in Pisidia, at an interval of 33 miles, Acts XIII. 6, 13, 14, and being cast out there, they migrated to Iconium for 24 miles, v. 51, in the year 47. Thence they went to Lystra, distant seven miles from Iconium, A.D. 48. From there they betook themselves to the Derbeans by a journey of 12 miles: and in turn returned by as many miles to the Lystrians, and from Lystra they returned seven miles to Iconium: and from Iconium for 24 miles to Antioch in Pisidia, confirming the souls of the disciples in those cities, and by votes creating Presbyters in each city: and from Antioch, having traveled through all Pisidia, they came at an interval of 33 miles to Perga in Pamphylia, from there indeed they descended six and a half miles into the city of Attalia, in the year 48, Acts XIV. Finally, setting sail from there in the year 49, they sailed to Antioch in Syria at an interval of 85 miles. In the year 51, at an interval of 70 miles from Antioch, they set out to Jerusalem for the Apostolic council, Acts XV, passing through Phoenicia and Samaria. Furthermore, Paul, Barnabas, Silas, and Judas betook themselves from Jerusalem to Antioch at an interval of 70 miles: which was done with 14 years of Paul's conversion completed, Gal. II. And thus far was the second journey of Paul through 475 miles.

The third follows, which Paul undertook with Silas, first departing from Antioch of Syria, and traveling through Cilicia, and arriving at Derbe at a distance of 100 miles in the year 51, and further to Lystra, 14 miles distant, and from there to Troas for 102 miles: from which they crossed into Samothrace for 29 miles and to Neapolis for 23 miles: arriving by foot journey at Philippi in Macedonia at an interval of six miles, Acts XVI, and being cast out there, they set out to Amphipolis, having completed 9 miles, from there they proceeded to Apollonia for 11 miles, and from there to Thessalonica, at an interval of 5 miles, and to Beroea at an interval of fifteen miles, Acts XVII, where Paul, having boarded a ship, came to Athens for 66 miles in the year 52. Then, having departed from Athens, coming to Corinth at an interval of 18 miles, he remained in that city for a year and six months, Acts XVIII. And at Cenchreae, at an interval of two miles from the same, shaving his head, he sailed from that port to Ephesus in the year 53 for 76 miles: from Ephesus further by ship he betook himself to Caesarea of Straton in Palestine for 170 miles, and from there to Jerusalem, for the sake of greeting the Church, for 8 miles: finally, from Jerusalem he returned 70 miles to Antioch in Syria in the year 54, Acts XVIII. Which journeys of the third Pauline pilgrimage make up seven hundred and twenty-two miles.

In the fourth journey of Paul, departing from Antioch, the metropolis of Syria, he first traveled through Galatia and Phrygia by a journey of 95 miles: then, having set out from Laodicea in the year 55, he came again to Ephesus at an interval of 70 miles, Acts XIX. In the year 57, having departed from Ephesus, he returned to Troas at a distance of 53 miles: from there, sailing into Macedonia at an interval of fifty-eight miles, he came to Philippi, and from Philippi through Greece

Having set out for Corinth by a journey of one hundred and twenty miles, in which he visited cities and churches, and wintered there 1 Cor. XVI. (according to Bünting) and with Spring now approaching, he did not sail from Corinth to Syria by a direct route, but, in order to escape the snares of the Jews, he returned to Philippi by an interval of 73 miles, and there celebrated the feast of the Passover in the year of Christ 58. Acts XX. and came by ship to Troas for 58 miles: from Troas he walked to Assos for 9 miles: from Assos he sailed to Mitylene for 40 miles: from the island of Mitylene he crossed to Chios by an interval of 16 miles Acts XX. and from the island of Chios he sailed to the island of Samos at a distance of 15 miles, staying at the island of Tragyllium in the territory of Samos: from whence they came to Miletus for 40 miles: to which place the elders of Ephesus were summoned by a journey of 10 miles Acts XX. From the city of Miletus, Paul and his companions crossed by a direct course for 15 miles to the island of Cos Acts XXI. thence to Rhodes for 21 miles, thence to Patara for 25 miles, thence to Tyre at an interval of 95 miles, leaving Cyprus to the left: thence to Ptolemais at a distance of 6 miles, thence to Caesarea of Straton by an interval of 11 miles Acts XXI. from which Paul went up to Jerusalem for 8 miles in the year of our Lord 58. Acts XXI. which journeys of the fourth Pauline pilgrimage make 823 miles.

Following the fifth journey of Paul, when he was being led as a prisoner to Rome by order of the tribune Claudius Lysias, first from Jerusalem to Antipatris for three miles Acts XXIII. and thence he was brought to Caesarea of Straton to the Roman governor Felix Acts XXIII.

In the year of our Lord 59, by Porcius Festus, the governor of the Jews, he was sent to Rome to Caesar Nero, with Autumn now approaching, and having boarded a ship from Caesarea of Straton, he sailed to Sidon for 21 miles Acts XXVII. Thence Paul and his companions, sailing under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary, having traversed the sea which is against Cilicia and Pamphylia for an interval of 120 miles, arrived at Myra Acts XXVII. From the city of Myra they sailed as far as Cnidus for 62 miles, thence driven by the wind, sailing towards Crete to the south, and also passing by the cities of that place, Salmone, Lasea, and Assos, they came to the port of Crete, Phoenix, which was distant from Cnidus by an interval of 45 miles towards the south-southwest.

From the port of Phoenix, driven back by a typhoon wind, which is called Euro-Aquilo, they are carried for a course of 13 miles to the island of Clauda, where they bound the skiff to the ship, fearing that they might fall into the Syrtis. From the island of Clauda, not without the greatest danger, not far from the great Syrtis, they crossed by an interval of 180 miles to the island of Melita; where, having suffered shipwreck, Paul wintered for three months, Acts XXVII. XXVIII. From the island of Melita they sailed to Syracuse in Sicily for 45 miles; and from Syracuse for 16 miles to the city of Rhegium: thence for 41 miles to Puteoli. From Puteoli to the Forum of Appius for 30 miles: from the Forum of Appius to the Three Taverns for one and a half miles: from the Three Taverns for 4 miles to Rome; in the year of our Lord 60, about the fiftieth year of Paul's age. Which journeys constitute five hundred and eighty-eight miles: but all of Paul's journeys, already designated, up to his first captivity in the city of Rome under Nero, make 3090 miles.

This is a succinct chronotaxis with an apostolic itinerary and a summary compilation of the book of the Acts of the Apostles: the scope and primary argument of which the blessed Luther rightly assigned in his German preface, to illustrate and confirm the article concerning our gratuitous justification with God through faith, without the works of the law, by the sermons of the Apostles and the examples of the converted. In the whole book of Acts, says the blessed Luther, Vol. IV. Jena Lat. in Commentary on Galatians III. 2. f. 56. In sum, nothing else is treated than that it is necessary for both Jews and Gentiles, both the righteous and sinners, to be justified by faith alone in Christ Jesus, without the law and works. This is indicated both by the sermons of the Apostles, Peter, Paul, Stephen, Philip, and others, and also by the examples of the Gentiles and Jews. For just as to the Gentiles, who lived without the law, God through the Gospel gave the Holy Spirit, so also to the Jews, not through the Law, not through the worship and sacrifices commanded in the law, but through the preaching of faith alone, He gave the Holy Spirit. But if the law could have justified, and the righteousness of the law had been necessary for salvation, then certainly the Holy Spirit would not have been given to the Gentiles, who had not kept the law, but manifest experience itself testified that the Spirit was given to them without the Law. And the Apostles, Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and others, saw this. Therefore, not the Law, but faith alone in Christ, which the Gospel preaches, justifies. Whence rightly St. Jerome to Paulinus, The Acts, he says, of the Apostles seem indeed to sound of a bare history and to weave the infancy of the nascent Church, but if we know that their writer Luke is a physician, whose praise is in the Gospel, we shall perceive likewise that all his words are medicine for languishing souls.

PART I. OF THE BOOK exhibiting the foundation of the Church in Judea and Samaria, performed mostly by the work of St. Peter.

Latin:

PRÆLOQUIUM.

Etsi Petri & Pauli acta imprimis hoc libro descri- bantur, non tamen in ἐπιγραφῇ Apostolorum nomi- ejus XXXIV. facta, fluxerunt, usque ad quartum Neronis, qui in annum Christi LX. incidit. De- scribens tum fundationem Ecclesiae in Judaea & Sa- maria juxta praeceptum Christi c. I. 8. parte priori usque ad cap. X. maxime S. Petri opera factam: tum propagationem Ecclesiae inter gentes per Sy- riam, Lycaoniam, Pamphyliam, Graeciam &c. im- primis a S. Paulo, cui Lucas comes fuit, susceptam; Postquam S. Petrus primum ad gentes monitu di- vino ingressus cap. X. Paulus vero cum Barnaba ad Evangelii propagationem segregatus esset. Ac Judaei Antiochiae Paulum reprobassent & verbum Evangelii a se repulissent Actor. XIII.

Chronotaxis Actuum cum ordine capitum in hoc libro descriptorum ita exhiberi potest. Anno Christi XXXIV. ascensio Christi 40. diebus post resurrectionem, & electio Matthiae in locum Judae facta Act. I. & missio Spiritus S. festo Pentecostes, conversis ad primam concionem tribus millibus hominum cap. II. Brevi post sanato claudo concio- ne Petrina altera conversi 5000. c. III. & IV. Post incarcerationem Petri & Johannis, eorumq; apolo- giam ac precationem totius coetus, Spiritu & παῤῥη- σίᾳ magna impleti sunt, ut eodem quarto capite refertur. Dehinc cap. V. Ananiae & Saphirae fur- tum ac poena, & post murmur Graecorum contra Ebraeos, creatio septem Diaconorum, & disputatio Stephani contra Judaeos ejusque exitus, lapidatio Stephani Protomartyris cap. VI. & VII. exponitur. Quae sub exitum anni facta creditur.

Anno sequente XXXV. dispersis ob persecu- tionem fidelibus per Judaeam & Samariam, Phi- lippus in Samaria praedicavit, & cum acceptarent ibi verbum, per Petrum & Johannem in fide con- firmati, ac Simon Magus a Petro publice confu- sus est: Eunuchus etiam, Aethiopiae primas, a Phi- lippo baptizatus cap. VIII.

Anno XXXVI. Paulus convertitur, Damasci praedicat, (inde abiit in Arabiam Gal. I. 17. Mox iterum Damascum revertens, ubi per triennium substitit: Petrus vero Lyddae Aeneam paralyticum sanat, & in Joppen Tabitham excitat cap. IX.

Anno XXXVII. visione coelesti conversionem gentilium instare monitus S. Petrus, ad Cornelium Centurionem Caesaream se confert, eumque cum familia baptizat cap. X. & ejus rei rationem reddit Actor. XI.

Anno Christi XXXIX. Paulus Damasci quaesi- tus a Judaeis, sporta per murum demittitur, & Hie- rosolymam abit, ut Petrum videat, Gal. I. 18. quam historiam cap. IX. inseruit S. Lucas.

Anno XLII. postquam adducto Antiochiam a Barnaba Paulo Ecclesia ibi incrementum per eos cepit, per annum uterque illic mansit, ac praedica- vit: Tum fames, ab Agabo praedicta, orta, & Antiochiae primum nominati Christiani sunt Acto- rum XI.

Anno XLIV. Iacobus ab Herode occisus; Pe- trus vero incarceratus, sed ab Angelo liberatus est Actor. XII.

Anno XLV. Barnabas, & Paulus Antiochiae segregantur ad Evangelium inter gentes praedi- candum Actor. XIII.

Anno XLVI. cum iidem Seleuciam peragras- sent, inde Cyprum navigassent, Salaminam venis- sent, & insulam totam permeassent in Paphos, Ma- go Elyma excaecato Sergium Proconsulem con- vertissent, inde in Pamphyliam appulerunt: postea Antiochiam se contulerunt, ibique praedicarunt, sed reprobati a Judaeis ad gentes se converterunt & Iconium contenderunt Actor. XIII.

Anno XLVII. Iconii Judaeorum & gentium multi per eos conversi sunt, ibique longo tempo- re perstiterunt Paulus & Barnabas; tandem vero Anno XLVIII. ob persecutionem perrexerunt in Lycaoniam, & apud Lystrenses pro Diis habiti, verum Deum annunciarunt, & excitata à Judæis seditione, lapidato Paulo, ut pro mortuo habere- tur, Derben venerunt, & inde vicissim Lystram, Ico- nium & Antiochiam se contulerunt, ac discipulos confortarunt, & per Pisidiam Pamphyliam adie- runt, & in Pergen prædicarunt, Attaliam dehinc profecti: & inde iterum Anno XLIX. post quin- quennalem peregrinationem Antiochiam naviga- runt, ibique non exiguo tempore, per biennium nempe, substiterunt Actor. XIV.

Anno Christi LI. primum Concilium Hierosoly- mis celebratum de controversia à Pseudo-Apo- stolis mota, an legis observatio ad salutem necessa- ria sit? Cujus decisionem Paulus, Barnabas, Silas & Iudas Antiochiam deferunt Actor. XV. Separa- tus autem Barnabas cum Iohanne Marco in Cy- prum contendit, Paulus Apostolus cum Sila, Sy- riam & Ciliciam perambulat, Ecclesias confir- mans: Actor. XV. & pervenit in Derben & Lystram, ubi Timotheum circumcidit & comitem sibi ad- junxit, ac per Phrygiam ac Galatiam, & Mysiam transeuntes, Troadam venerunt: ibique visione excitato Paulo Macedoniam contenderunt. Phi- lippis conversa Lydia ipsisque ob ejectum ex an- cilla Spiritum fatidicum carceratis, & per miracu- losam liberationem ipsorum ad fidem Christi per- ducto carceris præfecto Actor. XVI. Inde peram- bularunt Amphipolin & Apolloniam, & Thessaloni- cam venerunt, ibique prædicarunt, sed Judæorum seditione civitate exacti Beroeam profecti sunt, ubi multi ad fidem conversi, sed ob persecutionem à Judæis excitatam Paulus, ibi relicto Sila & Ti- motheo, Athenas contendit, Anno Christi LII. annunciavit illic Deum, quem ignotum cole- bant ipsi, & convertit inter alios Dionysium cum conjuge Actor. XVII. atque inde se Corinthum conferens, plures Judæos, & inter eos etiam Cry- spum synagogæ principem, & Græcos ad fidem perduxit & monitus per oraculum, per sesqui- annum ibi substitit Actor. XIIX.

Anno Christi LIII. à Judæis tumultuantibus ad tribunal Gallionis pertractus: dehinc in Syriam a- biturus ex voto, Cenchrea, qui portus Corinthi e- rat, caput totondit, & Ephesum pervenit.

Anno LIV. Paulus relicto Ephesi Aquila cum Priscilla, à quibus Apollo in fide uberius instructus Judæos potenter convicit, subiit Cæsaream, ac sa- lutata Ecclesia Hierosolymitana Antiochiam re- versus; peragrata Galatia & Phrygia discipulos undiquaque confirmavit Actor. XIIX.

Anno LV. Paulus, postquam superiores partes peragrasset, Ephesum iterum venit, ibique per duos annos & tres menses prædicavit, & plurima fecit miracula Actor. XIX.

Anno LVI. Ephesi occasione Iudæorum exorci- starum multi conversi sunt, multi etiam, qui Ma- gica sectati erant, libros attulerunt, & publice exusserunt, & valde crevit tum verbum Dei, Ti- motheus & Erastus in Macedoniam ablegati à Pau- lo sunt Actor. XIX.

Anno LVII. Tumultu à Demetrio Dianæ tem- pla argentea fabricante excitato, Paulus Epheso in Macedoniam profectus, inde in Græciam venit, ibiq; per tres menses commoratus, in Macedoniam per minorem Asiam profectus, in Troade Euty- chum à morte resuscitavit, tandem in urbem Mile- tum venit, & accersens eo Seniores Ephesinos, ora- tionem valedictoriam ad illos habuit Act. XX.

An. LVIII. Cæsaream venit, ubi Agabus ei vin- cula Hierosolymitana prædixit: inde Hierosoly- mam profectus, cum in templo se purificaret, à Ju- dæis captus, à tribuno erept9 Act. XXI. Apologiam instituit conversionem suam enarrans, c. XXII. ac ad Synedrium adductus, cum se ob resurrectionem mortuorum argui testaretur, dissidio facto inter ipsos Judæos, Pharisæos & Sadducæos judicium eva- sit, & ob insidias Judæorum à Tribuno Cæsaream abductus, à Felice acceptatur c. XXIII. Qui audita utraq; parte, Anania à Judæis misso, & Paulo, cau- sam protelavit, cum Drusilla uxore concionem Pauli audivit, eumq; Successori Portio Festo capti- vum post se reliquit, c. XXIV. A quo Paulus, cum Hi- erosolymis ille causam cognoscere in gratiam Judæ- orum vellet, ad Cæsarem appellavit c. XXV. & post- quam in præsentia Agrippæ Regis Apologiam suam instituisset c. xxvi. In Italiam ad Cæsarem mittitur, ac naufragium passus, ast superstites cum omnibus comitibus conservatus Melitam pervenit An. LIX. c. XXVII. In Insula Melita à vipera liberatus, Publii Parente aliisq; multis sanitati restitutis, Syracusas & Rhegium pervenit: ac postmodum per septiduu substitit Puteolis, & inde Romam tendit: ibi Judæis rationem fidei suæ exposuit, & per biennium sub custodia in suo conductu mansit, omnes suscipi- ens, libereque Christum prædicans c. XXVIII. exacto biennio à Nerone An. Christi LXI. tandem dimissus.

ITINERARIUM S. PETRI ET S. PAULI.

JUvat autem inde etiam peregrinationes & pro- fectiones Apostolorum, S. Petri imprimis, & S. Pauli exhibere, cum mensura itinerum, prouti à B. Büntingio eadem designata est, ad meliorem libri hujus intelligentiam, idque juxta Chronotaxin jam propositam.

S. Petrus itaq; cum Johanne An. Christi XXXV. Hierosolyma se contulerunt in Samariam per octo milliaria, ibique confirmarunt noviter conversos, & cum Simone Mago disputarunt Act. IIX. A. C. XXXVI. Petrus Lyddæ, quæ quinque milliaribus Hi- erosolyma distat, Æneam paralyticum sanavit, Act. IX. & porro in Joppen tribus quartis milliaribus Germanici à Lydda distantem accersitus, excitavit ibidem Tabitham, cap. eodem.

Ex Joppen Cæsaream Stratonis novem milliarium spatio vocatus à Cornelio, venit An. XXXVII. Act. X.

Cæsarea reversus est Hierosolymam octo millia- rium intercapedine, ubi se ob ingressum ad gentes excusavit Act. XI.

Postquam vero Petrus è carcere, in quem diebus Azymorum injectus An. XLIV. fuit, liberatus es- set, Hierosolymis discessit, sed quorsum, non liquet Act. XII. eo reversus post excessum Herodis: si qui- dem concilio Hierosolymitano interfuerit c. XV.

Hæc de Petri itineribus in Actis designatis: S. Pauli quid concernit itinera hic descripta, Hieroso- lymis, quæ à Patria ejus Tarso in Cilicia 76. milliari- bus distant, A. Dn. XXXVI. Damascum, 40. millia- rium dissitam, contendit, inque via conversus est Act. IX. mox in Arabiam se contulit Gal. I. 17. sed brevi post Damascum iterum ex Arabia rediit; do- nec ob Aretæ persequutionem per corbem dimis- sus effugerit, Act. IX. 25. 2. Cor. XI. & Hierosolymam ad Petrum se recepit Gal. I. 18. Act. IX. 26. quadra- ginta milliarium itinere. Sed & illic Judæorum insidiis expositus, Cæsaream à fratribus deductus per octo milliaria, Tarsum venit Act. IX. 30. sexa- ginta octo milliarium intervallo. Dehinc An- tiochiæ in Syria inventus legitur, Act. XI. 26. quæ distabat triginta milliaribus: ubi per annum moratus est. Postmodum per 70. milliaria ex Antiochia cum Barnaba Hierosolymam Eleemo- synas adduxere : iterum Antiochiam expleto E- leemosynæ ministerio reversus per totidem milli- aria. Atque hæc prima fuit Pauli peregrinatio per 482. milliaria.

Altera cum Barnaba suscepta, cum ad gentes mitteretur, Act. XIII. A. C. XLVI. Antiochia Syriæ metropoli primum Seleuciam venit, sex milliarium itinere, post navigio in Cyprum trajecerunt Salami- nam 24. milliartbus, Act. XIII. 4. 5. Anno XLVI. ac porro progressi in illa insula usque ad Paphum per 25. milliaria: ulterius in Pergen venerunt, Pamphi- liæ civitatem, in Asia minore sitam, 37. milliarium intercapedine : inde Antiochiam in Pisidia, inter- vallo 33. milliarium profecti sunt, Act. XIII. 6. 13. 14. ibique ejecti Iconium migrarunt per 24. milliaria, v. 51. An. XLVII. Dehinc Lystram adierunt millia- ribus septem ab Iconio distitam, A. D. XLIIX. inde ad Derbenses se contulerunt itinere 12. milliarium : ac vicissim totidem milliartbus remearunt ad Ly- strenses, & de Lystra septem milliartbus reversi sunt Iconium : & Iconio per 24. milliaria Antiochiam in Pisidia, confirmantes in civitatibus illis discipulo- rum animos, & per suffragia in singulis civitatibus creantes Presbyteros : ac ab Antiochia, peragrata universa Pisidia, venerunt 33. milliarium intervallo Pergam in Pamphyliam, inde vero descenderunt sex ac dimidio milliartbus in urbem Attaliam, Ann. XLIIX. Act. XIV. deniq; solventes inde Ann. XLIX Antiochiam in Syriam navigarunt 85. milliarium interstitjo. An. LI. 70. milliarium intervallo ab An- tiochia Hierosolymam profecti sunt, ad concilium Apostolicum, Act. XV. Phanicen ac Samariam per- transeuntes. Porro Hierosolyma Paulus, Barnabas, Silas & Judas Antiochiam 70. milliarium intersti- tio se contulerunt : quod factum completis 14. con- versionis Pauli annis Gall. II. Atque hactenus fuit secunda Pauli peregrinatio per 475. milliaria.

Sequitur tertia, quam Paulus cum Syla suscepit, ab Antiochia Syriæ primum egrediens, & Ciliciam perambulans, & in Derben 100. milliarium inter- capedine proveniens An. LI. & porro Lystram 14. milliartbus distantem, atque inde Troadem per 102. milliaria : è qua trajecerunt in Samothraciam milliartbus 29. & Neapolin per 23. milliaria : pedestri itinere Philippos in Macedoniam sex milliarium in- tervallo pervenientes, Act. XVI. ibique ejecti Am- phipolin profecti sunt, confectis 9. milliartbus, inde Apolloniam perrexerunt milliaribus 11. atque inde Thessalonicam, 5. milliarium interstitio, ac Beroeam per intervallum quindecim milliarium, Act. XVII. ubi navim ingressus Paulus per 66. milliaria Athe- nas venit An. D. LII. Dehinc Athenis egressus 18. milliarium interstitio Corinthum veniens, per an- num & sex menses in illa urbe permansit Actor. XIIX. & Cenchreis duorum milliarium ab eadem in- terstitio caput suum radens, ex portu illo Ephe- sum An. Dom. LIII. navigavit per 76. milliaria : ab Epheso porro navigio Cæsaream Stratonis in Pa- læstinam per 170. milliaria, & indę Hierosolymam, salutandi Ecclesiam causa, per 8. milliaria sese con- tulit : Hierosolymis denique 70. milliartbus Antio- chiam in Syria reversus An. LIV. Act. XIIX. Quæ itinera tertiæ peregrinationis Paulinæ conficiunt milliaria septingenta & viginti duo.

Quarta peregrinatione Pauli Antiochia Syriæ metropoli discedens primum 95. milliarium itine- re Galatiam ac Phrygiam peragravit: tum Laodi- cea profectus Anno LV. per 70. milliarium inter- stitium Ephesum iterum venit, Act. XIX. An. LVII. Epheso digressus 53. milliarium intercapedine Troadem reversus est: inde in Macedoniam na- vigans intervallo quinquaginta & octo mil- liarium Philippos venit, & Philippis per Græciam

Corinthum centum viginti milliarium itinere, in quo urbes & Ecclesias visitavit, profectus, ibique hybernavit 1. Cor. XVI. (juxta Büntingium) & in- stante jam Vere non recta via ex Corintho in Sy- riam solvit, sed, ut insidias Judæorum effugeret, 73. milliarium intercapedine Philippus remeavit, ibique Paschatos festum celebravit Anno Chri- sti LIIX. Act. XX. ac Troadem navigio venit per 58. milliaria: de Troade Assum ambulavit per 9. milliaria: ab Asso navigavit Mitylenem per 40. milliaria: ex Insula Mitylene 16. milliarium inter- stitio in Chium trajecit Actor. XX. & ex Insula Chium navigavit in Insulam Samum spatio 15. mil- liarium commorando Tragyllii Insula Samonice- na: unde Miletum per 40. milliaria venerunt: quo accersiti sunt 10. milliarium itinere Ephesini Seniores Act. XX. Ab urbe Mileto Paulus & co- mites ejus recto cursu trajecerunt 15. milliari­bus ad Insulam Coum Act. XXI. inde Rhodum 21. milliari- bus, inde Pataram 25. milliari­bus, inde Tyrum in- terstitio 95. milliarium relicta Cypro ad sinistram: inde Ptolemaidam spatio 6. milliarium, inde Cæsa- ream Stratonis 11. milliarium intercapedine Act. XXI. ex qua Hierosolymam afcendit Paulus per 8. milliaria Anno Domini LIIX. Act. XXI. quæ iti- nera quartæ peregrinationis Paulinæ milliaria ef- ficiunt 823.

Quinto itinera succedunt Pauli emensa, cum ca- ptivus Romam duceretur, jussu Cl. Lysiæ Tribuni, primum Hierosolyma Antipatridem per tria mil- liaria Act. XXII. & inde Cæsaream Stratonis ad Fe- licem Præsidem Romanum adductus Act. XXIII.

An. Domini LIX. à Portio Festo Judæorum præ- sule Romam, instante jam Autumno, ad Cæsarem Neronem missus, conscensa navi à Cæsarea Strato- nis Sidonem 21. milliari­bus navigavit Act. XXVII. Inde Paulus, & comites subnavigantes juxta Cy- prum, propterea quod essent venti contrarii e- mensi pelagus, quod est contra Ciliciam & Pam- phyliam intervallo 120. milliarium Myram perve- nerunt Act. XXVII. De civitate Myra ad Gnidum usque navigarunt per 62. milliaria, inde vento re- pulsi adnavigantes Cretæ versus Austrum, præter- legentes etiam civitates illius Salmonem, Lasæam & Asson, venerunt ad portum Cretæ Phœnicen, qui à Gnido abfuit interstitio 45. milliarium versus Austro-Africum.

De portu Phœnice repulsi vento Typhonico, qui Euro-Aquilo vocatur, devehuntur 13. milliarium curriculo ad Inf. Claudam, ubi Scapham navi alliga- runt, timentes, ne in Syrtim inciderent. Ab Insula Clauda non sine maximo periculo haud procul de Syrti magna, interstitio 180. milliarium trajece- runt ad Insulam Meliten; ubi naufragio facto Pau- lus per tres menses hybernavit, Act. XXVII. XXIX Ex Insula Melite Syracusas in Siciliam navigarunt 45. milliari­bus; & de Syracusis per 16. milliaria ad urbem Rhegium: inde per 41. milliaria Puteolos. Puteolis ad forum Appii per 30. milliaria: de foro Appii ad tres Tabernas milliari uno ac dimidio: de trib. tabernis per 4. milliaria Romam; Ann. Dom. LX. circa quinquagesimum ætatis Pauli annum. Quæ itinera constituunt milliaria quingenta, & octoginta octo: universa autem Pauli itinera, jam designata, usque ad primam in urbe Roma sub Ne- rone captivitatem, efficiunt milliaria 3090.

Hæc succincta Chronotaxis est cum itinerario A- postolico, & sumaria complexione libri Actorum Apostolicorum: cujus scopum & argumentum prima- rium B. Lutherus ex vero assignavit in præf. Germ. articulum de gratuita nostri justificatione cum Deo per fidem, absque operibus legis, concionibus Aposto- lorum, & exemplis conversorum illustrare & confir- mare. In toto libro Actorum, inquit B. Luth. T. IV. Jen. Lat. in Conc. ad Gal. III. 2. f. 56. In summa nihil alind agitur, quam oportere tam Judaeos quam Gen- tes, tam justos quam peccatores sola fide in Christum Jesum justificari, sine lege & operibus. Id quod indi- cant, tum Conciones Apostolorum, Petri, Pauli, Ste- phani, Philippi & aliorum, tum etiam Exempla Gen- tium & Judaeorum. Nam sicut Gentibus, quae sine lege vivebant, Deus per Evangelium Sp. S. dedit, ita & Judaeis, non per Legem, non per cultum & sacrificia in lege praecepta, sed per solam Fidei praedicationem dedit Sp. S. Si autem lex potuisset justificare, & justitia le- gis fuisset necessaria ad salutem, tum certe Sp. S. non fuiffet datus gentibus, quae non servaverant legem, sed ipsa manifesta experientia testabatur, illis dari Spi- ritum sine Lege. Hocque videbant Apostoli, Petrus, Paulus, Barnabas, & alii. Ergo non Lex, sed sola Fi- des in Christum, quam Evangelium praedicat, justifi- cat. Unde merito S. Hieron. ad Paulinum, Actus, in- quit, Apostolorum nudam quidem videntur sonare historiam, & nascentis Ecclesiae infantiam texere, sed si noverimus scriptorem eorum Lucam esse Medi- cum, cujus laus est in Evangelio, animadvertemus pariter, omnia verba illius animae languentes esse me- dicinam.

PARS I. LIBRI Fundationem Ecclesiae in Judaea & Sa- maria, maxime S. Petri opera fa- ctam, exhibens.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

With a brief preceding recapitulation of the Gospel of Luke, concerning the acts and sayings of Christ, up to the day of the assumption, and specifically concerning the apparitions made during 40 days after the passion, the final apparition of Christ is reported, and in it the command not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father: the conversation concerning the time of the restoration of the kingdom of Israel, and the ascension of Christ into heaven, with the angelic address concerning the same, and the return of the disciples, and their dwelling in Jerusalem, where, upon the proposal of Peter concerning the place of Judas, about whom he instituted a narrative and brought forward a Davidic prophecy, with two being presented, Joseph Barsabas and Matthias, the latter was chosen by lot after preceding prayers.

There are two parts: I. The account of the ascension of Christ into heaven, with the preceding and following events, up to verse 14. II. The election of Matthias, for what reason and how it was done, up to verse 26.

PART I. Concerning the ascension of Christ into heaven.

Vers. I. Τὸν μὲν πρῶτον λόγον) That is, former. See what was said at John the Evangelist 1. 15 and 30. λόγον, that is, a book; thus Galen said ἕβδομον λόγον.

Therefore the Vulgate is not sufficiently convenient: 'the first discourse I made.' The Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic more correctly translated it as 'book.' Yet the opinion of Camerarius, that λόγος denotes an exposition and commemoration of things, does not seem to be disapproved. Certainly it is more suitable than the version authentic to the Papists. Nor did the Vulgate render ἤρξατο ποιεῖν, 'began to do,' well, which Beza nevertheless followed. For it is a Hellenism, ἄρχεσθαι ποιεῖν for ποιεῖν: See Judges 13. 5, 20. 31, Acts 3. 8, 5. 21, 12. 45, 23. 30, which was also observed here by Grotius from Gen. 2. 3, Matt. 12. 1, Luke 3. 8, Acts 2. 4.

ὦ Θεόφιλε) See what was said in the preface to the Gospel of Luke.

ὧν ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησοῦς ποιεῖν τε κὴ διδάσκειν) That is, ἐποίησε κὴ ἐδί-

δαξε. Thus Gen. II. 3. ὧν ἤρξατο ὁ Θεὸς ποιῆσαι. Thus ἤξαντο ἰδεῖν. Matth. XII. 1. μείξετο λέγειν. Luc. III. 8. add also what is below II. 4. These words contain a brief description of the Gospel.

Latin:

CAPUT I. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Praevia brevi recapitulatione Evangelii Lucae, de actis & dictis Christi, usque ad diem as- sumtionis, & in specie de apparitionibus post passionem per 40. dies factis, refertur ultima apparitio Christi, & in ea manda- tum, ne Hierosolymis discederent, sed expe- ctarent promissum Patris: Colloquium de tempore restitutionis regni Israël, & ascen- sio Christi in caelum, cum concione angelica de eadem, & reversione discipulorum, ac commoratio in Ierusalem, ubi ad propositio- nem Petri in locum Iudae, de quo narratio- nem instituit, & vaticinium adduxit Da- vidicum, praesentatis duobus Iosepho Bar- saba, & Matthia, posterior praeviis preci- bus per sortem electus est.

Partes duae sunt: I. Relatio de ascensione Christi in caelum, cum antecedentibus, & consequentibus, usque ad v. 14. II. Electio Matthiae, quam ob causam, & quomodo facta, usque ad v. 26.

PARS I. De ascensione Christi in caelum.

Vers. I. Τὸν μὲν πρῶτον λόγον) Id est πρότερον. Vide, quae ad Joh. Evang. I. 15. & 30. λόγον, id est librum, sic ἕβδομον λόγον dixit Galenus.

Non ergo commode satis Vulgatus: primum quidem sermonem feci. Rectius Syrus, Arabs, & Aethiopicus librum verterunt. Non tamen impro- banda Camerarii sententia, quod λόγος expositio- nem & commemorationem rerum notet, videtur. Certe convenientior est versione Papistis authen- tica. Neque illud ἤρξατο ποιεῖν cepit facere, pro- be reddidit Vulgatus: quem tamen Beza sequu- tus est. Hellenismus enim est, ἄρχεσθαι ποιεῖν pro ποιεῖν: Vide Jud. XIII. 5. XX. 31. Act. III. 8. V. 21. XII. 45. XXIII 30. quod hic Grotio etiam observa- tum è Gen. II. 3. Matth. XII. 1. Luc. III. 8. Act. II. 4.

ὦ Θεόφιλε) Vide, quae dicta ad anteloquium Evang. Lucae.

ὧν ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησοῦς ποιεῖν τε κὴ διδάσκειν) Id est ἐποίησε κὴ ἐδί-

δαξε. Sic Gen. II. 3. ὧν ἤρξατο ὁ Θεὸς ποιῆσαι. Sic ἤξαντο ἰδεῖν. Matth. XII. 1. μείξετο λέγειν. Luc. III. 8. adde & quod inf. II. 4. Hæc verba brevem Evangelii descriptionem conti- nent.

## 1:2
Vers. 2. Until the day) Thus historians are accustomed to connect later books with earlier ones. Thus Herodotus at the beginning of Thalia: ἐπὶ τῦτον δὲ τὸν ἀμωσιν. At the beginning of Erato: Ἀρισταγόρας μὲν ἐν Ἰωνίης ἀποστήσας ἔτε τελευτᾷ. At the beginning of Urania: ταῦτα μὲν ὕτως λέγεται γίνεσθαι. Thucydides in Peloponnesian War II. ἄρχεται δὲ ὁ πόλεμος ἐνθένδε ἤδη Ἀθηναίων κὶ Πελοποννησίων. Who in like manner also connects the following books with the preceding ones. Thus also Luke here clearly looks back to the end of his former book.

Having given orders to the Apostles) Giving them many precepts, which for the sake of brevity are passed over here. You have a similar compendium of speech in 2 Sam. XVII. 2.

Through the Holy Spirit) This is also a concise expression: for he wishes to say: he gave orders, which they ought to carry out through the Holy Spirit, after, of course, they had received him.

whom he chose) A transposition of words: for this member refers to that which precedes, Apostles. Such transpositions are frequent in the sacred scriptures.

Sanctius and Beza invent another transposition, referring the word through the Holy Spirit to the verb he chose. But there is neither any example of this concise expression, and there is no need for a transposition here. For the words through the Holy Spirit do not pertain to the Apostles carrying out the orders through the Holy Spirit, which he gave; but to Christ, who gave orders to the Apostles through the Holy Spirit: which the Apostle explains, either that the precepts were spiritual, or that he gave them precepts through the Spirit, just as he cast out demons through the Spirit, or that he was nowhere nor did anything without the Holy Spirit, for wherever the Son acts, there also the Spirit as of one mind works and is present. However, that there were many precepts which were given to the Apostles is not indicated here; and although it is admitted that they are not recounted here, it is not believed, except rashly, with the Papists, that they are not contained in the Apostolic letters: that they are entirely different from the Scriptures, and that the tenor of them is nowhere held in Holy Scripture, is asserted with greater rashness: just as it is evident that the Pontificians wish to prop up their unwritten traditions from this passage as well. Moreover, these can be referred to the precepts recorded in Matth. XXIX. 19. 20. Marc. XVI. 16. Luc. XXIV. 47. 48. Joh. XX. 23., where among other things they are commanded in Luc. XXIV. 48. to wait in Jerusalem for the mission of the Holy Spirit. Compare Acts I. 4.

He was taken up) See what was said on Mark XVI. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ἀχρι ἧς ἡμέρας) Sic solent historiarum scriptores libros posteriores cum prioribus connectere. Sic Herodotus Thaliæ principio: ἐπὶ τῦτον δὲ τὸν ἀμωσιν. Principio Era- tus: Ἀρισταγόρας μὲν ἐν Ἰωνίης ἀποστήσας ἔτε τελευτᾷ. Initio Uraniæ: ταῦτα μὲν ὕτως λέγεται γίνεσθαι. Thucidides Pelo- ponnesiacôn II. ἄρχεται δὲ ὁ πόλεμος ἐνθένδε ἤδη Ἀθηναίων κὶ Πελοποννησίων. Qui pari modo & sequentes libros præce- dentibus connectit. Sic & respicit Lucas hic aperte finem libri sui prioris.

Ἐντειλάμενος τοῖς Ἀποσόλοις) Multa illis præcepta dans, quæ brevitatis causa hic reticentur. Simile dicendi com- pendium habes 2. Sam. XVII. 2.

Διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίε) Est & hæc compendiosa locutio: vult enim dicere: mandavit, quæ agere deberent per Spiri- tum Sanctum, postquam scilicet eum accepiffent.

ὣς ἐξελέξατο) Vocum trajectio: nam hoc membrum re- fertur ad id, quod præcesfit Ἀποσόλυς. Frequentes sunt ta- les in sacris scriptis trajectiones.

Aliam trajectionem Sanctius & Beza fingunt, vocem διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίε ad verbum τὸ ἐξελέ- ξατο referentes. Sed nec exemplum ullum est hu- jus compendiosæ locutionis, & nulla hic opus tra- jectione. Nam verba διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίε non ad Apostolos per Spiritum Sanctum mandata exe- quentes pertinent, quæ dedit; Sed ad Christum, qui per Spiritum S. mandata Apostolis dedit: quod explicat Apostolus, vel quod πνευματικά fuerint præcepta, vel quod per Spiritum præcepta eis de- derit,uti per SpiritumDæmonia ejecerit,vel quod non sine Spiritu S. fuerit uspiam aut fecerit quid- quam, ὅτι ἔνθα ἂν ὁ ὑὸς διαπράττηται ἐκεῖ κὶ τὸ πνεῦμα ὡς ὁμοΦανὲς ēνεργεῖ κὶ πάρεσι. Multa autem fuisse præcepta, quæ data Apostolis sunt, hic non indicatur; & quamvis ea hic non recense- ri admittatur, in literis tamen Apostolicis ea non contineri, non nisi temere, cum Papistis, creditur: à Scripturis plane diversa esse, nec uspiam in S.Scri- ptura eorundem tenorem haberi, majori temeri- tate statuitur: quemadmodum constat, Pontificios traditiones suas non-scriptas ex hoc etiam loco sta- cuminare velle. Referri autem hæc possunt ad præcepta Matth. XXIX. 19. 20. Marc. XVI. 16. Luc. XXIV. 47. 48. Joh. XX. 23. consignata, ubi in- ter alia jubentur Luc. XXIV. 48. expectare Hiero- solymis Spiritus S. missionem. Cons. Act. I. 4.

Ἀνελήφθη) Vide, quæ dicta ad Marcum XVI. 19.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. By many proofs) in here means with. With many miracles, some of which are recounted by John in the Gospel.

And speaking the things concerning the kingdom of God) How the Gospel was to reach all nations; through which God reigns in men, even in kings.

Christ undoubtedly spoke with the Apostles not only about the propagation of the Gospel to the nations, but also about other things pertaining to the kingdom of God: And not only about the kingdom of grace, but also about the kingdom of glory: which is also called the kingdom of God in Mark IX. 47. and Luke XXII. 16. However, it is not to be thought, with the Pontificians, that Christ handed down things which pertain to the Papal Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, as Lorinus does, or things which pertain to the matter and form of the seven Sacraments, which they invent, as Cornel. à Lapide wishes. For that Papal Hierarchy is utterly opposed to the Apostolic one described in 1 Cor. XII. v. 28. and Eph. IV. 11.: nor do the things which the Papists babble about the seven Sacraments and their matter and form agree with the Scriptures. But who would say that Christ handed down to the Apostles anything contrary to the Scriptures?

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ἐν πολλοῖς τεκμηρίοις) ἐν hic valet cum. Cum multis miraculis, quorum quædam referuntur à Johanne in Evangelio.

Καὶ λέγων τὰ περὶ τῆς βασιλείας τῦ Θεῦ) Quomodo ad omnes gentes perventurum esset Evangelium; per quod Deus in hominibus, etiam regibus, regnat.

Non tantum de Evangelii propagatione ad gentes, sed etiam de aliis ad regnum Dei pertinentibus, sine dubio locutus est cum Apostolis Christus: Nec solum de regno gratiæ, sed etiam de regno gloriæ: quod etiam regnum Dei vocatur Marc. IX. 47. & Luc. XXII. 16. Non autem cum Pontificiis putan- dum, quod Christus, quæ ad Hierarchiam Papa- lem Ecclesiasticam faciunt, ut Lorinus, vel quæ ad materiam & formam septem Sacramentorum, quæ fingunt, ut Cornel. à Lapide vult, tradiderit. Illa enim Hierarchia Papalis Apostolicæ 1. Cor. XII. v. 28. & Eph. IV. 11. descriptæ penitus adversa- tur: neque consonant Scripturis, quæ Papistæ de septem Sacramentis eorumque materia & forma nugantur. Christum autem Scripturis aliquid contrarium tradidisse Apostolis, quis dixerit?

## 1:4
Vers. 4. Καὶ συναλιζόμενος) Supply αὐτὸς, gathering them together into one, who had been dispersed, see John XXI. 2. It is passive in sound after the Attic custom, but active in sense. Herodotus Euterpe: τὰς γυναῖκας συναλίσαντες. When he had gathered all the women into one place.

See Camerarius for this sense. The Vulgate is wrong in saying 'eating with them,' nor can what Beza inserted by the authority of one codex, the words μετ' αυ̉́τω̃ν, be approved: which are found neither in other Greek nor in Latin texts, and were added by the Syrian, Arab, and Ethiopian only because, lacking compound verbs, they could not translate it otherwise.

Τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν του̃ πατρός) Luke XXIV. 49.

Η̃ν ἠκούσατέ με) A transition from indirect to direct speech, which is frequent in histories. Ἠκούσατέ με is a good Greek idiom, such as are many in this writer, who had read both medical and historical authors. Thus Xenophon: το̃το πολλοὶ ἐφη ἀδουσι.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ συναλιζόμενος) Supple αὐτὸς, ipsos in unum recolligens, qui dispersi fuerant, vide Joh. XXI. 2. Est Attico more passivum sono, sensu Activum. Herodo- tus Euterpe: τὰς γυναῖκας συναλίσαντες. Cum in unum lo- cum fæminas omnes congregasset.

Vide pro hoc sensu Camerarium. Perperam Vulg. convescens, nec probari potest, quod Beza unius Codicis autoritate inseruit verba μετ' αυ̉́τω̃ν: Quæ nec in aliis Græcis, nec in Latinis reperiuntur, & à Syro, Arabe, Æthiope addita tantum sunt, quia verbis compositis carentes aliter vertere non potuerunt.

Τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν του̃ πατρός) Lucæ XXIV. 49.

Η̃ν ἠκούσατέ με) Transitus à sermone indirecto ad directum, qui in historiis frequens. Ἠκούσατέ με, bene Græca locutio, quales multæ in hoc scriptore, qui & medicos & historicos legerat. Ita Xenophon: το̃το πολλοὶ ἐφη ἀδουσι.

## 1:5
Vers. 5.

Ἰωάννης μὲν ἐβάπτισεν ὔδατι) See Matt. III. 11, ἐν πνεύματι ἀγίω) It would have been sufficient to say πνεύματι ἀγίω, as the Latin here says Spiritu Sancto. But the Hellenists, after the manner of the Hebrew ב, add ἐν, as in the expression ἐν ὔδατι in the cited passage of Matthew. Βαπτίζεσθαι here means to be poured out abundantly, not to be lightly sprinkled. The Apostles received much more than the Prophets of old. See Gospel of John, ch. III. 34. This Spirit was πνευ̃μα ἀφέσεως καὶ πνευ̃μα κάυσεως, Is. IV. v. 7.

The passage John III. 34 does not treat of the Apostles, but of Christ. For the Apostles did not receive the Spirit οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου, but Christ alone, from whom the Apostles received the Spirit κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τη̃ς δωρεα̃ς, Eph. ch. IV. v. 7. Furthermore, the Holy Spirit in Eph. ch. IV. v. 4 is called πνευ̃μα κάυσεως, not because he was to be sent in the symbol of fire, but because he kindles the fire of devotion, faith, and love in our hearts, Luke XXIV. 32. Conf. Luke XII. 49. The Baptism of water is distinguished from the Baptism of the Holy Spirit, not because the Spirit was not dispensed in the former: for the baptism of water is also the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, Tit. III. 6. But because in the former are the common gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are granted to all the faithful; in the latter, however, the singular gifts of the Spirit, which were necessary for the Apostles for their office and were proper to the primitive Church, were poured out abundantly. B. Joh. Gerhard rightly explains the emphasis of the word. in h. l. p. 12. That miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit is called Baptism on account of the abundance and plenty of the gift; βαπτίζειν means to submerge: truly, therefore, the Apostles are said to be βαπτισθη̃ναι, because the house in which this was done was filled with the Holy Spirit, so that the Apostles seem to have been submerged into it as if into a certain pool. Conf. also Casaubon on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Ἰωάννης μὲν ἐβάπτισεν ὔδατι) Vide Matth. III. 11, ἐν πνεύματι ἀγίω) Satis fuerat dixisse πνεύματι ἀγίω, quomodo Latinus hic Spiritu Sancto. Sed Hellenistæ ad modum Hebræi ב addunt ἐν, quomodo ἐν ὔδατι dicto Matthæi loco. Βαπτίζεσθαι, hic est largiter profundi, non leviter aspergi. Multo plus accepere Apostoli, quam olim Prophetæ. Vide Evang. Johan. cap. III. 34. Hic Spiritus erat πνευ̃μα ἀφέσεως καὶ πνευ̃μα κάυσεως, Es. IV. v. 7.

Locus Joh. III. 34. non agit de Apostolis, sed de Christo. Non enim Apostoli Spiritum acceperunt οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου, sed solus Christus, à quo Apostoli κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τη̃ς δωρεα̃ς acceperunt Spiritum, Eph. cap. IV. v. 7. Cæterum Spiritus Sanctus Eph. cap. IV. v. 4. dicitur πνευ̃μα κάυσεως, non quod mittendus erat in symbolo ignis, sed quia ignem devotionis, fidei & amoris accendit in cordibus nostris, Luc. XXIV. 32. Conf. Luc. XII. 49. Distinguitur autem Baptismus aquæ à Baptismo Spiritus S. non quod illo Spiritus dispensatus non fuerit: Nam & baptismus aquæ lavacrum est regenerationis & renovationis Spiritus S. Tit. III. 6. Sed quod communia illic Spiritus S. dona, quæ omnibus fidelibus conceduntur; hic vero dona Spiritus singularia, quæ Apostolis ad officium erant necessaria, & primitivæ Ecclesiæ propria largiter effusa sint. Recte autem ἔμφασιν vocis explicat B. Joh. Gerhard. in h. l. p. 12. Miraculosa illa Spiritus S. effusio vocatur Baptismus propter copiam & abundantiam muneris; βαπτίζειν est mergere: Vere igitur Apostoli dicuntur βαπτισθη̃ναι, quia domus, in qua hoc factum est, Spiritus S. fuit repleta, ut in eam tanquam in κολυμβήθραν quandam Apostoli demersi videantur. Conf. & Casaubonus in h. l.

## 1:6
Vers. 6. Εἰν τω̃ χρόνω τούτω ἀποκαθιστάνεις τὴν βασιλείαν τώ Ἰσραήλ) אם, which often signifies 'whether,' just as the Greek interpreters often translate it by εἰ, so the Latin often translates it by 'si' (if). The Apostles refer to the passage of Daniel VII. 27. 'Do you restore,' that is, are you preparing to restore into its ancient dignity.

Concerning the restoration of the kingdom of Israel to its former dignity, nothing is held in Dan. VII. 27, where the discourse is rather concerning the spiritual kingdom of the Messiah. But what the Apostles understood by the ἀποκατάστασιν τη̃ς βασιλείας Ἰσραὴλ is ambiguous. They may still have indulged in a preconceived opinion about a worldly kingdom as being sufficiently ingrained, or, because Christ had already instructed the Apostles for 40 days concerning the kingdom of God, it is credible that the Apostles looked rather to the restoration of the spiritual kingdom, which had collapsed in Israel, than to the day of the final judgment, which the blessed Matthesius desires: inasmuch as they had been ordered to make the beginning of the proclamation of repentance and remission of sins in his name at Jerusalem, Luke XXIV. 47. From which they could gather that the kingdom of God was to be restored in Israel: and they desired to be informed concerning that ἀποκαταστάσει and the time of the ἀποκαταστάσεως. Just as CHRIST also taught them, not indeed concerning the time and occasion, or the manner of that restoration, because GOD reserves these to his own power, whether at once and together, or but successively, and at what time, with what success, and in what manner those things ought to be done, but that God is about to take up through them the Holy Spirit, those things which make for the restoration of the Kingdom of Israel, and that they are to testify of themselves concerning that very end not only in Jerusalem, but also in all Judea, and indeed even in Samaria, nay even unto the ends of the earth, not only by the proclamation of a living voice, but also by their own writings, to be divulged for the good of the whole world Joh. XXI. 24. 1. Joh. I. 3. 4. Apoc. I. 2. 3. indicating by this reason that an accession to the kingdom of Israel would come through their ministry from the nations throughout the whole earth.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Εἰν τω̃ χρόνω τούτω ἀποκαθιστάνεις τὴν βασιλείαν τω̃ Ἰσραήλ) אם quod sæpe an significat, ut Græci Interpretes per εἰ, ita Latinus per si sæpe vertit. Respiciunt Apostoli locum Danielis VII. 27. Restituis, id est, restituturus paras in veterem dignitatem.

De restitutione regni Israëlis in veterem dignitatem nihil habetur apud Dan. VII. 27. ubi de regno Messiæ spirituali potius sermo est. Quid vero Apostoli per ἀποκατάστασιν τη̃ς βασιλείας Ἰσραὴλ intellexerunt, ambiguum est. Indulsisse adhuc potuère præconceptæ de regno mundano opinioni ceu satis inolitæ, aut, quia Christus per 40. dies jam de regno Dei instituerat Apostolos, credibile est spiritualis regni, quod in Israële collapsum erat, restaurationem potius, quam extremi judicii diem, quod vult B. Matthesius, respexisse Apostolos: utpote qui jussi erant, præconii pœnitentiæ & remissionis peccatorum in nomine ejus instituendi initium facere Hierosolymis, Luc. XXIV. 47. Unde colligere poterant, restaurandum esse in Israële regnum Dei: ac de ἀποκαταστάσει illa & tempore ἀποκαταστάσεως informari desiderabant. Quemadmodum etiam CHRISTUS ipsos edocuit, non quidem de tempore & occasione, vel ratione instaurationis istius, quia hæc DEUS reservat potestati suæ, an simul ac semel, an vero successive, & quo tempore, quo successu, quove modo ea fieri debeat, sed quod per ipsos accipient Spiritum Sanctum ea, quæ ad restaurationem faciunt Regni Israëlis, Deus suscepturus sit, eaque fini ipsi non tantum Hierosolymis, sed in tota etiam Judea, imo & in Samaria testaturi sint de sese, quin etiam usque ad fines terræ, non vivæ tantum vocis præconio, sed scriptis etiam suis, totius orbis bono divulgandis Joh. XXI. 24. 1. Joh. I. 3. 4. Apoc. I. 2. 3. indicans hac ratione, regno Israëlis accessionem ipsorum ministerio futuram ex gentibus per universam terram.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. It is not for you to know the times or the seasons) In Daniel VII. 12. עד־זמן ועדן is translated ἕως χρόνου καὶ καιροῦ. It is a hendiadys, by which a certainly appointed time is signified. That time, however, was nearly three hundred years after these words. For then Christ, the offspring of David, began to reign on earth through Constantine, and subsequently through others and others, not only emperors, but also kings, who subjected their kingdom to Christ as King of Kings. Christians are the people of God, and therefore the true Israel, Gal. VI. 16. Christ is their head, an Israelite also according to the flesh. The Hebrews also say that it is hidden from men when the kingdom is to return to the house of David. Augustine translates seasons as tempestates, epist. 78.

Not some special time appointed by God, nor is the time of the reign of Constantine the Great precisely looked at here (for there is no indication of this matter here; why those things ought to be restricted to that time) but it is taught that in general the time and the seasons are reserved for divine mysteries: whence this general maxim is also rightly applied by Aug. l. XIIX. de Civ. Dei c. 53. to the time of the last day, even if it is not peculiarly about that which is treated here, but the times and seasons of the restoration of the kingdom of God are looked at, which had greatly collapsed, which was done then both by the Apostles and by their successors: to which you might perhaps also refer the conversion of many nations under the empire of Constantine the Great. What the Jews say about the kingdom returning to the house of David has little to do with this.

Which the Father hath put in his own power) It is the custom of Christ to refer secret dispensations to the Father, Matth. XX. 23. Marc. XIII. 32.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ὀὐχ ὑμῶν ἐστι γνῶναι χρόνους ἡ καιροὺς) In Daniele VII. 12. עד־זמן ועדן vertitur ἕως χρόνου καὶ καιροῦ. Est ἧς διὰ δυοῖν, quo significatur tempus certo constitutum. Id vero tempus fuit trecentis ferme post hæc verba annis. Tunc enim Christus Davidis stirps in terris regnare cœpit per Constantinum, ac deinceps per alios & alios, non imperatores tantum, sed & reges, qui regnum suum Christo ut Regi Regum subjecere. Christiani populus Dei, atque ideo verus Israël, Gal. VI. 16. Christus eorum caput Israëlita etiam secundum carnem. Occultum esse hominibus, quando regnum rediturum sit da domum Davidis, ajunt & Hebræi. Καιροὺς tempestates vertit Augustinus, epist. 78.

Non speciale quoddam tempus à Deo constitutum, nec præcise tempus regiminis Constantini M. hic respicitur (nullum enim hujus rei hic est indicium; cur ad id tempus ista restringi debeant) sed in genere χρόνος καὶ καιροὺς divinis arcanis reservari, docetur: unde generalis hæc gnome etiam ab August. l. XIIX. de Civ. Dei c. 53. recte applicatur ad tempus extremæ diei, etsi de illa peculiariter hic non agatur, sed χρόνοι καὶ καιροὶ respiciantur restaurationis regni Dei, quod valde collapsum erat, quæ tum ab Apostolis, tum à successoribus eorum facta est: ad quam etiam referre fortassis possis conversionem gentium plurimarum sub imperio Constantini M. Quæ Judæi de regno redituro ad domum Davidis, huc parum faciunt.

Οὓς ὁ πατὴρ ἔθετο ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ) Mos est Christi arcanas dispensationes ad Patrem referre, Matth. XX. 23. Marc. XIII. 32.

## 1:8
Vers. 8. But ye shall receive power) אורו חיל 1. Sam. II. 4. and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth) He proposes here the sum of all the Apostolic discourses, which this book will exhibit, Confer Mark XVI. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἀλλα᾿ λήψεσθε δύναμιν) אורו חיל 1. Sam. II. 4. καὶ ἔσεσθέ μοι μάρτυρες ἔν τε Ἰερουσαλὴμ, καὶ ἐν πάσῃ τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ, καὶ Σαμαρείᾳ, καὶ ἕως ἐχάτου τῇς γῆς) Summam hic proponit tot sermonem Apostolicorum, quos hic liber exhibebit, Confer Marci XVI. 20.

## 1:9
Vers. 9. He was taken up) he was carried up, Luke Evang. XXIV. 51. And a cloud received him) Elijah carried into heaven in a whirlwind, 2. Kings II. 1. 11. Christ in a peaceful cloud. See Luke c. IX. 54. 55.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ἐπήρθη) ἀνεφέρετο, Luc. Evang. XXIV. 51. Καὶ νεφέλη ὑπέλαβεν αὐτὸν) Elias in cœlum vectus in turbine, 2. Reg. II. 1. 11. Christus in nube placida. Vide Lucæ c. IX. 54. 55.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. In white apparel) See what was said at Matthew XVII. 2. The most ancient manuscript has in white garments, but that matters little. Moreover, it is a manner of speaking also customary to the Latins; thus in gold, in purple, Cato apud Gellium.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἐν ἐσθῆτι λευκῇ) Vide, quæ dicta ad Matthæi XVII. 2. Manuscriptus vetustissimus habet ἐν ἐσθήσεσι λευκαῖς, sed parum id refert. Est autem loquendi genus etiam Latinis usitatum; sic in auro, in purpura, Cato apud Gellium.

## 1:11
Vers. 11. So shall he come) he shall descend I. Thess. IV. 16. The Chaldean in the Canticles, and others at Joel III. 2. Zach. XIV. 4. think that the Israelites will rise again on the Mount of Olives.

A dream of the Jews and of the Papists, it has no foundation in the Prophetic places, nor does it agree with this of ours: for these things do not sound of the place of the return, but of the manner, that Christ is about to return in a cloud, and visibly, about to come to judgment.

What the Angel says, that Christ will come SIMILARLY, JUST AS they saw him going into heaven, that seems to look to both a visible return, as this departure was visible and conspicuous; and the Angelic retinue, which was without doubt present here, just as the fiery Angelic chariots were seen in the translation of Elijah, 2. Kings cap. II. vers. 11. conf. cap. VI. vers. 17. and the clangor and sound of the Angelic trumpets, with which the LORD is about to return, 1. Thess. cap. IV. vers. 16. 1. Cor. cap. XV. v. 52. such as the Holy Psalmist had predicted at the ascension of Christ, Psalm XLVII. v. 6. To these must be added the company of those who were taken up alive into heaven: for just as by the common opinion of the ancients the holy Patriarchs and Kings and Prophets, or whoever those were who came forth from the tombs alive after the resurrection of Christ, accompanied Christ in his ascension into heaven, so the same ones seem destined to accompany Christ from heaven when he returns for judgment, because his return will be similar to the ascension of Christ, together with Enoch, Moses, and Elijah who are already living in heaven in soul and body, Gen. ch. V. v. 24. 2. Kings ch. II. v. 11. Matt. ch. XVII. v. 3. and many myriads of Angels, Jude v. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Οὕτως ἐλεύσεται) καταβήσεται I. Thess. IV. 16. resurrecturos in monte olivarum Israëlitas sentit Chaldæus in Canticum, & alii ad Joël. III. 2. Zach. XIV. 4.

Somnium Judæorum, & Pontificiorum nec in Propheticis locis fundamentum habet, nec huic nostro congruit: non enim de τόπῳ vel loco reditus, sed de τρόπῳ vel modo, quod in nube, ac visibiliter Christus rediturus sit, venturus ad judicium, hæc sonant.

Quod Angelus ait, SIMILITER venturum Christum, SICUT viderunt ipsum πορευόμενον profectum in cælum, id tum visibilem reditum, ut hæc erat profectio visibilis & conspicua; tum Angelicum comitatum, qui hic fine dubio affuit, quemadmodum ignei currus Angelici visi sunt in Eliæ translatione, 2. Reg. cap. II. vers. 11. conf. cap. VI. vers. 17. tum buccinarum Angelicarum clangorem & sonitum, cum quo rediturus est DOMINUS, 1. Thess. cap. IV. vers. 16. 1. Cor. cap. XV. v. 52. qualem in ascensione Christi prædixerat Hiero-Psaltes, Psal. XLVII. v. 6. respicere videtur. Quibus comitatus addendus eorum, qui vivi in cælum recepti sunt: uti enim communi veterum sententia sancti Patriarchæ & Reges ac Prophetæ, vel quicunque illi fuerint, qui post resurrectionem Christi vivi è monumentis prodiere, Christum in ascensione in cælum comitati sunt, ita iidem Christum rediturum ad judicium, quia reditus similis futurus ascensui Christi, comitaturi videntur de cælo, cum Enoche, Mose, & Elia jam in cælo anima & corpore agentibus, Genes. cap. V. v. 24. 2. Reg. cap. II. v. 11. Matth. c. XVII. vers. 3. & multis Angelorum myriadibus, Jud. v. 15.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. Σαββάτου ἔχον ὁδὸν) Most Jews define a Sabbath day's journey as two thousand cubits, that is, one thousand paces, for a pace is a double cubit. A stadium, according to Pliny, is the eighth part of a thousand paces II. 23. Therefore a Sabbath day's journey would be eight stadia, which does not differ much from the opinion of the Syrian, who here put seven stadia. In Josephus it is explained as five stadia: but the reading is suspect, since Theophylact cites Josephus as saying seven stadia. But we gather from Luke XXIV. 50 that Christ was taken up from Bethany; and John XI. 18 places Bethany at a distance of fifteen stadia from the city. John seems to have had in mind a certain Jewish measure, which he calls a stadium, although it contained only about half of a Greek stadium; just as leagues are larger in one place and smaller in another: see what the most learned Selden has in book III. c. 9 of the Law of Nature and of Nations according to the Hebrews, following Drusius and Beza on this passage.

That a Sabbath day's journey was two thousand paces is taught in Sebbeleh recheth tr. 22. c. 1. de Sabb. and Targum on Ruth I. 16, as also in Hieronymus on Algas. q. X. Which some understand as smaller paces or cubits, of which two make one greater pace, so that thus they made a Sabbath day's journey of only one thousand greater paces, i.e., nearly seven stadia, as the Syrian renders it, only one Italian mile, which is the fourth part of a German mile: For according to Suidas, 7 1/2 stadia make an Italian mile: and one stadium is 125 paces, and the eighth part of an Italian mile. But the fact that Bethany is said to be situated at the Mount of Olives, Mark XI. 1, as if it were fifteen stadia away from Jerusalem, does not conflict with the present passage: since it could be said that Bethany was situated about eight stadia back from the root of the mountain on the mountain itself. Lud. de Dieu explains it thus, that they are said here to have returned from the mountain, that is, from the extreme side of the Mount of Olives, where the village of Bethany was, distant fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, whereas the beginning of the mountain was distant, according to Josephus, five (Greek) stadia, i.e., 7 1/2 Hebrew stadia, so that Bethany, situated on the extreme side of the mountain, was not further removed from its beginning than this was from Jerusalem. Conf. Joh. Buxtorf. Lex. Talm. Rabb. p. 25. 83. and B. Joh. Ern. Gerh. on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Σαββάτου ἔχον ὁδὸν) Iter Sabbati plerique Judæi definiunt bis mille ulnis, id est, mille passibus, nam passus duplex ulna. Stadium Plinio octava pars mille passuum II. 23. Ergo iter Sabbati essent stadia octo, quod non longe abit à Syri sententia, qui hic posuit stadia septem. In Josepho explicatur per stadia quinque: sed suspecta est lectio, cum Theophylactus Josephum citet de stadiis septem. At ex Bethania sublatum Christum colligimus ex Lucæ XXIV. 50. à Bethania vero ad urbem quindecim stadia ponit Johannes XI. 16. videtur Johannes in animo habuisse Judaicam quandam mensuram, quam stadium vocat, quanquam Græci stadii ferme dimidium tantum continebat; sic Leucæ alibi majores, alibi minores: vide, quæ habet doctissimus Seldenus, libro III. c. 9. de Jure naturali & gentium secundum Hebræos, post Drusium & Bezam hoc loco.

Iter Sabbati duorum millium passuum fuisse in Sebbeleh recheth tr. 22. c. 1. de Sabb. & Targum ad Ruth. I. 16. ut & apud Hieronym. ad Algas. q. X. docetur. Quod nonnulli de minoribus passibus seu cubitis intelligunt, quorum duo unum majorem passum conficiant, ut ita mille tantum passus majores fecerint iter Sabbati h. e. fere septem stadia, ut Syrus reddit, unum tantum milliare Italicum, quod est pars quarta milliaris Germanici: Nam secundum Suidam 7. stadia cum dimidio milliare Italicum faciunt: unumque stadium est 125. passuum, & octava pars milliaris Italici. Quod vero ad montem Oliveti sita Bethania, Marc. XI. 1. quasi XV. stadiis Hierosolymis abfuisset, dicitur, non pugnat cum præsenti loco: Siquidem dici possit Bethaniam octo fere stadiis retro à montis radice in ipso monte sitam fuisse. Lud. de Dieu ita explicat, reversos hic dici à monte, id est, à latere montis Oliveti extremo, ubi erat vicus Bethania, distante Hierosolymis XV. stadiis, quum initium montis distaret, secundum Josephum, quinque stadiis (Græcis, h. e. 7 1/2 stadiis Ebraicis) ut ita Bethania in montis extremo latere sita non longius ab ejus initio dissita fuerit, quam hoc Hierosolymis. Conf. Joh. Buxtorf. Lex. Talm. Rabb. p. 25. 83. & B. Joh. Ern. Gerh. in h. l.

## 1:13
Vers. 13. Εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον) See from what a small place, and from 120 men, the beginning of how great a thing was made; and compare what we had in Matt. XIII. 31.

Ὁ, τε Πέτρος) Who is here rightly named first, as being clearly designated by Christ as the leader of the Apostolic band: whence he also made the beginning of the speech, as the Greek interpreters note here. Oecumenius on Peter: having been entrusted with the leadership of the disciples. Theophylact: as the chief.

Order alone implies no leadership. See what is on Matt. X. 1.

Καὶ Ἰούδας Ἰακώβου) Brother, which the Arab adds here. But in the Syrian it is son of James. It could have happened that a father had a son with the same name as himself. This conjecture rests on no foundation. That he was the brother of James is also from the epistle of Jude v. 1. & Mark VI. 3. It is certain. The Syriac, as in other places, so also here, and Luke VI. 16, where it also inserts its own בר, could have erred: whom the Ethiopian has followed.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον) Vide ex quantillo loco, & hominibus CXX. quantæ rei factum sit exordium; & confer, quæ habuimus Matth. XIII. 31.

Ὁ, τε Πέτρος) Qui primus hic bono jure nominatur, utpote à Christo designatus non obscure προστάτης Apostolici cœtus: unde & loquendi exordium fecit, ut hic notant Græci interpretes. Oecumenius de Petro: τὴν προστασίαν τῶν μαθητῶν ἐγκεχειρισμέν[ος]. Theophylactus: ὡς κορυφαῖος.

Ordo solus nullam προστασίαν infert. Vid. quæ ad Matth. X. 1.

Καὶ Ἰούδας Ἰακώβου) Frater quod hic addit Arabs. At Syro est Jacobi filius. Fieri potuit, ut pater filium haberet sibi cognominem. Conjectura hæc nullo nititur fundamento. Fratrem fuisse Jacobi etiam ex epistola Judæ vers. 1. & Marc. VI. 3. constat. Syrus ut in aliis, ita & hic, & Luc. VI. 16. ubi etiam suum בר inserit, labi po-tuit: quem sequutus Æthiops est.

## 1:14
Verse 14. Σὺν γυναιξὶ) The Syriac and Arabic rightly understood this word concerning sex, not marriage. Those women are understood, whose mention is in Matthew XXVII. 55, and with them certain women of Jerusalem.

Why should we not understand wives, which the word properly signifies. Since the wives of the Apostles were without doubt also present, Matthew IV. 14, and all the Apostles, with John alone excepted, according to the testimony of Ambrose in 2 Cor. XI, had wives, if indeed Mary is counted separately.

Καὶ Μαρίᾳ τῇ μητρὶ τῦ Ἰησῦ) Who, as exceptional, deserved to be remembered singularly. See what we have said at Mark XVI. v. 7.

PART II. Concerning the election of Matthias.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Σὺν γυναιξὶ) De sexu, non de matrimonio hanc vocem recte cepere Syrus & Arabs. Intelliguntur mulie-res illæ, quarum mentio Matth. XXVII. 55. & cum iis Hi-erosolymitanæ quædam.

Cur non uxores, quod proprie vox sonat, intel-ligamus. Quum Apostolorum uxores procul du-bio etiam adfuerint, Matth. IV. 14. & omnes A-postoli, solo Johanne excepto, teste Ambrosio in 2. Cor. XI. uxores habuerint, siquidem Maria seor-sim numeretur.

Καὶ Μαρίᾳ τῇ μητρὶ τῦ Ἰησῦ) Quæ ut eximia singulariter memorari merebatur. Vide, quæ diximus ad Marcum XVI. v. 7.

PARS II. De electione Matthiæ.

## 1:15
Verse 15. ὄχλος ὀνομάτων) That to say names for men was a received manner of speaking among the Jews, appears from the Apocalypse.

ὡςἑκατὸν εἴκοσιν) As the Satraps of a new kingdom, which was to exist as much greater than the kingdom of Nabonidus, to whom there were 120 Satraps, Dan. VI. 2.

Darius the Mede, Dan. VI. 2, is not Nabonidus, but Cyaxares the son of Astyages, called Ahasuerus, as we have taught at Dan. VI. 2 and in the Biblical Chronicle.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὄχλος ὀνομάτων) Nomina dicere pro homi-nibus, receptum fuisse inter Judæos loquendi genus, ex A-pocalypsi apparet.

ὡςἑκατὸν εἴκοσιν) Tanquam Satrapæ novi regni, quod multo majus exstiturum, quam Nabonidi regnum, cui CXX. fuerunt Satrapæ, Dan. VI. 2.

Darius Medus Dan. VI. 2. non Nabonidus est, sed Cyaxares Astyagis, Asveri dicti, filius, ut ad Dan. VI. 2. & in Chronico Biblico docuimus.

## 1:16
Verse 16. ἔδει πληρωθῆναι) It was fitting that something similar should happen to Judas, as had happened to Ahithophel, whose treachery Judas had imitated. Thus we have said that πληρωθῆναι is often taken at Matthew I. v. 22.

That πληρωθῆναι does not look to the manner of the death of Judas, but to the death itself as a prophecy in Ps. LXIX. v. 27, that his house should become empty, and Ps. CIX. 8, that his office should have to yield to another. Concerning the method of perverting prophecies delivered at Matthew I. 12, we have already spoken there.

Latin:

Vers. 16. ἔδει πληρωθῆναι) Par erat Judæ simile quid eve-nire, quale Achitopheli evenerat, cujus perfidiam Judas erat imitatus. Sic πληρωθῆναι sæpe sumi diximus ad Matth. I. v. 22.

Illud πληρωθῆναι non respicit modum interitus Judæ, sed interitum ipsum ut vaticinium Ps. LXIX. v. 27. quod domus ejus vacua fieri & Ps. CIX. 8. quod officium ejus alteri cedere debuerit. De μεθοδείᾳ pervertendi vaticinia ad Matth. I. 12. tra-dita, ibi jam diximus.

## 1:17
Ver. 17. The lot of this ministry) A lot (κλῆρος) is called whatever falls to anyone, just as hereditary lands were divided by lot. There are certain lots of the saints (κλῆροι ἀγίων), to which all Christians belong, Col. 1:12; 1 Pet. 5:3; there are also lots of ministry (κλῆροι διακονίας), to which pastors belong: from this the name of clergy (clerici) was born.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Τὸν κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας ταύτης) κλῆρος dici-tur, quicquid alicui obvenit, sicut hæreditaria sola forte divi-debantur. Sunt quidam κλῆροι ἀγίων, ad quos omnes perti-nent Christiani, Coloss. I. 12. 1. Pet. V. 3. sunt & κλῆροι δια-κονίας, ad quos pastores: inde natum nomen clericorum.

## 1:18
Ver. 18. He acquired a field) That is, he left behind a monument of his crime, as we explained at Matt. 27:5; yet I do not object if anyone thinks that a certain use of the field, destined for the burials of foreigners, was granted to Judas, and that he expired there. See what Theophylact has here.

We have refuted that fabrication about the death of Judas in the aforementioned note on Matt. 27:5. Others, with Bede, explain 'he acquired' (ἐκτήσατο) by saying that Judas is said to possess, because he caused others to possess. See Casp. Barthius, Book III, Adversaria, ch. 13, p. 136 B; Joh. Gerh. in Harm., ch. 140, p. 1849. Others say that Judas is said to have possessed the field figuratively, because the field was bought from the money he had received, so that one does not look at what Judas intended, but at the outcome of his plans: as Beza holds. Dievius, however, thinks it could have happened that Judas wanted to spend this money on a field and had made a deal with the potter about it, which the priests, with the secret providence of God directing it, bought up when he himself refunded the money: These things are simpler than what Rabanus has here: Judas, having lost the land of the living, possessed the field of blood and death, a memory of his eternal crime and name.

And falling headlong he burst asunder) See regarding this matter what we said at Matt. 27:5.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ἐκτήσατο χωρίον) Id est, monumentum sceleris sui reliquit, ut explicavimus ad Matth. XXVII. 5. non ta-men obstem, si quis putet, fundi ad sepulchra externorum destinati usum quendam concessum Judæ, & ibi eum ex-spirasse. Vide, quæ hic habet Theophylactus.

Commentum illud de morte Judæ in prædicto ad Matth. XXVII. 5. reprobavimus. Ἐκτήσατο exponunt alii cum Beda, Judam dici possidere, quia fecit, ut alii possiderent. Vid. Casp. Barthius l. III. adversar. c. 13. p. 136. B. Joh. Gerh. in Harm. c. CXL. p. 1849. Alii, tropice possedisse agrum dici Judam, ajunt, quia ex pecunia, quam acceperat, ager emtus est, ut non spectetur, quid intenderit Judas, sed con-filiorum ejus eventus: ut Beza habet. Fieri ta-men potuisse, Dievius putat, ut pecuniam hanc agro impendere voluerit Judas, eaque de re cum figulo transegerit, quem refundente ipso pecu-niam Sacerdotes arcana Dei providentia ita diri-gente coëmerint: Quæ simpliciora sunt, quam quæ hic habet Rabanus: Judas amissa terra viven-tium agrum sanguinis & mortis æterna sceleris & no-minis sui memoriam possedit.

Καὶ πρηνὴς γενόμενος ἐλάκησε μέσος) Vide de hac re, quæ diximus ad Matth. XXVII. 5..

## 1:19
Ver. 19. In their own dialect) That the word 'dialect' (διαλέκτῳ) is not taken so strictly by Luke as to signify some difference in language, in the way the Greeks are accustomed to use this word, but rather for the language itself, is apparent from other places below: 2:6, 8; 21:40; 22:2; 26:14.

Aceldama) חקל דמא as the Syriac writes it here. The Jerusalem language of his time approached close to the Syriac.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Τῇ ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ αὐτῶν) Vocem διαλέκτω non tam arcte sumi à Luca, ut discrimen aliquod in lingua significet, quomodo Græci hac voce uti solent, sed pro ipsa lingua, apparet ex aliis locis infr. II. 6. 8. XXI. 40. XXII. 2. XXVI. 14.

Ἀκελδαμὰ) חקל דמא quomodo hic scribit Syrus. Hierosolymitana ejus temporis lingua prope ad Syriacam accedebat.

## 1:20
Ver. 20. Desolate (ἔρημος)) In the LXX it is 'made desolate' (ἠρημωμένη). Luke cited these things from memory from the LXX; those who do this often exchange word for word.

His bishopric (ἐπισκοπὴν)) And this is from the LXX; in the Hebrew it is פְּקֻדָּתוֹ. Moreover, 'פקודה' (pequdah) for the Hebrews is any office or duty, whether perpetual or temporary; as can be seen in Num. 3:32; 4:16; 7:2; 14:29; 16:29; 26:23; 1 Chron. 23:11, and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ἔρημος) In LXX. est ἠρημωμένη. Citavit hæc Lucas memoriter ex LXX. id qui faciunt sæpe verbum verbo commutant.

Τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν ἀυτᾶ) Et hoc ex LXX. in Hebræo פְּקֻדָּתוֹ. Est autem פְקֻדָּה Hebræis quodvis officium sive munus, sive perpetuum, sive temporarium; ut videre est Num. III. 32. IV. 16. VII. 2. XIV. 29. XVI. 29. XXVI. v. 23. 1. Paralip. XXIII. 11. & alibi.

## 1:21
Ver. 21. In which the Lord went in and out among us) That is, lived before us. By the word of entering and exiting, all acts of life, both public and private, are signified. See Zech. 8:10.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐν ᾧ ἐισῆλθε καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ἐφ' ἡμᾶς ὁ Κύριος) Id est, coram nobis vixit, Intrandi & exeundi vocabulo omnes vitæ actus, qua publici qua privati significantur. Vide Zach. IIX. 10.

## 1:22
Ver. 22. Beginning from the baptism of John) That is, from the time he was baptized by John. For that was the beginning for him of inaugurating his ministry. And from there the history of the Gospel begins, to which certain other things serve in the place of a preface, as we said at the inscription of the book of Matthew.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τῶ βαπτίσματος Ἰωάννα) Id est, ex quo ab Iohanne fuit baptizatus. Id enim ini- tium ei fuit auspicandi muneris. Et inde incipit Evange- lii historia, cui quædam alia præfationis vice inserviunt, ut diximus ad inscriptionem libri Matthæi.

## 1:23
Vers. 23. Him who is called Barsabas) בַּר שְׁבַע son of an oath.

Who was surnamed Justus) Perhaps he had received that name from the Romans on account of the integrity of his character.

And Matthias) Matthias is the same name, which is written more fully as Matathias, as Drusius noted, and we [noted] in the Maccabean [commentary].

Latin:

Vers. 23. Τὸν καλέμενον βαρσαβᾶν) בַּר שְׁבַע filium ju- ramenti.

Ὁς ἐπεκλήθη Ἰῦστος) Forte à Romanis id nomen accepe- rat ob morum integritatem.

Καὶ Ματθίαν) Ματθίας idem nomen, quod plenius scribitur Ματαθίας, ut notavit Drusius, & nos ad Mac- cabaica.

## 1:24
Vers. 24. You, Lord, who know the hearts) חֹקֵר לֵב Jer. XVII. vers. 10. To judge with certainty concerning the souls of men belongs to God alone.

Show which one you have chosen of these two) Which one you love more. For thus בָּחַר is often taken among the Hebrews.

Why should the proper meaning not be retained, which certainly fits the passage most aptly, [namely] whom you have chosen from the two, that he may receive the lot of the ministry and Apostleship, that is, Apostolic [ministry] by hendiadys.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Σὺ κύριε καρδιογνῶσα) חֹקֵר לֵב Jer. XVII. vers. 10. de animis hominum certo judicare, solius est Dei.

Ἀνάδειξον ὃν ἐξελέξω ἐκτέτων δύο, ἕνα) Utrum magis a- mes. Sic enim בָּחַר sæpe sumitur apud Hebræos.

Cur non retinenda propria significatio, quæ utique loco aptissime convenit, quem ex duobus bis elegeris, ut accipiat κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας καὶ Α'ποστολῆς, id est, Α'ποστολικῆς per Hendyaden.

## 1:25
Vers. 25. To take the lot of this ministry and Apostleship) To take, that is, that he may take. We had 'the lot of the ministry' also above [in verse] 17; here 'Apostleship' is added, surely a hendiadys for 'Apostolic [ministry]'. In that manuscript: 'the place of the ministry'.

from which Judas turned aside) עָבַר. Of which office Judas was a deserter.

to go to his own place) For 'to go'. The outcome is signified, which followed his crimes by the just judgment of God. 'His own', that is, which suited him better than the Apostolic office: that manuscript which I mentioned has 'to the just place', not badly.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Λαβεῖν τὸν κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας ταύτης καὶ Ἀπο- στολῆς) λαβεῖν, id est, ut accipiat. κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας ha- buimus & supra 17. hic additur, Ἀποστολῆς, nimirum ἓν διὰ δυοῖν pro Ἀποστολικῆς. In manuscripto illo: τὸν τό- πον τῆς διακονίας.

ἐξ ἧς παρέβη Ἰύδας) עָבַר. Cujus officii Judas desertor fuit.

πορευθῆναι εἰς τὸν τόπον τὸν ἴδιον) Pro εἰς τὸ πορευθῆναι. Si- gnificatur eventus scelera ipsius justo Dei judicio conse- cutus. Proprium, id est, qui ipsi melius conveniebat, quam Apostolica functio: manuscriptus ille, quem dixi, habet εἰς τὸν τόπον τὸν δίκαιον, non male.

## 1:26
Vers. 26. And they gave their lots) That is, they cast their names into an urn, and into another urn [they put] another slip having the name 'Apostle' inscribed: [and] another empty slip: then from each urn they drew out two slips equally, as in the division of the land. In that manner David had distributed the functions of the priests by lots, 1 Chron. ch. XXIV. 5. Josephus, [Book] IV of the Jewish War: 'they attempted to make the high priests by lot.' Then: 'there was a pretext of an ancient custom for the undertaking.' Virgil, Aeneid II: 'Laocoon, chosen by lot as priest for Neptune.'

Where Servius [says] from Euphormio: 'Laocoon, priest of Thymbraean Apollo, was chosen by lot: as is accustomed to be done when a certain priest is lacking.' Plato, Laws VI: 'Those things from the sacred [offerings], entrusting to God himself that the things which are pleasing be chosen by lot, thus are rendered to divine fortune.'

The lot fell) His name came out with the name of the Apostleship.

Καὶ συγκατεψηφίσθη) συγκατεψηφίσθη, נִמְנָה, which is elsewhere translated as ἐλογίσθη, elsewhere ἐξηριθμήθη. See above 17, where for the same it is said κατηριθμημένος ἦν.

Μετὰ τῶν ἕνδεκα Ἀποστόλων) See Matt. ch. XXVIII. v. 16. Mark XVI. 13. Luke I. 9. XXII. 9. XXIV. 33.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Καὶ ἔδωκαν κλήρους ἀυτῶν) Id est, conjecerunt nomina eorum in urnam, & in alteram urnam alteram schedam inscriptum habentem nomen Apostolus: alteram schedam vacuam: deinde ex utraque urna pariter eduxere binas schedas, ut in divisione terræ. Ad eum modum David sacerdotum functiones sortibus distribuerat, 1. Para- lip. c. XXIV. 5. Josephus IV. de bello Judaico: κληρωτὸς ἐπεχείρησαν ποιῆσαι τὺς ἀρχιερεῖς. Deinde: ἦν δὲ πρόχημα μὲν τῆς ἐπιβολῆς ἔθος ἀρχαῖον. Virgilius II. Æneidos: Laocoon ductus Neptuno forte Sacerdos.

Ubi Servius ex Euphormione: Laocoon Thymbræi Apollinis Sacerdos forte ductus est: ut solet fieri, cum deest sacerdos certus. Plato de Legibus VI. τὰ μὲν ἀπὸ τῶν ἱερῶν, τῷ Θεῷ ἐπιτρέ- ποντα ἀυτῷ τὰ κεχαρισμένα γενέσθαι κληρῶν, ὕτω τῇ θείᾳ τύχῃ ἀποδιδόνται.

Ἔπεσεν ὁ κλῆρος) Nomen ejus cum nomine Apostolatus exiit.

Καὶ συγκατεψηφίσθη) συγκατεψηφίσθη, נִמְנָה, quod a- libi vertitur ἐλογίσθη, alibi ἐξηριθμήθη. Vide supra 17. ubi pro eodem dicitur κατηριθμημένος ἦν.

Μετὰ τῶν ἕνδεκα Ἀποστόλων) Vide Matth. c. XXVIII. v. 16. Marc. XVI. 13. Luc. I. 9. XXII. 9. XXIV. 33.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

On the day of Pentecost, a wind having arisen, cloven tongues are seen, and the Holy Spirit sat upon the Apostles, and teaches them to speak in various languages, and a multitude having been gathered from various peoples, and each hearing them speaking in his own language, all are astonished, concerning these as Galileans, foreigners, and those speaking in various languages the mighty works of the Lord, while some wondered, others attributed these things to drunkenness: against whom Peter institutes an apology, and teaches that the prophecy of Joel concerning the outpouring of the Holy Spirit after Jesus was killed, and according to the oracle of David, that he should not see corruption, having been resurrected and exalted to the right hand of God, according to another Davidic prediction, has been fulfilled. With which he pierced the hearts of the hearers, and they were admonished concerning repentance, and receiving baptism, 3000 souls were baptized, and remained unanimous in the Apostolic doctrine and also in the communion of goods, among whom miracles were done, and by God, whom they glorified, many were subsequently added to the communion.
