XLIV. 22. ubi in Hebræo מחיתי. simili- tudo sumta ab iis, quæ in tabulis scripta delentur. ὅπως ἂν ἔλθωσι) ut veniant. Sic ὅπως sæpissime sumitur in his libris: & recte sensum assecuti sunt Syrus, Arabs. Ter- tullianus de resurrectione carnis citat: ut tempora nobis superveniant refrigerij. καιροὶ ἀναψύξεως). Exod. VIII. 15. הרוחה vertitur ἀνάψυξις. Sicut calamitates æstui comparantur, ita ab iis liberatio auræ refrigeranti. Sensus est: ut imminenti ex- cidio gentis eximanini. Tempora ἀναψύξεως non respiciunt liberatio- nem ab imminenti gentis Judaicæ excidio, sed re- focillationem in altero sæculo : ubi erit ἀποκατά-σασις πάντων v. 21. Matth. VIII. 18. tempus re- demtionis Luc. XXI. 24. Rom. VIII, 21. 23. recrea- tionis Apoc. VII. 17. cap. XIV. 13. exultationis Esa. LXV. 14. Job. XVI. 20. ἀναψύχειν est refrigerare, desiccare, & metaphorice refocillare, recreare, Psal. LXV. 12. Jer XLIX, 31. Hos. XII. 8.

## 3:20
Vers. 20. that he may send [him], that is, as soon as possible, for the removal of the evils of all the pious. Tertullian: If the representation of the Lord's kingdom pertains to the will of God and to our suspension, how do some demand a certain postponement of the age, when the kingdom of God, for whose coming we pray, tends toward the consummation of the age? We desire to reign sooner, and not to serve longer. Even if it were not predetermined in prayer to ask for the coming of the kingdom, we would have uttered that voice of our own accord, hastening to the embrace of our hope: the souls of the martyrs under the altar cry out to the Lord with envy: how long, O Lord, do you not avenge our blood upon the inhabitants of the earth? For their vengeance is surely directed from the end of the age. Rather, how quickly may your kingdom come, O Lord: the vow of Christians, the confusion of nations, the exultation of Angels, for which we struggle, or rather for which we pray. προκεχειρισμένον, which Tertullian translates as fore-designated, is also in that old codex in England. See below c. XXII. 13. & XXVI. 16. Exod. IV. 13. Jos. III. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 20. ὅπως ἐλθῃ τὸν προκεκηρυγμένον ὑμῖν Ἰησῦν Χρι- στὸν) mittat, quamprimum scilicet, ad tollenda omnium piorum mala. Tertullianus: Si ad DEI voluntatem & ad nostram suspensionem pertinet regni Dominici repræsentatio, quomodo quidam protrattum quendam sæculi postulant, cum regnum Dei quod ut adveniat oramus ad consummationem sæ- culi tendat? optamus maturius regnare, & non diutius ser- vire. Etiamsi præfinitum in oratione non esset, de postulando regni adventu, ultro eam vocem protulissēmus, festinantes ad spei nostræ complexum: clamant ad Dominum invidia animæ martyrum sub altari: quonam usq; non ulcisceris, Domine, sanguinem nostrum de incolis terræ? Nam utiq; ultio illorum a sæculi fine dirigitur. Imo quam celeriter veniat, Domine, re- gnum tuum: votum Christianorum, confusio nationum, exsul- tatio Angelorum, propter quod conflictamur, imo potius propter quod oramus. προκεχειρισμένον quod Tertullianus vertit prædesignatum, habet etiam vetus ille in Anglia codex, Vide infra c. XXII. 13. & XXVI. 16. Exod. IV. 13. Jos. III. 12.

## 3:21
Vers. 21. whom the heaven must receive) Nothing is rendered for that μὲν: but that aposiopesis is easily supplied from the words until the times of restoration; as if he were to say: when that time comes, he will return from heaven to earth, above c. I. 1.

until the times of the restoration of all things, of which God spoke) Restoration, for Plutarch, Columella, Numenius in Eusebius, Servius on Eclogue 4, the Gnostics in Irenaeus I. 13, and others, is the revolution of a star to its original focus: for historians, the quiet restored to troubled affairs. But since ἀποκαθίστασθαι also signifies to show, just as Capella calls the number five the restorative number, because when associated with other odd numbers or with its own kind, it always shows itself, they prefer this sense here. Until that time, he says, when those things which the Prophets had predicted in words concerning the destruction of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles will have been shown to the world: thus ἀποκαταστήσατε for καταστήσατε, Amos V. 15. Nor is ἀποκαθιστῶν taken otherwise, Mal. XVI. 5. And Oecumenius explains it thus, to be restored, to come to an end, all things.

from of old) that is, already long ago, Job XXIV. 2. Isa. LXIII. 16, 19.

Heaven does not receive Christ as if he were enclosed in it until his return for judgment, which the Calvinists and Socinians in the German Racovian version desire; but Christ had to receive heaven, to occupy it as his Royal Palace, or the principal seat of his kingdom, which is heaven, among the saints and the elect, so that he might reign from heaven over the whole world, because that word is best used for the occupation of the heavenly kingdom, since the verb δέξασθαι with its compounds is always taken actively in the New Testament; nor does a passive acceptance consist with the Accusative heaven; for thus it should have been said by heaven, whence Beza, Crocius, Tossanus, and the Tigurines do not render it to be captured by heaven, but whom heaven must capture. Aretius explains heaven to capture as to occupy heaven with full power. Nor is the verb used here for local reception, but it notes rather to take up of one's own accord, or to receive what is offered in any other way, as we have shown from other places in the N.T. and from exotic writers in Exam. doctr. Reform. de persona Christi page 534. Therefore, the majestic acceptance of the heavenly kingdom is noted, and that from the Hebrew idiom, by which the consequent is understood from the antecedent, so that it is implied: that Christ has occupied the heavenly kingdom, and occupies, manages, and administers it, as far as the economy of grace is concerned, which is usually conferred upon the kingdom of heaven, until the time of the restoration of all things, if the word until is taken terminatively, 1 Cor. XV. 25, or simply regarding the rule of Christ the God-man, which he exercises here and in the future age, because there is no end to his kingdom, as is evident, the particle until, from the observation of Nazianzen Orat. II. on the Son, is also taken for the final limit: see Ps. LXXII. 18, CX. 1. Matt. XIX. 10.

But this passage is very badly perverted when it is dragged to the time of the destruction of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles: of which there is no trace here. And what? Does Christ occupy heaven only until the time of the destruction of the Jews? Is not Grotius himself forced to admit that these words look to the time of his return for judgment? Nor does restoration import the showing of a prediction: but it notes a restoration to the whole; to the original place, as can be seen in the LXX Interpreters Jer. XXIII. 7, c. XLVII. 6, Ob. XI. 12, Job VIII. 6, c. V. 18, Gen. XXIX. 3, 1 Sam. V. 11; but concerning restoration to an original or better state, Gen. XL. 13, 21, c. XLI. 13, Job XXII. 18, c. XXXIII. v. 25, Ps. XVI. 5, Ps. XXXIV. 17, Amos V. 15, Mal. IV. 6, which restoration to a better state, condition, and lot is expected here on the last day. Which is comprehended afterwards by the word of blessing, which we obtain in Christ, v. 25, 26. For all things have been depraved and disturbed by sin, and labor under various disorder and infirmity, all of which will be restored through Christ, in whom, the curse having been removed, we obtain every blessing, and all things are restored, reintegrated, and repaired, 2 Cor. V. 17, Eph. I. 10. Yet a perfect restoration is expected finally at the last coming of Christ, 2 Peter III. 13, Rev. XXI. 1, 5. Compare Isa. LXV. 17, c. LXVI. 12. Therefore, the Vulgate and Beza rightly rendered the Greek word by restoration. Hesychius explains it as perfection: by which the sense of the Interpreters is commonly approved.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ὃν δεῖ μὲν ὁρανὸν δέξασθαι) Nihil redditur ad μὲν illud: sed ea ἀποσιώπησις facile suppletur ex verbis ἄχρι χρόνων ἀποκαταστάσεως; quasi dicat: ubi illud tempus ve- nerit, ex cœlo in terras redibit, supra c I. 1.

ἄχρι χρόνων ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων, ὧν ἐλάλησεν ὁ Θεὸς) Ἀποκατάστασις Plutarcho, Columellæ, Numenio apud Eu- sebiũ, Servio ad Eclogam 4. Gnosticis apud Irenæum I. 13. & aliis, est revolutio sideris in pristinum focum: histo- ricis, quies reddita rebus turbidis. Sed cum ἀποκαθίστασθαι etiam ostendere significet, sicut ἀποκαταστατικὸν numerum Capella vocat quinarium, quia cum aliis imparibus sive cum suo genere sociatus, se semper ostendit, hunc sensum hic præferant. Adusque tempus, inquit, illud cum exhi- bita rebus erunt ea, quæ Prophetæ verbis prædixerant de excidio Judæorum de vocatione gentium: sic ἀποκαταστή- σατε pro καταστήσατε, Amos V. 15. Nec aliter sumitur ἀπο- καθιστῶν, Mal. XVI. 5. & Oecumenius sic explicat, ἀποκα- ταστῆναι, εἰς πέρας ἐλθεῖν ἅπαντα.

ἀπ’ αἰῶνος) id est, jam olim מעולם, Job. XXIV. 2. Esa. LXIII. 16.19.

Non recipit Christum cœlum, quasi in eo con- cludatur usque ad reditum ad judicium, quod Cal- viniani volunt & Sociniani in versione Germani- ca Racov. sed Christus cœlum debuit δέξασθαι oc- cupare ceu Regiam suam, vel sedem regni præci- puam, quæ cœlum est, penes sanctos & electos, ut regnet de cœlo per universum orbem, quia ver- bum illud de regni cælestis occupatione optime adhi- betur, siquidem active verbum δέξασθαι cum com- positis semper accipiatur in Novo Testam. neque passiva acceptio cum Accusativo ὁρανὸν consistat; sic enim dicendum fuisset ὑπὸ ὁρανῦ, unde Beza, Crocius, Tossanus, & Tigurini non reddunt calo capi, sed quem oportet cælum capere. Aretius calos capere explicat, ex plena potestate cælum occupare. Nec de locali receptione hic verbum adhibetur, sed notat potius sponte sua suscipere, vel alio quo- cunque modo oblatum recipere, ut è locis aliis N.T. & exoticis scriptoribus ostendimus Exam. doctr. Reform. de persona Christi pag. 534. Notatur ergo majestatica regni cælestis acceptio, idque ex Ebraico idiotismo, quo ex antecedente intelligitur consequens, ut ita innuatur; Christum regnum cæleste occupasse, & occupatum gerere atq; administrare, quantum ad œconomiam gratiæ, quæ regno cœlorum conferri solet, usq; ad tempus restitutionis omnium, si termi- native accipiatur vox ἄχρι 1. Cor. XV. 25. vel sim- pliciter quoad regimen Christi θεανθρώπε, quod hic, & in futuro sæculo gerit, quia regni ejus non est finis, quemadmodum constat, particulam ἄχρι ex observatione Nazianzeni Orat. II. de Filio accipi etiam fine termino: vid. Ps. LXXII, 18, CX. 1. Matth. XIX. 10.

Pessime autem pervertitur hic locus, dum tra- hitur ad tempus excidii Judæorum, & vocationis gentium: de quo nullum hic vestigium. Et quid? Num Christus cœlum occupat tantum usque ad tempus excidii Judæorum? Annon Grotius ipse fa- teri cogitur, his verbis respici tempus reditus e- jus ad judicium? Neque ἀποκατάστασις ostensionem prædictionis importat: sed notat restitutionem in integrum; in pristinum locum, ut videre est apud LXX. Interpp. Jer. XXIII. 7. c. XLVII. 6. Of. XI. 12. Job. VIII. 6. c. V. 18. Gen. XXIX. 3. 1. Sam. V. 11. de restitutione vero in statum pristinum vel meliorem Gen. XL. 13. 21. c. XLI. 13. Job. XXII. 18. c. XXXIII. v. 25. Psal. XVI. 5. Ps. XXXIV. 17. Amos V. 15. Mal. IV. 6. quæ hic restitutio in statum, conditionem & sortem meliorem in novissimo die expectatur. Quæ comprehenditur postea benedictionis voce, quam in Christo consequimur, v. 25. 26. Omnia enim per peccatum depravata sunt & perturbata, variaque laborant ἀταξίᾳ & infirmitate, quæ o- mnia restituentur per Christum, in quo, sublata maledictione, omnem consequimur benedictio- nem, ac restituuntur, redintegrantur ac reparantur omnia, 2. Cor. V. 17. Eph. I. 10. Perfecta tamen ἀπο- κατάστασις expectatur demum in adventu Christi novissimo, 2. Petri III. 13. Apoc. XXI. 1. 5. Conf. Esa. LXV. 17. c. LXVI. 12. Recte ergo vocem Græcam & Vulgat. & Beza reddidit per restitutionem. He- sychius exponit τελείωσιν: quo sensus Interpre- tum communiter probatur.

## 3:22
V. 22. The Lord will raise up a prophet for you) Generally, this law of God pertains to this, that whoever Prophet shall have arisen among the people of God, doing miracles, or certainly predicting unknown future things, and not leading the people to false gods, he is to be obeyed, even if he should command something against the law. But it pertains especially to Jesus, than whom no one is more illustrious, by those signs through which God wished the prophets to be known. See what we have said on the place cited here, Deut. XVIII. 15.

We have uncovered and discussed this corruption in the Annotations on the loc. cit. Deut. This speech of Peter also clearly teaches that Moses prophesied of none other than Christ.

Latin:

V. 22. Προφήτην ὑμῖν ἀναστήσει ὁ Κύριος) Generaliter hæc Dei lex eo pertinet, ut quicunque Propheta in populo Dei surrexerit, miracula faciens, aut futura incognita certo prædicens, nec abducens populum ad deos falsos, ei pare- atur, etiamsi qui contra legem præcipiat. Eximie autem pertinet ad Jesum, quo nullus illustrior, illis signis, per quæ prophetas cognosci Deus voluit. Vide, quæ diximus ad citatum hic locum Deut. XVIII. 15.

Corruptelam hanc deteximus & discussimus in Annot. ad l. c. Deut. Non de aliis, quam Christo, Mosen vaticinari, hæc etiam oratio Petrina lucu- lenter docet.

## 3:23
Verse 23. ἐξολοθρευθήσεται ἐκ τοῦ λαοῦ) by a violent or untimely death: but the Rabbis also mystically refer this to punishments after this life.

This sense is not mystical, but proper and literal, because he who does not hear this great Prophet, and consequently does not believe in him, is already condemned, John 3:18; he who does not believe is condemned, Mark 16:16.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ἐξολοθρευθήσεται ἐκ τοῦ λαοῦ) morte violenta aut immatura: sed mystice etiam Rabbini hoc ad pœnas post hanc vitam referunt.

Sensus hic non mysticus est, sed proprius & lite- ralis, quia, qui non audit Prophetam hunc magnū, adeoq; non credit in ipsum, jam condemnatus est, Job. III. 18. qui non credit, condemnatur Mar. XVI. 16.

## 3:24
Verse 24. τῶν καθεξῆς ὅσοι) These are to be connected thus: κατήγγειλαν τὰς ἡμέρας ταύτας) The advent, miracles, and kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 24. τῶν καθεξῆς ὅσοι) Hæc ita connectenda sunt: κατήγγειλαν τὰς ἡμέρας ταύτας) Adventum, miracula & regnum.

## 3:25
Verse 25. ὑμεῖς ἐστε υἱοὶ τῶν προφητῶν) that is, you are those to whom those Prophets from Samuel onwards were sent. Thus υἱοὶ νυμφῶνος in Matthew 9:15, Mark 2:19, Luke 5:34.

καὶ τῆς διαθήκης) they are called sons of the covenant by the Hebrews, to whom the covenant pertains. God had promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that their posterity would never fail. This was the reason why God always preserved some in the greatest destructions. Among those some, there could now be those whom Peter addresses: they could say:

What forbids my name to be among the few?

The covenant entered into with Abraham and his posterity did not concern only the temporal preservation and blessing of this nation, but primarily spiritual and heavenly goods, which are comprehended by that promise, I WILL BE YOUR GOD: For our God is not only God in this life, but also in the future, Matthew 22:31-32, Revelation 21:7; nor does the blessing of Christ pertain primarily to this earthly happiness, but to the heavenly; indeed, nothing is held here in Peter's sermon regarding preservation in the greatest destructions, which is directed toward the conversion and eternal salvation of the hearers, and deliverance from eternal destruction. Compare what we said on Genesis 22:3.

καὶ ἐν τῷ σπέρματί σου ἐνευλογηθήσονται πᾶσαι αἱ πατριαὶ τῆς γῆς) See what was said on Genesis 12:3. Thus he who was promised to Abraham will do good to all nations, how much more to his own kinsmen, if only they remove the impediments.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ὑμεῖς ἐστε υἱοὶ τῶν προφητῶν) id est, vos estis ii, ad quos missi sunt Prophetæ illi à Samuele deinceps. Sic υἱοὶ νυμφῶνος apud Matth. IX. 15. Marc. II. 19. Luc. V. 34.

καὶ τῆς διαθήκης) filii pacti dicuntur Hebræis, ad quos pa- ctum pertinet. Promiserat Deus Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jaco- bo nunquam defecturam posteritatem ipsorum. Hæc cau- sa fuit, cur in maximis excidiis aliquos semper Deus serva- verit. Inter illos aliquos nunc esse poterant illi, quos allo- quitur Petrus: dicere poterant:

Quid vetat in paucis nomen inesse meum?

Pactum cum Abrahamo & posteris ejus initum non concernebat tantum gentis hujus temporalem conservationem, ac benedictionem, sed imprimis spiritualia & cœlestia bona, quæ promissione illa, ERO DEUS TUUS, comprehenduntur: Non enim Deus noster tantum Deus est in hac vita, sed etiam in futura, Matth. XXII. 31. 32. Apoc. XXI. 7. nec benedictio Christi præcipue ad hanc terrenam felicitatem, sed ad cœlestem pertinet; de conserva- tione vero in excidiis maximis hic nihil habetur in Petrina concione, quæ ad conversionem & æter- nam salutem auditorum directa est, & liberationē ab æterno exitio. Conf. quæ ad Gen. 22. 3. diximus.

καὶ ἐν τῷ σπέρματί σου ἐνευλογηθήσονται πᾶσαι αἱ πατριαὶ τῆς γῆς) Vide, quæ dicta ad Gen. XII. 3. Sic ille Abraha- mo promissus benefaciet omnibus gentibus, quanto magis consanguineis suis, si modo hi impedimenta auferant.

## 3:26
Verse 26. ὑμῖν πρῶτον) for Christ first proposed his word to the Jews by himself: then to the Gentiles through the Apostles. See Matthew 10:5, chapter 15:24.

ἀναστήσας τὸν παῖδα αὑτοῦ Ἰησοῦν) to raise up here is not to recall from the dead to life, but to make conspicuous, by prophecy and other gifts. For those things which preceded are looked back upon, 'a prophet will raise up for you.' Thus also to rise is attributed to the Prophets:

Deut. XIII, 1. ch. XXXIV. 10. Sirach XLVII. ch. XLVIII. 1. ἀπέστειλεν ἀυτὸν ἐυλογοῦντα ὑμᾶς) That is, doing good to your people through so many healings.

ἐν τῷ ἀποστρέφειν ἕκαστον ἀπὸ τῶν πονηριῶν ὑμῶν) He shows to what those benefits looked, namely that they might win authority for Jesus, and through it each one might be led to the amendment of life, such as Jesus was teaching and prefiguring. ἐν τῷ for εἰς τὸ. For our writers often interchange those particles. And thus the Latin [translator] understood it.

To raise up is not indeed to recall from death, but neither is it only to make conspicuous: for he was raised up when he was sent into these lands: just as the branch of David was said to be raised up, Jer. XXIII. 6. therefore he is said to be raised up from the seed of David, Acts XIII. 23. (Rom. I. 3.) Nor is that ἐυλογία to be restricted to bodily healing: for it embraces all that which we have by virtue of the promise Gen. XII. 3. in Christ, namely the taking away of every curse which came about through sin; and the bestowing of every kind of blessing, as being that which Christ acquired for us by his death, outside of whom there is no salvation, no blessing Acts IV. 12. Gal. III. 13. The particle ἐν is deservedly retained in its more famous and ordinary meaning. For not the least part of the blessing consists in this, that we are turned from malice, and so in turn can enjoy divine grace, the source and fountain of every blessing. For that gloss of Grotius is too jejune, and akin to Socinian inventions: That the benefits exhibited by Christ served to win authority for his precepts; because our conversion is not effected by moral persuasion alone, or by bare precepts, nor is it enough that we be merely persuaded of the authority of Christ, but there is need of efficacious grace and the operation of the Holy Spirit, whom, just as Christ acquired for us by his merit, so he confers upon us through the ministry of the word for our conversion and salvation.

i. πονηριῶν) רעות that word sometimes signifies every vicious habit generally, sometimes malice specifically: as Mark VII. 22. Luke XI. 39. Rom. I. 29. 1 Cor. V. 8. Cicero in the Tusculans: Contrary to virtue is vitiositas: for so I prefer to call it rather than malitia, which the Greeks call κακίαν. For malitia is the name of a certain specific vice: vitiositas of all.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ὑμῖν πρῶτον) nam Christus primum Judæis verbum suum proposuit per se: deinde gentibus per Apo- stolos. Vide Matth. X. 5. c. XV. 24.

ἀναστήσας τὸν παῖδα αὑτοῦ Ἰησοῦν) excitare hic non est è mortuis ad vitam revocare, sed conspicuum facere, prophe- tia aliisq; donis. Respiciuntur enim ea, quæ præcessere, προ- φήτην ὑμῖν ἀναστήσει. Sic & surgere tribuitur Prophetis:

Deutren. XIII, 1. c. XXXIV. 10. Sirach. XLVII. c. XLVIII. 1. ἀπέστειλεν ἀυτὸν ἐυλογοῦντα ὑμᾶς) Id est, benefacientem populo vestro per tot sanationes.

ἐν τῷ ἀποστρέφειν ἕκαστον ἀπὸ τῶν πονηριῶν ὑμῶν) Ostendit, quo illa beneficia spectaverint, nempe ut auctoritatem Jesu conciliarent, & per eam quisque ad vitæ emendationem, qualem Jesus præcipiebat & præmonstrabat, præduceretur. ἐν τῷ pro εἰς τὸ. Sæpe enim nostri scriptores istas particulas permutant. Et sic accepit Latinus.

Excitare non quidem revocare est à morte, sed nec solum conspicuum facere: nam excitatus est, quando in has terras missus: uti excitandum dicebatur germen Davidis Jer. XXIII. 6. ideo è semine Davidis excitatus dicitur, Act. XIII. 23. (Rom. I. 3.) Nec ἐυλογία illa ad sanationem corporalem restringenda: Nam complectitur omne illud, quod habemus vi promissionis Gen. XI. 3. in Christo, ablationem nempe omnis maledictionis, quæ per peccatum evenit; & collationem omnigenæ benedictionis, utpote quam Christus morte sua nobis acquisivit, extra quem nulla salus, nulla benedictio Act. IV. 12. Gal. III. 13. Particula ἐν merito retinetur famosiori & ordinario significatu. Nam non postrema benedictionis pars in eo consistit, quod convertamur à malitia, adeoq; vicissim frui possimus divina gratia, omnis benedictionis fonte ac scaturigine. Glossa enim illa Grotii nimis jejuna est, ac Socinianis commentis affinis: Quod beneficia à Christo exhibita fecerint ad conciliandam ejus præceptis autoritatem; quia non morali tantum suasione, aut nudis præceptis nostra conversio efficitur, neque satis est, ut persuasi simus tantum de autoritate Christi, sed opus est efficaci gratia & operatione Spiritus S. quem uti acquisivit nobis Christus merito suo, ita confert nobis per verbi ministerium ad nostri conversionem, & salutem.

i. πονηριῶν) רעות ea vox modo generaliter omnem vitiosam consuetudinem significat, modo specialiter malitiam: ut Marc. VII. 22. Luc. XI. 39. Rom. I. 8. 1 Cor. V. 8. Cicero in Tusculanis: Virtuti contraria est vitiositas: sic enim malo quam malitiam appellare, quam Græci κακίαν vocant. Nam malitia certi cujusdam vitii nomen est: vitiositas omnium.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The priests with the Sadducees, to whom the doctrine concerning the resurrection was hateful, imprison Peter and John, with very many hearers converted, and in the morning they are brought before the Sanhedrin, who, being asked by what power they healed the sick man, say that it was done in the name of Jesus, the cornerstone, rejected by the builders themselves, and that no one obtains salvation outside that name: A consultation having been initiated, since they could oppose nothing to that miracle, the Apostles are forbidden to preach the name of Jesus: they on the contrary say that God must be obeyed rather than men, and having been dismissed with a threat, they preach to their own with unanimous voice that, according to David's prophecy, Kings and Princes of the earth tumult in vain against the Lord and his Christ, praying that he may grant confidence of speaking, and stretch forth his hand through miracles; all filled with the Holy Spirit, persevering in unity and the communion of goods, to which Barnabas specifically contributed money received from a field sold off.

There are three parts: I. The dismissal of Peter and John examined before the Sanhedrin, with a threat, to v. 21. II. The prayer of the Church for boldness of speaking, to v. 31. III. The unity of the Church, and the communion of goods, and the contribution of Joses to the same, to v. 37.

PART I. The dismissal of Peter and John examined before the Sanhedrin with a threat.

Ver. 1.

Ἐπέστησαν αὐτοῖς οἱ ἱερεῖς) See Matt. XXI. 1.

and the captain of the temple) Whose duty it was to take care that no tumult should arise in the temple, such as they wished it to be thought they feared from this new preaching. See what we said on Matt. XXVI. 43, Luke XXII. 4.

and the Sadducees) Quite rigid in exacting punishments, as Josephus teaches us, who says the Pharisees were milder in those matters. Naturally, those who had placed all their hope in this life thought they must severely oppose all those things which could disturb the quiet of the people, in which their own quiet was also contained. Add that if Jesus had risen from the dead, in that controversy which they had with the Pharisees, the victory would have been with the Pharisees. See below XXIII. 6, 7.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Sacerdotes cum Sadducæis, quibus infesta erat doctrina de resurrectione, incarcerant Petrum & Johannem, auditoribus plurimis conversis, & mane sistuntur Synedrio, qui rogati, qua potestate ægrum sanarint, in nomine Jesu, lapidis angularis, ab ipsis Architectis rejecti, id factum ajunt, nec extra illud nomen salutem obtingere ulli: Consultatione inita, quam miraculo illi nihil opponere possent, interdicitur Apostolis, ne Jesu nomen prædicent: illi contra magis Deo obediendum dicunt, & cum comminatione dimissi, cu suis unanimi voce prædicant, quod juxta Davidis vaticinium frustra Reges & Principes terræ adversus Dominum & Christum ejus tumultuentur, precantes, ut fiducia loquendi concedat, manumq́; per miracula extendat; omnes Spir. S. repleti, in unitate & bonorum communione, ad quam nominatim Barnabas pecuniam ex agro divendito acceptam contulit, perseverantes.

Partes tres sunt: I. Petri, & Johannis coram Synedrio examinatorum, cum comminatione, dimissio, ad v. 21. II. Ecclesiæ pro παρρησίᾳ loquendi precatio, ad v. 31. III. Ecclesiæ unitas, & bonorum communio, Jolisque ad eandem collatio, ad v. 37.

PARS I. Petri & Iohannis coram Synedrio examinato- rum cum comminatione dimissio.

Vers. 1.

Ἐπέστησαν αὐτοῖς οἱ ἱερεῖς) Vide Matth. XXI. 1.

καὶ ὁ στρατηγὸς τῶν ἱεροῦ) Cujus erat munus cavere, ne quis tumultus in templo oriretur, qualem videri volebant time- re ex nova hac prædicatione. Vide quæ diximus Matth. XXVI. 43. Luc. XXII. 4.

κὴ οἱ Σαδδουκαῖοι) Rigidi admodum in pœnis exigendis, ut Josephus nos docet, qui Pharisæos ait fuisse in iis rebus leniores. Nimirum qui omnem spem in hac vita colloca- tam habebant, severe occcurrendum putabant omnibus iis, quæ turbare poterant quietem populi, in qua & ipsorum quies continebatur. Adde, quod si Jesus à mortuis resurre- xiffet, in ea controversia, quam habebant cumPharisæis ma- ximam, penes Pharisæos erat victoria. Vide infra XXIII. 6. 7.

## 4:3
Vers. 3. and they put them in hold) Thus also below V. 18, it is called τήρησις, which is usually φυλακή. See Jer. XX. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 3. κὴ ἔθεντο εἰς τήρησιν) Sic & infra V. 18. τήρησις vo- catur, quæ plerumque φυλακή. Vide Jer. XX. 2.

## 4:5
V. 5. the rulers) That is, those of whom the בית דין or Sanhedrin consisted, below 15. See Luke IV. 1, John III. 1, above II. 17.

and elders) The senators of the city.

and scribes) Assessors to both, men learned in the law.

Latin:

V. 5. τοὺς ἄρχοντας) Id est, eos, quibus constabat בית דין sive συνέδριον, infra 15. Vide Luc. IV. 1. Joh. III. 1. supra II. 17.

κὴ πρεσβυτέρους) Senatores urbis.

κὴ γραμματεῖς) Assessores utrorumq; viros legis peritos.

## 4:6
Vers. 6. and Annas the high priest and Caiaphas) See the Gospel of Luke III. 2.

John) יוחנן הכהן in the writings of the Rabbis.

and as many as were of the kindred of the high priest) Whose ancestors had not long before held the high priesthood, which great nobility had caused them to be enrolled in the great Sanhedrin.

by what power) By medical art or magical: For this also was an inquiry of the Sanhedrin.

or by what name) By what authority, if by chance they should say they had done it by prophetic right.

Latin:

Vers. 6. κὴ Ἄνναν τὸν ἀρχιερέα κὴ Καϊάφαν) Vide Evang. Lucæ III. 2.

Ἰωάννην) יוחנן הכהן in Rabbinorum scriptis.

κὴ ὅσοι ἦσαν ἐκ γένους ἀρχιερατικοῦ) Quorum majores sum- mo sacerdotio non ita pridem functi fuerant, quæ magna nobilitas fecerat, ut Synedrio magno adscriberentur.

ἐν ποίᾳ δυνάμει) Arte medica an magica: Nam & hæc in- quifitio erat Synedrii.

ἢ ἐν ποίῳ ὀνόματι) Qua auctoritate, si forte se id prophe- tico jure fecisse dicerent.

## 4:9
Vers. 9. if we this day be examined) are interrogated. Thus Tacitus: lest anyone should be interrogated in the future about any deed. Cicero pro domo: who has ever interrogated me by any law? You have ἀνακρίνεσθαι in this sense in Plato, Book VI of the Laws, Plutarch, and others. See below XII. 9, XXV. 26, XXVIII. 18. If here I take it in the common sense. If there is a question about this matter, an answer is ready for us.

ἐπὶ εὐεργεσίᾳ ἀνθρώπου ἀσθενοῦς) The genitive denotes sometimes the efficient cause, sometimes the thing or person receiving, as here.

ἐν τίνι) By whom. A similar manner of speaking in Ps. 108:14; 2 Sam. 22:30.

Latin:

Vers. 9. εἰ ἡμεῖς σήμερον ἀνακρινόμεθα) interrogamur. Sic Tacitus: ne cujus facti in posterum interrogaretur. Cicero pro domo: quis me unquam lege ulla interrogavit ? ἀνακρίνεσθαι hoc sensu habes apud Platonem VI. de Legibus, Plutar- chum & alios. Vide infra XII. 9. XXV. 26. XXVIII. 18. Si hic sumo in sensu vulgari. Si de hac re quæstio est, parata est nobis responsio.

ἐπὶ εὐεργεσίᾳ ἀνθρώπου ἀσθενοῦς) Genitivus modo causam efficientem, modo rem aut personam recipientem notat, ut hic.

ἐν τίνι) Per quem. Simile loquendi genus Pf. CVIII. 14. 2. Sam. XXII. 30.

## 4:10
Vers. 10. ὅτι ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ τοῦ Ναζωραίου, ὃν ὑμεῖς ἐσταυρώσατε, ὃν ὁ Θεὸς ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν) The words are as bold as they are full of gravity: whence we shall soon see boldness attributed to the Apostles. For what else was this than to accuse the highest Senate of the highest parricide?

παρέστηκεν) He stands by erect: as below 14.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ὅτι ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ τοῦ Ναζωραίου, ὃν ὑμεῖς ἐσταυρώσατε, ὃν ὁ Θεὸς ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν) Verba ut libera, ita plena gravitatis: unde mox videbimus παῤῥησίαν tribui A- postolis. Quid enim hoc erat aliud, quam summum Sena- tum arguere summi parricidii ?

παρέστηκεν) Adstat erectus: ut infra 14.

## 4:11
Vers. 11. ὁ λίθος ὁ ἐξουθενηθεὶς ὑφ̓ ὑμῶν τῶν οἰκοδομούντων) See Matt. 21:42.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ὁ λίθος ὁ ἐξουθενηθεὶς ὑφ̓ ὑμῶν τῶν οἰκοδομούντων) Vide Matth. XXI. 42.

## 4:12
Vers. 12. κὴ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἄλλῳ οὐδενὶ ἡ σωτηρία) In no one, namely of men, as the following indicates: for Peter does not exclude God.

ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανὸν) Of those who are seen on earth: not the Patriarch: not the Prophet: not the Priest: not the King.

Latin:

Vers. 12. κὴ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἄλλῳ οὐδενὶ ἡ σωτηρία) In nullo, nem- pe hominum, ut indicant sequentia: neque enim Deum ex- cludit Petrus.

ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανὸν) Eorum, qui in terris conspecti sunt: non Patriarchæ: non Prophetæ: non Sacerdotis: non Re- gis.

## 4:13
Vers. 13. ἀγράμματοί εἰσι) That is, not versed in Talmudic doctrines, such as the לא יודעי ספר are to the Hebrews: for the Apostles had both read the sacred scriptures and held them in memory.

κὴ ἰδιῶται) הדיוטים are to the Hebrews those who are neither magistrates nor learned in the law. Thus 1 Cor. 14:16, 23, 24, it is opposed to him who teaches: and 2 Cor. 11:6, ἰδιώτης τῷ λόγῳ, a man having nothing in speech above a commoner.

They were not indeed instructed in the Pharisaic school: yet they were not entirely rude, and were sufficiently instructed for these things by the Holy Spirit at the feast of Pentecost: so that it is in vain for the Anabaptists, Weigelians, and Quakers to appeal to them, being destitute of such instruction of the Holy Spirit; of which no promise was made to us, and which was especially proper to the time of the primitive Church and to the Apostles. Idiots are opposed to τοῖς πεπαιδευμένοις, the learned and literate, but this name does not refer to status or office: for idiots are sometimes in the magistracy.

ἐπεγίνωσκόν τε αὐτοὺς, ὅτι σὺν τῷ Ἰησοῦ ἦσαν) It is no wonder, when certain of the Senators had sometimes approached Jesus accompanied by his disciples and had spoken to him Matth. XXI. 23. Luc. XVIII. 18. Joh. XII. 42.

Latin:

Vers. 13. ἀγράμματοί εἰσι) Id est, non versati in doctri- nis Talmudicis, quales לא יודעי ספר Hebræis: nam scripturas sacras Apostoli & legerant, & memoria tene- bant.

κὴ ἰδιῶται) הדיוטים sunt Hebræis, qui neque ma- gistratus sunt, neque legisperiti. Sic 1. Corinth. XIV. 16. 23. 24. opponitur ei, qui docet: & 2. Corinth. XI. 6. ἰδιώ- της τῷ λόγῳ, homo in sermone nihil supra plebejum ha- bens.

Non erant quidem in schola Pharisæica infor- mati: nec tamen plane rudes, & ad hæc à Spiri- tu Sancto in festo Pentecostes affatim instructi: ut frustra ab Anabaptistis, Weigelianis & Quac- queris ad ipsos provocetur, tali Spiritus Sancti instructione destitutis; cujus nulla nobis facta promissio, quæque imprimis tempori primitivæ Ecclesiæ, & Apostolis erat propria. Idiotæ oppo- nuntur τοῖς πεπαιδευμένοις, doctis & literatis, non vero nomen hoc respicit statum, aut offi- cium: nam & idiotæ quandoque in magistratu sunt.

ἐπεγίνωσκόν τε αὐτοὺς, ὅτι σὺν τῷ Ἰησοῦ ἦσαν) Non mi- rum, cum Senatorum quidam interdum Jesum suis disci- pulis comitatum adiissent & allocuti essent Matth. XXI. 23. Luc. XVIII. 18. Joh. XII. 42.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. οὐδὲν εἶχον ἀντειπεῖν) אין מענה בפיהם Job. XXXII. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 14. οὐδὲν εἶχον ἀντειπεῖν) אין מענה בפיהם Job. XXXII. 5.

## 4:15
Vers. 15. ἔξω τοῦ συνεδρίου) The word συνεδρίου elsewhere signifies a college, elsewhere the place where colleagues met: thus also Church sometimes means people, sometimes the place.

συνέβαλον πρὸς ἀλλήλους) נועצו יחדו Nehem. VI. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἔξω τοῦ συνεδρίου) Vox συνεδρίου alibi collegium si- gnificat, alibi locum, quo collegæ conveniebant: sic & Ec- clesia interdum homines, interdum locum.

συνέβαλον πρὸς ἀλλήλους) נועצו יחדו Nehem. VI. 7.

## 4:17
Vers. 17. ἀπειλῇ ἀπειλησώμεθα) Let us threaten strictly.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ἀπειλῇ ἀπειλησώμεθα) Destricte interminemus.

## 4:18
Vers. 18. μὴ φθέγγεσθαι, μηδὲ διδάσκειν) Neither privately nor publicly to teach that dogma.

Latin:

Vers. 18. μὴ φθέγγεσθαι, μηδὲ διδάσκειν) Neque privatim, neque publice docere id dogma.

## 4:19
εἰ δίκαιόν ἐστιν ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὑμῶν ἀκούειν μᾶλλον ἢ τοῦ Θεοῦ, κρίνατε) The Apostles appeal simply to the common sense: as also below V. 29. This sentiment is frequent among the Rabbis. Herodotus: πρεσβύτερα ποιεῖν τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἢ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. I shall not repeat here what we collected on this matter in the second book of the Law of War and Peace, chapter XXVI, § 3, and in the annotations to that place.

Latin:

Vers. 19. εἰ δίκαιόν ἐστιν ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὑμῶν ἀκούειν μᾶλλον ἢ τοῦ Θεοῦ, κρίνατε) Provocant Apostoli simpliciter ad κοινὴν ἔννοιαν: ut & infra V. 29. Est hæc sententia frequens apud Rabbinos. Herodotus: πρεσβύτερα ποιεῖν τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἢ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. Non repetam hic, quæ de hac re colligimus II. li- bro de Jure Belli ac Pacis cap. XXVI. §. 3. & in annotatis ad eum locum.

## 4:20
V. 20. οὐ δυνάμεθα γὰρ ἡμεῖς ἃ εἴδομεν καὶ ἠκούσαμεν μὴ λαλεῖν) Here also δυνάμεθα is taken in a moral, not a physical sense, as above II. 24. If anyone denies the testimony of truth to a man, he sins: how much more he who denies it to God?

Latin:

V. 20. οὐ δυνάμεθα γὰρ ἡμεῖς ἃ εἴδομεν καὶ ἠκούσαμεν μὴ λαλεῖν) Hic quoque δυνάμεθα sumitur sensu non Physico, sed mora- li, ut supra II. 24. Si quis homini testimonium veri denegat, peccat: quanto magis qui Deo?

## 4:21
Vers. 21. ἀπολύσωσιν αὐτοὺς) Among the Hebrews there was no peremptory acquittal: the accused could always be recalled on the basis of new evidence.

μηδὲν εὑρίσκοντες, τὸ, πῶς κολάσωνται) There is an ellipsis not unlike that which we noted above III. 13 and Luc. XXII. 4.

PARS II. The prayer of the Church for boldness of speech.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἀπολύσωσιν αὐτοὺς) Apud Hebræos nulla absolu- tio erat peremptoria: semper repeti poterant rei ex novis probationibus.

μηδὲν εὑρίσκοντες, τὸ, πῶς κολάσωνται) Est ἔλλειψις non dis- similis ei, quam supra notavimus III. 13. & Luc. XXII. 4.

PARS II. Ecclesiæ pro παῤῥησίᾳ loquendi precatio.

## 4:24
V. 24. Δέσποτα σὺ ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ ποιήσας τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν) It is a Hellenistic locution, signifying the vocative by the interposed σὺ: as Genes. XLIX 8. Ps. II. 7. The sense is: O you, Lord, maker of heaven, earth and sea, and of all things that are in them. This universe is expressed among the Hebrews sometimes by three names, as here, sometimes by two, as heaven and earth.

Latin:

V. 24. Δέσποτα σὺ ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ ποιήσας τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν) Est locutio Hellenistica, per σὺ interpositum significans vo- cativum: ut Genes. XLIX 8. Ps. II. 7. sensus est: O tu, Do- mine, opifex cœli, terræ & maris, & omnium, quæ in iis. Universum hoc apud Hebræos modo tribus nominibus, ut hic, modo duobus ut cœli & terræ exprimitur.

## 4:25
V. 25. David your servant) your servant here means your slave: this is apparent from a comparison of the Hebrew with the Greek XIX. 18. and other places. In that old Manuscript it is: he who through the Holy Spirit of the mouth of David your servant, having said, where the words seem to have been transposed by the scribe, for: he who through the Holy Spirit of the mouth of David our father your servant. The Holy Spirit is of the mouth of David, who through the mouth of David was announcing future things.

But if the words were transposed by the scribe, that reading of the MS. Codex is certainly not sound. And that that single corrupt Codex is by no means sufficient evidence that those words 'through the Holy Spirit' and 'our father' were once added in codices of better quality, which in others have fallen out. Finally, that manner of speaking is unusual, 'the Holy Spirit of the mouth of David,' or of the mouth of Isaiah, or Jeremiah, of which no similar example will be given.

Why did the nations rage) Luke wrote down all these things word for word from the LXX.

Nay, Luke did not write these things down from the LXX Interpreters, but had them from the mouth of the praying holy communion, through divine inspiration: which the Holy Spirit also suggested to the Church in prayer, or inspired the Apostle leading the Church in these words, and Luke reporting this history.

Latin:

V. 25. Δαυὶδ τοῦ παιδός σου) παιδός σου hic valet servi tui: id apparet ex collatione Hebræi cum Græco XIX. 18. & aliis locis. In vetere illo Manuscripto est: ὁ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου στόματος Δαυὶδ παιδός σου, εἶπὼν ubi trans- positæ à scriba voces videntur, pro: ὁ διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου στόματος Δαυὶδ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν παιδός σου. Spiritus Sanctus oris Davidis est, qui per os Davidis futura pronuntiabat.

Sed si transpositæ à scriba voces sunt, lectio uti- que illa Codicis MS. proba non est. Et olim ad- dita fuisse ista διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου, & τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν in codicibus melioris commatis, quæ in aliis exciderint, corruptus ille unicus Codex sufficien- ti indicio minime est. Denique insolens est illa lo- quendi ratio, Spiritus Sanctus oris Davidis, aut oris Esaiæ, vel Jeremiæ, cujus nullam dabitur simile exemplum.

ἵνα τί ἐφρύαξαν ἔθνη) Hæc omnia Lucas κατὰ λέξιν descri- psit ex LXX.

Imo hæc non ex LXX. Interpp. descripsit Lucas, sed ex ore precantis communionis sacræ, per in- spirationem divinam habuit: quæ & Ecclesiæ sug- gessit in precatione Spiritus Sanctus, vel Aposto- lo Ecclesiæ in ista verba præeunti, & Lucæ histo- riam istam referenti inspiravit.

## 4:26
Vers. 26. the king) to the Hebrews [this word] means not only those who are properly kings, but also petty kings and governors, as we have often noted.

Latin:

Vers. 26. ὁ βασιλεὺς) מלכים Hebræis non tantum illi, qui proprie reges, sed & reguli, & præsides, ut sæpe notavimus.

## 4:27
Vers. 27. in truth) In that manuscript there is added here, in this city of yours.

your holy servant Jesus) See above III. 13. 26.

whom you anointed) Whom you had adorned with such great power, of healing diseases, of expelling demons, of raising the dead. The anointing of Christ, as also of David, had its degrees,

Concerning the anointing of David in Psalm II, nothing is held: for that Psalm treats only of Christ: which we proved against Grotius in the annotations to the book of Psalms. But the anointing of Christ has no degrees, because the gifts of the Spirit, with which he himself was instructed when he was anointed, were immense, for he was anointed not by measure, John III. 34. But where there is immensity, there are no degrees. Nor could the miraculous works or the acts of the Mediatorial and Redemptive work of Christ be performed by finite power, but there was need of infinite and immense power, as we showed in the Examination of Reformed doctrine concerning the perfection of Christ, Controv. V. p. 255.

with the nations) With the Romans, who were in the council or ministry of Pilate.

and the peoples of Israel) Judah and Benjamin, and those who dwelt in Judea from other tribes. In like manner you have nations and people opposed in Tobit XIV. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ἐπ' ἀληθείας) In illo manuscripto additur hic, ἐν τῇ πόλει σε ταύτῃ.

τὸν ἅγιον παῖδά σου Ἰησοῦν) Vide supra III. 13. 26.

ὃν ἔχρισας) Quem tanta potestate ornaveras, sanandi morbos, expellendi dæmones, mortuos resuscitandi. Un- ctio Christi ut & Davidis suos gradus habuit,

De Davidis unctione Psal. II. nihil habetur: A- git enim Psalmus ille solum de Christo: quod con- tra Grotium in annot. ad librum Psalmorum evici- mus. Unctio vero Christi gradus non habet, quia Spiritus dona, quibus instructus ipse fuit, cum unctus est, immensa fuere, unctus enim est οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου Joh. III.34. Ubi vero immensitas, ibi nulli gradus. Neque finita virtute vel opera miraculosa, vel actus Mediatorii & Redemtorii Christi perfici poterant, sed infinita & immensa virtute opus erat, ut in Exam. doctr. Reformat. de perf. Christi Contr. V. p. 255. ostendimus.

σὺν ἔθνεσι) Cum Romanis, qui in consilio aut ministerio erant Pilati.

καὶ λαοῖς Ἰσραήλ) Juda & Benjamin, & qui ex aliis tribu- bus in Judæa habitabant. Pari modo ἔθνη & λαὸς opposita habes Tobiæ XIV. 8.

## 4:28
V. 28. whatever your hand, and your counsel predestined to happen) See above II. 23. God, because He is omnipotent, therefore what He wills, He brings to effect: therefore the hand, that is, power, is placed here before counsel. The counsels of men, because they do not have such power, often fail. προορίζειν, in Hebrew כשר קדם.

It is certain that the hand and counsel of God imply His providence and power, by which all things are governed, which extends itself even to evil actions: in which, however, the action itself must be distinguished from the disorder and malice of the acts. For to the former He concurs by an active and direct influx, on account of the dependence of the secondary cause upon the first, but not so to the latter: But only by permitting, by setting limits to it, by directing it to a good end; whence the Apostles say, which your hand and counsel predestined, not that they might DO, but that they might BE DONE. Concerning which Beza himself warned in this place, that indeed the verb ποιῆσαι is not to be referred to the will and counsels of Pilate and Herod, but to the outcome of the counsels, and that the entire blame for the crimes is to be established in secondary causes, such as the Devil and wicked men. Nor can the Reformed obtain from this passage that the word προορίζειν is used in the scriptures to mean predestinate, in such a way that it also comprehends the decree of reprobation, which Beza, Polanus, Bucanus, Zanchius, and others strive to prove from this, because that word does not here denote reprobation to eternal destruction, as is clear, nor even predestination to evil: But the predestination of those things which, in order that they might be done, the hand and counsel of God had decreed: which does not indicate the operation of evil itself, or the impulse, or motion toward evil, much less such a motion that imports a necessity of malice, but the direction of that malice, foreseen and permitted, to a salutary end, the redemption of the human race, concerning which more fully treated in the cited places in Vol. II of the System of Theology.

Latin:

V. 28. ὅσα ἡ χείρ σου, καὶ ἡ βουλή σου προώρισε γενέσθαι) Vide supra II. 23. Deus, quia omnipotens est, ideo quod vult, effectum dat: ideo manus, id est, potentia præponitur hic consilio. Hominum, quia talem potentiam non habent, consilia sæpe fallunt. προορίζειν, Hebræis כשר קדם.

Manum & consilium Dei ejus providentiam & potentiam, qua gubernantur omnia, inferre cer- tum est, quæ porrigit sese etiam ad actiones malas: in quibus tamen actio ipsa ab ἀταξίᾳ & malitia actuum distinguenda. Nam ad illam concurrit æ- ctivo & directo influxu, ob dependensiam causæ se- cundæ a prima, ad hanc non item: Sed tantum permittendo, limites ei præfigendo, ad finem bonum dirigendo; unde Apostoli ajunt, quæ προώρισε ma- num & consilium tuum, non ut FACERENT, sed ut FIERENT. Quo de monuit ipse Beza in h. l. quod nempe verbum ποιῆσαι referendum non sit ad voluntatem & consilia Pilati & Herodis, sed ad consiliorum eventum, quodque scelerum culpa to- ta in secundis causis puta Diabolo & hominibus im- probis constituenda. Neque possunt Reformati ex hoc loco obtinere, vocem προορίζειν prædestinare adhiberi in sacris, ita, ut etiam reprobationis de- cretum comprehendat, quod Beza, Polanus, Bu- canus, Zanchius, alii hinc probare satagunt, quia vox illa non notat hic reprobationem ad æternum exitium, ut in aprico est, neque etiam prædestina- tionem ad malum: Sed προορισμὸν eorum, quæ ut fierent, Dei manus & consilium decreverat: qui non ipsam mali operationem, vel impulsum, aut motio- nem ad malum, nedum talem motum, qui necessi- tatem malitiæ importet, indicat, sed directionem malitiæ istius prævisæ & præmissæ, ad finem sa- lutarem, redemtionem humani generis, quo de in LL. CC. T. II. System. Theol. fusius actum.

## 4:29
Vers. 29. and now) עתה, which is translated by νῦν, among the Hebrews is a word of exhortation, Genesis XX. 7, XXI. 23, XXVII. 3, 8, 43, XXXI. 13 and often elsewhere.

with boldness) Without fear.

Latin:

Vers. 29. καὶ τὰ νῦν) עתה, quod per νῦν vertitur, apud He- bræos est excitantis, Genes. XX. 7. XXI. 23. XXVII. 3. 8. 43. XXXI, 13 & alibi sæpe.

μετὰ παῤῥησίας) Sine metu.

## 4:30
Vers. 30. in your stretching out your hand) The reason is explained, by which God might most greatly increase that confidence of speaking in the Apostles.

Latin:

Vers. 30. ἐν τῷ τὴν χεῖρά σου ἐκτείνειν) Explicatur ratio, per quam Deus maxime illam in Apostolis fiduciam lo- quendi augere possit.

Vers. 31. the place was shaken) A sign of God acting effectively, below XVI, 26. see XII. 26.
