Vers. 15. ὡσεὶ πρόσωπον ἀγγέλου) Id est, habebat gravita- tem cum summa suavitate conjunctam. Vide supra 8.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Stephen, having instituted his defense, repeating the calling of Abraham, with the promise made to him, and the covenant of circumcision, asserts the history of the departure of the Israelites into Egypt and their leading out of Egypt by Moses, along with the history of Moses' life in the court and in exile, and his calling, and the promise of a similar Prophet, and the received law, from which they had fallen away in the desert through calf-worship, serving at last the heavenly host, condemned to rejection beyond Babylon. But as for the place of worship, he professes that the tabernacle was erected in the desert and in the land of Canaan as a type until David, and upon his prayer, the temple was built by Solomon, but that God does not dwell in temples made with hands, much less is He bound to the Jerusalem temple; especially because they themselves always resisted the Holy Spirit with their fathers, and killed the prophets, who he openly professes had foretold the coming of that just one, Christ, but also that He was killed by the Jews, and that the law received among the ministries of angels was not kept by them. Whence they were at least exasperated; but Stephen, seeing heaven opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, testifies publicly concerning Him, but they, stopping their ears, cast him out of the city and stone him: who, having commended his spirit to the Lord Jesus, praying for them, falls asleep.

There are two parts: I. Stephen's Apologetic Speech: partly historical concerning the people of God, Moses, and the divine law, as also concerning the apostasy of that people, to v. 43, partly concerning the place of worship divinely instituted, to v. 47, then convincing refutatively that God does not dwell in a certain place, to v. 50, and correctively that the Jews have always resisted the Holy Spirit, and have killed Christ who was foretold by the Prophets, and have not kept the divine law, to v. 54. II. The stoning of Stephen, comforted by a vision of Jesus, on account of his confession, to v. 60.

PART I. Stephen's apologetic speech.

Ver. 1. εἰ ἄρα ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει;), Are those things true which these men testify concerning you? εἰ ἄρα הֲכָזֹאת.

Latin:

CAPUT VII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Stephanus Apologia instituta repetens vocati- onem Abrahami, cum promissione ei facta, & fœdere circumcisionis, historiam profe- ctionis Israelitarum in Ægyptum & edu- ctionis ex Ægypto, per Mosen, cum historia Mosaica vita in aula & in exilio, ac voca- tionis ejusdem, & promissionis similis Pro- phetæ, & accepta legis, asserit autoritatem Mosis & legis divinæ, à qua defecerint in deserto per μοσχολατρείαν, servientes tan- dem cœlesti exercitui, damnati ad rejectio- nem ultra Babyloniam. Quod vero ad lo- cum cultus, tabernaculum in deserto, & in terra Canaan in typum erectum usque ad Davidem, eo vero exorante, templum per Salomonem extructum esse profitetur, sed nec Deum habitare in templis manu fa- ctis, nedum ad templum Hierosolymita- num alligatum esse; imprimis quia ipsi semper cum Patribus restiterunt Spiritui Sancto, & Prophetas occiderunt, quos ad- ventum justi istius Christi prænunciasse, sed & illum à Judæis occisum, nec legem inter Angelorum ministeria acceptam ab iisdem servatam esse, palam profitetur. Unde illi exacerbati saltim sunt; Stepha- nus vero aperto cœlo Jesum videns à dexté- ris Dei stantem, de eo publice testatur, sed ipsi aures occludentes, ejectum ex urbe la- pidant: qui vero spiritu Domino Jesu com- mendato, pro ipsis orans obdormit.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Stephani Apologetica Oratio: historice partim de populo Dei, Mose, & lege divi- na, ut & de Apostasia illius, ad v. 43. partim de loco cultus divina instituta, ad v. 47. tum convincens e- lenctice, quod Deus non habitet in certo loco, ad v. 50. & epanorthotice, quod Judæi & Spiritui S. re- stiterint semper, & Christum à Prophetis prænun- ciatum interfecerint, & legem divinam non serva- rint, ad v. 54. II. Stephani, visione Jesu confortati, ob ejus confessionem lapidatio, ad v. 60.

PARS I. Apologetica Stephani oratio.

Vers. 1. εἰ ἄρα ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει;), Suntne vera, quæ isti de te testantur? εἰ ἄρα הֲכָזֹאת.

## 7:2
Ver. 2. ὁ δὲ ἔφη) Since Stephen was accused of two things, that he had predicted the destruction of the temple, and that he had predicted the calling of the Gentiles to God, in order to show that there is nothing unjust in it, he runs through all ancient history down to his own times and insinuates covertly that the favor of God had never been restricted to any place, not even to the Tabernacle or the Temple: then that the Jews, if they weighed well the deeds of their nation and their own, have nothing for which they should prefer themselves to foreigners.

Ἄνδρες ἀδελφοὶ) He says this to the people.

καὶ πατέρες) He says this to the Senators. Thus also the Roman Senators were called Fathers.

The God of glory) מלך הכבוד Ps. XXIV. 7. ὤφθη) That is, according to the tradition of the Hebrews, not from written history. Abarbaniel mentions this tradition. ὄντι ἐν τῇ Μεσοποταμίᾳ) It seems, therefore, that Ur was in Mesopotamia: nor does Ammianus book XXV contradict this, where he makes mention of Ur. For at that time the possession of Mesopotamia was being disputed by arms between the Romans and the Persians. It is possible, however, that ארם נהרים extended more widely for the Hebrews, and contained all those things which are irrigated not only by the Euphrates and the Tigris, but also by their branches.

Even if such a tradition should perhaps be found, it could still be a matter of doubt whether it was known at the time of Stephen: nor were the things which men inspired by God (θεόπνευστοι) commemorate outside of written history always known from traditions; for the Spirit of God, by whose impulse they spoke, suggested those things to them. But in truth, if one compares what Grotius notes below on v. 3, that the words of Gen. XII. 1 were spoken to Abraham in Ur of the Chaldeans, the things which Stephen relates concerning the calling of Abraham could have been had from there, and there was no need for tradition. As for the topographical doubt, since Stephen implies that he received the former calling in Mesopotamia, while Moses records in Gen. XI. 31 that he departed from Ur of the Chaldeans into Canaan, it is rightly observed by Grotius from Ammianus that Ur was in Mesopotamia, which Pliny also refers to Mesopotamia, book VI, ch. 26. Placing Nineveh and Babylon itself among the borders of Mesopotamia (although the latter is situated on this side of the confluence of the Euphrates, the former beyond the Tigris in the part of Assyria) as also Orrhoë, which Junius and Tremellius think is Ur. And Josephus also, book I, ch. IIX, reckons the Chaldeans among the Mesopotamians, and thus St. Stephen in this place takes Mesopotamia broadly for the whole region which is beyond the Euphrates, as he opposes it to the land of Canaan promised to the Israelites, which extended as far as the Euphrates, Deut. XI. 24. However, by those words in v. 2, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he had come into Charran, he does not establish Charran as outside of Mesopotamia, but specifically designates this place as being nearer to the Euphrates and Syria, even if it is also situated in Mesopotamia. There are not wanting those who wish Ur of the Chaldeans to be named not from the kingdom or region of Chaldea, but from those skilled in the art of Astrology, who were called Chaldeans because that art flourished most in Chaldea, and with whom that city of Ur abounded. Thus Ussher in the Annals of the O.T. p. 6. But this Ur, which with St. Stephen the Protomartyr (Acts VII. 2) Abarbaniel (in Gen. XI.) also places in Mesopotamia, was inhabited by Priests and Mathematicians who obtained the appellation of Chaldeans from the name of the city (by which name, even in Chaldea itself, the genethliacs are found to be distinguished from the rest of the Magi, Dan. II, 2, 10, ch. IV, 7, and VII). From whose company both Terah and his sons learned the worship of idols (Jos. XXIV. 2). Which not unlearned explanation, proved more fully by Ussher in his Sacred Chronology page 143, we leave to its own place.

ἐν χαῥῥάν) In Charris, which are also in Mesopotamia, Charra to Ptolemy, Charræ to Pliny, ennobled by the slaughter and blood of the Roman army routed by the Parthians in the fiftieth year before Christ: Today they hold the name Ophra, and are distant 84 miles from Ur of the Chaldeans.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ὁ δὲ ἔφη) Cum de duabus rebus accusaretur Ste- phanus, quod templi excidium prædixisset, & quod voca- tionem gentium ad Deum, ut ostendat nihil in eo esse ini- qui, omnem historiam veterem ad sua tempora percurrens insinuat κατὰ κρύψιν, Dei favorem nunquam adstrictum fuisse loco ulli, ne Tabernaculo quidem aut Templo: deinde Judæos, si gentis suæ & sua facta bene expenderent, nihil habere cur se alienigenis præferrent.

Ἄνδρες ἀδελφοὶ) Hoc populo dicit.

καὶ πατέρες) Hoc Senatoribus. Sic & Romani Senato- res vocabant Patres.

ὁ Θεὸς τῆς δόξης) מלך הכבוד Pf. XXIV. 7. ὤφθη) Hoc est, ex traditione Hebræorum, non ex scri- pta historia. Meminit hujus traditionis Abarbaniel. ὄντι ἐν τῇ Μεσοποταμίᾳ) Videtur ergo Ur fuisse in Meso- potamia: nec repugnat Ammianus libro XXV. ubi Uris facit mentionem. Nam eo tempore Mesopota miæ posses- sio inter Romanos & Persas disceptabatur armis. Fieri tamen potest ut ארם נהרים Hebræis latius patuerit, & omnia illa continuerit, quæ non Euphrate tantum & Ti- gride, sed & eorum divergis irrigantur.

Etiamsi talis traditio forte reperiatur, dubium tamen esse queat, num illa jam tempore Stephani nota fuerit: nec quæ viri θεόπνευστοι extra histo- riam scriptam commemorant, è traditionib. sem- per cognita fuére; suggessit quippe iisdem illa Spi- ritus Dei, cujus impulsu locuti sunt. Verum enim vero si conferatur, quod Grotius ad v. 3. infra no- tat, verba Gen. XII. 1. dicta ad Abrahamum esse in Ure Chaldæorum, exinde quæ de vocatione Abrahæ refert Stephanus, haberi potuēre, nec opus tradi- tione fuit. Quod ad dubium Topographicum, cum in Mesopotamia priorem vocationem ipsum acce- pisse, Stephanus innuit, quum ex Ure Chaldæorum ipsum profectum esse in Canaan, Moses tradat Gen. XI. 31. recte ex Ammiano observatum Gro- tio, Ur fuisse in Mesopotamia, quam ad Mesopota- miam etiam refert Plinius l. VI. c. 26. Ninum & Ba- byloniam ipsam collocans inter Mesopotamiæ ter- minos (licet hæc cis confluentem Euphratis, illa trans Tigrim in parte Assyriæ posita sit) ut & Or- rhoën, quam Urem esse putant Junius & Tremel- lius. Et accenset quoque Josephus l. I. c. IIX. Chal- dæos Mesopotamitis, atq; ita late Mesopotamiam accipit hoc loco S. Stephanus pro omni regione, quæ est trans Euphratem, utpote quam terræ Ca- naam Israélitis promissæ, quæ se extendebat usque ad Euphratem, Deut. XI. 24. opponit. Verbis au- tem illis v. 2. cum esset in Mesopotamia, antequam venisset in Charram, non constituit Charram ex- tra Mesopotamiam, sed locum hunc Euphrati & Sy- riæ viciniorem, etsi etiam in Mesopotamia situm, specialiter designat. Non desunt, qui Ur Caldæo- rum dici velint non à regno vel regione Chaldæa, sed ab artis Astrologicæ peritis, qui Chaldæi vocati sint, quod in Chaldæa eadẽ maxime viguerit, qui- bus civitas illa Ur abundarit. Ita Usserius in Ann. V. T. p. 6. Ur vero ista, quam in Mesopotamia cum Stephano Proto-Martyre Act. VII. 2. etiam Abarba- niel (in Gen. XI.) collocat, à Sacerdotibus & Mathe- maticis ex urbis vocabulo Chaldæorum appellatio- nem fortitis (quo nomine in ipsa etiam Chaldæa Ge- nethliaci à reliquis Magis distincti reperiuntur Dan. II, 2. 10. c. IV. 7. & VII.) habitata fuit. Ex quorum consortio & Terah & filii ejus idolorum cultum di- dicerunt (Jos. XXIV. 2.) Quam non ineruditam ex- plicationem ab Usserio in Chronologia Sacra pag. 143. uberius probatam suo loco relinqui- mus.

ἐν χαῥῥάν) In Charris, quæ & ipsæ in Mesopotamia, Charra Ptolomæo, Charræ Plinio, clade & cruo- re exercitus Romani à Parthis anno ante Christum stum quinquagesimo fusi nobilitatæ: Hodie no- men Ophræ obtinent, & 84. milliaribus ab Ur Chaldæorum distant.

## 7:3
Vers. 3. κὶ εἶπε πρὸς ἀυτὸν: ἔξελθε ἐκ τῆς γῆς σε) Those who reconcile these with Moses in Gen. XII. 1 think that in Moses ויאמר is pluperfect, and that what had been said in Ur is referred to there: such as are many hystera protera both in sacred and in profane histories. I praise those who untie all the knots: Yet if the memory of Luke has stumbled in the exact designation of an old place or time, the authority of the history which he wrote will not therefore perish. The Holy Spirit confirmed the Apostles and Evangelists in Evangelical doctrine: in other matters, if we believe Jerome, He left them, as men, to the things of men.

It is impiously attributed to Luke that he stumbled.

Therefore others [think] that there was a double calling and departure of Abraham, one from Ur of the Chaldeans, the other from Charran: that both are implied by Moses; the former indeed in Gen. XI. 31, the latter however in ch. XII. 4, and then are related by Stephen: the former in these words τότε ἐξελθὼν ἐκ γῆς χαλδαίων κατῴκησεν ἐν χάῥῥαν: the latter however by those which are added there κακεῖθεν μετα τὸ ἀποθανεῖν τὸν πατέρα αὐτῦ μετῴκησεν αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν γῆν ταύτην εἰς ἧν ὑμεῖς νῦν κατοικεῖτε. The time of the former departure is not defined: because he is said only to have departed into Charran, and to have lived there, without mention of the year or time of his habitation. But to the latter departure, instituted after the death of Terah, from Charran into Canaan, the seventy-fifth year of Abram's age is assigned by the LXX Interpreters. they say that the days of Terah ἐν τῇ χάῥῥαν became two hundred and five; But they wrongly confuse this with the time of his whole life, which they confuse with the days of his sojourn in Charran. Mercerus thinks he lived there for 23 years, but without solid foundation. Some, such as Petavius book IX, doctr. temp. ch. 18, Havillæus, Bonfrerius in Gen. XV, Thom. Pius with the Rabbis think that Abraham sojourned in Charran for five years, so that thus he was called from Ur of the Chaldeans in the 70th year of his age, in the 205th of Terah. Achior in Judith V says that those holy men fled into Mesopotamia, and lived there ἡμέρας πολλὰς many days: and Moses in Gen. XII. 5 testifies that Abraham and Lot acquired substance there, and made souls. But they nowhere find those five years defined. And therefore Ussher thinks that both the calling and the departure took place in the same year, and that Abraham stayed there for some time, at least for the sake of the aged old man detained there by weariness or sickness, so that he would not leave him destitute of help and comfort while he was breathing his last. Which opinion is favored by August. book XVI, de Civ. Dei ch. 16, Euthym., Salianus, Torniellus, Henr. Philippi the Jesuit in his Chronological Questions on Gen. ch. XII, and others.

To that point about the souls made in Haran, they respond who say that both callings were made in the same year, that this is to be understood of the servants and beasts of burden acquired in that same place.

But as for the words of Achior, that that Ammonite could have erred in that designation of many days, just as he erred when he asserted that the gods of his fathers, Terah and Abraham, worshipped in Chaldea, when it is established that the fathers and ancestors of Terah and Abraham were pious patriarchs, and not worshippers of idols; not to mention that that 'many days' is not found in the Chaldean text, which Jerome translated. Concerning which see Ussher in Chronol. S. p. 149. However, the narrative of Philo in his book on dreams seems preferable to this of Achior, that Abraham μὴ πολὺν χρόνον did not stay for a long time in Haran; as also Josephus in book I of Antiquities, ch. XV, who says that Abraham left Chaldea at 75 years of age, which would not be true if he had not departed from both Ur of the Chaldeans and Haran in the same year. To this opinion, therefore, we also add our vote in the Sacred Chronicle: and thus we determine that it was not so much an interrupted, double departure due to an intervening cause, as it was the same departure, because there was one calling, and one destination.

Therefore, as for that ἔξελθε ἐκ τῆς γῆς σε, although some, especially Ussher, resolve this difficulty without hysteron-proteron, namely that the tenor of the first calling is reported by Stephen, and that of the second calling by Moses, who strives to prove from Gen. XXIV. 4 that those words, 'go out from your land and your kindred,' also fit the calling made at Haran: because Nahor remained there with his family, and to that extent it is called his land and his kindred: nevertheless, it seems there is nothing absurd if hystero- logia is established with Masius, Pererius, Joh. Fernandius, & B. Gerhard, and thus those words of Moses, Gen. XII. v. 1. 2. 3. and the first clause of the fourth verse and the word ויאמר should be read as if in a parenthesis in the pluperfect, but the particle Vlau should be explained in a causal sense, in this way: For the Lord had said to Abraham, go out from your land and your kindred, and from your father's house, which description there is no doubt fits Ur of the Chaldeans more correctly than Haran: and let the first clause of verse 4 be taken concerning the departure for that calling made in Ur. But to the latter clause let there be subjoined, as if after the parenthesis is finished, Abraham's further departure from Haran after the death of Terah, mentioned before this parenthesis, was instituted; with the addition also of the character of time: Namely, that it was done in the 75th year of Abraham's age. Thus there will be one and the same calling of Abraham, which is described and reported by Moses, and by Stephen the Protomartyr in the same words, which, having been received in Ur of the Chaldeans, he carried out with Terah his parent and Lot; even though he was forced to stop for a short time in Haran, on account of the sickness and death of his parent; upon whose decease, in that same year, he set out from Haran further into the land which the Lord showed him. Which Moses reports after the mentioned death of Terah, and Stephen expressly declares was done after the death of Terah.

But if indeed anyone is convinced that a hysteron proteron in Moses does not sufficiently agree with the historical account (although that is not unusual in history), let him, with our permission, establish a double calling, one made in Ur, which Stephen describes, another in Haran, which Moses describes, to which latter a promise was added: that Terah having died in Haran and the patrimony having been divided between his sons Nahor and Abraham, Abram followed God calling him and migrated into Canaan, but the older brother Nahor, adhering to the old idolatry, remained in Haran with his own and the greater part of the paternal family, and thence in Gen. ch. XXIV. v. 10. the city of Haran is called the city of Nahor and v. 38. the house of Terah; if indeed it is certain from Josephus b. 1. ch. 14. that Nahor also set out with Terah to Haran from Ur of the Chaldeans: who lists there eight legitimate sons of Nahor, and four born of a concubine. Provided that this alone remains, that after the death of Terah in the 75th year of Abraham's age the departure from Haran took place, which Moses and Stephen clearly define. In which definition, so brilliantly made by the Holy Spirit, if curious minds were to persist, no difficulty would remain either in the Mosaic history or in the repetition of Stephen: But since, having abandoned the fountains of truth, they invent that Abraham was born in the 70th year of Terah, and thus, since the parent lived 205 years, that he was in his 135th year when he ended his life, an irreconcilable conflict emerges with the Mosaic narrative and the pronouncement of Stephen, that Abram departed from Haran only after the death of his parent, from which Moses with a resounding voice declares he departed not in his 135th year, but in his 75th. Therefore they either despair of a solution to this difficulty, which they have fashioned for themselves, not found in the Scriptures, and wish for Elias with Scaliger, or they cavil that Luke or Stephen erred through a lapse of memory; into which profane opinion Grotius has fallen along with a certain Scaligerian chronologist: in no way helping the authority of Scripture with this little exception, that the Holy Spirit confirmed the Apostles and Evangelists in Evangelical doctrine, but in other matters, as men, left to them what belongs to men; For once some falsehood is admitted into such a pinnacle of authority, no particle of those books will remain which will not in some way seem either difficult regarding morals or incredible regarding faith, as Augustine says in Ep. 118 to Jerome, Conf. which we have said against the similar impiety of the Socinians in Socinism Overthrown Sect. II. Membr. 1. contr. 141.

εἰς γῆν, ἧν ἂν σοι) He was therefore still far from Canaan when God said these things to him. God loved him, not the place to which He was leading him.

There are not wanting those who think these things were likewise said in Haran, which opinion Ussher strongly defends: But because Stephen openly testifies that this oracle was made to Abraham in Ur of the Chaldeans, nor is it likely that, when Abraham had been forced to stop for a time in Haran, he was so excited by that new oracle to continue his departure that the destination was again left indefinite: Therefore it seems better to establish only one calling, which Abram received in his fatherland: when he was altogether far from Canaan, just as the words of the same are used by Moses, which Stephen uses concerning the calling in Ur of the Chaldeans, than to admit a double calling; one made in Ur of the Chaldeans, the other in Haran, of which the former is described by Moses, the latter by Stephen, but in the same tenor of words; if indeed a departure can properly be considered one, even if it was interrupted for a short time on account of the sickness and death of Terah, and only one year has been assigned by Moses in the account of the calling of Abraham and the departure from Ur of the Chaldeans, the sojourn in Haran, the death of Terah, and the continued departure into Canaan, namely the 75th year of Abraham's age, as a new epochal ετισινὸς: and Josephus b. I. Antiq. c. XV. declares that in that year of his age Abraham chose Chaldea: But Abraham adopted Lot the son of his brother Aram, and the brother of his wife Sarah, not having a legitimate son, and left Chaldea, when he was seventy-five years old, at God's command, to migrate into Canaan. Who also cites Nicolaus of Damascus in the fourth book of his histories speaking thus: Abraham reigned in Damascus, coming as a stranger with an army from the land of the Chaldeans, which is called above Babylon. Therefore, after not much time, rising up also from this region with his people, he inhabited the land which is then called Canaan, but now Judaea. What of the fact that the Holy Spirit himself seems to commemorate only one calling and departure of Abram, both in Jos. XXIV. 2, where Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor, served other gods, when God took Abraham from the borders of Mesopotamia; but they served other gods in Ur of the Chaldeans: and in Nehem. ch. IX. 7, Thou thyself, O Lord God, who didst choose Abraham and didst lead him out of Ur of the Chaldeans. But that Abram is said to have dwelt in Haran, Gen. XI. 31. Acts VII. 2, 4, where Petavius and Harvillæus observe that the word κατοικῆσαι does not argue for such a short interval, Ussher rightly remarked that if it is posited that Terah and Abram departed from Ur of the Chaldeans in the summer, and afterwards Terah was detained by infirmity in Carrhae, and finally, upon his death there, Haran was left by Abram at the beginning of spring, enough space is left so that he could be said to have dwelt in Haran, even if he had stayed there with his people for only six months: such was the shorter dwelling of Jacob in Bethel, Gen. XXXV. 1, 16, and of Tamar the widow in her father's house, Gen. XXXVIII. 11. But as we warned before, whether one calling is posited or a double one, provided that the departure of Abraham both from Ur of the Chaldeans and from Haran is said to have occurred in the same year, which was the 75th of his age, and the historical account is correctly explained so that there is no need to ascribe mnemonic errors to Luke or Stephen, nor will sacred Chronology be endangered, while that fixed limit of the Abrahamic age remains, when he received the promise, from which the beginning of the new Epoch must be taken, which ought to be altogether certain and immovable.

Latin:

Vers. 3. κὶ εἶπε πρὸς ἀυτὸν: ἔξελθε ἐκ τῆς γῆς σε) Qui hæc conciliant cũ Mose Gen. XII. 1. existimant in Mose ויאמר esse plusquam perfectum, & perinάποδος ibi referri id, quod in Ure dictum fuerat: qualia ὑσερόπρωτα multa sunt & in sa- cris, & in profanis historiis. Laudo, qui omnes nodos tol- lunt: Neque tamen si in veteris loci, aut temporis exacta designatione memoria Lucæ titubaverit, ideo historiæ, quam scripsit, peribit auctoritas. Spiritus sanctus Apo- stolos & Evangelistas confirmavit in doctrina Evangelica: in cæteris rebus, si Hieronymo credimus, ut hominibus, re- liquit, quæ sunt hominum.

Impie tribuitur Lucæ titubatio.

itaque alii, geminam fuisse vocationem, & profe- ctionem Abrahami, alteram ex Ur Chaldæorum: alteram ex Charram: utrâmq; cum à Mose innui; illam quidem Gen. XI. 31. hanc autem c. XII. 4. tum à Stephano referri: priorem verbis istis τότε ἐξελ- θὼν ἐκ γῆς χαλδαίων κατῴκησεν ἐν χάῥῥαν: posteri- orem vero ab iis, quæ ibi adduntur κακεῖθεν μετα τὸ ἀποθανεῖν τὸν πατέρα αὐτῦ μετῴκησεν αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν γῆν ταύτην εἰς ἧν ὑμεῖς νῦν κατοικεῖτε. Priores illius profectionis tempus definitum non est: quia solum in Charram profectus, ibiq; habitasse dicitur, sine mentione anni aut temporis habitationis. Po- steriori autem profectioni, post mortem Tharæ in- stitutæ, è Carris in Canaan assignatum esse annum ætatis Abrami septuagesimum quintum LXX. qui- dem Interpp. dies Tharæ ἐν τῇ χάῥῥαν ducentos, quinque factos ajunt; Sed hoc totius vitæ ejus tem- pus, quod cum diebus commorationis in Carris perperam confundunt. Mercerus per 23. annos ibi- dem habitasse putat, sed sine solido fundamento. Nonnulli utpote Petavius l. IX. doctr. temp. c. 18. Havillæus, Bonfrerius in Cen. XV. Thom. Pius cum Rabbinis quinquennium in Carris commoratum fuisse Abrahamum putant, ut ita 70. ætatis suæ anno Tharæ ducentesimo ex Ure Chaldæorum vocatus sit. Achior Judith V. sanctos illos in Me- sopotamiam fugisse, ibiq; ἡμέρας πολλὰς dies mul- tos habitasse dicit: & Moses Gen. XII. 5. testatur, Abrahamum & Lothum ibi substantiam acquisi- visse, & animas fecisse. Sed nuspiam illos quinque annos definitos inveniunt. Ideoque Usserius, eodem anno utramque vocationem & profectionem fa- ctam, & Abrahamum saltem in gratiam senis gran- dævi vel lassitudine vel morbo istic detenti illic ali- quamdiu substitifse, ne eundem animam agentem auxilio & solatio destitueret, existimat. Cui senten- tiæ favet August. l. XVI. de Civ. Dei c. 16. Euthym. Salianus, Torniellus, Henr. Philippi Jesuita quæst. Chronol. in Gen. c. XII. aliique.

Ad illud de anima- bus in Charran factis respondent, qui eodem anno utramque vocationem factam ajunt, intelligen- dum id esse de servis & jumentis ibidem acquisitis.

Ad verba Achioris vero, quod Ammonita ille erra- re potuerit, in illa dierum multorum designatio- ne, æque uti erravit, cum Deos Patrum suorum Tharam & Abraham in Chaldæam coluisse asseruit, quum constet Patres & Majores Tharæ & Abra- ham pios fuisse Patriarchas, non vero Idolorum cultores; ut taceam, quod illud diebus multis non habeatur in textu Chaldæo, quem Hieronym. trans- tulit. De quod vid. Usserius in Chronol. S. p. 149. Præferenda autem huic Achioris videtur Philonis narratio in l. de somniis, Abrahamum μὴ πολὺν χρό- νον non multum temporis in Charræm moratum esse; ut & Josephi l. I. antiq. c. XV. qui Abrahamum an- nos natum 75. reliquisse Chaldæam ait, quod ve- rum non esset, si non eodem anno & Ure Chal- dæorum & Charane ille decessisset. Huic ergo sententiæ nos etiam calculum in Chronico S. adje- cimus: adeoque non tam interruptam, ob causam intervenientem, geminam, quam eandem profe- ctionem, quia una erat vocatio, unus terminus ad quem, statuimus.

Quod ergo illa ἔξελθε ἐκ τῆς γῆς σε, etsi citra ὑσεροπρώτων hanc difficultatem ex- pediant nonnulli, imprimis Usserius, quod nem- pe à Stephano tenor vocationis primæ, à Mose vo- cationis secundæ referatur, qui verba illa, exi è ter- ra tua & cognatione tua, Charani etiam factæ vo- cationi convenire è Gen. XXIV. 4. probare sata- git: quod Nachor ibidem cum familia sua manse- rit, atque eatenus terra ejus & cognationis ejus illa dicatur: nihil tamen absurdi videtur, si ὑσερο- logia cum Masio, Pererio, Joh. Fernandio, & B. Gerhardo statuatur, atque adeo velut in pa- renthesi legantur verba illa Mosis, Gen. XII. v. 1. 2. 3. & incisi primi versus quarti ac verbum ויאמר in plusquamperfecto, particula vero Vlau sensu causali exponatur h. m. Nam dixerat Do- minus Abrahamo, exi e terra tua & cognatione tua, & de domo patris tui, quam descriptionem rectius Uri Chaldaeorum convenire, quam Chara- ni, dubium nullum est: & versus 4. primum in- cisum accipiatur de partitione ad vocationem il- lam in Ure factam. Posteriori vero inciso sub- jungatur, veluti post parenthesin finitam, A- brahae ulterior profectio e Carris post mortem Tha- rae, ante hanc parenthesin commemoratam, in- stituta; addito etiam temporis charactere: Quod nempe anno aetatis Abrahae 75. facta sit. Ita una eademque vocatio erit Abrahae, quae a Mose, & quae a Stephano Proto-Martyre iisdem verbis descripta refertur, quam in Ur Chaldaeorum acceptam, cum Thara parente suo & Lotho exe- quutus est; etsi subsistere coactus ad breve tem- pus in Harran, ob morbum & mortem parentis; quo defuncto, eodem illo anno, ex Harrane porro in terram, quam ipsi monstravit Domi- nus, profectus est. Quod Moses post memora- tum obitum Tharae refert, ac Stephanus diserte fa- ctum perhibet post mortem Tharae.

Quod si vero quis, ὑστερολογίαν in Mose non satis convenire historiae relationi, persuasus sit (quamvis ea in historia non insolens sit) gemi- nam, per nos licet, statuat vocationem, alte- ram in Ur factam, quam Stephanus, alteram in Charane, quam Moses describat, cui posteriori promissio addita: quod Thara in Charane mortuo & patrimonio inter ejus filios Nacho- rem & Abrahamum diviso, Abram Deum vo- cantem secutus in Canaan migrarit, senior vero frater Nahor veteri Idololatriae adhaerescens cum sua & paternae familiae majore parte in Cha- rane permanserit, indeque Gen. cap. XXIV. v. 10. urbs Charan civitas Nahor dicatur & vers. 38. domus Thamar; siquidem ex Josepho l. 1. cap. 14. constet, etiam Nachorem cum Thara Chara- nem ex Ur Chaldaeorum profectum esse: qui octo Nachoris filios legitimos, quatuor de concu- bina natos ibi recenset. Dum id solum ma- neat, post mortem Tharae anno aetatis Abrahae 75. profectionem e Charane factam, quod clare Moses & Stephanus definiunt. In qua definitione, tam luculenter facta a Spiritu Sancto, si persi- sterent curiosa ingenia, nulla difficultas superf- set vel in Mosaica historia, vel in repetitione Ste- phani: Sed quum relictis veritatis fontibus com- miniscantur, Abrahamum 70. Tharae anno na- tum, adeoque quum Parens vivendo 205. annos fecerit, eo vitam finiente 135. annum egisse, irre- conciliabilis emergit pugna cum Mosaica narra- tione & pronunciato Stephani, quod Abram post mortem parentis sui demum Carris discesse- rit, quem non 135. aetatis anno, sed 75. inde di- scessisse, Moses sonora voce perhibet. Idcirco vel desperant difficultatis hujus, quam sibi finxere, non in Scripturis invenere, solutionem, & Eliam exoptant cum Scaligero, vel Lucam aut Stephanum memoria lapsum errasse cavillantur; in quam prophanam sententiam cum Scalige- riano quodam Chronologo prolapsus est Gro- tius: nequicquam autoritati Scripturae hac suc- currens exceptiuncula, quod Spiritus S. Apostolos & Evangelistas in doctrina Evangelica confirmarit, in caeteris, ut hominibus reliquerit, quae sunt homi- num; Nam admisso semel in tantum autoritatis faftigium aliquo mendacio, nulla illorum libro- rum particula remanebit, quæ non utcunque vide- bitur vel ad mores difficilis, vel ad fidem incredi- bilis, dicente Augustino Ep. IIX. ad Hieron. Conf. quæ contra Socinianorum similem impie- tatem diximus Socinismo profligato Sect. II. Membr. 1. contr. 141.

εἰς γῆν, ἧν ἂν σοι) Longe ergo'erat adhuc à Cananæa, cum Deus hæc ei diceret, Amabat ipsum Deus, non locum quo eum ducebat.

Non defunt, qui in Charris hæc itidem dicta censeant, quam sententiam maximopere propu- gnat Usserius: Sed quia Stephanus in Ur Chal- dæorum hoc oraculum Abrahamo factum aperte testatur, nec verisimile est, cum in Harane ad tem- pus subsistere coactus fuisset Abrahamus, ipsum novo illo oraculo ad continuandam profectio- nem ita excitatum, ut denuo terminus ad quem indefinitus relictus sit: Idcirco præstare vide- tur, unam tantum statuere vocationem, quam in patriâ acceperit Abram: cum longe omnino abesset à Cananæa, sicuti etiam à Mose ejusdem verba adhibita sunt, quæ Stephanus de vocatione in Ur Chaldæorum adhibet, quam geminam vo- cationem; alteram in Ure Chaldæorum, alteram in Harane factam, quarum prior à Mose, posterior à Stephano, sed eodem verborum tenore descri- batur, admittere; siquidem una proprie censeri possit profectio, etsi ad breve tempus ob morbum & mortem Tharæ interrupta, nec nisi unus annus à Mose adsignatus sit in relatione vocationis Abra- hæ & profectionis ex Ure Chaldæorum, commora- tionis in Carris, mortis Tharæ, & continuatæ in Ca- naan profectionis, annus 75. nempe ætatis Abraha- mi, ceu novæ Epochæo' ετισινὸς: & Josephus l. I. An- tiq. c. XV. illo ætatis anno Abrahamum Chaldæam elegisse perhibeat: Abraham vero Loth filium fratris sui Aram, uxoris vero suæ Saræ germanum adoptavit, filium legitimum non habens, dimisitque Chaldæam, cum septuaginta & quinque annorum esset, Deo jubente, ut migraret in Canaan. Qui al- legat etiam Nicolaum Damascenum in IV. histo- riarum libro sic loquentem: Abrahamus regna- vit in Damasco, veniens advena cum exercitu de terrâ Chaldæorum, quæ super Babylonem dicitur. Igitur post non multum tempus exurgens etiam de hac regione cum populo suo, terram, quæ tunc Cana- naa, nunc vero Judæa dicitur, habitavit. Quid quod ipse Spiritus S. non nisi unam vocationem, ac profectionem Abrami commemorare videa- tur, tum Jos. XXIV. 2. ubi Thara Pater Abrahami & Nahoris alienis Diis servirent, cum tulit Deus Ab- rahamum de Mesopotamiæ finibus; servierunt au- tem alienis Diis in Ure Chaldæorum: tum Nehem. c. IX. 7. Tu ipse Domine Deus, qui elegisti Abraham & eduxisti eum de Ure Chaldæorum. Quod autem in Charane habitasse dicitur Abram Genes. XI. 31. Act. VII. 2 4. ubi Petavius, ac Harvillæus observant verbum κατοικῆσαι, non adeo breve intervallum ar- guere, recte Usserius animadvertit, si ponatur, Tha- ran & Abramum Ure Chaldæorum æstate disces- sisse, postmodum Tharan infirmitate detentum fuisse in Carris, eoque demum ibi vita functo, sub initium Veris Charanem ab Abramo relictam esse, satis relinqui spatii, ut in Charane habitasse dici posset, etsi tantum per sex menses ibi cum suis sub- stitisset: cujusmodi brevior habitatio Jacobi inBe- thel fuit Gen. XXV. 1. 16. & Thamaræ viduæ in domo Patris sui Gen. XXXIIX. 11. Sed quod antea monui- mus, sive una statuatur vocatio, sive gemina, dum eodem anno solum facta dicatur Abrahæ & ex Ure Chaldæorum, & è Charane profectio, qui æ- tatis ejus fuit 75. & historica relatio recte expediri potest, ut opus non sit, Lucæ aut Stephano ἀμαρ- τήματα μνημονευτικὰ adscribere, nec periclita- bitur Chronologia sacra, manente fixo illo ætatis A- brahamicæ termino, dum ἐπαγγελίαν accepit, un- de novæ Epochæ sumendum Exordium est, quem omnino certum & immotum esse oportet.

Verse 4. He moved him) Gen. XII. 4.

## 7:5
Verse 5. nor a footstep) Thus Deuter. II. 5. כף רגל is translated.

when he had no child) He inserts this in passing, in order to commend the power of faith,

Latin:

Vers. 5. ὀυδὲ βῆμα ποδὸς) Sic Deuter. II. 5. transfertur כף רגל.

ὀυκ ὀντος ἀυτῷ τέκνυ) Hoc obiter inspergit, ut fidei vim commendet,

## 7:6
Verse 6. that his seed should be a sojourner) His children will be inhabitants. For so the Latins speak.

and shall enslave it, and shall afflict it four hundred years.) Thus in the Hebrew Gen. XV. 13. in the Greek a little more: and shall enslave them and shall afflict them, and shall humble them four hundred years. Theophylact in this place: and shall enslave it four hundred years. These things were born from different versions mixed together. But there is here in the Hebrew a brief expression, not well perceived by the interpreters. For the sense is that that calamity would last until almost the four-hundredth year from when the oracle had come to Abraham: as we have said at that place of Genesis: where all things which are predicted pertain to Egypt.

Grotius wishes the sense to be: that that calamity would last until almost the four-hundredth year (he meant to say four-hundredth) from when the oracle had come to Abraham: But the Holy Spirit does not treat of a calamity that would last for such a time, but joins these things, that the seed of Abraham would be a sojourner, and that they would serve and would be ill-treated, all of which he concludes in a period of four centuries: but the calculation of the same has been treated in the Chronicle and Commentary on Genesis. Briefly: the 400 years are counted either by the rounding of the number here and in Gen. XV. v. 13. Judith V. 9. with the centuries expressed, omitting the small number, or by the beginning made from the birth of Isaac, from which the years to the exodus are counted as 405, or from the mocking and casting out of Ishmael, which they say happened in the fifth year of Isaac, from which 400 years flowed precisely to the Exodus. Let one see Jerome in the Hebrew traditions on Genesis and Bede in this place. Acts VII. As to v. 6. nor a footstep, a doubt arises, because of the passage Gen. XXIII. 17. concerning the purchased field: of which Stephen himself also made mention in v. 16. Drusius distinguishes the times in book V. of his Praeterita, p. 168, that before the purchase of the field of Ephron he possessed nothing there. Others more correctly observe the emphasis of the Greek word κληρονομία, that he received nothing from God as an inheritance, so that his faith in the same promise of God might be exercised. Nor did that field serve the living, but was a tomb for the dead, and was to be a monument of the future fulfillment of the promise made, both concerning the land of Canaan to be inherited by his descendants, and concerning the blessed seed to be raised up in the same.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ὅτι ἔσαι τὸ σπέρμα ἀυτῦ πάροικον) Liberi ejus incolæ erunt. Ita enim loquuntur Latini.

κὴ δωλώσεσιν ἀυτὸ, κὴ κακώσεσιν ἔτη τετρακόσια.) Sic in He- bræo Gen. XV. 13. in Græco paulo amplius: κὴ δωλώσεσιν ἀυ- τὸς κὴ κακώσεσιν ἀυτὸς, κὴ ταπεινώσεσιν ἀυτὸς τετρακόσια ἔτη. Theophylactus hoc loco: κὴ δωλώσεσιν ἀυτὸ ἔτη τετρακόσια. Hæc nata sunt ex diversis versionibus inter se permixtis. Est autem hic in Hebræo brevis locutio, non bene percepta ab interpretibus. Sensus enim est, duraturam eam calamitatem usque ad annum ferme quadragesimum ex quo oraculum Abrahamo obtigerat: ut diximus ad illum Geneseos lo- cum: ubi, quæ prædicuntur, omnia ad Ægyptum pertinent.

Sensum esse vult Grotius: duraturam eam cala- mitatem usque ad annum ferme quadragesimum (di- cere voluit quadringentesimum) ex quo oraculum Abrahamo obtigerat: Sed Sp. S. non de calamitate per tantum tempus duratura agit, sed conjungit hæc, quod semen Abrahæ futurum sit πάροικον, quodque servituri sint & quod male habituri, quæ omnia quatuor seculorum periodo concludit: de computo vero ejusdem in Chronico & Commenta- rio in Genesin actum. Breviter: anni 400. numeran- tur vel rotundatione numeri hic & Gen. XV. v. 13. Judith. V. 9. expressis seculis, omisso minuto nume- ro, vel initio, facto à nativitate Isaaci, à qua anni ad exitum numerantur 405. aut ab irrisione & ejectio- ne Ismaëlis, quam anno quinto Isaaci factam dicunt, unde præcise 400. anni ad Exodum fluxere. Vi- deat. Hieronym. in tradit. Hebræis ad Gen. & Beda in h. l. Act. VII. Quod ad v. 6. ὀυδὲ βῆμα ποδὸς, dubium occurrit, ob locum Gen. XXIII. 17. de comparato agro: cujus etiam Stephanus ipse mentionem fecit v. 16. Drusius distinguit tempora lib. V. præterit. p. 168. quod ante emtum agrum Ephronis nihil ibi possederit. Rectius alii Græcæ vocis κληρονομία emphasin observant, quod à Deo nihil acceperit in hæreditatem, ut exerceretur fides ejusdem qua Dei promissionem. Neque ager ille vivo inserviebat, sed mortui tumulus, & futuræ adimpletionis factæ promissionis, tum de hæreditanda à posteris terra Canaan, tum de semine benedicto in eadem exci- tando, monumentum esse debebat.

## 7:7
Verse 7. and after these things they shall come out and shall serve me in this place) This agrees more in sense than in words. For in Genesis it is: they shall be equipped here.

Latin:

Vers. 7. κὴ μετὰ ταῦτα ἐξελέυσονται κὴ λατρέυσουσί μοι ἐν τῷ τόπῳ τέτῳ) Hoc magis sensu congruit quam verbis. Nam in Genesi est: ἀποσκευήσονται ὧδε.

## 7:8
Verse 8. and he gave him the covenant of circumcision) Namely, after those excellent promises. This also pertains to the purpose of Stephen, lest the obedience of circumcision be believed to have been the cause of the promises.

and so he begat Isaac) The promises were not given because of Isaac: But Isaac was given because of the promises, into the shadow of the grace to be given through the Gospel.

τὲς δώδεκα πατριάρχας) Authors of the tribes, as also in the following clause. Thus also Abraham is πατριάρχης, Heb. VII. 4. The terms φυλῆς and πατριᾶς are confused. Those whom we have mentioned are properly φυλάρχαι or φύλαρχοι: David is properly πατριάρχης, as above II. 27, because he was the author of the royal family, which is πατριὰ, Luke II. 4.

The Holy Spirit, the best master of speech, is wrongly accused of confusion of terms. But why should not the sons of Jacob, and why should not Abraham, be rightly called Patriarchs? And by what right shall we call only the royal family a πατριὰν, and not other families as well? Furthermore, is not Abraham, because he was the author of many families and tribes, and are not the sons of Jacob, because from them not only tribes but also families depended in each tribe of any Patriarch, rightly so named?

Latin:

Vers. 8. κὴ ἔδωκεν ἀυτῷ διαθήκην περιτομῆς) Nempe post illa eximia promissa. Hoc quoque ad propositum Stephani pertinet, ne crederetur circumcisionis obedientia causa fu- isse promissorum.

κὴ ὕτως ἐγέννησε τὸν Ἰσαάκ) Non propter Isaacum data sunt promissa: Sed Isaacus propter promissa datus, in umbram gratiæ per Evangelium dandæ.

τὲς δώδεκα πατριάρχας) Tribuum auctores ut & com- mate sequente. Sic & Abraham πατριάρχης, Hebr. VII. 4. Confunduntur voces φυλῆς & πατριᾶς. Illi quos diximus proprie φυλάρχαι vel φύλαρχοι: David proprie πατριάρχης, ut supra II. 27. quia auctor erat familiæ regalis, quæ πατριὰ, Luc. II. 4.

Male arguitur Spiritus S. confusionis vocum, optimus loquendi artifex. Quidni vero Jacobi filii, quidni & Abraham Patriarchæ recte voca- rentur? Et quo jure familiam tantum regiam πατριὰν, non vero alias etiam familias vocabi- mus? Tum annon Abraham, quia multarum fa- miliarum & tribuum autor fuit, annon Jacobi fi- lii, quia ab illis non tribus tantum, sed familiæ etiam dependebant in quaque tribu cujusvis Pa- triarchæ recte nuncupati.

## 7:9
Vers. 9. ζηλώσαντες τὸν Ἰωσὼφ) It is a κρῦψις (concealment). For he wishes to say, you in like manner betrayed Jesus to foreigners out of envy. ἀπέδοντο εἰς Αἴγυπτον) מכרו אתו אל מצרים, which Moses said concerning the Midianites, XXXII. 36; here he rightly transferred it to the Patriarchs, who had been the cause of that evil. In the Greek there it is, as here, ἀπέδοντο τὸν Ἰωσὴφ εἰς Αἴγυπτον. In almost the same way Aristophanes said ἀγοράζειν εἰς ἀγρὸν, that is, to buy in order that it may be carried into the field. κὶ ἧν ὁ Θεὸς μετ’ αὐτῶ) κὶ here signifies 'yet'. As if he were to say: it is not without precedent that God does good to those whom you harm the most.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ζηλώσαντες τὸν Ἰωσὼφ) Est κρῦψις. Vult enim di- cere, vos pari modo Jesum ex invidja tradidistis extraneis. ἀπέδοντο εἰς Αἴγυπτον) מכרו אתו אל מצרים, quod de Madianitis dixit Moses XXXII. 36. hic recte ad Patriar- chas transtulit, qui causa ejus mali fuerant. In Græco ibi est, ut hic, ἀπέδοντο τὸν Ἰωσὴφ εἰς Αἴγυπτον. Pari ferme modo ἀγοράζειν εἰς ἀγρὸν dixit Aristophanes, id est, emere ut fera- tur in agrum. κὶ ἧν ὁ Θεὸς μετ’ αὐτῶ) κὶ hic valet tamen. Quasi dicat: non est sine exemplo, quod Deus benefacit iis, quibus vos nocetis maxime.
