## 7:14
V. 14. ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε) This reading is old enough, as appears from the Syriac, Arabic, and Latin. And hence it happened that, just as in the repeated name of Cainan, the Greek books here also received a change from Christian copyists. For in Gen. ch. XLVI. 27, where in the Hebrew seventy souls are named, as Josephus and the Chaldean Interpreters also have it, the Greek texts now have ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε (seventy-five), with the addition of certain words which are missing in the Hebrew and pertain to completing this number. Indeed, even in Deuteronomy X. 22, where the same history is related, the same change was made in the Greek books after the times of Jerome. For he clearly signifies in his Questions on Genesis that the number seventy existed in that place. But just as in the name of Cainan, from one copy of Luke wrongly written, the error flowed into all that we have, so I believe it happened here also: and that the origin of the error was that after O, that is, seventy, there was noted E, to signify the fifth part of the section pertaining to Stephen.

We have dealt at length with Cainan in the Critici Sacri.

We have already examined the opinion of Grotius on Luke 3. It is surreptitious, but it has not, however, occupied all the Greek copies, as was shown in the Critici Sacri, p. 759 of the first edition. But that an error was committed in the number, which Calvin, Paraeus, Flacius, and Arcularius maintained, and that it originated from a marginal note, which Grotius contends, or that originally it was read not πέντε but πάντες, which Beza and Glassius think, is by no means to be admitted. For since all the copies read it so, that would be a universal corruption of the codices, which is repugnant to divine providence.

Nor is anything certain regarding those notes of the sections of Stephanus: and the number 75 of souls is correct, provided we apply our mind correctly to the words of Stephanus, who counts the number of those who were summoned by Joseph with Jacob into Egypt, which was not done by Moses, Genesis ch. 46, v. 27, inasmuch as he wove a different catalog, in which his descendants are included together with Jacob, but not the wives of the sons of Jacob, since he designates only those who came out of the loins of Jacob, v. 26, namely the souls of the house of Jacob, excluding the wives, but including Jacob, as the root of the family, who came into Egypt, whether with Jacob or before him. The words of Stephanus are as follows: Joseph sent and summoned his father his own, and all his kindred of seventy-five souls. See Critic. Sacr. page 746. and following, as also the Commentary on Genesis at ch. XLVI. v. 27. Our opinion is praised by the blessed Joh. Ernest. Gerhard, analect. on this passage. As also by the most famous English Polyhistor Joh. Selden, book II. on the Synedrion, page 409. who calls it accurate and ingenious: as also in the Addenda to page 148. line 30. although he does not correctly assign my name, calling me Calovius.

Latin:

V. 14. ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε) Vetus satis est hæc lectio, ut ex Syro, Arabe, Latino apparet. Et hinc factum, ut, sicut in Cainanis nomine repetito, libri Græci etiam hic mutatio- nem reciperent à Christianis exscriptoribus. Nam Gen. c. XLVI. 27. ubi in Hebræo septuaginta animæ nomi- an- tur, quomodo habet & Josephus & Chaldæi Interpretes, Græca nunc habent ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε, additis & vocibus quibusdam, quæ in Hebræo desunt, & ad explendum hunc numerum pertinent. Quin & in Deuteronomio X. 22. ubi eadem refertur historia, eadem mutatio in Græcis li- bris facta post tempora Hieronymi. Nam is eo in loco ex- stitisse numerum septuaginta aperte significat quæstioni- bus ad Genesim. Sicut autem in nomine Cainani ex uno exemplari Lucæ male scripto, error in omnia fluxit, quæ habemus, ita & hic factum arbitror: originemque erroris fuisse, quod post O, id est, septuaginta, annotatum fuit E, ad significandam quintam particulam sectionis ad Stepha- num pertinentis.

De Cainane in Critico sacro prolixe egimus.

Sententiam etiam Grotii ad Luc. III. jam expendi- mus. Irreptitius ille est, sed non occupavit tamen omnia exemplaria Græca, ut in Critico sacro p. 759. primæ editionis ostensum. Hic autem er- rorem in numero commissum esse, quod voluit Calvinus, Paræus, Flacius, Arcularius, eumque ex marginali nota ortum trahere, quod Grotius contendit, aut primitus non πέντε, sed πάντες lectum fuisse, quod Beza & Glassius putant, mi- nime admittendum. Quum enim omnia exem- plaria ita legant, universalis foret illa codicum corruptio, quæ repugnat divinæ providentiæ.

Neque de illis notis particularum sectionis Ste- phani quicquam constat: & numerus 75. anima- rum rectè se habet, modo animum recte verbis Stephani advertamus, qui eorum init nume- rum, qui cum Jacobo in Ægyptum accersiti à Jo- sepho sunt, quod à Mose non factum, Genes. cap. XLVI. v. 27. utpote qui catalogum texit alium, in quo una cum Jacobo posteri ejus com- prehenduntur, non autem filiorum Jacobi uxo- res, quum egressos solum è lumbis Jacobi desi- gnet v. 26. animas nempe domus Jacob, exceptis uxoribus, annumerato autem Jacobo, ut stir- pe familiæ, quæ in Ægyptum venerunt, seu cum Jacobo, seu ante eundem. Verba Stephani sic habent: Josephus misit & accersivit patrem suum, & omnem cognationem suam animarum septuaginta quinque. Vid. Critic. Sacr. pag. 746. &seqq. ut & Commentarium in Genesin ad c. XLVI. v. 27. Nostram sententiam laudat B. Joh. Ernest. Gerhard, analect. ad h. l. Nec non Clariss. An- glorum Polyhistor Joh. Seldenus l. II. de Synedr. pag. 409. qui eam accuratam, & ingeniosam vo- cat: ut & in Addendis ad pag. 148. l. 30. quamvis meum nomen non recte assignet, Calovium me appellans.

## 7:16
Vers. 16. And they were carried over into Sychem, and were laid in the sepulchre that Abraham bought for a sum of money of the sons of Emmor the son of Sychem) Both the Syriac and the Arabic teach us that those last words 'the son of Sychem' are wrongly added here. The meaning will be best if, for the word Emmor, you write the neighboring word Ephron. For it is from Ephron that Abraham bought the monument, Gen. ch. XXIII. 17. and in the same monument Jacob was buried: Gen. ch. L. v. 13. Joseph, however, was buried in Sychem: Jos. XXIV. v. 32. This, therefore, he says, that they, of whom he had spoken, were buried partly in Sychem, partly in the field which had been Ephron's. Jerome says in the Epitaph of Paula that the brothers of Joseph were buried in Sychem: but Joseph in that field which had been Ephron's, II. of ancient history IV. This passage provides us with an excellent reconciliation if we say that they were buried partly with Jacob, partly with Joseph, which is itself an argument that they had no fixed seat.

This Grotian correction is opposed by all the Greek Codices: whose authority ought to be sacred to us: For if that license to emend sacred codices is granted, what certainty will finally be left? Therefore, we cannot give our assent to others who feel that the name of Abraham was placed in the passage of Jacob by error, as Eugubinus does in Gen. ch. XXIII. and Masius in the last chapter of Joshua: even though from our own side the blessed Gesner and the blessed Rungius in Gen. XXXIII., as also the blessed Arcularius on this passage, have joined them: Jacob did not buy the field for a sepulchre, but for the use of an estate, nor did he acquire it for silver, which price Stephen names, but for a hundred lambs, Gen. XXIII. Therefore, it seems that the discourse in this passage is not about the purchase of Jacob, but of Abraham, which is commemorated in Gen. XXIII. 17.: for which reason also some prefer to insist on the opinion of Jerome in his Epistle to Pammachius on the best kind of interpreting, whom Gregory the Great followed in Epistle LV. Lyranus, Usiander on this passage, as also Bened. Pererius on Gen. XXIII. Disp. II. [argue] that indeed the father of Ephron was called by another name, Hemor, and his father was named Sychem: and thus it is not the history of Gen. XXXIII. that is being referred to, but that which stands described in ch. XXIII.; even though in that one those names Hemor and Sychem likewise recur: provided that under those names different persons are insinuated there in the history of Jacob in the purchase of the same estate; but others in the history of Abraham made here, in the purchase of the sepulchre. Therefore, according to this opinion, the father of Ephron was binominal, called Seor by Moses, and Hemor by Stephen: whose father's name, although Moses did not report it, Stephen nevertheless expressed here, that he was indeed called Sychem. Thus, therefore, the reconciliation of Joseph with Jerome handed down by Grotius can be left in place, that indeed a part of the brothers of Joseph were buried there where Joseph was, and a part in the field which Abraham bought from Ephron: provided that the received reading in this passage remains without prejudice, that this purchase was made from the sons of Emmor the son of Sychem, so that both are indicated by Stephen: that some were carried over into Sychem, where Joseph was then buried; but others were laid in the field acquired from the sons of Emmor (who is also called Seor), the son of Sychem, in the sepulchre of Abraham and Jacob: Therefore Emmor is not the same as Ephron, but the father of Ephron: who had several sons, since 'of the sons'

of Emmor, Stephen makes mention of the sons of Emmor, among whom, however, Moses commemorates Ephron as the chief, Gen. XXIII.

If, however, anyone should prefer the observation of Ludovicus de Dieu, since there is no article prefixed to the name Abraham, and it can be taken in another case just as well as the nominative, that the purchase was attributed by Stephen to Jacob and not to Abraham, yet that it is said to have been made for Abraham, there will be no need for that subtle interpretation that it was bought for Abraham himself as a pledge of the inheritance of the whole land promised to him: for it can be said more simply, for Abraham, that is, for the sake of Abraham, so that indeed the Patriarch Jacob may be said to have bought a certain estate in the land of Canaan, not indeed for Abraham, who had already died and was buried in the field of Ephron, but for the sake of Abraham, to whom the promise of that land was first made by God: just as Joseph, when he wished to be buried there, made mention of that promise, confirmed by an oath from God to Abraham, Gen. L. 24. By which method it will be confirmed from the words of Stephen what Jerome observed in the Epitaph of Paula, that the brothers of Joseph were buried in Sychem: that indeed they were carried to Sychem by their descendants who were already taking possession of the inheritance of the land. Finally, that same Ludovicus brings forward yet another explanation, with Cajetan leading the way, that the words 'from the sons of Emmor the son of Sychem' are to be construed not with the verb 'bought', but with the preceding 'were laid': in this sense; that the bodies of the deceased Patriarchs were first carried over into Sychem, into the estate of Jacob, and placed before the sons of Emmor the son of Sychem, so that with their help they might be transferred into the monument bought by Abraham, and thus were laid in the monument bought by Abraham, by the sons of Emmor the son of Sychem. For when, says Dievius, that burial of the peoples who were still strangers and powerful in Canaan happened, and thus a danger could have been created for the Hebrews, with the corpses of their fathers unburied, by the Canaanite inhabitants, they very prudently betook themselves first to Shechem and not only requested the help of the sons of Hamor, but also, so that the whole matter might be carried out more safely, they entrusted the whole thing to them, so that they might complete this business as their own. He confirms this opinion with the authority of Josephus: from book II of the Antiquities, chapter IV. 'But his brothers also died, when they had lived happily: whose bodies indeed their descendants and sons buried in Hebron after some time: but they transported the bones of Joseph afterwards, when the Hebrews migrated from Egypt into Canaan.' But if this account of Josephus stands, if it is to be accepted concerning all the brothers, the tradition of Jerome will be wiped out. But the authority of both, namely Jerome and Josephus, will be perfectly consistent with itself if the first explanation is retained, and the father of Hamor is established as having two names along with certain fathers, nor will it be necessary to say either that the field was bought by Jacob for the sake of Abraham, or that the Patriarchs were buried and interred by the sons of Hamor in the field bought by Abraham.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Καὶ μετετέθησαν εἰς Συχὲμ, καὶ ἐτέθησαν ἐν τῷ μνήματι, ᾧ ὠνήσατο Ἀβραὰμ τιμῆς ἀργυρίου παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἐμ- μὸρ τοῦ Συχέμ) Postrema illa τοῦ Συχὲμ male hic adscripta docent nos & Syrus & Arabs. Optima erit sententia, si pro Ἐμμὸρ vicina voce scribas Ἐφρὼν. Ab Ephrone enim est quod monumentum emit Abrahamus, Genes. c. XXIII. 17. & in eodem monumento sepultus fuit Jacob: Gen. cap. L. v. 13. Josephus autem sepultus fuit in Si- chem: Jos. XXIV. v. 32. Hoc ergo dicit, eos, de quibus erat locutus, partim in Sichem, partim in agro, qui Ephro- nis fuerat, sepultos. Fratres Josephi in Sichem sepul- tos ait Hieronymus in Paulæ Epitaphio: at Josephus in illo, qui Ephronis fuerat, agro, II. antiquæ historiæ IV. Optimam conciliaturam nobis hic locus suppeditat, si di- camus partim eos cum Jacobo, partim cum Josepho se- pultos, quod ipsum argumentum est nullam eis certam fu- risse sedem.

Correctio hæc Grotiana refragatur omnibus Codicibus Græcis: quorum auctoritas nobis sa- cra esse debet: Nam si ea concedatur emen- dandi sacros codices licentia, quid tandem cer- ti relinquetur? ideo nec aliis assensum præbere possumus, qui loco Jacobi nomen Abrahami positum per errorem esse cum Eugubino in Gen. c. XXIII. & Masio in cap. ult. Josuæ sentiunt: etsi iisdem e nostris B. Gesnerus, & B. Rungius in Gen. XXXIII. ut & B. Arcularius in h. l. accesse- rint: Non emit Jacob agrum in sepulchrum, sed in usum prædii, nec pro argento, quod pretium Stephanus nominat, sed pro centum agnis com- paravit, Gen. XXIII. Idcirco non de Jacobi, sed Abrahami emtione sermo hoc loco esse videtur, quæ Gen. XXIII. 17. commemoratur: ob quam etiam causam insistere nonnulli malunt Hierony- mi sententiæ Epist. Cl. de optim. genere interpret. ad Pammach. quem sequutus est Gregorius M. Epist. LV. Lyranus, Usiander in h. l. ut & Bened. Pererius ad Gen. XXIII. Disp. II. quod nempe Ephronis Pater alio nomine dictus fuerit Hemor, hujusque Pater nominatus sit Sichem: adeoque non historia Gen. XXXIII. sed quæ cap. XXIII. descripta extat, respiciatur; etsi in illa nomina ista Hemor & Sichem itidem recurrant: siqui- dem sub illis nominibus ibi diversæ personæ in Jacobi historia insinuentur in emtione prædii ejus- dem; aliæ vero in bistoria Abrahami hic facta, in emtione sepulchri. Pater ergo Ephronis juxta hanc sententiam binominis fuit à Mose Seor, à Stephano Hemor dictus: Cujus Patris nomen, etsi Moses non retulerit, Stephanus tamen hic expsserit, quod nempe Sichem nuncupatus fu- erit. Ita ergo Josephi cum Hieronymo conci- liaturæ à Grotio traditæ, locus relinqui potest, quod nempe pars fratrum Josephi ibi tumulata sit, ubi Josephus, pars in agro, quem emit Abraham ab Ephrone: dummodo salva manet lectio recepta in hoc loco, à filiis Emmor τοῦ Συχὲμ emtionem hanc factam esse, ut utrumque indicetur à Stephano: alios in Sichem translatos, ubi Joseph sepultus deinde est; alios vero in agro à filiis Emmor (qui & Seor dictus) filii Sichemi comparato, in sepulchro Abrahami & Jacobi, conditos: Non ergo Emmor idem est, qui Ephron, sed Pater Ephro- nis: qui plures habuit filios, quum τῶν υἱῶν

Ἑμμὼρ filiorum Emmor mentionem Stephanus fa- ciat, inter quos vero Ephronem ceu præcipuum commemorat Moses Gen. XXIII.

Si tamen quis Ludovici de Dieu observationem præferre malit, quum nomini Abraham nullus præfixus articulus sit, idque in alio æque ac nomi- nativo casu accipi queat, Jacobo non Abrahamo hic tributam à Sephano emtionem esse, eam ta- men Abrahamo factam dici, non opus erit subtili illa interpretatione, quod Abrahamo ipsi ceu pi- gnus hæreditatis totius terræ eidem promissæ, emtus sit: simplicius enim dici poterit, Abrahamo, id est, Abrahami causâ, ut nempe Jacobus Patri- archa dicatur emisse prædium quoddam in terrâ Canaan, non quidem Abrahamo, qui jam diem suum obierat & in agro Ephronis sepultus erat, sed Abrahami causâ, cui illius terræ promissio à Deo primum facta: quemadmodum ejus promissionis, juramento à Deo Abrahamo firmatæ, etiam Jose- phus, cum illic sepeliri vellet, mentionem fecit Gen. L. 24. Quo pacto è verbis Stephani confirma- bitur, quod Hieronymus in Paulæ Epitaphio obser- vavit, fratres Josephi in Sichem sepultos esse: quod nempe à posteris hæreditatem terræ jam capientibus Sichemam translati sint. Postremo adfert Ludovi- cus ille adhuc aliam explicationem, præeunte Ca- jetano, quod verba ita παρὰ τῶν ὑιῶν Ἑμμὸῤ t̄ Σv- χὲμ non cum verbo ὠνήσατο, sed cum præcedenti ἐτέθησαν construenda sint: hoc sensu; quod trans- lata primum corpora Patriarcharum defunctorum in Sichem sint, in prædium Jacobi, & posita coram filiis Emmor filii Sichemi, ut eorum adjumento in monu- mentum ab Abrahamo emtum transferrentur, & ita posita in monumento, ab Abraham emto, sint, à filiis Emmor filii Sichemi. Cum enim, inquit Die- vius, rerum adhuc in Cánanaą polientibus peregri- nis populis inhumatio ea contigerit, adeoque pericu- lum Hebreis, Patrum suorum cadavera inhumatu- ris, creari à Cananæa incolis potuisset, prudenter ad- modum Sichemum se primum contulerunt filiorumque Emmor non modo opem postularunt, sed & quo tutius perageretur, rem totam ipsis commiserunt, ut nego- tium hoc tanquam suum conficerent. Quam senten- tiam Josephi autoritate firmat: è libr. II. Archæol. c. IV. Moriuntur vero & fratres ejus, quum feliciter vixissent : quorum quidem corpora post tempus ali- quod posteri eorum & filii Hebrone sepeliverunt: Jo- sephi autem ossa postmodum, quum ex Ægypto mi- grarunt Hebrei in Cananæam transportarunt. Hæc vero Josephi relatione stante, si de omnibus fratri- bus ea accipienda, Hieronymi traditio in spongiam incumbet. Utriusque autem Hieronymi nempe & Josephi autoritas constabit sibi probé, si prima ex- plicatio retineatur, & Pater Emmori διώνυμος cum Patribus quibusdam constituatur, neque opus erit dicere vel quod Abrahami causâ emtus à Jacobo ager sit, vel quod à filiis Hemor conditi & sepulti sint Patriarchæ in agro ab Abrahamo emto.

## 7:17
Verse 17. The time of the promise) The end of the years somewhat above four hundred. See Exodus XII. 40. — which God swore) Moses Maimonides says that every vehement affirmation of God is called an oath. Such is; know for certain, Gen. XV. 15. But that codex which is in England has here ὡμολόγησεν, just as the Latin also reads.

There is no reason why we should either take the word for swearing as a vehement affirmation, or read ὡμολόγησεν instead of ὤμοσεν; since we have the express oath of God made to Abraham, Gen. XXII. 16, of which a repeated mention occurs, Gen. XXVI. 3, Ps. CV. 9, Heb. ch. VI. 13, 17, 18, and indeed in such a way that it is manifest that the discourse is not about a vehement affirmation only, but about an oath properly so called, which the Apostolic passage most explicitly teaches.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ὁ χρόνος τῆς ἐπαγγελίας) Finis annorum aliquan- to supra quadringentos. Vide Exodi XII. 40. -- ἧς ὤμοσεν ὁ Θεός) Omnem vehementem Dei affirmatio- nem juramentum dici ait Moses Maimonides. Tale est; cir- to cognosce, Gen. XV. 15. At codex ille, qui in Anglia, hic habet ὡμολόγησεν, quomodo legit & Latinus.

Non est, quod vel jurandi verbum de vehementi affirmatione accipiamus, vel loco ὤμοσεν ὡμολό- γησεν legamus; quum expressum habeamus Dei juramentum Abrahamo factum, Gen. XXII. 16. cu- jus iterata mentio occurrit, Gen. XXVI. 3. Ps. CV. 9. Ebr. c. VI. 13.17. 18. & ita quidem, ut manifestum sit, non de vehementi tantum affirmatione, sed de ju- ramento proprie dicto sermonem esse, quod locus Apostolicus disertissime docet.

## 7:18
Vers. 18. There arose another king, who knew not Joseph) These are the words of the LXX interpreters, Exodus I. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἀνέστη βασιλεὺς ἕτερος, ὃς οὐκ ᾔδει τὸν Ἰωσήφ) Verba sunt LXX. interpretum, Exodi I. 8.

## 7:19
Vers. 19. Dealing craftily with our race), Thus the LXX, Ex. I. 10. let us deal craftily with them, where in the Hebrew it is נתחכמה לו, let us act prudently against them. Moreover, this word also pertains to the labors imposed upon them, as history shows, and Judith c. V. 9. they dealt craftily with them in toil and in brick. You have the same sense in the same history, Ps. CV. 24. להתנכל בעבדיו where the Greeks: to deal deceitfully with his servants. Ezechiel the Tragedian: King Pharaoh devised much craft against us; afflicting mortals with brick-making and heavy buildings, and he built cities for their sake, the wretches. Then he proclaims to the race of the Hebrews to cast their males into the deep stream of the river. Thus concerning Antiochus, Daniel VIII. 20. understanding riddles. to make their infants exposed) So that they themselves were forced to expose their male infants, so that they might not be killed by the royal guards. This sense is suggested to us by the same word ἐκτιθέντα, which is repeated shortly after in 21. to the end that they might not live) This refers to that he afflicted. It was Pharaoh's purpose to extinguish the race. The Hellenists use ζωογονεῖν for to leave alive, החיה, as can be seen in Jud. VIII. 18. 1 Sam. II. 6. XXVII. 9. 11. 2 Kings VII. 4. here it refers to the whole race. For with the infants killed or dispersed, it was necessary for the race to perish. The opposite of this is Exodus c. II. v. 17. concerning the midwives ותחיין הילדים where in the Greek, and they kept the males alive.

Latin:

Vers. 19. κατασοφισάμενος τὸ γένος ἡμῶν), Sic LXX. Ex. I. 10. κατασοφισώμεθα αὐτοὺς, ubi in Hebræo נתחכמה לו, prudenter adversus eos agamus. Pertinet autem hæc vox etiam ad labores eis impositos, ut historia ostendit, & Ju- dith. c. V. 9. κατεσοφίσαντο αὐτοὺς ἐν πόνῳ καὶ ἐν πλίνθῳ. Eun- dem sensum in eadem historia habes, Ps. CV. 24. להתנכל בעבדיו ubi Græci: τοῦ δολιοῦσθαι ἐν τοῖς δούλοις αὐτοῦ. Ezechiel Tragicus: Δόλοισι καθ' ἡμῶν πολὺν ἐμηχανήσατο Βασιλεὺς Φαραώ· τοὺς μὲν ἐν πλινθεύμασιν, Οἰκοδομίαις τε βάρεσιν αἰκίζων βροτοὺς Πόλεις τ' ἐπύργου σφῶν ἕκατι δυσμόρων. Ἔπειτα κηρύσσει μὲν Ἑβραίων γένει Τ' ἄρσενικὰ ῥίπτειν ποταμοῦ εἰς βαθὺ ῥόον. Sic de Antiocho Daniel VIII. 20. συνίων προβλήματα. τοῦ ποιεῖν ἔκθετα τὰ βρέφη αὐτῶν) Ita ut ipsi cogerentur exponere infantes suos mares, ne à regiis satellitibus inter- ficerentur. Hunc sensum suggerit nobis vox eadem ἐκτι- θέντα, quæ repetitur mox 21. εἰς τὸ μὴ ζωογονεῖσθαι) Hoc refertur ad illud ἐκάκωσε. Pro- positum Pharaonis erat gentem extinguere. Ζωογονεῖν Hel- lenistæ usurpant pro in vita relinquere, החיה, ut videre est Jud. VIII. 18. 1 Sam. II. 6. XXVII. 9. 11. 2. Regum VII. 4. id hic ad totam gentem refertur. Nam interemptis aut disper- sis infantibus, necesse erat gentem perire. Contrarium hu- jus est Exodi c. II. v. 17. de obstetricibus ותחיין הילדים ubi in Græco, καὶ ἐζωογόνουν τὰ ἄρσενα.

## 7:20
Vers. 20. And he was fair to God) That ἀστεῖος is from the Greek of Exodus II. 2. where in the Hebrew it is טוב. That to God, which is added here, is a Hebraism לאלהים, that is, exceedingly. Thus: Nineveh was a great city to God, Jon. III. 3. thus also in the genitive נפתולי אלהים נפתלתי Gen. XXX. 8. thus cedars of God, and the like.

Latin:

Vers. 20. καὶ ἦν ἀστεῖος τῷ Θεῷ) Illud ἀστεῖος est ex Græ- co Exodi II. 2. ubi in Hebræo טוב. Illud τῷ Θεῷ, quod hic additur, est Hebraismus לאלהים, id est, valde. Sic: Νινευὴ ἦν πόλις μεγάλη τῷ Θεῷ, Jon. III. 3. sic & in Geniti- vo נפתולי אלהים נפתלתי Gen. XXX. 8. sic cedri Dei, & similia.

## 7:21
Vers. 21. And when he was exposed) Better in the manuscript: and when he was exposed, because of what follows. he took him up) Terence: Whatever she had brought forth, they decreed to take up. that is, not to suffer to perish. she brought him up for herself as a son) Exodus II. 10. Heb. XI. v. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ἐκτεθέντα δὲ αὐτὸν) Melius Manuscriptus: ἐκ- τεθέντος δὲ αὐτοῦ, ob id, quod sequitur. ἀνείλετο αὐτὸν) Terentius: Quicquid peperisset decreverunt, tollere. id est, non pati interire. ἀνεθρέψατο αὐτὸν ἑαυτῇ εἰς υἱὸν) Exodi II. 10. Hebr. XI. v. 4.

## 7:22
Vers. 22. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians) He did not write this about Moses: but the thing is credible in itself and confirmed by tradition, Ezechiel the Tragedian: He obtained all royal nourishment and instruction as if from the bowels of the earth. Certainly, skill in astrology and medicine appears everywhere in his laws. What the disciplines of the Egyptians were, can be learned from Clement of Alexandria, Strom. VI. Add the question to the Orthodox XXV. Although Moses did not write this about himself, we do not need to recur to tradition, nor is his wisdom to be estimated solely from the Mosaic laws, just as Grotius says that this is confirmed by tradition, and that skill in astrology and medicine appears everywhere in the laws of Moses: for he received wisdom and knowledge from the Holy Spirit, and by His inspiration he not only recorded the laws, but wrote everything that is read in his books. Therefore, those things have this author and teacher, not Egyptian masters, even if for the rest he was informed in Egypt regarding all wisdom by royal tutors. But what they had received from the Hebrews themselves and among these from the instruction of Joseph, Ps. CVI. 21. For wisdom did not pass first from the Egyptians to the Hebrews, but vice versa from the Hebrews to the Egyptians: which the Hebrews had from the Patriarchs of the later world, and these from Noah and other Patriarchs of the earlier world. That mathematical sciences flourished especially in Egypt is evident from Philo, book I. on the life of Moses, and Diodorus Siculus, book I.

Latin:

Vers. 22. καὶ ἐπαιδεύθη Μωσῆς πάσῃ σοφίᾳ Αἰγυπτίων) Non scripsit hoc de Moses: sed res per se est credibilis & traditione firmata, Ezechiel Tragicus: Τροφαῖσι βασιλικαῖσι καὶ παιδεύμασιν Ἅπαντ' ἐτύγχαν' ὡς ἀπὸ σπλάγχνων ἰῶν. Certe Astrologiæ & Medicinæ peritia passim in ejus legibus apparet. Quæ fuerint Ægyptiorum disciplinæ, discere est ex Clemente Alexandrino Strom. VI. Adde quæstionem ad Orthodoxos XXV. Etsi Moses hoc de se non scripserit, non tamen ad traditionem opus habemus recurrere, vel è le- gibus Mosaicis ejus sapientia solum æstimanda, quemadmodum Grotius è traditione hoc firmari, Astrologiæ etiam ac Medicinæ peritiam passim in legi- bus Mosis apparere, ait: nam à Spiritu S. acce- pit σόμα & Cοφίαν, ejusque inspiratione non leges tantum consignavit, sed scripsit omnia, quæ in li- bris ejus leguntur. Hunc ergo autorem & do- ctorem illa habent, non Ægyptiacos magistros, etsi de cætero quoad omnem sapientiam in Ægypto à præceptoribus regiis informatus fuerit. Quam vero illi ab ipsis Ebræis & inter hos è Josephi insti- tutione acceperant, Ps. CVI. 21 Non enim ab Ægy- ptiis ad Ebræos primum transiit sapientia, sed vice versa ab Ebræis ad Ægyptios: quam Ebræi à Patri- archis posterioris orbis, hi à Noah, & aliis prioris mundi Patriarchis habuere. Floruisse autem im- primis Mathematicas scientias in Ægypto è Philone lib. I. de vit. Mosis & Diodor. Siculo l. I. constat.

## 7:23
Vers. 23. And when a period of forty years was being fulfilled to him) This is not in the Holy Scripture, but is drawn from tradition, which is found in Midrash Rabba Bereshith. How many years Moses had when he killed the Egyptian, that Stephen drew from Jewish tradition, whence was it proved? Could not the Holy Spirit have suggested it to him without tradition? But it is likely that what is read in the Midrash flowed to the Christians from this account of Stephen.

Latin:

Vers. 23. ὡς δὲ ἐπληροῦτο αὐτῷ τεσσαρακονταετὴς χρόνος) Hoc non est in sacra scriptura, sed haustum est ex traditio- ne, quæ reperitur in Midrasch Rabba Bereschith. Quot annos habuerit Moses, cum Ægyptium interfecit, ex traditione Judaica Stephanum hau- sisse, unde probabatur? annon ea Spiritus S. ipsi suggerere potuit citra traditionem? Quæ vero in Midrasch leguntur, à Christianis ex hac Stephani relatione redundasse, verisimile est.

## 7:24
Ver. 24. And seeing one being wronged) Treated harshly with blows.

he defended) He protected the innocent.

having struck the Egyptian) Even to death, as appears below 28. The law of nature gives the right to the innocent, and to him who protects the innocent, against the guilty. See what we have said in book II. of the Law of War and Peace, 1. 6. and 10.

It is certain that Moses killed this Egyptian: however, the law of nature does not grant to an innocent person, or to one protecting an innocent person, the power of killing a guilty person, unless the moderation of blameless defense is observed: which some also posit here in the deed of Moses, with Ambrose, lib. 1. Offic. cap. 36, Paul of Burgos on Ex. II, Lipomanus in the Catena, and Thomas Aquinas, l. 2. q. 60. art. 6. ad 2. Others, however, think that Moses exceeded the limits of just defense, even if drawn by an affection of pity, such as B. Franzius against Smalc. disp. X. §. 74, which was also the opinion of Augustine, l. XXII. against Faustus the Manichaean, c. 70, but deservedly corrected and changed by him later, quæst. II. in Exod. For even from this passage we learn that it was not without divine instinct and from the consciousness of his calling to liberate his brothers that Moses performed this ἐκδίκησιν, as Stephen calls it: for he supposed that his brothers understood that GOD would give salvation to them by his hand: but they did not understand. Compare what we said on Exod. II.

Latin:

Ver. 24. καὶ ἰδών τινα ἀδικούμενον) Dure tractatum verberibus.

ἠμύνατο) Tutatus est innocentem.

πατάξας τὸν Αἰγύπτιον) Ad mortem usque, ut apparet infra 28. jus naturæ & innocenti, & innocentem tutanti, jus dat adversus nocentem. Vide, quæ diximus libro II. de Ju- re Belli ac Pacis, 1. 6. & 10.

Plane interfecisse Mosen hunc Ægyptium cer- tum est: non autem jus naturæ concedit innocenti, aut innocentem tutanti potestatem nocentem in- terficiendi, nisi moderamen inculpatæ tutelæ serve- tur: quod etiam hic ponunt nonnulli in Mosis fa- cto cum Ambrosio lib. 1. Offic. cap. 36. Paulo Burgenfi ad Ex. II. Lipomano in Catena, & Thoma de Aqui- no l. 2. q. 60. art. 6. ad 2. Alii vero excessisse justæ defensionis limites Mosen putant, etsi com- miserationis affectu tractum, utpote B. Franzius contra Smalc. disp. X. §. 74. quæ etiam Augustini sententia fuit, l. XXII. contra Faustum Manich. c. 70. sed merito ab eodem postea correcta & mutata, quæst. II. in Exod. Nam vel ex hoc loco discimus, non absque divino instinctu, & ex con- scientia vocationis suæ ad liberandos fratres Mo- sen hanc ἐκδίκησιν, ut vocat Stephanus, fecisse: existimabat enim intelligere fratres, quoniam DEUS per manum ipsius daret salutem illis: at illi non intellexerunt. Conf. quæ ad Exod. II. di- ximus.

## 7:25
Vers. 25. ἐνόμιζε δὲ συνιέναι τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς ἀυτοῦ) From his own prompt spirit to protect them.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἐνόμιζε δὲ συνιέναι τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς ἀυτοῦ) Ex tam prompto ipsius animo ad eos tutandos.

## 7:26
Vers. 26. μαχομένοις) The Seventy Elders have διαπληκτιζομένοις here. In the Hebrew נצים, which is also translated elsewhere as μάχεσθαι, as in Exodus XXI. 22, Leviticus XXIV. 10, Deuteronomy XXV. 2, 2 Samuel XIV. 6.

καὶ συνήλασεν ἀυτούς) The name of the effect is given to the attempt. Then the word, as if signifying force, signifies the agent's insistence, as ἀναγκάζειν in Luke XIV. 23 and παραβιάζεσθαι in Luke c. XXIV. 28.

εἰπών) He did not put the very words which are in Exodus, but he expressed the sense well. For there it is ὁ πλησίον, who here is ὁ διάφορος, a fellow countryman: born of the same ancestors.

Latin:

Vers. 26. μαχομένοις) διαπληκτιζομένοις habent hic LXX. Senes. In Hebræo נצים, quod & alibi per μά- χησθαι vertitur, ut Exodi XXI. 22. Levit. XXIV. 10. Deut. XXV. 2. 2. Sam. XIV. 6.

καὶ συνήλασεν ἀυτούς) Conatui datur nomen effectus. Deinde vox quasi vim significans agentis instantiam signi- ficat, ut ἀναγκάζειν Luc. XIV. 23. & παραβιάζεσθαι Luc. c. XXIV. 28.

εἰπών) Non ipsa verba posuit, quæ sunt in Exodo, sed sensum bene expressit. Nam ibi ὁ πλησίον, qui hic ὁ διαφόρ popularis: eisdem ortus majoribus.

## 7:27
Vers. 27. ὁ δὲ ἀδικῶν) Thus also the Seventy translated the Hebrew רשע in this history. In the Gospel, it is said in the same sense ὁ πονηρὸς, he who does an injury: ὁ ἀδικήσας ἐν χερσὶν ἀδίκως, as the Greeks speak. See book I. de Jure Belli ac Pacis II. 18.

τίς σε κατέστησεν ἄρχοντα, καὶ δικαστὴν ἐφ' ἡμᾶς) The words are the same in the version of the Seventy, except that there it is ἐφ' ἡμῶν, with the same sense.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ὁ δὲ ἀδικῶν) Sic & LXX. verterunt in hac historia Hebræum רשע. In Evangelio eodem sensu dicitur ὁ πονηρὸς, is qui injuriam facit: ὁ ἀδικήσας ἐν χερσὶν ἀδίκως, ut Græci loquuntur. Vide libro I. de Jure Belli ac Pacis II. 18.

τίς σε κατέστησεν ἄρχοντα, καὶ δικαστὴν ἐφ' ἡμᾶς) Eadem verba sunt in versione LXX. nisi quod ibi est ἐφ' ἡμῶν, sensu eodem.

## 7:29
Vers. 29. ἔφυγε δὲ Μωϋσῆς) Namely, understanding well that that slaughter of the Egyptian would create trouble for him, because the Egyptians held the Hebrews in the place of servants, or rather of cattle, against whom they did not want it to be believed that any injury could be committed.

ἐν γῇ Μαδιάμ) He always urges the purpose. God, just as in Mesopotamia and Egypt, so also in the land of Midian, was present with the pious. He is the same everywhere.

Latin:

Vers. 29. ἔφυγε δὲ Μωϋσῆς) Nempe satis intelligens cæ- dem illam Ægypti malum sibi creaturam, quod Ægyptii Ebræos servorum, imo pecudum haberent loco, in quos nullam cadere injuriam credi volebant.

ἐν γῇ Μαδιάμ) Semper urget propositum. Deus sicut in Mesopotamia & Ægypto ita & in terra Madianis adfuit piis. Est ubique idem.

## 7:30
Vers. 30. καὶ πληρωθέντων ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα) And this is from tradition.

Ἄγγελος Κυρίου) Truly an Angel: but instructed with divine commands and extraordinary power. See what we said at the beginning of the Decalogue.

That the Angel who appeared to Moses in the cloud was not created, but uncreated, we have shown with invincible proofs in Theolog. natur. & revel., as also in the annotations to Exod. ch. III. and T. IV. Syst. Theol., and we have asserted this against the Jews and Socinians no less than against Grotius and others who agree with them. Let those things be seen there. He who appeared to Moses testifies with a resounding voice that his name is Ehjeh Ascher Ehjeh, which befits none but God alone; he is taught by the proper and essential name of God, Jehovah; he is described as the true God by divine attributes, works, and axioms. Who, therefore, can doubt that he is the same true God?

ἐν φλογὶ πυρὸς) That manuscript, πυρὸς φλογὸς, as the Latin reads, both φλὸξ πυρὸς and πῦρ φλογὸς 2 Thess. I. 8. is flaming fire.

Latin:

Vers. 30. καὶ πληρωθέντων ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα) Et hoc est ex traditione.

Ἄγγελος Κυρίου) Vere Angelus: sed divinis mandatis, & extraordinaria potestate instructus. Vide, quæ diximus ad initium Decalogi.

Non creatum, sed increatum fuisse Angelum, qui Mosi in nube apparuit, in Theolog. natur. & revel. ut & annot. ad Exod. c. III. & T. IV. Syst. Theol. invictis documentis ostendimus, & adver- sus Judæos ac Socinianos non minus quam Grotium, aliosque ipsis astipulantes asseruimus. Quæ illic videantur. Testatur is, qui Mosi apparuit so- nora voce: quod nomen ipsi sit Ehjeh Ascher Ehjeh, quod nonnisi soli Deo convenit, docatur nomine Dei proprio & essentiali Jehovah, descri- bitur ceu verus Deus ab attributis, operibus & axiomasi divinis. Qui ergo dubium esse potest, eundem verum Deum esse?

ἐν φλογὶ πυρὸς) Manuscriptus ille, πυρὸς φλογὸς, quomo- do legit Latinus, tam φλὸξ πυρὸς, quam πῦρ φλογὸς 2. Thess. I. 8. est ignis flammans.

## 7:31
Vers. 31. ἐθαύμασε τὸ ὄραμα) He briefly signifies what he does not express, that the bush burned, yet was not consumed, which was an image of the Hebrew people who would be survivors in the greatest calamities.

ἐγένετο φωνὴ κυρίυ πρὸς ἀυτὸν) Here too there is some inversion of order, but it pertains nothing to the sum of the matter. For in Exodus Moses is commanded to loosen his sandals before God says to him that He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Latin:

Vers. 31. ἐθαύμασε τὸ ὄραμα) Breviter significat, quod non exprimit, rubum arsisse, nec ustum tamen, quæ imago erat populi Hebræi in summis calamitatibus futuri superstitis.

ἐγένετο φωνὴ κυρίυ πρὸς ἀυτὸν) Hic quoque est aliqua or- dinis inversio, sed ad summam rei nihil pertinens. Nam in Exodo Moses prius jubetur calceos solvere, quam Deus ei dicit, se Deum esse Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi.

## 7:32
Vers. 32. ὁυκ ἐτόλμα κατανοῆσαι) That is, to inspect, as it is in the Hebrew of Exodus, where the Greeks have κατεμβλέψαι. But κατανοεῖν is often used in the same sense for the word נבט, which is here in the Hebrew, as in Exodus 33. 8, Ps. 10. 14, Ps. 22. 19, Ps. 91. 8, Ps. 94. 9, Ps. 119. 15, 18, Ps. 142. 5; in a similar way in Exodus 19. 21 לראות is translated in the Greek as κατανοῆσαι. Naturally, words for internal and external senses are accustomed to be interchanged.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ὁυκ ἐτόλμα κατανοῆσαι) Id est, inspicere, ut est in Hebræo Exodi, ubi Græci κατεμβλέψαι. Sed κατανοεῖν eo- dẽ sensu, pro verbo נבט, quod hic in Hebræo est, sæpe po- nitur, ut Exodi 33. 8. Ps. 10. 14. Ps. 22. 19. Ps. 91. 8. Ps. 94. 9. Ps. 119. 15. 18. Ps. 142. 5. simili modo Exodi 19. 21. לראות in Græco vertitur κατανοῆσαι. Nimirum sensuum interno- rum & externorum vocabula inter se commutari solent.

## 7:33
Vers. 33. λύσον τὸ ὑπόδημα) See what we have brought to this passage of Exodus.

Latin:

Vers. 33. λύσον τὸ ὑπόδημα) Vide, quæ ad hunc Exodi lo- cum attulimus.

## 7:34
Vers. 34. ἰδὼν εἶδον τὴν κάκωσιν τῶ λαῶ με τῦ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ) The same words are in the Greek of the LXX. Seeing I have seen, that is, I have thoroughly perceived.

κὴ τῦ στεναγμῦ αὐτῶν ἤκουσα) In the version of the LXX it is τῦς στεναγμῦς. הנאקת is generally translated κραυγὴ: but in Job XXVII. 9, ὀδύνης.

κὴ κατέβην ἐξελέσθαι αὐτὺς) This also is from the version of the seventy. God is said to descend where He either protects His own or avenges Himself on enemies: to ascend where He ceases to do so.

κὴ νῦν δεῦρο) So it is also in the Greek of the LXX; in the Hebrew לכה, that is, come now.

Latin:

Vers. 34. ἰδὼν εἶδον τὴν κάκωσιν τῶ λαῶ με τῦ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ) Eadem verba sunt in Græco LXX. sidens vide, id est, peni- tus pervidi.

κὴ τῦ στεναγμῦ αὐτῶν ἤκουσα) In versione LXX. est τῦς stevo- γμῦς. הנאקת plerumque κραυγὴ vertitur: at Jobi XXVII. 9. ὀδύνης.

κὴ κατέβην ἐξελέσθαι αὐτὺς) Hoc quoque ex versione LXX. senum. Dicitur Deus descendere, ubi aut protegit suos, aut hostes ulciscitur: adscendere, ubi id facere definit.

κὴ νῦν δεῦρο) Sic quoque est in Græco LXX. in Hebræo לכה, id est, adesdum.

## 7:35
Vers. 35. ὃν ἠρνήσαντο) Whom they refused to acknowledge. See above 3. 13.

καὶ λυτρωτὴν) גאל is accustomed to be translated by this word, and it is used both of men and of God, even when He delivers someone with no price accepted, as can be seen in Ps. XIX. 15, Ps. LXXVIII. 35. Nor will the metaphor be harsher if you call it redeemer in Latin in this sense, than if you call it λυτρωτὴν in Greek, which comes ἀπὸ τῦ λύτρου. Naturally, for the elegance of a translation, an equal effect suffices.

ἐν χειρὶ Ἀγγέλου) This is to be referred to ἀπέσειλεν: He gave commands to him through an Angel.

Latin:

Vers. 35. ὃν ἠρνήσαντο) Quem noluerunt agnoscere. Vi- de supra 3. 13.

καὶ λυτρωτὴν) גאל hac voce verti solet, usurpaturque & de hominibus & de Deo, etiam cum nullo pretio accepto aliquem liberat, ut videre est Ps. XIX. 15. Ps. LXXVIII. 35. Nec durior erit metaphora, si Latine redemtorem hoc sen- su dicas, quam si Græce λυτρωτὴν, quod venit ἀπὸ τῦ λύτρου. Nimirum ad translationis elegantiam sufficit par effectus.

ἐν χειρὶ Ἀγγέλου) Hoc referendum est ad ἀπέσειλεν: man- data ei per Angelum dedit.

## 7:36
Vers. 36. He brought them out) He proclaims his late benefits, which Moses performed for the people, and the honors which he received from God, so that the contumacy of the people against him might be the more shameful, and it is less of a wonder if, born of such parents, they were ungrateful and savage toward Jesus.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ὗτος ἐξήγαγεν αὐτὺς) Late prædicat & benefi- cia, quæ Moses populo præstitit, & honores, quos à Deo ac- cepit, ut eo turpior sit populi in ipsum contumacia, minus- que mirum, si talibus orti parentibus, in Jesum ingrati & immanes fuerint.

## 7:37
Vers. 37. He who said to the sons of Israel. The Lord will raise up a prophet for you) He commended Jesus to you, with words that indeed pertain to other prophets to some extent, but pertain especially to Jesus. See what has been said on the passage of Deuteronomy, and what is above in chapter III. 22.

Let our remarks opposed to Grotius on chapter XIII of Deuteronomy also be seen. The discourse there is not about prophets in general, but about that great Prophet so called by way of excellence, and indeed according to the literal sense of the prophecy.

Latin:

Vers. 37. ὁ εἰπὼν τοῖς ὑἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ. Προφήτην ὑμῖν ἀνασήσει κύ- ριος) Ille vobis Jesum commendavit, verbis ad prophetas quidem alios aliquatenus, sed ad Jesum eximiè pertinenti- bus. Vide, quæ ad locum Deuteronomii dicta, & quæ su- pra c. III. 22.

Videantur & nostra Grotio ad Deut. XIII. cap. opposita. Non de Prophetis communiter, sed de magno illo Propheta κατ’ ἐξαίρετον λόγον ita dicto sermo ibi est, & quidem secundum literalem vati- cinii sensum.

## 7:38
Vers. 38. This is he who was in the church in the wilderness) Who was present with the Israelite people in all that very difficult journey, which is קהל in Hebrew, and ἐκκλησία in Greek.

with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai) Namely, in the name and by the special command of God. See what we have said at the beginning of the Decalogue.

The law was not promulgated through a created angel. For God himself promulgated it directly, as Moses testifies. Concerning which, see [my notes] on Exodus XIX and in Theol. nat. & revel. p. 377 et seqq.

who received the living word) Reference is made to the passage in Deut. XXXII. 47, where the law is said to be life, that is, the cause of a happy life, which is especially life to the Hebrews. Here ζῶντα is ζωοποιῦντα: just as βασιλεύον means to make to reign. This is frequent among the Hellenists.

We admit this, if it is understood of eternal life: but not in the Pelagian-Socinian sense, from which Grotius is not far removed, concerning the life of this age. For the law in itself is the word of life, when it is kept: that it cannot quicken us now after the fall, is not the fault of the law, but our own: because we are unable to fulfill the law. Conf. Luke X. 28.

Latin:

Vers. 38. ὗτός ἐstιν ὁ γενόμενος ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) Qui in omni isto perdifficili itinere adfuit populo Israeliti- co, qui קהל Hebraice, Græce ἐκκλησία.

μετὰ τῦ ἀγγέλου τῦ λαλῦντος αὐτῷ ἐν τῷ ὄρει Σινᾷ) Nempe Dei nomine & mandato speciali. Vide, quæ diximus ad ini- tium Decalogi.

Non per angelum creatum lex est promulgata. Nam Deus ipse ἀμέσως eandem promulgavit, te- ste Mose. De quo ad Exod. XIX. & in Theol. nat. & revel. p. 377. seqq.

ὃς ἐδέξατο λόγον ζῶντα) Respicitur locus Deut. XXXII. 47. ubi lex dicitur esse vita, id est, causa vitæ felicis, quæ eximie vita Hebræis. Hic ζῶντα est ζωοποιῦντα: sicut βασιλεύον fa- cere regnare. Frequens hoc Hellenistis.

Admittimus hoc, si de vita æterna intelligatur: non vero sensu Pelagio-Sociniano, à quo non abest Grotius, de vita hujus seculi. Nam lex per se ver- bum vitæ est, cum servatur: quod autem nos vivi- ficáre nunc post lapsum nequear, non culpa legis sit, sed nostra: quod legem implere nos nequea- mus. Conf. Luc. X. 28.

## 7:39
Vers. 39. And they turned in their hearts to Egypt) They returned to the customs which they had learned in Egypt.

Latin:

Vers. 39. καὶ ἐσράφησαν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν εἰς Αἴγυπτον) Rediere ad mores, quos in Ægypto didicerant.

## 7:40
Vers. 40. Make for us gods) The Egyptians, as we learn from Iamblichus and others, established degrees of gods: and through lesser gods, even greater ones were drawn into images: therefore the plural is used here and in Exodus.

V. 40. Who shall go before us) Who may show us the way and make it prosperous.

For this Moses, who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him) It is a Hebrew idiom, for τῷ γὰρ Μω- σῇ τούτῳ ἐκ οἴδαμεν τί γέγονε. So also in the LXX version, but there it is more, Μωϋσῆς ὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, and in the Hebrew משה האיש: as if they were saying: we do not want a mortal leader: we want an immortal one.

Latin:

Vers. 40. ποίησον ἡμῖν Θεὺς) Ægyptii, ut ex Jamblicho & aliis discimus, statuebant Deorum gradus: & per minores Deos etiam majores attrahi in simulacra: ideo pluralis po- nitur hic & in Exodo.

V. 40. οἳ προπορεύσονται ἡμῶν) Qui nobis iter monstrent ac prosperent.

ὁ γὰρ Μωϋσῆς ὗτος, ὃς ἐξήγαγεν ἡμᾶς ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου, ἐκ οἴ- δαμεν τί γέγονεν αὐτῷ) Est Hebraica locutio, pro τῷ γὰρ Μω- σῇ τούτῳ ἐκ οἴδαμεν τί γέγονε. Sic & in versione LXX, sed ibi amplius est Μωϋσῆς ὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, & in Hebræo משה האיש: quasi dicerent: mortalem ducem nolu- mus: immortalem volumus.

## 7:41
Vers. 41. ἐμοσχοποίησαν) Luke coined this word after the example of many which the LXX coined in that manner. It corresponds to the two Hebrew words עשו עגל, they made a calf, in imitation of the Egyptians: among whom the calf is very ancient. See Tacitus, Histories V, and Herodotus, book II.

τῷ εἰδώλῳ) To that molten calf, as if into it divine spirits had been drawn.

That was the persuasion of the Egyptians, that divine powers are drawn into idols. That the Hebrews had that intention here does not appear from history, Exod. XXXII. Rather, in the golden calf they were worshipping the God who had led them out of Egypt: and in that their idolatry consisted. For this too is a species of idolatry, when God is worshipped with a cult other than what He prescribed in His word, or certainly when He is worshipped in idols, which He expressly prohibited in the first commandment. You shall not make for yourself a carved image or likeness to bow yourself down before it, Deut. V. 8. 9.

καὶ εὐφραίνοντο ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις τῶν χειρῶν αὐτῶν) They rejoiced on account of that thing. ויפרו לצחק, they rose up to play, Exod. XXXII, 7.

Latin:

Vers. 41. ἐμοσχοποίησαν) Hanc vocem Lucas confinxit ad exemplum multarum quas ad eum modum finxere LXX. Respondet Hebræis duabus עשו עגל fecere autē juven- cum ad imitationem Ægyptiorum: apud quos不出 tus valde est vetus, Vide Tacitum historiarum V. & He- rodotum libro II.

τῷ εἰδώλῳ) Isti juvenco fusili, tanquam in quem deducti essent divini spiritus.

Ægyptiorum illa fuit persuasio, quod in idola Numina attrahantur. Ebræis eam hic mentem fuisse ex historia non apparet, Exod. XXXII. In vi- tulo potius aureo ipsi adorabant Deum, qui eos e- duxerat ex Ægypto: Et in eo consistebat ipsorum idololatria. Nam & hæc idololatriæ est species, cum Deus cultu alio, quam præscripsit in verbo suo, colitur, vel certe cum in idolis adoratur, quod diserte in primo præcepto ipse prohibuit. Non facies tibi sculptile vel imaginem ad incurvandum te coram illa, Deut. V. 8. 9.

καὶ εὐφραίνοντο ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις τῶν χειρῶν αὐτῶν) Lætifalta- runt ejus rei causa. ויפרו לצחק ἀνέστησαν παίζειν, Exod. XXXII, 7.

## 7:42
Vers. 42. ἔστρεψε δὲ ὁ Θεὸς) Turning away from them. Just as Virgil said: Aversa dea mens. And it is an active verb for a reciprocal one.

παρέδωκεν αὐτὲς λατρεύειν τῇ στρατιᾷ τῷ ὐρανῶ) He permitted them to slip from one evil cult into another: and to prostrate themselves not to one or another, but to many gods. This, however, is not to be referred to that time in the desert, but to later times. For, as we shall now see, because of these frequent and long-lasting sins they were delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans. See 2 Kings XVII. 16, ch. XXI. 3, ch. XXIII. 5.

μὴ σφάγια) The words are from the LXX, which we have interpreted thus regarding Amos: Did you not offer sacrifices to me daily in the desert, and yet I turned away from you, because of your stubbornness? How much more now, when you have added to your stubbornness these new cults of new gods?

καὶ θυσίας) מנחות. See what was said at Mark IX. 49.

Latin:

Vers. 42. ἔστρεψε δὲ ὁ Θεὸς) Adversans eos. Sicut Virgilius dixit: Aversa dea mens. & est verbū activum pro reciproco.

παρέδωκεν αὐτὲς λατρεύειν τῇ στρατιᾷ τῷ ὐρανῶ) Permisit eos ab uno malo cultu in alterum delabi: nec uni, aut alteri, sed plurimis diis se prosternere. Hoc autem non est refe- rendum ad illud tempus in deserto, sed ad tempora poste- riora. Nam, ut jam videbimus, propter hæc peccata fre- quentia & diuturna traditi sunt in manus Chaldæorum. Vi- de 2. Reg. XVII. 16. c. XXI. 3. c. XXIII. 5.

μὴ σφάγια) Verba sunt ex LXX. quæ ad Amosum sic in- terpretati sumus: Nonne in deserto quotidie mihi sacra ob- tulistis, & tamen vos aversatus sum, propter contumaci- am? quanto magis nunc, cum ad contumaciam adjeceri- tis hos novos cultus novorum Deorum?

καὶ θυσίας) מנחות. Vide quæ dicta ad Marc. IX. 49.

## 7:43
Vers. 43. ἀνελάβετε τὴν σκηνὴν τᾶ Μολόχ) We said that σκηνὴν in Amos is a small shrine, in which sat the image of the king of the Ammonites of old, from which name the Ammonites named the star of Saturn.

καὶ τὸ ἄστρον τῶ Θεῶ ὑμῶν Ῥεμφὰν) So many codices have it. And this reading seems to be restored also in the books of the LXX. For ῥεμφὰν is רפון Remuan in the Syriac pronunciation, for which the Masoretes read רמון, 1 Reg. V. 18. Thus the Syrians called Saturn, and worshipped him not in the form of a king, but in the form of a star. The name is taken from there, because that star is in the highest sphere, as Tacitus speaks: in the Hebrew it is כיון; which signifies the same star of Saturn, but to the Arabs it is the same thing.

The passage is Amos V. 25. Grotius considers Moloch, and Remphan as called by the Syrians, and Kion by the Arabs, to be the same minor deity, who was called Moloch when worshipped in the form of a King, and Kiun, or Kivan, when in the form of a star; namely, Saturn. Claudius Salmasius, and with him Ludovicus de Dieu, think that the LXX interpreters changed the Hebrew כיון, as being unknown to the Egyptians, into the Ῥεμφὰν which was very well known to them. The same Dievius makes the tabernacle the image of the heavens, Moloch the image of the Sun, and Kiun the image of Saturn, and he says that all these images were worshipped by the Israelites in the desert, and he thinks that Saturn was adored in the rite of the Egyptians in the form of an ox, because Saturn was believed by the ancient pagans to be the author and president of agriculture. Nor does any reason appear why an Arabic name should be attributed to an Egyptian idol, or why an unknown and exotic name of an idol should be used in Egypt by the LXX interpreters. And there are found not a few most learned interpreters who prefer the word כיון to be an appellative noun rather than a proper one. There are those who say that Moloch was indeed the Sun, and Remphan was the morning star; others make a different star out of Remphan, for instance Mars, or even Jupiter. It certainly cannot be held as indubitable, what Grotius holds as such, that Moloch and Remphan refer to the same star, as we have shown in the Annotations to Amos V.

Latin:

Vers. 43. ἀνελάβετε τὴν σκηνὴν τᾶ Μολόχ) σκηνὴν ad Amos surn diximus esse ναΐσκον, in quo sedebat imago regis quon- dam Ammonitarum, ex quo nomine Ammonitæ Saturni stellam nominabant.

καὶ τὸ ἄστρον τῶ Θεῶ ὑμῶν Ῥεμφὰν) Sic habent multi codices. Et hæc lectio videtur restituenda etiam in libris LXX. Nam ῥεμφὰν est רפון Remuan Syriaca pronunciatione, pro quo Masoritæ legunt 1 רמון. Reg. V. 18. Sic Saturnum vocabant Syri, colebantque non in forma regis, sed in for- ma stellæ. Nomen inde sumptum, quod ea stella sit altiffi- mo orbe, ut Tacitus loquitur: in Hebræo est כיון; quod eandem Saturni stellam fignificat, sed Arabibus res eadem.

Locus est Amos V. 25. Molochum, & Rempham Syris, Kion Arabibus dictum, pro eodem deastro habet Grotius, qui Moloch dictus, cum cultus in forma Regis, Kiun, vel Kivan cum in forma stellæ; Saturni nempe. Claud. Salmasius, & cum eo Lud. de Dieu, LXX. interpp. putant Ebræorum כיון ut- pote Ægyptiis ignotum in notissimum ipsis Ῥεμφὰν immutasse. Idem Dievius tabernaculum imaginem cœli, Moloch imaginem Solis, & Kiun imaginem Saturni facit, & has imagines omnes cultas ab Israe- litis in deserto, ait, ac Saturnum ritu Ægyptiorum in bove edoratum putat, quia antiquis gentilibus a- griculturæ autor & præses creditus Saturnus fuerit. Neque causa apparet, cur idolo Ægyptiaco no- men Arabicum tributum fit, vel in Ægypto adhi- bitum ignotum & exoticum idoli nomen à LXX. Interpp. Et reperiuntur non pauci doctiffimi in- terpretès, qui vocem כיון malunt appellativum esse nomen, quam proprium. Sunt, qui Moloch qui- dem Solem, ad Rempham luciferum fuisse dicant; alii aliam stellam è Remphan faciunt, Martem puta, vel etiam Jovem. Indubitatum certe haberi non potest, quod pro tali habet Grotius, Moloch & Remphan ad idem sidus referri, ut in Annot. ad Amos V. ostendimus.

## 7:43
μετοικιῶ ὑμᾶς ἐπέκεινα Βαβυλῶνος) In the Hebrew and Greek Amos: ἐπέκεινα Δαμάσκου. But the sense is well expressed. For Amos said less: he signified more. Assyria and Media, which are beyond Babylon, are much more beyond Damascus. Thus Isaiah 10:9, where in the Hebrew it is כרכמיש, the LXX translate, ἐπάνω Βαβυλῶνος.

This explanation is not to be disapproved. Compare what is at Amos 5:26. For the Israelites were not only in Syria, whose metropolis is Damascus, but were also led away beyond Babylon into Persia and Cassia, as can be seen from Ezra 8:17.

Latin:

μετοικιῶ ὑμᾶς ἐπέκεινα Βαβυλῶνος) In Amos Hebræo & Græco: ἐπέκεινα Δαμάσκου. Sed sensus bene expressus est. Minus enim dixit Amosus:plus significavit. Assyria & Media quæ ultra Babylonem sunt, multo magis sunt ultra Damascum. Sic Esaiæ X. 9. ubi in Hebræo est, כרכמיש, LXX. vertunt, ἐπάνω Βαβυλῶνος.

Non improbanda hæc explicatio. Confer. quæ ad Am. V. 26. Non enim in Syria tantum, cujus metropolis est Damascus, Israelitæ fuere, sed etiam trans Babylonem in Persiam & Cassiam abducti sunt, ut ex Esdr. VIII. 17. videre est.

## 7:44
Vers. 44. ἡ σκηνὴ τῷ μαρτυρίυ) He returns to the other part of his argument, which is about the place of worship: and he shows that it has varied. Jeremiah 12:12 argues with the same point.

κατὰ τὸν τύπον) Thus in the LXX version of Exodus 25:40, where in the Hebrew it is תבנית.

Latin:

Vers. 44. ἡ σκηνὴ τῷ μαρτυρίυ) Redit ad alteram partem argumenti sui, quod est de loco cultus: & ostendit cum variaffe. Eodem argumento pugnat Jeremias VII. 12.

κατὰ τὸν τύπον) Sic in versione LXX. Exodi XXV. 40. ubi in Hebræo תבנית.

## 7:45
Vers 45. διαδεξάμενοι) Received from those who had lived with Moses.

ἐν τῇ κατασχέσει τῶν ἐθνῶν) It is common for Hellenists to interchange ἐν and εἰς, because the Hebrews use the letter ב for both. κατάσχεσις ἐθνῶν is land possessed by nations. Thus the word κατάσχεσις is generally taken, corresponding to the Hebrew אחוזה.

ὧν ἔξωσεν ὁ Θεὸς) הוריש as in Exodus 34:24, Numbers 21:32, Deuteronomy 11:23, where in the Greek it is ἐκβάλλειν.

ἀπὸ προσώπυ τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν) At their arrival; this way of speaking is in Deuteronomy 2:21, 22, and often elsewhere. Those who made the inscription which Procopius saw in Africa imitated this expression: ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν οἱ φυγόντες ἀπὸ προσώπου Ἰησοῦ τῶ λῃστῇ υἱῦ Ναυῆ.

Latin:

Vers 45. διαδεξάμενοι) Acceptam ab iis, qui cum Mose vixerant.

ἐν τῇ κατασχέσει τῶν ἐθνῶν) Frequens Hellenistis permutare ἐν & εἰς, quia Hebræi pro utraque ב literam ponunt κατάσχεσις ἐθνῶν est terra à gentibus possessa. Sic vox κατάσχεσις plerumque sumitur, respondens Hebræo אחוזה.

ὧν ἔξωσεν ὁ Θεὸς) הוריש ut Exod. XXXIV 24. Num. XXI. 32. Deut. XI. 23. ubi in Græco ἐκβάλλειν.

ἀπὸ προσώπυ τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν) Ad eorum adventum; est hoc loquendi genus Deut. II. 21. 22. & alibi sæpe. Imitati sunt hanc locutionem ii, qui inscriptione eam fecere, quam in Africa vidit Procopius: ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν οἱ φυγόντες ἀπὸ προσώπου Ἰησοῦ τῶ λῃστῇ υἱῦ Ναυῆ.

χάριν) That is, therefore.

χάριν) Id est, propterea.

## 7:46
Vers. 46. ὃς εὗρε χάριν) מצא חן. See Luke 1:30.

ἠτήσατο εὑρεῖν σκήνωμα τῷ Θεῷ Ιακώβ) Permanently that εὑρεῖν is taken from Psalm 132:5. ἠτήσατο: שאל that is, he desired; thus שאל is translated by ἐπιθυμεῖν in Deuteronomy 15:26. σκήνωμα for the Hebrews משכן is any dwelling.

Latin:

Vers. 46. ὃς εὗρε χάριν) מצא חן. Vid. Luc. I. 30.

ἠτήσατο εὑρεῖν σκήνωμα τῷ Θεῷ Ιακώβ) Permanenter se dem illud εὑρεῖν est sumtu ex Pf. CXXXII. 5. ἠτήσατο: שאל id est, desideraverit, sic שאל per ἐπιθυμεῖν vertitur Deut. XV. v. 26. σκήνωμα Hebræis משכן est quælibet habitatio.

## 7:48
Vers. 48. ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὁ ὕψιστος ἐν χειροποιήτοις ναοῖς κατοικεῖ) Taken from the words of Solomon: 1 Kings 8:27, where κατοικήσει, in the Hebrew ישב, signifies it will be able to be contained. Euripides: Ποῖος δ’ ἂν οἶκος τεκτόνων πλασθεὶς ὑπὸ Δέμας τὸ θεῖον περιβάλοι τοίχων πτυχαῖς; Zeno, citing Clement of Alexandria and Origen: ἱερά τε οἰκοδομεῖν οὐδὲν δεήσει. ἱερὸν μὴ γὰρ πολλῶ ἄξιον κὴ ἅγιον, οἰκοδόμων ἔργον κό βαναύσων. You have ναὸν χειροποίητον also in Mark 14:58 and ἐν χειροποιήτοις ναοῖς below in chapter 17:24. The manuscript, however, which I mentioned, does not have the word ναοῖς here. Origen, Against Celsus III, VII, VIII, places images and temples in the same category: and he says they were first dedicated to demons, who, either induced by incantations or accustomed to certain places by themselves, would cling to them because of the odors. Thus also Caecilius concerning the Christians: Why do they have no altars, no temples, no known images? And M. Octavius acknowledges: The temple which I shall build for him, since this whole world fashioned by his work cannot contain him: Arnobius, in his constructions of temples, denies that God is honored by Christians. It appears they did not wish the places of Christian assemblies to be called temples; because a temple for Christians is a pure body: an altar is a holy mind: but images of every kind are mighty works. Origen felt that God, when he permitted a temple to be made for himself by Solomon, did so with the same purpose with which he also allowed an altar and victims, namely, to adapt himself to the character of the people, and to claim for himself those rites which the people were otherwise going to bestow upon false gods. The passages of Origen on this matter are worthy of reading, and not foreign to these things which Stephen says here. Christian Emperors also use the name of temples when it is a matter of pagans, as in the Code concerning pagans, sacrifices, and temples, not when it is a matter of Christians; thus also Zeno of Verona: what is the Church to you, if temples are to be approached? Jerome against Vigilantius: He would either destroy the basilicas or convert them into temples. Therefore, Christians called the places of their assemblies sometimes Churches by synecdoche, sometimes basilicas, and in the same sense houses of God: but they purposely abstained from the appellation of Temple.

Grotius wrongly praises Origen, because he felt that God, when he permitted a temple to be made for himself, did so with a purpose of indulgence, with which he also allowed an altar and victims, namely, to adapt himself to the character of the people, and to claim for himself those rites which the people were otherwise going to bestow upon false gods. Such a condescension to the rites of the Gentiles is certainly by no means sacred, and is utterly unworthy of God: who always recalled and dissuaded his people from the same. God did not imitate the Gentiles in temples, altars, and victims, but the Gentiles, through a perverse emulation by the instigation of the Devil, who is the ape of God, and wished to mock his worship in this way, wished to imitate the Israelites.

as the prophet says) Isaiah 66:1.

Latin:

Vers. 48. ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὁ ὕψιστος ἐν χειροποιήτοις ναοῖς κατοικεῖ) Depromptu ex Salomonis verbis: 1. Reg. VIII. 27. ubi κατοικήσει, in Hebræo ישב, significat contineri poterit. Euripides: Ποῖος δ’ ἂν οἶκος τεκτόνων πλασθεὶς ὑπὸ Δέμας τὸ θεῖον περιβάλοι τοίχων πτυχαῖς; Zeno citante Clemente Alexandrino & Origene: ἱερά τε οἰκοδομεῖν οὐδὲν δεήσει. ἱερὸν μὴ γὰρ πολλῶ ἄξιον κὴ ἅγιον, οἰκοδόμων ἔργον κό βαναύσων. Habes ναὸν χειροποίητον etiam Marc. 4. 58. & ἐν χειροποιήτοις ναοῖς inf. c. 17. 24. Manuscriptus tamen, quem dixi, vocem ναοῖς hic non habet. Origenes contra Celsum III, VII. VIII. pari loco ponit simulacra & templa: dicitq; ea primum dicata dæmonibus, qui aut carminib9 inducti, aut per se locis quibusdam affueti, ob nidores iis adhærescerent. Sic & Cæcilius de Christianis: Cur nullas aras habent, templa nulla, nulla nota simulacra? & agnoscit M. Octavius: Templum quod ei exstruam, cum totus hic Mundus ejus opere fabricatus eum capere non possit:& Arnobi9 templorum constructionibus, Deum à Christianis honorari negat. Apparet eos Christianorum conventuum loca templa dici noluisse; quod templum Christianis sit corpus purum: altare animus sanctus:simulacra vero omnis generis virtutes. Sensit Origenes Deum, cum templum sibi fieri permisit a Salomone, pari id fecisse proposito, quo & altare & victimas indulsit, nempe ut se populi ingenio aptaret, ac eos ritus sibi vindicaret, quos alioqui populus falsis diis erat impensurus. Loca Origenis ea de re digna sunt lectu, & ab his, quæ hic dicit Stephanus, non aliena. Imperatores etiam Christiani templorum nomen usurpant, ubi de paganis agitur, ut C. de paganis, sacrificiis & templis, non ubi de Christianis; sic & Zeno Veronensis: quo tibi Ecclesia, si adeunda sint templa? Hieronymus adversus Vigilantium: Basilicas aut destrueret aut in templa converteret. Vocabant ergo Christiani suorũ conventuum loca, modo Ecclesias κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν, modo basilicas, & eodem sensu domos Dei: Templi autem appellatione destinato abstinebant.

Perperam laudat Origenem Grotius, quod senserit Deum, cum templum sibi fieri permisit, pati id fecisse proposito, quo & altare & victimas indulsit, nempe ut se populi ingenio aptaret, ac eos ritus sibi vindicaret, quos alioqui populus falsis diis erat impensurus. Talis certe συγκατάβασις ad gentilium sacra minime sacra, Deo prorsus indigna est: qui ab eadem semper revocavit ac dehortatus est populu suum. Non imitatus est gentiles in templis, altaribus & victimis Deus, sed per κακοζηλίαν gentiles instinctu Diaboli, qui Dei est simia, ejusq; cultui sic illudere voluit, imitari voluere Israelitas.

καθὼς ὁ προφήτης λέγει) Esaias LXVI. I.

Verse 49. heaven is my throne) from the LXX. or what is the place of my rest? did not my hand make all these things) In the LXX. with words slightly different: or what is the place of my rest: for my hand made all these things.

Vers. 49. ὁ οὐρανός μοι θρόνος) ex LXX. ἤ τίς τόπος τῆς καταπαύσεώς μου; οὐχὶ ἡ χείρ μου ἐποίησε ταῦ- τα πάντα) In LXX. verbis paulum diversis: κὴ ποῖος τόπος τῆς καταπαύσεώς με: πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα ἐποίησεν ἡ χείρ με.

## 7:51
Verse 51. stiff-necked) This epithet is given to the Hebrews Ex. 33:3. ch. 34:9. Deut. 9:6, 13. Neh. 9:16. Add Bar. 2:30.

and uncircumcised in heart) Having a heart full of vicious affections. Lev. 26:41. Jer. 9:26.

and in your ears) Whose ears itch to hear those things which favor vices. Jer. 6:10.

you always resist the Holy Spirit) That is, you set yourselves crosswise against the warnings of God through the prophets, like those who obstruct a journey: which is to walk contrary, Lev. 26:21, 23, 24, 40, 41.

They are said to resist the Holy Spirit, where they are otherwise said to resist God, and to have provoked him, so that it may be taught that the Holy Spirit is God. See our Anti-Crellius page 506 seqq. And hence the irresistible grace of the Calvinists is rightly refuted. Conf. Ps. 45:8. Matt. 23:37.

and you) There is here a doubling of the word you, such as are many among the Hebrews.

Latin:

Vers. 51. σκληροτράχηλοι) Hoc elogium Hebræis datur Ex. 38.3. c. 39.9. Deut. 9.6.13. Neh. 9.6. Adde Bar. 2.30.

κὴ ἀπερίτμητοι τῆ καρδίᾳ) Cor habentes plenum vitiosis affectibus. Lev. XXIV. 41. Jer. IX. 26.

κὴ τοῖς ὠσὶν) Quibus pruriunt aures ad ea audienda, quæ vitiis favent. Jer. VI. 10.

ἀεὶ τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ ἀντιπίπτετε) Id est, Dei monitis per prophetas, transversos vos opponitis, ut qui iter impe- diunt: quod est הלך קרי πορεύεσθαι πλάγιον, Lev. XXVI. 21. 23. 24. 40. 41.

Spiritui S. resistere dicuntur, ubi resistere alias Deo dicti sunt, eumque irritasse, ut Spiritum S. esse Deum doceatur. Vid. Anti-Crellius noster pag. 506. seqq. Atque hinc recte Calvinianorum irresistibilis gratia redarguitur. Conf. Psal. XLV. 8. Matth. XXIII. 37.

κὴ ὑμεῖς) Est hic geminatio vocis ὑμεῖς, quales multæ a- pud Hebræos.

## 7:52
Verse 52. which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute) Matt. 5:12. ch. 21:35. ch. 23:31, 37. Luke 13:34.

of the Just One) Jesus, to whom this name especially belongs: See above c. III. 14.

of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers) It had been your duty to protect him, because the prophets were committed to your protection: on the contrary, however, you omitted nothing by which his death could be procured. See above c. III. 13.

Vers. 52. τίνα τῶν προφητῶν ὐκ ἐδίωξαν οἱ πατέρες ὑμῶν) Matth. V. 12. c. XXI. 35. c. XXIII. 31. 37. Luc. XIII. 34.

τῦ δικαίυ) Jesu, cui eximie hoc nomen competit: Vide supra c. III. 14.

ὗ νῦν ὑμεῖς προδόται κὴ φονεῖς γεγένησθε) Vestrum fuerat eum tueri, quia prophetæ vestræ tutelæ commissi sunt: contra vero nihil omisistis, quo ejus mors procurari posset. Vide supra c. III. 13.

## 7:53
Verse 53. at the dispositions of angels) εἰς for inter; he shows how magnificently the law was given among many hosts of Angels: for reference is made to the passage Deut. XXXIV. 2. διατάσσειν is a military term, as is evident in Judges III. 23 in the Greek: 1 Macc. VI. 35. 2 Macc. XII. v. 20.

We have already proved that interpretation in Theol. natur. & revel. page 387, before Grotius, with Franc. Junius, that the law was ordained among the middle ranks of the Angels accompanying [it] for the sake of honor and duty to their commander, or with the myriads of saints accompanying [it] Deut. XXXIII. 2, where the LXX have the word ἀγγέλων. We also weighed there other expositions of others, which he who wishes may compare here.

PART II. The stoning of Stephen, comforted by a vision of Jesus, because of his confession.

Vers. 53. εἰς διαταγὰς ἀγγέλων) εἰς pro inter; ostendit, quam magnifice data sit lex inter multas Angelorum turmas: re- spicitur enim locus Deut. XXXIV. 2. διατάσσειν vox est mi- litaris, ut patet Judicum III. 23. in Græco: 1. Macc. VI. 35. 2. Macc. XII. v. 20.

Probavimus jam eam interpretationem Theol. natur. & revel. pag. 387. ante Grotium cum Franc. Junio, quod inter medias acies Angelorum stipan- tium honoris & officii causa imperatorem suum lex ordinata sit, vel stipantibus myriadibus sancto- rum Deut. XXX. 2. ubi LXX. vocem ἀγγέλων ha- bent. Expendimus etiam illic alias aliorum ἐκθέ- σεις, quas conferre hic poterit, cui libuerit.

PARS II. Stephani, visione Jesu confortati, ob ejus con- fessionem lapidatio.

Verse 55. the glory of God) A certain brightness, by which the majesty of God was represented. See Exodus XXIV. 17. c. XXXIII. 18. 22. Ezekiel I. 1.
