## 8:30
V. 30. Reading the prophet Isaiah) With a clear voice. Do you then understand what you are reading?) An allusion such as that in the phrase 'I have read, I have understood.' Do you sufficiently perceive to what those things you read tend?

Latin:

V. 30. ἀναγινώσκοντα τὸν προφήτην Ἠσαΐαν) Clara voce. Ἀρά γε γινώσκεις ἃ ἀναγινώσκεις) Allusio qualis in illo ἀνέγνων, ἔγνων. Satisne percipis, quo tendant quæ legis?

## 8:31
Vers. 31. For how could I, unless someone guides me?) He did not think that Scripture was everywhere so clear, and had a sense exposed to everyone, as not only the uneducated but even women do now, who would act more rightly if they acknowledged that they had need of a guide.

These things were said for the sake of the Papists: But when we teach that Holy Scripture is clear, we do not exclude the parts or the office of interpreters and doctors of the word, but we remove only the necessity of a visible infallible interpreter, whom the Papists make their Pope ἄλεργραγῆς. Interpreters and doctors of the word are absolutely necessary for the more unlearned: not so an infallible interpreter sitting in the chair of Peter: and no privilege of infallibility has been granted by Christ to anyone outside the Apostles. Nor do interpreters have their expositions from elsewhere than from Scripture: for this is not of private interpretation, 2 Pet. 1:21, whence it is not permitted to conclude from interpreters to the obscurity, but rather to the perspicuity of Scripture. Which, if it were not luminous, could not be its own interpreter, or exhibit the true sense to interpreters. Finally, although in certain things, even in prophecies, before their fulfillment is known, Scripture is not always clear, yet in those things which are necessary for faith and the Christian life, it is sufficiently clear and luminous: just as the example of this Eunuch also teaches, since it does not appear that he was instructed about those things from anywhere else than from the Scriptures, even though he was still ignorant that Jesus of Nazareth was the promised Messiah. For in those things which are openly placed in the Scriptures are found all things that contain faith and the morals of living, as Augustine says, book II de doctrina Christiana, ch. 9, whence no one can be barred from the reading of Scripture, which is written for all and enjoined to be read by all: nor do they have any excuse who, with the Papists, bar the laity from it, John 5:39, Acts 17:30, Col. 3:16, 2 Tim. 3:15, 1 John 2:12 ff., 2 Pet. 1:10. It is manifest, says Claudius Espencaeus in ch. 2 of Titus, from the Apostle (Col. 3.) and the practice of the ancient Church, that the use of reading the Scriptures was granted to the people. Jerome praises Pamphilus the Martyr, book 1 against Ruffinus, because he handed over the Scriptures to be read not only to men but also to women. Cornelius à Lapide praises Marcella along with Jerome for the reading of Scripture. Compare Chrysostom, Homily XXXV on Genesis and Sermon III on Lazarus. Nor do I believe that Grotius either asked for or had a special faculty from the Pope, according to the Council of Trent, to read the Bible: even though he was a layman. Nor did the Eunuch have it from Peter, which the Papists themselves will undoubtedly admit. We learn from this, says Cornelius à Lapide on this passage, how useful it is to read pious books, especially Holy Scripture. For the Holy Spirit, their author, inserts Himself into this reading, and instills pious thoughts of the things read into the intellect, and affections into the will, by which a man is converted or urged toward greater holiness. Thus, from the reading of the life of St. Anthony, those two courtiers of the Emperor were converted, and St. Augustine himself, as he reports in book 8 of his Confessions, ch. 6 and 7. Indeed, when St. Athanasius, fleeing the Arians, had brought the life of St. Anthony written by himself to Rome, and had given it to be read, many Roman nobles, men and women, despising the world, embraced the religious life like St. Anthony: of whom the leader was St. Marcella, as St. Jerome testifies in her Epitaph, epistle 16 to her daughter Principia. If such is the use of the reading of Scripture, why should the laity be deprived of it, why should women be deprived of it, when they happen to be destitute of a guide! Although indeed the Eunuch, as a proselyte, and not yet sufficiently grounded in the Scriptures, here hesitates about which prophet he is speaking of, yet that passage in the Prophet is not therefore obscure, because it is sufficiently clear from it that he is speaking of none other than the Messiah, which even the Jews themselves acknowledged, just as Cyril Alex. professes that the meaning of these words is open; and on account of this prophecy, Isaiah was called by the ancients the Evangelist rather than a Prophet.

And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him) Here too is fulfilled mystically what Isaiah said in ch. LXVI. 20.

Indeed, this prophecy, which deals there with the conversion of the nations לפִנֵי הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, was fulfilled in the literal sense in the Eunuch and others, even though the Prophet used figurative words in that place. See our annotations on the loc. cit.

Latin:

Vers. 31. πῶς γὰρ ἂν δυναίμην, ἐὰν μή τις ὁδηγήσῃ με) Non putabat tam perspicuam ubique esse scripturam, & expositum omnibus habere sensum, ut nunc faciunt non sellularii tantum, sed & fœminæ, qui rectius facerent, si duce sibi opus esse agnoscerent.

Hæc in gratiam Pontificiorum dicta: Verum cum perspicuam esse docemus Scripturam S. non excludimus partes, vel officium Interpp. & Doctorũ verbi, sed removemus solum necessitatem visibilis infallibilis interpretis, quem Papistæ suum Papam ἄλεργραγῆς faciunt. Interpretibus, & doctorib. verbi omnino opus est ob rudiores: non item infallibili aliquo interprete, in cathedra Petri sedente: nulliq; extra Apostolos est infallibilitatis privilegiũ à Christo concessum. Neq; interpretes suas ἐκθέσεις aliunde habent, quam è Scriptura: hæc enim non est ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, 2. Pet. I. 21. unde ab interpretibus non concludere licet ad obscuritatem, sed poti9 ad perspicuitatem Scripturæ. Quæ si luculenta non sit, sui ipsius interpres esse, aut interpretib. verum sensum exhibere non poterit. Deniq; etsi in quibusdam, etiam in vaticiniis, antequam eorum complementum cognitum sit, non semper perspicua Scriptura sit, in his tamen, quæ ad fidem & vitam Christianam necessarīa sunt, satis est perspicua & luculenta: quemadmodum exemplum Eunuchi hujus etiam docet, utpote quē aliunde, quam è Scripturis de illis instructum non constat, etsi adhuc Jesum Nazarenum esse promissum Messiam ignoraret. In illis enim, quæ aperte in Scripturis posita sunt, inveniuntur omnia, quæ continent fidem moresq; vivendi, dicente August. l. II. de doctr. Christ. c. 9. unde à Scripturæ lectione, quæ omnib. scripta, omnibusq legenda injuncta est, nemo arceri potest: nec excusationem ullam habent, qui cum Papistis Laicos ab eadem arcent, Joh. 5. 39. Act. 17. 30. Col. 3. 16. 2. Tim. 3. 15. 1. Joh. 2. 12. seqq. 2. Petr. 1. 10. Manifestum est, inquit Claudius Espensæus in c. 2. Tit. ex Apostolo (Col. 3.) & Ecclesiæ antiquæ praxi, quod usus Scripturas legendi populo concedebatur. Hieron. laudat Pamphilum Martyr. l. 1. advers. Ruffin. quod Scripturas legendas tradiderit non tantum viris, sed & fœminis. Laudat cum Hieronymo ob Scripturæ lectionem Corn. à Lap. Marcellam. Conf. Chrysost. Hom XXXV. in Genesin & serm. III. de Laz. Neque credo, Grotium à Papa facultatem specialem, juxta Concil. Trident. vel petiisse vel habuisse legēdi Biblia: etsi Laicus fuerit. Nec à Petro eam habuit Eunuch9, quod sine dubio fatebūtur ipsimet Papistæ. Discimus hinc, inquit Corn. à Lapide ad h. l. quam utile sit legere libros pios præsertim S. Scripturam. Huic enim lectioni interserit se Spiritus S. eorum auctor, piasq; rerum lectarum cogitationes intellectui, & affectiones voluntati instillat, quib. homo conversatur, vel ad majorem sanctitatem probehatur. Ita ex lectione vita S. Antonii, conversi sunt duo illi aulici Imper. ipseq S. August uti ipse refert lib. 8. Confess. c. 6. & 7. Imo cum S. A- thanasius fugiens Arrianos, vitam S. Antonii a se scriptam Ro- mam detulisset, eamq; legendam dedisset, multi Romani nobiles, viri & fœminæ, spreto mundo, vitam religiosam instar S. An- tonii amplexi sunt: quorum dux fuit S. Marcella, teste S. Hie- ronym. in ejus Epitaphio epist. 16. ad Principiam ejus filiam. Si talis lectionis Scripturæ usus, cur eo privandi Laici, cur privandæ fœminæ, cum forte destituan- tur duce! Quanquam vero Eunuchus, utpote prose- lytus, nec satis adhuc in Scripturis fundatus, hic am- bigat, de quonam propheta loquatur, non tamē ideo locus ille in Propheta obscurus est, quia constat sa- tis ex eo, quod non de alio, quam de Messia loqua- tur, quod etiam agnovere ipsimet Judæi, quemad- modum Cyrill. Alex. apertam esse horum verborum sententiam profitetur; & ob hoc vaticiniū veterib. Esaias Evangelista potius dictus est, quam Propheta.

παρεκάλεσέ τε τὸν Φίλιππον ἀναβάντα καθίσαι σὺν ἀυτῷ) impletum & hic mystice quod dixit Esaias c. LXVI. 20.

Imo sensu literali impletum hoc vaticinium, quod ibi de conversione gentium לפִנֵי הַמִּקְדָּשׁ agit, in Eunucho, aliisque, etsi Propheta verbis figura- tis usus ibidem sit. Vid. annotata Nostra ad l. c.

## 8:32
Ver. 32. ἡ δὲ περιοχὴ τῆς γραφῆς) περιοχὴ is the same as περιόδω: nor does it have anything in common with the Hebrew פָּרָשָׁה except for a fortuitous similarity of sound. Cicero to Atticus: I did not even dictate to Tiro, who was accustomed to follow whole periods. ὡς πρόβατον) Luke brought forth this whole passage from the LXX, except that in the LXX it is κείροντος ἀυτὸν, and after τόμα, ἀυτῦ is not added, nor after ταπεινώσει, and τὴν γενεὰν is there without δε. But these two latter variations are not in the manuscript, which here agrees with the Greek version. Clement uses the same passage, but extended further: I think the Eunuch himself read the Prophet's passage in the Hebrew language, which he could have learned more easily from the many Jews who were in Ethiopia, from whom he had also received the religion.

Others think he read the Greek version of the LXX Interpreters himself. Cornel. à Lapide conjectures that perhaps by that time the Scripture had already been translated into the Ethiopian language: to which opinion, in the judgment of the blessed Johann Ernst Gerhard, it seems to favor that the Abyssinians even today firmly believe that their Kings trace their origin from Solomon, and that the Jewish religion also long ago prevailed in the Abyssinian kingdom. Who, however, not without reason, leaves it in the middle whether he read the authentic text of Isaiah or indeed the version? What is to be held concerning the Epistle of Clement will be said in the preface to the first to the Corinthians §. Θ.

Latin:

Vers. 32. ἡ δὲ περιοχὴ τῆς γραφῆς) περιοχὴ idem est, quod περιόδω: nec quicquā commune habet cū Hebræo פָּרָשָׁה præter fortuitam soni vicinitatem. Cicero ad Atticum: Ne Tironi quidem dictavi qui totas periochas persequi solebat. ὡς πρόβατον) Locum hunc totum ex LXX. protulit Lucas, nisi quod in LXX. est κείροντος ἀυτὸν, & post τόμα non affcri- bitur ἀυτῦ, nec post ταπεινώσει, & τὴν γενεὰν ibi est sine δε. Sed hæ duæ postremæ varietates non sunt in manuscripto, qui hic consonat versioni Græcæ. Utitur eodem loco, sed longius producto Clemens in epistola: ipsum Eunu- chum puto Prophetæ locum legisse in sermone Hebræo, quem facilius addiscere potuit a multis Judæis, qui in Æthi- opia erant, a quibus & religionem acceperat.

Versionem LXX. Interpp. Græcam ab ipso le- ctam alii putant. Cornel. à Lapide conjicit forte jam tum in linguam Æthiopicam conversam fuisse Scri- pturam: cui sententiæ, judicio B. Johannis Ernesti Gerhardi, favere videtur, quod hodienum Abysfini firmiter credant, Reges suos ortum trahere à Sa- lomone, ac religionem etiam Judaicam in regno Abyss. dudum obtinuisse. Qui tamen, nec imme- rito, in medio relinquit, num ipsum textum au- thenticum Esaiæ legerit, an vero versionem? Quid de Epistola Clementis habendum, in præloquio ad priorem ad Corinthios §. Θ. dicetur.

## 8:33
Ver. 33. ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει ἡ κρίσις ἀυτῦ ἤρθη) The LXX read בְּעֹצֶר מִשְׁפָּטוֹ לָקָח. The sense would now be: After he was depressed, the punishment was taken away from him. A different reading is not argued from there, which Grotius, with Ludov. Capellus in Critic. Sacr. p. 61, wishes to infer: since that translation of the LXX could have arisen from elsewhere: as they often looked to the sense and rendered word for word. However, the same sense remains: for if he was taken away from distress and anxiety (or enclosure or prison, which name the Syrian also has in the Acts in this place) and judgment, he must certainly have been depressed before, but the punishment taken away from him, or the judgment of the condemned taken away: therefore in both cases both his depression or emptying, and his liberation from the same, are designated.

"Who shall declare his generation?" (τὴν δὲ γενεὰν ἀυτῦ τίς διηγήσεται) generation (γενεὰ) signifies duration to the Greeks, as (דּוֹר) does to the Hebrews, or the times which are the measures of duration. See Isa. 34. 10, 17; ch. 51. 8. Explain from Heb. 7. 24.

ὅτι αἴρεται ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἡ ζωὴ ἀυτῦ) Because of the evils endured he will be honored with those highest rewards,

Regarding the sense of these words, see our annotations on Isaiah. It is not the duration of life, but rather the race of Christ or his spiritual generation that is designated: because it is to be so numerous that no one will be able to recount it, as the explanation of v. 10 added by the Prophet confirms. Nor can those words ὅτι αἴρεται ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἡ ζωὴ ἀυτῦ have any other sense than that which the Prophet's words render, because he was cut off from the land of the living. Therefore they are not to be explained as concerning the highest rewards after evils endured, but they deal with that extreme degree of emptying, when his life was taken from the earth, or he himself was cut off from the land of the living.

Latin:

Vers. 33. ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει ἡ κρίσις ἀυτῦ ἤρθη) Legerunt LXX. בְּעֹצֶר מִשְׁפָּטוֹ לָקָח. Sensus nunc esset: Post- quam depressus fuit, ablata est ab eo pœna. Non arguitur inde diversa lectio, quam cum Lu- dov. Capello in Critic. Sacr. p. 61. inferre vult Gro- tius: quum aliunde potuerit oriri illa LXX. trans- latio: utpote qui sensum sæpe respexere, & ver- bum verbo reddidere. Manet autem idem sensus: nam si ex angustia & anxietate (aut claustro seu car- cere, quod nomen Syrus in Actis h. l. etiam habet) & judicio sublatus est, oportet utique ipsum depres- sum quidem prius fuisse, sed ablatam ab ipso esse pœnam, vel sublatum judicium condemnato- rum: utrobique ergo & depressio ejus vel exina- nitio, & liberatio ex eadem designatur.

τὴν δὲ γενεὰν ἀυτῦ τίς διηγήσεται) γενεὰ Græcis ut דּוֹר He- bræis durationē significat, sive tempora, quæ mensuræ sunt durationis. Vid. Es. 34. 10. 17. c. 51. 8. Explica ex Hebr. 7. 24.

ὅτι αἴρεται ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἡ ζωὴ ἀυτῦ) Propter mala tolerata honorabitur summis illis præmiis,

De sensu horum verborum vid. annotata nostra ad Esai- Verba Es- am. Non duratio vitæ, sed potius genus Christi vel generatio coru. spiritualis designatur: quod tam numerosa ea futura sit, ut nemo eam enarraturus sit, uti explicatio v. 10. apud Pro- phetam addita confirmat. Neq; verba illa ὅτι αἴρεται ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἡ ζωὴ ἀυτῦ alium sensum habere possunt, quam quem Prophetæ verba reddunt, quia abscissus est de terra viventium. Non ergo explicanda sunt de præmiis summis post mala tole- rata, sed agunt de extremo illo exinanitionis gradu, cum subla- ta est vita ejus de terra, vel abscissus est ipse de viventium terra.

## 8:34
Ver. 34. περὶ ἑαυτῦ) For Isaiah also endured many evils in the time of Manasseh.

ἢ περὶ ἑτέρου τινὸς) Perhaps he was thinking of Jeremiah.

If his mind had been as perverse as Grotius', he could have thought of Jeremiah. But these thoughts, which occurred to Grotius, did not even enter the minds of the insane Jews of later times, as we noted at Isaiah ch. 58. Far be it, therefore, that we should attribute them to this proselyte. For how convoluted all those things are which Grotius devised so that the text might be snatched away to Jeremiah, has been sufficiently shown by us there.

Latin:

Vers. 34. περὶ ἑαυτῦ) Nam & Esaias multa pertulit ma- la Manassis tempore.

ἢ περὶ ἑτέρου τινὸς) Forte de Jeremia cogitavit.

Si mens ipsi tam laeva fuisset, quam Grotio, co- gitasse poterat de Jeremia. Sed hae cogitationes, quae Grotio, ne insanis quidem Judaeis sequiorum temporum in mentem venere. Ut ad Esaiae c. LVIII. monuimus. Absit ergo, ut huic proselyto eas affingamus. Quam contorta enim omnia illa sint, quae, ut ad Jeremiam abripiatur textus, excogita- vit Grotius, ibi ostensum satis a nobis est.

## 8:35
Ver. 35. εὐηγγελίσατο ἀυτῷ τὸν Ἰησοῦν) In whom all those words fit in an excellent manner.

Not only do all things fit in an excellent manner in Jesus, but they agree with no one but Jesus alone. Certainly no one (not even Jeremiah) can be set there as the subject to whom all the predicates apply in any way, not to mention κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν or according to the literal sense intended by the Holy Spirit. The eunuch was already sufficiently instructed about the Messiah, but now he is instructed by Philip that the same one is none other than Jesus of Nazareth.

Latin:

Vers. 35. εὐηγγελίσατο ἀυτῷ τὸν Ἰησοῦν) In quem omnia ista verba congruunt, eximio modo.

Non tantum eximio modo in Jesum omnia con- gruunt, sed non nisi uni Jesu conveniunt. Nullus certe (nec Jeremias) pro subjecto illic statui pot- est, cui omnia praedicata conveniant aliqua ratio- ne, ne dicam, κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν vel secundum literalem a Spiritu S. intentum sensum. Erat Eunuchus jam satis edoctus de Messia, sed nunc eundem nullum alium esse, quam Jesum Nazarenum, a Philippo edocetur.

## 8:36
Ver. 36. κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν) Along the paved road: thus Aquila translates כברת in Gen. 35:16 as καθ' ὁδὸν τῆς γῆς. Jerome mentions this in his Hebrew places and on Genesis, and interprets it as on the journey and near the road.

ἦλθον ἐπί τι ὕδωρ) To the spring which is in the village of Bethsora, in the tribe of Judah, for those going from Aelia to Hebron at the twentieth milestone. Thus Ado in the Martyrology.

Jerome had also noted this in his book on Hebrew places: There is today Bethsoron, Heb. בית צור, a village for us going from Aelia to Hebron at the twentieth milestone, near which a spring bubbling up at the roots of the mountain is swallowed by the same earth in which it is born. And the Acts of the Apostles report that the eunuch of Queen Candace was baptized by Philip in this place. Therefore, Beza's opinion is not to be approved, that he was baptized at the river Eleutherus, which river he teaches is located very close to Lebanon at the northern boundary, very far away, refuting Beza. Nic. Fuller, book II, Miscell. sacr. ch. 8.

τὶ κωλύει με βαπτισθῆναι;) From this we understand that the eunuch was also instructed about the necessity of baptism. Thus many things of the preceding are supplied from the subsequent.

Latin:

Vers. 36. κατὰ τὴν ὁδὸν) Per viam stratam: sic כברת Genes. XXXV. 16. vertit Aquila καθ' ὁδὸν τῆς γῆς. meminit Hieronymus in locis Hebraicis, & ad Genesin, interpreta- turque in itinere, & juxta viam.

ἦλθον ἐπί τι ὕδωρ) Ad fontem, qui est in vico Bethsora, in tribu Juda, euntibus ab Aelia ad Hebron in vigesimo lapi- de. Ita Ado in Martyrologio.

Notarat id etiam Hieronymus in libr. de locis He- braicis: Est hodie Bethsoron Ebr. בית צור. vicus eun- tibus nobis Aelia Chebron in vicesimo lapide, juxta quem fons ad radices montis ebulliens ab eadem, in qua gignitur, sorbetur humo. Et Apostolorum Acta referunt, Eunuchum Candacis Reginae in hac esse ba- ptizatum a Philippo. Non ergo probanda Bezae sententia, quod ad Eleutherum fluvium baptiza- tus sit, quem amnem proxime Libanum in Septen- trionali termino, longissime dissitum esse docet, Bezam refellens. Nic. Fuller. l. II. Miscell. sacr. c. 8.

τὶ κωλύει με βαπτισθῆναι;) Hinc intelligimus Eunuchum etiam de baptismi necessitate institutum. Sic multa praece- dentium ex subsequentibus supplentur.

## 8:37
Ver. 37. εἶπε δὲ Φίλιππος) In that manuscript which I often mention, this whole thing is missing, no less than in other codices as well as in the most ancient versions; wherefore nothing is more probable than that it was added by someone from what it was fitting to believe had happened.

The authority of this verse is asserted by approved codices, the 11 most ancient manuscripts of Robert Stephanus and Beza, and also those which Walton used, as well as the Arabic version, both the London and the Leiden. And it could more easily have fallen out of certain codices through carelessness than be added: because it was a matter of religious scruple for Christians (and not without reason) to add anything to the divine scriptures.

Latin:

Vers. 37. εἶπε δὲ Φίλιππος) In manuscripto illo, cujus sae- pe memini, deest hoc omnia, non minus, quam in aliis tum codicibus, tum versionibus antiquissimis; Quare nihil pro- babilius, quam ab aliquo additum, ex eo quod gestum cre- di par erat.

Αὐθεντίαν hujus commatis adserunt probati co- dices XI. MMSS. vetustissimi Rob. Stephani, ac Be- zae, nec non illi, quos Waltonus adhibuit, ut & versio Arabica, Londinensis ac Leydensis. Et facilius excidere potuit e quibusdam codicibus versus ille per incuriam, quam addi: quia religio fuit Chri- stianis (nec immerito) ad divinas literas aliquid adjicere.

## 8:38
Vers. 38. and he baptized him) Therefore also deacons have the right of baptizing, namely because the Apostles had permitted that to them, where they themselves were not present. Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans: It is not lawful without the bishop either to baptize or to offer. Tertullian on Baptism: It remains to conclude the little matter, to give notice also concerning the observance of giving and receiving baptism. The high priest, who is the Bishop, indeed has the right of giving, then presbyters and deacons: yet not without the authority of the Bishop, for the sake of the honor of the Church, by which being safe, peace is safe. Otherwise even laymen have the right: for what is received equally, can be given equally, unless the bishops or presbyters or deacons are already called disciples. The word of the Lord ought not to be hidden by anyone. Therefore also baptism, equally a census of God, can be exercised by all: but how much more does the discipline of shame and modesty rest upon laymen? Since these things belong to superiors, let them not take upon themselves the office of the Episcopate dedicated to Bishops. Emulation is the mother of schisms: the most holy Apostle said that all things are lawful, but not all things are expedient. Let it suffice, of course, that you use it in necessities, if ever the condition of place or time or person compels it. For then the constancy of the one helping is accepted, when the circumstance of the one in danger presses.

Latin:

Vers. 38. κὶ ἐβάπτισεν ἀυτὸν) Ergo & diaconis jus bapti- zandi, nempe quia Apostoli ipsis id permiserant, ubi ipsi non adessent Ignatius ad Smyrnaeenses: ἐκ ἐξόν ἐστι χωρὶς τῦ ἐπισκόπε ὔτε βαπτίζειν ὔτε προσφέρειν. Tertullianus de Ba- ptismo: Superest ad concludendam materiolam, de observatio- ne quoque dandi & accipiendi baptismum commonefacere. Dandi quidem habet jus summus sacerdos, qui est Episcopus, de- hinc presbyteri & diaconi: non tamen sine Episcopi auctoritate, propter Ecclesiae honorem, quo salvo, salva pax est. Alioqui et- iam laicis jus est: quod enim ex aequo accipitur, ex aequo dari pot- est, nisi Episcopi jam aut presbyteri aut diaconi vocantur discen- tes. Domini sermo non debet abscondi ab ullo. Proinde & ba- ptismus, aeque Dei census, ab omnibus exerceri potest: sed quanto magis laicis disciplina verecundiae & modestiae incumbit? Cum ea majoribus competant, ne sibi adsumant dicatum Episcopis of- ficium Episcopatus Aemulatio schismatum mater est: omnia li- cere dixit sanctissimus Apostolus, sed non omnia expedire. Suf- ficiat scilicet in necessitatibus utaris, sicubi aut loci aut temporis, aut personae conditio compellit. Tunc enim constantia succur- rentis excipitur, cum urget circumstantia periclitantis.

## 8:39
Vers. 39. the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, and the eunuch saw him no more) That old manuscript has it thus: the Holy Spirit fell upon the eunuch, but an Angel of the Lord caught away Philip, and he saw, etc. just as Erasmus and Beza noted that some other codices have it; and Jerome himself cites it thus in the Dialogue of the Orthodox and the Luciferian. It is difficult to say which reading is truer, since both the Syriac and the Arabic follow the received one. If we follow the manuscripts which I mentioned, the meaning will be that the gift of the Holy Spirit was anticipated in the Eunuch before any laying on of hands, clearly as in Cornelius and his household before baptism below X. 44. But that Philip was carried away elsewhere by an Angel, such a thing as the writer of the final addition to Daniel believed happened to Habakkuk.

There is no doubt that that reading, which is found in the received codices, as being in most and indeed the most approved manuscripts, and occurs in the Syriac, and Arabic, and add to that the Ethiopic, is more approved: which therefore Chrysostom and Oecumenius also followed. Those words could easily have crept in from the margin, added for the sake of memory by some reader from Acts X. 44. It is not worth the effort to compare here the deportation of Habakkuk, which only the apocryphal addition to Daniel hands down. For we have in the Canon a similar rapture of Elijah, 1 Kings XVIII. 12 and 2 Kings II. 16, which it will be proper to compare with the rapture of Philip.

for he went on his way rejoicing) That 'for he went on his way' gives the reason why the Eunuch did not see Philip anymore, because the Eunuch was pursuing his own way: Philip was being carried off elsewhere. But that 'rejoicing' is added only incidentally, and signifies the tranquility of mind which that Eunuch had obtained from the knowledge of the Gospel.

It is not added only incidentally, but of set purpose, so that the fruit of the Gospel and faith may be expressed: that he now traveled home with greater tranquility of heart, and joy, even though deprived of his Teacher, than he had when he began this journey. Cf. Rom. V. 1, c. XIV. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 39. πνεῦμα Κυρίου ἥρπασε τὸν Φίλιππον, κὶ ἐκ εἶδεν ἀυτὸν ὐκέτι ὁ ἐυνῦχος) Manuscriptus ille vetus sic habet. πνεῦμα ἅ- γιον ἐπέπεσεν ἐπὶ τὸν ἐυνῦχον, Ἄγγελος δὲ Κυρίου ἥρπασε † Φίλιπ- πον, κὶ ἐκ εἶδεν, &c. quomodo & alios quosdam habere co- dices notatum Erasmo & Beza; & sic citat ipse Hieronymus Dialogo Orthodoxi & Luciferiani. Difficile est dicere, utra lectio sit verior, cum receptam sequantur & Syrus & Arabs. Si Manuscriptos, quos dixi, sequimur, sensus erit ante ullam manuum impositionem anticipatum in Eunucho donum Spiritus S. plane ut in Cornelio Ce: tutione & domesticis ejus ante baptismum infra X. 44. Philippum autem ab An- gelo fuisse alio deportatum, quale quid Abacuco evenisse credidit scriptor accessionis ultimæ ad Danielem.

Lectionem illam, quæ & in receptis Codd. ut- pote plerisque & quidem probatissimis MMSS. consentaneis, reperitur, & in Syro, & Arabe, adde & Æthiope occurrit, probatiorem esse, dubitan- dum non est: quam proinde sequuti etiam sunt Chrysostomus & Oecumenius. Irrepere facile è margine verba ista potuere, addita memoriæ cau- sa à lectore aliquo ex Act. X. 44. Deportationem Abacuci, quam nonnisi apocryphum assumentum Danielis tradit, ut hic conferamus, non est operæ pretium. Habemus quippe in Canone raptum si- milem Eliæ 1. Reg. XVIII.12. & 2. Reg. II. 16. quem cum Philippi raptu conferre par erit.

ἐπορεύετο γὰρ τὴν ὁδὸν ἀυτᾶ χαίρων) Illud ἐπορεύετο γὰρ τὴν ὁδὸν ἀυτᾶ, causam reddit cur Philippum Eunuchus ultra non viderit, quia suam viam insistebat Eunuchus: Philippus alio auferebatur. Illud autem χαίρων obiter tantum additur, si- gnificatque tranquillitatem animi, quam Eunuchus ille ex Evangelii notitia erat consecutus.

Non obiter tantum additur, sed ex instituto, ut fructus Evangelii & fidei exprimatur: quod nunc majori cordis tranquillitate, ac gaudio, etsi orba- tus suo Doctore, domum contenderit, quam iter hoc ingressus fuit. Conf. Rom. V 1. c. XIV. 17.

## 8:40
Vers. 40. and Philip was found at Azotus) Again 'eis' for 'en', as above 23. 'eurethe', that is, was seen: thus we have 'matsa' for to see, Gen. IV. 13, 14, and often elsewhere: and so it is also translated by 'idein', Jerem. XXIII. 11, Lam. II. 9.

he preached the gospel in all the cities) The same construction as above 25.

till he came to Caesarea) Caesarea which is called Straton's, and is not far from Azotus. See Ptolemy.

That Caesarea in Palestine situated between Dora and Joppa, in which Cornelius was baptized, Acts X. Compare what is at chapter IX. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 40. Φίλιππος δὲ εὑρέθη εἰς Ἄζωτον) Rursum εἰς pro ἐν, ut supra 23. εὑρέθη, id est, conspectus fuit: sic מצא pro conspicere habemus Gen. IV. 13. 14. & alibi sæpe: itaque & per ἰδεῖν vertitur Jerem. XXIII 11. Thren. II. 9.

ἐυαγγελίζετο τὰς πόλεις πάσας) Eadem constructio quæ supra 25.

ἕως τᾶ ἐλθεῖν εἰς Καισάρειαν) Cæsaream quæ Stratonis di- citur, & non longe abest ab Azoto. Vide Ptolemæum.

Illa Cæsarea in Palæstina inter Doram & Joppen sita, in qua Cornelius baptizatus est Act. X. Con- fer, quæ ad cap. IX. 30.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Saul, breathing threats and slaughter, having received letters to inquire at Damascus for those converted to Christ, is converted on the way, surrounded by a light from heaven, and being blinded for three days, is led to Damascus, where he was ordered by a heavenly voice to go, to Ananias, by whom, having been instructed by a vision concerning Paul, a chosen vessel to carry the name of the Lord among the Gentiles, he is restored to sight, and is filled with the Holy Spirit, and preaches Christ in the synagogues, with everyone astonished; and he convinces the Jews of Damascus concerning Christ. When the Jews were lying in wait for him, he was let down in a basket from the wall and came to Jerusalem, received by Barnabas, who informed the other disciples of his conversion; where Paul preached freely and disputed with the Greeks: But on account of the plots he was accompanied to Caesarea and sent to Tarsus, and there was peace in the whole Church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria, and it was not a little edified: and as Peter was healing Aeneas the paralytic at Lydda, and raising Tabitha at Joppa, many in Lydda, Saron, and Joppa were converted to the Lord.

There are three parts: I. The miraculous conversion of Saul, to verse 19. II. The deliverance of the same, while preaching Jesus, from the plots of those in Damascus and Jerusalem, to verse 30. III. The Church in tranquility, edification, and the amplification of the Church through the miraculous healing of Aeneas by Peter, and the resuscitation of Tabitha, to the final verse 43.

PART I. The miraculous conversion of Saul.

Vers. 1. Ἔτι ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνε) ἐμπνέων, נשׁב. προσελθὼν τῷ Ἀρχιερεῖ) Who at that time was נשיא, that is, the prince of the Sanhedrin.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Saulus minas & cædes spirans acceptis literis, ut Damasci inquireret ad Christum conver- sos, in via luce de cælo circumfusus conver- titur, & ad triduum visu orbatus, Dama- scum, quo voce cælesti ire jussus est, ad Ana- niam adducitur, à quo visione de Paulo, va- se electo ad portandum nomen Domini in- ter gentes, edocto visui restituitur, & Sp. S. impletur, ac Christum in synagogis, stupen- tibus omnibus, prædicat: Judæosque Dama- scenos de Christo convincit. Cui cum insidi- arentur Judæi, demissus in sporta de muro Hierosolymam venit à Barnaba susceptus, qui alios discipulos de ejus conversione in- formavit; ubi libere prædicavit Paulus, & cum Græcis contulit: Sed ob insidias Cæsare- am comitatus Tarsum missus est, fuitq́; pax in tota Ecclesia per Judæam, Galilæam & Samariam, & non parum ædificata est: ac Petro Lyddæ Æneam paralyticum sanante, & in Joppen Tabeam resuscitante, multi in Lydda, Sarone, & Joppen ad Dominum con- versi sunt.

Partes sunt tres: I. Sauli miraculosa conversio, ad v. 19. II. Ejusdem Jesum prædicantis ab insidi- is Damascenis & Hierosolymitanis liberatio, ad v. 30. III. Ecclesia in tranquillitate ædificatio, & per miraculum sanati à Petro Æneæ, & resuscitatæ Tabex amplificatio, ad v. 43. finalem.

PARS I. Miraculosa Sauli conversio.

Vers. 1. Ἔτι ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνε) ἐμπνέων, נשׁב. προσελθὼν τῷ Ἀρχιερεῖ) Qui eo tempore erat נשיא, id est, princeps Synedrii.

## 9:2
Vers. 2. ἠτήσατο παρ’ αὐτῦ ἐπιστολὰς) From him as the prince of the Sanhedrin: this is evident below in XXIII. 5. εἰς Δαμασκὸν πρὸς τὰς συναγωγὰς) The Romans permitted the Sanhedrin the right of arrest and scourging, not only against the Jews of Palestine, but even outside Palestine, where there were Synagogues, which of their own accord acknowledged the jurisdiction of the Sanhedrin in matters pertaining to religion. τῆς ὁδὲ ὄντας) מדרך הוא, of that institution.

He received letters from the high priest, who at that time was נשיא, the prince of the Sanhedrin: which is clear from Acts XXIII. 5. For it was rightly observed by Grotius here, and at c. VIII. 3., that the Sanhedrin had the right not only of arrest, but also of scourging over the Jews by the permission of the Romans, and not only over the Jews of Palestine, but even outside Palestine, where there were Synagogues, which of their own accord acknowledged the jurisdiction of the Sanhedrin in matters pertaining to religion. However, the Jews did not have that power in all offenses, but only in those cases which concerned their religion.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἠτήσατο παρ’ αὐτῦ ἐπιστολὰς) Ab ipso ut Syne- drii principe: patet id infra XXIII. 5. εἰς Δαμασκὸν πρὸς τὰς συναγωγὰς) Romani Synedrio per- mittebant jus prehensionis & verberum, non tantum in Ju- dæos Palæstinæ, verum etiam extra Palæstinam, ubi erant Synagogæ, quæ sponte sua jurisdictionem Synedrii in re- bus ad religionem spectantibus agnoscebant. τῆς ὁδὲ ὄντας) מדרך הוא, illius instituti.

A Pontifice summo accepit literas, qui eo tem- pore נשיא princeps erat Synedrii: quod ex Act. XXIII. 5. liquet. Recte enim observatum Grotio hic, & ad c. VIII. 3. Synedrium non prehensionum tantum, sed & verberum jus in Judæos ex permissu Romanorum habuisse, nec solum in Judæos Palæstinæ, verum etiam extra Palæstinam, ubi erant Synago- gæ, quæ sponte sua Synedrii jurisdictionem in rebus ad religionem spectantibus agnoscebant. Non ta- men in omnibus delictis potestatem illam habe- bant Judæi, sed in illis solum causis, quæ religio- nem ipsorum concernebant.

## 9:3
Vers. 3. περιήστραψεν αὐτὸν( ברק עליו. Φῶς ἀπὸ τῦ ὐρανῦ) See below XXII. 6. & XXVI. 13. Add below XII. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 3. περιήστραψεν αὐτὸν( ברק עליו. Φῶς ἀπὸ τῦ ὐρανῦ) Vide infra XXII. 6. & XXVI. 13. Adde infra XII. 7.

## 9:4
Vers. 4. καὶ πεσὼν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν) As in Daniel VIII. 17. & X. 9. Σαὺλ Σαὺλ) He placed the Hebrew word itself here, without a Greek case.

τί με διώκεις) Because Christ and the Church make one body: and he who harms the kingdom, harms the king.

Latin:

Vers. 4. καὶ πεσὼν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν) Ut Daniel VIII. 17. & X. 9. Σαὺλ Σαὺλ) Ipsam vocem Hebræam hic posuit, sine ca- su Græco.

τί με διώκεις) Quia Christus & Ecclesia unum faciunt corpus: & qui regnum lædit, lædit regem.

## 9:5
Vers. 5. ὁ δὲ Κύριος εἶπε) In that Manuscript: ὁ δὲ ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ Ἰησῦς ὁ Ναζωραῖος ὃν σὺ διώκεις· ἀλλὰ ἀνάστηθι. How many other codices have this has been observed by others, who not incorrectly noted that these were added to this place by scribes from that which is below partly in XXII. 10. and partly in XXVI. 14., in which places this very history is recited more fully.

Therefore, it is not to be concluded immediately from a variation of readings that the true reading is doubtful, but then the more accurate codices are to be compared, and other means of certainty are not to be neglected. Furthermore, from this history of the Pauline conversion, the Calvinists rashly conclude the irresistible grace of conversion: for this was not an ordinary, but an extraordinary conversion, as Polanus in his Syntagma and Groffius in Vindic. Script. acknowledge: nor was the conversion of Saul itself irresistible, even if that irradiation which was prior to the conversion was irresistible, as we have taught elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ὁ δὲ Κύριος εἶπε) In Manuscripto illo: ὁ δὲ ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ Ἰησῦς ὁ Ναζωραῖος ὃν σὺ διώκεις· ἀλλὰ ἀνάστηθι. Quomo- do & multos alios habere codices observatum est ab aliis, qui non male notarunt à librariis hæc ad hunc locum ad- dita ex eo, quod infra est partim XXII. 10. partim XXVI. 14. quibus in locis hæc ipsa historia plenius recitatur.

Non ergo è lectionum variatione statim colli- gendum, dubiam esse veram lectionem, sed tum codices accuratiores imprimis conferendi, tum alia media certitudinis haud negligenda. Cæterum ex hac historia conversionis Paulinæ nonnisi te- mere Calviniani gratiam conversionis irresisti bi- lem colligunt: non enim hæc ordinaria, sed extra- ordinaria fuit conversio, ut Polanus in Syntagma- te & Groffius in Vindic. Script. agnoscunt: nec ir- resistibilem ipsammet Saulis conversionem fuisse, etsi illa irradiatio fuerit irresistibilis, quæ conver- sioni prævia erat, alibi docuimus.

## 9:6
Vers. 6. εἰς τὴν πόλιν) To Damascus. καὶ λαληθήσεταί σοι τί σε δεῖ ποιεῖν) Just as it was said to Saul the king of old הודעתי לך את אשר תעשה I will make known to you what you shall do.

Latin:

Vers. 6. εἰς τὴν πόλιν) Damascum. καὶ λαληθήσεταί σοι τί σε δεῖ ποιεῖν) Sicut Sauli olim regi di- ctum הודעתי לך את אשר תעשה γνωρίσω σοι ἅ ποιή- σεις.

## 9:7
Vers. 7. οἱ δὲ ἄνδρες οἱ συνοδεύοντες αὐτῷ εἰστήκεισαν ἐννεοὶ) So astonished that they lost their voice: how the Syrian understood it. See a similar case in Gen. XLV. 3. first fixed by stupor, then they fell down, as we learn below in XXVI. 14. ἀκούοντες μὲν τῆς φωνῆς) Hearing the sound confusedly, but not understanding the words, clearly as those in John XII. 28. which Maimonides also thinks happened to the people at Mount Sinai from the place in Exodus XIX. 9. compared with Deut. IV. 12. V. 23. below XXII. 9. φωνὴν ὐκ ἤκουσαν means, they did not understand. For the Hebrew שמע is often placed for to understand.

Μηδένα δὲ θεωρῦντες) Clearly as those who, with Daniel, were. Dan. X. 7.

There is no doubt that Christ appeared to Paul here, not through another, but in his own form, and was seen by him, even if he was not seen by his companions: Whence Paul appeals to this vision of Christ 1. Corinthians XV. 8. Therefore he is not so enclosed in heaven by his ascension into heaven, that he cannot present himself to be seen on earth in human flesh, which is to be observed here against the Calvinists. For not with

Zanchius, book II, on the Nature of God, ch. VI, Heidelberg edition, year 1572, page 138, column 2, is to be imagined, that Christ, by his Deity, by which he is everywhere, formed a new body for himself, and under it appeared to Paul on earth, his natural body meanwhile being left in heaven. Which impious fiction he himself corrected later, having been admonished by others.

Latin:

Vers. 7. οἱ δὲ ἄνδρες οἱ συνοδεύοντες αὐτῷ εἰστήκεισαν ἐννεοὶ) Ita attoniti ut vocem perderent: quomodo accepit Syrus. Si- mile vide Gen. XLV. 3. præ stupore primum defixi, deinde delapsi sunt, ut discimus infra XXVI. 14. ἀκούοντες μὲν τῆς φωνῆς) Sonum confuse audientes, non au- tem intelligentes verba, plane ut illi Joh. XII. 28. quod & populo ad montem Sinai evenisse putat Maimonides ex lo- co Exodi XIX. 9. collato cum Deut. IV. 12. V. 23. inf. XXII. 9. φωνὴν ὐκ ἤκουσαν est, non intellexerunt. Nam שמע He- bræum sæpe ponitur pro intelligere.

Μηδένα δὲ θεωρῦντες) Plane ut illi, qui cum Daniele e- tant. Dan. X. 7.

Christum Paulo hic apparuisse, non per alium, sed in forma propria, ab eoque visum esse nullum dubium est, etsi à comitibus ejus visus non sit: Unde Paulus ad hanc Christi visionem provocat 1. Corinth. XV. 8. Non ergo ita per ascensionem in cœlum conclusus cœlo est, ut non possit in terris se in humana carne visendum præbere, quod con- tra Calvinianos hic observandum. Non enim cum

Zanchio l. II. de Natur. Dei c. VI. edit. Heidelb. An- no 1572. pag. 138. col. 2. fingendum, Christum sua Deitate, qua ubique est, corpus sibi novum for- masse, atque sub illo in terris Paulo apparuisse suo naturali corpore interim in cœlo relicto. Quod impium commentum postea ab aliis admonitus ipse correxit.

## 9:8
V. 8. ἠγέρθη δὲ ὁ Σαῦλος ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς) As in Daniel VIII. 18. Ἀνεῳγμένων δὲ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτοῦ, οὐδένα ἔβλεπε) Thus the Syriac reads, not οὐδὲν, and many books have it so. The sense is: Although his eyes were open, he nevertheless saw nothing, and that sense is clearly expressed below in XXII. 11, where the same history is related: ὡς δὲ οὐκ ἐνέβλεπον ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης. Such was the image of Saul, as he had been before, having the appearance of a man learned in the law, when he was plainly blind in his mind.

χειραγωγοῦντες δὲ αὐτὸν) As is usually done for the blind. Thus Antigone is the guide of Oedipus in the Phoenissae: The guidance of a blind parent in Seneca.

The sense can be the same, even if οὐδένα is read, as it is held in the received Greek codices: As also in the Arabic version, London edition, and in Chrysostom. Because he saw no one, for the reason that he could see nothing, as is evident from the necessity of being led by the hand, and the parallel passage Act. XXII. 11. In the Latin text he is also said to have seen NOTHING. Regarding the reconciliation of that circumstance, that Paul's companions are said here to have heard a voice; but in Acts XXII. 9 they are denied to have, let B. Gerhardus be consulted on this passage. Grotius's explanation is not displeasing.

Latin:

V. 8. ἠγέρθη δὲ ὁ Σαῦλος ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς) Ut Daniel. VIII. 18. Ἀνεῳγμένων δὲ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτοῦ, οὐδένα ἔβλεπε) Sic le- git Syrus, non οὐδὲν, multique libri sic habent. Sensus est: Quanquam oculis erat apertis, nihil tamen conspiciebat, & is sensus clare exprimitur infra XXII. 11. ubi eadem histo- ria refertur: ὡς δὲ οὐκ ἐνέβλεπον ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης. Ea fuit imago Sauli, qualis antehac fuerat, speciem habens hominis eru- diti in lege, cum plane animo cæcus esset.

χειραγωγοῦντες δὲ αὐτὸν) Ut cæcis fieri solet. Sic Antigo- ne ποδηγὸς Oedipodis int hœnissis: Cæci parentis regimen apud Senecam.

Sensus idem esse potest, etiamsi legatur οὐδένα, ut in Græcis receptis codicibus habetur: Ut & in Arabica versione edit. Londinens. & apud Chry- sostomum. Quia neminem vidit, eo quod nihil videre potuerit, ut è χειραγωγίας necessitate, & loco parallelo Act. XXII. 11. constat. In Latino tex- tu etiam NIHIL vidisse dicitur. De conciliatio- ne illius circumstantiæ, quod vocem audivisse hic dicuntur Pauli comites; Act. vero XXII. 9. negan- tur, conferatur B. Gerhardus ad h. l. Non displicet, Grotiana explicatio.

## 9:9
Vers. 9. κὶ οὐκ ἔφαγεν οὐδὲ ἔπιεν) Thus showing repentance for the cruelty exercised against the Church. This is what the Hebrews call: Ταπεινοῦν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ.

Not because of repentance; but because of consternation and extreme weakness, on account of which he could neither eat nor drink.

Latin:

Vers. 9. κὶ οὐκ ἔφαγεν οὐδὲ ἔπιεν) Pœnitentiam sic ostendens sævitiæ in Ecclesiam exercitæ. Hoc est quod Hebræi dicunt. Ταπεινοῦν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ.

Non ob pœnitentiam; sed ob consternationem & infirmitatem summam, præ qua nec edere nec bibere potuit.

## 9:10
Vers. 10. Ἁνανίας) As likely to be a friend to Saul as the other Ananias had been to Daniel, Dan. I. 6. seqq.

ἐν ὁράματι) He appeared to him not in a dream, but ἐν ἐκστάσει, some Angel representing the form of Christ. Therefore Ananias had seen Christ before, being one of the seventy disciples, if we believe the ancients.

There is nothing in the text about an Angel representing the appearance of Christ. Therefore, a new ὅραμα (vision) is not to be established ἄτεγγραφῆς (without a record). And we nowhere read in the sacred writings that an Angel was seen in the form of Christ; Ananias heard Christ himself speaking with him αὐτοπροσώπως (in person) and sending him away, not an Angel sustaining the person of Christ; whether he had seen Christ before or not. For he could certainly recognize him from the manifestation, or even by an internal ἐλλάμψει (illumination).

Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ, Κύριε) That is, I am prepared to receive and perform commands. Concerning this manner of speaking, we have spoken at Matt. XXI. 30.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἁνανίας) Tam amicus Saulo futurus, quam al- ter Ananias fuerat Danieli Dan. I. 6. seqq.

ἐν ὁράματι) Apparuit illi non in somnio, sed ἐν ἐκστάσει, Angelus aliquis Christi speciem referens. Viderat ergo an- tehac Christum Ananias, quippe unus discipulorum LXX. si veteribus credimus.

Nihil in textu de Angelo speciem Christi referen- te. Non ergo ἄτεγγραφῆς novum ὅραμα constitu- endum. Et Angelum alicubi in Christi forma conspe- ctum nuspiam in sacris legimus; Christum ipsum αὐτοπροσώπως secum loquentem, seque ablegan- tem audivit Ananias, non Angelum, personam Christi sustinentem; sive viderit antea Christum, sive non. Nam è manifestatione utique agnoscere ipsum potuit, vel etiam interna ἐλλάμψει.

Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ, Κύριε) Id est paratus sum jussa accipere & face- re. De hoc loquendi genere diximus Matth. XXI. 30.

## 9:11
Vers. 11. Τὴν ῥύμην) Thus in Is. XV. 3. is translated שׁוּק, which elsewhere is πλατεῖα (street). And Pollux explains that word by this one. In the Glossary, ῥύμη is a street.

ἐν οἰκίᾳ Ἰούδα) With whom Saul seems to have had an old lodging.

Ταρσέα) Mystically fulfilled is that which is in Is. LXVI. 19, where in the Hebrew it is תַּרְשִׁישׁ, in the Greek Θαρσεῖς.

In Isaiah chapter LXVI. 19, that name is not proper but appellative, and it concerns the nations dwelling by the sea, which has nothing to do with Paul of Tarsus.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Τὴν ῥύμην) Sic Es. XV. 3. vertitur שׁוּק quod ali- bi πλατεῖα. Et Pollux illam vocem per hanc exponit. In Glossario ῥύμη vicus.

ἐν οἰκίᾳ Ἰούδα) Cum quo vetus hospitium Saulo videtur fuisse.

Ταρσέα) Mystice impletum quod est Es. LXVI. 19. ubi in Hebræo תַּרְשִׁישׁ in Græco Θαρσεῖς.

Apud Esaiam cap. LXVI. 19. nomen illud non proprium sed Appellativum est, & de gentibus maris accolis agitur, quod nihil ad Paulum Tar- sensem facit.

## 9:12
Vers. 12. κὶ εἶδεν ἐν ὁράματι) The Syriac took it as the continued words of God: Nor does what follows, 'a man by the name of Ananias', stand in the way: Because to Paul, who had not known him, that very name was indicated in the vision.

It is so; the words of God are continued entirely here, as observed by Piscator and the Vinarienses. Nor does it appear how these are to be taken otherwise, unless a parenthesis is invented by Luke, with the words of God inserted before the response of Ananias, which most Papist interpreters, Lorinus, Tirinus, Menochius, Corn. à Lapide, and Fromondus, maintain.

καὶ ἐπιθέντα αὐτῷ χεῖρα, ὅπως ἀναβλέψῃ) See the things said above at VIII. 17.

Latin:

Vers. 12. κὶ εἶδεν ἐν ὁράματι) Syrus accepit ut continuata Dei verba: Nec obstat, quod sequitur, Virum nomine Ananiam: Quia Paulo, qui illum non noverat, in viso id- ipsum nomen indicatum fuit.

Ita est; continuantur omnino hic Dei verba, ut Piscatori, & Vinariensibus observatum. Nec apparet, quomodo aliter hæc accipienda sint, nisi parenthesis fingatur à Luca verbis Dei insertis an- te responsionem Ananiæ, quod Pontificii inter- pretes plerique, Lorinus, Tirinus, Menochius; Corn. à Lapide, ac Fromondus volunt.

καὶ ἐπιθέντα αὐτῷ χεῖρα, ὅπως ἀναβλέψῃ) Vide dicta su- pra VIII. 17.

## 9:13
Vers. 13. Τοῖς ἁγίοις σου) To the true Nazarenes thus, and below 32 and 41.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Τοῖς ἁγίοις σου) Veris Nazarenis sic, & infra 32. & 41.

## 9:14
Vers. 14. ᾗ ὧδε ἔχει ἐξουσίαν) Ananias shows how unsafe it was for him to approach one who had received authority in the very city of Damascus to seize men of that profession to which Ananias belonged,

παρὰ τῶν ἀρχιερέων) This is a synecdoche. For the whole Sanhedrin is designated by its most noble part.

ἐπικαλουμένους τὸ ὄνομά σου) Just as Stephen had done in VII, 58. Pliny on the Christians of his time: That they were accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn and to sing a hymn to Christ, as if to a god, among themselves.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ᾗ ὧδε ἔχει ἐξουσίαν) Ostendit Ananias, quam non turum sibifit, eum accedere, qui potestatem acceperat in ipsa urbe Damasco capiendi homines ejus professionis,cu- jus erat Ananias,

παρὰ τῶν ἀρχιερέων) Est συνεκδοχή. Ex parte enim nobili- ssima designatur totum Synedrium.

ἐπικαλουμένους τὸ ὄνομά σου) Sicut Stephanus fecerat VII, 58. Plinius de Christianis sui temporis: Quod essent soliti stato die ante lucem convenire carmenque Christo, quasi Deo dicere secum invicem.

## 9:15
V. 15. Σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς μοί ἐστιν ὗτος) A Hebraism. Σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς for σκεῦος ἐκλεκτὸν, a most exquisite instrument. A vessel of God's use, says Rabbi Israel on Psalm LI. Nor does Polybius use the word σκεῦος otherwise when speaking of Damocles: 'He was a serviceable vessel and had many resources for the management of affairs.'

ἐνώπιον ἐθνῶν κὰι βασιλέων ὑῶν τε Ἰσραήλ) Reference is made to the passage in Ef. XLIX. 6. & Jerem. I. 10.

The passage of Jeremiah is not a twin to the other. For there the discourse is about Jeremiah himself, and about the time in which he lived. But in Ef. XLIX. 6. it concerns Christ and the time of the New Testament.

Latin:

V. 15. Σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς μοί ἐστιν ὗτος) Hebraismus. Σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς pro σκεῦος ἐκλεκτὸν, instrumentum exquifitissimum. Vas usus Dei, ait Rabbi Israël ad Psal. LI. Nec aliter vo- cem σκεῦος usurpat Polybius de Damocle loquens: ὁ δὲ ἧν ὑπηρετικὸν σκεῦος καὶ πολλὰς ἔχον ἀφορμὰς εἰς πραγμάτων οἰ- κονομίαν.

ἐνώπιον ἐθνῶν κὰι βασιλέων ὑῶν τε Ἰσραήλ) Respicitur ad lo- cum Ef. XLIX. 6. & Jerem. I. 10.

Locus Jeremiæ alteri geminus non est. Ibi enim de Jeremia ipso sermo est, & de tempore illo quo vixit. At Ef. XLIX. 6. de Christo agitur & tempo- re N. Testamenti.

## 9:16
V. 16. ὅσα δεῖ αὐτὸν ὑπὲρ τῶ ὀνόματός με παθεῖν) The hatreds of his countrymen, the fury of the nations, prison, scourges, hunger, thirst, shipwrecks, death. These things I will show him, and yet he will preach my name: What he did to others, he will willingly bear.

Latin:

V. 16. ὅσα δεῖ αὐτὸν ὑπὲρ τῶ ὀνόματός με παθεῖν) Odia po- pularium, furorem gentium, carcerem, flagra, famem, sitim, naufragia, mortem. Hæc illi ostendam, & tamen prædicabit nomen meum: Quæ aliis fecit, libenter feret.

## 9:17
Vers. 17. εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν) Of that Judas of whom [we spoke] above in 11.

Σαὺλ ἀδελφὲ) He calls him brother, as a companion in the faith; thus above in VI. 3.

κὰι πληơθῇς Πνεύματος ἁγίου) Which happened to him as soon as he recovered his sight, so that the internal reality might accompany the external sign. This was an anticipation of grace such as we noted above in VIII. 39. and shall have below in X. 44.

Why is it called an anticipation of grace? For could not the same have been conferred even outside of baptism, and outside of χειροθεσίαν? But because Saul is called brother by Ananias, although not yet baptized, it is rashly denied by the Papists that Catechumens, even if they have not yet received baptism, are true members of the Church. And since he became a participant of the gifts of the Holy Spirit through Ananias, this axiom is certainly not to be claimed for Bishops alone; because Ananias was certainly not a Bishop, nor for the Apostles alone, which was asserted by the Papist-leaning Grotius at chapter VIII.15, because Ananias was not an Apostle either.

Latin:

Vers. 17. εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν) Illius Judæ de quo supra 11.

Σαὺλ ἀδελφὲ) Fratrem eum vocat, ut consortem fidei; sic supra VI. 3.

κὰι πληơθῇς Πνεύματος ἁγίου) Quod ei evenit, simulat- que visum recuperavit, ut ad externum signum interna res accederet. Hæc fuit anticipatio gratiæ qualem supra nota- vimus VIII. 39. & habebimus infra X. 44.

Cur anticipatio dicitur gratiæ? Annon enim eadem conferri potuit etiam extra baptismum, & extra χειροθεσίαν? Quia vero frater vocatur ab Anania Saulus, etsi nondum baptizatus, Catechu- menos, utut nondum baptismum sulceperint, ve- ra Ecclesiæ membra esse temere à Pontificiis nega- tur. Et quum donorum S. S. particeps factus sit per Ananiam, utique non solis Episcopis hoc axio- ma vindicandum; quia Ananias certe non fuit E- piscopus, neque solis Apostolis, quod à Grotio Pa- pizante assertum ad cap. VIII.15. quia nec Aposto- lus fuit Ananias.

## 9:18
Verse 18. ὡσεὶ λεπίδες [as it were scales]) Shadowing forth that veil of which Paul treats in 2 Cor. III. 14.

ἐβαπτίσθη [he was baptized]) Ananias is of the same right in this as Philip the Deacon was before.

Latin:

Vers 18. ὡσεὶ λεπίδες) Adumbrantes velum illud de quo agit Paulus 2. Cor. III. 14.

ἐβαπτίσθη) Istus est pari jure Ananias, quo ante Philip- pus Diaconus,

## 9:19
Verse 19. κ̓αὶ λαβὼν τροφὴν ἐνίσχυσεν [and having taken food he was strengthened]) It is in the active voice, with a reciprocal sense: התחזק Genesis XLVIII. 2. Thus also ἰσχύειν, ἐνισχύειν, παλισχύειν often in the interpreters of the Old Testament and Sir. XLVIII. 25. and 1 Macc. I. 38. VII. 25. as also ἐνίσχυσε Luke XXIII. 5.

μετὰ τῶν ἐν Δαμάσκῳ μαθητῶν [with the disciples in Damascus]) Μαθηταὶ here as above I.15, who acknowledged Jesus as Master, not Hillel or Sameas, or others. Now there were quite a few such in Damascus from the time of that dispersion, of which above VIII. 1, 3.

PART II.

The deliverance of Saul, who was preaching Jesus, from the snares of Damascus and Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 19. κ̓αὶ λαβὼν τροφὴν ἐνίσχυσεν) Est sono activo, sensu reciproco: התחזק Genes. XLVIII. 2. sic & ἰσχύειν ἐνισχύειν παλισχύειν sæpe in interpretibus Veteris Testamenti & Sir. XLVIII. 25. & 1. Macc. I. 38. VII. 25. si & ἐνίσχυσε Luc. XXIII. 5.

μετὰ τῶν ἐν Δαμάσκῳ μαθητῶν) Μαθηταὶ hic ut supra I.15. qui Jesum Magistrum agnoscebant, non Hillelem aut Sa- meam, aut alios. Damasci autem tales aliquam multi erant à tempore dispersionis illius, de qua supra VIII. 1, 3.

PARS II.

Sauli Jesum prædicantis ab insidiis Damasce- nis & Hierofolymitanis liberatio.

## 9:20
Verse 20. ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς [in the synagogues]) For the Apostles always addressed the Jews first, so that they might either convert them, or take away from them every excuse.

ἐκήρυσσε τὸν χριστὸν, ὅτι ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τῦ Θεῦ [he preached Christ, that this is the Son of God]) Better in the manuscript: ἐκήρυσσε τὸν Ἰησῦν ὅτι [he preached Jesus that]. For Christ and the Son of God are put for the same thing, as we have said. The question was, whether Jesus of Nazareth was that Christ or Son of God.

The remaining codices are rashly corrected from one MS., with which the Arabic version agrees: it is falsely asserted that Christ and the Son of God are put for the same thing. We showed the contrary against the Socinians in Anti-Grellius p. 385. The name Son of God is the name of a person, but Christ is of an office.

Latin:

Vers. 20 ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς) Semper enim Apostoli Ju- dæos primum affati sunt, ut aut eos converterent, aut o- mnem eis excusationem adimerent.

ἐκήρυσσε τὸν χριστὸν, ὅτι ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τῦ Θεῦ) Melius in manufcripto : ἐκήρυσσε τὸν Ἰησῦν ὅτι. Nam Christus & Dei Filius pro eodem ponitur, ut diximus. Quæstio erat, an Jesus Nazarenus esset ille Christus sive Dei Filius,

Temere ex uno MS. reliqui codices corrigun- tur, quibus Arabica versio consonat: Christum, & Dei Filium pro eodem poni falso asseritur. Con- trarium contra Socinianos ostendimus in Anti- Grellio p. 385. Nomen Filii Dei personæ nomen est, Christi vero officii.

## 9:21
Verse 21. Οὐχ ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ πορθήσας ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ τὺς ἐπικαλ- λυμένυς τὸ ὄνομα τῦτο [Is this not he who destroyed in Jerusalem those who call upon this name]) As if they were saying: Is Saul also among the Prophets 1 Samuel X.11. πορθεῖν here is to harass. Paul uses the same word in this very history Gal. I. 13, 23.

— πρὸς ὅδε τῦτο ἐλήλυθει [for this he had come]) ὧδε [hither] is used by the Greeks also for motion to a place, thus in Matth. VIII. 29. XIV. 8. Luke XIV. 21. John XX. 27. Rev. IV. 1.

ἐπὶ τὺς ἀρχιερεῖς) See above 14.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Οὐχ ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ πορθήσας ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ τὺς ἐπικαλ- λυμένυς τὸ ὄνομα τῦτο) Quasi dicerent: An etiam Saul in- ter Prophetas 1 Samuel. X.II. πορθεῖν hic est vexare. Uti- tur eouem vocabulo in eadem hac historia Paulus Gal. I. 13.23.

— πρὸς ὅδε τῦτο ἐλήλυθει) ὧδε Græcis etiam motionem ad locum sic ing theat Matth. VIII. 29. XIV. 8. Luc. XIV.21. Joh. XX. 27. Apoc. IV. 1.

ἐπὶ τὺς ἀρχιερεῖς) Vide supra 14.

## 9:22
Vers. 22. Ἐνεδυναμῦτο) He was becoming stronger day by day. Thus Rom. IV, 20. Eph. VI. 10. 2. Timoth. I. II. Heb. XI. 34. It corresponds to the Hebrew זוע as appears in Ps. LII. 9.

Others more correctly understand here the Caesarea of Philip, situated at the root of Mount Lebanon not far from Damascus, inasmuch as it was once called Lachis and Dan, concerning which Josephus, book II of the Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 8, from which Paul could arrive in his homeland of Cilicia by a land journey. Compare Acts 16:15. In the preceding chapter, the last verse, it treats of Caesarea of Straton situated by the Mediterranean Sea, concerning which Josephus, book I of the Jewish War, chapters 3 and 16, which was restored by Herod the Ascalonite in honor of Caesar Augustus. See what is in Acts 10:1.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Ἐνεδυναμῦτο) Fortior fiebat indies. Sic Rom. IV,20. Eph. VI. 10. 2. Timoth. I.II. Ebr. XI. 34. Respon- det Hebræo זוע ut apparet Pf. LII. 9.

ream Philippi alii rectius hic intelligunt, ad radi- cem montis Libani haud procul a Damasco sitam, utpote quæ olim Lachis & Dan dicta, de qua Jo- seph. l. II. Ant. Jud. cap. 8. ex qua Paulus itinere terrestri in Ciliciam patriam suam pervenire po- tuit. Conf. Actor. XVI.15. In præcedente v. capite v. ult. de Cæsarea Stratonis ad mare mediterrane- um sita agitur, de qua Josephus libro I. de Bell. Jud. cap. 3. & 16. quæ ab Herode Ascalonita in hono- rem Cæsaris Augusti restaurata est. Vide quæ Act. X. 1.

## 9:30
εἰς Ταρσόν) Where he could be safer from ambushes among many who were his kin and acquaintances.

It was the metropolis of Cilicia, which Jerome in his Hebrew places says was built by Tarsus, son of Javan. Solinus, book 47, called it the mother of cities.

PART III. The building up of the Church in tranquility, and its expansion through the healing of Aeneas by miracles and the raising of Tabitha.

Latin:

εἰς Ταρσόν) Ubi inter multos sibi propinquos & notos tu- tior ab insidiis esse posset.

Metropolis ea Ciliciæ fuit quam Hieron. in loc. Ebraic. a Tarso filio Javan exstructam dicit. Solinus l. 47. matrem urbium appellavit.

PARS III. Ecclesiæ in tranquillitate ædificatio & per mi- racula sanati Æneæ, & resuscitata Ta- bithæ amplificatio.

## 9:31
Verse 31.

ἔσχον εἰρήνην) With many having gone into exile, the persecution had burned out, that is, what the Christians called peace. See our annotations to book I of The Law of War and Peace, chapter 2, near the end.

They attribute this quiet to Tiberius; concerning whom Tertullian in his Apology, chapter V, and Eusebius in his Chronicle report that, hearing of the wonders which Christ had performed, he threatened death to the accusers of Christians by public edict.

Οἰκοδομούμεναι) This word is translated in a similar way to the Latin 'instruere' [to build up/instruct]. See 1 Corinthians 8:10, 10:23, 14:4.

It is more correctly explained by the blessed Luther regarding building up, because the Church is the building and house of God, Psalm 27:4, 69:10, 24:5, 92:17, Ephesians 2:19, 22, 1 Timothy 3:4, Hebrews 3:3, 6.

καὶ πορευόμεναι τῷ φόβῳ τῷ Κυρίου) A similar construction in 1 Maccabees 6:23, πορευέσθαι τοῖς ὑπ' αὐτῦ λεγομένοις, and 59, πορευθῶσι τοῖς νομίμοις αὐτῶν.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

ἔσχον εἰρήνην) Multis in exilium egressis deflagraverat ve- xatio, id est, quod Christiani pacem vocabant. Vide an- notata nostra ad r. I. de lure Belli & Pacis c. 2. circa finem.

Hanc quietem Tiberio tribuunt; de quo Ter- tull. in Apol. c. V. & Euseb. in Chronic. perhibent, quod mira, quæ Christus gesserat, audiens, pu- blico edicto Christianorum accusatoribus mor- tem comminatus fuerit.

Οἰκοδομούμεναι) Est hæc vox simili modo translata, quo Latinum instruere. Vide I. Corinth. VIII. 10. X. 23. XIV. v. 4.

Rectius de ædificatione a B. Luthero explica- tur, quia Ecclesia ædificium & domus Dei Psal. XXVII. 4. LXIX. 10. XXIV. 5. XCII. 17. Ephes. II. 19. 22. 1. Tim. III. 4. Ebr. III. 3. 6.

καὶ πορευόμεναι τῷ φόβῳ τῷ Κυρίου) Similis constructio 1. Maccab. VI. 23. πορευέσθαι τοῖς ὑπ' αὐτῦ λεγομένοις. & 59. πορευθῶσι τοῖς νομίμοις αὐτῶν.

## 9:32
Verse 32.

τοὺς κατοικοῦντας Λύδδαν) This is a village of Palestine to the west of the Jordan. See Pliny and Ptolemy. In Syriac, לוד, as also in Hebrew, 1 Chronicles 8:12. Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 20.5, calls it a village not inferior to a city in size. See what was said on Mark 1:38.

Lydda was then called Diospolis, and finally Ruma, by which name it is known today, as Adrichomius notes. Bunting observes that it is five miles distant from Jerusalem, part II of the Itinerary of the Holy Land. The Synod of Lydda and Diospolis against Pelagius, convened in the time of Augustine, is famous.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

τοὺς κατοικοῦντας Λύδδαν) Est is vicus Palæstinæ ad occa- sum lordanis. Vide Plinium & Ptolemæum. In Syriaco לוד ut & in Ebræo I. Paral. VIII. 12. Iosephus antiquæ historiæ XX. 5. vocat κώμην πόλεως τὸ μέγεθος ἐκ ἀποδέυσαν. Vide quæ dicta ad Marcum I. 38.

Dicta deinde Lydda est Diospolis, ac denique Ruma, quo nomine hodie venit notante Adricho- mio. Hierosolyma quinque eam milliaribus dista- re observat Bunting. parte II. Itiner. terræ san- ctæ. Celebris est Synodus Lyddensis & Diospolita- na contra Pelagium, coacta Augustini tem- pore.

## 9:33
Verse 33.

Αἰνέαν ὀνόματι) The name Αἰνίας and Αἰνέας is the same; but the former is genuine, as it is placed here: the latter is poetic, because otherwise that word could not enter heroic verse, therefore it is written Αἰνέας in iambics. Sophocles in Laocoon: Νῦν δ' ἐν πύλαισιν Αἰνέας ὁ τῆς θεᾶ. And hence also the heroic poets say Αἰνειάδας, and the Latins Aeneadas with the second syllable shortened. I do not doubt that the Aeneas who is treated of here was a Jew: he was called Aeneas among the Greeks, to whom Luke accommodates himself here. In Hebrew, Hillel, like that noble teacher in Jerusalem.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

Αἰνέαν ὀνόματι) Idem est nomen Αἰνίας & Αἰνέας; sed illud genuinum, ut hic est positum: Hoc Poëti- cum, quia aliter ea vox heroïcum intrare non poterat, ideo in Iambicis scribitur Αἰνέας. Sophocles Laoco- onte: Νῦν δ' ἐν πύλαισιν Αἰνέας ὁ τῆς θεᾶ. Et hinc etiam Heroïci dicunt Αἰνειάδας, & Latini Ænea- das secunda correpta. Æneas de quo hic agitur, non du- bito, quin fuerit Iudæus: dictus inter Græcos, quibus Lu- cas hic se accommodat, Αἰνέας. Hebræis הילל Hillel, ut ille Hierosolymis nobilis magister.

## 9:34
Verse 34.

ἰᾶταί σε ὁ Κύριος Ἰησοῦς χρισὸς) That manuscript has ἰᾶται, and the Syriac reads it thus. He does not pray; but he promises with certainty.

Not only the Syriac, but also the Arabic favors this reading. We judge that ἰᾶται, which Leudensis, as well as Beza and Erasmus, approve—and which Erasmus Schmid prefers to the other as more accepted—and which the Ethiopic and the Latin Vulgate follow, is altogether to be preferred.

ἀνάσηθι) קום לך Στρῶσον σεαυτῷ) The bed which others previously made for you, make for yourself, as a sign of restored health. You have a similar, though not identical, passage in Mark 2:19, John 5:8.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

ἰᾶταί σε ὁ Κύριος Ἰησοῦς χρισὸς) Ἰᾶται habet & Manuscri- ptu ille, & sic legit Syrus. Non precatur; sed certo pro- mittit.

Lectioni huic non Syrus tantum, sed & Arabs faveredit. Leudensis, ut & Beza, & Erasmus, quam ceu receptiorem alteri ab Erasmo Schmi- dio probatæ ἰᾶται sanet, quam Æthiops & Vulg. Latin. sequuntur, omnino preferendam cense- mus.

ἀνάσηθι) קום לך Στρῶσον σεαυτῷ) Lectum quem antehac straverunt tibi alii, tute tibi sterne, in signum restitutæ valetudinis. Simi- le, non idem, habes Marci II. 19. Ioh. V. 8.

## 9:35
Verse 35.

καὶ τὸν Σαρωνᾶν) In the manuscript, τὸν Σάρῥωνα. Neither is wrong; the latter is Hebrew, the former is Syriac. Saron is a pasture field lying wide open. See 1 Chronicles 5:16, 27:29, Isaiah 33:9, John 5:8.

Others understand it as a city situated on a mountain in the tribe of Ephraim, with the author of the Glossa Ordinaria, Dionysius the Carthusian, Andreas Masius, and Benedictus Arias Montanus on chapter 12 of Joshua. However, that opinion which wishes a region to be indicated is approved by Lorinus, Fromundus, and Ludovicus de Dieu, who should be consulted here in particular.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

καὶ τὸν Σαρωνᾶν) In Manuscripto τὸν Σάρῥωνα. Neutrum male, hoc est Hebræum, illud Syriacum. Saron est ager pascuus late patens, Vide 1. Par. V. 16. XXVII. 29. Es. XXIII. 9. Iohan. V. 8.

Alii pro urbe in tribu Ephraim in monte sita intelligunt cum autore Glossæ ordinar. Dionysio Carthus. Andr. Masio ac Benedicto Ariemonta- no in cap. XII. Jos. Illam tamen sententiam, quæ regionem notari vult probat Lorinus, Fromun. dus & Ludov. de Dieu, qui hic imprimis videa- tur.

## 9:36
Verse 36.

Tabitha) In Syriac טביתא. The learned rightly warn that פ is often placed by the Syrians where there is a ב in Hebrew. In Hebrew, צבי is δορκάς. Deuteronomy 12:15, 22; chapter 14:5; chapter 15:22; 2 Samuel chapter 2:18; 1 Kings chapter 4:23; 1 Chronicles chapter 12:8; Proverbs chapter 6:5; Song of Songs chapter 2:9; chapter 4:3; chapter 7:3; chapter 8:14.

which is interpreted is called Dorcas) She was so called among the Greeks, just as Thomas is Didymus, Cephas is Peter. See below 39.

Full of good works) A Hebrew idiom such as Isaiah 50:21, John 1:14, below 13:10.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

Tabitha) In Syriaco טביתא. Recte monent eruditi Syris sæpe פ poni ubi in Hebræo est ב. Hebræis צבי est δορκάς. Deuter. XII 15.22. cap. XIV. 5. cap. XV. 22 2. Sam. cap.II.18. 1.Reg. cap. IV.23. I. Paral.cap. XII. 8. Proverb. cap. VI. 5. Cantic. cap. II. 9. cap. IV. 3. cap. VII. 3. cap. VIII. 14.

ἡ διερμηνευομένη λέγεται Δορκάς) Sic vocabatur inter Græcos, quomodo Thomas Δίδυμος, Cephas Πέτρ@- Vi- de infra 39.

Πλήρης ἔργων ἀγαθῶν) Loquutio Hebræa qualis Esaiz L 21. Ioh. 1. 14. infra XIII. 10.

## 9:37
Vers. 37.

And having washed her) It was permitted to wash corpses for those nearby: Servius on Book IV of the Aeneid regarding that line of Virgil: 'Give water for the wounds --- I will wash, etc.' The same Virgil, IV: 'And they wash the body of the cold one and anoint it.' That the custom of washing the bodies of the deceased was accepted not only among the Romans, but also among the Greeks, is evident from Aelian, Book IV of Various History, Book I, and Plato in the Phaedo. That it also flourished among the Jews, we learn here, and Rabbi Moses Maimonides records it in the treatise on mourning, chapter IV. That it was accepted among Christians is clear from Tertullian, Apology, chapter 42, and Eusebius, Book VII of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 17.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

Λούσαντες δὲ αὐτὴν) Lavare cadavera proximis concede- batur: Servius ad IV. Æneidos ad illud Virgilii: Date vulnera lymphis --- Abluam &c. Idem Virgilius IV. Corpusque lavant frigentis & unguunt. Non apud Romanos tantum, sed & Græcos mo- rem abluendi defunctorum corpora receptum fuisse ex Æliano l. IV. var. Histor. L. I. & Plato- ne in Phædone constat. Quem etiam apud Judæos viguisse, hic discimus, traditque R. Moses May- monid. tr. de luctu cap. IV. Apud. Christianos eum receptum è Tertullian. Apol. c. XLII. Euseb. 1. VII. Histor. Eccl. c. 17. liquet.

## 9:38
And Lydda being near to Joppa) This is apparent from Ptolemy.

Latin:

Ἐγγὺς δὲ ἔσης Λύδδης τῇ Ἰόππη) Apparet id ex Ptolo- mæo.

## 9:39
Vers. 39.

Weeping) As in Mark 5:38. Showing the tunics and garments, as many as Dorcas made while she was with them) You see that what Euripides said is true: 'Virtue, even if someone dies, does not perish.' Chiton is the inner garment; himation the outer.

Latin:

Vers. 39.

Κλαίουσαι) Ut Marci V. 38. Ἐπιδεικνύμεναι χιτῶνας καὶ ἱμάτια, ὅσα ἐποίει μετ' αὐ- τῶν ὖσα ἡ Δορκάς) Vides verum esse quod dixit Euripi- des: Ἀρετὴ δὲ, κἂν ἀποθάνῃ τις, ἐκ ἀπόλλυται χιτὼν interior vestis; ἱμάτιον exterior.

## 9:40
Vers. 40.

But Peter having cast everyone out) Lest he seem to be hunting for fame; he had learned this also from the Master, Mark 5:40.

This was done primarily so that he might pour out more ardent prayers to GOD, which Lyranus observed, and that he might not be disturbed in them by the crowd of people, as Chrysostom advised. Compare 2 Kings 4:33, Matthew 9:25.

Having placed his knees) See above 7:60. Regarding this rite and gesture used in prayers, see Matthew 17:14, chapter 23:29, Mark 1:40, chapter 10:17, chapter 15:19, Acts 20:36, chapter 21:5. It was a sign of humility and penitence or contrition for a fall, just as conversely, the ancient Christians praying on Sundays and the feast of Easter did not bend their knees as a sign of the resurrection obtained by Christ. See Justin, 99, and response number 115.

To the body) Properly. For the ancients observe that Homer does not use soma except for a dead body.

Ἀνάσθηθι) קומי as in Mark 5:41. Ὁμοιώθητι τῇ Δορκάδι (Be made like unto Dorcas) Cant. 8, at the end.

ἡ δὲ ἤνοιξε τῆς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτῆς (And she opened her eyes) A sign of one reviving.

Latin:

Vers. 40.

ἐκβαλὼν δὲ ἔξω πάντας ὁ Πέτρ@-) Ne famam aucupari vide- retur; didicerat & hoc a Magistro Marci V. 40.

Imprimis hoc factum, ut eo ardentiores pre- ces ad DEUM funderet, quod Lyranus obser- vavit, nec à populi concursu in illis turbaretur, ut monuit Chrysostom. Conf. 2. Reg. IV. 33. Matth. IX. 25.

Θεὶς τὰ γόνατα) Vide supra VII. 60. De hoc ritu, & gestu in precibus adhibito Matth. XVII. 14. cap. XXIII. 29. Marci 1.40. cap. X. 17. cap. XV. 19. Actorum XX. 36. cap. XXI. 5. Si- gnum erat humilitatis & pœnitentiæ vel contritionis ob lapsum, quemadmodum vice versa Christia- ni veteres diebus Dominicis ac festo Paschatos orantes non flectebant genua in fignum resurre- ctionis a Christo comparatæ. Vid. Justin. 99. & resp. n. CXV.

Πρὸς τὸ σῶμα) Proprie. Nam Homerum non usurpare σῶμα nisi de corpore mortuo, observant veteres.

Ἀνάσθηθι) קומי ut Marci V. 41. Ὁμοιώθητι τῇ Δορκάδι Cant. VIII. in fine.

ἡ δὲ ἤνοιξε τῆς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτῆς) Signum reviviscentis.

Vers. 41.

Παρέστησεν αὐτὴν ζῶσαν (He presented her alive) He exhibited.
