## 9:42
γνωστὸν δὲ ἐγένετο καθ' ὅλης τῆς Ἰόππης (And it became known throughout all Joppa) Celebrated in Joppa.

Bar-Jonas is more than Jonas. Jonas was resuscitated from the whale. Bar-Jonas is the resuscitator of Talitha from the underworld.

By both miracles the people of Joppa were invited to the Church. Therefore, here too, many believed in Christ. For Joppa was formerly called Japho. Jon. I. 3. 1. Macc. X. 2. Macc. XII. concerning which see Joseph. b. IX. Antiq. ch. 2. Strabo b. XVI.

and many believed in the Lord) They placed their trust in Christ.

Latin:

γνωστὸν δὲ ἐγένετο καθ' ὅλης τῆς Ἰόππης) Celebratus Ioppe

Barjonas plus quam Jonas. Jonas è ceto resuscicatus. Barjonas Talithæ ex orco resuscitator.

Utroque miraculo Joppenses ad Ecclesiam invitati fuere. Ideo etiam hic multi in Christum crediderunt. Joppe enim olim Japho dicta. Jon. I. 3. 1. Macc. X. 2. Macc. XII. de qua Vid. Joseph. l. IX. Antiq. c. 2. Strabo l. XVI.

καὶ πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν ἐπὶ τὸν Κύριον) In Christo fiduciam suam posuere.

## 9:43
Verse 43.

with a certain Simon a tanner) In the Glossary: βυρσεὺς is a tanner; more elegant Greeks would say βυρσοδέψης.

PART II. OF THE BOOK concerning the extension of the Church among the Gentiles through Syria, Lycaonia, Pamphylia, Greece, etc., undertaken mainly by St. Paul.

Latin:

Vers. 43.

παρά τινι Σίμωνι βυρσεῖ) In Glossario: βυρσεὺς coriarius Græci elegantiores βυρσοδέψης dicerent.

PARS II. LIBRI PROROGATIONEM ECCLESIÆ inter Gentes per Syriam, Lycaoniam, Pamphyliam, Græciam &c. maxime à S. Paulo susceptam concernens.

## 10:1 Argument
CHAPTER X. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The first entry to the Gentiles, with Cornelius at Caesarea ordered by a vision to summon Peter from Joppa: and Peter meanwhile, having been taught by a vision and a heavenly voice about not considering that impure which GOD has cleansed, and about going to Cornelius: To whom Cornelius explained the heavenly command, whence, after Peter's sermon was delivered concerning the announcement of peace prepared through Christ throughout Judea, whom GOD had anointed with the Holy Spirit; who was killed and resuscitated, and who, having been shown alive, commanded the Apostles to testify that He is appointed Judge of the living and the dead, and that through His name they who believe in Him obtain remission of sins, by the testimony of all the Prophets; the Holy Spirit fell upon the Gentiles in the house of Cornelius; with the Jews being astonished that the Spirit had been poured out upon them also, so that they spoke in various tongues. And Peter baptized them in the name of the Lord, and remained there for some days.

There are three parts: I. Of Cornelius, whose piety is described, and the vision about summoning Peter; to verse 9. II. Peter's instruction through a vision about cleansing the unclean, and his instruction to depart with the same when the messengers of Cornelius appeared; to verse 24. III. Peter's reception by Cornelius, and the sermon held in his house, with the consequences of the same; to verse 48.

PART I. The vision of Cornelius about summoning Peter.

Verse 1.

by name Cornelius) A Roman with a Roman name, perhaps from the Scipios or the Sullas.

Ἑκατοντάρχης) In the Glossary: Centurion: Ἑκατόνταρχος.

Ἐκ σπείρης) That σπείρην in these books is not a legion but a cohort is apparent from Matt. XXVII. 27, Mark XV. 16, John XVIII. 3, 12, where he who is in charge of it is called χιλίαρχος, as also below in XXI. 31.

Τῆς καλυμένης Ἰταλικῆς) That is, of the Italian legion. The Italian legion is on an ancient stone, which Lipsius mentions in his notes on Tacitus, Hist. II, and Tacitus himself often does.

Latin:

CAPUT X. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Primus ad gentes ingressus Cornelio Cæsarea visionem jusso Petrum Joppæ advocare: Petroque interea visione & voce cœlesti de non habendo impuro, quod DEUS mundavit, deque adeundo Cornelio, edocto: Cui exposuit Cornelius mandatum cœleste, unde concione Petri de annunciatione pacis per Christum paratæ per Judæam facta, quam DEUS Spiritu S. unxerat; occiso, resuscitato, qui vivus demonstratus Apostolos jussit testari, quod constitutus Judex sit vivorum & mortuorum, quodque testimonio omnium Prophetarum per nomen ejus remissionem consequantur, in ipsum credentes; Spiritus S. in gentiles in ædibus Cornelii cecidit; Judæis obstupescentibus, quod etiam in eos Spiritus effusus esset, ut variis linguis loquerentur. Et baptizavit eos Petrus in nomine Domini, ibique ad aliquot dies mansit.

Partes sunt tres I. Cornelii, cujus pietas describitur, de accersendo Petro visio; ad vers. 9. II. Petri de immundis mundandis per visionem informatio, ejusdemque, comparentibus nunciis Cornelii, ad proficiscendum cum iisdem instructio, ad v. 24. III. Petri à Cornelio exceptio, & in ædibus ejus habita concio, cum ejusdem consequentibus, ad v. 48.

PARS I. Cornelii de accersendo Petro visio.

Vers. 1.

Ὀνόματι Κορνήλιος) Romanus Romano nomine ex Scipionibus aut Sullis forte.

Ἑκατοντάρχης) In Glossario: Centurio: Ἑκατόνταρχος.

Ἐκ σπείρης) Σπείρην in his libris esse non legionem sed cohortem apparet ex Matt. XXVII. 27. Marci XV. 16. Joh. XVIII. 3. 12. ubi qui ei præest, χιλίαρχος vocatur, ut & infra XXI. 31.

Τῆς καλυμένης Ἰταλικῆς) Id est, legionis Italicæ. Legio Italica est in veteri lapide, cujus meminit Lipsius ad Tacitum Hist. II. & ipse Tacitus sæpe.

## 10:2
Vers. 2.

Εὐσεβὴς κὶ φοβύμενος τὸν Θεόν) Uncircumcised; but one who, having abandoned idolatry, had given himself to the one God, and followed what he judged to be consistent with piety; such as are called חסידי אומות by the Talmudists, and σεβόμενοι ἄνδρες below in XVII. 4. Many such had once lived in Judea, but they were bound by certain rules, about which a man of the greatest erudition, Selden, has produced many things useful to read. After the Jews were forced to bear the yoke of the nations, and having with difficulty preserved for themselves the freedom of their sacred rites, had lost jurisdiction over the foreigners living among them, and therefore could not restrain them within those rules, the wise men instituted that the Jews should entirely avoid the company of foreigners, because they were either idolaters, or at least were not thought to keep the precepts of Noah; and the Apostles would have followed this perpetually, nor would they have admitted any non-Jew by birth or proselyte of the law into their familiarity, unless God had expressly shown to Peter first, and then also to Paul, that it pleased Him for this to be done. And the cause of that institution of the wise men ceased; because such foreigners, by joining themselves to the Church through baptism, by that very act testified that they were departing far not only from idolatry, but from all wickedness, and promised a life much purer than that of those who followed the precepts of Noah.

That Cornelius was uncircumcised, who nevertheless, having abandoned idolatry, had given himself to the one God, we easily acknowledge, nor do we reject that distinction between proselytes of the law, such as are called by the Hebrews גרי צדק, proselytes of justice, of truth, or of the true [God], and גרי ברית, proselytes of the covenant, who undertook circumcision and the whole law of Moses; and גרי שער, proselytes of the Gate, who did not undertake Jewish rites, which is approved everywhere by great men. See Buxtorf, Lex. Rabb. Talm. p. 467; Drusius, lib. V. praeter. p. 156; Ludov. de Dieu on the IV Gospels; Camero, Tom. III, praelect. p. 39; Selden, de jure Natur. & gent. lib. II, c. 2; Schindler, Lex. Pentagl. p. 297. But as for the precepts of Noah, to which the Jews say the proselytes of the gate were bound, which they assign as seven; handed down to the sons of Noah: I. Judgments, that they should observe public judgment, and in this, justice. II. Blessing, that they should bless God. III. Cultum alienum seu idololatriam vitarent. III. That they should avoid strange worship or idolatry. IV. Revelation of nakedness, or that they should beware of wandering lusts, so that they might abstain from the incest of relatives. V. Shedding of blood or homicide, that they should abstain from slaughter. VI. Rapine, that they should abstain from robbery. VII. A member from a living creature, that they should not take a member from an animal; we judge these to pertain to Rabbinical inventions. For whatever may be the case regarding the seventh, there is no doubt that the others flourished already before Noah, nor is it evident by any document that these seven precepts were handed down by Noah to his sons; indeed, both the law of nature inscribed [on the heart] and the frequent manifestations of God made to the Patriarchs teach that the entire decalogue was to be observed in the first world, and thus was observed by the holy Patriarchs and other faithful ones.

Moreover, Schindler assigns yet a third kind of those who joined themselves to the people of God, who were indeed not circumcised, nor did they undertake the whole law, whom nevertheless he distinguishes from the proselytes of the gate, and says they sent gifts to the temple: counting among them Cornelius and those ἐνλαβεῖς, of whom there is mention in Acts II. 5. With whom Grotius seems to agree here. But there is no reason why we should admit three kinds here, since proselytes are adequately distinguished into circumcised and uncircumcised. And the things that are handed down from the Hebrews by Schindler and others concerning proselytes of the law, that they are compelled I. to observe the Sabbath, II. not to stay overnight among the nations, III. to observe the precepts, IV. not to worship idols, V. that they have four punishments, VI. that they have a house of burial: these are so constituted that they are not undeservedly reckoned among the trifles of the Rabbis. For why should one not stay overnight among the nations? Why are proselytes of the law bound only to the 613 precepts & not also to the ten commandments comprised in the decalogue, which Schindler in his Lexicon on page 1120 distinguishes from these according to the opinion of the Rabbis, or why from the decalogue were only those two things concerning the non-worship of idols and the observance of the Sabbath prescribed to them? Nor are those things solid, or worthy of consideration, which are said concerning the institutions of the wise among the Jews, about avoiding all commerce whatsoever with foreigners, and that the Apostles approved of those things before Peter was sent to Cornelius. abhorred spiritual commerce with the Gentiles who remained in Gentilism, yet it will not be taught that they avoided all commerce with foreigners, nor that they admitted no one who was not a Jew by birth or a proselyte of the law into their familiarity.

But setting those things aside, we observe this rather: that Cornelius, who is here eminently proclaimed for piety and fear of God, as well as for beneficence toward the needy and assiduity in prayers, had already been entirely converted and justified, which even the Papists acknowledge here, and Cornelius à Lapide proves at length, primarily because he is said to have been acceptable to God by working righteousness, verse 34. Even though he feigns that he was justified by the law of nature and charity, which is diametrically contrary to the Scriptures, since no one can be justified by the law, much less by the law of nature alone, Romans ch. III, verse 20; Galatians ch. II, verse 21. Although Cornelius did not yet have certain knowledge of the Messiah already exhibited, for which reason Peter was to be sent to him, he did not, however, have only an implicit faith in Christ the Mediator, as the Papists wish, because no one has ever attained salvation without explicit faith in Christ the Mediator, whether before or after his advent into this world, Acts IV, verse 12; ch. X, verse 43; ch. XV, verse 10. Cornelius à Lapide himself confesses that the truer and more common opinion of theologians is that after the sufficient promulgation of the Gospel, no one can be justified or saved except through explicit faith in Christ the Mediator, and thus he refutes Melchior Cano, and from him Dominicus Bannes 2. 2. q. 2. articul. 8., who separate salvation from justice and teach that Cornelius and those like him could have been justified without explicit faith in Christ, but not saved. For justice, he says, and grace is the seed of glory, so that whoever dies in grace is certain of salvation and eternal glory. He also acknowledges it to be necessary, not only by necessity of precept, as Beza and Dominicus Soto wished, but also by necessity of means, that one must believe explicitly in Jesus. Therefore, as regards earlier times, we readily admit that a distinction must be made between the object of saving faith, which is Christ, regarding those things which were to be believed concerning his person and office after the promulgation of the Proto-Evangelium, and the object of historical faith, which is that Jesus of Nazareth is that promised Messiah; which application to this individual, born under Augustus Caesar, was not necessary to be believed until after the promulgation of the Gospel concerning Jesus of Nazareth throughout the world. There is no need for us to speak in this place about the contentions and contradictions of the Papists concerning explicit and implicit faith in the Mediator.

Doing many alms to the people) To the Jews, whom he loved for this reason, that they worshipped the one God.

And praying to God always) Assiduous in pouring out prayers to the one and true God.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Εὐσεβὴς κὶ φοβύμενος τὸν Θεόν) Incircumcisus; sed qui idololatria relicta, uni Deo se dederat, & quæ pietati con- sentaneæ judicabat, sequebatur quales חסידי אומות dicuntur Talmudicis σεβόμενοι ἄνδρες infra XVII. 4. multi olim tales in Judæa vixerant sed certis adstricti regulis, de quibus plurima lectu utilia prodidit vir maximæ eruditionis Seldenus. Postquam Judæi gentium jugum ferre coacti, ægre servata sibi sacrorum libertate, jurisdictionem in alienigenas secum habitantes amiserant, ideoque eos intra istas regulas coërcere non poterant, instituere sapientes, ut Judæi plane alienigenarum commercium devitarent, quia aut idololatræ erant, aut certe Noæ præcepta non putabantur servare, & hoc perpetuo sequuti essent Apostoli, neque ullum non Judæum gente aut proselytum legis admisissent ad suam familiaritatem, nisi Deus diserte Petro primum, deinde & Paulo ostendisset, id fieri sibi placere. Et cessabat causa instituti illius sapientum; quia tales alienigenæ aggregantes se Ecclesiæ per baptismum, eo ipso testabantur, se non modo ab idololatria, sed ab omnibus flagitiis longe discedere, vitamque pollicebantur multo puriorem, quam illa, Noæ præcepta sequentium fuerat.

Incircumcisum fuisse Cornelium, qui tamen idololatria relicta uni Deo se dederit, facile annuimus, neque distinctionem illam inter proselytos legis, quales Ebræis dicti גרי צדק proselyti justitiæ, veritatis vel veri, & גרי ברית proselyti fœderis, qui circumcisionem & totam legem Mosis suscepere; atque גרי שער roselytos Portæ, qui non suscipiebant ritus Judaicos, quæ passim viris magnis probata, reprobamus, Vid. Buxtorff. Lex. Rabb. Talm. pag. 467. Drus. l. V. præter. pag. 156. Ludov. de Dieu in IV. Evangel. Camero Tom. III. prælect. pag. 39. Seldenus de jure Natur. & gent. l. II. c. 2. Schindl. Lex. Pentagl. pag. 297. Quod vero ad præcepta Noæ, quibus proselytos portæ adstrictos fuisse, Judæi dicunt, quæ septem assignant; filiis Noæ tradita I. judicia, ut servarent judicium publicum, & in hoc justitiam. II. Benedictionem, ut Deum benedicerent. III. Cultum alienum seu idololatriam vitarent. IV. Revelationem nuditatum seu vagas libidines caverent, ut ab incestu propinquorum abstinerent. V. Effusionem sanguinis seu homicidium, ut à cæde. VI. Rapinam, ut à rapina abstinerent. VII. Membrum de vivo, ne tollerent membrum de animali; Hæc ad commenta Rabbinica pertinere judicamus. Nam quicquid de septimo sit, cætera ante Noam jam viguisse, dubitandum non est, neque ullo patet documento, septem hæc præcepta à Noa filiis tradita esse, imo decalogum integrum observandum in primo mundo, adeoque à sanctis Patriarchis aliisque fidelibus observatum fuisse tum lex naturæ inscripta, tum crebræ Dei manifestationes, Patriarchis factæ, docent.

Cæterum assignat Schindlerus adhuc tertium genus eorum, qui se populo Dei adjunxere, qui non circumcisi quidem fuerint, nec totam legem susceperint, quos tamen à proselytis portæ distinguit, & misisse ad templum dona ait: Annumerans illis Cornelium & ἐνλαβεῖς illos, quorum Actor. II 5. mentio sit. Cum quo facere hic videtur Grotius. Sed nulla est causa cur tria hic admittamus genera, cum adæquate distinguantur proselyti in circumcisos, & incircumcisos. Et quæ de proselytis legis traduntur ex Ebræis à Schindlero & aliis, quod cogantur I. observare sabbatum. II. non pernoctare apud gentes. III. observare præcepta, IV. Non colere idola. V. quod habeant quatuor supplicia. VI. quod habeant domum sepulturæ: Ita comparata sunt, ut nugis Rabbinorum non immerito accenseantur. Cur enim non pernoctandum apud gentes? Cur tantum præceptis 613. & non etiam præceptis decem in decalogo comprehensis, quæ ab istis distinguit ex mente Rabbinorum Schindlerus in Lexico pag. 1120. obligati proselyti legis, aut cur ex decalogo tantum duo illa de non colendis idolis & de ob- servando sabbato ipsis præscripta sunt? Nec so- lida sunt, aut calculum merentur illa, quæ de sa- pientum institutis apud Judæos dicuntur, de vi- tando omni prorsus alienigenarum commercio, & quod Apostoli illa probarint, antequam Pe- trus ad Cornelium mitteretur. Nam quamvis à spirituali cum gentibus in gentilismo manenti- bus commercio abhorruerint Apostoli, tamen commercium omne cum alienigenis eos devitas- se, nec ullum non Judæum gente aut prosely- tum legis ad suam familiaritatem admisisse, non docebitur.

Sed missis illis, id potius observamus, Corne- lium, qui à pietate & timore Dei nec non bene- ficentia erga egenos & assiduitate in precibus exi- mie hic prædicatur, omnino jam conversum fuis- se ac justificatum, quod agnoscunt etiam hic Papistæ & prolixe probat Cornelius à Lapide, imprimis, quia operatus justitiam Deo gratus fuisse dicitur vers. 34. etsi fingat, quod per legem naturæ & charitatis justificatus sit, quod Scri- pturæ è diametro contrarium, cum nemo per legem, nedum per solam naturæ regem justifi- cari possit Roman. cap. III. vers. 20. Galat. cap. II. vers. 21. Licet vero nondum habuerit certam de Messia jam exhibito notitiam Corneiius, cujus rei gratia ad eum mittendus erat Petrus, non tamen Christi Mediatoris implicitam tantum fi- dem habuit, quod Papistæ volunt, quia sine expli- cita fide Christi Mediatoris nemo unquam salu- tem est adeptus, seu ante, seu post adventum ejus in hunc mundum Actorum IV. vers. 12. cap. X. vers. 43. cap. XV. vers. 10. Post sufficientem Evangelii promulgationem neminem posse ju- stificari aut salvari nisi per explicitam fidem Chri- sti Mediatoris, veriorem & communiorem Theo- logorum sententiam esse fatetur ipse Cornelius La- pideensis, adeoque Melchiorem Canum, & ex eo Dominicum Bannes 2. 2. q. 2. articul. 8. sepa- rantes salutem à justitia, docentesque Corne- lium & similes sine fide explicita Christi potuisse justificari, sed non salvari, refellit. Justitia e- nim, inquit, & gratia est semen gloriæ, ut, qui- cunque moritur in gratia, certus sit de salute & gloria æterna. Agnofcit quoque necessarium, non tantum necessitate præceptis, ut Beza & Do- minicus Soto voluere, sed etiam medii necessita- te, ut explicite in Jesum credatur. Quod itaque ad priora tempora distinguendum inter objectum fidei salvificæ, quod est Christus, quoad ea, quæ de persona & officio ejus credenda fuere, in- de post promulgatum Prot-Evangelium, & ob- jectum fidei historicæ, quod nempe Jesus Naza- renus sit ille promissus Messias; quam applicatio- nem ad hoc Individuum, sub Augusto Cæsare natum, non fuisse necessariam creditu, nisi post Evangelii de Jesu Nazareno per orbem promul- gationem, ultro admittimus. De concertationi- bus & contradictionibus Pontificiorum circa fi- dem Mediatoris explicitam & implicitam non est ut hoc loco dicamus.

Ποιῶν τε ἐλεημοσύνας πολλὰς τῷ λαῷ) Judæis quos ideo amabat, quod unum Deum colerent.

κὴ δεόμεν@ τοῦ Θεοῦ διαπαντός) Assiduus in precibus fun- dendis ad unum & verum Deum.

## 10:3
Vers. 3.

About the ninth hour) Around the time of the evening sacrifice. See above III. 1.

An angel of God) See how good God is, who gives both an angel and an Apostle to one who uses his gifts so well, so that he might teach him that way which henceforth was the only way to salvation, the word of the cross.

From the fact that the prayers of Cornelius are commended, which are also said to have ascended to GOD in verse 4, some Papists gather that unregenerate men can dispose themselves toward grace. But Cornelius was not unregenerate, nor outside of grace, but justified and in grace, nor had he in any way disposed himself for justification through the powers of nature, but he attained faith through the grace of God alone and was reborn through the word, and was justified through faith, out of grace, without merits or his own disposition, solely on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by true faith. For if it is by grace, it is not by works, Romans XI, verse 6. Concerning which, see August. lib. de prædestinat. sanct. cap. VII. Whatever Cornelius did well before he believed, and when he believed, and after he had believed, is all to be given to God, lest anyone be exalted. And Gregory the Great, Homily XIX in Ezekiel. Cornelius the Centurion, whose alms were praised before baptism, did not come to faith through works, but came to works through faith.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ὡσεὶ ὥραν ἐνάτην) Circa tempus sacrificii vespertini. Vi- de supra III. 1.

Ἄγγελον τοῦ Θεοῦ) Vide quam bonus sit Deus, qui tam bene utenti datis & Angelum mittit, & Apostolum, ut eum doceat eam viam, quæ posthac unica erat ad salutem, ver- bum crucis.

Ex eo quod preces Cornelii commendantur, quæ etiam ad DEUM afcendisse vers. 4. dicuntur, Pontificii nonnulli colligunt, homines irregenitos se posse disponere ad gratiam. Sed Cornelius non erat irregenitus, nec extra gratiam, sed justificatus, & in gratia, neque ullatenus disposuerat se per vires naturæ ad justificationem, sed per solius Dei gratiam & renatus per verbum fidem adeptus est, & per fidem justificatus est, ex gratia, citra merita, vel dispositionem propriam, unice propter meritum Christi vera fide apprehensum. Si enim ex gratia, non ex operibus Roman. XI. vers. 6. Quo de August. l. de prædestinat. sanct. cap. VII. Quicquid Cornelius antequam crederet & cum crederet & postquam credidisset, bene operatus est, totum Deo dandum est, ne quis extollatur. Et Gregorius M. Homil. XIX. in Ezech. Cornelius Centurio, cujus eleemosynæ ante baptismum laudatæ sunt, non operibus venit ad fidem, sed fide venit ad opera.

## 10:4
Ver. 4.

Τί ἐστι Κύριε) Thus he addresses him honorifically as someone greater than a man.

Ἀνέβησαν εἰς μνημόσυνον) This is a simile taken from the legal incense: for that is properly called אזכרה, in Greek μνημόσυνον in Leviticus II and elsewhere. And it is said of incense that it ἀναβαίνειν (ascends) in Revelation VIII. Moreover, that incense was a symbol of prayers. Revelation V, ver. 8, chap. VIII, ver. 3. The ancients say that prayer is carried up on two wings, fasting and works of mercy.

Ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ) Not bad. Nor is the Manuscript Ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Θεοῦ bad either.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Τί ἐστι Κύριε) Sic eum appellat honorifice ut homine majorem.

Ἀνέβησαν εἰς μνημόσυνον) Est similitudo sumpta à suffitu legali: nam is propriè vocatur אזכרה, Græce μνημόσυνον Levitici II. & alibi. Et de suffitu dicitur ἀναβαίνειν Apocal. IV. Is autem suffitus symbolum erat precum. Apocal. V. vers. 8. cap. VIII. vers. 3. precationem subvehi alis duabus ajunt veteres, jejunio & misericordiæ operibus.

Ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ) Non male. Nec male etiam Manuscriptus Ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Θεοῦ.

## 10:5
Ver. 5.

καὶ μετάπεμψαι Σίμωνα) The Apostolic embassy was greater than the Angelic. The Angel points out the Apostle, the Apostle points out Christ; such honor did Christ have for his witnesses.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

καὶ μετάπεμψαι Σίμωνα) Major erat legatio Apostolica, quam Angelica. Angelus Apostolum monstrat, Apostolus Christum; tantum honorem testibus suis habuit Christus.

## 10:7
Ver. 7.

Στρατιώτην εὐσεβῆ) A rare epithet.

We see, however, from this, as also from the example of Cornelius and other soldiers commended in the scriptures for their piety, that the military state is not at odds with piety, which the Anabaptists and Socinians in part maintain. It did no harm, says Jerome, Ep. IX to Sab., for the soldier to have a military cloak, a belt, and a crowd of attendants, because under the habit of one he was serving another, etc.

Τῶν προσκαρτερούντων αὐτῷ) To those who were appearing to him. And I think the Latin Interpreter wrote it thus.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Στρατιώτην εὐσεβῆ) Rarum ἐπίθετον.

Videmus tamen inde, ut & exemplo Cornelii & aliorum militum in sacris à pietate commendatorum, non pugnare cum pietate statum militarem, quod Anabaptistæ, & Sociniani ex parte statuere. Nihil nocuit, inquit Hieron. Ep. IX. ad Sab. militanti paludamentum & baltheus & apparitorum caterva, quia sub habitu alterius alteri militabat &c.

Τῶν προσκαρτερούντων αὐτῷ) Iis qui illi apparebant. Et sic scripsisse puto Latinum Interpretem.

## 10:9
Ver. 9.

Ἐπὶ τὸ δῶμα) From where there would be a clear view toward the temple. For in such places the Jews were accustomed to pray, Dan. VI. 11.

περὶ ὥραν ἕκτην) Which is one of the hours appointed for prayer, as we said above III, 1.

PART II. Peter's instruction concerning his journey to Cornelius.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ἐπὶ τὸ δῶμα) Unde liber conspectus esset templum versus. Talibus enim in locis precari solebant Judæi Dan. VI. 11.

περὶ ὥραν ἕκτην) Quæ una horarum dicararum precationi, ut diximus supra III, 1.

PARS II. Petri de profectione ad Cornelium instructio.

## 10:10
Vers. 10.

Ἐγένετο δὲ πρόσπεινος) It is no wonder that he was hungry at midday, who had risen early in the morning, as is credible.

ἤθελε γεύσασθαι) We have γεύσασθαι without an added accusative also in Jonah chapter III, verse 7, and below XX, verse 11. γευσάμενος can be taken in the same way or referred to ἄρτον, which word preceded it.

Ἔκστασις) This word sometimes signifies horror, sometimes madness: in this place, the state of a man rapt out of himself. Thus Lucan on Apollo: --- He expelled his former mind and commanded the man to yield his whole breast to him.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἐγένετο δὲ πρόσπεινος) Esuriisse non mirum est meridie eum, qui mane summo, ut credibile est, surrexerat.

ἤθελε γεύσασθαι) γεύσασθαι non addito Accusativo habemus & Jonæ cap. III. vers. 7. infra XX. vers. 11. γευσάμενος potest eodem modo sumi aut referri ad ἄρτον quæ vox præcessit.

Ἔκστασις) Hæc vox interdum horrorem, interdum insaniam significat: hoc loco constitutionem hominis extra se rapti. Sic de Appolline Lucanus: --- Mentemque priorem Expulit atque hominem toto sibi cedere jussit Pectore

## 10:11
Vers. 11.

τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγμένον) See what was said above VII. 56. and Matt. III. 16.

Σκεῦός τι ὡς ὀθόνην μεγάλην) כלי among the Hebrews, which the Greeks translate σκεῦος, and the Syrians מאנא, signifies everything that is for domestic use, even of linen or wool. The word ὀθόνης or ὀθονίου is general enough, as appears in Hosea II. 3, 9. The writer of the responses to the orthodox called it a sindon; and in this place, Oecumenius.

Τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς δεδεμένον) He calls the corners ἀρχαῖς, as the Syrian explains. Moreover, that linen cloth seemed to hang from heaven, so that the liberty granted from heaven might be signified.

Interpreters think the four corners of the world are thus indicated, since the Gospel was to be propagated throughout the whole world, and the Church was bound to embrace all nations in its bosom. See August. serm. XXVI. de divers. Oecumenius, Beda in h. l.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγμένον) Vide quæ dicta supra VII. 56. & Matth. III. 16.

Σκεῦός τι ὡς ὀθόνην μεγάλην) כלי Hebræis, quod σκεῦος vertunt Græci, Syri מאנא, significat omne id, quod in usu est domestico, etiam è lino aut lana. ὀθόνης vel ὀθονίου vox satis generalis, ut apparet Os. II. 3. 9. Sindonem dixit scriptor responsorum ad orthodoxos; & hoc loco Oecumenius.

Τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς δεδεμένον) Ἀρχὰς vocat angulos, ut explicat Syrus. Videbatur autem linteum illud à cælo pendere, ut significaretur libertas cœlitus indulta.

Quatuor mundi plagas ita indigitari putant interpretes, quum Evangelium per totum orbem propagandum fuerit, & Ecclesia debuerit omnes gentes sinu suo complecti. V. August. serm. XXVI. de divers. Oecumenius, Beda in h. l.

## 10:12
Vers. 12.

Πάντα τὰ τετράποδα τῆς γῆς) בהמה, where it is placed without anything added, usually signifies living creatures clean according to the Law. καὶ τὰ θηρία) חיה, of which many are unclean, Levit. XI. v. 27. καὶ τὰ ἑρπετά) שרץ, by which name fish are also included among the Hebrews. Many of these are unclean, as appears in the said place of Leviticus. καὶ τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) עוף, of which kind many are likewise unclean.

The author of the questions and answers among Justin, Quæst. LXXXIX., believed that only unclean living creatures were contained in this sheet. If clean ones had also been present, Peter could certainly have slaughtered and eaten them. The word 'all' must therefore be taken in a qualified sense, as in Matth. IV. 23, Luc. XI. 42.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Πάντα τὰ τετράποδα τῆς γῆς) בהמה ubi nullo addito ponitur, significare solet animantia ex Lege munda. καὶ τὰ θηρία) חיה, quorum multa immunda, Levit. XI. v. 27. καὶ τὰ ἑρπετά) שרץ quo nomine etiam pisces comprehenduntur apud Hebræos. Horum multa immunda, ut dicto loco Levitici apparet. καὶ τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) עוף, cujus generis multa item immunda.

Immunda tantum hoc linteo comprehensa animantia auct. quæstion. & respons. apud Justin. Quæst. LXXXIX. credidit. Si munda quoque adfuissent, utique Petrus ea mactare ac comedere potuisset. Vox ergo πάντα κατά τι accipienda, ut Matth. IV. 23. Luc. XI. 42.

## 10:13
Vers. 13.

θῦσον καὶ φάγε) i. e. slaughter all those things, and eat of all.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

θῦσον καὶ φάγε) i. e. macta omnia ista, & de omnibus ede.

## 10:14
Vers. 14.

μηδαμῶς Κύριε) Thus חלילה is usually translated, which elsewhere is μὴ γένοιτο, elsewhere ἵλεως; concerning which word we have spoken at Matth. X. 22. Πᾶν κοινὸν ἢ ἀκάθαρτον) The one explains the other. For a pig is called טמא, which is translated ἀκάθαρτον, Levit. XI. 7. The same is among κοινὰ, I. Maccab. I. v. 65. Common is that which the nations commonly use, not also the people sanctified to God. Seneca relates that in the time of Tiberius, foreign rites forbidden at Rome were a sign of abstinence from certain animals.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

μηδαμῶς Κύριε) Sic verti solet חלילה, quod alibi μὴ γένοιτο, alibi ἵλεως; de qua voce diximus ad Matth. X. 22. Πᾶν κοινὸν ἢ ἀκάθαρτον) Alterum per alterum explicat. Nam sus dicitur טמא, quod vertitur ἀκάθαρτον, Levit. XI. 7. Eadem inter κοινὰ, I. Maccab. I. v. 65. Commune est, quo vulgo utuntur gentes, non etiam populus Deo sanctificatus. Narrat Seneca Tiberii tempore vetita Romæ sacra externa signum fuisse, abstinentiam à certis animalibus.

## 10:15
Vers. 15.

Ἃ ὁ Θεὸς ἐκαθάρισε, σὺ μὴ κοίνου) The verb טהר, which is here translated κοινοῦν, is properly to pollute, improperly to hold as polluted. That is frequent in verbs. Peter could have believed that by this vision it was only indicated that foods forbidden by the Law were now permitted, which some Jews even believed could be lawfully consumed outside the land of Judea, because the reason of health required it in Judea and in certain neighboring places: whence also the Egyptians once abstained from swine, and the Ethiopians, not Judaizing, from almost all those foods which the Law forbids. But Peter, because that sheet had come from heaven and had been received into heaven, first suspected that something greater lay hidden, below 17. Then, when at the same time he was summoned by Cornelius and commanded by God to go to him μηδὲν διακρινόμενος, he understood what mystery was here: Namely, it was clearly persuaded to the Jews that by unclean animals were signified impious men, as the epistle of Barnabas shows, produced by us in book IV. of the truth of the Christian religion, Clemens Stromatum II. v: Eleazar in Eusebius's Evangelical Preparation; Origen against Celsus and Josephus Albo; and just as they said of an animal: So they said of such a man טמא חזיר. Hence he understood that that sheet which had descended from heaven was the Church gathered from heaven, Apocal. XXI. v. ., and about to return to heaven. Into this Church must be gathered not only clean animals, by which name the Jews called themselves, but also unclean, by which name the Jews called foreigners, but namely after they had repented of idolatry and depraved morals and had devoted themselves to piety, which Cornelius had done and was about to do more, and after him many others having faith in the Gospel. These are they whom God has cleansed; nor are they involved in the Church unless already cleansed. See below 34. 35. To kill is to take away in them what remains of the old man: To eat is to unite to oneself.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ἃ ὁ Θεὸς ἐκαθάρισε, σὺ μὴ κοίνου) Verbum טהר, quod hic vertitur κοινοῦν proprie est polluere, improprie pro polluto habere. Frequens id in verbis. Potuerat credere Petrus, hoc viso tantum indicari, permitti jam cibos lege vetitos, quos extra terram Judæam licite sumi etiam Judæi quidam credidere, quia ratio valetudinis id in Judæa exigebat, & in vicinis quibusdam locis: unde & Ægyptii a sue abstinuere olim, & Æthiopes non Iudaizantes à cibis ferme illis omnibus, quos lex vetat. Sed Petrus, quod linteum illud de cælo venisset, & in cælum receptum esset, primum suspicatus est, majus aliquid latere, infra 17. Deinde cum eodem tempore à Cornelio accerseretur, & à Deo juberetur ad eum ire μηδὲν διακρινόμενος, intellexit quid hic esset mysterii: Nempe Iudæis persuasum plane erat, per animalia immunda significari homines impios, ut ostendit Barnabæ epistola, producta nobis ad librum IV. de veritate religionis Christianæ, Clemens Stromatum II. v: Eleazar apud Eusebium præparatione Evangelica; Origenes contra Celsum & Iosephus Albo; ac sicut de animali: Ita de tali homine dicebant טמא חזיר. Hinc intellexit linteum illud de cælo delapsum esse Ecclesiam cœlitus collectam, Apocal. XXI. v. . & in cælum redituram. In hanc Ecclesiam colligi debent non tantum animalia munda, quo modo se Judæi vocabant, sed & immunda, quo nomine Iudæi appellabant alienigenas, sed nempe postquam cœlesti ope ab idololatria & pravis moribus resipuissent ac pietati se dedissent, quod fecerat Cornelius ampliusque facturus erat & post eum multi alii Evangelio fidem habentes. Hi sunt quos Deus mundavit; nec in Ecclesiam involvuntur, nisi jam mundati. Vide infra 34. 35. Occidere, est tollere in eis quod restat de veteri homine: Manducare, sibi adunare.

## 10:16
Verse 16.

τοῦτο δὲ ἐγένετο ἐπὶ τρὶς) Visions and oracles which God wishes to be deeply fixed in the mind are accustomed to be repeated. Moreover, the number three is proper to Christians. Below c. X. v. 16. XI. 10. 2. Cor. XII. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

τοῦτο δὲ ἐγένετο ἐπὶ τρὶς) Solent visa & oracula, quæ penitus animo infigi Deus vult, repeti. Ternarius autem numerus Christianorum proprius. Infra c. X. v. 16. XI. 10. 2. Cor. XII. 8.

## 10:17
Verse 17.

τὴν οἰκίαν Σίμωνος) Namely, of the tanner, as above 6. Therefore in the following verse it is said: Σίμων ὁ ἐπικαλούμενος Πέτρος. ἐπὶ τὸν πυλῶνα) Concerning this word, see at Matthew XXVI. 72. Verse 19. εἶπεν αὐτῷ τὸ πνεῦμα) i.e., God, not through a vision, but through inspiration.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

τὴν οἰκίαν Σίμωνος) Nempe coriarii ut supra 6. Ideo in sequenti commate dicitur: Σίμων ὁ ἐπικαλούμενος Πέτρος. ἐπὶ τὸν πυλῶνα) De hac voce ad Matth. XXVI. 72. Vers. 19. εἶπεν αὐτῷ τὸ πνεῦμα) i. e. Deus non per visum, sed per afflatum.

## 10:20
μηδὲν διακρινόμενος) Thus also below c. XI. 12. Hesitating nothing, namely because those to whom you are being summoned are not Jews. Thus διακρίνειν is taken in Matthew XXI. 31. Mark XI. 23. Romans IV. 20. James I. 6. c. II. 4.

Ἐγὼ ἀπέσταλκα ἀυτοὺς) The active for a double active, that is, I caused them to be sent.

Latin:

μηδὲν διακρινόμενος) Sic & infra c. XI. 12. Nihil hæ- sitans, nempe ideo quod illi ad quos accerseris, Judæi non sunt. Ita διακρίνειν sumitur Matth. XXI. 31. Marci XI. 23. Rom. IV. 20. Jac. I. 6. c. II. 4.

Ἐγὼ ἀπέσταλκα ἀυτοὺς) Activum pro duplici activo, id est, feci ut mitterentur.

## 10:21
Verse 21.

Vers. 24.

## 10:25
Vers. 25.

Εἰσελθεῖν τὸν Πέτρον) When he was on the point of entering the doors.

Προσκύνησεν) The Jews indeed and other nations of the East showed this honor not only to Kings, but also to others placed in dignity. But among the Greeks and Romans this custom was reserved for the honor of the gods: whence Peter understood that he was thought by Cornelius to be an Angel, just as the Lystrians held Paul and Barnabas for gods c. XIV. 12. 13. at the end; therefore Peter turns away from that honor, which his words that follow demonstrate.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

Εἰσελθεῖν τὸν Πέτρον) Cum in eo esset, ut fores intraret.

Προσκύνησεν) Judæi quidem & alia gentess Orientis eum honorem exhibebant non Regibus tantum; sed & ali- is in dignitate positis. At Græcis & Romanis is mos deo- rum honori reservatus: unde intellexit Petrus, se Cornelio Angelum putari, quomodo Lystrenses pro diis habuere Paulum & Barnabam c. XIV. 12. 13. in fine; ideo eum ho- norem Petrus aversatur, quod ostendunt, quæ sequuntur, ejus verba.

## 10:26
Vers. 26.

Κἀγὼ ἀυτὸς ἄνθρωπός εἰμι) To you ὁμοιοπαθής (of like passions).

The word προσκύνησις implies not only civil honor, but religious, especially in the N.T., which therefore Peter declines here, and the Angels themselves refuse it in Apoc. XIX. 10. c. XXII. 9. and teach that it is owed to God alone. It seems therefore that Cornelius wished to worship God in Peter in that way: but since that is not permitted either, he is corrected by Peter. Grotius himself acknowledges at Acts XII. 23. that Peter here left his honor unimpaired to God, when he refused the προσκύνησις.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

Κἀγὼ ἀυτὸς ἄνθρωπός εἰμι) Tibi ὁμοιοπαθής.

Non civilem tantum honorem, sed religiosum importat verbum προσκυνήσεως, imprimis in N.T. quem proinde declinat hic Petrus, Angelique ipsi recusant Apoc. XIX. 10. c. XXII. 9. soli Deo deberi docent. Videtur ergo voluisse Cornelius in Petro Deum ita colere: sed cum nec illud licitum sit, à Petro corrigitur. Agnofcit Grotius ipse ad Act. XII. 23. Petrum hic Deo illibatum reliquisse suum honorem, cum προσκύνησιν recusavit.

## 10:28
Vers. 28.

Ὡς ἀθέμιτόν ἐστι ἀνδρὶ Ἰουδαίῳ) You have the word ἀθεμίτου in 2 Maccabees 6:5 and 7:7. It corresponds to the Rabbinic אסור, illicit not by the law of Moses, but by the decree of the wise, which was held in the same place as the law. But besides the fact that God is the Lord not only of such decrees but also of His own law, the reason for the decree ceased here. The decree had been made against idolaters and men of evil life, such as Cornelius was not. And hereafter the gathering into the Church was to be a most clear mark by which good foreigners would be distinguished from the bad.

Who will concede that the decrees of the wise were held by the Apostles in the same place as the law of Moses? Those are merely human: This was divine. Concerning the former: In vain they worship me, says the Lord, teaching doctrines ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων (commandments of men), Matthew 15:9. But concerning the latter: You shall not add to it, nor take anything away from it, Deuteronomy 12:32, 4:2, Proverbs 30:6.

Ἀλλοφύλῳ) Under this name were not included proselytes of the law (for they were naturalized citizens), but all others outside of Jews by birth and such proselytes. The word ἀλλόφυλος corresponds to the Hebrew פלשתי Isaiah 2:6, 6:5, 2 Maccabees 10:2, 5, whence ἀλλοφυλισμὸς 2 Maccabees 4:13, 6:24.

Κολλᾶσθαι) to live together familiarly, as above in chapter 9:26.

Ἢ προσέρχεσθαι) Indeed, even to approach beyond necessary uses προσέρχεσθαι שׁרת.

If that ἀθέμιτον (unlawful thing) concerning the ἀλλοφύλῳ (foreigner) does not concern the proselytes of the law, such as Cornelius was, why did Peter have need of that preface here? Is it not rather, because the Apostle used it by design, that it is evident that ἀλλόφυλον in this place is to be understood in such a way that Cornelius could also be included under that word? For this is an Ἀντυποφορά (counter-objection). Although it is considered not consistent with the custom of the Jews to associate familiarly with foreigners, God nevertheless taught me otherwise, namely, to call no one common or unclean. He does not therefore approve of the decree or the custom of the Jews regarding avoiding all association with Gentiles, but rather teaches that that distinction of clean and unclean peoples now ceases, since God wishes even those Gentiles who were considered most unclean to be called to the communion of the Church. Μηδένα κοινὸν ἢ ἀκάθαρτον λέγειν ἄνθρωπον (to call no man common or unclean) namely, commanded by God, as he explains below in verse 35. This was an Ἀλληγορία (allegory) of animals.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

Ὡς ἀθέμιτόν ἐστι ἀνδρὶ Ἰουδαίῳ) Vocem ἀθεμίτου habes 2. Maccab. VI. 5. & VII. 7. Respondet Rabbinico אסור, illicitum non lege Mosis, sed decreio sapientum, quod pari loco tum lege habebatur. Sed præterquam quod Deus non talium tantum decretorum, sed & suæ legis est Dominus, cessabat hic ratio decreti. Decretum factum erat contra idololatras, malæque vitæ homines, qualis non erat Cornelius. Et posthac aggregatio ad Ecclesiam apertissi- ma futura erat nota, qua alienigenæ boni à malis discerne- rentur.

Decreta sapientum pari cum lege Mosis loco ab Apostolis habita ecquis concedet? Illa mere humana sunt: Hæc divina fuit. De illis: Frustra me colunt, inquit Dominus, docentes doctrinas ἐν- τάλματα ἀνθρώπων Matth. XV. 9. De hac vero: non addetis, nec detrahetis ei quicquam, Deut. XII. v. 32. c. IV. 2. Prov. XXX. 6.

Ἀλλοφύλῳ) Sub hoc nomine non comprehendebantur proselyti legis (ii namque erant cives adscititii) sed alii o- mnes extra Judæos ortu & tales proselytos. Vox ἀλλόφυλος respondet Hebræo פלשתי Esa. II. 6. VI. 5. 2. Maccab. X. v. 2. 5. unde ἀλλοφυλισμὸς 2. Macc. IV. 13. c. VI. 24.

Κολλᾶσθαι) familiariter convivere, ut supra c. IX 26.

Ἢ προσέρχεσθαι) Imo etiam adire extra necessarios usus προσέρχεσθαι שׁרת.

Si ἀθέμιτον illud de ἀλλοφύλῳ non concernit proselytos legis, qualis Cornelius fuit, cur illa præfatione hic opus habuit Petrus? Annon po- tius, quia ea ex instituto usus est Apostolus, patet ἀλλόφυλον hoc loco accipiendum esse, ut sub ea voce comprehendi potuerit etiam Cornelius? Est enim hic Ἀντυποφορά. Quamvis non conveniens ex more Judæorum habeatur, cum alienigenis con- versari familiariter, Deus tamen aliud me docuit, nimirum neminem communem vel immundum dicere. Non approbat ergo sive decretum sive morem Judæorum de vitando omni consortio cum genti- libus, sed docet potius, nunc cessare discrimen illud mundorum & immundorum populorum, cum Deus etiam gentes maxime immundas habi- tas vocatas velit ad communionem Ecclesiæ. Μηδένα κοινὸν ἢ ἀκάθαρτον λέγειν ἄνθρωπον) nempe à Deo mandatum, ut explicat infra 35. Hæc erat Ἀλληγορία, animalium.

## 10:33
Verse 33.

Ἐξ αὐτῆς (immediately) At once. This word is used here and below ch. XLII. ch. XXIII. 30. Mark VI. v. 25. Philip. II. 23. Philo also uses it regarding those renamed, and Procopius in his Vandalic War. Σύ τε καλῶς ἐποίησας παραγενόμενος (and you have done well to come) It is the expression of one giving thanks, as 'benigne' (kindly) in Horace, as noted twice by the Scholiast on Epistle 1. 7. Thus καλῶς ἐποιήσατε (you did well) Phil. IV. 14. Καλῶς ποιήσεις (you will do well) John Epist. III. v. 6. Aristophanes in the Acharnians, καλῶς ποιῶν, ὅςις πορ ἦν (doing well, whoever he was). Archytas also uses it in Laërtius, as do Demosthenes and Dionysius of Halicarnassus. Thus what Aristophanes said in the Plutus: Νὴ διὰ καλῶς τοίνυν ποιῶν ἀπόλωλας (By Zeus, you have perished doing well). Pliny said in his 6th Epistle: 'Benefecit Regulus, quod est mortuus' (Regulus did well, in that he is dead). Donatus also noted this way of speaking on Terence. Ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεῦ πάρεσμεν (we are present before God) Since both the Syriac and the Latin read ἐνώπιόν σου (before you), I think that reading is older. Ἐνώπιόν σου, that is, we are in your power. The same way of speaking in Gen. XIII. v. 9. לפניך (before you) where the Greeks use ἐνώπιόν σε (before you) in the same sense.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

Ἐξ αὐτῆς) Illico. Hic usurpatur hæc vox & infra c. XLII. c. XXIII. 30. Marci VI. v. 25. Philip. II. 23. Utiuur & Philo de transnominatis. & Procopius Vandalicis. Σύ τε καλῶς ἐποίησας παραγενόμενος) Est gratias agentis, ut benigne apud Horatium, notante bis Scholiaste ad Epi- stolam 1. 7. Sic καλῶς ἐποιήσατε Phil. IV. 14. Καλῶς ποιή- σεις Joh. Epist. III. v. 6. Aristophanes Acharnensibus, κα- λῶς ποιῶν, ὅςις πορ ἦν Utuntur & Architas apud Laërtium, Demosthenes & Dionysius Halicarnassensis. Sic quod Ari- stophanes dixit Pluto: Νὴ διὰ καλῶς τοίνυν ποιῶν ἀπόλωταψ Plinius dixit VI. Epistola: Benefecit Regulus, quod est mortuus. Notavit hoc genus loquendi etiam Donatus ad Terentium. Ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεῦ πάρεσμεν) Cum & Syrus & Latinus le- gerin· ἐνώπιόν σου, puto eam Lectionem esse vetustiorem. Ἐνώπιόν σου, id est, in tua sumus potestate. Idem loquendi genus Gen. XIII. v. 9. לפניך ubi Græci ἐνωπίον σε eodem sensu.

## 10:36
Verse 36.

The word, which he sent to the sons of Israel) A Hebraism for which word he sent, which message God announced to the Israelites through Jesus, as follows: Formerly indeed this had been hinted at by the examples of Melchizedek, Job, Naaman, Cyrus: but through Jesus he opened this general decree of his to the Israelites themselves. This appears in Matt. VIII. 12. John XI. 32. which words, however, the Apostles themselves did not fully grasp before these revelations.

We believe that this sermon, or message, should not be restricted to those things which were predicted concerning the calling of the Gentiles: Nor was it merely hinted at in the Old Testament by examples, but announced beforehand by the clearest prophecies. But who that word is, is partly indicated here, namely that God preached peace through Jesus Christ; and it is partly explained subsequently concerning the anointing, office, crucifixion and resurrection, and the coming judgment of Christ, through whom we have remission of sins through faith in his name. For Grotius observed below that this is the explanation of that report, of which Peter had begun to speak at verse 38. Heinsius's explanation is also incongruous, understanding by word here the hypostatic Word, because in the text word is distinguished as the object of the announcement from Christ as the cause, through whom the announcement was made.

Preaching peace through Jesus Christ) which the Angels had predicted in Luke II. 14. and Christ gave in John XIV. v. 27. Namely, Christ's disciples ought to live among themselves in the highest peace, and indeed in love, and for this Christ gives his Spirit; they ought to be in one linen cloth, that is, in one Church.

Peace announced by the Angels in Luke II. 14. given by Christ in John XIV. 27. and preached in the Gospel, implies not only peace between us mutually and with our neighbor, but primarily peace above us with God, who has been reconciled to us through Christ, and within us with our own conscience, not reproving us, which is the tranquility of the soul, because we know that we now have God propitious, Rom. V. v. 1. Phil. IV. 7. Rejoicing in this internal peace, they pursue external peace with others, striving to cultivate harmony with all men, as much as lies in them, Rom. XII. 18. Heb. XII. 14.

He is Lord of all) Matt. XXVIII. 16. shows the fulfillment of Daniel's prophecy concerning the eternal empire.

Therefore, Daniel's prophecy dealt with the kingdom of Christ and his eternal empire, chap. VII. 14. seqq. And no one other than Christ is that Son of man, seen there in the Prophetic vision. Which is to be noted against the depravation of Grotius, by which he understood the Roman people through the Son of man. Let what we said there be compared.

Latin:

Vers. 36.

Τὸν λόγον, ὃν ἀπέστειλε τοῖς ὑοῖς Ἰσραὴλ) Hebraismus pro ὃν λόγον ἀπέστειλε quem nuntium nunciavit Ifraelitis Deus per Jesum, ut sequitur: Olim quidem id inuerat exem- plis Melchisedeci, Jobi, Naamanis, Cyri: sed per Jesum decretum hoc suum generale aperuit ipsis Israelitis. Ap- paret id Matth. VIII. 12. Joh. XI. 32. quæ tamen verba ipsi Apostoli non plene assequuti sunt ante has revelationes.

Sermonem istum, vel nuncium non restringen- dum censemus ad ea, quæ de vocatione gentium prædicta sunt: Nec in Veteri Testamento ea in- sinuata exemplis tantum est, sed clarissimis vatici- niis prænunciata. Quis autem ille λόγος sit, par- tim hic indicatur, quod nempe Deus pacem evange- lizavit per Christum Jesum; partim deinceps ex- plicatur de unctione, officio, crucifixione & resur- rectione, ac judicio venturo Christi, per quem habe- mus remissionem peccatorum per fidem in nomen ejus. Hanc enim esse ἐξήγησιν illius famæ, de qua loqui cœperat Petrus ad vers. 38. observavit infra Grotius. Incongrua etiam est Heinsii explicatio, per λόγον hic intelligentis Verbum hypostaticum, quia in textu distinguitur λόγος tanquam obje- ctum annunciationis à Christo ceu causa, per quem facta annunciatio.

Εὐαγγελιζόμενος εἰρήνην διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) quam Angeli præ- dixerant Luc. II. 14. & Christus dedit Joh. XIV. v. 27. Nempe Christi discipuli inter se in summa pace, imo & di- lectione debent vivere, & ad id dat Christus Spiritum su- um; in uno linteo, id est, in una Ecclesia esse debent.

Pax ab Angelis annunciata Luc. II. 14. à Chri- sto data Joh. XIV. 27. & in Evangelio prædicata non tantum pacem inter nos mutuam & cum pro- ximo, sed imprimis pacem supra nos cum Deo, qui per Christum reconciliatus nobis est, & intra nos cum conscientia propria, nos non redarguente, quæ est tranquillitas animæ, quod sciamus, nos Deum jam habere propitium, importat, Rom. V. v. 1. Phil. IV. 7. Qua interna pace gaudentes pro- sequuntur externam pacem cum aliis, cum omni- bus hominibus concordiam colere satagentes, quantum in ipsis est, Rom. XII. 18. Ebr. XII. 14.

Οὗτός ἐστι πάντων Κύριος) Matth. XXVIII. 16. ostendit impletum Danielis vaticinium de imperio æterno.

De regno ergo Christi, & æterno ejus imperio Danielis vaticinium egit, cap. VII. 14. seqq. Nec alius quam Christus est ille Filius hominis, ibi con- spectus in visione Prophetica. Quod contra de- pravationem Grotianam, qua per Filium hominis Romanum populum intellexit, observandum. Conferantur, quæ illic diximus.

Verse 37.

after the baptism which John preached) See above ch. I, 22.

Vers. 37.

Ὑμεῖς οἴδατε τὸ γενόμενον ῥῆμα) Ῥῆμα vocat famam de Jesu.

μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα ὃ ἐκήρυξεν Ἰωάννης) Vide supra c. I, 22.

## 10:38
Vers. 38.

Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit) A Hebraism for how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit. This is the explanation of that fame of which he had begun to speak. Reference is made, however, to the passage of Isaiah LXI. 1, cited in Luke IV. 18.

and with power) is a hendiadys for Spirit and power, that is, with a most powerful Spirit. Similar to Luke I. 17, 35; thus also elsewhere power for Spirit, as above ch. I. 8.

who went about doing good) In a similar sense we had the noun of well-doing above ch. IV. 9.

and healing all who were oppressed by the Devil) Therefore he liberated those corporally possessed by the Devil, so that it might be understood that he was also going to liberate the human race spiritually besieged by the Devil, and would truly be one who executes judgment for the oppressed, as it is in Psalm CXLVI. 7. See Matt. XXII. 29, Luke X. 10.

From these things it is understood that the passage of Isaiah LXI. 1 cannot be accepted otherwise than concerning Christ. By which very thing the throat of the glosses invented for the Prophetic passage is cut by Grotius. See what is said on that passage. That comparison also with Luke I. v. 37 is foreign. For a hendiadys does not occur there, but distinct predicates are attributed to the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, which also occur as subjects in different clauses; they are not, however, joined immediately as in a hendiadys.

that God was with him) For God always loved, Matt. III. 17, always heard, John XI. 42.

Too thin and jejune an explanation. God was not only with him with the affection of love, but by hypostatic union and communion, because this is the cause of that anointing by which Christ, according to his human nature, was anointed with the Holy Spirit not by measure, Ps. 45:7; John 3:34. For unless the human nature were a participant in the divine, neither would πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος dwell in Christ, Col. 2:9; certainly the flesh of Christ could not have been enriched with immense and infinite gifts, nor by divine and infinite power could he have either performed those miracles and liberated those corporally obsessed by demons, or redeemed the human race spiritually obsessed by the Devil, 1 John 3:2; Heb. 2:14; Col. 1:13. Cf. our Anti-Crellius p. 256.

## 10:39
Verse 39.

καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν μάρτυρες πάντων ὧν ἐποίησε) That manuscript, ὑμεῖς μάρτυρες πάντων, is not bad: so that Peter may distinguish the deeds before the resurrection and the deeds after the resurrection, and may say that the Apostles are witnesses of the latter, but all the people of the former.

It is wrong to correct the others from one manuscript, with which the versions also agree, and therefore that distinction and Grotian gloss is null. Peter speaks of himself and the other Apostles, and asserts his own testimony as that of witnesses not who heard, but who saw.

κρεμάσαντες ἐπὶ ξύλυ) see above ch. 5:30. The Jews have the less reason to complain about the calling of the Gentiles, because they themselves treated Jesus so cruelly.

These things are said not to repel the complaint of the Jews, but to inform the house of Cornelius: and they pertain to the object of faith: because the holy Apostle wished here to set forth in summary, as it were, the instruction of that family and the firstfruits of the Gentiles, concerning those things which are primarily to be believed about Christ, to which the article concerning the crucifixion and death of Christ entirely pertains, Rom. 4:24.

## 10:44
Vers. 44.

the Holy Spirit fell upon all who were hearing the word) Grace anticipated again, as above c. VIII. 39. c. IX. 17. this dispensation was, however, clearly necessary, so that Peter, and through Peter the Apostles, might learn that the baptism of water was not to be denied to those to whom God also imparted the baptism of the Spirit. A matter so new could not be obtained with less authority; the following verse teaches us this: ἐπιπίπτειν is said of the Holy Spirit above c. VIII. 16. c. XI. 15. it is also said concerning a trance as above 10. so also concerning fear.

Why do we say this grace was anticipated, since God did not bind himself to baptism, or to the imposition of hands, so that he would not confer the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit except either in baptism or with the laying on of hands of the Apostles. Nor did he have to learn this only then, namely from the baptism of the Spirit, that the baptism of water or of the river, as they call it, was not to be denied to that Cornelius and his family. For he had that from the institution of Baptism, as he knew it was not left to free dispensation, but was necessary, by the force of the same, Matth. XXVIII. 19. which Grotius has confessed more than once. But Grotius seems here to have followed the Papists, who deny that the preached Word is the ordinary medium through which the Holy Spirit is conferred. Which, however, is sufficiently confirmed not only from this passage and c. XI. 14. but also Joh. XVII. 20. Rom. X. 17. 1. Cor. IV. 15. Gal. III. 2. 1. Petr. I. 23. Jac. I. 18. See what [is written] against the Jesuit Hagerus, by the Blessed Lord Father-in-law Dr. Hülsemann in Manual. Aug. Conf. p. 234. 971. It seems probable to some, however, that the Holy Spirit was poured out here upon the Gentiles just as upon the Jews at the feast of Pentecost Act. II. namely in the visible symbol of tongues of fire: which we leave in its place.

IX. 17. erat autem hæc dispensatio plane necessaria, ut disceret Pe- trus & per Petrum Apostoli, non negandum illis aquæ ba- ptismum, quibus etiam Spiritus baptismum Deus imparti- ret. Minori auctoritate res tam nova obtineri non poterat; docet id nos comma sequens: ἐπιπίπτειν dicitur de Spiritu S. supra c. VIII. 16. c. XI. 15. dicitur & περὶ ἐκσάσεως ut supra 10. sic & de timore.

Cur anticipatam dicamus hanc gratiam, cum non ad baptismum, vel ad manuum impositionem Deus eadem se alligarit, ut non nisi vel in bapti- smo vel cum χειροθεσίᾳ Apostolorum dona mira- culosa Spiritus S. conferret. Neque inde potius demum discere hoc habuit, nempe è baptismo flaminis, baptismum aquæ vel fluminis, quem vo- cant, non denegandum isti Cornelio & familiæ ejus. Id enim habebat ex institutione Baptismi, utpote quem non liberæ dispensationi relictum, sed necessarium esse noverat, vi ejusdem, Matth. XXVIII. 19. quod non semel confessus est Grotius. Videtur autem Grotius hic Papistas sequutus, qui negant Verbum prædicatum esse ordinarium me- dium, per quod Spiritus S. conferatur. Quod ve- ro non ex hoc solum loco & cap. XI. 14. sed etiam Joh. XVII. 20. Rom. X. 17. 1. Cor. IV. 15. Gal. III. 2. 1. Petr. I. 23. Jac. I. 18. satis firmatur. Vid. quæ con- tra Jesuitam Hagerum, B. Dn. Socer D. Hülse- mannus in Manual. Aug. Conf. p. 234. 971. Veri- simile autem nonnullis videtur ita effusum hic su- per gentes fuisse Spiritus S. uti super Judæos in fe- sto Pentecostes Act. II. sc. in symbolo linguarum ignearum visibili: quod suo loco relinquimus.

XXIII. 6. Sirach IV. 26. Luke VI. 29. ## 10:48
Verse 48.

and he commanded them to be baptized) The Apostles also used the work of others to baptize men. He who does something through another does it himself.

That the Apostles used the work of others can be admitted; but not that of laymen, as Joh. Volckel the Socinian gathers from this passage in 'Solutio nodorum Gordianorum' page 19. For the administration of baptism was entrusted not to just anyone, but to the Apostles as ministers of the word, Matt. XXVIII. 19. Nor do we read here that Peter baptized through laymen: and St. Peter could have had other ministers of the word with him, through whom he administered baptism, since in Acts XI. 12 he is read to have had six with him in the house of Cornelius, and it is not established that they were all laymen: Although it is not even read here that Peter baptized through others; it is only said that he commanded that they be baptized, whether by himself or by others, whence Lorinus says: Nothing, he says, prevents Peter from having wished to baptize the distinguished person of Cornelius, or the rest of his household as well.

in the name of the Lord Jesus) From the name of Christ, He who anointed, the Father, and the Spirit by whom He was anointed are tacitly understood. See above c. II. 38. below c. XIX. 25. Rom. VI. 3. Gal. III. 27.

The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity is rightly gathered from the name of Christ, with Basil the Great and Ambrose leading the way. Yet the formula of the administration of baptism is not designated by this phrase 'in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ' (although not all copies have these names added, but some and the more recent ones read simply 'in the name of the Lord,' which Blessed Luther also followed), which is expressed in Matt. XXVIII. 19; but the author and principal cause, in whose name and authority baptism was administered, is designated.

Then they asked him to stay for some days) Cornelius, and those with him, asked Peter that he might be both their guest and their dinner companion, in which matter Peter complied with them XI. 3. And thus Peter showed that he was released by God from those precepts of the Sages concerning avoiding familiarity with the uncircumcised. I do not think, however, that he used foods forbidden by the law. For that is not objected to him in the following chapter. Nor do I think that any Jew converted to Christ did that, while it was permitted to enjoy those things of the fatherland.

Petrus alios verbi ministros, per quos baptismum administra- rit, quum Act. ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τῦ Κυρίε Ἰησῦ) Ex nomine Christi tacite in- telligitur & qui unxit, Pater, & Spiritus quo unctus est. Vi- de supra c. II. 38. infra c. XIX. 25. Rom. VI. 3. Gal. III. 27.

Recte colligitur è nomine Christi Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis mysterium, præeunte Basilio Magno & Ambrosio. Non tamen hac phrasi in nomine Do- mini Jesu Christi (quamvis nec omnia exemplaria hæc nomina addita habeant, sed nonnulla & rece- ptiora simpliciter legant in nomine Domini, quæ sequutus est etiam B. Lutherus) formula designa- tur administrati baptismi, quæ Matth. XXVIII. 19. expressa; sed autor & causa princeps, cujus nomi- ne & autoritate administratus est baptismus.

Τότε ἠρώτησαν ἀυτὸν ἐπιμεῖναι ἡμέρας τινάς) Cornelius, & qui cum eo, Petrum rogarunt, ut & hospes ipsorum & conviva esset, qua in re obsecutus est eis Petrus XI. 3. Nec puto quemquam judæum ad Chri- stum conversum id fecisse, dum patria istis frui licuit.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Peter, being compelled to give an account of why he had entered unto the Gentiles, recounts his heavenly vision, the warning of the Holy Spirit, and his calling made through an angelic apparition, as well as the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Caesarean assembly, according to Christ's promise concerning the baptism of the Holy Spirit: having heard these things, all praise God, because He had also granted repentance unto eternal life to the Gentiles. But when those who had been dispersed because of the tribulation of Stephen as far as Phoenicia, and Cyprus, and Antioch, had there also announced Jesus to the Greeks, with many having entered unto the Lord, Barnabas was sent from Jerusalem to Antioch, that he might confirm them in the faith, and a great multitude was added to the Lord. And Barnabas brought Paul from Tarsus, and for a whole year both taught there, and the disciples were first named Christians there. But Agabus predicting a great famine, the disciples sent relief for the ministry to the brethren in Judea by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.

There are three parts: I. Peter's apology concerning his entry unto the Gentiles, with the celebration of the Lord received, to verse 18. II. The conversion of the Antiochenes, and the ἐπωνυμία of the Christians, to verse 27. III. The collection sent to the brethren in Judea for the great famine impending, to verse 20.

PART I. Peter's apology concerning his entry unto the Gentiles.

V. 1. Τὰ ἔθνη) Uncircumcised men, whom the Jews call [Hebrew: גוים].

Latin:

CAPUT XI. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Petrus rationem reddere adactus, cur ad gen- tes ingressus sit, visionem suam cœlestem, Spir. S. monitum, & vocationem per Ange- licam apparitionem factam, nec non effu- sionem Spir. S. ad concionem Cæsariensem, juxta Christi de baptismo Spir. S. promif- sum, recenset: quibus auditis omnes Deum prædicant, quod etiam gentibus pœnitenti- am ad vitam æternam dederit. Cum vero il- li, qui ob Stephani tribulationem dispersi e- rant usque ad Phœnicen, & Cyprum & An- tiochiam, ibidem quoque Græcis Jesum an- nunciarint, multis ad Dominum ingressis, missus Hierosolymis fuit Antiochiam Bar- nabas, ut eos confirmaret in fide, & apposita est multa turba Domino. Adduxitq́; Bar- nabas Paulum Tarso, & per totum annum ambo illic docuerunt, primumque ibi disci- puli Christiani nominati sint. Agabo au- tem famem magnam prædicente, discipuli fratribus in Judæa per manus Barnabæ & Saulis in ministerium subsidia miserunt.

Partes sunt tres: I. Petri de ingressu ad gentes apologia, cum celebratione Domini suscepta, ad v. 18. II. Antiochenorum conversio, & Christiano- rum ἐπωνυμία, ad v. 27. III. Collecta fratribus in Judæa ad famem magnam imminentem transmif- sa, ad v. 20.

PARS I. Petri de ingressu suo ad gentes apologia.

V. 1. Τὰ ἔθνη) Homines incircumcisi, quos Judæi [Hebrew: גוים] vocant.

## 11:2
Vers. 2. Διεκοίνοντο) they disputed. Not the Apostles, inasmuch as they had been commanded to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles; but other believers from the circumcision. For although they had scattered after the stoning of Stephen, there is no doubt that some returned later to Jerusalem, and others were even newly converted to the Christian faith there. Nor do they seem to have disputed whether the Gentiles were to be called or converted, which perhaps was not unknown from the Prophets themselves; but whether they were to be admitted without circumcision and the observance of the Mosaic law.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Διεκοίνοντο) disputabant. Non Apostoli, utpote qui jussi erant gentibus prædicare Evangelium; sed alii fideles è circum- cisione. Nam licet dilapsi fuerint post lapidatio- nem Stephani, fideles, reversos tamen postmo- dum nonnullos Hierosolymam, aliosque etiam de novo ad Christianam fidem ibidem conversos, dubium nullum est. Neque adeo disceptasse illi videntur, anne vocandi aut convertendi sint gen- tiles, quod forsan è Prophetis ipsis non fuit igno- tum; sed an admittendi sint sine circumcisione, & Mosaicæ legis observatione.

## 11:3
Vers 3. ὅτι) understand: We complain of this. εἰσῆλθες κὴ συνέφαγες ἀυτοῖς) Contrary to the decree of the wise. Peter in any case scorns the authority of such decrees, but opposes the express command of God. What is to be thought of that decree, which Grotius so often inculcates, we have said before. That the Jews were not averse to all conversation with the Gentiles, so that they would not even walk with them or enter their houses, but only to familiar and closer conversation, has been rightly observed by the blessed Joh. Ern. Gerhard, who should be compared here.

Latin:

Vers 3. ὅτι) subintellige: Hoc querimur. εἰσῆλθες κὴ συνέφαγες ἀυτοῖς) Contra decretum sapien- tum. Petrus utcunque spernit talium decretorum auto- ritatem, sed disertum Dei mandatum opponit. Quid de decreto illo, quod toties inculcat Gro- tius, habendum, diximus antea. Non omnem conversationem cum gentilibus aversatos fuisse Judæos, ita ut nec ambulare cum ipsis, aut eorum ædes ingredi voluerint, sed tantum familiarem & arctiorem conversationem recte observatum B. Joh. Ern. Gerharde, qui hic conferatur.

Vers. 10. Ἀνεσπάσθη) [Hebrew: עלה] just as [Hebrew: עולי] Ἀνέσπασε Hab. I, 15. above c. X. 16. placed for the same ἀνελήφθη, [Hebrew: נלקח].
