Vers. 10. Ἀνεσπάσθη) [Hebrew: עלה] sicut [Hebrew: עולי] Ἀνέσπασε Abac. I, 15. supra c. X. 16. pro eodem positum ἀνελήφθη, [Hebrew: נלקח].

## 11:12
Vers. 12. κἀγὼ οἱ ἕξ ἀδελφοὶ ὗτοι) who could testify that the gifts of the Holy Spirit were poured out by God upon Cornelius and his household.

Latin:

Vers. 12. κἀγὼ οἱ ἕξ ἀδελφοὶ ὗτοι) qui testari poterant à Deo dona Spiritus S. in Cornelium & domesticos ejus effusa.

## 11:14
Vers. 14. ἐν οἷς σωθήσῃ σὺ κὴ πᾶς ὁ οἶκός σε) After Christ was sent, God did not want there to be any other way to salvation than through knowledge of him. Therefore, he did not leave Cornelius in that state of the Noahides. And note that it is not only for them, but also for his house that good is done by God. Thus Philo in the history of the angels who had turned aside to Abraham: "It must be believed that upon their entry all parts of the house would increase even more toward the better, with virtue having been prayed for at the same time."

Having dismissed the fiction concerning the precepts of the Noahides, which has its origin from the Rabbinic gloss on the book of Ruth, as Schindler observed in his Lexicon under the word [Hebrew: גור]: it is certain that not even through the precepts of the Mosaic Law, let alone those fictitious ones of the Noahides, could anyone ever have attained salvation, nor were the faithful of old saved otherwise than through the grace of Christ, Acts XV. v. 10. But after Jesus was manifested, salvation was obtained solely through faith in his name. Moreover, however these words in Acts X. v. 22 are not referred to as having been spoken by an Angel, that passage can nevertheless be completed from this parallel, since it is evident from it concerning the words which Peter was about to speak, of what power they were to be held. From which it also appears that the preached word is truly a means of salvation, Rom. I. 16, ch. X. 17, 1 Cor. I. 18, 21. The preposition ἐν is put for διὰ, through, as in Rom. VIII. 9, Gal. I. 16, ch. III. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ἐν οἷς σωθήσῃ σὺ κὴ πᾶς ὁ οἶκός σε) Post missum Christum noluit Deus aliam esse viam ad salutem, quam per ejus co- gnitionem. Ideo Cornelium in illo statu Noahidarum non reliquit. Et nota non ipsi tantum, sed & domui ipsius bene à Deo fieri. Sic Philo in historia Angelorum qui ad Abra- hamum diverterant Νομιστέον μὲν τοι κατὰ τὴν εἴσοδον ἀυτῶν ἔτι μᾶλλον ἐπιδώσειν πάντα τὰ μέρη τῆς οἰκίας πρὸς τὸ βέλτισον, ἅμα την τελευτάτη ἀρετῆς ἐπιπευξθείσης.

Misso commento de præceptis Noahidarum, quod è glossa Rabbinica in lib. Ruth. originem ha- bet, ut Schindlerus in Lex. in voce [Hebrew: גור] observa- vit: certum est, ne quidem per præcepta Legis Mosaicæ, nedum Noahidarum illa fictitia quem- quam salutem unquam consequi potuisse, nec fideles olim aliter quam per gratiam Christi sal- vatos esse, Actor. XV. v. 10. postquam vero Jesus manifestatus fuit, unice per fidem in ejus nomine salutem obtigisse. Cæterum utut hæc verba Act. X. v. 22. non referantur, ceu ab Angelo dicta, com- pleri tamen locus ille ex hoc parallelo potest, quum inde constet de verbis, quæ Petrus dicturus erat, cujusnam illa virtutis habenda. Ex quo et- iam apparet, quod verbum prædicatum vere me- dium salutis sit, Rom. I. 16. cap. X. 17. 1. Cor. I. 18. 21. Præpositio ἐν ponitur pro diα per, ut Rom. VIII. 9. Gal. I. 16. cap. III. 21.

## 11:15
Vers. 15. ἐν δὲ τῷ ἄρξασθαί με λαλεῖν) that is, ἐν τῷ με λαλεῖν, while I am speaking, as above ch. I. 1. Compare ch. X. 44, and add the Canon from the Grammar of the Holy Scriptures by B. Glassius, page 237. Inchoative verbs are sometimes to be understood as completive, Gen. IX. 20, Num. XXV. v. 1, Matt. XVI. 22, Luke XV. 24, ch. XXI. 28.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἐν δὲ τῷ ἄρξασθαί με λαλεῖν) id est, ἐν τῷ με λαλεῖν, dum loquor, ut supra c. I. I. Conf. c. X. 44. & adde Canonem è B. Glassii Gramm. S. pag. 237. Verba inchoativa completive aliquando intelligenda sunt, Gen. IX. 20. Num. XXV. v. 1. Matth. XVI. 22. Luc. XV. 24. c. XXI. 28.

## 11:16
Vers. 16. τοῦ ῥήματος Κυρίου) these are properly the words of John the Baptist that follow, Matt. III. 11, Mark I. 8, Luke III. 16, John I. v. 26, but what John had said, Christ approved, Matt. XI. 9. Grotius is mistaken. These words are not properly those of the Proto-baptist, but of the Lord himself, Acts I. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 16. τοῦ ῥήματος Κυρίου) sunt proprie, quæ sequuntur Jo- hannis Baptistæ verba Matth. III. 11. Marc. I. 8. Luc. III. 16. Joh. I. v. 26. sed quæ Johannes dixerat, probavit Christus Matth. XI. 9. Fallitur Grotius. Verba hæc non Proto-bapti- stæ proprie sunt, sed ipsius Domini, Act. I. 5.

## 11:17
Vers. 17. ἐγὼ δὲ τίς ἤμην δυνατὸς κωλῦσαι τὸν Θεὸν) for ἵνα δυνατὸς ὦ. Who then was I, that I could withstand God? God called them as such to salvation, not I.

Latin:

Vers. 17. ἐγὼ δὲ τίς ἤμην δυνατὸς κωλῦσαι τὸν Θεὸν) pro ἵνα δυνατὸς ὦ. Quis ergo eram, ut Deo possim obsistere? Deus eos tales vocavit ad salutem, non ego.

## 11:18
Vers. 18. Ἡσύχασαν) They complained no further, but were overcome. Ἄραγε) therefore. τὴν μετάνοιαν ἔδωκεν) that repentance is given, here is to forgive beautifully: to give the effect of repentance. There is no reason why we should depart from the literal meaning of the words. For even for repentance the grace of God is necessary, not only for the forgiveness of sins. For it is God who converts us. Even the Papists themselves will acknowledge that repentance is to be ascribed not to our own powers, but to divine grace, Johan. Hoffmeister and Libertus Fromond on this passage.

The conversion of the Antiochenes, and the naming of Christians.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ἡσύχασαν) Nihil ultra conquesti sunt, victi vero. Ἄραγε) ergo. τὴν μετάνοιαν ἔδωκεν) dari pœnitentiam, hic est belle igno- scere: dare effectum pœnitentiæ. Non est, cur à proprietate verborum disceda- mus. Nam & ad pœnitentiam gratia Dei opus est, non solum ad peccatorum veniam. Deus enim est, qui nos convertit. Agnoscent etiam ipsimet Pa- pistæ, non nostris viribus, sed divinæ gratiæ adscri- bendam esse pœnitentiam, Johan. Hoffmeisterus & Libertus Fromond. in h. l.

Antiochenorum conversio, & Christianorum nuncupatio.

## 11:19
Vers. 19. οἱ μὲν ὖν διασπαρέντες) those of whom [we spoke] above VIII, 1 and 4. διῆλθον ἕως Φοινίκης κὴ Κύπρε κὴ Ἀντιοχείας) he explains more broadly what he had said briefly in the aforementioned place, ch. VIII. 4. From these passages we have said in the second epistle to the Thessalonians that certain relatives of Silas and Timothy came into Macedonia. Moreover, the Antioch to be understood here is not that of Pisidia, which is in Acts XIII. v. 14, but that of Syria, which was once called Emath, according to B. Luther, Tom. IV. of his German works, Altenb. ed., p. 337. μηδενὶ λαλῦντες τὸν λόγον εἰ μὴ μόνον Ἰυδαίοις) because they had not learned the Greek language.

This is not the reason which Grotius gives, since the Greek language was not unknown to them, being widely accepted and very common: but because they believed that the word of the Gospel did not pertain except to the Jews, and those who had approached them and had taken up their rites as proselytes, which was then generally believed by the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 19. οἱ μὲν ὖν διασπαρέντες) illi, de quibus supra VIII, 1. & 4. διῆλθον ἕως Φοινίκης κὴ Κύπρε κὴ Ἀντιοχείας) latius expli- cat, quod breviter dixerat dicto loco c. VIII. 4. Ex his locis quosdam porro Silæ & Timothei propinquos in Macedo- niam venisse diximus in secundam ad Thessalonicenses. Cæterum Antiochia hic intelligenda non Pi- sidiæ, quæ Act. XIII. v. 14. Sed Syriæ, quæ Emath olim dicta, juxta B. Luther. Tom. IV. oper. Germ. edit. Altenb. p. 337. μηδενὶ λαλῦντες τὸν λόγον εἰ μὴ μόνον Ἰυδαίοις) quia sermo- nem Græcum non didicerant.

Non hæc causa est, quam Grotius reddit, siqui- dem non ignota fuerit Græca lingua utpote pas- sim recepta, & usitatissima: sed quod crediderint illi, non pertinere verbum Evangelii nisi ad Ju- dæos, & qui ad illos accesserant, eorumque ritus susceperant proselytos, quod tum Judæis persuasum fere erat.

## 11:20
Verse 20.

Κύπριοι καὶ κυρηναῖοι) Known in those places where the Greek language was frequent. For Cyprus and Cyrene were long connected to the Egyptian kingdom, in which that language was much used, especially at Alexandria.

Indeed, they seem to have been instructed more correctly than the rest, since they understood the mystery concerning the calling of the Gentiles.

ἐλάλουν πρὸς τοὺς Ἑλληνιστάς) It must certainly be read πρὸς ἕλληνας, as that manuscript in England has it. And the Syriac reads it so. For it translates it as 'with the Greeks': not with those speaking Greek, as above in ch. IX. 22. The Latin and the Arab read it in the same way. ἕλληνες, from the time of the Greek, that is, Macedonian empire, were already called by the Jews all uncircumcised persons from the predominant party. Thus that word is taken in 2 Macc. IV. 36. And hence ἑλληνικὸς χαρακτὴρ 2 Macc. X. 2, ἑλληνικαὶ δόξαι 16. 15, τὰ ἑλληνικὰ 2 Macc. VI. 9, ch. XI. 24, that is, foreign customs: and often in Paul. Moreover, it can rightly be taken properly here. For at Antioch there were many of Greek origin. See 2 Macc. VI and what is said there.

· εὐαγγελίζόμενοι τὸν Κύριον) telling of his deeds as above in ch. V. 42.

Vain is the suspicion concerning the corruption of the Greek text and its reckless alteration, since all the codices agree, and Walton noted no variation. Nor does the Syriac and the Arab argue against it, since they are accustomed to express those words in the same manner at times; meanwhile, by ἑλληνιστὰς here I understand Greek Gentiles, not indeed Jews who were only Greek by nation, or who had read the Holy Scripture in the Greek language. The opposition of the Jews, to whom the word was preached by others, and the Hellenists, to whom the Cypriots and Cyrenians preached it, sufficiently teaches this: nor do Chrysostom, Lyra, Hugo, Cajetan, Lorinus, Tirinus, Drusius, and the Vinarienses understand anything other than Greek Gentiles by Hellenists. Although, for the rest, it must not be denied that Jews using the Greek language and the version of the LXX Interpreters were also sometimes called Hellenists, concerning which see Ludovicus de Dieu on Acts X. v. 19 and Bart. Majer, Prodrom. Philolog. Sacr. Nor is there any reason why we should explain this as referring to Greek proselytes, because they were mixed and aggregated with the Jews, and when the word was preached to these, it was certainly already preached to them as well, because they participated in the same communion; indeed, the Jews did not even refuse marriages with them.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Κύπριοι καὶ κυρηναῖοι) Noti illis in locis, in quibus fre- quens sermo Græcus. Nam Cyprus & Cyrene connexa diu regno Ægyptio, in quo multus ille sermo, præsertim Alexandriæ.

Imo videntur illi potius rectius instituti, quam reliqui, siquidem intellexerunt mysterium de vo- catione gentium.

ἐλάλουν πρὸς τοὺς Ἑλληνιστάς) Certo legendum προς ἕλληνας, quomodo habet ille in Anglia manuscriptus. Et ita legit Syrus. Vertit enim cum Græcis : non cum Græce loquen- tibus, ut supra c. IX. 22. legit eodem modo & Latinus & Arabs, ἕλληνες jam à tempore imperii Græci, id est, Ma- cedonici, dicebantur Judæis omnes incircumcisi à parte prædominante. Sic sumitur ea vox 2.Macc.IV.36. Et hinc ἑλληνικὸς χαρακτὴρ 2.Macc. X .2. ἑλληνικαὶ δόξαι 16.15. τὰ ἑλλην- νικὰ 2. Macc. VI. 9. c. XI. 24. instituta scilicet extranea: & apud Paulum sæpe. Cæterum hic proprie sumi recte potest. Nam Antiochiæ multi erant Græcæ originis. Vid. 2. Macc. Vf. & ibi dicta.

· εὐαγγελίζόμενοι τὸν Κύριον) ejus res narrantes ut supra c. V. 42.

Vana est suspicio de corruptione textus Græci & immutatio ejus temeraria, quum omnes codi- ces consentiant, neque ullam varietatem notarir Waltonus. Nec Syrus, & Arabs eam arguit, quum eadem ratione voces illas exprimere quandoque soleant, interim per ἑλληνιστὰς hic intelligo Græcos gentiles, non vero Judæos, qui natione tantum Græci, aut Græca lingua Scripturam S. legerant. Oppositio Judæorum, quibus verbum prædicatum est ab aliis, & Hellenistarum, quibus Cyprii, & Cy- reniaci id prædicarunt, satis docet: nec alios per Hellenistas, quam Græcos gentiles intelligunt Chry- sostomus, Lyranus, Hugo, Cajetanus, Lorinus, Ti- rinus, Drusius, Vinarienses. Etsi de cætero negan- dum non sit, alias Hellenistas etiam vocatos Ju- dæos Græca lingua & versione LXX. Interpretum utentes, quo de vid. Ludovicus de Dieu ad Act. X. v. 19. & Bart. Majer. Prodrom. Philolog. Sacr. Ne- que vero est, quod de Græcis proselytis hæc ex- plicemus, quia illi admixti & aggregati erant Ju- dæis & cum his verbum prædicatum est, illis uti- que jam etiam idem prædicatum est, quia uni in- tererant communioni, imo etiam matrimonia cum iisdem non detrectabant Judæi.

Verse 21.

Ἐπέστρεψεν) they turned themselves. The active for the reciprocal.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Ἐπέστρεψεν) converterunt se. Activum pro reciproco.

Verse 23.

Ἰδὼν τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ) by the grace of God understand here the increase of the Church.

Τῇ προθέσει τῆς καρδίας) with a firm purpose, in which way πρόθεσις is also taken in 2 Tim. III. 10.

Latin:

Vers 23.

Ἰδὼν τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ) per gratiam Dei intellige Lic in- crementum Ecclesiæ.

Τῇ προθέσει τῆς καρδίας) firmo proposito, quomodo πρό- θεσις sumitur etiam 2. Tim. III. 10.

## 11:25
Vers. 25.

Ἀναζητῆσαι Σαῦλον) An old friend and one affected by a kindness from him, see above IX. 27.

Vers. 25.

Ἀναζητῆσαι Σαῦλον) Amicum veterem & beneficio à se affectum, supra IX. 27.

## 11:26
Vers. 26.

χρηματίσαι τε πρῶτον) χρηματίζειν for 'to be named' is a word of better Greek, which Polybius also uses more than once, a writer read by Luke, and Paul in Rom. VIII. 7.

ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ) where the seat of his kingdom had been, which is Magog to Ezekiel, the Northern kingdom to Daniel, and had been overturned before the coming of Christ according to the oracles.

Grotius did not explain here what those oracles are concerning the Antioch of Magog and the Northern kingdom of Daniel. However, his inventions concerning Magog in Ezekiel, and those which he proposed in Daniel, have already been discussed in their proper places. Antioch was rather the seat of the Christian Church and not the last Patriarchate, since three Patriarchal Sees were once numbered: Roman, Antiochene, and Alexandrian, to which was added later the Jerusalemite, and afterwards the Constantinopolitan. Finally, some add a sixth, the Aquileian, a See erected there by Mark the Evangelist after the Alexandrian: whose Patriarch, however, after Aquileia was destroyed, resides at Venice, as Hieronymus Megiserus observes in the 'Paradiso delitiarum', that is, the description of Venice, p. 222.

Χριστιανὸς) After the custom of the Greeks who named disciples from their masters, such as Pythagoreans, Platonists, Aristotelians, Epicureans.

They were previously called μαθηταὶ, disciples, Acts VI. 2, 17, ch. IX. 1, 19, 25, 26, 38. But at Antioch they received this new name from Christ towards the end of the seventy weeks of Daniel, as we have observed in the Sacred Chronicle. Chrysostom, in Photius' Bibliotheca, p. 270, says: Paul came into the city of Antioch and planted such a great multitude of the faithful that then for the first time the appellation of Christians flourished. Concerning this prerogative of Antioch over Rome, see B. Luther, Vol. VIII of the German works, Altenburg edition, p. 451.

PART III. The collection sent to the brethren in Judea on account of the famine.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

χρηματίσαι τε πρῶτον) χρηματίζειν pro nominari est vox meli ris Græcitatis, quam & Polybius non semel usurpat, feriptor Lucæ lectus, & Paulus Rom.VIII.7.

ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ) ubi sedes fuerat regni ejus, quod Magog Ezechieli, Septentrionale Danieli, & eversum erat ante ad- ventum Christi secundum oracula.

Quænam oracula illa sint de Antiochia Magogi & Septentrionalis Danielis regni non exposuit hic Grotius. Commenta autem ejus de Magog in E- zechiele, & quæ in Daniele proposuit, suis discussa jam sunt locis. Sedes potius Ecclesiæ Christianæ & Patriarchæ non postremi Antiochia fuit, quum tres olim numeratæ sint Patriarchales Sedes, Ro- mana, Antiochena, & Alexandrina, quibus acces- sit deinde Hierosolymitana, ac postmodum Constan- tinopolitana. Addunt denique sextam Aquilejien- sem nonnulli a Marco Evangelista ibidem post Ale- xandrinam erectam Sedem: cujus tamen Patriar- cham, post eversam Aquilejam Venetiis residere Hier. Megiserus in Paradiso delitiarum, h. e. Vene- tiarum descriptione p. 222. observat.

Χριστιανὸς) Græcorum more qui à magistris discipulos nominabant, ut Pythagoreos, Platonicos, Aristotelicos, Epicureos.

Dicti antea sunt μαθηταὶ discipuli Act. VI. 2. 17. cap. IX. 1. 19. 25. 26. 38. Antiochiæ autem novum hoc nomen accepere à Christo sub exitum septima- narum LXX. Danielis, uti in Chronico sacro ob- servavimus. Chrysost. apud Photium in Biblioth. pag. 270. Venit, inquit, in Antiochiam urbem Paulus tantamque fidelium multitudinem plantavit, ut tum primum Christianorum appellatio floruerit. De qua Antiochiæ præ Roma prærogativa vid. B. Luth. Tom. VIII. oper Germ. edit. Altenburg. p. 451.

PARS III. Collecta fratribus in Judæa ob famem missa.

## 11:28
Vers. 28. Ἄγαβος) עגב, whence the Greek ἀγάπη. Dorotheus in his Synopsis hands down that he was of the number of the seventy disciples.

ὅς τις καὶ ἐγένετο ἐπὶ Κλαυδίε Καίσαρος) Suetonius and Dio mention it under Claudius: and Josephus XX. 2.

See also Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book III, chapter 4. Nicephorus, History, Book II, who writes that in the time of that famine, Helena, Queen of the Adiabeni, having purchased grain in Egypt with a vast sum of money, sent it to those in need. Luke teaches that this famine came upon the whole inhabited world; which Grotius wrongly explains by synecdoche in Matthew XXIV, p. 400, as referring to Judea, observing that it is familiar to the Jews to call it Palestine: a point which he will prove with no evidence, and therefore others more correctly understand it as the whole orb of the earth, as far as the Roman Empire extended. See Luke II. 1, Acts XXIV, Matthew XXIV. 14. That the famine prevailed even outside Judea is sufficiently testified by the external writers cited here by Grotius himself.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Ἄγαβος) עגב, unde Græcum ἀγάπη. Quem è numero LXX discipulorum fuisse, tra- dit Dorotheus in Synopsi.

ὅς τις καὶ ἐγένετο ἐπὶ Κλαυδίε Καίσαρος) meminere Sue- tonius & Dion Claudio : & Joseph. XX. 2.

Vid. & Eusebius III. Hist. Eccles. cap. 4. Niceph. lib. II. Histor. l. II. qui scribit, tempore illius famis Reginam gentis Adiabenorum Helenam ingenti pecunia frumento in Ægypto comparato indigen- tibus id transmisisse. Ἐφ᾽ ὅλην τὴν οἰκεμένην eam famem venisse Lucas docet; quam perperam Gro- tius per synecdochen ad Matth. XXIV. p. 400. de Judæa explicat, ita Judæis familiare esse Palæstinam vocare, observans: quod vero nullo documento probabit, ideoque alii totum terrarum orbem, quousque Romanorum imperium se extendebat, rectius intelligunt. Vid. Luc. II. 1. Actor. XXIV, Matth. XXIV. 14. Extra Judæam etiam famem in- valuisse scriptores exteri hic à Grotio ipso laudati satis testantur.

## 11:29
Verse 29.

ὥσπερ ὑπορετό τις) כמצאת ידו די Lev. XXV. 18.

εἰς διακονίαν) for the relief of the poor. It is called διακονία above VI. 1, Rom. XII. 7, 2 Cor. VIII. 4, ch. IX. 1, 12, 13, ch. XI. 8.

τοῖς κατοικῦσιν ἐν τῇ Ἰεδαίᾳ ἀδελφοῖς) who were for the most part poor. Wherefore Paul often commends them, now to the Achaeans, now to the Macedonians.

The brethren in Judea were in need beyond the rest, and many had voluntarily contributed their resources to the common fund, Acts II & IV; many also had suffered the plundering of their goods, Heb. X. 34, 1 Thess. II. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

ὥσπερ ὑπορετό τις) כמצאת ידו די Lev. XXV. 18.

εἰς διακονίαν) ad levamentum pauperum. Id διακονία dicitur supra VI. 1. Rom. XII. 7. 2. Cor. VIII. 4. c. IX. 1. 12. 13. c. XI. 8.

τοῖς κατοικῦσιν ἐν τῇ Ἰεδαίᾳ ἀδελφοῖς) qui pauperes ferme erant. Quare sæpe eos Paulus modo Achæis, modo Ma- cedonibus commendat.

Indigi erant præ reliquis fratres in Judæa, ac facultates suas multi in commune sponte contule- rant Act. II. & IV. multi etiam rapinam bonorum suorum passi erant. Ebr. X. 34. 1. Thess. II, 14.

## 11:30
Verse 30.

πρὸς τὺς πρεσβυτέρυς) This is the first mention of presbyters in the Church. They were called זקנים by the Jews, not only those who presided over public judgments, but also those who presided over individual synagogues. The second law in the Theodosian Code concerning the Jews translates them as presbyters: in another law they are called Fathers of the synagogues. Moreover, the entire government of the Churches of Christ was fashioned after the model of the synagogues. But also among the Greeks, the ancients were accustomed to call the best men and the elders πρεσβυτέρυς κὶ τὺς ἀρίσυς, κὶ τὺς γέροντας, says Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book II.

These things were said without doubt in favor of the Papal Ecclesiastical Polity. But the Jewish Synagogue had a high priest by divine institution. The primitive Christian Church, however, had no high priest, nor did God institute any in it. And who were the Patriarchs in the Jewish Synagogue, such as we have said existed in the Christian Church? Who were the Bishops there, who the Archbishops? To say nothing now of other differences.

διὰ χειρὸς Βαρνάβα κὶ Πάυλυ) by Paul and Barnabas sent there: for 'by' the Hebrews say ביד.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

πρὸς τὺς πρεσβυτέρυς) Hæc prima est presbyterorum in Ecclesia mentio. Judæis זקנים dicti, non solum, qui ju- diciis publicis, sed & qui synagogis singulis præerant. Pres- byteros vertit lex secunda codice Theodosiano de Judæis : in alia lege dicuntur Patres synagogarum. Totum autem regimen Ecclesiarum Christi, conformatum fuit ad Syna- gogarum exemplar. Sed & apud Græcos πρεσβυτέρυς κὶ τὺς ἀρίσυς, κὶ τὺς γέροντας εἰώθασιν οἱ παλαιοὶ λέγειν, ait Hali- carnaffensis Dionysius lib. II.

Hæc in gratiam Papalis Politiæ Ecclesiasticæ si- ne dubio dicta. At habuit Synagoga Judaica Sa- cerdotem summum ex institutione divina. Nullum vero summum Sacerdotem habuit primitiva Ec- clesia Christiana, nullum instituit in ea Deus. Et quinam Patriarchæ fuere in Synagoga Judaica, quales in Christiana Ecclesia jam fuisse diximus? Quinam ibi Episcopi, quinam Archi-Episcopi? ut alia jam discrimina taceamus.

διὰ χειρὸς Βαρνάβα κὶ Πάυλυ) per Paulum & Barnabam eo missos: pro per Hebræi dicunt ביד.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The persecution of the Church by Herod in Judea, by whom James was killed with the sword, Peter was imprisoned, so that after the feast of the Passover, which was then being celebrated, he might be brought forth, but being freed by an Angel through the prayers of the Church, the miracle of his liberation having been reported to the faithful, he departed elsewhere: Herod, having made an inquiry concerning the guards of the prison, departing for Caesarea, and because of his pride being struck by an Angel, and consumed by worms: but the Word of the Lord increasing, Barnabas and Saul having returned to Jerusalem, having taken with them John, surnamed Mark.

There are three parts: I. The Herodian persecution, to v. 17. II. The striking of Herod, to v. 23. III. The propagation of the Word of God, to v. 25.

PART I. The Herodian persecution.

Vers. 1. Herod the king laid hands) It is the Hebrew שלח יד, which is often translated ἐπιβάλλειν χεῖρα, sometimes ἐκτείνειν; and it signifies to devote effort to some matter, Gen. III 21. Deut. XII. 7. and elsewhere. The Syrian rightly explains Herod here as Agrippa, namely the son of Herod the Great, from which family as many as there were, were called by the common name Herod.

κακῶσαί τινας) It is accustomed to be translated here by the Hebrew ענו.

There was also another Herod called Agrippa, Acts XXVI. 2, the son of this one. But this Herod Agrippa Major was the great-grandson of Herod Antipas, the grandson of Herod Antipater, the grandson of Herod the Great, and was the son of Aristobulus.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Herodis persecutio Ecclesiae in Iudaea, à quo Ia- cobus gladio casus, Petrus incarceratus, ut post Paschatos festum, quod tum agebatur, sisteretur, sed precibus Ecclesiae per Ange- lum liberatus, relato fidelibus miraculo li- berationis, aliorsum profectus est: Herode, facta de carceris custodibus inquisitione, Caesaream proficiscente, & ob fastum ab Angelo percusso, atque à vermibus consum- to: Verbo autem Domini crescente, Barnaba & Saulo Hierosolymam reversis, assumto Iohanne, Marco cognominato.

Partes sunt tres: I. Herodiana persecutio, ad v. 17. II. Herodis percussio, ad v. 23. III. Verbi Dei pro- pagatio, ad v. 25.

PARS I. Herodiana persecutio.

Vers. 1. Ἐπέβαλεν Ἡρώδης ὁ βασιλεὺς τὰς χεῖρας) Hebræum est שלח יד, quod sæpe vertitur ἐπιβάλλειν χεῖρα, nonnun- quam ἐκτείνειν; & significat studium alicui rei impendere, Gen. III 21. Deut. XII. 7. & alibi. Herodem hic recte Sy- rus explicat Agrippam, filium nempe magni Herodis, ex qua familiâ quotquot erant, communi nomine Herodes vocabantur.

κακῶσαί τινας) Solet hic verti ענו Hebræum.

Fuit & alius Herodes Agrippa dictus Actor. XXVI. 2. hujus filius. Hic vero Herodes Agrippa Major dictus Herodis Antipa abnepos, Herodis Antipatris pronepos, Herodis Magni nepos, & Aristobuli filius extitit.

## 12:2
Vers. 2. and he killed James the brother of John with the sword) the son of Zebedee; the son of thunder, that is, eminent among the Apostles, and therefore more suspicious to Herod. Thus that cup befell him, of which Christ had spoken in Matthew XX. 23. With the sword, however, because in ancient times kings used this punishment alone for those who were sources of trouble. These things were done at Jerusalem. For besides other tetrarchies, he also received Judea properly so called from Claudius Agrippa, as Josephus testifies XIX. 4. see below 19.

This son of Zebedee by Salome, the brother of John, called James the Greater, of intimate admission to Christ, Matth. XVII. c. XXVI. 37. The other James, the son of Alphaeus, Matth. X. v. 3, Bishop of Jerusalem, mentioned in Acts XV and in this chapter v. 17, is said to have been stoned. See Josephus book XX. c. X. Whence Ludovicus Capellus errs in Spicil. thinking that this James killed by Herod was the son of Alphaeus. For he is said here in v. 2 expressly to be the brother of John. Conf. Matth. IV. 21. chap. X. v. 2. That beheading was also in use among the Jews, or the punishment of the sword, is evident from Rabbi Solomon on Exodus XXII. 16. Conf. Selden on the Sanhedrin book II. c. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 2. ἀνεῖλε δὲ Ἰάκωβον τὸν ἀδελφὸν Ἰωάννου μαχαίρᾳ) filium Zebedæi; ὑιὸν βροντῆς, id est, eximium inter Aposto- los, eoque Herodi suspectiorem. Ita contigit ei calix ille, de quo Christus erat locutus Matth. XX. 23. Gladio autem, quia antiquitus Reges hoc solo supplicio in fontes uteban- tur. Hæc Hierosolymis acta sunt. Nam præter alias te- trarchias etiam Judæam proprie dictam à Claudio Agrippa accepit, teste Josepho XIX. 4. vide infra 19.

Hic Zebedæi ex Salome filius, Johannis frater, Jacobus Major dictus, intimæ apud Christum ad- missionis, Matth. XVII. c. XXVI. 37. Alter Jaco- bus Alphæi filius Matth. X. v. 3. Hierosolymitanus Episcopus, Act. XV. hoc capite v. 17. commemo- ratus, lapidatus dicitur. Vid. Josephus lib. XX. c. X. Unde errat Ludovicus capellus in Spicil. existi- mans hunc Jacobum ab Herode interfectum Al- phæi filium fuisse. Dicitur enim hic v. 2. diserte frater Johannis. Conf. Matth. IV. 21. cap. X. v. 2. Decollationem autem etiam apud Judæos in usu fuisse, seu pœnam gladii à Rabbi Salomone ad E- xod. XXII. 16. constat. Conf. Seldenus de Synedrio lib. II. c. 13.

## 12:3
Vers. 3.

καὶ ἰδὼν ὅτι ἀρεστόν ἐστι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις) The descendants of Herod, following the example of Herod the Great, directed all their actions toward this, partly to be pleasing to the Caesars, partly to the Jewish people, being entirely unconcerned whether what they were doing was right or not.

προσέθετο συλλαβεῖν καὶ Πέτρον) a Hebrew idiom, such as Luke XX. 12. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

καὶ ἰδὼν ὅτι ἀρεστόν ἐστι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις) Herodis posteri, He- rodis Magni exemplo omnes actus suos in id dirigebant, partim ut Cæsaribus, partim ut populo Judaico grati essent, rectumne esset quod agerent, annon plane securi.

προσέθετο συλλαβεῖν καὶ Πέτρον) locutio Hebræa, qualis Luc. XX. 12. & alibi.

## 12:3
ἦσαν δὲ ἡμέραι τῶν Ἀζύμων) The beginning of the feast or of the eight days. The unleavened bread begins before the Passover, as we said at Matt. XXVI. 18.

Latin:

ἦσαν δὲ ἡμέραι τῶν Ἀζύμων) Initium τῆς ἑορτῆς sive octo dierum. Azyma incipiunt ante Pascha, ut diximus ad Matth. XXVI. 18.

## 12:4
Vers. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

## 12:4
τέσσαρσι τετραδίοις) In the Glosses: τετράδιον is a quaternion; they guarded him in turns of four.

βουλόμενος μετὰ τὸ Πάσχα ἀναγαγεῖν ἀυτὸν) After the day on which the lamb was eaten, which, on account of the joy, was exempt from punishments. See what we wrote at Matt. XXVI. 5. ἀναγαγεῖν here and shortly after προάγειν, means to bring forth, to show to the public.

Latin:

τέσσαρσι τετραδίοις) In Glossis : τετράδιον quaternio; quaterni per vicis eum servabant.

βουλόμενος μετὰ τὸ Πάσχα ἀναγαγεῖν ἀυτὸν) Post diem eum, quo agnus edebatur, qui ob lætitiam exemptus sup- pliciis. Vide, quæ ad Matth. XXVI. 5 Ἀναγαγεῖν hic & mox προάγειν, est producere, publico ostendere.

## 12:12
to the house of Mary the mother of John who is called Mark) The mother is called here by the son as the more well-known person. Thus Matt. XX. 20. ch. XXVII. 55. Mark XV. 40. But why I think this John Mark is a different person from him who wrote the Gospel, I have said at the beginning of that Gospel.

where many were gathered together and praying) For many assemblies were held, and in many houses.

What is to be thought of this Mark, we have said likewise at the beginning of the Gospel of St. Mark. Mention of this Mark is made also in v. 25 below, and ch. XIII. 13. ch. XV. 37. Col. IV. 10. Concerning Mark the Evangelist see 1 Peter Epist. V. v. 13. and Blessed Joh. Gerhard on that passage. But those assemblies and domestic churches, such as were also Rom. XVI. 15. 1 Corinth. XVI. 15. Coloss. IV. 15. were instituted for divine worship; which consisted in the reading of the word Acts XIII. 17. and preaching Acts XX. 7. in psalmody and prayer ch. III. 1. ch. XVI. 16. in the administration of the sacraments ch. XX. 7. 1 Cor. XI. v. 33. as also in the collection and distribution of alms 1 Cor. XVI. 2.

Latin:

ἐπὶ τὴν οἰκίαν Μαρίας τῆς μητρὸς Ἰωάννη τοῦ ἐπικαλουμένου Μάρκου) Mater hic à filio ut notiore appellatur. Sic Matth. XX. 20. c. XXVII. 55. Marc. XV. 40. Johannem autem hunc Marcum cur alium esse putem ab eo, qui scripsit Ev- angelium, dixi ad initium illius Evangelii.

ὦ ἦσαν ἱκανοὶ συνηθροισμένοι καὶ προσευχόμενοι) Multi enim cœtus & multis in domibus habebantur.

Quid de Marco hoc habendum, diximus iti- dem ad initium Evangelii S.Marci. Mentio hujus Marci fit etiam v. 25. infra, & cap. XIII. 13. c. XV. 37. Col. IV. 10. de Marco Evangelista vide 1. Petri Epist. V. v. 13. & B. Joh. Gerhard. ad eum locum. Con- ventus autem illi & Ecclesiæ domesticæ, quales & Rom. XVI. 15. 1. Corinth. XVI. 15. Coloss. IV. 15. ob cultum divinum instituebantur; qui consistebat in verbi lectione Actor. XIII. 17. & prædicatione Act. XX. 7. in Psalmodia & oratione cap. III. 1. cap. XVI. 16. in Sacramentorum administratione cap. XX. 7. 1. Cor. XI. v. 33. ut & in Eleemosynarum collectione & erogatione 1. Cor. XVI. 2.

## 12:13
Vers. 13.

the door of the gate) That door by which the courtyard lying before the house was closed. See above ch. X. 7. Matt. XXVI, v. 7.

a maidservant came to answer) She came so that she might recognize by the voice who it was, lest she admit someone rashly.

by name Rhoda) In Hebrew חבצלת Cant. II. 1. many names of women are from flowers, herbs, trees, as Susanna from the lily, Hadessa from the myrtle. The Greek name Ῥόδη is also in the fragments of Menander.

Compare concerning similar names Blessed Joh. Ernest. Gerhard on this passage.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

τὴν θύραν τοῦ πυλῶνος) Ostium illud, quo area domui præjacens claudebatur. Vide supra cap. X. 7. Matth. XXVI, v. 7.

προσῆλθε παιδίσκη ὑπακοῦσαι) Venit ut ex voce cogno- sceret, quis esset, ne quem temere admitteret.

ὀνόματι Ῥόδη) Hebraice חבצלת Cant. II. 1. multa muli- erum nomina à floribus, herbis, arboribus, ut Susanna a li- lio, Hadessa à myrto. Græcum nomen Ῥόδη est etiam in Menandri fragmentis.

Conf. de similibus nominibus B. Joh. Ernest. Gerhard. ad h. l.

## 12:15
Vers. 15. his angel it is) From the opinion of the masters, about which we have spoken at Matt. XVIII. 10. See Gen. XLVIII. 16.

The passage Gen. XLVIII. 16 is rashly drawn here. For there not a created, but an uncreated angel is understood. But what is to be held concerning that commonly received opinion of the Jews, that an angel of his own is assigned to each person, according to which ὁ ἄγγελος αὐτοῦ seems to Blessed Joh. Gerhard to be an angel appearing in his form, we have said in Vol. IV. Syst. Theol. page 77. The Papists themselves, although they accede to the opinion of the Jews, scarcely dare to establish that angels appear in the person of those whose angels they are: as can be seen from Johannes Hoffmeister on this passage: but whether, he says, such an angel is accustomed to appear in some visible form and especially that of the one to whom he is deputed, it is not certain to me, nor does an example of that thing occur to me now. Nor is the singularity of Joh. Cameron in his lectures Vol. II. page 471 to be approved, who understands by ἄγγελον a messenger here. For Rhoda heard the voice of Peter, and she had testified without doubt that she had heard it. Therefore it could not be a presumption about a messenger of Peter.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ὁ ἄγγελος αὐτοῦ ἐστι) Ex opinione magistrorum, de qua diximus ad Matth. XIIX. 10. Vid. Gen. XLVIII. 16.

Temere huc trahitur locus Gen. XLVIII. 16. Ibi enim non creatus, sed increatus angelus intelli- gitur. Quod vero de illa opinione Judæorum communiter recepta, quod cuique Angelus suus assignatus sit, juxta quam ὁ ἄγγελος αὐτοῦ B. Joh. Gerhardo videtur esse angelus in forma ejus appa- rens, habendum sit, diximus Tom. IV. Syst. Theol. pag. 77. Papistæ ipsi, etsi Judæorum opinioni acce- dunt, vix audent statuere, angelos in persona eo- rum, quorum Angeli sunt, apparere: uti è Johan- ne Hoffmeistero in h. l. videre est: an vero, inquit, talis angelus apparere soleat visibili quadam specie & præcipue ejus, cui deputatus est, mihi pro certo non constat nec ejus rei mihi jam aliquid succurrit exemplum. Neque probanda Joh. Cameronis in prælect. Tom. II. pag. 471. singularitas, qui per ἄγγε- λον nuncium hic intelligit. Audivit enim Rode vocem Petri, eamque sine dubio se audivisse testa- ta erat. Non ergo præsumtio esse poterat de nun- cio Petri.

## 12:17
Vers. 17. but having beckoned to them with his hand) It is a good Greek word, which Luke also uses elsewhere ch. XIII. 16. ch. XIX. 33. ch. XXI. 40. Ovid, however, describes it thus: --- who after he had suppressed the murmurs with his voice and hand. Persius: --- to have made silence for the hot crowd by the majesty of his hand. Heliodorus: stretching out his hand, he calmed the turbulence of the people for the sake of silence.

σιγᾶν) that is, εἰς τὸ σιγᾶν.

ἀπαγγείλατε Ἰακώβῳ) To the brother, that is, to the kinsman of the Lord, whose epistle we have. Josephus calls him, τὸν ἀδελφὸν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ λεγομένου χριστοῦ. Ἰάκωβος ὄνομα αὐτῷ. Antiquities XX. 8.

If this author James is the kinsman of the Lord of the Jacobean Epistle, why does Grotius deny that James the son of Alphaeus is the author of the same, in his annotations to James I. 1? For James the son of Alphaeus is he who was called the brother of the Lord, Matt. XIII. 55. Mark VI. 3. Gal. I. 19.

καὶ τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς) To those who were not present in that place at that time. For they held assemblies in many places, lest a crowd too large gathered into one might make them more suspicious.

καὶ ἐξελθὼν ἐπορεύθη εἰς ἕτερον τόπον) Lest by chance he should be sought where many had gathered.

PART II The striking of Herod.

Latin:

Vers. 17. κατασείσας δὲ αὐτοῖς τῇ χειρὶ) Vox est bene Græ- ca, quam & alibi Lucas usurpat cap. XIII. 16. c. XIX. 33. c. XXI. 40. Ovidius autem ita circunscribit: --- qui postquam voce manuque Murmura compressit. Persius: --- Calidæ fecisse silentia turbæ Majestate manus. Heliodorus: τὴν χεῖρα προτείνας πρὸς ἡσυχίαν τὸ κλυδώνιον τοῦ δήμου κατέστειλε.

σιγᾶν) id est, εἰς τὸ σιγᾶν.

ἀπαγγείλατε Ἰακώβῳ) Fratri, id est, consanguineo Do- mini, cujus est quam habemus epistola. Josephus hunc vocat, τὸν ἀδελφὸν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ λεγομένου χριστοῦ. Ἰάκωβος ὄνομα αὐτῷ. Antiquæ historiæ XX. 8.

Si autor hic Jacobus consanguineus Domini est Epistolæ Jacobææ, cur negat Grotius, Jaco- bum Alphæi filium autorem ejusdem esse annot. ad Jac. I. 1. Nam Jacobus Alphæi est, qui vocatus est frater Domini, Matth. XIII. 55. Marc. VI. 3. Gal. I. 19.

καὶ τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς) Iis qui in eo loco tunc non aderant. Mul- tis enim in locis cœtus habebant, ne nimia multitudo in u- num conglobata suspectiores eos faceret.

καὶ ἐξελθὼν ἐπορεύθη εἰς ἕτερον τόπον) Ne forte ibi quo mul- ti convenerant quæreretur.

PARS II Herodis percussio.

## 12:19
Vers. 19. ἀνακρίνας τοὺς φύλακας) An examination having been held concerning them. See above ch. IV. 9. below ch. XXVIII. 18. & ch. II. 5. 16.

ἐκέλευσεν ἀπαχθῆναι) Luke said this in the Roman manner: he ordered them to be led away, namely to execution. Seneca on Anger, book 15. Piso climbs the tribunal in a rage, and orders both to be led away.

Guilb. Budaeus teaches in his commentaries on the Greek language that the word ἀπαχθῆναι is used simply in this way among the Greeks: and Chrysostom and Oecumenius also understand it thus in this place. Proclus in his oration on the binding of Peter, and Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechism XIV. Others, however, explain it as being led into prison, such as Rabanus and Cajetan; or they think the guards were led to Caesarea, where Herod was about to come, and they say that a little later, after Herod was killed, those guards were dismissed, God thus softening Herod's mind, so that Peter's release might not harm anyone, or be the cause of death for the guards. In a doubtful matter and an ambiguous word, with history failing us, we leave these things in the middle.

καὶ κατελθὼν ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰουδαίας εἰς τὴν Καισάρειαν) Josephus also mentions this journey in XIX. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἀνακρίνας τοὺς φύλακας) Quæstione de eis habi- ta. Vide supra c. IV. 9. infra c. XXVIII. 18. & c. II. 5. 16.

ἐκέλευσεν ἀπαχθῆναι) Romano more hoc dixit Lucas: duci jussit, nempe ad supplicium. Seneca de Ira l. 15. Con- scandit tribunal furens Piso, ac jubet duci utrumque.

Ita vocem ἀπαχθῆναι simpliciter adhiberi apud Græcos, Guilb. Budæus in comment. Græcæ ling. docet: atque ita accipit etiam hic Chrysost. & Oecu- men. in h. l. Proclus orat. de vinc. Petri & Cyrillus Hierosol. Catech. XIV. Alii tamen per duci in carcerem exponunt, ut R职务banus & Cajetanus; aut Cæsaream, quo Herodes venturus erat, deductos custodes putant, ac paulo post, Herode occiso, custodes illos dimissos esse, ajunt, Deo ita Hero- dis animum emolliente, ne Petri solutio alicui no- ceret, aut custodibus necis causa esset. Nos in re dubia & voce ambigua, deficiente Historia, hæc in medio relinquimus.

καὶ κατελθὼν ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰουδαίας εἰς τὴν Καισάρειαν) Hujus iti- neris meminit & Josephus XIX. 7.

## 12:20
Vers. 20. θυμομαχῶν) Luke took this word also from Polybius. Diodorus Siculus and others also use it, and it signifies to be eager to fight.

Τυρίοις καὶ Σιδωνίοις) Which cities were then under the Romans, but with some shadow of liberty.

ὁμοθυμαδὸν δὲ παρῆσαν πρὸς αὐτὸν) Envoys by the common decree of both cities.

τὸν ἐπὶ τοῦ κοιτῶνος τοῦ βασιλέως) Suetonius calls those performing this office chamberlains, both in Nero and in Domitian; a name which Cicero and the jurist Alfenus also use when dealing with a private house. Later Greeks also say κυβικουλαρίους, as Leontius Scholasticus in an epigram; Cedrenus, Menander the protector, and the writer of the Etymologicum. Codinus said κοιτωνάριον.

διὰ τὸ τρέφεσθαι αὐτῶν τὴν χώραν ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλικῆς) The territory of Sidon and Tyre was too narrow to be able to feed those populous cities with its own grain and wine. Therefore they had need to purchase such things from Judea, Galilee, and other regions that belonged to Herod. See what we have said on Isaiah ch. XXIII. 18.

Luke seems to have inserted this history, both to manifest the truculent spirit of Herod, who was hostile not only to Christians but also to others without cause, and also to note here his pride and ambition, stirred by which he was meditating the subjugation of the cities of the Tyrians and Sidonians, which were very populous and wealthy: not indeed as Baronius rashly suggests, that the Sidonians had admitted Peter after he escaped from prison, and having been made Christians by him, had received a bishop. For no testimony can be brought forward for that matter.

Latin:

Vers. 20. θυμομαχῶν) Hanc quoque vocem de Poly- bio sumpsit Lucas. Utitur & Diodorus Siculus, & alii, si- gnificatque, pugnaturire.

Τυρίοις καὶ Σιδωνίοις) Quæ civitates tunc sub Romanis erant, sed cum umbra aliqua libertatis.

ὁμοθυμαδὸν δὲ παρῆσαν πρὸς αὐτὸν) Legati ex communi utriusque civitatis decreto.

τὸν ἐπὶ τοῦ κοιτῶνος τοῦ βασιλέως) Hoc officio fungentes Suetonius & in Nerone & in Domitiano cubicularios vo- cat; quo nomine etiam de privata domo agentes utuntur Cicero & Jurisconsultus Alfenus. Dicunt & Græci poste- riores κυβικουλαρίους, ut Leontius Scholasticus in Epigram- mate; Cedrenus, Menander protector, Etymologici scriptor. Codinus dixit κοιτωνάριον.

διὰ τὸ τρέφεσθαι αὐτῶν τὴν χώραν ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλικῆς) Ter- ritorium Sidonis & Tyri angustius erat, quam ut illas civi- tates populosas alere frumento suo & vino posset. Itaque opus habebant ex Judæa, Galilæa & aliis regionibus. Quæ Herodis erant, talia coëmere. Vide, quæ diximus ad E- saiam c. XXIII. 18.

Historiam hanc inseruisse videtur Lucas, cum ut truculentum Herodis animum manifestaret; qui non Christianis solum, sed aliis etiam citra cau- sam infensus esset, tum ut fastum ejus & ambitio- nem hic quoque notaret, qua excitatus debellatio- nem Tyriorum & Sidoniorum urbium maxime populosarum & opulentarum meditabatur: non vero ut temere Baronius, quod Sidonii Petrum è carcere elapsum admisissent, ab eoque Christiani fa- cti, Episcopum suscepissent. Ejus enim rei nullum proferri potest testimonium.

## 12:21
Vers. 21. τακτῇ δὲ ἡμέρᾳ) On the day appointed for this, namely the second day of the games which he was exhibiting in honor of Claudius Caesar. Thus Josephus XIX. 7.

ἐνδυσάμενος ἐσθῆτα βασιλικὴν) Woven from silver with rare art, which, when the rays of the sun fell upon it, gave off an admirable splendor: the same Josephus.

καὶ καθίσας ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος) βῆμα here is a platform placed in the theater, as we learn from Josephus. Every elevated place is called βῆμα by the Greeks, as also by the Syrians כומרא, which word the Syrian interpreter uses here.

ἐδημηγόρει πρὸς αὐτούς) With a certain singular eloquence.

Latin:

Vers. 21. τακτῇ δὲ ἡμέρᾳ) Die ad hoc constituta, secunda nempe ludorum, quos exhibebat in honorem Claudii Cæsaris. Ita Josephus XIX. 7.

ἐνδυσάμενος ἐσθῆτα βασιλικὴν) Ex argento rara arte tex- tam, quæ Solis radiis in eam incidentibus splendorem de se edebat admirabilem: idem Josephus.

καὶ καθίσας ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος) βῆμα hic est suggestum po- situm in theatro, ut ex Josepho discimus. Omnis locus e- ditior βῆμα Græcis dicitur, ut & Syris כומרא, qua voce Sy- rus interpres hic utitur.

ἐδημηγόρει πρὸς αὐτούς) Singulari quadam facundia.

## 12:22
Vers. 22. ὁ δὲ δῆμος ἐπεφώνει) As the flatterers of the court were making a beginning.

Some think that Herod wished to propose publicly the response to the demands of the Tyrians and Sidonians. Thus also the Weimar Paraphrasts, since the history concerning the Tyrians and Sidonians had been premised here by Luke.

Θεοῦ φωνὴ καὶ οὐκ ἀνθρώπου) The Hebrews called that revelation which occurred through a voice בת קול, which word the Syrian uses here. The flatterers attribute this to Herod in these words, calling him a god, says Josephus. It was not the custom among the Hebrews to call kings gods because of the danger of the word, almost all the surrounding peoples honoring kings partly living, partly dead, with that honor which was proper to the gods. In the whole college of Senators, there was not the same danger. And so we find them, but not the kings, called אלהים.

Tremellius on this passage: Frequently, he says, you may find in the ancient writings of the Hebrews the daughter of the voice used for a voice sent down from heaven, by which men are admonished concerning the will of God. Compare Drusius in praeter. page 6, on Matthew III, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ὁ δὲ δῆμος ἐπεφώνει) Principium facientibus aulæ assentatoribus.

Nonnulli putant Herodem responsum ad Ty- riorum & Sidoniorum postulata publice propo- nere voluisse. Sic & Vinarienses Paraphrastæ, quum historia de Tyriis & Sidoniis præmissa à Luca hic fuerit.

Θεοῦ φωνὴ καὶ οὐκ ἀνθρώπου) Hebræi eam revelationem, quæ per vocem fiebat, vocabant בת קול, qua voce hic Sy- rus utitur. Id his verbis Herodi tribuunt assentatores, Θεὸν προσαγορεύοντες, ait Josephus. Non erat Hebræis mos reges Deos appellare ob periculum vocis, cunctis ferme- circumpopulis, reges partim vivos, partim mortuos, colen- tibus honore eo, qui diis erat proprius. In collegio toto Senatorum, non idem erat periculis. Itaque eos, non autem reges, invenimus dictos אלהים.

Tremellius in h. l. Frequenter, inquit, invenias in antiquis Hebræorum scriptis filiam vocis pro voce cœlitus demissa poni, qua homines de voluntate Dei admoneantur. Conf. Drusius in præter. pag. 6. ad Matth. III, 17.

## 12:23
Verse 23.

παραχρῆμα δὲ ἐπάταξεν αὐτὸν Ἄγγελος κυρίου) With severe pain around the heart and through the whole abdomen. See Josephus. God often uses the ministry of angels in sending diseases, Exodus XII, 27; 2 Samuel XXIV, 16.

ἀνθ᾽ ὧν ἐκ ἔδωκε τὴν δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ) He did not leave to God His unblemished honor. He did not do what Peter did above in chapter X, 26, and Paul and Barnabas below in XIV, 14, 15.

Lorinus says that the ministry of an evil angel was employed here by God: but Cornelius à Lapide, as also B. Arcularius, say that the good angel, whom God used in delivering Peter, was employed to punish Herod. Bede seems to favor Lorinus, who also says that Herod saw the angel imminent over his head, and immediately sensed that he was the minister of his destruction.

κὴ γενόμενος σκωληκόβρωτος) After the example of Antiochus, 2 Maccabees IX, 9. Thus God shows to those who breathe more than a human spirit that they are men, that is, food for worms.

ἐξέψυξεν) ויפח as above in chapter V, 5.

They judge him to have been made subject to the disease which physicians call Phthiriasis, or the louse disease. They designate the year of Herod's death as the 12th after the resurrection of Christ, the 55th of Herod's age, and the 3rd of the reign of Claudius. See Eusebius, book II, Ecclesiastical History, 10; Josephus, book XIX, Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 2, and book II of the Jewish War, chapter 4.

PART III. The propagation of the Word of God.

Vers. 23.

παραχρῆμα δὲ ἐπάταξεν αὐτὸν Ἄγγελος κυρίου) Gravi do- lore circa cor & per ventrem omnem. Sis Josephus. In morbis immittendis sæpe Angelorum ministerio Deus utitur, Exod. XII, 27. 2. Sam. XXIV, 16.

ἀνθ᾽ ὧν ἐκ ἔδωκε τὴν δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ) Non reliquit Deo il- libatum suum honorem. Non fecit quod Petrus supra cap. X, 26. & Paulus & Barnabas infra XIV, 14. 15.

Angeli mali ministerium à Deo adhibitum hic fuisse Lorinus: at Corn. à Lapide, ut & B. Arcula- rius bonum illum angelum, quo in Petro liberan- do Deus usus est ad Herodem puniendum adhibi- tum dicunt. Lorino favere Beda videtur, qui etiam Herodem vidisse imminentem capiti suo an- gelum, esse exitii sui ministrum eum statim sensisse, ait.

κὴ γενόμενος σκωληκόβρωτος) Ad exemplum Antiochi 2. Macc. IX, 9. Ostendit sic Deus iis, qui plus homine spi- rant, homines eos esse, id est, vermium escam.

ἐξέψυξεν) ויפח ut supra c. V. 5.

Obnoxium factum morbo, quem medici Phti- riasin nuncupant, seu pedicularem, censent. An- num obitus Herodis designant XII. post resurre- ctionem Christi, ætatis Herodis LV. Imperii Clau- dii III. Vid. Euseb. l. II. Histor. Eccles. 10. Josephus l. XIX. Ant. Jud. c. 2. & libr. de Bell. Jud. II. c. 4.

Verse 24.
