Therefore, justification is claimed solely for faith in Christ, in whom we have that which was impossible for us by the law, as being both the fulfillment of all things which God commanded us, and the merit of obedience, because the works of Christ's obedience were not owed to the law, but were spontaneously performed for us for the law; and also the substitution of Christ for us, when he offered himself as a sacrifice for our sins, and satisfied for us by his passion and death; whence a man is justified in him, through faith, when the merit and satisfaction of Christ, or his obedience both active and passive, is imputed to him, and thus not only the remission of sins, but also true and perfect righteousness is obtained in Christ. Furthermore, Grotius did not teach, nor could he teach, by any testimony that τὸ δικαιῦν (to justify) is to be purged, that is, to be freed from the habit of sinning. The passage Job ch. IV v. 17. Shall a man be

Shall a man be justified before God, or shall he be cleansed before his maker? It admits very well the customary meaning of the word, if indeed a man wishes to contend with God, that not man, but God will be justified, as it is said in Job IX. 2. 3.: I know it is so of a truth: but how should man be just with God, &c. Nor is it necessary that we say the word to be cleansed is an explanation of the former. In Daniel ch. VIII. 14. the sanctuary is said to be justified, that is, cleansed, but that liberation from the habit of sinning cannot have a place there: much less will that meaning be proven from the N. T. Furthermore: That heavenly gifts were not promised in the O. T. and that by the power of those promises made in the N. T. man is liberated from the habit of sinning or justified, are Socinian-Pelagian hypotheses. But concerning these in the preface to the Epistle to the Romans. The evangelical axiom, which is comprised in this proclamation, teaches that the discourse is about justification through faith, and not about the avoidance of the habit of sinning: In this everyone who believes is justified: Cf. Rom. X. 4.

Latin:

Vers. 39. κὲ ἀπὸ πάντων ὧν ὐκ ἠδυνήθητε ἐν τῷ νόμῳ Μώσεως δικαιωθῆναι, ἐν τύτῳ πᾶς ὁ πισεύων δικαιῦται) Non est idem, quod præcessit, sed aliud beneficium. Nam צָדַק, quod plerumque Græce est δικαιῦν significat & purgare. Vertiturque צָדַק καθαρὸς ἔσται, Job. IV. 17. κα- θαρισθήσεται, Dan. VIII. 14. purgatur à criminibus, qui à peccandi consuetudine liberatur, id ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ per legem non fiebat, Hebr. X. 23. Causa est, quia lex promissa non habebat cœlestia. Hæc autem attulit Christus, ideoque corda purificavit.

Non hæc duo diversa beneficia proponuntur, nec usus rerum id admittit. Sed remissio peccato- rum, quæ ipsa est justificatio & forma ejusdem, explicatur uberius. Quod per Christum remif- sio peccatorum fiat, & quidem omnium peccato- rum, à quibus nos justificari, vel quorum remissio- nem consequi non possumus in lege Mofis: ut ostenda- tur omnium peccatorum remissionem in Evange- lio propositam, simulque doceatur, per legem Mo- sis ejusque observationem justificari à peccatis nos minime posse, quod ipsum est thema illud, quod prolixius exequutus est Apostolus in Epistolis ad Romanos, ad Galatas, ad Ephesios, ad Philippen- ses, hic ἐπιτομικῶς propositum.

Observandum autem hic (1) Verba γνωςὸν ἖ν ἔσω ὑμῖν, notum igitur sit vobis, indicare quid, quod maxime scitu est necessarium, sive fuerit antea co- gnitum, sive non; quia etiam de re antea cognita, minimeq; obscura adhiberi potest hæc comone- factio, ut ea quam maxime attendatur, ceu impri- mis necessaria; Quanquam vero ea res, quod per Messiam unice remissionem peccatorum conse- quantur, qui credunt in ipsum, in V. T. ab omnibus Prophetis credita, adeoque notissima esse potu- erit, Act. X. 43. quia tamen maxime obscurata hæc salutaris doctrina fuerat penes Judæos, & præterea nunc in Evangelio annunciandum ab Apostolis id erat, quod Jesus Nazarenus Filius Dei ab æterno ex essentia ejus genitus, à Deo excitatus, & missus, ac post mortem resuscitatus, ne videret corruptio- nem, sit ille, in quo fidelia Davidi & Patriarchis an- te ipsum promissa impleta sunt, per quem oportet nos remissionem peccatorum & justificationem consequi, idcirco annunciat hoc palam Apostolus, ut in ipsum credant, eumque vera fide suspiciant Judæi, si justificari, & salutem adipisci velint. (2) Textum ita distingui in tribus Erasmianis editioni- bus, ut & Basilœensi, Tigurina & Stephanea, observa- vit B. Erasm. Schmidius, quibus consonat Casau- boni editio, ut post δικαιωθῆναι comma tantum ha- beatur, idquerecte, quum verba illa ἐν τούτῳ πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων δικαιοῦται non faciant hic, aut inchoent novam sententiam, sed cum antecedente sententia cohæreant; Quam distinctionem firmat etiam Dn. D. Seb. Schmidts Colleg. Bibl. post p. 207. quod ea ra- tione nulla ellipsi vel supplemento opus sit; quod- que non satis conveniat ad nomen ἄφεσις remissio præpositio ἀπὸ. (3) Duo itaque vult Apostolus Ju- dæis nota esse: 1.quod per & propter Jesum Nazare- num annuncietur ipsis remissio peccatorum. 2. Et quod ἀπὸ πάντων ab omnibus, ὧν à quibus non potuerint in lege Mosis (vel iis, quæ in lege tradidit Moses) justi- ficari, vel absolvi in hoc Christo Jesu (vel iis, quæ ipse fecit, & passus est) omnis, qui credit (in ipsum) justificetur. In illo ὧν pro ἀφ’ ὧν Ellipsin Atticam notat Erasm.Schmied. repeti autem potest è priori, ἀπὸ πάντων. Græci enim id in usu habent, ut quan- do præpositio cum relativo repetenda est, omitta- tur, posito tantum relativo. 4) Prius concernit cau- sam justificationis meritoriam: quod nempe per Je- sum in mortem traditum, in quo nulla mortis causa inventa est, & à mortuis resuscitatum remissio pec- catorum obtineatur; posterius ad causam organicam spectat: quod sc. unice per fidem in Christum justifi- cari oporteat; nec in iis, quæ in lege continentur, justificari quisquam possit, sed in hoc Christ. Jesu, & iis, quæ ipse pro nobis egit, aut passus est, cum fide apprehenduntur, omnes qui credunt, justificantur. Quæ in lege continentur, & præcipiuntur, sunt ope- ra legis tum moralia, tum ceremonialia, tum politica, per quæ justificari nemo poterat. Modus, quo lex Judæis videbatur justificare, duplex est: unus per impletionem præceptorum, alter per substitutionem, si per sacrificia mactata, eorumque sanguinem Deo satisfieret, ita ut peccata in ipsis amplius non pu- niret. Alius justificationis forensis modus de le- ge ne quidem fingi potest. At neuter possibilis e- rat; non prior, quia legem nemo implere potest, ne- dum quicquam per impletionem legis, utpote ali- as debitam, mereri; non posterior, quia per san- guinem hircorum & vitulorum nulla fieri potest expiatio. Fidei ergo in Christum unice vindicatur justificatio, in quo, quod lege impossibile nobis fuit, habemus, utpote tum impletionem omnium, quæ Deus nobis præcepit, & meritum obedientiæ, quia non erant opera obedientiæ Christi legi de- bita, sed sponte legi pro nobis præstita; tum substi- tutionem Christi pro nobis, cum seipsum obtulit in sacrificium pro peccatis nostris, & passione ac morte sua pro nobis satisfecit; unde homo justifi- catur in ipso, per fidem, cum meritum & satisfa- ctio Christi, vel obedientia ejus tum activa tum passiva ei imputatur, adeoque non tantum remis- sio peccatorum, sed etiam vera & perfecta justitia in Christo obtinetur. Porro, τὸ δικαιῦν esse pur- gari, id est, liberari à consuetudine peccandi, nul- lo testimonio docuit, aut docere potuit Gro- tius. Locus Job. c. IV. v. 17. Numquid homo præ

Deo justificabitur, an prae factore suo mundabitur vir? optime admittit consuetam vocis significatio- nem, si nempe homo cum Deo contendere ve- lit, non hominem, sed Deum justificatum iri, ut Jobi IX. 2. 3. dicitur: vere novi, quod ita sit & quod non justificabit se homo cum Deo, &c. Neque necessum est, ut dicamus verbum mundari esse prioris ἐξηγητικὸν. Apud Danielem V. c. IIX. 14. sanctuarium justificari, id est, expiari dicitur, non vero ibi locum habere potest illa à consue- tudine peccandi liberatio: multo minus è N. T. ea significatio probabitur. Porro: In V. T. non promissa fuisse dona cœlestia & vi promissorum istorum in N. T. factorum hominem liberari à consuetudine peccandi seu justificari, hypotheses sunt Sociniano-Pelagianae. Sed de his in praefat. ad Epistol. ad Roman. De justificatione per fidem, non vero de vitatione consuetudinis peccandi ser- monem esse docet ἀξίωμα Evangelicum, quod in hoc praeconio comprehensum est: Ἐκ τούτῳ πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων δικαιῦται: Conf. Rom. X. 4.

## 13:40
Vers. 40. That which is spoken in the prophets) In that volume, which is called by the Hebrews תְּרֵי עֲשַׂר. See that the same thing does not happen to you, which once happened to your parents when the city and Temple were destroyed, and they themselves were deported because of their contempt for the benefits of God. See Habakkuk and what is said there.

Latin:

Vers. 40. Τὸ εἰρημένον ἐν τοῖς προφήταις) In eo volumi- ne, quod ab Ebraeis dicitur תְּרֵי עֲשַׂר. Videte ne, idem vobis eveniat, quod olim parentibus vestris urbe & Templo exciso, ipsis deportatis ob contemptum benefi- ciorum Dei. Vide Abacucum & ibi dicta.

## 13:41
Vers. 41. Behold, you despisers) Hab. ch. I. v. 5. you shall see, you who despise so many warnings, what I am about to do. It is true what Beza conjectured, that the LXX Elders read בֹּגְדִים instead of בַגּוֹיִם, for also in the same Habakkuk II. 5. בּוֹגֵד is translated as despisers.

And wonder) Luke contracted the Greek while preserving the sense, which is as follows: and look and wonder at wonders.

and perish) Namely the faces, as in Matt. VI. 16. grow pale. How the LXX Elders seem to have read the Hebrew here, we have said to the Prophet himself.

For I work a work) In the LXX, instead of ὅτι there is διότι. It appears that Luke did not write these from a manuscript, but as much as his memory supplied.

Work) This repetition of the word is not in the Greek, but it explains the matter effectively.

Vain are those conjectures as to what the LXX Elders read, inasmuch as it is established that they do not vary because of a different reading, but mostly because of other causes, nor do they render the text word for word, about which we have often warned. Moreover, Luke did not transcribe these from a manuscript, nor did he draw them from memory, but he committed them to writing from the suggestion and inspiration of the divine Spirit, if Paul is to be believed, that ALL Scripture is God-breathed or divinely written, 2 Tim. III. v. 16. and Peter, that holy men of God spoke, and therefore also wrote, being carried by the Holy Spirit, 2 Ep. I. 21.

Ὧι ὗ μὴ πιστεύσητε) Other manuscripts have ὃ, just as the Codex of the LXX Interpreters does.

PART III.

The abandonment of the Jews who reject the Word, and the conversion of the Gentiles who receive the Word.

Latin:

Vers. 41. Ἴδετε οἱ καταφρονηταὶ) Abac. c. I. v. 5. vide- bitis vos, qui tot monita contemnitis, quid sim facturus. Verum est, quod conjecit Beza LXX. Senes pro בַגּוֹיִם legisse בֹּגְדִים nam & in eodem Abacuco II. 5. בּוֹגֵד vertitur καταφρονητής.

Καὶ θαυμάσατε) Contraxit Lucas salvo sensu Graeca, quae sic habent: καὶ ἐπιβλέψατε καὶ θαυμάσατε θαυμά- σια.

καὶ ἀφανίσθητε) Nempe τὰ πρόσωπα, ut Matth. VI. 16. expallescite. Quomodo LXX. Senes hic in Hebræo le- gisse videantur, diximus ad Prophetam ipsum.

Ὅτι ἔργον ἐγὼ ἐργάζομαι) In LXX. pro ὅτι est διότι. Ap- paret à Luca haec non ex Codice scripta, sed quantum memoria suppeditabat.

Ἔργον) Haec repetitio vocis in Graeco non est, sed rem efficaciter exponit.

Vanae sunt illae conjecturae quid legerint LXX. Senes, utpote quos constat non variare ob diver- sam lectionem, sed plerumque ob alias causas, nec κατὰ πόδα reddere textum, de quo saepius mo- nuimus. Cœterum nec è Codice haec descripsit Lu- cas, nec è memoria depromsit, sed ex suggestione & inspiratione divini Spiritus id literis consigna- vit, si Paulo credendum, quod OMNIS Scriptura sit θεόπνευστος vel divinitus conscripta, 2. Tim. III. v. 16. & Petr. quod ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίς φερόμενοι loquuti sint, adeoque & scripserint sancti Dei homines, 2. Ep. I. 21.

Ὧι ὗ μὴ πιστεύσητε) Alii Codices habent ὃ, quomodo & Codex LXX. Interpretum.

PARS III.

Judaeorum Verbum repellentium relictio, & ad gentes Verbum suscipientes conversio.

## 13:42
Ver. 42. They besought the Gentiles) Those Pisidians.

Εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ σάββατον) It must be read entirely as ὡς τὸ μεταξὺ σαββάτων, the time between two Sabbaths. They say this because they saw the Apostles were free on the Sabbaths to instruct the Jews, as is clear above XIII. 14, below 44, XVI. 13. Formerly, the long O and the short O were written in the same or a similar form.

Scaliger intended almost the same thing, collecting the Greek text likewise, that it should be amended in book VI of his De emendatione temporum, p. 259, namely, that it should be read εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ Σαββατὸν, which opinion Casaubon explains in his notes, and B. Glassius does not seem to disapprove in his Grammat. S. p. 494, and Er. Schmidius. But the received reading is deservedly retained by the unanimous consent of the codices, and is rendered with Vatablus as 'in the intervening Sabbath' or 'the intermediate Sabbath.' The Latin version can be understood in the same sense, 'the FOLLOWING Sabbath,' with which the Syriac and Tigurine agree, as well as Pagninus, and also Oecumenius. Casaubon has this to say about it: 'The form of speech εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ σάββατον is certainly unusual, which, if you look at the custom of the Greek language, could signify nothing other than some middle Sabbath.' Interpreters, however, think the following Sabbath is meant: just as τῷ ἐρχομένῳ σαββάτῳ follows shortly after. The Syrian simply interpreted it as another Sabbath. If, therefore, the greatest assent is given here to Casaubon in that he indicates not the following Sabbath, but the intermediate time of the week, to which B. Luther's version also leans, as well as Er. Schmidius's new translation, 'the intervening week,' with Beza's version also agreeing, 'within the next following Sabbath': there is still no need for us to change the original text on that account; since τὸ σάββατον also denotes the whole week at times, as in Luke ch. XVIII, 12. And what certainty of the text will there finally be, if you once begin to change it? For Scaliger reads Σαββάτων, to Camerarius it seems it should be read σαββάτων instead of σάββατον: Grotius [reads] εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ σαββάτων: even though neither he, nor they, nor this one relies on any codex. Others will find other things, if it is permissible to devise something without the authority of the codices.

Latin:

Vers. 42. Παρεκάλουν τὰ ἔθνη) Pisidae isti.

Εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ σάββατον) Omnino legendum ὡς τὸ μεταξὺ σαββάτων, medio tempore inter duo Sabbata. Id ideo dicunt, quia videbant Apostolos per Sabbata Judæis instituendis vacare, ut patet supra XIII. 14. infra 44. XVI. 13. olim O longum & O breve ad eandem aut supparem formam scribebatur.

Idem fere voluit Scaliger, textum Graecum pa- riter colligens, emendandum esse l. VI. de emendat. temp. p. 259. sc. ut legatur εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ Σαββατὸν, quam sententiam explicat Casaubonus in notis, nec improbare videtur B. Glassius in Grammat. S. p. 494. & Er. Schmidius. Sed merito in una- nimi consensu codicum retinetur recepta lectio, ac cum Vatablo redditur, intercurrente, vel intermedia Sabbato. Sensu eodem accipi potest Latina versio, SEQUENTI Sabbato, cui consonat Syriaca, & Tigurina, nec non Pagnini, ut & Oecumenius. Casaubonus ita de eo habet: Insolens sane loquendi genus εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ σάββατον, quod si Graeci sermonis consuetudinem spectes, nihil aliud significare possit, quam medium aliquod Sabbatum. Interpretes autem sequens Sabbatum putant intelligi: sicut sequitur mox τῷ ἐρχομένῳ σαββάτῳ. Simpliciter Syrus de alio Sabbato interpretatus est. Si ergo maxime Casaubono hic in eo assensus praebeatur, quod non Sabbatum sequens, sed intermedium tempus septimanae innuatur, quo etiam B. Lutheri versio abit, nec non Er. Schmidii nova translatio, interjecta septimana, consentiente quoque Bezae versione intra proxime sequens Sabbatum: non tamen opus est, ut ideo textum mutemus originalem: quum τὸ σάββατον etiam totam septimanam quandoque notet, ut Luc. c. XIIX, 12. Et quae tandem certitudo textus erit, si semel eundem immutare coeperis. Scaliger enim legit Σαββατῶν, Camerario legendum videtur σαββάτων pro σάββατον: Grotius εἰς τὸ μεταξὺ σαββάτων: etsi nec illi, nec isti, nec hic aliquo nitatur codice. Alii alia invenient, si integrum sit, sine autoritate codicum aliquid excogitare.

## 13:43
Ver. 43. Of the devout proselytes) Not of the common people, but of those who had submitted themselves to the law of Moses, גרי צדק.

Οἵτινες) Paul and Barnabas.

Προσλαλοῦντες αὐτοῖς) To those Jews and proselytes.

Ἐπιμένειν τῇ χάριτι τοῦ Θεοῦ) Thus, by metonymy, the Evangelical doctrine is called, which came to us by the supreme benefit of God; so Heb. XII, 15; 1 Pet. V, 12.

Latin:

Vers. 43. Τῶν σεβομένων προσηλύτων) Non τῶν ἰδιωτῶν sed eorum, qui legi Mosis se subdiderant גרי צדק.

Οἵτινες) Paulus & Barnabas.

Προσλαλοῦντες αὐτοῖς) Illis Judaeis & proselytis.

Ἐπιμένειν τῇ χάριτι τοῦ Θεοῦ) Ita per Metonymiam vocatur doctrina Evangelica, quae summo Dei beneficio nobis contigit; sic Ebr. XII, 15. 1. Pet. V, 12.

## 13:44
Ver. 44. On the next Sabbath) The Manuscript is better: Τῷ δὲ ἐχομένῳ σαββάτῳ, that is, on the next Sabbath: Thus τῇ ἐχομένῃ below XX, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 44. Τῷ δὲ ἐρχομένῳ σαββάτῳ) Melius Manuscriptus: Τῷ δὲ ἐχομένῳ σαββάτῳ, id est σαββάτῳ proximo: Sic τῇ ἐχομένῃ infra XX, 15.

## 13:45
Ver. 45. But when the Jews saw the crowds) Those from the Gentiles, to whom they could not bear to be made equal. This is what he calls envy.

Ἀντέλεγον τοῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ Παύλου λεγομένοις ἀντιλέγοντες καὶ βλασφημοῦντες) Those words 'contradicting and' are missing, just as they are in many other books, so also in that excellent manuscript. The Syrian, Latin, and Arab [translators] used codices that likewise have them.

Grotius did not indicate which those books are and of what faith they are, except for one MS Codex. The Latin Vulgate lies in error in countless other places. Therefore, the Greek text is not to be emended from it. Nor is that safely done from the Syriac translation. But it agrees here with the received Arabic codices. This word added in the source is in the Hebrew manner, not without emphasis.

Latin:

Vers. 45. Ἰδόντες δὲ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι τοὺς ὄχλους) Illos ex gentibus, quibus ferre non poterant se aequari. Hoc est quod ζῆλον vocat.

Ἀντέλεγον τοῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ Παύλου λεγομένοις ἀντιλέγοντες καὶ βλασφημοῦντες) Illa ἀντιλέγοντες καὶ, sicut in multis aliis libris desunt, ita & in illo optimo manuscripto. Pariter habentibus codicibus usi sunt Syrus, Latinus, Arabs.

Quinam libri illi & cujus fidei sint non indicavit Grotius praeter unum Cod. MS. Latina Vulgata aliis innumeris locis in mendo cubat. Ex ea ergo non est emendandus Graecus textus. Nec id tuto fit e Syriaco translatione. Arabico vero hic receptis codicibus consonat. Additum hoc verbum in fonte est more Ebraeo non sine emphasi.

## 13:46
Vers. 46. παῤῥησιασάμενοι) Not at all terrified by their insults.

ὑμῖν ἦν ἀναγκαῖον πρῶτον λαληθῆναι τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ) ἀναγκαῖον ἦν, that is, it was necessary according to the precept and example of Christ, Matt. X, v. 24. XV, 6. Luke XXIV, v. 47. above I, v. 8.

ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἀπωθεῖσθε αὐτὸν) כרם תמאסוהו you disdain. מאס is translated in very many places of the Old Testament as ἀπωθεῖν, sometimes ἐξουθενεῖν, φαuλίζειν, and other words. See above VII, 39. 1 Tim. I, 19.

καὶ οὐκ ἀξίους κρίνετε ἑαυτοὺς αἰωνίου ζωῆς) It is the same manner of speaking, l. Judices Cod. de dignitatibus book XII. nor let them flatter themselves henceforth about that honor, of which they have judged themselves unworthy. That is, they showed it no less clearly than a judge who pronounces a sentence. It is customary for names of other actions to be attributed to actions whose effects are equal. See what was said in book II of De Jure Belli ac Pacis XX, 2. Matt. XXVI, 12. See also Ps. CVI, 24. Prov. c. VIII, 36. XVII, 19.

Latin:

Vers. 46. παῤῥησιασάμενοι) Nihil territi ipsorum contumeliis.

ὑμῖν ἦν ἀναγκαῖον πρῶτον λαληθῆναι τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ) ἀναγκαῖον ἦν, id est, oportebat ex Christi praecepto & exemplo, Matth. X, v. 24. XV, 6. Luc. XXIV, v. 47. supra I, v. 8.

ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἀπωθεῖσθε αὐτὸν) כרם תמאסוהו fastiditis. מאס plurimis in locis veteris testamenti vertitur ἀπωθεῖν, interdum ἐξουθενεῖν, φαuλίζειν, aliisque verbis, Vide supra VII, 39. 1. Tim. I, 19.

καὶ οὐκ ἀξίους κρίνετε ἑαυτοὺς αἰωνίου ζωῆς) Est idem loquendi genus, l. Judices Cod. de dignitatibus libro XII. nec sibi posthac de eo honore blandiantur, quo seipsos indignos judicaverunt. Id est, ostenderunt non minus clare, quam judex, qui sententiam pronunciat. Solent actionibus nomina tribui aliarum actionum, quarum pares sunt effectus. Vide quae dicta libro II. de Jure Belli ac Pacis XX, 2. Matth. XXVI, 12. Vide & Ps. CVI, 24. Prov. c. VIII, 36. XVII, 19.

## 13:47
Vers. 47. 'For so the Lord has commanded us.' Christ in the said place, above I. 8. Matt. XXVIII. v. 19. Mark XVI. v. 15. Luke XXIV. 43.

'I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you should be for salvation to the ends of the earth.' In the LXX version, Is. XLIX. 6: 'I have given you as a covenant to the people, as a light to the Gentiles, that you should be for salvation to the ends of the earth.' This, said of Isaiah, fits Christ much more, who is said to have done what He did through the Apostles. Moreover, this citation is placed absolutely, so that before it one must understand, 'as it is written,' which the Syriac and Arabic correctly supply.

We see [this] concerning the passage of Isaiah in the annotations on the same. Isaiah did not speak about himself, nor do those things predicted fit him; he prophesied solely about Christ. Which, because it was proven there, there is no need to prove here.

Latin:

Vers. 47. ὕτω γὰρ ἐντέταλται ἡμῖν ὁ Κύριος.) Christus dicto loco, supra I. 8. Matth. XXVIII. v. 19. Marc. XVI. v. 15. Luc. XXIV. 43.

τέθεικά σε εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν, τῆ εἶναί σε εἰς σωτηρίαν ἕως ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς.) In versione LXX, Es. XLIX. 6. δέδωκά σε εἰς διαθή- κην γένος, εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν τῆ εἶναί σε εἰς σωτηρίαν ἕως ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς. Hoc de Esaia dictum, multo magis Christo conve- nit, qui fecisse dicitur, quod fecit per Apostolos. Est au- tem allegatio hæc absolute posita, ita ut ante eam subau- diatur, sicut scriptum est, quod recte supplent Syrus & Arabs.

De loco Esaiæ in annot. ad Eundem videmus. Non de se loquutus est Esaias, nec ei prædi- cata illa conveniunt, unice vaticinatus est de Christo. Quod, quia illic probatum, hic pro- bare opus non est.

## 13:48
Vers. 48. 'And the Gentiles hearing' [the] Pisidians: that the same honor was held for them by God as for the Jews, who called themselves alone the people of God.

And they glorified the word of the Lord: They praised the goodness of God appearing in the Gospel.

More correctly 'at the foot': They glorified the Word of the Lord. Which shine with their own light, and do not need interpretation.

And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. It is not here προωρισμένοι, which would be 'predestined,' nor even προτεταγμένοι: but rather τεταγμένοι. And clearly these 'ordained' to eternal life are opposed to those who had judged themselves unworthy of that life, that is, had shown [themselves to be]. Τάττειν is worth שום, which is also often translated by τιθέναι, and among other things signifies to prepare. Then indeed it is frequent for the Hebrews that the passive form is put for the reciprocal, Niphal for Hitpahel. The grammarians of the Hebrews note that, Lev. XXV. 29, 2 Sam. XX. 10, and the Hellenists follow it. Thus 2 Macc. XIV. 3, μεμολυσμένος is he who had defiled himself; thus Rom. X. 3, Οὐκ ὑπετάγησαν, they did not subject themselves, and Heb. XII. 9, ὑποταγησόμεθα, we shall subject ourselves, Jas. IV. 7, and 1 Pet. V. 5, ὑποτάγητε, subject yourselves, and 10, ταπεινώθητε, humble yourselves, which word you have in a similar sense, 1 Pet. V. 6. They prepare themselves for eternal life, who, if the hope of it is given, are willing for that reason to do and suffer the most grievous things. Such are εὔθετοι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, as Luke speaks IX. 62, and they easily believe the Gospel, John VII. 17. When we say these things, we do not exclude preventing grace: for men are said to do that which they do when excited by the grace of God, just as they are said to convert themselves. For there is a certain grace even before faith, which is called the drawing of the Father. They see nothing who refer these words to predestination, and indeed absolute [predestination], as they say. For neither do all the predestined of one place believe at the same time, nor are all who believe predestined in that sense. Nor was that mystery concerning individuals, who were to arrive at salvation and who were not, revealed to Luke.

Grotius correctly notes against the Calvinists that it is not here προωρισμένοι, which would be 'predestined.' But neither προτεταγμένοι, nor τεταγμένοι; And that clearly τὸ τεταγμένοι is opposed to those who had judged themselves unworthy of life, that is, had shown [it]. Nothing, therefore, does this passage do for an absolute decree of predestination. Nothing, he says, do they see, who refer these words to predestination, and indeed absolute, as they say. For neither do all the predestined of one place believe at the same time, nor are all who believe predestined in that sense. Nor was that mystery concerning individuals, who were to arrive at salvation and who were not, revealed to Luke. It cannot be proven, however, that he explains τάττειν as 'to prepare,' and says the passive form is put for the reciprocal in the Hebrew manner. For although ὑποταγησαν, Rom. X. 3, and ὑποταγησόμεθα, Heb. XII. 9, as also ὑποτάγητε, Luke IV. 7, 1 Pet. V. 5, is taken reciprocally, so that they denote 'to subject oneself,' it does not follow that the reciprocal sense is obtained here. For no one can prepare or dispose himself for faith. They could be said to subject themselves, but in this sense, that they did not resist or do the same things as those who resist, and

do not subject themselves, Rom. X. 3. Which is, alas, too much in our power! But not that anyone is able to dispose or prepare himself for faith, 1 Cor. ch. II. v. 14, Heb. ch. III. v. 5. But they prepare, says Grotius, themselves for eternal life, who, if the hope of it is given, are willing for that reason to do and suffer the most grievous things. Such are εὔθετοι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, as Luke speaks ch. IX. v. 62, and they easily believe the Gospel, John VII. 17. Resp. The mere promise of eternal life does not cause us to be willing to do and suffer the most grievous things: nor is preventing grace sufficient for that, as this Grotius thinks: 'when we say these things, we do not exclude preventing grace: for men are said to do that which they do when excited by the grace of God, just as they are said to convert themselves. For there is a certain grace even before faith, which is called the drawing of the Father.' For in order that we may believe, and do the will of God, and suffer for the faith, there is need of divine grace not only preventing and exciting, but operating and cooperating, as grace is wont to be distinguished from Phil. II. 13, ch. I. 29. It is not of our own powers, even if we are excited by the preventing grace of God; which, however, Grotius, with the Arminians, places only in the promise of eternal life, so that we may be rendered εὔθετοι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, if these things are taken concerning eternal life, or so that we may believe the Gospel. Although in Luke IX. 62, through βασιλείαν τοῦ

By Θεοῦ [of God] let not eternal life be understood, but the spiritual kingdom of God, to which those are inept, not εὔθετοι [fit], to serve in the sacred ministry, who have put their hand to the plow, as it is said, and look back. But that we may be rendered more and more certain concerning divine doctrine, if we strive to do the will of God, John.

VII. v. 12. does nothing for our preparation for faith, as if we could dispose ourselves to the same. But concerning these things in the Socinianism overthrown and in the consideration of Arminianism.

The word Τεταγμένοι [ordained/disposed] respects the divine order, because GOD does not act by absolute grace in the business of salvation: but He has prescribed a certain Τάξιν [order] of means, which those who do not exclude, but admit—namely by hearing the word, by not stopping their ears and hearts to it, by not resisting the Holy Spirit willing to work through it—they are τεταγμένοι [ordained]. Nor indeed are we taught that they are τεταγμένοι by themselves, but rather this belongs to God or to divine grace and the power of the divine word, by which alone we are rendered τεταγμένοι and εὔθετοι [fit], while we leave place for it and do not repudiate or exclude the τάξιν [order] of divine means, but observe it. That this pertains to pedagogical acts, as they call them, and is thus in our own powers, is not denied. And thus τεταγμένοι are distinguished from ἀτάκτοις [the disorderly]. For these are they who do not keep the order prescribed by God, reject or neglect the τάξιν [order], or disturb it, to the Holy Spirit they resist, they spurn the counsels of God against themselves, they render themselves unworthy of the kingdom of God, 1 Thess. c. V. 24. 2 Thess. III. 6. 7. Matt. XXIII. 37. Luke VII. v. 30. Acts VII. 51. Those truly, who keep the order prescribed by God, are further ordained by divine grace, so that they may obtain the good which is offered in the word. For to him who has, it shall be given, Mark IV. 25. Cornelius à Lapide explains the word τεταγμένος as ordained, and disposed like soldiers in a battle line and in their order, so that they might be placed at that time in the order and way to eternal life. For thus τάξεις [orders] are called military orders. And Emperor Leo wrote τακτικὰ [tactics], that is, precepts and the method of instructing a battle line for battle; so that the sense may be: They believed, as many as were already ordained and disposed to eternal life, as many, that is, as had a true desire for eternal life implanted in them by God, as many as were zealous for their own salvation, as many as were searching for the manner and the way by which they might save themselves and attain to eternal life. Which can be admitted in a sound sense.

Latin:

Vers. 48. ἀκούοντα δὲ τὰ ἔθνη) Pisidæ: parem sibi à Deo honorem haberi cum Judæis, qui se solos populum Dei vo- cabant.

καὶ ἐδόξαζον τὸν λόγον τοῦ Κυρίου) Laudarunt Dei bonita- tem in Evangelio apparentem.

Rectius κατὰ πόδα: Glorificarunt Verbum Do- mini. Qui sua luce radiant, nec interpretatione indigent.

καὶ ἐπίστευσαν ὅσοι ἦσαν τεταγμένοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον) Non est hic προωρισμένοι, quod esset prædestinati, sed nec προτε- ταγμένοι: Verum τεταγμένοι. Et manifeste hi τεταγμένοι ad vitam æternam opponuntur, eis, qui se ea vita indignos judicaverant, id est, ostenderant. Τάττειν valet שום, quod & per τιθέναι sæpe vertitur, & inter alia significat pa- rare. Tum vero frequens est Hebræis, ut ponatur forma passiva pro reciproca, Niphal pro Hitpahel. Notant id Hebræorum Grammatici, Lev. XXV. 29. 2. Sam. XX. 10. & sequuntur Hellenistæ. Sic 2. Macc. XIV. 3. μεμολυσμένος est qui se polluerat; sic Rom X. 3. Οὐκ ὑπετάγησαν se non sub- jecerunt, & Hebr. XII. 9. ὑποταγησόμεθα subjiciemus nos- met, Jac. IV. 7. & 1. Petr. V. 5. ὑποτάγητε subjicite vosmet & 10. ταπεινώθητε humiliate vosmet, quod verbum pari sen- su habes. 1. Pet. V. 6. Farant se vitæ æternæ, qui si ejus spes detur gravissima ob id velint facere ac pati. Tales sunt εὔθετοι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ut Lucas loquitur IX. 62., & facile credunt Evangelio, Joh. VII. 17. Cum hæc dicimus, non excludimus prævenientem gratiam: Facere enim ho- mines dicuntur id, quod faciunt per Dei gratiamexcitati, si- cut se dicuntur convertere. Est enim quædam gratia etiam ante fidem, quæ patris tractio vocatur. Nihil vident qui ad prædestinationem, & quidem absolutam, ut loquuntur, hæc verba referunt. Nam neque prædestinati omnes unius loci credunt eodem tempore, neque omnes qui credunt, sunt eo sensu prædestinati. Neque id arcanum de singulis, qui ad salutem perventuri essent, qui non, Lucæ erat re- velatum.

Recte notat Grotius contra Calvinianos, non esse hic προωρισμένοι, quod essent prædestinati. Sed nec προτεταγμένοι, neque τεταγμένοι; Quodque manifeste τὸ τεταγμένοι opponitur eis, qui sese vita indignos judicaverant, id est, ostende- rant. Nihil ergo hunc locum pro absoluto prædestinationis decreto facere. Nihil, in- quit, vident, qui ad prædestinationem & quidem absolutam, ut loquuntur, hæc verba referunt. Nam neque prædestinati omnes unius loci credunt eodem tempore, neque omnes, qui credunt, sunt eo sensu prædestinati. Neque id arcanum de singu- lis, qui ad salutem perventuri essent, qui non, Lucæ erat revelatum. Non probari tamen potest, quod τάττειν pro parare explicat, & formam passi- vam pro reciproca more Ebræo poni, ait. Licet enim ὑποταγησαν, Rom. X. 3. & ὑποταγησόμε- θα, Ebr. XII. 9. ut & ὑποτάγητε, Luc. IV. 7. 1. Pet. V. 5. reciproce accipiatur, ut se subjicere notent, hic tamen sensum reciprocum obtinere, non sequi- tur. Non enim quis ad fidem semetipsum pa- rare aut disponere potest. Subjicere sese dici possent, sed hoc sensu, quod non reluctati sint aut paria fecerint cum illis, qui resistunt, &

non subjiciunt seie, Rom. X. 3. Quod in pote- state sane nostra eheu! nimium est. Sed non quod quisquam sese valeat ipsum disponere, aut præparare ad fidem, 1. Cor. cap. II. v. 14. Ebr. cap. III. v. 5. At parant, inquit Grotius, se vi- tæ æternæ, qui si ejus spes detur gravissima ob id velint facere ac pati. Tales sunt εὔθετοι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ut Lucas loquitur c. IX. v. 62. & facile credunt Evangelio, Joh. VII. 17. Resp. Sola promissio æternæ vitæ non efficit, ut veli- mus gravissima quæque facere ac pati: nec ad id præveniens gratia sufficit, uti putat hic Grotius: cum hæc dicimus, non excludimus prævenientem Gratiam: facere enim homines dicuntur id, quod faciunt per gratiam Dei excitati, sicut se dicuntur convertere. Est enim quædam gratia etiam ante fidem, quæ patris tractio vocatur. Nam ad id ut credamus, & voluntatem Dei faciamus ac pro fide patiamur, opus est divina gratia non præve- niente tantum & excitante, sed operante, & coope- rante, uti solet distingui gratia è Phil. II. 13. c. I. 29. Non nostrarum virium est, etiamsi excitemur, per gratiam Dei prævenientem; quam vero Grotius cùm Arminianis solum ponit in vitæ æternæ promissione, ut reddamur εὔθετοι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, si hæc de vitâ æterna accipiantur, vel ut credamus Evangelio. Quanquam Luc. IX. 62. per βασιλείαν τοῦ

Θεοῦ non æterna vita, sed regnum Dei spirituale in- telligatur, ad quod inepti sunt, non εὔθετοι, ut mi- nisterio sacro inserviant, qui manum aratro, quod dicitur, admoverunt, & retro respiciunt. Quod au- tem magis magisque de doctrina divina certi red- damur, si satagamus voluntatem Dei facere, Joh.

VII. v. 12. non facit quidquam pro præparatione nostri ad fidem, quasi nos ipsos ad eandem dispo- nere possimus. Sed de his in Socinianismo prosli- gato & in consideratione Arminianismi.

Vox Τεταγμένοι respicit ordinem divinum, quia non absoluta DEUS agit gratia in ne- gotio salutis: sed certam Τάξιν mediorum præ- scripsit, quam qui non excludunt, sed ad- mittunt, verbum nempe audiendo, ad illud aures & corda non obturando, Spiritui Sancto per illud operari volenti non resistendo, illi τε- ταγμένοι sunt. Nec vero docemur, quod à se- ipsis sint τεταγμένοι, quin potius Deo vel divinæ gratiæ & verbi divini virtuti hoc convenit, quæ sola nos reddimur τεταγμένοι & εὔθετοι, dum ei locum relinquimus & τάξιν mediorum divino- rum non repudiamus aut excludimus, sed observa- mus. Quod ad actus pædagogicos, quos vocant, per- tinere, & in nostris adeo viribus esse, non nega- tur. Et distinguuntur ita τεταγμένοι ab ἀτάκτοις. Hi enim sunt, qui ordinem à Deo præscriptum non servant, τάξιν reprobant aut negligunt, vel turbant, Spiritui S. resistunt, consilia Dei adversus se spernunt, semetipsos regno Dei indignos red- dunt, 1. Thess. c. V. 24. 2. Thess. III. 6. 7. Matth. XXIII. 37. Luc. VII. v. 30. Act. VII. 51. Illi vero, qui ordinem à Deo præscriptum servant, gratia divina porro ordinantur, ut bonum, quod in verbo offertur, consequantur. Habenti enim dabitur, Marc. IV. 25. Cornel. à Lapide explicat vocem τεταγμένος ordi- nati, ac dispositi veluti milites in acie & ordine suo, ut videlicet eo tempore ponerentur in ordine ac via ad vitam æternam. Sic enim τάξεις vocantur ordines militares. Et Leo Imper. scripsit τακτικὰ, id est, præcepta & modum instruendi aciem ad prælium; ut sensus sit: Crediderunt, quotquot jam ordinati & dispositi erant ad vitam æternam, quotquot scilicet habebant verum vitæ æternæ deside- rium sibi à Deo injectum, quotquot studebant suæ sa- luti, quoquot vestigabant modum & iter, quo se sal- vare & ad vitam æternam pertingere possent. Quæ sano sensu admitti possunt.

## 13:49
Ver. 49. And the word of the Lord was spread abroad) That discourse of which Luke had spoken above in 48.

Latin:

Vers. 49. Διεφέρετο δὲ ὁ λόγος τοῦ Κυρίου) Ille sermo de quo loquutus erat Lucas supra 48.

## 13:50
Ver. 50. The devout women) Proselytes. For there were also proselytes in that city, as we heard above in 43.

And the honorable) Those proselytes were stirring up other honorable women, known to them. We have had the name of honorable in this sense also in Matt. XV. 43, and we shall have it again concerning women below in XVII, 2. The Greeks in this place interpret honorable women with the Roman term matrons: Not badly. Clement concerning the acts of Peter: The most illustrious of the noble, and those whom the word knows to call matrons. Cedrenus: They called chaste women matrons.

and the chief men of the city) Those matrons were inciting their husbands. You have the chief men of the city also in Justinian's Novella CXXIII. Thus the first of the decurions are called in Latin Principales, as in Tertullian and the Theodosian Code. These were in some places five, in others ten, in others twenty.

and raised a persecution) See Matt. V. 10, 11, 12. XIII. 21. above VIII. 1.

and cast them out of their borders) They ordered them to leave by authority. Thus that word is used, Matt. IX. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 50. Τὰς σεβομένας γυναῖκας) Proselytas. Nam erant & proselyti in ea urbe, ut audivimus supra 43.

Καὶ τὰς εὐσχήμονας) Illæ proselytas alias fœminas hono- ratas, notas sibi, concitabant. Nomen εὐσχήμονος hoc sensu habuimus & Matth. XV. 43. & habebimus rursum de fœ- minis infra XVII, 2. Græci hoc loco εὐσχήμονας γυναῖκας Romano vocabulo matronas interpretantur: Non male. Clemens de rebus Petri: Τῶν εὐγενῶν τὰς ἐπιφανεστάτας, κἀι ἃς ὁ λόγος, ματρώνας οἶδε καλεῖν. Cedrenus: Τὰς σώφρονας γυναῖκας ματρώνας ἐκάλουν.

καὶ τοὺς πρώτους τῆς πόλεως) Illæ matronæ maritos suos incitabant. Τοὺς πρώτους τῆς πόλεως habes & in Novella Iusti- niani CXXIII. Ita vocantur decurionum primi Latine Principales, ut apud Tertullianum & Cod. Theodosiano. Hi erant alibi quinque, alibi decem alibi viginti.

καὶ ἐπήγειραν διωγμὸν) Vid. Matth. V. 10, 11, 12. XIII. 21. supra VIII. 1.

καὶ ἐξέβαλον αὐτοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρίων αὐτῶν) Exire jusserunt pro imperio. Sic verbum id sumitur, Matth. IX. 25.

## 13:51
Ver. 51. But they shook off the dust of their feet) They observed not only the matter, but also the symbol of the matter according to the Lord's words in Matt. X. 14, where see what is said.

Against them) Against them; as a testimony against them, as it is in Luke IX. 5.

to Iconium) A city of Lycaonia. Strabo XII. It is a famous city by Mount Taurus, in Lycaonia. See Pliny book V. ch. 27. There is another of the same name in Cilicia distinct from this.

Latin:

Vers. 51. Οἱ δὲ ἐκτιναξάμενοι τὸν κονιορτὸν τῶν ποδῶν αὐτῶν) Non rem tantum, sed & rei symbolum observarunt juxta Domini verba Matth. X. 14. ubi dicta vide.

Ἐπ᾽ αὐτοὺς) Adversus ipsos; in testimonium contra ipsos, ut est Luc. IX. 5.

εἰς Ἰκόνιον) Urbem Lycaoniæ. Strabo XII. Urbs est celebris ad montem Taurum, in Lycao- nia. Vid. Plinius l. V. c. 27. Ab hac alia est e- jusdem nominis in Cilicia.

## 13:52
Ver. 52. And the disciples) Who had believed the Gospel in Perga.

Were filled with joy) On account of the received remission of sins, and the heavenly promises.

and of the Holy Spirit) By gifts for the sealing of the faith.

Latin:

Vers. 52. Οἱ δὲ μαθηταὶ) Qui Pergis Evangelio credi- derant.

Ἐπληροῦντο χαρᾶς) Ob acceptam peccatorum remissio- nem, & promissa cœlestia.

καὶ Πνεύματος ἁγίου) Donis ad obsignandam fidem.

## 14:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIV.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

At Iconium, upon the preaching of the Apostles, many Jews and Greeks were converted; the unbelieving Jews, stirring up the Gentiles against the brethren, caused a dissension in the city, some adhering to the Jews, others to the Apostles: whence Barnabas and Paul, understanding that they were to be stoned, fled into Lycaonia; preaching the Gospel at Lystra, where, after a man lame from his mother's womb was healed by Paul, they were held by the Lycaonians to be gods, Jupiter and Mercury, who, wishing to sacrifice to them, were restrained, and were admonished concerning the announcement and conversion from those false gods to the living God, and creator of heaven, who had not left himself without witness to them. The Jews of Antioch and Iconium stirring up the people, by whom Paul was stoned almost to death, he departed thence with Barnabas to Derbe, preaching the Gospel likewise there, and confirming the neighbors, and having appointed elders here and there, coming through Pisidia into Pamphylia, and proposing the word of God in Perga, thence going to Attalia, and from there sailing to Antioch, from which they had been sent out, he announces what a door the Lord had opened for him among the Gentiles.

There are three parts: I. The success of Barnabas and Paul at Iconium, to verse 5. II. The miraculous healing of the lame man,

and the refusal of divine worship among the Lystrians, to verse 18. III. Paul being stoned at Lystra, the churches being confirmed and ordered here and there in the Derbian vicinity, the return to the Antiochians, and the report made there concerning the progress of the Gospel among the Gentiles, to the final verse 28.

PART I. The success of Barnabas and Paul at Iconium.

Vers. 1. And it came to pass in Iconium) Here Timothy was present with Paul, 2 Tim. III. 10, also known to Paul before, and often a companion of his journeys, while he was still a boy or a youth. The Latin interpreter said 'in Iconio' here, following the Greek. Thus in Berenice, in Hispalis according to Pliny: but where the name of a city or town follows.

Both Jews and Greeks are said to have believed there. By whom Chrysostom understands Gentiles; but because they appeared in the Synagogue with the Jews, they were without doubt proselytes. The Papists assert that Thecla and Tryphena and Tryphosa, who are mentioned in Rom. XVI. 12, were converted there, but from the apocryphal acts of St. Thecla. See Cornel. à Lapid. in this place.

at the same time) Together as above II. 1, namely Paul and Barnabas, and their companions, among whom was Timothy, entered the Synagogue equally.

Latin:

CAPUT XIV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Iconii ad præconium Apostolorum multis Iu- dæis & Græcis conversis, Iudæis incre- dulis, gentes adversus fratres concitanti- bus, dissidium in civitate exoritur, aliis Iudæis, Apostolis aliis adhærentibus: Unde lapidandos sese intelligentes Barnabas & Paulus in Lycaoniam fugerunt; Lystris ev- angelizantes, ubi sanato à Paulo viro ex utero matris claudo, à Lycaoniis pro diis, Iove, & Mercurio, habebantur, qui ipsis sacrificare volentes retundebantur, & de annunciatione, ac conversione à falsis istis diis ad Deum vivum, atque cæli creato- rem, qui se non ἀμάρτυρον ipsis reliquerat, monebantur. Iudæis Antiochenis & Ico- niis populum excitantibus, à quo ferme ad mortem lapidatus Paulus inde cum Bar- naba in Derben profectus Evangelium itidem ibi prædicans, & vicinos confir- mans, ac senioribus hinc inde constitu- tis per Pisidiam in Pamphiliam veniens, & in Pergen verbum Dei proponens, de- hinc Attaliam adiens, & inde Antiochi- am navigans, ex qua emissi fuerant, quam sibi Dominus inter gentes januam aperu- erit, annunciat.

Partes tres sunt: I. Successus Barnabæ & Pau- li Iconiensis, ad v. 5. II. Miraculosa sanatio claudi,

& cultus divini declinatio apud Lystrenses, ad v. 18. III. Pauli Lystris lapidati, confirmatis & ordinatis passim in vicinia Derbensi Ecclesiis, ad Antiochenos reditus, ibidem facta de progressu Evangelii inter gentes relatio, ad vers. final. 28.

PARS I. Successus Barnabae & Pauli Iconiensis.

Vers. 1. Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν τῷ Ἰκονίῳ) Hic Paulo adfuit Timo- theus 2. Tim. III. 10. etiam ante Paulo notus, & saepe itine- rum ejus comes, adhuc puer aut adolescens cum esset. La- tinus interpres in Iconio hic dixit, Graecum secutus. Sic in Berenice, in Hispali apud Plinium : sed ubi vox urbis aut oppidi sequitur.

Credidisse ibi dicuntur & Judaei & Graeci. Per quos gentiles Chrysostomus intelligit; sed quia in Synagoga cum Judaeis comparuere, proselyti sine dubio fuerunt. Theclam & Tryphenam & Trypho- sam, quarum mentio fit Rom. XVI. 12. ibi conver- sas esse Pontificii asserunt, sed ex actis S. Theclae a- pocryphis. Vid. Cornel. à Lapid. in h. l.

κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ) Simul ut supra II. 1. nempe Paulus & Bar- nabas, & eorum comites, in quibus Timotheus, pariter in- gressi sunt Synagogam.

## 14:2
Vers. 2. They embittered the souls of the Gentiles) He said 'kakoun' which others call 'kakunein'. Dioscorides also speaks thus sometimes.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ἐκάκωσαν τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν ἐθνῶν) Κακοῦν dixit quod alii κακύνειν. Loquitur sic & Dioscorides aliquo- ties.

## 14:3
Vers. 3. To the one bearing witness to the word) God giving authority to the sermon. Thus also below XV. 8. John V. 37.

Of the grace) Thus also below XX. 24. 32. gospel of grace. And more briefly through the grace, that is, through the Gospel below XVIII. v. 27. because that message proceeded from the supreme goodness of God.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Τῷ μαρτυροῦντι τῷ λόγῳ) Autoritatem Deo dan- te sermoni. Sic & infra XV. 8. Ioh. V. 37.

Τῆς χάριτος) Sic & infra XX. 24. 32. ἐυαγγέλιον χάριτος. Et brevius διὰ τῆς χάριτος, id est per Evangelium inf. XVIII. v. 27. quod ex summa Dei bonitate nuntius is proces- sit.

## 14:4
Vers. 4. And the multitude of the city was divided) Similar to John VII. v. 43.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἐσχίσθη δὲ τὸ πλῆθος τῆς πόλεως) Simile Ioh. VII. v. 43.

## 14:5
Vers. 5. Assault) It corresponds to the Hebrew שואה which signifies a tumult.

With their rulers) Above XIII. 50.

to insult and stone them) That similar passage in Matt. XXII. they insulted and killed. See also 1 Thess. II, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ὁρμὴ) Respondet Hebraeo שואה quod tumul- tum significat.

Σὺν τοῖς ἄρχουσιν ἀυτῶν) Supra XIII. 50.

ὑβρίσαι κᾲ λιθοβολῆσαι ἀυτούς) Simile illud Matth. XXII. ὕβρισαν καὶ ἀπέκτειναν. Vide & 1. Thess. II, 2.

## 14:6
Vers. 6. they fled into the cities) Not so much for the sake of their own life, as lest time should be wasted more uselessly, which could be spent more fruitfully elsewhere. See Matt. X, 23.

Nay rather, especially for the sake of their own life. Because to take flight on account of personal persecutions is not illicit. What? It is even commanded, as is clear even from the cited passage Matt. X, 23.

Lystra and Derbe) Ptolemy mentions Derbe. Stephanus has Lystra among the cities. Here he declines it sometimes as Lystra, Lystrae, sometimes as Lystra, Lystrorum.

Latin:

Vers. 6. κατέφυγον εἰς τὰς πόλεις) Non tam suae vitae cau- sa, quam ne tempus inutilior periret, quod alibi fructuosius impendi poterat. Vid. Matth. X, 23.

Quin imo praecipue vitae suae causa. Quia ob persecutiones personales fugam capessere non est il- licitum. Quid? etiam demandatur, ut vel è lo- co laudato Matth. X, 23. liquet.

Λύστραν καὶ Δέρβην) Derbes meminit Ptolemaeus. Λύ- στρα habet Stephanus in urbibus. Hic modo Λύστρα Λύστρας, modo Λύστρα Λύστρων declinat.

## 14:8
Vers. 8. Impotent in his feet) He did not err who translated it weak, Maecenas: Make him weak in hand, weak in foot, in hip. See the controversy of Seneca, which is inscribed the one weakening those exposed.

That it ought rather to be rendered impotent or invalid, who namely could not stand or walk on his feet, Corn. à Lapide, although he otherwise acknowledges himself a defender of the Vulgate.

PART II. The healing of the lame man by a miracle, and the refusal of divine worship offered to Paul on that account among the Lystrians.

Χωλὸς ἐκ κοιλίας μητρὸς ἀυτοῦ) A similar manner of speaking, Matt. XIX. 12. & above III. 7. those vices are incurable by human aid, which having been born with someone, have grown up with him.

ὃς ὀυδέποτε περιπεπατήκει) The manuscript has περιεπάτησε.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἀδύνατος τοῖς ποσὶν) Nihil peccavit, qui vertit debilis, Maecenas : Debilem facito manu, Debilem pede, coxâ. Vide controversiam Senecae, quae inscribitur debilitans ex- positos.

Impotentem potius reddi debere aut invalidum, qui scilicet pedibus non potuerit consistere aut ambulare, Corn. à Lapide etsi alias Vulgatae hype- raspistes agnoscit.

PARS II. Miraculo claudi sanatio, & cultus divini ideo Pauli delati declinatio apud Lystrenses.

Χωλὸς ἐκ κοιλίας μητρὸς ἀυτοῦ) Simile loquendi genus, Matth. XIX. 12. & supra III. 7. incurabilia sunt humana ope vitia, quae cum aliquo nata, cum eo adoleverunt.

ὃς ὀυδέποτε περιπεπατήκει) Manuscriptus περιεπά- τησε.

## 14:9
Vers. 9. Ὅτι πίστιν ἔχει τοῦ σωθῆναι) Namely, from his infirmity. See Matt. IX. 28. & what is said there.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ὅτι πίστιν ἔχει τοῦ σωθῆναι) Nempe à malo suo. Vid. Matth. IX. 28. & ibi dicta.

## 14:10
Vers. 10. Ἀνάστηθι ἐπὶ τοὺς πόδας σου ὀρθὸς) A similar locution above III. 6.

καὶ ἥλλετο) See above III. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἀνάστηθι ἐπὶ τοὺς πόδας σου ὀρθὸς) Similis loquu- tio supra III. 6.

καὶ ἥλλετο) Vide supra III. 8.

## 14:11
Vers. 11. Λυκαονιστὶ) The language of the Cappadocians.

λέγοντες. οἱ Θεοὶ ὁμοιωθέντες ἀνθρώποις κατέβησαν πρὸς ἡμᾶς) The nations sometimes believed that this happened. Homer:

Καίτε θεοὶ ξείνοισιν ἐοικότες ἀλλοδαποῖσι Παντοῖοι τελέθοντες ἐπιστρωφῶσι πόληας.

Catullus: For the heaven-dwellers were accustomed to visit chaste homes in person more often, and to show themselves to the mortal assembly, before piety was spurned,

Jupiter in Ovid, in the first book of the Metamorphoses: And I, a god, survey the lands under a human image.

Grotius cites Homer, Catullus, and Ovid. But without doubt the Devil wished to mock the mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God through such fictions about gods who were made men.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Λυκαονιστὶ) Lingua Cappadocum.

λέγοντες. οἱ Θεοὶ ὁμοιωθέντες ἀνθρώποις κατέβησαν πρὸς ἡ- μᾶς) Id interdum factum credebant gentes. Home- rus :

Καίτε θεοὶ ξείνοισιν ἐοικότες ἀλλοδαποῖσι Παντοῖοι τελέθοντες ἐπιστρωφῶσι πόληας.

Catullus: Praesentes namque ante domus invisere castas Saepius, & sese mortali ostendere coetu Coelicolae nondum spreta pietate solebant,

Jupiter apud Ovidium primo Metamorphoseon: Et Deus humana lustro sub imagine terras.

Adfert Grotius Homerum, Catullum, Ovidium. Sine dubio autem Diabolus ludificari voluit per ejusmodi commenta de Diis, qui homines fa- cti sunt, mysterium incarnationis Filii Dei.

## 14:12
Verse 12. And Paul Hermes) For Jupiter was accustomed to take Mercury with him, as you see in Plautus's Amphitruo: Aristides on Demosthenes: whom I would call Hermes the eloquent, having come down among men as a model of eloquence. Themistius, Oration I: as if Hermes, leaving Zeus and heaven, having put on a small body, wanders about in our city. Since he himself was the leader of the word) That is, he spoke a great deal. It seems there may be an allusion to the surname of Mercury, hegemon. Philo on Mercury: the interpreter and prophet of divine things, from whom also he is named Hermes. Justin in his Second Apology: Hermes, the word, the interpreter and teacher of all.

They bring forward reasons for this comparison and naming, that Mercury was considered the son of Jupiter and the god of eloquence, and Barnabas was older in age and stood by Paul with his gravity. See here Corn. à Lapide.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Τὸν δὲ Παῦλον Ἑρμῆν) Solebat enim Iupiter Mercurium secum ducere, ut vides in Amphitruone Plauti: Aristides de Demosthene: ὃν ἐγὼ φαίην ἂν Ἑρμῆ λογίῳ λογίῳ τύπον εἰς ἀνθρώπους κατελθεῖν. Themistius Orat. I. ὡς ἄρα ὁ Ἑρμῆς καταλιπὼν τὸν Δία τε κὴ τὸν ὠρανὸν σαρκία μικρὰ περιθέμενος ἐν τῇ πόλει ἡμῶν περινοσῶ. ἐπειδὴ αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ ἡγέμενος τῦ λόγου) Id est, plurimum loquebatur. Allusum videri potest ad cognomen Mercu- rii, ἡγεμών. Philo de Mercurio: τὸν ἑρμηνέα κὴ προφήτην τῶν θείων, ἀφ' ὗ κὴ Ἑρμῆς ὠνόμαται. Justinus Apologeti- co secundo: Ἑρμῆν μὲν λόγον τὸν ἑρμηνευτικὸν κὴ πάντων δι- δάσκαλον.

Rationes adferunt hujus comparationis & de- nominationis, quod Mercurius Jovis filius & Deus eloquentiae habitus sit, Barnabas aetate grandior fu- erit & gravitate sua Paulo adstiterit. Vid. hic Corn. à Lapid.

## 14:13
Verse 13. Of Zeus, who was before their city) According to the custom of the nations, he gave the name of Zeus to the image of Zeus. Before the city, that is, at the gate, beside the door of the city, 2 Kings 7:3, 10. Thus Venus outside the city in Plautus's Rudens.

Bulls) And the greatest bull... victim. Virgil.

and garlands) Crowns, which they would place upon the gods themselves, Epistle of Jeremiah 8: they construct crowns upon the heads of their gods; see the things brought forward by us at that place. That Diana of Ephesus was also crowned, Pausanias and Dionysius of Halicarnassus are witnesses.

They did not crown the image, but the victim. The priest brought bulls and crowns, that is, by hendiadys, crowned bulls. See Corn. à Lapide.

At the gates) Before the doors of the houses in which Paul and Barnabas were staying.

wished to sacrifice) To immolate, to slaughter, to offer, in the way it was accustomed to be done to the gods.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Τῶ Διὸς, τῶ ὄντος πρὸ τῆς πόλεως ἀυτῶν) More gentium Jovis simulacro Jovis nomen decit. Πρὸ τῆς πό- λεως, id est, ad portam, παρὰ τὴν θύραν τῆς πόλεως, 2 Reg. VII. 3. 10. Sic Venus extra urbem a Rudente Plautina.

Ταύρους) Et maxima taurus --- Victima. Virgilius.

κὴ στέμματα) Coronas, quas ipsis diis imponerent, Epi- stola Jeremiae 8. κατασκευάζουσι στεφάνες ἐπὶ τὰς κεφαλὰς τῶν θεῶν ἀυτῶν; ad quem locum allata à nobis vide. Etiam Dianam Ephesiam fuisse coronatam, testes sunt Pausanias & Dionysius Halicarnassensis.

Non simulacrum coronarunt, sed victimam. Tauros & coronas attulit Sacerdos, id est, per hendyaden tauros coronatos. Vid. Corn. a Lapid.

Ἐπὶ τὼς πυλῶνας) Ante fores aedium, in quibus Paulus & Barnabas diversabantur.

ἤθελε θύειν) Immolare, mactare, porricere, quomodo Diis fieri solebat.

## 14:14
Verse 14. Tearing their garments) As in the greatest grief. See the things said at Matthew 26:56.

They rushed into the crowd) They went to meet those who wished to enter with that pomp.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Διαῤῥήξαντες τὰ ἱμάτια ἀυτῶν) Ut in summo dolore. Vide dicta ad Matth. XXVI. 56.

Εἰσεπήδησαν εἰς τὸν ὄχλον) Intrare cum illa pompa vo- lentibus ivere obviam.

## 14:15
Vers. 15. Men, why do you do these things) Empedocles would not have done this, who strove, as Horace says, to be considered an immortal God, and wrote of himself: 'But I am to you an immortal God, no longer a mortal.' And we are men of like passions with you) Thus James 5:17, 'Elijah was a man of like passions with you,' that is, in need of food and drink, subject to diseases and death. Thus the Hebrew Sage said ὁμοιοπαθῆ γῆν in 7:3, and Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus use the same word.

From these vain things) Μάταια אלילים Zechariah 11:17, 1 הבלים Kings 16:13, and often elsewhere: כזבים Amos 2:4, by which names the Hebrews call the gods of the nations, being as they are empty inventions of men, gods without substance.

To the living God) Who does not die, like those Kings consecrated as gods, but always lives and acts.

Who made the heaven, and the earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them) As above in 4:24, by this mark God is best distinguished from false gods, Jeremiah 10:11. We have here an excellent form of speech which those ought to imitate who preach the Gospel among peoples educated in idolatry.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ἄνδρες, τὶ ταῦτα ποιεῖτε) Non hoc fecisset Em- pedocles, qui studuit, ut ait Horatius, Deus immortalis ha- beri, & de se scripsit: Ἐγὼ δ' ὑμῖν Θεὸς ἄμβροτος ἐκέτι θνητός. Καὶ ἡμεῖς ὁμοιοπαθεῖς ἐσμὲν ὑμῖν ἄνθρωποι) Sic Jac. V. 17. Ἠλιας ἄνθρωπος ἦν ὁμοιοπαθὴς ὑμῖν, id est, cibi & potus in- digi, morbis mortique obnoxii. Sic ὁμοιοπαθῆ γῆν dixit Sapiens Hebraeus VII. 3. utunturque eadem voce Plato, Aristoteles, Theophrastus.

Ἀπὸ τέτων τῶν ματαίων) Μάταια אלילים Zachar. XI. 17. 1 הבלים Reg. XVI. 13. & alibi saepe : כזבים Amos II. 4. quibus nominibus Hebraei Deos gentium vo- cant, quippe inania hominum commenta, Deos sine re.

Ἐπὶ τὸν Θεὸν τὸν ζῶντα) Qui non moritur, ut Reges illi in Deos consecrati, sed semper vivit agitque.

Ὃς ἐποίησε τὸν ὠρανὸν, κὴ τὴν γῆν, κὴ τὴν θάλασσαν, κὴ πάντα τὰ ἐν ἀυτοῖς) Ut supra IV. 24. hac nota optime Deus dis stinguitur à Diis falsis Jer. X. 11. egregiam hic habemus formam orationis quam imitari debeant, qui apud populos in idololatria educatos Evangelium praedicant.

## 14:16
Vers. 16. Who in the past generations) For a long time now, since Joseph, the son of Jacob, lived.

He allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways) This is said comparatively, as the following things show. He neither gave them a law by which he might restrain their wicked cults, nor Prophets,

GOD was not more absent after the times of Joseph, such as under Nebuchadnezzar, Cyrus, and other Gentile monarchs, than in the very time of Joseph; meanwhile, speaking comparatively, they did not have the word of God, the Law, and the Prophets, as far as the ordinary ministry is concerned, in the same way as the Jews, Psalm 147:20, 'He has not dealt so with any nation.'

Latin:

Vers. 16. Ὃς ἐν ταῖς παρωχημέναις γενεαῖς) Longo jam tempore, ex quo vixit Josephus, Jacobi filius.

Εἴασε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη πορέυεσθαι ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἀυτῶν) Hoc comparate dictum ut sequentia ostendunt. Nec legem illis dedit, quibus pravos cultus compesceret, nec Pro- phetas,

Non defuit DEUS magis post tempora Jo- sephi, utpote sub Nebucadnezare, Cyro & aliis monarchis gentilibus, quam ipso Josephi tem- pore; interim συγκριτικῶς loquendo non ha- buerunt ita verbum Dei, Legem & Prophetas, quantum ad ordinarium ministerium, quemad- modum Judaei, tf. CXLVII. 20. Non fecit Deus ta- liter omni nationi.

## 14:17
Vers. 17. Nevertheless he did not leave himself without witness) He gave, however, that from which they might learn, although not as much as to the Hebrews, an excellent writer on the calling of the Gentiles, book 5. Although therefore this and many similar things the scripture of truth declares, we believe according to it, and most piously confess, that the divine providence has never lacked care for the totality of men, which, although it directed its chosen people with special institutions for piety, nevertheless withdrew the gifts of its goodness from no nation of men, so that they might be convinced that they had received prophetic voices and legal precepts in the obedience and testimonies of the elements, whence they also became inexcusable, because they made gods for themselves, and what were created for use, they venerated for worship. And 2:4. For although by the special care and indulgence of God, it is established that the Israelite people were chosen, and all other nations were permitted to walk in their own ways, that is, to live according to their own will, yet the eternal goodness of the Creator did not so depart from those men that it did not admonish them by no signs to know and fear him. For heaven and earth, and sea, and every creature that can be seen and understood, was disposed especially for this utility of the human race, so that the rational nature might be imbued from the contemplation of so many species, from the experience of so many goods, from the perception of so many gifts, to the worship and love of its author, the Spirit of God filling all things, in whom we are, move, and exist. And 10. For many authorities of divine utterances have served, and the continuous experiments of all ages have taught, that the just mercy of God, and his merciful justice, have never been lacking either in feeding the bodies of men, or in teaching and helping their minds. For he always rained upon the good and the evil, he always made his Sun to rise upon the just and the unjust, he always provided the breezes, he always ministered the successions of day and night, he always bestowed abundance for fields, multiplication for seeds, and fertility for the generation of men. And 15. For there has always been applied to all men a certain supernal measure of doctrine, which, of a more sparing and hidden grace, is yet sufficient, as the Lord has judged, for some as a remedy, for all as a testimony. Plotinus says if we were to hear the voice of the world, it would say nothing else than that God made me, not the Cretan Jupiter, or the Arcadian Mercury, but that unknown God, of whom Paul speaks to the Athenians.

Ἀγαθοποιῶν) מטיב. For הטיב is translated by ἀγαθοποιεῖν, Num. X. 32. Jud. XVII. 13. The same word exists, Tob. XII. 14. 1. Macc. XI. 33. 2. Macc. I. 2. Mark III. 4. Luke VI. 9. 33. also in Peter & John. For the same ἀγαθεργεῖν, I. Tim. VI. 18. and this manuscript has ἀγαθεργῶν. Moreover, this word connects very well with the preceding. For he has sufficiently inscribed the memory of himself in the minds of those, who does not cease to do good to them perpetually.

giving us rain from heaven) Aratus: Of water coming from Zeus.

and fruitful seasons) Spring, summer, autumn,

filling with food) With grain.

and gladness) That is, with wine. Sirach XXXI. 33.

Doubtless Paul described there the state of the nations, both by reason of the lacking testimony of the heavenly Word or the special revelation of God made in His word, which He allowed all nations constituted outside the polity of Israel, Ephes. ch. II. verse 12. to walk in their own ways, not announcing His word, nor manifesting His judgments to them, Psal. CXLVII. verses 18. 20. and by reason of the divine testimony or general revelation made through His benefits; which among those nations, which were destitute in past generations of the revelation of the divine word's testimony, God by no means left himself altogether ἀμάρτυρον [unwitnessed] intestatum, or declared by no testimony, but rather made himself testified by manifold benefits exhibited to them from heaven, from which he could also be recognized by them as the living God of heaven, earth, the sea, and all things that are in them, the artificer and creator. in Theol. natur. & revelat. p. 114. first from the method of the Apostolic address, which was most accommodated to the grasp of the Lystrians. They worshipped Jupiter, who was believed by most of the Gentiles to be the God of gods, of whom Orpheus, the most ancient of poets, according to Lactantius l. 1. de fals. relig. c. 5. had taught that he is the parent of all gods and the creator of heaven, and by nature and reason leading, understanding that there is given a most excellent power, the creator of heaven and earth. Varro according to August. l. IV. de C. D. cap. 9. & 11. & l. VII. c. 9. shows that Jupiter was so worshipped by the Gentiles that in Jupiter they comprehended all the gods, citing to that opinion Valerius Soranus on the worship of the gods. Moreover, the Lystrians had appointed a priest who offered sacrifices to Jupiter, and when they saw the miraculous healing of the lame man performed by Barnabas and Paul, they wanted a sacrifice to be offered to them, believing Barnabas to be Jupiter and Paul to be Mercury, and that they had descended from heaven and come to men. Whence they said οἱ θεοὶ ὁμοιωθέντες ἀνθρώποις κατέβησαν πρὸς ἡμᾶς [the gods, having become like men, have come down to us], thinking perhaps and alluding to that of the poet, οἱ θεοὶ ἀνθρώποισιν ὁμοιωθέντες εἰς ἡμᾶς ἤλυθον [the gods, having become like men, have come to us]. From that the Apostle took the occasion of recalling those Gentiles from the vain things which they served to the living God. When he attempted this, he proposed to them the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them. not only to intimate that this is that one and only true God who made these things, but that by this περιφράσει [periphrasis] he might at the same time involve an argument from which they could know that the same is the only true God, and that he alone as the true God is to be looked up to with religious worship: since even from the intuition and consideration of this work of the universe and the most orderly disposition of the pole, the sun, and the sea, they could arrive at that, that not Jupiter and other fictitious divinities, or mortal men, ought to be treated with divine worship, but that he at last is the living and true God who exists as the artificer and author of all these things, as being of heaven, and earth, and sea, and all things that are in them: since they depend and were produced from some principle, and do not exist from themselves: so that thus the Lystrians might be convinced that he alone is to be followed with sacrifices and other religious worships, and with true devotion of mind. For by the intuition of these things the Gentiles were led to the recognition of the creator: as Sophocles sang: One, in truth one is God, who fashioned heaven and the long earth, and the rough swellings of the sea; and before him Orpheus according to Clement of Alexandria: God is the Lord of heaven and hell and sea and earth. Hence also Virgil asserted that he goes through all lands and tracts of the sea, and the deep heaven, l. 4. Georg. But the voice of the poets is the voice of the people, to whose ears they generally accommodated their songs. Plutarch, however, concluded from thence thus: Let us not adore the elements, heaven, the sun, the moon, etc. Let these be mirrors in which we may behold the singular art of him who founded and adorned this world. Nor is the world anything other than his temple.

The second [argument] is from the common testimony of divinity, which the Apostle teaches is proposed to all, and revealed even to the Gentiles destitute of the testimony of the divine Word, by whose benefit all could have been led into the knowledge of God, even though they lacked the revealed Word of God. Hence we conclude thus: To whomsoever God did not leave himself ἀμάρτυρον [unwitnessed], they could altogether know God by some reason. But to the Gentiles, destitute of the testimony of the divine Word, God did not leave himself ἀμάρτυρον. Therefore, those Gentiles also could altogether know GOD by some reason, who did not have the testimony of the divine Word. The third [argument] is from the mode of divine attestation. For the Apostle declares by what reason God made himself testified to the Gentiles walking in their own ways: not by the relation of the Word, which they lacked; not by immediate apparition, or even by tradition concerning divine apparitions and some fame spread about himself; but by his works and benefits, through which he could be recognized himself as the giver and author of benefits. But he proposes those things then in general, that God made himself manifest by ἀγαθοποιῶν [doing good], since he is also in himself supremely good and the fountain and source of all good: then in particular he explains certain things, that namely GOD made himself testified by granting rains from heaven, by bestowing fruitful seasons, and by filling the hearts of men with food and gladness. For he who sends rains from heaven, bestows fruitful seasons, fills us with food, and gladness, him it surely behooves to be the true and living God. Therefore also the sounder Gentiles acknowledged that there is some Divinity, which they called τὸ ἀγαθὸν [the good] or Goodness itself and the Goodness of goods, and also the source and principle of all goods, as is abundantly evident from the example of Trismegistus, Plato, and most of the followers of Plato. They acknowledged, moreover, a Divinity that both made heaven and earth and disposed the seasons of the year, so that all things might germinate with certainty, as Aratus sang. Plutarch, l. III. cap. 6. de placit. Philosoph., among various modes from which men have had knowledge of God, also names τὴν μαρτυρίαν ἐκ τῶν φαινομένων καὶ μετεώρων [the testimony from things appearing and celestial phenomena], to which are also added τὰ ὑπὸ τῆς γῆς ζωογονούμενα καὶ καρπογονούμενα [things brought to life and fruit-bearing by the earth], to which opinion Tullius can also be seen, l. I. de Nat. Deor. Hence it is that they described Jupiter in such a way that he is ὄμβριος καὶ ὑέτιος [rainy and rain-giver]; ἐπικάρπιος [fruit-bearing]: ὁ ἀρτοδότης [bread-giver], as also δωτὴρ ἐάων [giver of good things] and epithets that occur similar to these. For through those testimonies by which God testifies of himself to the Gentiles, through them also as certain means of θεογνωσίας [knowledge of God], the Gentiles could be led into the knowledge of God. And yet, through his benefits in general and in particular through the sending of rains, the granting of fruitful seasons, the bestowing of food, and the donation of all joy and happiness, God testifies of himself to the Gentiles. Therefore, etc. It has pleased us to repeat these things from the praised book, perhaps not now obvious to many, because they contribute much to the illustration of the present passage.

PART III. The report made there by Paul, returning to the Antiochians after being stoned at Lystra and having confirmed and ordained churches throughout the vicinity of Derbe, concerning the progress of the Gospel among the Gentiles.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Καίτοιγε ἐκ ἀμάρτυρον ἑαυτὸν ἀφῆκεν) Dedit tamen, unde discerent, quanquam non tanta, quanta He- brais, Scriptor egregius de vocatione gentium, 1. 5. Quam- vis ergo haec & multa similia veritatis scriptura pronuntiet, secundum tamen ipsam credimus, & piissime confitemur, quod nunquam universitati hominum divina providentia cura defuerit, quae licet exceptum sibi populum specialibus ad pietatem direxerit institutis, nulli tamen nationi hominum bonitatis suae dona subtraxit, ut propheticas voces & praece- pta legalia convincerentur in elementorum obsequiis ac testi- moniis accepisse, unde & inexcusabiles facti sunt, quia Deos- sibi dona fecerunt, & quae creata sunt ad utendum, vene- rati sunt ad colendum Et II. 4. Quamvis enim speciali cura & indulgentia Dei, populum Israeliticum constat electum, o- mnesque alias nationes vias suas ingredi, hoc est, secun- dum propriam permissae sunt vivere voluntatem, non tata- men se aeterna Creatoris bonitas ab illis hominibus abert ut eos ad cognoscendum se atque metuendum, nullis signifi- cationibus admoneret. Caelum quippe ac terra, ac mare, omniaque creatura, quae videri atque intelligi potest, ad hanc praecipue disposita est humani generis utilitatem, ut natura rationalis de contemplatione tot specierum, de expe- rimento tot bonorum, de perceptione tot munerum, ad cul- tum & dilectionem sui imbueretur autoris, implente omnia Spiritu Dei, in quo sumus, movemur, & sumus. Et 10. Ministrarunt enim divinorum eloquiorum multa autorita- tes, & continua omnium seculorum experimenta docuerunt, ju- stam Dei misericordiam, misericordemq; justitiam, nec alendis unquam corporibus hominum, nec docendis, jubandisque eo- rum mentibus defuisse. Semper enim pluit super bonos & malos, semper suum Solem oriri fecit super justos & injustos, semper bis les auras praebuit, semper dies & noctis vicissitu- dines ministravit, ubertatem agris, multiplicationem semi- nibus, foecunditatem generandu hominibus semper impendit. Et 15. Adhibita enim semper est universis hominibus que- dam superna mensura doctrinae, quae parcioris, occultiorisque gratiae, sufficit tamen, sicut Dominus judicavit, quibusdam ad remedium, omnibus ad testimonium. Ait Ploti- nus si mundi vo em audiremus, nihil aliud eum dice- re, quam Deus me fecit, Non Cretenfis Jupiter, aut Arcas Mercurius, sed Deus ille ἄγνωστος, de quo Paulus ad Athenienses.

Ἀγαθοποιῶν) מטיב. Nam הטיב vertitur per ἀγαθο- ποιεῖν, Num. X. 32. Iud. XVII. 13. Exstat idem verbum, Tob. XII. 14. 1. Macc. XI. 33. 2. Macc. I. 2. Marc. III. 4. Luc. VI. 9. 33. apud Petrum etiam & Johannem. Pro eodem ἀγαθεργεῖν, I. Tim. VI. 18. & hic manuscriptus ille habet ἀγαθεργῶν. Optime autem haec vox connectentis cum superioribus. Satis enim memoriam sui insculpsit illorum animis, qui non cessat perpetuo eis benefa- cere.

ὠρανόθεν ἡμῖν ὑετὼς διδὲς) Aratus : Ὕδατος ἐρχομένοιο Διὸς παρά.

κὴ καιρὼς καρποφόρους) Ver, aestatem, autumnum,

ἐμπιπλῶν τροφῆς) Frumento.

κὴ ἐυφροσύνης) Id est, vino. Sirach. XXXI. 33.

Nimirum descripsit Paulus ibi gentium sta- tum tum ratione carentis testimonii Verbi cale- stis seu patefactionis Dei specialis in verbo suo factae, quod omnes gentes extra politiam Israe- lis constitutas, Ephes. cap. II. vers. 12. dimiserit ingredi vias suas, non annuncians verbum suum, nec manifestans eis judicia sua, Psal. CXLVII. vers. 18. 20. tum ratione testificatio- nis divinae seu patefactionis generalis per be- neficia sua factae; quod apud gentes illas, quae destitutae fuere praeteritis generationibus re- velatione testimonii verbi divini, haudquaquam prorsus ἀμάρτυρον intestatum, vel nullo testimonio declaratum sese reliquerit Deus, sed potius testa- tum semetipsum fecerit multivariis beneficiis iis- dem cœlitus exhibitis, è quibus agnosci quoque potuerit ab iisdem, ut vivus Deus cœli, terræ, maris & omnium, quæ in iis sunt, opifex & condi- tor. Unde θεογνωσίαν naturalem deduximus in Theol. natur. & revelat. p. 114. primum à concionis Apostolicæ methodo, quæ maxime! accomodata erat ad Lystrensium captum. Colebant illi Jo- vem, qui plerisque gentilium Deus Deorum crede- batur, de quo Orpheus, Poëtarum vetustissimus apud Lactantium l. 1. de fals. relig. c. 5. docuerat, quod sit omnium Deorum parens & cæli conditor naturæ & ratione ducente intelligens, dari præstan- tissimam potentiam, cæli ac terræ conditricem. Varro apud August. l. IV. de C. D. cap. 9. & 11. & l. VII. c. 9. ostendit, Jovem ita à gentilibus cultum fuis- se, ut in Jove comprehenderent omnes Deos, addu- cens in eam sententiam Valerium Soranum de cul- tu Deorum. Cæterum Lystrenses constituerant Sacerdotem, qui Jovi sacrificia offerebat, & quum miraculosam sanationem claudi à Barnaba & Pau- lo peractam viderent, sacrificium offerri ipsis vole- bant, credentes Barnabam esse Jovem, & Paulum Mercurium, eosque de cœlo descendisse, & ad ho- mines venisse. Unde dicebant οἱ θεοὶ ὁμοιωθέντες ἀνθρώποις κατέβησαν πρὸς ἡμᾶς, cogitantes forte & alludentes illud Poëtæ, οἱ θεοὶ ἀνθρώποισιν ὁ- μοιωθέντες εἰς ἡμᾶς ἤλυθον. Ex eo capiebat Apo- stolus occasionem, gentiles istos à vanis rebus, qui- bus serviebant, revocandi ad Deum vivum. Quod cum conaretur, proposuit illis vivum Deum, qui fe- cit cælum & terram & mare & omnia, quæ in illis sunt. non modo ut innueret, hunc esse unum illum & solum verum Deum, qui ea fecit, sed ut hac περι- φράσει simul argumentum involveret, unde co- gnoscere illi poterant. eundem esse solum verum Deum, solumque ut Deum verum cultu religioso suspiciendum esse: quandoquidem vel ex intui- tu & consideratione opificii hujus universi & di- spositionis ordinatissimæ poli, soli & sali eo per- venire queant, non Jovem, aliaque Numina ficti- tia, vel mortales homines divino cultu affici de- bere, sed eum demum esse vivum & verum Deum, qui istorum omnium opifex & autor exsistat, utpote cœli, terræque & maris & omnium, quæ in illis sunt: quippe quæ dependeant & pro- ducta sint ab aliquo principio, non à seipsis exsistant: ut ita Lystrenses convincerentur, il- lum solum sacrificiis aliisque cultibus religiosis, veraque mentis devotione prosequendum esse. Horum namque intuitu ad agnitionem condi- toris deducti sunt gentiles: ut Sophocles cecinit: Unus revera unus est Deus, qui cælum fabricavit & terram longam, marisque truces tumores; & ante eum Orpheus apud Clementem Alexandr. cæli & inferni & maris terræque Dominus est Deus. Hinc etiam Virgilius eum ire per omnes Terrasque tra- ctusque maris, cælumque profundum asseruit l. 4. Georg. Vox autem Poëtarum vox populi, ad cu- jus aures suos plerumque cantus accomodabant. Plutarchus vero inde ita conclusit: Ne adoremus Elementa, cælum, Solem, Lunam, &c. Specula sint hæc, in quibus artem illius singularem intu- eamur, qui mundum hunc condidit & adorna- vit. Nec est aliud mundus, quam templum ejus.

Secundum à communi divinitatis testimonio, quod omnibus propositum esse, gentibusque etiam, testimonio Verbi divini destitutis, pate- factum, docet Apostolus, cujus beneficio o- mnes in cognitionem Dei deduci potuerint, utut Verbo revelato Dei caruerint. Hinc ita con- cludimus; Quibuscunque Deus sese non reli- quit ἀμάρτυρον, illo omnino Deum potuere co- gnoscere aliqua ratione. At gentibus, Verbi divini testimonio destitutis, Deus sese non reli- . quit ἀμάρτυρον. Proinde etiam gentes illae po- tuere omnino DEUM aliqua ratione cogno- scere, quae Verbi divini testimonium non ha- buere. Tertium à testificationis divinae modo. De- clarat enim Apostolus, qua ratione Deus sese gentibus in viis suis incedentibus testatum fece- rit: non Verbi relatione, qua caruerunt; non immediata apparitione, vel etiam traditione de apparitionibus divinis & fama quadam de sese sparsa; sed operibus suis & beneficiis, per quae agnosci potuerit ipse ut beneficiorum dator & autor. Ea autem tum in genere proponit, quod Deus ἀγαθοποιῶν benefaciendo sese pate- fecerit, quippe & in sese summe bonus & o- mnis boni fons & scaturigo: tum in specie quae- dam exponit, quod nempe testatum se fecerit DEUS, pluvias de cælo concedendo, tempora fru- gifera largiendo, ciboque & lætitia corda homi- num implendo. Qui enim pluvias de cœlo im- mittit, tempora largitur frugifera, cibis nos replet, & lætitia, eum utique oportet esse ve- rum & vivum Deum. Ideo etiam saniores gen- tiles agnoverunt, esse Numen aliquod, quod τὸ ἀγαθὸν vel Bonum ipsum dixerunt & Bonita- tem bonitatum, nec non scaturiginem & prin- cipium omnium bonorum, ut exemplo Trismegi- sti, Platonis & plerorumque sectatorum Plato- nis abunde constat. Agnoverunt insuper Nu- men, quod & cælum terramque fecerit & tem- pestates anni disposuerit, ut omnia certo germi- nent, ut cecinit Aratus. Plutarchus l. III. cap. 6. de placit. Philosoph. inter varios modos, unde homines cognitionem Dei habuerint, nominat quoque τὴν μαρτυρίαν ἐκ τῶν φαινομένων καὶ με- τεώρων quibus adduntur quoque τὰ ὑπὸ τῆς γῆς ζωογονούμενα καὶ καρπογονούμενα, in quam senten- tiam videri etiam potest Tullius l. I. de Nat. Deor. Hinc est quod Jovem ita descripserint, quod sit ὄμβριος καὶ ὑέτιος pluvius & pluviator; ἐπικάρπιος frugipotens: ὁ ἀρτοδότης, ut & δωτὴρ ἐάων & quae his gemina occurrunt Epitheta. Per quae enim testimonia Deus de seipso testatur gentilibus, per ea etiam ceu media θεογνωσίας certa, genti- les potuere in cognitionem Dei deduci.
