Atqui per beneficia sua in genere & in specie per pluvi- arum immissionem, temporum fœcundorum con- cessionem, ciborum largitionem, omnis lætitiae & felicitatis donationem Deus de seipso testatur gentilibus. Ergo &c. Hæc nostra è libro laudato non multis forte jam obvio repetere placuit, quia ad loci præsen- tis illustrationem multum faciunt.

PARS III. Pauli Lystris lapidati confirmatis & ordina- tis passim in vicinia Derbensi Ecclesiis ad Antiochenos redeuntis, ibidem facta de progressu Evangelii inter gentes relatio.

## 14:19
Vers. 19. Ἀπὸ Ἀντιοχείας καὶ Ἰκονίου) From Antioch of Pisidia and Iconium, cities of Lycaonia, came some of those who had already adopted a hostile mind against the Apostles. Above XIII. 50. XIV. 2. add 2. Tim. III. 11. where the history of this chapter is touched upon.

καὶ λιθάσαντες τὸν Παῦλον) In the manuscript, λιθοβολήσαντες. It is the same, whichever you read. For both λιθάζειν and λιθοβολεῖν are in use among the Greeks, even in these books. What is narrated here is that which Paul mentions in 1 Cor. 11:25.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ἀπὸ Ἀντιοχείας καὶ Ἰκονίου) Ab Antiochia Pisidiae & Iconio Lycaoniae urbibus venere aliqui eorum, qui jam hostilem animum in Apostolos induerant. Supra XIII. 50. XIV. 2. adde 2. Tim. III. 11. ubi hujus capitis historia attingitur.

καὶ λιθάσαντες τὸν Παῦλον) In Manuscripto, λιθοβολήσαν- τες. Perinde est, utrum legas. Nam & λιθάζειν & λιθοβο- λεῖν in usu est Græcorum, etiam in his libris. Quod hic narratur, id est, cujus meminit Paulus 1. Cor. XI. 25.

## 14:20
Vers. 20.

ἀναστὰς) from that place where he had lain as dead. εἰς Δέρβην) concerning which see above 6. The disciples are said to have surrounded Paul, who had been stoned, which was done either to bury him, whom they believed dead, which is what Cajetan wants, or to cover him while alive and hide him from the Jews, as seemed good to Lyranus and Hugo. But he AROSE, because God miraculously and immediately restored those strengths to Paul, so that on the next day he was able to proceed to Derbe as if strong and healthy.

Circumdedisse autem dicuntur Paulum lapida- tum discipuli, quod factum vel ut sepelirent, quem mortuum credebant, quod vult Cajetanus, vel ut vivum tegerent & Judæis absconderent, uti Lyra- no & Hugoni visum. SURREXIT autem, quia miraculose Deus confestim Paulo eas restituit vires, ut postridie quasi valens validusque in Derben pergere potuerit.

## 14:22
Vers. 22.

καὶ ὅτι διὰ πολλῶν θλίψεων δεῖ ἡμᾶς εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ) Rom. 8, and 2 Cor. passim. The troubles of the journey through the desert in the time of Moses had prefigured this. IT IS NECESSARY, this is a hypothetical [statement] from the hypothesis of divine preordination and our conformation with Christ, Rom. 8:29, as well as the due mortification of our flesh, and thus the corruption of the exterior, 2 Cor. 4:16, as also the perpetual persecution of the infernal serpent. Gen. 3:15, 2 Tim. 3:13.

Vers. 22.

καὶ ὅτι διὰ πολλῶν θλίψεων δεῖ ἡμᾶς εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασι- λείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ) Rom. VIII, & 2. Cor. passim. Hoc præfigura- verant molestiæ itineris per desertum Mosis tempore. OPORTET hoc est hypotheticum ex hypo- thesi divinæ præordinationis & nostræ cum Christo conformationis, Rom. VIII. 29. nec non debitæ car- nis nostræ mortificationis, & sic exterioris corruptio- nis 2. Cor. IV. 16. ut & perpetuæ serpentis infernalis persecutionis. Gen. III. 15. 2. Tim. III. 13.

## 14:23
v. 23. χειροτονήσαντες) χειροτονεῖν is indeed accustomed to be taken for any election, even that which is made by one or a few. But it is also credible that the consent of the people was added to the election which is being discussed, on account of that which we had above in a lesser matter, 6:2, 8.

These things are to be noted against the Papists, who exclude the congregation from this χειροτονία of the presbyters, and contend that it was done, and ought to be done, by Bishops alone, to such an extent that χειροτονία does not even befit Presbyters, as can be seen in Cornelius a Lapide on this passage. But it is clear from 1 Tim. 4:14 that χειροθεσία also befits Presbyters; now indeed χειροτονία in the New Testament according to Cornelius is χειροθεσία, or ordination to the Holy Ministries. But that the same man appeals to the perpetual practice of the Church, that it constitutes ministers through the imposition of the hands of a Bishop, not through the votes of the people, that has been sufficiently discussed by the blessed Dn. D. Hülsemann in his Apology for the ordination of ministers. Certainly, the Papists have not yet been able to bring forward any passage from the Holy Scriptures in which χειροτονία is attributed to the office proper to a Priest, with the minister being superior to other Presbyters, except for this present one in Acts 14. But that ordination is understood here by χειροτονία has not yet been shown: our people have taught that election and proposal are rather to be understood, by which the Apostles proposed to the Churches those whom they judged suitable, and with the vote of the Church added, the calling would be ratified; the blessed Chemnitz on Can. 7, sess. 13 of the Council of Trent, part 2 of the Examination, Brentius, Pomeranus, Justus Jonas, Sarcerius in the Catena of Marloratus, Arcularius, Osiander in his notes on this passage. Calvin, although he accepts this passage regarding the rite of ordination, nevertheless observes that the Greek word χειροτονεῖν signifies to decree something with hands raised, as is accustomed to be done in the assemblies of the people. For by this form of speaking, the legitimate method in creating pastors is best expressed: Paul and Barnabas are said to elect presbyters. Do they do this alone by private office? Rather, they permit the matter to the votes of all. Therefore, in creating pastors, the election of the people was free. Nor indeed can the people be excluded from this χειροτονία any more than from the fellowship of fasting and prayers: because the same ones are said to have appointed presbyters who are said to have prayed and fasted, v. 29. As therefore in the elections of magistrates and civil ministers the common people were accustomed to extend their hand on high to indicate their vote or approval: so in the presentation of future Presbyters or ministers of the word made by Barnabas and Paul to the congregation, the congregation or the people are said to have raised their hand to vote for those presented. Erasmus interprets this word as 'chosen by votes.' Salmero says, χειροτονεῖν signifies the calling of a magistrate, because it was done with that ceremony of the elevation of hands, and thus it was the custom of the Greeks of old to grant their votes to someone. And furthermore: Paul and Barnabas gave the believers the power to show and choose a Bishop in their own city as well: whom they themselves afterwards consecrated with prayers and fastings and the imposition of hands, although no peculiar mention of this is made in this place. Gratian himself, in Can. 1, dist. 62, says that no reason allows those to be held as Bishops who have neither been elected by the Clergy nor requested by the people; which he confirms with many testimonies.

Whether indeed by Presbyters here are understood those lower in rank than Bishops, or whether Bishops are included at the same time, is not agreed upon even among the Papists themselves: John Gagnejus says that it cannot be defined here; for in the Glossa ordinaria it is held thus: When they had constituted, that is, had ordained in their stead, those who were about to depart. At that time, however, Bishops and Presbyters were of the same name. Lyranus says that by the name of Presbyters, other ministers of the Church are also understood here, such as Bishops, Deacons, and the like. Lapidensis says that Bishops are included here under the name of Presbyters.

Παρέθεντο αὐτοὺς τῷ Κυρίῳ) to Jesus, the best guardian.

Latin:

v. 23. χειροτονήσαντες) solet quidem χειροτονεῖν sumi de quavis electione, etiam quæ ab uno vel paucis fit. Sed & electioni, de qua agitur, accessisse consensum plebis cre- dibile est, ob id quod in re minori supra habuimus, VI. 2. 8.

Notanda hæc contra Pontificios, qui ab hac χει- ροτονίᾳ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων excludunt communio- nem, eamque à solis Episcopis factam, & fieri de- bere, adeo ut nec Presbyteris conveniat ἡ χειροτο- νία, contendunt, ut videre est apud Cornelium La- pidensem in h. l. At Presbyteris etiam χειροθεσίαν convenire liquet è 1. Tim. IV. 14. jam vero χειρο- τονία in Novo Testamento secundum Cornelium est χειροθεσία, vel ordinatio ad S. Ministeria. Quod autem idem provocat ad praxin Ecclesiæ perpe- tuam, quod ea ministros constituat per impositio- nem manuum Episcopi, non per suffragia populi, ea satis discussa à B. Dn. D. Hülsemanno in Apolo- gia ministri ordinationis. Nullum certe locum è S. literis proferre potuerunt hactenus Papistæ, quo χειροτονία ad officium Sacerdotis proprium, mini- stro aliis Presbyteris superiori tribuatur, præter hunc præsentem Actor. XIV. At ordinationem hic intelligi per χειροτονίαν, nondum ostensum est: ele- Etionem & propositionem, qua Ecclesiis Apostoli eos, quos judicabant idoneos, proposuere, & ac- cedente suffragio Ecclesiæ rata esset vocatio, in- telligendam potius esse nostrates docuere, B. Che- mnitius ad Can. VII. sess. XIII. Concil. Trid. part. II. Exam. Brentius, Pomeranus, Justus Jonas, Sarce- rius in Catena Marlorati, Arcularius, Osiander in not. ad h. l. Calvinus etsi de ordinationis ritu hunc locum accipiat, observat tamen verbum Græcum χειροτονεῖν significare, aliquid manibus sublatis de- cernere, qualiter in comitiis populi fieri solet. Hac enim loquendi forma optime exprimitur legitima in creandis pastorib. ratio: Presbyteros eligere dicuntur Paulus & Barnabas. An soli hoc privato officio fa- ciunt? quin potius rem permittunt omnium suffra- giis. Ergo in pastoribus creandis libera fuit populi electio. Nec vero magis populus excludi potest ab hac χειροτονίᾳ quam à societate jejunii & orationum: quia iidem dicuntur constituisse presbyteros, qui di- cuntur orasse & jejunasse v. 29. Ut ergo in electio- nibus Magistratuum, & ministrorum civilium plebs solebat manum in altum extendere, ad indican- dum suffragium sive approbationem suam: ita in præsentatione futurorum Presbyterorum seu mini- strorum verbi à Barnaba & Paulo ad plebem facta communio, vel populus extulisse dicitur manum ad suffragandum præsentatis. Erasmus hanc vocem interpretatur per suffragiis delectos. Salmero χειροτονεῖν, inquit, vocationem Magistratus significat, eo quod cum illa cæremonia elevationis manuum fieret, & ita moris erat olim Græcis suffragia sua alicui tribuere. Et porro: Paulus & Barnabas dederunt credentibus facultatem, ut monstrarent ac eligerent in sua quoque civitate Episcopum: quem ipsi postea orationibus & jejuniis, & manuum impositione, quanquam hujus hoc loco non fiat peculiaris mentio, consecrabant. Gratianus ipse, in Can. I. dist. LXII. Nullam rationem sinere, ait, ut inter Episcopos habeantur, qui nec à Clericis electi sunt, nec à plebibus expetiti; quod multis confirmat testimoniis.

An vero per Presbyteros hic intelligantur gradu inferiores Episcopis, aut comprehendantur simul Episcopi, inter Pontificios ipsos non constat: Joh. Gagnejus id definiri hic non posse ait; in Glossa enim ordinaria ita habetur: Cum constituissent, id est, ordinassent pro se, qui erant migraturi. Illo autem tempore ejusdem nominis erant Episcopi, & Presbyteri. Lyranus, nomine Presbyterorum, inquit, hic intelliguntur etiam alii Ecclesiæ ministri, ut Episcopi, Diaconi, & hujusmodi. Episcopos nomine Presbyterorum hic comprehendi, ait Lapidensis.

Παρέθεντο αὐτοὺς τῷ Κυρίῳ) Jesu optimo custodi.

## 14:24
Ver. 24.

ἦλθον εἰς Παμφυλίαν) retracing their own footsteps. See above c. XIII. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ἦλθον εἰς Παμφυλίαν) sua vestigia retro legentes. Vide supra c. XIII. 13.

## 14:25
κατέβησαν εἰς Ἀττάλειαν) Ptolemy places Attalia on the seacoast of Pamphylia after Lycia. So also Strabo. Others attribute it to Lycia. But the boundaries of provinces were often changed by the Romans: it has its name from Attalus, one of the kings of the kingdom of Gog, as the Hebrews speak.

Latin:

κατέβησαν εἰς Ἀττάλειαν) Attaliam Ptolemæus in ora maritima Pamphyliæ ponit post Lyciam. Sic & Strabo. Alii Lyciæ attribuunt. Sed provinciarum fines à Romanis sæpe mutati: nomen habet ab Attalo uno regum regni Gog ut Hebræi loquuntur.

Ver. 26.

## 14:27
Ver. 27. ὅσα ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς μετ' αὐτῶν) that is, with how much honor God had affected them through the conversion of so many men. A similar expression is in Ps. CXIX. 123. Luke I. 71. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 27. ὅσα ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς μετ' αὐτῶν) id est, quanto honore eos affecisset Deus per tot hominum conversionem. Similis locutio Psal. CXIX. 123. Luc. I. 71. & alibi.

## 14:28
Ver. 28. κ, ὅτι ἤνοιξε τοῖς ἔθνεσι θύραν πίστεως) that is, He gave an opportunity for believing in Himself: the same kind of speaking is in 1 Cor. XVI. 9. 2 Cor. II. 12. Coloss. IV. 3.

Paronius thinks that Barnabas and Paul consumed five years in this work of pilgrimage. For they went out from Antioch to preach in the year of Christ 44, which was the 2nd or 3rd of the Emperor Claudius, but returned in the year of Christ 49. After their return, however, they remained at Antioch for two years until the Council of Jerusalem, which was celebrated in the year 51. For they are said to have stayed there for no small time, v. 29.

Latin:

Vers. 28. κ, ὅτι ἤνοιξε τοῖς ἔθνεσι θύραν πίστεως) id est, occasionem dedit in se credendi: idem loquendi genus 1. Cor. XVI. 9. 2. Cor. II. 12 Coloss. IV. 3.

Paronius putat Barnabam & Paulum in hoc opere peregrinationis quinque annos consumpsisse. Exivisse enim Antiochia ad prædicandum Anno Christi 44. qui fuit Claudii Imper. II. vel III. reversos vero esse anno Christi XLIX. Post reditum vero mansisse Antiochiæ per biennium usque ad Concilium Hierosolymitanum, quod celebratum anno LI. Dicuntur enim ibi morati tempus non modicum v. 29.

## 15:1 Argument
CHAPTER XV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

When some coming from Judea taught concerning the necessity of circumcision, and contention arose therefrom, Paul, Barnabas, and others sent for that reason to Jerusalem, bring joy to the brethren in Phoenicia and Samaria because of the conversion of the Gentiles, are received at Jerusalem by the Apostles and elders and report the same, and when certain of the sect of the Pharisees who had believed arose, who urged the necessity of circumcision and of keeping the Mosaic law in the council. After various disputation, Peter, having testified concerning the Gospel preached among the Gentiles, with no distinction made by God between them and the Jews, their hearts having been purified by faith, that the unbearable yoke of the law was by no means to be imposed upon the disciples, but teaches that we are to be saved, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the same way as the Fathers. But after Paul and Barnabas had recounted those things which had been done among the Gentiles, James, confirming the report concerning the Gentiles who had been taken in from the Prophets (Amos IX. 11.) that they would acknowledge the name of the Lord, concluded that the converted Gentiles were not to be troubled, but only to be warned to abstain from idols, fornication, and things strangled, whence it pleased Paul and Barnabas to join Judas Barsabas and Silas, to whom they entrusted synodical letters to the brethren in Antioch, Syria, etc. letters, which were read with joy at Antioch, Silas remaining there with Paul and Barnabas, who, when they wished to visit the neighboring churches, Paul refused to take John, called Mark, for that work, though Barnabas advised it in vain, whence Barnabas also separated himself from Paul, sailing with Mark to Cyprus. But Paul chose Silas for himself, traveling through Syria and Cilicia, and confirming the churches.

There are three parts: I. The description of the Jerusalem council, to verse 21. II. The sending, reception, and dismissal of the legates to the Antiochene brethren with synodical letters, to verse 34. III. The journey of Paul, separated from Barnabas, who took Mark, through Syria and Cilicia, to the final verse 41.

PART I. Description of the Jerusalem Council.

Verse 1.

καί τινες) Certain ones from the Antiochene Jews: certain Jews, not all, felt this way, that no man could be saved unless he were circumcised and submitted himself to the whole law of Moses as the only way to salvation, as this passage is explained in the constitutions which are called those of Clement VI. 12. Others, however, felt that even those who were חסידי אומות could be saved, namely because circumcision itself was not commanded except to the descendants of Abraham, Gen. XVII. 10. 11. 12. Nor was the law of Moses, except to the Israelites. Ananias the Jew said to Izates of Adiabene in Josephus XX. 2. that he could worship the divine even without circumcision. Tryphon speaks hesitantly in Justin: for if you remain in that manner of philosophy and live blamelessly, a hope of a better lot remained for me. Of these two opinions, God approved the milder one.

τῷ ἔθει Μωσέως) כדרך אשר according to the customs of Moses. Circumcision was indeed older, but it was also commanded by Moses, John VII. 22.

That controversy is sometimes proposed simply concerning circumcision, as here in verse 1, and sometimes mention is also added concerning the keeping or observation of the law of Moses, verse 5. Because he who is circumcised renders himself subject to the law of Moses, Gal. V. 3. Grotius rightly understands this controversy as concerning the whole law; even though he wished to curry favor with the Papists in this Council as well: who indeed say that there was a discussion only concerning the Ceremonial law. But although the converts from the Jews moved the litigation concerning the observance of the Ceremonial law, the first lie, nevertheless it was theirs, that through the observance of the law, and thus through works and one's own righteousness, the way to salvation was uniquely opened, as Grotius does not deny, that they believed this was the only way to salvation. Indeed, they did not believe that they obtained salvation through the righteousness of Christ imputed, and through faith in Christ, or the apprehension or application of the active and passive obedience of Christ: but through their own obedience or observance of the whole Mosaic law: requiring indeed the knowledge of Jesus, so that he might be held as the Messiah and Prophet of the Lord, but ascribing salvation to their own works: which was a mixture and syncretism of Judaism and Christianity. For they urged circumcision for this reason, because they judged the whole law to be necessary for salvation, just as by the observance of circumcision they truly rendered themselves obligated to observe the whole law. Which is further evident from the fact that they are said to have been from the sect of the Pharisees, who were the cause of this contention. But that this was the heresy of the Pharisees, that a man is justified by works or the observance of the commandments of the law, is certain from Matt. V, Rom. IX, X, Phil. III, and other places of Scripture. It is added that the Apostles, desiring to remove the controversy and doubts raised from the foundation, not only do not teach that circumcision is necessary, nor that the observation of ceremonial laws is necessary, even if they wish some things to be observed for the sake of avoiding scandal according to the condition of that Church, which they specifically express, which were either ceremonial or are to be held as indifferent, but they also openly define that no one, whether a Jew or a Gentile by birth, is saved by the law or the obedience performed to the law, but whoever are saved, or have ever been saved, they are saved or have been saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that the law was an unbearable yoke, which neither the fathers could bear, nor can it now be borne by anyone, whence it is impossible for anyone to obtain salvation through the observance of the law: that hearts are purified from sins by faith alone, that salvation is obtained by faith alone in the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, namely that which was procured by his passion and death, so that thus faith and justification, which is described by the remission of sins and the purification of the heart, by which our hearts are cleansed from all sin by the blood of JESUS Christ, 1 John 1 v. 7, and eternal salvation and blessedness consist: because we cannot be saved by the grace of our Lord JESUS Christ, except by the faith by which we apprehend the same, and make it our own through faithful apprehension, Roman. IV v. 25, Gal. II v. 20, concerning which see S. Augustin. c. I. contr. two Epist. Pelag. cap. XXI. However great you may proclaim the virtue of the ancient righteous to have been, it did not save them, except for the faith of the mediator, who shed his blood for the remission of sins. Conf. B. Luther. comment. in Epist. ad Galat. 1538. in cap. III. Tom. IV. Jenens. Lat. fol. 68. & I. von den Conciliis und Kirchen Tom. VII. Jenens. Germ. as well as our dissertation on the faith of the ancients, page 31. Furthermore, among those who troubled the Antiochians with their sermons, to add this in passing, Epiphanius writes that Cerinthus was also present, heresy XXVIII, concerning whom see the diatribe on the heresy denying the divinity and satisfaction of Christ.

Latin:

CAPUT XV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Quum aliqui è Judæa venientes de circumcisionis necessitate docerent, & contentio inde oriretur, Paulus, Barnabas, & alii ideo missi Hierosolymam, in Phœnicia & Samaria ob conversationem gentium fratribus gaudium conciliant, Hierosolymis ab Apostolis & senioribus excepti eadem nuntiant, & surgentibus quibusdam de secta Pharisæorum conversis, qui necessitatem circumcisionis, & servandæ legis Mosaicæ urgebant in concilio. Post variam disceptationem Petrus de Evangelio, inter gentes prædicato, nullo discrimine à Deo inter ipsas, & Judæos facto, cordibus per fidem purgatis, testatus, ju- gum legis ἀβάςακτον haud imponendum di- scipulis, quin credere sese, docet, per gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi, similiter sicut Pa- tres, salvatum nos iri. Postquam vero Pau- lus & Barnabas ea quæ inter gentes gesta sint, recensuissent, Iacobus relationem de as- sumtis gentibus è Prophetis (Amos IX. 11.) quod nomen Domini agnituræ sint, confir- mans, conclusit, gentes conversas turban- das non esse, sed monendas solum, ut ab ido- lis, scortatione & suffocato abstineant, un- de placuit Paulo & Barnabæ, Iudam Barsa- bas, & Silan adjungere, quibus synodicas ad fratres in Antiochia, Syria &c. literas commisere, quæ cum lætitia Antiochiæ le- ctæ sunt, Sila ibidem remanente cum Paulo & Barnaba, qui cum vellent Ecclesias vici- nas visitare, ad opus illud Iohannem, Mar- cum, nequicquam consulente Barnaba, Pau- lus assumere renuit, unde Barnabas sese et- iam à Paulo separavit, cum Marco in Cy- prum trajiciens. Paulus vero adoptavit sibi Silam, per Syriam & Ciliciam proficiscens, & Ecclesias confirmans.

Partes sunt tres: I. Hierosolymitani concilii de- scriptio, ad v. 21. II. Legatorum ad Antiochenos fratres cum literis synodicis destinatio, susceptio & dimissio, ad v. 34. III. Pauli cum Sila separati à Barnaba, Marcum assumente, per Syriam & Cili- ciam profectio, ad v. 41. finalem.

PARS I. Hierosolymitani Concilii descriptio.

Vers. 1.

καί τινες) Quidam ex Judæis Antiochensibus: quidam Judæi, non omnes, ita sentiebant, neminem hominum ser- vari posse nisi circumcideretur, totique Mosis legi, ut unicæ ad salutem viæ, se subjiceret, quomodo hic locus explica- tur in constitutionibus, quæ dicuntur Clementis VI. 12. alii tamen sentiebant etiam eos qui erant חסידי אומות posse servari, nimirum quia ipsa circumcisio non erat im- perata, nisi Abrahami posteris, Gen. XVII. 10. 11. 12. Nec lex Mosis, nisi Israëlitis. Ananias Judæus Izati Adiabeno apud Josephum XX. 2. δυνάμενον δὲ αὐτὸν ἔφη κὰι χω- ρὶς τῆς περιτομῆς τὸ θεῖον σέβειν. Tryphon hæsitanter lo- quitur apud Justinum: μένοιτι γάρ σοι ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ τῆς φιλοσο- φίας τρόπῳ κὰι ζῶντι ἀμέμπτως ἐλπὶς ὑπελείπετο ἀμείνονός μοί ρας. Ex his duabus sententiis leniorem Deus probavit.

τῷ ἔθει Μωσέως) כדרך אשר secundum Mosis insti- tuta. Erat quidem circumcisio antiquior, sed à Mose etiam præcepta, Ioh. VII. 22.

Controversia illa modo simpliciter proponitur de circumcisione, ut hic v. 1. modo etiam additur mentio de τηρήσει vel observatione legis Mosis, v. 5. Quia qui circumciditur, legi Mosis obnoxium se red- dit, Gal. V. 3. De tota etiam lege recte Grotius hanc controversiam accipit; utut Papistis alias etiam in hoc Concilio velificari voluerit: qui vero de lege Ceremoniali solum συζήτησιν fuisse ajunt. Sed quamvis de lege Ceremoniali observanda liti- gium moverint conversi è Judæis, τὸ πρῶτον ψεῦδος, tamen eorum erat, quod per observantiam legis, adeoq; opera & justitiam propriam unice ad salutem pateret via, uti non diffitetur Grotius, unicam hanc ad salutem viam ipsos credidisse. Nimirum non per justitiam Christi imputatam, & per fidem in Chri- stum, seu apprehensionem, vel applicationem obedientiæ Christi activæ & passivæ salutem se consequi credebant: sed per propriam obedien- tiam seu observantiam totius legis Mosaicæ: re- quirentes quidem cognitionem Jesu, ut nempe ipse haberetur pro Messia & Propheta Domini, sed sa- lutem adscribentes propriis operibus: quæ erat mixtura, & Syncretismus Iudaismi & Christiani- smi. Idcirco enim circumcisionem urgebant, quia legem universam observatu necessariam esse ad salutem censebant, uti per circumcisionis obser- vantiam se ad totam legem observandam obliga- tos revera reddebant. Quod porro inde constat, quia ἀπὸ τῆς αἱρέσεως τῶν Φαρισαίων fuisse dicun- tur, qui hujus contentionis causa erant. Pharisaeo- rum autem hanc fuisse haeresin, quod homo justifi- cetur per opera, vel observantiam mandatorum legis e Matth. V. Rom. IX. X. Phil. III. aliisque lo- cis Scripturae certum est. Accedit, quod Apostoli controversiam & dubia mota e fundamento tolle- re discupientes, non modo non necessariam cir- cumcisionem, non necessariam legum ceremonia- lium observationem doceant, etsi nonnulla pro- pter scandalum vitandum pro ratione status istius Ecclesiae observari velint, quae nominatim expri- munt, quae vel ceremonialia erant, vel pro indiffe- rentibus quasi habeantur, sed etiam palam defi- niunt, non per legem, seu obedientiam legi praesti- tam servari quenquam seu Judaeum, seu gentilem natu, sed quicunque servantur, aut servati un- quam sunt, eos per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi servari, aut servatos esse: legem fuisse ju- gum ἀβάστακτον, quod neque patres portare potuere, neque nunc portari a quoquam possit, unde impos- sibile, per legis observantiam quenquam salutem consequi: sola fide purificari corda a peccatis, sola fide in gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi, passione scilicet & morte ejus partam, salutem obtineri, ut ita fides & justificatio, quae remissione peccato- rum, & cordis purificatione, qua sanguine JESU Christi corda nostra mundantur ab omni peccato, 1. Johan. 1. v. 7. describitur, & salus ac beatitudo aeterna constet: quia gratia Domini nostri JESU Christi salvari non possumus, nisi qua fide ean- dem apprehendimus, nostramque per fiduclalem apprehensionem facimus, Roman. IV. v. 25. Gal. II. v. 20. de quo S. Augustin. c. I. contr. duas Epist. Pelag. cap. XXI. Quantalibet fuisse virtutis anti- quos praedices justos, non eos salvos fecit, nisi fides mediatoris, qui in remissionem peccatorum sangui- nem fudit. Conf. B. Luther. comment. in Epist. ad Galat. 1538. in cap. III. Tom. IV. Jenens. Lat. fol. 68. & I. von den Conciliis und Kirchen Tom. VII. Jenens. Germ. nec non dissert. nostram de fide ve- terum pag. 31. Caeterum inter hos, qui sermoni- stus suis Antiochenos turbarunt, ut hoc obiter addam, fuisse etiam Cerinthum scribit Epiphanius haeres. XXVIII. de quo vid. diatribe de Haeresi Deitatem, & satisfactionem Christi abnegante.

## 15:2
Verse 2.

γενομένης ὖν σάσεως) arising from the exasperation of minds. Thus, in the Hebrew, it is sometimes translated as sedition, sometimes as provocation.

κὰι συζητήσεως ὐκ ὀλίγης τῷ Παύλῳ κὰι Βαρνάβα) These datives pertain to the discussion, not to the sedition. A necessity was imposed upon Paul and Barnabas of disputing with those men. Paul could have used those things which the prophets had said to Naaman, Nebuchadnezzar, and Cyrus.

The Vulgate omits the words ὼ συζητήσεως, which, however, are not omitted in the Greek codices and Oriental versions, as also in Chrysostom, and are necessary, lest the sedition be attributed to Paul and Barnabas.

ἔταξαν) the brethren, the whole Church.

πρὸς τὺς Ἀποσόλυς κό πρεσβυτέρυς) Although the Apostles had sufficient right in themselves, and gifts of God, and authority, they taught by their example that bishops should do nothing without the counsel of the presbyters, approving the praiseworthy custom of the Synagogue.

περὶ ζητήματος τύτυ) if any question arose among the Jews, from which there was a fear of schism, the Sanhedrin was approached, instructed by most learned men, and that according to the law which is in Deuteronomy XVII and following. Thus the Christians, when such a thing had arisen among them, went to consult at Jerusalem, where

Peter was there, and John and James, and perhaps also certain other of the Apostles and distinguished elders. What Jerusalem was then as a city, that Rome became after Jerusalem was destroyed, where there was a great abundance of learned men, both those who lived in the city and those who arrived there from elsewhere, so that a Roman Synod might to some extent contain within itself the force of a universal council (such as could not be held except under Christian Emperors, nor always even under them), and all the more so, because Bishops of other regions were also accustomed to be consulted by that Synod through letters.

Therefore, Presbyters are not to be excluded from Synods, nor are Synods or definitive votes in them to be restricted to Bishops alone, as the Papists wish, against whom it has been treated at length in the Critico sacro, page 895. Naturally, not only the Apostles gathered, but also the Presbyters, and indeed all of them for this purpose, that they might examine the controversy that had arisen at Antioch, not so that these at least might merely offer counsel, or, as the adversaries would rather have it, that they might serve with their ministry while others consulted and decreed, and they themselves decided and defined: but so that both these and those might look into that matter, or weigh it, and test it against the word of God. Furthermore, much is said to have been done there, a συζήτησις, and a disquisition, v. 7, not only among the Apostles, but also the Presbyters, and indeed the whole Church, or the communion present, until, with Peter speaking, and also Paul and Barnabas narrating the miracles divinely performed among the Gentiles, ἐσίγησε πᾶν τὸ πλῆθος, the whole multitude fell silent, v. 13. But after they had also heard James, who was bringing forth his opinion and confirming it with the Scriptures, then at last it seemed good not only to the Apostles, but also to the Presbyters, and not to these alone, but furthermore to THE WHOLE CHURCH, to send certain ones to Antioch, with Synodal letters established by all those present in the Council, with the persons to be sent, and written in the name, knowledge, consent, and votes of all, that Synodal Epistle, verses 22, 23. Therefore, not only the Apostles concluded in the Synod, but the Apostles and Presbyters σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, and neither regarding the question that had arisen, nor the persons destined for the embassy, nor the Synodal letters, is it held as the conclusion of the Synod what seemed good only to the Apostles, but what also seemed good to the Presbyters, and what seemed good to the whole Church; therefore, not only does Luke assert that it seemed so to all of them, or that it was thus judged and defined by all, but the Synodal letters themselves also testify to this, the beginning of which is, The Apostles, Presbyters, and brothers, verse 23; in the narrative, however, it is reported ἔδοξεν ἡμῖν γενομένοις ὁμοθυμαδὸν, It seemed good to us, having gathered WITH UNANIMOUS SENTIMENT, that is, we all thought together, having gathered, as the Syrian interpreter has it, v. 25, and again v. 28, it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us, namely, to all those aforementioned. Finally, lest any doubt remain, the Holy Spirit calls, Acts 16:4, those constitutions of the Synod δόγματα τὰ κεκριμένα, decrees, which were DECREED by the Apostles and Presbyters who were at Jerusalem. Therefore, not only the Apostles decreed, but all the Presbyters equally with them. But what Grotius adds for the sake of the Roman Catholics, both that the city of Jerusalem was once accustomed to be visited, and that Rome was subsequently held in that place, does not at all agree with history. What then, he says, was the city of Jerusalem, that Rome became after Jerusalem was destroyed, where there was a great abundance of learned men, both those who lived in the city and those who arrived there from elsewhere, so that a Roman Synod might to some extent contain within itself the force of a universal council (such as could not be held except under Christian Emperors, nor always even under them): and all the more so, because Bishops of other regions were also accustomed to be consulted by that Synod through letters. Although this first Council was held at Jerusalem, yet Synods were not tied to that place because of any dignity or holiness: but they gathered there because the controversy moved about the Jews was in the chief seat of the Jews; especially because the Apostles were present there, it had to be decided there. Now, if Peter was then the Bishop of Rome, should those things not have been decided at Rome instead? Furthermore, the reason for other Councils, whether celebrated at Rome or elsewhere, is not the same as this Jerusalem one. For the Apostles, directed by the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, presided over this one, which it is evident was neither permitted to nor happened to anyone after the departure of the Apostles. Nor indeed do the Tomes of the Councils teach that Councils were held at Rome after this first Apostolic Synod, but rather that they were more frequently celebrated outside of it. But it is said rashly that Roman Synods had the force of a universal Council above others, nor could it be proven by historical documents.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

γενομένης ὖν σάσεως) ex acerbatlone animorum orta. Ita רוב modo σάσις vertitur, modo παραπικρασμός.

κὰι συζητήσεως ὐκ ὀλίγης τῷ Παύλῳ κὰι Βαρνάβα) Hi da- tivi ad συζήτησιν pertinent, non ad σάσιν. Paulo & Barna- bae imposita necessitas, cum illis hominibus disputandi. Uti potuit Paulus iis, quae Prophetae dixerant Nehemani, Nabuchodonosori, Cyro.

Vulgatus verba ὼ συζητήσεως omittit, quae vero in Graecis codicibus & versionibus Orientali- bus, ut & apud Chrysostomum non omittuntur, & necessaria sunt, ne Paulo & Barnabae tribuatur seditio.

ἔταξαν) οἱ ἀδελφοὶ, tota Ecclesia.

πρὸς τὺς Ἀποσόλυς κό πρεσβυτέρυς) Apostoli quanquam in se juris satis haberent & donorum Dei, & auctoritatis, exemplo suo docebant Episcopos nihil agere sine presby- terorum consilio, probantes laudabilem Synagogae morem.

περὶ ζητήματος τύτυ) si qua inter Judaeos quaestio ori- retur, unde justus erat schismatis metus, adibatur Syne- drium, instructum viris doctissimis, idque ex lege qua est Deuter. XVII. & seqq. Sic Christiani, ubi tale quid inter ipsos ortum esset, ibant consultatum Hierosolyma, ubi

Petrus erat, & Johannes & Jacobus, forte & alii quidam Apostolorum & seniores egregii. Quod tunc fuit urbs Hie- rosolyma, id destructis Hierosolymis facta est Roma, ubi magna copia eruditorum, tum qui in urbe habitabant, tum qui aliunde eo adventabant, ita ut Synodus Romana con- cilii universalis, (quale nisi sub Imperatoribus Christianis haberi non potuit, nec sub illis semper) vim aliquatenus in se contineret, eoque magis, quod ab ea Synodo etiam alia- rum regionum Episcopi per Epistolas consuli solerent.

Non ergo Presbyteri excludendi à Synodis, non restringendæ Synodi aut suffragia definitiva in il- lis ad solos Episcopos, uti Papistæ volunt, contra quos in Critico sacro pag. 895. prolixe actum. Ni- mirum convenerunt non tantum Apostoli, sed & Presbyteri, & quidem omnes hi eo fine, ut de con- troversia Antiochiæ exorta dispicerent, non ut hi quidem saltim in medium consulerent, vel, quod potius volunt adversarii, ut ministerio suo infer- virent cæteris consultantibus, & decernentibus, illi autem deciderent, ac definirent: sed ut tam hi, quam illi de re illa viderent, vel eam expenderent, & ad Dei verbum exigerent. Adhæc multa dici- tur ibidem facta συζήτησις, & disquisitio v. 7. non solum inter Apostolos, sed & Presbyteros imo to- tam Ecclesiam, vel communionem præsentem, donec Petro loquente, nec non Paulo & Barnaba narrantibus de miraculis divinitus factis inter gentiles, ἐσίγησε πᾶν τὸ πλῆθος, conticuit univer- sa multitudo, v. 13. Postquam vero etiam Jaco- bum audivissent, sententiam suam proferentem & Scripturis confirmantem, tunc demum visum fuit non solum Apostolis, sed & Presbyteris, nec his tantum, sed insuper TOTI ECCLESIÆ, quos- dam ablegare Antiochiam, cum literis Synodicis constitutis ab omnibus in Concilio præsentibus, personis ablegandis, scriptaque nomine, scitu, consensu, & suffragiis omnium Epistola illa Syno- dica vers. 22. 23. Non ergo concluserunt in Syno- do soli Apostoli, sed Apostoli & Presbyteri σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, nec vel de quæstione exorta, vel de personis legationi destinandis, vel de literis Syno- dicis, quid visum solum Apostolis, sed quid etiam Presbyteris, quid toti Ecclesiæ, pro conclusione Synodi habetur; ideo non tantum Lucas ita omni- bus illis visum, seu ab omnibus sic judicatum & definitum esse asserit, sed ipsæ literæ Synodales id quoque testantur, quorum exordium est, Aposto- li, Presbyteri & fratres vers. 23. in narratione vero refertur ἔδοξεν ἡμῖν γενομένοις ὁμοθυμαδὸν, Visum est nobis coactis UNANIMI SENTENTIA, id est, cogitavimus omnes nos simul congregati, ut ha- bet Syrus interpres v. 25. & rursus v. 28. visum est Spiritus S. & nobis, sc. præmemoratis omnibus. Tandem, ne ulla supersit dubitatio, vocat Spiri- tus S. Act. XVI. 4. eas constitutiones Synodi δόγμα- τα τὰ κεκριμένα, placita, quæ DECRETA erant ab Apostolis, & Presbyteris, qui erant Hieroso- lymis. Non ergo decernebant soli Apostoli, sed juxta cum iis omnes Presbyteri. Quod vero Gro- tius in gratiam Romano - Catholicorum addit, tum quod adiri olim urbs Hierosolyma consueve- rit, tum quod deinde Roma eo loco habita sit, historiæ nequaquam convenit. Quod tunc, inquit, fuit urbs Hierosolyma, id destructis Hierosolymis facta est Roma, ubi magna copia eruditorum, tum qui in urbe habitabant, tum qui aliunde eo adven- tabant, ita ut Synodus Romana Concilii univer- salis (quale nisi sub Imperatoribus Christianis ha- beri non potuit, nec sub illis semper) vim aliqua- tenus in se contineret: eoque magis quod ab ea Synodo etiam aliarum regionum Episcopi per e- pistolas consuli solerent. Etsi autem Hierosolymis primum hoc Concilium habitum sit, non tamen ad locum illum ob dignitatem aut sanctitatem aliquam alligatæ fuere Synodi: sed convenere illic, quia de Judæis mota controversia in præcipua Judæorum sede; maxime quia præsentes ibi erant Apostoli, decidenda ibidem erat. Jam vero si Petrus Romæ tum fuit Episcopus, annon Romæ decidenda ea potius fuissent? Porro non eadem ratio aliorum sive Romæ eà celebrata, sive alibi, Conciliorum, quæ hujus Hierosolymitani. Huic enim præfuerunt Apostoli immediato Spiritus S. afflatu directi, quod post Apostolorum excessum nulli aut permissum fuisse, aut contigisse constat. Neque vero Concilia post primam hanc Apostolicam Synodum Romæ habita, sed frequentius extra eam celebrata esse, Tomi Conciliorum satis docent. Romanas autem Synodos præ aliis vim Concilii universalis habuisse temere dicitur, nec documentis Historicis probari potuit.

Thus also B. Luther rendered it: Others, however, think that they are simply said to have been sent by the Church, not also escorted for some distance. τὴν ἐπιστροφὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν) to God: Namely, of the Cornelius, the Antiochenes, the Cyprians, the Pisidians, the Pamphylians, the Lycaonians, the Lycians. κ᪀ ἐποίουν χαρὰν μεγάλην πᾶσι τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς) because of such great growth of the Church.
