## 15:10
Now therefore why do you test God) Why do you offend God? As above ch. 5:9, he who offends God tests His patience: but he offends who resists His will sufficiently revealed.

Indeed, they also test God who attempt to do something or impose upon others that which is far beyond their own strength and has not been commanded by God, such as that imposition of the yoke of the law and the observation of the commandments as necessary for obtaining salvation: Rightly the blessed Gerhard the elder: It is, however, to test God to depart from the word of God and to pervert by one's own rashness the order established by divine wisdom. This, therefore, Peter wishes to say. Those who urge the works of the law as necessary for salvation, these depart from the purpose of God, who, since He had brought the law for this reason, that through it they might be led to the acknowledgment of sin to seek the Mediator, they themselves change the counsel of God by their own rashness and audacity, and strive to be justified partly by the grace of God, partly by their own works.

ἐπιθεῖναι ζυγὸν ἐπὶ τὸν τράχηλον) this is said concerning servitude, as in Jer. 28:14. The Rabbis use it concerning a doctrine that inculcates that something must be done at all costs. See what we have said at Matt. 23:4. For the same thing the Rabbis say סרשׁ, that is, βαρύνειν, to which the contrary is קלל κουφίζειν, for teaching that something is not necessary.

ὃν ὔτε οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν, ὔτε ἡμεῖς ἰσχύσαμεν βαστάσαι) that is, we bore it, but with trouble, because of that huge number of ritual precepts, which you can see in Moses of Coucy; we are said to be unable, because it is very difficult, as in Matt. 6:24, Mark 1:45, Luke 11:7, John 6:60. He shows how hard it is for such a troublesome burden to be imposed on those whom God wishes to be free from it.

It is not dealing here only with ceremonial laws, but primarily also with moral precepts: 1. because the proposition of the state of the controversy was made generally, v. 5, ὅτι δεῖ περιτέμνειν αὐτὸς, παραγγέλλειν τε τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον Μωϋσέως: it is not dealing here with the ceremonial law alone, but generally with the law of Moses. Therefore, it is not appropriate to restrict these to the ceremonial law. 2. because the acceptance of circumcision brought with it the necessity of observing the whole law, Gal. 5:3. But those from the opposition were urging that. 3. because this must be explained according to the opinion and mind of the Pharisees, who indeed required for salvation the observation not only of the ceremonial, but primarily also of the moral law. 4. because Peter makes mention of faith alone regarding the purification of the heart, v. 9, so as to exclude the necessity of the works of the law and the observation of the precepts of the law: because they contribute nothing to the purification of the heart: since those are cleansed from all sin by the blood of Christ alone, apprehended by true faith, 1 John 1:7, Heb. 9:14. For faith and works, or the observation of laws, are opposed to each other in the article of Justification, Rom. 3:28. 5. because salvation is attributed to the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. But if it is by grace, then it is not by works, otherwise grace would not be grace, Rom. 11:6. 6. because the moral law is properly an ἀβάςακτον yoke, and can be fulfilled by no one after the fall, John 7:19, Rom. 3:19, 20, ch. 8:4. Ceremonial laws cannot properly be called such: because the Jews were indeed able to keep them: but there is no one who can fulfill the moral law completely. Which Grotius acknowledges, when he perverts the words of Peter with the Papists thus: He does not say IT IS IMPOSSIBLE, at least it is very difficult, not impossible: but that is δυσβάςακτον, difficult to carry, but the other is ἀβάςακτον, impossible to carry. Peter affirms not the former, but the latter concerning the law. Finally, Stapleton himself acknowledges in his antidotes, page 325, that because of the multitude of ceremonies attached to the moral law, the burden was difficult: Just as Christ himself, comparing the precepts of the ceremonial and moral law among themselves, calls these βαρύτερα, Matt. 23:23, Luke 11:24. Cf. Rom. 7:14 seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 10. νῦν οὖν τί πειράζετε τὸν Θεόν) Cur Deum offenditis? ut supra c. V. 9. qui Deum offendit, patientiam ejus tentat: offendit autem qui voluntati ejus fufficienter revelatæ obstrepit.

Imo tentant etiam Deum, qui conantur aliquid facere vel aliis imponere, quod longe supra ipsorum vires, nec à Deo mandatum est, qualis erat illa jugi legis impositio, & observationis mandatorum, ceu necessariæ ad consequendam salutem: Recte B. Gerhardus senior: Est autem tentare Deum discedere à verbo Dei, & ordinem divina sapientia fancitum propria temeritate pervertere. Hoc proinde vult Petrus dicere. Qui legis opera urgent, ut necessaria ad salutem, hi discedunt à proposito Dei, qui cum legem ideo tulisset, ut per eam ad agnitionem peccati deducti ad quærendum dum Mediatorem adigeremur, ipsi consilium Dei propria temeritate & audacia mutant, ac par- tim Dei gratia, partim ex operibus propriis justi- ficari satagunt.

ἐπιθεῖναι ζυγὸν ἐπὶ τὸν τράχηλον) dicitur hoc de servitu- te, ut Ier. XXVIII. 14. Rahbini usurpant de doctrina quæ aliquid omnino faciendum inculcat. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXIII. 4. dicunt pro eodem Rabbini סרשׁ, id est, βαρύνειν, cui contrarium est קלל κουφίζειν, pro docere ali- quid non esse necessarium.

ὃν ὔτε οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν, ὔτε ἡμεῖς ἰσχύσαμεν βαστάσαι) id est, tulimus, sed cum molestia, ob ingentem illum nume- rum præceptorum ritualium, quem videre potes apud Mosem de Kotzi; dicimur non posse, quod perdifficile est, ut Matth. VI. 24. Marc. I. 45. Luc. XI. 7. Ioh. VI. 60. Ostendit quam durum sit, onus tam molestum iis imponi, quos Deus ab eo velit esse liberos.

Non de ceremonialibus tantum legibus, sed imprimis etiam de moralibus præceptis hic agi- tur: 1. quia generatim propositio facta est status con- troversiæ, v. 5. ὅτι δεῖ περιτέμνειν αὐτὸς, πα- ραγγέλλειν τε τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον Μωϋσέως: non hic ceremoniali solum lege, sed generaliter de lege Mosis agitur. Non ergo convenit hæc ad legem ceremonialem restringere. 2. quia circumcisio- nis susceptio inferebat necessitatem observationis totius legis Gal. V. 3. At illam urgebant οἱ ἐξ ἐναν- τίας. 3. quia ex Pharisæorum sententia, ac mente hæc explicanda, qui vero non solum ceremonialis, sed imprimis etiam moralis legis observationem ad salutem requirebant. 4. quia solius fidei men- tionem facit Petrus, quoad cordis purificationem v. 9. ut excludat necessitatem operum legis, & ob- servationis præceptorum legis: quod ad purifica- tionem cordis ea nihil faciat: utpote quæ solo Christi sanguine vera fide apprehenso mundantur ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. v. 7. Ebr. IX. 14. Fides enim & opera, vel observatio legum sibi opponun- tur in articulo de Justificatione, Roman. III. v. 28. 5. quia gratiæ Domini nostri Jesu Christi tribuitur salus. Si autem ex gratia, utique non ex operibus, alioqui gratia non esset gratia, Rom. XI. 6. 6. quia lex moralis proprie est jugum ἀβάςακτον, & à ne- mine impleri potest post lapsum, Joh. VII. 19. Rom. III. 19. 20. c. VIII. 4. Ceremoniales leges ita vo- cari proprie non possunt: quia eas servare utique potuere Judæi: sed legem moralem nemo est qui implere ex asse possit. Quod agnoscit Grotius, quando cum Papistis verba Petri sic pervertit; Non dicit NON POSSE, perdifficile saltem est, non impossibile: at illud est δυσβάςακτον difficile portatu, aliud vero ἀβάςακτον impossibile portatu. Non illud, sed hoc de lege affirmat Petrus. Deni- que agnoscit ipse Stapletonus in antidotis pag. 325. propter adjunctam legem moralem ceremoniarum multitudinem onus difficile fuisse: Quemadmodum Christus ipse præcepta legis ceremonialis, & moralis inter se conferens hæc dicit βαρύτερα, Matth XXIII. v. 23. Luc. XI. 24. Conf. Rom. VII. v. 14. seqq.

## 15:13
V. 13. Ἀπεκρίθη) he began to speak as above in 3:12 and elsewhere.

Ἰάκωβος) Because Peter was no less accused on account of Cornelius than Paul was on account of others admitted to the Church: it was for James, who held the authority next to Peter, to speak the first opinion.

Latin:

V. 13. Ἀπεκρίθη) loqui cœpit ut supra III. 12. & alibi.

Ἰάκωβος) Quia non minus Petrus ob Cornelium, quam Paulus ob alios ad Ecclesiam admissos accusabatur: Iacobi, qui proximam Petro habebat autoritatem, erat primam sententiam dicere.

## 15:14
Vers. 14.

Συμεὼν) It is the Hebrew name שמעון Gen. 29:33, it is written in Greek letters Συμεὼν, as in Luke 2:8, with υ placed for Hirik, and ε for Scheva, but the Greeks used for it the Greek name of similar sound Σίμων, as in Sirach 50:1, Josephus, and our writers. But here Luke followed the Hebrew pronunciation, because he introduces a Hebrew speaking to Hebrews. The Syriac here and elsewhere expressed that name in the same way. They are mistaken who think this concerns that Simeon whom Luke mentions in the said chapter 2. James briefly repeats what was said by Peter.

Πρῶτον) namely in the person of Cornelius.

ἐπεσκέψατο λαβεῖν) A similar expression is in Jer. XXXII. 41,

κ̔, ἐπιστέψομαι τῶ ἀγαθῶσαι αὐτὺς, where in Hebrew וששתי עליהם להטיב אותם I will rejoice over them, by doing good to them.

ἐξ ἐθνῶν λαὸν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι ἁυτῦ) Before there were some among the nations who called upon God, and were called those who fear God, but they did not form a congregation.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Συμεὼν) Hebræorum nomen est שמעון Gen. XXIX. 33. id Græcis literis scribitur Συμεὼν, ut Luc. II. 8. posito υ pro Hirik, & ε pro Scheva, Græci vero pro eo usurparunt no- men Græcum soni similis Σίμων, ut Sirach. L. I. Iosephus & nostri scriptores. Sed hic Lucas Hebraicam pronuncia- tionem sequutus est, quia Hebraicam inducit loquentem Hebræis. Syrus & hic & alibi eodem modo id nomen ex- pressit. Errant qui de Simeone illo agi putant, cujus Lu- cas meminit dicto capite II. breviter repetit Iacobus à Pe- tro dicta.

Πρῶτον) nempe in persona Cornelii.

ἐπεσκέψατο λαβεῖν) Similis est loquutio Ier. XXXII. 41,

κ̔, ἐπιστέψομαι τῶ ἀγαθῶσαι αὐτὺς, ubi in Hebræo וששתי עליהם להטיב אותם gaudebo de ipfis, benefa- ciendo ipfis.

ἐξ ἐθνῶν λαὸν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι ἁυτῦ) Ante erant quidam in gentibus, qui Deum invocabant, & Dei timentes di- cebantur, sed cœtum non faciebant.

## 15:16
Verf. 16.

μετὰ ταῦτα ἀναστρέψω, κ̔ὶ ἀνοικοδομήσω τὴν σκηνὴν Δαβὶδ τὴν πεπτωκυῖαν κ̔ὶ τὰ κατεσκαμμένα αὐτῆς ἀνοικοδομήσω) A Hebrew expression, which signifies this: I will restore the collapsed house of David. For to the Hebrews every dwelling is called σκηνὴ, because that is the most ancient habitation. He wished to explain more clearly what the LXX translated thus: ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἀναστήσω τὴν σκηνὴν Δαβὶδ τὴν πεπτωκῦαν, κ̔ὶ τὰ κατεσκαμμένα αὐτῆς ἀναστήσω.

κ̔ὶ ἀνορθώσω αὐτὴν) in the LXX. in the same sense, closer to the Hebrew words: κ̔ὶ οἰκοδομήσω ἀυτὴν καθὼς αἱ ἡμέραι τῦ αἰῶνος. I will restore it, as it was of old. God promises less: He does more. For He restores the house of David in Jesus, and to a much greater splendor.

Latin:

Verf. 16.

μετὰ ταῦτα ἀναστρέψω, κ̔ὶ ἀνοικοδομήσω τὴν σκηνὴν Δαβὶδ τὴν πεπτωκυῖαν κ̔ὶ τὰ κατεσκαμμένα αὐτῆς ἀνοικοδομήσω) Lo- cutio Hebraica, quæ hoc fignificat: reponam domum Da- vidis collapfam. Nam Hebræis omne habitaculum σκηνὴ dicitur, quia ea habitatio vetustissima, Clarius explicare voluit quod fic verterunt LXX: ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ ἀναστή- σω τὴν σκηνὴν Δαβὶδ τὴν πεπτωκῦαν, κ̔ὶ τὰ κατεσκαμμένα αὐτῆς ἀναστήσω.

κ̔ὶ ἀνορθώσω αὐτὴν) in LXX. eodem sensu, propius ad verba Hebraica: κ̔ὶ οἰκοδομήσω ἀυτὴν καθὼς αἱ ἡμέραι τῦ αἰ- ῶνος. Restituam eam, qualis olim fuit. Deus minus pro- mittit: plus facit. Restituit enim domum Davidis in Iesu, & ad splendorem multo majorem.

## 15:17
Verf. 17.

ὅπως ἂν ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸν Κύριον) He added ἂν for the sake of purer speech, and Κύριον for the sake of greater clarity to the version of the seventy elders: for that which the Masoretes placed as אדום the seventy elders read אדם and took the singular for the plural: which is not rare where it concerns the whole genus.

κ̔ὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη ἐφ̓ ὇ς ἐπικέκληται τὸ ὄνομά μυ ἐπ̓ αὐτύς) These are word for word from the LXX. It appears the construction is according to the meaning, ἔθνη, ἐπ̓ αὐτὺς, as if he had said ἀνθρώπυς. Who are called by the name in Him, that is, who will be those who fear God. See what we said on Matt. V. 9.

λέγει Κύριος ὁ ποιῶν πάντα ταῦτα) These, says Amos, are the words of God Himself, who will also bring them to pass.

Therefore Amos c. IX. did not treat of Zerubbabel, but of Christ; not of the return from the Babylonian captivity, but of the spiritual reparation of the Church, to which the calling of the nations pertained. See what we said on Amos against Grotius. However, it does not sufficiently accord with the truth of God that He should perform something other than what He promises; if indeed the exactness of promises, or of prophecies, and the harmony of the fulfillment, or of the event, ought to be. Doubtless, that restoration of the house of David in the divine promise is to be understood conformably to other prophecies concerning the calling of the nations, which was to be to the Church of the Jews; which is promised everywhere in the O.T.

Latin:

Verf. 17.

ὅπως ἂν ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸν Κύ- ριον) addidit ἂν purioris sermonis, & Κύριον majoris per- spicuitatis causa ad versionem LXX. senum: pro eo quod Masoretici posuerunt אדום LXX. senes legerunt אדם & sumpserunt singulare pro plurali: quod non ra- rum est ubi de genere toto agitur.

κ̔ὶ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη ἐφ̓ ὇ς ἐπικέκληται τὸ ὄνομά μυ ἐπ̓ αὐ- τύς) Hæc verbotenus ex LXX. apparet constructionem esse κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον, ἔθνη, ἐπ̓ αὐτὺς, quasi dixisset ἀνθρώ- πυς. qui vocantur de nomine in eo, id est, qui erunt σεβό- μενοι θεόν. Vide quæ ad Matth. V. 9.

λέγει Κύριος ὁ ποιῶν πάντα ταῦτα) Hæc, ait Amosus, sunt Dei ipsius dicta, qui & ea dabit effecta.

Non ergo Amos c. IX. de Zorobabele, sed de Christo, non de reductione è captivitate Babylonica, sed de spirituali reparatione Ecclesiæ egit, ad quam vocatio gentium pertinebat. Vid. quæ ad Amo- sum contra Grotium diximus. Non autem Dei ve- ritati satis consonat, quod aliud præstet quam pro- mittat; siquidem vi illius exacta debeat esse pro- missionum, vel vaticiniorum, & complementi, vel eventus harmoniæ. Nimirum restitutio illa domus Davidis in promissione divina conformiter intel- ligenda est aliis vaticiniis de vocatione gentium, quæ ad Ecclesiam Judæorum futura erat; quæ pas- sim in V. T. promissa.

## 15:18
Ver. 18.

Known from eternity are to God all his works) It is no wonder that God in the times of Amos foreknew what he had decreed to do, and had prefigured it both by those things of which Amos treats, and by his own words being fulfilled more eminently in the times of the Messiah than ever before. When God gave a small land to the descendants of Jacob, when he allowed first ten, then two tribes to be scattered into distant shores, he was revolving something greater in his mind. He wished to be both known and worshipped more widely. In certain manuscripts and in that one in England it is γνωσὸν and ἔργον.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

Γνωσὰ ἀπ̓ αἰῶνός ἐσι Θεῷ πάντα τὰ ἔργα ἀυτῦ) Non mi- rum est Deum Amosi temporibus prænosse, quod facere decreverat, atque id præfigurasse tum rebus illis, de quibus agit Amosus, tum ipsius verbis eminentius implendis Mes- siæ temporibus, quam unquam ante. Deus cum exiguam terram dedit Jacobi posteris, cum primum decem, deinde duas tribus spargi sivit in oras longinquas, majus aliquid a- nimo agitabat. Volebat latius & nosci & coli. In Manu- scriptis quibusdam & illo in Anglia est γνωσὸν & ἔργον.

## 15:19
Ver. 19.

Therefore I judge) that is, I am of this opinion, in the way that Roman Senators concluded the delivery of their opinion. See the third, fifth, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, thirteenth, and fourteenth Philippics of Cicero, all near the end.

Not to trouble those from the nations who are turning to God) Unnecessary burdens were not to be imposed upon them, lest by such means the approach to Christianity might be precluded for many.

Latin:

Verf. 19.

Διὸ ἐγὼ κρίνω) id est, ita censeo, quomodo Romani Se- natores sententiæ dictionem concludebant. Vide Philippi- cam Ciceronis tertiam, quintam, octavam, nonam, deci- mam, undecimam, decimam tertiam, decimam quartam, omnes circa finem.

Μὴ παρενοχλεῖν τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν ἐπισρέφυσιν ἐπὶ τὸν Θεόν) Non imponendas illis molestias non necessarias, ne sic multis aditus ad Christianismum præcluderetur.

## 15:20
Ver. 20.

But to write to them) with that authority of which we spoke above. To abstain from the pollutions of idols) He does not think that the pious from the nations need to be admonished about those things which they had sufficiently learned: that God is to be worshipped, the one and true God, not false ones: that all reverence is to be shown to him: that one must abstain from murders, robberies, injuries, adulteries, and incests known by the law of nations: that justice is to be rendered to everyone: but he admonishes them about those things which seemed to admit of dispute, and which could offend the Jews and prevent the pious from the nations from coalescing with the pious Hebrews into one Church: among these, the first place is held by the pollutions of idols, that is, those things which are called below things sacrificed to idols, Mal. I. 7. in the Greek of the LXX it is, bread polluted, where Aquila and Symmachus have, defiled, Sirach XL. v. 33. he will pollute his soul with strange meats. See on Dan. I. 8. The writer of the Constitutions, which bear the name of Clement, VI. 12. explains pollutions by things sacrificed to idols. Christians, as Justin says while disputing with Trypho: every un-

ANNOTATIONS ON THE ACTS

and punishment even to the last death they endure for the sake of neither practicing idolatry nor eating things sacrificed to idols. And when Trypho had said that there were some who were called Christians and ate things sacrificed to idols, and said that the soul is not defiled by that matter, he says that they indeed usurp that name: but teach those things which are from the seducing Spirit, things sacrificed to idols, from which James wishes one to abstain, are of two kinds: the one, where at the very table a part of the bread and the entrails is cast into the hearth, (for that word is proper to this matter) and wine is sprinkled upon the fire, the name of some god being invoked for it: the other, where one who has performed sacred rites to the gods in a temple, signifying this to friends, calls them to the entrails, of which custom there is mention several times in Plautus. Theocritus to those traveling; - - - and having sacrificed this to the nymphs, Morson, send the fine meat immediately. Ovid Metam. XII. They brought their sacred rites: the rest of the part was given to the tables. To this pertains that of Juvenal: And to set birthday lard for a kinsman, with the addition of new meat, if the victim gave any. That part of the entrails which was given to the altar or hearth is called by the Greeks akrothinia, by the Latins prosecta or prosiciae: through that part the rest also were sacred to the gods. In whichever of these ways one might eat of things sacrificed, that matter is reckoned as idolatry. Tertullian on Idolatry: If I stand by having been called on account of a sacrifice, I shall be a participant in idolatry. In the same book: Therefore the Holy Spirit, the Apostles then consulting, relaxed the bond and yoke for us, that we might be free to avoid idolatry. And on the Crown: by a bare word the condition (that is, the creature of God) is polluted, as the Apostle teaches: but if anyone shall say, this is a thing sacrificed to idols, do not touch it. The same on spectacles: Nor do we eat of things sacrificed and offered to the dead. Among Minucius, Caecilius: You abhor foods taken beforehand and drinks tasted by the altars. Soon Octavius: We despise the remains of sacrifices and cups tasted by the altars. Clem. Alexandrinus Pædag. II. 1. Here one must be reminded also concerning those called things sacrificed to idols. How ever it is commanded that one must abstain from these: Those things seem to me foul and abominable, over which souls fly, with the blood of dead corpses. For the Apostle says I do not want us to become partners of demons. One must therefore abstain from these, being afraid. For there is no power in them; but because of our conscience, which is holy, and because of the abomination of the demons, to whom they are named, we loathe them. That one should abstain from things sacrificed to idols not simply because those things are made evil, but for just causes, says Origen against Celsus VIII.

and of fornication) among the precepts given to Adam and Noah the Jews do not place a prohibition of whoring; and those who were thought the wisest among the nations did not indeed deny that harlots act basely because they were harlots, as Ulpian speaks. L. idem D. de condit. ob turpem causam: and that there is a penalty in the very profession of the disgrace, as Tacitus speaks in Annals II, yet they did not think that those who used women already for sale sinned, as appears from the opinion of Cato which is in Horace, and the law of Solon, which Philemon praises in the comedy Delphis, in those verses which we have brought into the Excerpta, as also the verses of Eubulus in Nannius of a similar argument, to which can be added the Epigram of Argentarius, in Anthology III. 6. Cicero for M. Caelius dealing with this matter: For when has this not been done? When has it been censured? When has it not been permitted? But the law of Christ, commanding brotherly love toward all, does not allow anyone to use the baseness of another, and thus to foster it: since even the law of Moses had forbidden that way of life to all Hebrew women. Lactantius VI. 23. And it commanded that one must abstain not only from the beds of others, which it is not permitted to touch, but also from public and common bodies. It pertained much to those from the nations being associated with the Hebrews, if they saw that the girls of the Hebrews, in the praise of chastity, yielded nothing to the Hebrew girls: and that the men also tempered themselves from all lust outside of marriage.

Although it may be granted that abstinence from things sacrificed to idols and from whoring is commanded on account of the scandal of the Jews, lest they be deterred from the commerce of the nations: yet that communion with things sacrificed to idols, or even whoring, was not prohibited by Moses at last, much less by Christ, but that the law of nature itself dictated that one must abstain from all idolatry and whoring. Nor does Scripture know of the precepts which the Jews pretend were given to Adam and Noah, by which whoring was not prohibited: but concerning the nations, even the wisest, the Apostle teaches that they became fools, for the reason that they served the creature beside the Creator, and because knowing God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor give thanks, Rom. I. 21. seqq. Because therefore even the wisest among the nations did not think that those who used harlots sinned, from there the Apostles judged it necessary to prohibit this peculiarly, since whoring excludes one from the fellowship of the kingdom of God, equally as other grave sins, 1. Cor. VI. 9. 10.

and of things strangled and of blood) there were already long ago codices in which 'things strangled' was missing; there were also those in which after 'blood' was added both here and below in Epist. 29. 'and whatever they do not wish to happen to themselves, not to do to others.' But in most codices, and in all versions and among Origen lib. VII, against Celsus, and others, this is absent, but that is present. The former certainly pertains here, as we shall soon show, not the latter. For if anyone should wish to say that all the precepts of the Gospel are comprehended in this sum of words, he is mistaken, since the precept about worshipping one God through Christ, about the denial of self, and the undergoing of the cross, are not within this scope: other things also can only be referred here very obscurely. But it was asked from what things, besides crimes known to all, the uncircumcised ought to guard themselves, so that without offense to the Jews they might coalesce with the Jews into one Church. The law which is in Gen. IX. v. 4, given to the human race after the flood, which the Jews commonly interpret as not eating a limb of a living animal, the ancients understood as not eating flesh together with the blood of that flesh. Josephus makes this manifest in Antiquities I. 4, and the versions of the LXX, Aquila, and Symmachus. And the Babylonian Gemara on the title of the Sanhedrin says that Rabbi Ananias, son of Gamaliel, and certain others thought so. Nor does it stand in the way that the law permits the inhabitants to eat of an animal that died of itself to the uncircumcised, Deut. XIV. 21. For that could be done with the blood removed, no less than in those animals which were killed for the sake of food. This law, no less than others given to Adam and Noah, was observed for a long time by other peoples outside the Hebrew; until they lapsed into idolatry. Therefore the writer of the constitutions of Clement says that the pious are here referred to the imitation of Melchizedek, Job, and the like. In a later age, the observation of that law was reduced to the inhabitants of the land of Judea, who did not obtain the right of hospitality and friendship except under the condition of that law being observed among others: and to a few pious ones, who, although cohabiting with idolaters, nevertheless abstained from idolatry. But from the time when the Macedonians, and then the Romans, held Judea with supreme power, or Judea had kings subject to the Romans, the wise Jews, when they saw that they no longer had the right to compel the inhabitants to observe those things which had been commanded by God to Adam and Noah, found no other remedy, lest that license should creep to the Jews, than to keep the Jews away from all closer association with all the inhabitants (for the pious could no longer be distinguished from the impious). Hence that, μὴ συγχρᾶσθαι, μὴ συγκολλᾶσθαι, μὴ συνεσθίειν with such people: which you often have both in the sacred scriptures and in Josephus. After the Apostles began to gather a new Church from the precept of Christ, pious foreigners could now again, as of old, be distinguished from idolaters, by the very fact that they added themselves to the Church. But the reason why James wanted these called from the Gentiles to abstain from blood, this has been believed by the truer Christians, because they were not bound by the precepts of Moses, which had been given to the Israelites, nor by the law of circumcision, which bound only the descendants of Abraham, but they were not free from those things which God had commanded Adam and Noah, to which Christ added some things, and took away nothing. Tertullian. on Monogamy: And thus in Christ all things are recalled to the beginning, so that faith also has returned from circumcision to the integrity of that flesh, as it was from the beginning: and the freedom of foods and the abstinence from blood alone, as it was from the beginning: and the indivisibility of marriage, as it was from the beginning; and the prohibition of divorce, which was not from the beginning, and finally the whole man is recalled into paradise, where he was from the beginning: and in the book on Fasting: Likewise after the flood in the reformation of the human race it sufficed for a time to have one law to abstain from blood, with the use of other things permitted. Looking to this, Emperor Leo, where he forbids blood to be eaten stuffed into intestines, as if into tunics, says that both in the time of the old and the new grace, that matter was held to be wicked. And certainly the observation of that precept, just as it is not too superstitious, is easy, so the reasons are very honorable. For if we look at what is natural, peoples who use such food are accustomed to become brutalized, which has been observed especially in America: but if we look at what is moral, it is the best and most open signification that one must abstain from vengeance. For he who avenges himself is said to be fed by blood. Origen adds another reason, that demons were believed to be fed by blood. Nor did the ancient Christians accept this precept as if it were given for that one reason, that the offense of the Jews might be avoided. For if that were the case, they would not have observed that precept with certain danger to their lives, even where Jews were not present: but it is certain that they did this. Biblis, in Eusebius, History V. 1. πῶς ἂν παιδία φάγοιεν οἱ τοιῦτοι οἷς μηδὲ ἀλόγων ζώων αἷμα φαγεῖν ἐξόν; A witness also is Tertullian in the Apology: Let your error blush before the Christians, who do not even have the blood of animals in our edible feasts: who for that reason also abstain from things strangled and from carcasses, lest we be contaminated by any blood, either buried within the viscera. Finally, among the temptations of the Christians, you even bring forward sausages distended with blood, being most certain that it is illicit among them, by which you wish them to go astray. Furthermore, what kind of thing is it that you believe those whom you trust to shudder at the blood of cattle, to be panting after human blood? Octavius in Minucius: and we so much abstain from human blood, that we do not even know the blood of cattle as food. In the Apostolic canons, which book contains the most ancient customs of the Christians, we read: If any bishop, or presbyter, or deacon, or at all of the priestly list, eats meat in the blood of its soul, or that which is caught by beasts or dead of itself, let him be deposed; for the law has forbidden this; but if he be a layman, let him be excommunicated. Nor indeed was this observation included in the beginnings of Christianity, but it was transmitted with great solicitude to the following centuries. For the East, let the Synod of Gangra be a witness, Can. II. If any one eats meat, without blood and things sacrificed to idols and things strangled, with reverence and faith, let him be anathema if he condemns him as having no hope because of partaking. The Synod in Trullo, Can. LXVII, renewed this interdict, and Emperor Leo, as I just began to say, Novella LVIII. For the West, we have the testimony of the Synod of Worms under Louis the Pious c. LXV, and the letter of Pope Zachary to Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz: Adam of Bremen c. XX, and several books of penitentials, which impose canonical punishments on those who eat blood. And these things indeed concerning blood. But why is πνικτὸν added? Doubtless because the Greeks, and other nations, as we learn from Athenaeus in two places, were accustomed to have as a delicacy τὰ πνικτὰ, that is, meats in which the blood had been preserved with exact diligence, so that they might be cooked with that blood retained inside, which itself was also against the law concerning not eating blood. For this reason, there is also express mention of πνικτοῦ in the Synod of Gangra, as also of εἰδωλοθύτου, from this precept of the Apostles, of course. It may seem more strange that θνησιμαῖον is added in the so-called Apostolic Canon: and that Justin says, except meat in blood which is νεκριμαῖον, when, as we just showed from Deuteronomy, it was permitted to the pious uncircumcised to eat נבלה, which the LXX translate as θνησιμαῖον, which is the same as νεκριμαῖον, so that the Scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds interprets θνησιμαῖα as νεκριμαῖα: but this prohibition is to be understood concerning that which is dead of itself or even snatched by wild beasts (for the said canon also adds θηριόβρωτα) to which the undrained blood would adhere, as was usually the case. Tertullian in Apologeticus c. IV, when he had spoken about blood: for which reason we also abstain from things strangled and carcasses: which two he places as equals, and the Hebrew book called Chulin. The edicts concerning blood handed down in the law through Moses, I do not bring here, because they obligated no one, except Israelites, or those who voluntarily subjected themselves to the law. If the Church, out of reverence for the Apostles and antiquity, wishes to recall this Canon into use, I will not resist. Let superstition be absent, and let it be guarded against that, on purpose, a large quantity of blood, either in the meat or outside the meat, be preserved for the delicacies of diet. For that it was not rigidly observed concerning things strangled in Africa in his time, Augustine is a witness against Faustus XXXII. 13. And Zonaras, on the Gangrenous Canon, interprets blood as that which is boiled or coagulated on purpose. Balsamon: without intentional blood.

The discussion of our blessed Dorscheus on these matters explains. Hug. Grot. on Acts XV. 20, on blood and things strangled, published at Rostock 1665. Scripture has nothing concerning those laws of Adam and Noah. And it is doubtful whether all the precepts given to Adam and Noah obligated the nations perpetually, as the precept concerning sacrificing is an example, and whether the Apostles here wished the nations to be obligated to the precepts given to Noah, which Selden denies in book 7 de jur. natur. et gent. c. 72, because the laws given to the sons of Noah are said only to have made a proselyte of the gate, who could converse outwardly with the Jews, not a proselyte of righteousness, who would have been in the inner communion, of which account is taken here. Tertull. lib. de Monogam., written by him after he had fallen into the heresy of Montanus, as B. Rhenanus noted, and the abstinence from blood is falsely recounted among those things which were in the paradisiacal beginning: although it may be admitted that it was introduced at the beginning of sacrifices, Lev. XVII. 11. Nor does Tertull. de Jejun. teach that the law concerning abstinence from blood should have lasted perpetually. Leo's Novella arose from a sinister understanding of the Mosaic or Apostolic law: and it seems to have been issued so that the Jews might the more willingly pass over to the custom with the Christians. Experience did not teach that men were made more savage by the eating of blood. Americans eat raw meat with blood. Those desirous of vengeance feed their eyes, not their belly, with blood. But how could Origen's error concerning demons have given cause to the law? Nor is it sufficiently certain that the ancient Christians did not believe that that precept was given solely so that the offense of the Jews might be avoided: nor that they always determined that the eating of blood was forbidden in such a way, or that they abstained from divine interdict, not from Christian liberty. Can that also be licit or not licit which is such by human assent or consensus? See Acts II. 29, ch. XXI. v. 37, ch. XXII. v. 21. John XVIII. v. 31. They could have abstained because of the scandal of the Jews, who were dispersed throughout the whole world: or also so that the Christians might be the more separated from the Gentiles, because they did not abstain: and Tertullian notes in Apolog. that the Apostolic Canons are of no authority and that the first one seems suspect in many ways, as the blessed Dorscheus shows in the cited place. But the Gangrenous Canon does not say anathema to him who eats blood, but to him who takes away all hope of salvation from the one eating. See concerning Eustathius, Nicephorus book IX. Histor. Eccles. cap. 16.

Moreover, the Apostles prohibited the eating of things strangled and blood only for a time, until the minds of the Jews and Gentiles might coalesce, and the Synagogue might be buried with honor, because it was strictly forbidden to the Jews to feed upon blood or things strangled. Consult Augustine, Epist. IX, where it is taught that a triple time is to be observed in Mosaic ceremonies. One of life before the passion of Christ, in which they were necessary for the Jews by God's command, and ordained for the life of the pious, and flourished until John, Matt. XI. v. 13. Another of the struggle from John the Baptist, or the passion of Christ, to the plenary promulgation of the Gospel into the whole world, and the constitution of the Churches of the New Testament, in which they were free and near to death, or even dead, having no force for life, but not deadly, because according to the reason of the infirm they could be used without the operation of the mind and necessity. The third of death, from the time of the promulgated Gospel and the constituted Churches, when they were made and are to be considered deadly, as well as the rest, then especially those which pertained to shadowing forth the truth of the body in Christ, for the reason that he who wished them to be necessary would consequently deny that Christ had come in the flesh, Galat. V. v. 2, 3, & 4, Roman. X. v. 4, 5. Whence Blessed Gerhard notes that that custom lasted until the times of Tertullian, as is gathered from the book de Pudic.: and that Leo Imper. Constit. LVIII established penalties against those who provide blood stuffed into intestines for the belly: he rightly warned that this is contrary to Christian liberty, 1 Cor. X. 25. But why that Canon, the Jewish Synagogue now being buried, should be recalled into use, does not appear. It was prescribed by the Apostles only because of the state of that time, for the sake of avoiding scandal among the infirm, which reason now expires. Therefore those three heads are not said to be necessary in the same way: namely, because they were necessary for the peace of the Church, which then existed, on account of the infirm, but not always and everywhere necessary: however, the flight from fornication is simply necessary for all, therefore joined only to the others, because it was held by the Gentiles as a thing indifferent. Augustine, lib. XXXII. contra Faustum cap. 13. When that time had passed, he says, in which those two walls, one coming from circumcision, the other from uncircumcision, although they agreed in the cornerstone, nevertheless stood out more distinctly by their own certain properties: and where the Church of the Gentiles was made such, that in it no carnal Israelite may appear, who now among Christians observes this, so as not to touch thrushes or smaller birds, unless their blood has been poured out? Or does not eat a hare, if it was struck by hand on the neck and killed without any bloody wound? And those who perhaps still fear to touch these things are mocked by the rest. Beza's gloss on spiritual fornication, as departing from the letter of the Synod and the Synodal Epistle, deserves no consideration.

Latin:

Verf. 20.

Ἀλλ̓ ἐπισεῖλαι ἀυτοῖς) ea autoritate, de qua diximus supra. τῦ ἀπέχεσθαι ἀπὸ τῶν ἀλισγημάτων τῶν εἰδώλων) Non censet monendos pios ex gentibus de iis, quæ satis didicerant: Deum colendum, unum, & verum, non falsos: ei omnem exhibendam reverentiam: abstinendum à cædibus, rapinis, injuriis, adulteriis, & incestis jure gentium cognitis: jus cui- que reddendum: sed de iis monet quæ disputationem reci- pere videbantur, & quæ Judæos poterant offendere, & im- pedire quo minus pii ex gentibus cum piis Hebræis in unam Ecclesiam coalescerent: in his primum locum obtinet τὰ ἀλισγήματα τῶν εἰδώλων, id est, ea quæ infra vocantur ἐιδωλό- θυτα, Mal. I. 7. in Græco LXX. senum est, ἄρτυς ἠλισγημένυς, ubi Aquila & Symmachus, μεμολυσμένυς, Sirach. XL. v. 33. ἀλισγήσεσι τὴν ψυχὴν ἁυτῦ ἐν ἐδέσμασιν ἀλλοτρίοις. Vide ad Dan. I. 8. Scriptor Constitutionum, quæ Clementis nomen præferunt, VI. 12. ἀλισγήματα exponit per εἰδωλόθυτον. Chri- stiani, ut ait Justinus cum Tryphone disputans: πᾶσαν ἀδι-

ANNOTATA AD ACTA

κὶαν κὴ τιμωρίαν μέχρις ἐσχάτε θανάτε ὑπομένεσι περὶ τῶ μήτε εἰδωλολατρῆσαι μήτε εἰδωλόθυτα φαγεῖν. Et cum Trypho di- xiffet, effe quosdam qui Christiani dicerentur, & ederent εἰδωλόθυτα, dicerentque ea re animum non obstringi, dicit eos id quidem nomen usurpare: sed ea docere quæ sunt à Spiritu seductore, εἰδωλόθυτα, à quibus abstineri vult Jaco- bus, duum sunt generum: alia, ubi ad ipsam mensam pars de pane & extis in focum porricitur, (ea enim vox huic rei propria) & vinum igni inspergitur, Dei alicujus nomine in id advocato: alia, ubi qui diis in templo sacra fecit, id ami- cis significans,eos vocat ad exta, cujus moris apud Plautum aliquoties est mentio. Theocritus iter facientibus; - - - κὴ τὸ δὲ θύσας ταῖς νύμφαις Μόρσων καλὸν κρέας αὐτίκα πέμψον. Ovidius Metam. XII. Sacra tulere suam: pars est data cætera mensis. Huc illud pertinet Juvenalis: Et natalitium cognato ponere lardum Accedente nova, si quam dabat hostia, carne. Pars illa extorum quæ in aram vel focum dabatur, Græcis dicitur ἀκροθίνια, Latinis prosecta aut prosiciæ:per eam par- tem cætera quoque diis sacra erant. Utro horum modo- rum quis de immolatitiis edat, ea res idololatriæ deputatur. Tertullianus de Idololatria: Si propter sacrificium vocatus assistam,ero particeps idololatriæ. Eodem libro: Propterea Spiritus S. consultantibus tunc Apostolis, vinculum & ju- gum nobis relaxavit, ut idololatriæ devitandæ vacaremus. Et de Corona: verbo nudo conditio (id est, creatura Dei) polluitur, ut Apostolus docet: si quis autem dixerit, hoc idolothytum est, ne contigeris. Idem de spectaculis: Ne- que de sacrificato, & parentato edimus. Apud Minutium Cæcilius: Præcerptos cibos & delibatos altaribus potus abhorretis. MoxOctavius: Sacrificiorum reliquias & pocu- la delibata contemnimus. Clem. Alexandrinus Pædag.II.1. Ἐνταῦθα ὑπομνητέον κὴ περὶ τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων καλωμένων. ὅ- πως πότ᾽ ἄρα παραγγέλλεται ἀποχεσθαι δεῖν τέτων· Μιαρὰ δο- κεῖ μοι κὴ βδελυρὰ ἐκεῖνα, ὧν ἐφίπτανται, τοῖς ἅιμασι ψυχαὶ ὑπὲρ ἐρείσεις νεκύων κατατεθνειώτων. ὀ γὰρ θέλω ἡμᾶς κοινωνὲς δαιμονίων γίνεσθ᾿ ὁ ἈπόστολΘ λέγει. Ἀφοίκτεον τοίνυν τέτων ἐδεδιότας. Οὐ γὰρ ἐσί τις ἐν ἀυτοῖς δυνάμις· διὰ δὲ τὴν συνείδη- σιν τὴν ἡμετέραν, ἁγίαν ὖσαν, κὴ τῶν δαιμονίων διὰ τὴν βδε- λυρίαν, οἷς ἐπικατωνόμαται μυσαττομένες· Abstineri ab im- molatitiis non simpliciter,quod res illæ malæ sint factæ,sed ob justas causas dicit Origenes contra Celsum VIII.

κὴ τῆς πορνείας) inter præcepta Adamo & Noæ data Judæi non ponunt interdictum scortandi; & qui inter gentes pu- tabantur sapientissimi, non negabant quidem meretrices turpiter facere quod meretrices essent, ut loquitur Ulpia- nus. L. idem D. de condit. ob turpem causam: & pœnam esse in ipsa professione flagitii, ut loquitur Tacitus Anna- lium II. attamen non putabant peccare, qui fœminis ad- huc venalibus uterentur, ut apparet ex Catonis sententia quæ apud Horatium est, & Solonis lege, quam Philemon laudat in Comœdia Delphis, iis versibus quos in Excerpta retulimus, ut & Eubuli in Nannio versus paris argumenti, quibus addi potest Argentarii Epigramma, in Anthologia III. 6. Cicero pro M. Cælio hac de re agens: Quando enim hoc factum non est? Quando reprehensum? Quando non permissum? At lex Christi, dilectionem in omnes frater- nam imperans,non sinit,quenquam aliena uti turpitudine, & sic eam fovere: quippe cum & lex Mosis omnibus He- bræis fœminis id vitæ genus interdixisset. Lactantius VI. 23. Nec tantum alienis toris, quos attingere non licet,ve- rum etiam publicis vulgatisque corporibus abstinendum esse præcepit. Multum pertinebat ad illos ex gentibus cum Hebræis consociandos, si viderent Hebræis ipsorum puel- las, castitatis laude Hebræis puellis nihil concedere: viros quoque, sibi ab omni venere extra nuptias temperare.

Etsi concedi possit, abstinentiam ab Idolothytis & à scortationibus ob scandalum Judæorum man- dari, ne absterrerentur à gentilium commerciis: non tamen illa communio cum Idolothytis, aut etiam scortatio à Mose demum, nedum à Christo prohibita,quin ipsa lege naturæ dictante abstinen- dum fuerit ob omni idololatria,& scortatione. Ne- que de præceptis, quæ Judæi fingunt Adamo & Noæ data, novit Scriptura, quibus scortatio prohi- bita non fuerit: de gentilibus vero etiam sapientis- simis docet Apostolus, quod stulti facti sint, ideo quia creaturæ serviere παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα, & quia γνῶντες τὸν Θεὸν, ἐχ ὡς Θεὸν ἐδόξασαν, ἤ ἐυχαρί- στησαν, Rom.I.21.seqq. Quia ergo etiam sapientissi- mi inter gentes non putabant peccare,qui meretri cibus uterentur,indeApostoli necessarium judica- runt hoc peculiariter prohibere, siquidem scor- tatio excludat à consortio regni Dei, æque ut alia gravia peccata, 1. Cor. VI. 9. 10.

καὶ τῶν πνικτῶν καὶ τῶ αἵματος) fuere jam olim codices, in quibus deerat πνικτῶν; fuere & in quibus post αἷματος addi- tum & hic & infra in Epist. 29. καὶ ὅσα μὴ θέλωσιν ἁυτοῖς γε- νέσθαι ἑτέροις μὴ ποιεῖν. Sed in plurimis codicibus, inque ver- sionibus omnibus & apud Origenem lib. VII, contra Cel- sum, aliosq; hoc abest, illud vero adest. Est certe prius illud huc pertinet, ut mox ostendemus, non & alterum. Nam si quis dicere velit hac verboru summa comprehendi omnia Evangelii præcepta, fallitur, cum præceptum de uno Deo colendo per Christum, de abnegatione sui, & subeunda cruce, non sint intra hunc ambitum: alia etiam non nisi obscure admodum huc referri possint. Sed id quærebatur à quibus rebus, præter nota omnibus scelera, cavere sibi de- berent incircumcisi, ut sine offensa Judæorum cum Judæis in unam Ecclesiam coalescerent. Legem quæ est Gen. IX. v. 4. post diluvium datam humano generi, quam vulgo interpretantur Judæi de membro animalis vivi non eden- do, vetustiores intellexere de non edenda carne simul cum ejus carnis sanguine. Manifestum id facit Josephus antiquæ Historiæ I. 4. & versiones LXX. senum, Aquilæ & Symma- chi. Et sic sensisse Rabbinum Ananiam Gamalielis filium & aliosquosdam, ait Gemara Babylonica ad titulum de Sy- nedrio. Nec obstat quod incolæ incircumciso permittit lex morticino vesci, Deut. XIV. 21. Id enim fieri poterat de- tracto sanguine, non minus quam in eis animalibus, quæ victus causa occidebantur. Hanc legem non minus, quam alias Adamo & Noæ datas observavere diu populi alii extra Hebræum; donec ad idololatriam sunt prolapsi. Ideo scri- ptor constitutionum Clementis ait pios hic remitti ad imi- tationem Melchisedeci, Jobi & similium. Seriore ævo, le- gis illius observatio redacta est ad incolas terræ Judææ, qui non nisi sub conditione ejus legis inter cæteras observandæ jus hospitii, & amicitiæ impetrabant: & ad paucos pios, qui, quamvis idololatris cohabitantes, ab idololatria tamen se abstinebant. Ex quo vero Macedones, deinde Romani summo imperio Judæam tenuere, aut Judæa Reges habuit Romanis obnoxios, Judæi sapientes cum viderent, sibi ultra jus non esse cogendi incolas ad observanda ea quæ Adamo & Noæ præcepta à Deo fuerant, non aliud reme- dium, ne ista licentia ad Judæos serperet, invenere, quam ut ob omni propiore consuetudine, cum incolis omnibus (neque enim pii amplius ab impiis distingui poterant) Ju- dæos arcerent. Hinc illud, μὴ συγχρᾶσθαι, μὴ συγκολλᾶσθαι, μὴ συνεσθίειν cum talibus: quæ sæpe habes & in sacris scri- ptis, & apud Josephum. Postquam novam Ecclesiam ex Christi præcepto Apostoli colligere cœperunt, potuere jam iterum, ut olim, peregrini pii ab idololatris distingui, eo ipso quod se illi addebant Ecclesiæ. Causa autem cur Ja- cobus voluerit, hos ex gentibus vocatos abstinere à san- guine, hæc credita est à verioribus Christianis, quod illi Mosis quidem præceptis, quæ Israëlitis data erant, non te- nebantur, neque circumcisionis lege, quæ solos Abrahami obstringebat posteros, liberi autem non erant ab iis quæ Adamo & Noæ Deus præceperat, ad quæ addidit quædam Christus, dempsit nihil. Tertullian. de Monogamia: Et ædeo in Christo omnia revocantur ad initium, ut & fides reversa sit à circumcisione ad integritatem carnis illius, sicut ab initio fuit: & libertas ciborum & sanguinis solius abstinentia, sicut ab initio fuit: & matrimonii individuistas, sicut ab initio fuit; & repudii cohibitio, quod ab initio non fuit, & postremo totus homo in paradisum revocatur, ubi ab initio fuit: & in libro de Jejuniis: Æque post diluvium in reformatione generis hu- mani suffecisse unam interim legem à sanguine abstinendi, per- misso usu cæterorum. Huc respiciens Leo Imperator, ubi vetat sanguinem edi intestinis, velut tunicis, infarctum, ait tum veteris tum novæ Gratiæ tempore, rem illam habitam nefariam. Et certe præcepti illius, sicut observatio, non nimis superstitiosa, est facilis, ita causæ honestæ admo- dum. Nam si quod naturale est spectamus, solent quæ tali alimento utuntur gentes, efferari, quod in America maxi- me perspectum est: si vero id quod morale est, optima & apertissima significatio est, à vindicta abstinendum. Nam qui se vindicat, pasci sanguine dicitur. Addit Origenes aliam causam, quod Dæmones pasci sanguine crederentur. Neque vero Christiani veteres hoc præceptum accepere tanquam datum ea una ex causa, ut Judæorum offensa vitaretur. Nam si id esset, non observassent id præceptum cum certo vitæ periculo, etiam ubi non aderant Judæi: at hoc fecisse eos constat. Biblis, apud Eusebium, Historiæ V. 1. πῶς ἂν παιδία φάγοιεν οἱ τοιῦτοι οἷς μηδὲ ἀλόγων ζώων αἷμα φαγεῖν ἐξόν; Testis & Tertullianus Apologetico: Erubescat error vester Christianis, qui ne animalium quidem sanguinem in epulis esculentis habemus: qui propterea quoque suffocatis, & morticinis abstinemus, ne quo sanguine contami- nemur, vel intra viscera sepulto. Denique inter tentamenta Christianorum, botulos etiam cruore distentos admovetis, cer- tissimi scilicet illicitum esse penes illos, per quod exorbitare eos vultis. Porro quale est, ut quos sanguinem pecoris horrere con- fiditis, humano inhiare credatis? Octavius apud Minutium: tantumque ab humano sanguine cavemus, ut nec edulium peco- rum in cibis sanguinem noverimus. In canonibus Apostolicis, qui liber antiquissimos Christianorum mores continet, le- gimus: εἴ τις ἐπίσκοπος, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, ἢ ὅλως τοῦ καταλόγου τοῦ ἱερατικοῦ Φάγῃ κρέα ἐν αἵματι ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ, ἢ θηριάλωτον ἢ θνησιμαῖον, καθαιρείσθω; τοῦτο γὰρ ὁ νόμος ἀπεῖπεν· εἰ δὲ λαϊκὸς εἴη, ἀφοριζέσθω. Neque vero initiis Christianismi inclusa fuit hæc observatio, sed magna folli- citudine ad sequentia secula transmissa est. Pro Oriente te- stis sit Gangrensis Synodus Can. II. εἴτις ἐσθίοι κρέα, χωρὶς αἵματος καὶ εἰδωλοθύτου καὶ πνικτοῦ, μετ’ εὐλαβείας καὶ πίστεως, κατακρίνοι ὡς ἂν διὰ τὸ μεταλαμβάνειν ἐλπίδα μὴ ἔχοντα, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω. Renovavit hoc interdictum Synodus in Trul- lo, Can. LXVII. & Leo Imperator, ut modo cœpi dicere, Novella LVIII. Pro Occidente testimonium habemus Synodi Wormatiensis sub Ludovico Pio c. LXV. & Papæ Zachariæ epistolam ad Bonifacium, Archiepiscopum Mo- guntinum: Adamum Bremensem c. XX. & libros pœniten- tiariorum complures, qui sanguine vescentibus pœnas im- ponunt canonicas. Et hæc quidem de sanguine. Sed cur πνικτὸν additur? Nimirum quia solebant Græci, & gentes a- liæ, ut ex Athenæo duobus in locis discimus, in deliciis ha- bere τὰ πνικτὰ, id est, carnes in quibus exacta diligentia as- servatus erat sanguis, ut ita cum eo sanguine, intus retento, coquerentur, quod & ipsum erat contra legem de sanguine non edendo. Hæc de causa & in Gangrensi Synodo πνικτοῦ diserte sit mentio, ut & εἰδωλοθύτου, ex hoc scilicet Aposto- lorum præcepto. Magis mirum videri potest quod θνησι- μαῖον additur in Apostolico qui dicitur Canone: & quod Ju- stinus ait, πλὴν κρέας ἐν αἵματι ὅπερ ἐστι νεκριμαῖον, cum, ut modo ex Deuteronomio ostendimus, pio incircumciso li- cuerit edere נבלה, quod θνησιμαῖον vertunt LXX. quod idem est cum νεκριμαῖον, ita ut θνησιμαῖα apud Aristophanem Avibus Scholiastes interpretetur νεκριμαῖα: sed intelligenda est hæc prohibitio de morticino aut etiam a feris rapto (nam & θηριόβρωτα adjicit dictus canon) quibus adhæreret non deductus sanguis, ut plerunqne fieri solebat. Tertullia- nus Apologetico c. IV. cum de sanguine locutus esset: qui propterea quoque suffocato & morticinis abstinemus: quæ duo ut paria ponit & Hebræus liber dictus Chulin. Quæ sunt de sanguine edicta in lege per Mosem tradita, huc non adfero, quia ea nullos, nisi Israëlitas, aut qui sponte se legi subjicerent, obligabat. Hunc Canonem si Ecclesia, Apo- stolorum & antiquitatis reverentia, in usum revocare velit, non reluctabor. Absit superstitio, & id caveatur ne de in- dustria, magna sanguinis copia, aut in carne aut extra car- nem ad victus delicias asservetur. Nam rigide illud de suf- focato non observatum in Africa suo tempore testis est Au- gustinus contra Faustum XXXII. 13. Et Zonaras ad Gan- grensem Canonem, sanguinem interpretatur ἐξεπίτηδες ἑψόμενον ἢ πηγνύμενον. Balsamo: χωρὶς ἐπιτηδευτοῦ αἵματος.

Videnda de his B. Dorfchei nostri discussio ex- plicat. Hug. Grot. ad Act. XV. 20. de sanguine & suf- focato edita Rostoch. 1665. De legibus illis Ada- mi & Noæ Scriptura nihil habet. Et dubium est, an omnia Adamo & Noæ data præcepta perpetuo gentes obligarint, uti exemplo est præceptum de sacrificando, & an hic Apostoli ad præcepta Noæ data obligari gentes voluerint, quod negat Selde- nus l. 7. de jur. natur. & gent. c. 72. quia leges filiis Noæ datæ dicuntur tantum fecisse proselytum por- tæ, qui exterius cum Judæis conversari potuerit, non proselytum justitiæ, qui in interiori commu- nione, cujus hic ratio habetur, fuerit. Tertull. lib. de Monogam. scriptus ab illo in hæresin Monta- ni prolapso, ut notavit B. Rhenanus, & falso san- guinis abstinentia recensetur inter ea, quæ in initio paradisíaco fuerunt: etsi initio sacrificiorum in- troductorum fuisse, admitti possit, Lev. XVII. 11. Neque Tertull. de Jejun. docet, legem de absti- nentia sanguinis perpetuo durare debuisse. Leonis Novella ex sinistro legis Mosaicæ, aut Apostolicæ intellectu orta: & lata videtur, ut eo lubentius Judæi ad consuetudinem cum Christianis trans- irent. Sanguinis esu efferatiores homines factos esse, non docuit experientia. Americani crudo car- vescuntur sanguine. Vindictæ cupidi oculos non ventrem sanguine pascunt. Origenis autem error de Dæmonibus quomodo legi potuit causam dare? Neque id satis constat, Christianos veteres haud credidisse præceptum illud unice datum, ut Judæorum offensa vitaretur: nec quod semper statuerint vetitum taliter sanguinis esum esse, aut quod abstinuerint ex interdicto divino, non e libertate Christiana. Num ἔξὸς licitum etiam id esse, aut non licitum potest, quod tale est ex as- sensu humano, aut consensu. Vid. Actor. II. 29. cap. XXI. v. 37. cap. XXII. v. 21. Iohan. XVIII. v. 31. Potuere abstinere ob scandalum Judæorum, qui per totum orbem dispersi: aut etiam ut eo magis à gentilibus separarentur Christiani, quia illi non abstinebant: & notat Tertullianus in Apolog. Ca- nones Apostolicos nullius autoritatis esse & pri- mus ille multis modis suspectus esse videtur, o- stendente l. c. B. Dorscheo. Canon vero Gangrenus non dicit anathema illi, qui sanguinem comedit, sed qui comedenti omnem spem salutis adimit. Vid. de Eustathio Nicephorus lib. IX. Histor. Eccles. cap. 16.

Cæterum suffocatum & sanguinem non nisi ad tempus Apostoli prohibuerunt comedere, donec coalescerent animi Judæorum, & gentilium, & Synagoga cum honore sepeliretur, quia Judæis severe interdictum erat, ne sanguine aut suffoca- to vescerentur. Cons. Augustin. Epist. IX. ubi do- cetur, triplex in ceremoniis Mosaicis observan- dum esse tempus. Unum vitæ ante Christi passio- nem, in quo erant Judæis ob Dei mandatum ne- cessariæ, & ad vitam piorum ordinatæ, vigebant- que usque ad Johannem, Matth. II. v. 13. Alterum agonis à Johanne Baptista, vel passione Christi ad plenariam Evangelii in orbem universum pro- mulgationem, Ecclesiarumque Novi Testamenti constitutionem, in quo erant liberæ ac mortuis vi- cinæ, vel etiam mortuæ, nullam vim ad vitam ha- bentes, sed non mortiferæ, quia pro ratione infir- morum poterant usurpari citra operationem mentis & necessitatis. Tertium mortis, à tempore promulgati Evangelii & constitutarum Ecclesia- rum, quando factæ & censendæ sunt mortiferæ cum reliquæ, tum imprimis illæ, quæ ad verita- tem corporis in Christo adumbrandam pertine- bant, eo quod qui illas necessarias esse volebat, consequenter Christum in carnem venisse nega- ret, Galat. V. v. 2. 3. & 4. Roman. X. v. 4. 5. Unde B. Gerhardus notat consuetudinem illam durasse usque ad Tertulliani tempora, ut ex libro de Pu- dic. colligitur: & quod Leo Imper. Constit. LVIII. pœnas in eos statuerit, qui intestinis tunicis san- guinem infarctũ ventri præbeant: id adversari libertati Christianæ recte monuit ille 1. Cor. X. 25. Cur autem Canon ille Judaica Synagoga jam se- pulta in usum revocandus sit, non apparet. Ob temporis istius statum præscriptus solum ab Apo- stolis fuit, evitandi scandali penes infirmos causa, quæ ratio jam expirat. Tria ergo illa capita neces- saria dicuntur non eodem modo: nimirum quia ad pacem Ecclesiæ, quæ tunc erat, necessaria fuere pro- pter infirmos, non autem semper & ubique necessa- ria: scortationis autem fuga simpliciter necessa- ria est omnibus, ideo cæteris solum juncta, quia à gentibus habebatur pro re adiaphora. Augustin. lib. XXXII. contra Faustum cap. 13. Transacto, in- quit, illo tempore, quo illi duo parietes, unus ex circumcisione, alter ex præputio venientes, quam- vis in angulari lapide concordarent, tamen suis quibusdam proprietatibus distinctius eminebant: & ubi Ecclesia gentium talis effecta est, ut in ca nullus Israëlita carnalis appareat, quis jam hoc Christianus observat, ut turdos vel minu- tiores aviculas non attingat, nisi quarum san- guis effusus est? aut leporem non edat, si manu à cervice percussus nullo cruento vulnere occisus est? & qui forte pauci adhuc tangere ista for- midant, à cæteris irridentur. Glossa Bezæ de scortatione spirituali, utpote à litera discedens Synodi, & Epistolæ Synodicæ, nullum meretur calculum.

## 15:21
Verse 21.

For Moses from ancient generations has in every city those who preach him in the synagogues, being read every Sabbath. The sense here seems to me to be by way of anticipation. For as far as Moses is concerned, those who are from the Jews cannot complain that he is despised by the foreigners of our flock, since in our assemblies, no less than in the Jewish ones, Moses is read, just as has been done from of old, and indeed on Sabbaths. By the name of synagogues, the churches of the Christians also come, as also in James II, verse 2. In Theophilus of Antioch, 'synagogues are called churches.' It is an ancient custom of Christians, which remained for a very long time in the East, to assemble no less on the Sabbath than on the Lord's days. Clement, Constitutions VII. 24: 'Celebrate the Sabbath and the Lord's day; for the one is a memorial of creation, the other of the resurrection.' He has similar things in VIII. 33 and 67. Asterius, Bishop of Amasea, in his homily on divorce, calls the Sabbath and the Lord's day a 'beautiful pair.' Gregory of Nyssa calls them 'sister days.' Balsamon: 'By the holy fathers, the Sabbaths were made equal to the Lord's days in almost everything,' therefore Constantine forbade Christians from working on the Sabbath no less than on the Lord's day, as Eusebius testifies. Hence also arose that custom, that just as on the Lord's days, as days of joy, one did not fast, as the Synod of Gangra teaches in Canon XVIII, so neither on the Sabbaths, except for one before Easter. Thus Zonaras interprets 'feasts' in the Apostolic Canon 53. Ignatius to the Philippians: 'If anyone fasts on the Lord's day or the Sabbath, except for one Sabbath, he is a murderer of Christ.' Tertullian, in his work on fasting, says the Sabbath should never be fasted except at Easter; and also against Marcion IV, he says the privilege granted to the Sabbath from the beginning of the world is a pardon from fasting. Wherefore, when Justin and Tertullian deny that those fathers before Moses kept the Sabbath, this is to be understood not of assemblies, but of rigid idleness throughout the whole day. Ignatius to the Magnesians: 'Let us no longer keep the Sabbath in a Jewish manner, delighting in idleness.' However, on the Sabbaths in those first Christian assemblies, the Gospels were not read, but the parashah of Moses, exactly as among the Judaizing Jews. The Synod of Laodicea first changed this, and willed that the Gospels, no less than the ancient scriptures, be read on Sabbaths in Canon XIX. The custom still remains from of old among Christian churches that on the Sabbath before Easter the history of the creation is read, exactly as among the Hebrews. James therefore says that in this part the Jews have nothing to complain about, since in every city where there were assemblies of Christians, Moses was read on the Sabbaths 'from ancient generations,' that is, as of old, with nothing changed in this custom. It is believed to have been instituted by Moses that the law should be read on the Sabbath. 'To preach' is to pronounce with a loud voice, as in Exodus XXXII. 5, Matthew III. 1, and often elsewhere.

What Grotius's opinion was regarding the idleness on the Sabbath day not observed of old, and what should be thought of it, we have already explained in the Annotations on Exodus XX. The other historical matters are not uselessly observed. Yet that reason for the mention of the reading of Moses made here, which Grotius provides, is not necessary: rather, the blessed Gerhard more correctly says, 'The reason is given,' he says, 'why the Gentiles ought to conform themselves to the Jews in abstinence from blood and things strangled, namely because they were already accustomed to ceremonial laws of old, and because every Sabbath the Mosaic law is still read in their own synagogues.'

PART II. The sending, reception, and dismissal of the envoys to the brothers at Antioch with the Synodal letters.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Μωσῆς γὰρ ἐκ γενεῶν ἀρχαίων κατὰ πόλιν τὺς κηρύσσοντας αὐτὸν ἔχει ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινω- σκόμενον) Sensus mihi hic videtur esse per ἀνθυποφορὰν. Nam quod ad Mosen attinet, non possunt qui ex Judæis sunt queri eum sperni ab alienigenis nostri gregis, quando in nostris non minus quam in Judaicis conventibus, Moses, ita ut ab antiquo factum est, legitur, & quidem Sabbatis. Συνα- γωγῶν nomine veniunt etiam Christianorum Ecclesiæ, ut & Jacobi II. vers. 2. Theophilo Antiocheno, Συναγωγαὶ αἱ καλέμεναι ἐκκλησίαι Christianorum mos vetus, qui diutis- sime mansit in Oriente, convenire non minus Sabbati quam Dominicis diebus. Clemens Constitutionum VII. 24. τὸ σάββατον μέν τοι καὶ τὴν κυριακὴν ἑορτάζετε· ὅτι τὸ μὲν δη- μιεργίας ἐστιν ὑπόμνημα, ἡ δὲ ἀναστάσεως. Paria habet VIII. 33. & 67. Asterius Amaseæ Episcopus in homilia de repudio: καλὴν συνωρίδα vocat σαββάτυ καὶ τῆς κυριακῆς. Gregorius Nys- senus ἡμέρας ἀδελφάς. Balsamo: παρὰ τῶν ἁγίων πατέρων ἐξι- σώθησαν δι’ ὅλε χεδὸν ταῖς κυριακαῖς τὰ σάββατα, ideo Con- stantinus Christianos non minus in Sabbatum, quam in diem Dominicum vadari vetuit, teste Eusebio. Hinc etiam ortum illud, ut sicut diebus Dominicis tanquam lætitiæ diebus non jejunabatur, sicut docet Gangrensis Synodus Canone XVIII. ita nec Sabbatis, excepto uno ante Pascha. Sic ἑορτὰς interpretatur Zonaras ad Canonem Apostoli- cum 53. Ignatius ad Philippenses εἴτις κυριακὴν ἢ σάββα- τον νησεύει, πλὴν ἑνὸς σαββάτε, χρισοκτόνος ἐστι. Sabbatum nunquam nisi in Pascha jejunandum ait Tertullianus de jejuniis: qui & adversus Marcionem IV. privilegium do- natum Sabbato à primordio mundi, dicit, veniam jeju- nii. Quare cum Justinus, & Tertullianus patres illos an- te Mosem negant sabbatizasse, id intelligendum, non de conventibus, sed de rigido per totum diem otio. Ignatius ad Magnesios : μηκέτι ὦν σαββατίζωμεν Ἰδαϊκῶς ἀργίαις χαίροντες. Sabbatis autem in illis primorum Christiano- rum conventibus, non Evangelia legebantur, sed Mosis פרשת, plane ut apud Judæos Judaizantes. Primo id mutavit Synodus Laodicena, voluitque Sabbatis Evange- lia non minus, quam veteres scripturas legi Canone XIX. Manet & nunc ex antiquo mos apud Christianas Ecclesias, ut in Sabbato ante Pascha legatur historia creationis, pla- ne ut apud Hebræos. Dicit ergo Jacobus hac in parte non habere quod querantur Judæi, cum in singulis urbibus, ubi conventus erant Christianorum, in Sabbatis legeretur Moses ἐκ γενεῶν ἀρχαίων, id est, ut olim, nihil in hoc im- mutato more. Creditur à Mose fuisse institutum ut lex in Sabbato legeretur. κηρύσσειν, est alte voce pronuntiare, ut Exodi XXXII. 5. Matth. III. 1. & alibi sæpe.

Quæ de otio in die Sabbati olim non observato sententia fuerit Grotio, & quid de ea habendum, in Annotat. ad Exod. XX. jam exposuimus. Cæte- ra historica non inutiliter observata. Nec tamen illa ratio mentionis lectionis Mosis hic factæ, quam Grotius reddit, necessaria est: imo rectius B. Gerhardus, Redditur, inquit, ratio, quare gen- tiles Judæis in abstinentia à sanguine & suffocato se- se conformare debeant, quia scilicet jam olim legibus ceremonialibus assueverunt, & quia singulis Sab- batis lex Mosaica in ipsorum Synagogis adhuc le- gitur.

PARS II. Legatorum ad Antiochenos fratres cum li- teris Synodicis destinatio, susceptio & dimissio.

## 15:22
Verse 22.

Then to the Apostles and the elders) See above II. 'With the whole church') They approve the opinion of the Apostles and elders. Thus the laity used to subscribe to the Acts of Synods in this way: 'consenting, I have subscribed.' See below XVI. 4, where only the Apostles with the elders are named.

Therefore, neither Presbyters nor even the Laity are excluded from Synods and their subscription, as the Papists contend. But Bellarmine urges in Book I on Councils, chapter 16, that only the Apostles and Presbyters were called, which he says is evident from the fact that it is said: 'The Apostles and Elders came together to consider this matter,' with no mention made of the people. Then, that both the Apostles and the Elders spoke while the controversy was being discussed, he gathers from those words ('and when there had been much disputation'), but that only the Apostles spoke the definitive sentences after the disputation, he elicits from the fact that only Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and James are introduced by Luke as speaking. But the context easily refutes these little arguments. For if those words are to be taken exclusively, 'The Apostles and Elders came together,' so that the people are excluded because there is no mention of them, it would have to be said that the people did not even come together, not just that they were not summoned. But that the common people were present is testified most evidently by the account of Luke, and Bellarmine himself concedes it. Wherefore the multitude of the common people cannot be excluded by these words, but with the more important ones named, the others are connoted. Furthermore, that great discussion held in this Council is rashly restricted by Bellarmine to the Apostles and Presbyters; it is more ineptly gathered from the words, when a great discussion was taking place, that the same was held by the Apostles and Presbyters alone. For why? Perhaps it was great because it was by men of great authority, such as they were! Nay, Luke says a great discussion was held: therefore if it is to be gathered in that way, it was held by the multitude of the common people. Which is certainly more sure, because afterwards the whole multitude is said to have kept silent, and to have listened to Barnabas and Paul. Wherefore it had spoken before, and at the same time conferred opinions. There is also no doubt that a disputation was held with the Pharisees and converted Jews as the opposing party. For some are said to have risen up from the heresy of the Pharisees, who had believed, or had been converted to Christ, saying that it was necessary for them to be circumcised, and to command them to observe the law of Moses, v. 5. Since therefore the assembly was held ἰδεῖν περὶ τοῦ λόγου, that it might be examined concerning this word, or concerning this matter, who will doubt that those who were then present at Jerusalem, and were stirring up this controversy, were heard and admitted to the discussion? Among the Apostles and Presbyters themselves, there does not seem to have been need for such a laborious discussion: but because a great and many-sided συζήτη- σις was held, it is permitted to gather that the Pharisees contended with them, and attempted to defend their own cause. Which equity itself also teaches, and the custom of Synods confirms, in which it is most well known that the opposing party is accustomed to be heard. Therefore also Peter, having heard their disputation, refuted them, and contradicted them to their face and in their presence. Why therefore do you tempt God? verse 10. Finally, that the Apostles, who are introduced speaking after the disputation, gave a definitive sentence, and indeed alone, for the reason that they alone are introduced by Luke as speaking, that is entirely ἀνακόλουθον, because neither were their opinions definitive, just as the adversaries indeed make the sentences definitive, nor are the Presbyters or others of the common people present excluded from the conclusion and definitive sentence of the Synod, but are expressly included, as has been shown. Therefore, to speak here is not the same as to pass a decisive sentence. Barnabas and Paul are also reported to have spoken, but did they pass a definitive sentence? Bellarmine indeed says so, but Luke contradicts this, reporting only that they recounted the miracles done among the Gentiles. The Petrine speech also is not so much a definitive conclusion as a commemoration concerning the calling of the Gentiles, and a conviction of the opposing party concerning the ἀδυναμίᾳ of fulfilling the law. James, however, finally uses the word for judging, and the conclusion is attributed to him, not to Peter, not to others. But will the Papists say that the rest of the Apostles were excluded from the definitive sentence because of that? Wherefore, is it not more correctly gathered from the conclusion of the Synod commemorated by Luke, and the tenor of the Synodal letters, who made the Synodal decree? Namely, not the Apostles alone, nor the Presbyters only with the Apostles, but the Apostles and Presbyters σὺν ὄλῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ with the whole Church, or the remaining multitude.

Judas called Barsabas) The brother of that Joseph of whom above I. 23.

and Silas) He was among the first of the Christians at Jerusalem, also called Silvanus, as we noted above XIII. 9.

Leading men among the brethren) Eminent men ראשים.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Τότε Ἀποστόλοις τὺ τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις) Vide supra II. σὺν ὅλη τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ) Approbant Apostolorum & pres- byterorum sententiam. Sic Laici Synodorum Actis sub- scribebant, hoc modo: consentiens subscripsi. Vide in- fra XVI. 4. ubi soli Apostoli cum presbyteris nominan- tur.

Non exclusi ergo vel Presbyteri, vel etiam Laici a Synodis, earumque subscriptione, quod conten- dunt Papistae. At urget Bellarm. l. I. de Concil. c. 16. quod Apostoli tantum & Presbyteri vocati sint, quod ex eo patere ait, quod dicatur: Conveniant A- postoli, & Seniores videre de verbo hoc, nulla facta plebis mentione. Deinde quod tam Apostoli, quam Seniores loquuti sint, donec discutiebatur contro- versia, colligit ex verbis illis (& cum magna dis- quisitio fieret) quod vero post disquisitionem soli Apostoli sententias definitivas dixerint, ex eo eli- cit, quod soli Petrus, Paulus, Barnabas & Jacobus introducantur a Luca loquentes. Verum facile has ratiunculas discutit contextus. Si enim verba illa exclusiue accipienda sunt, Convenerunt Apostoli & Seniores, ita ut plebs excludatur, quia ejus nulla sit mentio, ne convenisse quidem plebem dicendum erit, non tantum, haud convocatum esse. At in- terfuisse plebem & relatio Lucae testatur eviden- tissime, & concedit ipse Bellarminus. Quo circa non excludi potest istis verbis multitudo plebis, sed potioribus nominatis, caeteri connotantur. Porro disquisitio illa magna facta in hoc Concilio, teme- re restringitur a Bellarm. ad Apostolos, & Presby- teros; ineptius colligitur ex verbis, cum fieret ma- gna disquisitio, eandem a solis Apostolis & Pres- byteris factam. Quid enim? an forte ideo magna, quod a magnae autoritatis viris, quales illi fuere! Imo multam disquisitionem factam dicit Lucas: Ergo si ita colligendum, a multitudine plebis facta. Quod utique certius, quia postea conticuisse di- citur multitudo universa, & Barnabae ac Paulo au- scultasse. Quocirca loquuta erat antea, simulque contulit sententias. Disceptationem quoque fa- ctam cum Pharisaeis & Judaeis conversis ceu parte adversa, nullum dubium est. Surrexisse enim di- cuntur nonnulli de haeresi Pharisaeorum, qui cre- diderant, seu conversi erant ad Christum, dicen- tes, quod oporteat eos circumcidi, & jubere ob- servare legem Mosis, v. 5. Quum ergo conventus celebratus sit ἰδεῖν περὶ τοῦ λόγου, ut dispiceretur de hoc sermone, vel de hac re, quis ambiget, illos, qui tum praesentes erant Hierosolymis, & controver- siam hanc movebant, auditos, & ad disquisitio- nem admissos fuisse? Inter ipsos certe Apostolos, & Presbyteros tam operosa disquisitione non vi- detur opus fuisse: sed quia multa & magna συζήτη- σις facta, colligere licet, contendisse cum iisdem Pharisaeos, causamque suam propugnare conatos esse. Quod etiam aequitas ipsa docet, & consuetudo Synodorum confirmat, in quibus partem adver- sam audiri solitam, notissimum. Ideo etiam Petrus audita eorum disceptatione ipsos redarguit, iisque coram & in os contradicit. Quid ergo tentatis Deum? vers. 10. Tandem quod Apostoli, qui post disputationem loquentes introducuntur, senten- tiam definitivam dixerint, & quidem soli, eo quod soli a Luca introducantur loquentes, id prorsus ἀνακόλουθον, quia nec illorum sententiae fuere defi- nitivae, prouti quidem adversarii definitivas faciunt sententias, nec excluduntur a conclusione & defi- nitiva sententia Synodi Presbyteri vel caeteri, de ple- be praesentes, sed diserte includuntur, ut osten- sum. Non ergo idem est hic loqui, & sententiam ferre decisivam. Barnabas, & Paulus loquuti e- tiam referuntur, sed an sententiam tulerunt defi- nitivam? Id quidem Bellarminus dicit, at con- tradidit Lucas, qui refert tantum eos enarrasse miracula inter gentes facta. Petrina quoque ora- tio non tam definitiva conclusio est, quam com- memoratio de gentium vocatione, & partis adver- sæ convictio, de ἀδυναμίᾳ implendi legem. Jaco- bus autem demum utitur verbo judicandi, eique tribuitur conclusio, non Petro, non aliis. Num autem inde cæteros Apostolos exclusos à definiti- va sententia dicent Pontificii? Quocirca rectius è conclusione Synodi à Luca commemorata, & tenore literarum Synodalium colligitur, quinam decretum fecerint Synodale? Nempe non soli Apostoli, nec Presbyteri tantum cum Apostolis, sed Apostoli & Presbyteri σὺν ὄλῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ cum tota Ecclesia, seu multitudine reliqua.

Ἰύδαν τὸν ἐπικαλύμενον Βαρσαβᾶν) Fratrem illius Josephi de quo supra I. 23.

κὴ Σίλαν) Fuit hic inter primos Christianorum Hieroso- lymis, dictus & Silvanus, ut notavimus supra XIII. 9.

Ἄνδρας ἡγυμένυς ἐν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς) Viros eximios ראשים.

To those from the Gentiles) To the uncircumcised. These things pertain in no way to the faithful Jews.

greetings) Thus Luke translates the Hebrew שלום.

## 15:24
v. 24. unsettling your souls) He said ἀνασκευάζειν, which the Hebrews say הכיא לב, which the LXX translate as to pervert the minds Num. XXXII. 7, to turn away the heart Num. XXXII. 9. The sense is: shaking the minds.

saying to be circumcised) An infinitive for a gerund, saying that they must be circumcised, namely the faithful.

and to keep the law) And that the law must be observed by them, that is, those precepts which Moses added to the old precepts; for they were complaining about those alone.

They were not complaining about the ceremonial precepts alone. But because, beyond and against the doctrine concerning the righteousness of faith handed down by the Apostles, some Syncretist Pharisees from among the Jews required for justification and salvation also the observance of the Mosaic law. Grotius ought to have been mindful of those things which he had said above at v. 1, that these Jews had felt that no man could be saved unless he were circumcised, and submitted himself to the WHOLE law of Moses, as the ONLY way to salvation. But he, with shameful ἑαυτομαχίᾳ, wished here to sail with the wind for the Papists.

To whom we gave no such commandment) We gave no such mandates. They were falsely prescribing the authority of the Apostles for their own dogmas.

Latin:

v. 24. ἀνασκευάζοντες τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν) ἀνασκευάζειν dixit, quod Hebræi הכיא לב quod LXX. vertunt διαστρέφειν διάνοιας Num. XXXII. 7. ἀφίσασθαι καρδίαν Num. XXXII. 9. sensus est: labefactantes animos.

λέγοντες περιτέμνεσθαι) Infinitivus pro gerundio, dicentes circumcidendos, nempe fideles.

κὴ τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον) Et observandam ipsis legem, id est, illa præcepta, quæ Moses addidit ad præcepta vetera de iis enim solis querebantur.

Non de solis ceremonialibus præceptis quere- bantur. Sed quod præter & contra doctrinam de fidei justitia ab Apostolis traditam Syncretistæ nonnulli è Judæis Pharisaizantes ad justificatio- nem & salutem requirerent etiam legis Mosaicæ observantiam. Memor esse debebat Grotius eo- rum quæ supra ad v. 1. dixerat, Judæos hos ita sensisse, neminem hominum servari posse, nisi circum- cideretur, TOTIQUE Mosis legi, ut UNICÆ ad salutem viæ, se subjiceret. Sed ille cum turpi etiam ἑαυτομαχίᾳ hic Papistis velificari voluit.

Οἷς ἐ διεστειλάμεθα) Mandata talia non dedimus. Auto- ritatem Apostolorum falso illi suis dogmatibus præscribe- bant.

## 15:25
V. 25. Γενομένοις ὁμοθυμαδὸν) See above II. 1. V. 12. A unanimous opinion adds no small weight to a decree.
