Salvianus at the end of book VIII: But in that city these were not so much the benefits of men as of the laws. For the decrees of the XII Tables forbade any man whatsoever from being killed while uncondemned.

ἀνθρώπυς Ῥωμαίυς ὐπάρχοντας) This is a synecdoche, such as in Matthew 28:44. For Paul alone possessed the right of Roman citizenship, as we shall see below in 22:25. It was not permitted by the Porcian and Sempronian laws to beat a Roman citizen with rods at all: how much less when the case was unheard? Paul knew how to use even the laws for the protection of his innocence and good cause.

It is also established that by the ancient law of the Romans it was a sacrilege to subject a Roman citizen to scourging: which Valerius Publicola first established by a passed law, according to Valerius Maximus, book IV, chapter 1, and this was confirmed by the Porcian law and the Sempronian law, as witnessed by Cicero in his speech for Rabirius.

οὐ γὰρ) Aposiopesis. For it is not right that it be done in such a way. ἡμα̃ς ἐξαγαγέτωσαν) As innocent men. Thus the magistrates come to soothe Apuleius, Metamorphoses III.

From this it appears that Paul, after having taken food in the keeper's house, returned to the prison so that the magistrate might find him there, and pronounce him innocent, and lead him out as such. Moreover, this is the heroic magnanimity of Paul, that he does not wish to leave the prison unless the magistrate passes judgment on his innocence, and that publicly.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

δείραντες ἡμᾶς δημοσίᾳ) dicuntur duumviri fecisse,

ANNOT. AD ACTA APOSTOL.

quod fieri jufferant. Et multum auget injuriam, quod facta erat in publico. Vide L. prætor in fine D. de injuriis.

Non præcipitarant tantum fententiam, sed mul- tum etiam in ea deliquerant, tum qua personam, tum qua causam ipsam: quod ob expulsum è mu- liere Pythonem dæmonem, adeoque ob benefi- cium in eam totamque urbem collatum tam male Paulum excepissent. Forte etiam ideo pœni- tentia ducti, quod de miraculo terræ motus, Pau- lique innocentia, & lætitia in carcere ac libera- tione divina edocti sint, Deo hic ita moderante, ne prædicationis Pauli cursus inhiberetur: uti quidam Græci Codices hæc addidere: Die autem facto convenerunt magistratus in concilium & memores terræ motum factum timuerunt ac mi- serunt lictores, quibus verbis innuitur terra mo- tum non fuisse tantum in carcere, sed per totam urbem.

ἀκατακρίτυς) Contra jus gentium & Romanorum: de jure gentium audi Hesiodum: Μηδὲ δίκην δικάσῃς πρὶν ἀμφοῖν μῦθον ἀκούσῃς. Et Senecam Medea: Qui statuit aliquid parte inaudita altera, Æquum licet statuerit, haut æquus fuit. De jure Romano testis Cicero: causa cognita possunt multi absolvi, incognita nemo condemnari potest. Et Tacitus Hi- storiarum I. inauditi atque indefensi tanquam innocentes pe- rierant: Et Historiarum III. quamvis invisum & nocentem, more tamen audiendum. Testis & Tertullianus peritus sane Romani juris in Apologetico: inauditum si damnant, invi- diam iniquitatis merebuntur. Idem adversus nationes: Quando non licet indefensos & inauditos omnino damnari. Apulejus IX. Milesiarum: Nec adinstar barbaricæ feritatis, vel tyrannicæ impotentiæ damnaretur aliquis inauditus. Sal- vianus fine libri VIII. Sed in urbe illa non tam hominum fu- erunt hæc beneficia, quam legum. Interfici enim indemnatum quemcunque hominem, etiam XII. tabularum decreta ve- tuerunt.

ἀνθρώπυς Ῥωμαίυς ὐπάρχοντας) Est Synecdoche, qualis Matth. XXVIII. 44. Nam jus civitatis Romanæ solus habe- bat Paulus, ut videbimus infra XXII. 25. Civem Romanum omnino virgis cædere non licebat per leges Porcias & Sem- pronias: quanto minus causa indicta? norat Paulus ad inno- centiæ & bonæ causæ præsidium etiam legibus uti.

Antiquo etiam jure Romanorum nefas fuisse civem Romanorum subjicere flagellis constat: quod primum lata lege statuit Valerius Publicola apud Valer. Maxim. l. IV. c. 1. idque confirmatum est lege Porcia, & lege Sempronia, teste Cicerone pro Rabirio.

οὐ γὰρ) Ἀποσιώπησις. Non enim ita agi rectum est. ἡμα̃ς ἐξαγαγέτωσαν) Tanquam innoxios. Sic magistra- tus Apulejum solatum veniunt, Milesiarum III.

Ex eo apparet, Paulum post cibum in domo custodis sumtum rediisse ad carcerem, ut ibi eum magistratus inveniret, & innocentem pronuncia- ret ac ceu talem educeret. Est autem hæc heroica magnanimitas Pauli, quod carcere egredi non vult, nisi magistratus sententiam ferat de ejus in- nocentia idque publice.

## 16:38
Verse 38. And they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans. See a similar passage below in 22:29. They feared the crime of treason, which Cicero threatens Verres with near the end of the final Verrine oration. For the laws had so established that when a Roman citizen was harmed, the very majesty of the Roman people was believed to be harmed.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Καὶ ἐφοβήθησαν ἀκούσαντες ὅτι Ῥωμαι̃οί εἰσι) Simi- le vide infra XXII, 29. Metuebant majestatis crimen, quod Verri minatur Cicero circa finem Verrinæ ultimæ. Ita enim constituerant leges, ut in cive Romano læso, ipsa populi Romani majestas læsa crederetur.

## 16:39
Verse 39. They comforted them, saying that they were unworthy of the injury which they had received. See Terence, Adelphi, Act II, Scene I.

ἠρώτων ἐξελθει̃ν τη̃ς πόλεως) Under this pretext, so that they might not suffer anything grievous from the angry populace.

The Vulgate rendered: They besought them. Some Greek codices add the words which they used: We were ignorant of your status and that you are just. Furthermore, adding these things and leading them out, they asked them, saying: Go out from this city, lest by chance they rush upon you again and shout against you. Thus, therefore, Paul made his judges suppliants to himself.

Latin:

Vers. 39. Παρεκάλεσαν αὐτής) Consolati sunt eos, di- centes, indignos eos esse ea, quam accepissent, injuria. Vide Terentium Adelphis Act. II. Sc. I.

ἠρώτων ἐξελθει̃ν τη̃ς πόλεως) Hoc obtentu, ne quid tristè ab irata plebe paterentur.

Vulgata reddidit: Deprecati sunt eos. Græci Codd. nonnulli addunt verba, quibus usi sint: Ignoravimus statum vestrum & quod estis justi. Hæc porro subjungentes, & educentes eos roga- verunt dicentes: Exite ex hac urbe, ne forte rursus irruant in vos, & vociferentur contra vos. Ita ergo Paulus suos judices fecit sibi sup- plices.

## 16:40
Vers. 40. εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὴν Λυδίαν) That is, into the house of Lydia. Thus in the Comedies: Let us go to my house.

παρεκάλεσαν αὐτὸς) They exhorted them to remain constant in the faith, although they themselves were departing,

ἐξῆλθον) Namely, both so that they would not expose themselves to unnecessary dangers, and because Macedonia, which God had commended to them, lay open more widely.

Having seen the brothers, they comforted them. Luke is indicated, Timothy, and if there were any other companions of Paul. Some Greek codices add, they recounted whatever the Lord did for them.

Latin:

Vers. 40. εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὴν Λυδίαν) Id est in Lydiæ do- mum. Sic in Comœdiis: Eamus ad me.

παρεκάλεσαν αὐτὸς) Hortati eos sunt, ut in fide constan- tes manerent, quanquam se abeuntibus,

ἐξῆλθον) Nempe tum ne periculis se ingererent non necessariis, tum quia Macedonia, quam ipsis Deus com- mendaverat, latius patebat.

Visis fratribus consolati sunt eos. Lucas in- digitatur, Timotheus, & si qui alii Pauli erant so- cii. Addunt quidam Græci Codices, narrâve- runt quæcunque fecit Dominus illis.

## 17:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Paul and Silas, traveling through Amphipolis and Apollonia, come to Thessalonica, and there announce Jesus, from which some of the Jews and Greeks are converted. But with the stubborn Jews causing a riot, and their host Jason dragged before the leaders of the city, they are accused of acting against Caesar by saying that Jesus is King; however, after satisfaction was rendered, Jason is dismissed, and Paul and Silas betake themselves to Beroea, where many receive the word, but on account of the Jews rioting there, Paul is led away from Thessalonica to Athens, with Silas and Timothy left behind there; being stirred up on account of the idolatry of the Athenians, yet teaching daily in the synagogue and in the marketplace, with Epicureans and Stoics disputing, and others slandering him as if he were announcing new Gods, because he was preaching the Gospel about Jesus and the resurrection. And when the Athenians, as if desirous of new things, wished to hear him, on the occasion of the altar inscribed to the unknown God, he announced the true God, creator and Lord of the world, who is not worshipped with human hands, being in need of anything, but gives life and breath to all, who made every race of men from one blood, dwelling on the whole earth, so that they might seek him, of whom, according to the gentile poets, we are the offspring, whence the Deity cannot be like statues: Who now commands all men to repent, because he is about to judge the whole world through one man, whom he raised from the dead. Which sermon some mocked because of the mention of the resurrection, some said they would hear him further, some adhered to him, and among them Dionysius the Senator, with his wife, named Damaris.

There are three parts: I. Paul's sermons at Thessalonica, along with the danger to his host Jason, up to v. 9. II. The success at Beroea, up to v. 14. III. The success at Athens, which includes the disputation and sermon of Paul concerning the unknown God and Jesus as Judge of the human race, the judgments of the hearers, and the conversion of some.

PART I. Paul's sermons at Thessalonica.

Vers. 1. Διοδεύσαντες δὲ τὴν Ἀμφίπολιν) A city near Philippi, as is clear from Ptolemy.

A colony of the Athenians founded by Cimon, according to Cornelius Nepos; called Amphipolis because it is surrounded by waters on all sides, connected only by an isthmus of land, as Pollux has it in book IX.

Apollonia.) That which Ptolemy calls Mygdonia. It was situated by the sea, a colony of the Corinthians and Corcyraeans, which Caesar describes in Book III of the Civil War, and Strabo in Book VII. ἦλθον εἰς Θεσσαλονίκην) It is a famous city of Macedonia on the Thermaic Gulf, as can be known from Strabo and Ptolemy, founded by Philip the son of Amyntas after his victory over the Thessalians, whence the city gets its name. Now by apocope it is called Salonica, in which the Jews have a synagogue, a printing press, and dominion, as Cornelius notes from Stephanus in his book on cities.

ὅπου ἧν ἡ συναγωγὴ τῶν Ἰυδαίων) The added article signifies that there were no synagogues in Philippi, Amphipolis, and Apollonia: but if there were any Jews there, they went to the Thessalonian synagogue.

Latin:

CAPUT XVII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Paulus & Silas per Amphipolin, & Apolloniam proficiscentes, Thessalonicam veniunt, ibi- que Jesum annuntiant, unde convertuntur nonnulli è Judæis & Græcis. Sed contuma- cibus Judæis tumultuantibus, hospite Jaso- ne ad primores urbis protracto, arguuntur, quod contra Cæsarem agant, Jesum Regem dicentes; Reddita tamen satisfactione di- mittitur Jason, & Paulus, ac Sila Berrhœam se conferunt, ubi multi verbum suscipiunt, sed ob tumultuantes ibidem Judæos Thessa- lonica Athenas Paulus deducitur, relictis illic Sila & Timotheo; ob idololatriam A- theniensium incitatus, in Synagoga tamen & in foro quotidie docens, Epicureis & Stoicis disputantibus, aliis calumnianti- bus, quasi novos Deos annunciaret, quod Evangelium de Jesu, & resurrectionem prædicaret. Et cum Anthenienses, ceu cupi- di rerum novarum ipsum audire vellent, occasione de ara ignoto Deo inscripta, Deum verum creatorem ac Dominum mundi an- nunciavit, qui non humanis manibus coli- tur, indigens aliquo, sed omnibus dat vi- tam, & spiritum, qui ex uno sanguine o- mne genus hominum, habitans in tota ter- ra, fecit, ut quærerent ipsum, cujus, juxta Poetas gentiles, genus nos sumus, unde Dei- tas statuis similis, esse nequeat: Qui jam omnibus hominibus præcipit pœnitentiam, quod judicaturus totum orbem per unum virum sit, quem è mortuis resuscitavit. Quam concionem aliqui ob mentionem re- surrectionis irridebant, aliqui seipsum porro audituros dicebant, nonnulli ipsi ad- hærebant, & inter eos Dionysius Senator, cum conjuge, Damaris nomine.

Partes tres sunt: I. Conciones Pauli Thessaloni- censes, cum hospitis ipsius Jasonis periculo, ad v. 9. II. Successus Berrhœensis, ad v. 14. III. Successus Athe- niensis, qua disputationem & concionem Pauli de ignoto Deo & Jesu Judice humani generis judicia auditorum & conversionem nonnullorum.

PARS I. Conciones Pauli Thessalonicenses.

Vers. 1. Διοδεύσαντες δὲ τὴν Ἀμφίπολιν) Urbem vicinam Philippis, ut ex Ptolemæo liquet.

Colonia Atheniensium condita à Cimone, au- ctore Cornel. Nepote; Amphipolis dicta, quod aquis undiquaque sit cincta, isthmo tantum terræ cohærens, ut habet Pollux l. IX.

ἡάπολλωνία·) Eam quam Mygdoniam vocat Ptolemæus. Erat mari adsita, Corinthiorum & Corcyræorum Colonia, quam describit Cæsar III. belli civilis, & Strabo L. VII. ἦλθον εἰς Θεσσαλονίκην) Est urbs præclara Macedoniæ ad sinum Thermaicum, ut ex Strabone, & Ptolemæo cognoscere est, condita à Philippo Amyntæ filio post victoriam de Thessalis, unde urbi nomen. Nunc per Apocopen Salonica vocatur, in qua Judæi habent Synagogam, Typographiam & dominium, ut è Stephano libr. de urbibus notat Cornelius.

ὅπου ἧν ἡ συναγωγὴ τῶν Ἰυδαίων) Articulus additus significat Philippis, Amphipoli & Apolloniæ nullas fuisse Synagogas: sed si qui ibi essent Judæi, eos Synagogam adiisse Thessalonicensem.

## 17:2
Vers. 2. κατὰ δὲ τὸ εἰωθὸς τῷ Παύλῳ εἰσῆλθε πρὸς αὐτὺς) A Hebraism for: ὁ δὲ Παῦλος κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ εἰσῆλθε. It was Paul's custom to approach the Jews first and bring the word of the Gospel to them, above XIII. 46.

But why did Paul enter the synagogues, when he had already protested before in Acts XIII. v. 46: behold, we turn to the Gentiles? Surely the Apostle did not mean there that he wished to leave the Jews immediately, or to turn himself away entirely from all Jews, but that the unbelief of the Jews provided an occasion for transferring the kingdom of Christ to the Gentiles. And since the writings of the Prophets were read in the synagogues, and Gentile proselytes also attended them, the Apostle thought he should use that occasion so that they might be informed about Christ from the Scriptures.

Latin:

Vers. 2. κατὰ δὲ τὸ εἰωθὸς τῷ Παύλῳ εἰσῆλθε πρὸς αὐτὺς) Hebraïsmus pro: ὁ δὲ Παῦλος κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ εἰσῆλθε. Mos erat Paulo primum adire Judæos & ipsis afferre Evangelii sermonem, Supra XIII. 46.

Cur vero ingressus Synagogas Paulus, quum protestatus antea jam fuerit Act. XIII. v. 46. ecce convertimur ad gentes? Nimirum non id voluit illic Apostolus, quod illico Judæos relinquere, vel plane à Judæis universis se avertere velit, sed quod Judæorum ἀπισία occasionem præbeat regnum Christi ad gentes transferendi. Et quum in Synagogis prælecta fuerint Scripta Prophetarum, iis​que interfuerint etiam gentiles proselyti, ea occasione utendum duxit Apostolus, ut è Scripturis informarentur de Christo.

## 17:3
Vers. 3. διαλέγετο αὐτοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν διανοίγων κὴ παρατιθέμενος, ὅτι τὸν χριστὸν ἔδει παθεῖν κό ἀναστῆναι ἐκ νεκρῶν) I think it is better distinguished: διαλέγετο αὐτοῖς, ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν διανοίγων κάη παρατιθέμενος. He reasoned with them, and from the Scriptures he made it plain and set before their eyes that Christ had to suffer. Understand παρατιθέμενος as ἐνὼπιον αὐτῶν. Which full expression is found in Exodus XIX. 7, XXI. 1, Deut. IV. 44. Paul used the same places of Scripture that Christ used in the same matter in Luke XXIV. 16, 27.

The Greek text does not support this distinction, which was also approved by Price, in which the second verse ends with the words ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν, and the third verse begins with the following διανοίγων. Nor is there need for innovation. For to have reasoned ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν is from the Scriptures, as the Tigurines and Pagninus have it: or also concerning the Scriptures, as the Vulgate has it: for the preposition ἀπὸ is not only from, but also out of and concerning, both regarding the subject matter and the object, Matt. III. 4, Luke IIX. 2. Διανοίγων is opening: because the Scripture is a book closed to the natural man, 1 Cor. II. 14, needing opening, which is done by the ministers of the word through the Holy Spirit, Acts XVI. 14. παρατιθέμειν is as if setting before the eyes. Compare Gal. III. 1.

ὃν ἐγὼ καταγγέλλω ὑμῖν) A transition from indirect to direct speech, frequent both in others and especially in our own writers. Vers. 4. κὴ προσεκληρώθησαν τῷ Παύλῳ κὴρ τῷ Σίλα) נלווו, they were added to Paul and Silas. But there is somewhat more in προσεκληρώθησαν, and it signifies that they were clearly addicted to Paul and Silas, like hereditary property among the Hebrews. Lucian also uses this verb. Aristides said συγκληρῶσαι for the same thing.

Latin:

Vers. 3. διαλέγετο αὐτοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν διανοίγων κὴ παρατιθέμενος, ὅτι τὸν χριστὸν ἔδει παθεῖν κό ἀναστῆναι ἐκ νεκρῶν) Puto rectius disti gui: διελέγετο ἐυτοῖς,ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν διανοίγων κάη παρατιθέμενος. Multa cum illis disferebat, & ex Scripturis apertum faciebat, & ob oculos ponebat Christum debuisse pati. Παρατιθέμενος intellige ἐνὼπιον αὐτῶν. Quæ plena locutio reperitur Exodi XIX. 7. XXI. 1. Deut. IV. 44. Locis Scripturæ iisdem usus est Paulus, quibus Christus in eadem re Luc. XXIV. 16. 27.

Non fert hanc distinctionem, Priceo etiam probatam, textus Græcus, in quo verbis ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν versus secundus finitur, & sequentibus διανοίγων versus tertius inchoatur. Nec opus est innovatione. Nam disseruisse ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν est è Scripturis, ut Tigurini & Pagninus: vel etiam de Scripturis, ut Vulgata habet: Nam præpositio ἀπὸ, non tantum est ab, sed etiam ex & de, tum de materia, tum de objecto, Matth. III. 4. Luc. IIX. 2. Διανοίγων est adaperiens: quia Scripturæ liber clausus est homini animali, 1. Cor. II. 14. apertione indigens, quæ fit per verbi ministros à Spiritu S. Act. XVI. 14. παρατιθέμειν est quasi ob oculos ponens. Conf. Gal. III. 1.

ὃν ἐγὼ καταγγέλλω ὑμῖν) Transitio ab oratione aliqua de directam frequens & aliis, & nostris maxime Scriptoribus. Vers. 4. κὴ προσεκληρώθησαν τῷ Παύλῳ κὴρ τῷ Σίλα) נלווו, additi fuere, Paulo & Silæ. Sed in προσεκληρώθησαν plus aliquanto est, & significat plane illis addictos fuisse Paulo & Silæ, sicut res hæreditaria apnd Hebræos. Utitur hoc verbo & Lucianus. Συγκληρῶσαι pro eodem dixit Aristides.

## 17:4
τῶν τέ σεβομένων Ἑλλήνων πολὺ πλῆθος) Here the σεβόμενοι Ἕλληνες are the same as those whom the Hebrews call חסידי אומות, the pious from among the nations, who indeed had not accepted the law of Moses, but having left idolatry and wicked morals, worshipped one God, and did injury to no one, which was a step toward Christianity.

γυναικῶν τε τῶν πρώτων) Of the matrons. See above XIII. v. 50.

Why he understands proselytes of that kind, who are commonly called proselytes of the gate, does not appear: since these attended the synagogues of the Jews, and without doubt, having been aggregated to the Jews, had accepted their laws: for in the synagogue of the Jews, while Paul was preaching for three Sabbaths, they were converted to Jesus.

Latin:

τῶν τέ σεβομένων Ἑλλήνων πολὺ πλῆθος) Hic σεβόμενοι Ἕλληνες sunt iidem quos Hebræi vocant חסידי אומות pii ex gentibus, qui legem quidem Mosis non susceperant, sed idololatria & pravis moribus relictis, unum colebant Deum, & nemini faciebant injuriam, qui gradus erat ad Christianisnum.

γυναικῶν τε τῶν πρώτων) Ex matronis. Vide supra XIII. v. 50.

Cur illius generis proselytos intelligat, qui vulgo proselyti portæ vocati sunt, non apparet: quum Synagogæ Judæorum hi interfuerint, & sine dubio Judæis aggregati leges eorum susceperint: nam in Synagoga Judæorum prædicante Paulo per tria Sabbata ad Jesum conversi sunt.

## 17:5
Vers. 5. Τῶν ἀγοραίων τινὰς) Ammonius: Ἀγόραιοι, when applied to those who are forward, signifies a wicked man who has been reared in the marketplace; but when applied to those who are sent forward, it signifies one who is honored in the marketplace. These are those whom the Latins call circumforanei,

Livy, book IX, the forum faction; Plautus, the buffoons in the Trinummus, whom he depicts so graphically: There is nothing surely more foolish, nor more stupid. Nor more mendacious, nor more cunning: Nor more confident, nor more perjured: Than urban, assiduous citizens, whom they call buffoons. ἀγόραιοι σύρφακες [market-place rabble] in Clement of Alexandria: ἤθη ἀγόραια [market-place manners] in Theophrastus. For more on this word see Price and from him: Wale. Posidippus in Athenaeus calls it ὄχλω ῥακείαν [a ragged crowd]. Tacitus, the sordid mob accustomed to the circus and theaters: Cicero in the oration for Sylla, the dregs and filth of the state: which Price observes illustrates Luke perfectly: because here follows τὴν πόλιν ἐθορύβουν [they threw the city into an uproar]. Cicero in Pro Flacco: What business is it to stir up the shopkeepers, and all that filth of the state?

ὀχλοποιήσαντες [having gathered a crowd]) ὀχλοποιεῖν is ישק, which is translated as συντροφὴ [gathering] in Amos.

τῇ οἰκίᾳ Ἰάσονος [at the house of Jason]) Jews, who in Hebrew are ישוע. This man was one of those Christian Jews who had come from Judea to Syria, and from Syria to Macedonia.

But who were those Christian Jews, and when had they come from Syria to Macedonia? These things are stated without Scripture, without testimony of antiquity. See what we observe regarding the preface to the former Epistle to the Thessalonians.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Τῶν ἀγοραίων τινὰς) Ammonius: Ἀγόραιοι ἐπὶ προπεπεξυτότων, σημαίνει τὸν πονηρὸν τὸν ἐν ἀγορᾷ τεθραμμένον· ἐπὶ δὲ προπεπομπένων σημαίνει τὸν ἐν ἀγορᾷ τιμώμενον. Hi sunt quos circumforaneos vocant Latini,

Livius l. IX. forensem factionem, Plautus scurras Tri- nummo, quos sic graphice depingit: Nihil est profecto stultius, neque stolidius. Neque mendaciloquius, neque argutum magis: Neque confidentiloquius, neque perjurius: Quam urbani assidui cives, quos scurras vocant. ἀγόραιοι σύρφακες Clementi Alexandrino : ἤθη ἀγόραια : Theophrasto. Plura de hac voce vid. apud Pricæum & ex eo : Waleum. Posidippus apud Athenæum ὄχλω ῥα- κείαν vocat. Tacitus sordidam plebem circo & theatris assuetam: Cicero in or. pro Sylla cænum fæcemque civitatis: quæ optime Lucam illustrare observat Pricæus: quia sequitur hic τὴν πόλιν ἐθο- ρύβουν. Cicero in Pro Flacco: Opifices tabernarii, atque omnem illam civitatis fæcem quid est negoti concitare?

ὀχλοποιήσαντες) ὀχλοποιεῖν est ישק, quod συντροφὴ πα- ϊν vertitur apud Amosum.

τῇ οἰκίᾳ Ἰάσονος) Judæi, qui Hebraice ישוע. Hic fuit ex Judæis illis Christianis, qui ex Judæa in Syriam, ex Syria in Macedoniam venerant.

Quinam vero illi Judæi Christiani, & quando ex Syria in Macedoniam venerant? Dicuntur hæc sine Scriptura, sine antiquitatis testimonio. Vid. quæ ad præloquium prioris Epistolæ ad Thessa- lonic. observamus.

## 17:6
Verse 6. ἐπὶ τοὺς πολιτάρχας [to the city authorities]) A Greek word formed in the same way as Βοιωτάρχαι [Boeotarchs]. The latter are the prefects of a city; the former, of the Boeotian nation.

οἱ τὴν οἰκουμένην ἀναστατώσαντες [those who have turned the world upside down]) Those who have stirred up the world to revolution: Thus ἀναστατῶν [one who stirs up] is also used below in XXI. 38. Politicians, who often do not know how to distinguish true dogmas from false, or healthy from harmful, hold all new things as suspect; this would have vehemently opposed the Gospel, had not God dispersed those counsels with a mighty Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 6. ἐπὶ τοὺς πολιτάρχας) Vox Græca eodem modo facta quomodo Βοιωτάρχαι. Illi urbis præfecti: hi gentis Bœoticæ.

οἱ τὴν οἰκουμένην ἀναστατώσαντες) Qui terrarum orbem ad res novas excitarunt: Sic ἀναστατῶν & infra sumitur XXI. 38. Politici qui sæpe dogmata vera à falsis, salubria à no- xiis non norunt distinguere, omnia nova suspecta habent, id Evangelio vehementer obstitisset, nisi Deus ingenti Spi- ritu difflasset ista consilia.

## 17:7
Verse 7. ὃς ὑποδέδεκται [who has received]) In the Glossaries, ὑποδέχομαι means I receive, I welcome. Thus this word is used in Tobit ch. VII, v. 9, and 1 Macc. XVI. 15. It is a frequent word in this sense both among poets and among Greek historians.

ἀπέναντι τῶν δογμάτων Καίσαρος πράττουσι [they act contrary to the decrees of Caesar]) For neither the Roman people of old, nor the Caesars afterwards, permitted anyone in conquered regions to be called king, except by their permission. Livy records that Masinissa gave thanks to the Senate because Scipio had called him king: and Cicero in Pro Deiotaro, and in the Responses of the Haruspices, and in his Letters, says more than once that Deiotarus was called king by the Senate. Sallust in the Jugurthine War relates that it was not granted to the grandson of Masinissa by Metellus to place a chair beside him, because that honor belonged only to those whom the Roman people had called kings. Caesar teaches us in his Commentaries that Ariovistus was called King by the Roman people: in which history Dion says: τὴν κύρωσιν τῆς βασιλείας παρὰ τῶν Ῥωμαίων εἰλήφει [he had received the confirmation of the kingdom from the Romans]: who also says of Juba, βασιλεὺς προσηγορεύθη [he was addressed as king]. Valerius Maximus reports that the son of Ariobarzanes was called king by Pompey.

βασιλέα λέγοντες ἕτερον εἶναι Ἰησοῦν [saying that there is another king, Jesus]) Not just of Judea, regarding which Jesus had been accused before Pilate, but of the whole human race. For Christians called Jesus Lord, which occurs often in this book, and very often in the Pauline letters. But this means the same thing as king. Rev. I. 8, XV. 3, XVII. 14. These Macedonians understood no more than Pilate that the kingdom of Christ was of such a nature that it did not oppose the kings of this world, but rather strengthened their empires in many ways. See a similar passage in John XVIII. 36, 37. ἕτερον [another], that is, one other than Caesar, who called himself Lord of the world, as it is in L. Ἀξίωσις D. ad legem Rhodiam.

For others, ἀνάστασις is an insurrection, by which some rise up against others: and ἀναστατώσαντες are those who stir up to sedition.

Latin:

Vers. 7. ὃς ὑποδέδεκται) In Glossis ὑποδέχομαι susci- pio, excipio. Sic usurpatur hæc vox Tobiæ c. VII. v. 9. 1. Macc. XVI. 15. frequens vox hoc sensu & apud Poëtas, & apud historiarum Scriptores Græcos.

ἀπέναντι τῶν δογμάτων Καίσαρος πράττουσι) Neque enim aut olim populus Romanus, aut postea Cæsares permi- sere in regionibus devictis, quemquam regem dici, nisi suo permissu. Livius commemorat à Masinissa gratias actas Senatui, quod Scipio eum regem appellasset: & Cicero pro Deiotaro, & in Aruspicum responsis, & in Epi- stolis, non semel Deiotarum ait à Senatu regem appel- latum. Sallustius in bello Jugurthino narrat Masinissæ nepoti à Metello non concessum ut sellam juxta eum po- neret, quod is honos eorum modo foret, quos populus Ro- manus reges appellavisset. Ariovistum à populo Roma- no Regem appellatum docet nos in Commentariis suis Cæsar: in qua historia Dion. τὴν κύρωσιν τῆς βασιλείας παρὰ τῶν Ῥωμαίων εἰλήφει : qui & de Juba, βασιλεὺς προσηγορεύθη. Valerius Maximus refert à Pompejo Ariobarzanis filium regem appellatum.

βασιλέα λέγοντες ἕτερον εἶναι Ἰησοῦν) Non Judææ tan- tum, de quo apud Pilatum accusatus Jesus fuerat, sed to- tius humani generis. Nam Christiani Jesum vocabant Κύριον, quod in hoc libro sæpe, sæpissime vero in Pau- linis literis occurrit. Hoc autem idem valet quod βα- σιλεύς. Apoc. I. 8. XV. 3. XVII. 14. Non magis quam Pi- latus intelligebant isti Macedones, regnum Christi ejus esse ingenii, ut regibus mundi hujus non obstaret, imo & illorum firmaret imperia multis modis. Simile vide Joh. XVIII. 36. 37. ἕτερον, id est, alium à Cæsare, qui se κόσμου Κύριον dicebat, ut est in L. Ἀξίωσις D. ad legem Rho- diam.

Aliis ἀνάστασις est insurrectio, qua alii adver- sus alios insurgunt: & ἀνασταζώσαντες sunt, qui ad seditionem excitant.

## 17:8
Verse 8. Ἐτάραξαν δὲ τὸν ὄχλον καὶ τοὺς πολιτάρχας [And they troubled the crowd and the city authorities]) That is, they disturbed the minds of both the people and the magistrates not a little, for fear that they might commit some offense against the Roman empire.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἐτάραξαν δὲ τὸν ὄχλον καὶ τοὺς πολιτάρχας) Id est, animos & populi, & Magistratuum non parum commo- verunt, metu ne quid in imperium Romanum committe- rent.

## 17:9
Verse 9.

and having taken the security from Jason) is a Roman expression of law, to accept security, to which corresponds to give security, whence satisdatio ἱκανοδοσία [security/bail] in Theophilus: just as satisfacere [to satisfy] ἱκανὸν ποῖῆσαι [to do enough] Mark ch. XV. 15. For these are said in a like manner L. I. D. [Digest, Book 1] who are compelled to give security. To accept security is frequent in law, as at the beginning of L.I.D. as in the possession of legacies. He accepts security, to whom it is guaranteed, as much as is enough for the law or the judge or a good man. Jason here, and his friends gave security for Paul and Silas to be produced in court, if there were need, which did not happen. Thus both the Syrian and the Arab have correctly interpreted this passage.

Others take it concerning satisfaction. The Vulgate, having received satisfaction: B. Luther rendered it Verantwortung [answer/defense]. Yet the version of the Syrian (and Arab): And they received sureties. To B. Gerhard, the interpretation concerning the caution interposed seemed more convenient: who praises the opinion of Cajetan here: I would believe that some surety was given by Jason and other Christians, who had been dragged with Jason to the princes of the city, concerning fidelity toward Caesar and the Roman Empire. Salmero teaches that a pecuniary caution was made from Peter Martyr of Alexandria, concerning appearing in court, with sureties given at the same time. Similarly, Pricaeus thinks it is safer to explain it concerning security to be produced in court.

PART II. The success of the Pauline ministry in Berrhoea.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

καὶ λαβόντες τὸ ἱκανὸν παρὰ τοῦ Ἰάσονος) Est vox Romani juris, satis accipere, cui respondet satisdare, unde satisdatio ἱκανοδοσία Theophilo: sicut satisfacere ἱκανὸν ποῖῆσαι Marc. c. XV. 15. Sunt enim hæc pari modo dicta L. I. D. qui sa- tisdare cogantur. Satis accipere frequens in jure, ut initio L.I.D. ut in possessionem legatorum. Satis accipit, cui ca- vetur, quantum legi aut judici aut viro bono satis est. Iason hic, & amici ejus satis dederunt judicio sisti Paulum & Si- lam, si opus esset, quod non evenit. Ita interpretati sunt hunc locum recte & Syrus & Arabs.

Alii de satisfactione accipiunt. Vulgata, ac- cepta satisfactione: B. Lutherus reddidit Ver- antwortung. Syri tamen (& Arabis) versio: Et acceperunt fidejussores. B. Gerhardo visa conve- nientior de interposita cautione, interpretatio: qui Cajetani sententiam hic laudat: Crediderim ego fidejussionem aliqam datam à Jasone & aliis Christianis, qui cum Jasone tracti fuerant ad prin- cipes civitatis de fidelitate erga Cæsarem & Roma- num Imperium. Pecuniariam cautionem è Petro Martyre Alexandrino, de comparendo in judicio, datis simul fidejussoribus factam esse, Salmero do- cet. Similiter Pricæus tutius explicari censet de satisdatione judicio sisti.

PARS II. Successus ministerii Paulini Berrhoensis.

## 17:10
Verse 10. εἰς Βέῤῥοιαν [to Berrhoea]) It is a city of Macedonia not far from Pella, Plin. IV. 10. Ptolemy in Macedonia. οἵτινες [who]) Paul and Silas.

παραγενόμενοι [having arrived]) When they had come to Beroea.

Latin:

Vers. 10. εἰς Βέῤῥοιαν) Est urbs Macedoniæ non procul à Polla, Plin. IV. 10. Ptolemæus in Macedonia. οἵτινες) Paulus & Silas.

παραγενόμενοι) Ubi Berœam venerant.

## 17:11
Verse 11. ὗτοι δὲ [but these]) Namely the Beroean Jews. For τῶν Ἰυδαίων [of the Jews] preceded after the mention of Beroea. Therefore that ὗτοι [these] refers to this.

Εὐγενέςεροι ἄλλων τῶν ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ [More noble than others who were in Thessalonica]) The genitive here signifies the other member of the comparison. But the Greek Fathers interpret Εὐγενέςεροι [more noble] as ἐπιεικέτεροι [more reasonable/gentle]. They were not of an equally hard spirit: they listened patiently: they thought about the matter: they inquired. They were εὐθετότεροι πρὸς τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ [more fit for the kingdom of God]: They were more τεταγμένοι πρὸς τὴν ζωὴν αἰώνιον [disposed toward eternal life]. They wanted to do the will of the Father, and by that they knew better concerning the word, John ch. VII. v. 17. In the Glossary, ἐυγενὴς [noble], ingenuous. However it has a primitive meaning concerning origin, transferred to the mind. Thus also the Latins say ingenium liberale [a liberal disposition]. Josephus concerning those who did not obey the impious commands of Antiochus XII. 7. οἱ δὲ δοκιμώτατοι καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἐυγενεῖς ἐκ ἐφρόντισαν ἀυτᾶ [but the most approved and noble in soul did not care for him]. Plutarch in the Homeric questions: ἔτι δὲ τῶν ἀυτῶν Φιλοσόφων δόγμα, κὴ τὸ διδακτὸν εἶναι τὴν ἀρετὴν, ἔχυσαν μετὰ ἀρχὴν τὴν ἐυγένειαν, ὑπὸ δὲ παιθείας εἰς τὸ τελειον προαγομένην [and it is a dogma of the same philosophers, that virtue is teachable, having nobility from the beginning, but being led to perfection by education].

οἵτινες [who]) Which Beroean Jews.

ἐδέξαντο τὸν λόγον [they received the word]) That is, they believed the word, as the Greeks explain here. The same expression above XI. 1.

μετὰ πάσης προθυμίας [with all readiness]) בכל לבב [with all heart]: with a ready mind. Thus προθυμία [readiness] is taken Sir. XLV. 32. 2 Cor. VIII. 11. 19. ch. IX. v. 2.

It is not that Beroea, which is now called Aleppo, as the Arab judged, rendering it to the city of Haleb (which Ludov. de Dieu teaches to be that Beroea) but this Beroea of ours is a city of Macedonia not far from Thessalonica, as Pliny testifies book IV. ch. 10, whereas that one is situated not far from Damascus, and in hollow Syria according to Pliny book V. ch. 23. Furthermore, Erasmus explains ἐυγενεςέρας [more noble] as born of the highest rank among those who were in Thessalonica: as if those were the most noble of the Thessalonians, as the Vulgate: For these were more noble than those who are in Thessalonica, or concerning primary and excellent men, superlatively also Stapleton in his Antidotes, Josephus à Costa, etc. But Beza correctly notes that the Thessalonians are not compared simply with the Beroeans, but the Jews of both cities among themselves, so that the Beroean Jews are said to have been far more ready than the Thessalonians. For they themselves immediately embraced the word: because the Thessalonians, not content with having rejected [him], pursued Paul as far as Beroea. Therefore (Beza continues) Luke does not say ἐυγενέςεροι Θεσσαλονικέων, but τῶν ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ, so that it may appear that the Jews are distinguished from the true inhabitants, with the anaphoric force of the article preserved. Then, since Luke has already led Paul and Silas to Beroea, why would he return to the history of the Thessalonians? Furthermore, the following verse declares that the Jews are being dealt with separately here, where mention is made separately of the native citizens, both men and women. Therefore, I preferred to preserve the proper meaning of the comparative. But although εὐγενὴς is properly said of birth; yet since the comparison here seems to be instituted not of birth (for all those were Jews) but of virtue and piety, I preferred to interpret it as 'more generous' rather than 'more noble': since it is established among the Greeks that, figuratively, τὴν εὐγένειαν is adapted to morals and to the mind, so that μεγαλοπρεπὴς, εὐγενὴς, [and] γενναῖος are often synonyms. The Syriac and Arabic interpreters, however, clearly confirm my opinion. This is Beza. The Syriac has it thus: 'Those Jews who were there were more noble than those Jews who were at Thessalonica.' Hence, therefore, it is established that the reading of Scripture was by no means forbidden to the laity: because they are praised as more generous, who were comparing, or where they were searching the Holy Scriptures.

searching the scriptures whether these things were so) Not that they doubted the truthfulness of Paul and Silas, but so that by comparing the Prophetic writings with their words, they might be confirmed more and more in the truth, and have [the means] from which to convince others. Ἀνακρίνειν here is what ἐρευνᾷν is in John 5:39, חקר. For it is translated by both those Greek words.

Beza, literally 'judging,' that is, diligent, and weighing each thing with judgment applied: to whom are opposed those who approach the reading of the Scriptures with prejudices, or rashly accept anything in them.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ὗτοι δὲ) Nempe Judæi Berœenses. Nam præ- cessit τῶν Ἰυδαίων post Berœæ mentionem. Huc ergo re- fertur illud ὗτοι.

Εὐγενέςεροι ἄλλων τῶν ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ) Genitivus hic si- gnificat alterum membrum comparationis. Εὐγενέςεροι autem Patres Græci interpretantur ἐπιεικέτεροι. Non æque duro erant animo: audiebant patienter: cogitabant de re: inquirebant. Erant εὐθετότεροι πρὸς τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ: Erant magis τεταγμένοι πρὸς τὴν ζωὴν αἰώνιον. Volebant facere voluntatem Patris, eoque melius cognoscebant de verbo, Ioh. c. VII. v. 17. In Glossario. ἐυγενὴς, ingenuus. Utcunque primitivam significationem habet de origine, translatam ad animum. Sic & Latini dicunt ingenium li- berale. Iosephus de iis qui Antiochum impiis jussis non ob- sequebantur XII. 7. οἱ δὲ δοκιμώτατοι καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἐυγενεῖς ἐκ ἐφρόντισαν ἀυτᾶ. Plutarchus in Homericis quæstioni- bus: ἔτι δὲ τῶν ἀυτῶν Φιλοσόφων δόγμα, κὴ τὸ διδακτὸν εἶναι τὴν ἀρετὴν, ἔχυσαν μετὰ ἀρχὴν τὴν ἐυγένειαν, ὑπὸ δὲ παιθείας εἰς τὸ τελειον προαγομένην.

οἵτινες) Qui Judæi Berœenses.

ἐδέξαντο τὸν λόγον) Id est, crediderunt verbo, ut hic ex- plicant Græci. Eadem locutio supra XI. 1.

μετὰ πάσης προθυμίας) בכל לבב : animo alacri. Sic προθυμία sumitur Sir. XLV. 32. 2. Cor. VIII. 11. 19. c. IX. v. 2.

Non est Beræa illa, quæ nunc Aleppo vocatur, ut Arabs censuit, reddens ad urbem Haleb (quam Beræam illam esse docet Ludov. de Dieu) sed hæc nostra Berœa Macedoniæ urbs est non pro- cul à Thessaloniça, teste Plinio l. IV. c. 10. quum illa non procul à Damasco, & in cava Syria juxta Plinium l. V. c. 23. sita sit. Cæterum Berœenses ἐυγενεςέρας summo genere natos inter eos, qui erant Thessalonicæ, Erasmus exponit: quasi Thessa- lonicensium illi nobilissimi fuerint, ut Vulgata: Hic enim erant nobiliores eorum, qui sunt Thef- salonicæ, vel de primariis & excellentibus vi- ris, superlative etiam Stapletonus in Antidotis, Josephus à Costa, &c. Sed recte notat Beza, non comparari simpliciter Thessalonicenses cum Berœ- ensibus, sed utriusque urbis Judæos inter se, ita ut Beræenses Judæi dicantur longe fuisse alacriores Thessalonicensibus. Statim enim ipsi amplexi sunt verbum: quod Thessalonicenses non contenti repu- diasse, Paulum Berœam usque sunt persecuti. Itaque (pergit Beza) non dicit Lucas ἐυγενέςεροι Θεσσαλο- νικέων, sed τῶν ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ, ut Judæos appareat à veris incolis discerni, servata vi articuli ἀνα- δοχικῇ. Deinde cum Lucas jam deduxerit Paulum & Silam Beraeam, cur ad Thessalonicensium histo- riam reverteretur? Praeterea de Judaeis seorsim hic agi declarat sequens versiculus, ubi seorsim fit men- tio indigenarum civium, tum virorum, tum mu- lierum. Itaque propriam comparativi significa- tionem servare malui. Sed quamvis εὐγενὴς de genere proprie dicatur; tamen cum comparatio hic videatur instituta non generis (erant enim o- mnes isti Judaei) sed virtutis ac pietatis, generosio- res malui interpretari, quam nobiliores: cum con- stet apud Graecos translalitie τὴν εὐγένειαν ad mores & ad animum accommodari, ita ut μεγαλοπρε- πὴς, εὐγενὴς, γενναῖος, saepe sint Synonyma. Syrus autem & Arabs interpretes manifeste sententiam meam confirmant. Haec Beza. Syrus ita habet: Nobiliores erant illi Judaei, qui illic erant, quam Ju- daei illi, qui erant Thessalonicae. Hinc ergo lectio- nem Scripturae laicis minime prohibitam fuisse, con- stat: quia eos ceu generosiores laudatos, qui con- ferrent, seu ubi S. literas easque scrutarentur.

ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς εἰ ἔχει ταῦτα οὕτως) Non quod dubitarent de veracitate Pauli & Silas, sed ut Prophetica scripta cum illorum verbis conferendo, magis magisque, in veritate confirmarentur, & haberent unde alios convin- cerent. Ἀνακρίνειν hic est quod ἐρευνᾷν Joh. V. 39. חקר. Nam id utraque illa Graeca voce vertitur.

Beza, ad verbum dijudicantes, id est diligen- tes, & adhibito judicio singula perpendentes: quibus opponuntur, qui ad Scripturarum lectio- nem cum praejudiciis accedunt, vel temere quod- vis in iis accipiunt.

## 17:12
Verse 12. Many therefore of them believed) Some of the Jews [following] the example of others.

and of the Greek women of high standing) Some also of the Macedonian matrons. See above XIII, 30.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Πολλοὶ μὲν οὖν ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐπίστευσαν) Ex Judaeis alii aliorum exemplo.

καὶ τῶν ἑλληνίδων γυναικῶν τῶν ἐυσχημόνων) Quaedam etiam ex Macedonicis matronis. Vide supra XIII, 30.

## 17:13
Verse 13. Stirring up the crowds) σαλεύειν corresponds to many Hebrew words. Here it is worth as much as σειειν, הסית, to incite, to irritate against someone.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Σαλεύοντες τοὺς ὄχλους) σαλεύειν multis vocibus Hebraeis respondet. Hic tantundem valet, quantum σειειν הסית concitare, irritare adversus aliquem.

## 17:14
Verse 14. To go as if to the sea) That Manuscript and others indeed have ἕως: but I judge ὡς to be more true, and that Paul was indeed led to the seashore as if he were about to sail, and the rumor was spread in that way, but that in reality he hastened to Athens by a land journey.

It rightly deserts the Vulgate, which rendered it 'as far as the sea'; as if ὡς were either read as ἕως or is to be taken as such. Beza also deserted it, rendering it 'as if to go to the sea.' Doubtless, this plan seems to have been given to Paul, so that the Jews might cease to pursue him, as if he had boarded a ship and sailed away from those regions. For that he came to Athens from Philippi by sea cannot be elicited in any way from the context of this history: but rather the contrary. Whence that ὡς was not to be neglected by the Syrian, the Arab, [and] the Ethiopian. Nor is it to be considered as redundant, as Lud. de Dieu [does].

PART III.

The success of Paul the Athenian, in which [are] the disputations, and the sermon about the unknown God, and Jesus as judge of the human race, the judgments of the hearers, and the conversion of some.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Πορεύεσθαι ὡς ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν) Habet quidem Manuscriptus ille & alii, ἕως: sed ὡς verius arbitror, & de- ductum quidem Paulum ad oram maris tanquam naviga- turum, & famam ita sparsam, caeterum reipsa properasse eum terrestri itinere Athenas.

Vulgatam merito deserit, quae reddidit, usque ad mare; quasi ὡς pro ἕως aut lectum sit, aut accipia- tur. Deseruit & Beza reddens, ut iret velut ad mare. Nimirum Paulo hoc datum videtur con- silium, ut illum Judaei persequi desinerent, quasi navi conscensa ex illis regionibus enavigasset. Mari enim illum Athenas Philippis venisse ex hu- jus historiae contextu elici nullo modo potest: Sed contrarium potius. Unde illud ὡς negligen- dum non erat, à Syro, Arabe, Aethiope. Neque enim id tanquam παρέλκον redundans cum Lud. de Dieu habendum.

PARS III.

Successus Pauli Atheniensis, qua disputationes, & concionem de ignoto Deo, & Jesu judice humani generis, judicia auditorum, & conversionem nonnullorum.

## 17:15
Verse 15. And those who were conducting Paul) Who were leading Paul by the mandate of the Thessalonians. In the Manuscript it is καθιστάνοντες.

and having received a commandment) From Paul.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Οἱ δὲ καθιστῶντες τὸν Παυλον) Qui Paulum de- ducebant mandatu Thessalonicensium. In Manuscripto est καθιστάνοντες.

καὶ λαβόντες ἐντολὴν) A Paulo.

## 17:16
Vers. 16.

his spirit was provoked within him) His spirit was moved for him. ישתמם לב Ps. CXLIV. 4 where the Greeks [say] ἐταράχθη ἡ καρδία. A similar expression [is found in] John XII. 27, chap. XIII. 21. c. XIV. 1.

However, to Beza and Camerarius, it does not seem that the leading away is denoted simply by the word καθεςῶντες, but that Paul was established in a safer place: so that καθεςῶντες is placed for εἰς ἀσφαλὲς καθισῶντες; whence he rendered: But those who were following Paul to be established in a safer place. Nor does our blessed Gerhard disagree.

κατείδωλον ὖσαν τὴν πόλιν) Luke coined the word κατείδωλον, after the example of the word κατάθεος, which is, according to the interpreter Pollux, worshipping gods. What the Greeks called gods, Christians called εἴδωλα. Paul would have said in Hebrew, עובדי עבודת זרה. Athens is a city filled with shrines, according to Cicero in his speech On the Responses of the Soothsayers.

It is more correctly explained with the Syrian as a city filled with idols, rather than given over to idolatry: just as places are called by geographers κατὰ δένδρα, where there are many trees, as Camerarius, Casaubon, blessed Gerhard, and others have observed. How truly Luke wrote this, says Beza, one may understand even from the Greek writers themselves. For Pausanias, in this one city, commemorates more idols than in the rest of Greece: and speaking of the Athenians, he writes, τέτοις δὲ ὐ τὰ εἰς Φιλανθρωπίαν μόνον καθέςηκεν (for a little before he had dealt with the altar of mercy) ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς Θεὸς εὐσεβεῖν ἄλλων πλέον, καὶ γὰρ Αἰδὲς σφίσι βωμός ἐςι, καὶ Φήμης καὶ Ὁρμῆς, that is, For these men, not only have those things been established which pertain to the duties of humanity, but they also have a greater care for piety toward the gods than others. For there exists among them even an altar of Shame and of Fame and of Appetite. But also Xenophon in his Republic of the Athenians says, ἄγωσιν, ἑορτὰς διπλασίας ἢ οἱ ἄλλοι: that is, They celebrate twice as many festivals as others.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

παρωξύνετο τὸ πνεῦμα ἑαυτῷ ἐν ἑαυτῷ) Commotus ei fuit animus. ישתמם לב Ps. CXLIV. 4 ubi Graeci ἐτα- ράχθη ἡ καρδία. Similis locutio Ioh. XII. 27, cap. XIII. 21. c. XIV. 1.

Bezae tamen & Camerario non simpliciter de- ductio per vocem καθεςῶντες denotari videtur, sed quod constitutus fuerit Paulus tutiori loco: ut καθεςῶντες positum sit pro εἰς ἀσφαλὲς κα- θισῶντες; unde reddidit: Qui vero Paulum se- quebantur tutiori loco constituendum. Nec ab- nuit B. Gerhardus noster.

κατείδωλον ὖσαν τὴν πόλιν) Vocem κατείδωλον finxit Lucas, ad exemplum vocis κατάθεος, quod est inter- prete Polluce λατρεύων θεοῖς. Quos Deos vocabant Graeci, eos Christiani εἴδωλα. Paulus Hebraice dixerit, עובדי עבודת זרה. Athenae urbs fanorum referta, Cicerone de Aruspicum responsis.

Rectius exponitur cum Syro urbs idolis re- ferta, quam idololatriae dedita: sicut a Geogra- phis loci vocantur κατὰ δένδρα, ubi multae sunt arbores, ut observarunt Camerarius, Casaubonus, B. Gerhardus, alii. Quam vere hoc scripserit Lucas, inquit Beza, vel ex ipsis Graecis scriptori- bus licet intelligere. Nam Pausanias in hac una urbe plura bene idola, quam in reliqua Graecia commemorat: & de Atheniensibus loquens scribit, τέτοις δὲ ὐ τὰ εἰς Φιλανθρωπίαν μόνον καθέ- ςηκεν (nam paulo ante egerat de misericordiae ara) ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς Θεὸς εὐσεβεῖν ἄλλων πλέον, καὶ γὰρ Αἰδὲς σφίσι βωμός ἐςι, καὶ Φήμης καὶ Ὁρμῆς, id est, Istis vero non modo constituta sint quae ad hu- manitatis officia pertinent, sed majorem etiam quam alii pietatis in Deos curam habent. Nam etiam Pudoris & Famae & Appetitionis ara apud ipsos exstat. Sed & Xenophon in Atheniensium republica, ἄγωσιν, inquit, ἑορτὰς διπλασίας ἢ οἱ ἄλλοι: id est, Festa duplo plura agitant quam alii.

## 17:17
Vers. 17.

καὶ τοῖς σεβομένοις) Namely, of the Greeks. As above in 4.

κὴ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ) Where things were for sale, and where the people gathered most. Ἀγορὰ τόπος ἔνθα πιπράσκεται τὰ ὤνια, says the Scholiast on the Acharnians.

Thus ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐντυγχάνοντες, Plutarch in Apophthegmata, whence Beza, with anyone met in the forum.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

καὶ τοῖς σεβομένοις) Nempe τῶν Ἑλλήνων. Ut supra 4.

κὴ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ) Ubi res erant venales, & quo maxime populus coibat. Ἀγορὰ τόπος ἔνθα πιπράσκεται τὰ ὤνια, ait Scholiastes ad Acharnenses.

Sic ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἐντυγχάνοντες Plutarch. in Apopht. unde Beza, cum quibusvis in foro ob- viis.

## 17:18
Vers. 18.

τινὲς δὲ τῶν Ἐπικυρείων) He names two kinds of philosophers, most alien to the Christian religion. For the Epicureans believed neither that the world was created by God, nor that God had any care for human affairs, nor that there were any rewards or punishments after death, nor any good other than what was perceived by the senses.

κὴ Στωϊκῶν) The Stoics, however, were κενῆς οἰήσεως ἔμπλεοι ἄσκοι. They denied that their wise man yielded anything to Jupiter: that he owed nothing to God for the fact that he was wise: that Jupiter could do no more than a good man: that Jupiter is good for a longer time, but the wise man esteems himself no less, because his virtues are contained in a shorter span, which you have in Seneca, Epistle LXXIII. That death should be sought by one's own hand rather than enduring slavery, insults, or severe diseases.

συνέβαλον ἀυτῷ) They engaged with him. The translation is taken from battles, as appears in Luke 12:31; Polybius, whom Luke loves to follow, uses it often. Tertullian, in his Prescriptions against Heretics, speaking of Paul: he had been at Athens, and he knew that human wisdom, the affecter and interpolator of truth, from his engagements.

People generally are accustomed to call Epicureans (פוקירוס or אפיקורוס) those who either despise or deny the foundations of true wisdom and religion, and they hold them in the same place as the מינים, the heretics: to whom there is no portion in the world to come. Luke, however, has not used the word with this breadth here, even though Heinsius inclines toward it: because he distinguishes the Epicureans from the Stoics, and proposes two distinct sects here. From the Stoics, Seneca, among other things, speaks very turgidly, nay impiously: There is something by which the wise man precedes

God. He is wise by the benefit of nature, not his own. Behold a great thing, to possess the weakness of a man and the security of God! Doubtless, they said that virtue, in which they place the highest good, is in the power of each person, and that there is no need for it to be sought from God. Furthermore, they taught that one who offends should not be forgiven, and that one should not be pitied, for the reason that pity is a passion and a sickness of the soul, which does not befall a wise man. Therefore, Cicero in his Pro Murena says that no one among the Stoics is merciful, except the foolish and the light-minded. Add to these opinions of the Stoics, above all, the fatal necessity of all things, which they themselves established, that all things which happen, and which are to be, are defined fatally from all eternity, as Cicero said in De Divinatione. Just as, on the contrary, the Epicureans attributed all things to the liberty of those acting, or to the fortuitous confluence of causes, and thus excluded divine providence, removing God from the care of things, and establishing Him in perpetual rest, οὔτε αὐτὸν πράγματα ἔχοντα, οὔτε ἄλλῳ παρέχοντα, neither having any business himself, nor providing it for another, not involved in any occupations, not undertaking any works, rejoicing in his own wisdom and virtue in security and freedom from cares. That death pertains nothing to us: for that which is dissolved is also devoid of sensation: that happiness is situated in the will. For this is the beginning and the end of living well and of a blessed life, as can be seen in Laërtius. Let the Calvinian heterodoxy be compared in B. Micrelius, Disp. III, Thes. IX, et seqq.

ὁ σπερμολόγος ὗτος) Σπερμολόγοι are properly birds that eat up seeds, as the Scholiast says on the Birds of Aristophanes. From this it began to be transferred to those who would take away things placed on altars; as Ulpian says on Demosthenes' Oration on the Crown, where this name is given to Aeschines. It began to be transferred further to all who sustain themselves by dishonest gain. Hence σπερμολόγων ῥήματα, and σπερμολογία ναυτικὴ, in Plutarch. Eustathius on the Odyssey, E: It must be known that just as it was said here figuratively, a seed of fire, so also the word σπερμολογεῖν has been turned to those who boast without method about subjects from certain hearsay. Eupolis is said to have mocked the natural philosopher Protagoras in the passage: who boasts, being a scoundrel, about the heavens, but eats things from the ground. ὁ δὲ κυρίως, φασὶ, σπερμο- λόγος, κὶ σπερμονόμος· is a kind of bird that damages seeds, from which the Attics called those who spend their time around markets and shops spermologoi, because they say they gather what flows out from the loads and live off that. From this, the same name fell to those who are worth no account. Tatian joins together phlenaphas (triflers) and spermologoi.

The Syriac translator explains it as a collector of words: Beza as a babbler. Because, as Eustathius testifies, this word among the Attics, when transferred to men, denotes those who busy themselves around markets and forums, so that they may collect what flows down from sacks and live from that, nothing prevents it from being used as another metaphor to describe vain men who, crawling through forums, catch the words of others, and collect what falls from the mouth of each, like grains from a sack, so that they may feed their own mind with those things, and have something to gossip and chatter about, as Lud. de Dieu observes. Pricaeus cites an old Onomasticon to that effect: σπερμολογῶ, I talk loquaciously; σπερμόλογος, loquacious; σπερμολογία, empty talk. Plutarch on the flatterer: Διαμελλώμενος ὑπερβάλλεσθαι βωμολογία καὶ σπερμολογίᾳ. Camerarius says: there is a certain little bird among the Greeks, the spermologos, a seed-gatherer, small and vile, neither suitable for food nor for pleasure, which is accustomed to gather things thrown away in the crossroads. For this reason, they called futile and worthless men by this name. By this name, however, is signified a vain trifler, and a futile and light-minded peddler. And from this, Gregory used the verb in his first oration on the Son: πολλά δ' ἂν ἔτι σπερμολογίσας. Many more things you would still bring forth or collect by babbling ineptly. Arator, who translated this book into Latin verses, thus: -- -- From what shores, he says, does this sower of words flow? The ignorant crowd calls Paul a sower of seeds, and enjoys the master's error, speaking true things.

So far Camerarius. But Beza notes that those birds troublesome with their perpetual chattering are so called παρὰ τὸ λέγειν σπέρματα, as if seed-gatherers, you might say, because they graze upon things sown in the fields, but not παρὰ τὸ σπείρειν τὰς λόγες, as some think, being doubly deceived, namely both in the etymology (for it should have been said λογοσπόρον) and in the fact that they sought in this word a proper meaning, and one leaning on a false etymology, instead of a metaphorical one: Moreover, regarding the passage from the oration περὶ ςεφάνε, Camerarius observes that it is cited falsely, since the true Scripture is ὁ σπερμόλογος εἰρονευομένε τὂ ῥήτορος.

he seems to be a proclaimer of foreign deities) That was not valid at Athens, to admit foreign divinities by public decree. Strabo concerning the Athenians: πολλὰ τῶν ξενικῶν ἱερῶν παρεδέξαντο. Privately it was not allowed; therefore Socrates was accused, as if ἕτερα κὴ καινὰ δαιμόνια εἰσηγύμενος, as Laërtius speaks.

that he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection to them) Under resurrection understand also all power in heaven and on earth, and of judging the dead and the living, which Paul attributed to Jesus. See below 31.

Selden, with Chrysostom, maintains that they interpreted the sacred words wrongly, having thought that Paul wished to indicate both Anastasis and Jesus as a demon or deity to be worshipped and a God.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

τινὲς δὲ τῶν Ἐπικυρείων) Duo genera Philosophorum no- minat, maxime alienorum a Christiana religione. Nam Epicurei neque mundum conditum a Deo credebant, neque Deo curam esse rerum humanarum, neque ulla prae- mia aut poenas post mortem, neque bonum aliud quam quod sensibus perciperetur.

κὴ Στωϊκῶν) Stoici vero erant κενῆς οἰήσεως ἔμπλεοι ἄσκοι. Negabant sapientem suum quicquam Jovi ce- dere: nihil eum Deo debere ob id quod saperet: Jovem plus non posse quam bonum virum: Jovem diutius bo- num esse, at sapientem nihilo minoris se aestimare, quod virtutes ejus spatio breviori clauduntur, quae habes apud Senecam Epistola LXXIII. Manu quaerendam mortem potius quam ferendam servitutem, contumelias aut gra- ves morbos.

συνέβαλον ἀυτῷ) Congressi sunt cum eo. Translatio est de praeliis sumta, ut apparet Luc. XII, 31. utitur ita saepe Polybius, quem sequi amat Lucas. Tertullianus de Haere- ticorum praescriptionibus, de Paulo locutus: fuerat Athe- nis, & istam sapientiam humanam affectatricem, & in- terpolatricem veritatis, de congressibus noverat.

Epicureos פוקירוס, vel אפיקורוס generaliter dicere solent eos, qui verae sapientiae & religio- nis fundamenta vel spernunt, vel negant, & eodem illos loco cum מינים haereticis habent: quibus nulla seculi futuri pars est. Hac tamen am- plitudine vocis hic non usus est Lucas, etsi eo inclinet Heinsius: quia Epicureos a Stoicis distin- guit, & duas distinctas sectas hic proponit. E Stoicis Seneca ita inter alia perquam turgide, imo impie habet: Est aliquid, quo sapiens antecedat

Deum. Ille naturæ beneficio, non suo sapiens est. Ecce res magna haberi imbecillitatem hominis, securitatem Dei! Nimirum virtutem in qua summum bonum penetrant, in cujusque pote- state esse dicebant, nec opus esse, ut à Deo eadem petatur. Adhæc docebant, non es- se ignoscendum ei, qui offendit, non esse mise- rendum, eo quod misericordia sit passio & ægri- tudo animi, quæ in sapientem non cadit. Ideo Cicero pro Murena ex Stoicis neminem misericor- dem esse, ait, nisi stultum & levem. Adde his sen- tentiis Stoicorum imprimis fatalem rerum o- mnium necessitatem, quam ipsi statuebant, omnia quæ fiunt, quæque futura sunt, ex omni æternitate definita esse fataliter, dixit Cicero de divinat. Quemadmodum ex adverso Epicurei libertati agentium, aut fortuitis causarum confluxibus o- mnia tribuerunt, adeoque divinam providentiam excluserunt, Deum à cura rerum removentes, in perpetua quiete constituerunt, οὔτε αὐτὸν πράγ- ματα ἔχοντα, οὔτε ἄλλῳ παρέχοντα, nec ipsum quis- quam negotii habentem, nec exhibentem alteri, nul- lis occupationibus implicari, nulla opera moliri, sua sapientia & virtute gaudere in securitate, curarum- que vacatione. Mortem nihil ad nos pertinere: quod enim dissolutum est, id sensus etiam expers: feli- citatem sitam esse in voluntate. Hanc enim initium & finem esse bene vivendi vitæque beatæ, ut apud Laërtium videre est. Conferatur heterodoxia Calviniana B. Micrelii Disp. III. Thes. IX. seqq.

ὁ σπερμολόγος ὗτος) Σπερμολόγοι proprie aves, quæ sata depascuntur, ut ait Scholiastes ad aves Aristophanis. Cœpit hinc transferri ad eos, qui aris imposita auferrent; ut ait Ulpianus ad Demosthenis Orationem de Corona, ubi Æschini hoc nomen datur. Longius transferri cœpit ad o- mnes inhonesto quæstu se sustentantes. Hinc σπερμολόγων ῥήματα, & σπερμολογία ναυτικὴ, apud Plutarchum. Eu- stathius ad E. Odysseæ. Ἰσέον δὲ ὅτι ὥσπερ ἐνταῦθα τροπι- κῶς ἐῥῥήθη, σπέρμα πυρὸς, οὕτω τέτρεπται καὶ τὸ σπέρμαλο- γεῖν ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλαζονευομένων ἀμεθόδως ἐπὶ μαθήμασιν ἔκ τινων παρακουσμάτων. Εὔπολις λέγεται τὸν Φυσικὸν Πρωταγόραν διακωμῳδῶν ἐν τῷ· ὃς ἀλαζονεύεται· μὲν ἀλιτήριος περὶ τῶν μετεώρων, τὰ δὲ χαμᾶθεν ἐσθίει. ὁ δὲ κυρίως, φασὶ, σπερμο- λόγος, κὶ σπερμονόμος· εἶδός ἐστιν ὀρνέου λωβώμενον τὰ σπέρμα- τα, ἐξ ὗ Ἀττικοὶ σπερμολόγους ἐκάλουν τὺς περὶ ἐμπόρια καὶ ἀγορὰς διατρίβοντας, διὸ τὸ ἀναλέγεσθαι τὰ ἐκ τῶν φορτίων, φασιν, ἀποῥῥέοντα καὶ διαζῇν. Ἐκ τύτυ δὲ τὴν αὐτὴν ἐλάγ- χανον κλῆσιν καὶ οἱ οὐδενὸς λόγυ ἄξιοι. Tatianus conjungit Φληνάφυς καὶ σπερμολόγους.

Syrus collectorem verborum: Beza blaterato- rem exponit. Quia teste Eustathio vox hæc apud Atticos ad homines translata notat eos, qui circa mercatur & fora versantur, ut quæ ex saccis de- fluunt colligant, atque inde vivant, nihil impedit, quo minus ita alia metaphora aliis describantur vani homines, qui fora perreptantes dicta aliorum captant, & quæ ex ore cujusque, velut grana è sacco, excidunt, colligunt, ut animum suum istis pascant, & habeant, quod fabulentur, & garriant, observante Lud. de Dieu. Allegat in eam sententiam Pricæus Onomasticum vetus, σπερμο- λογῶ, loquacito, σπερμόλογος, loquax σπερμολο- γία vaniloquentia. Plutarchum de adulatore Δια- μελλώμενος ὑπερβάλλεσθαι βωμολογία καὶ σπερμολογίᾳ. Camerarius, avicula, inquit, Græcis quædam est σπερμόλογος feminilega, parva & vi- lis, neque ad cibum neque ad delectationem idonea, quæ solet abjecta femina in triviis colligere. Propterea futiles & nihili homines hoc nomine appellabant. Significatur autem nomine hoc, vanus nugator, & circulator futilis ac levis. Et inde facto ver- bo usus est Gregorius in oratione priore περὶ ὑἷῦ: πολλά δ' ἂν ἔτι σπερμολογίσας. Multa adhuc autem garriendo inepte protuleris sive colle- geris. Arator, qui hunc librum in Latinos ver- sus transtulit, ita: -- -- Quibus, inquit, ab oris Verborum fluit iste sator? Plebs nescia Paulum Semina ferre, vocat, fruiturque errore magistro, Vera loquens.

Hactenus Camerarius. Notat autem Beza aves il- las perpetuo garritu molestas sic vocatas παρὰ τὸ λέγειν σπέρματα, quasi seminilegas, dicas, quod sata in agris depascantur, non autem παρὰ τὸ σπείρειν τὰς λόγες, uti existimant nonnulli dupliciter decepti, nempe tum in etymo (dicen- dum enim fuisset λογοσπόρον) tum in eo quod propriam eamque etymo falso innitentem signi- ficationem, loco Metaphoricæ, in hoc vocabu- lo quæsiverunt: Cæterum de loco ex oratione περὶ ςεφάνε observat Camerarius, falso eum ad- duci, cum vera Scriptura sit ὁ σπερμόλογος εἰρονευομένε τὂ ῥήτορος.

ξένων δαιμονίων δοκεῖ καταγγελεὺς εἶναι) Non ratum id Athenis, publico scito extranea numina admittere. Stra- bo de Atheniensibus: πολλὰ τῶν ξενικῶν ἱερῶν παρεδέξαντο. Privatim id non licebat; ideo Socrates accusatus, tan- quam ἕτερα κὴ καινὰ δαιμόνια εἰσηγύμενος, ut Laërtius lo- quitur.

ὅτι τὸν Ἰησῦν κὴ τὴν ἀνάςασιν αὐτοῖς εὐηγγελίζετο) Sub re- surrectione intellige etiam omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra, & judicandi mortuos & vivos, quam Jesu Paulus tribuebat. Vide infra 31.

Perperam eos verba sacra interpretatos, tam Anastasin, quam Jesum Dæmonium seu Nu- men adorandum & Deum esse Paulum indicare voluisse opinatos esse, cum Chrysostomo Seldenus statuit.

## 17:19
Vers. 19.

And having taken hold of him) Gently taken by the hand.

they led him to the Areopagus) Not for judgment, but because many learned men, senators, orators, and others were accustomed to be there. See below 34.

may we know) Is it permitted for us to learn from you what your dogma is, of which sect you are in philosophy?

The Vulgate retains the Greek Areopagus, which was preserved by Cicero himself; Erasmus explains it as the Martian quarter: But Beza with Camerarius notes that πάγον is not a quarter, but a hillock. Nor was that the name of a quarter, but of a court, according to Beza, in which the judges were accustomed to meet: whence the Areopagite judgment in Tacitus book II. Therefore they were called Areopagites, who indeed were permanent, and took cognizance of capital crimes, and specifically indeed of impiety. Hither therefore Paul was dragged, if you listen to him, so that he might be prosecuted as guilty of ἀσεβείας. Although indeed Beza says that Paul was dragged by them to judgment, it does not seem, in his judgment, that Paul pleaded his case before the judges themselves, but when he had been dragged there through a tumult, he later escaped by the wonderful providence of GOD, the adversaries having been dispersed; But because nothing of this miracle appears in the text, it is said more simply that he was not dragged to judgment. Camerarius teaches that that hill was opposite the citadel of the Athenians. And he adds: the Greeks say that Paul was not dragged to judgment, but to that place where there was a greater gathering of men. But Paul's oration is directed especially against the Epicureans, τὰς ἀπρονοήτα λέγοντας εἶναι τὰ πάντα: Asserting that all things are devoid of providence.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Ἐπιλαβόμενοί τε ἀυτὸν) Manu leniter prehen- sum.

ἐπὶ τὸν Ἄρειον πάγον ἤγαγον) Non ad judicium, sed quod ibi multi esse solerent homines eruditi, senatores, oratores & alii. Vide infra 34.

δυνάμεθα γνῶναι) Licetne nobis per te discere, quod sit tuum dogma, cujus sis in Philosophia sectæ?

Vulgata retinet Græcum Areopagum, quod ab ipso Cicerone servatum; Erasmus exponit Martium vicum: Sed Beza cum Camerario notat, πάγον non esse vicum, sed colliculum. Neque id nomen vici erat, sed curiæ, secun- dum Bezam, in qua coire solebant judices: unde Arcum judicium apud Tacitum l. II. Idcir- co vocati Areopagitæ, qui quidem perpetui erant, & de summis criminibus cognosce- bant, ac nominatim quidem de impietate. Huc igitur pertractus est Paulus, si ipsum au- dias, ut ἀσεβείας reus perageretur. Quan- quam vero Beza Paulum ab his ad judicium ra- ptum dicat, non videtur, ejus judicio, Paulus coram ipsis judicibus causam dixisse, sed cum illuc per tumultum raptus esset, postea mirabili DEI providentia dissipatis adversariis evasisse; Sed quia de hoc miraculo nihil in textu comparet, simplicius dicitur, non raptum fuisse ad judi- cium. Camerarius collem illum oppositum fu- isse arci Atheniensium docet. Additque: non in judicium Paulum raptum fuisse, Græci ajunt, sed eo, ubi esset conventus hominum major. O- ratio autem Pauli adversus Epicureos potissi- mum dirigitur, τὰς ἀπρονοήτα λέγοντας εἶναι τὰ πάντα: Perhibentes expertia esse providentiæ omnia.

## 17:20
Ξενίζοντα γάρ τινα) Strange things. Thus the writer of 2 Macc. IX. 6 said ξενιζούσαις συμφο- ραῖς βασανίσαντα (having tormented with strange calamities). τί ἂν θέλοι ταῦτα εἶναι) We had the same form of expression above II. 21.

Latin:

Ξενίζοντα γάρ τινα) Non audita. Sic ξενιζούσαις συμφο- ραῖς βασανίσαντα dixit Scriptor 2. Macc. IX. 6. τί ἂν θέλοι ταῦτα εἶναι) Idem loquendi genus habuimus supra II. 21.

## 17:21
Verse 21.

καὶ οἱ ἐπιδημοῦντες ξένοι ) Foreigners, who were staying there for a time, easily imbibed the vices of the citizens as well.

εἰς ὀυδὲν ἕτερον εὐκαίρουν ) They had leisure. Thus also Mark VI. v. 31.

ἢ λέγειν τι καὶ ἀκούειν καινότερον) Demosthenes, Philipp. c. IV: 'You are as eager as you are sitting listening if anything newer is reported.' The same in his response to the letter of Philip: 'But we, for the truth shall be told, sit here doing nothing, always delaying and voting, and inquiring in the marketplace if anything newer is said.' You see there that νεώτερον is used, just as here καινότερον is a comparative used for a positive. Thus also in Plato: 'What is newer, O Socrates?'

Latin:

Vers. 21.

καὶ οἱ ἐπιδημοῦντες ξένοι ) Peregrini, qui ibi ad tem- pus diversabantur, facile & hi imbibebant civium vi- tia.

εἰς ὀυδὲν ἕτερον εὐκαίρουν ) Vacabant. Sic & Marci VI. v. 31.

ἢ λέγειν τι καὶ ἀκούειν καινότερον) Demosthenes Philipp. c. IV. Τοσοῦτον χρόνον σπουδάζετε, ὅσον ἂν καθῆσθε ἀκούοντες ἢν προσαγγελθῇ τι νεώτερον. Idem in responso ad episto- lam Philippi : Ἡμεῖς δὲ, εἰρήσεται γάρ τ' ἀληθὲς, ὀυδὲν ποιοῦντες ἐνθάδε καθήμεθα, μέλλοντες ἀεὶ καὶ ψηφιζόμενοι, καὶ πυνθανόμενοι κατὰ τὴν ἀγορὰν, εἴτι λέγεται νεώτερον. Vides illic dici νεώτερον, quomodo hic καινότερον compa- rativum pro positivo. Sic & apud Platonem : Τί καινό- τερον, ὦ Σώκρατες.

## 17:22
Verse 22.

κατὰ πάντα ὡς δεισιδαιμονεστέρους ὑμᾶς θεωρῶ) δεισιδαίμων is a neutral word. Plutarch says δεισιδαιμονία ἥψατο τῆς πόλεως: religion invaded the city. He wished to praise the Athenians because they were religious according to the abundance of their knowledge, so that by that insinuation he might prepare a way for himself to teach them better things. Now this praise was proper to the Athenians: to surpass other peoples in the study of religion. Josephus against Apion II: 'For it was fitting to imitate the ignorance of Apion, who considered neither the fortunes of the Athenians nor those of the Lacedaemonians, whom everyone calls the bravest and the most pious of the Greeks, respectively.' Sophocles in Oedipus at Colonus:

Ὅδ' ἕνεψ' ὥτις γῆ Θεὸς ἐπίσταται Τιμαῖς σεβίζειν, ἥτε τῶδ' ὑπερφέρει.

Lycurgus the orator against Leocrates: 'For you do not know, Athenians, that in which you differ most from other men is in being pious toward the gods,' etc. Pausanias I: 'It has been said by me before, that the Athenians have more zeal for divine things than others.' Philostratus IV: 'Since he saw that the Athenians were fond of sacrificing.'

The religiosity of the Athenians is not being commended, but as the Vulgate rightly implies, it is being reproved that they seemed superstitious in all things. For there is a certain, albeit tacit, correction here. That others, such as the pagan Sophocles in Oedipus at Colonus, the orator Lycurgus against Leocrates, Philostratus, and Pausanias, celebrated their religion, as Josephus testifies in Book II against Apion, does not make for true praise of religion, but for mere superstition. For what true worship (λατρεία) was there among the Pagans, to whom the Jews—a people addicted to true religion and subject to superstition—were considered contrary in their religions, in the judgment of Tacitus, Histories IV? The Arab rendered it: 'I see you fearing demons in every way.' The Ethiopian: 'I see you are insane in all things.'

Latin:

Vers. 22.

κατὰ πάντα ὡς δεισιδαιμονεστέρους ὑμᾶς θεωρῶ) δεισιδαίμων vox est media. δεισιδαιμονία ἥψατο τῆς πόλεως Plutarchus: religio civitatem invasit. Laudare voluit Athenienses quod pro copia cognitionis suæ religiosi essent, ut ea in- sinuatione aditum sibi pararet ad eos docendos rectiora. Erat autem hæc laus propria Aheniensium : religionis stu- dio alios populos vincere. Josephus adversus Appionem II. Μιμεῖσθαι γὰρ ἦ προσῆκεν τὴν Ἀπίωνος ἀπαιδευσίαν, ὃς ὔτε τὰς Ἀθηναίων τύχας, ὔτε τὰς Λακεδαιμονίων ἐνενόησεν, ὧν τὺς μὲν ἀνδρειοτάτους, τὺς δὲ εὐσεβεστάτους τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἅπαν- τες λέγουσιν. Sophocles Oedipode Coloneo:

Ὅδ' ἕνεψ' ὥτις γῆ Θεὸς ἐπίσταται Τιμαῖς σεβίζειν, ἥτε τῶδ' ὑπερφέρει.

Lycurgus Orator adversus Leocratem οὐ γὰρ ἴστε Ἀθηναῖοι, ὅτι ᾧ πλεῖστον διαφέρετε τῶν ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων τῷ πρός τε τὼς Θεὸς εὐσεβῶς ἔχειν. &c. Pausanias I. λέλεκται δέ μοι καὶ πρό- τερον, ὡς Ἀθηναίοις περισσότερόν τι ἢ τοῖς ἄλλοις εἰς τὰ θεῖά ἐσι σπουδῆς. Philostratus IV. Ἐπειδὴ φιλοθύτας τὺς Ἀθηναίους εἶδεν.

Non religiositas Atheniensium commendatur, sed ut recte Vulgatus innuit, id reprehenditur, quod per omnia superstitiosi visi sint. Habetur enim quædam hic, etsi tacita ἐπανόρθωσις. Quod ipsorum religionem teste Josepho l. II. advers. Ap- pion. celebrarunt alii pagani, Sophocles, Oedipode, Coloneo, Lycurgus orator adversus Leocratem, Phi- lostratus Pausanias, non ad veram religionis lau- dem, sed ad meram superstitionem facit. Quæ enim vera λατρεία apud Paganos, quibus Judæi, veræ addicti religioni superstitioni obnoxia gens, adversa religionibus, judice Tacito Histor. IV. cen- sebantur? Arabs reddidit : video vos quibus- cunque modis Dæmones verentes. Æthiops : video vos insanire in omnibus.

## 17:23
Verse 23.

διερχόμενος γὰρ) Passing through the city. Τὰ σεβάσματα ὑμῶν) Σεβάσματα, or in Philo σεβασμοὶ, are those things through which gods are worshipped, whence the Latin translator not badly rendered it as 'objects of worship' (culturas). We spoke about this word in the second letter to the Thessalonians.

Nay, σέβασμα is rather that very thing which is worshipped: and because among the Athenians, who were very superstitious, these were images, Ludov. de Dieu rightly observes that 'your deities' is best rendered, as in the Book of Wisdom chapter XIV, verse 20, σέβασμα is a deity: as also in chapter XV, verse 17, and likewise in the History of the Dragon. Thus also Paul understood the word in 2 Thess. chapter II, v. 4, ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον Θεὸν, ἢ σέβασμα, over everything that is called GOD or a Deity. The Syriac and Arabic translate it as temples, Beza as 'your sacred things', in preference to which the Vulgate and the Ethiopic more fittingly rendered it 'your images'.

To an unknown God) Lucian: By the unknown one in Athens. And the unknown one in Athens. Wherefore it should not be doubted that there were certain inscriptions in the singular, To an unknown God. Just as Laërtius, narrating the origin of this matter, says that the Athenians were warned by Epimenides to perform sacrifices to the proper God, that is, to that God to whom that matter pertained, without adding a name, so the Romans: If you are a God, if you are a Goddess. Macrobius III. 9. When Pausanias says there were altars in Athens to unknown Gods, he means this, that there were many altars with such an inscription To an unknown God, although there could also have been others inscribed in the plural, others in the singular.

Jerome on chapter 1 of Titus says that the inscriptions were read only in the plural: however, the author of the Philopatris not only swears by an unknown God, but also testifies that he found him in Athens and worshipped him. Others, along with Grotius and Vossius, hand down another occasion for this inscription. Namely, that the Athenians, oppressed by a grave plague, when they had wearied themselves in vain by worshipping their ancestral gods, and feared that some deity had been overlooked by them, wished to have built this altar To the unknown God. Others, when the Persians had invaded Greece with an immense force, and help had been sought from the Spartans, say that the image of Pan occurred to Philippides, who was being sent, around the mountain which is named Parthenius, who complained that he was neglected and promised help: whom, since they were ignorant of him, they meanwhile gratefully inscribed an altar To an unknown God. Concerning which Pelusiota is also to be consulted; whence the occasion which the Apostle used appears. For when, having experienced a benefit, they were blind and senseless as to whom they owed it, and therefore worshipped an unknown God and supplicated him, by this occasion he leads them to the true source of every good and the author of the benefit, no otherwise than by the hand, as Heinsius is the author in this place. Compare Oecumenius on this passage.

Whom therefore you worship in ignorance) Note that eusebein is active. Thus in Plutarch from an ancient poet: No labor is to worship God. With a similar construction, with the sense slightly inclined, Paul said to worship one's own house in 1 Timothy 5:4.

This one I proclaim to you) Lucan: And Judea gave to the rites of an uncertain God; that is, to an unknown God. The Samaritans in a letter to Antiochus Epiphanes: Having established an anonymous temple on the mountain called Garizim. Dion Cassius calls the GOD of the Jews ineffable and invisible. To Josephus, the GOD of the Jews is unbegotten, eternal, timeless, unchangeable, unknown in essence. He had no name known to the nations: but that by which he was called by the Jews, it was not permitted to pronounce in public. The nations either did not believe that there was a God who had created the world, or they confessed that they were ignorant of who he was. Ovid: Thus when he, whoever of the gods he was, had separated the arranged mass. See what will now follow, and what is above in chapter 14, verse 15. Just as that one, so also this speech prescribes an excellent form for those whose business it is to recall idolaters to the right path.

Vossius also noted, and Walæus from him, that the Athenians worshipped the same deity under the name of the unknown, which the Jews venerated. How openly Paul says here that the Athenians worshipped that deity which he himself was about to announce, so that they might subsequently recognize him! Nor when we read in Lucan in the second book of the Pharsalia, The uncertain God of the Jews—: that uncertain one is none other than the true GOD of Israel: but he is called Uncertain by the poet, because he could not say whether it was Saturn, or Jupiter, or Mars, or by what name he finally rejoiced. Which proceeds from a double cause. For the Jews did not commonly utter the tetragrammaton name of God, lest it be exposed to the mockery of the nations, or even become cheapened among the people of God. Nor could the nations gather anything certain from the Jewish cult, which differed greatly from the cult of the gentile gods. For what Plutarch conjectured in his problems from the feast of Tabernacles, that it was Bacchus, is too rotten to deserve to be refuted. There is no doubt, therefore, that he who is unknown to the Athenians is the same as the uncertain God to Lucan: meanwhile, known in some way: known confusedly and in potentiality; unknown distinctly and in act. Which, unless they are taken dexterously, cannot be admitted. For the gentiles did not say an unknown God in the same sense as the Jews said ineffable or unknown in essence; for the former were completely ignorant of the true God, who alone is Jehovah Elohim, that is, God one in essence, three in persons: but the latter said that the nature of that one true God is incomprehensible and inexplicable to us. Nor does it suffice that the gentiles worshipped the same God as the Jews, because the God of the Jews, as we have said, is none other than Jehovah Elohim: whom the gentiles could not worship, since they were not informed about God. The Apostle therefore only wishes this, that they, even though ignorant of that one true God, have hitherto worshipped one God by this inscription of the altar and religion of worship: and thus, besides other deities which they worshipped by their own names, they acknowledged that there was still a God who was indeed unknown to them, but most distinct from those deities. Therefore, so that they might know who, besides other deities designated by their own names, is the uniquely true God who is truly unknown to them, whom they themselves, while ignorant, worshipped as God, who alone could avert the plague or grant victory, he testifies that he is now about to announce him to them. The Athenians therefore had some knowledge of God, even though they were destitute of the Word of God: It was known to them: That there is a God, even though they were ignorant of who that true God was. It was known that God must be worshipped religiously, even though they did not know the true worship of God. But the Apostle also asserts that they worshipped in ignorance that God whom he himself was preaching, that is, that one true God. Because when they venerated many gods and goddesses, they nevertheless placed one above them all as the supreme God, whom they worshipped above the rest as the author of every good, even though they did not know which one out of such a multitude of gods that God was to be considered; and therefore they called him unknown. For, as we noted before, the altar was not inscribed in the plural number, which kind of inscription Jerome thinks it was, perhaps having itself in this way: To the gods of Asia, and Europe, and Africa, to the unknown and foreign gods; but in the singular number, as Paul expressly testifies, this was the inscription, To an unknown God.
