ὀυκ ἐν χειροποιήτοις ναοῖς κατοικεῖ) Vide supra cap. VII. 48. & ibi dicta.

## 17:25
Verse 25. Neither is he served by human hands, needing anything) The sense is: he is not worshipped by the pious because he himself has need of that worship, but because it is our duty: the same sense is in Psalm 50:10, 11, 12, 13. Euripides in Hercules Furens: 'For God, if he is truly God, needs nothing. These are the wretched words of poets.'

Ludovicus de Dieu rightly observes that θεραπεύεσθαι here is rather 'to be served' than 'to be worshipped,' because 'to worship' pertains to honor, which is not considered here, since it is owed to God and accepted by Him; but 'to serve' properly pertains to utility, since God is not only in need of nothing, but also gives all things to all, so that in the preceding verse the incomprehensibility and infinity of God are asserted, and here His perfection and αὐτάρκεια (self-sufficiency): there is no doubt, however, that that honor is also considered which is shown through temples erected and in temples to God, which, as it is not precisely owed to God and was freely instituted by God, so the worship of God is not situated primarily in that which is prepared by the hands of men, but in the soul.

He himself gives to all life and breath in all things) life and breath, that is, the breath of life, as appears from Genesis 2:7, and we said at John 3:5. God is the Father of spirits, Numbers 16:23, that is, the cause of living for all living things: but especially of men, as those who have received the dominion of themselves and other things from God.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ὀδὲ ὑπὸ χειρῶν ἀνθρώπων θεραπεύεται προσδεόμενός τινος) Sensus est: non ideo à piis colitur, quod eo cultu ipse opus habeat, sed quia id nostri est: officii: idem sensus in Psal. L. 10. 11. 12. 13. Euripides Hercule furente: Δεῖται γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς, εἶπερ ἴσ᾽ ὄντως Θεὸς Ὀδενὸς. ἀοιδῶν οἵδε δύστηνοι λόγοι.

Recte quidem observat Ludov. de Dieu θεραπεύεσθαι hic esse potius ministratur, quam colitur, quia τὸ colere honoris est, qui hic non respicitur, quippe qui Deo debetur, & ab ipso admittitur; ministrare autem proprie utilitatis est, quum Deus non modo nullius rei indigens sit, sed & omnibus det omnia, ut præcedenti versu Dei incomprehensibilitas, & infinitas, hic ejus perfećtio & αὐτάρκεια asseratur: nullum tamen dubium est, honorem etiam illum respici, qui per templa erecta, & in templis Deo exhibetur, qui uti præcise non debetur Deo, & libere à Deo institutus est, ita in eo non præcipue cultus Dei situs est, quod manibus hominum paratur, sed in anima.

αὐτὸς διδὺς πᾶσι ζωὴν καὶ πνοὴν κατὰ πάντα) ζωὴν κὲ πνοὴν, id est, πνοὴν ζωῆς, ut apparet ex Gen. II. 7. & diximus ad Joh. III. 5. Deus Pater πνευμάτων Num. XVI. 23. id est, omnibus animantibus causa vivendi: eximie vero hominum, ut qui & sui, & aliarum rerum dominium adinistat Dei acceperint.

## 17:26
Verse 26.

And he made from one blood every nation) From the seed of one Adam, so that in that way also he might bind us all together by a certain bond of natural kinship. My father brings forward this reason and others, to show that God could have the whole world in one man: so that God might be more rightly understood to be one: so that there might be greater admiration in such a diversity of forms and languages.

To dwell upon all the face of the earth) From Genesis 11:8. Moreover, 'the face of the earth' is that which we commonly call the surface of the earth, whereas jurists call that which is built upon 'the surface,' but 'the face of the earth' is the soil.

Having determined the appointed times) With a certain great providence He took care that where any nation had begun to overflow, new lands would open up to it, with no one hindering.

And the boundaries of their habitation) ὁροθεσίαν, גבלות, Deuteronomy 32:9, where the Greeks have ὅρια. Thus He attributed sufficient boundaries to each, so that they would not have a need to invade the boundaries of others; nor indeed would they have been permitted to do so, unless God had wished to punish certain peoples for grave crimes.

By 'appointed times' new possessions of land are not noted, because the boundaries of habitation are expressed by the following word, and this word properly denotes times, whence commentators distinguish them in such a way that by the former word are designated the prefixed times, when and how long, and by the latter the prefixed limits of regions, as each people is to dwell. Which Ludovicus de Dieu rightly observed; but he is less correct in calling into doubt whether by 'the boundaries of habitation' the limits of habitation are denoted, and inclining toward the view that they should rather be understood as the set limits of the life of each individual, as the Ethiopian rendered it, 'and he ordained the times and his years, how long they should dwell.' For ὁροθεσίαι are properly limits, not of life, but of a defined space or place: and κατοικία properly denotes habitation, not age or life. Therefore, that controversy concerning the term of life, whether it is fixed or movable, is not defined here. But just as the times have been preordained by God, so also the Apostle taught that the boundaries of habitation have been divinely defined. We have therefore here some heads of natural knowledge of God, from which the Apostle, as if from principles conceded by the Athenians, tried to lead them as if by the hand to the saving knowledge of the true God. For every treatment, and every disputation, which is undertaken with right reason, γίνεται ἐκ προϋπαρχούσης γνώσεως, as the Philosopher says; and it is necessary for convincing an adversary to use principles which are conceded, lest the proof become τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ αἴτησις. Such principles are those common notions which the Apostle introduces, some of which follow from others, such as: (1.) That God exists. (2.) That God made the world and all things which are in the world. (3.) That God is the Lord of heaven and earth. (4.) That the immense God is not circumscribed by temples made by hand. (5.) That God, being in need of nothing, is not to be conciliated or appeased by the hands of men. (6.) That God gives to all life, and breath, and all things. (7.) That God is the author of the whole human race. (8.) That God has granted the whole earth as a habitation to men. (9.) That God has defined the appointed times. (10.) That God has established the boundaries of habitation. (11.) That God is not far from any one of us. (12.) That in God we live, and move, and are.

From these principles, as if sufficiently known, the Apostle refutes the first worship of the Athenians, and convicts them of idolatry, who do not hesitate to compare the creature to the creator, to circumscribe the incomprehensible, to assimilate the maker of all things and the parent of the human race to human handiwork, to conciliate the giver of all good things with gifts, and to assign a certain habitation to Him who gave the whole earth to the human race, and defined the limits of habitation for all, and is nowhere absent by the immensity of His essence and the goodness of His providence. Afterwards the Apostle leads his hearers as if by the hand, and that most prudently, by the benefit of these principles as if they were most certain and well-known postulates, to the saving knowledge of God, setting before them then the command, then the decree, then the Catholic benefit of God: The former, by which He denounces to all men everywhere that they should repent: The latter, by which He has appointed a day on which He is about to judge the world justly, and indeed through the man whom He has defined; the last, finally, by which He deigns to provide faith to all, or causes every man to be converted to faith in Him, after He raised Him from the dead, as the Syrian, the Arab, and also the Vulgate Interpreter render it.

Although indeed those aforementioned axioms about God were not all so well known to the Athenians, as far as actual, explicit, and distinct knowledge is concerned, they were nevertheless used by the Apostle as conceded, both because they were known in potentiality, by implicit and confused knowledge, and therefore were assumed as known by nature and obvious to all who use sound reason; and because they had been expressly handed down by their own writers, that is, the Gentile Philosophers, who by the benefit of reason alone discovered them to be most certain. Whence those very principles are found here and there in the writings of the Gentiles: that God indeed exists, as all assert: but that God is δημιουργὸν τῶν ἁπάντων, the maker of all things, not only Plato acknowledging it in the Timaeus, the Epistle to Dionysius, Hermeas, and Coriscus, as also his disciple Aristotle testifies, and likewise Cicero, Plutarch, Laertius, etc. but also before Plato, Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, Thales the Milesian, and others more ancient, concerning whom Justin Martyr, Clement and Cyril of Alexandria, and others bear witness. Similarly, that God is the Lord of heaven and earth, Hesiod professed: For He Himself is the king and ruler of all,

For He (God) Himself is the King and Lord of all: that God is not contained in temples, Heraclitus taught, to whose sentiment Heinsius judges the Apostle to have alluded; That God is not worshipped or delineated by the hands of men (οὐδὲ ὑπὸ χειρῶν ἀνθρώπων θεραπεύεται) Zaleucus expressed in express words, whom Scaliger made a follower of Pythagoras: ὃ τιμᾶται Θεὸς ὑπ᾽ ἀνθρώπῳ φαύλῳ, οὐδὲ θεραπέυεται δαπάναις, God is not honored by a wicked man, nor is He worshipped or delineated by expenses. That God is not in need of anything, Plato and Jamblichus and Proclus, and other followers established, preaching Him as self-sufficient and the good, and the excess or superabundance of all things. That God gives life, and breath, and all things to all, did not escape Pythagoras, who called God the principle of all things, and the animation, and the motion of the universe, as attested by Cicero, Plutarch, and Clement of Alexandria. That He is the parent of the human race, the Apostle himself teaches from Aratus. That finally God perfects, constitutes, and defines all things, being everywhere present, it appears from that of Orpheus, which Clement of Alexandria produces, to have been known to the Gentiles; ἔστι δὲ πάντη αὐτὸς ἐπουράνιὸς καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ πάντα τελευτᾷ, He is indeed everywhere heavenly, and on earth He perfects all things. But since among the Athenians those sects of the Stoics and Epicureans especially opposed themselves to Paul, the Apostle proposed those things which overthrew both the fatal necessity of the Stoics and the fortuitous confluence of things of the Epicureans, without the providence of the Divine.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

ἐποίησέ τε ἐξ ἑνὸς αἵματος πᾶν ἔθνος) Ex semine unius Adami, ut ea quoque modo nos omnes quodam naturalis cognationis vinculo colligaret. Mihi pater hanc causam adfert & alias, ut ostenderet Deus totum mundum posse esse in uno homine: ut sic rectius Deum esse unum intelligeretur: ut major esset admiratio in tanta formarum ac vocum diversitate.

κατοικεῖν ἐπὶ πᾶν τὸ πρόσωπον τῆς γῆς) Ex Gen. XI. 8. est autem πρόσωπον τῆς γῆς, id quod vulgo dicimus superficiem terræ, cum Jurisconsulti id quod inædificatur vocent superficiem, τὸ πρόσωπον vero γῆς, solum.

ὁρίσας προτεταγμένους καιρούς) Magna quadam providentia curavit, ut ubi gens aliqua cœpisset exundare, terræ ei novæ patescerent, nemine prohibente.

καὶ τὰς ὁροθεσίας τῆς κατοικίας αὐτῶν) ὁροθεσίαν גבלות Deut. XXXII. 9. ubi Græci ὅρια. Ita sufficiens cuique fines attribuit, ut non necesse haberent alienos fines invadere; neque vero id permissæ fuissent facere, nisi Deus populos quosdam ob gravia facinora punire voluisset.

Per προτεταγμένους καιροὺς non notantur novæ terræ possessiones, quia termini habitationis voce sequenti expressi sunt, & hæc vox proprie tempora notat, unde ita illa distinguunt commentatores, ut per priorem vocem præfixa tempora, quando & quamdiu, per posteriorem præfixi regionum limites, uti quisque populus habitaturus designentur. Quod recte observavit Ludov. de Dieu; at minus recte in dubium revocans num per ὁροθεσίας τῆς κατοικίας denotati sint termini habitationis, eoque inclinans, quod potius intelligendi sint positi limites vitæ uniuscujusque, uti Æthiops reddidit, & ordinavit tempora & annos sios, quamdiu habitarent. ὁροθεσίαι enim proprie limites sunt, non vitæ, sed spatij vel loci definiti: & κατοικία proprie habitationem, non vero ætatem, vel vitam notat. Non ergo definitur hic illa controversia de termino vitæ, fixusne sit, an mobilis? Sed uti tempora à Deo præordinata sunt, ita etiam terminos habitatio- nis divinitus esse definitos Apostolus docuit. Ha- bemus ergo hic capita nonnulla cognitionis Dei naturalis, è quibus Apostolus ceu principiis con- cessis ab Atheniensibus eos deducere veluti manu conabatur ad veri Dei cognitionem salutiferam. Omnis enim tractatio, omnisque disputatio, quæ cum recta ratione suscipiturer έκ προυπαρχόσης γίνε- ται γνώσεως, dicente Philosopho; & oportet ad adversarium convincendum uti principiis, quæ con- ceduntur, ne probatio fiat τῶ ἐν ἀρχῇ αἴτησις. Talia principia sunt communes illæ notiones, quas inducit Apostolus, quarum aliæ ex aliis con- sequuntur, utpote: (1.) Deum esse. (2.) Deum fecisse mundum & omnia, quæ in mundo sunt. (3.) Deum illum cæli & terræ Dominum esse. (4.) Deum immensum non circumscribi templis manu- factis. (5.) Deum nullius rei indigum haud conci- liari vel deliniri manibus hominum. (6.) Deum dare omnibus vitam, & halitum, & omnia. (7.) Deum universi generis humani auctorem esse. (8.) Deum universam terram concessisse habitationem hominibus. (9.) Deum stata definivisse tempora. (10.) Deum terminos habitationis constituisse. (11.) Non abesse Deum longe ab unoquoque nostrum. (12.) In Deo nos vivere, moveri, & esse.

Ex hisce principiis veluti satis notis refellit Apostolus primum cultum Atheniensium, eosque idololatrías convincit, qui creaturam creatori comparare, incomprehensibilem circumscribe- re, factorem rerum omnium, generisque humani parentem facturis humanis assimilare, datorem o- mnium bonorum donis conciliare, illique certam habitationem adsignare non dubitent, qui huma- no generi terram universam dedit, omnibusque limites habitationis definivit, nec uspiam abest immensitate essentiæ ac bonitate providentiæ. Postmodum deducit Apostolus auditores veluti manu, idque prudentissime, horum principiorum ceu αἰτημάτων certissimorum, notissimorumque beneficio, ad salutiferam Dei notitiam, sistens il- lis tum mandatum, tum decretum, tum beneficium Dei Catholicum: Illud, quo denunciat omnibus ubique hominibus, ut resipiscant: Istud, quo consti- tuit diem, quo juste judicaturus est terrarum or- bem, & quidem per virum, quem definiit; hoc de- nique, quo fidem præbere dignatur omnibus, vel converti facit omnem hominem ad fidem ejus, post- quam excitavit eum à mortuis, ut Syrus, Arabs, nec non vulgatus Interpres reddunt.

Quanquam vero superiora ista axiomata de Deo omnia haud fuerint ita nota Atheniensibus, quantum ad cognitionem actualem, explicitam, & distinctam, adhibita tamen sunt ab Apostolo ceu concessa, tum quod potentia nota essent, cogni- tione implicita, & confusa, ideoque ceu natura nota, omnibusque sana ratione utentibus obvia, assumuntur; tum quod à propriis ipsorum scri- ptoribus, hoc est, gentilibus Philosophis expresse tradita fuerint, qui solo rationis beneficio ea de- prehenderunt certissima. Unde illa ipsa princi- pia passim reperta in gentilium scriptis: Deum quidem esse omnibus asserentibus: Deum vero δη- μιυργὸν τῶν ἁπάντων opificem rerum omnium, non Platone tantum agnoscente in Timæo, Epistola ad Dionys. Hermeam, & Coriscum, teste quoque Aristotele discipulo, itemque Cicerone, Plutarcho, Laërtio, &c. sed & ante Platonem Anaxagora, Py- thagora, Thalete, Milesio aliisque antiquioribus, de quibus Justinus Martyr, Clemens & Cyrillus Alexan- drin. aliique testimonium perhibent. Similiter Deum esse cæli terræque Dominum, professus est Hesio- dus: Αὐτὸς γὰρ πάντων βασιλεὺς καὶ κοίρανός ἐστιν,

Ipse enim (Deus) omnium Rex & Dominus est: Deum non conclusum esse in templis, Heraclitus docuit, cujus sententiam allusisse Apostolum censet Heinsius; Quod Deus manibus hominum non colatur vel deliniatur (οὐδὲ ὑπὸ χειρῶν ἀνθρώ- πων θεραπεύεται) expressit Zaleucus disertis ver- bis, quem Pythagorae sectatorem fecit Scaliger: ὃ τιμᾶται Θεὸς ὑπ᾽ ἀνθρώπῳ φαύλῳ, οὐδὲ θεραπέ- υεται δαπάναις, non honoratur ab improbo homine, neque sumptibus colitur, vel delinitur, Deus. Quod Deus non indigeat re ulla, Plato & Jamblichus & Proclus, aliique sectatores statuerunt, eundem ceu αὐταρκῆ & τὸ ἀγαθὸν, & ὑπερβολὴν vel ex- uperantiam omnium rerum praedicantes. Quod Deus vitam, & halitum & omnia det omnibus, non latuit Pythagoram, qui Deum principium omnium rerum dixit, & animationem, & mo- tum universi, teste Cicerone, Plutarcho, Cle- mente Alexandrino. Quod humani generis pa- rens sit, ex Arato docet ipse Apostolus. Quod denique Deus omnia perficiat, constituas, defi- niat, ubique praesens, ex illo Orphei, quod Clemens Alexandr. producit, gentilibus cognitum fuisse apparet; ἔστι δὲ πάντη αὐτὸς ἐπουράνιὸς καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ πάντα τελευτᾷ, Est vero ubique ipse caelestis, & in terra perficit omnia. Quum vero inter Atheni- enses sectae illae Stoicorum, & Epicureorum imprimis sese opposuerint Paulo, ea proposuit Apostolus, quae cum Stoicorum fatalem necessitatem, tum Epicureorum fortuitum rerum confluxum, sine providentia Numinis profligarunt.

## 17:27
Vers. 27.

ζητεῖν τὸν κύριον) In the Manuscript τὸν Θεὸν, because κύριος in these books is for the most part Jesus.

No change of the text is to be granted here. For the Greek codices consistently read κύριον. Which name is not attributed to Christ alone in the N.T. but also expresses God simply.

εἰ ἄραγε ψηλαφήσειαν αὐτὸν καὶ εὕροιεν) Again ἓν διὰ δυοῖν, for ψηλαφήσαντες ὕυροιεν; He did all these things, so that He might give them an opportunity of finding Him as if by groping. And by εἰ ἄραγε ψηλαφήσειαν, he shows some difficulty in the matter. For to grope is either for the blind (see the groped wall of Quintilian) or for those walking at night.

It is implied that God, incorporeal by nature, as if made corporeal in those visible things, offered Himself to be known in a certain way by the very act of touching; that God the creator can be as it were groped for from those things which He created, and primarily from the production of the human race, from the concession of the habitation of the whole earth, from the determination of times, and from the definition of limits, and periods, kingdoms and polities, all of which proclaim the supreme Lord of all things, and the principle of all, τὸ ὄντων ὂν with a clamorous silence, and in reality exhibit Him to be handled by all, not by the contact of the body, but by the apprehension of the mind. The depravation of the passage, which Socinus attempted in his praelect. c. II., that to seek the Lord is nothing else than to live holily; but to find Him is to experience Him as propitious to oneself, we have overthrown in Theol. nat. & revel. page 101.

seqq. But the verb ψηλαφάω is properly indeed to grope, as the blind are accustomed to grope with their hands, just as the LXX use this verb in Is. LIX. 10. we have groped like the blind for the wall, and as if without eyes we have touched; and Deut. XXIX. 28. you shall grope in the midday, as the blind gropes: but metaphorically it signifies to search or to attain by apprehension of the mind, especially indeed, when the truth is manifest and obvious, so that it can be as it were handled with the hands. This agrees excellently with the Gentiles: because just as the blind do not see those things which are nearest to them, and therefore attempt to grope for them with their hands; so the Gentiles, who lived in the times of ignorance, placed in darkness Is. IX. 1. and blind Rom. II. 19. destitute of the light of the Word of God illuminating the eyes, Ps. XIX. 9. although they could not behold God, with eyes not illuminated; yet they could as it were grope for God with their hands, who is not far from each one of us. Concerning which Hermes Trismegistus says in the Pimander: 'God cannot indeed be penetrated by human sight, yet He can be touched by the hands; And Jamblichus de Myst. cap. I. teaches that we apprehend God by a certain kind of contact.

καίτοιγε ὐ μακρὰν ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἑκάσυ ἡμῶν ὑπάρχοντα) Namely by the power of His might: for Paul does not call the Athenians to subtle disputes about the essential presence of God, about which there were various opinions of Philosophers and Jews and Christians, but to those things which were perceived by the things, Porphyry cites the oracle:

Πάντα Θεῶ πλήρη· πάντη Θεός ἐσι Φανήθα.

Josephus, when he explains the words of Solomon concerning the temple: For you, he said, have an eternal house, O Lord, and we know that the heaven, and the air, and the earth, and the sea, were made from those things which you brought forth for yourself, through all of which, not even content with these, you have contained. Aristaeus in the same Josephus: For both they (namely the Jews) and we (the Greeks) worship the God who established the whole, having understood the invocation to him from the life innate in all things. The opinion of Zeno in Diogenes Laertius: That the mind extends through every part of the world, just as it does in us. Seneca, Epistle XLI: God is near to you: he is with you: he is within. LXXIII. Do you wonder that a man goes to the gods? God comes to men: nay, what is closer, he comes into men. LXXXIII. Nothing is closed to God: he is present in our minds, and intervenes in our thoughts. Dio Chrysostom: For as being not far nor outside of God, but having been born in him, in the midst of him. Soon being filled from all sides with the divine Nature. Proclus on the Timaeus: For the divine is distant from nothing, but is present equally to all. The same sense among Christian writers. Minucius Felix: We live not only in the eyes of God, but also in his bosom. The same: He is everywhere not only near to us, but infused. Clement, Stromata II, concerning God: Standing very near. Arnobius I: For that we walk, that we breathe and live, does it not come to us from him? The same VII: Nothing at all is long to God, to whom the earth is a point, and all things are established under his nod. Salvian II: Teaching that our substance is implanted among the sacred virtues. If anyone wishes for more, let him consult Arrian of the Epicteteans I. 14, Nazianzen in Oration I, Ambrose on Psalm XVIII.

That not only the presence of grace—which seems to Grotius, along with the Socinians, Arminians, Vorstius, and indeed even certain Calvinists, to be denoted without substantial omnipresence—is clear both from the text and from a comparison with the sounder Gentiles, to whom the immensity of the divine substance was not denied. Their opinions have been adduced in part by Grotius. Nor indeed is it right to evade by the name of subtlety those things whose denial easily leads to Atheism, and which were known to the Gentiles even from the light of nature. Certainly by those words, that God is not far from each one of us, it is not denoted that God is present to those living holily, which is the Socinian gloss, but that he is present to all: since the Apostle is addressing the Athenians, who certainly were not living holily; and he conceives the words universally, ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἑκάσε ἡμῶν, from each one of us, and the hexameter which he subjoins deals with all men, as Socinus himself admits, when he says: For this very thing, that we both live, and move, and are, we all have from him: But it is one and the same subject when the Apostle says that God is not far from each one of us, and when he says that we live, move, and are in him. Whence we argue: God is not far from those who live, move, and are in God. But all men live, move, and are in GOD. Therefore, concerning all men, not only those who live holily, it is certain that God is not far from them. Furthermore, those from whom God is not far can find God by feeling to find. All, therefore, not only those who live holily, can find God by feeling after Him. Furthermore, the very evidence of the words teaches that God is said not to be far from us, by reason of a general presence, by which He is at hand to all, and can be found by all, not by reason of a special presence, by which He is present to the Church, and to the faithful, and to His saints; because in respect of this it is not said, οὐ μακρὰν ὑπάρχει ἀφ' ἡμῶν, not far from us, but ἐν μέσῳ ἡμῶν, in the midst of us, Matt. XVIII. 20, and μεθ' ὑμῶν, with you, Matt. XXVIII. 20. But in respect of the former, it is said that God is not from afar, Jerem. XXIII. 23. The coherence of the text also teaches this: because it treats of that presence by virtue of which all things are administered, and life, and breath, and all things are granted to all, and the times for everyone are defined, and the terms and limits for empires are established, according to those things which precede: as also by virtue of which we live, and move, and have our being in Him, according to the things which follow. But that is a general presence, and the governance and administration of all things, not a special care toward the saints: of this, nothing at all is delivered here; all the benefits here are general and common, and therefore Crellius acknowledges in his book on God and the divine attributes, chap. 27, page 276, with these words, 'He is not far off,' that a universal presence is expressed. Nor indeed is that divine presence without the substantial presence of God. For the power of God is not abstracted from His essence. Nor does God act upon created things, or preserve or govern them, while absent, but while present: not by virtual contact only, but by substantial presence: as it is commonly said: Enter praesenter Deus hic & ubique potenter. Nor do they bring in the presence of power only, but of the substance itself, which Grotius himself cited. Let them only be weighed accurately; Porphyry, he says, cites the oracle:

Πάντα Θεῶ πλήρη· πάντη Θεός ἐσι Φανήθη.

Add also what we previously observed that Clement of Alexandria produced from Orpheus: ἐςὶ δὲ πάντη αὐτὸς ἐπικράνιος, κἠπὶ χθονὶ πάντα. He is indeed everywhere heavenly, and on earth he perfects all things: And what we produced from ecclesiastical antiquity in Vol. II of the System of Theology, page 399. Cyprian on the Vanity of Idols: 'But what temple can God have, whose temple the whole world is? God is one, and is diffused everywhere in His entirety.' Athanasius against the followers of Sabellius: 'Do not seek a magnitude of place so spacious that it can contain the magnitude of GOD; for that which is immeasurable ought not to be contained in that which is measured. Since He measures the heaven in His palm, etc.' Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechism VI: 'God is to be believed to be perfect in all things, not defined by place, but the maker of places, who is in all things, and is circumscribed by none.' Chrysostom, Homily V on chapter II of Colossians: 'Either God circumscribes the world, or less.' If less, He Himself is circumscribed. But if He circumscribes, He is infinite by nature. Cyril of Alexandria, book XI of Commentaries on John: 'It is fitting for God to be everywhere and in an inexplicable way to fill heaven, to fill earth, to contain all things, and to be contained by none. For God cannot be comprehended by place, nor circumscribed by spaces.' And book I of the Thesaurus, chap. VII: 'God is in all things, and penetrates all things, yet we do not believe that He is connected to bodies. For God remains in His purity, nor is He mixed with others, although He is everywhere and penetrates all things.' Augustine, book VII of The City of God, chap. XXX: He says that God is everywhere, acting, filling heaven

and earth by His presence, with His nature not absent. Epistle VII to Dardanus: 'Therefore He is said to be everywhere, because He is absent from no part of things; therefore He is whole, because He does not offer part of Himself present to one part of things, and another part to another part, equal to equal, but less to less, and greater to greater, but He is present as a whole equally not only to the totality of creation, but also to any part whatsoever. How everywhere, if in Himself? Everywhere, namely, because He is nowhere absent: But in Himself, because He is not contained by those things to which He is present.' Fulgentius against the sermon of Fastidiosus, chap. VI: 'Thus He is immense, whom no creature can enclose, and because He is immense, He is whole everywhere, because He is neither contained by place, nor extended, or contracted by space.'

Latin:

Vers. 27.

ζητεῖν τὸν κύριον) In Manuscripto τὸν Θεὸν, quia κύριος in his libris plerumque est Jesus.

Nulla hic concedenda textus mutatio. Codices enim Graeci constanter legunt κύριον. Quod no- men non soli Christo tribuitur in N. T. sed etiam Deum simpliciter exprimit.

εἰ ἄραγε ψηλαφήσειαν αὐτὸν καὶ εὕροιεν) Iterum ἓν διὰ δυοῖν, pro ψηλαφήσαντες ὕυροιεν· fecit haec omnia, ut occasionem illis daret se inveniendi velut palpando. Et per εἰ ἄραγε ψη- λαφήσειαν, ostendit aliquam rei difficultatem. Nam pal- pare aut caecorum est (vide parietem palmatum Quinti- liani) aut noctu incedentium.

Id innuitur, Deum natura incorporeum quasi corporeum in rebus illis aspectabilibus factum, sese attrectatione quodammodo ipsa cognoscen- dum praebuisse; Deum conditorem veluti palpa- ri posse ex iis, quae condidit, & cum primis e gene- ris humani productione, e terrae universae inhabitatio- nem concessione, e temporum determinatione, e li- mitum, & periodorum, regnorum & politiarum definitione, quae omnia supremum rerum omnium Dominum, & principium omnium, τὸ ὄντων ὂν clamoso silentio produnt, & reapse omnibus con- trectandum exhibent, non contactu corporis, sed apprehensione mentis. Depravationem loci, quem Socinus in praelect. c. II. tentavit, quod quae- rere Dominum nihil aliud sit, quam sancte vivere; eum autem invenire, sit, illum sibi propitium ex- periri, profligavimus Theol. nat. & revel. pag 101.

seqq. Est autem verbum ψηλαφάω proprie qui- dem palpo, ut caeci solent manibus palpare, quem- admodum verbum hoc adhibent LXX. Es. LIX. 10. palpavimus sicuti caeci parietem, & veluti absque ocu- lis attrectavimus; & Deut. XXIX. 28. palpabis in meridie, ut caecus palpat: tralatitie vero significat scrutari vel apprehensione mentis assequi, praesertim vero, cum veritas est manifestaria & obvia, ut veluti palpari possit manibus. Convenit id egregie gentilibus: quia non secus atque caeci ea, quae proxima ipsis sunt, non vident, ideoque manibus ea palpare conantur; ita gentiles, qui vixere tem- poribus ignorantiæ, in tenebris positi Esa. IX. 1. & cæci Rom. II. 19. destituti lumine Verbi Dei oculos illumi- nantis, Pf. XIX. 9. tametsi non potuere intueri Deum, oculis haud illustratis; manibus tamen veluti palpare Deum poterant, qui non longe abest ab unoquoque nostrum. De quo Hermes Trismegi- stus ait in Pimandro: 'Deus humana acie pene- trari quidem non potest, attamen manibus con- trectari potest; Et Jamblichus de Myst. cap. I. do- cet, nos quodam quasi contactu Deum apprehen- dere.

καίτοιγε ὐ μακρὰν ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἑκάσυ ἡμῶν ὑπάρχοντα) Nem- pe vi potentiæ suæ: neque enim ad subtiles disputationes de præsentia essentiali Dei, de qua variæ fuere & Philoso- phorum & Judæorum & Christianorum sententiæ, Athe- nienfes vocat Paulus, sed ad ea quæ rebus sentiebantur, Porphyrius oraculum citat:

Πάντα Θεῶ πλήρη· πάντη Θεός ἐσι Φανήθα.

Josephus ubi verba Salomon.s de templo explicat: Σὺ γὰρ, ἔιπεν, οἶκον μὲν αἰώνιον ἔχεις, ὦ δεσπότα, κἀξ ὧν σαυτῷ ἐξηγά- σω γεγονότα τὸν ἐρανὸν οἴδαμεν κὼ ἀέρα, κὼ γῆν κὼ θάλασ- σαν, δι ὧν ἁπάντων, ὐδὲ τέτοις ἀρκύμενος, κεχώρηκας. Apud eundem Josephum Aristaus: τὸν γὰρ ἅπαντα συσησάμενον Θεὸν κὼ ὗτοι (Judæi scilicet) κὼ ἡμεῖς (Græci) σεβόμεθα, ἑτοί- μως ἀπὸ τῶ σύμπασιν ἐμφύσιν τὸ ζῆν, τὴν ἐπίκλησιν ἀυτῷ νοήσαν- τες. Zenonis sententia apud Diogenem Laertium: εἰς ἅπαν τῶ κόσμω μέρος διήκειν τὸν νῦν καθάπερ ἐφ' ἡμῶν. Seneca Epistola XLI: prope est à te Deus: tecum est: intus est. LXXIII. Miraris hominem ad Deos ire? Deus ad homines venit: imo quod propius est, in homines venit. LXXXIII. Nihil Deo clu- sum est: interest animis nostris, & cogitationibus mediis inter- venit. Dion Chrysostomus: ἅτε γὰρ ὐ μακρὰν ὐδ' ἔξω τῶ Θεῶ διωκισμένοι, ἀλλ' ἐν αυτῷ μέσῳ πεφυκότες ἐκείνῳ. Mox πανταχόθεν ἐμπιπλάμενοι τῆς θείας Φύσεως. Proclus ad Ti- mæum: ὐδενὸς γὰρ ἀφέσηκε τὸ θεῖον, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ἐξίσε πά- ρεσιν. Idem sensus apud scriptores Christianos. Minutius Felix: Non solum in oculis Dei, sed & in sinu vivimus, Idem; ubique non tantum nobis proximus, sed infusus est. Clemens Strom. II. de Deo: ἐγγυτάτω βεβηκων. Arnobius I. Nam quod incedimus, quod spiramus & vivimus, ab eo ad nos venit? Idem VII. Deo longum nihil omnino est, cui punctum terra est, & sub nutu omnia con ft tuta. Salvianus II. Docens insitam inter virtutes sacras nostram esse substantiam. Si quis plura velit, consulat Arrianum Epicteteorum I. 14. Nazianze- num oratione I. Ambrosium in Psal. XVIII.

Non solam gratiæ præsentiam, quod Grotio cum Socinianis, Arminianis, Vorstio, imo & Calvinianis quibusdam videtur, citra ανςαςα- σίαν substantialem notari, cum è textu liquet, tum è collatione saniorum gentilium, quibus non negata divinæ substantiæ immensitas. Quo- rum sententiæ ex parte à Grotio adductæ sunt. Nec vero subtilitatis nomine eludere fas est ea, quorum inficiatio facile ad Atheismum ducit, quæque vel è lumine naturæ gentibus nota fue- runt. Verbis certe illis, quod Deus non absit procul ab unoquoque nostrum, non notatur, quod Deus sancte viventibus præsto sit, quæ So- ciniana est Glossa, sed quod omnibus: quum alloquatur Apostolus Athenienses, qui utique sancte non vivebant; & verba universaliter conci- piat, ἀπὸ ἑνὸς ἑκάσε ἡμῶν ab unoquoque nostrum, & senarius, quem subjungit, de omnibus homini- bus agat, fatente ipso Socino, dum ait: Hoc enim ipsum, quod & vivimus, & movemur, & sumus, ab ipso omnes habemus: Est autem unum idem- que subjectum, quando dicit Apostolus, quod non absit Deus ab unoquoque nostrum, & cum ait, quod in ipso vivamus, moveamur, & simus. Unde arguimus: Ab illis Deus non abest, qui in Deo vivunt, moventur, & sunt. At omnes homines in DEO vivunt, moventur, & sunt. De omnibus ergo hominibus, non tantum de iis, qui sancte vivunt, certum est, quod Deus non longe ab iis absit. Porro à quibus Deus non longe abest, illi possunt Deum palpando inve- invenire. Omnes ergo, non solum qui sancte vivunt, Deum palpando invenire possunt. Prae- terea docet ipsa verborum evidentia, Deum dici non abesse procul a nobis, ratione praesentiae ge- neralis, qua omnibus praesto est, & ab omni- bus inveniri potest, non ratione praesentiae spe- cialis, qua adest Ecclesiae, & fidelibus, sanctisque suis; quia hujus respectu non dicitur, 8' μακρὰν ὑπάρχει ἀφ' ἡμῶν non longe abesse a nobis, sed ἐν μέσῳ ἡμῶν in medio nostrum Matth. XVIII. 20. & μεθ' ὑμῶν nobiscum esse Matth. XXVIII. 20. illius au- tem respectu dicitur Deus non de longinquo esse, Jerem. XXIII. 23. Docet id quoque textus cohae- rentia : quia de ea praesentia agitur, vi cujus ad- ministrantur omnia, & conceduntur omnibus vita, & halitus, & omnia, definiuntur qui- busvis tempora, constituuntur imperiis termi- ni, & limites, juxta ea, quae antecedunt: ut & vi cujus nos in ipso & vivimus, & move- mur, & sumus, juxta consequentia. Ea au- tem generalis est praesentia, rerumque omnium gubernatio, & administratio, non specialis cu- ra erga sanctos: De hac nihil omnino hic tra- ditur; omnia beneficia hic sunt generalia & communia, ideoque agnoscit Crellius lib. de Deo, & attrib. div. cap. 27. pag. 276. verbis il- lis, Non longe abest, universalem praesentiam ex- primi. Nec vero illa praesentia divina est sine substantiali Dei adessentia. Non enim potentia Dei est abstracta ab ejus essentia. Nec agit Deus in res creatas, aut conservando seu gu- bernando easdem absens, sed praesens: non per virtualem tantum contactum, sed praesentia sub- stantiali: ut vulgo dicitur: Enter praesenter Deus hic & ubique potenter. Nec potentiae solum, sed ipsius substantiae praesentiam infe- runt, quae Grotius ipse attulit. Expendantur modo accurate; Porphyrius, inquit, oraculum citat:

Πάντα Θεῶ πλήρη· πάντη Θεός ἐσι Φανήθη.

Adde & quae ex Orpheo Clementem Alexan- drinum produxisse antea observavimus : ἐςὶ δὲ πάντη αὐτὸς ἐπικράνιος, κἠπὶ χθονὶ πάντα. Est vero ubique caelestis, & in terra perficit omnia : Et quae ex antiquitate Ecclesiastica produximus Tom. II. Syst. Theol. pag. 399. Cyprianus de Idolor. vanit. Quod vero templum Deus habere possit, cujus templum totus est mundus ? Deus unus est, & ubique totus diffusus est. Athanasius contr. Scabell. gregal. Ne requiras magnitudinem loci tam spatiosam, quae capere possit DEI magnitudi- nem; non enim id, quod immensurabile est, in men- surato contineri oportet. Quoniam in palmo suo me- titur caelum, &c. Cyrillus Hierosolym. Catech. VI. Perfectus in omnibus credendus est Deus, non definitus loco, sed locorum opifex, qui in omnibus est, & a nullo circumscribitur. Chrysostomus homil. V. in cap. II. Col. Aut circumscribit Deus orbem, aut minus. Si minus, ipse circum- scribitur. Si vero circumscribit, infinitus est natu- ra. Cyrillus Alexandr. lib. XI. Commentar. in Joh. Deo conveniens est esse ubique & inexplicabili mo- do implere caelum, implere terram, capere omnia, & a nullo capi. Non enim comprehendi loco po- test Deus, neque spatiis circumscribi. & lib. I. Thesaur. cap. VII. Deus est in omnibus, & pene- trat omnia, nec tamen connecti corporibus ipsum credemus. Manet enim in sua sinceritate Deus, nec aliis commiscetur, quamvis ubique sit, omnia penetret. Augustin. lib. VII. de C. D. cap. XXX. Deum esse ubique ait, actum, implentem caelum

& terram præsentia, non absente natura. Epist. VII. ad Dardan. Ideo ubique esse dicitur, quia nulli parti rerum absens est; ideo totus, quia non parti rerum partem suam præsentem præbet, & alteri parti alteram partem, æquales æqualibus, minori vero minorem, majorique majorem, sed non solum universitati creaturæ, verum etiam cuilibet parti totus pariter adest. Quomodo ubi- que, si in seipso? Ubique scil. quia nusquam est ab- sens: In seipso autem, quia non continetur ab eis, quibus est præsens. Fulgentius contr. sermon. fastidios. cap. VI. Sic est immensus, quem nulla potest concludere creatura, & quia immensum ubique totus, quia nec continetur loco, nec disten- ditur, aut contrahitur spatio.

## 17:28
Verse 28.

ἐν αὐτῷ γὰρ ῶμεν, καὶ κινύμεθα, καὶ ἐσμέν) It is a Hebraism. In Him, that is, through Him, by His benefit. Through Him we exist: He gave us life congruent to man, and movements responding to such a life.

There is no need to abandon the customary meaning of the preposition ἐν. Not only is the origin indicated, that we are FROM HIM, but also the divine περιχώρησις: that we both live, and move, and have our being IN HIM. Which sense the preceding words confirm. For God is not absent from any one of us. Compare, Jerem. XXIII. v. 23.

ὡς καί τινες τῶν καθ' ὑμᾶς ποιητῶν εἰρήκασι) It is no wonder if Paul the Cilician had read the Cilician Aratus, or in honor of their common fatherland.

τῦ γὰρ κὴ γένος ἐσμὲν) In spirit, namely. You have a paraphrase of this Aratean passage in Festus Avienus, where these things are among others:

The flower and flame of the soul, which, as the course of the primal mind runs through, resolving the divine inner chambers, has filled the veins, having worked with abundant love.

What Aratus had said about Jove, Paul truly adapts to God, because the wiser Greeks also understood the supreme God by Jove. Thus Aristeas, in Josephus, says that the God of the Jews is the God of the universe, whom the Greeks call Ζῆνα.

It is so: He applies to God what he had said about Jove. For thus Aratus had begun his poem, ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα, Let us begin from Jove, etc., where he also taught that the crossroads, and the gatherings of men, and the sea, and the harbors were full of Jove, and he handed down other things consonant with the previous assertions of the Apostle, to which it is likely the Apostle intended to refer, having cited a few of his words. To some it seems that the preceding words of the Apostle, ἐν αὐτῷ γὰρ ζῶμεν καὶ κινώμεθα καὶ ἐσμὲν, For in him we live and move and are, also exhibit a senarius of an ancient poet, ζῶμεν δ' ἐν αὐτῷ θνητὰ καὶ κινώμεθα, καὶ ἐσμὲν, since he speaks in the plural number, as also some of your own poets have said. But Aratus does not say that we are the offspring of God only in mind: because our whole being is from God: nor is our origin to be attributed to him only with regard to the soul. And man is the offspring of God, because he was created in the image of God: whence he is also called the Son of God.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ἐν αὐτῷ γὰρ ῶμεν, καὶ κινύμεθα, καὶ ἐσμέν) Est Hebraismus. In ipso, id est, per ipsum, ipsius beneficio. Per ipsum exi- stimuss: ipse nobis vitam homini congruentem, & motus tali vitæ respondentes dedit.

Non opus est relinquere usitatam præpositio- nis ἐν significationem. Non origo tantum in- dicatur, quod AB IPSO simus, sed περιχώ- ρησις etiam divina: quod IN IPSO & vivamus, & moveamur, & simus. Quem sensum verba antecedentia firmant. Non enim abest Deus ab unoquoque nostrum. Confer, Jerem. XXIII. v. 23.

ὡς καί τινες τῶν καθ' ὑμᾶς ποιητῶν εἰρήκασι) Non mirum si Cilix Paulus Cilicem Aratum, vel in patriæ communis honorem, legerat.

τῦ γὰρ κὴ γένος ἐσμὲν) Animo scil. Loci hujus Arateï paraphrasin habes apud Festum Aviennum, ubi hæc in- ter alia:

Flos & flamma animæ qui discurrente meatu Mentis primigenæ penetralia dia resolvens Implevit largo venas operatus amore.

Quod de Jove dixerat Aratus, id vero Deo aptat Paulus, quia & sapientiores Græci per Jovem Deum summum intelligebant. Sic Aristæus apud Josephum ait Deum Judæorum esse Deum universi, quem Ζῆνα vocant Græci.

Ita est: Ad Deum applicat, quod ille de Jo- ve dixerat. Ita enim orsus erat Aratus carmen suum, ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα, Ab Jove principium &c. ubi etiam docuit, & compita, & hominum cæ- tus, & mare, & portus esset Jovis plenos, aliaque tradidit, superioribus Apostoli assertionibus con- sona, quo remisisse Apostolum voluisse, pau- cis ejusdem verbis adductis, verisimile est. Non- nullis videtur, præcedentia quoque Apostoli verba ἐν αὐτῷ γὰρ ζῶμεν καὶ κινώμεθα καὶ ἐσμὲν. In ipso enim vivimus, movemur & sumus, Poëtæ veteris senarium exhibere, ζῶμεν δ' ἐν αὐτῷ θνητὰ καὶ κινώμεθα, καὶ ἐσμὲν, quandoquidem in plurali numero dicat ὡς καί τινες τῶν καθ' ὑμᾶς ποιητῶν εἰρήκασι. Non autem Aratus tantum animo nos Dei genus esse dicit: Quia totum esse nostrum à Deo est: nec tantum quoad animum origo ei accepta ferenda. Et genus Dei homo est, quia creatus ad imaginem Dei: unde Dei et- iam Filius dicitur.

## 17:29
V. 29. γένος ὖν ὑπάρχοντες τῦ Θεῦ) Paul adapts himself to poetic speech. He signifies, however, that we approach God most of all by the mind, and on account of this likeness we are called his children. See what we have said at the end of Luke III. In the New Testament, however, we are called his children for a weightier reason, because we imitate his goodness: again, in another way, through his resurrection we shall be children by the fellowship of blessedness.

But did not the pious faithful also in the Old Testament, for example, Abraham, Moses, David, and other Patriarchs and Prophets and Saints, imitate the divine goodness? How then is their piety set before us as an example? See Hebrews chapter XI.

We ought not to think that the Divine is like unto gold or silver or stone, a graven thing of art and man's device. Two things are looked at in images: matter and work. Matter, even the most excellent, such as gold, silver, marble, is far inferior to man: the work cannot but be more ignoble than the workman: many therefore are deceived who think such things are suitable for the honor of God, since the purest honor of God is in a worship withdrawn from all things that fall under the senses. See what we have brought forward on this matter at Deut. 4. λίθῳ here is marble, as in Isaiah XXXVII. 19. Jeremiah II. 27. chapter III. 9. Concerning marble images see Pliny. χάραγμα is that which is sculpted: for χαράσσειν is to sculpt, 2 Kings XVII. 11 in the Greek. He wished to express the Hebrew פסλ. τέχνης, such as the works of Praxiteles or Polycletus. τέχνης ἐμμελέτημα, Wisdom XIII. 10. ἔργον χειροτέχνιτος, Deut. XXVII. 5. and of man's device: some things not fashioned from art according to some model, but made according to whim, such as those bodiless persons, concerning whom Arnobius speaks in the aforementioned place. What is here called ἐνθύμησις, that is in the Greek of Ezekiel ἐνθύμημα in many places, where in the Hebrew it is גלוליו. τὸ θεῖον εἶναι ὅμοιον: for many nations thought that there were such gods in heaven as the images exhibited. Arnobius, Book VI: All these images are likenesses of the superior deities. Therefore, God also must be said to dwell in heaven, to whose form and appearance the likeness of this image has been directed.

Heinsius says that the mention of man's device is added, because the artist gives the form which he imagines: He gives the form which he fashions and devises; not of God, whom he does not know, but of the art and of the device, the art and thought which he conceives; and therefore not the true one. Whence Isaiah XXXI. 7, the things made by hands, made into sin, are spoken of.

Latin:

V. 29. γένος ὖν ὑπάρχοντες τῦ Θεῦ) Accommodat se Poë- ticæ loquutioni Paulus. Significat autem nos mente potissi- mum ad Deum accedere, ac propter hunc similitudinem filios ejus dici. Vide quæ diximus ad finem III. Lucæ. In Novo vero Testamento graviore de causa filii ejus dicimur, quod bonitatem ejus imitemur: Rursum alia- ter per resurrectionem ejus filii erimus beatitudinis con- sortio.

Annon vero etiam pii fideles in Veteri Testa- mento, exempli causa, Abraham, Moses Da- vid, aliique Patriarchæ & Prophetæ ac Sancti bo- nitatem divinam imitati sunt? Quomodo ergo eorum pietas nobis in exemplum sistitur? Vide Ebr. XI. caput.

ὐκ ὀφείλομεν νομίζειν, χρυσῷ ἡ ἀργύρῳ ἢ λίθῳ, χαράγ- ματι τέχνης καὶ ἐνθυμήσεως ἀνθρώπου, τὸ θεῖον εἶναι ὅμοιον) Duo spectantur in simulacris: materia & opus. Materia etiam praestantissima, ut aurum, argentum, marmor, multo inferiora sunt homine: opus non potest non ignobi- lius esse opifice: multum ergo falluntur qui putant talia ad honorem Dei esse idonea, cum purissimus Dei honos sit in cultu abducto ab omnibus rebus sub sensum cadentibus. Vide quæ de ea re attulimus ad Deut. 4. λίθῳ hic est marmor, ut Esaæ XXXVII. 19. Jerem. II. 27. cap. III. 9. De marmoreis simulacris vide Plinium. χάραγμα est id, quod sculptitur: nam χαράσσειν sculpere 2. Reg. XVII. 11. in Græco. Exprimere voluit Hebræum פסל. τέχνης qualia opera Praxitelis vel Polycleti. τέχνης ἐμμελέτημα, Sap. XIII. 10. ἔργον χειροτέχνιτος Deut. XXVII. 5. κὶ ἐνθυμήσεως ἀνθρώ- πε: quædam non ex arte ad aliquod exemplar ficta, sed fa- cta pro libitu, quales illæ personæ sine corpore, de quibus dicto loco Arnobius. Quod hic ἐνθύμησις dicitur, id in Græco Ezechielis ἐνθύμημα multis in locis, ubi in Hebræo גלוליו τὸ θεῖον ἔναι ὅμοιον: nam multæ gentes putabant tales in cœlo esse Deos, quales simulacra exhibebant. Ar- nobius Libro VI: Simulacra hæc omnia superiorum sunt ima- gines numinum. Ergo & in cœlo habitare dicendus est Deus talis ad cujus formam & speciem simulacri hujus similitudo dire- cta est.

Heinsius ἐνθυμήσεως ἀνθρώπυ mentionem ad- ditam ait, quia artifex dat formam quam imagina- tur: Formam dat quam fingit & excogitat; non Dei, quam ignorat, sed τῆς τέχνης καὶ τῆς ἐνθυ- μήσεως, artis atque cogitationis quam concipit; ideoque non veram. Unde Esa. XXXI. 7. τὰ χει- ροποίητα, in peccatum facta, dicuntur.

## 17:30
Vers. 30.

The times of ignorance therefore) Thus he calls the former times, compared to the light of the Gospel.

God having overlooked) ὑπεριδεῖν is to dissemble, as if you do not see. התעלם Deut. XXII. 1, 3, 4. God is said to have dissembled idolatry, because he did not threaten the punishment of Gehenna to those practicing it, as in the Gospel.

Now he commands all men everywhere to repent) He strictly denounces to all that they should correct themselves.

Beza also explained it as having dissembled by conniving. But the Vulgate 'despising' is more correct. This word also properly signifies, as Lud. de Dieu notes, that which is used by the LXX for קוט to be indignant, to detest, מאס to reject, התעבר to be angry, Deut. III. 26, Psalm LXXVIII. 59, 62, as also for עלם to hide oneself, as Deut. XXI. 1, so that the sense may be that in the times of ignorance God was angry, or hid himself, which is the cause given here why now, under the Gospel of light, and not indeed in the ancient times of ignorance, repentance is preached to all men: if indeed God was angry with them, or by his just judgment hid himself from them. Dn. D. Sebastian Schmidius in colleg. Bibl. after page 269, says that ὑπεριδὼν comprises two things in itself: 1. That God was so long-suffering toward the ignorance of men, even the most gross, that although he had many causes for destroying men, he nevertheless did not do this, but waited for the times of the New Testament, under which the Gospel was to be preached to all, if even then they would do penance for their ignorance. 2. That at the same time in Christ he decreed to forgive the sins of ignorance, even the most gross, to those doing penance, and permitted access to repentance. And thus it could happen that saving repentance could be preached to all men. That God formerly did not threaten Gehenna, but that this was only done in the New Testament, is an erroneous hypothesis, already refuted more than once.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

τὺς μὲν ὖν χρόνυς τῆς ἀγνοίας) Sic vocat tempora priora, comparata ad lucem Evangelii.

ὑπεριδὼν ὁ Θεός) ὑπεριδεῖν est dissimulare, quasi non vi- deas. התעלם Deut. XXII. 1. 3. 4. dicitur Deus dissimulas- se idololatriam, quia eam factantibus non minabantur pœnam Gehennæ, ut in Evangelio.

τὰ νῦν παραγγέλλει τοῖς ἀνθρώποις πᾶσι πανταχῦ μετανοεῖν) Destricte omnibus denunciat, ut se corrigant.

Dissimilasse connivendo etiam Beza exposuit. Sed rectius Vulgata despiciens. Hoc etiam proprie verbum significat, notante Lud. de Dieu, quod à LXX. usurpatur pro קוט indignari, detestari, מאס reprobare, התעבר irasci Deut. III. 26. Psal. LXXVIII. 59. 62 ut & pro עלם abscondere se, ut Deut. XXI. 1. ut sensus sit, temporibus ignorantiæ Deum iratum fuisse se, vel abscondisse se, quæ causa hic datur, cur jam hisce, sub Evangelio lucis, non vero antiquis ignorantiæ temporibus omnibus hominibus prædicata resipiscentia: siquidem Deus iratus ipsis fuerit, vel justo se judicio ab iis abscon- derit. Dn. D. Sebastian Schmidius in colleg. Bibl. post pag. 269. τὸ ὑπεριδὼν duo in se complecti ait: 1. Quod Deus erga hominum ignorantiam etiam crassissimam adeo fuerit longanimis, ut licet causas multas habuerit delendi homines, hoc ta- men non fecerit, sed tempora N. Test. sub quo E- vangelium omnibus prædicandum expectaverit, si vel tum de ignorantia sua pœnitentiam agerent. 2. Quod simul in Christo peccata ignorantiæ et- iam crassissimæ pœnitentiam agentibus remittere decreverit, & ad pœnitentiam aditum permiserit. Atque sic fieri potuit, ut omnibus hominibus pœ- nitentia salutaris prædicari potuerit. Olim Deum non comminatum fuisse gehennam, sed id de- mum in Novo Testamento factum esse, hypo- thesis erronea est, plus vice simplici jam pro- fligata.

## 17:31
Vers. 31.

Because he has appointed a day) He appointed it with himself: but he made men certain that there would be some day of judgment, even if he concealed from his most beloved friends when it would be.

By that man.

πίστιν παρασχὼν πᾶσιν) Because the matter was hardly credible, he brings forward an excellent argument. Thus הורעתי נאמנה. Hos. V. v. 9.

ἀναστήσας αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν) God, by raising Jesus from the dead, provided the greatest testimony he could for his doctrine. Moreover, in that doctrine this also was included, that he would be the judge of the human race, Matt. XXV. 31. & seqq. John V. v. 25.

Concerning the faith in the future universal judgment made, or provided, through the resurrection of Christ from the dead, even the Calvinists, Tossanus, Ludov. de Dieu, and others have expounded: But where is God said to have 'made faith' in the sense of a confirmation of a thing to be believed! The word παρασχών implies something else. He provided, namely, faith to all, supplying or furnishing those things by which they might attain it through faith. For thus, what was in him, he is deservedly said to have provided faith to us all. Thus the Vulgate rendered it, 'fidem præbens omnibus' [providing faith to all]. What πίστις is in these books is known. That this word is commonly accepted as saving faith in Christ, who was raised from the dead for our justification, so that through faith in him we might have true righteousness, does not need proof. And since repentance, which God has seen to be announced to all men everywhere, is not salutary without faith, which indeed is not of everyone 2 Thess. III. 2. & is to be given to us by God Phil. I. 29. John VI. 29. therefore it was necessary that faith should also be provided to all by God.

The Syrian translates: And he caused every man to turn to his faith. See B. D. Danhavverus in Hodosoph. page 1306. & Dn. D. Sebastian Schmidius loc. cit. who notes that the word παρέχειν signifies to give, to exhibit, to make. But πίστιν, especially in the matter of repentance, signifies the faith by which we believe, justifying: and he wishes δι’ αὐτὸν to be understood, namely, the man by whom he has defined; i.e., Because he is about to judge the world through the Man whom he has defined, exhibiting faith through him; after he raised him from the dead: and furthermore he warns that the word παρέχειν denotes not only some external offering, but also a real bestowal or work, Matt. XXVI. 10. Luke XI, 7. chap. XVIII. 5. Acts XXII. 2. chap. XXVIII. 2. 1. Timothy VI. 7. But what is said about the world being judged in righteousness, Dn. D. Schmidius takes under a hypothesis, unless they have repented, understanding it as rigorous justice, page 389. although he does not reject the opinion of others, that God will judge the world in righteousness, being about to give eternal life to the penitent, and eternal ignominy to the impenitent: Which is the explanation of Brentius and others, and in our judgment is to be preferred.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

διότι ἔστησεν ἐν ἡμέραν) Apud se constituit: Homines vero certos fecit aliquam diem judicii fore, etsi quando ea futura esset, etiam amicissimos celavetit.

ἐν ἀνδρὶ) Per eum hominem.

πίστιν παρασχὼν πᾶσιν) Quia res erat vix credibilis, argu- mentum adfert eximium. sic הורעתי נאמנה. Ose. V. v. 9.

ἀναστήσας αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν) Deus Jesum resuscitando è mortuis, maximum quod potuit doctrinæ ejus testimo- nium præbuit. In ea autem doctrina & hoc erat, se fore ju- dicem humani generis, Matth. XXV. 31. & seqq. Joh. V. v. 25.

De fide futuro universali judicio per resuscita- tionem Christi ex mortuis facta, vel præbita, etiam Calviniani, Tossanus, Ludov. de Dieu, alii ex- posuere: Sed ubi fecisse fidem sensu confirmatio- nis rei credendæ, dicitur Deus! Aliud verbum παρασχών importat. Præbuit nempe fidem omni- bus, sufficiens vel subministrans ea, quæ per fi- dem ipsi consequi possint. Sic enim, quod in ipso erat, fidem nobis omnibus præbuisse meri- to dicitur. Ita Vulgatus reddidit, fidem præbens omnibus. Quid sit πίστις in hisce libris, notum est. Quam vocem de fide salvifica in Christum, ideo propter justitiam nostram à mortuis resusci- tatum, ut per fidem in ipsum veram haberemus justitiam, communiter accipi, probatione non indiget. Et cum μετάνοια, quam omnibus ho- minibus ubique annunciari curavit Deus, nulla salutaris sit, sine fide, quæ vero non est cujusvis 2. Thess. III. 2. & à Deo donanda nobis est Phil. I. 29. Johan. VI. 29. idcirco opus erat, ut omnibus etiam à Deo præberetur fides.

Syrus, vertit: Et converti fecit omnem homi- nem ad fidem ejus. Vid. B. D. Danhavverus in Hodosoph. pag. 1306. & Dn. D. Sebastian Schmi- dius loc. cit. qui notat verbum παρέχειν significa- re dare, exhibere, facere. Πίστιν vero impri- mis in materia de pœnitentia significare fidem, qua nos credimus, justificantem: & subaudiri vult δι’ αὐτὸν scilicet ἄνδρα, ᾧ ὥρισεν: h. m. Quia judicaturus est orbem terrarum per Virum, quem definiit, exhibens per hunc fidem; postquam susci- tavit eum ex mortuis: ac præterea monet, quod verbum παρέχειν non tantum externam aliquam oblationem, sed realem etiam collationem aut opus notet, Matth. XXVI. 10. Luc. XI, 7. cap. XVIII. 5. Actorum. XXII. 2. cap. XXVIII. 2. 1. Timoth. VI. 7. Quod vero de orbe terrarum judicando in justitia di- citur, sub hypothesi accipit Dn. D. Schmidius, nisi pœnitentiam egerint, justitiam rigorosam in- telligens, pag. 389. etsi non rejiciat aliorum sen- tentiam, judicaturum Deum esse orbem in justi- tia, daturus pœnitentibus vitam æternam, im- pœnitentibus æternam ignominiam: Quæ Bren- tii explicatio & aliorum, nostroque judicio præ- ferenda est.

## 17:32
Vers. 32.

οἱ μὲν ἐχλεύαζον) No doubt the Epicureans. οἱ δὲ εἶπον· ἀκουσόμεθά σου πάλιν περὶ τούτου) Namely the Stoics, who did not think the restoration of a dead man impossible, as we showed in book II of the Truth of the Christian Religion.

Latin:

Vers. 32.

οἱ μὲν ἐχλεύαζον) Non dubium quin Epicurei. οἱ δὲ εἶπον· ἀκουσόμεθά σου πάλιν περὶ τούτου) Nempe Stoi- ci qui hominis mortui restitutionem non putabant impos- sibilem, ut ostendimus ad librum II. de Veritate Religionis Christianæ.

## 17:33
Vers. 33.

καὶ οὕτως ὁ Παῦλος ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ μέσου αὐτῶν) Deferred to another day.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

καὶ οὕτως ὁ Παῦλος ἐξῆλθεν ἐκ μέσου αὐτῶν) Dilatus in alium diem.

## 17:34
Vers. 34.

Τινὲς δὲ ἄνδρες κολληθέντες αὐτῷ) When they had insinuated themselves into a closer familiarity with him. Thus κολλᾶσθαι is taken, above chap. V. 13. c. IX. 26. c. X. 28.

Among whom also Dionysius) Not he who suffered martyrdom in Gaul: For that happened while Decius was ruling the Romans, as the most learned man Jacobus Sirmondus made clear.

Areopagite) One from that most noble Senate, which both had much authority in the Republic, and judged concerning murders and wounds. The Greeks call it the most venerable and most just court. Valerius Maximus II. 6 calls it a most holy council, and he also proclaims its wisdom VIII. 1. Tacitus in Annals II called it the Arean Judgment; without doubt the conversion of a man so grave and approved by public testimony was of much benefit to the Gospel.

On Dionysius, Cornelius à Lapide is mistaken: This is he who wrote those sublime books on the celestial and Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, on the Divine Names, on Mystical Theology, etc. He praises Baronius and Delrio, who learnedly defended him against the calumnies of the heretics, as he calls them, Erasmus and Scaliger. But not only did Erasmus and Scaliger doubt or deny that the aforementioned books belong to this Dionysius; others did as well. Laurentius Valla mocked these works as forged, as Erasmus notes at this place: William Grocyn the Englishman, although he had previously publicly refuted Valla on this account, did not hesitate afterwards, having perceived the author's genius more closely and familiarly, to recant his former opinion, as Erasmus reports in his Scholium on Jerome's De Ecclesiasticis Scriptoribus and in his Declaration to the Censure of the Paris Theologians, title 31, number 91. Cajetan, in his commentary on this place, says: whether that Dionysius is the one (the Areopagite) who wrote the books on the Divine Names, is not certain: such things are also found in Bellarmine, book II, De Confirmatione, chapter 7. Possevinus in his Apparatus Sacer, under the word Photius, says: The works of Dionysius, he says, seem to be noted by Photius as pseudepigrapha. Nor is it possible to find any mention of them in Eusebius, Jerome, or Sophronius; indeed, Bellarmine, in his Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, denies that the writings of Dionysius were known to the world before the times of Gregory the Great: And that Gregory did not wish to acquiesce to the authority of Dionysius, nor did he wish for the Hierarchy and the orders of the Angels, nor other most serious Greek and Latin Fathers to follow him, Fr. Ribera admits in his Epistle to the Hebrews. The style also is too subtle, inflated, and affected, not simple and sincere, not such as would befit the age of Dionysius, but one which began to be in use at least three hundred years after the departure of the Apostles, as Flacius notes: And since in the book on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy concerning temples, altars, sacred places, the Choir, the establishing of Catechumens outside the doors of the temple, as well as many things concerning Monks, which it is evident do not befit the time of Dionysius, furthermore, Ignatius's Epistle to the Romans is alleged, and in the book on the Divine Names it is said that this Dionysius was present at the funeral of Mary, which must have been celebrated before the conversion of Dionysius. This Dionysius also alleges Clement of Alexandria; how can he be considered the Areopagite? See the Censure of Ancient Writers by Robertus Loci, and the Criticus Sacer of Andr. Rivetus, book I, chapter IX. What Cornelius handed down concerning the conversion, Episcopate, and martyrdom of the Senator and primary judge, the Areopagite, we leave to its own place. Most things rest on doubtful witnesses. But that Damaris was the wife of this Dionysius, which Chrysostom in book IV De Sacerdotio claims, does not appear from this passage: for it is not said γυνὴ ἀυτῶ, but simply γυνὴ. Grotius also rashly suspects his name to be corrupted, as if it should be read Δάμαλις. For no Codex reads it so: and who does not know that names are various, and very many are close to one another, yet not the same.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

Τινὲς δὲ ἄνδρες κολληθέντες αὐτῷ) Cum in propiorem se ejus familiaritatem insinuassent. Sic κολλᾶσθαι sumitur, supra cap. V. 13. c. IX. 26. c. X. 28.

ἐν οἷς καὶ Διονύσιος) Non ille qui in Gallia martyrium passus est: Id enim Decio Romanis imperante conti- git, ut perspicuum fecit vir doctissimus Jacobus Sirmon- dus.

Ἀρεοπαγίτης) Unus ex illo nobilissimo Senatu, qui & in Republica multum habebat auctoritatis, & de cæ- dibus & vulneribus judicabat. Græci vocant σεμνότατον, καὶ δικαιότατον δικαστήριον. Sanctissimum consilium Vale- rius Maximus II. 6. qui & sapientiam ejus prædicat VIII. 1. Areum Judicium dixit Tacitus Annalium II. multum pro- cul dubio profuit Evangelio, viri tam gravis & publico te- stimonio probati conversio.

De Dionysio perperam Cornelius à Lapide: Hic est ille, qui sublimes illos libros scripsit de cæ- testi & Ecclesiastica hierarchia, de divinis no- minibus, de mystica Theologia, &c. Laudat Baronium, & Delrionem, qui à calumniis ha- reticorum, quos vocat, Erasmi & Scaligeri eru- dite eum defenderint. At non Erasmus, & Sca- liger solum dubitarunt, aut negarunt libros prædictos hujus esse Dionysii; sed etiam alii. Laurentius Valla hæc opera ut conficta derisit, notante ad hunc locum Erasmo: Guilhelmus Grocinus Anglus cum prius publice refutasset ob id Vallam, non dubitavit postea propius ac fami- liarius autoris ingenio perspecto priorem senten- tiam παλινωδεῖν, ut refert Erasmus Schol. in Hieronym. de Eccles. Script. & Declar. ad Cen- sur. Paris. Theol. titul. 31. num. 91. Cajetanus, an istimet (Areopagita) sit ille Dionysius, in- quit ad h. l. qui scripsit libros de divinis nomini- bus, certum non est: qualia etiam habentur a- pud Bellarmin. lib. II. de Confirm. cap. 7. Pos- sevinus in appar. sacr. verbo Photius: Opera, inquit, Dionysii ut Pseudepigrapha videntur à Photio notari. Neque ullam eorum mentionem reperire licet apud Eusebium, Hieronymum, So- phronium; imo Bellarmin. Catal. Script. Ec- cles. negat, Scripta Dionysii ante tempora Grego- rii M. mundo nota fuisse: Nec Gregorium Dio- nysii autoritati acquieviscere voluisse, aut Hierar- chiam & ordines Angelorum, nec alios gra- vissimos Patres Græcos & Latinos eum sequi voluisse, Fr. Ribera in Epist. ad Ebræos fate- tur. Stylus etiam argutus nimis, inflatus, & affectatus est, non simplex, & sincerus, non qualis Dionysii ætati conveniat, sed qui trecentis ad minimum annis post excessum Apostolorum in usu esse cœperit, notante Flacio: Et quum libr. de Hierarch. Ecclesiast. de templis, de altaribus, de locis sacris, de Choro, de Catechumenis extra fores templi statuendis, ut & de Monachis mul- ta habeantur, quæ constat Dionysii tempori non convenire, adhæc allegetur Ignatii Epist. ad Rom. & libr. de Divin. nominibus dicatur Dionysius hic suse funeri Mariæ interfuisse, quod ante conversionem Dionysii celebratum esse oportet. Clementem etiam Alexandrinum al- leget hic Dionysius, quomodo is Areopagita haberi potest? Vid. Censura Scriptor. veter. Ro- berti loci, & Andr. Riveti Critic. sacer lib. I. cap. IX. Quæ Cornelius de Areopagitæ Senatoris & judicis primarii conversione, Episcopatu, & martyrio tradidit, suo relinquimus loco. Ple- raque testibus dubiis nituntur. Damarin au- tem uxorem hujus Dionysii fuisse, quod Chry- sostom. lib. IV. de Sacerd. vult, ex hoc loco non apparet: non enim γυνὴ ἀυτῶ dicitur, sed sim- pliciter γυνὴ. Nomen etiam ejus temere suspi- catur corruptum esse Grotius, quasi legendum sit Δάμαλις. Nullus enim Codex ita legit: & quis nescit, nomina varia esse, ac plurima inter se vicina, non tamen eadem.

## 18:1 Argument
CHAPTER XVIII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Paul stays in Corinth with Aquila and Priscilla, and especially upon the return of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia, he testifies that Jesus is the Christ. But when the Jews contradicted and blasphemed, having shaken out his garments, he said, Your blood be upon your own head, I am clean: From this I will go to the Gentiles, and having entered the house of Justus, a pious man near the Synagogue, whose ruler Crispus, with many Corinthians, believed and were baptized; he was warned by a vision to preach fearlessly, because God has a great people in this city, and so he sat there for a year and a half, and was dragged by the Jews to the tribunal of Gallio, who, however, doing nothing about matters of religion, repelled them, and did not care that Sosthenes was beaten by the Greeks before the tribunal. Finally, Paul, about to sail into Syria, shaved his head in Cenchreae, and coming to Ephesus, he dealt with the Jews, and when he was asked to stay there, he promised a return, hastening to Jerusalem because of the approaching feast, having left Aquila and Priscilla there. He confirmed the brethren in Caesarea, Antioch, in Galatia and Phrygia. But at Ephesus, Apollos, teaching about the Lord, was more fully informed about the way of God by Aquila and Priscilla, who, instructed by letters of recommendation, coming into Achaia, contributed much to those who had believed among the Jews, convincing them through the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

There are two parts: I. The unsuccessful success of Paul among the Corinthians with the Jews, and his successful success among the Gentiles, with the proceedings before Gallio, up to verse 18. II. The Ephesian deeds, with the journeys of Paul, and the information of Apollos by Aquila, and the confirmation of the faithful in Achaia, up to the last verse.

PART I. The unsuccessful success of Paul among the Corinthians with the Jews, and his successful success among the Gentiles, with the proceedings before Gallio.

Verse 1.

χωρισθεὶς ὁ Παῦλος) When he had departed. It corresponds to the Hebrew ירד as appears in Judges IV. 1. Thus also in the following clause and above in Acts I. 4.

ἦλθεν εἰς Κόρινθον) Once the light of Greece, as Cicero calls it, indeed razed by Mummius, but flourishing again with time.

It was situated in Achaia, or the Peloponnese, which is now called the Morea, and was once its metropolis; a noble emporium with two harbors, of which Lechaeum overlooks the Ionian Sea, and Schoenus the Aegean: whence they called Corinth 'two-seaed'. Formerly named Ephyra, according to Strabo, book VIII, and later, when it was restored by Corinthus, son of Marathon, or as Suidas wishes, son of Pelops, it was named Corinth. Because of the convenience of its location and its commerce, and because it was rich in metals and especially in bronze, just as the Corinthian bronze was most excellent, it reached such a point of power that it scarcely yielded to the city of Rome. It also abounded in philosophers and orators, and for that reason was very famous: whence Paul went to it, so that in a city so populous, he might disseminate the celebrated Gospel, and he converted many there to Christ. This Cornelius thinks that the Apostle wrote the first Epistle to the Thessalonians in this city, but it was given at Athens before he departed from there, as the subscription of the same testifies.

Latin:

CAPUT XVIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Paulus Corinthi divertit apud Aquilam & Priscillam ac redeunte imprimis è Macedo- nia Sila, & Timotheo testificatur Jesum esse Christum. Judæis autem contradi- centibus, & blasphemantibus, excussis ve- stimentis, sanguis vester, dixit, super ca- put vestrum, mundus ego: Ex hoc ad gen- tes vadam, & ingressus domum Iusti, viri pii prope Synagogam, cujus præfectus Cri- spus, cum multis Corinthiis credebant, & baptizabantur; Visione monebatur, ut in- trepide prædicaret, quod Deus magnum po- pulum in hac civitate habeat, adeoque per sesquiennium ibi sedit, & a Iudæis ad Gallionis tribunal pertractus fuit, qui ve- ro nihil faciens causas religionis, ipsos repel- lebat, Sosthenem a Græcis coram tribuna- li percuti, nihil curabat. Tandem in Sy- riam navigaturus Paulus in Cenchris caput totondit, Ephesumque veniens cum Iudæis egit, & cum rogaretur, ut illic maneret, Hierosolymam, ob festum imminens pro- perans, reditum promisit, relictis ibidem A- quila & Priscilla. Cæsarea Antiochia, in Galatia & Phrygia fratres confirmavit. Ephesi autem Apollo docens de Domino uberius de via Dei informabatur ab A- quila & Priscilla, qui literis systaticis instructus in Achaiam veniens multum contulit his, qui crediderunt Judæis, per Scripturas convincens Jesum esse Chri- stum.

Partes sunt duæ I. Successus Pauli apud Corin- thios infelix penes Judæos, felix penes gentes cum actis coram Gallione, ad v. 18. II. Gesta Ephe- sina, cum profectionibus Pauli, & Apollinis ab Aquila informatione, ac fidelium in Achaia con- firmatione, ad v. ult.

PARS I. Successus Pauli apud Corinthios infelix pe- nes Judæos, felix penes gentes, cum actis coram Gallione.

Vers. 1.

χωρισθεὶς ὁ Παῦλος) Cum abiisset. Respondet Hebræo ירד ut apparet Iud. IV. 1. Sic & commate sequente & su- pra Actor. I. 4.

ἦλθεν εἰς Κόρινθον) Græciæ quondam lumen, ut eam Ci- cero vocat, excisam quidem a Mummio, sed cum tempore reflorescentem.

Sita fuit in Achaia, sive Peloponeso, quæ nunc Morea dicitur, ejusque erat quondam me- tropolis; emporium nobile duobus portubus, quorum Lechæum Jonio, Schonus Ægeo immi- net mari: unde Corinthum bimarem dixerunt. Olim Corcya nominata Strab. lib. VIII. post Ephy- ræ, & ubi a Corintho Marathonis, seu ut Suidas vult, Pelopis filio restaurata, Corinthus nuncupa- ta. Ob situs opportunitatem, & mercimoniam, quia metallis ac potissimum ære, quemadmo- dum æs Corinthiacum præstantissimum fuit, eo pervenit potentiæ, ut vix Romanæ urbi conce- deret. Abundabat & Philosophis, atque Orato- ribus, eoque nomine valde celebris fuit: unde Paulus eam adiit, ut in urbe tam frequenti, ad celebri Evangelium disseminaret, ac multos ibi ad Christum convertit. In hac urbe Apostolum scripsisse Epistolam priorem ad Thessalonicenses putat hic Cornelius, sed ea Athenis data est, an- tequam inde egrederetur, teste subscriptione ejusdem.

## 18:2
Vers. 2.

ὀνόματι Ἀκύλαν) The Hebrew name עקיל the Latins translated as Aquila. It is also written עקילס and אנקילס. Some think it was the same name as the noble Chaldean interpreter, because with the insertion of נ, which is frequent among the Chaldeans, it is called אונקלוס.

Pontic by race) Born of Pontic parents. For there are many Jews in Pontus. See 1 Pet. 1:1.

lately) Recently בקרב, Ezek. 11:3.

Priscilla) In Hebrew קדסה.

Besides this Onkelos the Chaldean paraphrast and the present Aquila, there was still another Aquila, likewise a Pontic, who translated from Hebrew into Greek. V. Test. under the Emperor Hadrian, who was first a Christian from a Gentile, but finally became a Jew from a Christian. See Epiphanius, book on Weights and Measures, and Philastrius, heresy 90; concerning this one of ours, see 1 Cor. 16:19 and 2 Tim. 4:19.

because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome) Suetonius mentions this; Josephus does not mention it: whence it appears that that edict was not observed for long at Rome, which can also be gathered from the end of this book.

The cause of the edict seems to Cornelius à Lapide to have been the contention of the Jews and Christians concerning the coming of the Messiah, whence both were ordered to leave Rome, so that a riot might not arise. But Hugo and Lyranus more correctly observe another cause for the expulsion, namely that they had enticed Agrippina, the wife of Claudius, to Judaism. Just as Tiberius also, a little before, had proscribed the same from Rome because they had drawn Fulvia, the wife of the Senator Saturninus, to Judaism, as Josephus testifies, book 18, chapter 1 and 5.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ὀνόματι Ἀκύλαν) Hebræum nomen עקיל Latini verte- re Aquilam. Scribitur & עקילס & אנקילס. Quidam pu- tant idem nomen fuisse nobili interpreti Chaldæo, quia in- terposito נ, quod frequens Chaldæis, dicitur אונקלוס.

ποντικὸν τῷ γένει) Ortum parentibus Ponticis. Nam in Ponto multi Judæi. Vide 1. Petr. I, v. 1.

προσφάτως) Recens בקרב, Ezech. XI, 3.

Πρίσκιλλαν) Hebraice קדסה.

Præter hunc Onkelum Chaldæum Paraphra- sten & præsentem Aquilam fuit adhuc alius Aqui- la, itidem Ponticus, qui ex Ebræo in Græcum transtulit. V. Test. sub Adriano Imper. qui primum ex gentili Christianus, tandem vero è Christiano Judæus factus est. Vid. Epiph. libr. de Mensur. & Philastr. hær. XC. de hoc nostro vid. 1. Cor. XVI. 19. & 2. Tim. IV. 19.

διὰ τὸ διατεταχέναι Κλαύδιον, χωρίζεσθαι πάντας τὸς Ἰυ- δαίυς ἐκ τῆς ῥώμης) Meminit Suetonius: Josephus non me- minit: unde apparet non diu Romæ observatum illud edi- ctum, quod & ex fine hujus libri colligere est.

Edicti causa Cornelio à Lapide videtur fuisse Judæorum & Christianorum de Messiæ adventu contentio, unde utrique jussi Roma excedere, ne tumultus oriretur. Sed aliam expulsionis cau- sam rectius Hugo, & Lyranus observant, quod nempe Agrippinam Claudii uxorem ad Judai- smum pellexerint. Sicut etiam Tiberius paulo ante eosdem Roma proscripserat, quod Ful- viam Saturnini Senatoris uxorem ad Judaismum traduxissent, teste Joseph. lib. XVIII. cap. 1. & V.

## 18:3
Verse 3.

and he worked) Which custom Paul had imposed upon himself from the beginning of his preaching, 1 Cor. 4:12, 1 Thess. 2:9, 2 Thess. 3:8.

for they were tentmakers by trade) Makers of tents for military use. It was the custom even for the most learned of the Jews to learn some craft, whence, when circumstances required, they might support themselves. They were furriers, cobblers, garland-weavers, bakers, copyists. Thinking, no doubt, of that saying of Hesiod: 'Work is no disgrace.'

Concerning Asinaeus and Asidaeus, Jews in Babylonia, Josephus 18:12. 'Their mother commanded them to learn weaving, for work is not a disgrace, unseemly to the locals, so that the men might do wool-work among them.' Thus the Apostles after the resurrection of Christ were fishermen. And Minucius concerning the Christians: 'Unskilled in the arts, except for the base ones'; and concerning Octavius: 'Chief among bakers.' Epiphanius, heresy 80: 'All those who are servants of God, who labor for righteousness with their own hands, so as to provide also for those in need.' Theodoret, sermon 7: 'Tanners and weavers and coppersmiths, and others who practice trades.'

Because tents were made from skins, Origen called Paul a skin-stitcher, homily 17 on Numbers, who was called from stitching earthly tents to stitching eternal ones. Compare 2 Thess. 3:8. The Apostle wished to work with his hands, not because it is illicit to receive a stipend, 1 Cor. 9:12 ff., but partly because in a church not yet established there were as yet no ordered stipends, and partly because the pseudo-apostles, intruding themselves and not requiring stipends, could easily have seized the opportunity, as if he were teaching the Gospel for the sake of his belly and idleness.

ἦσαν γὰρ σκηνοποιοὶ τὴν τέχνην) Tentoriorum opifices in usum militarem. Mos erat etiam doctissimis Judæorum opificium aliquod discere, unde, ubi res ferret, se sustenta- rent. Erant pelliones, sutores, στεφανοπλόκοι, pistores, li- brarii. Nimirum Hesiodum illud cogitantes: ἔργον δ' ὐδὲν ὄνειδος.

De Asinæo & Asidæo in Babylonia Judæis Josephus XVIII. 12. Αὐτοῖς ἡ μήτηρ προσέταξεν ἱστῶν μαθήσεις, ποίη- σεως ἐκ ὄνειδος ἀπρεπῶς τοῖς ἐπιχωρίοις ὥστε τὺς ἄνδρας ταλά- σιεργεῖν παρ' αὐτοῖς. Sic Apostoli post resurrectionem Chri- sti piscatores. Et Minutius de Christianis: Expertes artium nisi seffilium: & de Octavio: Pistorum præcipuus. Epiphanius hæres. LXXX. Πάντων τῶν τῷ Θεῷ δύλων τῶν εἰς δικαιοσύνην καυνόντων ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσὶν εἰς τὸ ἐπαρκεῖν κὲ τοῖς ἐνδεομένοις. Theodoretus sermone VII. Σκύτιας κό ὑφάντας κὲ χαλκοτύ- πυς, κὲ τὺς ἄλλυς ὅσοι τὰς τέχνας μέταχειρίζουσι.

Quia tentoria è pellibus fiebant, Origenes Pau- lum pellium sutorem dixit hom. XVII. in Numeros, qui à terrenorum tentoriorum futura ad æterna confuenda vocatus. Confer. 2. Thess. III. 8. Opera- ri autem manibus voluit Apostolus, non quod illicitum sit stipendium accipere, 1. Cor. VI. 12. seqq. sed partim quia in Ecclesia nondum constituta nulla adhuc ordinata stipendia erant, partim quia Pseud-Apostoli se ingerentes, nec stipendia re- quirentes facile occasionem arripere potuissent, quasi ventris & otii causa Evangelium doce- ret.

In the Vulgate, these words are redundant here: Interposing the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Which are found neither in the Greek nor in the Syriac Codices.

## 18:5
Verse 5.

And when Silas and Timothy had come down from Macedonia) Whom Paul had ordered to follow him, chapter XVII. 15. Paul had signified to them, through those who had brought him to Athens, where he was directing his journey further.

Paul was constrained by the Spirit) He was agitated, full of the divine Spirit. Thus συνεχόμενος αὐτῷ Jerem. XXII. 9. עצר, that is, as if placed outside himself. συνεχόμενος φόβῳ Job III. 24. Thus Plutarch says that superstitious women were συνέχεσθαι by the Bacchic frenzy in Solon; but I think it is read more correctly as πνεύματι than λόγῳ, although that Manuscript has λόγῳ.

testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ) The Manuscript also has it thus. It is, however, a transposition for τὸν Ἰησῦν εἶναι χριστὸν. Similar below v. 28.

Not only the fullness of the divine Spirit and the agitation

of Paul is noted: nor is the Latin INSTABAT sufficiently apt; for what he adds, VERBO, is foreign, as Grotius acknowledges here: and Cornelius himself confesses, having set aside the authority of the Vulgate, that it is better rendered as he was stirred up in spirit, that is, with a zeal so ardent that he could hardly contain himself, and he was constrained by the spirit by others. Compare c. XVII. v. 16.
