συνείχετο τῷ πνεύματι ὁ Παῦλος) Plenus divino Spiritu agitabatur. Sic συνεχόμενος αὐτῷ Jerem. XXII. 9. עצר, id est, velut extra se positus. συνεχόμενος φόβῳ Job. III. 24. sic Plu- tarchus feminas superstitiosas συνέχεσθαι ait τῷ βαχχισμῷ in Solone rectius autem legi puto πνεύματι quam λόγῳ, quan- quam λόγῳ habet ille Manuscriptus.

διαμαρτυρόμενος τοῖς Ἰυδαίοις εἶναι τὸν χριστὸν Ἰησῦν) Sic habet & Manuscriptus. Est autem transpolitio pro τὸν Ἰησῦν εἶναι χριστὸν. Similis infra v. 28.

Non sola plenitudo divini Spiritus & agitatio

Pauli notatur: neque satis apposite Latinus IN- STABAT; nam quod addit VERBO, alie- num est, ut agnoscit hic Grotius: & fatetur Cornelius ipse, posthabita autoritate Vulgatæ, melius reddi concitabatur spiritu, id est, zelo adeo ardente, ut fere ipsum non caperet, & ab aliis comprimebatur spiritu. Confer. c. XVII. v. 16.

## 18:6
Verse 6.

shaking out his garments) Namely, so that no dust might adhere. See above c. XIII. 51. your blood be upon your own head) Thus 2 Sam. I. 16 in the Greek, your blood be upon your head. That is, you pay the penalty owed for homicide: for it is properly said of homicide, as also in Matt. XXVII. 25, and improperly of other sins. The sense is: if any evil happens to you, know that it happened by your own fault. I am clean) I stood on the watchtower and cried out. It refers to the passage of Ezekiel XXXIII. 4, where in the Greek, his blood shall be upon his own head. And v. 8, you have delivered his soul. from now on I will go to the Gentiles) As above c. XIII. 46.

That hypothetical gloss is not sufficient, if any evil happens, destruction is indicated openly, and that eternal, which certainly awaits the despisers of the Gospel. The phrase, blood upon your head, seems to have arisen from the fact that among the Jews, witnesses were accustomed to lay hands upon the head of the guilty party, so that the punishment might be committed to him: just as hands were also accustomed to be laid upon the head of the beast which was destined for a sacrifice, because it was held to bear the guilt of those who offered the sacrifice.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ἐκτιναξάμενος τὰ ἱμάτια) Nempe ne quid pulveris adhæ- resceret. Vide supra c. XIII. 51. τὸ αἷμα ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ὑμῶν) Sic 2. Sam. I. 16. in Græco τὸ αἷμά σου ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλήν σου. Id est, luis pœnam debitam homicidio: proprie enim de homicidio dicitur, ut & Matth. XXVII. 25. improprie de peccatis aliis. Sensus est; si quid vobis mali evenerit, scitote id vestra culpa evenisse. καθαρὸς ἐγώ) Steti in specula & clamavi. Respicitur lo- cus Ezechielis XXXIII. 4. ubi in Græco, τὸ αἷμα ἀυτοῦ ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς ἀυτοῦ ἔσται. Et v. 8. σὺ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀυτοῦ ἐξήρησαι. ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν εἰς τὰ ἔθνη πορεύσομαι) Ut supra c. XIII. 46.

Non sufficit illa Glossa hypothetica, si quid ma- li evenerit, indicatur palam exitium, idque sem- piternum, quod certe manet contemtores Evan- gelii. Phrasis, sanguis super caput vestrum inde quibusdam orta videtur, quod apud Judæos testes solebant manus imponere capiti rei, ut ita suppli- cio committeretur: quemadmodum etiam manus capiti pecudis, quæ in hostiam destinabatur, imponi consueverant, quia culpam ferre tenebatur eo- rum, qui hostiam offerebant.

Most Greek manuscripts do not recognize the name of Titus. It seems to have been written in the margin by someone by chance, and to have crept subsequently into certain manuscripts.

## 18:9
Verse 9. εἶπε δὲ ὁ κύριος) through an Angel in the figure of Christ. δι' ὁράματος ἐν νυκτὶ) As above, chapter XVI. 9.

Why through an Angel? Why not immediately? And where is it read that an Angel ever appeared in the form of Christ? Would not such an appearance offer a danger of angel-worship?

μὴ Φοβοῦ, ἀλλὰ λάλει καὶ μὴ σιωπήσῃς) Act as Isaiah did once, chapter LXII. 1.

Those words are not Isaiah's, but the Lord's, which is evident from verse 6, where it cannot be denied that the Lord is speaking. But it is one continuous speech of the same person.

Latin:

Vers. 9. εἶπε δὲ ὁ κύριος) per Angelum in Christi figura. δι' ὁράματος ἐν νυκτὶ) Ut supra c. XVI. 9.

Cur per Angelum? Cur non immediate? Et ubi legitur Angelum in forma Christi unquam apparuisse? annon periculum Angelolatriæ præ- beret talis apparitio?

μὴ Φοβοῦ, ἀλλὰ λάλει καὶ μὴ σιωπήσῃς) Fac ut olim Esaias c. LXII. 1.

Non Esaiæ illa verba sunt, sed Domini, quod è v. 6. patet, ubi Dominum loqui negari nequit. At una est, & continua ejusdem personæ ora- tio.

## 18:10
Verse 10. διότι ἐγώ εἰμι μετὰ σοῦ) That is, I am a help to you. See what was said at Matthew XXVIII. 20. Reference is made to what God had said in Jeremiah I. 18. διότι μετὰ σοῦ ἐγώ εἰμι.

καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐπιθήσεταί σοι) Namely, hands. Thus Achilles in Homer's Iliad A: 'so long as I live and look upon the earth, no one shall lay heavy hands upon you beside the hollow ships.'

The Vulgate, therefore, must be corrected, which rendered it passively: 'And no one shall be set upon you.' That it must be rendered actively, 'no one shall lay or cast hands upon you,' was acknowledged even by Cornelius à Lapide.

τοῦ κακῶσαί σε) That he may harm you. Similar to the aforementioned place, Jeremiah I. 18, 19. διότι λαός ἐστί μοι πολὺς ἐν τῇ πόλει ταύτῃ) Those who could easily become the people of Christ are called this people, like the sheep in John X. 16. As names are given here from the future, so elsewhere they are given from the past: as in Matthew XXI. 31. The prophecy of Isaiah chapter LIV. 15 seems to be referenced.

Latin:

Vers. 10. διότι ἐγώ εἰμι μετὰ σοῦ) Id est sum tibi auxilio. Vide quæ dicta Matt. XXVIII. 20. Respicitur id, quod Deus dixerat Jer. I. 18. διότι μετὰ σοῦ ἐγώ εἰμι.

καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐπιθήσεταί σοι) Nempe χεῖρας. Sic Achilles apud Homerum Iliados A. ὄφρα ἐμεῦ ζῶντος καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ δερκομένοιο Σοὶ κοίλης παρὰ νηυσὶ βαρείας χεῖρας ἐποίσει.

Corrigendus ergo Vulgatus, qui passive reddi- dit: Et nemo apponetur tibi. Reddendum esse acti- ve, nemo imponet, vel injiciet tibi manus, agnovit etiam Cornelius à Lapide.

τοῦ κακῶσαί σε) Ut tibi noceat. Simile dict. loc. Jer. I. 18. 19. διότι λαός ἐστί μοι πολὺς ἐν τῇ πόλει ταύτῃ) Populus hic di- cuntur ii qui facile Christi populus fieri poterant, ut oves Joh. X. 16. Ut hic ex futuro, ita alibi ex præterito dantur nomina: ut Matth. XXI. 31. Respici videtur vaticinium Esaiæ c. LIV. 15.

## 18:11
Verse 11. ἐκάθισέ τε ἐνιαυτὸν καὶ μῆνας ἕξ) That is, he made a delay: for the Hebrew ישב is taken in this way, to which καθίζω corresponds, which is also translated elsewhere as διατρίβω, μένω, διαμένω, καταμόνω, παραμένω, παύω, ἀναπαύω. You have here the word ἐνιαυτὸν which Luke also uses elsewhere in chapter IV. 19, and John and Paul and the writer to the Hebrews and James. It also exists very frequently in the Greek versions of the Old Testament. Besides the poets, Plato, Xenophon, and Aristophanes also use it.

Latin:

Vers. 11. ἐκάθισέ τε ἐνιαυτὸν καὶ μῆνας ἕξ) Id est, moram fecit: nam ita sumitur Hebræum ישב, cui respondet κα- θίζω, quod & alibi vertitur διατρίβω, μένω, διαμένω, καταμό- νω, παραμένω, παύω, ἀναπαύω. Habes hic vocem ἐνιαυτὸ qua & alibi Lucas utitur c. IV. 19. & Johannes & Paulus & scriptor ad Hebræos & Jacobus. Exstat & sæpissime in Græ- cis versionibus Veteris Testamenti. utuntur &, præter Poëtas, Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes.

## 18:12
V. 12. And when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia) This man was called the brother of the great Seneca, since he was the younger Novatus, but was later adopted by Junius Gallio. Statius says of this man of ours: And to have begotten the sweet Gallio. This is the brother whom Seneca says attained honors, writing to his mother at these very times. Achaia was a proconsular province under Augustus. Tiberius joined it to Macedonia and made it Caesarian. But Claudius returned these provinces to the Senate, that is, he made them proconsular again, as Suetonius testifies in the life of Claudius 25 and Dio LX.

For these were three brothers: M. Annaeus Novatus (of whom Eusebius in the Chronicle: Junius Annaeus Seneca Gallio, an outstanding declaimer), L. Annaeus Seneca, Nero's tutor, and Lucius Annaeus Mela, the father of the poet Lucan. See Lipsius, preface to Seneca, ch. II. Through this Gallio, to whom he proved his case, it seems the friendship between Paul and Seneca was reconciled, since Augustine mentions the exchange of letters in Ep. LIV and Jerome in his book on Ecclesiastical Writers. Those, however, which are circulated today are supposititious, as Cornelius à Lapide admits here, and Possevinus in his Apparatus, with Sixtus Senensis thinking otherwise to no avail.

κατεπέστησαν ὁμοθυμαδὸν) That is, they set upon him with one accord, as above in 6.

ἐπὶ τὸ βῆμα) To the proconsular tribunal as a defendant of a serious crime.

Latin:

V. 12. Γαλλίων® δὲ ἀνθυπατεύοντος τῆς Ἀχαΐας) Erat hic frater magni Senecæ dictus cum junior esset Novatus, sed adoptatus postea à Junio Gallione. Statius de hoc nostro: Et dulcem generasse Gallionem. Hic est frater, quem honores confecutum dicit Seneca ad matrem his ipsis temporibus scribens. Achaia erat provin- cia proconsularis sub Augusto. Tiberius Macedoniæ adjun- xit, & Cæsarianam fecit. Sed Claudius has provincias Se- natui reddidit, id est, rursus fecit proconsulares, teste Sue- tonio in vita Claudii 25. & Dione LX.

Hi enim tres fuerunt fratres, M. Annæus No- vatus, (de quo Euseb. in Chronic. Junius An- næus Seneca Gallio, egregius declamator) L. Annæus Seneca, Neronis præceptor: & Lucius Annæus Mela, Pater Lucani poëtæ. Vid. Lipsius proæm. in Senecam c. II. Per hunc Gallionem, cui causam suam probavit, videtur conciliata amicitia inter Paulum & Senecam, quum literas amœbæas me- moret August. Ep. LIV. & Hieron. l. de Scriptor. Ecclesiast. Illæ tamen quæ hodie circumferuntur supposetitiæ sunt, fatente Cornelio à Lapide hic, & Possevino in Apparatu, nequicquam secus sentien- te Sixto Senensi.

κατεπέστησαν ὁμοθυμαδὸν) Id est, ἀντελάβοντο, ut supra 6.

ἐπὶ τὸ βῆμα) Ad tribunal proconsulare ut gravis crimi- nis reum.

## 18:13
Vers. 13.

παρὰ τὸν νόμον ἀναπείθει τὸς ἀνθρώπυς σέβεσθαι τὸν Θεὸν) They mean this: It is granted to the Jews by the Romans to live even in Greece according to the law of Moses; but this man neither adds himself to you Romans in religion, nor follows the law of Moses, and he disturbs the Jews. This accusation took its pretext from the fact that the Apostles, who were Jews, admitted the uncircumcised to their assembly; the Jews approach the proconsul for this reason, because in Achaia they did not have jurisdiction over their own countrymen, such as they had in Judea and neighboring regions.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

παρὰ τὸν νόμον ἀναπείθει τὸς ἀνθρώπυς σέβεσθαι τὸν Θεὸν) Hoc volunt: Judæis concessum est à Romanis etiam in Græcia vivere secundum legem Mosis: hic vero neque vo- bis Romanis in religione se addit, neque legem Mosis se- quitur & turbat judæos. Hæc accusatio inde obtentum sumebat, quod Apostoli, qui Judæi erant, incircumcisos ad suum cœtum admittebant; ideo autem proconsulem accedunt Judæi, quia in Achaia animadversiones in popu- lares suos non habebant, qualem habebant in Judæa & vicinis regionibus.

## 18:14
Vers. 14.

εἰ μὲν ὖν ἦν ἀδίκημά τι) Suppose homicide, wounding, theft, which come under the human terms פשע עשק עול עון, all of which are accustomed to be rendered by ἀδίκημα.

ρἱῥᾳδιόργημα πονηρὸν) Such as is fraud. See above XIII. 10.

κατὰ λόγον ἂν ἠνεχόμην ὑμῶν) It would be right for me to bear with you, that I should suffer you as much as you wished to speak; this would have been my duty; Plato uses the phrase κατὰ λόγον in Epistle VII.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

εἰ μὲν ὖν ἦν ἀδίκημά τι) Puta homicidium, vulneratio, furtum, quæ veniunt sub hominibus פשע עשק עול עון, quæ omnia per ἀδίκημα reddi solent.

ρἱῥᾳδιόργημα πονηρὸν) Quale est falsimonium. Vide su- pra XIII. 10.

κατὰ λόγον ἂν ἠνεχόμην ὑμῶν) Merito vos ferrem æquum esset, ut vos paterer quantum velletis dicere: fuisset hoc mei officii, usurpat sic serme κατὰ λόγον Plato Epistola VII.

## 18:15
Vers. 15.

εἰ δὲ ζήτημά ἐστι περὶ λόγε) That is, about matters that admit of dispute. Thus Demosthenes, Theophrastus, and others use the word λόγυ.

καὶ ὀνομάτων) Consider whether Jesus should be called the Christ.

καὶ νόμε) Whether your law condemns all the uncircumcised.

ὄψεσθε αὐτοὶ) See to it yourselves. The same manner of speaking as in Matthew 27:4.

κριτὴς γὰρ ἐγὼ τύτων ὐ βύλομαι εἶναι) A well-turned answer, as from a gentle man: as if he were to say: The Romans have indeed granted freedom of religion to the Jews even in Greece, but if any controversies arise among them concerning religion, let them either settle them among themselves, or dispute as much as they like. It is not for Roman magistrates to involve themselves in them, no more than in the disputes between Stoics and Epicureans.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

εἰ δὲ ζήτημά ἐστι περὶ λόγε) Id est, de rebus quæ disputa- tionem recipiunt. Sic λόγυ vocem usurpant Demosthenes, Theophrastus & alii.

καὶ ὀνομάτων) Puta an Jesus dicendus sit Christus.

καὶ νόμε) An lex vestra omnes incircumcisos damnet.

ὄψεσθε αὐτοὶ) Vos videritis. Idem loquendi genus quod Matth. XXVII. 4.

κριτὴς γὰρ ἐγὼ τύτων ὐ βύλομαι εἶναι) Bene responsum ut ab homine dulci: quasi dicat: Romani quidem libertatem religionis Judæis etiam in Græcia concessere, sed si quæ in- ter ipsos de religione oriuntur controversiæ, aut eas com- ponant inter se, aut disputent quantum libet. Romanorum Magistratuum non est eis se immiscere, non magis quam Stoicorum & Epicureorum inter se disceptationibus.

## 18:16
Verse 16.

καὶ ἀπήλασεν αὐτὸς ἀπὸ τῦ βήματος) He removed them from the threshold of the judgment seat, as bringing forward nothing that belonged to his court.

This action of Gallio is not to be praised: because he did not deign to investigate or hear, let alone judge, causes of religion: as if religion did not pertain at all to the magistrate: just as the Papists exclude the magistrate entirely from the care of religion and sacred matters. But GOD has enjoined something else upon the magistrate, as one who ought to be the guardian of both tables, Deut. 17:18, Psalm 2:10, 11, 12, 24:2, upon whom also, according to the prescription of Aristotle, the ἐπιμέλεια περὶ τὸ θεῖον (care concerning the divine) devolves, Politics Book VII, ch. 2, and according to Plato, the chief care ought to be about religion, Republic Book II. It was indeed to be praised in this Gallio that he did not wish to judge concerning unknown matters, but his atheistic ἀμέλεια (negligence) and ἀπραξία (inactivity) in causes of religion are not to be praised, concerning which see B. Dannhauer in Salve Reformat. page 627 et seqq. B. Gerhard on these matters, Vol. I.

περὶ λόγε καὶ ὀνομάτων takes it concerning λογομαχίᾳ (word-strife): and this, he says, is usually the judgment of the world and of politicians concerning controversies of religion, that they are vain λογομαχίαι (word-strifes).

Latin:

Vers. 16.

καὶ ἀπήλασεν αὐτὸς ἀπὸ τῦ βήματος) Removit eos à li- mine judicii, tanquam nihil adferentes, quod sui esset fori.

Non laudandum hoc factum Gallionis: quod causas religionis non indagare, vel audire, ne- dum judicare dignatus: quasi religio non atti- neret quicquam ad Magistratum: quemadmo- dum Pontificii Magistratum à cura religionis & sa- crorum prorsus excludunt. Aliud autem injunxit Magistratui DEUS, utpote qui custos esse debet utriusque tabulæ, Deut. XVII. 18. Psal. II. 10.11.12. XXIV. 2. cui etiam ex Aristotelis præscripto ἐπι- μέλεια περὶ τὸ θεῖον incumbit l. VII. Polit. c. 2. & juxta Platonem præcipua cura de Religione esse debet l. II. de Rep. Laudandum quidem in hoc Gallione erat, quod de ignotis rebus judicare nolebat, sed non laudanda ἀμέλεια atheistica, & ἀπραξία in causis religionis, de quo vid. B. Dannhauerum in Salve Reformat. pag. 627. seqq. B. Gerhardus ista Tom. I.

περὶ λόγε καὶ ὀνομάτων de λογομαχίᾳ accipit: atque hoc, inquit, solet esse mundi & politicorum de controversiis religionis judicium, quod sint λογομαχίαι frustraneae.

## 18:17
Verse 17.

ἐπιλαβόμενοι) This word is neutral. In this place it signifies that seizing which is done with force.

πάντες οἱ Ἕλληνες) Ἕλληνες is not in that Manuscript. Nor does the Latin read it in his. I think it is an addition by some interpreter, sufficiently appropriate to the matter. For the Corinthians who were standing by the tribunal, when they saw that the Jews were being driven away from the tribunal with contempt because they had obstructed the Proconsul—who was occupied with other matters—with the petty questions of their law, they themselves also, as if to do a favor to the Proconsul, inflicted blows upon the Jews, so that they might leave more quickly: thus it was the custom of provincials, especially Greeks, to adapt their actions to those things which pleased the powerful. Cicero, in a letter to his brother, says that the Greeks were trained by long-standing servitude to excessive flattery.

The word ἕλληνες, whatever may be the case regarding Grotius's manuscript, is found in any Greek codices whatsoever, nor can it be considered an addition. That beating is not said to have been done by the Corinthians or by ministers, nor are the Jews reported to have been beaten, but mention is made only of Sosthenes, whom Chrysostom confuses with Gaius mentioned in 1 Corinthians 1:14: whether he was still a Jew at that time, which seemed to be the view of Bede and Hugo, or whether, as others think, he was already a Christian in spirit, having been converted by Paul, we leave in the middle; it is certainly believed not without reason that he favored Paul; and for that reason, at the instigation of the Jews, he seems to have been beaten by the Gentiles themselves, not to please Gallio, but out of hatred toward Paul: whence Chrysostom thinks that Paul himself was also beaten in this tumult.

Σωσθένην τὸν ἀρχισυνάγωγον) Namely, of a synagogue other than the one over which Crispus presided: for in large cities there were several synagogues, and each had its own archisynagogue. For the same reason, formerly in Rome, Antioch, and other large cities, except for Alexandria, where Epiphanius says another custom always prevailed, there were several bishops for the different regions of the cities and the assemblies of Christians; the Synod of Nicaea later forbade this. The name Sosthenes seems to have been Hebrew, שׁושׁ, whence also the feminine name Susanna.

Others place Sosthenes in charge not of another, but of the same synagogue over which Crispus had presided before he was converted to Christ. Although we do not deny that there were several bishops in the same city, Phil. 1:1, yet not in the sense that the dignity of bishops is different from the presbytery, did one city have several bishops, but in the sense that presbyters are called bishops.

PART II. The Ephesian deeds with the journeys of Paul and Apollos with information from Aquila, and the confirmation of the faithful in Achaia.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ἐπιλαβόμενοι) Haec vox media est. Hoc loco eam prehensionem, quae cum vi fiat, significat.

πάντες οἱ Ἕλληνες) Non est Ἕλληνες in illo Manuscripto. Neque Latinus in suis legit. Puto esse additamentum alicujus interpretis, rei satis conveniens. Nam Corinthii homines qui tribunali astabant, cum viderent Judaeos ideo a tribunali cum contemptu abigi, quod suae legis quaestiunculis obstrepuissent Proconsuli, aliis rebus occupato, ipsi quoque velut Proconsuli gratum facturi, verbera ingessere Judaeis, quo abirent celerius: ita mos erat provincialium, praesertim Graecorum, actus suos aptare ad ea quae placerent potentibus. Cicero in epistola ad fratrem, Graecos ait diuturna servitute ad nimiam assentationem eruditos.

Vox ἕλληνες, quicquid sit de manuscripto Grotii, in Codicibus Graecis quibusvis reperitur, nec pro additamento haberi potest. Neque a Corinthiis, aut ministris percussio illa facta dicitur, neque percussi perhibentur Judaei, sed solius Sosthenis mentio sit, quem cum Cajo 1. Corinth. I. 17. memorato confundit Chrysostomus: an Judaeus tum adhuc fuerit, quod Beda & Hugoni visum, an vero, quod alii censent, a Paulo conversus animo jam fuerit Christianus, quod in medio relinquimus; favisse certe Paulo non abs re creditur; atque ideo instigantibus Judaeis ab ipsis etiam Ethnicis incredulus percussus videtur, non in gratiam Gallionis, sed ex odio adversus Paulum: unde Paulum ipsum hoc etiam tumultu percussum fuisse Chrysostomus putat.

Σωσθένην τὸν ἀρχισυνάγωγον) Nempe Synagogae alterius ab ea cui praeerat Crispus: nam in magnis urbibus plures erant Synagogae, & singulis sui archisynagogi. Eadem de causa olim Romae, Antiochiae & aliis magnis in urbibus, excepta Alexandria, ubi morem alium semper obtinuisse ait Epiphanius, plures fuere Episcopi pro diversis urbium regionibus conventibusque Christianorum; id in posterum vetuit Synodus Nicaena. Sostheni nomen Hebraeum videtur fuisse שׁושׁ. unde & feminae nomen Susanna.

Non alteri, sed eidem Synagogae, cui Crispus, antequam converteretur, ad Christum, praefuerat, Sosthenem alii praeficiunt. Plures autem in eadem urbe Episcopos fuisse etsi non diffiteamur Phil. I. 1. non tamen qua Episcoporum dignitas a Presbyterio diversa est, una civitas plures habuit Episcopos, sed qua Episcopi dicuntur Presbyteri.

PARS II. Gesta Ephesina cum profectionibus Pauli & Appollo ab Aquila informatione, ac fide- lium in Achaia confirmatione.

## 18:18
Vers. 18.

ἀποταξάμενος) Having said farewell, you have this word in Mark 6:46, Luke 9:61, 2 Cor. 2:13.

κὶ σὺν αὐτῷ Πρίσκιλλα κὶ Ἀκύλας, κειράμενος τὴν κεφαλὴν ἐν κεγχρεαῖς. εἶχε γὰρ εὐχήν) He named Priscilla first because he had something to add about Aquila: namely, that before he undertook the journey, he had fulfilled a vow at Cenchreae, having shaved his head. Understand the vow of Naziriteship from the law in Num. 6:18. When the people were in the desert, hair had to be shaved near the tent, and after the land was possessed, at Jerusalem, with a victim being brought: but these precepts, like others concerning sacrifices, did not bind those who lived outside Judea. Εὐχὴ is called the vow of Naziriteship by excellence. εὐχὴ μεγάλη to Philo, as we said at Matt. 2:23. Cenchreae is the port of the Corinthians, as Piraeus is of the Athenians. This port is on the Saronic Gulf. It appears there was a church of Christians there, Rom. 16:1. Ovid, Tristia book 1, said Cenchris for Cenchreae by contraction.

Isidore also understands the vow to be about Aquila, book 2, De Officiis. The office chapter on Tysracia, as also Baronius. But Augustine, Epistle XIX, Jerome, Epistle XI, Bede, and most others understand this more correctly of Paul: Nor can the Greek text be explained otherwise: because those words, καὶ σὺν ἀυτῷ ῾Πρίσκιλλα καὶ ᾿Ακύλας, are enclosed in a parenthesis, and the reason is given why Paul sailed into Syria, because, namely, he had made a vow which had to be fulfilled in the Jerusalem temple, see chapter XXI. 24. He had done this, however, so that he would not alienate the Jews from himself, as if he were utterly opposed to legal requirements, because he wished to become all things to all men through a pious συγκατάβασιν (condescension), without prejudice, however, to the faith and Christian liberty. See 1 Corinthians VIII. 20, 21; Numbers VI. 13. Therefore the Vulgate is wrong, as is the Ethiopic, in omitting those words δεῖ με πάντων τὴν ἑορτὴν τὴν ἐρχομένην ποιῆσαι εἰς ῾Ιεροσόλυμα. The Greek codices consistently have them, as do the Syriac and Arabic. Chrysostom, Oecumenius, Vatablus, and Cajetan also read them, as Cornelius à Lapide admits. κἀκείνως κατέλιπεν ἀυτῶ) The Syriac, if I am not mistaken, correctly transposed these words after those words ἀνακάμψω πρὸς ὑμᾶς.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

ἀποταξάμενος) Valedicto, habes hanc vocem Marci VI. 46. Luc. IX. 61. 2. Cor. II. 13.

κὶ σὺν αὐτῷ Πρίσκιλλα κὶ Ἀκύλας, κειράμενος τὴν κεφαλὴν ἐν κεγχρεαῖς. εἶχε γὰρ εὐχήν) Ideo Priscillam prius nominavit, quia de Aquila aliquid addendum habebat: nempe eum antequam iter aggrederetur, voto se solvisse Cenchreis, raso capite. Votum intellige Nazaraeatus ex lege Num. VI. 18. Cum in deserto esset populus, capillus radi debebat apud tentorium, & post terram possessam, Hierosolymis, accedente victima: sed haec praecepta ut alia de sacrificiis, eos non obligabant qui extra Judaeam agebant. Εὐχὴ per excellentiam dicitur votum Nazaratus. εὐχὴ μεγάλη Philoni, ut diximus ad Matth. II. 23. Cenchreae portus est Corinthiorum, ut Piraeus Atheniensium. Est autem is portus ad sinum Saronicum. Apparet ibi Ecclesiam fuisse Christianorum Rom. XVI. 1. Cenchris pro Cenchreis contracte dixit Ovidius Tristium l. 9.

De Aquila etiam intelligit votum Isidorus l. II. Offic. Offic. cap. de Tysracia, ut & Baronius. Sed rectiùs de Paulo id accipiunt Augustinus Epistol. XIX. Hie- ronymus Epistol. XI. Beda, & plerique alii: Nec aliter explicari textus Græcus potest: quia ver- ba illa, καὶ σὺν ἀυτῷ ῾Πρίσκιλλα καὶ ᾿Ακύλας, in- clusa sunt parenthesi, & causa redditur, cur Paulus navigarit in Syriam, quia sc. votum fecerat, quod expleri debebat in templo Hierosolymitano Cons. cap. XXI. 24. Fecerat autem id, ut Judæos à se, quasi prorsus aversante legalia, non averteret, quia omnibus omnia fieri voluit per piam συγκα- τάβασιν, salva tamen fide, & libertate Christiana. Cons. 1. Corinth. VIII. 20. 21. Num. VI. 13. Per- peram ergo Vulgata, ut & Æthiops omisit illa δεῖ με πάντων τὴν ἑορτὴν τὴν ἐρχομένην ποιῆσαι εἰς ῾Ιεροσόλυμα. Habent ea constanter Græci Codices, Syrus item & Arabs. Legit ea etiam Chrysostomus, Oecum. Vatabl. & Cajetanus, fatente Cornel. à La- pide. κἀκείνως κατέλιπεν ἀυτῶ) Syrus recte, ni fallor, hæc verba trajecit post illa ἀνακάμψω πρὸς ὑμᾶς.

## 18:20
Verse 20.

Ἐρωτώντων δὲ ἀυτῶν) Aquila and Priscilla.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Ἐρωτώντων δὲ ἀυτῶν) Aquila & Priscilla.

## 18:21
Verse 21.

ἑορτὴν τὴν ἐρχομένην) Where ἑορτὴ is said simply, the Passover is understood. ποιῆσαι) A type of speaking such as above XV. 33 and below 23. εἰς ῾Ιεροσόλυμα) εἰς for ἐν ῾Ιεροσολύμοις. πάλιν δὲ ἀνακάμψω) πάλιν is redundant, as in Plato's Timaeus, πάλιν ἐπανελθεῖν. Τῦ Θεῦ θέλοντος) An excellent caution of the Christians, to promise nothing of the future unless expressly adding, if God wills, so that they might signify that in all things, but especially those of the pious, the providence of God intervenes. Thus also Paul, 1 Corinthians IV. 19, and James IV. 15 admonishes all Christians concerning it. κἀνήχθη ἀπὸ τῆς Ἐφέσε) Ἀνήχθη in this place is indeed sailed, as the Syriac explains. Thus also Luke VIII. 22.

## 18:22
Verse 22.

καὶ κατελθὼν εἰς Καισάρειαν) Namely, from the ship. For Caesarea is a maritime city. Thus also below XXVII. 5, κατήχθημεν is used. ἀναβάς) Namely, to Jerusalem: which is always understood whenever Hebrews speak of a journey through Judea, John VII. 8, 10; XII. 20. καὶ ἀσπασάμενος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν) The apostles and the faithful who were at Jerusalem.

Not the Caesarea of Cappadocia, as Jerome, Beza, Rabanus, and Lyranus wish, but of Palestine, or Straton's. It is ridiculous, says Beza, that Jerome interprets these things of the Caesarea of Cappadocia, whom at least it behooved to consider the word ἀνήχθη, which is said of those who sail. Yet one must not approve of Beza, because he inserted the word Jerusalem into the text: and when he had descended to Caesarea, and had ascended to Jerusalem: concerning which Ludov. de Dieu rightly says: Beza understands Ἱεροσολήμ, Jerusalem, after ἀναβὰς, and says it is expressed in the Syriac interpretation. The most learned Tremellius deceived the man, who, when he thought the passage demanded it, supplied it, and did not distinguish it with a different typeface from the Syriac text itself. The Syriac editions do not have it, nor does the sense demand it, which seems to be entirely that he entered that Caesarea, ascended to the church of that place, and greeted it. Nor is there any reason why the word for ascending should offend anyone: for it does not always signify climbing from a lower place to a higher one, but often simply moving oneself in a place, as we showed at Luke V. 2; nor will anyone think it inept that the assembly of the Church was held in a higher part of the city, to which it was necessary for Paul to ascend. The Ethiopic did not understand it otherwise when it translated, and he descended to Caesarea, and ascended into the house of the Christians (that is, the Church) and greeted them, and went to Antioch. Therefore, from Ephesus, a city of Asia Minor, Paul sailed a distance of 170 miles to Caesarea Stratonis in Palestine; and from there, by a journey of sixty miles, he returned to Antioch in Syria,

κατέβη εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν] To Antioch in Syria. Beda, Rabanus, and Lyranus understand it as Antioch in Pisidia. But it is more correctly understood, with Chrysostom, as Antioch in Syria, which is accustomed to be referred to by this name alone, where the disciples were first called Christians: which the Apostle therefore loved.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

καὶ κατελθὼν εἰς Καισάρειαν) Nempe è navi. Est enim Cæsarea maritima urbs. Sic & infra XXVII. 5. sumitur κα- τήχθημεν. ἀναβάς) Nempe Hierosolyma: quod semper intelligi- tur, quoties de itinere per Judæam Hebræi loquuntur, Joh. VII. 8. 10. XII. 20. καὶ ἀσπασάμενος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν) Apostolos & fideles qui erant Hierosolymis.

Non Cæsaream Cappadociæ, ut Hieronym. Be- za, Rabanus, Lyranus volunt, sed Palestinæ, vel Stratonis. Ridiculum est, inquit Beza, quod Hie- ronymus de Cæsarea Cappadociæ ista interpretatur, quem saltem oportuerat considerare verbum ἀνήχ- θη de iis, qui navigant, dici. Nec tamen proban- dum est in Beza; quod textui ingesserit vocem Hierosolyma: cumque descendisset Cæsaream, ascen- dissetque Hierosolymam: de quo recte Ludov. de Dieu: Beza post ἀναβὰς subintelligit Ἱεροσολήμ, Hierosolymam, dicitque in Syriæ interpretatione exprimi. Fefellit virum doctiss. Tremellius, qui quum locum id postulare existimaret, supplevit, neque diverso charactere ab ipso textu Syri distinxit. E- ditiones Syriacæ non habent, nec sensus postulat, qui omnino esse videtur, eam Cæsaream ingressum, ad Ecclesiam illius loci ascendisse, eamque salutasse. Nec est quod ascendendi vox quenquam offendat: ea enim non semper ex depressiori loco in altio- rem conscendere, sed sæpe simpliciter loco se mo- vere significat, ut ostendimus ad Luc. V. 2. neque inepte sentiet quis, in editiori urbis loco conven- tum Ecclesiæ fuisse habitum, ad quem ascendere Paulus necesse habuerit. Æthiopicus non aliter ac- cepit, quum vertit, & descendit Cæsaream, & ascen- dit in domum Christianorum (id est Ecclesiam) & salutavit eos, & abiit Antiochiam. Ab Epheso ergo Asiæ minoris urbe Paulus interstitio 170. millia- rium Cæsaream Stratonis in Palæstinam navigavit; & inde sexaginta milliarium itinere Antiochiam in Syriam reversus est,

κατέβη εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν] Syriæ ad Orontem. Antiochiam Pisidiæ Beda, Rabanus & Lyranus intelligunt. Sed rectius cum Chrysost. Antiochia Syriæ intelligitur, quæ absoluto hoc nomine veni- re solet, ubi primum discipuli cognominati sunt Christiani: quam proinde amabat Apostolus.

V. 25. ὗτος ἦν κατηχημένος τὴν ὁδὸν κυρίου) He had received the first elements of Christianity. See Luke I. 4. and what we said at Matt. XXVIII. 19. 20. Add Gal. VI. 6. ζέων τῷ πνεύματι) The same kind of expression Rom. XII. 11. καὶ ἐδίδασκεν ἀκριβῶς τὰ περὶ Κυρίου) Namely, according to the measure of knowledge which he had received. ἀκριβῶς with the best faith. ἐπιστάμενος μόνον τὸ βάπτισμα Ἰωάννου) ἐπιστάμενος that is, experienced, as it is taken by the Hebrews ידע Isaiah LIII. 3. He had not been baptized in the Christian manner, and therefore had not received the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Although some among Oecumenius also wish this Apollos to be the Apelles, of whom Rom. XVI. 10., others however more correctly prefer to distinguish these two. He is mentioned, however, here 1 Cor. I. 12. III. 6. But because he is called a Catechumen, or indeed instructed in the beginnings of the Christian faith, but to have known only the Baptism of John, Cornelius à Lapide infers that he was not yet a Christian: but from a false hypothesis, as if the baptism of John were different in substance from the baptism instituted by Christ in Matt. XXVIII., when yet the Baptism of John was equally a means of regeneration, and was dispensed for the remission of sins John III. 5. Luke III. as was Christ's baptism Acts II. 38. Tit. III. 5. Moreover, here the Baptism of John is opposed not to the Sacrament of baptism instituted by Christ, or to the Baptism of water, of which Matt. XXVIII., but to the baptism of the Spirit, of which he knew nothing, as it was not yet accustomed to happen in the primitive Church concerning the extraordinary outpouring of gifts, much less had he received it, such an opposition as is had in Matt. III. 11. Mark I. 21. Luke III. 12. John I. 26. Acts I. 5. Others think that the Johannine doctrine is understood synecdochically with baptism by the baptism of John, but the doctrine of John was not different from the doctrine of Christ; others judge that this is indicated, that John baptized into Christ who was to come: But Apollos without doubt not only knew that Christ ought to come, but was also informed about him, that Christ had already come, even if he was still to be more fully informed and confirmed concerning the Lord Jesus, that he is the promised Messiah. For he had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and taught diligently those things which are of Jesus, and began to act with confidence in the Synagogue, even if the way of the Lord was still more diligently explained to him by Priscilla and Aquila, so that he could afterwards vehemently and publicly refute the Jews, and show and demonstrate through the Scriptures of the Old Testament, in which he was powerful, that Jesus is the Christ.

Test. in quibus potens erat, Jesum esse Christum.

## 18:27
Verse 27.

into Achaia) To Corinth. the brethren encouraging) Voluntarily urging him to fulfill such a strong purpose. through grace) The Syrian refers this to 'he helped'. And rightly so. He profited the Church much through the gifts which he had received after his baptism into the name of Christ, the grace of God anticipating the Apostolic hands. Grotius seems to hint that he had been baptized again with water-baptism, because he also said at verse 23 that Apollos had not been baptized in the Christian manner before, and he says that now baptism into the name of Christ was conferred upon him. But those who have once received water-baptism had no need to be baptized with water again, nor were they baptized. Although, therefore, Apollos could have received extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, nothing, however, is read about that here, nor is it certain that by the word 'grace' extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit are designated here, since grace is also needed for those who wish to be useful with ordinary gifts, and they are useful to the Church. But he rightly retained that 'through grace', even though it is not held in the Vulgate. Because the Syrian, the Arab, and the Ethiopian agree in these words with almost all the Greek codices.

for mightily) Luke uses this word, and it exists in the Gospel XXIII, 10, and in the Greek of Joshua VI. 8; you will rightly translate it 'acutely'. Hesychius explains it by 'strongly'. he thoroughly refuted) הוכיח which is translated by 'to refute', 'to argue against', 'to convict'. showing by the scriptures) 'showing' here is what 'explaining' was above in XVII. 3. The word 'he thoroughly refuted' is, with great contention and efficacy he was convincing the Jews more and more: for the preposition increases the meaning of the verb. But the word 'showing' imports a clear and invincible demonstration, so that that which is shown or demonstrated can be grasped as if by the eyes themselves. Compare Luke XXIV. 40, XX. 24, Acts IX. 39. Whence it is clear that in the Old Testament the mysteries concerning Christ were handed down not only obscurely, as the Calixtines wish, but clearly enough, if indeed Apollos demonstrated them clearly from the same, and convinced the Jews of their truth.

## 19:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIX. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Paul, coming to Ephesus, instructed twelve disciples baptized by John who were ignorant of the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit, conferred the Holy Spirit upon them through the laying on of hands, and taught there for three months in the School. But as most were hardened, departing from them, he preached the Word in the school of Tyrannus for two years to the Jews and Greeks throughout Asia, God working great things through the hands of Paul and through his handkerchiefs. And when some Jewish exorcists used the name of Jesus, especially the seven sons of Sceva the High Priest, but the demon prevailed against them, fear fell upon all, and many of the believers confessed their deeds, and many also publicly burned their superstitious books, the word of the Lord growing and being strengthened. Paul, however, proposing to himself to go to Jerusalem through Macedonia and Achaia, and afterwards also to see Rome, with Timothy and Erastus sent into

Macedonia, stayed for a time in Asia. And when a tumult was stirred up on account of Demetrius the silversmith, who made silver temples of Diana, from whose profit much was lost because of the despised Diana, hitherto worshipped throughout all Asia, with many shouting, 'Great is Diana of the Ephesians', and Paul's companions, Gaius and Aristarchus, were seized, and Paul was not permitted to go into the public, Alexander the Chancellor, admitted with difficulty to speak because of the tumult, settles the same, warning that the accusation of Demetrius and his men should be instituted in order, because on account of this tumult they could easily be accused of sedition.

There are three parts: I. The instruction of the disciples of John by Paul with the conferring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the biennial Ephesian sermons confirmed by miracles, to verse 12. II. The confusion of certain exorcists, and the conversion of the superstitious and many others, to verse 20. III. The sedition of Demetrius on account of the despised Diana, and the settlement of the same made by Alexander, to verse 40.

PART I. The instruction of the disciples of John, and the Ephesian sermons of Paul.

V. 1. Apollos) An ancient accusative of the fourth declension among the Greeks: thus Theocritus: 'Athos' Rhodopen. And Virgil from him: 'Either Athos or Rhodope': and Livy: 'Mount Athos'.

the upper parts) the more northern ones, Pontus and Bithynia.

Others render 'upper parts' word for word with the Vulgate, and understand Galatia and Phrygia.

Latin:

CAPUT XIX. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Paulus Ephesum veniens duodecim discipulos donorum miraculosorum S. S. nescios à Jo- hanne baptizatos, instruxit, ipsis per χειρο- θεσίαν S. S. contulit, ibique per tres menses in Schola docuit. Plerisque autem induratis recedens ab illis, in Schola tyranni, per bien- nium Judaeis, & Graecis per Asiam, Verbum praedicavit, Deo per manus Pauli & per su- daria ejus, magna operante. Et quum exor- cistae nonnulli Judaei nomen Jesu adhiberent, imprimis filii septem Scevae Pontificis, qui- bus vero praevaluit daemonium, timor super omnes cecidit, multique credentium confessi sunt actus suos, multi etiam libros suos su- perstitiosos publice combusserunt, crescente & confortato verbo Domini. Paulus autem sibi proponens per Macedoniam & Achiam Hierosolymam tendere, & postmodum et- iam Romam videre, Timotheo & Erasto in

Macedoniam missis substitit ad tempus in Asia. Et quum tumultus, ob Demetrium au- rifabrum, Dianæ argentea templa fabrican- tem, cujus lucro multum, ob contemptam Dianam, hactenus per totam Asiam cultam, decedebat, excitaretur, clamantibus pluri- mis, Magna est Diana Ephesiorum, & comi- tes Pauli, Gajus & Aristarchus, apprehen- derentur, nec permitteretur Paulus in pu- blicum ire, Alexander Concellarius ægre ad dicendum præ tumultu admissus, eundem se- dat, monens, ut accusatio Demetrii, & suo- rum ordine instituatur, quia ob tumultum istum facile argui seditionis possint.

Partes tres sunt: I. Paulina discipulorum Jo- hannis informatio cum collatione donorum S. S. & conciones Ephesinæ biennales miraculis firmatæ, ad v. 12. II. Exorcistarum quorundam confusio, & conversio superstitiosorum, & aliorum multo- rum, ad v. 20. III. Seditio Demetrii ob Dianam con- temtam, ejusdemque compositio ab Alexandro facta, ad v. 40.

PARS I. Discipulorum Iohannis informatio, & con- ciones Ephesinæ Pauli.
