## 19:3
V. 3. 'unto what then were ye baptized?' 'unto what' for 'in what'. How were you baptized?

'And they said, Unto John's baptism' That is, 'in John's baptism'.

It is likely, as some think with Chrysostom, that these men were baptized by John in Judea about twenty years earlier, while they had gone up to Jerusalem for the feast according to custom, but soon returning home to Asia, they had not perceived those things concerning the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, which were sometimes wont to be conferred even in baptism. Whence they are here informed about it by Paul. But the Papists rashly attempt to excuse the Sacrament of Confirmation from this; because it is hinted here that the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and those extraordinary ones, were accustomed to be conferred not in another Sacrament, but in Baptism itself: which Grotius also observed at v. 6. Therefore, Cornelius a Lapide says in vain that Paul doubted whether they had been confirmed, even if he thought they had been baptized with the baptism of Christ: From where will it be taught that the Apostle thought this, or that the fictitious Sacrament of Confirmation came into his mind? What need would there have been to ask, 'in what were you baptized,' if he had thought they were baptized with the baptism of Christ? But Grotius rightly rendered that 'in what' as 'how were you baptized?' Because Paul was asking this: whether they themselves, as others frequently were, had been so baptized that they had received the baptism of the Spirit at the same time? Grotius, who is otherwise papistical, also rightly departs from the Papists here, who think it is evident from this that the baptism of John was different from the baptism of Christ; which, while we concede it, when by the baptism of Christ is understood the baptism of the Spirit, or of the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, it is by no means to be conceded according to the definition of the Council of Trent, Session VII, c. 1, on Baptism, in which water-baptism is [distinguished] from

It is understood to be instituted by Christ in Matt. XXVIII. For although baptism was conferred according to the institution of Christ in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, whence those who were so baptized could not be ignorant whether there is a Holy Spirit as regards ὑπόςασιν & ἰσίαν, person and nature or divine essence: nevertheless, some who were so baptized could be ignorant whether there is a Holy Spirit as regards such miraculous and extraordinary gifts, which Grotius acknowledges are designated here by the voice of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

V. 3. εἰς τί οὖν ἐβαπτίσθητε) εἰς τί pro ἐν τίνι. quomodo baptizati estis?

οἱ δὲ εἶπον, εἰς τὸ Ἰωάνου βάπτισμα) Id est, ἐν τῷ Ἰωάνου βαπτίσματι. baptismate Johannis.

Verisimile est, quod nonnulli cum Chrysostomo censent hos à Johanne in Judæa ante annos viginti circiter baptizatos, dum ex Asia Hierosolymam pro more ad festum ascenderunt, mox autem in Asiam domum redeuntes illa de extraordinariis do- nis Spiritus S. quandoque etiam in baptismo, con- ferri solitis haud percepisse. Unde hic de eo infor- mantur à Paulo. Temere autem Papistæ hinc Sa- cramentum Confirmationis excusare conantur; quia non in alio Sacramento, sed in ipso Baptismo con- ferri consuevisse dona S. S. eaque extraordinaria hic innuitur: quod Grotius etiam ad v. 6. observa- vit. Frustra itaque Cornelius Lapidensis ait, Paulum dubitasse an confirmati essent, etsi putarit eos bapti- zatos baptismo Christi: Hoc putasse Apostolum, vel in mentem ei venisse fictitium Confirmationis Sacramentum unde docebitur? Quid opus habuis- set quærere, in quo baptizati estis, si putasset, ba- ptismo Christi eosdem baptizatos esse? Recte au- tem Grotius illud ἐν τίνι reddidit, quomodo baptizati estis? Quia id quærebat Paulus, annon etiam ipsi, uti frequenter alii sic baptizati sint, ut baptismum simul flaminis acceperint? Recte etiam discedit à Papistis Grotius alias papizans, qui hic patere pu- tant baptismum Johannis à Christi baptismo diver- sum fuisse, quod uti concedimus, cum per baptis- mum Christi baptismus flaminis, seu donorum ex- traordinariorum S. S. intelligitur, ita minime con- cedendum juxta definitionem Concilii Tridentini Sess. VII. c. 1. de Baptis. in qua ὑδατοβαπτισμὸς à

Christo Matt. XXVIII. institutus intelligitur. Nam etsi baptismus juxta institutionem Christi in nomi- ne Patris & Filii & Sp. S. conferebatur, unde qui ita baptizati, ignorare non poterant, an sit Spir. S. quoad ὑπόςασιν & ἰσίαν, personam & naturam vel essentiam divinam: Ignorare tamen nonnulli sic baptizati poterant, an sit Spiritus S. quoad dona e- jusmodi miraculosa, & extraordinaria, quæ voce S. S. hic designari agnoscit Grotius.

## 19:4
V. 4. John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance) This μὲν does not cohere with that which follows, ἀκέσαςτες δὲ, as many have thought: but it is placed as καὶ ἀποσύνδεσιν as above III. 21. Thus, on the contrary, Donatus notes in Terence that 'sed tamen' is placed where 'quidem' has not preceded. The sense is: he indeed baptized into repentance, that is, he exhorted those whom he baptized that they should amend themselves, and thus escape the impending evils, but not into the promised Holy Spirit, which distinction between both baptisms is hinted at also in Matt. III, 11. In this book I. 5. The writer of the responses to the orthodox: τὸ βάπτισμα τῷ Ἰωάννα προοίμιον ἦν τῷ ἐυαγγελία τῆς χάριτος. Saying to the people, that they should believe in him who was coming after him) That they might receive the full precepts of the heavenly kingdom from him who was about to appear to the Israelite people after him. For with this mark John the Baptist had depicted Christ, Matt. III, 11. where see the things said, a more perfect dogma demanded a more perfect baptism. See the Greek Fathers on this passage, and Tertullian on Baptism, where he says that the baptism of John provided nothing heavenly, but ministered to heavenly things, and adds: Thus afterwards in the Acts of the Apostles we find that those who had the baptism of John had not received the Holy Spirit, whom they had not even heard of; therefore it was not heavenly, because it did not exhibit heavenly things.

Latin:

V. 4. Ἰωάννης μὲν ἐβάπτισε βάπτισμα μετανοίας) Non co- hæret hoc μὲν cum eo quod sequitur ἀκέσαςτες δὲ, ut multi putarant: sed positum est καὶ ἀποσύνδεσιν ut supra III. 21. Sic contra apud Terentium Donatus notat, sed tamen poni, ubi quidem non præcessit. Sensus est: baptizavit ille quidem in pœnitentiam, id est, hortatus est eos, quos baptizavit, ut se emendarent, & sic mala imminentia evaderent, sed non in promissum Spirit, S. quæ distinctio inter utrumque bapti- sma innuiter & Matth. III, 11. hoc lib. I. 5. Scriptor respon- sionum ad orthodoxos: τὸ βάπτισμα τῷ Ἰωάννα προοίμιον ἦν τῷ ἐυαγγελία τῆς χάριτος. τῷ λαῷ λέγων, ἐἰς τὸν ἐρχόμενον μετ᾿ ἀὐτὸν ἵνα πιστεύσωσι) Ut plena præcepta regni cœlestis acciperent ab eo qui post ip- sum populo Israelitico appariturus esset. Hæc enim nota Jo- hannes Baptista Christum depinxerat, Matt. III, 11. ubi di- cta vide, perfectius dogma perfectiorem exigebat baptis- mum. Vide Græcos Patres hoc loco, & Tertullianum de Ba- ptismo, ubi baptismum Johannis ait nihil cœleste præstitis- se, sed cœlestibus præministrasse, & addit: Adeo postea in a- ctis Apostolorum invenimus, quoniam qui Johannis baptismum habebant, non accepiffent Spiritum S. quem ne auditu quidem noberant, ergo non erat cæleste, quod cælestia non exhibebat.

## 19:5
V. 5. And having heard) Namely those to whom Paul was speaking: for these are the words of Luke. Thus the Latin, the Syriac, the Arabic, and all the ancients before Marnixius have accepted it. Into the name of the Lord Jesus) That is, into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. See what we have said on Matt. XXVIII. 19.

That ἀνανταπόδοτον is feigned in vain. We do not deny that μὲν occurs alone somewhere, but when in the text there is at the same time another particle δὲ responding to it, which happens here, an ἀνανταπόδοτον is not to be feigned; rather, an adversative sense always obtains then, whence it is permitted to conclude firmly that because μὲν in the protasis speaks beyond controversy about the baptism of John, similarly δὲ in the apodosis must be understood as speaking of nothing but the same thing, so that the coherence may be integrated; otherwise it cannot be that the very συνέχεια itself is not ἐπισεσῃρμένη, gaping in its middle part, and finally a λόγος ἐκκρεμὴς or a hanging sentence emerges: as rightly B. D. Georg. König in Vind. Sacr. Disp. XXX. p. 536. Who therefore observes this συνέχειαν of the speech: Paul, he says p. 540, understanding from the Ephesian disciples that they did not know whether there is a Holy Spirit, that is, whether the Holy Spirit is poured out abundantly and miraculously, proceeded to inquire with what baptism they had been baptized? at the beginning, without doubt, deciding with himself that they had been baptized by the Apostles, and consequently also, as was commonly done then, had participated in the miraculous effusion of the Holy Spirit: but when they spontaneously and publicly professed that they were baptized into the baptism of John, that is, in the phrase of Scripture, 1 Cor. X. 2, by John, Paul seized this occasion and instituted a more exact dissertation about the baptism of John, not to alienate the twelve from their former baptism and incite them to receive a new one, but rather to extol and praise the baptism of John, that it was indeed an effective medium of repentance, consisting of a right institution and a subsequent application of the saving wave into the name of Christ: for which name that baptism is to be highly esteemed. Although indeed the miraculous effusion of the Holy Spirit did not follow it, being reserved for the glorification of Christ, John VII. 39. nevertheless this also remains a beaten path. And when these things were finished, Paul had laid hands upon them, it happened suddenly that they also became miraculous participants of the Holy Spirit. This is D. König. Indeed, that entire fourth verse recounts only what the Proto-baptist formerly observed regarding the candidates for Baptism, namely that he first informed them so that they would believe in him who was about to come, i.e., in Christ Jesus, and afterwards, when they had given ear, he conferred the baptism upon them in the name of Christ, and therefore that verse is to be explained not in a διχρόνῳ but in an ὁμοχρόνῳ sense: but in the following fifth verse Luke subjoins what Paul did for the present, namely that through the imposition of hands he made the believing Ephesians participants of the singular gifts of the Holy Spirit. There are certainly not lacking those among our own who explain the later words of v. 4, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, as referring to a baptism not of water, but of the Spirit, dispensed to the Ephesians, to which the χειροθεσία was joined in v. 5, such as Osiander and the paraphrast Franzius T. II. Disp. Witenb. p. 739. But in this way, beyond the necessity of the word 'they were baptized,' the propriety is left behind, and it is taken in an improper sense: and the adversative δὲ is violently torn from the preceding μὲν, indeed a new ἔλλειψις is introduced, and consequently the apodosis is doubled in the analysis, in this way: John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, but Christ (which is the first apodosis supplying the ἔλλειψιν and the ἀνανταπόδοτον) with the Holy Spirit and fire. But they (which is the second apodosis), having heard these things, were baptized with the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit. According to our interpretation, however, neither is the propriety of the letter deserted, nor is there need for an ἔλλειψις, nor is the natural nexus between the particles responding to each other, μὲν and δὲ, violated. And so neither is any defense left for Anabaptism, nor is anything detracted from the Baptism of John; nay, its authority and efficacy are openly asserted, the Apostle himself defining it. Nor is Beza inelegant here: It is necessary to admit that this does not concern some peculiar history of twelve men who were, by the Apostle, either baptized or rebaptized: nor does it concern baptism, but the beginnings of the Ephesian Church, when before there had been no orderly constituted assemblies of the pious there: and therefore the Apostle is inquiring about the gifts with which God was accustomed to adorn those who were moved to the governance of the Churches: namely, whether hands had already been laid upon them, or whether they themselves were at least endowed with those gifts of the Holy Spirit, from which it might be gathered that they were divinely called to the sacred ministry, such as the gift of tongues and prophecy.

It is no wonder, however, that the Interpreters did not notice this sense. For the Vulgate omitted the particle δὲ, and translated: 'having heard these things,' as if it had read ἀκούσαντες ταῦτα, whereas all the most approved Codices have ἀκούσαντες δὲ ἐβαπτίσθησαν. That omitted particle provided the ancients with the greatest occasion for a double error, so that those who, believing on that account that these were the words of Luke, fell into the error of thinking that the baptism of John was something other than that of Christ, and that those baptized by John ought to have been rebaptized in the name of Christ—a not light error. But the particle δὲ is read in all Greek Codices with the highest consensus, as Beza notes, which necessarily corresponds to the particle μὲν, and in no way allows us to tear apart the series of this discourse, as if the prior part were to be attributed to Luke a little later than the latter. But that Grotius-like sense, that John baptized into repentance, that he did nothing else than exhort them to amend themselves, that he did not baptize into the promise of the Holy Spirit, can neither be gathered from those places in Matt. III. 11, Acts I. 5, nor is it indeed consistent. For in those places it is not taught that Christ would dispense the baptism of water into the promise of the Holy Spirit through his disciples, which John dispensed only into repentance: But that Christ would provide another baptism, namely the effusion of the Holy Spirit, which is distinct from the ὑδατοβαπτισμῷ (water-baptism) and not tied to the same, by which extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit [are given]: Although in the baptism of water, administered not only by the Apostles and their successors, but also by St. John, the Holy Spirit was entirely poured out as regards sanctifying (not ministering) gifts, because baptism is the washing of regeneration.

& of renewal Tit. III. 5. & by the same they are regenerated from water & Spirit, baptized by John, just as we also are regenerated: But that which is born of the Spirit, is Spirit, Joh. III. 5. 6. And the baptism of St. John is said to be dispensed not only unto repentance, but also unto the remission of sins: and not in that sense alone, that a preaching of repentance was joined to the baptism, but that the Baptism itself effectively worked repentance, conversion, & remission of sins; Whence those who rejected it, are said to have rejected the counsel of God concerning salvation Luc. III. 3. VII. 30. nor was it said to the people by John for that reason, that they should believe in him who was to come after him, so that they might receive the full precepts of the heavenly kingdom from him: for they did not receive only semi-full ones from John, or even from the Prophets themselves; but he himself with the Prophets delivered the counsel of God concerning salvation entire: and the Apostles testified that they taught nothing outside of those things which Moses & the Prophets wrote Act. XXVI. 21. nor did Christ hesitate to remit the cause of the counsel concerning salvation to Moses & the Prophets Luc. XVI. 29. Joh. V. 39. which can be had through the Scriptures themselves 2. Tim. III. 15. Those who among the Greek Fathers might agree here with Grotius, are neither cited, nor could they delay us more than Tertullian, although it is nevertheless too clear from the Holy Scriptures that the baptism of John was by no means different from the Baptism of Christ. See Exeg A. Conf. art. IX.

Latin:

V. 5. ἀκέσαςτες δὲ) Nempe illi ad quos Paulus loqueba- tur: sunt enim hæc Lucæ verba. Sic accepere Latinus, Sy- rus, Arabs, & veteres omnes ante Marnixium. ἐἰς τὸ ὄνομα τῶ Κυρία Ἰησᾶ) Id est, in nomen Patris & Filii & Spiritus Sancti. Vide quæ diximus ad Matt. XXVIII. 19.

Illud ἀνανταπόδοτον frustra fingitur. Non nega- mus alicubi solum μὲν occurrere, sed quando in textu habetur simul altera ei respondens particula δὲ, quod hic fit, non est fingendum ἀνανταπόδοτον, imo semper tum adversativus sensus obtinet, unde firmiter concludere licet, quia μὲν in προτάσει ex- tra controversiam de Baptismo Johannis loquitur, similiter δὲ in ἀποδόσει non nisi de eodem intelligi oportere, ut integreur cohærentia, alioquin aliter fieri non posse, quin ipsa συνέχεια sit, ἐπισεσῃρμένη media sui parte hiulca, & tandem λόγος ἐκκρεμὴς sive sententia pendula prodeat: ut recte B. D. Georg. König in Vind. Sacr. Disp. XXX. p. 536. Qui proin- de observat hanc orationis συνέχειαν: Paulus, in- quit p. 540. ex discipulis Ephesinis intelligens, nescire eos, an fit Spir. S. hoc est, an Spir. S. ubertim & admi- raculum effundatur, perrexit inquirere, quonam baptismo essent baptizati? sub initium procul dubio secum statuens, ipsos ab Apostolis baptizatos, conse- quenter etiam, prout communiter tum fieri solebat, miraculosam Sp. S. effusionem participasse: at ubi sponte ac publice professi sunt, se in Johannis bapti- smum, id est, phrasi Scripturæ, 1. Cor. X. 2. à Johanne esse baptizatos, arripuit Paulus hanc occasionem, & exactiorem de baptismate Johannis instituit disserta- tiumculam, non ut duodecim à pristino baptismo ab- alienaret, & ad novum suscipiendum instigaret, sed potius, ut baptismum Johannis attolleret & depredi- caret, fuisse videlicet efficax resipiscentiæ medium, constans recta institutione, & subsequente unda salu- taris in nomen Christi applicatione: quo nomine ille baptismus magni sit faciendus. Licet vero eum non consecuta fuerit miraculosa Sp. S. effusio, quippe ad Christi glorificationem reservata, Joh. VII. 39. tamen hoc etiam tritam restare viam. Et cum his finitis Paulus illis imposuisset manus, factum est dere- pente, ut etiam Spiritus S. miraculose participes fa- cti sint. Hæc D. König. Nimirum integer ille versi- culus quartus recenset solum, quod olim Protobapti- sta circa Baptismi candidatos observavit, quod nem- pe prius illos informarit, ut crederent in eum, qui ven- turus esset, h. e. in Christum Jesum, & postmodum, ubi auditum præbuissent, in nomen Christi Bapti- smum ipsis contulerit, ideoque versus ille explicandus est non διχρόνῳ sed ὁμοχρόνῳ sensu: sequenti vero quinto versu Lucas subjungit, quid Paulus impræ- sentiarum egerit, nimirum quod per impositionem manuum singularium donorum S. S. Ephesios cre- dentes participes reddiderit. Non desunt sane è no- stris, qui verba posteriora v. 4. baptizati sunt in no- men Domini Jesu, de baptismo non aquæ, sed flami- nis Ephesiis dispensato explicant, cui conjuncta fuerit χειροθεσία v. 5. utpote Osiander & paraphr. Franzius T. II. Disp. Witenb. p. 739. Sed ita præter necessitatem verbi baptizati sunt, proprietas relin- quitur, idque sensu improprio accipitur: & adver- sativa δὲ τὶ præcedenti μὲν violenter discerpitur, imo nova ἔλλειψις invehitur, ac consequenter ἀπόδοσις in analysi duplicatur, hoc modo Johannes quidem baptizavit, baptismo resipiscentiæ, Christus ve- ro (quæ prior ἀπόδοσις τὴν ἔλλειψιν κ᾿ ἀνανταπό- δοτον supplens) Spiritu S. & igne. Illi vero, (quæ alte- ra ἀπόδοσις) his auditis baptizati sunt extraordina- riis S. S. donis. Juxta nostram vero interpretatio- nem neque literæ proprietas deseritur, neque i- λείψες opus est, nec naturalis nexus inter particu- las sibi respondentes, μὲν, & δὲ, violatur; adeoque nec Ἀναβαπτισμῷ patrocinium relinquitur, ne- que Baptismo Johannis quicquam derogatur, imo autoritas & efficacia ejusdem aperte adseritur, ipso Apostolo eam definiente. Nec inconcinne hic Beza: Necesse est fateri hic non agi de peculiari qua- piam duodecim hominum historia, qui sint ab Apo- stolo, seu baptizati, seu rebaptizati: neque de bapti- smo, sed de Ephesinæ Ecclesiæ primordiis, cum antea nulli fuissent illic ordine constituti piorum conven- tus: ac proinde Apostolum percontari de donis, quibus illos peculiariter solebat Deus ornare, qui gubernacu- lis Ecclesiarum admovebantur: num videlicet jam essent illis manus impositæ, vel essent ipsi iis saltem Spiritus Sancti donis præditi, ex quibus colligetur il- los ad sacrum ministerium divinitus vocari, veluti dono linguarum, & prophetiæ.

Non mirum autem Interpretes hunc sensum non animadvertisse. Vulgata enim omisit particu- lam δὲ, & vertit: his auditis, quasi legerit ἀκούσαν- τες ταῦτα, quum probatissimi quique Codices habeant ἀκούσαντες δὲ ἐβαπτίσθησαν. Illa particula omissa veteribus præbuit maxime duplicis erroris occasionem, ut qui propterea Lucæ hæc esse ver- ba credentes eo sunt delapsi, ut aliud fuisse bapti- sma Johannis quam Christi, & à Johanne baptiza- tos oportuisse in Christi nomine rebaptizari existi- maverint errore non levi. Atqui particula δὲ in Græcis Codicibus omnibus summo consensu, no- tanteBeza, legitur, quæ particulæ μὲν necessario re- spondet, ac nullo modo patitur, ut hujus orationis seriem discerpamus, quasi prior pars paulo poste- rior ipsi Lucæ tribuenda sit. Sensus vero ille Gro- tianus, Johannem baptizasse in pœnitentiam, nihil aliud quam hortatum cum esse, ut se emendarent, non in promissum Spiritus S. baptizarit, neque è locis illis Matth. III. 11. Act. I. 5. colligi potest, neque vero consentaneus est. Nam in locis illis non id docetur, Christum aquæ baptismum in promissum Spiritus S. per discipulos suos dispensaturum: quem Johan- nes solum in pœnitentiam dispensavit: Sed Chri- stum alium baptismum, effusionem nempe Spiritus S. quæ ab ὑδατοβαπτισμῷ distincta, nec ad eundem alligata est, qua dona Spiritus S. extraordinaria, præbiturum: Etsi in baptismo aquæ non tantum ab Apostolis, eorumque successoribus, sed etiam à S. Johanne administrato, omnino Spiritus S. quo- ad dona sanctificantia (non ministrantia) effusus sit, quia baptismus est lavacrum regenerationis

& renovationis S. S. Tit. III. 5. & per eundem ex a- qua & Spiritu regeniti sunt, a Johanne baptizati, quemadmodum & nos regeneramur: Quod autem ex Spiritu natum est, Spiritus est, Joh. III. 5. 6. Nec tantum in poenitentiam, sed etiam in remissionem peccatorum dispensatus dicitur a S. Johanne Bapti- smus: nec eo solum sensu, quod concio poenitentiae baptismo adjuncta fuerit, sed quod ipse Baptismus efficaciter operatus sit poenitentiam, conversionem, & remissionem peccatorum; Unde qui illum spreve- runt, consilium Dei de salute spreviffe dicuntur Luc. III. 3. VII. 30. nec ea ratione populo dictum a Iohanne, ut credat in eum, qui post ipsum venturus erat, ut ple- na praecepta regni coelestis ab ipso acciperent: nam a Johanne, aut etiam ab ipsis Prophetis non accepe- runt tantum semiplena; sed tradidit ipse cum Pro- phetis consilium Dei de salute integrum: atque te- stati sunt Apostoli, se nihil docere extra ea, quae Mo- ses & Prophetae scripsere Act. XXVI. 21. neque dubi- tavit Christus remittere consilii de salute causa ad Mosen & Prophetas Luc. XVI. 29. Joh. V. 39. quae haberi potest per ipsas Scripturas 2. Tim. III. 15. Qui e Graecis Patribus hic cum Grotio faciant, nec ad- ducti sunt, nec magis nos morari possent, quam Tertullianus, quum tamen nimis clarum sit e Scri- pturis S. baptismum Johannis a Baptismo Christi minime diversum fuisse. Vid. Exeg A. Conf. art. IX.

## 19:6
V. 6. and when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them) They had been baptized by another Christian: but God, to commend the Apostolic office, did not wish to communicate the gifts of His Spirit to them before the Apostolic hand had touched them. This was for the most part done so. God, however, not being bound to that law, just as Apollos had conferred those gifts before the imposition of Apostolic hands, so [He did] to Cornelius before baptism itself.

and they spoke with tongues and prophesied) They received not ordinary gifts, but both many and greatest, to be useful for founding Churches throughout Asia. See Esa. LIV. 13. 14. LXII. 1.

It is evident from what precedes that they were baptized not by any private person, but rather by John himself; in which baptism they without doubt received the gifts of the H. Spirit: but they are not said here to have received the gifts of the H. Spirit through the laying on of hands of Paul, [this] pertains to the ministering and extraordinary gifts, which were accustomed to be conferred in the primitive Church through the imposition of hands, for the founding of Churches, and that not by the Apostles alone: for Ananias, who laid hands on Paul Act. IX. 12. certainly was not an Apostle.

Latin:

V. 6. καὶ ἐπιθέντος αὐτοῖς τοῦ Παύλου τὰς χεῖρας, ἦλθε τὸ πνεῦ- μα τὸ ἅγιον ἐπ᾿ αὐτοὺς) Baptizati erant ab alio Christiano: sed Deus ad commendandum munus Apostolicum, non ante eis Spiritus sui dona communicare voluit, quam Apo- stolica manus eos tetigiffet. Hoc plerumque ita factum est. Deus tamen illi legi non adstrictus, sicut Apollo illa dona ante impositionem Apostolicarum manuum contulerat, ita Cornelio ante ipsum baptisma.

ἐλάλουν τε γλώσσαις καὶ προεφήτευον) Non vulgaria dona, sed & complura & maxima accepere, utiles futuri ad fun- dandas per Asiam Ecclesias. Vide Esa. LIV. 13. 14. LXII. 1.

Non ab aliquo privato, sed a Johanne potius ipso baptizatos illos fuisse ex antegressis constat; in quo baptismo dona Sp S. sine dubio accepere: non autem hic dona Spir. S. per χειροθεσίαν Pauli accepisse dicuntur, pertinet ad dona ministrantia, & extraordinaria, quae solebant in primitiva Eccle- sia per impositionem manuum conferri, ad fun- dandas Ecclesias, idque non per solos Apostolos: nam Ananias, qui Paulo imposuit manus Act. IX. 12. certe non fuit Apostolus.

## 19:8
V. 8. and persuading the things concerning the kingdom of God) See above XVIII. 4. where the same verb to persuade, but with the accusative of the person: it is signified that many were drawn into assent, although not all, as the following things show.

Latin:

V. 8. καὶ πείθων τὰ περὶ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ Θεοῦ) Vide supra XVIII. 4. ubi idem verbum πείθειν, sed cum accusativo per- sonae: significatur multos tractos in assensum, etsi non o- mnes, ut ostendunt sequentia.

## 19:9
V. 9. but as some) Of the Jews.

speaking evil of the way) The dogma of Christ XVIII. 25. 26. below 23. XXII. 4. XXIV. 23.

departing from them he separated the disciples) And he himself went out from the Synagogue, and led away those who had believed, because they were not going to be safe in the Synagogue.

in the school of a certain Tyrannus) A sophist or declaimer, whose name was Tyrannus: so Suidas. This name belonged also to a certain bodyguard of Herod, as can be seen in Josephus XVI. 16.

Some take the word Tyrannus as an Appellative, noting from Strabo some royal family among the Ephesians, to whom Pricaeus rises: But such, in the judgment of Casaubon, could no more be called Tyrants than he who among the Romans was called the sacrificial King, and among the Athenians also there was one, who was similarly called king. For all these were Kings in name only, but in fact were sacrificial priests. See Plutarch. quaest LXIII. There is therefore no reason why we should, with Lyranus, Cajetan, Vatablus, take the word Tyrant for a Prince, and the School for a hall or portico, into which that Prince was accustomed to withdraw for the sake of leisure: as Cornel. a Lap. trifles, feigning that he was from the stock of Androclus, King of the Athenians.

Latin:

V. 9. ὡς δέ τινες) Judaeorum.

κακολογοῦντες τὴν ὁδὸν) Dogma Christi XVIII. 25. 26. infra 23. XXII. 4. XXIV. 23.

ἀποστὰς ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν ἀφώρισε τοὺς μαθητὰς) Et ipse e Sy- nagoga exiit, & eos qui crediderant, abduxit, eo quod in Synagoga tuti non erant futuri.

ἐν τῇ σχολῇ Τυράννου τινὸς) Sophistae sive declamatoris, cui nomen Tyranno: ita Suidas. Fuit hoc nomen & cuidam satelliti Herodis, ut videre est apud Josephum XVI. 16.

Vocem Τυράννου quidam ceu Appellativam acci- piunt, ex Strabone notantes regiam aliquam apud Ephesios familiam, quibus assurgit Pricaeus: Sed tales, Casaubono judice, non magis potuere Tyranni appellari, quam qui apud Romanos Rex sacrificulus vocabatur, & apud Athenienses quoque fuit, qui simi- liter βασιλεὺς diceretur. Nam hi omnes nomine tan- tum Reges, re autem sacrificuli fuerunt. Vid. Plu- tarch. quaest LXIII. Non ergo est, quod cum Lyra- no, Cajet. Vatablo, vocem Tyranni pro Principe ac- cipiamus, & Scholam pro aula vel porticu, in quam Princeps ille otii causa secedere solitus sit: uti nu- gatur Cornel. a Lap. eum ex stirpe Androchi Regis Athenarum fuisse, fingens.

## 19:10
V. 10. all those dwelling in Asia) Who were accustomed to come to Ephesus for the sake of sacred rites. For that temple was common to Asia, whence also the name of Asiarchs; Jews also from other cities of Asia often came there for the sake of trade or lawsuits.

Latin:

V. 10. πάντας τοὺς κατοικοῦντας τὴν Ἀσίαν) Qui sacrorum causa Ephesum venire solebant. Erat enim templum illud commune Asiæ, unde & nomen Ἀσιαρχῶν, Judæi quoque ex aliis Asiæ urbibus sæpe eo veniebant mercatus causâ aut judiciorum.

## 19:11
V. 11. and mighty works not the ordinary ones) A very Greek expression. Dionysius Longinus on Moses: not an ordinary man. But that word mighty works is geburoth as above II. 22.

Latin:

V. 11. δυνάμεις τε ὀὐ τὰς τυχύσας) Locutio bene Græca. Dionysius Longinus de Mose : ὀὐχ’ ὁ τυχὼν ἀνήρ. Illud au- tem δυνάμεις est גבורות ut supra II. 22.

## 19:12
v. 12. sudaria) concerning this word we have spoken at Luke xix. 20, John xi. 44. simikinthia) There is a Lemma in Martial, semicinctium, with this couplet: You give a tunic, rich man: I could gird you: If I were wealthy, I would give both gifts. In the Glossaries: semicinctum emizonion. Elsewhere: semicinctum hypozoma. Suidas: simikinthion phakelia, zonaria; he wishes to say that phakelia are small bands. The word simikinthion is also in the Catechesis of Cyril, and in Nicetas Paphlagon.

and that diseases were removed from them) Thus was performed what Christ had said in John XIV. 12. See also above V. 15.

Concerning that expression not the ordinary ones, Camerarius: God did not effect fortuitous or common faculties of miracles for Paul as his minister. That is, singular and extraordinary, by the figure of litotes. As: I sing of things not uncertain. That is, things explored and altogether about to happen. Furthermore, Beza took sudarium and semicinctium for the same thing, just as these are also read as synonyms in Suidas: but they are more correctly distinguished: because it is not likely that two words were joined thus by Luke through tautology, and it makes for the amplification of Paul's miracles that he exercised power through both sudaria and semicinctia. Hesychius indeed translates simikinthia as phakelia, but adds zonaria horaria ton hiereon, the horary girdles of the priests: Whence Lud. de Dieu says, I understand girdles, with which they would gird themselves when they performed sacred rites. For since he was clothed in long robes, that they were not accustomed to be free for sacred rites unless girded is clear from Exod. XXXIX. 29, Lev. XIV. 6, 1. Sam. II. 18. Paul undoubtedly used such girdles also, so that he might both walk and perform his tasks more expeditiously, which are rightly called semicinctia, because they gird the middle of the body in the middle of the garment. Camerarius says sudaria and simicinthia are foreign words. Sudaria are indeed clearly Latin. Simicinctia also, from cinctus, seems to be a name of the same language. To Suidas these are the same as sudaria. By both are signified small linens and bands, with which they would both gird themselves and wipe away sweat.

PART II.

The confusion of certain exorcists, and the conversion of some superstitious persons and others.

Latin:

v. 12. συδάρια) de hac voce diximus Luc. xix. 20. Ioh. xi. 44. σιμικίνθια) Est apud Martialem Lemma, semicinctium, cum hoc disticho: Dei tunicam dives: ego te præcingere possum: Essem si locuples, munus utrumque darem. In Glossis: semicinctum ἐμιζώνιον. Alibi: semicinctum ὑπόζω- μα. Suidas : σιμικίνθιον φακεώλια, ζωνάρια, illud φακεώλια vult dicere fasciolas. Est vox σιμικίνθιον & in Catechesi Cy- rilli, & in Niceta, Paphlagone.

κὰὶ ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι ἀπ’ αὐτῶν τὰς νόσυς) Ita præstitum quod dixerat Christus Joh. XIV. 12. Vide & supra V. 15.

De locutione illa ὀὐ τὰς τυχύσας Camerarius: Non fortuitas neque communes miraculorum facultates ef- ficiebat Deus Paulo administro. Id est, singulares & eximias, figura λιτότητος. Ut: Haud incerta cano. Id est, explorata & omnino eventura. Porro Beza su- darium & semicinctium pro eodem accepit, uti e- tiam hæc tanquam Synonyma leguntur apud Sui- dam: sed rectius distinguuntur: quia à Luca duo vocabula per ταυτολογίαν sic conjuncta fuisse non est verisimile, & ad amplificationem miraculorum Pauli facit, quod & per sudaria, & per semicinctia virtutem exercuerit. Hesychius quidem σιμικίνθια vertit Φακεώλια, sed addit ζωνάρια ὡράρια τῶν ἱερέων, Cingula horaria sacerdotum: Unde Lud. de Dieu cingula, inquit, intelligo, quibus se accingerent cum sacra facerent. Cum enim talaribus indueretur vestibus, non nisi succinctos solere sacris vacare, liquet ex Exod. XXXIX. 29. Lev. XIV. 6. 1. Sam. II. 18. Ta- libus quoque cingulis, quo expeditius & incederet & sua perageret, usus procul dubio fuit Paulus, quæ semicinctia recte dicuntur, quia in medio corporis medium vestis accingunt. Camerarius sudaria, in- quit, & simicinthia, externa sunt vocabula. Sudaria quidem manifeste Latina. Simicinctia quoque à cinctus, ejusdem linguæ nomen videtur. Suidæ hæc eadem suda- ria sunt. Significantur ambobus linteola & fasciolæ, quibus & præcingerentur, & detergerent sudorem.

PARS II.

Exorcistarum quorundam confusio, & superstitioso- rum nonnullorum aliorumque conversio.

## 19:13
v. 13. Of the wandering Jewish exorcists) Concerning whom see what we have brought forward at Matt. XII. 27. But he calls them wandering, because they did not stay in one place, but ran hither and thither hunting for gain, such as were called agyrtai among the Greeks and circulators among the Latins.

we adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches) See a similar case at Mark IX. 38, Luke IX. 49.

Latin:

v. 13. Ἀπό τῶν περιερχομένων Ἰυδαίων ἐξορκιστῶν) De quibus vide quæ attulimus Matth. XII. 27. περιερχομένυς autem vo- cat, quod non uno in loco subsisterent, sed huc illuc cursi- tarent quæstui aucupando, quales apud Græcos ἀγύρται apud Latinos circulatores.

ὁρκίζομεν ὑμᾶς τὸν Ἰησῦν ὃν ὁ Παῦλος κηρύσσει) Simile vide Marc. IX. 38. Luc. IX. 49.

## 19:14
V. 14. sons of Sceva) Sheba as here in the Syriac. A name said to be from an oath.

Jewish high priest) Sons of the prince of some priestly family: for we showed at Matt. II. 4 that such are also called high priests.

Selden, however, praised more than once by Grotius, preferred to understand them as those who, on account of the dignity of their ancestors and the proximity of blood, had a hope of succeeding by established law, and that they were also sometimes called ἀρχιερεῖς or High Priests, in almost the same way as in some regions formerly the sons of Kings were called Kings, and the sons of Dukes and Counts were called Dukes and Counts: and thus also Sceva the Jew was called High Priest, even though he never held the High Priesthood: just as also Gamala, son of Jesus, is called High Priest by Josephus.

Latin:

V. 14. ὑοὶ σκευᾶ) שבעא ut hic Syrus. à jurejurando dictum nomen.

Ἰυδαίυ ἀρχιερέως) Filii principis familiæ alicujus sacerdo- talis: nam & tales dici ἀρχιερέας oftendimus Matth. II. 4.

Seldenus tamen Grotio non semel laudatus de illis intelligere maluit, quibus ob majorum digni- tatem, & sanguinis proximitatem spes erat ex jure recepto succedendi, quodque etiam ἀρχιερεῖς seu Pontifices interdum dicti sint, non aliter ferme, ac in nonnulli olim regionibus Regum filii Reges, ac Ducum & Comitum filii Duces ac Comites: atque ita etiam Scevam Judæum Pontificem dictum, etsi nun- quam Pontificatum gesserit: quemadmodum e- tiam Gamala Jesus F. Pontifex Josepho dictus.

## 19:15
v. 15. ἀποκριθὲν δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ πονηρὸν εἶπε. τὸν Ἰησῦν γινώσκω κὰι τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίσταμαι) By God's compulsion. Tertullian in his Apology: Believe them when they speak the truth about themselves, you who believe them when they lie. No one lies to their own disgrace; rather, they do so for their honor. See the whole passage if you please.

ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνες ἐστε) As if he were saying: you certainly have nothing to do with them.

Latin:

v. 15. ἀποκριθὲν δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ πονηρὸν εἶπε. τὸν Ἰησῦν γινώ- σκω κὰι τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίσταμαι) Deo cogente. Tertullianus in Apologetico. Credite illis cum verum de se loquantur, qui mentientibus creditis. Nemo ad suum dedecus mentitur? quin potius ad honorem. Vide si placet totum locum.

ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνες ἐστε) Quasi dicat: vos certe nihil ad illos per- tinetis.

## 19:16
v. 16. κὰὶ κατακυριεύσας αὐτῶν) That manuscript also has ἀμφοτέρων instead of αὐτῶν. Therefore, two of the seven sons of Sceva were present there. But the speech shifts strangely from the man to the the Spirit, because what that man was doing, he was doing not by his own power, but by the power of an unclean spirit. See Matt. VIII. 28.

The Vulgate, and that of one MS., does not have such authority that it deserves to be preferred to all other codices; therefore, it cannot be asserted with certainty that two of the seven sons were present, since it is not contained in the source.

Latin:

v. 16. κὰὶ κατακυριεύσας αὐτῶν) ἀμφοτέρων pro αὐτῶν ha- bet & ille Manuscriptus. Ergo de septem Scevæ filiis duo ibi adfuere. Mire autem transit oratio ab homine ad ipsum Spiritum, quia quod ille homo agebat, id agebat non sua, sed Spiritus impuri vi. Vid. Matth. VIII. 28.

Vulgata, & unius MS. tanta non est autoritas, ut praeferri omnibus aliis Codicibus mereatur, duos ergo de septem filiis adfuisse certo asseri non potest, quum in fonte id non habeatur.

## 19:17
v. 17. And fear fell upon them all) As above V. 11. And the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified) It is customary to say of God, 'May Thy name be magnified,' as in 2 Sam. VII. 26.

Latin:

v. 17. καὶ ἐπέπεσε φόβος ἐπὶ πάντας αὐτούς) Ut supra V. 11. καὶ ἐμεγαλύνετο τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ) Solet de Deo dici μεγαλυνθείη τὸ ὄνομά σε ut 2. Sam. VII. 26.

## 19:18
v. 18. They came confessing) They came to the Apostles, confessing how badly they had led their lives until then, with even more serious crimes being commemorated, like those who had come to John the Baptist, Matt. III. 6, where see the stated things. The Greeks say in this place: 'Every believer ought to tell his own sins, and to renounce them, by changing himself, so as not to do the same things anymore, according to what was said: Tell your sins first, that you may be justified, and that: A just man is his own accuser in the first speech.'

Latin:

v. 18. ἤρχοντο ἐξομολογούμενοι) Venerunt ad Apostolos, confitentes quam male vitam hactenus traduxissent, commemoratis etiam criminibus gravioribus, ut illi, qui ad Johannem Baptistam venerant Matth. III. 6. ubi dicta vide Graeci hoc loco: Δεῖ πάντα πιστὸν λέγειν τὰς ἑαυτοῦ ἁμαρτίας, καὶ ἀποτάττεσθαι, διὰ τοῦ ἑαυτὸν διαλλάγχειν, τοῦ ἔτι μὴ ποιεῖν τὰ αὐτά, κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον· λέγε σὺ τὰς ἁμαρτίας σε πρῶτος, ἵνα δικαιωθῇς καὶ τὸ, δίκαιος ἑαυτοῦ κατήγορος ἐν πρωτολογία.

## 19:19
v. 19. And many of those who practiced curious arts) You will understand what 'curious' (perierga) are from Irenaeus I. 2, concerning the Simonians: 'Love charms also, and incantations, and those who are called familiars, and dream-senders, and whatever other curious things (it is wrongly written parerga) are zealously practiced among them.' Philosophers called these 'curious' and 'sorceries' and 'wonders,' as Porphyry does in Book II of 'On Abstinence from Animal Food,' where he also places love charms and erotic things in this class. The Greek Fathers have 'sorcerous books' here, but Christians truly called these things Diabolical. But Luke is content to use the word received at Ephesus. Ephesus was devoted to these wicked studies before other cities; Plutarch mentions the Magicians who were at Ephesus in his 'Alexander.' Menander in 'The Child': 'He walks about saying Ephesian charms to those who are marrying, as antidotes.' Interpret this from Apuleius in his 'Herbarium': 'If anyone has been bewitched and bound at his wedding, you will release him in this way.' Anaxilaus in Athenaeus: 'And besides these, wearing beautiful Ephesian letters sewn into small leather pouches.' Plutarch in 'Symposiacs' VII: 'The magicians order those who are possessed by demons to recite and name the Ephesian letters to themselves.' Clement of Alexandria, 'Stromata' I: 'Some, more mythical, say that the so-called Idaean Dactyls were the first to become wise, to whom the discovery of the so-called Ephesian letters and the musical rhythms is attributed.' And 'Stromata' V: 'Androcydes the Pythagorean says that the so-called Ephesian letters, which are very famous in many places, have the order of symbols; and that Askion signifies darkness, for it has no shadow. Lix is the earth, for it is an ancient name; and Tetras is the year, because of the seasons; and Damnameneus is the Sun, the one who tames; and the Aisia are the true voice.' Eustathius also mentions them in his commentary on Odyssey phi, who also says that Ephesian letters were inscribed obscurely and enigmatically on the feet and girdle and crown of the Ephesian Diana herself, as do Hesychius and Suidas.

bringing the books together, they burned them before all) It is not enough to conceive repentance in the mind; it must also be shown by deeds, Matt. III. 8.

Compare what Walaeus brings forward here from the blessed Quistorpius the Elder, my former host, and my promoter in the doctoral act 35 years ago, and also from Stephanus Bald.

and they found fifty thousand pieces of silver) I think Luke did not reduce this price to Roman or Greek or Asiatic currency, but to Jewish, and that 'silver' corresponds to the Hebrew 'kesef,' which is used for a silver shekel, and is translated as such in Num. VII. 85, Deut. XXII. 19, 2 Kings XV. 20, Is. VII. 23, Jer. XXXII. 9. Those believers burned those books: they did not sell them, so as to bring the price to the Apostles: for it would have been like the price of a prostitute, which ought not to be offered, Deut. XXIII. 18.

Ludovicus de Dieu on this passage has it thus: 'The Vulgate, They found 50,000 denarii. Beza also translates silver as denarii. The Arab as drachmas, which were worth about as much as denarii. The Syrian as kespa. Just as the LXX mostly use silver for kesef; sometimes, however, they use didrachma of silver, as in Deut. XXII. 29, sometimes didrachma absolutely, as in Gen. XX. 16, sometimes shekel, as in Numbers VII. 85, Deut. XXII. 19, 2 Kings XV. 20, Is. VII. 23, Jer. XXXII. 9. But the common shekel is understood, worth a didrachmon, two drachmas. Just as the Chaldean is accustomed to say sela, a shekel, for kesef. From this calculation, the sum is fifty thousand shekels. Greater by another amount than denarii. For a common shekel comprises two denarii.' This is Ludov. de Dieu. What is to be held concerning the distinction of the shekel into common and sacred, we have said in our treatise on coins; where it was dealt with in the 'Bibl. Illustr. V. T.' p. 179 concerning this passage. Those 50,000 silver pieces, or Roman denarii and Attic drachmas, amounted to 6,250 Joachim thalers or Valley thalers, which we call Imperials.

PART III. The sedition of Demetrius because of Diana being held in contempt, and the settlement of the same made by Alexander.

Latin:

v. 19. ἱκανοὶ δὲ τῶν τὰ περίεργα πραξάντων) περίεργα quae sint intelliges ex Irenaeo I. 2. de Simonianis: amatoria quoque, & agogima, & qui dicuntur paredri, & oniropompi, & quaecunque sunt alia perierga(male scribitur parerga)apud eos studiose exercentur. Haec Philosophi vocabant περίεργα & γοητείας & τερατουργίας, ut Porphyrius II. de abstinendo ab animatis, ubi & φίλτρα & ἐρωτικὰ ponit in hac classe. γοητικὰς βίβλους habent hic Patres Graeci, Christiani vero Diabolica haec vocarunt. Sed Lucas recepta Ephesi voce uti, contentus est. Ephesus ante alias civitates his pravis studiis dedita, Magorum qui erant Ephesi meminit Plutarchus Alexandro. Menander παιδίῳ. Ἐφέσια τοῖς γαμοῦσιν οὗτος περιπατεῖ Λέγων ἀλεξιφάρμακα. quod interpretare ex Apulejo in Herbario; Si quis defotus defixusque fuerit in ejus nuptiis eum sic resolves. Anaxilaus apud Athenaeum: καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ἐν σκυταρίοις ῥαπτοῖσι φορῶν Ἐφεσήϊα γράμματα καλά. Plutarchus Symposiacorum VII. οἱ μάγοι τοὺς δαιμονιζομένους κελεύουσι τὰ Ἐφέσια γράμματα πρὸς αὑτοὺς καταλέγειν καὶ ὀνομάζειν. Clemens Alexandr. Strom. I. τινὲς δὲ μυθικώτεροι τῶν ἰδαίων καλουμένων δακτύλων, σοφούς τινας πρώτως γενέσθαι λέγουσιν, εἰς οὓς ἥτε τῶν Ἐφεσίων λεγομένων γραμμάτων καὶ ἡ κατὰ μουσικὴν εὕρεσις ῥυθμῶν ἀναφέρεται. Et Strom. V. Ἀνδροκύδης γ’ οὖν ὁ Πυθαγορικὸς τὰ Ἐφέσια καλούμενα γράμματα, ἐν πολλοῖς δὲ πολυθρύλητα ὄντα συμβόλων ἔχειν φησὶ τάξιν· σημαίνειν δὲ Ἄσκιον μὲν τὸ σκότος. μὴ γὰρ ἔχειν τοῦτο σκιάν. λὶξ δέ ἐστιν ἡ γῆ γὰρ ἀρχαίαν ἐπωνυμίαν· κᾀτετρὰς ὁ ἐνιαυτὸς διὰ τὰς ὥρας· δαμναμενεὺς δὲ ὁ Ἥλιος. ὁ δαμάζων· τὰ Αἴσιά τε ἡ ἀληθὴς φωνή. Meminere & Eustathius ad Odysseae φ, qui etiam pedibus & zonae & coronae ipsius Dianae Ephesiae inscriptas ait fuisse literas Ephesias ἀσαφῶς καὶ αἰνιγματωδῶς, & Hesychius & Suidas.

συνενέγκαντες τὰς βίβλους κατέκαιον ἐνώπιον πάντων) Non satis est poenitentiam animo concipere; factis quoque ostendenda est Matth. III. 8.

Confer quae hic è B. Quistorpio Seniore, meo quondam hospite, & in actu Doctorali ante 35. annos promotore, nec non è Stephano Bald. Walaeus hic adducit.

καὶ εὗρον ἀργυρίου μυριάδας πέντε) Puto Lucam hoc pretium non ad Romanum aut Graecum, aut Asiaticum, sed ad Judaicum redegisse, & ἀργυρίου respondere Hebraeo כסף quod pro siclo argenteo ponitur, atque ita vertitur Num. VII. 85. Deut. XXII. 19. 2. Reg. XV. 20. Es. VII. 23. Jerem. XXXII. 9. Usserunt isti fideles libros illos: non vendiderunt, ut pretium ad Apostolos afferrent: fuisse enim id velut pretium scorti, quod offerri non debet, Deut. XXIII. 18.

Ludovicus de Dieu ad h. l. ita habet: Vulgatus, Invenerunt denariorum 50. millia. Beza quoq; ἀργύριον per denarios vertit. Arabs per drachmas, quae tantunde fere valebant atq; denarii. Syrus כספא. Sicut LXX. plerumque pro כסף ponunt ἀργύριον; interdum tamen δίδραχμα ἀργυρίου, ut Deut. XXII. 29. interdum δίδραχμα absolute, ut Gen. XX. 16. aliquando σίκλος siclus, ut Numer. VII. 85. Deut. XXII. 19. 2. Reg. XV. 20. Es. VII. 23. Jer. XXXII. 9. intelligitur autem siclus communis, valens δίδραχμον duas drachmas. quomodo & Chaldaeus pro כסף solet dicere סלעא, siclus. ex hac supputatione, summa est, siclorum quinquaginta millia. altero major quam denariorum. Siclus enim communis duos denarios comprehendit. Haec Ludov. de Dieu. Quid de distinctione Sicli in vulgarem & sacrum habendum, diximus tract. de numis; ubi in Bibl. Illustr. V. T. p. 179. de hoc loco actum. Illi 50000. argenteorum, vel denariorum Romanorum & drach- marum Atticarum effecerunt 6250. Joachamicos vel Vallenses, quos Imperiales vocamus.

PARS III. Seditio Demetrii ob Dianam contemtam, e- jusdemque ab Alexandro facta compositio.

## 19:21
v. 21. ἔθετο ὁ Παῦλος ἐν τῷ πνεύματι) The learned rightly note that this is a Hebrew idiom שׂם על לבו which the Greeks translate as ἔθετο ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ. Moreover, it is not surprising that πνεῦμα with the article is used for the mind. See I Cor. II. 11. V. 5. VI. 20. Eph. IV. 23. Heb. IV. 12.

δεῖ με κᾀ Ῥώμην ἰδεῖν) Paul was seeking those cities where he hoped for the greatest harvest.

Others, including B. Luth., explain it as: he proposed in the Spirit: Not badly: because this plan was certainly undertaken by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, Acts XX. 1. It is not new for simple verbs to be used for compound ones, both among the Hebrews and in the N.T., which not infrequently Hebraizes. See Glassius, Gramm. S. p. 211. seqq. Thus ἔθετο is said for προέθετο, as Beza in the former edition, which he had no need to change in the latter, in our judgment. Whence Camerarius, most learned in Greek, explained it: προέθετο he proposed in his mind, or rather by the instinct of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

v. 21. ἔθετο ὁ Παῦλος ἐν τῷ πνεύματι) Bene notant eruditi esse locutionem Hebraicam שׂם על לבו quod Græci ver- tunt ἔθετο ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ. Non mirum autem πνεῦμα cum ar- ticulo poni pro animo. Vide I. Cor. II. 11. V. 5. VI. 20. Eph. IV. 23. Hebr. IV. 12.

δεῖ με κᾀ Ῥώμην ἰδεῖν) Quærebat eas urbes Paulus, ubi ma- ximam sperabat messem.

Alii, etiam B. Luth. exponunt, proposuit in Spi- ritu: Non male: quia Spiritus S. impulsu utique hoc consilium ceptum est Act. XX. 1. Non novum est verba simplicia poni pro compositis, tum apud E- bræos, tum in N. T. quod non raro Ebraizat. Vid. Glassii Gramm. S. p. 211. seqq. Sic ἔθετο dictum pro προέθετο, ut Beza in priori editione, quod in altera mutare opus non habuit, nostro judicio. Unde Ca- merarius Græce doctissimus exposuit: προέθετο proposuit animo suo, vel potius de Spir. S. instinctu.

## 19:22
v. 22. κᾀ Ἔραστον) Not the one whose mention is in Rom. XVI. 25. But another whose mention is in 2 Tim. IV. 20. Perhaps he was a Hebrew, whose name was David.

ἐπέσχε χρόνον εἰς τὴν Ἀσίαν) for ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ, which change is frequent among the Hellenists.

And Camerarius: ἐπέσχε χρόνον εἰς τὴν Ἀσίαν. He stayed for a time in Asia. ἐπεῖχεν ἐπὶ χρόνον ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ, with a change not unusual in these writings.

Latin:

v. 22. κᾀ Ἔραστον) Non eum cujus mentio Rom. XVI. 25. Sed alterum cujus mentio 2. Tim. IV. 20. forte Hebræus fuerit, cui nomen David.

ἐπέσχε χρόνον εἰς τὴν Ἀσίαν) pro ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ, quæ mutatio frequens Hellenistis.

Et Camerarius: ἐπέσχε χρόνον εἰς τὴν Ἀσίαν. In- stitit ad tempus in Asia. ἐπεῖχεν ἐπὶ χρόνον ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ non inusitata in his scriptis mutatione.

## 19:23
v. 23. Τάραχος οὐκ ὀλίγος) No light tumult. Τάραχος and ταραχὴ and θόρυβος are accustomed to be used for the Hebrew מהומה.

περὶ τῆς ὁδῦ) By occasion of the Gospel.

Latin:

v. 23. Τάραχος οὐκ ὀλίγος) Non levis tumultus. Τάρα- χος & ταραχὴ & θόρυβος poni solent pro Hebræo מהומה.

περὶ τῆς ὁδῦ) Occasione Evangelii.

## 19:24
v. 24. Ἀργυροκόπος) This word is correctly translated in the Glossary as silversmith.

ποιῶν ναοὺς ἀργυροῦς Ἀρτέμιδος) That is, small silver shrines, and in them an image of Diana after the likeness of the true temple and image. Pliny XXXVI. 5 mentions such a shrine of the Cnidian Venus. Polybius calls them Naidia. Dion calls them μικροὺς νεὼς, the makers of which the interpreter of Aristotle calls ναοποιοὺς, as Salmasius observed in his notes on Solinus.

Camerarius notes that the Greeks called them κιβώρια, a name which they used for ecclesiastical vessels. And from Athenaeus, book XI, he observes that he made mention of such vessels, which were named from a shape similar to the Egyptian bean, as they called it both κιβώριον and κολοκάσιον. Beza taught that coins were designated: but that does not please Casaubon: This opinion, he says, although it is probable, yet because no one of the ancients mentions these coins which were called ναοὶ: I for my part do not doubt that ναὸς is used in this place for small shrines made of silver or gold, in which were stored small images of Diana, which were commonly bought by others who visited the Ephesian Diana. And perhaps those shrines represented the workmanship of the Ephesian temple, etc. Compare what Walæus brings forward here from Pricæus and Salmasius.

παρέχετο τοῖς τεχνίταις ἐργασίαν οὐκ ὀλίγην) By 'craftsmen' he calls the workmen of Demetrius to whom he gave work to do. The Syriac called them sons of his art.

Latin:

v. 24. Ἀργυροκόπος) Hæc vox in Glossario recte verti- tur faber argentarius.

ποιῶν ναοὺς ἀργυροῦς Ἀρτέμιδος) Id est, exiguas ædiculas argenteas, & in iis simulacrum Dianæ ad effigiem veri tem- pli & simulacri. Talis ædiculæ Veneris Cnidiæ meminit Pli- nius XXXVI. 5. Naidia vocat Polybius. Dion Νεως μικρους, quorum fabros ναοποιοὺς vocat Aristotelis interpres, ut ob- servavit Salmasius ad Solinum.

Græcos vocasse κιβώρια notat Camerarius, quod nomen de Ecclesiasticis vasis usurparunt. Et ex A- thenæi l. XI. observat, quod mentionem talium va- sorum fecerit, quæ sit appellata à forma simili fabæ Ægyptiacæ, utpote quam & κιβώριον & κολοκάσιον dixere. Beza nummos designari docuit: sed id non placet Casaubono: Hæc sententia, inquit, etsi proba- bilis est, tamen quia horum nummorum, qui ναοὶ ap- pellarentur, nemo veterum meminit: non dubito equi- dem ναὸς vocari hoc loco, ædiculas ex argento vel au- ro factas, in quas recondebantur Dianæ parva simula- chra, quæ vulgo ab aliis emebantur, qui Dianam Ephesinam visebant. Et fortasse referebant ista ædi- culæ templi Ephesini artificium, &c. Conf. quæ ex Pricæo & Salmasio hic adducit Walæus.

παρέχετο τοῖς τεχνίταις ἐργασίαν οὐκ ὀλίγην) τεχνίταις his vocat operas Demetrii quibus ille dabat, quod agerent. Filios artis suæ dixit Syrus.

## 19:25
v. 25. τὲς περὶ ταῦτα ἐργάτας) Others like himself and of the same trade.

ὅτι ἐκ ταύτης τῆς ἐργασίας ἡ εὐπορία ἡμῶν ἐστι) From this craft there is gain for us; hence we are enriched. He did not wish to seem false, because it was profitable to him.

Latin:

v. 25. τὲς περὶ ταῦτα ἐργάτας) Alios sibi similes & quæ- stus ejusdem.

ὅτι ἐκ ταύτης τῆς ἐργασίας ἡ εὐπορία ἡμῶν ἐστι) Ex hoc opi- ficio quæstus est nobis; hinc ditamur. Nolebat falsum vi- deri, quod ipsi proderat.

## 19:26
v. 26. λέγων ὅτι ἐκ εἰσὶ θεοὶ οἱ διὰ χειρῶν γινόμενοι) He denied that there was any divine power in images. He was saying things consistent with Ps. CXV. 4. and following, and Jer. X. 3. and following.

Latin:

v. 26. λέγων ὅτι ἐκ εἰσὶ θεοὶ οἱ διὰ χειρῶν γινόμενοι) Nega- bat ullam esse vim divinam in simulacris. Dicebat congru- entia Ps. CXV. 4. & sequentibus & Jer. X. 3. & sequentibus.

## 19:27
v. 27. ὀ μόνον δὲ τῦτο κινδυνεύει ὑμῖν τὸ μέρος ἀπελεγμὸν ἐλθεῖν) It must be read ἡμῶν entirely, just as I believe the Syriac and the Arab read it. The sense is: There is a danger not only that that which concerns us (that is, our craft) may come into contempt. Τὸ ἡμῶν μέρος, that which touches us, a known expression. Ἀπελεγμός, however, is the same as ὀνειδισμός, and signifies contempt by metonymy: and therefore ὀνειδισμὸς and ἔλεγχός interpret one another in Is. XXXVI. 3.

No necessity appears why the text should be emended. Nor has anything of the sort been observed either by the Greek Fathers or by the most learned Greek philologists. And the sense is consistent both in the Greek and among the Syrian and the Arab, without any change. Not only does this part of ours run the risk of being brought into disrepute, the Vulgate rendered: This part is rendered by the Syriac and Arabic as this thing, or this business, as in 2 Cor. IX. 3. τὸ μέρος seems to be accepted: as also Col. II. 16. and 1 Pet. IV. 16.

but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis should be considered as nothing) as if he were saying, it is a small matter about our gain: The whole religion is in danger here. That the temple of Diana existed at Ephesus before the times of Liber Pater and the Amazons, the Ephesians teach us in Tacitus, Annals III. That it was built commonly by the cities of Asia, Livy is the author, book 1. hence Martial: Nor let the soft Ionians be praised for the temple of Trivia. Aristophanes: And thou, blessed Ephesus, hast an all-golden house in which the maidens of the Lydians greatly worship thee. Great Diana is called here that Ephesian one, as Pausanias's first-throned.

Concerning this temple see what Camerarius says on this passage and Walaeus from Salmasius. The city of Ephesus was once situated at the time of Croesus in such a way that it was seven stadia from the temple, which are almost a thousand paces. But when at one time the city was being besieged by Croesus, then the Ephesians, as Herodotus has it, consecrated their city to Diana, with a rope attached from the walls to the temple.

her majesty) The Latin rightly [translates it] Majesty. The Glossary [defines] μεγαλειότης as Majesty, you could also translate it as divinity.

whom all Asia and the world worships) he does not say this falsely. For among the few gods who could be instituted as heirs by Roman testators, this Ephesian Diana was one, as Ulpian teaches us in the Institutes, title XXII.

Pricaeus and from him Walaeus [cite] these things from Pausanias and Apuleius concerning Diana: Pausanias in the Messeniaca: All cities and men privately hold the Ephesian Artemis in the greatest honor among the gods: with the following. Apuleius book II concerning this same one: Whose single divinity the whole world worships in manifold form, with varied rite, and by many names.

Latin:

v. 27. ὀ μόνον δὲ τῦτο κινδυνεύει ὑμῖν τὸ μέρος ἀπελεγμὸν ἐλθεῖν) omnino legendum est ἡμῶν quomodo & Syrum & A- rabem arbitror legisse. Sensus est: Periculum est non modo ne id quod nos contingit(id est,ars nostra)in contemptum veniat Τὸ ἡμῶν μέρος id quod nos tangit, nota locutio. Ἀπελεγμός autem, idem quod ὀνειδισμός, per μετωνυμίαν con- temptum significat: ideoque ὀνειδισμὸς & ἔλεγχός se mutuo interpretantur Es. XXXVI. 3.

Nulla apparet necessitatis, cur textus emen- detur. Nec quicquam tale vel Græcis Patribus vel Græcis doctissimis Philologis observatum. Et constat sibi sensus cum in Græco, tum apud Syrum, & Arabem, sine ulla mutatione. Non solum hoc periclitabitur nobis pars in redargutionem venire, reddidit Vulgata: Hæc pars Syro & Arabi redditur hæc res, vel hoc negotium, uti 2. Cor. IX. 3. τὸ μέρος accipi videtur: ut & Col. II. 16. & 1. Petr. IV. 16.

ἀλλὰ κὶ τὸ τῆς μεγάλης θεᾶς ᾿Αρτέμιδος ἱερὸν εἰς ὐδὸν λογι- θῆναι) quasi dicat, parum est de nostro quæstu: Tota re- ligio hic periclitatur. Templum Dianæ fuisse Ephesi ante Liberi Patris & Amazonum tempora, docent nos Ephesii apud Tacitum Annalium III. Majus factum communiter ab Asiæ civitatibus, Livius auctor est lib. 1. ideo Martialis: Nec Triviæ templo molles laudentur Iones. Aristophanes: Ἡ τ᾽ Ἐφέσυ μάκαιρα πάγχρυσον ἔχεις οἶκον ἐν ὧ κόραι σε Λυδῶν μεγάλως σέβυσιν. Magna Diana hic di- citur illa Ephesia, ut Pausaniæ πρωτοθρονία.

De hoc templo vid. quæ Camerarius ad h. l. & Walæus è Salmasio. Fuit Ephesi urbs olim ad tem- pus Crœsi ita sita, ut à templo abesset stadiis se- ptem, qui sunt propemodum mille passus. Cum vero quodam tempore urbs à Crœso oppugnare- tur, ibi tum Ephesii, ut habet Herodotus, conse- crarunt urbem suam Dianæ, annexo è mœnibus fune ad templum.

τὴν μεγαλειότητα αὐτῆς) Bene Latinus Majestatem. Glos- sarium μεγαλειότης Majestas, posses & numen vertere.

ἣν ὅλη ἡ ᾿Ασία κό οἰκυμένη σέβεται) non falso hoc dicit. Nam & inter paucos Deos qui à Romanis testatoribus hæ- redes institui poterant, erat hæc Diana Ephesia, ut nos do- cet Ulpianus institutionum tit. XXII.

Pricæus & ex eo Walæus hæc è Pausania, & Apulejo de Diana: Pausanias Messeniacis: ᾿Εφε- σίαν ᾿Αρτεμιν πόλεις τε ὀνομάζυσιν αἱ πᾶσαι κό ἄνδρες ἰδίᾳ θεῶν μάλισα ἄγυσιν ἐν τιμῇ: cum seqq. Apulejus lib. II. de eadem ista: Cujus numen unicum multiformi specie, ritu vario, nomine multi- jugo totus veneratur orbis.

## 19:29
V. 29. And the whole city was filled with confusion) the same as τάραχος above. For just as מהומה is translated as τάραχος, so also is σύγχυσις. And shortly it will be said a confused assembly.

Ὡρμησάν τε ὁμοθυμαδὸν) εἰς τὸ θέατρον, to which the people were accustomed to run together. Diodorus Siculus, book XVI: ὁ δὲ δῆμος ἅπας ἅμ᾽ ἡμέρᾳ συνέδραμεν εἰς τὸ θέατρον. Plutarch, Aratus: Κατέβαινεν εἰς τὸ θέατρον ἀπὸ τῆς ἄκρας πλήθος ἀθρόον ἐπιρρέοντος ἐπιθυμίᾳ, τῆς ὄψεως αὐτῶν καὶ τῶν λόγων. Juvenal concerning Demosthenes: Et pleni moderantem subla theatri. The same Plutarch makes mention of this same custom in his Timoleon, as does he who wrote his life in Latin. See also other passages which the diligence of Heraldus has collected on this matter in his Adversaria.

Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians) This Gaius was indeed a Thessalonian, but by origin a Derbean, as we learn below in ch. XX. 4. There is mention of others of this name, very frequent among the Romans, in the writings of Paul and John. Mention of this Aristarchus is below in ch. XX. 4, XXVI. 2, Col. IV. 10, Philem. 24. The name is famous among the Greeks and common to many writers as well.

Latin:

V. 29. Καὶ ἐπλήσθη ἡ πόλις ὅλη συγχύσεως)idem quod su- pra τάραχος. Nam מהומה sicut τάραχος vertitur, ita & σύγχυσις. Et mox dicetur ἐκκλησία συγκεχυμένη.

Ὡρμησάν τε ὁμοθυμαδὸν) εἰς τὸ θέατρον, quo concurrere populus solebat. Diodorus Siculus lib. XVI. ὁ δὲ δῆμος ἅπας ἅμ᾽ ἡμέρᾳ συνέδραμεν εἰς τὸ θέατρον. Plutarch. Arato: Κατέβαινεν εἰς τὸ θέατρον ἀπὸ τῆς ἄκρας πλήθος ἀπότρο ἐπιρρέ- οντος ἐπιθυμίᾳ, τῆς ὄψεως αὐτῶν κό τῶν λόγων. Juvenalis de Demosthene: Et pleni moderantem bela theatri. Meminit ejusdem moris idem Plutarchus in Timoleonte, & is qui vi- tam scripsit Latine. Vide & alia loca quæ in hanc rem congessit Heraldidiligentia in Adversariis.

Γάϊον κό ᾿Αρίςαρχον Μακεδόνας) Cajus hic erat quidem Thessalonicensis, sed origine Derbæus, ut discimus infra c. XX. 4. Mentio & aliorum hujus nominis, inter Roma- nos per frequentis, in scriptis Pauli & Johannis. Aristarchi hujus mentio infra c. XX. 4. XXVI. 2. Col. IV. 10. Phi- lem. 24. Nomen est apud Græcos celebre ac commune multis etiam scriptoribus.

ver. 30. the disciples did not allow him) they were dissuading him with prayers.

vers. 30. ἐκ εἴων οἱ μαθηταὶ) precibus eum dimo- vebant.

## 19:31
v. 31. τῶν ᾿Ασιαρχῶν) Just as the Phoenician-archate and Syrian-archate were priesthoods: Code de Nat. lib. L. 1. so also the Asian-archate, which is called the priesthood of Asia L. in honoribus D. de vacatione & excusatione munerum: so that Ulpian in L. si duas §. Gentium D. de excus. calls this dignity the prefecture of Asia: and Strabo calls the Asiarchs πρατεύοντας κατὰ τὴν ἐπαρχίαν (those holding first place in the province): who also teaches us this, that they were chosen from the principal cities of Asia, among which Tralles was one, and so the Latin interpreter in this place calls the Asiarchs the princes of Asia. After the Emperors became Christians, that honor and the ancient insignia remained for those provincial priests, without the sacrifices: but the only function that remained for them was to provide games at their own expense, whence Ruffinus in the martyrdom of Polycarp in Eusebius interprets Asiarchs as providers of games (munerarios). Their expenses were great, nor were they restricted by the laws that reduced the costs of other games L. cunctos C. Theod. de expensis ludorum; and therefore they are reckoned among the burdens of patrimonies L. Nec protostasiæ C. de muneribus patrimoniorum & L. 1. Cod. de periculo successionum parentis, and an excuse was granted concerning them to professors of the arts L. si duas §. est autem D. de Excusat. Tutor. There is mention of the Asiarchs in the Arundelian marbles.

μὴ δῦναι ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸ θέατρον) lest the anger of the stirred-up people should harm him.

they administered the office, but because perhaps those who had already performed that office were also called by that name. Nor were they only princes of the priests, or of one city, but they were considered the primates of the entire assembly and council of the province, and they held a magistracy, not only a priesthood. Which magistracy, however, was usually created especially for the duties of providing games in honor of the gods, when they also took up the priesthood at the same time. Whence Ruffinus renders Ἀσιάρχην as a provider of games (munerarium).

Latin:

v. 31. τῶν ᾿Ασιαρχῶν) Sicut Phœnicarchia & Syriarchia sacerdotia fuere: Codice de Nat. lib. L. 1. sic & Asiarchia, quod sacerdotium Asiæ vocatur L. in honoribus D. de va- catione & excusatione munerum: ita ut Ulpianus in L.si duas §. Gentium D. de excus. dignitatem hanc præfidatum Asiæ vocet:&Asiarchas πρατεύοντας κατὰ τὴν ἐπαρχίαν dicat Strabo: qui & hoc nos docet, lectos ex præcipuis Asiæ civi- tatibus, inter quas fuisse & Tralles, sic & Latinus interpres hoc loco Asiarchas vocat Asiæ principes. Postquam Chri- stiani facti sunt Imperatores, mansit sacerdotibus illis pro- vincialibus, sine sacrificiis, honos & insignia vetera: functio autem unica eis mansit ludos edere suo sumptu, unde Asiar- chas, munerarios interpretatur Ruffinus in Policarpi mar- tyrio apud Eusebium. Horum impendia magna erant, nec adstricta legibus ludorum aliorum sumptus ad modum re- digentibus L. cunctos C. Theod. de expensis ludorum; & ideo patrimoniorum oneribus accensentur L. Nec proto- stasiæ C. de muneribus patrimoniorum & L. 1. Cod. de pe- riculo succeslionum parentis, debaturque de eis excusatio artium professoribus L. si duas §. est autem D. de Excusat. Tutor. Est Asiarcharum mentio in marmorib. Arundelianis.

μὴ δῦναι ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸ θέατρον) ne populi concitati ira ei noceret.

munus administrarint, sed quod illi fortasse etiam sic appellati, qui jam eo munere functi fuerant. Nec sacerdotum tantum illi erant principes, aut unius civitatis, sed Consessus & consilii totius pro- vinciae primates habebantur, & magistratum ge- rebant, non sacerdotium solum. Qui tamen ma- gistratus praecipue creari solebat ad munera ad lu- dos edendos in honorem deorum, quum & sacer- dotium simul capessebant. Unde Ruffinus Ἀσιάρ- χην reddit munerarium.

## 19:32
v. 32. ἦν γὰρ ἡ ἐκκλησία συγκεχυμένη) ἐκκλησία here signifies any gathering whatsoever, since in Latin a concio is nothing but a multitude called together by a magistrate according to the laws. Plutarch in Coriolanus said ἐκκλησίαν θορυβώδη (a tumultuous assembly), and in Phocion ἐκκλησίαν παμμιγῆ καὶ ἄτακτον (a confused and disorderly assembly).

Latin:

v. 32. ἦν γὰρ ἡ ἐκκλησία συγκεχυμένη) ἐκκλησία hic קהל cœtum quemvis significat, cum concio Latine non sit nisi à magistratu secundùm leges convocata multitudo. Plutar- chus in Coriolano dixit ἐκκλησίαν θορυβώδη, & in Phocio- ne ἐκκλησίαν παμμιγῆ καὶ ἄτακτον.

## 19:33
v. 33. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ὄχλου προεβίβασαν Ἀλέξανδρον) τινες (some) is understood, as in Matt. XXIII. 34, John XVI. 17, and elsewhere. προεβίβασαν, that is, they moved him forward out of the crowd to that place from which he could be heard by all.

προβαλόντων ἀυτὸν τῶν Ἰουδαίων) The Jews were putting him forward as a suitable accuser of Paul, as one who knew all his doctrines and had defected from them. For this seems to be Alexander the coppersmith, of whom Paul complains in 1 Tim. I. v. 20, 2 Tim. IV. 14. But in this way the Jews wanted to remove all this hatred from themselves, since they knew that they too were hated as enemies of the gods.

κατασείσας τὴν χεῖρα) See above ch. XII. 17, XIII. 16.

ἤθελεν ἀπολογεῖσθαι τῷ δήμῳ) To separate the cause of the Jews from the cause of Paul.

Although there are not wanting those who think that this Alexander stood on the side of Paul and the pious, I easily agree, however, that he was an enemy of the truth, of whom 2 Tim. IV. 14 speaks. And it is likely, with Beza as author, that he was produced by the Jews for this reason, because he was from the number of the craftsmen from whom this sedition had arisen, and that he would have excused the Jews (unless divine providence had stood in the way), if the power of speaking had been granted to him, in such a way that he would have turned the whole rage of the people onto the head of Paul and the pious.

Latin:

v. 33. ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ὄχλου προεβίβασαν Ἀλέξανδρον) subau- ditur τινες, ut Matth. XXIII. 34. Joh. XVI. 17. & alibi. προε- βίβασαν, id est, promoverunt eum extra turbam in eum lo- cum, unde ab omnibus exaudiri posset.

προβαλόντων ἀυτὸν τῶν Ἰουδαίων) Judæi eum propone- bant tanquam idoneum Pauli accusatorem, ut qui ipsius dogmata nosset omnia, & ab iis descivisset. Videtur enim hic esse Alexander faber ærarius, de quo queritur Paulus 1. Tim. I. v. 20. 2. Tim. IV. 14. Hoc autem modo Judæi volebant odium omne hoc à se amovere, cum scirent se quoque invisos esse tanquam inimicos deorum.

κατασείσας τὴν χεῖρα) Vide supra c. XII. 17. XIII. 16.

ἤθελεν ἀπολογεῖσθαι τῷ δήμῳ) Judæorum causam è Pauli causa segregare.

Etsi non desint, qui Alexandrum hunc à Pauli & piorum partibus stetisse censeant, facile tamen annuo, fuisse illum hostem veritatis, de quo 2. Tim. IV. 14. Et verisimile est, autore Beza, propterea illum à Judæis productum, quod esset ex fabro- rum numero, à quibus orta hæc seditio fuerat, Judæos (nisi divina providentia obstitisset) sic ex- cusaturum, si facta nisi fuisset dicendi potestas, ut totam populi rabiem fuerit in Pauli, & piorum caput conversurus.

## 19:35
Vers. 35.

καταστείλας δὲ ὁ γραμματεὺς τὸν ὄχλον) γραμματεὺς here is the scribe of the city, ὁ εἰωθὼς ἐν τῷ δήμῳ τὰ τοῦ δήμου γράμματα ἀναγινώσκειν (he who is accustomed to read the writings of the people in the assembly), says the Scholiast of Thucydides. Among the Romans, as he who wrote the lives of the Emperors in Latin says, scribes were considered mercenaries: But among the Greeks, no one was admitted to that office unless he was known for an honorable position, and for fidelity and industry.

The Vulgate, as here Ludov. de Dieu, the Ethiopic and Beza translate γραμματεὺς word for word as Scribe. The Syriac and Arabic, the chief of the city: which I do not reject. The Glossary, γραμματεὺς Scribe Tesserarius: now a Tesserarius is one who distributes tallies, and gives symbols to soldiers, which among us in garrisoned cities belongs to the Governor, in others to the chief Consul. Papias: Tesserarius is the one in charge of chariots, who announces war. Plutarch, Τεσσεράριοι καλοῦνται; οἱ δὲ ἀγγέλων ἢ διοπτήρων ὑπηρεσίας τελοῦντες, Tesserarii are called those who perform services through messengers and scouts. Since therefore here in the city of Ephesus someone is designated, who is absolutely called ὁ γραμματεὺς, he is deservedly understood as the prefect, who prescribes symbols and duties to the soldiers. This is Dievius. Camerarius did not depart from the opinion of Grotius, why γραμματεὺς is the Master of public letters. Baronius thinks he was Alexander the Jew: but others more correctly call him a Gentile, and he is distinguished here from Alexander.

the city of the Ephesians being the temple-warden of the great Artemis) concerning Enna Cicero: So that to me not the citizens of that city, but all the priests, all the neighbors and overseers seemed to be the others: The word νεωκόρος is in this sense also in the Arundel marbles: and often on coins, as in that one of the Magnesians temple-wardens of Artemis, in another: Of the Ephesians twice temple-wardens and of Artemis, where the Ephesians are called twice temple-wardens on account of the games twice held in honor of Caesar, but perpetual ones for Diana.

Concerning the title of the temple-wardens Sam. Petitus [wrote] many things, which Walaeus presented in his annotations. But Camerarius succinctly conveyed the meaning of the word: he calls the city of the Ephesians a temple-warden

to Diana, as if serving in a special ministry to her worship, and caring for the temple. For there are neokoroi and zakoroi, temple-wardens, because they care for sacred things and sacred buildings. For korein is to adorn, and to beautify, that is, to decorate and equip and add an appearance of beauty. And of the heaven-fallen) namely, the statue. It was made of vine-wood, as Pliny handed down on the authority of Mucianus: but because its manufacture exceeded all memory, therefore the priests easily persuaded the common people that it had fallen from heaven, as Suidas notes under the word diopetes. Thus Euripides concerning the Tauric statue of Diana: To take the statue of the goddess which they say fell here from heaven into this temple. He later calls it the heaven-fallen statue. Thus also Plutarch concerning the ancile, a heaven-fallen shield. There is also in Herodian a heaven-fallen statue. That Jupiter is said for heaven is frequent among the Greeks: thus also Horace under the cold Jupiter. That it is of vine-wood, says Salmasius, although others reported it was of ebony, Mucianus had written. Vine-wood, which is made from a vine, just as oleagineum from an olive tree. But Vitruvius mentions cedar, as also for coffered ceilings, book II, chapter 9. Xenophon, which you may rightly wonder at, reports that it was not of ebony, not of cedar, nor of vine-wood, but of gold: book V, Anabasis of Cyrus. It is credible that Xenophon knew what the appearance of the statue of the Ephesian Diana was, and from what material it was made, and had even seen it. However, in the Vulgate, the name diopetes is wrongly rendered as the offspring of Jupiter.

Latin:

Vers. 35.

καταστείλας δὲ ὁ γραμματεὺς τὸν ὄχλον) γραμματεὺς est hic scriba civitatis, ὁ εἰωθὼς ἐν τῷ δήμῳ τὰ τοῦ δήμου γράμμα- τα ἀναγινώσκειν, ait Scholiastes Thucydidis. Apud Roma- nos, ut ait is, qui vitas Imperatorum Latine scripsit, scribæ mercenarii existimabantur: At apud Grajos nemo ad id officium admittebatur, nisi honesto loco & fide & in- dustria cognitus.

Vulgatus, ut hic Ludov. de Dieu, Æthiopicus & Beza vertunt γραμματεὺς ad verbum Scriba. Sy- rus & Arabs, primarius civitatis: quod non reji- cio. Glossarium, γραμματεὺς Scriba Tesserarius: est autem Tesserarius, qui tesseras tribuit, & mi- litibus symbola dat, quod apud nos in urbibus præsidiariis Gubernatoris est, in cæteris primarii Consulis. Papias: Tesserarius præpositus curruum, qui bellum nunciat. Plutarchus, Τεσσεράριοι κα- λοῦνται; οἱ δὲ ἀγγέλων ἢ διοπτήρων ὑπηρεσίας τε- λοῦντες, Tesserarii vocantur, qui per nuncios & specu- latores ministeria peragunt. Quum ergo hic in urbe Epheso designatur aliquis, qui absolute vocatur ὁ γραμματεὺς, merito intelligitur præfectus, qui militibus symbola & munia præscribit. Hæc Die- vius. Camerarius à Grotii haud abiit sententia, cur γραμματεὺς Magister est publicarum literarum. Baronius putat eum fuisse Alexandrum Judæum: sed rectius alii eum gentilem dicunt, & distingui- tur hic ab Alexandro.

τὴν Ἐφεσίων πόλιν νεωκόρον οὖσαν τῆς μεγάλης Ἀρτέ- μιδος) de Enna Cicero: Vt mihi non cives illius civitatis, sed omnes sacerdotes, omnes accola atque antistites Ceteris vi- derentur: Est νεωκόρος vox hoc sensu etiam in marmoribus Arundelianis: & in nummis sæpe, ut in illo Μαγνήτων νεω- κόρων Ἀρτέμιδος, in alio: Ἐφεσίων δὶς νεωκόρων καὶ τῆς Ἀρτέ- μιδος, ubi bis νεωκόροι vocantur Ephesii ob bis editos lu- dos in honorem Cæsaris, Dianæ autem perpetuos.

De τῶν νεωκόρων nuncupatione Sam. Petitus mul- ta, quæ in annotationibus suis exhibuit Walæus. Significationem autem vocis succincte Camerar. tradidit: νεωκόρον vocat civitatem Ephesiorum

Dianæ, quasi peculiari ministerio servientem cul- tui illius, & templum curantem. Sunt enim νεωκόροι & ζακόροι æditimi, quod sacra & ædes sacras cu- rent. κορεῖν γὰρ τὸ κοσμεῖν, καὶ καλλύνειν, id est, or- nare instruereque & addere speciem pulcritudinis. καὶ τοῦ διοπετοῦς) nempe ἀγάλματος. Erat id ex vite fa- ctum, ut Muciano auctore tradidit Plinius: sed quia fabrica- tio ejus omnem memoriam excedebat, ideo facile sacerdo- tes plebi persuadere esse de cœlo delapsum, ut Suidas notat in voce διοπετής. Sic de Taurica Dianæ simulacro Euripides: Λαβεῖν τ' ἄγαλμα θεᾶς ὃ φάσιν ἐνθάδε Εἰς τᾶς δε ναὸς ὐρανᾶ πεσεῖν ἄπο. idem postea vocat διοπετὲς ἄγαλμα. Sic & de ancili Plutar- chus διοπετὲς πόλτης. Est & apud Herodianum διοπετὲς ἄγαλμα. Jovem pro cœlo dici frequens Græcis: sic & Horatius sub Jove frigido. Vitigineum esse, ait Salmasius, cum cæteri ex he- beno traderent, Mucianus scripserat. Vitigineum quod ex vite est factum, ut oleagineum ex olea. At Vitruvius cedrinum ut & lacunaria, lib. II. cap. 9. Xenophon, quod jure mireris, non habeninum, non cedrinum, nec vitigineum fuisse prodit, sed aureum: lib. V. Κύρα 'Αναϐ. credibile est, Xenophontem scisse quali facie esset simulacrum Dianæ Ephesiæ, & ex qua materia factum, illud etiam vidisse. Perperam autem in Vulgata nomen διοπετὲς per Jovis pro- lem redditur.

## 19:36
V. 36. these things being undeniable) He means this: those who speak concerning things made by hands, they do not harm this statue which is acknowledged to be not made by hands, but heaven-fallen. to exist in a settled manner) the Latin translator well renders it as 'sedated'. The Glossary defines katastello as 'I sedate', as above 35. Thus Virgil: Latinus answers him, with sedated heart.

and to do nothing rashly) The Latin translator, 'to do nothing rashly'. Well: thus 'do not swear rashly', in the Law 'if he says' in the Digest on oaths: in the Glossary propetes is 'rash'. Plutarch, Camillus: 'having used battle rashly', when they had fought rashly.

Latin:

V. 36. ἀναντιῤῥήτων ὧν ὄντων τότων) Hoc vult: qui περὶ τῶν χειροποιήτων loquuntur, ii nihil lædunt hoc simulacrum quod constat esse non χειροποίητον, sed διοπετές. κατεσταλμένως ὑπάρχειν) bene Latinus sedatos vertit. Glossarium κατασέλκω sedo, ut supra 35. sic Virgilius: Olli respondet, sedato corde Latinus.

καὶ μηδὲν προπετὲς πράττειν) Latinus, nihil temere agere. Bene: sic προπετῶς μὴ ὄμνυε temere ne jura. L. si dicit D. de jur. jurando: in Glossario προπετὴς temerarius. Plutarch. Camill.: προπετῶς μάχῃ χρησαμένων. cum temere pugnassent.

## 19:37
v. 37. not temple-robbers) because they had not even entered the temple. not blaspheming your goddess) because they had not specifically named the Ephesian Diana. Josephus in the second book against Apion: 'For it is our ancestral custom to guard our own things, and to accuse others, and as for not mocking or blaspheming the gods considered as such by others, the lawgiver has expressly forbidden us.' Namely, the Jews did not by name curse this or that god of the nations, because they did not pronounce the very names of those gods; yet the law means one thing, and Josephus tries to persuade the Romans of another. As we said in III, On the Law of War and Peace, V. 2.

Whether it was forbidden to name the gods of the nations specifically? The Rabbis inquire. Selden reports various opinions about it: some that the simple naming of them is illicit, even if no mention is made of their divinity: others, that their proper names are not forbidden, provided that divinity is not attributed to them: others, he observes, establish that only vows and oaths in their name are forbidden. But those who do not admit simple mention understand it to mean that they are not to be named except with contumely and detestation. Therefore, what Grotius adds next from Josephus, Against Apion, book II: 'Namely, the Jews did not by name curse this or that god of the nations, because they did not pronounce the very names of those gods,' is mere superstition. He rightly acknowledges that the law means one thing, and Josephus in book II, Against Apion, tries to persuade the Romans of another. For thus Exodus XXII, v. 28. You shall not revile the gods; the discourse is about magistrates, not about the gods of the nations.

Latin:

v. 37. ὄτε ἱεροσύλες) quia ne intraverant quidem templum. ὄτε βλασφημοῦντας τὴν Θεὰν ὑμῶν) quia Dianam Ephe- siam speciatim non nominaverant.
