Josephus secundo con- tra Appionem: Τὰ γὰρ αὐτῶν ἡμῖν φυλάττειν πάτριόν ἐστι, κ᾿ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων κατηγορεῖν, κ᾿ περὶ γε τῷ μήτε χλευάζειν, μήτε βλασφημεῖν τὲς νομιζομένες Θεὺς παρ' ἑτέροις, ἄντικρυς ἡμῖν ὁ νομοθέτης ἀπείρηκεν. Nempe Judæi nominatim non male- dicebant huic vel illi gentium Deo, quia nomina ipsa eorum Deorum non pronunciabant, aliud tamen vult lex, aliud Josephus Romanis persuadere conatur. Ut diximus III. de Jure Belli & Pacis V. 2.

An nominare speciatim gentium Deos prohi- bitum fuerit? Rabbini disquirunt. Seldenus refert diversas de eo sententias: alios simplicem eorum nominationem illicitam esse, etiamsi ne divinitatis quidem eorum mentio fiat: alios, non vetari pro- pria eorum nomina, dum modo non tribuatur iis divinitas: alios, vota solum ac juramenta in eo- rum nomine fieri prohibita esse, statuere observat. Sed qui simplicem memoriam non admittunt, id intelligunt, non esse nominandos, nisi cum con- tumelia & detestatione. Quod ergo addit dein- ceps Grotius è Josephi II. contt. Appion. Nempe, Judæi nominatim non maledicebant huic vel illi gen- tium Deo, quia nomina ipsa eorum Deorum non pro- nunciabant, è mera est superstitione. Aliud etiam velle legem, aliud Josephum lib. II. contr. Appion. Romanis persuadere merito agnoscit. Ita enim Exod. XXII. v. 28. Diis non detrahes; de Magistra- tibus sermo est, non de Diis gentilium.

## 19:38
V. 38. have a matter against anyone) namely, of complaint. Thus 'if anyone has a complaint against anyone', 2 Cor. VII. 1. Thus dabar, which properly sounds 'a word', is translated as 'contradiction' in Exodus XVIII, v. 16, and 'judgment' in Exodus XVIII, 22. 'Court days are held' should be written 'agoraioi' if we follow Suidas and the Glossary: where we read: 'When the law is agitated: when the court day is,' where Casaubon noted that 'day' is to be understood. There are, he says, days on which legal business is conducted, which the Romans call fasti.

There is no need for an emendation of the text. Camerarius explains 'agoraioi syllogoi', or 'synodoi', that court assemblies or congresses are held. And the Vulgate also translates it thus, 'they hold court assemblies, there are proconsuls, let them accuse one another.' Which explanation is more consistent than if you take the word with Pricaeus as referring to the time and place of the assembly, or with others judge that it means lawyers, or with the Syrian and Arabic interpreter translate it as 'only those workmen', namely Demetrius and his companions. Which agrees sufficiently with neither the words nor the purpose.

and there are proconsuls) is a catachresis. For when he said proconsuls, he understands both him who is truly proconsul, and his legate. Thus we showed above in XIII. 7 and XVI. 20 that names of greater offices were given. Concerning the legate of the proconsul, see Law 'all' § 'at the legate', Law 'they are accustomed' § 'legates', Law 'of the legates' in the Digest on the office of the proconsul.

let them accuse one another) Let them plead among themselves. Enkalein is properly said of an accuser: but here it signifies to dispute: in which way it is also taken in Plutarch's Alcibiades.

Latin:

V. 38. πρός τινα λόγον ἔχουσιν) nempe μομφῆς. Sic ἐάν τις πρός τινα ἔχῃ μομφὴν, 2. Cor. VII. 1. Sic דּבר, quod pro- prie λόγον sonat, vertitur ἀντιλογία Exod. XVIII. v. 16. & κρίμα Exod. XVIII. 22. ἀγοραῖοι ἄγονται Ἀγόραιοι scribendum, si Suidam sequi- mur & Glossarium: ubi legimus: Cum lex agitatur: ὅτε ἡ ἀγόραιός ἐστιν, ubi subaudiri ἡμέρα notavit Casaubonus. Sunt, inquit, dies, quibus lege agitur, quos fastos Romani vocant.

Non opus est emendatione textus. Camerarius explicat ἀγοραῖοι σύλλογοι, seu σύνοδοι aguntur conventus, seu congressus forenses. Atque ita vertit etiam Vulgatus, conventus forenses agunt, proconsules sunt, accusent invicem. Quæ explicatio concin- nio:, quam si cum Pricæo de tempore & loco conven- tus vocem accipias, vel cum aliis judices aut causi- dicos intelligas, vel cum Syro & Arabe interprete- ris, tantummodo illi operarii sunt, Demetrius nem- pe, ejusque sodales. Quæ nec verbis, nec institu- to satis conveniunt.

κὴ ἀνθύπατοί εἰσιν) est κατάχρησις. Nam proconsules cum dixit, intelligit & eum, qui vere proconsul, & legatum ejus. Sic magistratib. nomina data majora ostendimus supra XIII. 7. & XVI. 20. De Legato proconsulis vide L. omnes §.apud legatum L. solent §. legatos, L. legati D. de offic. procon- sulis.

ἐγκαλείτωσαν ἀλλήλοις) Lege inter se agant. Ἐγκαλεῖν proprie de accusatore dicitur: sed hic valet disceptare: quo- modo & apud Plutarchum sumitur Alcibiade.

## 19:39
v. 39. but if you seek anything concerning other matters) If you desire anything of those things which pertain to the government of the city, under which the care of the temple was also included. Many cities under the Romans had a certain restricted autonomy, as can be seen from the letters of Pliny.

Baronius understands the synagogue of the Jews. But Cornelius refutes this: because in that way that scribe would have more irritated the raging people, who hated the Jews greatly as enemies of their Diana. The same Cornelius notes at v. 40 of this place that there is deep silence here in Luke concerning the Antiochene and Roman Chair of Peter. Which who would wonder at: since it was the purpose of St. Luke to write not fables but histories?

in the lawful assembly) ἔννομος ἐκκλησία is a legitimate gathering, which is called together and governed by the magistrate of the city: A meeting, as we just said.

Latin:

v. 39. εἰ δέ τι περὶ ἑτέρων ἐπιζητεῖτε) Si quicquam desi- deratis eorum, quæ ad civitatis regimen pertinent, sub quo & templi cura comprehendebatur. Civitates multæ sub Ro- manis habebant quandam restrictam ἀυτονομίαν, ut ex Pli- nii epistolis videre est.

Baronius Synagogam Judæorum intelligit. Sed refellit hoc Cornelius: quia sic scriba ille magis ir- ritasset furentem populum, qui Judæos ceu Dianæ suæ hostes maximopere oderat. Notat idem Cor- nelius ad v. 40. h. l. altum hic esse apud Lucam de Cathedra Petri Antiochena & Romana silentium. Quod quis miretur: quum non fabulas sed histo- rias scribere S. Lucæ propositum fuerit?

ἐν τῇ ἐννόμῳ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἐπιλυθήσεται) ἔννομος ἐκκλησία le- gitimus cœtus est, qui à magistratu civitatis convocatur & regitur: Concio, ut modo diximus.

## 19:40
V. 40. We are in danger of being accused of sedition) We are all in danger, who are here, of being made guilty of sedition before the proconsul P. Suilius.

of this gathering) Of that concourse. Seneca also uses this word in this sense. Sulpitius Victor: According to that law, let him who has made a gathering and a concourse be punished with death. There were certain exceptions, such as in the arrival of enemies, fire, and similar matters. Therefore he says that no cause can be given for this concourse.

Latin:

V. 40. Κινδυνέυομεν ἐγκαλεῖσθαι στάσεως) Periclitamur o- mnes, qui hic sumus, rei fieri seditionis apud proconsulem P. Suilium.

τῆς συστροφῆς ταύτης) Concursus istius. Utitur & Seneca hac voce hoc sensu. Sulpitius Victor: Secundum legem illam qui cœtum & concursum fecerit, capite puniatur. Erant exceptio- nes quædam, ut in adventu hostium, incendio, & rebus si- milibus. Ideo dicit nullā concursus hujus causā posse reddi.

## 19:41
He dismissed the assembly) He ordered everyone to go home.

Latin:

Ἀπέλυσε τὴν ἐκκλησίαν) Jussit quemque domum ire.

## 20:1 Argument
CHAPTER XX. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION,

Paul sets out into Macedonia and Greece, staying for three months on account of the plots of the Jews, heading into Asia with Sopater, Aristarchus, and others, in Troas raising Eutychus from the dead, summoning the Ephesian Elders to Miletus, he held a valedictory address to them, repeating in it how he had served the Lord there amidst various persecutions, and had withheld nothing useful, but publicly announced to all Jews and Greeks, preaching repentance and faith in the Lord Jesus. And concerning his departure towards Jerusalem, where chains and tribulations await him to finish his course and ministry with joy, testifying, he gravely warns them to pay attention to themselves and to the flock redeemed by the blood of God, and because of encroaching wolves, and because of men speaking perverse things, who would arise from among themselves, to be vigilant by his three-year example, commending them to God, and to the word of grace, and he exhorts them to support the weak and the needy, mindful of the word of the Lord: It is more blessed to give than to receive: And so with tears he was dismissed.

There are two parts: I. The miracle of Eutychus raised from the dead in Troas, after Paul had stayed for three months in Greece and was setting out into Asia, to v. 12. II. His valedictory sermon held to the Ephesian Elders at Miletus, to v. 38 inclusive.

PART I.

The raising of Eutychus from the dead in Troas.

V. 1. and having embraced) The Syrian translated, and kissed, in the manner of those nations, Luke VII. 45. Rom. XVI. 10. 1 Cor. XVI. 20. 2 Cor. XIII. 12. 1 Thess. V. 26. v. 2. εἰς [τὴν Ἑλλάδα) into that part where Athens is. See Ptolemy on Achaia. v. 3. ποιήσας τε μῆνας τρεῖς) A locution like that above XV. 33. XVIII. 21. 23. γενομένης αὐτῷ ἐπιβουλῆς ὑπὸ τῶν Ἰουδαίων) As often happens: above IX. 23. XIII. 10. XIV. 2, 5. XVII. 5. 2 Cor. XI. 26. that which is said in Ps. XXVII. 12, 13 is often fulfilled around Paul. v. 4. ἄχρι τῆς Ἀσίας) some say even beyond: for ἄχρι does not exclude further points. See similar things in Matt. I. 25. Σώπατρος Βεροιαῖος) Σώπατρος and Σωσίπατρος are the same name: and there were also historians, rhetoricians, and grammarians by this name. In that old manuscript, as in many others, it is here Σώπατρος Πύρῥου βεροιαῖος. Pyrrhus is a frequent name in Thessaly and neighboring regions. Σώπατρος is אבישוע as we shall say at Rom. XVI. 21. Beroea is a city of Macedonia, about which see above XVII. 10. 13. And of the Thessalonians Aristarchus) about whom see above XIX. 19. The Syriac thinks these were the only two Thessalonians. To me, this seems to pertain to the four names that follow. See what is above XIX. 27. καὶ Γάϊος Δερβαῖος) who is a Derbaean by origin, born in Macedonia. καὶ Τιμόθεος) he is reckoned among the Thessalonians because his ancestors were from the Jews who had once lived in Thessalonica. See what we said in the Appendix concerning the Antichrist. Ἀσιανοὶ δὲ) that is, from Ephesus, as is said below concerning Trophimus, and is gathered concerning Tychicus, 2 Tim. II. 12. Τυχικὸς) who is named not only in the aforementioned place to Timothy, but also Eph. VI. 21. Tit. III. 12. Col. IV. 7. καὶ Τρόφιμος) whose mention is below XXI. 28. 2 Tim. IV. 20.

The Vulgate wrongly omits the words ἄχρι τ' Ἀσίας, v. 4. For Luke signifies that these men had then decided to accompany Paul, not as far as Syria, but only as far as Asia, Paul, whose followers they were, undoubtedly decreeing this, so that as the custom of the churches required, they might stop here or there, and be sent here or there. But to the word Σώπατρος the Vulgate rashly adds the name of Pyrrhus, as if Sopater were the son of that Pyrrhus; which is read neither in the Greek, nor in the Syriac, Arabic, or Ethiopic: for one swallow does not make a spring; so neither does one MS of Grotius, with the others resisting, establish authority. At the end of the verse after καὶ Τιμόθεος the Syriac and Arabic add, who was from Lystra, but without the authority of the Greek codices. Furthermore, Beza notes that that ἄχρι τ' Ἀσίας does not pertain to the last two, from what is said about Trophimus in ch. XXI. 29. and therefore he thought this particle should be connected with προελθόντες, as if the pronoun ὗτοι were redundant: but the Asians Tychicus and Trophimus, when they had known beforehand, waited for us at Troas. That city was called both Antigonia and Alexandria. It was a Roman colony.

Latin:

CAPUT XX. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO,

Paulus proficiscitur in Macedoniā & Græciā, per tres menses subsistens ob insidias Judæo- rum, in Asiam cum Sopatro, Aristarcho, & aliis tendens, in Troade Eutychum à mortuis resuscitas, Miletum Ephesinos Seniores ac- cersens, concionem ad ipsos habuit valedi- ctoriam, repetens in ea, quomodo Domino ibi inter varias persecutiones serviverit, nihilque utilium subtraxerit, quin publice annunciaret omnibus Judæis & Græcis, pre- dicans pœnitentiam & fidem in Dominum Jesum. Et de profectione sua versus Jerosoly- mam, ubi expectent sese vincula & tribula- tiones ad consummandum cum gaudio cur- sum & ministerium, testificans, graviter monet, ut sibi & gregi sanguine Dei redem- pto attendant, & ob lupos ingruentes, & ob viros perversa loquentes, ex ipsis orituros, exemplo suo triennali vigilent, commen- dans eos Deo, & verbo gratiæ, hortaturque, ut infirmos & egenos suscipiant memores verbi Domini: Beatius est dare, quam acci- pere: Atque ita cum lacrymis dimissus est.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Pauli postquam tribus men- sibus in Græcia hæsisset, in Asiam proficiscentis miraculum in Troade resuscitati Eutychi, ad v. 12. II. Sermo ejus valedictorius ad Ephesinos Seniores Mileti habitus, ad v. 38. final.

PARS I.

Eutychi in Troade ex mortuis resuscitatio.

V. 1. κὴ ἀσπασάμενος) Syrus transtulit, & osculatus, ex more illarum gentium, Luc. VII. 45. Rom. XVI. 10. 1. Cor. XVI. 20. 2. Cor. XIII. 12. 1. Thess. V. 26. v. 2. εἰς [τὴν Ἑλλάδα) in illam partem, ubi Athenæ. Vi- de Ptolemæum in Achaia. v. 3. ποιήσας τε μῆνας τρεῖς) Locutio quæ supra XV. 33. XVIII. 21. 23. γενομένης αὐτῷ ἐπιβουλῆς ὑπὸ τῶν Ἰουδαίων) Ut sæpe evenit: supra IX. 23. XIII. 10. XIV. 2, 5. XVII. 5. 2. Cor. XI. 26. im- pletum sæpe circa Paulum id quod dicitur Ps. XXVII. 12, 13. v. 4. ἄχρι τῆς Ἀσίας) quidam & ultra: neque enim ἄχρι excludit ulteriora. Similia vide Matth. I. 25. Σώπατρος Βεροιαῖος) idem nomen est Σώπατρος & Σωσίπατρος: ac fuere hoc nomine etiam Historici, Rheto- res, Grammatici. In Manuscripto illo vetere, ut in multis aliis, est hic Σώπατρος Πύρῥου βεροιαῖος. Pyrrhus nomen est frequens in Thessalia & vicinis regionibus. Σώπατρος est אבישוע ut dicemus ad Rom. XVI. 21. Berœa urbs Mace- doniz est, de qua supra XVII. 10. 13. Θεσσαλονικέων δὲ Ἀρίσταρχος) de quo supra XIX. 19. Hos duos tantum Thessalonicenses fuisse putat Syrus. Mihi videtur hoc ad quatuor quæ sequuntur nomina pertinere. Vide quæ supra XIX. 27. καὶ Γάϊος Δερβαῖος) qui origine Derbæus, natus in Ma- cedonia. καὶ Τιμόθεος) hic Thessalonicensibus accensetur, quia majores ejus ex Judæis erant, qui Thessalonicæ quondam vixerant. Vide quæ diximus in Appendice de Antichristo. Ἀσιανοὶ δὲ) id est, ex Epheso ut infra de Trophimo dici- tur, & de Tychico colligitur, 2. Tim. II. 12. Τυχικὸς) qui nominatur non tantum dicto ad Timo- theum loco, sed & Eph. VI. 21. Tit. III. 12. Col. IV. 7. καὶ Τρόφιμος) cujus mentio infra XXI. 28. 2. Tim. IV. 20.

Vulgata perperam omittit verba ἄχρι τ' Ἀσίας, v. 4. Significat enim Lucas istos tunc constituisse Paulum comitari, non in Syriam usque, sed tantum in Asiam, sic procul dubio decernente Paulo, cujus erant asseclæ, ut prout usus Ecclesiarum ferebat, hic vel illic subsisterent, & huc vel illuc mitteren- tur. Ad voce autem Σώπατρος temere addit Vulga- tus nomen Pyrrhi, quasi Sopater illius Pyrrhi filius fuerit; quod neque in Græco, neque apud Syrum, Arabem aut Æthiopem legitur: una enim hirundo non facit ver; ita nec unus MS. Grotii, cæteribus re- pugnantibus αὐθεντίαν conciliat. In fine vero ver- sus post κὶ Τιμόθεος Syrus & Arabs addunt, qui erat ex Lystra, sed citra codicum Græcorum autorita- tem. Cæterum illud ἄχρι τ' Ἀσίας ad duos postre- mos non pertinere notat Beza ex eo, quod de Tro- phimo dicitur c. XXI. 29. ideoque hanc particulam censuit connectendam cum προελθόντες, quasi re- dundante pronomine ὗτοι: Asiani vero Tychicus, & Trophimus, quum prænossent, expectarunt nos Troa- de. Dicta est civitas illa & Antigonia & Alexan- dria. Fuit Colonia Romana.

## 20:5
v. 5. ἔμενον ἡμᾶς) Here Luke signifies in passing, which he does not express, that he was a companion of Paul on this journey and the following ones as far as Rome. ἐν Τρωάδι) it can sometimes be doubted whether it is the name of a region or a city: for Τρωὰς is also a city, according to Pliny: ἐν Τρωάδι as ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, Eph. I. 1. 1 Tim. I. 3. 2 Tim. I. 18. ἐν Κορινθῳ above XIX. 1. 1 Cor. I. 1. 2 Cor. II. 11. 2 Tim. IV. 20.

Here without doubt the city is noted. For in it they roused Paul with other companions, as Grotius admits at v. 7.

Latin:

v. 5. ἔμενον ἡμᾶς) Hic obiter Lucas significat, quod non exprimit, se Paulo comitem fuisse hujus itineris & sequen- tium Romam usque. ἐν Τρωάδι) dubitari interdum potest, sitne nomen re- gionis an urbis: nam Τρωὰς etiam urbs, Plinio teste: ἐν Τρωάδι ut ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, Eph. I. 1. 1. Tim. I. 3. 2. Tim. I. 18. ἐν Κο- ρίνθῳ supra XIX. 1. 1. Cor. I. 1. 2. Cor. II. 11. 2. Tim. IV. 20.

Hic sine dubio urbs notatur. In ea enim excita- runt Paulu cū aliis sociis, ut ad v. 7. fatetur Grotius.

## 20:6
v. 6. ἐξεπλεύσαμεν) by river first, then by sea. μετὰ τὰς ἡμέρας τῶν Ἀζύμων) Paul defended the freedom of those called from the Gentiles: yet he himself observed the feast days of the Jews. See above XVIII. 21. below XX. 16. 1 Cor. XVI. 8. ἀπὸ Φιλίππων) about which city see above XVI. 12. ἄχρις ἡμερῶν πέντε) πλεύσαντες is understood, from that which preceded ἐξεπλεύσαμεν: thus often the construction is more according to sense than to words. Ὧ) in which city, namely Troas. v. 7. ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων) See Matt. XXVIII. v. 1. that day is proper for the assembly of Christians, 1 Cor. XVI. 2. the Lord's day, Apoc. I. 10. Justin concerning the same day in Apology II. τῇ τοῦ Ἡλίου λεγομένη ἡμέρᾳ πάντων κατὰ πόλεις ἢ ἀγροὺς μενόντων ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ συνέλευσις γίνεται. συνηγμένων τῶν μαθητῶν τοῦ κλᾶσαι ἄρτον) The Eucharist, says the Syriac. Understand the agapes which were concluded by the Eucharist. In the MS. συνηγμένων ἡμῶν, and soon: ἦμεν συνηγμένοι, not badly. Not all other codices are to be recalled to the norm of one MS. By ἀρτοκλασίαν the Arab also understands the Eucharist, rendering it, so that we might distribute the body of Christ. But Grotius, while he prefers to understand the agapes by the argument of the Papists, which they seek from here for communion under one kind, cuts the nerve. Nor did Bellarmine dare to seek proof from this place. Cajetan, however, doubts whether it should be understood of spiritual or bodily food. Lorinus says this weapon is doubtful; Lyranus explains it expressly as a bodily refreshment, as does the Historia Scholastica. The sacramental Eucharist did not conclude the agapes, but the Eucharistic hymn. If you understand it most of all with Chrysostom, Bede, and Augustine in Epistle LXXXVI as the Sacrament, it will be a synecdochical description, but not an exclusion of the use of the cup. But it is better to take it as a common supper. Sermons were not instituted after the Eucharist originally, but before it, as Cornelius a Lapide admits.

Latin:

v. 6. ἐξεπλεύσαμεν) amne primum, deinde mari. μετὰ τὰς ἡμέρας τῶν Ἀζύμων) Paulus vocatorum ex gen- tibus libertatem tuebatur: ipse tamen dies Judæorum festos observabat. Vid. supra XVIII. 21. infra XX. 16. 1. Cor. XVI. 8. ἀπὸ Φιλίππων) de qua urbe supra XVI. 12. ἄχρις ἡμερῶν πέντε) Subauditur πλεύσαντες, ex eo quod præcessit ἐξεπλεύσαμεν : ita sæpe constructio magis sit ad sensum, quam ad verba. Ὧ) in qua urbe, nempe Troade. v. 7. ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων) Vide Matth. XXVIII. v. 1. is dies conventus Christianis proprius, 1. Cor. XVI. 2. dies κυριακὴ, Apoc. I. 10. Iustinus de eadem die Apologeti- co II. τῇ τοῦ Ἡλίου λεγομένη ἡμέρᾳ πάντων κατὰ πόλεις ἢ ἀγροὺς μενόντων ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ συνέλευσις γίνεται. συνηγμένων τῶν μαθητῶν τοῦ κλᾶσαι ἄρτον) Eucharistiam, Syrus. Intellige agapas quæ Eucharistiā claudebantur. In MS. συνηγμένων ἡμῶν, & mox : ἦμεν συνηγμένοι, non male. Non revocandi alii codices omnes ad unius MS. normam. Per ἀρτοκλασίαν Arabs etiam intelligit Eucharistiam, reddens, ut distribueremus cor- pus Christi. Grotius vero dum Agapas intelligere mavult Papistarum argumento, quod pro commu- nione sub una hinc petunt, nervum incidit. Neque ausus est Bellarm. ex hoc loco probationem petere. Cajetanus vero dubitat, de spirituali, an corporali intelligendus sit cibo. Lorinus anceps dicit hoc te- lum; Lyranus expresse de refectione corporali ex- plicat, ut & Historia Scholastica. Non Eucharistia sacramentalis claudebat agapas, sed hymnus Ev- charisticus. Si maxime cum Chrysoft. Beda & Au- gustino Epist. LXXXVI. de Sacramento intelligas, synecdochica erit descriptio, non vero usus cali- cis exclusio. Sed præstat de vulgari cœna accipere. Non post Eucharistiam sermones instituebantur primitus, sed ante eandem fatente Cornel. a Lapide.

## 20:7
ὁ Παῦλος διελέγετο αὐτοῖς) After supper, as Christ in John XIII. 31. and following. Mark XVI. 14. Luke XXII. 13. μέλλων ἐξιέναι τῇ ἐπαύριον) about to leave the city of Troas the next day.

Latin:

ὁ Παῦλος διελέγετο αὐτοῖς) Post cœnam, ut Christus Joh. XIII. 31. & seqq. Marc. XVI. 14. Luc. XXII. 13. μέλλων ἐξιέναι τῇ ἐπαύριον) postridie exiturus ex urbe Troade.

## 20:8
v. 8. ἐν τῷ ὑπερῴῳ) in which was the assembly, as above I. 13. v. 9. ὀνόματι Εὔτυχος) It would be written more correctly and more analogically Εὐτυχὴς: for that name is not rare in Greece.

Grotius is very rash, while he dares to correct the letter of the text at his own discretion, instructed by the authority of no codex. But who does not know how much proper names vary? Luke said after τὸν παῖδα, so that this young man is to be understood as having been quite young, that is, still of boyish age.

ἀπὸ τῶ τριστέγω) He calls the third story τρίστεγον, beginning from the bottom. Conversely, in Genesis it is begun from the top and the bottom is called τρίστεγον, as we said in ch. VI. 16.

Latin:

v. 8. ἐν τῷ ὑπερῴῳ) in quo erat conventus, ut supra. I. 13. v. 9. ὀνόματι Εὔτυχος) Rectius & ἀναλογικώτερον scri- beretur Εὐτυχὴς: id enim nomen non rarum in Græcia.

Valde temerarius est Grotius, dum audet corri- gere literam textus pro arbitrio, nullius codicis in- structus autoritate. Ecquis vero nescit, quanto- pere varient nomina propria? Lucas post τὸν παῖ- δα dixit, ut admodum fuisse hunc adolescentem intelligendum sit, id est, adhuc ætate puerili.

ἀπὸ τῶ τριστέγω) τρίστεγον vocat tertiam contignationem incipiendo ab imo. Contra in Genesi a summo incipitur & imum vocatur τρίστεγον, ut diximus c. VI. 16.

## 20:10
v. 10. ἔπεσεν αὐτῷ) just as is said of Elisha, 2 Kings IV. verse 34. Συνέκαμψεν ἐπὶ τὸ παιδάριον: where other interpreters [say] ἐνεφύσησεν ἡ γὰρ ψυχὴ αὐτᾶ ἐν αὐτῷ ἐστι) that is, even now as I speak, life has returned to him.

Eutyches, overwhelmed by deep sleep, fell from the third story, from the ὑπερῴῳ, the upper room, which, as Heinsius notes, was assigned here and elsewhere to the Apostles as the cheapest part of the house, as they were strangers and of slender means. The Vulgate wrongly [translates it] as the third upper room: because the third story is indicated. In the word καταφερόμενος ὕπνῳ there is a signification of a vehement impulse: and physicians called a heavy καταφορὰν, not from a rotting brain, what they called by other names κατοχὴν, and καρὸν, and ἀποπληξίαν. Chrysostom makes the Devil the author of this fall, so that he might disturb this feast and joy of the Christians and the fruit of Paul's sermon, and make it mournful with such a sad event. Those words ἐπὶ πλεῖον pertain to διαλεγομένε, Paul delaying a little longer, that is, for a longer time, not as Erasmus [applies it] to the following words κατενεχθεὶς ἀπὸ τᾶ ὕπνε, which, as Budaeus says, is 'overcome by sleep': For the comma distinction does not allow that, and we have [evidence] of a longer sermon of the Apostle below in ch. XXVIII. 23.

Latin:

v. 10. ἔπεσεν αὐτῷ) sicut de Elisæo dicitur, 2. Reg. IV. vers. 34. Συνέκαμψεν ἐπὶ τὸ παιδάριον: ubi alii interpretes ἐνεφύσησεν ἡ γὰρ ψυχὴ αὐτᾶ ἐν αὐτῷ ἐστι) id est, jam nunc cum lo- quor vita ei rediit.

Eutyches obrutus somno profundo de tertia contignatione cecidit de ὑπερῴῳ cænaculo, quod notante Heinsio, tanquam vilissima ædium pars hic & alibi Apostolis, ut peregrinis, ac fortunæ tenuis, tributum. Vulgatus perperam de tertio cœ- naculo: quia tertia contignatio indicatur. In verbo καταφερόμενος ὕπνῳ est significatio vehementis impetus: & Medici καταφορὰν βαρεῖαν non pu- trescente cerebro eam vocarunt, quam aliis nomi- nibus κατοχὴν, & καρὸν, & ἀποπληξίαν. Chrysost. Diabolum hujus casus autorem facit, ut festum hoc, gaudiumque Christianorum, & fructum concio- nis Paulinæ interturbaret, & tam tristi eventu fu- nestraret. Illa ἐπὶ πλεῖον ad διαλεγομένε perti- nent differente paulo diutius, id est, longiori tem- pore Paulo, non ut Erasmus ad sequentia κατενε- χθεὶς ἀπὸ τᾶ ὕπνε, quod dicente Budæo est victus a somno: Non enim id distinctio commatica per- mittit, & de longiore concione Apostoli habemus infra c. XXVIII. 23.

## 20:11
v. 11. καὶ γευσάμενος) See above X. 10. This was a morning meal.

It is added ὕτως ἐξῆλθεν: where ὕτως is not a particle of similitude, but it subjoins the consequent to the antecedent, whence the Syriac and Arabic render it 'so'. See Job VI. 6, ch. VII. 8, Psalm LXI. 9. Paul is said to have departed, namely, by a journey on foot, while the others were to travel by ship, as appears from verse 13: therefore the Syriac and Arabic, for the sake of explanation, have 'that he might go by dry land', that is, by land. The word παρεκλήθησαν means 'they received comfort', which the Vulgate barbarously [translates as] 'they were comforted'.

PART II. The valedictory sermon held to the Ephesian elders at Miletus.

Latin:

v. 11. καὶ γευσάμενος) Vide supra X. 10. hic erat cibus matutinus.

Additur ὕτως ἐξῆλθεν: ubi ὕτως non similitudi- nis particula est, sed subjurgit antecedenti conse- quens, unde Syrus & Arabs reddunt tam. Vid. Job. VI. 6. c. VII. 8. Psal. LXI. 9. Exiisse autem dicitur Paulus itinere sc. pedestri, cæteris navituris ut è vers. 13. apparet: ideo Syrus & Arabs explicationis ergo habent, ut iret per aridam, id est, terram. Verbum παρεκλήθησαν est solamen acceperunt, quod Vulgatus barbare consolati sunt.

PARS II. Valedictoria ad Ephesios seniores Mileti habita concio.

## 20:13
v. 13. ἀνήχθημεν) See above XVIII. 21. πεζεύειν) to go on foot, as the ancient Latins used to speak: peditare, as the glossary [says].

Latin:

v. 13. ἀνήχθημεν) Vide supra XVIII. 21. πεζεύειν) pedare, ut loquebantur veteres Latini: pedi- tare, ut glossarium.

## 20:14
v. 14. εἰς τὴν Ἄσσον) a city of the Troad, Strabo XIII. From here to the city of Troas, the journey was short, both by land and by sea.

The Syriac, 'and we sailed to the port of Thesos', implying that the city of Assos, which is also called Apollonia, was a maritime one, and a suitable port for ships. However, ϑάσον is read incorrectly. Not only do the Greek codices commonly, but the Arab also, and the Ethiopian have Ἄσσον. Πεζεύειν ἀπὸ τῆς πέζης, by which the sole of the foot is signified, is to make a journey on foot, and πεζὸς is pedestrian: in the following verse ὡς δὲ συνέβαλεν ἡμῖν, the Vulgate rendered, 'and when he had met us at Assos.' Κατὰ πόδα is, 'and when he joined (himself) with us' or 'met us.'

εἰς Μιτυλήνην) The chief city of the island of Lesbos, whence came Pittacus, Alcaeus, Sappho.

Latin:

v. 14. εἰς τὴν Ἄσσον) urbem Troadis, Strabo XIII. Huc Troade urbe, tam terra, quam mari breve erat iter.

Syrus, & navigavimus ad portum Thesos innu- ens urbem Asson, quæ etiam Apollonia dicta, ma- ritimam fuisse, aptumque portum navibus. Male autem legitur ϑάσον. Non Græci tantum co- dices communiter, sed Arabs etiam, & Æthiops habent Ἄσσον. Πεζεύειν ἀπὸ τῆς πέζης, quo pedis planta significatur, est pedibus facere iter, & πεζὸς pedester est: sequenti versu ὡς δὲ συνέβαλεν ἡμῖν, Vulgatus reddidit, cum autem convenissemus in Asson. Κατὰ πόδα est, ut autem conjunxit (sese) nobiscum vel convenit nos.

εἰς Μιτυλήνην) Lesbi insulæ urbem præcipuam, unde Pittacus, Alcæus, Sappho.

## 20:15
V. 15. ἀντικρὺ Χίο) A well-known island between Lesbos and Samos. Ἀντικρὺ among other things signifies both 'deeply' and 'utterly,' and 'directly.' We met, that is, we arrived directly at Chios. A well-known name of an island fertile in good wine and mastic, which it still retains today.

εἰς Σάμον) Of Ionia. For there is another island of that name in the Ambracian Gulf, and another near Thrace.

The verb παρεβάλομεν (εἰς Σάμον) 'we approached,' occurs in this sense in Plato in the Lysis and book VIII of the Republic: There is also the nautical παραβαλέσθαι in the Frogs of Aristophanes, παραβαλεῖν τῷ κωπίῳ 'I bring the ship to land by rowing': so that it is permitted to interpret these things thus. On the next day we arrived at Samos.

κὰ μείναντες ἐν Τρωγυλλίῳ) which is a promontory of Ionia, not far from Samos. Strabo and Ptolemy are witnesses.

It is 40 stadia away, that is, about 5000 paces, according to Strabo: but those words are wrongly omitted in the Vulgate Latin edition. The sense is, although they had stayed at Trogyllium, the day after they had set sail from Samos, they had arrived at Miletus.

εἰς Μίλητον) A city of Ionia, whence came Thales, Anaximander, and others. Hence the Milesiaca, written about love affairs.

Latin:

V. 15. ἀντικρὺ Χίο) Nota est insula interLesbum &Samū. Ἀντικρὺ inter alia & penitus & prorsus, & dire- cte significat. Occurrimus, id est, devenimus re- cta in Chium. Notum nomen insulæ feracis boni vini, & mastyches, quod nunc quoque illa retinet.

εἰς Σάμον) Ioniæ. Nam est altera ejus nominis insula in Ambracio sinu, & alia apud Thraciam.

Verbum παρεβάλομεν (εἰς Σάμον) accessimus, apud Platonem in Lyside & lib. VIII. Rerum publ. hoc sensu occurrit: Est & nauticum παραβαλέσθαι in Ranis Aristophanis, παραβαλεῖν τῷ κωπίῳ appel- lito navem remigio: ut liceat hæc ita interpretari. Altera die appulimus ad Samum.

κὰ μείναντες ἐν Τρωγυλλίῳ) quod Ioniæ est promonto- rium, non longe à Samo. Testes Strabo & Ptolemæus.

Abest stadiis 40. id est, ad passus circiter 5000. secundum Strabonem: perperam autem verba illa omissa in vulgata editione Latina. Sensus est, quamvis Trogyllii diversati essent, postridie, quam à Samo solverant, Miletum ipsos appulisse.

εἰς Μίλητον) Ioniæ urbem, unde Thales, Anaximander, & alii. Hinc Milesiaca, de amoribus scripta.

## 20:16
V. 16. χρονοτριβῆσαι) Aristotle uses this verb. The Hebrews would say התמהמה.

Latin:

V. 16. χρονοτριβῆσαι) Utitur hoc verbo Aristoteles. Hebræi dicerent התמהמה.

## 20:17
V. 17. ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς Μιλήτυ πέμψας εἰς Ἔφεσον) These cities are not so far apart, as appears from Ptolemy.

χρονοτριβῆσαι is to waste time. Paul did not want this in Asia, so that he might be present at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost; having sent messengers from Miletus to Ephesus, he approached the Elders of the Church. That interval between Ephesus and Miletus was about 400 stadia, which make nearly fifty thousand paces, as Camerarius notes here.

μετεκαλέσατο) He called to himself, thus above c. VII. 14. c. X. 32. c. XXII. 25.

the elders of the Church) זקנים. See above XI. v. 30. c. XIV. 23. c. XV. 4, 6. 22. 23. c. XVI. 4. The same are called also ἐπίσκοποι, namely because they were inspectors of the flock, as is said below in verse 28. But he who was the leader was called by way of excellence ὁ ἐπίσκοπος, to whom corresponded the High Priest in the temple, but in the synagogue the Archisynagogus. This is the Angel of Ephesus in the Apocalypse, because he spoke words in the name of God to the people, and for the people to God. It seems, however, that at this time the leader of the Ephesian presbytery was Timothy, and that he had come to Paul with his fellow-presbyters.

There was therefore no difference then between the terms Bishop and Presbyter, unless the former perhaps denoted by way of eminence the leader of the presbytery, whom we now call a Superintendent; which meaning, however, it is not permitted to prove from the Scriptures, by which the eminence of jurisdiction and power, which the Papists claim for Bishops over Presbyters, and which they contend is sometimes of divine right, is maintained without law or testimony of Scripture. Here, certainly, several Bishops of the one city of Ephesus are noted. But according to the Pontifical Canons, several Bishops of one city are forbidden. Here, therefore, the Bishops are none other than Presbyters. Cornelius à Lapide acknowledges this: He calls, he says, the primary presbyters bishops.

Latin:

V. 17. ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς Μιλήτυ πέμψας εἰς Ἔφεσον) Non ita longe distant hæ urbes, ut ex Ptolemæo apparet.

χρονοτριβῆσαι est tempus terere. Id noluit Pau- lus in Asia, ut die Pentecostes adesset Hierosoly- mis; missis autem Mileto nunciis Ephesum, ac- cessivit Seniores Ecclesiæ. Intervallum illud inter Ephesum & Miletum erat ad stadia circiter 400. quæ efficiunt prope quinquaginta millia passuum, notante hic Camerario.

μετεκαλέσατο) Ad se vocavit, sic supra c. VII. 14. c. X. 32. c. XXII. 25.

τὺς πρεσβυτέρυς τῆς Ἐκκλησίας) זקנים. Vide supra XI. v. 30. c. XIV. 23. c. XV. 4, 6. 22. 23. c. XVI. 4. vocantur iidem & ἐπίσκοποι, nempe quia inspectores erant gregis, ut infra dicitur 28. Sed is, qui princeps erat, excellenter vo- cabatur ὁ ἐπίσκοπος, cui respondebat summus Sacerdos in templo, in synagoga vero Archisynagogus. Hic est Angelus Ephesi in Apocalypsi, quia Dei nomine verba faciebat ad populum, & pro populo ad Deum. Videtur autem hoc tempore Ephesini presbyterii princeps fuisse Timotheus, & cum compresbyteris venisse ad Paulum.

Nulla ergo tum erat inter voces Episcopi, & Presbyteri differentia, nisi cum illa forte ἐξοχικῶς principem notabat presbyterii, quem Superinten- dentem nunc dicimus; quam tamen significationem è Scripturis non licet probare, qua jurisdictionis & potestatis ἐξοχὴν, quam Episcopis præ Presby- teris vindicant Papistæ, eamque juris divini esse quandoque, sed sine lege vel testimonioScripturæ, contendunt. Hic sane unius civitatis Ephesi plures notantur Episcopi. At juxta Pontificios Canones plures unius civitatis Episcopi esse vetantur. Hic ergo Episcopi nulli alii, nisi Presbyteri. Agnoscit id Cornelius à Lapide: Episcopos, inquit, vocat primarios presbyteros.

## 20:18
v. 18. εἶπεν αὐτοῖς) This is an excellent form, which a good Bishop might use when bidding farewell to his Church for necessary reasons.

Πῶς μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν πάντα χρόνον ἐγενόμην) That is, how I have conducted myself toward you. In almost the same way you have ἐγενήθημεν, 1 Thess. II. 5 & 10. Thus γίνομαί σοι δι᾽ ἔχθρας in Thucydides.

Latin:

v. 18. εἶπεν αὐτοῖς) Est hic egregia forma, qua uti possit bo- nus Episcopus ex causis necessariis valedicens Ecclesiæ suæ.

Πῶς μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν πάντα χρόνον ἐγενόμην) Id est, quomodo me erga vos gesserim. Pari fere modo habes ἐγενήθημεν, 1. Thess. II. 5. & 10. Sic γίνομαί σοι δι᾽ ἔχθρας apud Thucyd.

## 20:19
v. 19. μετὰ πάσης ταπεινοφροσύνης) The Apostles, placed at such a height of calling, nevertheless displayed nothing grand about themselves.

CAP. XX. v. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. 21. 22.

but they associated equally even with the least. Paul would not have boasted of this about himself had he not needed to leave a pattern of life for his successors.

Latin:

v. 19. μετὰ πάσης ταπεινοφροσύνης) Apostoli in tanto vo- cationis culmine positi, nihil tamen grande præ se ferebant

CAP. XX. v. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. 21. 22.

sed cum minimis etiam æqualiter versabantur. Ne hoc qui- dem de se prædicasset Paulus nisi successoribus formam vi- tæ relinquere debuisset.

## 20:20
V. 20. ὡς ὀυδὲν ὑπεστειλάμην τῶν συμφερόντων) Nothing of those things which ought to be believed, hoped for, and done to prepare for eternal life. ὑποστέλλειν here and below in verse 27 is to withdraw: that Greek word is used for the Hebrew נחש and for עפר. τῷ μὴ ἀναγγεῖλαι ὑμῖν) so as not to announce that to you. We have spoken of this locution several times.

The word ὑποστέλλεσθαι, says Camerarius, signifies to tergiversate, to hesitate, to delay, to conceal. Demosthenes: ἐ μὴν οἶμαι δεῖν τὴν ἰδίαν ἀσφάλειαν σκοπῶντα ὑποστέλασθαι περὶ ὧν ὑμῖν συμφέρειν ἡγῦμαι: I do not think, however, that looking to my own safety, I ought to tergiversate in those things which I consider to be to your advantage, or to dissemble them. And Hippocrates says: ἐν τοῖσι παροξυσμοῖσι ὑποστέλλεσθαι χρή. In the exacerbations of diseases it is necessary to delay or hesitate. Therefore, these things, as I think, may be interpreted thus: That I have concealed or dissembled nothing of all things which would be to your advantage, so as not to explain them to you, and teach them publicly and privately. So much for him.

Suidas says that ὑποστειλάμενος means having concealed. τὰ συμφέροντα are those things which conduce to salvation. Therefore, all those things which make for salvation have been announced by the Apostle. But he preached nothing outside of those things which were written in Moses and the Prophets, Acts XXVI. 22. Therefore, all things which make for salvation must exist in the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament as well. Compare Acts XX. 27.

καὶ διδάξαι ὑμᾶς δημοσίᾳ) in the assembly. Above XVIII. 29. καὶ κατ' οἴκως) to individuals when the occasion was given.

Latin:

V. 20. ὡς ὀυδὲν ὑπεστειλάμην τῶν συμφερόντων) Nihil eo- rum, quæ ad vitam æternam parandam credi, sperari, fieri debent. ὑποστέλλειν hic & infra 27. est subducere: ponitur ea vox Græca pro Hebræo נחש & pro עפר. τῷ μὴ ἀναγγεῖλαι ὑμῖν) ne id vobis annunciarem. De hac locutione diximus aliquoties.

Verbum ὑποστέλλεσθαι, ait Camerarius, significat tergiversari, cunctari, insistere, celare. Demosthen. ἐ μὴν οἶμαι δεῖν τὴν ἰδίαν ἀσφάλειαν σκοπῶντα ὑποστέλασθαι περὶ ὧν ὑμῖν συμφέρειν ἡγῦμαι: Non arbitror tamen spectantem me ut sim ipse intuto, tergiversari in iis, aut dissimulare ea debere, quæ con- ducere vobis duco. Et Hippocrat. ait: ἐν τοῖσι παρο- ξυσμοῖσι ὑποστέλλεσθαι χρή. In morborum tantatio- nibus insistere s. cunctari oportet. Itaque hæc, ut opi- nor, sic liceat interpretari: Quod nihil celaverim aut dissimulaverim omnium, quæ vobis conducerent, quo minus exponerem vobis, doceremque publice & privatim. Hæc ille.

Suidas ὑποστειλάμενος, inquit, ἀποκρυψάμενος τὰ συμφέροντα sunt, quæ conducunt ad salutem. Ea ergo omnia quę ad salutem faciunt, annunciata ab Apostolo sunt. At nihil ille prædicavit extra ea, quæ in Mose & Prophetis scripta, Actor. XXVI. 22. omnia ergo quę ad salutem faciunt, in Scripturis S. etiam V.T. extare oportet. Conf. Act. XX. 27.

καὶ διδάξαι ὑμᾶς δημοσίᾳ) in conventu. Supra XVIII. 29. καὶ κατ' οἴκως) singulos occasione data.

## 20:21
V. 21. testifying to both Jews and Greeks repentance toward God) We have had διαμαρτύρεσθαι before, sometimes without an adjunct, sometimes with an infinitive, or with ὅτι following. Here with an accusative, as also shortly in 24, and c. XXIII. 11, and c. XXVIII. 23, and Exod. XVIII. 20, Ezech. XVI. 8, c. XX. 4, where in the Hebrew it is הודיע. The sense is, he certainly affirmed to them that there was a place for repentance: that is, that repentance would not be useless: thus διδόναι μετάνοιαν in XI. 18. And that faith in Christ is true and saving.

The distribution of Jews and Greeks is frequent. For all peoples who were alien to the Jewish polity are called Greeks in the N.T., whom Onkelos and the Syriac interpreter call Aramaeans or Syrians, because the Jews have no closer Gentiles than the Syrians, from whom they even learned idolatry.

Latin:

V. 21. διαμαρτυρόμενος Ἰουδαίοις τε καὶ Ἕλλησι τὴν εἰς τὸν Θεὸν μετάνοιαν) διαμαρτύρεσθαι supra habuimus, modo sine adjuncto, modo infinitivo, aut ὅτι subsequente. Hic cum accusativo, ut & mox 24. & c. XXIII. 11. & c. XXVIII. 23. & Exod. XVIII. 20. Ezech. XVI. 8. c. XX. 4. ubi in Hebræo הודיע. Sensus est, certo affirmavit illis esse locum pœni- tentiæ: id est, pœnitentiam non fore inutilem: sic διδόναι με- τάνοιαν XI. 18. Et fidem in Christum esse veram ac salutare.

Distributio Judæorum & Græcorum frequens est. Omnes enim populi, qui à politia Judaica ali- eni erant, Græci dicuntur. in N.T. quos Onkelos & Syrus interpres Aramæos sive Syros vocat, quod Judæi nullos gentiles viciniores habeant, quam Syros, à quibus etiam idololatriam didicere.

## 20:22
V. 22. bound in the spirit) Foreseeing bonds by the Spirit. For those things which are to come are presented to the minds of the prophets as if they were present: he explains this more fully in what follows.

Heinsius explains it as saddened in spirit, and as it were constrained. Neither is convenient: for he is not said to be bound in spirit who foresees bonds, nor was Paul saddened here for that reason. Therefore Pricaeus rightly prefers the opinion of Camerarius and Beza, that he is said to be bound in spirit because he did this by the impulse of the Holy Spirit. Cf. Acts XIX. 21, c. XIII. 4, Matt. IV. v. 1, Luke II. v. 27. The interpretation of Chrysostom, who places a period at this participle, 'Behold I am now bound, because I know by the indication of the Spirit that bonds await me there, I set out for Jerusalem,' does not deserve approval: since that arrangement of words is harsh, and one should not depart from the common punctuation. It is doubtful, however, how he went to Jerusalem by the impulse of the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit dissuaded that journey, c. XXI. 4. But this dissuasion must be understood κατά τι, unless, that is, he wishes to bear bonds and chains, as is gathered from v. 11 of the same chapter: which indeed Paul did not so much refuse, that when he was asked on that account not to go to Jerusalem, he testified with great παῤῥησίᾳ his readiness even to undergo death, v. 13.

the things that will happen to me in it) what the cause, what the manner, what the outcome of the bonds will be, still remains hidden from me. τὰ συναντήσοντά μοι is מה יפגע לי for פגע means to happen, Ruth I. 16.

Concerning which Theophylact: Since the Apostle was not ignorant of other things, he says that this one thing was unknown to him, what the end would be. And this was the ambiguity of the spirit, so that in the fear of the weakness of the flesh he might pray to God to be delivered from temptations.

Latin:

V. 22. δεδεμέν[ος] τῷ πνέυματι) Spiritu vincula præsen- tiens. Nam quæ futura sunt, ea prophetis tanquam præsen- tia menti obversantur: id in sequentibus fusius explicat.

Heinsius contristatum spiritu, & quasi constri- ctum exponit. Neutrum commode: nam nec spi- ritu vinctus dicitur, qui præsentit vincula, nec Pau- lus hic contrutatus ideo fuit. Ideo merito Camera- rii & Bezæ sententiam præfert Pricæus, vinctum dici spiritu, quia impulsu Spiritus S. hoc egit. Conf. Act. XIX. 21. c. XIII. 4. Matth. IV. v. 1. Luc. II. v. 27. Chrysostomi punctum ponentis ad hoc participium interpretatio, Ecce ego jam vinctus, quod Spiritus indicio me vincula ibi manere sciam Hierosolyma proficiscor; non meretur calculum: cum dura sit illa verborum dispositio, neque recedendum à communi distinctione. Dubium tamen est quomo- do Spiritus impulsu Hierosolymam ierit, siquidem Spiritus id iter dissuaserit, c. XXI. 4. Sed hæc dis- suasio κατά τι intelligenda, nisi sc. velit vincula & catenas ferre, ut è v. 11. ejusdem capitis colligitur: quæ vero adeo non detrectavit Paulus, ut cum eo nomine rogaretur, ne Hierosolymam iret, prom- titudinem suam etiam mortem subeundi, magna παῤῥησίᾳ testatus sit, v. 13.

τὰ ἐν ἀυτῇ συναντήσοντά μοι εἰδὼς) quæ causa, qui modus, quis exitus futurus sit vinculorum, adhuc me latet. τὰ συ- ναντήσοντά μοι מה יפגע לי nam פגע evenire, Ruth. I. 16.

De quo Theophylactus: Cum alia non ignoraret Apostolus, ignorari à se unum hoc ait, qui finis fu- turus esset. Et hoc fuit ambiguum spiritus, ut in me- tu imbecillitatis carnis precaretur Deum liberari ex tentationibus.

## 20:24
Verse 24.

ἀλλ’ ὐδενὸς λόγον ποιῦμαι) These evils are not of such account to me that they should deter me from the preaching of the Gospel.

As this of Theocritus: ὅ δέ μευ λόγον ὐδένα ποιῇ He cares nothing for me, or has no regard for me. So that it may be: τούτων ὐδένα λόγον ποιῦμαι. I care nothing for these things. Or, these things do not move me: as here Camerarius.

ὐδὲ ἔχω τὴν ψυχήν μου τιμίαν ἐμαυτῷ) The word ὕτως is understood here, to which the following ὡς corresponds: I am so far from fearing bonds, that I do not even flee from death. Among the Hebrews, he is said to hold his life precious who spares it, 2 Sam. 1:13, 14. Conversely, to hold it at no price is to not spare it. Ezek. 36:5.

ὡς τελειῶσαι τὸν δρόμον με) I do not care so much for life as to complete my course. The course signifies great and assiduous labor, above ch. 13:25, 1 Cor. 9:24. You have τελεῖν τὸν δρόμον also in 2 Tim. 4:7.

μετὰ χαρᾶς) Paul often calls by this name the tranquility of mind arising from a good conscience, as Rom. 5:3, 2 Cor. 7:10, 1 Thess. 5:16, and elsewhere.

καὶ τὴν διακονίαν ἧν ἔλαβον) See above ch. 1:17, 25, ch. 6:4.

τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον τῆς χάριτος τῦ Θεῦ) See above 14:3.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

ἀλλ’ ὐδενὸς λόγον ποιῦμαι) Non tanti sunt mihi ista mala, ut ea me ab Evangelii prædicatione deterreant.

Ut hoc Theocriti: ὅ δέ μευ λόγον ὐδένα ποιῇ Nihil ille me curat, seu nullam habet mei rationem. Ut sit: τούτων ὐδένα λόγον ποιῦμαι. Nihil ista curo. Aut, nihil me ista movent: ut hic Camerarius.

ὐδὲ ἔχω τὴν ψυχήν μου τιμίαν ἐμαυτῷ) Subauditur hic ὕτως, cui respondet quod sequitur ὡς: tantum abest vincula metuam, ne mortem quidem defugio. Hebræis pretiosam habere vitam dicitur qui ei parcit, 2. Reg. I. 13. 14. Contra nullo pretio habere qui non parcit. Ezech. XXXVI. 5.

ὡς τελειῶσαι τὸν δρόμον με) non tam vitam cur, quam complere cursum. Cursus laborem magnum & assiduum significat, supra c. XIII. 25. 1. Cor. IX. 24. τελεῖν τὸν δρόμον habes & 2. Tim. IV. 7.

μετὰ χαρᾶς) Sæpe Paulus hoc nomine appellat animi ex bona conscientia tranquillitatem, ut Rom. V. 3. 2. Cor. VII v. 10. 1. Thess. V. 16. & alibi.

καὶ τὴν διακονίαν ἧν ἔλαβον) Vide supra c. I. 17. 25. c. VI. 4.

τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον τῆς χάριτος τῦ Θεῦ) Vide supra XIV. 3.

## 20:25
V. 25. ὅτι ὐκ ἐτι ὄψεσθε τὸ πρόσωπόν με) as if he were saying: This is the last time, by fate, that I address you.

ὑμεῖς πάντες) You all, Asians. A Hebraism. You all shall not see, that is, none of you.

Quidni vero sensus, quem Latina versio reddidit, retineri possit: Amplius non videbitis faciem meam vos omnes? It is possible that some among them may have existed who still saw the face of the Apostle. We do not wish to touch here upon that controversy, whether Paul returned to the East and Ephesus after the release from his first Roman captivity. For there are those who wish these things to be said by Paul only conjecturally, and from human supposition, from a comparison with Phil. 1:19.

ἐν οἷς διῆλθον κηρύσσων τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ) See above ch. 8:12.

Latin:

V. 25. ὅτι ὐκ ἐτι ὄψεσθε τὸ πρόσωπόν με) quasi diceret: Extremum fato quod te alloquor, hoc est.

ὑμεῖς πάντες) Vos omnes Asiatici. Hebraïsmus. Non videbitis vos omnes, id est, nemo vestrum.

Quidni vero sensus, quem Latina versio reddidit, retineri possit: Amplius non videbitis faciem meam vos omnes? Potuere fortassis aliqui inter ipsos extitisse, qui adhuc Apostoli faciem viderint. Controversiam illam, anne reversus in Orientem, & Ephesum Paulus post primæ captivitatis Romanæ solutionem sit, hic tangere nolumus. Sunt enim, qui hæc tantum στοχαστικῶς, & ex humana conjectura dicta velint à Paulo è collatione Phil. I. v. 19.

ἐν οἷς διῆλθον κηρύσσων τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ) Vide supra c. VIII. 12.

## 20:26
V. 26 μαρτύρομαι ὑμῖν) that is, I testify before you. Thus Gal. V. 3. μαρτύρομαι δὲ πάλιν παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ περιτετμημένῳ.

ὅτι καθαρὸς ἐγὼ ἀπὸ τῦ αἵματος πάντων) See above c. XVIII. 6. & Matth. XXVII. 24. & what is said there.

Latin:

V. 26 μαρτύρομαι ὑμῖν) id est, coram vobis testificor. Sic Gal. V. 3. μαρτύρομαι δὲ πάλιν παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ περιτετμημένῳ.

ὅτι καθαρὸς ἐγὼ ἀπὸ τῦ αἵματος πάντων) Vide supra c. XVIII. 6. & Matth. XXVII. 24. & ibi dicta.

## 20:27
V. 27. ὐ γὰρ ὑπεσειλάμην τῦ μὴ ἀναγγεῖλαι ὑμῖν) Something is understood. See above 20.

πᾶσαν τὴν βυλὴν τῦ Θεῦ) By the name of will, it signifies here metonymically everything that God wishes to be performed by individuals, so that salvation may be reached. A usage not unlike Luke VII. 30. He calls the same thing here τὴν βυλὴν τῦ Θεῦ which he just called τὰ συμφέροντα.

Indeed, the counsel of God concerning our salvation concerns not only those things which God requires of us, but primarily those things which He Himself wishes to exhibit to us, or the gracious will of God revealed to us in the Gospel, that He wishes to grant the remission of sins and salvation to all who have believed in Christ. Compare John III. 16. c. VI. 40. From Luke VII. 30 we learn that the means, which He deigned to institute for the sake of our salvation, also pertain to this counsel of God.

Latin:

V. 27. ὐ γὰρ ὑπεσειλάμην τῦ μὴ ἀναγγεῖλαι ὑμῖν) Subauditur τι. Vide supra 20.

πᾶσαν τὴν βυλὴν τῦ Θεῦ) voluntatis nomine μετωνυμικῶς hic significat omne id, quod à singulis præstari vult Deus, ut ad salutem perveniatur. Usus non dissimilis Luc. VII. 30. idem hic vocat τὴν βυλὴν τῦ Θεῦ quod modo τὰ συμφέροντα.

Imo consilium Dei de salute nostra non ea tantum concernit, quæ à nobis requirit Deus, sed imprimis ea, quæ nobis ipse exhibere vult, seu voluntate Dei gratiosam erga nos in Evangelio revelatam, quod remissionem peccatorum & salutem omnibus concedere velit, qui in Christum crediderint. Conf. Joh. III. 16. c. VI. 40. Ad quod Dei consilium etiam media, quę salutis nostræ causa instituere dignatus est, pertinere, è Luc. VII. 30. discimus.

## 20:28
V. 28. προσέχετε ὖν ἑαυτοῖς καὶ πάντι τῷ ποιμνίῳ) He cannot attend to the flock who has not attended to himself.

ἐν ᾧ ὑμᾶς τὸ πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἔθετο ἐπισκόπυς) He explains the name of the office, which was פקידי עדר: for Pastors are ἐπίσκοποι ποιμνίε, פקידי עדר. He says, however, that they were appointed by the Holy Spirit because they were appointed by the Apostles full of the Holy Spirit, although with the approval of the people. See above XIV. 23.

ποιμαίνειν) a frequent brevity among the Hebrews for εἰς τὸ ποιμαίνειν.

Therefore, the wish and vote of the people in the election of ministers of the word is not to be entirely excluded, since not even the Apostles excluded it. Which I would wish to be observed against the Papists.

τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τῦ Θεῦ) That manuscript has τῦ Κυρίε, as do many others. And the Syriac reads thus, which translates Christ. An easy slip of abbreviated writing θῦ for χῦ. The Apostles mostly call Christ Κύριον, but the Father God.

Grotius is too easy in admitting slips and errors in the Holy Scriptures. That that abbreviated writing was used, and that those sufficiently different letters were swapped, how, I ask, will it be proven? Even if the Apostles mostly call Christ Κύριον, they nevertheless also called Him God, as is evident from John I. 1. c. XX. 28. Rom. IX. 5. 1. Tim. III. 16. Tit. II. 13. 1. John V. 20. and other places. Nor did Enjedinus or Socinus move a dispute here about the word Θεῦ, who nevertheless tried everything to overturn the statements about the Deity of Christ: because they preferred to establish that the blood of Christ is called the blood of God the Father by appropriation, or that an ellipsis of the word ὑῦ occurs here, blood of His own (Son), or that the word of blood is put for the Son, although ineptly. See Enjed. annot. p. 254. Socin. in Anti-Wujek. &c. Beza's suspicion would rather have a place here, even if he is otherwise prone to the errors of scribes: In five copies it is read Κυρίου καὶ Θεῦ, of the Lord & of God. I suspect, however, that τῦ Κυρίυ was initially written in the margin by someone who was explaining the word of God in this way against the Anthropomorphites, lest Paul seem to attribute blood to the divinity itself: then when this had crept into the context, and those Κυρίε Θεῦ did not seem to cohere well, the particle καὶ was interposed.

We have treated this argument more fully in the ἀπόδειξις (demonstration) of the Deity of Christ, from which it is pleasing here to repeat the vindications of the present passage. For those have not yet seen the light. Our κατασκευὴ (construction) stands thus: He who is here called ὁ Θεὸς (God), he is truly that one God by nature. But Christ is here called ὁ Θεὸς. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because not only does the name of God occur absolutely and simply, which denotes none but that one God, but the article is also added, by the addition of which adversaries concede that that one God is always designated: furthermore, the name of God is used subjectively, when ὁ Θεὸς (God) is said to have acquired the Church for Himself with His own blood: but when it is used subjectively, adversaries again assert and maintain that that true and one God is always designated: Finally, that God is pointed out whose the Church is: But the Church is ascribed to no other God in the Holy Scriptures, except to that one true God, the God of Israel. The minor premise is confirmed from this: that the περιποίησις (acquisition) of the Church, and indeed made διὰ τῦ ἰδίε αἵματος (through His own blood), belongs to no one else but Christ. He alone redeemed the Church with His own blood, as Scripture testifies throughout, Rom. III. 24, 25, 1 Cor. VI. 10, ch. VII. 23, Eph. I. 7, 1 Pet. I. 19, 2 Pet. II. 1. Whence also the Syrian, as well as the Arabic interpreter, looking not so much to the words as to the sense, explained the word of God by the name of Christ: since it was manifest that the discourse was about Christ. Which opinion, that the Son of God is understood here, the universal Church has most constantly maintained, nor could Enjedinus reject it, conceding that He is understood by the word God, even though he denies that it can be concluded from thence that Christ is that one true God.

Here, however, the adversaries move everything possible, so that they may, if not snatch away this illustrious testimony, at least render it doubtful for us. Schmalzius in his refutation of the disputation on the Incarnation of Gravius, page 25, with his teacher Socinus leading the way, opposes this very Syriac reading, which has Christ instead of God, from which he thinks it can rightly be gathered that there was some difference in the copies from the beginning, and that either this word, or another similar to it, existed in at least some copies, which he says Beza also confirms, while he says that in five copies it is read as Lord and God. (2.) Enjedinus in his Explanation of passages, p. 255, invents an ellipsis of the word Son, and thus provides this gloss: He acquired with the blood of His (or His own), understand Son, because the word Son is sometimes accustomed to be omitted, as in Luke III, Matt. IV, and similar substantives, John XIII, v. 1, Matt. X. 42. (3.) Furthermore, the same Enjedinus, not content with the former torture, wishes the word blood to be put for Son, as in Homer, Theocritus, Virgil, and therefore that it can not inconveniently be said that God redeemed the Church with His own blood, that is, with His own Son. (4) Again, he says that the blood of Jesus Christ can be called the blood of God, because it was sacred to God, just as the blood of victims was sanctified to God. (5.) Furthermore, he contends that this same blood of Christ is called God's, not because God has blood, but because He reckons it as His own: and it is as precious to Him as if it were His own; comparing Zech. 2:8, Matt. 25:40, Acts 9:14. Which is also the Gloss of Socinus against Wujek, p. 354. That the name God ought not to be referred to Christ, but to God the Father Himself, whose Blood he is said to be, which He also poured out, by that figure by which Zech. 2:8 says, He who touches the people of God is said to touch the apple of God's eye. He adds that even the words spoken about God the Father, 'they shall look on him whom they pierced,' Zech. 12:10, are adapted to Christ, John 19:37, because of the highest and most perfect union between God the Father and Christ, and because God the Father possesses this blood of the lamb, just as He possesses the lamb himself, and gives it as His own thing together with the lamb himself for the expiation of our sins. Schlichting, disp. de Trin. p. 342, adds that the blood of Christ is the blood of the Father, because it is of His right and dominion, and was produced by Him in the womb of the virgin by the efficacy of the Holy Spirit. Smalcius, in the cited place, repeating the words of Socinus, adds that the spirits and bodies of the faithful are also said to be God's, 1 Cor. 6:20, between whom and God there is by no means as great a union as between Christ and the Father. Finally, he subjoins the consent of Erasmus, whom he afterwards extols with many words. (6.) Finally, Enjedinus says that nothing else can be obtained from this than that Christ is God, which he concedes: but he adds, not immediately that he who is God is also the eternal and omnipotent creator of heaven and earth.

These, therefore, are the more important exceptions of the Socinians, to which it will now be necessary to respond in the same order. To (1.) I respond: The Greek Codices most constantly, without any dissension, retain the word τοῦ Θεῦ; no one is found who has the word 'Christ' in its place, nor has it been found by any of the critics who have most diligently compared the copies, nor finally is such a reading observed in the allegations of the ancients: But rather, both Greeks and Latins confirm this received reading. Moreover, the Greek text alone is authentic, and infallible in establishing the dogmas of the faith. Nor indeed do we admit the consequence that there was a difference in the Greek copies from the beginning, and that either this word 'Christ' or another similar to it existed (in place of the word τοῦ Θεῦ), and that the word משיחא 'Messiah' is read in the Syriac, because there could be another cause for this translation, namely that the interpreter wished to express that the discourse was about the Messiah, especially since the Syriac does not always render words strictly, sometimes having regard to the sense, and even adding certain words: as in Acts 27:9 the name ליהודיא 'of the Jews' is added, Rom. 4:5 the particle בלחוד, 'only' or 'alone', 1 Cor. 7:7 the word ברכיותא, 'in chastity', Mark 2:4 'they ascended onto the roof', which are not found in the Greek codices; or it substitutes other things different from the Greek text, as in Matt. 2:19, ch. 14:6 (Mark 6:21), Matt. 27:37, Mark 4:10, ch. 15:22. Thus, when in Luke 2:49 it is held in the Greek ἐν τοῖς τῦ πατρός μȣ, the Syriac explained it לביתא דאבי 'in the house of my Father'; Luke 2:30 τὸ σωτήριόν σου it renders חנך, which Tremellius translated 'your gracious one'. Boderian: 'your merciful one'. Lud. de Dieu, Comm. in Evang. p. 258, more correctly 'your mercy'; John 8:23 the Greek ὁ λόγος ὁ ἐμὸς ὐ χωρεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν, the Syriac rendered: 'you do not suffice for my word'; looking to the sense, not expressing the words; John 19:42 διὰ τὴν παρασκευὴν τῶν Ἰυδαίων, the Syriac rendered, 'because the Sabbath was entering', and thus in these

& others, he handed down not so much a translation as an explanation, of which kind many more could be noted. But shall we admit in those and similar places that the Greek Codices varied (against their own constant consensus), because they are rendered otherwise (as to the words) by the Syriac interpreter? not to mention that some things are omitted in the Syriac interpretation, such as in Mark 1:2 that ἔμπροσθέν σου, and in John 8 the story of the adulteress (which, although Lud. de Dieu, Comm. ad Evang. p. 445, produced it from a manuscript received from the Archbishop of Armagh, James Ussher, the same manuscript nevertheless prefixes this inscription to it: 'a reading which is about the sinful woman, which reading is not in the simple [version]'; that is, which is not in the commonly received one, and simply without controversy admitted by all the Syriac Churches as the accepted copy, as Ludov. de Dieu interprets in the cited place) and many other things, which are read constantly without discrepancy of Codices in the Greek text, so that the defects of the Syriac interpretation do not prejudice the authority of the Greek text in the same.

But as for the diverse reading of the Greek Codices, which was annotated by Beza (observed by Stephanus), that by no means confirms that the word τοῦ Θεῦ was once omitted in some copies, or another read in its place, but rather teaches that in all the Codices collated by Stephanus and Beza the word τοῦ Θεῦ existed, although the Complutensian edition, according to the most ancient copies once printed, together with other older Codices, prefixed the word κυρίου to four, and thus read τοῦ κυρίου τοῦ Θεῦ, the cause of which variety, explained by conjecture, see in the annotations of Beza on this passage. That reading, however, is by no means adverse to our demonstration: rather, it confirms the same also, because by the name τοῦ Θεῦ is understood the true and natural God, since nowhere are these names τοῦ κυρίου τοῦ Θεῦ said conjunctively of any other than of Jehovah, that one true God.

Smalcius's evasion, that once that reading concerning the Lord, that is, Jesus Christ, is admitted, it is properly said (what is brought forth here, he acquired the Church with his own blood) of the true God (the Father) improperly, is utterly vain: because it will not be taught by any example perhaps, that those names τοῦ κυρίου καὶ Θεῦ, where no other is added to it, are to be distinguished in such a way that one is to be understood of Christ, and the other of God the Father; nor can it be that the same predicate once placed in the same passage has a double and most diverse sense at the same time, both proper and improper. The passage which is drawn here from Rev. 1:4, that John prays for grace from God properly, and from the seven spirits improperly, is controversial; nor do we admit that grace is wished for improperly from the seven spirits; but properly, even if the seven spirits are understood improperly and metonymically of the Holy Spirit in his septiform gift. Conf. our Anti-Crell. §. 528. seqq.

To (2.) Resp. Who would not wonder at, who would not detest that impudent audacity of Enjedinus, by which he wishes to insert the word ἁιῦ into the text beyond and against the custom of Scripture, to pervert a most clear testimony? The text itself vindicates itself by its own evidence, τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ Θεῦ, ἣν περιεποιήσατο διὰ τοῦ ἰδία αἵματος., the Church of God, which he acquired through his own blood. What cause, I pray, can be given here for admitting an ellipsis, what necessity can be imagined for it? Furthermore, no suitable example of this ellipsis can be brought forward from the Scriptures; that the word ὑιὸς is to be understood in Luke 3:23, the genealogy itself teaches, since the parents are commemorated, although the word ἁιὸς can also be repeated ἀπὸ κοινῦ from verse 23, Matt. 4:12, Ἰακωβὸν τὸν τοῦ Ζεβεδαίου, ὑιὸν is to be understood from that customary way of speaking

It is manifest from the formula of the Greeks, by which, with the name of the Father placed in the Genitive case, they understand the noun υἱᾶ. But what does this have to do with the present passage? Is God referred to here as the Father of Christ, or is a genealogy being woven here? That the other examples, Job XIII. 1, c. I. 12, Matth. X. 42, are entirely dissimilar, everyone sees. What if, in texts that are entirely clear without an ellipsis, it were permissible to invent an ellipsis, so insolent and foreign to the Scriptures, what finally would remain certain in Holy Scripture? We add no more, because other Anti-Trinitarians, Socinus, and his disciples, have long since been ashamed of this gloss.

To (3.) Resp. Here indeed one must again detest the extreme impudence, or rather impiety, of Enjed., because he dared to pervert this text in such a way, transforming the word αἵματος into the word υἱᾶ: which corruption, as it rests on no reason, nor could it be supported by any example in the Scriptures; whence it was necessary to leap over to the Heathen Poets, although even those things which are produced from Homer do not contribute anything to this; thus it is also contrary to Scripture, which teaches that redemption was made with τῷ αἵματι blood, it does not understand the Son, but the blood of the Son, nay, it is also joined with blasphemy; as if God had a Son begotten from His own blood, just as the sons of men are begotten, who for that reason are called the blood of their parents, metonymically.

To (4.) Resp. It is not said that the Church was acquired by the sacred or sanctified blood of God, in the way that sacred victims were to God, but διὰ τᾶ ἰδίε αἵματος, through the proper blood of God. The blood of victims, even if they were sacred to God, is nowhere called τὸ ἴδιον αἷμα the proper blood of God Himself, but just as that blood was the proper blood of the victims themselves, e.g., of sacrificial lambs, so this blood, by which the Church was redeemed, is called the blood of God Himself. But that was truly and without figure the proper blood of the same, and therefore this also is to be understood as truly and without figure the proper blood of God. For no necessity compels us to abandon the proper sense of the words and admit a figurative one.

To (5.) Resp. That the name τᾶ Θεᾶ is to be referred here to Christ and not to the Father is easily evident, both because Blood is ascribed to Christ in the Holy Scriptures, but nowhere throughout the whole of Scripture to God the Father, and because the Father does not have τὸ ἴδιον αἷμα proper blood, but the Son, who was made a partaker of our flesh and blood, Heb. II. 14, and because the shedding of proper blood is said everywhere of Christ, but nowhere and never of God the Father, and because the περιποίησις acquisition of the Church made by proper blood is vindicated to no one but Christ in the Holy Scriptures, and by no means to God the Father, and finally, because the Scripture of the New Testament, when it celebrates the benefits of the redemption and acquisition of the Church, nowhere commemorates the Father alone, with no mention made of the Son, but ascribes the redemption, acquisition, and things similar to these, to the Son. Therefore the blessed Gravverus had urged this Argument. As often as the Scripture of the New Testament teaches us that we have been redeemed by blood, it speaks of Christ, nor can the adversaries show any contrary passage, Heb. IX. 12, Apoc. V. 9, Eph. I. 7, 1 Petr. I. 19, Apoc. I. 6. Whence he concluded, undoubtedly, that by the name God in the subject of Acts XX. 28, is understood He to whom the predicate is otherwise expressly attributed in the Holy Scriptures, and not He to whom the predicate is otherwise nowhere attributed. But Christ is He to whom the predicate is otherwise attributed, Heb. IX. 12, Apoc. I. 9, 2 Cor. V. 15, etc. Even if redemption is attributed somewhere to God the Father, yet God the Father is not said to have redeemed us for Himself by His own or proper blood, which has been demonstrated from Heb. IX. 12, 2 Cor. V. 15, to be said of Christ. But Smalcius objects that redemption is also ascribed to God the Father, Luke I. 68, 2 Petr. II. 1, l. c. page 28.

But in the latter passage Christ is openly understood, and not the Father (concerning whom elsewhere); in the former, God of Israel is said not to have redeemed, but to have made redemption, by which name, however, it can be taught from a comparison of verse 78 that Christ can also be understood. For He is understood o̔ ἐπισκεψάμενο, who visited us. But ἐπισκεύατο visited us the dayspring from on high, that is the Son of God, that He might appear to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. Conf. Mal. IV. 2, Zachar. III. 8, cap. VI. 12, which passages are annotated in the margin so that they may be compared. Which very thing is also shown from a comparison of Luke I. 16: namely, that by the name of the God of Israel who visited us, Christ is understood, since John had to go before His face and prepare the way for Him, concerning which likewise more fully elsewhere. 2. The reasons which are brought forward, why the Blood of Christ is called the Blood of God, such as on account of kinship, estimation, right and dominion, as also on account of origin, are by no means to be admitted. Because it is gratuitously invented here that blood is attributed here to God the Father, which is against and beyond the custom of Holy Scripture. Furthermore (2.) it has already been shown that mention is made of the Son, and not of the Father. Nor (3.) does anything stand in the way of our understanding the Son of God by the name τoῦ Θεoῦ: which is set forth in the Holy Scriptures not only concerning the Father, but also concerning the Son. What Smalcius urges on page 27, that it can be taught in no place of the Holy Scriptures that the word God, when it holds the place of the subject, is predicated of Christ without any controversy even once, that is entirely vain: because whatever passage is brought forward, the Socinians will stir up controversy about it, as we see being done in this case. The passage is also clear in itself 1. 1 Tim. III. 15, where the word God is taken subjectively to denote the Son of God: the word Θεoῦ is likewise taken subjectively in Eph. IV. 5, 7, Heb. I. 8, as also in Tit. II. 14, which may also be said of Isa. IX. 6, John XX. 28; nor does it produce any diversity in meaning, whether that word holds the place of subject or of predicate, which, when placed absolutely and in its proper sense, implies the true and natural God, of whom we have treated in Theol. nat. & revel. chap. 3, p. 474 seq. Finally, if no other passages were given besides this one itself (which, however, is otherwise), Smalcius ought to have remembered what he had written a little before; that instances of all locutions are not given, both reason itself teaches, and most learned philosophers also confirm: for it is enough that similar modes of speaking exist. Thus Smalcius. Furthermore (4.) not only is God said to have acquired the Church with his own blood, but διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος by HIS OWN blood. Therefore, that God (or that divine person) is understood who has his own blood. But the Father does not have his own blood, but the Son. Smalcius replies, loc. cit., that the Greek word ἰδίου often signifies the same as the Latin suus, and therefore there is no greater force in the word 'own' than there is in the word 'his'. But he brought forward no examples of this. Nor is the consequence valid: it is often the same as 'his', therefore it is so here too. Moreover, all Greeks, whose authority is more important to us than Smalcius's groundless contraction, acknowledge a greater emphasis in the word ἰδίου; especially because no reasons persuade us that the proper emphasis of the word should be rejected here. We therefore still press our adversaries, that this blood is

attributed to God not through a mere σχέσιν [relation], but as His own blood: and that nowhere in Holy Scripture is his own blood attributed to God the Father, much less is it said that God the Father redeemed the Church with his own blood. We still challenge the same persons to show even one single passage, if they can; which Smalcius himself freely acknowledges cannot be produced, and confesses that such a locution does not exist in Holy Scripture: Therefore he resorts to the claim that instances of all locutions cannot be given: which, as we readily admit, it is nevertheless certain that when examples are given, and those even commonly met with, or analogous passages, that sense which relies on the analogy of Scripture is to be preferred to the other, which, without any example from Scripture, produces a new and unusual formula of speaking, so that the evident sense, and one obvious to all, is obscured or rendered doubtful; and that those who introduce a new formula of speaking are rightly and deservedly urged to support the same with examples. That similar modes of speaking exist by which this could be excused, as Smalcius says, has not yet been shown. For those that are brought forward are not very similar, but are much different, concerning which later. Add to these (5.) that that sense, by which Christ is understood by the name of God, is proper, but the other (even if it had similar examples, which it does not) is figurative and improper: The former is commonly met with in the Scriptures, but no passages for the latter can be brought forward, which Smalcius admits in both cases l. c. I answer, he says, those passages in which it is properly said that Christ redeemed us by his blood, washed us from sins, and acquired his people, cannot prevent it from being said elsewhere improperly that God acquired us by his blood. But Socinus had warned Fr. David in vol. Epist. pag. 188 that one should not rashly depart from the customary or proper signification of words. and that one should not resort to figures unless some necessity compels it, Smalcius inculcated above on page 9 that this is a sober rule of theology. Therefore, what Smalcius says here, that the matter itself and the circumstance of the passage can easily teach everyone that the words cannot be understood here otherwise than improperly concerning God the Father, this had to be demonstrated evidently. But he has no other proof except that the word God here holds the place of the subject, which how frivolous it is, has already been demonstrated. Since therefore no compelling cause can be brought forward why, having abandoned the proper and native sense, and likewise the one familiar to Scripture and commonly obvious, an improper and figurative one, entirely alien to the use and custom of Scripture, should be admitted, we rightly and deservedly adhere to the former, even with the adversaries themselves as judges. (6.) We deny that the blood of Christ is called God's own blood solely because of Christ's kinship with God the Father: since Christ is not only joined to God the Father, but is one with the Father. John X. 30. and indeed in such a way as the Holy Spirit is one with the Father. John V. 7. and likewise God is said to be blessed above all as the Father Rom. IX. 5. Nor are similar examples given: The spirits and bodies of the faithful are indeed said to be God's, because of the mystical union 1. Corinthians VI. 20. But nowhere does Scripture name God's spirit or God's body, indicating the soul or body of the faithful, which are God's, much less does it name them God's own spirit or God's own body. (7.) Furthermore, estimation indeed causes God to reckon that what happens to the faithful happens to himself; he who touches his people is said to touch even the apple of his eye; he who persecutes his Church asserts that he is persecuting himself; he who shows a kindness to the faithful of Christ asserts that he is showing it to himself; but from this it cannot be inferred that such estimation is the cause that God the Father's own blood is posited, and Christ's blood is understood. For those things are far different. Let it be shown where the apple of our eye is ascribed to God, or another part of our body, because God esteems it as his own, just as the adversaries wish the blood of Christ (and that properly spoken) to be claimed for God here, and indeed as his own blood, because of the estimation that God reckons it as his own; not to mention that here, in addition, the shedding of his own blood and the acquisition made by that shedding are ascribed to God: For which a genuine example, where the discourse is about God the Father, could not be brought forward from the whole of Scripture. For as to the passage Zach. XII. 10. where Jehovah is said to be pierced, that it is to be understood not of God the Father, but of the Son of God himself, is evident from the very comparison with John XIX. Apoc. 1. and has been proven in the Annotations on Zechariah. Add that where God reckons that what happens to the faithful happens to himself, it is expressly indicated and expressed, as is evident from the cited passages. Here, however, no indication of such estimation is expressed. Whence again a great diversity of passages shines forth. (8.) Nor can the possession, right, and dominion, that God possesses this blood of the lamb and gives it for expiating our sins, help the adversaries. Because nowhere does Scripture speak in such a way about any thing that God possesses by right of dominion, nor about the lamb of God, or the blood of the lamb: God possesses our souls, our bodies, and even our blood by right of dominion: But nowhere is God's own soul indicated, or God's own body, or God's own blood, to signify our souls, our bodies, or our blood because of that possession, right, and dominion. Add that not only is regard had here to some right and dominion, but the blood is appropriated to God, so that it is also intimated that God poured out the same, so that He thus acquired the Church with His own blood, which the force of the words themselves imports, and the comparison of other passages teaches. For who is the God who acquired the Church with His own blood? Is it not that Christ poured out His own blood to acquire the Church? Who therefore does not see that the shedding of blood is connoted? But that presupposes not only some right and dominion, but such a pouring out of blood, by which he who pours out his blood acknowledges it as a part of his body, in which sense not God (the Father), but Christ, who was man, and had blood and poured it out from His body, acquired the Church with His own blood. As Schlichtingius himself confesses in these very words in De Trinit. page 343. Ostorodus also in Disput. German. Tradel. opposita page 244. He says that God (the Father) can neither have nor pour out blood. How then is it to be understood of God the Father, that He acquired the Church with His own (poured out) blood? Add that His own blood is opposed to the blood of another, which the High Priest of the Old Testament was accustomed to offer. Since therefore the Apostle says that God acquired the Church not with the blood of another but with His own, he does not point out 'own' in a gross and general way, by reason of dominion and right, in which manner even the blood of victims was His own, nay, all created things are His own, but specially or singularly, by reason of possession and appropriation hypostatically, in that he was made a partaker of our flesh and blood Heb. II. 14. and in that he shed that own blood of his for our sake. To this contributes the parallel passage Heb. IX. 12. where in a similar phrase it is said of Christ, that διὰ τῶ ἰδίε αἵματος through his own blood he entered once into the sanctuary, having found eternal redemption. For as here by HIS OWN blood is understood not own generally, by reason of dominion, but specially, because it pertains to Christ, no less properly than our blood pertains to us, so also here τὸ ἴδιον αἷμα must be understood as own blood. (9.) As far as the origin is concerned, that the blood of Christ is called the own blood of God, because it was produced by God, by the power of the Holy Spirit, is a vain empty-talk.
