Paul, beginning to speak about the integrity of his conduct, is struck by the order of the High Priest, whom he therefore calls a whitewashed wall, but he excuses himself because he did not know that he was the High Priest. And when he said that he was a Pharisee and was being accused because of the asserted resurrection, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees concerning the same, with the former excusing him. Because of the violent tumults, however, he is led away by the tribune, and the Lord appears to him in the barracks, strengthening him, that just as he had testified about the Lord in Jerusalem, so he ought to testify in Rome also. The Jews, however, conspire to kill him, which the son of his sister reveals to him, and by his warning to the tribune, who through two centurions takes care for him to be led to Caesarea with a letter to Felix, which is referred to here, where he is kept in custody.

There are three parts: I. The proceedings before the council, with Ananias the High Priest striking Paul undeservedly, and the Pharisees dissenting from the Sadducees. II. The apparition of Jesus made to Paul in the barracks, to v. 11. III. The abduction of Paul to Felix after the conspiracy against him was detected, to v. 35.

PART I. Proceedings with Paul before the council.

Vers. 1. Ἀτενίσας δὲ ὁ Παῦλος τῷ συνεδρίῳ) Concerning this verb see Luke 4:20, 22:56, above 3:4, 12, 6:15, 11:6, 13:9, 14:9.

By this verb is designated Paul's freedom, spirit, and confidence: as well as the consciousness of his innocence; as well as prudence and prudent circumspection, so that he might adapt himself and his speech and gesture to the minds and ears of his hearers, as being his enemies.

ἐγὼ πάσῃ συνειδήσει ἀγαθῇ πεπολίτευμαι τῷ Θεῷ) Now indeed according to Christ: but before, as much as I had been able to draw from the Pharisee teachers. This he opposes to those by whom he was held for an impious man and an enemy of God. Πολιτεύεσθαι, to Greek writers, is to follow a way of life. Thus 2 Macc. 6:1, 11:25. It is taken in a passive sense in Canon XIV of the Synod of Sardica. Τῷ Θεῷ is before God, as the Syrian translates. He cites the searcher of minds as a witness.

His conscience or conduct was not good when he was still acting in Pharisaism, for he himself acknowledges that he was πρῶτον τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν, 1 Tim. 1:15. And therefore these things are to be understood concerning the conduct of his office: that he served God with a good conscience of mind in that duty which was entrusted to him. Conf. 2 Cor. 1:12.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Paulus de conversationis suæ integritate loqui incipiens percutitur jussu Pontificis, quem ideo parietem dealbatum dicit, sed excusat se, quod nescierit, ipsum esse Pontificem. Et cum se Pharisæum esse, atque ob assertam resurrectionem accusari diceret, orta inter Pharisæos, & Saducæos est dissensio de eo- dem, illis eum excusantibus. Ob tumultus autem vehementes subducitur à tribuno, & apparet ei Dominus in castris confor- tans ipsum, quod ut Hierosolymis testifica- tus erat de Domino, ita & Romæ eum testi- ficari oportere. Judæi autem conspirant de eo interficiendo, quod ei detegit filius soro- ris ipsius, & monitu ejus tribuno, qui per duos centuriones eum Cæsaream duci curat cum literis ad Felicem, quæ hic referuntur, ubi custoditur.

Partes tres sunt I. Acta coram concilio, Anania Pontifice Paulum immerito percutiente, & Phari- sæis à Saducæis dissentientibus. II. Apparitio Jesu Paulo in castris facta, ad v. 11. III. Abductio Pauli ad Felicem post detectam conspirationem adversus eum, ad v. 35.

PARS I. Acta cum Paulo coram concilio.

Vers. 1. Ἀτενίσας δὲ ὁ Παῦλος τῷ συνεδρίῳ) De hoc verbo vide Lucam IV. 20, XXII. 56. supra III. 4. 12. VI. 15. XI. 6. XIII. 9. XIV. 9.

Verbo hoc designatur Pauli tum libertas, ani- mositas & confidentia: tum innocentiæ conscien- tia; tum prudentia & prudens circumspectio, ut se suamque orationem & gestum auditorum, utpo- te hostium suorum mentibus & auribus attem- peraret.

ἐγὼ πάσῃ συνειδήσει ἀγαθῇ πεπολίτευμαι τῷ Θεῷ) Nunc quidem secundum Christum: ante vero quantum ex Pha- risæis magistris haurire potueram, Hoc illis opponit, à qui- bus pro impio, Deique hoste habebatur. Πολιτεύεσθαι, Græcis Scriptoribus est vitæ genus sequi. Sic 2. Macc. VI. 1. XI. 25. passivo sensu sumitur Canone XIV. Sardicensis Synodi. Τῷ Θεῷ est coram Deo, ut vertit Syrus. Testem citat menti- um introspectorem.

Non bona fuit conscientia, aut conversatio, cum in Pharifaismo adhuc ageret, Nam se fuisse πρῶτον τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν agnoscit ipse, 1. Tim. I. 15. Ideoq; hæc de officii πολιτεία intelligenda: quod animi conscientia bona Deo serviverit in eo mu- nere, quod ipsi creditum fuit. Conf. 2. Cor. I. 12.

## 23:2
Ver. 2. But the High Priest Ananias) The son of Nebedaeus according to Josephus, Antiquities VIII. 3. Perhaps in Josephus c. XX. 6. for "to the High Priest Jonathan," one should write "Ananias." For Ananias seems to have returned from Rome, whither he had been sent with Cumanus. Ananias, who succeeded Josephus son of Camydus, is a different person from this one.

Others make this Ananias the last son of Annas the High Priest, inasmuch as he killed James the brother of the Lord after five years, and for that reason was deprived of the priesthood by King Agrippa: who, according to the testimony of Josephus, book XX, ch. 8, was bold, fierce, savage, and a Sadducee by sect.

He commanded those standing by him) The attendants, who are the שׂוֹטְרִים (shoterim) to the Hebrews.

To strike his mouth) In this also the fortune of the disciple is equal to the master, John XVIII. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ὁ δὲ Ἀρχιερεὺς Ἀνανίας) Nebedæi filius juxta Iosephum antiquæ historiæ VIII. 3. Forte apud Iosephum c. XX. 6. pro πρὸς τὸν Ἀρχιερέα τὸν Ἰωνάθην, scribendum Ἀνανίαν. Nam à Roma, quo cum Cumano missus fuerat, rediisse Ananias videtur. Alius ab hoc est Ananias qui Iosepho Cabæi successit.

Alii Ananiam ultimum Annæ Pontificis filium hunc faciunt, utpote qui post quinquennium Ja- cobum fratrem Domini occidit, & ob id ab A- grippa Rege Pontificatu privatus fuit : qui teste Iosepho l. XX. c. 8. audax, ferus, sævus & secta Sad- ducæus fuit.

Ἐπέταξε τοῖς παρεστῶσιν αὐτῷ) Apparitoribus, qui שׂוֹטְרִים Hebræis.

Τύπτειν αὐτοῦ τὸ στόμα) In hoc quoque par fortuna disci- puli cum magistro, Ioh. XVIII. 23.

## 23:2
Ver. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

## 23:3
Ver. 3. God is about to strike you) He uses the right of a Prophet. See what we have said on Luke XIII. 32, and add the response to the orthodox 125. Similar is that of Isaiah LII. 11: In sorrow you shall lie down. See also what Isaiah predicts of Shebna, XXII. 17, 18, and what we have noted there: And what Jeremiah says concerning King Jeconiah, XXIII. 30. Whether Ananias was dead or removed is uncertain; not long after this time, Ishmael son of Phabi was substituted.

Whited wall) An excellent simile to express impious men, who for the sake of honor or profit pretend to be pious.

Foul within, beautiful with a fair skin. Seneca uses a similar comparison: They are miserable, sordid, foul, and adorned on the outside after the likeness of their walls. This also belongs to the Prophets, to rebuke freely not only men who are Princes, but also Kings. See examples 1 Kings XVIII. v. 18, 2 Kings III. 13.

That the Apostle uses the right of a Prophet, as Isaiah ch. LII. 11, ch. XXII. 17, 18, and Jeremiah ch. XXIII. v. 30, he observes. Truly it was not railing, but a grave rebuke of hypocrisy, and a prediction of divine vengeance, both of which were of the Prophetic and Apostolic Spirit. Compare 1 Kings XVIII. v. 18, ch. XX. v. 39, 2 Kings III. 13, and therefore the Apostle would have needed no excuse, who nevertheless thought the fierce man should be softened later with kind words, v. 5. For this offense was not light, but enormous, and it was being committed publicly, therefore it was deservedly rebuked. 1 Tim. V. 20, for to strike a man without hearing the case is a grave transgression. He therefore called him a whited wall, not with the intention of railing, but to strike the man's conscience: just as Christ compared the Pharisees to whited sepulchres. Which simile excellently expresses an impious man pretending to be pious for the sake of honor or profit: as Seneca says: they are miserable, he says, sordid, foul, and adorned on the outside after the likeness of their walls. Who also pronounced philosophers teaching honest things, but living foully, to be like the boxes of certain apothecaries, whose labels promise a remedy, while poison lurks within.

And do you sit judging me according to the law) The judicial law remained as long as the republic remained: and according to it, Hebrew judges were bound to judge, within those limits of jurisdiction which the Romans granted to them.

And acting contrary to the law do you command me to be struck) The case not yet heard. See what we have said on the cited passage of John and above ch. XVI. ver. 32. παρανομῶν (acting contrary to the law) is the מעל (ma'al) of Psalm LXXI. v. 4.

It is contrary not only to the Mosaic judicial law, but to the very law of nature, that punishment be inflicted before the case is heard, and thus an innocent person be struck, which the Gentiles themselves acknowledged, Acts XXV. 16. Compare John XVIII. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Τύπτειν σε μέλλει ὁ Θεὸς) Utitur jure Prophetæ. Vide quæ diximus ad Luc. XIII. 32. & adde responsum ad orthodoxos 125. Simile illud Esaiæ LII. 11. In dolore cu- babitis. Vide & quæ Sobnæ prædicit Esaias XXII. 17. 18 & quæ ibi à nobis notata : Et quæ de Rege Iechonia Ieremias XXIII. 30. Ananiæ incertum mortuo an amoto, non mul- to post hoc tempus suffectus est Ismael Phabi.

Τοῖχε κεκονιαμένε) Egregia similitudo ad exprimendos homines impios, qui honoris aut commodi causa pios se simulant.

Introrsum turpes, speciosi pelle decora. Pari comparatione utitur Seneca: Miseri sunt, sordidi, turpes. & ad similitudinem parietum suorum extrinsecus culti. Etiam hoc Prophetarum est libere reprehendere, non viros tan- tum Principes, sed & Reges. Exempla vide 1. Reg. XVIII. v. 18. 2. Reg. III. 13.

Uti Apostolum Jure Prophetæ, ut Esaiam c. LII. 11. c. XXII. 17. 18. & Jeremiam cap. XXIII. v. 30. observat. Nimirum non erat convitium, sed gravis reprehensio hypocrisœos, & prædictio divi- næ vindictæ, quæ utraque Spiritus fuit Prophetici & Apostolici. Conf. 1. Reg. XVIII. v. 18. c. XX. v. 39. 2. Reg. III. 13. ideoque nulla excusatione opus ha- buisset Apostolus, qui tamen benignis verbis ho- minem ferocem postea leniendum duxit v. 5. Deli- ctum enim hoc nec leve fuit, sed enorme, & publi- ce hic committebatur, ideo merito reprehensum est. 1. Tim. V. 20. nam non audita causa hominem percutere, gravis est transgressio. Parietem de- albatum ergo dixit non convitiandi animo, sed ut feriret hominis conscientiam : quemadmodum Christus Pharisæos sepulchris dealbatis compara- vit. Quæ similitudo egregie exprimit hominem impium honoris aut commodi causa pium se si- mulantem: uti Seneca: miseri sunt, inquit, sor- didi, turpes, & ad similitudinem parietum suorum extrinsecus culti. Qui etiam Philosophos ho- nesta docentes, at turpiter viventes, similes pro- nunciavit quorundam Pharmacoporum pyxidi- bus, quarum tituli remedium pollicentur, cum intus venenum latitet.

κὺ σὺ κάθῃ κρίνων με κατὰ νόμον) Manebat lex judicialis, quamdiu manebat respublica: & secundum eam judicare tenebantur Hebræi judices, intra eos cognitionis limites, quos Romani ipsis concedebant.

κὺ παρανομῶν κελεύεις με τύπτεσθαι) Nondum dicta cau- sa. Vide quæ diximus ad dictum Iohannis locum & supra cap. XVI. vers. 32. παρανομῶν est מעל Psalmi LXXI. v. 4.

Non id tantum legi judiciali Mosaica, sed ipsi naturæ legi adversatur, causa nondum di- cta pœnam inferri, adeoque innocentem percuti, quod gentiles ipsi agnovere Act. XXV. 16. Conf. Iob. XVIII. 23.

## 23:4
Ver. 4.

Do you revile the High Priest of God?) He was leaving behind a sharp sense of his own meaning, the reproach drawing much from the truth. See a similar instance in Luke ch. XI. ver. 45. Here λοιδορεῖς, just as there ὑβρίζεις.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

τὸν Ἀρχιερέα τῦ Θεῦ λοιδορεῖς) Acrem sui sensum relin- quebat, multum de vero trahens exprobratio. Simile vide Luc. cap. XI. vers. 45. Hic λοιδορεῖς, quod ibi ὑβρί- ζεις.

## 23:5
I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest) He wished to soothe a fierce man with kind words, as Nathan did before Josephus: 'Be of good courage; for you are a sensible man, having considered that kings, when they fall into anger, do not bestow more than this upon the just.' Ananias and the officers took these words of Paul as if Paul were excusing himself, that, being placed in such evils, it had not sufficiently come to his mind with whom he was dealing. For ידע is often to consider, ἐπισκοπεῖν, as in Esth. II. 11. But a more hidden meaning lay beneath, that he was not a priest or Prince of the council who had purchased those dignities with money. For Paul had learned this from Gamaliel, that a judge who has given money for the sake of obtaining an honor is in reality neither a judge, nor to be honored, but is to be held in the place of an ass, as it is in the Talmudic title concerning the Sanhedrin. The Jews specifically call such magistrates golden and silver gods, and deny that they are to be adored. Paul did not bring forward a true defense, having used his prophetic right, because that would not have been believed of him, nor would it have profited anything in that place.

For it is written) As if he were to say: I know from the Scriptures that this reverence is owed to those placed in that honor, lest they be provoked by curses, even true ones. See what we have said in book I. of the Law of War and Peace, ch. IV. 7.

You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people) The very words of the LXX of Exodus XXII. 28, where in the Hebrew it is נשיא, which is how the prince of the council was accustomed to be called, which office in those times the high priest mostly occupied. You have here ἐρεῖς κακῶς, with the Accusative, as also κακολογεῖν in 2 Macc. IV. 1.

Grotius notes that Ananias and the officers took these words as if Paul were excusing himself, that, being placed in such evils, it had not sufficiently come to his mind with whom he was dealing: because ידע is often to consider, ἐπισκοπεῖν, as in Esth. II. 11. Some even do not fear to affirm that Paul suffered something human here, and was destitute of grace; which Heinsius observed regarding certain (Reformed) theologians. Lorinus the Jesuit says that Paul speaks ironically and mockingly: as if to say, I did not know he was the Pontiff, because from his furious manner of speaking he does not seem to be a Pontiff, but a tyrant: which Cornelius does not disapprove of with this scheme: namely, that Paul was prudently playing the fox with foxes, acting craftily with the crafty, and that this seems to agree with his pleasant and versatile genius and talent. But these things are worthy of Jesuits, and of their genius and talent. And the Jesuit does not seem to trust this answer sufficiently, therefore more simply from Chrysostom. He thinks it is answered to Lyranus and Dionysius that Paul did not recognize the Pontiff because he had been absent from Jerusalem for a long time, and this Pontiff was new, and he was surrounded by many standing by; and from Sanctius he adds that Paul heard the voice, but because of the crowd did not know from whom it had been emitted, especially because this council seems to have been convened not in the ordinary place, for instance in the temple, but in the fortress Antonia, where they were sitting tumultuously and confusedly. Capellus in his vindication for Casaubon, book III. 2, from the monuments of the Hebrews concerning the houses of judgment, also observes this, that there were two primary judges, namely the high priest, and he who is called NASI properly so called, that is, Prince, just as in the time of Christ Annas was NASI, and Caiphas was AB, or Father, and both were called ἀρχιερεὺς: whence Baronius thinks that Paul could easily have been ignorant of which of the two was the high priest, if by chance he saw them sitting on high. But Andreas Rivetus, on Exod. XXII. v. 28, thinks that this does not resolve the difficulty, since Paul could not have been ignorant that the one he was addressing was a judge; and when he thus addresses him, 'You sit to judge according to the law,' v. 3. But that law in Exod. XXII does not only regard the princes of the people, or of the council, but judges in general, who are those gods whom one must not revile: Therefore with Augustine, and He replies to others that it is an ironic speech, not indeed one which is covered by the artifice of deception, but one which figuratively designates the matter in question in such a way that it stings more sharply: which the Pontiff either did not weigh at the time, or, driven by the stings of conscience, dissembled, God so moderating the matter that no greater harm resulted from it to Paul. Similarly, however, Grotius here: A more latent sense, he says, lay beneath: that he was not a priest, or prince of the Senate, who had obtained those dignities for a price. For Paul had learned this from Gamaliel, that a judge who had given money for the sake of obtaining honor is in reality neither a judge, nor to be honored, but is to be held in the place of an ass: as it is in the Talmudic title concerning the Sanhedrin. The Jews peculiarly call such magistrates golden and silver gods, and deny that they are to be adored. He adds: Paul did not bring forward a true defense, that he had used prophetic right, because that would not have been believed of him, nor would that have profited anything in this place. But as we acknowledge this to be true, so it is no less to be judged that what was said by Paul was true, that he did not acknowledge the high priest: which he said indeed not for the sake of an excuse, as if he himself had acted against the law of Exod. XXII, who reproves another transgressing the law, but that he might soothe with kind, yet most true words, a fierce man and the whole multitude stirred up by fury, as if he were to say that he by no means wished to strike the Pontiff himself, inasmuch as he did not know him, and therefore is falsely accused that he wished of set purpose to λοιδορεῖν a priest of God: but that he had only reproved one of the sitting judges for this iniquity publicly brought upon him. For although it is said in general, You shall not speak evil of the gods, and you shall not curse the Prince of your people, yet the reason is different in the judgment of a Prince, or President, and any assessor, since not individuals, but all or the greatest part finally complete the judgment, whereas the President represents the judgment by a certain reason. Therefore, he who reproves one of the assessors, carried away by ἀμετρίᾳ τῆς ἀυτολῆς and the fervor or fury of his affections, does not immediately detract from the judgment against the law. And for that reason, what Heinsius has here holds place: It is certain that there was such ἀναρχία then, that the Pontiffs were as if they were not from day to day: than which confusion as nothing is more foul, so nothing is more just, after Truth had been condemned by the faction and lies of the high priests themselves, the Hope of the fathers condemned, the high Priest of all condemned. Paul therefore, as he spoke bitterly, so he spoke truly what he felt, I did not know that he was, or was present, the Pontiff.

Latin:

Οὐκ ᾔδειν, ἀδελφοὶ, ὄτι ἐστὶν ἀρχιερεὺς) Benignis verbis le- nire hominem ferocem voluit, ut Nathan apud Jose- phum: Ἀτιθω· ὧν κὶ συνετὸς ἀνὴρ, λογισάμενος ὡς οἱ βασι- λεῖς ὅταν εἰς ὀργὴν ἐμπέσωσι ταύτη πλέον ἡ τῷ δικαίῳ νέμουσι. Hæc Pauli verba Ananias & apparitores sic accipiebant, quasi excusaret Paulus, quod sibi in istis malis constitu- to, non satis in mentem venisset, qui cum sibi res esset. Nam ידע sæpe est considerare ἐπισκοπεῖν, ut Esth. II. 11. Verum latentior sensus suberat, non esse eum sacerdotem aut Principem senatus, qui eas dignitates pretio compa- rasset. Didicerat enim hoc à Gamaliele Paulus, Judicem qui honoris consequendi causa pecunias dederit, revera neque Judicem esse, neque honorandum, sed asini ha- bendum loco, ut est in titulo Talmudico de Synedrio. Judæi peculiariter tales magistratus vocant Deos aureos & argenteos, eosque adorandos negant. Veram defen- sionem non attulit Paulus, prophetico jure se usum, quia id ei non fuisset creditum, nec id quicquam isto loco profuisset.

Γέγραπται γὰρ) Quasi dicat: Scio ex Scripturis, in eo honore positis deberi hanc reverentiam, ne, maledictis, etiam veris, lacessantur. Vide quæ diximus l. I. de Jure Belli & Pacis c. IV. 7.

Ἄρχοντα τῦ λαῦ συ ἐκ ἐρεῖς κακῶς) Verba ipsa LXX. Exodi XXII. 28. ubi in Hebræo est נשיא, quomodo vo- cari solebat princeps senatus, quem locum istis temporibus plerumque occupabat sacerdos summus. Habes hic ἐρεῖς κακῶς, cum Accusativo, ut & κακολογεῖν 2. Macc. IV. 1.

Hæc verba Anania & apparitores sic accepisse notat Grotius, quasi excusaret Paulus, quod sibi in istis malis constituto non satis in mentem venisset, qui cum sibi res esset: quia ידע sæpe est considerare, ἐπι- σκοπεῖν, ut Esth. II. 11. Nonnulli etiam humani quid passum hic esse Paulum, & à gratia destitutum fuisse affirmare non verentur; quod de Theologis qui- busdam (Reformatis) observavit Heinsius. Lori- nus Jesuita Ironice & irrisorie loqui Paulum ait: q. d. Nesciebam eum esse Pontificem, quia ex modo loquendi furioso non videtur esse Pontifex, sed Tyran- nus: quod non improbat Cornelius hoc Schemate: Paulum nempe prudenter cum vulpibus vulpinari, cum versutis versute agere, idque genio & ingenio ejus amæno & versatili congruum videri. Sed hæc Je- suitis digna, & eorum genio & ingenio. Neque satis fidere Jesuita videtur huic responsioni, ideo simplicius à Chrysost. Lyrano & Dionysio responderi censet, Paulum non agnovisse Pontificem, quia diu- tinus Hierosolyma abfuerat, & novus erat hic Ponti- fex, ac multis astantibus cingebatur; & è Sanctio ad- dit, Paulum audiisse vocem, sed præ turba nescisse, à quo emissa esset, præsertim quia concilium hoc co- actum videtur non in loco ordinario, puta in tem- plo, sed in arce Antonia, ubi tumultuarie & confuse sedebant. Capellus in vind. pro Casaub. l. III. 2. ex E- bræorum monumentis, de domibus judiciorum & hoc observat, duos fuisse primarios Judices, nempe summum Pontificem, & eum, qui appellatur NASI proprie sic dictus, id est, Princeps, quemadmodum tempore Christi NASI fuerit Annas, AB autem, sive Pater, Caiphas, & uterque dictus sit ἀρχιερεὺς: un- de Baronius putat facile ignorare potuisse Paulum, quisnam duorum, si forte in sublimi eos sedentes vidit, summus sacerdos esset. Sed id difficultatem non expedire censet Andr. Rivetus ad Exod. XXII. v. 28. siquidem non potuerit ignorare Paulus, eum quem alloquebatur, fuisse judicem; & quum ita compellet ipsum, Tu sedes, ut judices secundum legem, v. 3. Lex autem illa Exod. XXII. non tan- tum respiciat principes populi, vel concilii, sed in genere judices, qui sunt dii illi, quibus non detrahendum: Itaque cum Augustino, & aliis respondet, Ironicam orationem esse, non eam quidem, quæ fallendi artificio tegitur, sed quæ sic figurate rem, de qua agitur, designat, ut acrius pun- gat: quam vero vel non expenderit tum Pontifex, vel stimulis conscientiæ actus dissimulaverit, Deo ita rem moderante, ut majus incommodum inde non redundarit ad Paulum. Similiter vero Grotius hic: Latentior, inquit, sensus suberat: non esse eum sa- cerdotem, aut principem Senatus, qui eas dignitates pretio comparasset. Didicerat enim hoc à Gamaliele Paulus, judicem qui honoris consequendi causa pecu- nias dederit, revera neque judicem esse, neque hono- randum, sed asini habendum loco: ut est in titulo Thalmudico de Synedrio. Judæi peculiariter tales magistratus vocant deos aureos, & argenteos, eosque adorandos negant. Addit: Veram defensionem non attulit Paulus, prophetico jure se usum, quia id ei non fuisset creditum, nec id quicquam isto loco pro- fuisset. Sed uti hoc verum esse agnoscimus, ita non minus quoque censendum vere à Paulo dictum illud esse, quid non agnoverit Sacerdotem summum: id quod vero non excusationis causa dixit, quasi ipse contra legem Exod. XXII. egerit, qui alium le- gem transgredientem reprehendit, sed ut homi- nem ferocem, totamque multitudinem furore perci- tam verbis benignis, verissimis tamen leniret, quasi dicat, se neutiquam ipsum Pontificem summum ferire voluisse, utpote quem non noverit, adeoque falso argui, quod ex proposito sacerdotem Dei λοιδορεῖν voluerit: quin aliquem è judicibus assi- dentibus, ob hanc iniquitatem, sibi publice illa- tam injuriam solum redarguisse. Nam etsi in ge- nere dictum, Diis non deroges, & Principi populi tui ne maledicas, dispar tamen ratio est in judicio Principis, vel Præsidis, & assessoris cujusvis, quum non singuli, sed omnes aut maxima pars demum judicium absolvant, Præses autem judicium certa ratione repræsentet. Non ergo statim judicio de- trahit contra legem, qui aliquem assessorum ἀμε- τρίᾳ τῆς ἀυτολῆς & affectuum fervore an furore ab- reptum redarguit. Atque ea ratione locum habent, quæ hic habet Heinsius: Constat tantum tum fu- isse ἀναρχίαν, ut in diem quasi essent Pontifices aut non essent: qua confusione ut nihil fœdius, ita nihil justius, postquam factione summorum quoque sacer- dotum & mendaciis damnata Veritas, damnata pa- trum Spes, damnatus esset summus omnium Sacer- dos. Paulum ergo ut acerbe ita vere quod sentiret dixisse, Nesciebam esse, vel adesse, Pontificem.

## 23:6
v. 6. But Paul knowing that one part were Sadducees, and the other Pharisees) That there were Pharisees in the Sanhedrin appears in Matt. XXI. 45. Sadducees also above IV. 1. and V. 17. Paul did not lack human prudence either, by which, using it for the good of the Gospel, he usefully mixed the serpent with the dove and enjoyed the dissensions of his enemies.

I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee) Of a more accurate sect, as he said above c. XXII. 23. In the Manuscript it is son of Pharisees, that is, born of a father and mother of that institution. Thus Hebrew of Hebrews, as touching the law a Pharisee, Phil. III. 5.

concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am judged) It is ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. It would have been correct to say concerning the hope of the resurrection, I am called into judgment because of the hope concerning the resurrection. See what we said above c. XVII. 25. and John III. 5.

Others understand by hope the promised Christ, who is the hope of Israel Acts XXVIII. 29. But it is rightly established by the Syriac, which the Syrian expressed: I am judged concerning the hope of the resurrection of the dead; for the hope of Christians is nothing other than the resurrection of the dead, as Tertullian says, which, because the Apostle was preaching it in the resurrected Christ (who is the firstfruits of those who rise), he could openly say that he was accused concerning the resurrection of the dead brought about by the merit of Christ, and confirmed by the resurrection of Christ: because the question with the Jews was especially about him, whether Christ was resurrected from the dead? But no syncretism of Paul with the Pharisees is to be carved out here: because he did not simply call himself a Pharisee, but in a certain article, concerning the resurrection, in which they thought rightly, because it was better to commit himself to those he knew than to subject himself and the truth to the most present danger. And he wished thus to bring into the light the wickedness of the judges, that they conspire for the oppression of the truth, meanwhile being themselves distracted from one another by mutual discords.

Latin:

v. 6. Γνοὺς δὲ ὁ Παῦλος ὅτι τὸ ἓν μέρος ἐστὶ Σαδδουκαίων, τὸ δὲ ἕτερον Φαρισαίων) Pharisæos fuisse in Synedrio apparet Matth. XXI. 45. Sadducæos quoque supra IV. 1. & V. 17. Non deerat Paulo humana etiam prudentia, qua in bonum Evangelii utens, columbæ serpentem utiliter miscebat & inimicorum dissidiis fruebatur.

ἐγὼ Φαρισαῖός εἰμι, υἱὸς Φαρισαίου) Accuratioris sectæ, ut dixit supra c. XXII. 23. In Manuscripto est υἱὸς Φαρισαίων, id est, ex patre & matre natus ejus instituti. Sic Ἑβραῖος ἐξ Ἑβραίων, κατὰ νόμον Φαρισαῖος, Phil. III. 5.

περὶ ἐλπίδος καὶ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν ἐγὼ κρίνομαι) Est ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. Rectum fuerat περὶ ἐλπίδος ἀναστάσεως, ob spem de resurrectione in judicium vocor. Vide quæ diximus supra c. XVII. 25. & Joh. III. 5.

Alii per spem intelligunt Christum promissum, qui spes Israelis Act. XXVIII. 29. Sed recte bendya- de statuitur, quam expressit Syrus: De spe resurre- ctionis mortuorum judicor; spes enim Christia- norum non est alia, quam resurrectio mortuorum, ut ait Tertullianus, quam quia in Christo resusci- tato prædicabat Apostolus, (qui primitiæ resur- gentium) aperte dicere potuit, se accusari de resur- rectione mortuorum Christi merito parta, & resur- rectione Christi confirmata: quia de eo maxime quæstio erat cum Judæis, num Christus à mor- tuis resuscitatus sit? Non autem hic Syncretismus aliquis Pauli cum Pharisaeis exsculpetur: quia non simpliciter se Pharisaeum dixit, sed in certo articulo, de resurrectione, in quo illi recte sentiebant, quia melius erat eos notis se committere, quam sese & veritatem periculo praesentissimo subjicere. Et in lucem ita producere voluit improbitatem judicum, quod ad veritatis oppressio nem conspirent, ipsimet interim mutuis discordiis a se invicem distracti.

## 23:7
v. 7. there arose a dissension) that is, a disagreement, as above XV. 2. the multitude was divided) the same as in John VII. 43. and X. 19. there was a division. By a similar locution Virgil said: the crowd is divided. The multitude here is, עדה, the assembly of the Senators itself, with its assessors.

Latin:

v. 7. ἐγένετο στάσις) id est, dissidium, ut supra XV. 2. ἐσχίσθη τὸ πλῆθος) idem quod apud Johannem VII. 43. & X. 19. σχίσμα ἐγένετο. Simili locutione Virgilius dixit: scinditur vulgus. πλῆθος hic est, עדה, ipse coetus Senatorum, cum suis assessoribus.

## 23:8
v. 8. For the Sadducees indeed say that there is no resurrection, neither angel, nor spirit) They believed that God exists; but besides him nothing that was not perceived by the senses, that angels do not exist, that souls do not survive the bodies, and therefore that there would be no resurrection. See what we said on Matthew XXI. 27.

But the Pharisees confess both) he joined here the opinion concerning angels and concerning the spirit as one. The observation of Beza, brought from Budaeus, makes for this, that the word ἀμφότερον is said even of more than two, but only then when they constitute two kinds. Thus Cicero 2. against Catiline, not differing about two citizens, but about two kinds of citizens, I place both, he says, Quirites, in the same kind of predators and plunderers. Thus therefore Luke in this place also divides those errors of the Sadducees into two members. For because the nature of angels and souls is similar, or at least like, it seems to have been one error, to deny the existence of angels and souls. Josephus indeed writes expressly that the Sadducees thought that souls perish with the bodies. Doubtless Luke joins the angel and the spirit, as if one thing, and of the same kind and reason, and opposes them to the resurrection, which is of the body, as Chrysostom and Oecumenius have noted. Cajetan, however, less correctly thinks that the spirit, that is, the rational soul, is considered one with the resurrection and is opposed to an angel. There are indeed those who, with Scaliger, take πνεῦμα indefinitely, so that the sense is: they are so far from believing in an angel that they do not even believe in any spirit; since they even called God himself corporeal. But because the denial of the resurrection of the dead, of an angel, and of a spirit is proposed in the same way, μηδὲ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν, μηδὲ ἄγγελον, μηδὲ πνεῦμα, that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, that interpretation is simpler by which the soul released from the body is understood by spirit; for they denied that the soul of man exists separately, and said that it is nothing other than a crasis, or a certain temperament of the humors, in which error, as Theodore testifies, many physicians were, whence, as Abraham Zacuto of Salamanca teaches, they determined that the soul dies with the body.

Latin:

v. 8. Σαδδουκαῖοι μὲν γὰρ λέγουσι μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν, μηδὲ ἄγγελον, μηδὲ πνεῦμα) Deum esse credebant; sed praeter eum nihil quod non sensibus perciperetur, non Angelos ὑφεστάναι, non superesse corporibus animos, ideoq; nec fore ἀνάστασιν. Vide quae diximus ad Matthaeum XXI. 27.

Φαρισαῖοι δὲ ὁμολογοῦσι τὰ ἀμφότερα) conjunxit hic opinionem de angelis, & de spiritu tanquam unam, Facit huc observatio Bezae, e Budaeo adducta, vocem ἀμφότερον etiam de pluribus quam duobus dici, sed tum demum cum duo genera constituunt. Sic Cicero 2. in Catilinam, non de duobus civibus, sed de duobus civium generibus differens, Utrosque, inquit, Quirites, in eodem genere praedatorum direptorumque pono. Sic igitur Lucas hoc etiam loco errores istos Sadducaeorum in duo membra dividit. Nam quia similis est, aut certe παρόμοιος Angelorum ac animarum natura, unus error fuisse videtur, Angelorum & animarum ὑπόστασιν negare. Diserte vero scribit Josephus arbitratos fuisse Sadducaeos, animas cum corporibus interire. Nimirum Lucas Angelum & spiritum, quasi unum quid, & ejusdem generis ac rationis conjungit, & resurrectioni, quae corporis est, opponit, ut Chrysost. & Oecumen. notarunt. Minus autem recte Cajetanus spiritum, id est, animam rationalem putat unum censeri cum resurrectione, & opponi angelo. Sunt quidem qui cum Scaligero πνεῦμα indefinite accipiunt, ut sensus sit, tantum abest, ut Angelum credant, ut ne spiritum quidem ullum: siquidem & Deum ipsum corporeum dixerint: sed quia negatio resurrectionis mortuorum. Angeli, spiritus eodem modo proponitur, μηδὲ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν, μηδὲ ἄγγελον, μηδὲ πνεῦμα, non esse resurrectionem, neq; Angelum, neque spiritum, simplicior est illa interpretatio, qua per spiritum anima a corpore soluta intelligitur: negarunt enim animam hominis separatim exsistere, eamque nihil aliud esse, quam Crasin, seu temperamentum quoddam humorum dixerunt, in quo errore etiam, Theodoro teste, Medici multi fuere, unde Abrahamo Zachuth Salmaticensi docente, statuerunt, animam mori cum corpore.

## 23:9
v. 9. οἱ γραμματεῖς) Experts in the Law, assessors of the Senators. See what [is said] at Matt. II. 4. διεμάχοντο) they contended with others רבו. εἰ δὲ πνεῦμα ἐλάλησεν αὐτῷ) a certain inspiration penetrating the mind in a wonderful way, which is also ἐπίπνοια to the Greeks. See above X. 19. XI. 12. 28. XVI. 17. XX. 23. ἢ ἄγγελος) as Matt. I. 20. II. 13. Luke I. 11. above V. 19. VIII. 26. X. 3. 7. 22. XII. 7. 8. 9. 10. μὴ θεομαχῶμεν) It is a good Greek word which exists also in 2 Maccab. VII. 19. so also the noun θεομάχος above c. V. 39. where see what was said by us.

By πνεῦμα the Holy Spirit is understood here, not a certain unsubstantial inspiration; because to speak is an act; but actions belong to subjects. Therefore, a revelation made through the Holy Spirit is opposed to a revelation made through an angel. Grotius correctly acknowledges that that clause μὴ θεομαχῶμεν was wrongly omitted by the Vulgate; Cornelius a Lapide rashly asserts that it crept in from a marginal note. For Greek codices, and those the older ones, consistently have it.

PART II. The apparition of Jesus to Paul made in the camp.

Latin:

v. 9. οἱ γραμματεῖς) Legisperiti, assessores Senatorum. Vide quae ad Matth. II. 4. διεμάχοντο) contendebant cum aliis רבו. εἰ δὲ πνεῦμα ἐλάλησεν αὐτῷ) afflatus quidam in animum miro modo penetrans, qui & ἐπίπνοια Graecis. Vide supra X. 19. XI. 12. 28. XVI. 17. XX. 23. ἢ ἄγγελος) ut Matth. I. 20. II. 13. Luc. I. 11. supra V. 19. VIII. 26. X. 3. 7. 22. XII. 7. 8. 9. 10. μὴ θεομαχῶμεν) Vox est bene Graeca quae exstat & 2. Maccab. VII. 19. sic & nomen θεομάχος supra c. V. 39. ubi dicta a nobis vide.

Per πνεῦμα Spiritus S. hic intelligitur, non afflatus quidam ἀνυπόστατος: quia loqui actus est; Actiones autem suppositorum sunt. Itaque revelatio per Spiritum S. facta opponitur revelationi factae per Angelum. Perperam vero omissam illam particulam μὴ θεομαχῶμεν a Vulgato esse, Grotius recte agnoscit: quam irrepsisse e nota marginali, temere asserit Cornel. a Lapide. Habent enim eam constanter Gr. codices, iiq; vetustiores.

PARS II. Apparitio Iesu Paulo in castris facta.

## 23:10
v. 10. μὴ διασπαθῇ ὁ Παῦλος ὑπ’ αὐτῶν) Lest they should tear him to pieces, as the Thracian women did Orpheus, in which story Isocrates uses the word διασπασθῆναι. Lucian: 'They nearly tore me to pieces.' This is a description of fierce anger.

ἐκέλευσε τὸ στράτευμα καταβῆναι) He led the whole band of soldiers down from the Antonia into that chamber near the Temple where the Sanhedrin was held.

εἰς τὴν παρεμβολὴν) into the Antonia, as above.

But the assembly was not in the ordinary place near the temple, but at the Antonia. For there Paul could easily have been torn to pieces before the band of soldiers could be sent there from the Antonia. And Luke hints that Claudius had called the Sanhedrin to himself, ch. XXII, last verse, as we said there.

Latin:

v. 10. μὴ διασπαθῇ ὁ Παῦλος ὑπ’ αὐτῶν) Ne eum dis- cerperent, ut Orphea Thressæ, in qua historia vocem δια- σπασθῆναι usurpat Isocrates. Lucianus: μικρῷ γῦν με διεσπά- σαντο Atrocis iræ est hæc descriptio.

ἐκέλευσε τὸ στράτευμα καταβῆναι) Totam militum ma- num ab Antonia deduxit in conclave illud apud Tem- plum, in quo Senatus habebatur.

εἰς τὴν παρεμβολὴν) in Antoniam, ut supra.

At congregatio non erat in loco ordinario apud templum, sed penes Antoniam. Nam illic discerpi facile potuisset Paulus, antequam manus militum ab Antonia eo mitteretur. Et ad se vocasse Syne- drium Claudium, c. XXII, v. ult. Lucas innuit, ut ibi diximus.

## 23:11
v. 11. ἐπιστὰς αὐτῷ ὁ Κύριος) concerning this word see Luke II. v. 9, XXIV. 4, above XII. 7. The Lord appeared to him through an Angel, as several times above.

Nothing is held here concerning an Angel: therefore he is not to be thrust into the text. Nor are angelophanies and christophanies to be confused. Paul himself affirms in 1 Cor. XV that Christ appeared to him in person, who also was seen by Stephen when he was undergoing martyrdom, Acts VII; whence it is rightly taught against the Calvinists and Jesuits that Christ is not enclosed in the heavens in his body, so that he cannot be present with us on earth and appear whenever he wishes. How could an Angel speak thus, 'as you have testified of me' (τὰ περὶ ἐμοῦ), those things which it was necessary to testify of me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify at Rome? Did Paul testify of an Angel in Jerusalem, or was he bound to testify of an Angel at Rome? But he of whom he had testified is said here to have 'come upon' or 'stood by' him (ἐπιστάς). Nor is the Lord (ὁ Κύριος) ever said to have appeared, stood by, or come upon anyone when an Angel is appearing, assisting, or coming upon them.

Θάρσει Παῦλε) The Lord gives him assurance that all that violence of the stirred-up mob will do him no harm. When the wicked plots against the just and gnashes his teeth, God laughs at him, Psalm XXXVII, v. 12, and does not advance his evil counsels, Psalm CXL. 9. But he protects the pious against those who lie in wait. Psalm XII, 6.

Οὕτω σε δεῖ κὰι εἰς ῥώμην μαρτυρῆσαι) That 'must' (δεῖ) signifies here a future event, as in Matthew XVI, v. 21, where see what is said. Nor does the Syriac interpret it otherwise here.

PART III. The abduction of Paul to Felix.

Latin:

v. 11. ἐπιστὰς αὐτῷ ὁ Κύριος) de hoc verbo vide Luc. II. v. 9. XXIV. 4. supra XII. 7. Dominus ei apparuit per An- gelum, ut supra aliquoties.

Nihil hic de Angelo habetur: non ergo ille in- gerendus textui. Nec confundendæ sunt ἀγγελο- φίαι & χριστοφανίαι. Apparuisse sibi Christum αὐ- τοπροσώπως Paulus ipse affirmat 1. Cor. XV. qui et- iam Stephano visus est, cum martyrium subiret, Actor. VII. unde contra Calvinos & Jesuitas recte docetur, Christum non esse in cœlis conclusum corpore, quo minus nobis in terra præsto sit, & apparere possit, quando velit. Quomodo Ange- lus ita loqui poterat, sicut testificatus es DE ME τὰ περὶ ἐμῦ, ea quæ de me testari oportebat in Jeru- salem, sic te oportet & Romæ testificari. Num de Angelo testatus erat Hierosolymis Paulus, aut te- stari debuit Romæ! Is autem de quo testatus erat, eidem hic ἐπισὰς supervenisse vel astitisse dicitur. Neque uspiam Angelo apparente, vel assistente, & superveniente, apparuisse, astitisse, aut super- venisse dicitur ὁ Κύριος Dominus.

Θάρσει Παῦλε) Certum eum facit Dominus omnem istam commotæ plebis violentiam nihil ipsi nocituram. Cum improbus adversus justum cogitat, frenditque denti- bus, Deus eum irridet, Psal. XXXVII, v. 12. & mala consi- lia non provehit, Psal. CXL. 9. Sed pios tutatur contra insi- diatores. Psal. XII, 6.

Οὕτω σε δεῖ κὰι εἰς ῥώμην μαρτυρῆσαι) Δεῖ illud rem fu- turam hic significat, ut Matth. XVI, v. 21. ubi dicta vide. Nec aliter hic interpretatur Syrus.

## 23:15
Vers. 15.

make known to the tribune) signify. For הודיע is translated to make known, Exod. XXXIII. v. 13. thus also below 22. Heb. XI. v. 14.

with the Sanhedrin) that is, not you alone, but together with your colleagues, so that there may be greater authority for the notification.

The Vulgate is obscure, Now therefore you make known to the tribune with Cornelius: the Syriac is clearer, You therefore with the council: that is, you and the council judge [it best] to the tribune. Beza, now therefore you prepare yourselves before the tribune from the will of the assembly. that he may bring him down to you tomorrow) Namely from the Antonia into the chamber; in which the Senate was held. as intending to inquire more accurately the things concerning him) more accurately than in the first examination. For defendants are accustomed to be heard more often at intervals of time, either because something new has become known to the judge, or so that it may be explored whether they are consistent with themselves. before he comes near to you) before he comes to you: Syriac, But it is signified more fully, that they wish to perpetrate the slaughter on the way, far enough from that place in which the Senate was held, so that the Senate could not be accused on that account. we are ready to kill him) Here also the τοῦ is redundant, as it is sometimes. For above he said, I am ready to die. Thus also below 20. they agreed to ask. Because they had decided to perpetrate the slaughter on the way, far enough from that place in which the Senate was held, they did not seek that Paul should be sent down from the Antonia, a higher place, into the chamber of that fortress which was lower, but into that chamber near the temple, in which the Senate was ordinarily held.

σὺν τῷ συνεδρίῳ) id est, non vos soli, sed una cum col- legis vestris, quo major significationi sit auctoritas.

Obscura est Vulgata, Nunc ergo vos notum faci- te tribuno cum Cornelio : luculentior Syrus, Vos igitur cum concilio : id est, vos & concilium judi- cate tribuno. Solent enim rei per inter- valla temporum saepius audiri, sive quod novi aliquid ju- dici innotuerit, sive ut exploretur an sibi constent. πρὸς τὸ ἐγγίσαι αὐτὸν) antequam ad vos veniat: Syrus, Sed amplius significatur, velle se caedem perpetrare in via, satis longe ab eo loco, in quo Senatus habebatur, ne Sena- tus eo nomine argui posset. ἕτοιμοί ἐσμεν τῦ ἀνελεῖν ἀὐτόν) Hic quoque τῦ abundat, ut aliquoties. Nam supra dixit, ἑτοίμως ἔχω ἀποθανεῖν. Sic & infra 20. συνέθεντο τῦ ἐρωτῆσαι. Quia in via perpetrare caedem constituerant, satis longe ab eo loco, in quo Senatus habebatur, non id expetebant, ut ex Antonia loco superiori in conclave arcis illius inferius dimitteretur Pau- lus, sed in conclave illud apud templum, in quo Se- natus ordinarie habebatur.

Verse 21.

Do not therefore be persuaded by them) The youth added this, out of pious affection for his uncle. and now they are ready) they are prepared, namely to kill him. Above 15. awaiting the promise from you) the message from you. For thus 'promise' is taken: Esther IV. 7 & Ezech. VII. v. 26 & 'to announce', to announce: Sirach XVI. 26. Vulgate, and now they are ready, awaiting your promise: So also the Syrian: in this sense, that when you have promised this to them, that you will by no means refuse them, they wait until you send him to be slaughtered. The sense perhaps comes to the same thing.

Vers. 21.

Σὺ ἶν μὴ πεισθῇς αὐτοῖς) Hoc juvenis addidit, ex pio in avunculum affectu. καὶ νῦν ἕτοιμοί εἰσι) parati sunt, nempe ad eum occiden- dum. Supra 15. προσδεχόμενοι τὴν ἀπὸ σῦ ἐπαγγελίαν) nuntium abs te. Sic enim ἐπαγγελία sumitur: Esther IV. 7. & Ezech. VII. v. 26. & ἐπαγγέλλειν, annunciare : Sirach. XVI. 26. Sensus forte eodem recidit.

## 23:22
Verse 22.

He dismissed the youth) he sent the youth away from him. Having commanded to tell no one that you have reported these things to me) The transition from indirect speech to direct is frequent for the Hebrews, but also for other writers.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

᾿Απέλυσε τὸν νεανίαν) dimisit a se juvenem. Παραγγείλας μηδενὶ ἐκλαλῆσαι ὅτι ταῦτα ἐνεφάνισας πρός με) Transitio ab indirecta oratione ad directam frequens Hebraeis, sed & aliis scriptoribus.

## 23:23
Verse 23.

Certain two of the centurions, he said, prepare two hundred soldiers) each one hundred soldiers, who were under him. Martial: Vare Paratonias Latia modo vite per urbes Nobilis, & centum dux memorande viris. and seventy horsemen) It is customary for cavalry to be assigned to infantry, to be a guard for them. This number makes a little more than two squadrons. and two hundred spearmen) Manuscript: two hundred javelin-throwers. To the Roman legions were attached auxiliaries from foreign soldiers, armed more lightly: Among these, besides slingers, there were those who threw weapons. These could seem to be called 'spearmen', nor do the Syrian and Arab read and understand it otherwise. But Suidas and the author of the Etymologies interpret 'spearmen' as guards. Meursius thinks those are meant who guarded those given to prison, and seized those who were ordered to be seized. Constantine Porphyrogenitus: οἱ δὲ λεγόμενοι τυρμάρχαι εἰς ὑπερ- γίαν τῶν σρατηγῶν ἐτάχθησαν, σημαίνει δὲ τοιῦτον ἀξίωμα τὸν

having under him five hundred archers, and three hundred peltasts and one hundred spearmen. But it is possible that from this passage of Luke, poorly read and understood, that name penetrated into the military of a later age.

Grotius maintains the ancient reading, amending the text from the authority of one codex. Which, however, is by no means to be conceded. Nor is there need here for any other than the received reading. For Suidas explains dexio-labous as guards, as Grotius himself observes, or bodyguards who do not depart from one's side, whether one chooses to take this of the tribune's own bodyguards, or whether they are so called to whom Paul was properly committed, so that as long as he was outside of danger, they would not depart from his side. For very often in this kind of speaking, the right is not opposed to the left, but in general declares the side. Beza observes that the Vulgate therefore translates them as lancers, because, forsooth, they are also called by the Greeks doryphoroi, the bodyguards of princes: whence he himself rendered it bodyguards. Paul was therefore led by 470 guards. For the tribune feared that those forty, who were conspiring for the death of Paul, might drag him away with a large crowd of the people.

from the third hour of the night) It is frequent in Syria to travel by night on account of the daytime heat. But here this plan had this purpose, that ambushes might not be made on the journey itself, Paul being led away before the news of that matter could reach the conspirators.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

Δύο τινὰς τῶν ἑκατοντάρχων, ἔπεν, ἑτοιμάσατε σρατιώτας δια- κοσίυς) quisque centum milites, qui sub se erant. Martialis: Vare Paratonias Latia modo vite per urbes Nobilis, & centum dux memorande viris. καὶ ἱππεῖς ἑβδομήκοντα) Solent peditibus equites attribui, qui eis praesidio sint. Hic numerus paulo plus, quam duas turmas facit. καὶ δεξιολάβυς διακοσίυς ) Manuscriptus: δεξιοβόλυς δια- κοσίυς. Legionibus Romanis aderant auxilia e milite exteri- no, armata levius: In iis praeter funditores, erant qui tela manumitterent, Hi videri possent dicti δεξιοβόλοι, nec ali- ter legere & accipere Syrus & Arabs. Verum Suidas & Ety- mologiae scriptor δεξιολάβυς interpretantur παραφύλακας, Putat Meursius intelligi eos qui carceri daros asservabant, & prehendebant eos qui prehendi jubebantur. Constanti- nus Porphyrogenneta: οἱ δὲ λεγόμενοι τυρμάρχαι εἰς ὑπερ- γίαν τῶν σρατηγῶν ἐτάχθησαν, σημαίνει δὲ τοιῦτον ἀξίωμα τὸν

ἔχοντα ὑφ' ἑαυτὸ ὁπλίτας τοξοφόρους πεντακοσίους, καὶ πελτα- στὰς τριακοσίους καὶ δεξιολάβους ἑκατόν. Sed fieri potuit, ut ex hoc loco Lucæ male lecto & intellecto id nomen in serioris ævi militiam penetraverit.

Antiquum obtinet Grotius, è versionibus e- mendans textum unius Codicis autoritate. Quod pèro minime concedendum. Neque hic opus est alia, quam recepta lectione. Nam δεξιολάβους παραφύλακας explicat Suidas, observante ipsomet Grotio, vel stipatores, qui à latere non discedunt, sive de ipsius Tribuni stipatoribus id accipere li- beat, sive ita vocentur, quibus proprie commit- tebatur Paulus, ut quoad extra periculum esset, ab ejus latere non discederent. Nam sæpissime dex- tra in hujusmodi genere loquendi non opponitur sinistræ, sed in genere latus declarat. Vulgatam ideo lancearios exponere observat Beza, quia ni- mirum à Græcis etiam dicuntur δορυφόροι princi- pum stipatores: unde ipse stipatores reddidit. De- ductus ergo Paulus à Præsidiariis 470. Timebat enim Tribunus, ne illi quadraginta, qui in necem Pauli conspirant, sicum traherent multo populi agmine.

ἀπὸ τρίτης ὥρας τῆς νυκτὸς) Frequens est in Syria noctibus iter facere ob calores diurnos. Verum hic hoc consilium eo pertinebat, ne in ipsu itinere insidiæ fierent, ante deducto Paulo, quam ad conjuratos ejus rei notitia perveniret.

## 23:24
Verse 24.

And to provide beasts) Contrary to what has just happened here, the discourse shifts from direct to indirect.

that having put Paul on board) See Luke 10:34, 19:35.

to Felix the governor) This Felix was the brother of Pallas, who had all power with Claudius, placed over Judea and thinking all evil deeds done by him would go unpunished, being supported by such great power, as Tacitus says in Annals 12, who also says of the same in Histories 5: Antonius Felix, through all cruelty and lust, exercised royal power with a servile mind. Nothing less than descended from the kings of Arcadia, which their flatterers wanted to persuade the common people of. And yet this man, servile in both origin and character, was placed over not only cohorts and others, and the province of Judea, but was also the husband of three queens, according to Suetonius in the Life of Claudius 28; which understand not at the same time, as some wrongly interpret that 'husband of one wife' in Paul; but one dead, another: and understand queens as daughters and granddaughters of kings, just as Antigone and Electra are 'queens' among the tragic poets. One of these queens was Drusilla, named below in 24:24. Sister of King Agrippa; to whom, for the sake of obtaining the favor of the Caesars, a name was given from that family which was then ruling, whence Agrippa himself also had his name.

the governor) The procurator of Judea, in place of the president. See what is said at Matthew 27:2.

Concerning the words of Paul, that 'husband of one wife' does not suppose successive polygamy, but simultaneous, it will be seen in its own place with God, that is, at 1 Timothy 3:2.

Vers. 24.

Κτήνη τε παραστῆσαι) Contra quam modo transit hic o- ratio à directa in indirectam.

ἵνα ἐπιβιβάσαντες τὸν Παῦλον) Vide Luc. X. 34. XIX. 35.

πρὸς Φήλικα τὸν ἡγεμόνα) Felix hic Pallantis, qui apud Claudium omnia potuit, frater fuit, Judææ impositus & cuncta male facta sibi impune ratus, tanta potentia subni- xo, ut ait Tacitus Annalium XII. qui de eodem Historia- rum V. Antonius Felix per omnem sævitiam ac libidinem, jus regium servili ingenio exercuit. Nihil minus quam Ar- cadiæ regibus ortus, quod illorum adulatores plebi per- suadere volebant. Et hic tamen homo, servili & ortu & in- genio, non cohortibus tantum, aliisque, & provinciæ Judææ præpositus fuit, sed & trium reginarum maritus, reste Sue- tonio in Claudii vita 28. quod intellige non eodem tem- pore, sicut quidam male interpretantur illud μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα apud Paulum; sed alia mortua aliam: & reginas in- tellige regum filias & neptes, quomodo Antigone & Ele- ctra ἄνασσαι apud Tragicos. Harum reginarum una fuit Drusilla infra nominata XXIV. v. 24. Agrippæ Regis soror; cui ad adipiscendam Cæsarum gratiam nomen datum ex ea familia quæ tum imperabat, unde & Agrippa ipse habebat nomen.

τὸν ἡγεμόνα) Judææ procuratorem, vice præsidis. Vi- de quæ dicta ad Matth. XXVII. 2.

De Pauli verbis, quod μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα non supposuerit polygamiæ successivæ, sed simulta- neæ, suo loco videbitur cum Deo, hoc est, ad 1. Tim. III. v. 2.

Verse 27.

τῷ μέλλοντα ἀναιρεῖσθαι ὑπ' αὐτῶν) that is, when it was already near that he should be killed by them. In this sense μέλλειν is found also in Thucydides, Demosthenes, and others.

ἐπιστὰς σὺν τῷ στρατεύματι; It is well translated as 'coming upon' or 'supervening', as above in chapter 4:1.

μαθὼν ὅτι Ῥωμαῖός ἐστι) This aorist designates no certain time: and it is worth as much as καὶ ἔμαθον.

Thus there is no need to accuse Claudius of a lie, which is done here by Cornel. à Lapide and Beza, and by the former indeed, on account of the Vulgate version, 'knowing that he is a Roman'. For when he snatched Paul from the hands of the Jews, he did not yet know that he was a Roman.

## 23:30
Verse 30.

But when it was reported to me that a plot was about to be against the man) he began the speech as if he were going to say μελλόυσης; but he said μέλλειν, as if μηνυθέντος δέ μοι ἐπιβυλὴν had preceded. Thus the construction is often according to the sense rather than the words, as we said at Eph. I. 3.

Here Ludov. de Dieu notes Beza, who had said that he did not see how these things cohere: There seems, he says, to be no anomaly of syntax here, since it is permitted to translate word for word: But when the plots were indicated to me, this man, that it would be that they would be made by the Jews; nor do I think these things should be translated otherwise. For they were indicated to him when they were only conceived in the mind, not yet done, since they were only to be put into effect the next day. It is also to be observed that μέλλω, although it contains the signification of the future in itself, and thus is accustomed to be constructed only with the present, or an aorist having the signification of the present, and to give it the force of the future, is here nevertheless constructed with the future. Which we have not observed elsewhere in these books, and in this book indeed with only ἔσεσθαι, namely here, and Acts II. 28. and XXIV. 15. 16. and XXVII. v. 10. Among other authors, however, it sometimes happens with other verbs also, as in Demosth. pro Cor. What was I about to command or what was I about to advise him to do? See other examples from Synesius and Thucydides among the lexicographers. These are Dievius's words.

Having commanded also the accusers to speak the things against him before you) According to Roman custom, below 35. XXV. 16.

ἔῥῥωσο) which is the solemn closing of letters. See above c. XV. 29.

Latin:

Vers. 30.

μηνυθέντος δέ μοι ἐπιβυλῆς εἰς τὸν ἄνδρα μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι) serinonem ita incepit quasi dicturus esset μελλόυσης· dixit an- tem μέλλειν, quasi præcessisset μηνυθέντος δέ μοι ἐπιβυλὴν. ita sæpe constructio sit ad sensum magis quam ad verba, ut diximus Eph. I. 3.

Notat hic Bezam Ludov. de Dieu, qui dixerat se non videre quomodo hæc cohæreant: Nulla, inquit, hic videtur esse syntaxeos anomalia, quum ad verbum vertere liceat: Indicatis autem mihi insidiis, hunc virum, fore ut fierent à Judæis; nec aliter hæc vertenda censeo. Indicata enim ipsi fuere, quum mente concepta solum, nondum facta essent, quippe postridie demum effectui danda. Observan- dum quoque μέλλω, etsi futuri significationem in se contineat, adeoque non nisi cum præsenti, aut aoristo præsentis significationem habente, construi, eique futuri vim dare soleat, hic tamen cum futu- ro construi. quod alibi in hisce libris non obser- vavimus, & in hoc quidem libro cum solo ἔσεσθαι, nempe hic, & Act. II. 28. & XXIV. 15. 16. & XXVII. v. 10. Apud alios tamen autores cum aliis etiam verbis interdum contingit, ut apud Demosth. pro Cor. τί ἔμελλον κελεύσειν ἢ τί συμβυλεύσειν αὐτῇ ποιεῖν; quid jussurus essem, aut quid consulturus ei facere? alia exempla ex Synesio & Thucydide vi- de apud Lexicographos. Hæc Dievius.

παραγγείλας κὶ τοῖς κατηγοροῖς λέγειν τὰ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐπὶ σῦ) Ex more Romano, infra 35. XXV. 16.

ἔῥῥωσο) quæ solennis epistolarum clausula. Vide supra c. XV. 29.

εἰς τὴν Ἀντιπατρίδα) It is a city of Judea to the west of the Jordan. See Ptolemy.

It was distant from Jerusalem by an interval of three miles, from where to Caesarea Stratonis there remained still seven miles. That place was previously called Capharfalam, later built by King Herod it received its name from his father Antipater; today it is a village, which is called Assur, as noted by Brocardus and Adrichomius. Conf. Joseph. lib. XVI. c. V.

Distabat ab Hierosolymis trium milliarium in- tercapedine, unde ad Cæsaream Stratonis super- erant adhuc septem milliaria. Illa prius Capharfa- lama dicta, post ab Herode Rege extructa à Patre Antipatro nomen accepit; hodie villa est, quæ As- sur dicitur, notante Brocardo & Adrichomio. Conf. Joseph. lib. XVI. c. V.

## 23:33
v. 33. οἵ τινες) This is to be referred to the more remote, that is, to the horsemen.

εἰσελθόντες εἰς Καισάρειαν) where Felix happened to be at that time, as governors were accustomed to travel through the province, namely Caesarea Stratonis.

Παρέσησαν κὲ τὸν Παῦλον αὐτῷ) It is well translated as 'they set him'. Thus, where in the Digest it is 'to set before a court' (judicio sistere), the Greek Basilica have παρισᾶν. Paul did not say to the centurions or the horsemen that what they were doing was unlawful, but he made use of the benefit of public protection. The Fathers in the African Council, ch. 83: 'Against whose fury we can obtain no unusual safeguards, nor any other than those from the Scriptures, just as the Apostle Paul, as is known to the faithful in the Acts of the Apostles, removed the conspiracy of the factious even with military aid.'

v. 33. οἵ τινες) Hoc ad remotius, id est, ad equites refe- rendum.

εἰσελθόντες εἰς Καισάρειαν) ubi tum forte erat Felix, ut so- lebant præsides provinciam perambulare, Cæsaream nem- pe Stratonis.

Παρέσησαν κὲ τὸν Παῦλον αὐτῷ) Bene vertitur stiterunt. Sic ubi in digestis est judicio sistere, Græca Basilica habent παρισᾶν. Paulus non dixit centurionibus aut equitibus illi- citum esse quod agebant, sed usus est beneficio publicæ tu- telæ. Patres in Africano Concilio cap. 83. Quorum contra furorem possimus non insolita, nec à Scripturis impetrare alte- ra præsidia, quomodo Apostolus Paulus, sicut in Apostolorum actibus fidelibus notum est, factiosorum conspirationem militari etiam submovit auxilio.

## 23:34
v. 34. ἐκ ποίας ἐπαρχίας ἐσὶ) Ἐπαρχία is a province, also below ch. XXV. v. 1. Nor do the Greeks who wrote about Roman affairs call a province anything else. Also in the Glossary: Ἐπαρχία, a province.

v. 34. ἐκ ποίας ἐπαρχίας ἐσὶ) Ἐπαρχία est provincia etiam infra c. XXV. v. 1. Nec aliter appellant provinciam Græci, qui Romanas res scripsere. In Glossario quoque: Ἐπαρχία provincia.

## 23:35
v. 35. διακύσομαί συ, ἔφη, ὅταν κό οἱ κατήγοροί συ παρα- γίνωνται) according to the old saying: 'Do not judge a case before you hear the story of both sides.' Moreover, διακύειν is the same as ἀκύειν, as appears in Deut. I. 16, Job IX. 33. Both Plato and Plutarch use it in this way.

ἐν τῷ πραιτωρίῳ τῦ Ἡρώδε) Namely, that which was in Caesarea. See above XII. 17. & seqq. Praetorium takes its name from the Roman praetor, that is, the Emperor: but as is wont to happen, the use of that word began to be extended more broadly to all the houses of illustrious men. See Matt. XXVII. 27, Mark XV. 16, John XVIII. 28, 33, XIX. 9, Phil. I. 13. And among the writers on rural affairs, the praetorium is the part of a villa in which the master dwells.

Latin:

v. 35. διακύσομαί συ, ἔφη, ὅταν κό οἱ κατήγοροί συ παρα- γίνωνται) juxta dictum vetus: Μηδὲ δίκην δικάσῃς, πρὶν ἀμφοῖν μῦθον ἀκύσῃς. Est autem διακύειν idem, quod ἀκύειν, ut apparet Deut. I. 16. Job. IX. 33. Utuntur sic & Plato & Plutarchus.

ἐν τῷ πραιτωρίῳ τῦ Ἡρώδε) Nempe quod erat Cæsarea. Vide supra XII. 17. & seqq. Prætorium à prætore Roma- no, id est, Imperatore nomen habet: sed ut fieri solet cœpit proferri latius ejus vocis usus ad omnes domos viro- rum illustrium. Vide Matth. XXVII. 27. Marci XV. 16. Joh. XVIII. 28. 33. XIX. 9. Phil. I. 13. Et apud rusticæ rei scripto- res prætorium est pars villæ, in qua dominus habitat.

## 24:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXIV. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Paul, accused by Ananias and the Elders through Tertullus of sedition and the profanation of the temple, institutes his defense before Felix, that his adversaries can prove no such thing. He professes, however, his faith in Jesus to be in agreement with Moses and the Prophets, and his hope of the resurrection, and his zeal to keep a blameless conscience, and how he was found in the temple on the occasion of his purification, challenging them to explain if they should find any iniquity in him. But Felix, to whom that religion was unknown, deferred the matter until the arrival of the tribune Lysias. But afterwards, when Felix had at some time heard Paul speaking with his wife Drusilla about faith, about justice, and about chastity, and the future judgment, and expected money from Paul in vain, he left him to his successor Festus.

There are two parts: I. The accusation of Paul before Felix, and his defense, to v. 23. II. Paul's courtly sermon before Felix and Drusilla, and its consequence, to v. 27.

PART I. The accusation of Paul before Felix, and his defense.

μετὰ δὲ πέντε ἡμέρας) in the Manuscript: μετὰ δέ τινας ἡμέρας.

κατέβη) those who go from Jerusalem toward the sea are said to descend.

The customary reading is to be retained: However, the five days are not to be understood from the capture of Paul with Cajetan, but from his arrival in Caesarea. Conf. chap. XXI. 17.

Ἀνανίας μετὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων) The Manuscript is better: μετὰ πρεσβυτέρων τινων, with some from the Senate, above XXIII. 14.

But why is it better thus? Does not the same sense remain according to the received reading, so that there is no need for correction? For that expression μετὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων can also be taken indefinitely, only of those who had been deputed and represented the whole College.

καὶ ῥήτορος Τερτύλλε τινὸς) A Roman man, who would know both the Roman language and the formulas of legal actions better. ῥήτωρ, to the Greeks is an orator: the Latins use that Greek word more for teachers of speaking, whom the Greeks call σοφιστάς.

οἵτινες ἐνεφάνισαν τῷ ἡγεμόνι) ἐμφανίζειν is to make an information, as we saw above c. XXIII. 13. 22. and Esther II. 22. in the Glossary: ἐμφανίζω I allege, I intimate. Wherefore I judge the sense here to be: they brought an accusation, they declared Paul a defendant, they registered him as a criminal in the Roman manner.

Latin:

CAPUT XXIV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Paulus accusatus ab Anania & Senioribus per Tertullum, objeditionem & templi propha- nationem, apologiam instituit coram Felice, quod nihil tale docere possint adversarii. Profitetur autem fidem suam de Jesu, Mosi & Prophetis consentaneam, & spem resur- rectionis, ac studium servandi immacula- tam conscientiam, & quomodo occasione pu- rificationis suae in templo inventus fuerit, provocans, ut, si quid iniqui in ipso repere- rint, edisserant. Sed Felix, cui ignota religio illa erat, rem differebat ad Lysis tribuni ad- ventum. Postea vero cum aliquando Felix cum conjuge sua Drusilla Paulum de fide, de justitia, & de castitate, ac futuro judicio audivisset dicentem, & frustra expectaret a Paulo pecuniam, reliquit eum Festo suc- cessori.

Partes duae sunt: I. Pauli accusatio coram Fe- lice, ejusdemque apologia, ad v. 23. II. Pauli aulica concio coram Felice & Drusilla, ejusque consequentia, ad v. 27.

PARS I. Pauli coram Felice accusatio, ejusdemque apologia.

μετὰ δὲ πέντε ἡμέρας) in Manuscripto: μετὰ δέ τινας ἡμέρας.

κατέβη) ab Hierosolymis mare versus qui eunt descen- dere dicuntur.

Retinenda consueta lectio: Non autem intel- ligendi sunt quinque dies a captura Pauli cum Ca- jetano: sed ab adventu ejus in Caesaream. Conf. cap. XXI. 17.

Ἀνανίας μετὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων) Melius Manuscriptus: μετὰ πρεσβυτέρων τινων, cum aliquibus e Senatu, supra XXIII. 14.

Cur vero melius ita? Annon idem manet sen- sus juxta receptam lectionem, ut nulla opus sit correctione? nam indefinite accipi potest etiam illa locutio μετὰ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, tantum eo- rum, qui deputati fuerant, & totum Collegium re- praesentabant.

καὶ ῥήτορος Τερτύλλε τινὸς) Homine Romano, qui & lin- guam Romanam, & actionum formulas melius nosset. ῥήτωρ, Graecis est orator: Latini eam vocem Graecam ma- gis de dicendi magistris usurpant, quos Gr. σοφιστὰς vocant.

οἵτινες ἐνεφάνισαν τῷ ἡγεμόνι) ἐμφανίζειν est indicium facere, ut vidimus supra c. XXIII. 13. 22. & Esther II. 22. in Glossario: ἐμφανίζω allego, intimo. Quare hic sensum esse arbitror: accusationem attulere, reum egere Paulum, inscripsere in crimen more Romano.

Vers. 2.

κληθέντος δὲ αὐτῦ) that is, having been ordered to be brought. For he was being kept under military guard.

Vers. 2.

κληθέντος δὲ αὐτῦ) id est, adduci jusso. Nam sub mili- tari custodia servabatur.

## 24:3
Vers. 3.

Πολλῆς εἰρήνης τυγχάνοντες διὰ σῦ) Among the rhetorical precepts is that of making the judge well-disposed toward oneself by praising him, which Paul did not ignore, as appears below 10. & XXVI. v. 2. 3. See Cicero's exordia in Pro Roscio Amerino, Pro Milone, and others. Ambrose, book VI of De Sacramentis, last chapter: 'Whence also those wise orators have this discipline, that they present the judge as a supporter to themselves: for they begin with his praises, so that they may make the examiner well-disposed toward them.'

κὶ κατορθωμάτων γινομένων τῷ ἔθνει τύτῳ διὰ τῆς σῆς προ- νοίας) The manuscript is better with διορθωμάτων. κατόρθωμα among the philosophers, as Cicero teaches us, is a deed exacted according to the most perfect rule of wisdom. But by the word διορθωμάτων it is signified that many things in matters pertaining to the Jews were restored for the better by Felix: for this is what διορθῦν is to the Hebrews תקן, and the Syriac took it thus.

No reason appears again for departing from the common reading: which is not even right for the sake of a single codex. Since κατορθώματα are called those things which are accomplished by someone with both the greatest virtue and success, according to Beza, with whom Camerarius agrees: The word, he says, κατορθῶσαι has the meaning of perfection, and of a thing done well and excellently. Polybius lib. 1: ὡς δι' αὐτὸν καὶ διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν πρόνοιαν κατωρ- θωκώς. As if he himself had managed the matter well through his own providence. And the Stoics called a perfect duty a κατόρθωμα. According to Dievius from Ps. XCVI. 1, 1 Par. XVI. 30, Prov. XII. 3, 19, & ch. IV. 19, it could be rendered: establishments. Finally, according to the Glossary, κατορθῶ is to correct, as the Vulgate not inconveniently [renders it]; and many things are corrected through your providence.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Πολλῆς εἰρήνης τυγχάνοντες διὰ σῦ) Inter praecepta Rhe- torica est judicem sibi laudando benevolum reddere, quod nec Paulus ignoravit, ut apparet infra 10. & XXVI. v. 2. 3. Vide Ciceronis exordia pro Roscio Amerino, pro Milone, & alia. Ambrosius libro VI. de Sacramentis capite ultimo, Vnde & oratores isti sapientes hanc habent disciplinam, ut ju- dicem sibi fautorem praestent: Incipiunt enim a laudibus ejus, ut benevolum sibi faciant cognitorem.

κὶ κατορθωμάτων γινομένων τῷ ἔθνει τύτῳ διὰ τῆς σῆς προ- νοίας) Melius Manuscriptus, διορθωμάτων. κατόρθωμα apud Philosophos, ut Cicero nos docet, est factum exactum ad perfectissimam sapientiae regulam. Sed voce διορθωμάτων significatur, multa a Felice in rebus ad Judaeos pertinentib. suisse in melius restituta: nam hoc est διορθῦν Hebraeis תקן & ita accepit Syrus.

Nulla iterum apparet causa discedendi a com- muni lectione: quod nec fas est in unius codicis gratiam. Quum κατορθώματα dicantur, quæ sum- ma tum virtute tum felicitate ab aliquo perficiun- tur, secundum Bezam, cui consonat Camerarius: Verbum, inquit, κατορθῶσαι significationem habet perfectionis, & rei bene ac preclare gestæ. Polybius lib. 1. ὡς δι' αὐτὸν καὶ διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν πρόνοιαν κατωρ- θωκώς. Quasi ipse per & sua providentia rem bene gessisset. Et Stoici κατόρθωμα vocarunt officium per- fectum. Secundum Dievium è Psal. XCVI. 1. Par. XVI. 30. Prov. XII. 3. 19. & cap. IV. 19. reddi possit, stabilimenta: Denique juxta Glossar. κατορθῶ est corrigo, ut nonTx incommode Vulgata; & multa corrigantur per tuam providentiam.

## 24:4
Vers. 4.

ἵνα δὲ μὴ ἐπὶ πλεῖόν σε ἐγκόπτω) in the Glossary: ἐγκόπτω is to hinder: and Paul takes it thus in Rom. XV. 22, Galat. V. v. 7, I. Thess. II. v. 18. But he hinders the President from business who detains him by speaking to him for a long time. This also is among the rhetorical artifices, to promise that one will be brief, especially before busy people.

τῇ σῇ ἐπιεικείᾳ) with that kindness which is your custom. ἐπιείκεια and πραότης are accustomed to be joined. Here is understood the ability and patience in listening.

Vers. 4.

ἵνα δὲ μὴ ἐπὶ πλεῖόν σε ἐγκόπτω) in Glossario: ἐγκόπτω impedio: & ita sumit Paulus Rom XV. 22. Galat. V. v. 7. I. Thess. II. v. 18. Impedit autem a negotiis Præsidem, qui diu alloquendo eum detinet. Est & hoc inter Rhetorica artificia, polliceri se brevem fore, præsertim apud occu- patos.

τῇ σῇ ἐπιεικείᾳ) ea humanitate qua soles. Solent con- jungi ἐπιείκεια & πραότης. intelligitur hic facultas & pa- tientia in audiendo.

## 24:5
Vers. 5.

εὑρόντες γὰρ τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον λοιμὸν) Thus Cicero said: plague of the state, in Pro Rabirio: plague of the fatherland, in Pro Sextio: plague of the Empire, in Pro Deiotaro.

καὶ κινεῖντα στάσιν πᾶσι τοῖς ἰουδαίοις, τοῖς κατὰ τὴν οἰκουμένην) the same sense as above XVII. 6.

πρωτοστάτην τε) in the Glossary πρωτοστάτης is a leader. Thus are called those who in art, who in a banquet, who in judgment or in any other matter hold the primary place. Thus Cyprian in the proconsular sentence is called the author of an iniquitous name and a standard-bearer.

of the sect of the Nazarenes) thus they were called in Judea, who outside Judea were called Christians, namely from their Lord Jesus the Nazarene. And so today also Jews and Mahometans call Christians. See what we have said at the beginning of Matthew.

In the Glossary: πρωτοστάτης is rendered as ὁ τάγματος ἡγούμενος, the Vulgate [renders it] author of sedition, factionary. Furthermore, they call the faithful Nazarenes also, John 1:11, Acts 2:12, ch. 3:6, ch. 4:10; indeed the Holy Spirit Himself calls Christ so, Matt. 2:last verse, nor did Christ hesitate to call Himself by this name, Acts 22:8, since it had been predicted long ago that the Messiah would be called by that name.

Vers. 5.

εὑρόντες γὰρ τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον λοιμὸν) Sic Cicero dixit; pe- stem civitatis, pro Rabirio: pestem patriæ, pro Sextio: pe- stes Imperii, pro Deiotaro.

καὶ κινεῖντα στάσιν πᾶσι τοῖς ἰουδαίοις, τοῖς κατὰ τὴν οἰκουμένην) idem sensus qui supra XVII. 6.

πρωτοστάτην τε) in Glossario πρωτοστάτης princeps. Sic vocantur qui in arte, qui in convivio, qui in judicio aut re quavis alia primarium locum obtinent. Sic Cyprianus in sententia proconsulari dicitur, auctor iniqui nominis & si- gnifer.

τῆς τῶν Ναζαραίων αἱρέσεως) ita in Judæa vocabantur, qui extra Judæam Christiani, nempe à Domino ipsorum Jesu Nazareno. Et sic hodie quoque Judæi & Mahumetistæ Christianos appellant. Vide quæ diximus ad initium Mat- thæi.

In Glossario: πρωτοστάτης redditur ὁ τάγμα- τος ἡγούμενος, Vulgat. autor seditionis, factiona- rius. Porro Nazaræos vocant etiam fideles, Job. I. v. 11. Actor. II. 12. c. III. 6. c. IV. 10. imo vocat ita Christum ipse Spiritus S. Matth. II. v. ult. neque Christus Actor. XXII. 8. ab hoc nomine sese dubi- tavit nuncupare, quum olim eo nomine vocatum iri Messiam prædictum fuerit.

## 24:6
v. 6. who also tried to profane the temple) by introducing foreigners. A false charge.

whom also we took) The correct phrasing would have been: we ourselves took. Otherwise it is an anacoluthon, and that word 'finding' has no verb that corresponds to it. But similar things are found everywhere in good authors, and especially in our own. We noted something similar in Eph. 1:13.

and according to our law we wanted to judge) Namely, as one who had brought foreigners into the temple: in which crime the execution of capital punishment was permitted to them; as we said above at 21:28.

Latin:

v. 6. ὃς καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν ἐπείρασε βεβηλῶσαι) introductis alie- nigenis. Falsum crimen.

ὃν καὶ ἐκρατήσαμεν) Recta locutio fuerat: αὐτοὶ ἐκρατή- σαμεν. Alioqui est ἀνακόλουθον, nec illud εὑρόντες verbum habet quod ei respondeat. Sed similia passim apud bonos auctores reperiuntur, maxime vero apud nostros. Simile quid notavimus Eph. I. 13.

καὶ κατὰ τὸν ἡμέτερον νόμον ἠθελήσαμεν κρίνειν) Nempe tanquam eum qui alienigenas in templum induxisset: in quo crimine capitalis pœnæ ipsis permissa erat exsecutio; ut diximus supra XXI. 28.

## 24:7
Vers. 7.

but Lysias coming up) The same as 'standing by' above at 23:27. The scholiast of Thucydides: 'coming upon' is used for strangers; 'coming up' for one's own people: elsewhere: 'the stranger comes upon; the citizen comes up.' The same: 'to come up' signifies 'to come forward': thus also Athenaeus: 'I came forward shamelessly.'

with great violence took him away out of our hands) they call violence the help of one who prevents violence.

Vers. 7.

παρελθὼν δὲ Λυσίας) Idem quod ἐπιστὰς supra XXIII. 27. Scholiastes Thucydidis: ἐπελθόντες, ἐπὶ ξένων. παρελθόντες, ἐπὶ ἰδίων: alibi: ἐπέρχεται ὁ ξένος. παρέρχεται ὁ πολίτης. idem: τὸ παρελθεῖν, τὸ ἀντίκα δηλοῖ: sic & Athenæus: ἀναιδῶ δὲ παρῆλθον.

βίᾳ πολλῇ ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν ἡμῶν ἀφείλετο) vim vocant o- pem vim prohibentis.

Vers. 8.

Vers. 8.

παρ' οὗ) à quo, nempe Paulo.

## 24:9
Verse 9.

συνέθεντο δὲ καὶ οἱ ἰουδαῖοι) Ananias and the Senators approved the words of their orator. In the Glossary συντίθημι, συναινῶ: Pausanias: Ἀῤῥιανῷ μὲν ἔν ἔγωγε οὐδαμῶς κατά γε τοῦτο συνθήσομαι.

Chrysostom rightly observes here that the order of the trial is perverted, since the Jews wish to be both the accusers of Paul and the witnesses of the crime here: so that, namely, by their authority and their multitude they might overwhelm him.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

συνέθεντο δὲ καὶ οἱ ἰουδαῖοι) Ananias & Senatores oratoris sui dicta approbabant. In Glossario συντίθημι, συναινῶ: Pausanias: Ἀῤῥιανῷ μὲν ἔν ἔγωγε οὐδαμῶς κατά γε τοῦτο συν- θήσομαι.

Recte hic observat Chrysostomus, ordinem ju- dicii perverti, siquidem Judæi & accusatores Pauli fuerint, & testes hic criminis esse velint: ut scil. auctoritate, ac multitudine sua ipsum opprimant.

Verse 10.

Νεύσαντος αὐτῷ τοῦ ἡγεμόνος λέγειν) the power of speaking having been granted to him. See above XXI. 39. XXVI. 1.

Ἐκ πολλῶν ἐτῶν) for these things were done toward the end of this procuratorship of Felix: as is evident below XXVI.

Ὄντα σε κριτὴν) that is, a ruler. For שׁבט κρίνειν among the Hebrews also means to rule.

Τῷ ἔθνει τούτῳ) of Judea, Galilee, Samaria, Perea. Josephus, Jewish War II. 21. For Agrippa had Batanea, Trachonitis, Gaulonitis, and the kingdom of Lysanias and the prefecture which Varus had added.

Εὐθυμότερον τὰ περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ ἀπολογοῦμαι) It is fitting for a defendant to show confidence in his countenance and words.

Vers. 10.

Ὄντα σε κριτὴν) id est, rectorem. Nam שׁבט κρίνειν Hebraeis est etiam regere.

Τῷ ἔθνει τούτῳ) Judaeae, Galilaeae, Samariae, Peraeae. Josephus Belli Judaici II. 21. Nam Agrippa habebat Batanaeam, Trachonitidem, Gaulonitidem, & regnum Lysaniae & praefecturam, quam Varus addiderat.

Εὐθυμότερον τὰ περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ ἀπολογοῦμαι) Reo convenit, vultu ac verbis prae se ferre fiduciam.

Verse 11. Δυναμένου σου γνῶναι) from witnesses.

Προσκυνήσων εἰς Ἱερουσαλὴμ) not to profane the temple, but to worship God with the other Jews.

Vers. 11. Δυναμένου σου γνῶναι) ex testibus.

Ὅτι οὐ πλείους εἰσί μοι ἡμέραι ἢ δεκαδύο) Vide supra XXI. 27.
