ἡμέρας μέσης) Supra XXII. 6.

ὑπὲρ τὴν λαμπρότητα τοῦ ἡλίου) Si Christi in terris agentis vultus, ut Sol luxit, Matth. XVII. 2. æquum fuit magis eum lucere jam in cælo regnantis. Et si justi ut Sol splende- bunt: Dan. XII. 13. Matth. XIII. 43. quanto magis omni- um justorum Princeps?

## 26:14
Verse 14.

In the Hebrew dialect) Take as above XXI. v. 40. XXII. 2.

it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks) He recounts the history more fully than it had been recounted above in chapter IX. This proverb, however, concerning those who attempt things that will turn out badly for them, had come to the Jews from the Greeks: Aeschylus first in Agamemnon: Do not kick against the pricks, lest you suffer by striking. The same in Prometheus: You will stretch your leg against the pricks. Euripides in the Bacchae: I, a mortal, would kick against the pricks to a god. The same in Pelias: Do not kick against the pricks to those who rule you. Zenobius in the Proverbs: to kick against the pricks. Julian to Sallust: nor what the proverb says, to kick against the pricks. The Latins followed: Terence in Phormio I. 2. --- for it is ignorance, to kick against the goad. Sosipater Charisius also has it in book IV. Ammianus Marcellinus in book XVIII: lest he kick against the points. The Hebrews would say בעט על קטב. The Syrian here למבעטו לעוקסא.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Τῇ Ἑβραΐδι διαλέκτῳ) Sume ut supra XXI. v. 40. XXII. 2.

σκληρόν σοι πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζειν) Plenius historiam reci- tat, quam supra castpe IX. recitata fuerat. Proverbium au- tem hoc, de his qui res sibi male cessuras moliuntur, ad Judæos à Græcis venerat: primus Æschylus Agamemno- ne: Πρὸς κέντρα μὴ λάκτιζε, μὴ, πήσας μογῇς. idem Prometheo: Πρὸς κέντρα κῶλον ἐκτενεῖς. Euripides Bacchis: Πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζοιμι θνητὸς ὢν Θεῷ. Idem Peliasi: Πρὸς κέντρα μὴ λάκτιζε τοῖς κρατοῦσί σου Zenobius in Proverbiis: πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζειν. Julianus ad Sallustium: μηδὲ ὅ φήσιν ἡ παροιμία, πρὸς κέντρα λακτί- ζειν. Secuti Latini Terentius Phormione I. 2. - - - namque inscitia est, Adversus stimulum calces. Habet & Sosipater Charisius libro IV. Ammianus. Marcel- linus libro XVIII. ne contra acumina calcitrayet. Hebræi di- cerent בעט על קטב. Syrus hic למבעטו לעוקסא.

## 26:16
Verse 16.

and stand upon thy feet) as Dan. X. 10.

to appoint thee) That is, that I may appoint thee. See above XXII. 14.

of those things in which I will appear unto thee) Of those things through which I will appear to you. Paul's many visions are referred to; above XVIII. 9. XXIII. 11. 2 Cor. XII. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

κᾀ στῆθ᾽ ἐπὶ τοὺς πόδας σοῦ) ut Dan. X. 10.

προχειρίσασθαί σε) Id est, ἵνα σε προχειρίσω. Vide supra XXII. 14.

ὧν τε ὀφθήσομαί σοι) Eorum per quæ tibi apparebo. Re- spiciuntur visa Pauli plurima; supra XVIII. 9. XXIII. 11. 2. Cor. XII. 2.

## 26:16
v. 16. I was not disobedient) That calling was so powerful, yet it did not take away from him the power of resisting. God desires free obedience, not coerced. I was not disobedient, I did not resist contumaciously: thus the Syriac here. It refers to the passage in Isaiah 50:5, The discipline of the Lord opens my ears, and I do not disobey, nor do I speak against.

It is rightly asserted that even in this so powerful and extraordinary a conversion, the power of resisting was not taken away from Paul: or that the grace of God was not simply irresistible, which the Calvinists maintain even regarding the ordinary grace of conversion itself. One must be careful, however, not to be carried away to the other extreme of the Pelagian or Semi-Pelagian heresy, as if man has it in his own power to convert himself or not to convert; concerning which, against the Arminians in the Consideration of this sect, and the Calixtines in the Calixtine-Heretical Harmony, in their proper place.

to the heavenly vision) to the vision of God, Ezekiel 8:3. For heaven is known to be put for God. Daniel's interpreter Theodotion everywhere puts ὀπτασίαν, others ὅραμα or ὅρασιν.

Latin:

v. 16. ὐκ ἐγενόμην ἀπειθὴς) Tam potens illa vocatio, tamen non adimebat ei obsistendi potentiam. Deus libera vult obsequia, non coacta. ὐκ ἐγενόμην ἀπειθὴς non obstiti contumaciter: ita hic Syrus. Respicitur locus Esaiz L. 5. ἡ παιδεία τῦ Κυρίε ἀνοίγει μοι τὰ ὦτα, ἐγὼ δὲ ὐκ ἀπειθῶ, ὐδὲ ἀντιλέγω.

Recte asseritur etiam in hac tam potenti atque extraordinaria conversione non ademtam Paulo obsistendi potentiam: vel gratiam Dei non fuisse simpliciter irresistibilem, quod Calviniani volunt de ipsa quoque ordinaria conversionis gratia. Ca- vendum tamen ne ad alterum extremum Pelagia- næ, vel Semi-Pelagianæ hæreseos hæc abripian- tur, quasi homo in sua potestate habeat sese con- vertere, vel non convertere; de quo contra Armi- nianos in Consideratione hujus sectæ, & Calixtinos in Harmonia Calixtino-Hæretica suo loco.

τῇ ὐρανίῳ ὀπτασίᾳ) ὁράσει Θεῦ, Ezech. VIII, 3. Nam cœ- lum pro Deo poninotum est. Danielis interpres Theodo- tion ubique ponit ὀπτασίαν, alii ὅραμα aut ὅρασιν.

## 26:17
v. 17. delivering thee) Present for future, that is, about to deliver you from the hands of the Jews and the Gentiles; we had this word thus above VII. 10. 34. XII. 11.

Latin:

v. 17. ἐξαιρούμενός σε) Præsens pro futuro, id est, exem- pturus te manibus Judæorum & gentium, ita verbum hoc habuimus supra VII. 10. 34. XII. II.

## 26:18
v. 18. to open their eyes) You will perform in them spiritually what will happen to you corporally. to turn) 'For the purpose of' is understood. from darkness to light) Which is signified by that brightness of Christ.

Beza took this verb transitively, so that you may convert them with an ellipsis of the pronoun: but because it is usually taken intransitively, to be converted, there is no need for that ellipsis, if it is rendered with the Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic as that they may be converted.

and of the power of Satan) Thus he calls idolatry, see Luke 10:18.

Not only is idolatry noted: but what the words signify, that the Gentiles are truly under the power of Satan, both because they obey him in sins, and especially also in idolatry, and because he has right and dominion over them, 2 Peter 2:19. Just as all outside of Christ are under his power, Hebrews 2:14, Luke 1:71.

that they may receive forgiveness of sins) See above 10:43. It signifies that their former sins, however grave, will in no way hinder their salvation.

These do not refer only to past crimes and sins committed during heathenism: because we are bound to seek the remission of sins daily, which is obtained only in Christ.

and an inheritance among those who are sanctified) A right to eternal life with the other pious. ἐν for among, as Matthew 20:26. faith in me) Through which hearts are purified.

Grotius understands this as sanctification. But through faith we are not only sanctified, but primarily justified, with hearts purified by the blood of Jesus Christ apprehended by true faith, Acts 15:9, Hebrews 9:14, 1 John 1:7.

Latin:

v. 18. ἀνοῖξαι ὀφθαλμὺς αὐτῶν) Præstabis in ipsis spiri- tualiter, quod tibi corporaliter eveniet. τῦ ἐπιστρέψαι) Subauditur ἕνεκα. ἀπὸ σκότυς εἰς φῶς) Quod illo Christi fulgore significa- tur.

Beza hoc verbum transitive accepit, ut conver- tas cum ellipsi pronominis eos: sed quia plerum- que intransitive accipi solet, converti, ea ellipsi o- pus non est, si cum Vulg. Syr. & Arabe reddatur ut convertantur.

κὶ τῆς ἐξυσίας τῦ Σατανᾶ) Sic vocat idololatriam, Vi- de Luc. X. 10.

Non idololatria solum notatur: sed quod verba sonant, quod gentiles vere sub potestate Satanæ sint, tum quod ei parvant peccatis, & imprimis e- tiam idololatria, tum quod jus & dominium in eos habeat, 2. Petr. II. 19. Quomodo omnes ex- tra Christum sub ejus potestate sunt Ebr. II. 14. Luc. I. 71.

τῦ λαβεῖν αὐτὺς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν) Vide supra X. 43. si- gnificat peccata ipsorum priora, quamvis gravia, nihil ob- stitura ipsorum saluti.

Non hæc præterita tantum sub gentilisimo pa- trata crimina & peccata respiciunt: quia quotidie remissionem peccatorum petere tenemur, quæ non nisi in Christo obtinetur.

κὶ κλῆρον ἐν τοῖς ἡγιασμένοις) Jus ad vitam æternam cum piis cæteris. ἐν pro inter, ut Matth. XX. 26. πίσει τῇ εἰς ἐμὲ) Per quam purgantur corda.

Intelligit sanctificationem Grotius. At per fi- dem non tantum sanctificamur, sed imprimis ju- stificamur, purgatis per sanguinem Jesu Christi vera fide apprehensum cordibus, Act. XV. 9. Ebr. IX. 14. 1. Joh. I. 7.

## 26:20
v. 20. and to turn to God) Rightly: for the Gentiles had worshipped false gods: the Jews the true God, but not as they ought.

works worthy of repentance) See Matthew 3:8.

Latin:

v. 20. κό ἐπιστρέφειν ἐπὶ τὸν Θεὸν) Recte: nam gentes falsos coluerant Deos: Judæi verum Deum, sed non sicut opor- tebat.

ἄξια τῆς μετανοίας ἔργα πράσσοντας) Vide Matth. III. 8.

## 26:21
v. 21. they tried to kill me) As before the Lord, above 5:30, where the same word is used.

Herodotus uses this word θαλείᾳ· εἰδὼς δὲ ἀδύνατον ἐν δύο διαχειρίσασθαι βασιλέας, since he knew it was impossible to kill two kings.

Latin:

v. 21. ἐπειρῶντο διαχειρίσασθαι) Ut ante Dominum. su- pra V. 30. ubi idem verbum.

Adhibet hoc verbum Herodotus θαλείᾳ· εἰδὼς δὲ ἀδύνατον ἐν δύο διαχειρίσασθαι βασιλέας, cum sciret fieri non posse, ut duos Reges interimeret.

## 26:22
v. 22. having obtained help from God) Psalm 18:19. The Lord became my support.

testifying to both small and great) Instructing men of every kind. A Hebrew manner of speaking, Deut. 1:17, 1 Sam. 5:8, 30:2, 19, 2 Kings 23:2, 25:22.

of those things which the prophets spoke would come to pass, and Moses) See Luke 24:26.

They note here the third argument in Paul's apologetic speech. The first was from the testimony of the fathers, v. 6. The second from the vision of Christ illuminating his eyes and mind, v. 13. The third from the oracles concerning Christ, which predicted those things which Paul now

was preaching. But if Paul said nothing outside of those things which Moses and the Prophets spoke, unwritten traditions are vain: since the Papists pretend that certain things were handed down by the Apostles which are not found in the Scriptures. These things are openly contrary to Paul's protestation.

Latin:

v. 22. ἐπικυρίας ὖν τυχὼν τῆς παρὰ Θεῦ) Psal. XVIII. 19. κό ἐγένετο Κύριος ἀντιστήριγμά μυ.

μαρτυρόμενος μικρῷ τε κό μεγάλῳ) Instituens omnis ge- neris homines. Genus loquendi Hebraicum Deut. I. 17. I. Sam. V. 8. XXX. 2. 19. 2. Reg. XXIII. 2. XXV. 22.

ὧν τε οἱ Προφῆται ἐλάλησαν μελλόντων γίνεσθαι, κό Μωσῆς) Vide Lucæ XXIV. 26.

Notant hic tertium argumentum in oratione Pauli apologetica. Primum fuit ex testimonio Pa- trum v. 6. Alterum ex visione Christi oculos & mentem illustrantis, v. 13. Tertium ex oraculis de Christo, quæ prædixerunt ea, quæ Paulus jam fa-

cta prædicabat. Si autem nihil dixit Paulus extra ea quæ Moses & Prophetæ loquuti sunt, vanæ sunt traditiones non-scriptæ: cum Papistæ fingunt ab Apostolis tradita esse quædam, quæ in Scripturis non habeantur. Contrariantur hæc aperte Pauli protestationi.

## 26:23
v. 23. εἰ παθητὸς ὁ χριστὸς) A double impropriety. For both εἰ for ὅτι, as above 18, and παθητὸς for him who was to suffer, as appears in the said place of the Gospel of Luke. See Dan. IX. 2. Tryphon the Jew, disputing with Justin, clearly acknowledges what the Jews now deny. For he says: παθητὸν μὲν τὸν χριστὸν, ὅτι αἱ γραφαὶ κηρύσσουσι, φανερόν ἐστι.

There is no reason why we should take the εἰ improperly. It is a known figure of speech, which those who are inquiring or discussing some matter are accustomed to use, affirming that which is said. Regarding the word παθητὸς, Beza is correct that it is not only significant of power, but also of activity. For the Jews did not doubt that the Messiah would be a true man, and therefore passible, but they had conceived in their minds a Messiah, such as they imagine even today, that is, one whose kingdom would be of this world; Paul says in opposition that it was predicted by the Prophets that the Messiah would be παθητὸς, that is, destined for the bearing of our calamities and the punishments of our sins, who nevertheless would be the first to rise again into eternal glory, which he is to communicate to the faithful by the power of his passion and resurrection.

εἰ πρῶτος ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν) The first raised to immortal life, therefore called the firstborn from the dead, Coloss. I. 18. Apoc. I. 5.

Φῶς μέλλει καταγγέλλειν τῷ λαῷ καὶ τοῖς ἔθνεσι) From Isaiah XLII. 6. Light is the most open doctrine for salvation. Luke II. 32.

The doctrine, therefore, which is handed down in the Scriptures is not obscure, but most perspicuous and clear. For the Holy Scriptures would not be light, but darkness, to the Jewish people and the nations, if the Papists' accusation concerning the obscurity of Scripture were true. Surely the Jews and nations ought to have been taught by writings no less than by the proclamation of a living voice; there was need, therefore, for perspicuity in both, since he had to announce a light or doctrine that was most clear.

PART II. Paul's defense against Festus with an appeal to the judgment of Agrippa, and the judgment of the latter.

Latin:

v. 23. εἰ παθητὸς ὁ χριστὸς) Duplex improprietas. nam & εἰ pro ὅτι, ut supra 18. & παθητὸς pro eo qui debebat pati, ut apparet dicto loco Evangelii Lucæ. Vide Dan. IX. 2. Tryphon Judæus cum Justino disputans, plane agnoscit quod Judæi nunc negant. Ait enim: παθητὸν μὲν τὸν χριστὸν, ὅτι αἱ γραφαὶ κηρύσσουσι, φανερόν ἐστι.

Non est cur improprie τὸ εἰ accipiamus. Nota est sermonis figura, qua solent de aliqua re quærentes sive disserentes uti, id quod dicitur affirmando. De verbo παθητὸς Beza recte, quod non sit δυνάμεως tantum, sed etiam ἐνεργείας σημαντικὸν. Neque enim ambigebant Judæi, quin Messias esset verus homo futurus, adeoque passibilis, sed Messiam animo conceperant, qualem hodie quoque imaginantur, id est, cujus regnum esset ex hoc mundo, dicit contra Paulus prædictum esse à Prophetis Messiam fore παθητὸν, id est ferendis nostris calamitatibus & peccatorum nostrorum pœnis destinatum, qui tamen in æternam gloriam primus esset resurrecturus, quam virtute passionis & resurrectionis suæ cum fidelibus communicaturus sit.

εἰ πρῶτος ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν) Primus resuscitatus ad vitam immortalem, ideo dictus πρωτότοκος ἐκ νεκρῶν, Coloss. I. 18. Apoc. I. 5.

Φῶς μέλλει καταγγέλλειν τῷ λαῷ καὶ τοῖς ἔθνεσι) Ex Esaia XLII.6 Lux est doctrina apertissima ad salutem. Luc. II. 32.

Doctrina ergo non obscura, sed maxime perspicua est, & dilucida, quæ in Scripturis traditur. Non enim lux, sed tenebræ essent S. literæ populo Judaico, & gentibus, si verum foret ἔγκλημα Papistarum de obscuritate Scripturæ. Non minus sane scriptis doceri debuere Judæi & gentes, quam vivæ vocis præconio; In utriusque ergo opus erat perspicuitate, quum lucem seu doctrinam maxime dilucidam annunciare debuerit.

PARS II. Pauli adversus Festum defensio cum provocatione ad judicium Agrippæ, hujusque judicio.

## 26:24
v. 24. Τὰ πολλά σε γράμματα εἰς μανίαν περιτρέπει) Thus Theognetus the Comic poet: Ἐπαριστερ᾽ ἔμαθες, ὦ πόνηρε, γράμματα, Ἀντεστροφέν σε τ᾽ βίον τὰ βιβλία. Paul was learned not only in the law, but also in the traditions, which taught more openly of the resurrection and the goods of the other life. He knew the Hebrew, Syriac, Greek, and Latin languages; he had also read the poets.

Latin:

v. 24. Τὰ πολλά σε γράμματα εἰς μανίαν περιτρέπει) Sic Theognetus Comicus: Ἐπαριστερ᾽ ἔμαθες, ὦ πόνηρε, γράμματα, Ἀντεστροφέν σε τ᾽ βίον τὰ βιβλία. Eruditus erat Paulus non in lege tantum, sed & in traditionibus, quæ resurrectionem, & bona vitæ alterius apertius docebant. Norat linguas Hebræam, Syriacam, Græcam, Latinam; legerat & Poëtas.

## 26:25
v. 25. Κράτιστε Φῆστε) As above XXIV. 3.

ἀλλὰ ἀληθείας καὶ σωφροσύνης ῥήματα ἀποφθέγγομαι) The things I say, I say both with sincere faith and being of sound mind. Thus Homer: Ἀλλὰ σωφροσυνήσι νοήματα πατρὸς ἄκουθεν. And the origin agrees. For σώφρων is he who keeps his mind sound. Thus also he who is of sound mind is opposed to him who is possessed by a demon. Mark V. 15 and Luke VIII. 35.

Latin:

v. 25. Κράτιστε Φῆστε) Ut supra XXIV. 3.

ἀλλὰ ἀληθείας καὶ σωφροσύνης ῥήματα ἀποφθέγγομαι) Quæ dico ea dico & sincera fide & bene animi compos. Sic Homerus: Ἀλλὰ σωφροσυνήσι νοήματα πατρὸς ἄκουθεν. Et convenit origo. Nam σώφρων est ὁ σώζων τὴν φρένα. Sic etiam ὁ σωφρονῶν opponitur τῷ δαιμονιζομένῳ. Marc. V. 15. & Luc. VIII. 35.

## 26:26
v. 26. ἐπίσταται γὰρ περὶ τούτων ὁ βασιλεὺς) Concerning the miracles performed by Jesus and his disciples.

πρὸς ὃν καὶ παῤῥησιαζόμενος λαλῶ) I speak with confidence.

Latin:

v. 26. ἐπίσταται γὰρ περὶ τούτων ὁ βασιλεὺς) De miraculis factis per Jesum & discipulos ejus.

πρὸς ὃν καὶ παῤῥησιαζόμενος λαλῶ) Cum fiducia loquor.

## 26:27
v. 27. For this is not done in a corner) That is, in hidden places, as the Syrian interprets it here. Thus Terence in the Adelphi: Meanwhile I shall go off into some corner.

Latin:

v. 27. οὐδὲ γάρ ἐστι γωνίᾳ πεπραγμένον τοῦτό ἐστι) Id est, in locis occultis, ut hic interpretatur Syrus. Sic Terentius Adelphis: Interea in angulum aliquo abeam.

## 26:28
v. 28. King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe) Not only orators, but Paul also has this habit, that they often ask others questions, and immediately answer them themselves.

Thus Lucian, Dialogues of the Courtesans: What do you say? Will you do these things? I know you will do them. Pliny, Book IX, Epistle XII: Have you never done anything that could be rebuked by your father? I say you have. Cicero, Book on the Nature of the Gods: Or do you think God is like me, or like you? You certainly do not think so.

in a little you persuade me to become a Christian) You are not far from persuading me to become a Christian. It is a very Greek expression. For Plato also said in the Apology: I would have known about the poets also in a little [time] this. I learned almost the same thing about the poets. In the manuscript, to make me a Christian, as if you were to make me a Christian.

Latin:

v. 28. πιστεύεις βασιλεῦ Ἀγρίππα τοῖς προφήταις; οἶδα ὅτι πιστεύεις) Non oratores tantum, sed & Paulus hunc habet morem, ut sæpe alios interrogent, & mox sibi respondeant.

Sic Lucian. Dial. Meretr. τὶ φῇς; ποιήσεις ταῦτα; ποιήσεις οἶδα. Plinius l. IX. Epist. XII. Nunquam fecisti quod à Patre corripi possit? fecisti dico. Cicero l. de Natur. Deor. An tu mei similem putas esse, aut tui Deum? profecto non putas.

ἐν ὀλίγῳ με πείθεις χριστιανὸν γενέσθαι) Parum abest, quin mihi persuadeas ut fiam Christianus. Est locutio bene Gra- ca. Nam & Plato dixit in Apologetico: ἔγνων ἂν καὶ περὶ τῶν ποιητῶν ἐν ὀλίγῳ τῦτο. prope idem de poëtis cognovi. In Manu- scripto, χριστιανὸν ποιῆσαι, ut me Christianum facias.

## 26:29
v. 29. In a little and in much) That is, not only almost, but altogether. Therefore he adds in much, because the other had said in a little. For he preserves the same manner of speaking. In the manuscript: in little and in great, without in.

such as I am, except for these bonds) I wish for them all things that are in me, except for the inconveniences. He calls the guards placed around him bonds. For common speech does not take bonds as strictly as the Jurisconsults in the law 'It is true' in the Digest on the meaning of words. Such is that of Virgil: -- And Claelia swam across with bonds broken. For hostages are never bound, says Servius.

Heinsius is singular here, as he is elsewhere. Nor does Walaeus disapprove. He does not believe Agrippa uttered such a confession in such a place and assembly. What then? He wants this to be what Agrippa means: Do you wish that in so short a space I should become a Christian? But is the will and efficacy of the word so incredible? There is nothing in the text about a short space of time. He quibbles in vain, however, that the Apostle's wish, according to the received interpretation, would be this meaning, that they might be in a little, that is, almost Christians, or as it were Christians, or in part Christians, and he substitutes this sense, that they might be Christians both at that time and in every way. Beza had already settled that: For 'almost' and 'altogether' are not contradictory, but merely different. For this is just as if Paul were saying, Almost (as you say) I persuade you to become a Christian: I would indeed that it were even as you say, that is, that you are very close to Christianity: and even more than that, namely that you might be entirely what I am: and I wish this not only for him, but for all of you who hear me speaking here.

Latin:

v. 29. ἐν ὀλίγῳ καὶ ἐν πολλῷ) Id est, non propemodum tantum, sed plane. Ideo addit ἐν πολλῷ, quia alter ἐν ὀλίγῳ dixerat. Servat enim idem dicendi genus. In Manuscripto: ὀλίγῳ καὶ μεγάλῳ, sine ἐν.

ὁποῖος κἀγώ εἰμι, παρεκτὸς τῶν δεσμῶν τύτων) Omnia il- lis opto, quæ in me sunt, præterincommoda. Vincula autem vocat, custodias sibi circůndatas. Popularis enim sermo vincula non tam stricte sumit quam Jurisconsulti L. Verum est D. de verbor. signif. Tale est illud Virgilii: -- Et vinclis innaret Clœlia ruptis. non enim obsides unquam ligantur, ait Servius.

Singularis hic, ut alias est Heinsius. Nec im- probat Walæus. Non credit Agrippam talem con- fessionem in tali loco ac conventu effudisse. Quid ergo? Hoc vult Agrippam velle: Vis ut tantillo spatio Christianus fiam? At an vis & efficacia ver- bi tam incredibilis est? de spatio temporis exiguo nihil in textu. Nequicquam vero tricatur, Apo- stoli voto juxta receptam interpretationem hanc fore sententiam, ut ἐν ὀλίγῳ, id est propemodum Christiani, aut quasi Christiani, aut ex parte Chri- stiani essent, & hunc substituit sensum, ut & illo tempore, & omni sint Christiani. Expedierat id jam Beza: Neque vero Propemodum & Admodum sunt repugnantia, sed diversa duntaxat. Nam perinde hoc est, ac si diceret Paulus, Propemo- dum (ut inquis) tibi persuadeo, ut fias Christia- nus: utinam vero & ita sit ut dicis, id est proxime absis à Christianismo: atque adeo aliquid amplius, nempe ut prorsus id sis quod ego sum: neque vero illi duntaxat, sed etiam vobis omnibus id exopto qui me hic loquentem auditis.

## 26:30
v. 30. And the governor) Festus. See above XXIII. 24. And those who sat with them) The council of the President. Above XXV. 12.

Latin:

v. 30. κὶ ὁ ἡγεμὼν) Festus. Vide supra XXIII. 24. κὶ οἱ συγκαθήμενοι αὐτοῖς) Consilium Præsidis. Supra XXV. 12.

## 26:31
v. 31. Having withdrawn) When they had returned to their own homes. He acts) He deals with the conduct of life. Such also is that above XXV. 11. For if I am doing wrong.

Latin:

v. 31. ἀναχωρήσαντες) Cum in suas domos se recepif- sent. πράσσει) Agit de vitæ instituto. Tale & illud supra XXV. 11. εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἀδικῶ.

## 26:32
v. 32. He could have been released.) He could have been absolved. If he had not appealed to Caesar) For by an appeal, the power of the judge from whom the appeal is made ceases to absolve, no less than to condemn. For crimes must be kept intact for the cognizance of the superior.

This excuse is bald. He could have dismissed Paul even so, although he had appealed. Because he had appealed under compulsion: and by the appeal he had sought only his dismissal. Wherefore if Porcius Festus had granted it, Paul would have voluntarily withdrawn his appeal. But the President did not wish to offend the Jews by dismissing Paul, and therefore he preferred to send him to Nero Caesar, to whom he had appealed.

Latin:

v. 32. ἀπολελύσθαι ἐδύνατο.) Potuisset absolvi. εἰ μὴ ἐπεκέκλητο Καίσαρα) Nam appellatione potestas Judicis à quo appellatum est, cessare incipit ad absolven- dum, non minus quam ad condemnandum. Crimina enim integra servanda sunt cognitioni superioris.

Calva est hæc excusatio. Dimittere etiam ita poterat Paulum, tametsi appellarit. Quia coa- ctus appellarat: & appellatione dimissionem so- lum quæsierat. Quare si eam præstitisset Portius Festus, ultro appellatione sua cessisset Paulus. Sed Judæos nolebat offendere Præses, Paulum dimit- tendo, idcirco mittere eum maluit ad Neronem Cæsarem, ad quem provocarat.

## 27:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Paul the prisoner, with others, is committed to a ship under the Centurion Julius, by whom he is treated kindly; he visits friends in Sidon, afterwards at Myra in Lycia they board an Alexandrian ship heading for Italy, and when the voyage proceeded slowly, near Lasea, despite Paul’s warnings in vain that they should winter there because of extreme danger, and as they strove to proceed to Phoenix, a grave tempest arises, from which, the ship being tossed about in various ways, they despair of life. But Paul, instructed by a heavenly vision that no one would perish, encourages them, and when the sailors wished to escape, he orders them to be restrained, and to take food

while he encourages. Having taken which they unload the ship, yet they suffer shipwreck, and all escape safe.

There are three parts: I. A long and dangerous voyage, to v. 20. II. Paul's consolatory speech with an exhortation to take food; to v. 37. III. The salvation of all from the shipwreck, to v. 44.

PART I. A long and dangerous voyage.

v. 1. Ὡς δὲ ἐκρίθη) It was determined as above II. 16. XXV. 25.

τοῦ ἀποπλεῖν ἡμᾶς) A construction such as above III. 12. 1. Corinth. II. 2.

παρεδίδουν τόν τε Παῦλον) Namely Festus and those who had received that command from him. It is frequent among the Hebrews to understand the nominative matching the verb. But the Manuscript has παρεδίδου, so that the speech refers to Festus alone.

καί τινας ἑτέρους δεσμώτας) The Latin translates it as 'custodias' [guards/prisoners], very well. Thus Suetonius in Domitian, Paul in L. Carcer, and Venulejus in L. Ne quis D. de custodia & exhibitione reorum use the word 'custodia'.

ἑκατοντάρχῃ) See above XI.

ὀνόματι Ἰουλίῳ) A freedman, I believe, of the Julian house. See what is said regarding Luke. Thus Earinus, called Flavius. In the Manuscript, however, below it is Ἰουλιάνος.

σπείρης Σεβαστῆς) The Latin well translates it as the Augustan cohort. But understand that the cohort was from the Augustan legion, just as that of Cornelius was from the Italian legion above XI. For Augusta is the name of a legion in an ancient stone inscription in Lipsius on the second book of Tacitus' Histories.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Paulus captivus cum aliis navigio sub Cen- turione Iulio, à quo comiter habetur, com- mittitur, in Sidone amicos visitat, postea Myræ in Lycia navem Alexandrinam, in Italiam tendentem ipsis ingressis, cùm tarde navigatio succederet, prope Lasa- am, frustra monitis à Paulo, ut illic ob extremum periculum hyemarent, & Phœnicem pergere contendentibus oritur gravis tempestas, unde varie jactata navi desperant de vita. Sed Paulus visione cœ- lesti edoctus, neminem periturum, erigit eosdem, & cum effugere nautæ vellent, retineri illos jubet, & ad cibum sumen-

dum hortatur. Quo sumpto navem exone- rant, naufragium tamen patiuntur, & omnes salvi evadunt.

Partes tres sunt 1. Navigatio diuturna & peri- culosa, ad v. 20. II. Oratio Pauli consolatoria cum exhortatione ad sumendum cibum; ad v. 37. III. Omnium e naufragio salvatio, ad v. 44.

PARS I. Diuturna & periculosa navigatio.

v. 1. Ὡς δὲ ἐκρίθη) Constitutum fuit ut supra II. 16. XXV. 25.

τοῦ ἀποπλεῖν ἡμᾶς) Constructio qualis supra III. 12. 1. Corinth. II. 2.

παρεδίδουν τόν τε Παῦλον) Nempe Festus & qui ab eo id mandatum acceperant. Frequens est apudHebraeos subau- dire nominativum verbo congruentem. At Manuscriptus παρεδίδου, ut ad unum Festum se referat oratio.

καί τινας ἑτέρους δεσμώτας) Latinus vertit custodias, bene admodum. Sic vocem custodiae usurpant SuetoniusDomi- tiano, Paulus in L. Carcer, & Venulejus L. Ne quis D. de custodia & exhibitione reorum.

ἑκατοντάρχῃ) Vide supra XI.

ὀνόματι Ἰουλίῳ) Liberto, credo, Juliae domus. Vide quae ad Lucam. Sic Earinus, dictus Flavius. In Manuscripto tamen infra est Ἰουλιάνος.

σπείρης Σεβαστῆς) Bene Latinus cohortis Augustae. Sed intellige cohortem fuisse ex legione Augusta, quomodo illa Cornelii ex legione Italica supra XI. Nam Augusta nomen legionis in Antiquo lapide apud Lipsum ad Taciti secun- dum Historiarum.

## 27:2
v. 2. πλοίῳ Ἀδραμυττηνῷ) There are many cities called חצר מות Ἀδράμυττος, Ἀδράμυττα, Ἀτράμυττος, Ἀτραμύττηον. For this name is written in so many ways in Stephanus and others. The most famous of all is the maritime city of Africa, about which Procopius writes in Vandalicorum II, which Jerome rightly judges to be indicated here. This ship seems to have carried African goods to Syria, then Syrian goods to Lycia, so that it might receive there 'Vina Syra reparata merce' [Syrian wines in exchange for goods], as Horace says. Thus ships from Athens were accustomed to go first to Mende or Scione, then to the Bosphorus: and it is still customary even now that cargoes are changed twice or three times or more often. The African city of Adrumetum is called Hadrumetus by Jerome. According to Drusius, the word is purely Punic, חדר מות, for the Hebrews חצר מות, which sounds in Latin like the atrium of Dis, or of death, because of the pestilential air of that coast. To others, however, it seems that a certain city in Asia, which Stephanus calls Adramytteum, is indicated. To which Camerarius also inclines: since it is an excellent port in Phrygia.

μέλλοντες πλεῖν τοὺς κατὰ τὴν Ἀσίαν τόπους) Manuscriptus μέλλοντι πλεῖν. A ship was coming from Africa. It was reading the coast of Asia and was visiting certain maritime cities for the sake of its business. πλεῖν τόπους, just as Virgil says 'Tyrrhenum navigat aequor' [he sails the Tyrrhenian sea]. Thus Demosthenes says πλεῖν τὴν θάλασσαν τόπους, that is, parts, namely of the sea.

ἀνήχθημεν) As above XVI. 11. XVIII. 2. XX. 1. 2. & below 4. ὄντος σὺν ἡμῖν Ἀριστάρχου Μακεδόνος Θεσσαλονικέως) This Aristarchus, having become a Christian, had accompanied Paul from Macedonia all the way to Judea. Above XIX. 29. XX. 4. The same man, out of love for him and the truth, wished of his own accord to accompany Paul, now given over to custody, and was first his helper at Rome: Philem. 24. then a sharer in his bonds. Col. IV. 10.

Latin:

v. 2. πλοίῳ Ἀδραμυττηνῷ) Multae sunt urbes dictae חצר מות Ἀδράμυττος, Ἀδράμυττα, Ἀτράμυττος, Ἀτραμύτ- τηον. Nam tot modis hoc nomen scribitur apud Stephanum & apud alios. Celeberrima omnium est urbs Africae mariti- ma, de qua Procopius Vandalicorum II. quam hic indicari recte censetHieronymus. Navis haec videtur Africanas mer- ces in Syriam, deinde Syriacas in Lyciam portasse, ut ibi acciperet Vina Syra reparata merce. ut loquiturHoratius. Sic solebant Athenis ire naves primum Menden aut Scionem, deinde in Bosphorum: idque etiam nunc fieri solet ut onera bis terve aut saepius mutentur. Adrumetum Africae urbs Hieronymo dicitur Hadrumetus. Secundum Drusium vox est mere Punica חדר מות Ebraeis חצר מות quod Latine sonat Ditis, aut mortis atrium, ob pestilentem aërem illius orae. Aliis tamen videtur urbs quae- dam in Asiae, quam Stephanus Adramytteum vo- cat, indicari. Quo etiam inclinat Camerarius: quum egregius portus sit in Phrygia.

μέλλοντες πλεῖν τοὺς κατὰ τὴν Ἀσίαν τόπους) Manuscriptus μέλλοντι πλεῖν. Ab Africa veniebat navis. legebat oram Asiae & urbes quasdam maritimas negotiorum suorum causa a- dibat. πλεῖν τόπους quomodo Virgilius Tyrrhenum navigat aequor. Sic πλεῖν τὴν θάλασσαν Demosthenes τόπως, id est, μέρη, maris nempe.

ἀνήχθημεν) Ut supra XVI. 11. XVIII. 2. XX. 1. 2. & infra 4. ὄντος σὺν ἡμῖν Ἀριστάρχου Μακεδόνος Θεσσαλονικέως) Hic A- ristarchus Christianus factus Paulum ex Macedonia in Ju- daam usque comitatus fuerat. supra XIX. 29. XX. 4. Idem Paulum jam custodiae datum ex amore in ipsum & verita- tem comitari sponte voluit, Romaeque primum adjutor e- jus: Philem. 24. deinde vinculorum particeps fuit. Col. IV. 10.

## 27:3
Vers. 3. εἰς Σιδῶνα) Which is quite near to Caesarea. That is apparent from Ptolemy. Buntingius in his itinerary says that those sailing from the city of Caesarea Stratonis to Sidon covered twenty-one miles.

φιλανθρώπως τε ὁ Ἰούλιος τῷ Παύλῳ χρησάμενος) By the example of Felix XXIV. 23.

πρὸς τοὺς Φίλους πορευθέντα) With a soldier.

ἐπιμελείας τυχεῖν) To be treated with care. Thus Galen said ἐπιμέλειαν σώματος [care of the body].

Latin:

Vers. 3. εἰς Σιδῶνα) Quae satis propinqua Caesareae. Apparet id ex Ptolemaeo. Buntingius in itinerario à Caesarea Stratonis ur- be Sidonem navigantes absolvisse, ait, milliaria vi- ginti & unum.

φιλανθρώπως τε ὁ Ἰούλιος τῷ Παύλῳ χρησάμενος) Exemplo Felicis XXIV. 23.

πρὸς τοὺς Φίλους πορευθέντα) Cum milite.

ἐπιμελείας τυχεῖν) Cum cura haberi. Sic ἐπιμέλειαν σώμα- τος dixit Galenus.

## 27:4
v. 4. ὑπεπλεύσαμεν τὴν Κύπρον διὰ τοὺς ἀνέμους εἶναι ἐναν- τίους) Luke describes this whole voyage quite accurately. We sailed, he says, in such a way that we were not far from Cyprus: Not that the direct route led there, but because the contrary wind compelled them to deviate both their course and their path. Thus also below XXVII. 7. Properly it is, we sailed under Cyprus: for by deviating their course they had to turn below the island, leaving it to the left, and thus in a way to sail around the island. Whence the Syrian and the Arab, we sailed around near Cyprus.

Latin:

v. 4. ὑπεπλεύσαμεν τὴν Κύπρον διὰ τοὺς ἀνέμους εἶναι ἐναν- τίους) Accurate admodum totam hanc navigationem de- scribit Lucas. Navigavimus, inquit, ita ut a Cypro non lon- ge abessemus: Non quod rectum iter eo ferret, sed quod ventus adversus cogeret & finus & iter obliquare. Sic & infra XXVII. 7. Proprie est, navigavimus infra Cyprum : obli- quantes enim cursum infra insulam declinare de- buerunt, relicta ea ad sinistram, adeoque insulam quodammodo circuire. Unde Syrus & Arabs, cir- cuivimus juxta Cyprum.

## 27:5
v. 5. τό τε πέλαγος τὸ κατὰ τὴν Κιλικίαν καὶ Παμφυλίαν διαπλεύσαντες) Πέλαγος here signifies the high sea which is far from land, as also in Matt. XVIII, 6. and 2 Macc. V, 21.

κατήχθημεν) κατάγειν is to land, Luke V, 11. above IV, 30. XXI, 3. below XXVIII, in the Glossary: καταγωγή arrival: κατάγω I am brought to land.

εἰς Μύρα τῆς Λυκίας) Manuscript and others: Λύστρα. Both words are corrupt, namely for Λίμυρα, which is the name both of a river and of a city situated on the river in Lycia. Myra lies further inland. Lystra is in Lycaonia.

The Vulgate also has Lystram, and the same has been amended by the Romans. Which is rightly rejected here. But there is no reason why we should reject Myra. Not only Greek Codices read it thus, but also the Syrian. Chrysostom, Isidore, Hugo, and Vatablus also read it thus. Strabo book XIV counts Myra among the principal cities of Lycia. Lystra is situated far from the sea on the continent: The interval from Sidonia to Myra is 120 miles: which is situated about half a mile from the Mediterranean sea, at the river Limyrus.

Latin:

v. 5. τό τε πέλαγος τὸ κατὰ τὴν Κιλικίαν καὶ Παμφυλίαν διαπλεύσαντες) Πέλαγος hic significat altum mare quod procul à terra est, ut & Matth. XVIII, 6. & 2. Macc. V, 21.

κατήχθημεν) κατάγειν est appellere Lucæ V, 11. supra IV, 30. XXI, 3. infra XXVIII, in Glossario: καταγωγή adve- ctio: κατάγω advehor.

εἰς Μύρα τῆς Λυκίας) Manuscriptus & alii: Λύστρα. Vox utraque corrupta, videlicet pro Λίμυρα quod nomen & amni, & urbi ad amnem sitæ in Lycia. Myra interius jacet. Lystra in Lycaonia est.

Lystram habet & Vulgata, eademque à Romanis emendata. Quæ merito hic rejicitur. Sed Myran cur reprobemus causa non est. Legunt ita non Græci tantum Codices, sed etiam Syrus. Legerunt quoque sic Chrysostomus, Isidorus, Hugo & Vatablus. Strabo l. XIV. numerat Myram inter præcipuas Ly- ciæ urbes. Lystra procul à mari sita in continente est: Intervallum à Sidonia Myram usque est 120. milliarium: quæ dimidio circiter milliafi à mari mediterraneo sita, ad flumen Limyrum.

## 27:6
v. 6. πλοῖον Ἀλεξανδρῖνον πλέον εἰς τὴν Ἰταλίαν) Many ships from Alexandria were heading for Italy, and were bringing grain from Egypt and Persian and Indian goods. Therefore they alone had the right to land at the coast without lowering their mainsails. They usually landed at Puteoli. And the Alexandrian state contributed to the repairing and maintaining of the Puteolan lighthouse, as we learn from inscriptions. The Alexandrian fleet, the Niliacus cataplus [Nile-voyage] of Martial.

ἐνεβίβασεν ἡμᾶς εἰς αὐτό) ἐμβιβάζειν is a good Greek word, and used even by Plato in his Epistles, for putting someone on board a ship.

Latin:

v. 6. πλοῖον Ἀλεξανδρῖνον πλέον εἰς τὴν Ἰταλίαν) Multæ naves ex Alexandria Italiam petebant, advehebantque fru- mentum ab Ægypto & Persicas Indicasque merces. Ideo soli jus habebant ad oram appellere non demissis supparis. Ap- pellebant autem plerumque Puteolos. Et ad Pharum Pu- teolanam reficiendam fovendamque Alexandrina civitas contulit, ut ex inscriptionibus discimus. Classis Alexandri- na, Niliacus cataplus Martiali.

ἐνεβίβασεν ἡμᾶς εἰς αὐτό) ἐμβιβάζειν est vox bene Græca, & Platoni etiam in Epistolis usitata, pro imponere in navem.

## 27:7
v. 7. βραδυπλοῦντες) Because of a heavy load, as the Syriac takes it.

Not because of the magnitude of the load, but because of adverse winds, having traversed such a small stretch of sea in so many days.

μόλις γενόμενοι κατὰ τὴν Κνίδον) An island lying off Caria and noble for the image and worship of Venus.

It is distant from the city of Jerusalem 123 miles towards the summer sunset, at the extreme corner of the peninsula of Doris, Caria, and Asia Minor adhering to it, today called Cabo Crio. From the city of Myra to Cnidus there are 62 miles.

μὴ προσῶντος ἡμᾶς τοῦ ἀνέμου) The wind not permitting us, namely to keep a straight course, εὐθυδρομεῖν: thus the Syriac here supplies this ellipsis.

ὑπεπλεύσαμεν τὴν Κρήτην) See above 4.

κατὰ Σαλμώνην) In that part in which is the village of Salmone, whence the promontory Salmonium [is known] to Strabo and Ptolemy, [and] Dionysius Periegetes: Κρήτης αἱ ὑπὸ πῖπται οἶδμα Μάκρον ἐπ' ἀντολίην Σαλμωνίδος ἄχρι καρῆνυ.

Latin:

v. 7. βραδυπλοῦντες) Ob multum onus, ut accipit Syrus.

Non ob oneris magnitudinem, sed ob ventos adversos, spatium maris tantillum tot diebus e- mensum.

μόλις γενόμενοι κατὰ τὴν Κνίδον) Insulam Cariæ objectam & Veneris simulacro ac cultu nobilem.

Dissita illa ab urbe Hierosolyma milliaribus 123. versus occasum æstivum, in extremo cornu penin- sulæ Doridis, Cariæ, & Asiæ minoris adhærentis, ho- die Cabo Crio dicta. A civitate Myra ad Gnidum miliaria sunt 62.

μὴ προσῶντος ἡμᾶς τοῦ ἀνέμου) Non sinente vento, nempe rectum nos tenere cursum, εὐθυδρομεῖν: ita hanc ἔλλειψιν supplet hic Syrus.

ὑπεπλεύσαμεν τὴν Κρήτην) Vide supra 4.

κατὰ Σαλμώνην) In eam partem in qua vicus est Salmo- ne, unde promontorium Salmonium Straboni & Ptole- mæo, Dionysius Periegetes: Κρήτης αἱ ὑπὸ πῖπται οἶδμα Μά- κρον ἐπ' ἀντολίην Σαλμωνίδος ἄχρι καρῆνυ.

## 27:8
v. 8. μόλις τε παραλεγόμενοι αὐτήν) When we had sailed past that place with difficulty. Μόλις often signifies difficulty, as 1 Peter IV, 18; Sirach XXVI, 24. παραλέγεσθαι here and below 13 is to sail past. Virgil: — — — Et crebris legimus freta concita terris. That is, we pass by, says Servius.

καλούμενον καλοὺς λιμένας) That name remains even today. To Stephanus it is καλὴ ἀκτὴ in the same sense. For that is called a good shore by sailors which is full of harbors.

ᾧ ἐγγὺς πόλις Λασαία) In the Manuscript ᾧ ἐγγὺς πόλις ἦν Ἄλασσα. And I think this is the true reading, and that the Arab and Latin did not read otherwise, although in the former Alasia is read, and in the latter Thalassa, a change not departing much from the correct [reading].

Nor does Λασαία depart much from the word Ἄλασσα; and who does not know that related names have often belonged to the same city! We ought not to be so ready for the alteration of the authentic sacred text; otherwise there will be no measure or end to suspicions. Jerome names it Larea, Camerarius Laceam. Beza cites Lissan from Ptolemy, but adds, I would more willingly read ἐλαίαν; [a city] numbered by Pliny among the primary maritime cities of Crete. Buntingius makes Lasea a city on the island of Crete, called Lasa by Pliny.

Latin:

v. 8. μόλις τε παραλεγόμενοι αὐτήν) Cum difficulter eum lo- cum præternavigassemus. Μόλις difficultatem sæpe signi- ficat ut 1. Petri IV, 18. Sirach. XXVI, 24. παραλέγεσθαι hic & infra 13. est prætervehi. Virgilius: - - - Et crebris legimus freta concita terris. id est, præterimus, ait Servius.

καλούμενον καλοὺς λιμένας) Manet hodieque id no- men. Stephano est καλὴ ἀκτὴ eodem sensu. Nam bona ora nautis dicitur ea quæ est portuosa.

ᾧ ἐγγὺς πόλις Λασαία) In Manuscripto ᾧ ἐγγὺς πόλις ἦν Ἄλασσα. Et puto hanc veram esse lectionem, nec aliter le- gisse Arabem & Latinum, quanquam in illo Alasia, in hoc Thalassa, mutatione non multum à recto abeunte legitur.

Nec multum abit Λασαία à voce Ἄλασσα; & quis nescit, cognata sæpe nomina eidem fuisse civi- tati! Non tam faciles esse debemus in mutationem textus sacri authentici; alias suspicionum nullus modus vel finis erit. Hieronymus Laream, Came- rarius Laceam nominat. Beza à Ptolemæo Lissan adducit, sed addit, libentius ego ἐλαίαν legerem; in- ter primarias maritimas Cretæ urbes à Plinio nume- ratam. Buntingius Laseam civitatem facit in Insu- la Creta Plinio Lasam dictam.

## 27:9
v. 9. καὶ ὄντος ἤδη ἐπισφαλοῦς τοῦ πλοὸς διὰ τὸ καὶ τὴν νηστείαν ἤδη παρεληλυθέναι) Nηστεία by way of eminence is the day of יום כפורים, the day of atonement, the tenth of Tisri. See Levit. XXIII. Tisri corresponds partly to September, partly to October. Vegetius notes that the seas are closed in the month of November.

The Jesuit Sanctius approves this with the Syrian and Oecumenius, and confirms it with many arguments: because, to wit, this fast was public and solemn; and these things are said to the Jews, with whom the ship was full. Whence Bellarmine, in book II of Good Works, ch. 19, wrongly attempted to prove the fast of the four seasons from this passage: an argument upon which not even Cornelius a Lapide thought it safe to rely: although he understands the fast not of October, but of December, which was accustomed to be celebrated by the Jews in that month, Zech. 8:19.

Paul advised) Warned by God.

Latin:

v. 9. καὶ ὄντος ἤδη ἐπισφαλοῦς τοῦ πλοὸς διὰ τὸ καὶ τὴν νη- στείαν ἤδη παρεληλυθέναι) Nηστεία per excellentiam dies יום כפורים ἐξιλασμοῦ, decima Tisri. Vide Levit. XXIII Tisri partim cum Septembri, partim cum Octobri congruit. Mense Novembri claudi maria notas Vegetius.

Quod cum Syro & Oecumenio approbat San- ctius Jesuita, & multis confirmat: quia scil. jeju- nium hoc fuit publicum & solenne; & Judæis hæc dicuntur, quibus plena erat navis. Unde perperam Bellarminus lib. II. de Bon. Oper. c. 19. ex hoc loco jejunium quatuor temporum probare conatus est: cui argumento ne Cornelius quidem Lapidensis inniti tutum censuit: etsi jejunium non Octobris, sed Decembris intelligat à Judæis eo mense cele- brari solitum, Zach. IIX. 19.

παρῄνει ὁ Παῦλος) A Deo monitus.

## 27:10
v. 10. with injury and much loss) These two joined together are also found below in verse 21. Injury refers more to the person, loss to things. And it is a sufficiently elegant catachresis, in the way the Latins say, the injury of the sky.

of the cargo) That is, of the freight. Both Athenagoras and Eustathius have called a ship's cargo phorton: the Latins call it onus: whence that shameful saying of Julia: You will never take a passenger unless the ship is full. Full, supply of cargo.

but also of our lives) That is, of the persons, who are affected by great evils. Thus we have had this noun also above in 2:41, and we shall have it below in 27:37.

Grotius omitted those words, that the voyage is about to be. Ludovicus de Dieu has it thus regarding them: For that the voyage is about to be. To which Erasmus and Beza did not pay attention, since it contains a manifest solecism, unless it be excused. I say, therefore, that 'that' is not to be taken here from a Grecism specifically, for the Latin 'that', so that you translate word for word, I see that the navigation is about to be. For thus, without doubt, it should have been said, that the navigation is about to be. But from a Hellenism significantly, so that it is most common in Greek and Latin for it to be redundant from a Hebraism among the Hellenists, after verbs of saying, hearing, seeing, etc., to use 'that' pleonastically, to designate only that which has been said, heard, and seen. And it could be translated 'namely', as in Matt. 26:72. And again he swore with an oath, that I do not know the man, Namely I do not know the man. It indicates only what Peter swore. Take a closer example from Mark 12:19. Moses wrote, that if any man's brother die, etc., that his brother should take. The construction is, he wrote that he should take, for which you may also rightly say he wrote to take, 'that' intervenes to indicate what he wrote. So also in this passage, I perceive that the navigation is about to be. They cohere in the construction I perceive to be about to be. 'That' only intervenes, to indicate what he saw, namely the future navigation. Or 'that', as often 'ki' among the Hebrews, is an affirmative particle, meaning 'truly', as in 1 John 3:20, that God is greater than our heart, truly God is greater than our heart. Thus in this passage, I see truly the future navigation, etc., that pleases me most.

Latin:

v. 10. μετὰ ὕβρεως κὴ πολλῆς ζημίας) Hæc duo conjuncta & infra habentur 21. ὕβρις ad personam, ζημία ad res magis re- fertur. Et est κατάχρησις satis elegans, quomodo Latini di- cunt, cæli injuriam.

τῦ φορτίυ) Id est, γόμου. Ναὸς φόρτον dixere & Athenago- ras & Eustathius: onus Latini: unde illud Juliæ iuverecun- dum: Nunquam nisi nave plena tolles vectorem. Plena, sup- ple oneris.

ἀλλὰ κὴ 𝝉͂ ψυχῶν ἡμῶν) Id est, personarum, quæ magnis malis affectæ. Sic hoc nomen habuimus & supra II. 41. & habebimus infra 37.

Verba illa prætermisit Grotius μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι 𝝉 πλῦν. Ad ea Lud. de Dieu ita habet: Pro μέλλειν ἔ- σεσθαι ὁ πλῦς. Ad quod Erasmus & Beza non anim- adverterunt, quum manifestum habeat Solœcismum, nisi excusetur. Dico ergo, ὅτι non esse hic ex Græcis- mo accipiendum εἰδικῶς, pro Latino quod, ut ad ver- bum vertas, video quod futura sit navigatio. Sic enim procul dubio dicendum fuisset ὅτι μέλλει ἔσεσθαι ὁ πλῦς. Sed ex Hellenismo σημαντικῶς, sic ut Græce & Latine redundet V sit atissimum est ex Hebraismo Helle- nistis, post verba dicendi, audiendi, videndi &c. adhibe- re pleonastice ὅτι, ad designandum solummodo id quod dictum, auditum, & visum est. Et posset verti nem- pe, ut Matth. XXVI. 72. Et rursus juravit cum ju- ramento, ὅτι ἐκ οἶδα 𝝉 ἄνθρωπον, Nempe non novi hominem. Indicat tantum quid juraverit Petrus. Accipe exemplum vicinius ex Marc. XII. 19. Μωσῆς ἔγραψε, ὅτι ἐάν τινὸς ἀδελφὸς ἀποθάνῃ &c. ἵνα λάβῃ ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἀυτῦ. Constructio est, ἔγραψε ἵνα λαβῃ, pro quo recte etiam dicas ἔγραψε λαβεῖν, intervenit ὅτι ad innuendum quid scripserit. Ita quoque hoc loco, θεωρῶ ὅτι μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι 𝝉 πλῦν. Cohærent constru- ctione θεωρῶ μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι. Intervenit tantum ὅτι, ad indicandum quid viderit, nempe futuram naviga- tionem. Vel ὅτι, ut sæpe כי apud Hebræos, particula est affirmativa, valens ὄντως, ut 1. Joh. III. 20. ὅτι μείζων ἐσιν ὁ θεὸς 𝝉 καρδίας ἡμῶν, utique major est Deus corde nostro. Sic hoc loco, video utique futu- ram navigationem &c. id maxime arridet.

## 27:11
Vers. 11. to the pilot and to the shipmaster) The pilot is he who directs the ship with the rudder. But shipmaster is rightly translated in the Glossary as 'navicularius', a word which Cicero uses several times, and Plautus retained the Greek word. The name 'navicularius' extends more broadly than 'magister'. For the 'magister' is finally he whom the owners have placed in charge of the ship: the 'navicularius' is also he who is in charge of his own ship. The pilot followed his own conjectures; the shipmaster followed the authority of this man.

Latin:

Vers. 11. τῷ κυβερνήτῃ κὴ τῷ ναυκλήρῳ) Κυβερνήτης est qui navem gubernaculo regit. Ναύκληρος vero in Glossario re- cte vertitur navicularius, qua voce aliquoties utitur Cicero, Græcam Plautus retinuit. Latius patet navicularii nomen quam magistri. Nam magisteris demum est quem exercito- res navi præfecere: Navicularius etiam qui suæ navi præest. Gubernator suas conjecturas sequebatur; hujus auctorita- tem navicularius.

## 27:12
Vers. 12. and the harbor being not suitable for wintering) Just as 'euthetos' is suitable, Ps. 32:6, Luke 9:62, 14:32. So 'aneuthetos' is not suitable, inconvenient. To be tempest-tossed is to be tossed by storms, to winter is to avoid storms. This, therefore, he says; that harbor was not suitable for avoiding the storm.

This also pleases Heinsius: but by no means the ancients, or even Camerarius, Beza, or Pricaeus: who says, it is wonderful that those words, for wintering, are explained by such great men with such consensus as 'to avoid the storm': since, although it is a slow and less safe navigation, yet no mention of a storm appears here. The old and the more recent have satisfied me, who translate it 'to winter' or 'to hibernate'. Glosses: I winter, I hibernate. Wintering, hibernation, winter quarters. Another Glossary. I hibernate, I winter. Virgil, 4. Hibernam Lyciam. Where Servius says: Not rough, but suitable for those wishing to winter. See also below 28:11. There is no cause for departing from the common and received interpretation: especially because that passage in ch. 27:11 is manifest for the meaning of wintering.

to Phoenix) Ptolemy has in the southern side of Crete the city of Phoenix, the harbor of Phoenicus.

It was distant from Cnidus by an interval of 45 miles towards the south-southwest, Crete, in which this harbor was, is the land commonly called Candia, whose inhabitants were once called Curetes, as Strabo testifies in book 12. In this island of Crete were situated the cities of Salmone and Lasaea, which is called Lasas by Pliny. And in the middle of these two cities was found a place, which is named Fair Havens, Acts 27. There Paul wished to persuade those who were with him in the ship to winter in that same place in Crete; but the centurion believed the pilot and the shipmaster more than those things which were said by Paul, whence they also fell into the greatest danger of body and life. The cities of Salmone and Lasaea, with Fair Havens, were situated on the southern shore of Crete. Thence Paul and his companions sailed more towards the west, where on the same southern shore of this island was situated the town of Asson, which Pliny calls Asum. There, when the ship was being turned toward the North, to the port of Phoenix, so that they might winter there in Crete, with the South wind now blowing, a Typhonic wind suddenly arose, as Bünting has it, p. 247. Concerning the island of Crete, see Salmasius in Plin. Exerc. in Solin. Polyhist.

βλέποντα κατὰ λίβα) Lips, in Latin Africus, blows from the winter sunset.

καὶ κατὰ χῶρον) χῶρος is a word not Greek in origin but Latin, Corus or Caurus, to the Greeks ἀργέσης. It blows from the summer sunset, or, as others wish, the solstice; therefore this port, situated in a corner, presented its two horns to different seas and winds.

Latin:

Vers. 12. ἀνευθέτου δὲ τῦ λιμένος ὑπάρχοντος πρὸς παρα- χειμασίαν) Sicut ἔυθετος est idoneus Ps. XXXII. 6. Luc. IX. v. 62. XIV. 32. Ita ἀνέυθετος non idoneus, incommodus χειμάζεσθαι est jactari tempestatibus, παραχειμάζεσθαι vitare tempestates. Hoc igitur dicit; non erat portus ille idoneus ad vitandam tempestatem.

Placet id etiam Heinsio: neutiquam vero vete- ribus, vel Camerario etiam, Beza aut Pricæo: qui illa, inquit, πρὸς παραχειμασίαν mirabile est tanto à magnis Viris consensu exponi, ad tempestatem vi- tandam: cum tarda, minusque tuta navigationis qui- dem, at nondum ulla hic mentio tempestatis appareat. Satisfecerunt mihi vetus cum recentiore, qui ad hie- mandum, vel hibernandum. Glossæ: παραχειμά- ζω, hiberno. Παραχειμασία, hiematio, hibernium. Aliud Glossarium. Hiemo, παραχειμάζω. Vir- gil. 4. Hibernam Lyciam. Ubi Servius; Non asperam sed aptam hiemare cupientibus. Vide & infra XXVIII, 11. Non est causadiscedendi a com- muni & recepta interpretatione: imprimis quia lo- cus ille c. XXIX. 11. manifestus est pro significatu hybernandi.

εἰς Φοίνικα) Habet in Austrino Cretæ latere Ptolemæus urbem Phœnicis, portum Phœnicunta.

Abfuit a Cnido interstitio 45. milljarium versus Austrum Africum, Creta in qua portus hic fuit terra Candida vulgo Candia dicta, cujus habitato- res olim Curētes vocati teste Strabone l. XII. Sitæ fuerunt in hac insula Creta civitates Salmone & La- sæa, quæ Lasas a Plinio vocatur. Et in medio ha- rum duarum urbium inventus est locus, qui no- minatur Pulcher portus, Act.XXVII.Ibi Paulus illis, qui cum ipso in navi erant, persuadere voluit, ut ibidem in Creta hyemarent; centurio autem gu- bernatori & nauclero magis credebat, quam his quæ a Paulo dicebantur, unde in maximum etiam periculum corporis & vitæ inciderunt. Sitæ fu- erunt urbes Salmona & Lasæa, cum Pulchro por- tu, in australi littore Cretæ. Inde Paulus & comites ipsius magis versus occasum navigarunt, ubi in eo- dem littore australi hujus insulæ, situm erat Asson oppidum, quod Plinius Asum vocat. Ibi cum ver- sus Boream navis flecteretur, ad portum Phœni- cen, ut ibidem in Creta hybernarent, aspirante jam Austro, coortus est subito ventus Typhonicus, ut habet Bünting. p. 247. De insula Creta vid. Sal- masius in Plin. Exerc. in Solin. Polyhist.

βλέποντα κατὰ λίβα) Λίψ, Latine Africus, flat ab occasu brumali.

καὶ κατὰ χῶρον) χῶρος vox est non Græca origine sed Lati- na, Corus vel Caurus, Græcis ἀργέσης. Flat ab occasu æstivo, aut, ut alii volunt, solstitiali, Portus ergo iste in angulo situs duo mari ventisque diversis objiciebat cornua.

## 27:13
V. 13. ὑποπνεύσαντος δὲ νότου) ὑπὸ often diminishes the meaning in composition. And so ὑποπνεῖν is to blow gently. Such are ὑπόκωφος, ὑποκρίνω, ὑπολαλέω, and similar ones.

δόξαντες τῆς προθέσεως κεκρατηκέναι) The sailors, that is. κρατεῖν προθέσεως is to obtain one's desire. They thought this because the South wind had strengthened for those wishing to sail along the southern shore of Crete.

ἄραντες) When they had set sail, namely from Phoenix or the Phoenicean port.

ἆσσον παρελέγοντο τὴν Κρήτην) Thus it must be distinguished. That is: they were sailing as close as possible to the coast of Crete. חדרי מוקב this is the Syrian. Not fearing, that is, that they would be driven onto the shore, because the South wind was very gentle, as we learned from the aforementioned. I shall not repeat at length what others have rightly shown here, that it was wrongly thought by some that this name was the proper name of the place Asson.

Beza is more prolix against this opinion about the city of Asson: Yet it is not disapproved by Camerarius: But if Assum, he says, is the name of the place, just as it appears in Latin books, and is read in Pliny among the inland cities of Crete, perhaps it may be permitted to interpret these things thus: Having sailed past Assum. However, there was another city, Assus of Phrygia, which was mentioned above. And Heinsius refutes the interpretation of Beza and Grotius primarily with the argument that ἆσσον, when it signifies 'nearer', is peculiar to the poets. He understands it, however, as Aso, which Stephanus places in Crete, and calls a πολίχνιον or small town. The Vulgate also took it as a city, which the Pontifical interpreters follow, B. Luther, Bünting, and others of our own, from whom we do not see a solid reason why we should depart.

Latin:

V. 13. ὑποπνεύσαντος δὲ νότου) ὑπὸ sæpe in composi- tione rem imminuit. Itaque ὑποπνεῖν est leniter flare. Talia sint ὑπόκωφος, ὑποκρίνω, ὑπολαλέω & similia.

δόξαντες τῆς προθέσεως κεκρατηκέναι) Nautæ scil. κρατεῖν προθέσεως est voto potiri. Id ideo existimabant, quia Austra- le Cretæ litrus legere volentibus Auster obrigerat.

ἄραντες) Cum solvissent, nempe a Phœnice aut Phœni- cunte portu.

ἆσσον παρελέγοντο τὴν Κρήτην) Ita distinguendum est. Id est: quam proxime oram Cretæ legebant. חדרי מוקב hic Syrus. Non metuentes scil. ne in littus impingerentur, ideo quod lenis admodum esset Auster, ut ex antedictis co- gnovimus. Non repetam multis quod alii recte hic osten- derunt male a nonnullis putatum nomen hoc esse pro- prium loci Asson.

Prolixius est adversus hanc sententiam de Asson civitate Beza: Non improbatur tamen illa Came- rario: Quod si Assum, inquit, loci nomen sit, quemad- modum extat in Latinis libris, & inter mediterra- neas urbes Cretæ in Plinio legitur, liceat fortasse ita hæc interpretari: Prætervecti Assum. Fuit autem a- lia urbs Assus Phrygiæ, cujus supra mentio facta est. Et refellit Bezæ & Grotii interpretationem Hein- sius eo imprimis argumento, quod ἆσσον, cum si- gnificat propius, Poëtarum proprium sit. Intelligit autem de Aso, quam in Creta reponit Stephanus, & πολίχνιον sive urbeculam vocat. De urbe etiam accepit Vulgatus, quem Pontificii interpretes se- quuntur, B. Lutherus Büntingius, & alii e nostris, a quibus cur discedendum sit solidam rationem non videmus.

## 27:14
v. 14. ἄνεμος τυφωνικός) What τυφὼν is, we noted above from those who described the Meteora. But to the Hellenistic Jews, τυφὼς is any rather violent storm. For thus certain interpreters translate in Ps. CXLVIII. 8. רוח סערה: where others translate πνεῦμα καταιγίδος, a stormy wind. Just as the same name סערה is translated καταιγὶς in Ps. LV, 9. LXXXIII. 16. CVII. 27. 29. Is. XXIX. 6. XL. 24. XLI. 16. and elsewhere κλύδων, as in Jonah 1. 4. 11. 12.

ὁ καλόμενος Εὐροκλύδων) The manuscript has Εὐρακύλων, with no obscure substitution of λ for δ, the strokes of which letters are very similar in manuscripts. The true reading is that which the Latin interpreter followed, Εὐροακύλων. In like manner

It is called Euronotus; and Eurocercius in Vitruvius. Nor is it new for words of Greek origin to coalesce with Latin ones. Such are biclinium, epitogium, Anticæto, noted by Quintilian I. 9. which proceeds much more easily where that Greek word has been adopted into Latin, as Eurus. But not in vain did Luke, not content with having said a stormy wind, wish to add from where it was blowing, which could be none other than Euroaquilo, more adverse to those making for Italy. It could be said that with such a stormy wind standing from the East and North, that which is in Lucan, Nor shall the raft touch the Hesperian, nor the shipwrecked shores: This very Cornelius à Lapide the Jesuit, not daring to prefer the Vulgate to the received Greek text, although he is very prolix about this wind, and even brings in Phil. Cluverius, who contends in book II of the Antiquities of Sicily c. XVI that it must be read entirely as ευρακύλων in the Greek; But he rather reconciles both texts. In Greek Ευροκλύδων, that is, stormy and surging Eurus, and one stirring up waves and whirlpools in the sea, like the North wind. Pricæus, although he considers the arguments which are brought forward for Ευροακύλων to be probable, nevertheless says that our reading is not to be spurned except upon deliberation.

Latin:

v. 14. ἄνεμος τυφωνικός) τυφὼν quid sit, supra notavimus ex iis qui Meteora descripsere. At Judæis Hellenistis τυφὼς est quævis violentior procella. Nam sic interpretes quidam ver- tunt in Ps. CXLVIII. 8. רוח סערה: ubi alii πνεῦμα καται- γίδος, ventus procellosus. Sicut & idem nomen סערה ver- titur καταιγὶς Ps. LV, 9. LXXXIII. 16. CVII. 27. 29. Es. XXIX. 6. XL. 24. XLI. 16. alibi κλύδων, ut Jonæ 1. 4.11.12.

ὁ καλόμενος Εὐροκλύδων) Manuscriptus Εὐρακύλων, haud obscura commutatione λ in δquarum literarum perquam vicini sunt ductus in Manuscriptis. Vera lectio est, quam secutus est Latinus interpres, Εὐροακύλων. Pari modo

dicitur Euronotus; & Eurocercius apud Vitruvium. Nec novum vocabula Graecæ originis cum Latinis coale- fcere. Talia sunt, biclinium, epitogium, Anticæto, notata Quintiliano I. 9. quod multo facilius procedit, ubi vox illa Græca in Latium adoptata est, ut Eurus. Non frustra autem Lucas, non contentus dixisse conrtum ventum procello- sum, adjicere voluit unde is flaret, quod nullus esse posset Euro aquilone magis adversus Italiam petentibus. Dici po- terat vento tam procelloso stante ab Ortu & Septentrione, id quod apud Lucanum est, Nec ratis Hesperias tanget, neque naufragus oras: Non ausus hic ipse Cornelius à Lapide Jesuita Vulgatam præferre recepto Græco textui, etsi valde prolixus sit de hoc vento, ac Phil. Cluverium etiam adducat, omnino legendum in Græco esse ευρακύλων l. II. de Antiqu. Siciliæ c. XVI. conten- dentem; Sed conciliat potius utrumque textum. Græce Ευροκλύδων, id est, Eurus tempestuosus, & fluctuosus, excitansque in mari fluctus & vertices, instar Aquilonis. Pricæus etsi probabilia argu- menta censeat, quæ pro Ευροακύλων adferuntur, nostram tamen lectionem non nisi deliberato sper- nendam dicit.

## 27:15
Verse 15.

the ship being caught) Carried away from Crete. καὶ μὴ δυναμένου ἀντοφθαλμεῖν τῷ ἀνέμῳ) An excellent translation. Ἀντοφθαλμεῖν properly is to look against; improperly to struggle against: as when Plutarch denies that Demosthenes could ἀντοφθαλμεῖν the money, and when Polybius in more than one place denies that these or those could ἀντοφθαλμεῖν the enemies: in which sense the son of Sirach also uses this word XII. 14. Thus also Josephus uses ἀντιβλέπειν, as in Antiquities VI, to the sufferings which it was no longer possible to look against: and in the second against Apion: they did not look against the ordinances concerning diet. The Syriac rightly translates it to resist the wind. Deservedly, therefore, did Camerarius note the Greek interpreters here: The Greeks note this figure by the name of ἀκυρολεξία, when that is said of a ship which is properly of men. And, they add: that one ought not always to demand literal speech from Scripture. That a proper expression is not always to be demanded from Scripture. But not every metaphor is also an ἀκυρολεξία. The verb, however, signifies to look with opposing eyes. Which is in Theocritus: to look with straight eyes. But by this very gesture and such a countenance is indicated the confidence of the mind, of those not yielding to violent aggression, and of those who are not frightened by danger, nor dismayed. Polybius book IV concerning the Messenians: when they themselves by themselves were able to look against the weight of the Lacedaemonians: Nor could they themselves by themselves sustain the heavy force of the Lacedaemonians. And again: being able to look against the onset. That which Luke has now transferred to the ship. ἐπιδιδόντες ἐφερόμεθα) ἐπιδιδόντες, namely to the wind, which noun preceded. Yielding to the wind we were carried. Thus also Ovid describes a storm in Tristia I. 3. The sailor, having confessed his cold fear with pallor, now follows the wind, he does not rule the raft with art. Thus not where he wished, but where the force of the wave snatches it, I see the charioteer has given the sails to the raft.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

συναρπασθέντος δὲ τοῦ πλοίου) Abrepto à Creta. καὶ μὴ δυναμένου ἀντοφθαλμεῖν τῷ ἀνέμῳ) Egregia transla- tio. Ἀντοφθαλμεῖν proprie est contra tueri; improprie ob- niti: ut cum Plutarchus negat Demosthenem potuisse ἀντο- φθαλμεῖν τῷ ἀργυρίῳ, & cum Polybius non uno loco negat hos aut illos potuisse hostibus ἀντοφθαλμεῖν: quo sensu hoc verbo utitur & Sirachides XII. 14. Sic & ἀντιβλέπειν usur- pat Josephus, ut Antiquæ historiæ VI. παθήμασιν οἷς οὐκ ἔτι ἦν ἀντιβλέψαι: & secundo contra Appionem: τοῖς προστάγ- μασι τοῖς περὶ διαίτης οὐκ ἀντέβλεψαν. Syrus recte vertit vento obsistere. Merito ergo hic Græcos Interpretes notavit Camerarius: Græci notant hanc figuram ἀκυρολε- ξίας nomine, cum de navi id dicatur quod proprie est hominum. Et, addunt: ὅτι οὐ δεῖ κυριολεκτεῖν ἀεὶ ἀπαιτεῖν τὴν γραφήν. Quod non semper à Scriptura postulanda sit propria locutio. Sed non est omnis με- ταφορὰ etiam ἀκυρολεξία. Verbum autem signifi- cat, adversis oculis intueri. Quod Theocrito est: ὄμ- μασι τοῖς ὀρθοῖσι ποτιβλέπειν. Hoc ipso autem gestu & tali facie indicatur animi confidentia, non ceden- tium violentæ aggressioni, & eorum qui non terrentur periculo, neque consternuntur. Polybius libro IV. de Messenius: ὅτ' αὐτοὶ δι' αὐτῶν ἀντοφθαλμεῖν ἠδύ- ναντο πρὸς τὸ βάρος τῶν Λακεδαιμονίων: Neque ipsi per se gravem vim Lacedæmoniorum sustinere po- terant. Et rursum: ἠδυνάμενοι δὲ πρὸς τὴν ὁρμὴν ἀντοφθαλμεῖν. Id quod nunc Lucas ad navigium transtulit. ἐπιδιδόντες ἐφερόμεθα) ἐπιδιδόντες, nempe τῷ ἀνέμῳ, quod nomen præcessit. Cedentes vento ferebamur. Sic & Ovidius tempestatem describit I. Tristium. 3. Navita confessus gelidum pallore timorem, Iam sequitur dictus, non regit arte ratem. Sic non quo voluit, sed quo rapit impetus undæ, Aurigam video vela dedisse rati.

## 27:16
Verse 16.

And running under a certain small island) That is, when we had come near the island; in which sense we had the verb ὑποπλεῖν above XXVII. 4. and 7. καλούμενον Κλαύδην) Which is Κλαῦδος in Ptolemy, Κλαύδιος in Athenaeus. In the Syriac it is כודא, but it is believed to be written for קודא. For Strabo said the same island, as is believed, was Γαῦδος, and Suidas reads Καυδὼ in this place: Pliny, Solinus, Stephanus, Procopius name it Gaudon: which the learned judge to be this very one, with the pronunciation varying, as it is wont to do. This island is distant from the port of Phoenix, from which they were driven by the Typhonic wind, thirteen miles. μόλις ἰσχύσαμεν περικρατεῖς γενέσθαι τῆς σκάφης) We were barely able to lift the skiff from the sea into the ship. See below 30. that it was done so that the skiff, struck against the ship, might not damage it. Bünting says the skiff was towed with the ship seized, so that they might not fall into the Syrtis.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Νησίον δέ τι ὑποδραμόντες) Id est, cum prope insu- lam venissemus; quo sensu verbum ὑποπλεῖν habuimus su- pra XXVII. 4. & 7. καλούμενον Κλαύδην) Quæ Κλαῦδος Ptolemæo, Κλαύ- διος Athenæo. In Syro est כודא, sed creditur scriptum pro קודא. Nam Γαῦδος eandem, ut creditur, insulam dixit Strabo, & Suidas Καυδὼ legit hoc loco: Gaudon Pli- nius, Solinus, Stephanus, Procopius nominant: quam hanc ipsam esse censent eruditi, variante, ut solet, pronunti- atione. Distat hæc insula à portu Phænice, à quo re- pulsi fuere vento Typhonico, milliaribus tre- decim. μόλις ἰσχύσαμεν περικρατεῖς γενέσθαι τῆς σκάφης) Ægre potuimus scapham ex mari in navem attollere. Vide infra 30. factum id ne scapha incussa navi eam læde- ret. Büntingius scapham apprehensa navi allega- tam dicit, ne in Syrtim inciderent.

## 27:17
Which having lifted) Which having been drawn up. αἴρειν σκαφὴν and χαλᾶν are opposites.

they used helps) He calls those helps which the Latins call ministries. For that word signifies the naval crew. Germanicus uses it thus in Capricorn, where he calls them helps if anyone sees them.

binding the ship with cables, lest it should fly apart by the force of the winds and waves.

and fearing lest they should fall into the Syrtis) Lest the ship together with them should be driven into the Syrtis. Thus all shallow places are called from two sandy bays in Africa called by this name. Ἐκπέσωσι, from the deep sea, that is, into the shallows.

χαλάσαντες τὸ σκεῦος) With the mast lowered. For this mast is called σκεῦος by way of eminence: as observed by Heraldus. Thus also the Syrian understood it. It is customary for the mast to be lowered or even, in sudden danger, to be cut away, so that the wind may not drive the ship on that side. Papianus said to throw down the tree, L. cum arbor D. on the Rhodian law.

οὕτως ἐφέροντο) Namely, without the mast. A similar use of the little word οὕτως, John IV. 6.

Heinsius argues laboriously indeed against Beza, who translated it as 'with sails lowered,' that χαλᾷν τὸ σκεῦος here denotes the casting away of the mast: he doubts, however, whether they might not have first loosened the mast, which was then cast away. But Pricaeus rightly observes that, although it is true that in escaping storms masts are accustomed to be cut or cast away; yet it scarcely occurs in that sense as χαλᾷν, and therefore he sides with those who translate it as 'lowered,' as below in v. 30, and interpret σκεῦος not as the mast, but as the yard with the sail attached. Ovid: 'The lowered yard escapes the wintry storms.' Seneca: 'As often as the wind has increased, and is greater than is expedient, the yard is lowered.' We have 'to withdraw sails from a storm' in Petronius. They are not accustomed to lower the mast immediately in dangers, but the yard first: at the last, however, the mast. Furthermore, it is observed that the name σκεῦος correctly comprehends the tackle or instruments of a ship, of which the yard with the mast and sails are the principal. Here, however, with Chrysostom, Bede, and Mariana, we understand the yard with the sails, not denied by Camerarius, who explains Χαλάσαντες τὸ σκεῦος thus: 'With the tackle loosened.' These words sound as if they then used the sail differently than before. And in Theophylact it is: Χαλάσαντες τὸ σκεῦος, that is, the sails, for when the wind is violent, this is done. 'With the tackle loosened,' that is, the sails. For this happens in a stormy wind. The Vulgate, however, interprets it less conveniently as 'with the vessel lowered.'

Latin:

ἣν ἄραντες) Qui subducta. Contraria sunt αἴρειν σκα- φὴν & χαλᾶν.

βοηθείαις ἐχρῶντο) βοηθείας vocat quas Latini ministe- ria. Ea enim vox plebem navalem significat. Utitur sic Germanicus in Capricorno, ubi a nobis dicta videant si queis vocat.

ὑποζωννῦντες τὸ πλοῖον) Funibus navem ligantes, ne vi ventorum & fluctuum dissiliret.

φοβούμενοί τε μὴ εἰς τὴν Σύρτιν ἐκπέσωσι) Ne navis una cum ipsis impingeretur in Syrtim. Sic vocantur loca omnia vadosa a duobus in Africa arenosis sinibus dictis hoc no- mine. Ἐκπέσωσι, ex mari profundo scilicet in brevia.

χαλάσαντες τὸ σκεῦος) Demisso malo. Nam malus hic κατ’ ἐξοχὴν dicitur σκεῦος: ut observatum Heraldo. Sic & Syrus accepit. Solet demitti malus aut etiam in re- pentino periculo abscindi, ne ventus ea parte navem ur- geat. Arborem dejicere dixit Papianus L. cum arbor D. ad legem Rhodiam.

οὕτως ἐφέροντο) Nempe sine malo. Similis usus voculæ οὕτως, Joh. IV. 6.

Operose quidem adversus Bezam, qui reddi- dit demissis velis, disputat Heinsius χαλᾷν τὸ σκεῦος, hic jactum mali notare: ambigit tamen, annon prius laxaverint malum, qui deinde ejectus fuerit. Sed recte Pricæus observat, quanquam verum sit evadendis procellis cædi malos, vel re- jici solere; vix tamen eo sensu χαλᾷν occurrere, ideoque cum iis facit, qui demisso vertunt, ut infra v. 30. & σκεῦος non malum, sed cum appenso velo antemnam interpretantur. Ovidius: Effugit hibernas demissa antemna procellas. Seneca: Quoties ventus increbuit, majorque est quam expedit, antemna demittitur. Vela tempesta- ti subducere, apud Petronium habemus. Non solent malum statim in periculis demittere, sed antemnam prius: ad extremum autem malum. De cætero recte nomine σκεῦος comprehendi armamenta vel instrumenta navis, observatur, e quibus antemna cum malo & velis præcipua sunt. Hic vero cum Chrysostomo, Beda, Mariana ante- mnam intelligimus cum velis, non abnuente Ca- merario, qui sic exponit Χαλάσαντες τὸ σκεῦος: Laxato armamento: Ita hæc sonant, quasi tunc aliter atque antea usi sint velo. Et in Theophy- lacteis est: Χαλάσαντες τὸ σκεῦος, τουτέστι τὰ ἱστία, ὅταν γὰρ σφοδρὸς ὁ ἄνεμος ᾖ, τοῦτο γίνεται. Laxato armamento, id est, velis. Hoc enim fit in procelloso vento. Minus autem commode Vul- gata summisso vase interpretatur.

## 27:18
Ver. 18.

σφοδρῶς δὲ χειμαζομένων ἡμῶν) χειμάζεσθαι is, as we just said, to be tossed by a storm.

τῇ ἑξῆς ἐκβολὴν ἐποιοῦντο) They made a casting away, that is, the sailors. Ἐκβολὴ is 'a casting' in the Glossary: and it is so taken in Jonah I. 5, both words being proper to this matter. See the title of the Digest on the Rhodian law concerning casting away. Hermenopolus translates 'to make a casting' as ἐκβάλλειν, ἀποβάλλειν, ῥίπτειν. This is done for the sake of lightening the ship, as the first law in the said title speaks. This order is usually observed, which we also have in this history. First, the merchandise is cast away, as in this place: then the tackle, as follows immediately: finally, even the provisions, as below in 38.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

σφοδρῶς δὲ χειμαζομένων ἡμῶν) χειμάζεσθαι est, ut modo diximus, tempestati jactari.

τῇ ἑξῆς ἐκβολὴν ἐποιοῦντο) Jactum fecere, nautæ scilicet. Ἐκβολὴ jactus in Glossario: & sic sumitur Jonæ I. 5. vox utraque propria huic rei. Vide titulum Digestorum ad le- gem Rhodiam de jactu. Jactum facere Hermenopolus vertit ἐκβάλλειν, ἀποβάλλειν, ῥίπτειν. Fit id levandæ navis gratia, ut loquitur lex prima dicto titulo. Solet autem hic ordo servari, quem & in hac historia habemus. Primum jaciuntur merces, ut hoc loco: deinde armamenta ut sta- tim sequitur: postremo & cibaria, ut infra 38.

## 27:19
Ver. 19.

αὐτόχειρες τὴν σκευὴν τοῦ πλοίου ἐῤῥίψαμεν) That Manuscript has ἐῤῥίψαν, nor does the Latin read otherwise, ἡ σκευὴ is that with which each thing is equipped. In this place the Latin well translates: 'tackle.' In the Glossary, Armamenta is ἄρμενα. Not only poets use this word in that sense, but also historians, as see Tacitus, Histories V: 'Tackle accustomed to Liburnian ships': Julian the Jurisconsult, L. Navis D. on the Rhodian law.

Heinsius interprets the former part: 'but when the storm was intensified, they cast the loosened (mast, that is) into the sea.' Because he thinks the mast being loosened is indicated by the preceding words. But we have already said why that opinion is not to be approved. Nor is that order found here which Grotius assigns. Neither in ver. 18 are the objects of the casting away merchandise, nor in the following verses are the 'tackle,' as they call it, of the ship indicated by τὴν σκευὴν:

The goods are cast out not so much by the sailors as by those to whom they belong: and these are designated by the word σκευὴ, which those very owners, to whom they belonged, cast away, whence the Manuscript, and the Vulgate here is by no means to be preferred to the received Greek Codices: For thus τὰ σκέυη and αἱ σκευαὶ are distinguished: The former are called those things which pertain to the ship, τὰ ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ ἀνήκοντα, by the jurists ἐξαρτὶς, by the Latins armamenta and arma, whence in the laws a ship is said to be disarmed when it is despoiled of them. The latter, however, pertain to the merchants or passengers. The former are cast out by the sailors. But when goods are to be cast out, this very thing is usually done either by the owners, or not without consulting them by the ship-master. As the law holds: If the ship-master thinks about casting out goods, let him consult the passengers: whose, to wit, the money and goods are. Therefore, that which is said here of the sailors, ἐκβολὴν ἐποιῦντο, they made a casting out, you may not inappropriately understand of the tackle otherwise necessary for loading the ship, so that the ship might be lightened by them; but you would more correctly explain σκευὴν as referring to the merchandise. Tackle is not read to have been cast out, for the anchors also pertain to the same, four of which were lowered, v. 29.

PART II. Paul's consolatory speech with an exhortation to take food.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

αὐτόχειρες τὴν σκευὴν τοῦ πλοίου ἐῤῥίψαμεν) ἐῤῥίψαν habet Manuscriptus ille, nec aliter Latinus legit, ἡ σκευὴ est id quo res quæque instruitur. Bene hoc loco Latinus vertit: armamenta. In Glossario Armamenta ἄρμενα. Utuntur hac voce eo sensu non poëtæ tantum, sed & historici, ut ecce Tacitus Histor. V. Armamenta Liburnicis solita: Ju- lianus Jurisconsultus L. Navis D. de lege Rhodia.

Heinsius priora interpretatur: cum vero in- tenderetur tempestas, laxatum (malum scilicet) in mare abjecerunt. Quia verbis antegressis malum laxatum indicari putat. Sed cur ea sen- tentia non probanda, jam diximus. Neque ordo ille hic deprehenditur, quem assignat Grotius. Non nec vers. 18. objectum ἐκβολῆς merces sunt, aut vers. seqq. per τὴν σκευὴν ar- mamenta, quæ vocant, navis indigitantur:

Merces non tam nautæ, quam illi, ad quos spe- ctant, ejiciunt: eæque designantur voce σκευὴ, quas αὐτόχειρες illi, quarum erant, rejecerunt, unde Manuscriptus, & Vulgatus hic minime præferen dus Codicibus Græcis receptis: Nam ita discrimi- nantur τὰ σκέυη, & αἱ σκευαὶ: Illa dicuntur, quæ ad navem spectant, τὰ ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ ἀνήκοντα, Juris- consultis ἐξαρτὶς, Latinis armamenta, & arma, un- de in legibus exarmari navem est, cum illis spolia- tur. Hæc vero ad mercatores aut vectores perti- nent. Illa à nautis ejiciuntur. Cum autem merces ejiciendæ, hoc ipsum vel à possessoribus, vel non nisi consultis illis ab exercitore fieri solet. Uti lex habet: Si de ejiciendis mercibus exercitor cogitet, vecto- res consulat: quorum sc. pecuniæ & merces sunt. Quod ergo hic ἐκβολὴν ἐποιῦντο jactum fecére de nautis dicitur de sarcinis ad navem onerandam alias neces- sariis, ut illis exoneraretur jam navis, non incomo- de intelligas: τ̄ σκευὴν vèro de mercibus rectius explices. Armamenta ejecta non leguntur, nam & Anchoræ ad eadem spectant, quarum quatuor demissæ, v. 29.

PARS II. Oratio Pauli consolatoria cum exhortatione ad sumendum cibum.

## 27:20
v. 20. Neither sun nor stars appearing for many days) A solemn description of more severe storms. Thus in Virgil: Black night broods over the sea.

In Lucan: That was not the night of the sky, the air lies hidden, / With the pallor of the infernal house, and weighed down by clouds / It is pressed low, and the wave receives rain in the clouds, / Even the feared light perishes, nor do clear lightnings run, / But the cloudy air bursts asunder in darkness.

In Statius: Thence, horror on the waters & the day snatched from every / Sun, sent forth darkness.

concerning the word ἐπιφαίνειν see what we have said at Matt. XXVIII. 1.

and no small storm lying upon us) χειμὼν is sometimes winter, sometimes a storm, as here and Matt. XVI, 3. Imitating this, Latin poets use the word hiems for a storm. Ἐπικεῖσθαι here is to lie upon, to brood over, as we have already had from Virgil: Black night broods over the sea. And elsewhere: --- Winds as if a column were formed, / Where a gate is given they rush, & overturn the lands with a whirlwind: / They have brooded over the sea,

Quintilian book V. When a great force of wind has brooded over the sea.

Beza understood it of an imminent storm: but it is more correctly said to have already brooded: just as the Syrian also interpreted it. Thus ἐπικεῖσθαι is taken when someone is actually being pressed, or something is lying upon them, Luke V. 1. John c. XI. 8. Acts XXVIII. 2.

all hope of our being saved was taken away) This is a statement κατὰ φάσιν, according to what appeared, such as are many both in common and in sacred speech. In Syriac: Hope cut off.

Latin:

v. 20. Μήτε δὲ ἡλίου) μήτε ἄτρων ἐπιφαινόντων ἐπὶ πλείονας ἡμέρας) Solennis descriptio graviorum tempestatum. Sic apud Virgilium: Ponto nox incubat atra.

Apud Lucanum: Non cæli nox illa fuit, latet obfitus aër, Inferna pallore domus, nimbisque gravatus Deprimitur, fluctusque in nubibus accipit imbrem, Lux etiam metuenda perit, nec fulgura currunt Clara, sed obscurum nimbosus dissilit aër.

Apud Statium: Inde, horror aquis & raptus ab omni Sole dies, misset tenebras.

de verbo ἐπιφαίνειν vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXVIII. 1.

χειμῶνός τε ὐκ ὀλίγου ἐπικειμένου) χειμὼν interdum hiems, interdum tempestas, ut hic & Matth. XVI, 3. Id imitantes Latini Poëtæ hiemis vocem ponunt pro tempestate. Ἐπι- κεῖσθαι hic est incumbere, incubare, quomodo ex Virgilio jam habuimus: Ponto nox incubat atra Et alibi: --- Venti velut agmine facto, Qua data porta ruunt, & terras turbine bersant: Incubuere mari,

Quintilianus lib. V. Cum magna vis venti in mare incubuit.
