De imminente tempestate Beza intellexit: sed rectius incubuisse jam dicitur: uti etiam Syrus in- terpretatus est. Sic ἐπικεῖσθαι accipitur cum actu premitur quis, aut aliquid incumbit, Luc. V. 1. Joh. c. XI. 8. Act. XXVIII. 2.

λοιπὸν περιῃρεῖτο πᾶσα ἐλπὶς τῦ σώζεσθαι ἡμᾶς) Dictum hoc κατὰ φάσιν, secundum id quod videbatur, qualia multa & in communi, & in sacro sermone. In Syriaco: Abscissa spes.

## 27:21
V. 21. But much abstinence existing) Not that food was lacking, as we shall soon see, but that that huge tossing takes away all appetite, and on the contrary produces a loathing of food.

having obeyed me) To me, namely, saying nothing in this matter that is not divinely inspired.

not to set sail from Crete) Do not set sail from Crete. See above 2. 4. 12.

and to gain this injury and loss) A very Greek expression. For the Greek epigrammatists and Lucian speak in a similar way. The Latin translator also eruditely translated it as 'to gain' (lucrifacere). Thus, 'what injury you gain' (quam ille injuriam lucrifacis), Plin. VII. 39. Thus Tertullian spoke of the 'gaining of evils' (lucrationem malorum). Such also is that: 'Gain the censor's mark' (Lucri fac censoriarn notam). The reason for this way of speaking is that he who avoids a loss seems to make a gain, according to Aristotle. Concerning the words ὕβρεως and ζημίας, see above 10.

Pricaeus distinguishes these things thus: Ζημία here is the loss of goods and precious things. Theodorus Priscianus. Ships pressed by a burden, when they are tossed by a severe storm, have only a remedy from the loss. ὕβρις denotes the inconveniences and injuries of a storm. Thus in Pollux's Onomasticon, ὕβρισὴς ἄνεμος: and in Caesar, if I remember correctly, the 'insult' (contumelia) of the winds.

Latin:

V. 21. πολλῆς δὲ ἀσιτίας ὑπαρχύσης) Non quod alimenta deeffent, ut mox videbimus, sed quod ingens illa jactatio omnem adimat appetitum, ac contra cibi fastidium pariat.

πειθαρχήσαντάς μοι) Mihi, nempe nihil hac in re non di- vinitus dicenti.

μὴ ἀνάγεσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς Κρήτης) Non solvere à Creta. Vide supra 2. 4. 12.

κερδῆσαί τε τὴν ὕβριν ταύτην κὴ τὴν ζημίαν) Locutio bene Græca. Nam simili modo loquuntur Epigrammatici Græci & Lucianus. Latinus quoque interpres erudite transtulit lucrifacere. Sic quam ille injuriam lucrifecis, Plin. VII. 39. Sic lucrationem malorum dixit Tertullianus. Tale & il- lud: Lucri fac censoriarn notam. Causa loquendi inde, quod lucrum facere videtur, & qui damnum evitat, auctore Ari- stotele. De vocibus ὕβρεως & ζημίας vide supra 10.

Pricæus hæc ita distinguit: Ζημία hic est mer- cium & rerum pretiosarum damnum. Theodorus Priscianus. Naves pressæ onere, cum gravi tempe- state jactantur, solum habent ex damno reme- dium. ὕβρις, tempestatis incommoda & injurias notat. Sic in Pollucis Onomastico ὕβρισὴς ἄνεμος: & apud Cæsarem, si recte memini, ventorum contu- melia.

## 27:22
Verse 22. for there will be no loss of life among you) Namely, if you listen to me. Which condition is easily understood from the preceding speech. Such are the expressions found everywhere in Holy Scripture which have a tacit condition within them, from the preceding and following context: or one easily understood from the very nature of the thing, 1 Sam. II. 30, XIII. 13, 14.

except the ship) An exceptive particle in place of an adversative, as in Luke XXIII. 28, John I. 9 in the Greek, 1 Cor. XI. 1, Phil. I. 8, III. 16, IV. 12, Rev. II. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 22. ἀποβολὴ γὰρ ψυχῆς οὐδεμία ἔσται ἐξ ὑμῶν) Nem- pe, si me audiatis. Quæ conditio ex superiori oratione fa- tis intelligitur. Tales passim in Sacra Scriptura sunt locu- tiones quæ tacitam in se conditionem habent, ex antece- dentibus & consequentibus: aut ex ipsa rei natura intelligi facilem 1. Sam. II. 30. XIII. 13. 14.

πλὴν τοῦ πλοίου) Particula exceptiva loco adversativæ, ut Luc. XXIII. 28. Joh. I 9. in Græco, 1. Cor. XI. 1. Philipp. I. 8. III. 16. IV. 12. Apoc. II. 25.

## 27:23
Verse 23. of the God whose I am and whom I serve) Paul could say this of himself much more rightly than Jonah in a similar danger, Jonah I. 9. And for that reason Jonah's companions were saved by his being cast out: Paul's companions were saved by his being kept.

Latin:

Vers. 23. τοῦ Θεοῦ ὧν εἰμι ᾧ καὶ λατρεύω) Multo rectius hoc de se Paulus potuit dicere, quam in simili periculo Jonas I. 9. Et propterea Jonæ comites eo servati sunt ejecto: Pauli co- mites per eum retentum.

## 27:24
V. 24. You must stand before Caesar) Take δεῖ as above XXIII. 11. παραστῆναι, however, is judicial here, to stand. Rom. XIV. 10, for which above 'I am standing' (ἑσὼς εἰμι). XXV. 10, the active 'to present' (παραστῆσαι) above XXIII. 33. Horace: '...if I should delay, whether I have the strength to stand or know civil laws.' Where the Scholiast says: If I have the strength to stand in judgment.

God has granted you all those who sail with you) We have here χαρίζεσθαι in the opposite sense to that twice above in XXV. 11, 16; there it meant to deliver to destruction: here, to save in life. He gives to you, that is, for your sake He saves them. One sometimes loses a ship, one sometimes saves a ship. The same happens in a Republic.

God has given to you: Therefore they were all already lost, that is, certainly to be lost, both by the course of nature, on account of the force of the storm, as Oecumenius says, and by the vengeance of God, on account of their crimes. Whence Chrysostom explains it thus, as if he were saying: They were indeed worthy to perish, since they were disobedient: nevertheless, for your sake I will save them. Therefore Chrysostom continues: Let us keep the Saints among us, he says, and there will be no storm: nay, even if there is a storm, there will be serenity and tranquility, and deliverance from danger. Since that widow had a Saint as a guest, even the death of her son was undone, and she received the boy back to life, etc. Furthermore, because of Paul, Chrysostom continues, see that all these things happen, so that the prisoners, the soldiers, and the centurion might believe. All of whom he implies were converted to Christ by Paul. For even if they had been stones, because of the oracles, miracles, and benefits of Paul, they would surely have thought great things of him. And Cornelius a Lapide thinks this is implied by the words, 'God has given you all,' namely, as much regarding the salvation of the soul as of the body. But the literal sense (τὸ ῥητὸν) of those words only implies that they are all to be preserved in this life: as Paul himself had understood, v. 22, 25, 26. And Cornelius wrongly concludes from this: If Paul obtained salvation from God for souls in this life, therefore, now glorious, he will be able to obtain much more, enjoying the same in heaven. Because there he saw the necessity, but here he is ignorant of our necessities, Isa. LXIV. 16. Furthermore, when in v. 23 the angel of God, whom Paul served, is named, Salmero tries to prove 'angel-worship' (Ἀγγελολατρείαν) from it: But Cajetan, Lorinus, Cornelius a Lapide, and Estius, along with the interlinear Gloss and Lyranus, acknowledge that that pronoun does not pertain to the angel, but to God as the immediately preceding name.

Latin:

V. 24. Καίσαρί σε δεῖ παραστῆναι) Δεῖ sume ut supra XXIII. 11. παραστῆναι autem hic judiciale est, stare. Rom. XIV. 10. pro quo supra ἑσὼς εἰμι. XXV. 10. activum παραστῆσαι supra XXIII. 33. Horatius. - - - differeam si Aut valeo stare aut novi civilia jura. Ubi Scholiastes: Si habeo vires ut stem in judicio.

Κεχάρισταί σοι ὁ Θεὸς πάντας τοὺς πλέοντας μετὰ σοῦ) Sensu contrario hic habemus χαρίζεσθαι ei qui bis supra XXV. 11. 16. ibi in perniciem tradere: hic in vita servare. Tibi dat, id est, tui causa eos servat. Unus interdum na- vem perdit, unus interdum navem servat. Idem contin- git in Republica.

Donavit tibi Deus: Ergo omnes jam perditi erant, id est, certo perdendi, tum cursu naturæ, ob vim tempestatis, uti ait Oecumenius, tum ultione Dei, ob eorum scelera. Unde Chrysostomus sic explicat, quasi dicat: Digni quidem erant qui peri- rent, quoniam inobedientes fuerunt: verumtamen in tui gratiam servabo eos. Ideo Chrysost. porro: Retineamus, inquit, apud nos Sanctos, nec erit tem- pestas: imo etiamsi fuerit tempestas, erit serenitas ac tranquillitas, & a periculo liberatio. Quoniam vi- dua illa Sanctum hospitio habebat, etiam filii ejus mors soluta est, & redivivum accepit puerum, &c. Porro propter Paulum, ita pergit Chrysostomus, hæc omnia vide fieri, ut credant vincti, milites, ac cen- turio. Quos omnes innuit esse a Paulo ad Chri- stum conversos. Nam etiamsi lapides fuissent, pro- pter oracula, miracula & beneficia Pauli, de illo ma- gna utique cogitassent. Et hoc innui censet Cornel. a Lapide per verba, donavit tibi Deus omnes, scil. tam quoad animæ, quam corporis salutem. Sed τὸ ῥητὸν verborum illorum id solum infert, quod in hac vita conservandi sint omnes: uti acceperat ipse Paulus v. 22. 25. 26. Et perperam Cornelius hinc colligit: Si Paulus in hac vita 267. animabus salu- tem a Deo impetravit: ergo multo plura poterit jam gloriosus impetrare eodem fruens in cælo. Quia illic necessitatem vidit, hic vero necessitates nostras ignorat, Es. LXIV. 16. Porro cum v. 23. angelus Dei, cui servivit Paulus, nominatur, Salmero ̓Αγγελολα- τρείαν inde probare conatur: Sed pronomen illud non pertinere ad angelum, sed ad Deum ceu im- mediate antecedens nomen, Cajetanus, Lorinus, Cornelius a Lap. Estius cum Gloss. interl. & Lyrano agnoscunt.

## 27:25
Verse 25. take heart) As above 22. This is what is called 'to be of good courage' (θαρσεῖν) elsewhere, as above XXIII. 11. 'For I believe God that it will be so') God often requires faith even for obtaining the benefits of this life, to show that it is much more necessary for obtaining eternal life.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ἐνθυμεῖτε) Ut supra 22. Hoc est quod alibi dici- tur θαρσεῖν, ut supra XXIII. 11. πιστεύω γὰρ τῷ Θεῷ ὅτι οὕτως ἔσται) Fidem Deus etiam ad consequenda hujus vitæ beneficia sæpe requirit, ut osten- dat eam multo magis ad consequendam æternam esse ne- cessariam.

## 27:26
v. 26. εἰς νῆσον δέ τινα) Not νησίον such as Claude, but a proper island, such as Melite. δεῖ ἡμᾶς ἐκπεσεῖν) δεῖ again as just now 42. ἐκπεσεῖν as above. 17.

Latin:

v. 26. εἰς νῆσον δέ τινα) Non νησίον qualis Claude, sed justam insulam, qualis Melite. δεῖ ἡμᾶς ἐκπεσεῖν) δεῖ rursum ut modo 42. ἐκπεσεῖν ut supra. 17.

## 27:27
Vers. 27.

διαφερομένων ἡμῶν) Plutarch also used διαφέρεσθαι for being carried hither and thither.

ἐν τῷ Ἀδρίᾳ. That learned men have noted here from Strabo, Ovid, Statius, and Ptolemy that the Adriatic began to be called so for the whole Ionian sea is true. And so Procopius calls the sea from Methone to Sicily, and elsewhere from Cephalenia to Calabria, the Adriatic, and in another place makes a part of the Adriatic a gulf, and expressly in the first book of the Vandalic War he places Gaulon, which he locates in the Adriatic, rather than Melite.

προσάγειν τινὰ αὐτοῖς χώραν) To bring some land to oneself. Sailors are accustomed to speak in this way. Such is that passage in Virgil, Aeneid III: We are carried from the harbor: and the lands and cities recede. The Adriatic Sea is said to be named from Adria, an ancient town and port at the river Po, founded by the Tuscans, as Pliny testifies in book III, chapter XVI. But here it denotes not only that sea which penetrates from the Ceraunian mountains as far as Venice, but it also includes the Ionian Sea, which washes Epirus and the parts lying below it, which in the age of Strabo, when these things almost happened, had already become accustomed to being included under the Adriatic Sea taken more generally, as the same author testifies in book VII, and Ptolemy in book III. Bochart distinguishes between Adria or the Adriatic Sea and the Adriatic gulf. For he defines the latter with Illyricum. But the Adriatic Sea is the same as the Ionian.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

διαφερομένων ἡμῶν) διαφέρεσθαι pro huc & illuc ferri usurpavit & Plutarchus.

ἐν τῷ Ἀδρίᾳ. Quod notarunt hic viri eruditi ex Strabo- ne, Ovidio, Statio & Ptolemæo, Adriam cœpisse dici, pro to- to Ionio, verum est. Itaque Procopius mare a Methone ad Siciliam, & alibi a Cephalenia ad Calabriam, Adriam, vo- cat, & alio loco partem Adriæ facit sinum, & diserte Vanda- licorum primo ᾤκει Gaulon quam Meliten in Adria locat.

προσάγειν τινὰ αὐτοῖς χώραν) Accedere sibi terram ali- quam. Ita solent nautæ loqui. Tale illud apud Virgilium III. Æneidos: Provehimur portu: terræque urbesque recedunt. Mare Adriaticum ab Adria veteri oppido & Portu ad Padum fluvium à Tuscis conditio dicitur teste Plinio l. III.c. XVI. Hic vero non tantum mare illud, quod à Cerauniis montibus intus Venetias usque penetrat, notat, sed complectitur quoq; ma- re Ionium, quod Epirum & subjectas partes alluit, quod ætate Strabonis, qua hæc fere contigere, jam sub Adriatico mari generalius accepto compre- hendi consuevit, teste Eodem l. VII. & Ptolemæo l. III. Bochartus distinguit inter Adriam seu Adria- ticum mare & sinum Adriaticum. Hoc enim cum Illyrico definit. At mare Adriaticum idem est cum Ionio.

## 27:28
Vers. 28. Βολίσαντες) βολὶς, which is καταπειρατηρία in Herodotus, Euterpe, a rope with lead which, when cast down, sailors use to explore the depth of the sea, which is called βολίζειν. Lucilius called it a catapiraten in those verses which are corrupt in Isidore XIX. 14. Hence let a boy bring a catapiraten, a small piece of lead anointed, and a thread of linen, where he explained a nautical term not known to everyone with popular words. εὗρον ὀργυιὰς εἴκοσι) ὀργυιὰ is as much as the outstretched hands extend, whence the name for a pace. Sailors are accustomed to use this measure. εὗρον ὀργυιὰς δεκαπέντε) That was a sign that they were approaching land. Luke describes all these naval matters accurately and neatly. Glossary: Bolis is a small bronze and lead vessel with a chain, which sailors fill with grease and lower into the sea to explore whether the places are rocky, where a ship might stand, or sandy, or those which destroy a ship. Others call it a nautical plumb line, by which they explore the depth of the sea, so that it may not be dashed against the shallows. Dicitur communiter hodie plumbum: It is commonly called lead today: whence when the sailors had found the depth of the sea to be twenty fathoms, fearing that the ship might fall into rough places, sands, and reefs, they cast four anchors from the stern, so that they might stop the ship and make it firm until the day should shine, so that they might see in what place they were, and where they ought to turn again.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Βολίσαντες) βολὶς quæ καταπειρατηρία Hero- doto Euterpe, funis cum plumbo quo dejecto nautæ maris altitudinem explorant, quod βολίζειν dicitur. Catapiraten dixit Lucillius illis versibus qui corrupti apud Isodorum XIX. 14. Hinc Catapiraten puer eodem deferat, unctum Plumbi pauxillum raudus linique metaxam. ubi vocem nauticam non omnibus notam expusuit verbis popularibus. εὗρον ὀργυιὰς εἴκοσι) ὀργυιὰ est quantum patent passæ ma- nus, unde passui nomen. Hac mensura uti nautæ solent. εὗρον ὀργυιὰς δεκαπέντε) Id signum erat propius accedere terram. Omnia hæc navalia accurate & nitide describit Lucas. Glossarium: Bolis est vasculum æneum & plum- beum cum catena, quod nautæ implent adipe & submittunt in mare ad explorandum, an loca pe- trosa, ubi navis stare possit: an arenosa, s. quæ navim perdunt. Alii nauticum perpendiculum, quo altitu- dinem maris explorant, ne vadis illidatur. Dicitur communiter hodie plumbum: unde cum invene- rint usque ad fundum maris passus viginti navitæ timentes ne in aspera loca, arenas, & scopulos inci- deret vavis, jecerunt de puppi quatuor anchoras, ut navim sisterent, & firmarent, donec dies illuce- sceret, ut viderent quo loco essent, & quo rursum flectere deberent.

## 27:29
v. 29. Εἰς τραχεῖς τόπους) He calls rocky places rough, as the Syriac rightly explains here, such as are accustomed to be many around islands. Others call them χοιράδας. ἐκ πρύμνης ῥίψαντες ἀγκύρας τέσσαρας) Thus Virgil: The anchor is cast from the prow. But there is need of more anchors when the sea rages. ηὔχοντο ἡμέραν γενέσθαι) So that they might be able to see more easily where they were located.

Latin:

v. 29. Εἰς τραχεῖς τόπους) Aspera loca vocat saxosa, ut hic recte explicat Syrus, qualia multa esse circa insulas so- lent. χοιράδας dicunt alii. ἐκ πρύμνης ῥίψαντες ἀγκύρας τέσσαρας) Sic Virgilius: Anchora de prora jacitur. Pluribus autem opus anchoris, ubi sævit mare. ηὔχοντο ἡμέραν γενέσθαι) Ut facilius despicere possent, ubi essent locorum.

## 27:30
v. 30. χαλασάντων τὴν σκάφην εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν) Namely, so that having slipped into it and abandoned the ship, they might consult for their own safety. Cicero II de inventione: Some time later the storm began to toss them more violently, and not so much that the master of the ship, since he was also the pilot, would flee into the skiff. Προφάσει ὡς ἐκ πρώρας μελλόντων ἀγκύρας ἐκτείνειν) They used this pretext that they wanted to use the skiff, so that they might fix the anchors further from the prow with the rope extended that far. Note the expression προφάσει μελλόντων ἐκτείνειν ἀγκύρας: under the pretense that they were about to extend the anchors further.

Latin:

v. 30. χαλασάντων τὴν σκάφην εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν) Nimirum ut in eam delapsi derelicto navi saluti suæ consulerent. Cicero II. de inventione: Postea aliquanto ipsos quoque tempestas vehe- mentius jactare cœpit, neque adeo, ut dominus navis, cum idem gubernator esset, in scapham confugeret. Προφάσει ὡς ἐκ πρώρας μελλόντων ἀγκύρας ἐκτείνειν) Hoc utebantur prætextu velle se scapha uti, ut anchoras longius à prora figerent fune eo usque prolato. Nota locutionem προφάσει μελλόντων ἐκτείνειν ἀγκύρας: specie longius sensurorum anchoras.

## 27:31
v. 31. τῷ ἑκατοντάρχῃ) Of whom above 1. ἐὰν μὴ οὗτοι) He said this pointing to the sailors with his finger. ὑμεῖς σωθῆναι ὀὐ δύνασθε) How this does not conflict with those things which were said above 22, see in that place.

Latin:

v. 31. τῷ ἑκατοντάρχῃ) De quo supra 1. ἐὰν μὴ οὗτοι) Dixit hoc nautas digito monstrans. ὑμεῖς σωθῆναι ὀὐ δύνασθε) Quomodo hoc non pugnet cum iis, quæ dicta supra 22, vide illo loco.

## 27:32
Vers. 32. Ἀπέκοψαν τὰ σχοινία τῆς σκάφης, καὶ εἴασαν αὐτὴν ἐκπεσεῖν) The ropes having been cut, they let the skiff be carried away. Ἐκπίπτειν is said here with respect to the ship: above twice with respect to the sea. Thus ἐκπίπτειν τῆς ἀγορᾶς, ἐκπίπτειν τῆς πόλεως in Plutarch.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Ἀπέκοψαν τὰ σχοινία τῆς σκάφης, καὶ εἴασαν αὐτὴν ἐκπεσεῖν) Abscissis funibus sivere scapham auferri. Ἐκπίπτειν hic dicitur respectu navis: supra bis respectu maris. Sic ἐκπί- πτειν τῆς ἀγορᾶς, ἐκπίπτειν τῆς πόλεως apud Plutarchum.

## 27:33
v. 33. ἄσιτοι διατελεῖτε) It is said thus as in 1 Macc. III. 17: we are exhausted fasting today: it is to be understood in such a way that most had taken hardly any nourishment, as has been rightly noted by others. Hippocrates in his book on Flesh and other physicians teach that a healthy man cannot live without food beyond seven days. Sick people, however, in whom natural heat languishes and phlegm abounds, by which heat is fed, could prolong the fast longer. Therefore there is nothing here, or as if nothing: or nothing by way of a set and proper lunch or dinner, but rather tasting some things bit by bit rather than eating.

Latin:

v. 33. ἄσιτοι διατελεῖτε) Sic dictum quomodo I. Macc. III. 17 ἐκλελύμεθα ἀσιτοῦντες σήμερον: id ita intelligendum, quod vix quicquam aumenti cepissent plerique recte notatum aliis. Hippocrates libr. de Carnibus aliique Medici do- cent, hominem sanum non posse sine cibo ultra se- ptem dies vivere. Ægri tamen, quibus calor natura- lis languet, & abundat phlegma, quo calor pasca- tur, diutius inediam prorogare possint. Nihil ergo hic est perparum aut quasi nihil: vel nihil per mo- dum stati justique prandii aut cœnæ, sed carptim quædam libantes potius quam comedentes.

## 27:34
Vers. 34. παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς προσλαβεῖν τροφῆς) Namely, so that they might be stronger to endure the labors for which there was need. See 1 Sam. XIV. 28, 29. He exhorted them to take food for the sake of satisfying hunger: which, along with the Fathers, Jerome, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, Bede, and with the Glossa Ordinaria, and Peter Comestor, Salmero, Lorinus, Cornelius, and Fromondus in this place, as also Vasquez in 3 Thom. disp. 216, and most other Papists acknowledge, and it is most manifest from the circumstances; whence the inept Cochleus in his 25 reasons concerning one species asserts that the Eucharist was celebrated here under one.

οὐδενὸς γὰρ ὑμῶν θρὶξ ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς πεσεῖται) A proverbial expression, just as it could be said in Latin: Not even a whit will be harmed to you. See Luke XXI. 18. Understand this again under the condition, if you follow my counsels.

Latin:

Vers. 34. παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς προσλαβεῖν τροφῆς) Nempe ut firmiores effent ad perferendos labores quibus erat opus. Vide 1. Sam. XIV. 28. 29. Hortatus est ad cibum capiendum famis sedandæ causa: quod cum Patribus, Hier: Chrysost. Oecum. Beda & cum Glossa ordinaria, ac Petro Comestore, Salmero, Lorinus, Cornelius & Fromondus in h. l. ut & Vasquez in 3. Thom. disp. 216. & plerique alii Pontificii agnoscunt, & e circumstantiis manifestissimum est; Unde ineptus Cochleus in 25. rationibus de una specie, Eucharistiam hic sub una celebratam esse, asserit

οὐδενὸς γὰρ ὑμῶν θρὶξ ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς πεσεῖται) Proverbialis locutio, sicut Latine dici posset: Ne hilum quidem vobis nocebitur. Vide Luc. XXI. 18. intellige hoc rursus sub conditione, si consilia mea sequamini.

## 27:35
Vers. 35. εὐχαρίστησε τῷ Θεῷ) See Matt. XV. 36, Mark ch. VIII. 6, John VI. 11.

ἐνώπιον πάντων) Giving an example which they might imitate.

καὶ κλάσας) As in Matt. XIV. 19. XV. 36. Mark VIII. 6. 19. Luke XXIV. 30.

ἤρξατο ἐσθίειν) That is, he eats, as above in line 1.

Latin:

Vers. 35. εὐχαρίστησε τῷ Θεῷ) Vide Matth. XV. 36. Marc. c VIII. 6. Joh. VI. 11.

ἐνώπιον πάντων) Exemplum dans quod imitarentur.

καὶ κλάσας) Ut Matth. XIV. 19. XV. 36. Marc. VIII. 6. 19. Luc. XXIV. 30.

ἤρξατο ἐσθίειν) Id est, edit, ut supra l. 1.

## 27:36
Vers. 36. ἔνθυμοι δὲ γενόμενοι πάντες) From that very serious assertion of Paul, a man not given to levity.

Latin:

Vers. 36. ἔνθυμοι δὲ γενόμενοι πάντες) Ex ista tam seria Pauli, viri non levis, asseveratione.

## 27:37
v. 37. αἱ πᾶσαι ψυχαὶ) Persons: as above in II. 41. and here in X. 29.

PART III. The salvation of all of Paul's companions from the shipwreck.

Latin:

v. 37. αἱ πᾶσαι ψυχαὶ) Personæ: ut supr. II. 41. & h. c. X. 29.

PARS III. Omnium Pauli comitum e naufragio salvatio.

## 27:38
Vers. 38. κορεσθέντες δὲ τροφῆς) That is, after hunger was removed by the feast, as Virgil speaks.

ἐκούφιζον τὸ πλοῖον) They lightened the ship, as Paulus the Jurisconsult and Callistratus speak.

ἐκβαλλόμενοι τὸν σῖτον) By casting out the provisions. For this also is accustomed to be done. See L. si laborante §. cum in eandem D. ad l. Rhodiam. This was the third casting out, as we just observed.

Latin:

Vers. 38. κορεσθέντες δὲ τροφῆς) Id est, postquam exempta fames epulis, ut Virgilius loquitur.

ἐκούφιζον τὸ πλοῖον) Levarunt navem, ut loquuntur Paulus Jurisconsultus & Callistratus.

ἐκβαλλόμενοι τὸν σῖτον) Jactando cibaria. Nam & hoc fieri solet. Vide L. si laborante §. cum in eandem D. ad l. Rhodiam. Hic tertius fuit jactus, ut modo observavimus.

## 27:39
Vers. 39. Τὴν γῆν οὐκ ἐπεγίνωσκον) They did not know whether the land was a continent or an island, and what it was.

κόλπον δέ τινα κατενόουν) That is, they caught sight of, as above in VII. 31. κόλπος in Greek, sinus in Latin, is said sometimes of land, sometimes of the sea, as here. For it is distinguished from the shore.

ἔχοντα αἰγιαλὸν) This is not added in vain. For there are certain bays of the sea that do not have a shore, but are surrounded by steep cliffs.

ἐξῶσαι τὸ πλοῖον) to drive ashore. Thucydides uses it in this way.

Latin:

Vers. 39. Τὴν γῆν οὐκ ἐπεγίνωσκον) Nesciebant terra esset continens an insula, & quæ.

κόλπον δέ τινα κατενόουν) Id est, conspexere, ut supra VII. 31. κόλπος Græce, Latine sinus, modo de terra, modo de mari dicitur, ut hic. Distinguitur enim a littore.

ἔχοντα αἰγιαλὸν) Non frustra hoc additur. Sunt enim sinus quidam maris qui littus non habent, sed præruptis rupibus cinguntur.

ἐξῶσαι τὸ πλοῖον) appellere. Utitur sic Thucydides.

## 27:40
Vers. 40. καὶ τὰς ἀγκύρας περιελόντες) That is, with the anchors lifted on all sides. He said this indeed because there were several. Above at 29, they wanted to use the wind, which they could not do unless the anchors were lifted.

εἴων εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν) It is a brief expression for εἴων τὸ πλοῖον ἰέναι εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν; they allowed the ship to go into the sea, namely that which lay between the place where the ship had been fixed and the shore.

ἅμα ἀνέντες τὰς ζευκτηρίας τῶν πηδαλίων) In ancient ships there were two rudders, one for each side, as we showed in the Aratean images Cratinus ὀδυξζεῦσι· ὡς ἂν μᾶλλον τοῖς πηδαλίοις ἡ ναῦς ἡμῖν πειθαρχῇ. Those rudders were attached to the ship by certain bonds, which Luke here in Greek calls ζευκτηρίας; the Latin calls them joints, just as in the Glossary ζεῦξις is a joint. When those bonds are loosened, then the rudders descend much into the waters and by their own weight hold the ship, so that it is not overturned by the winds.

καὶ ἐπάραντες τὸν ἀρτέμονα τῇ πνεούσῃ) Luke here calls the artemon, from ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀρτᾶσθαι, that sail nearest the prow, which Pollux calls the dolon, and Livy in two places. The artemon is an addition rather than a part of the ship, says Javolenus L. Malum D. de verborum signif. Sailors are accustomed to use it when they fear that the larger sails might catch more wind than is sufficient and urge the ship too much. It was, however, more necessary here for the reason that we heard above that the mast had already been cast down. Regarding that τῇ πνεούσῃ, I would think that ἀὔρᾳ or πνοῇ is to be understood, nor is it more strange to say πνοὴν πνεῖν than πλοῖον πλεῖν.

Camerarius says, Artemon is either a machine in a ship, or, what I notice is more approved by the learned, a certain type of sail. And this seems to agree with the present exposition, because, desiring the land eagerly, they are carried forward with sails and oars, as the saying goes. I think, however, that the mark of distinction is rightly placed after πνεούσῃ: So that it may be, ἐπάραντας τὸν ἀρτέμονα τῇ πνεούσῃ. With the artemon offered to the blowing breeze. So that this artemon may be understood as turned and directed according to the blowing wind. Vitruvius in book X, in a machine, calls a certain pulley by this Latin name, which the Greeks call ἐπάγοντα.

καθεῖχον εἰς τὸν αἰγιαλὸν) Both Herodotus and Plutarch use καθέχειν to mean 'to steer towards'.

Latin:

Vers. 40. καὶ τὰς ἀγκύρας περιελόντες) Id est, anchoris undique sublatis. Id vero ideo dixit, quia plures erant. Supra 29. volebant vento uti quod non poterant nisi sublatis anchoris.

εἴων εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν) Est brevis locutio pro εἴων τὸ πλοῖον ἰέναι εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν; siverunt navem in mare ire, illud scil. quod inter locum in quo defixa fuerat navis, & littus intererat.

ἅμα ἀνέντες τὰς ζευκτηρίας τῶν πηδαλίων) In antiquis navibus bina erant gubernacula, suum cuique lateri, ut ostendimus in imaginibus Arateis Cratinus ὀδυξζεῦσι· ὡς ἂν μᾶλλον τοῖς πηδαλίοις ἡ ναῦς ἡμῖν πειθαρχῇ. Ea gubernacula vinculis quibusdam annectebantur navi, quas hic Græce Lucas ζευκτηρίας vocat: Latinus juncturas quomodo in Glossario ζεῦξις junctura. Cum laxantur ea vincula, tunc gubernacula multum in aquas descendunt & pondere suo navem retinent, quo minus a ventis evertatur.

καὶ ἐπάραντες τὸν ἀρτέμονα τῇ πνεούσῃ) Artemonem vocat hic Lucas ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀρτᾶσθαι velum illud proræ proximum, quod dolona Pollux vocat, & Livius duobus locis. Artemo adjectamentum potius quam pars navis est, ait Javolenus L. Malum D. de verborum signif. Eo uti solent nautæ ubi metuunt ne vela majora plus satis venti concipiant, navemque nimis urgeant. Erat autem ideo magis hic necessarium quod arborem dejectam jam supra audivimus. Ad illud τῇ πνεούσῃ subintelligi putem ἀὔρᾳ vel πνοῇ, nec magis mirum dici πνοὴν πνεῖν, quam πλοῖον πλεῖν.

Camerarius Artemon, inquit, vel machina in navi, vel quod eruditis magis probari animadverto, certum veli genus. Et convenire hoc expositione præsenti videtur, quia appetentes cupide terram velis & remis, ut dici solet, provehuntur. Recte autem distinctionis notam poni existimo post πνεούσῃ: Ut sit, ἐπάραντας τὸν ἀρτέμονα τῇ πνεούσῃ. Oblato artemone flanti auræ. Ut secundum ventum spirantem conversum directumque istum artemonem intelligatur. Vitruvius lib. X in machina sic vocat trochleam quandam Latino nomine, quem Græci ἐπάγοντα appellent.

καθεῖχον εἰς τὸν αἰγιαλὸν) καθέχειν pro tendere usurpant & Herodotus & Plutarchus.

## 27:41
Vers. 41. εἰς τόπον διθάλασσον) He understands a sandbar, such as are often found not far from the shore, yet in such a way that the sea flows between them and the shore.

Τόπον διθάλασσον, ait Camerarius, he calls a piece of rising ground that is washed by the sea on both sides: they call it an Isthmus: and the people of Malta still show this place, and call it lacala di San Paulo, that is, Paul's landing place: namely, the one to which Paul first swam. See Philipp. Cluver. l. II. de Antiqu. Sicil. c. 16. & Octav. Cajetan. Isagoges c. XIX. In a place with two seas, because the land cuts the sea, a shipwreck is wont to be certain. That place of two seas, as Beza rightly notes here, is by no means to be understood as if it were the shore itself (for why would they throw themselves into the sea if the prow of the ship had struck the shore itself?) but they were what are called shallows, sandbars placed in the way of the approach, upon which they were shipwrecked: since ἐποκέλλειν is not said of just any arrival, but declares a very great impact as well. Regarding the force of this word, Camerarius says: This verb signifies a violent arrival. Polybius l. I. ἢ τοῖς βραχέσι περιπίπτον ἐκάθισε τὴν πρύμναν, ἢ πρὸς τὴν γῆν φερόμενον ἐπώκελλε. Either the ship, falling into the shallows, settled at the stern, or, being carried towards the land, it ran aground.

ἐπώκειλαν τὴν ναῦν) The Latin translator well renders it: he drove it against. Thus Lucan: And the labor of Fortune, that drove you against our sands.

καὶ ἡ μὲν πρώρα ἐρείσασα) When it had stuck on the sandbar.

ἔμεινεν ἀσάλευτος) It remained unshaken. 'They strengthen them like the wave of the sea,' Sir. XXIX. 21.

ἡ δὲ πρύμνα ἐλύετο) The stern was broken up by the waves, because it could not be carried up onto the land. Lucan sings something similar about the Argo: The smaller Argo, with its stern snatched away, was drawn down from the mountains.

Latin:

Vers. 41. εἰς τόπον διθάλασσον) Tæniam intelligit, quales multæ solent esse non procul a littore, ita tamen, ut inter eas & littus mare interluat.

Τόπον διθάλασσον, ait Camerarius, vocat solum eminens, quod utrique mari allueretur: Isthmum di- cunt: & locum hunc etiamnum Melitenses osten- dunt, & lacala di San Paulo, id est, Pauli descensum vocant: nempe eum, in quem primum Paulus ena- tavit. Vid. Philipp. Cluver. l. II. de Antiqu. Sicil. c. 16. & Octav. Cajetan. Isagoges c. XIX. In clithalasso ob terram mare secantem certum solet esset naufra- gium. Locus iste bimaris, quod recte hic Beza notat, nequaquam sic accipiendus est, quasi littus ipsum fuerit (nam quorsum isti sese in mare projicerent, si in ipsum littus impegerat navis prora?) sed fue- runt Brevia quæ vocant, ipsi sinus aditui objecta, ad quæ naufragium fecerunt: siquidem ἐποκέλλειν non de quovis appulsu dicitur, sed maximum etiam impetum declarat. De qua vi vocis Camerarius: Si- gnificatur verbo hoc appulsio vehemens. Polybius l. I. ἢ τοῖς βραχέσι περιπίπτον ἐκάθισε τὴν πρύμναν, ἢ πρὸς τὴν γῆν φερόμενον ἐπώκελλε. Aut incidens navigium in brevia subsidebat ad puppim, aut, cum deferebatur terram versus appulsum hærebat.

ἐπώκειλαν τὴν ναῦν) Bene Latinus: impegit. Sic Lucanus: Laborque Fortunæ, quod te nostris impegit arenis.

καὶ ἡ μὲν πρώρα ἐρείσασα) Cum hæsisset in tænia.

ἔμεινεν ἀσάλευτος) Mansit inconcussa. ἰσχύουσιν ἀυτὰς ὡς κῦμα θαλάσσης, Sir. XXIX. 21.

ἡ δὲ πρύμνα ἐλύετο) Dissoluta est a fluctibus puppis, quia in terram subvehi non potuerat. Simile de Argo canit Luca- nus: Rapta puppe minor subducta est montibus Argo

## 27:42
V. 42. τῶν δὲ στρατιωτῶν βουλὴ ἐγένετο) βουλὴ denotes a plan, which is immediately [called] βόλημα. Thus we also often read that captives in war were slaughtered in similar danger.

μή τις ἐκκολυμβήσας) Namely, from the ship to the shore, which was not far away.

Latin:

V. 42. τῶν δὲ στρατιωτῶν βουλὴ ἐγένετο) βουλὴ dicit volun- tatem, quod statim βόλημα. Sic & bello captos in simili periculo trucidatos sæpe legimus.

μή τις ἐκκολυμβήσας) Nempe e navi in littus non longe absitum.

## 27:43
βουλόμενος διασῶσαι τὸν Παῦλον) As a Roman citizen.

τοὺς δυναμένους κολυμβᾷν) Such as the sailors, and if any others had learned to swim.

Ἀποῤῥίψαντας πρώτους) With the bodies cast from the ship into the sea.

ἐξιέναι) To go out from the sea onto the shore.

This was Paul's fourth shipwreck. For he himself recounted the previous three in 2 Cor. 11:25, since that Epistle was written long before this journey.

Latin:

βουλόμενος διασῶσαι τὸν Παῦλον) Ut civem Romanum.

τοὺς δυναμένους κολυμβᾷν) Ut nautas, & si qui alii nare didi- cerant.

Ἀποῤῥίψαντας πρώτους) Dejectis e navi in mare corporibus.

ἐξιέναι) Exire e mari in littus.

Quartum hoc erat Pauli naufragium. Nam priora tria recensuit ipse 2. Cor. XI. 25. quum Epi- stola illa longe ante iter hoc scripta sit.

## 27:44
Vers. 44. ὥς μὲν ἐπὶ σανίσιν) Cicero, Book II of De Officiis: If he has snatched a plank from a shipwreck, and to Atticus: This one plank delights me from this shipwreck:

ἐπί τινων τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ πλοίου) Suppose by oars snatched up.

The second voyage is surely what is called, if one fails with the sails, to sail with the oars.

Latin:

Vers. 44. ὥς μὲν ἐπὶ σανίσιν) Cicero II. Officiorum: Si ta- bulam de naufragio arripuerit, & ad Atticum: Hæc una me ex hoc naufragio tabula delectat:

ἐπί τινων τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ πλοίου) Puta remis arreptis.

Ὁ δεύτερος πλοῦς ἐστὶ δήπου λεγόμενος, Ἂν ποὸς ἀποτύχῃ τις, ἐν κώπαισι πλεῖν.

## 28:1 Argument
CHAPTER XXVIII. & LAST. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

When they were humanely received on the island of Malta, Paul, picking up a viper with his hand and remaining unharmed, is believed to be a god, and staying with Publius, he heals his father and many others from that island. From there they set out in another ship, and having found brothers at Puteoli, they remain with them for seven days, and thus arrive at Rome. But the brothers go to meet Paul and his companions: And to him is granted by the tribune free power of going, who, having called together the chief of the Jews, clears himself of the separation of captivity, and testifies that he is bound for the hope of Israel. They profess that they have heard nothing about him, but that this sect is spoken against everywhere; they appoint a day for him, however, on which they are to hear him. But as Paul informs them about Jesus from Moses and the Prophets, with some believing and others not believing, a dissension having arisen, they depart, when Paul teaches that the Holy Spirit truly prophesied through Isaiah (c. VI. 9.) about their blindness, and from there that that saving message of God had been sent to the Gentiles, the same as the hearers. But Paul, remaining in his own rented lodging, continues to preach freely about Jesus for two years.

I. The miracles of Paul unharmed by the viper and of various healings on the island of Malta, to v. 10.

II. The sermons held by Paul after being brought to Rome, to v. 31, the end.

PART I. The miracles of Paul on the island of Malta.

Vers. 1. Καὶ διασωθέντες) When they had escaped. ὅτι Μελίτη ἡ νῆσος καλεῖται) That Melite which is not far from Africa.

Latin:

CAPUT XXVIII. & ULTIMUM. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Cum in insula Melita humaniter exciperentur, Pau- lus viperam manu tollens illæsus, Deus credi- tur, & penes Publium divertens, patrem ejus & multos alios ex ista insula sanat. De hinc navigio alterius profecti, & Puteolis fratribus inventis per septiduum sbi permanent, atque ita Romam perveniunt. Obviam autem Paulo & comitibus eunt fratres: Illique a tribuno libera eundi potestas conceditur, qui convocatis Judæorum præcipuis seferatione captivitatis purgat, & ob spem Israelis vinctum testatur. Illi nihil se de ipso audivisse, se- ctæ autem isti ubique contradici profitentur, diem tamen ei dicunt, quo ipsum audituri sint. Infor- mante autem Paulo ipsos de Jesu e Mose & Pro- phetis, aliis credentibus, aliis non credentibus, dis- sensione orta discedunt, cum Paulus S. S. vere de ipsorum excæcatione per Esaiam (c. VI. 9.) vati- cinatum esse, inde salutare illud Dei gentibus idem auditoris missum doceret. Paulus verò manens in suo conducto porro per biennium libere de Jesu prædicat.

I. Miracula Pauli illæsi à vipera & sana- tionum variarum in insula Melita, ad v. 10.

II. Pauli Ro- mam deducti ibidem habitæ conciones, ad v. 31. fin.

PARS I. Miracula Pauli in insula Melita.

Vers. 1. Καὶ διασωθέντες) Cum evasisset. ὅτι Μελίτη ἡ νῆσος καλεῖται) Illa Melite quæ non longè ab Africa.

## 28:2
v. 2. οἱ δὲ βάρβαροι) Africans, who, being powerful at sea, held the neighboring islands.

ἐ τὴν τυχοῦσαν φιλανθρωπίαν) Concerning this expression, see above ch. XIX, 11.

That this Melite was situated between Africa and Sicily, which is today called Malta, and is likewise called Maltan by the Arab here, and not the other one called Meletina, is clear from the fact that Luke leads Paul from it to Syracuse, and thence to Rhegium within the straits of the Sicilian sea, as Beza observes here. Bochart, however, argues at length against Constantine Porphyrogenitus, who explains this passage as referring to the Illyrian Melite, and Walæus follows him on this passage, as does Phil. Cluv. l. II. de Antiqu. Sic. l. c. XVI. God undoubtedly arranged these things in such a way that Paul was brought to this island, so that the saving doctrine might be preached in it for the conversion of the Melitians. For Paul stayed in the same place for three months together with his companions Luke, Aristarchus, Trophimus, and others. Furthermore, this island of Malta is distant from the island mentioned in v. 16 of the preceding chapter, Clauda, by an interval of 180 miles. Μελίτη called, as if honey-flowing, because the most excellent honey, surpassing all honey in the world, is found there. The bishop in that island is called the Milevitan bishop, whence the Council of Milevis.

Vers. 2. Ἀνάψαντες γὰρ πυρὰν) A pile of wood. προσελάβοντο πάντας ἡμᾶς) אספו. They received us with hospitality. For that is how it is usually translated, as is לקח and the like. διὰ τὸν ὑετὸν τὸν ἐφεστῶτα) Because of the rain which had come upon us. After great winds, rains are accustomed to follow. καὶ διὰ τὸ ψύχος) The cold was present both from the time of year and was increased by the wind and the rains. And those who had swum through the sea could not but be cold. Plautus: By Pollux, Neptune, you are a cold bath-attendant: since I left you with my clothes on, I am shivering.

Latin:

v. 2. οἱ δὲ βάρβαροι) Afri, qui mari potentes vicinas insu- las tenuere.

ἐ τὴν τυχοῦσαν φιλανθρωπίαν) De hac locutione vide su- pra c. XIX, 11.

Melitem hanc fuisse inter Africam & Siciliam sitam, quæ hodie Malta dicitur, hic ab Arabe Maltan itidem vocata, non vero alteram, Meleti- nam dictam ex eo liquet, quod ex ea Paulum Lu- cas deducat Syracusas, & inde Rhegium intra Sicu- li freti angustias, observante hic Beza. Prolixe au- tem contra Constantinum Prophyrogonnetam de Illyrica Melita locum hunc explicantem disputat Bochartus & ex eo Walæus ad h. l. ut & Phil. Cluv. l. II. de Antiqu. Sic. l. c. XVI. Disposuit autem hæc sine dubio ita Deus, ut in hanc insulam deferretur Pau- lus, ut in ea prædicaretur doctrina salvifica, ad Me- litensium conversionem. Siquidem Paulus per tres menses una cum sociis Luca, Aristarcho, Trophimo & aliis in eadem commoratus fuerit. Cæterum di- stat hæc insula Malta ab Insula de qua v. 16. c. præ- cedent. Clauda interstitio 180. milliarium. Μελίτη vocata, quasi melliflua, quia ibi præstantissimum mel omnia in orbe mella superans, reperitur. Epi- scopus in illa Insula dictus est Milevitanus, unde Concilium Milevitanum.

Vers. 2. Ἀνάψαντες γὰρ πυρὰν) Lignorum struem. προσελάβοντο πάντας ἡμᾶς) אספו. Hospitio excepere. Id enim sic verti solet, ut & לקח & similia. διὰ τὸν ὑετὸν τὸν ἐφεστῶτα) Propter imbrem qui superve- nerat. Post ingentes ventos solent imbres sequi. καὶ διὰ τὸ ψύχος) Frigus & ex anni tempore aderat, & vento atque imbribus augebatur. Et non poterant non frigere qui per mare nataverant. Plautus: Edepol, Neptune, es balneator frigidus: Cum vestimentis postquam abs te abii, algeo.

## 28:3
v. 3. συστρέψαντος δὲ τῦ Παύλε φρυγάνων πλῆθος) In the manuscript: φρυγάνων τι πλῆθος. When he had gathered some brushwood. Namely, that which lay ready nearby. Φρύγανον is fomes in the Glossary: Fomes is whatever feeds a fire: ἔχιδνα ἐκ τῆς θέρμης ἐξελθῦσα) In the Glossary: Θέρμη is heat, fervor, burning. Thucydides uses it thus in his description of the plague. As soon as the viper had felt the heat of the fire, it wanted to escape. In the manuscript it is ἀπὸ τῆς θέρμης, which is clearer. Thus ἀπὸ τᾶ ἰδε ἀπὸ τῆς λύπης is often used among the Greeks to signify a cause.

The received reading is to be approved entirely. For it is indicated that the viper was grasped by the Apostle along with the sticks, and crawled out toward the heat when the branches were being placed by him onto the pyre.

Latin:

v. 3. συστρέψαντος δὲ τῦ Παύλε φρυγάνων πλῆθος) In Ma- nuscripto: φρυγάνων τι πλῆθος. Cum virgulta quædam colle- gisset. Nempe quæ in proximo parata jacebant. Φρύγανον so- mes in Glossario: Fomes est, quicquid ignem alit: ἔχιδνα ἐκ τῆς θέρμης ἐξελθῦσα) In Glossario: Θέρμη calor, fervor, æstus. Utitur sic Thucydides in pestilentiæ descrip- tione. Ignis calorem ut senserat vipera, effugere volebat. In Manuscripto est, ἀπὸ τῆς θέρμης, quod clarius. Sic ἀπὸ τᾶ ἰδε ἀπὸ τῆς λύπης in causæ significatu sæpe apud Græcos.

Recepta lectio probanda omnino est. Nam in- dicatur viperam cum festucis ab Apostolo fuisse comprehensam, & prorepsisse ad calorem, cum sarmenta ab ipso imponerentur in rogum.

## 28:4
v. 4. τὸ θηρίον) Thus are beasts that harm with poison accustomed to be called, in which vipers excel, whence the name θηριακὴ ἀντίδοτος (theriac antidote) comes. Ambrose in the Hexaëmeron: The viper is a most wicked kind of beast. Hence, "breathing a viperous soul," in Virgil.

Πάντως φονέυς ἐσιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος) They thought he was convicted of the crime for which he had been given into custody. ἡ δίκη ζῇς ἐκ εἴασεν) δίκη here is divine vengeance, concerning which there is that old saying: --- For in time Justice sees all things brought to light for mortals. And many other things in Stobæus under the title VII on the nature of things. Hesiod: --- But Justice holds sway over insolence, having reached the end. And the fool, having suffered, has learned. ζῆν ἐκ εἴασεν) Thus in a Greek epigram Sarapis says to a murderer: If I have not let you die now, you have indeed escaped a painless death for now. But know that you are being kept for the cross.

Latin:

v. 4. τὸ θηρίον) Sic solent vocati bestiæ quæ veneno nocent, in quibus excellunt viperæ, unde θηριακὴ ἀντίδοτος nomen habet. Ambrosius in Hexaëmero: Vipera nequissimum ge- nus bestiæ. Inde Vipeream inspirans animam, apud Virgilium.

Πάντως φονέυς ἐσιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος) Putabant convictum cri- minis, ob quod custodiæ erat datus. ἡ δίκη ζῇς ἐκ εἴασεν) δίκη hic divina ultio, de qua illud ve- tus: - - - Ὁρᾷ γὰρ ἐν χρόνῳ Δίκην ἄπαθ᾽ ἄγκιζαν εἰς Φάος βροτοῖς. Et alia multa apud Stobæum de rerum natura titulo VII. Hesiodus: - - - Δίκη δ᾽ ὑπὲρ ὕβριδος ἴσχει Ἐς τέλος ἐξελθῦσα. παθὼν δὲ τε νήπιος ἔγνω. ζῆν ἐκ εἴασεν) Sic in Epigrammate Græco Sarapis dicit homicidæ: Εἰ μὴ νῦν σε μεθῆκα θανεῖν, θάνατον μὲν ἄλυπον Νῦν ἔφυγες. Σταυρῷ δ᾽ ἴσθι φυλασσόμενος.

## 28:6
Vers. 6. οἱ δὲ προσεδόκων αὐτὸν μέλλειν πίμπρασθαι) To be swollen by the sea: Nicander describing one injured by a viper: But the frequent blisters on their limbs, thin pustules, as it were, soften above the skin forged by fire.

Then: Πᾶν δὲ ἐπὶ δριμεῖα δάκος καταβόζεται ἄτη Ὀξεῖα πυργολένα. ἣ καταπίπτειν ἄφνω νεκρὸν) For the poison of a viper is in certain places very rapid.

μηδὲν ἄτοπον) Nothing inconvenient. In this sense the word ἄτοπος is used in the Greek version of Job IV. 8 and in Theophrastus IV. 15.

μεταβαλλόμενοι) With their opinion changed, as is the custom of the mob: - - It follows fortune, as always, and hates the condemned.

ἔλεγον θεὸν ἀυτὸν εἶναι) I think Hercules the averter of evil, who was worshipped on the island of Melita.

They report that snakes and scorpions in Melita, as well those born there as those brought there, deposit poison, and that the Melitan earth heals any poisonous bites whatsoever; which benefit Cornelius à Lapide rashly and not piously enough asserts was bestowed upon Melita along with many others. Compare Beza on this passage concerning τῷ θηρίῳ, and Heinsius concerning Hercules.

Latin:

Vers. 6. οἱ δὲ προσεδόκων αὐτὸν μέλλειν πίμπρασθαι) Inflari mari: Nicander describens læsum à vipera: Αἰ δὲ θαμειναὶ Πομφόλυγες τοῖς ἐν γείνωσι, φλύκταιναι ἀραιαὶ Οἷα πυρικμήτοιο χροὸς πλαδόωσι ὕπερθεν

Deinde: Πᾶν δὲ ἐπὶ δριμεῖα δάκος καταβόζεται ἄτη Ὀξεῖα πυργολένα. ἣ καταπίπτειν ἄφνω νεκρὸν) Venenum enim viperæ quibusdam in locis valde rapidum est.

μηδὲν ἄτοπον) Nihil incommodi. Hoc sensu vox ἄτοπος est in Græca versione Job. IV. 8. & apud Theophrastum IV. 15.

μεταβαλλόμενοι) Mutata sententia, ut mos vulgi: - - Sequitur fortunam, ut semper, & odit Damnatos.

ἔλεγον θεὸν ἀυτὸν εἶναι) Herculem puto ἀλεξίκακον, qui in Melite insula colebatur.

Referunt quod Melitæ serpentes & scorpiones tam illic nati, quam eo illati ponant venenum, quodque terra Melitensis morsus quoslibet venenatos sanet, quod beneficium cum aliis multis contulisse Melitæ temere nec satis pie asserit Corn. à Lapide. Conf. Beza ad hunc locum de τῷ θηρίῳ, & de Hercule Heinsius.

## 28:7
V. 7. ὑπῆρχε χωρία τῷ πρώτῳ τῆς νήσου, ὀνόματι Ποπλίῳ) Wealthy Romans had estates in the provinces, especially in Africa. Perhaps this man was a freedman of Augustus. For that Syrus the Mime was likewise a freedman, called Publius without another name. Moreover, πρῶτος Μελιταίων is the name of a magistrate. This is apparent from an inscription found on the island of Melita. Λ. Κ. ΚΙΟΣ. ΚΥΡ. ΠΡΟΥΔΗΝΣ. ἹΠΠΕΥΣ. ΡΩΜ. ΠΡΩΤΟΣ. ΜΕΛΙΤΑΙΩΝ. ΚΑΙ. ΠΑΤΡΩΝ. ΑΡΞΑΣ. ΚΑΙ. ΑΜΦΙΠΟΛΕΥΣΑΣ. ΘΕΩ. ΑΥΓΟΥΣΤΩ.

ὃς ἀναδεξάμενος ἡμᾶς) Namely, having been ordered to move from the public inn into his house.

φιλοφρόνως ἐξένιζεν) Even then ordained to eternal life, and having certain shadows of Christian virtues. See Matt. XXV. 35.

There lies hidden here an Arminian-Pelagian heresy, because he calls this pagan Publius ordained to eternal life. Compare what is said on Acts XIII. Moreover, Ado in his Martyrology for Jan. 21 and Bede for Jan. 18 say that Publius was created bishop of this island: who later became bishop of Athens. But we leave these matters in the middle.

Latin:

V. 7. ὑπῆρχε χωρία τῷ πρώτῳ τῆς νήσου, ὀνόματι Ποπλίῳ) Romani divites in provinciis fundos habebant, maxime in Africa. Forte hic libertus fuerit Augusti. Nam & Syrus ille Mimus itidem libertus, dictus Publius sine alio nomine. Est autem πρῶτος Μελιταίων nomen Magistratus. Apparet id ex inscriptione in insula Melite reperta. Λ. Κ. ΚΙΟΣ. ΚΥΡ. ΠΡΟΥΔΗΝΣ. ἹΠΠΕΥΣ. ΡΩΜ. ΠΡΩΤΟΣ. ΜΕΛΙΤΑΙΩΝ. ΚΑΙ. ΠΑΤΡΩΝ. ΑΡΞΑΣ. ΚΑΙ. ΑΜΦΙΠΟΛΕΥΣΑΣ. ΘΕΩ. ΑΥΓΟΥΣΤΩ.

ὃς ἀναδεξάμενος ἡμᾶς) Nempe jussos transire ex diversorio publico in suam domum.

φιλοφρόνως ἐξένιζεν) Jam tum τεταγμένος εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, & umbras quasdam habens virtutum Christianarum. Vide Matth. XXV. 35.

Latet hic Arminiano - Pelagiana hæresis, quod Publium hunc gentilem τεταγμένον εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον dicat. Conf. quæ ad Actor. XIII. Creatum autem Publium Episcopum huic Insulæ Ado in Martyrol. ad d. 21. Jan. & Beda ad 18. Jan. dicunt: qui postea Atheniensis factus sit Episcopus. Sed nos hæc in medio relinquimus.

## 28:8
Vers. 8. πυρετοῖς κὴ δυσεντερίᾳ) Celsus IV. 15 translates δυσεντερίαν as gripes. That disease, if it lasts, usually leads to fevers.

συνεχόμενον) Matt. IV. 24. Luke IV. 38. Galen also uses this expression. Rightly, for συνέχειν is to bind, and diseases are certain bonds, Luke XIII. 16.

κατακεῖσθαι, Cubat, i. e. he is sick, the Scholiast on that line of Horace - - - Cubat hic in Colle Quirini.

and having prayed, having laid his hands upon him) See Matt. IX. 18. c. XIX. 13. Mark VI. 5. c. VII. 32. c. XVI. 18. Luke IV. 40. c. XIII. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 8. πυρετοῖς κὴ δυσεντερίᾳ) δυσεντερίαν tormina vertit Celsus IV. 15. Is morbus, si duret, plerumq; ad febres adfert.

συνεχόμενον) Matth. IV. 24. Luc. IV. 38. Utitur hac locutione & Galenus. Recte Nam συνέχειν est vincire, Et morbi vincula quædam Luc, XIII. 16.

κατακεῖσθαι, Cubat, i. e. ægrotat, Scholiastes ad illud Horat. - - - Cubat hic in Colle Quirini.

κὴ προσευξάμενος ἐπιθεὶς τὰς χεῖρας ἀυτῷ) Vid. Matt. IX. 18. c. XIX. 13. Marc. VI. 5. c. VII. 32. c. XVI. 18. Luc. IV. 40. c. XIII. 13.

## 28:9
v. 9. having infirmities) As Luke XIII. 11. 12. John V. 5. c. XI. 4.

Latin:

v. 9. ἔχοντες ἀσθενείας) Ut Luc. XIII. 11. 12. Joh. V. 5. c. XI. 4.

## 28:10
vers. 10. to those setting sail they loaded the things for the need) He mixed expressions about those sailing and about the ship, as is wont to happen. For ἀναγομένοις pertains to those sailing, ἐπέθεντο to the ship. Τὰ πρὸς τὴν χρείαν, those things which were necessary, namely provisions. In the Manuscript τὸ πρὸς τὰς χρείας in the plural as above c. XX. 34.

PART II.

The sermons held by Paul in the same place after he was brought to Rome.

Latin:

vers. 10. ἀναγομένοις ἐπέθεντο τὰ πρὸς τὴν χρείαν) Permiscuit locutiones de navigantib. & de navi, ut fieri solet. Nam ἀναγομένοις ad navigantes, ἐπέθεντο ad navim pertinet. Τὰ πρὸς τὴν χρείαν, ea quæ erant opus, cibaria scilicet. In Manuscripto τὸ πρὸς τὰς χρείας pluraliter ut supra c. XX. 34.

PARS II.

Pauli Romam deducti ibidem habitæ conciones.

## 28:11
Vers. 11. having wintered in the island) Because he had avoided the storm in Melita, as above c. XXVII. 12. for the winter had not yet passed.

It is exceedingly manifest that this word is to be understood here not of the avoidance of a storm, but of wintering. For what sense would that be? The Alexandrian ship had avoided the storm in that island, just as Paul with his companions wintered there after the shipwreck, so also that ship had wintered there; in which, therefore, at the beginning of Spring they were carried to Syracuse.

Alexandrian) See what was said above c. XVII. 6.

with the sign of the Dioscuri) A sign (parasemon) is one thing, a tutelary deity (tutela) is another. The tutelary deity is on the stern, like Minerva on the Argo: the sign or emblem (parasemon) is on the prow. Thus in the ship in which Ovid was carried, the tutelary deity was Minerva, the sign was a Helmet, and from that the name, just as Pistrix, Centaurus. The learned Latin translates: which had the sign of the Castors. Thus Pliny X. 43. above the temple of the Castors. Tertullian. Phantasms of the Castors. Arnobius book II. The Tyndarid Castors. book IV. Three kinds of Castors. Minutius: As also when the Castors were seen with horses. And Cyprian on the vanity of idols: The Castors die alternately.

Parasemon, says Turnebus, gave the name to the ship. The tutelary deity was always a god or goddess, the parasemon a god or goddess, or a hero or animal, or something else.

The Dioscuri are the Castors, just as the twin brothers, sons of Jupiter and Leda, are called, about whom Cornelius Lapide fabulates more here from the Poets: not denying the invocation of the Blessed Virgin, whom they ineptly call Star of the sea, and of S. Paul in dangers of the sea, that the pagan invocation of the twins or Castors has succeeded: to whom, however, the Papists join S. Clement, S. Nicholas, and from the new little saints canonized by the Pope, Francis Xavier the Loyolite. Some ignorantly read with the Gloss the sign of the Castra.

Latin:

Vers. 11. παρακεχειμακότι ἐν τῇ νήσῳ) Quod in Melite tempestatem vitaverat, ut supra c. XXVII. 12. nam hiems nondum exierat.

Non de tempestatis vitatione, sed de hyematione hoc verbum hic accipiendum esse, oppido manifestum est. Quis enim sensus ille? Navis Alexandrina in insula illa tempestatem evitaverat, ut Paulus cum sociis in ea post naufragium hyemavit, ita navis etiam ista ibi hyemaverat; in qua proinde ineunte Vere provecti sunt Syracusas.

Ἀλεξανδρίνῳ) Vide quæ dicta supra c. XVII. 6.

παρασήμῳ Διοσκούροις) Aliud est παράσημον, aliud tutela. Tutela in puppi, ut Minerva in Argo: παράσημον sive insigne in prora. Sic in navi, qua vectus Ovidius, tutela erat Minerva, insigne Cassis, & inde nomen, quomodo Pistrix, Centaurus. Erudite Latinus vertit: cui erat insigne Castorum. Sic Plinius X. 43. supra Castorum ædem. Tertullian. Phantasmata Castorum. Arnob. l. II. Tyndarida Castores. l. IV. Tria genera Castorum. Minutius: Vt & cum equis Castores viderentur. Et Cyprian. de Idolor. vanitate: Castores alternis moriuntur.

Parasemon, inquit Turnebus, navi nomen dabat. Tutela semper erat Deus aut dea, Parasemon Deus aut dea, aut heros aut animal, aut aliud quid.

Διόσκουροι Castores sunt, quemadmodum fratres ge- mini Jovis & Ledæ filii appellati, de quibus plura hic è Poëtis fabulatur Cornelius Lapidensis: non negans invocationem B. Virginis, quam inepte Stel- lam maris vocant, & S. Pauli in periculis maris, in- vocationi geminorum seu Castorum pagana succef- sisse: quibus tamen jungunt Papicolæ S. Clementem, S. Nicolaum, & è novellis Sanctulis à Papa Cano- nizatis Franciscum Xavericum Lojolitam. Non- nulli inscite cum Glossa legunt insigne Castrorum.

## 28:12
Vers. 12. having been driven to Syracuse) Namely to unload certain goods of the Alexandrian ship.

Syracuse is the greatest and most beautiful city of Sicily, situated under Mount Pachynus: the fatherland of Archimedes. Sailing hither, Paul and his companions completed 45 miles from the island of Malta: from there, however, to the city of Rhegium, sixteen miles.

Latin:

Vers. 12. παταχθέντες εἰς Συρακόσας) Nempe ad expo- nendas merces quasdam Alexandrini navigii.

Syracusa Siciliæ est civitas maxima, & pulcher- rima sub Pachino monte sita: Patria Archimedis. Huc navigantes Paulus & Socii ex Insula Melita confecerunt 45. milliaria: inde vero ad urbem Rhegium sedecim milliaria.

## 28:13
Verse 13. εἰς Ρήγιον) The Greeks write Ρήγνον and the people ῥηγόνυς, and they all add that the origin of the name is because Sicily had been cut off there from the side of Italy. Rhegium, however, by its Latin name, is a town of Cisalpine Gaul.

From ῥηγύναι, to break off: because by an earthquake or an inundation of the sea this city was broken off from Sicily, to which it was contiguous, or rather continuous, in which Cornel. à Lapide reports that the first Bishop was St. Stephen, a companion of Paul, created by Paul, which, however, the Papists otherwise claim for Peter as the prerogative of creating Bishops. This city was distant from Jerusalem 339 miles, towards the setting of the sun.

δευτεραῖοι) A very good Greek expression, which both Herodotus and Xenophon use. It is attributed to the person, which belongs to the thing. Such is that: Socrates is said to have been accustomed to stand in a stubborn posture for a day and a night, in Gellius II. 1.

εἰς Ποτιόλες) For Alexandrian ships were accustomed to put in at Puteoli: Seneca teaches us this in Epistle 77 and a decree in Gruter's inscriptions. Statius: - - - modo nam trans æquora terris Prima Dicarcheis Pharium gravis intulit annum. For the old name of Puteoli is Δικαιάρχεια, whence the poets make Dicarchea.

It is a city of Campania near Naples, so called from the stench of the hot water boiling there, or from the multitude of wells made for the sake of those same waters. It was 42 miles distant from Rhegium.

Latin:

Vers. 13. εἰς Ρήγιον) Ρήγνον scribunt Græci & populum ῥηγόνυς, adduntque omnes originem esse nominis, quod ibi ab Italiæ latere abscissa esset Sicilia. Rhegium vero, Latino nomine, oppidum est Galliæ Cisalpinæ.

Ἀπὸ τῶν ῥηγύναι abrumpere: eo quod terræ motu, vel maris eluvione abrupta sit hæc civitas à Sicilia, cui erat contigua, imo continua, in qua primum Episcopum fuisse comitem Pauli S. Stephanum à Paulo creatum refert Cornel. à Lapide, quod ta- men ἀξίωμα Episcopos creandi Petro alias vendi- cant Papicolæ. Distabat hæc civitas ab Hierosoly- ma 339. milliaribus, versus Solis occasum.

δευτεραῖοι) Locutio bene Græca, qua & Herodotus & Xenophon utuntur. Tribuitur personæ, quod est rei. Tale illud: Stare solitus Socrates dicitur pertinaci statu perdius & pernox, apud Gellium II. 1.

εἰς Ποτιόλες) Puteolos enim appellere solebant naves Ale- xandrinæ: docet id nos Seneca Epistola 77. & decretum in Gruteri inscriptionibus. Statius: - - - modo nam trans æquora terris Prima Dicarcheis Pharium gravis intulit annum. Puteolis enim vetus nomen Δικαιάρχεια, unde Poëtæ fa- ciunt Dicarcheam.

Urbs est Campaniæ juxta Neapolin ab aquæ ca- lidæ ibi ebullientis putore, vel à multitudine pu- teorum earundem aquarum gratia factorum ita vocata. Distabat Rhegio 42. milliaribus.

## 28:14
Verse 14. ᾗ ἑυρόντες ἀδελφοὺς) Therefore, there were Christians already not only at Rome, but also at Puteoli.

παρεκλήθημεν) We were asked. Thus this word is also taken above in ch. XVI. 12, ch. XXV. 3.

ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐπιμεῖναι) The manuscript has παρ αὐτοῖς.

That ἐπὶ is deservedly retained, which, although it is rare for παρὰ, is not, however, entirely unusual: as ἐπὶ ταῖς θύραις, at the doors, by the gate, used by almost all writers; and in Thucydides book III, ἡν ἐπὶ ποταμῷ: it was situated by the river. But if anyone does not wish for this, ἐπὶ very frequently means because of, for the sake of, on account of: as when they say, ἐπὶ τῷ κέρδει, he did this for the sake of gain. Thus here, we were asked to stay for seven days for their sake, as Ludov. de Dieu has it here.

εἰς τὴν ῥώμην ἤλθομεν) We were going to Rome. Thus the Syriac rightly understood it here; the Hellenistic Jews translate πορέυεσθαι and ἔρχεσθαι interchangeably.

The Vulgate and Erasmus have 'we came', but Beza more correctly has 'we were proceeding to Rome', we set ourselves on the way, with this observation added: τὸ ἔρχεσθαι in this place declares nothing other than τὸ ἰέναι ἢ πορέυεσθαι, as in that of Homer, ἔρχεσθον κλισίην, Iliad 1, in which way it is also taken in John VI. 17. That this was not observed was the reason why some placed the Forum of Appius, of which mention is made in the next verse, in the city itself: (since, as Erasmus rightly observes) it is further from the city of Rome than Aricia. See Luke XV. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 14. ᾗ ἑυρόντες ἀδελφοὺς) Ergo non Romæ tantum, sed & Puteolis jam erant Christiani.

παρεκλήθημεν) Rogati sumus. Sic hoc verbum & supra sumitur c. XVI. 12. c. XXV. 3.

ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐπιμεῖναι) Manuscriptus παρ αὐτοῖς.

Merito retinetur illud ἐπὶ, quod etsi rarum sit pro παρὰ, non tamen omnino insolens: ut ἐπὶ ταῖς θύραις, ad fores, apud Januam, omnibus fere Scri- ptoribus usitatum; & apud Thucid. lib. III. ἡν ἐπὶ πο- ταμῷ: Situs erat apud fluvium. Quod si quis hoc non velit, ἐπὶ frequentissime valet propter, causa, gratia: ut cum dicunt, ἐπὶ τῷ κέρδει, lucri causa hoc fecit. Ita hic, rogati sumus ut ipsorum causa mane- remus septem dies, ut hic habet Ludov. de Dieu.

εἰς τὴν ῥώμην ἤλθομεν) Romam ibamus. Ita hic bene ac- cepit Syrus, Judzi Hellenistæ אזל modo per πορέυεσθαι, mo- do per ἔρχεσθαι vertunt promiscue.

Vulgat. & Erasmus habent venimus, sed rectius Beza contendimus Romam, dedimus nos in viam, hac addita observatione: τὸ ἔρχεσθαι hoc loco nihil aliud declarat quam τὸ ἰέναι ἢ πορέυεσθαι, ut in illo Homeri ἔρχεσθον κλισίην, Illiad. ά. quo modo etiam accipitur Joh. VI. 17. Id vero non observa- tum, causa fuit, cur nonnulli Appii forum, cujus sit mentio proximo versiculo, in ipsa urbe collocarint: (cum ut recte observat Erasmus) longius absit ab urbe Roma quam Aritia. Vide Luc. XV. 20.

## 28:15
Vers. 15. ἄχρις Ἀππίου Φόρου κὶ Τρίων Ταβερνῶν) That is, some came to meet them at the Forum of Appius, others at the Three Taverns: the former earlier, the latter later. For the Three Taverns are nearer to Rome, as is evident from the maps and the letter of Cicero to Atticus II. 10. Many places in the Roman Empire then had names, some of a forum, others of a tavern; of a forum, from the trade of all kinds of goods; of a tavern, because wine and food were offered for sale there.

Büntingius has it thus in Itiner. p. 242. From Puteoli they proceeded at an interval of thirty miles to the Forum of Appius, where some Christians went to meet Paul, five and a half miles from the city of Rome, receiving him very kindly, Acts 28. From the Forum of Appius those Christians accompanied Paul on foot on the Appian Way, for one and a half miles, to the Three Taverns, where more Christians from the city of Rome came out to meet them, Acts 28. And thus Paul was led from the Three Taverns, at an interval of four miles, to Rome, about the fiftieth year of his age, in the twenty-seventh year after Christ's resurrection, but in the sixtieth year after the true birth of the same our Savior.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἄχρις Ἀππίου Φόρου κὶ Τρίων Ταβερνῶν) Id est, alii obviam venerunt ad Forum Appii, alii ad Tres Tabernas: illi prius, hi serius. Nam Tres Tabernæ propiores Romæ, ut apertum sit ex tabulis & epistola Ciceronis ad Atticum II. 10. Multa tum loca in Romano Imperio habebant no- men alia fori, alia tabernæ; fori ab omnium rerum merca- tu: tabernæ, quod ibi vinum & esculenta venum proposita essent.

Büntingius ita habet in Itinet. p. 242. De Puteo- lis progressi sunt triginta milliarium interstitio ad Appii forum, ubi nonnulli Christiani obviam pro- gressi sunt Paulo, milliaribus quinque ac dimidio ex urbe Roma perhumaniter eum excipientes, Act. 28. De foro Appii pedestri itinere Christiani illi Paulum comitati sunt in via Appia, milliari uno ac dimidio, ad Tres Tabernas, ubi plures Christiani ex urbe Roma, illis in occursum prodierunt, Act. 28. Atque ita Paulus de Tribus Tabernis, intervallo quatuor milliarium, Romam ductus est, circa quin- quagesimum annum ætate suæ, vigesimo septimo anno post Christi resurrectionem, post veram autem ejus- dem Salvatoris nostri nativitatem anno sexagesimo.

## 28:16
V. 16. ὅτε δὲ ἤλθομεν εἰς Ῥώμην) The manuscript has εἰσήλθομεν, which is clearer.

τῷ ςρατοπεδάρχῃ) Burro. For learned men rightly interpret this as the Prefect of the Praetorium. For from the times of Tiberius the Praetorian soldier was kept in the camp, as Tacitus testifies in Annals IV. And that the custody of the accused was under his care is proven by many passages of the same Tacitus.

σὺν τῷ φυλάσσοντι αὐτὸν ςρατιώτῃ) And in the Roman manner. The scholiast of Juvenal says a camp prison is spoken of when captives are handed over in chains. But understand it in such a way that the same chain also bound the soldier. Josephus XVIII on Agrippa, later King: ἐνετέταλτο δ᾽ ἀυτῷ παρὰ τῦ Μάκρωνος ςρατιωτῶν τε μετρίων ἀνδρῶν; οἳ παραφυλάξειαν ἀυτὸν ἐν φροντίσιν, κᾀ ἑκατοντάρχῃ. ἐφεσηκότι τε ἐκείνοις, κᾀ συνδέτῳ ἐσομένῳ, λυῖρά τε καθ᾿ ἡμέραν συγχωρεῖν, κᾀ ἀπολούσεσυν κᾀ φίλων εἰσόδως, τήν τε ἄλλην ἰατρώνην τῷ σώματι γίνεσθ᾿ ἕν. Seneca referred to this in De Tranquillitate I, 10. The same custody surrounded everyone, and those who bound them are also bound, unless perhaps you think the chain on the left hand is lighter. And Ep. V. Just as the same chain joins both the guard and the soldier: so those things, which are so dissimilar, proceed together. Thus Athenaeus on Manius Aquilius: σύνδετον ἔχων ἁλύσει μακρᾷ Βατάτην πενταπήχυν, πεζὸς ὑπὸ ἱππέως ἤγεῖτο. This is the chain which Paul mentions shortly after, showing it, v. 20, and Eph. VI. 20. Since the chain was long, which held both the soldier and Paul, we now easily understand how Paul, although bound, could walk here and there. This is what Paul understands by the name δεσμὸν. Coloss. IV. 18. Phil. I. 7. 13. 14. 16. 2. Tim. II. 6. Philem. X. 13.

μόνον καθ' ἑαυτὸν Without others. It is translated thus in Gen. XXX. 41, c. XLIII. 32, Zach. XII. 12, c. XIII. 14, which is translated elsewhere as καταμόνας.

The Vulgate has 'to himself', Erasmus 'alone', Beza 'separately', the Glossary καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν as 'in himself, with himself', Hesychius ἀυτὸν δι ἑαυτῶ as 'himself by himself'. Thus also Camerarius 'by himself', that is, alone, together with the soldier guard. Philippica IV. κᾀ γεγόνασι καθ' ἀυτὲς ἕκατοι. He says that the individual peoples, whom Demosthenes names there, separated from others and alone, also managed their own affairs. The Syrian, Arab, and Ethiopian are different, however, who translated it as 'where he wished'. They took καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν for 'according to himself', that is, according to the judgment of his own mind, καθ᾿ ἑαυτῶ γνώμην. In the Latin, those words are missing: The centurion handed over the bound, or captives, to the Master of the camp or the prefect.

Latin:

V. 16. ὅτε δὲ ἤλθομεν εἰς Ῥώμην) Manuscriptus εἰσήλθομεν, quod planius.

τῷ ςρατοπεδάρχῃ) Burro. Recte enim viri docti interpre- tantur Præfectum Prætorio. Nam à Tiberii temporibus Prætorianus miles in castris habitus, teste Tacito Annalium IV. Et sub hujus cura fuisse reorum custodias, multis ejus- dem Taciti locis evincitur.

σὺν τῷ φυλάσσοντι αὐτὸν ςρατιώτῃ) Et more Romano. Scho- liastes Juvenalis castrensem carcerem dici ait, quando capti- vi traduntur catenati. Sed intellige ita, ut eadem catena & militem constringeret. Josephus XVIII. de Agrippa postea Rege: ἐνετέταλτο δ᾽ ἀυτῷ παρὰ τῦ Μάκρωνος ςρατιωτῶν τε με- τρίων ἀνδρῶν; οἳ παραφυλάξειαν ἀυτὸν ἐν φροντίσιν, κᾀ ἑκατον- τάρχῃ. ἐφεσηκότι τε ἐκείνοις, κᾀ συνδέτῳ ἐσομένῳ, λυῖρά τε καθ᾿ ἡμέραν συγχωρεῖν, κᾀ ἀπολούσεσυν κᾀ φίλων εἰσόδως, τήν τε ἄλλην ἰατρώνην τῷ σώματι γίνεσθ᾿ ἕν. Seneca huc respexit de Tranquillitate I, 10. Eadem custodia universos circumdedit, alligatisque sunt etiam qui alligaverunt, nisi tu forte leviorem in sinistra catenam putas. Et Ep. V. Quemadmodum eadem cate- na & custodiam & militem copulat: sic ista, quæ tam dissimilia sunt, pariter incedunt. Sic de Manio Aquilio Athenæus: σύν- δετον ἔχων ἁλύσει μακρᾷ Βατάτην πενταπήχυν, πεζὸς ὑπὸ ἱππέως ἤγεῖτο. Hæc est catena cujus mox meminit eam monstrans Paulus v. 20. & Eph. VI. 20. Cum catena longa fuerit, quæ & militem & Paulum tenebat, facile jam intelligimus, quo- modo Paulus, quanquam vinctus, huc illuc ambulare po- tuerit. Hoc est, quod δεσμὸν nomine Paulus intelligit. Co- loss. IV. 18. Phil. I. 7. 13. 14. 16. 2. Tim. II. 6. Philem. X. 13.

μόνον καθ' ἑαυτὸν Sine aliis. Ita vertitur מלבד Gen. XXX. 41. c. XLIII. 32. Zach. XII. 12. c. XIII. 14. quod alibi verti- tur καταμόνας.

Vulgatus sibi, Erasmus solus, Beza seorsim, Glos- sarium καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν in se, secum, Hesychius ἀυτὸν δι ἑαυτῶ ipse per se. Ita & Camerarius per se, id est so- lum, una cum milite custode. Philippica IV. κᾀ γεγό- νασι καθ' ἀυτὲς ἕκατοι. Singulos, ait, populos, quos ibi nominat Demosthenes, separatos ab aliis & solos, suas quoque res egisse. Aliter tamen Syrus, Arabs & Æthiopicus, qui verterunt, ubi vellet. καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν ac- ceperunt pro secundum se, id est, secundum animi sui sententiam, καθ᾿ ἑαυτῶ γνώμην. In Latino desi- derantur illa, Centurio tradidit vinctos, seu capti- vos Magistro castrorum seu præfecto.

## 28:17
V. 17. τῶν ἰεδαίων πρώτες) The more prominent ones. For the Jews do not seem to have had a synagogue in Rome at that time.

παρεδόθην) As Christ before, above c. XXI. 11, where see what is said. But he was handed over to the Romans when he was accused by the Jews before Felix.

Latin:

V. 17. τῶν ἰεδαίων πρώτες) Eminentiores. Neque enim Synagogam Romæ videntur habuisse Judæi eo tempore.

παρεδόθην) Ut ante Christus, Supra c. XXI. 11. ubi dicta vi- de. Traditus autem est Romanis, cum à Iudæis apud Feli- cem accusatus est.

## 28:18
Vers. 18. ἀνακρίναντές με) By a certain preliminary examination. See above c. XXV. 26.

ἐβέλοντο ἀπολῦσαι) They wanted to release me, that is, unless I had appealed. A similar expression in Matt. XXVI. 39, where we spoke about it.

διὰ τὸ μηδεμίαν αἰτίαν θανάτε ὑπάρχειν ἐν ἐμοὶ) Above c. XXV. 25, c. XXVI. 31. Thus the servant, no less than the Master, bore witness to his innocence from the unbelievers.

Latin:

Vers. 18. ἀνακρίναντές με) Prævio quodam examine. Vi- de supra c. XXV. 26.

ἐβέλοντο ἀπολῦσαι) Voluerunt me dimittere, nempe nisi ap- pellassem. Similis locutio Matt. XXVI. 39. ubi de ea diximus

διὰ τὸ μηδεμίαν αἰτίαν θανάτε ὑπάρχειν ἐν ἐμοὶ) Supra c. XXV. 25. c. XXVI. 31. Sic servus non minus quam Domi- nus ab incredulis testimonium retulit suæ innocentiæ.

## 28:19
V. 19. But when the Jews opposed) When they were acting in such a way as to drag me to the judgment of the Sanhedrin, and it seemed that Festus wished to do them a favor.

I was compelled to appeal to Caesar) Namely, so that this might not happen. Not that I have anything to accuse my nation of) I am being accused, I am not accusing, nor do I have any lawsuit against the whole nation.

Latin:

V. 19. ἀντιλεγόντων δὲ τῶν Ἰυδαίων) Cum illi hoc agerent, ut me ad Synedrii cognitionem traherent, videreturque Fe- stus illis velle gratificari.

ἠναγκάσθην ἐπικαλέσασθαι Καίσαρα) Nempe ne hoc fieret. ὀχ᾿ ὡς τῶ ἔθνες με ἔχων τι κατηγορῆσαι) Accusor, non ac- cuso, nec contra totam gentem ulla lis mihi est.

## 28:20
Vers. 20. I called for you to see) I called, that I might see you. And to speak with you) To speak as with friends. For the sake of the hope of Israel) Because of the faith concerning the resurrection. As above c. XXIII. 6. c. XXIV. 15. c. XXVI. 6. 7.

Others understand the hope of Israel as being about Christ, expected by Israel, or they wish for the hope of Israel to be designated in the abstract as that expectation of the faithful, by which they were awaiting the coming of the Messiah, which interpretation is more convenient, as if he were saying, I am bound by this chain, because I preach that Jesus is the Christ, and that in him the remission of sins and salvation is to be hoped for, or that the liberation has already arrived, which the pious anxiously expected, with the Savior sent, formerly promised to Israel, and hoped for by true Israelites, Gen. XLIX. 10. Ps. XIV. 7. Luke II. 25. 38. For this was the sum of the Apostolic proclamation. Acts X. 43. Conf. Col. I. 17. 1 Tim. I. 1. I am bound with this chain) See above v. 16. v. 21. Neither did we receive letters about you) Namely, which would deal with you by name, and warn us to oppose you. Nor did any of the brothers arrive) Anyone from our nation. For the Jews called one another brothers. See above c. VII. 2. 37. c. XIII. 26. 38. c. XXIII. 1. 5. 6. Vers. 22. For concerning this sect) Of the Nazarenes: Above c. XXIV. 5. of which sect, namely, you profess to be. It is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against) Namely, because of those letters written by the Sanhedrin shortly after Christ's departure from the earth, about which we spoke at Matt. XXVII. 63. The Jews say that a copy of those letters is preserved at the most ancient synagogue which is in Worms of the Vangiones. Vers. 23. And having appointed him a day) On the appointed day. They came to him at his lodging) The house in which he was staying. Josephus also uses the word lodging in this way. He was setting forth and testifying the kingdom of God) He was explaining the future kingdom of God, having brought forward proofs, both from the sacred scriptures and from those things which were seen in the Lord Jesus. Thus we had 'testifying' above in chapter X. 42. and elsewhere. Instead of 'testifying' in the Manuscript it is 'setting forth'. as above c. XVII. 3. And persuading them) 'To persuade' here is taken as an attempt, as above c. XIX. 8. in the Glossary: I persuade, I advise, I urge, I counsel. The things concerning Jesus both from the law of Moses and the Prophets) For he was showing that every matter of Jesus was predicted or prefigured by Moses and the Prophets, Luke XXIV. 27. above c. III. 18. 24. c. XIII. v. 27. c. XV. 15. c. XXII. 14. c. XXVI. 22. The discourse was prolonged from morning until evening: because he was not satisfied with speaking about Christ; he was not wearied in his preaching; his zeal and thirst for the salvation of the Jews took away from him every memory of bodily thirst and hunger. Vers. 24. Some were persuaded by the things said, but others disbelieved) As it usually happens, as above c. XIV. 4. c. XVII. 34. c. XIX. 9. Vers. 25. They were departing) 'To depart' for 'to leave' is a Polybian expression. It is also found in Exod. XXXIII. 11. One word) That is, as they were leaving he said this one thing. Priceus not badly here: That is, after he had said this one thing, after so many of his warnings were rejected, to note their incredulity. It is usually said in this way about those who wish to close and as it were seal their preceding sermon with some notable saying. Dio in the Excerpts: 'And having said this one thing at the end, I will declare all his both folly and greed.' Moreover, the Apostle attributes these things to the Holy Spirit, which were said in Isaiah by the Lord of hosts: Well indeed did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the Prophet to our fathers saying: whence also the person and Deity of the Holy Spirit has been asserted by us elsewhere against the Socinians. V. 27. For it has been made fat) Luke follows the LXX Interpreters of Is. VI. 10. as he is accustomed: he only added 'their' after 'the eyes'. Concerning the sense, see what was said at Matt. XIII. 15. But as to how much the Jews hardened after the Gospel was rejected, see at Rom. 2. v. 28. That the salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles) In the Manuscript 'this salvation'. Salvation as a substantive is a Hellenistic word as in Is. XII. 3. c. XXVI. 1. c. XXXIII. 20. c. XXXVIII. 11. c. LX. 6. 18. c. LXI. 10. c. LXII. 1. c. LXIII. 1. 1 Sam. II. 1. 1 Chron. XVI. 23. in the Psalms very often. It is referred sometimes to a person, as Luke II. 30. sometimes to a thing, as here to the word of the Gospel. God could have sent that word to the Gentiles, even if the Jews had sinned in nothing. But he cut off every complaint from them, when he did not do that until after very many Jews had despised that benefit offered to them. See above c. XIII. 46. c. XVIII. 6. Others take this also concerning a person, and understand Christ, who is frequently called 'salvation', with Basil in Psalm LXX and Augustine book I against the adversaries of the law and the prophets c. XV. 'For it is the custom of Scripture to call the Christ of God salvation,' says Basil. For Scripture is accustomed to call Christ the salvation of God. They themselves

αὐτοὶ κῂ ἀκύσονται) They will not only hear, but also obey. For ἀκύειν is used here in the sense of obeying, as very often שמע is among the Hebrews, which is translated sometimes by ἀκύειν, sometimes by ὑπακύειν. Thus we have ἀκύειν with the accusative in Matt. XI. v. 14, elsewhere with the genitive, as Matt. XVIII. 15, 16, Luke VI. 47, 1 Pet. IV. 6. What Paul had experienced in many cities of Asia and Europe, that the harvest of the word might be more successful among the Gentiles, he foresaw would happen now as well.

We append what Lud. de Dieu has to say about the placement of the particle κῂ: It seems to me that the Evangelist, for the sake of greater emphasis, purposely placed κῂ after, which I think should be preserved and translated, 'they also will hear.' The Syriac effectively says, 'for they also will hear.' The Arabic has words which must be translated, 'know therefore now this, that this salvation, the salvation of God, has been sent to the Gentiles, that they may obey it.' That greatly diminishes the emphasis. So says Dievius.

Latin:

Vers. 20. παρεκάλεσα ὑμᾶς ἰδεῖν) Vocavi, ut vos viderem. κᾀ προσλαλῆσαι) Loqui ut cum amicis. ἕνεκεν γὰρ ἐλπίδος τῶ ἰσραὴλ) Propter fidem de resurre- ctione. Ut supra c. XXIII. 6. c. XXIV. 15. c. XXVI. 6. 7.

Alii spem Israelis de Christo intelligunt, ab Israe- le expectato, vel spem Israelis in abstracto expecta- tionem illam fidelium, qua adventum Messiæ præ- stolabantur, designari volunt, quæ interpretatio convenientior est, quasi dicat, ego hac catena vin- ctus sum, quia prædico Jesum esse Christum, & in eo sperandam esse remissionem peccatorum & salu- tem, vel advenisse jam liberationem, quam pii ex- spectarunt anxie, misso Salvatore, Israeli quondam promisso, & à veris Israelitis sperato, Gen. XLIX. 10. Ps. XIV. 7. Luc. II. 25. 38. Hæc enim summa erat præ- conii Apostolici. Act. X. 43. Conf. Col. I. 17. 1. Tim. I. 1. τὴν ἅλυσιν ταύτην περίκειμαι) Vide supra v. 16. v. 21. ὔτε γράμματα περὶ σῦ ἐδεξάμεθα) Nempe quæ de te nominatim agerent, & nos monerent, ut tibi adversaremur. ὔτε παραγενόμενός τις τῶν ἀδελφῶν) Aliquis de gente no- stra. Judæi enim alii alios fratres vocabant. Vide supra c. VII. 2. 37. c. XIII. 26. 38. c. XXIII. 1. 5. 6. Vers. 22. περὶ μὲν γὰρ τῆς αἱρέσεως ταύτης) Nazaræorum: Supra c. XXIV. 5. cujus scilicet sectæ te esse profiteris. γνωστὸν ἐσιν ἡμῖν ὅτι πανταχῦ ἀντιλέγεται) Nimirum propter literas istas scriptas à Synedrio paulo post Christi abitum ex terris, de quibus diximus ad Matth. XXVII. 63. ajunt Judæi earum literarum exemplum asservari apud Synagogam ve- tustissimam quæ est Borbetomagi Vangionum. Vers. 23. ταξάμενοι δὲ αὐτῷ ἡμέραν) Condicta die. ἧκον πρὸς αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν ξενίαν) Domum in qua divertebat. Utitur sic voce ξενίας & Josephus. ἐξετίθετο διαμαρτυρόμενος τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ) Expone- bat futurum Dei regnum, adhibitis probationibus, tum ex sacris literis, tum ex iis, quæ in Domino Jesu erant conspe- cta. Ita διαμαρτύρεσθαι habuimus supra cap. X. 42. & alibi. Pro διαμαρτυρόμενος in Manuscripto est παρατιθέμενος. quo- modo supra c. XVII. 3. πείθων τε αὐτὸς) πείθειν hic de conatu sumitur, ut supra c. XIX. 8. in Glossario: Suadeo, παραινῶ, πείθω, συμβελεύω. τὰ περὶ τῦ Ἰησῦ ἀπό τε τῦ νόμῦ Μωσέως καὶ τῶν Προφητῶν) Ostendebat enim omnis res Jesu prædictas aut præfigura- tas à Mose & Prophetis, Luc. XXIV. 27. supra c. III. 18. 24. c. XIII. v. 27. c. XV. 15. c. XXII. 14. c. XXVI. 22. Protracta fuit concio à mane usque ad vesperam: quia de Christo loqui non satiabatur; in ejus præ- dicatione non fatigabatur; zelus & sitis salutis Ju- dæorum omnem ei corporalis sitis & famis me- moriam adimebat. Vers. 24. οἱ μὲν ἐπείθοντο τοῖς λεγομένοις, οἱ δὲ ἠπίστουν) Ut plerunque evenit, ut supra c. XIV. 4. c. XVII. 34. c. XIX. 9. Vers. 25. ἀπελύοντο) ἀπολύεσθαι pro discedere est locutio Polybiana. Invenitur & Exod. XXXIII. 11. ῥῆμα ἕν) Id est, abeuntibus hoc unum dixit. Priceus non male hîc: Id est, postquam unum hoc, post tot monita ejus rejecta ad notandam eorum incredulitatem, dixisset. Sic dici solet de iis, qui præcedentem sermonem suum insigni aliquo dicto claudere & quasi signare volunt. Dio in Excerptis: κὼ τέλος ἓν τῦτο εἰπὼν, πᾶσαν αὐτῦ κὼ τὴν πιεφθίαν, κὼ τὴν ἀπλησίαν δηλώσω. Tribuit autem hæc Apo- stolus Spiritus S. quæ in Esaia à Domino exercituum dicta sunt: Bene sane Spiritus S. loquutus est per Esaiam Prophetam ad Patres nostros dicens: unde & persona & Deitas Spiritus S. adversus Socinia- nos alias à nobis asserta est.
